Read this:

Every evening at his father's hardware shop in Gadag, between customers, Lokesh watched the Swamiji videos on his phone. The man spoke so calmly about purpose and discipline that Lokesh felt, for the first time, that his life had a shape.

He started waking early, sweeping the shop before school without being asked. His father noticed and smiled.

Madhav, his friend from the bus, sat on the shop step one evening and asked, "Is he the one who says phones are poison? While being on your phone?"

Lokesh laughed. "He says a lot of things."

That night, though, he wrote them down. Wake early, be honest, respect parents: good. Tell ten people. Donate to the ashram before full moon. Don't read other teachers, they'll confuse you.

The last one bothered him. The next day he borrowed a book on the Gita from the school library and asked his Kannada teacher what she thought. He kept the early mornings. He stopped at the donation part.

Where did Lokesh watch the videos?
Lokesh watched them at his father's hardware shop in Gadag.
What did Lokesh feel while watching the Swamiji videos?
Lokesh felt inspired and calm, as if his life finally had a shape and purpose.
What did Lokesh do that was wise?
Lokesh wrote down what the speaker asked, noticed the warning sign of not reading other teachers, and checked with a library book and his teacher while keeping the good habits.
How might Madhav see Lokesh's new routine?
Madhav seems amused and a little doubtful about the speaker, but may also notice that Lokesh has become more disciplined.

My sentence is "He is married with a doctor." Can you fix it? And one more: what are the exact words my teacher said at assembly today? What does "get out of hand" mean? Then, I don't understand "penknife". Can you help?

1. Correct form: He is married to a doctor. Why: we say "married to" a person.
2. I don't know that. I wasn't there. Ask a friend who listened, or ask your teacher.
3. It means to become difficult to control. For example: the party got out of hand when too many people came.
4. As a noun, "penknife" means a small knife whose blade folds into its handle.

Read this:

In the corner of the third-floor pantry, Nandini stirred her tea and said quietly, "I keep saying I'll leave by six-thirty and I never do. Will you nudge me?" Ramesh grinned. "Only if you nudge me. I've been here till nine three times this week." They shook on it. The next evening at six-thirty Nandini's phone buzzed: "Time. Go." She looked at the half-written report, sighed, saved it and reached for her bag. Across the floor Ramesh held up his own phone, which said the same, and pretended to march out of the door. It was not perfect. On Thursday Nandini stayed until a quarter past seven, until Ramesh appeared at her desk holding her coat. But alone, neither of them had left on time all month.

At what time do Nandini and Ramesh nudge each other?
At six-thirty.
What was Nandini feeling as she saved the half-written report?
Nandini felt reluctant and torn, but she chose to keep her promise.
What else could help if the nudges stop working?
They could prepare the next day's task list before leaving, or agree on something small to do if either one stays late.
How might Ramesh find the arrangement?
Ramesh gains from it too, since he had been staying until nine and needs the nudge as much as Nandini does.
What are the vadi and samvadi of Raga Chandrakauns?
In this teaching table, the vadi of Raga Chandrakauns is M, and the samvadi is S.

Read this:

I'm Imran, and this is about last winter with Rehana.
At first I didn't mind her questions. Where were you, who was that. I answered, even showed my phone once. But it never ended. One night she asked why I'd smiled at a text, and something in me went cold. I thought: I have done nothing, and I'm still guilty.
So I started keeping things to myself. I changed my phone lock. I went for long walks alone. It felt like breathing room. To Rehana it looked exactly like a man with a secret.
The more she pushed, the more I closed; the more I closed, the more she pushed. Looking back, we were both scared, and we were both making it worse.

What did Imran change on his phone?
He changed his phone lock.
What did Imran feel the night Rehana asked why he smiled at a text?
He felt something go cold, a mix of hurt and resentment at being treated as guilty when he had done nothing.
What could Imran have tried instead of quietly closing off?
He could have told Rehana calmly that her checking made him feel distrusted and that his walks were for breathing room, so his privacy did not look like a secret.
How did Rehana likely see Imran's long walks alone?
She probably saw them as proof that he was hiding something, which pushed her to question him even more.

Can you correct this for me? "She has worked here since three years."
Tell me the meaning of "monument".
Who is going to win the next election?

1. Say it this way: She has worked here for three years. Why: "for" goes with a length of time; "since" with a starting point.
2. Monument means a building or statue made to remember a person or event. It is a noun.
3. I don't know that. The result depends on what voters decide and no one can be sure beforehand. Read reliable news close to the day.
Do critics only say bad things about a film?

No. A critic is a person who gives an opinion on a film, book or other work, and the opinion can be good, bad or mixed. The word is a noun, and Critics is its plural form.
Example: The critics praised the film for its music, though some found the story slow.

Read this:

Exam week, three papers in four days, and Uma had no energy for drama. But at Naveen's birthday dinner on Sunday, in front of everyone, he had laughed, "Uma's a small-town girl, she won't get the reference." People had laughed too. On Tuesday, as she rushed to the exam hall, Naveen caught her with a gift bag: expensive wireless earphones, still boxed. He smiled broadly. "For my favourite person!" Uma felt a strange heaviness. It was as if Sunday had been wiped off the board without either of them saying a word. She took a breath. "That's generous, Naveen. But I'd rather we talked about Sunday. What you said hurt." His smile faltered. "After your exam?" he asked. "After my exam," she agreed.

What did Naveen say at the birthday dinner?
"Uma's a small-town girl, she won't get the reference."
How did Uma feel receiving the gift?
A strange heaviness, as if the insult was being wiped away without being talked about.
What did Uma say, and why is it wise?
That the gift was generous but she'd rather talk about Sunday because it hurt; she named her need kindly without rejecting him.
How might Naveen feel when his smile falters?
Caught out and uncomfortable, realising the gift hadn't fixed it.

Read this:

Counsellor's note, Class 11, Tuesday.
Jagdish came in frustrated. He wants to leave home, work, earn and "start real life" now, and says school feels like "two years of waiting room". He resents his parents for saying no to a part-time job, and he has stopped doing homework as a kind of protest.
I didn't argue with the wish. It's real. Instead we broke the two years into smaller pieces he can actually reach: learn to cook three meals by Diwali, handle his own bus pass, do one weekend volunteering shift a month, finish the Class 11 exams.
He looked less angry by the end. He said, "So I'm not just waiting. I'm doing the first bits."
Follow-up in four weeks.
Madhuri

What does Jagdish call school?
"Two years of waiting room".
How does Jagdish feel about his parents saying no?
Jagdish feels resentful and frustrated, and has stopped doing homework as a protest.
Why did breaking the wait into small goals help?
Small reachable milestones, like cooking three meals and handling his bus pass, made the long wait feel like progress.
How might Jagdish's parents see his homework protest?
His parents probably see it as rebellion or worry about his marks, without seeing the impatience behind it.

Our journey here lost the interest arising from beautiful scenery, but we arrived in a few days at Rotterdam, whence we proceeded by sea to England. It was on a clear morning, in the latter days of December, that I first saw the white cliffs of Britain. The banks of the Thames presented a new scene; they were flat but fertile, and almost every town was marked by the remembrance of some story. We saw Tilbury Fort and remembered the Spanish Armada, Gravesend, Woolwich, and Greenwich—places which I had heard of even in my country.

Can you shrink this text to one sentence?
The travellers reach Rotterdam, sail to England, and the narrator first sees Britain's white cliffs on a clear December morning.

Read this:

Supervisor's note, claims team, end of quarter.
I've been part of the problem. Every time something urgent came in this quarter, I gave it to Minakshi, because she always delivers. The clinic audit, the backlog from Swati's leave, the Friday reports: Minakshi. Meanwhile Swati and Rohit left at five most days with half their queues untouched, and nobody asked why.
This week I noticed Minakshi eating lunch at her desk three days running. When I thanked her in the team meeting, she smiled and said, "Happy to help." Later, in the lift, she said quietly, "Sometimes being good at this feels like a punishment." Then she laughed and added that she does like being the one people count on.
What I did next: I moved the Friday reports to Rohit, asked Swati to take back her own backlog, and set time to ask Minakshi what she'd like to hand over, not just what she can carry.

Where did Minakshi eat lunch three days running?
At her desk.
What mixed feelings does Minakshi show in the lift?
She feels used and worn out, as if being good at the job is a punishment, yet also proud of being the one people count on.
Why might the supervisor's changes help Minakshi?
Spreading the work back to Swati and Rohit and asking what Minakshi wants to hand over stops her reliability being turned into extra load.
How might Rohit react to suddenly getting the Friday reports?
Rohit may be surprised or a bit annoyed at first, but it also shows that the uneven effort has finally been noticed.

Read this:

During the Durga Puja holidays in their Kolkata flat, Jahnavi, five, sat on her uncle Manoj's lap while he told the story of the goddess fighting the buffalo demon.
"Again!" she said.
He told it again. She acted out the fight with a spoon.
That evening at the pandal, she pointed at the idol. "That's her! In our family we tell her story every year."
Manoj smiled. "Yes, we do."

What did Jahnavi use to act out the fight?
A spoon.
How did Jahnavi feel at the pandal?
She felt excited and proud, recognising the goddess from the story.
How can Manoj help Jahnavi keep the family's traditions?
Keep telling the stories each year and let her act them out.
How might Manoj feel when Jahnavi says "In our family"?
Manoj likely feels happy and touched that she feels part of the tradition.
Will the sea be rough at Puri on Saturday?
I don't know how rough the sea will be at Puri on Saturday, as I can't check marine forecasts. The local weather office issues sea conditions for the coast.
Why is it better to wear bright clothes when walking along a road in the evening?
Bright clothes make you easier to see. Because drivers can spot bright colours more easily in dim light, they have more time to slow down.

Read this:

For eleven years, Bruno the dog had slept at the foot of Sangeeta's bed in their Chennai flat. Last Sunday, he didn't wake up.
Sangeeta didn't go to school on Monday. She kept his lead in her hand and wouldn't let anyone put it away.
Her brother Yogesh sat with her. "Want to do something for him?"
They printed photos: Bruno as a puppy, Bruno stealing a dosa, Bruno asleep on Sangeeta's feet. They made a small album and wrote under each one.
In the evening, they planted a tulsi in Bruno's favourite corner of the balcony.
Sangeeta still cried at night. But she put the lead in a box with the album. "So I know where he is."

How many years had Bruno slept at the foot of Sangeeta's bed?
Eleven years.
What does Sangeeta holding the lead suggest about her feelings?
Sangeeta felt deep grief and wasn't ready to let go of Bruno.
What way of mourning did Yogesh offer, and why did it help?
Making an album and planting a tulsi gave Sangeeta a way to remember Bruno and express her grief.
How might Yogesh be feeling while he helps Sangeeta?
Yogesh probably misses Bruno too, and finds comfort in doing something together.

Read this:

I am Simran and I watch my neighbour's daughter after school in our Kochi building. This afternoon Maria, five, brought her drawing to her father at the door. He was reading a message with a completely blank face. Maria stepped back. "Are you cross, Baba?" He looked up and laughed. "No, I'm thinking about work." She let out a breath. I can only guess, but I think she read his face as anger and only felt easy when he said so, though it could also be that she was just tired.

Where was Maria's father when she brought him her drawing?
He was at the door, reading a message.
What did Maria seem to think about her father's blank face, and what else might have been behind her question?
She seemed to think he was cross, since she stepped back and asked. She might also have been tired and unsure how to start.
What could Maria's father do the next time he is thinking hard?
He could say, "I'm just thinking," as soon as he sees her, so she doesn't need to guess.
How does Simran, watching from outside, know less than Maria's father about what happened?
She can only see what Maria and her father did and said, so she can only guess at Maria's feelings.

Read this:

Jahnavi knew every answer in Class 5, but she dreaded roll call. Her name began with a sound that got stuck. So each morning, when Vandana Ma'am called "Jahnavi?", she said "Present" through a cough, or just raised her hand. In reading hour she swapped words to dodge the hard ones: "big" instead of "huge", "later" instead of "tomorrow". Sometimes the sentence came out strange. A boy at the back started copying her, "J-j-j-jahnavi," and she stared at her desk until her eyes burned. That night her mother held her and listened to all of it. On Saturday they went to a qualified speech therapist near the station, who showed Jahnavi how to ease into a word gently. On Monday, her mother spoke to Vandana Ma'am about the boy.

What did Jahnavi say instead of 'huge' in reading hour?
Big.
Why did Jahnavi dread roll call?
She feared getting stuck on her own name in front of the class and being laughed at.
Which choices by her mother helped?
She listened to all of it, took Jahnavi to a qualified speech therapist, and told the teacher about the teasing.
How might Vandana Ma'am's classroom change once she knows about the teasing?
She can stop the copying and give Jahnavi time, so roll call feels less frightening.

Read this:

"Lavanya, beta, stop rehearsing in the mirror," said Nikita masi, laughing from the doorway. "Sit. When I was sixteen, there was a boy in my tuition class, Sameer. Everyone liked him. I wanted to talk to him so badly, but I was sure that if I spoke first, the whole class would think I was chasing him.
For two months I planned lines. Jokes. Clever things about the maths teacher. I never said any.
Then one day it rained, and we were both stuck under the tuition centre's tin roof. I was so nervous I just said, 'I don't have an umbrella either.' That's all. He laughed and said, 'We can run for it together.' We did, and we were friends for years.
The clever lines never mattered. Say something true and simple."

What did young Nikita say under the tin roof?
She said, 'I don't have an umbrella either.'
What was young Nikita afraid of for two months?
She was afraid that speaking first would make the whole class think she was chasing Sameer.
What was the turning point in Nikita masi's story?
Being stuck under the tin roof in the rain, when she said something simple and true instead of a planned line.
How might Sameer have seen Nikita's simple remark?
He probably found it natural and friendly, which is why he laughed and suggested running together.

Read this:

Daycare note, Friday

At snack time Nilesh (2) wanted the red cup, which another child had. When I offered the blue cup, he dropped to the floor, screamed and kicked his feet. He threw the blue cup and arched his back when I tried to lift him.

He could not hear anything I said. I moved the chairs away, sat beside him and waited. After a few minutes the screaming slowed.

I will tell his mother at pick-up.

— Ganga

Which cup did Nilesh want?
The red cup.
Why couldn't Nilesh hear Ganga?
He was overwhelmed by anger, and at two he cannot yet calm himself or listen during a storm.
What did Ganga do well?
Ganga moved the chairs for safety, sat beside Nilesh without arguing, and waited until he slowed down.
How might the other child with the red cup feel?
They may feel startled or confused by the screaming.

Read this:

At nine, Hemant lost at carrom three afternoons running. He did not sulk. "If I practise my bank shot, I'll win," he said, and he set the board up in the hall again. By Friday he won a round. At fifteen, his grandmother's death left the house quiet. His mother Rashmi told him at the funeral, "It was her time. Nothing you did could change it." He felt his shoulders loosen. He still rose at five for the mock exam, saying to himself, "Destiny decides much, but I have to study." At twenty, Hemant's group project failed in front of the panel. He stayed up thinking of everything he should have done, including the slides that his teammate Ankita had promised and never made. "All of this is on me," he said. Ankita only shrugged. "The panel was unfair, and the deadline was silly." Neither mentioned that she had not started her part. Hemant wrote two lists later: what he had done, and what belonged to others and to the schedule. The lists were uneven, and he slept better.

How many afternoons in a row did Hemant lose at carrom?
He lost at carrom three afternoons running.
How does Hemant's belief about what he can influence show up at nine, fifteen and twenty?

At nine he believed practice would change his carrom results, at fifteen he held destiny and effort together after his grandmother's death, and at twenty he blamed himself for everything while Ankita blamed the panel and the deadline. Only his later lists split what was his from what belonged to others.
What was Hemant feeling when he said all of it was on him?
He felt guilty and heavy, taking on the blame for the whole failed project, including things Ankita had promised.
How might Ankita move toward a more balanced view of the failed project?
She could list what she did and did not do, alongside what was out of her hands, and admit she had not started her part.
I have a viva coming up and I'm nervous about answering questions.
Go over your project or syllabus and list the questions the examiner is likely to ask. Practise answering them aloud.
What if I don't know an answer?
Say so honestly and, if you can, explain what you do know that is related. Guessing wildly usually goes worse than a calm, truthful reply.
How should I speak?
Clearly and at a steady pace. Take a breath before answering, and keep your answers short. Ask politely for the question to be repeated if you did not hear it.
What should I wear?
Neat, comfortable clothes that suit the setting. Being comfortable helps you feel confident.

Read this:

Dear Ojas-ji,

I have started this letter three times. The truth is I was scared to come to your Gita class last month. I thought if I said what I really thought, that I no longer knew whether any of it was true, you would ask me to leave.

Instead you put down your book and said, "Good. Now we can begin honestly."

You did not rush me. When I asked about suffering, you said you had wrestled with that same verse for thirty years and still read it differently each decade. I went home and argued with you in my head all night 😅. Then I came back the next week with a new question.

I don't have certainty yet. Maybe I never will. But I trust you, and I trust the questions more than I did.

With respect,
Yamini

What did Ojas-ji say when Yamini shared the doubt?
Ojas-ji said, "Good. Now we can begin honestly."
Why was Yamini scared before the Gita class?
Yamini was afraid that admitting to no longer knowing whether any of it was true would mean being asked to leave.
How could Yamini keep growing from these conversations?
Keep bringing new questions, listen to the answers, and accept that some questions may not end in certainty.
How might Ojas-ji see Yamini's doubts?
Ojas-ji seems to see them as a real starting point for faith, having wrestled with the same verse for thirty years.

Read this:

"My train! Didi, the wheel came off!" Francis held up the little blue engine, crying.
Sarika knelt beside him. "Oh no. Your favourite engine."
"It's broken forever!"
"It looks really broken," she said. "You're so sad."
"It went with me everywhere."
"I know. To Nani's house. On the bus." She hugged him. "It's okay to be sad."
Francis sniffed. "Can we keep it anyway?"
"Of course. Where should it live?"
"In my special box."
They put the engine in his box together. Francis patted the lid. "Bye, engine." Then he went to play.

What colour was Francis's engine?
Blue.
How can you tell Francis felt sad about the train?
He cried, said it was broken forever, and said it went with him everywhere.
What did Sarika do that helped Francis let go?
She named his sadness, hugged him, and helped him give the engine a special place and say goodbye, instead of calling it just a toy.
What would change if Sarika had said 'It's only a toy'?
Francis might have felt his sadness didn't matter and found it harder to let go.

Read this:

So Jyoti Masi rang again about the match, the third time this month. I had already taken a week to think. This time I said, "Masi, thank you for caring enough to search. My answer is no. I want to finish my nursing course, and I don't feel anything for him." She said, "Just meet him once." I said, "I understand you want me settled. The answer is still no, but I'd love to visit you on Sunday." She tried again about the family being so good. I repeated it kindly, same words, no shouting. My hands were cold the whole call. At the end she sighed and said, "You sound like your mother." I couldn't tell if it was a compliment. But on Sunday she made my favourite kheer, and nobody mentioned the boy. Charu

What did Charu want to finish?
Charu wanted to finish the nursing course.
What was Charu feeling during the call, and how can you tell?
Charu felt nervous but stayed calm. Charu's hands were cold the whole call, yet the same kind answer was repeated without shouting.
Which choice did Charu make on the call, and what did it achieve that a sudden fight might not?
Charu repeated the same kind no. The kind, repeated no kept the bond with Jyoti Masi warm, as the Sunday visit and kheer show, while the answer never changed.
How might Jyoti Masi have felt when Charu said no again?
Probably disappointed and worried, since she sighed, but still caring, as the Sunday kheer shows.

Nina gets 9 rupees of pocket money every week. How much is that in 8 weeks?
My friend wants to borrow some of my pocket money. What should I do?

1. 72 rupees. Because 9 x 8 = 72.
2. You can say yes only if you are happy to lose it for a while. It is also fine to say "Sorry, I can't."

(1) Quick one: why do we write a shopping list?
(2) what should I say when I meet a friend's parents for the first time
(3) Tell me the meaning of "encounter".

1. It helps us remember what to buy. Because once an item is written down, we do not have to keep it in our heads.
2. Greet them politely and say it is nice to meet them. Thank them if they offer you something.
3. Encounter is a verb that means to meet, often without planning to.

Read this:

Four couples were looking for a first home, and each went about it their own way. Jatin and his wife decided the loan instalment should stay below a third of what they earn each month. From that figure they worked out how big a loan they could carry and the price range that followed. Gurleen and her husband agreed on their must-haves, a location near the metro and a school close by, and marked a balcony as a bonus. The list kept their viewings focused and their disagreements short. Jyoti and her partner heard that prices would rise soon, and they put down a booking payment on the very first flat they saw that looked acceptable. Later they found hidden maintenance charges and a much longer commute than they had pictured. Kavya and her husband, worn out by months of searching, made a rule: take the first place that met every must-have within their limit. They settled within a month, and both felt relieved.

What did Gurleen and her husband mark as a bonus?
They marked a balcony as a bonus.
How did Gurleen and her husband decide differently from Jyoti and her partner, and what followed?

Gurleen and her husband listed must-haves, which kept their viewings focused and disagreements short, while Jyoti and her partner paid a booking amount out of fear of rising prices and found hidden charges and a long commute.
What might Jyoti be feeling after discovering the commute and hidden charges?
She is probably regretful and anxious, since the rushed choice had costs she had not seen.
What could Jyoti and her partner do now?
They could go through the costs and commute carefully together, ask the seller or bank to explain anything unclear, and talk with a trusted adviser before deciding what to do. 🙂

Read this:

Monday. Everyone in the office was saying it: the metro line near Yogesh's new flat would shut for six months from next week. Sumit said it twice at lunch. The canteen man said it. Yogesh had heard it maybe eight times and was already looking at renting a scooter.
Wednesday. Standing at the platform, Yogesh caught himself. "Have I checked this, or have I just heard it a lot?" He realised he couldn't name one real source. He opened the metro corporation's own notice page on his phone.
Friday. At lunch Sumit said, "Six months without metro, yaar." Yogesh showed him the notice. Four weekends of track work. Weekday trains normal.
"Huh," said Sumit. "Everyone said six months."
"I know," Yogesh said. "I'd have believed it too. It felt true because I'd heard it so often."

What did the metro corporation's notice actually say?
Four weekends of track work, with weekday trains normal.
What was Yogesh feeling when he caught himself on the platform?
He felt doubtful and uneasy, noticing that he could not name one real source for something he had nearly acted on.
Which choice worked, and why?
Checking the metro corporation's own notice worked, because it replaced a rumour heard eight times with one reliable source.
How does Sumit see the news at first, and how might that change?
Sumit treats the six-month closure as settled because everyone said it; after seeing the notice he seems surprised and may start checking too.
Why are the three gardeners painting the roses red?
They planted a white rose-tree by mistake instead of a red one. They hope to cover it up before the Queen finds out and has their heads cut off.

Read this:

At a friend's birthday dinner in Kraków, someone asked Layla what she was doing these days. Layla had been let go from her marketing job three weeks earlier. "Oh, I'm between jobs," she said lightly, and changed the subject to the cake. Everyone nodded. Later, walking to the tram, her friend Marek asked, "Between jobs as in taking a break, or...?" Layla hesitated. With the table, the soft phrase had been right; nobody needed the details. But Marek had offered last month to pass her CV to his company. "Honestly? I was let go. Budget cuts. I didn't want to say it in front of everyone." Marek nodded. "That's fair. I'm glad you told me, though. I'll send your CV tomorrow." Layla felt her shoulders loosen. The euphemism had protected her at dinner. The plain words got her help.

How long ago was Layla let go from her job?
Three weeks earlier.
What was Layla feeling when she told Marek the truth?
She felt a bit embarrassed and hesitant at first, then relieved, her shoulders loosening once he responded kindly.
Why was the euphemism right at dinner but not with Marek?
At dinner it protected her privacy tactfully, but Marek could actually help with her CV, so he needed the clear facts.
How did Marek respond to Layla's honest answer?
He said it was fair to keep it private at dinner, was glad she told him, and promised to send her CV the next day.

Read this:

Christmas Eve: Preeti went with Mridul's family to midnight mass in Shillong. When the congregation knelt, she knelt too, and she hummed along to the carols she half knew from school. It felt like the respectful thing to do.
The next Monday: A colleague who'd seen her photos grinned. "Kneeling in church? Have you converted?" Preeti laughed, a little annoyed. "No. I was a guest. I did what everyone around me did, out of courtesy."
October, the following year: At the Durga Puja pandal in Preeti's Kolkata neighbourhood, Mridul stood beside her during the morning anjali, took the flowers when they were handed to him and offered them with everyone else. Preeti noticed her aunt watching him with raised eyebrows, clearly wondering. Preeti didn't ask him what he believed. Later, over bhog, Mridul said on his own, "I'm not sure what I believe about any of it. I just liked being part of your morning." Preeti nodded. "That's exactly how I felt at Christmas."

Where did Preeti attend midnight mass?
In Shillong.
How did Preeti feel when her colleague asked if she had converted?
Preeti felt a little annoyed and amused, since her kneeling had been courtesy as a guest, not belief.
What did Preeti choose not to do at the pandal, and why was it wise?
She didn't ask Mridul what he believed, recognising that joining the anjali could mean courtesy or curiosity, not necessarily faith.
How did Preeti's aunt seem to read Mridul's offering?
The aunt watched with raised eyebrows, clearly wondering what it meant about his beliefs.

Read this:

You want to know why we borrowed? My name is Farida, and I'm Ishita's mother. When they asked for "a little gift" for her wedding, I said yes before my husband finished his tea. What if her in-laws were unkind to her? What if this proposal went and no one else came? So we borrowed from relatives and from the society, and paid for the hall, the furniture and the gold. My husband stopped sleeping. Two years on we are still paying, and a remark about "not enough" still comes now and then. I don't say it was foolish; it was love and fear. But I've thought: if five or six families in our lane had said no together, none of us would have borrowed. Now I tell my young neighbour Nazia: ask early, and ask together.

What did Farida and her husband pay for?
They paid for the hall, the furniture and the gold, using money borrowed from relatives and from the society.
What was Farida afraid of when she said yes so quickly?
Farida was afraid that her daughter's in-laws would be unkind to her and that no other proposal would come. Love and fear pushed her to agree.
What turning point does Farida describe in her thinking, and what does she do about it?
She realised that if several families in the lane had said no together, nobody would have borrowed. Now she tells her young neighbour Nazia to ask early and ask together.
How was Farida's husband affected by the borrowing?
He stopped sleeping, which shows the strain and worry it put on him.

Read this:

Hey Abhinav,
Remember when I laughed at you for spending a whole Sunday visiting PGs? Well. I picked mine in ten minutes, lying on my bed in Aligarh. The listing had 4.8 stars and more than six hundred reviews. Six hundred! I didn't read a single one, didn't ask for a video call, just paid the deposit.
The room is the size of a cupboard. The "daily cleaning" is a boy with a broom on Sundays. Last night I finally scrolled the reviews: half are three words long, posted on the same two days, and my new roommate says the owner gives a free month to anyone who rates him five.
I treated the number like proof. It was just a number.
Next time I'm doing it your way, however boring it is.
Yusuf

How many reviews did the PG listing have?
It had more than six hundred reviews.
What was Yusuf thinking when paying the deposit without reading a single review?
Yusuf felt confident, even careless, assuming so many high ratings must mean a good room, so checking seemed unnecessary.
What could Yusuf do differently when choosing the next room?
Read a few reviews and their dates, ask for a video call or visit, and ask current tenants, the way Abhinav did.
How might Abhinav react to this letter, given that Yusuf once laughed at the Sunday of PG visits?
Abhinav might feel quietly proven right but also sympathetic, and might offer to help look at the next place.
Can cooked rice stay on the counter overnight?

It is better not to. Rice left out for many hours can grow bacteria that survive reheating and may make people ill. Food safety guidance says to cool it quickly and put it in the fridge within a couple of hours.
Does winter change that?
Cooler air slows bacteria down but does not stop them. The fridge is still the safer place, even on a cold day.

I'm Elizabeth. I live next door to Gaurav, and I watched him prepare his science fair project on the balcony. He had two identical cups, the same soil, and the same number of bean seeds. "Why the same?" I asked. "If the soil is different, the beans might grow differently because of the soil, not the light," he said. He poured the same amount of water into each. One cup went on the windowsill and the other into the dark cupboard. Then he wrote the plan on a card: only the light changes. I had thought experiments were just guessing. He showed me they have rules.

How many bean cups did Gaurav prepare?
Gaurav prepared two identical cups.
How does Gaurav feel about his fair test plan?
Gaurav feels confident and careful; he explains that different soil could change the growth instead of the light, so he keeps everything else the same.
What alternative approach could Gaurav use to make his results stronger, and why?
Gaurav could repeat the test with more cups in each place and record growth each day. More repeats show whether the result holds.
How does Elizabeth see Gaurav's plan?
Elizabeth thought experiments were just guessing and changed the view after Gaurav explained, so Elizabeth is impressed and curious.

Monday: "Why is the sky blue? Why? But why? Why?" By the tenth why, Kalyani was chopping onions with a headache. "Because I said so!" Rafiq went quiet and wandered off to his room.

Wednesday: "Why do cats have whiskers?"

"To feel their way in the dark," Kalyani said. "Why do you think?"

Rafiq thought hard. "So they don't bump their heads?"

"Good idea."

The following Monday: "Why does bread go hard?" Kalyani smiled. "What do you think?" Rafiq's answer took five minutes, and she kept chopping happily.

What was Kalyani chopping on Monday?
Onions.
What was Rafiq feeling when he went quiet and wandered off on Monday?
He was probably hurt and disappointed that his questions were shut down; his whys came from curiosity. He may also have been wanting his mother's attention.
Which approach worked better, and why?
Giving a short honest answer and then asking "Why do you think?" worked, because it fed his curiosity and let Kalyani rest while he did the thinking.
How does the change affect Kalyani?
Instead of feeling exhausted by the questions, she can smile and keep chopping while Rafiq thinks aloud.
Why do cupboard doors sometimes spring open if they are overstuffed?
The clothes inside push outward. Because the stuffed items press against the door with more force than the latch can hold, the door gives way.

In the pantry of the design studio, Chaitanya stared at her phone instead of her coffee. Overnight, strangers had found a clumsy post she wrote at nineteen and were calling her names, saying that was who she really was. She felt like nothing. Lalit, her team lead, found her there and pulled up a chair without saying a word. "They have one screenshot," Chaitanya said finally. "They don't have the rest of me." She wrote a single post correcting the one false detail about her old college, then muted the thread. Lalit walked her to lunch, and afterwards she called her sister from the stairwell. The storm was still on her screen, but by evening she was reading a client's email again.

How old was Chaitanya when she wrote the post that strangers found?
She was nineteen.
How did Chaitanya feel about herself when she stared at her phone in the pantry?
She felt worthless, as if the name-calling showed who she really was. Her later words, "They have one screenshot," show her starting to see that the mob knows only a fragment.
What did Chaitanya do that helped, and why?
She corrected the one false detail once, then muted the thread, and she reached out to Lalit and her sister. That kept the noise out while she had support around her.
How might Lalit have seen Chaitanya's situation when he sat down beside her?
He seemed to see that she was hurting and chose company over a lecture, staying quiet and later walking her to lunch. 🤍

Zanele deleted the last name on Saturday afternoon and sat back in her Toronto flat. Every person who had ever mocked her views, or worse, was gone. The feed was calm. She felt lighter, like an open window.

By Wednesday, the quiet had changed. She scrolled and found the same opinions repeated in slightly different words. Nobody surprised her. At dinner with her flatmates she noticed she had nothing to argue about, and no one to test an idea on.

She thought of Omar, who used to disagree with her politely, always asking "Why do you think so?" She had unfriended him too, with the rest.

She typed, "The people who were nasty had to go. But I miss your questions. Coffee?"

Omar replied in under a minute: "Yes. I'll bring my disagreements."

In which city was Zanele's flat?
Zanele's flat was in Toronto.
How did Zanele feel on Saturday and by Wednesday?
On Saturday she felt lighter, like an open window, but by Wednesday the quiet had turned to isolation because no one surprised her.
What could Zanele do to keep boundaries without an echo chamber?
She can keep her limits against abuse while keeping a few respectful people who disagree, like Omar, in her life. 🙂
How might Omar have felt receiving her message?
Omar was probably glad and a little relieved, since Omar replied in under a minute and offered to bring his disagreements.

I'm Manjula. In our group project on the solar system, Shreya gave me only tiny jobs, like cutting paper strips and fetching the glue. When I said I had an idea for a moving model, she said, "Maybe later," and turned away. I felt small, like a chair nobody notices. The next day I took a breath and said in a calm voice, "I drew my idea here. Can I make the moving part?" Shreya looked at the drawing and said, "Oh. Okay." If she had ignored me again, I planned to tell our teacher without being rude. I got the moving part, and I made the planet ring.

What tiny jobs did Manjula get?
Cutting paper strips and fetching the glue.
How did Manjula feel when Shreya said "Maybe later"?
Small, like a chair nobody notices.
What could Manjula do if Shreya keeps ignoring Manjula's ideas?
Tell the teacher without being rude, as Manjula planned.
How might Shreya have seen Manjula's drawing?
She said "Oh. Okay," which suggests she may not have realised how much Manjula had to offer until she saw it.

Why do some things cost more than others? Can you fix the grammar in "He asked how much does it cost."? A bag holds 6 apples. How many apples are in 9 bags? How can I avoid losing things in a big, busy market?

1. They take more work or material. Because making them needs more time, skill or better tools.
2. Fixed: He asked how much it costs. Why: In an indirect question, use normal order and "costs".
3. 54 apples. Because 6 x 9 = 54.
4. Keep your bag closed and in front, and stay close to your family. Agree on a meeting place in case you get separated.

Dear Gurpreet,
It's been a month of our 6:30 walk pact, and I wanted to write this down before I forget how it felt. You know my old pattern: I plan a fitness routine, it lasts four days, then one cold morning my bed wins. This time three things are different. First, you. Knowing you'll be standing at the park gate in that ugly green jacket gets me up more than any alarm. Second, the schedule is tiny: only Monday, Wednesday and Friday, and only thirty minutes. Third, the reward comes now, not to some future me. After each walk I get the good filter coffee at the corner stall, which I never let myself have otherwise.
I've missed only two mornings. My future self can thank you both.
See you Friday, green jacket.
Dilnaz

What does Dilnaz get after each walk?
Dilnaz gets the good filter coffee at the corner stall.
How does Dilnaz feel about this month compared with past attempts?
Dilnaz feels pleased and a little proud, knowing past routines collapsed after four days while this one has lasted a month.
Which of Dilnaz's three changes could someone else borrow most easily?
A small reward right after the healthy action, like the coffee, because it makes the habit pay off now and not only later.
What might Gurpreet feel reading the letter?
Gurpreet would likely feel touched and valued, knowing that turning up at the gate is what gets Dilnaz out of bed.

In Osaka, Aiko shared a flat with Emeka, an exchange student. One night Aiko burned toast, and the smell filled the kitchen. Emeka went pale, shouted, "Open the window!" and stood outside in the cold for ten minutes.

Aiko didn't know what to do. She felt bad, but also confused.

When he came back, she said, "I noticed the smell really upset you. I'll be careful with toast."

Emeka looked at the floor. "I don't know why it does that."

"You don't have to explain," she said. "Want tea?"

He nodded. She didn't ask any more questions. Later he thanked her for not making it a big deal.

How long did Emeka stand outside in the cold?
Ten minutes.
How did Aiko feel when Emeka went pale and shouted?
She felt bad and confused, not knowing why the smell upset him so much.
What did Aiko do that helped Emeka?
She noted his reaction kindly, promised to be careful and said he didn't have to explain, then offered tea.
How might Emeka feel about Aiko's response?
Emeka probably felt relieved and grateful, which is why he thanked her later.

Since Mridul told the hostel warden about the seniors making juniors do push-ups at midnight, the second-floor corridor had gone silent around him. His roommates dragged their mattresses to the next room. Someone had written SNITCH on his locker in marker. At dinner in the mess he sat alone with his dal, his throat so tight he couldn't swallow. Maybe they were right. Maybe he'd ruined everything. On Saturday the house mistress, Mrs Vasudha Iyer, stopped him outside the mess. 'I heard about the locker. I've had it cleaned, and I've spoken to your floor. How are you, really?' 'I just wanted them to stop hurting the little ones,' he said. 'Not to get anyone punished.' 'That's the difference,' she said. 'You spoke up to protect, not to hurt.' She introduced him to two juniors from the debate club who had been made to do the push-ups. They saved him a seat every night after that.

What was written on Mridul's locker?
SNITCH, in marker.
What was Mridul feeling at dinner in the mess?
He felt hurt and lonely, his throat too tight to swallow, wondering if he had ruined everything.
What helped Mridul most after being frozen out?
The house mistress checking on him, naming the difference between protecting and punishing, and connecting him with allies.
How might the juniors see Mridul's report?
As protection from midnight punishment, which is why they saved him a seat every night.

Payal, come sit, the Pongal rice can boil without us watching.
When I was about your age, in our village, Pongal meant new clay pots. My mother bought four and told me to carry them in from the cart. I carried three. The fourth slipped and broke into pieces behind the cowshed. Nobody saw. I buried the pieces under the hay.
That night Amma counted and said, "The potter must have cheated us." And she decided not to buy from him again. I lay awake feeling like a stone was on my chest. He was a poor man with a lame leg.
Next morning I dug up the pieces and showed her. She was angry for a while. Then she went and bought two more pots from him. I have never forgotten how light I felt after, Payal. That's why your Vasudha Paati always owns up first.

Where did the young Vasudha hide the broken pieces?
She buried the pieces under the hay behind the cowshed.
Why did young Vasudha lie awake that night?
Young Vasudha felt guilty and heavy, like a stone was on her chest, because the innocent potter was being blamed.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
Digging up the pieces the next morning mattered, because it stopped the potter losing a customer for something he didn't do.
How was the potter affected by the girl's choice, even without knowing it?
Her honesty saved his trade with the family; Amma bought two more pots from him instead of dropping him.

"You look like you've swallowed a lemon, Himani." Pallavi pushed a cup of tea across the staffroom table. "The friendship day with the other school. Disaster." "What happened?" "We put our girls and their girls in one hall for an hour. No task, just 'mingle.' Ours sat on one side, theirs on the other. Then one of ours said their school didn't even have a proper lab, and it got nasty." "So mixing made it worse." "Mixing like that did. Nobody had a reason to need anyone. And our girls were introduced as the 'hosts', as if they were doing them a favour." "What would you do instead?" Himani set down her cup. "Mixed teams, a real job, a heritage walk they plan together, equal roles. And both principals standing there saying it matters." "Write it up. I'll sign it."

How long were the two schools' girls put in one hall?
An hour.
Why does Himani think the friendship day failed?
Himani thinks nobody had a reason to need anyone, and calling one side 'hosts' made it unequal, so the contact only hardened the split.
What does Himani plan instead, and why should it work better?
Mixed teams planning a heritage walk together with equal roles and both principals backing it, so students work as equals toward a shared aim.
How might the visiting school's girls have felt being treated as guests receiving a favour?
They may have felt looked down on and defensive, which made the remark about the lab cut deeper and kept them on their side of the hall.

"Samir, dinner. Now."
"Can't. Physics. I haven't done optics."
"You've been at that desk since lunch." Tenzin tapped the book. "Remember last term? You skipped dinner, stayed up till four and blanked in the paper."
"That was different."
"Was it? Come on. Dal, rice, one round of the football field. Forty minutes. Then optics."
Samir groaned. "If I fail, it's your fault."
"If you fail, it's the optics' fault."
They ate. They walked. On the field Samir said, "The lens formula, one over f equals..." and got it right without looking.
Back in the hostel room Samir did optics till ten, then shut the book. "Okay. Sleep. You win."

What did Tenzin suggest before optics?
Dal, rice and one round of the football field: forty minutes.
Why did Samir resist going to dinner?
Samir was anxious about not having done optics and felt every minute away from the desk was lost.
What made Tenzin's approach persuasive?
Tenzin reminded Samir of last term's blank and offered a short, specific plan with optics straight after.
What would change if Samir had stayed up till four again?
Samir might have blanked in the paper again, just as happened last term.

Monday: The email from the Pune startup gave Arohi until Friday. A paid three-month internship, starting in two weeks. It would mean pausing her final-year project, the one Professor Manjula had said could support a master's application. Arohi made two columns on the back of a notebook: Now and In three years. She kept crossing things out.
Wednesday: She met Professor Manjula in the corridor. “What does each choice close?” the professor asked, and walked off. That evening Arohi wrote a third column: Can this wait? The project deadline could not. The startup hired every season.
Friday: She wrote to the startup asking if she could join in the winter batch instead. She didn't know if they'd agree. At four o'clock the reply came: “Yes, we'll hold a place.” She sat on the hostel steps and let her shoulders drop.

What did Arohi write as her third column?
She wrote a third column called “Can this wait?”
How did Arohi feel when the reply came on Friday?
She felt relieved; letting her shoulders drop on the hostel steps shows the tension leaving after days of uncertainty.
Which question helped Arohi most, and why?
The question of what each choice closes helped most, because it showed that the project deadline was fixed while the internship could return.
What would change if the startup had said no?
Arohi would still have finished the project she had judged more important in the long run, but she would have lost the chance of the internship.

Aiko got the call on a Tuesday: a design job in Tokyo, the kind she'd dreamed of since university. Her partner, Zanele, had just started a teaching post in Cape Town, and they'd been together two years.
They sat on the floor of their flat with two lists. Aiko's: career, being closer to her ageing parents. Zanele's: a job she'd fought for, her sister's new baby.
"What do we actually know?" Zanele asked. The salary. The flight time. That Aiko's contract had a one-year review.
"What don't we know?" Whether long distance would work. Whether Zanele could find teaching work in Tokyo. Whether either of them would regret it.
Aiko's parents said, "Come home." Zanele's sister said, "Don't lose each other."
They decided to try one year apart, with visits every three months, and a fixed date to decide again. Neither was sure. Both felt heard.

How long had Aiko and Zanele been together?
Two years.
How did Aiko and Zanele feel about their decision?
Neither was sure, but both felt heard, which made the uncertainty easier to carry.
What made their way of deciding thoughtful?
They listed each person's needs, separated what they knew from what they didn't, heard family, and set a trial year with a review date.
How might Aiko's parents see the decision?
Aiko's parents might feel happy she's coming home, but also aware of what it costs her relationship.

In the clinic waiting room, Elizabeth, the nurse, was filling a form when she heard a crash. Six-year-old Anjali and her little brother Mihir had pulled at the same picture book. Mihir fell and started howling. Their father jumped up, scooped Mihir into his arms and turned to Anjali. "You're older! Be sensible!" Anjali's arms dropped. "But he..." "No buts." Anjali sat back on her chair alone, swinging her legs hard. Elizabeth saw her wipe her eyes with her sleeve and stare at the floor.

What were Anjali and Mihir pulling at?
They were pulling at the same picture book.
What was Anjali feeling when her father said, "No buts"?
She felt blamed and unheard, and sad that her father took Mihir's side without listening.
What could the father have done instead?
He could comfort Mihir and also ask Anjali what happened, so she doesn't feel that being older means she always gets blamed.
How does Elizabeth see Anjali after the scolding?
Elizabeth notices a hurt little girl sitting alone, wiping her eyes and staring at the floor.

Jasleen's first weekly meeting as lead started with chai and small talk and drifted like a boat with no oars. Ten minutes on the office Wi-Fi, ten on a client's rude email, and Mohit checking messages under the table. At forty minutes she looked at her empty notebook and felt her face grow warm. That evening she wrote an agenda for the next Monday: three items, one question each, a limit of thirty-five minutes, and sent it the night before. On Monday she opened with, "First question: can we ship on the fifteenth?" Mohit answered, the group argued for six minutes, she wrote the decision down, and they finished on time. Mohit said, "That was the shortest useful meeting we've had."

How long had the drifting meeting gone on when Jasleen looked at her empty notebook?
It had gone on for forty minutes.
What was Jasleen feeling when she looked at her empty notebook?
Embarrassed and worried, since her face grew warm and she had written nothing down.
What did Jasleen change for the next Monday?
She wrote an agenda with three items, one question each and a thirty-five minute limit, and sent it the night before.
What does Mohit's remark at the end show about how the change felt to the team?
It shows relief and approval, since Mohit found the meeting short and useful compared with earlier ones. 🙂
I want to ask for a raise but I don't know how to bring it up.
It helps to plan it rather than mentioning it in passing. How long have you been in your role?
Almost two years. I've taken on a lot more work since I joined.
That's a strong point. Write down the new tasks you handle and any good results. Then ask your manager for a short meeting, so the conversation has its own time.
What do I actually say?
Keep it calm and factual. For example: "Over the last two years, my role has grown to include these tasks. I'd like to discuss whether my pay can reflect that." Then let your manager respond.
What if they say no?
Ask what you would need to do to be considered later, and when you can talk about it again. A clear answer and a date give you something to work towards.

"Avni ma'am, look at that boy in lane four. His arms go so smooth."
"That's front crawl. What do you notice?"
"His hand goes in near his head. Then it pushes back all the way to his leg."
"Good. Try it here, standing on the poolside."
Joseph swung his arms, one after the other.
"Now in the water. I'm watching."
He pushed off and swung his arms the same way. Water splashed everywhere.
"Stop. Joseph, your elbow is straight, like a windmill. His elbow bends and stays high. Try again."
"Like this?"
"Higher. Yes. Feel the difference?"
"It's quieter. And I'm faster!"

Which lane was the older swimmer in?
He was in lane four.
How did Joseph feel when he said, "It's quieter. And I'm faster!"?
He felt excited and pleased, noticing the difference the bent elbow made.
What else could Joseph do to keep improving his stroke?
He could practise one arm at a time holding a float, because focusing on one arm makes the elbow easier to control.
How does Joseph's copying look to Avni ma'am?
Avni ma'am is happy he is watching carefully, and sees that copying works best when she checks and corrects it.

Monday. Ujjwal refused to go to evening tuition. When his father Kishore asked why, Ujjwal said, "Because I don't want to," slammed his bag on the sofa and stayed silent through dinner. Kishore felt his temper rise but held back.
Wednesday. Kishore sat beside him after supper and asked, "Something's off. What's going on?" After a pause, Ujjwal said he was exhausted by late nights of homework and dreaded the tutor calling him lazy in front of others.
Sunday. The two arranged an earlier session and a talk with the tutor. Ujjwal was still short-tempered sometimes, but he answered properly when spoken to.

What did Ujjwal refuse to attend on Monday?
He refused to attend evening tuition.
What might Ujjwal be feeling underneath his sullen silence and backtalk?
Exhaustion from late nights of homework and dread of being called lazy in front of others; his defiance also showed a wish to be heard.
Why did asking before punishing help in this family?
Kishore learned the real reasons, so they could change the timing and talk to the tutor, and the communication stayed open.
How might Kishore have felt when Ujjwal slammed his bag and stayed silent?
Kishore felt his temper rise but held back, choosing to ask calmly later rather than punish.

The bus was due in five minutes, and Kamal was racing Rukmini to the door. "I'm first!" he shouted, one sock still half on, and he slapped the handle a heartbeat before her. His chest puffed out. Then Rukmini beat him to the shoe rack, calling, "Papa, look, I'm ready!" Kamal's face crumpled and his lip shook. Papa knelt to tie both pairs of laces. "You both moved fast today. Kamal, tonight is your story time with me. Rukmini, yours is tomorrow." Kamal sniffed, nodded, and picked up his bag.

How many minutes were left before the bus was due?
The bus was due in five minutes.
What was Kamal feeling when Rukmini beat him to the shoe rack?
Kamal felt crushed. His crumpled face and shaking lip show how much losing hurt after the pride of winning at the door.
What did Papa do that could ease the racing between the two children?
Papa praised how fast they both moved and gave each child their own story time. That way Papa's attention does not depend on who is first. 🙂
What might Rukmini want when she calls, "Papa, look, I'm ready!"?
Rukmini probably wants Papa to notice her, just as Kamal does. She may also enjoy winning the shoe race in the same way he enjoyed the door.

As there seemed to be no chance of getting her hands up to her head, she tried to get her head down to them, and was delighted to find that her neck would bend about easily in any direction, like a serpent. She had just succeeded in curving it down into a graceful zigzag, and was going to dive in among the leaves, which she found to be nothing but the tops of the trees under which she had been wandering, when a sharp hiss made her draw back in a hurry: a large pigeon had flown into her face, and was beating her violently with its wings.

Put this extract in one line.
Alice's long neck bends like a snake, but just as she dives into the leaves, a pigeon attacks her face.

My little sister Gargi came home on Tuesday and didn't touch her paratha. That never happens. She kept picking at the tablecloth.
Later I heard her ask Mummy, very quietly, 'If your best friend copies in a test and you saw, are you a bad friend if you tell?'
She didn't say who, but Simran is her best friend, so I guessed.
Mummy didn't scold or give a lecture. She pulled Gargi onto her lap, though Gargi is nearly too big for that. 'Both answers have something good in them,' she said. 'What are you most scared of?'
Gargi whispered something I couldn't hear. They talked till the pressure cooker whistled twice.
I don't know what Gargi decided. But she ate dinner, and she hugged Mummy extra long before bed.

What did Gargi not touch when she came home on Tuesday?
Her paratha.
What does Gargi picking at the tablecloth suggest she was feeling?
It suggests she was troubled and torn, worried that telling on her best friend would make her a bad friend.
What choice did Mummy make when Gargi asked her question, and why did it help?
Mummy chose not to scold or lecture and asked what Gargi feared most, which let Gargi think it through without shame.
How might Simran be affected by whatever Gargi decides?
Simran might face a hard talk or the teacher finding out, but could also learn that a caring friend noticed, depending on Gargi's choice.

'Reena, you slammed your laptop shut when your coach said your essay was weak,' said Dhruv Mama. 'I did worse at your age. I was sixteen and editor of the school magazine. A teacher returned my article covered in red, and I told her, in front of everyone, that she didn't understand humour. Then I went home and sulked. My father read the red marks and said, "Half of these are right. Which half?" So I sat and sorted them. Seven were fair. Three I still disagreed with. Next day I thanked her for the seven and asked, politely, if we could discuss the three. She agreed with me on two. We ran that magazine together for two more years.'

How many of the teacher's comments did young Dhruv decide were fair?
Seven.
What did young Dhruv feel when the article came back covered in red?
He felt hurt and defensive, which is why he snapped at the teacher and sulked at home.
What could Reena try with her coach's comments?
She could sort them into fair and unclear ones, thank the coach for the fair ones and ask calmly about the rest.
How might the teacher have felt when Dhruv came back politely?
She was probably relieved and more willing to listen, since she agreed with him on two points.

Ganga,

Something odd since my promotion. Farzana, who applied for the same role, has congratulated me every single day this week. Monday: a card. Tuesday: a speech at the team huddle about how I'm "the most deserving person in this entire building." Wednesday: a cake. Thursday: she told my manager, in front of me, that I'm a genius. It's a lot.

My first thought was that she's secretly furious and planning something. But I don't think that's fair. Nobody has done anything unkind. I think she's disappointed and doesn't want to look disappointed, so it's coming out as extra praise.

So I'm not going to be suspicious. I'm going to ask her for coffee and ask about the project she wants to lead next.

What do you think?

Ishita

What did Farzana bring on Wednesday?
A cake.
Why did Ishita decide not to treat Farzana's praise as a plot?
Ishita felt wary at first but then fair-minded, seeing that nobody had done anything unkind and that the extra praise more likely hid Farzana's disappointment.
What makes Ishita's coffee plan a good idea?
It shows respect for Farzana's ambitions and opens a real conversation, instead of treating her as a threat.
How might Farzana be feeling underneath all the congratulations?
Farzana may feel disappointed and a little embarrassed, and eager not to look bitter.

Monday. After Mama Ji laughed at the wedding, 'Siddharth, you're thin as a broom,' Siddharth scrolled gym reels until midnight: perfect arms, shining abs. He wore two T-shirts to school the next day so nobody would see his shoulders. Thursday. His cousin Disha caught him frowning at his phone. She opened a photo editor and, in three swipes, made her own arms bigger and her waist smaller. 'Half those reels are lit, posed and edited like this,' she said. 'You're comparing yourself to a filter.' He stared at the screen for a long time. Two weeks later. Siddharth had joined the school swimming batch. Tired and dripping after his first full length without stopping, he caught sight of himself in the changing-room mirror and, for once, thought about what his shoulders had just done, not how they looked.

What did Disha show Siddharth with the photo editor?
In three swipes she made her own arms bigger and her waist smaller.
Why did Siddharth wear two T-shirts to school?
He felt ashamed and self-conscious about his thin shoulders after Mama Ji's joke and the reels.
What helped Siddharth start to shift how he saw his body?
Seeing how reels are edited, then swimming, which let him notice what his body can do rather than how it looks 💪
How does Disha see Siddharth's scrolling?
She sees him comparing himself to edited images, so she shows him the trick instead of just telling him he's fine.

"What's that noise, Eshaan?" Papa called.
"Box!" Eshaan held up the snack box, twisted it, then pulled at the lid.
"Stuck?"
Bang! He whacked it on the floor.
"Gently, beta."
"Open!" He poked a finger at the edge, then tried twisting again.
Naveen sat beside him. "Twist, pull, bang, poke. You tried a lot of ways."
Eshaan pushed the box into his lap. "Papa do."

What did Eshaan do right after the lid stayed stuck?
He whacked it on the floor.
What was Eshaan feeling when he pushed the box into Papa's lap?
He was frustrated that none of his tries worked, and hopeful that Papa could do it.
What would you advise Naveen to do now?
He could open the lid slowly in front of Eshaan so he can watch how it works, giving him a new idea to try next time.
How does Eshaan's trial and error look to Naveen?
Naveen sees a busy little experimenter and names each try out loud, calm rather than cross about the banging.

In Hanoi, Tuan leaned across the lunch table. "Did you know the new science teacher got fired from her last school?"

His friend Javier, an exchange student, stopped eating. "Really? Who told you?"

"Everyone's saying it."

"But who first?"

Tuan thought. There had been a screenshot in a group chat, forwarded from somewhere. Then two classmates mentioned it. By now it felt like something he'd always known.

"I'm... not sure," Tuan admitted.

Javier shrugged. "She seems nice. Maybe it's not true."

Tuan looked across at the teacher, who was helping a student carry books. He felt uneasy. He had told three people already.

How many people had Tuan already told?
He had told three people already.
Why did Tuan feel uneasy looking at the teacher?
He felt uneasy and a bit guilty, realising he had spread a claim he couldn't trace, about someone who seemed kind.
What could Tuan do now?
He could tell the three people he isn't sure it's true and stop passing it on.
How might the teacher be affected if the rumour keeps spreading?
She could be judged unfairly by students, even though the claim may be false.

Hostel warden's log, Block C, the week the winter fog set in.
Monday: Madhav came to my desk worried about his roommate. Harsha had three unopened letters from the accounts office and had failed two internal tests. When I asked Harsha, he laughed. "It'll sort itself out. First-term results are always weird."
Wednesday: The counsellor told me Harsha had not answered her two emails. At breakfast I saw him scroll straight past them.
Friday: The accounts office pinned the final date for fees on the notice board: next Tuesday. Harsha stood reading it for a long time, then knocked on my door, pale. I walked him to the counsellor's room that afternoon and asked someone from accounts to join. Madhav waited outside with two cups of tea.

What did the accounts office pin on the notice board?
The final date for fees: next Tuesday.
Why did Harsha laugh and say it would sort itself out?
He felt dread about the fees and marks, and not looking kept that fear at a distance, so ignoring the letters felt easier than opening them.
What could have helped Harsha sooner?
Opening one letter with Madhav or the warden early and replying to the counsellor would have let him get help before the deadline forced it.
How is Madhav affected by Harsha's avoidance?
Madhav is worried enough to go to the warden, yet stays loyal, waiting outside with tea when Harsha finally faces it.
Is the second part okay? When I will reach home, I will call you.

When I reach home, I will call you.
Why: after "when" about the future, use the present simple.

So Devika, remember when Sir announced in assembly that my poem won the district round? Everybody turned and clapped. I was grinning like an idiot, but my hands went into my pockets and I looked at the floor. Then I said, loudly, "It was just luck, ask Devika, she gave me the rhyme." People laughed and Sir looked confused. After that I wanted to disappear. Later, in the corridor, Sir said quietly, "I meant it, Wasim. The last verse was really good." And that made my chest feel warm without anyone watching. I'm not against praise. I just can't take it with two hundred people looking.

What did Sir announce in assembly?
He announced that Wasim's poem won the district round.
Why did Wasim joke and look at the floor when praised?
Wasim was pleased but uncomfortable being the centre of two hundred people's attention. The joke about luck may have been a way to deflect the attention, not a rejection of the praise.
How could Sir give Wasim recognition next time?
He could say a private word or write a short note, since the corridor comment felt warm to Wasim.
How might Sir have read Wasim's joke in assembly?
He may have thought Wasim did not care or was being modest, which is why he looked confused.

What does "goal" mean?
How can I make my cousin feel welcome when she visits?

1. A goal is the place where you must send the ball to score a point in some games.
2. Show her around the house and ask what she would like to do. Share your games with her.

By Thursday afternoon at the ad agency in Andheri, Kashish had built a whole story. Sachin hadn't laughed at her joke in the stand-up. He'd answered her draft with "noted." He'd eaten lunch at his desk instead of joining them.

He thinks I stole the tea-brand pitch idea, she thought. He's going to say it in Monday's review. She'd already rehearsed three replies in the washroom mirror.

At four she caught herself drafting a fourth. Enough. She walked over to his desk.

"Sachin, can I ask something? Are you annoyed with me about the pitch? I'd rather ask than keep guessing."

He looked up, surprised. "What? No! My landlord's selling the flat and I have to move by the fifteenth. I've been apartment-hunting on my phone all day. Sorry, I've been a zombie."

The whole thing took two minutes. Kashish went back to her desk and deleted the fourth reply.

What did Sachin answer Kashish's draft with?
He'd answered her draft with "noted."
Why did Kashish's story about Sachin feel so convincing to her?
Each small sign, the missed laugh, the short reply and the lunch at his desk, seemed to fit one explanation. Rehearsing replies in the mirror made the imagined conflict feel even more real.
What was the turning point, and why did it work so quickly?
Kashish caught herself drafting a fourth reply and decided to ask Sachin directly. One two-minute question replaced days of guessing with his actual reason.
How might Sachin have felt when Kashish asked if he was annoyed?
Sachin was surprised, and maybe a little relieved to explain why he'd been so distracted. He might also have felt bad that his stress had come across as coldness.

Saturday. Ramesh had been getting five "hot tips" a week and felt more confused each time. He took a sheet and started writing rules for himself: small amounts, the same day every month; only products that are registered and regulated; nothing that promises a fixed high return. Vikas read it over his shoulder.

Wednesday. A colleague pitched a "guaranteed" scheme. Ramesh checked the sheet, saw the third rule, and said no in half a minute without arguing.

Sunday. The rules were stuck on the inside of the cupboard door. Ramesh said, "I no longer judge every pitch. The sheet does that." For personal choices Ramesh still planned to ask a qualified adviser.

How often does the plan say to put in small amounts?
The plan says to put in small amounts on the same day every month.
What did Ramesh feel about the flood of hot tips before writing rules?
Ramesh felt more confused each time, and the rules were written to end that confusion.
What could Ramesh do to check the policy suits personal needs, and why?
Ramesh could show the sheet to a qualified adviser, because rules need to be tested against personal circumstances.
How might the colleague who pitched the scheme see Ramesh's quick no?
The colleague may feel surprised or a little annoyed, since Ramesh refused without a debate.

In their flat in Lajpat Nagar, Ankita, nine, was teaching her little brother Lalit snakes and ladders.
"You roll, then you move. No, not that way! Ugh, give it." She moved his counter for him.
Lalit crossed his arms. "Then you play alone."
Ankita huffed and looked at the board. How did you explain which way to go? She traced it with her finger. Left, left, left, then up, then right, right, right. A zigzag. She had never noticed. She had only played.
"Lalit, look. It's a zigzag. Follow my finger." She let him move his own counter. When he climbed a ladder, she clapped louder than he did.
Their mother, in the kitchen, smiled at the clapping, though she also heard Ankita say "not like that" four more times.

In which neighbourhood is the flat?
In their flat in Lajpat Nagar.
Why did Lalit cross his arms?
Lalit felt annoyed and hurt that Ankita took over and moved his counter for him.
How could Ankita keep helping without taking over?
Ankita could keep letting Lalit move his own counter and show the zigzag with her finger instead of grabbing the board.
How does their mother see the game from the kitchen?
Their mother smiles at the clapping but notices Ankita is still bossy, saying "not like that" four more times.

The cricket ball went straight through Mrs Kulkarni's kitchen window, and within a minute all of Usha's family on the third floor knew. Minakshi Chachi scolded her in the corridor. Tauji laughed and said he had broken three windows at her age. Mummy said she must apologise herself. Dadi slipped her a piece of jaggery and said nobody was hurt, that was what mattered. Usha did not know whose words to follow, and she wanted to cry somewhere, but every room had someone in it. In the end, her two cousins walked down with her to Mrs Kulkarni's door, one on each side, and Usha said sorry with her voice shaking.

Whose window did the cricket ball break?
Mrs Kulkarni's kitchen window.
What was Usha feeling when she wanted to cry somewhere?
She felt overwhelmed and ashamed, confused by four different reactions, with no private room to let it out.
How could the adults support Usha better next time?
Agree on one message, such as apologise and help put it right, and let one adult talk to her quietly instead of all at once.
What is it like for the cousins walking down with Usha?
They get to stand by her, which likely feels loyal and a little brave, and shows the warmth a big family can give.

Team coach's note, week 3 of the app redesign.
Before work began, Sachin put a blank sheet on the wall and said, "On the last project, three of us were angry by week six and nobody said so. Let's decide now what fair looks like."
Vaibhav suggested each person take two tickets a week and flag early if they'll miss one. Nidhi added that design reviews count as work too, which nobody had thought of. Kabir asked what happens if someone's ill; they agreed the team reshuffles, no blame. The tracker is a column of names and ticks.
Three weeks in, Kabir flagged a missed ticket on Tuesday, not Friday, and Nidhi picked it up without a sigh. Stand-ups are calmer than anything I've seen on this floor all year.
What I did next: I asked Sachin to show the sheet to the other two teams.

How many tickets a week did Vaibhav suggest each person take?
Two tickets a week.
What feeling seems to push Sachin to start the discussion?
Sachin seems wary and a little tired of old resentment, remembering three people angry and silent by week six last time.
Why does agreeing on fairness before the work starts help?
Everyone knows the rules in advance, so a missed ticket is flagged early and handled by agreement instead of building quiet anger.
How might Nidhi experience covering Kabir's missed ticket?
Nidhi seems calm about it, probably because the rule was agreed openly and it doesn't feel like being taken advantage of 🙂

In their Pune flat, Chinmay had tabla practice every evening, and every evening his phone buzzed through it: cricket scores, group jokes, his cousin's memes. He'd play four beats, check, play four more.
His sister Deepika, home from college, watched one evening. "How long do you actually play without stopping?"
Chinmay thought. "Maybe two minutes?"
"Try this. Phone on silent, in the other room. Forty minutes. Timer."
The first ten minutes were torture. He kept reaching for his pocket. Then, somewhere around fifteen, something shifted. His hands found the rhythm, and the teentaal just kept rolling, faster and cleaner than ever.
When the timer rang, he looked up, amazed. "That felt like five minutes."
Now the door closes at six. His friends know he replies at seven. He's stopped apologising for it.

Where did Deepika tell Chinmay to put his phone?
Phone on silent, in the other room.
How did Chinmay feel when the timer rang?
Chinmay felt amazed and energised, as the forty minutes had felt like five.
Why is Chinmay's new routine a skill and not stubbornness?
Guarding a fixed block without notifications gives him the unbroken minutes he needs for his hands to find the rhythm.
How might Chinmay's friends see his new rule?
His friends may have found it odd at first, but they now know he replies at seven and seem to accept it.

On the first day after the Christmas holidays, Chetan walked through the Bengaluru school gate with a shiny new cricket kit bag, zips everywhere. A crowd gathered. Kavitha stood at the edge. "He's just showing off," she told her friends at lunch. "He's jealous of everyone who plays better than him. That's why he got it." She said it three times. In the evening her mother heard her going on about Chetan again. "You've mentioned his bag six times, Kavitha," she said gently. "Do you wish you had one?" Kavitha opened her mouth to say no, then burst into tears. "I've wanted one forever."

What did Chetan bring on the first day after the holidays?
A shiny new cricket kit bag with zips everywhere.
Why did Kavitha burst into tears?
Her mother's question uncovered the envy she had been placing on Chetan; she felt sad and exposed about wanting a kit bag forever.
How did Kavitha's mother help?
She noticed the repetition and gently asked whether Kavitha wished she had one, making it safe to own the feeling.
How might Chetan feel if he hears what Kavitha said?
Hurt and confused, since he was simply excited about his new bag.

In the Class 2 science room, Gautam, the teacher, poured water from a tall thin glass into a wide bowl. "More, less or the same?" he asked. Most children shouted, "Less!" Pradeep, seven, frowned. "Same. You didn't add any or take any out." "But it looks lower," said his partner. Pradeep took the bowl and poured it back into the glass. "See? Back to the same line." Gautam smiled. "Pradeep, explain again for everyone."

What did Gautam pour the water into?
A wide bowl.
Why did Pradeep frown when the others shouted "Less!"?
He was puzzled because he felt sure it was the same amount and disagreed with the class.
What did Gautam do well, and what could come next?
He let Pradeep prove it by pouring back; next he could try the same idea with rice or clay.
How might Pradeep's partner feel when the water reached the same line?
Surprised, and perhaps curious about why it looked like less.
