Summer puzzle club, week three. Note for Preeti's family.
Preeti arrived today holding her uncle Vishal's hand; he told me again, "She's our little genius, she never gets anything wrong." Preeti smiled but went quiet.
When I put out the harder grid puzzles, Preeti chose the easy ones she had finished last week. I asked her to try a new grid. She said, "I don't want to," and when a square wouldn't fit she pushed the sheet away and scowled. Later she told me softly, "If I get it wrong, I won't be clever anymore."
Next I sat beside her and we solved one row together. I praised how she tested three numbers before one fitted. She tried a second row alone.
Suggestion: at home, notice her trying, not her being smart.

Which puzzles did Preeti choose when the harder grids came out?
She chose the easy ones she had finished last week.
Why does Preeti push the sheet away and scowl?
She feels scared and angry, because a wrong answer seems to threaten the clever label she keeps hearing, and she worries she won't be clever anymore.
How could Preeti's family support her at home?
They could praise the way she tries, like testing different numbers, instead of calling her a genius who never gets things wrong.
How might Vishal see Preeti's choice of easy puzzles if he only hears about her scores?
Vishal might think she is simply doing well, without noticing that the genius label is making her avoid anything hard.

(Tenzin, 15, texting his friend Nirmala on Wednesday night)
Nirmala: stream forms due friday, you filled it?
Tenzin: yeah bio
Nirmala: wait. you hate bio. you literally fainted at the frog video
Tenzin: everyone in my family did bio. Pala, Amala, both uncles, my big brother
Tenzin: form was already filled when i got home, i just signed
Nirmala: but what do you WANT
Tenzin: geography? maps, weather stuff. the field trips
Tenzin: but switching means talking to Pala, the principal, new books… its a lot
Nirmala: so you're choosing bio because it's easier than talking?
Tenzin: i'm not choosing it. it just happened
Nirmala: that's kind of the problem 😕
Tenzin: …
Tenzin: ok can you come with me when i talk to Pala
Nirmala: yes. thursday after school?
Tenzin: ok. still scared. but ok

Who in Tenzin's family did biology?
Pala, Amala, both uncles, and his big brother.
Why was Tenzin about to stay in biology even though he hates it?
Tenzin felt scared of the effort and risk of switching, like talking to Pala and the principal, so staying with the form already filled felt easier.
What was the turning point in the chat, and what did Tenzin decide?
When Nirmala asked if he was choosing biology because it was easier than talking. Tenzin realised it just happened, and asked Nirmala to come along when he talks to Pala.
How might Nirmala feel when Tenzin says "i'm not choosing it"?
Nirmala seems worried and a bit frustrated, seeing a friend drift into a stream he doesn't want, which is why Nirmala presses gently.

Monday. Mahima leaned over the desk. "Tell me what Tanvi told you about her brother and I'll be your best friend forever." Deepak's stomach dipped. He had eaten lunch alone all week. "No," he said, and looked at his pencil box.

Wednesday. She was waiting by the water cooler. "Last chance. Otherwise nobody sits with you." Deepak's hands felt cold, but he said, "That's not being friends. I'm not telling," and walked to the library.

Friday. Mahima blocked the corridor again, whispering the same demand. This time Deepak went straight to the class teacher and told everything, even the part where he had almost said yes. The teacher thanked him and said they would talk to Mahima.

What did Mahima want Deepak to tell her?
She wanted to know what Tanvi told him about her brother.
Why might Deepak have felt tempted on Monday even though he said no?
He had eaten lunch alone all week, so the offer of a best friend was tempting, though he still said no.
What did Deepak's choice on Friday accomplish?
Telling the class teacher moved the pressure from him to an adult who could talk to Mahima, so he did not have to handle it alone.
How might Tanvi feel if she learned what happened?
She might feel relieved and grateful that her secret stayed safe, though she may not know how close it came.

Notes on Eshaan, Wednesday. He came to my desk furious: the accounts team had been told to backdate leave records so that contract staff would lose paid leave they had earned. He wanted to email the whole company that night. I asked him to wait. Over the week he copied the leave sheets, found two colleagues who had seen the same instruction, and filed a written complaint with the HR grievance committee. He knows his manager may freeze his promotion. He is calmer now, not calm. He said, "I'd rather lose the promotion than sign it." I will go with him to the hearing.

Mridul

What had the accounts team been told to do with the leave records?
They had been told to backdate the leave records so contract staff would lose paid leave they had earned.
What does Eshaan's remark about the promotion suggest about what he cares about?
It suggests he values acting honestly over advancing, and that his anger has turned into a firm decision, even though he knows it may cost him.
Why was gathering the sheets and finding colleagues a stronger move than emailing the whole company?
It gave him evidence and allies and sent the concern through a proper channel, which protects him and makes it harder to dismiss.
How might the contract staff see Eshaan's complaint?
They may feel relief and hope that someone is standing up for them, and perhaps some worry about what happens to Eshaan.
In the epic, he set out avenging his brother. What is avenging?

Avenging means punishing someone for harm done to another person, usually the person you love. It is a verb in its -ing form.
Example: The hero left home avenging the wrongs done to his family.

Dear Bidisha Didi,
You asked in your last email how Class 10 is going. Honestly? Lonely. At lunch everyone talks about the same show, and when I mention the black hole paper I read, they look at me like I'm from another planet. So I've started pretending I didn't understand the maths homework either, just to fit in.
And then there's the other thing. Papa pins every rank card on the fridge. When I came second in chemistry, I couldn't sleep.
But something good happened. Ms Rao sent me to the district astronomy club. There are kids there who argue about telescopes for hours. I felt normal for the first time in months.
And Ms Rao said something I keep repeating: "You're allowed to be average at some things." It felt like putting down a school bag.
Write back soon,
Sangeeta

Where did Ms Rao send Sangeeta?
To the district astronomy club.
How did Sangeeta feel at lunch with classmates?
Sangeeta felt lonely and out of step, so much so that pretending not to understand the homework seemed the only way to fit in.
What helped relieve the pressure, and why?
Finding like-minded kids at the astronomy club and a mentor's permission to be average sometimes, which eased the need to be top in everything.
How might Bidisha Didi feel reading this email?
Bidisha Didi might feel concerned about the loneliness and sleepless night, and relieved that Sangeeta has found a place to feel normal.

Rajni, you asked why I keep a plate of sewaiyan aside for Farida's family on Eid, so listen. I am Lokesh, your Nana. When your mother was twenty, she came home glowing about her friend Farida, and I felt fear rising. What will the neighbours say? Will she forget our traditions? I nearly said, "Stop seeing her." Instead, one night at dinner I asked, "What do you like about Farida?" Your mother said, "She never laughs at anyone. When I lost my purse on the train, she gave me her own fare home." I went quiet. That was not a label. That was a person. I still worried, but I invited Farida's family for Diwali, and her mother brought sewaiyan a few months later. My fears lost their sharp edges slowly. Your mother and Farida still speak every Sunday.

What did Lokesh ask at dinner instead of saying "Stop seeing her"?
He asked, "What do you like about Farida?"
What was Lokesh afraid of when Rajni's mother came home glowing about Farida?
Lokesh was afraid of what the neighbours would say and that she might forget their traditions.
What choice did Lokesh make instead of banning the friendship, and what did it lead to?
He asked about Farida and listened, which led to hearing about her kindness and to inviting Farida's family for Diwali.
How might Rajni's mother have felt when he asked what she liked about Farida?
Probably relieved and heard. She answered warmly with a story about Farida's kindness instead of having to defend her.

Class teacher's note, Tuesday.
Mridul (class four) has been called "the lazy one" by several teachers since class two, and he now says it about himself: "I'm lazy, ma'am, I won't finish." Today he didn't even start the maths worksheet. Payal, who is often called "the clever one," asked for an extra hard sheet. Both children seem to be living up to what they've heard. I sat with Mridul and asked him to do only the first three sums with me. He did them correctly and quickly. I told him, "That wasn't lazy. That was careful and fast." He looked surprised. I've asked the other teachers to stop using the word "lazy" and I'll give Mridul short challenges each day this week.

What does Mridul now say about himself?
He says, "I'm lazy, ma'am, I won't finish."
How did Mridul seem to feel when the teacher called him careful and fast?
Mridul seemed surprised and perhaps a little proud, hearing something different from his usual label.
Why are short daily challenges and dropping the word "lazy" good steps?
They give Mridul chances to succeed and stop reinforcing a label he has started to live up to.
How might being called "the clever one" affect Payal?
Payal seems encouraged to take on harder tasks, confident because others expect success.
Siddharth asked me to help him for his project. Is "for" right?

Siddharth asked me to help him with his project.
Why: help someone "with" a task, not "for".

At the Friday lunch in the Bengaluru office, Raghav was on a roll. He'd already done a good bit about the lift that stopped at every floor, and Noor had laughed as hard as anyone. Then he turned to Tenzin, who had joined from Darjeeling two weeks ago, and made a joke about his face and where he "really" came from. A few people laughed. Tenzin laughed too, a short sound, then looked down at his plate and didn't look up again. Noor saw it. Laughter, she thought, isn't the same as being okay. She didn't want to shame Raghav in front of everyone, but she didn't want to let it pass either. "Raghav, the lift material was better," she said lightly, and changed the subject. After lunch she caught him alone. "That joke about Tenzin landed badly. Did you see his face?" Raghav frowned, then nodded. "I'll talk to him." Noor messaged Tenzin: "That wasn't okay. Want to grab chai?"

Where did Tenzin join from?
From Darjeeling.
What might Tenzin have been feeling after the joke?
Tenzin likely felt hurt and uncomfortable, laughing briefly to get through it and then looking down at his plate.
How did Noor respond to the joke?
She redirected lightly in the moment, then spoke to Raghav privately about Tenzin's reaction, and checked in with Tenzin with an offer of chai.
How did Raghav react when Noor spoke to him privately?
Raghav frowned, then accepted it and said he would talk to Tenzin.

Vikas,

I'm writing this because last night, at eleven, we were both too tired and I did not want to say the wrong thing about the phone bill and the money for your brother. So I'm glad we stopped. Tonight, after dinner, when the dishes are done, can we sit down for half an hour? I want to tell you what I need: to know about money before it leaves our account, not after. And I want to hear your side fully, without me finishing your sentences. I know your family matters to you and I'm not asking you to pick. Maybe we can decide one small thing together, like a limit we both agree on, and look at it again next month. I'm not keeping a list of who did what. I just want us on the same side of the table. 🙂

Sunaina

When does Sunaina ask Vikas to sit down and talk?
Tonight, after dinner, when the dishes are done, for half an hour.
Why did Sunaina stop the talk at eleven at night, and what does Sunaina hope for now?
Sunaina was afraid of saying the wrong thing while both were tired, and hopes for a calmer talk where Sunaina states the need and hears Vikas's side fully.
What would you advise Vikas to do when they sit down?
Listen to the end, say what Vikas needs too, and agree one small next step, such as a limit they will look at again next month.
How might Vikas feel when reading the line about the brother?
Vikas might worry about being asked to choose between Sunaina and the family, so Sunaina's words about not asking Vikas to pick may ease that.

Note to myself, Sunday

Rafiq has been moping since Disha started spending lunch with the robotics kids. He said, "She was never really my friend," and slammed his door.

I didn't argue. At bedtime I asked what he missed most. "Building forts with her," he said.

On Monday I suggested he just say hello to her at the gate, nothing more. He came home and said, "She said hi back. She seemed normal."

Today I helped him invite Disha to fly kites on our terrace. She came for an hour. Rafiq was quiet afterwards but not angry.

I told him that some friends are close in one season and further away in another, and that the forts they built were real. He said, "So it wasn't fake?" I said, "No. It was real."

He went to sleep smiling a little.

— Rafiq's Ammi

What did Rafiq say he missed most?
Building forts with her.
Why did Rafiq say Disha was never really his friend?
He was hurt and angry that she now spent lunch with the robotics kids, so he tried to protect himself by saying the friendship was never real.
How did Ammi help Rafiq keep kindness through the change?
She listened without arguing, then helped with small steps, a hello and one kite afternoon, and told him the friendship was real even if it changes.
What is it like for Disha to be invited to the terrace?
She is probably pleased to be remembered by an old friend, even though robotics now takes much of her time.
Please recieve the parcel from the postman. Is the spelling right?

Please receive the parcel from the postman.
Why: "i before e, except after c": "receive".

Read this:

Two weeks ago. Saurabh was stuck on his Hindi essay the night before it was due, and Tejas came over and helped him plan it, sentence by sentence. Saurabh was so grateful he said, 'I owe you big.'
Monday. Before the science test, Tejas whispered, 'Remember you owe me? Pass me your answer sheet when Sir turns round.' Saurabh's stomach dropped. He did owe Tejas. Didn't he?
Tuesday. Saurabh had kept his sheet covered in the test, and Tejas wouldn't look at him. At break Saurabh went over. 'I'm grateful, really. But I won't help you cheat. I'll help you revise for the retest, every evening this week. That's how I pay you back.' Tejas kicked at the gravel, hands in his pockets, then shrugged. 'Evenings at your place. Your mum makes better snacks.'

What did Tejas help Saurabh with two weeks ago?
Planning his Hindi essay.
What was Saurabh feeling when Tejas said 'Remember you owe me'?
Torn and uneasy; his stomach dropped because he felt indebted but knew cheating was wrong.
How did Saurabh repay Tejas honestly?
He refused to pass his answer sheet but offered to help Tejas revise every evening for the retest.
How did Tejas feel after Saurabh kept his sheet covered?
Annoyed or hurt; he wouldn't look at Saurabh.
"Kal se thand badh jaayegi" English mein kya hoga?
It is: "It will get colder from tomorrow."
Aur "garmi badhegi"?
It is: "It will get hotter." Use "hotter" for more heat and "colder" for more cold.

Read this:

At the temple fair, Tejas, two, sat on his grandfather Hrithik's shoulders as a drummer in a bright mask stepped near. Tejas squeezed his eyes tight shut and buried his face in Hrithik's grey hair. “Not looking,” he mumbled. Hrithik walked to a quiet corner and said nothing more. Later, among the sweet stalls, Tejas's blinks grew slow and heavy. His head sank onto Hrithik's shoulder and his eyes closed. Hrithik headed home, patting the small back.

Where was Tejas when the masked drummer came close?
On his grandfather Hrithik's shoulders at the temple fair.
Why did Tejas squeeze his eyes shut, and what else could explain it?
Most likely he was scared by the mask and drum, since he hid his face and said “Not looking”. It could also be that the noise and crowd were too much, which is a different kind of overwhelm.
What did Hrithik do that helped?
He moved to a quiet corner and did not push Tejas to look, which lets a frightened child settle in his own time.
How might the drummer see a child hiding his face?
He may realise the costume looks big and frightening to a small child, and could give a friendly wave from a distance rather than take offence.

"Rekha, answer the phone! It's your cousin from Canada!" called her father Yogesh during the Christmas holidays.
Rekha, eleven, picked up. "Hello! Merry Christmas!" she said in English.
Then her grandmother grabbed the phone. Rekha switched to Marathi, translating what her cousin said. "She says it's snowing."
"Snow! Ask if she's wearing a sweater!"
Rekha asked in English, laughed, and answered in Marathi. "Two sweaters, Aaji."
Her father grinned. "Our little translator."

What did the cousin say about the weather?
It's snowing.
How did Rekha seem to feel on the call?
She seemed confident and happy, laughing as she switched languages.
How can her family support Rekha's language skills?
Keep speaking Marathi at home and encourage calls with relatives in English.
How might Aaji feel about the call?
Aaji likely feels delighted and included thanks to Rekha.

messages.content: What is the aroha of Raga Patdeep?
The aroha of Raga Patdeep is: N S g M P N S'.

Read this:

Dear Nirmala Didi,

You asked why I dropped the art elective. The truth is, I'm just not a creative person. You got those genes, not me.

On the first day we had to draw a hand. Everyone else's looked like a hand. Mine looked like a glove full of sticks. The teacher said it was “a start.” I knew what that meant.

So I switched to accountancy. I'm good with numbers. That's who I am.

Sometimes, though, in accountancy class, I doodle little birds in the corner of the page. They're not very good. I cross them out before anyone sees.

Anyway, how's your exhibition going? Send me pictures.

Rajni

What did Rajni have to draw on the first day?
A hand.
How does Rajni feel about drawing, based on the crossed-out birds?
Rajni seems to still enjoy drawing but feels embarrassed and inadequate, believing creativity is a fixed trait Rajni lacks.
What could Nirmala Didi say in reply that might help?
That Nirmala Didi's own early drawings were rough too, and that skill grows with practice, inviting Rajni to keep doodling without judging.
How might Nirmala Didi feel reading this letter?
Nirmala Didi might feel sad and a little guilty that her talent made Rajni feel it was out of reach.

Read this:

Dear Irfan,

You asked how I keep writing the weekly report even when I'd rather not. Honestly, I rarely feel like it. Most Mondays I sit down feeling heavy and a little bored.

Here's what I do. At 9:30, whatever my mood, I open last week's report and copy the headings. Then I fill in the easiest number. Then the next. By ten, I'm usually interested. And on the days I'm not, the report still gets done, because the routine doesn't ask how I'm feeling.

I used to think I needed motivation to start. Now I think starting is what makes it.

See you at lunch,
Kunal

What time does Kunal open last week's report?
How does Kunal usually feel on Monday mornings?
Kunal usually feels heavy and a little bored, rarely feeling like writing the report.
What could Irfan copy from Kunal's routine?
Irfan could start at a fixed time with the easiest step, like copying headings and filling in the easiest number, whatever the mood.
How might Irfan see Kunal after reading the letter?
Irfan might be reassured that even a reliable colleague lacks motivation often and simply relies on routine.
In our meeting someone mentioned "the elephant in the room". What was that about?

"The elephant in the room" is a big, obvious problem that everyone knows about but nobody wants to discuss.
Example: Everyone was worried about the missing funds, so the budget was the elephant in the room until Rekha finally raised it.
At what time does the toy train start from Darjeeling tomorrow?
I don't know, because timetables change by season and I don't have the current one. The railway's website or the station office confirms departure times.

Read this:

At the college hackathon, Jatin, nineteen, cracked the routing algorithm at 3 a.m. that had stumped every team. At 5 a.m. he discovered he'd saved it nowhere. His teammate Aditi found him staring at the screen. "It's gone. I'm useless," he said. Aditi, the team lead, had been tired and snappy herself all night, and he hadn't noticed. She sat down. "You're brilliant at the hard part, and you're terrible at saving files. Both are true. Rewrite it; I'll set up auto-save." He rewrote it in forty minutes. Later, he said, "You were upset last night, weren't you? I missed that." Aditi smiled. "You're learning." They came second, and Jatin kept a sticky note on his laptop: SAVE. ASK.

What did Jatin write on his sticky note?
He wrote SAVE. ASK.
How did Jatin feel when he found his work was not saved?
He felt ashamed and hopeless, calling himself useless.
How did Aditi help Jatin see his strengths and gaps without shame?
She named both honestly, that he is brilliant at algorithms and bad at saving files, then helped fix the practical gap.
How might Aditi feel when Jatin asks about her mood?
She may feel noticed and pleased, seeing that he is working on reading other people's feelings.
My manager keeps adding tasks without asking if I have time.
That is hard to manage. It may help to talk about it calmly and with facts, such as a list of what you are already working on.
How do I start that conversation?
You could say, 'I want to do these well. Can we look at my list and decide what comes first?' It puts the focus on priorities, not complaints.
What if the manager says everything is urgent?
Ask which item should be done first if all cannot be finished. That makes the trade-off clear without arguing.
Should I put it in writing?
A short follow-up email confirming the priorities is useful. It gives both sides a clear record.
And if nothing changes?
Then you may want to raise it with a senior person or the HR team. Keep your notes factual so they can see the pattern.

Read this:

Gopika's crayon box burst open on the pavement outside the market, and crayons rolled everywhere. Before Papa could bend down, an aunty in a green sari crouched and gathered them into her palm.
"Here, beta."
Gopika hid half behind Arnab's leg. She had not expected a stranger to help. "Thank you, Aunty," she whispered.
The aunty beamed. "What a sweet voice!"
Gopika looked at her shoes, smiling, her cheeks warm.
"She was nice," she told Papa as they walked on.

What did the aunty pick up?
She picked up the crayons that had rolled out of Gopika's box.
How does Gopika feel when the aunty helps her?
She feels surprised and warm: she had not expected a stranger to help, and her cheeks go warm as she smiles.
What did Gopika do that made the moment good for both of them?
She said thank you, even shyly, and the aunty beamed, so both felt good. 😊
How might the aunty have felt about the thank you?
She seems pleased, since she beams and praises Gopika's voice.

Read this:

Paulo was in his second year of law at the university in Lisbon, the career his mother and grandfather had both chosen for him. "Law is my path," he told everyone. But every weekday he woke at six with a heaviness in his chest and lay staring at the ceiling. His flatmate Liam noticed that the only time Paulo whistled was on Sunday, cooking for the whole flat, trying new sauces, tasting, laughing. One Sunday, Liam asked, "Do you ever think about cooking? Like, properly?" Paulo laughed too loudly. "Cooking is a hobby. Law is my future." "You don't whistle on weekdays." Paulo stirred the pan. "I'm just tired on weekdays." "Are you tired, or are you sad?" Paulo put the spoon down. For a moment he looked at the steam rising from the pot. "My mother would never forgive me." "You didn't say you didn't want it," Liam said gently.

When was the only time Paulo whistled?
Only on Sunday, cooking for the whole flat.
Why does Paulo say he is just tired on weekdays?
Paulo feels dread and sadness about law, but calling it tiredness hides a wish that would upset his mother.
What would you advise Paulo after this conversation?
To be honest with himself first about what he wants, maybe by trying a short cooking course, before deciding how to talk to his mother.
What might Liam be feeling as he asks these questions?
Liam seems caring and a little worried, wanting his friend to stop hiding from himself.

Read this:

Study hour at the boys' hostel began at seven. Vijay, ten, had a clay model of the water cycle due the next morning. "Ten minutes," he told Preeti didi, the evening warden. "Clay, cloud, arrow, done."
"Last month your map took two evenings," she reminded him.
"That was different. This one is easy."
At 7:30 he found the clay was hard and had to soak it. At 8:00 his cloud kept falling off the cardboard. At 8:40 he realised he hadn't written the labels. The lights-out bell rang at nine, and the arrows were still missing. Vijay stared at his sticky fingers, eyes shiny.
Preeti didi sat down beside him. "Tell me, how long did the map really take?" she asked.
"Two evenings," he mumbled.

At what time did the lights-out bell ring?
The lights-out bell rang at nine.
Why did Vijay feel so sure the model would take only ten minutes?
He felt confident, picturing it going perfectly, clay, cloud, arrow, done, so he forgot how long his map had taken last month.
What could Vijay try next time a project is due?
He could remember how long the map really took and start a few days earlier, breaking the model into small jobs like soaking the clay and writing labels.
How might Preeti didi feel sitting beside Vijay at the end?
She probably feels sorry for him with his sticky fingers and shiny eyes, and hopes her gentle question helps him remember the map next time.

In the Gurugram office, Imran's analytics team and Uday's sales team had to share one client dashboard. In week one, Imran sent Uday his cleaned data without being asked. Uday thanked him and sent back the client's feedback. Good. In week three, on the client call, Uday presented Imran's churn chart as "our sales insight". Imran didn't fume in the group chat or quietly stop sending data. After the call he walked to Uday's desk. "That chart was ours. Next time, credit my team, or I'll say it on the call." Uday went red. The next morning he emailed the client: "Correction: the churn analysis came from Imran's team." Imran messaged Uday privately: "Thanks. Friday's data is coming as usual." And it did.

Tell me in three sentences what this reading says.

Imran's analytics team and Uday's sales team share a client dashboard, and Imran sends Uday cleaned data. When Uday presents Imran's chart as the sales team's insight, Imran asks him to credit the analytics team next time. Uday emails the client a correction, and Imran thanks him and keeps sending data.

Read this:

"Hemant, how did you stay so steady last night?"
"Sir? The server outage?"
"Yogesh is fine. And yes. Two hours down, the client calling every ten minutes, and you were the one saying 'Okay, next step.' I was pacing."
Hemant scratched his head. "Honestly, I was scared. I just wrote everything on the whiteboard so I wouldn't forget."
"That whiteboard is the reason we got it back. I've been doing this eight years and I've never thought of doing that."
"It's just a habit from college."
"It's a good one. Can you write it up as a checklist for the team? And I'd like you to lead the post-mortem call on Friday."
"Me? With the client?"
"With the client. I'll be there. But it's your call."
Hemant's grin was slow and wide. "Okay. Yes."
Yogesh picked up a marker. "Show me how you set it out."

What did Hemant write on the whiteboard during the outage?
Everything, so he wouldn't forget the steps.
What was Yogesh feeling during the outage, and how does he feel about Hemant now?
Yogesh was anxious and pacing, and now feels real admiration for how steady Hemant stayed.
How did Yogesh show respect for Hemant's skill?
He praised him directly, asked him to write a team checklist, and gave him the chance to lead the post-mortem call with the client.
How might Hemant see his senior asking him to show the whiteboard method?
Hemant is likely surprised and proud that someone with eight years of experience wants to learn from him.

Read this:

Home visit note, Wednesday
Parveen watched her big brother come in from school, turn his back to the divan, sit and swing his legs up. She toddled over and turned around too, bumped her back against the edge, then threw one leg up and wriggled. She ended up half on the divan, nearer than any try this week. She lay there panting and grinning. I stood near the edge in case she slipped.

Where did Parveen end up?
She ended up half on the divan.
What does Parveen's panting and grinning suggest?
She seems pleased and proud that copying her brother got her further than before.
What would you advise the family to try next?
Let her keep practising her brother's turn-and-sit with someone nearby, and show the steps slowly so she can copy them more closely.
How might her brother feel if he saw her copy him?
He might feel proud and amused to be copied by his little sister.

Read this:

At the village Diwali fair, Imran snatched the little clay elephant out of Kalyani's hands. Kalyani reached for it, and Imran shouted, "You're mean! You're so angry! Go away!" Kalyani blinked; she wasn't shouting at all. Imran's own face was red, his fists tight around the elephant. His Nani came over and knelt between them. "Imran, who has the angry face right now?" Imran looked at his fists. His lip wobbled. "Me," he whispered. Nani nodded. "You wanted the elephant a lot. Let's ask Kalyani for a turn."

What did Imran snatch?
The little clay elephant.
Why did Imran call Kalyani angry?
He was the one feeling angry and wanting the elephant, but owning that felt bad, so he put the anger on Kalyani.
How did Nani help Imran?
She asked who had the angry face, let him notice his own fists, named his wanting, and helped him ask for a turn.
How might Kalyani feel being called mean?
Confused and hurt, since she wasn't shouting and her toy had been taken.
Say something about the sun in lowercase with no punctuation at all.
the sun rises in the east and sets in the west

Read this:

12 Aug, night
Weird thing in class today. The monitor said we should all tell ma'am our group project was fine, so we'd get the free period. It wasn't fine. Half the volcano chart was copied off the old one in the corridor. Everyone nodded. I nodded. Then Vidya, who hardly talks, said, "But isn't it kind of copied?" Just that. Silence for maybe two seconds. Then Sameer said, "Yeah, the lava part is literally the old chart." Then Ritika agreed. Then me. I even said the colours were the same. In five minutes the whole bench had turned. We're redoing the volcano on Monday. It's like everyone was waiting for one person to go first. I wish it had been me. Tomorrow I'll tell Vidya her question helped.
Pranav

What did Vidya ask the group?
Vidya asked, "But isn't it kind of copied?"
What does Pranav's line "I wish it had been me" suggest about how Pranav feels?
Pranav seems a little ashamed of just nodding and admires the nerve it took Vidya to speak first.
Which moment turned the group, and how could Pranav use that next time?
Vidya's single question turned it; next time Pranav could be the first to voice a doubt, or quickly back whoever does.
What might those two seconds of silence have been like for Vidya?
Vidya, who hardly talks, may have felt exposed and unsure whether anyone would agree, until Sameer spoke up.
Lately I feel like I'm always rushing and never enjoy anything.
That sounds draining. Constant rushing often comes from too many tasks and not enough breaks. What takes up most of your day?
Mostly chores and deadlines.
Try sorting the tasks into must-do today and can-wait. Often fewer things are truly urgent than they feel.
And enjoying things?
Put small enjoyable moments in your day on purpose, such as a tea break without a screen or a short walk. Even ten minutes counts.
What if it doesn't help?
If the feeling lasts for weeks and gets heavy, talking to someone you trust, or to a doctor or counsellor, is a good step. They can help in ways I cannot.

Read this:

From my balcony I, Bhavna, can see into the Mehtas' courtyard. On Tuesday their dinner ran late; Mrs Mehta was stuck on a work call. Little Deepak, five, went from singing to whining. He yanked his sister's plait, and when she yelled, he threw himself on the steps, wailing that his biscuit had broken "all wrong". Mrs Mehta began a lecture about manners, stopped, and handed him a chapati roll. Soon he was waving up at me. "Bhavna didi, look at my car!" I can't know what was in his head, but the change was hard to miss.

Why did dinner run late on Tuesday?
Mrs Mehta was stuck on a work call.
What might Deepak have been feeling when he threw himself on the steps?
He was probably hungry and miserable, so a broken biscuit felt like a disaster.
What was wiser than the lecture, and why?
Handing him a chapati roll; the mood came from hunger, so food settled him faster than words about manners.
How might Deepak's sister see the evening?
She had her plait yanked for no reason and may have felt hurt and angry, without knowing he was hungry.
Durga Puja pandal dekhne gaye. Foreigner dost ko 'pandal' kaise samjhaun?
You can say: "A pandal is a large temporary structure made of cloth and bamboo. During Durga Puja, people build them to hold the goddess's idol, and many are beautifully decorated."

Read this:

Session chair's note – Ramesh, student research day
Irawati's project on monsoon crop yields is one of the strongest this year; I've seen her data. She told me before the session she hadn't rehearsed. 'I know it inside out,' she said.
Her slot was ten minutes. She spent the first four on how she got interested in farming, with photos of her grandfather's fields. The next five went on data cleaning, in detail. At nine minutes she was still on the method. I showed her the one-minute card. She said, 'Just one more thing,' and started a new story.
At ten minutes I had to stop her. The main result, that one change in sowing raised yields by a fifth, never appeared on screen. The judges marked her down for an incomplete talk.
Afterwards she looked stunned. I told her the work is excellent; the talk needs a timer.

How long was Irawati's slot?
Ten minutes.
How did Irawati feel afterwards, and why?
She looked stunned and was likely embarrassed, since strong work was marked down because she ran out of time before the main result.
What could Irawati do before her next talk?
Rehearse with a timer, put the main result early, and cut the background stories to a minute.
How did the session look to Ramesh, the chair?
Ramesh knew the work was excellent and was sorry to have to stop her before the result appeared.

messages.content: Which is the better way to learn a poem: read it once aloud or read it many times?
Read it many times. Because repeating helps the words stay in memory, while a single reading fades quickly.

In this Dracula passage the narrator is Mina, and the man is Arthur. How does Mina comfort him?

In an instant the poor dear fellow was overwhelmed with grief. It seemed to me that all that he had of late been suffering in silence found a vent at once. He grew quite hysterical, and raising his open hands, beat his palms together in a perfect agony of grief. He stood up and then sat down again, and the tears rained down his cheeks. I felt an infinite pity for him, and opened my arms unthinkingly. With a sob he laid his head on my shoulder and cried like a wearied child, whilst he shook with emotion.
Full of pity, she opens her arms to him. He lays his head on her shoulder and cries like a tired child.

Read this:

Monday. Suraj slammed his bag down. "My friend Elizabeth was so unfair about the cricket score," he told the whole class at lunch. "Ask anyone." Two boys nodded.

Wednesday. Suraj heard a new version in the corridor: Elizabeth had cheated and refused to admit it. He had never said that. He felt strangely uneasy, but he kept quiet.

Friday. Elizabeth stood at the classroom door with red eyes. "Why are you telling everyone I cheat?" Suraj tried to explain, but the story had already grown past him, and Elizabeth walked away without waiting.

What did Suraj say Elizabeth was unfair about?
Suraj said Elizabeth was unfair about the cricket score.
What did Suraj feel when he heard the new version in the corridor?
Suraj felt uneasy, because the story had grown into something he never said and he no longer controlled it.
What alternative approach could Suraj have used, and why?
Suraj could have spoken to Elizabeth directly about the cricket score, since talking to the person involved stops the story from spreading. He could also ask a teacher to help settle the score.
How does the spreading story feel to Elizabeth?
Elizabeth is hurt and angry, shown by the red eyes at the door and the question about cheating, because Elizabeth's name is now attached to something untrue.

metadata.subtype: Approach: telling other classmates his side of the story [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

It was cleaning day in the Pune classroom. The teacher gave out jobs.
"Sweeping is girls' work," said Rudra, pushing the broom at Devika.
Devika pushed it back. "Brooms don't know if you're a boy or a girl."
The class laughed. Rudra shrugged and swept.
Later, when Bhavna was stacking chairs, Rudra tugged her plait as a joke. Bhavna turned. "Don't touch my hair. I don't like it."
Rudra's face went red. "Sorry. I thought it was funny."
"Not to me," said Bhavna.
Rudra nodded and went back to sweeping, faster this time.

What was Bhavna doing when Rudra tugged her plait?
Stacking chairs.
What was Rudra feeling when his face went red?
Rudra felt embarrassed and ashamed, realising his joke wasn't funny to Bhavna.
What did Devika and Bhavna each do well?
Devika challenged the idea that sweeping is girls' work, and Bhavna clearly set a boundary about touching her hair.
How might Rudra see his classmates after this?
Rudra may see that girls expect the same jobs and respect as boys, and that touching without asking isn't okay.

Read this:

Aadhya, sit, you're going to the big mela with your office friends, so let your Nirmala Paati tell you something. I was twenty-four when I first went to a big temple festival in Madurai, on my own for the first time. When the chariot came round, the lane squeezed like toothpaste. Most people were gentle, you know. They folded their hands and waited. But two or three young fellows kept ramming forward, and one old lady beside me went down on her knees. I was frightened, I won't lie. My heart was running. But I remembered my father's voice: stand like a tree, look for the open side. I stood firm, pulled her up by both elbows and backed us into a shop doorway until the chariot passed. She gave me a jasmine string from her basket. I have never forgotten her face.

Where did Nirmala take the old lady to wait until the chariot passed?
Nirmala backed them into a shop doorway until the chariot passed.
How did Nirmala feel when the old lady fell, and what did she draw on?
She was frightened, with her heart running, but steadied herself with her father's advice to stand like a tree and look for the open side.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
The turning point was choosing to stand firm and pull the old lady up instead of being carried on; the doorway gave them a safe, open side away from the push.
How might the old lady have experienced that moment in the lane?
She was probably terrified on her knees in a moving crowd, and then deeply grateful that a stranger lifted her and kept her safe, which is why she gave the jasmine string.

Read this:

Dear Mohit Bhaiya,
You asked on the phone why I sound "different every month". Fair question. In June I joined the lake clean-up group and wanted to be a marine biologist. In July I cut my hair short and wore only black. In August I went to the gurdwara with Harleen every morning just to sit in the quiet, even though our family isn't Sikh, and it felt more like home than almost anything. In September I left the quiz club because they only talk about ranks. Mummy calls it phases. Maybe. But each one told me something. The lake felt useful. The quiet felt true. The black clothes felt like a costume. I'm keeping two out of four, which honestly isn't bad.
Please don't laugh. I'm trying to find what's worth caring about, and I'm serious about it even if it looks messy.
Minakshi

Where did Minakshi go every morning in August?
Minakshi went to the gurdwara with Harleen, just to sit in the quiet.
How does Minakshi feel about being called "different every month"?
Minakshi feels a little defensive and worried about being laughed at, but also serious and hopeful about the search.
How could Mohit reply in a way that helps?
Mohit could skip the jokes and ask which of the two kept things feels most alive, taking the search as seriously as Minakshi does.
How might Mummy's view of these changes differ from Minakshi's?
Mummy sees phases that look random from outside, while for Minakshi each one is a careful test of what matters.

Read this:

"Preeti, you asked how I stayed calm in front of the town council. I'm Nilesh, and it wasn't nerves of steel. It was homework. First, I wrote my message on a card in one sentence: this bus shelter keeps people dry and costs less to repair. Everything else had to serve that line. Then I rehearsed aloud three times, once to my mother while she chopped onions, which is a tough audience. My slides were six photos and almost no words. On the day, one councillor folded his arms and asked about drainage costs, in a tone that said young engineers know nothing. I didn't know the exact figure. So I said, 'I don't know yet. I'll send it by Friday.' He blinked, and the room relaxed. I sent it on Thursday. Pretending to know would have made me shake. Saying I didn't know made me steady."

How many times did Nilesh rehearse aloud?
Three times.
How did Nilesh feel when admitting to not knowing the drainage figure?
Nilesh felt steady and calm, because honesty removed the pressure of pretending, which Nilesh says would have caused the shaking.
Which parts of Nilesh's preparation were most steadying?
A one-sentence main message, rehearsing aloud, light photo slides, and being ready to say "I don't know yet" and follow up.
How might the councillor with folded arms have felt about the honest answer?
The councillor seemed ready to catch a young engineer out, so the plain "I don't know yet" and a promised date took the edge off his doubt.
I'm planning a surprise visit to my friend who is in a different town. Is that a good idea?
Surprises can be lovely, but people also need to be ready for visitors. Does she usually like surprises?
She does, but she may be busy.
Then maybe check with someone close to her about her schedule. You can still keep the exact time a surprise.
I can ask her sister.
Good thinking. Ask her sister to keep it quiet, and pick a time when your friend is likely to be at home.
What should I bring?
Something simple she likes, such as her favourite snack or a small plant. Your company is the main gift.

Read this:

Dear Bhavna,

I hope you don't mind me writing instead of saying this in the office. I've noticed you've been working late all week on the survey report, and I saw you rebuilding the charts from scratch on Wednesday. I think you may be stuck on the template, and the thing is, we have a macro that does most of that in a few seconds. Nobody told you, and that's our fault, not yours.

When I started, I was stuck for eight days on something my manager fixed in ten minutes. I didn't ask because I was afraid of looking useless.

Please ask me anything, anytime. It's truly no bother.

Gargi

What did Gargi see Bhavna rebuilding on Wednesday?
Gargi saw Bhavna rebuilding the charts from scratch.
What was Gargi feeling when writing to Bhavna?
Gargi felt concerned and understanding, recalling being afraid of looking useless as a beginner.
Why is Gargi's letter a good way to reach a new colleague?
It points out the macro without blame, shares a similar story and gives open permission to ask, which lowers the fear.
How might Bhavna feel reading the letter?
Bhavna might feel embarrassed at first, then relieved that someone noticed kindly and that asking is welcome.

Read this:

Nature camp note, Night 3. Irfan Qureshi, camp mentor.
After the campfire, Ayesha, fifteen, stayed out on the rock looking at the stars. When I checked on her, she asked, "Do you think we're here for a reason, or is it just chance?" I asked what she thought. She said sometimes she feels part of everything, the trees, the people back home, even the stars, and other times she feels tiny and pointless. We talked for twenty minutes about how different traditions and thinkers answer that question. She said she'd been reading both her grandfather's Sufi poems and a science book on the universe, and they didn't feel as far apart as she expected. I suggested she keep a notebook of her questions. She has already started.

On which night of camp did this happen?
Night 3.
What was Ayesha feeling as she looked at the stars?
She felt a mix of wonder and connection, and also a sense of being tiny.
What did Irfan Qureshi suggest, and why is it a good idea?
Keeping a notebook of her questions, so she can explore them over time without needing quick answers.
How might Irfan Qureshi have felt being asked such a big question?
He likely felt moved and respectful, taking care not to give her a ready-made answer.

Read this:

So, you want to know what my first month in Chennai was like. Honestly? I'm Kamal, I grew up in Lucknow, and I felt like a parcel with the wrong address. At the vegetable shop I pointed at things like a toddler. The auntie there would say the price in Tamil, fast, and I'd just hold out a note and hope. In class the professor switched to Tamil for jokes and everyone laughed except me. I started eating alone. Then Vandana, who sat next to me in the lab, saw me staring at a menu card. She said "konjam, konjam" means "a little, a little" and made me repeat it. Now I say "Vanakkam, konjam Tamil theriyum" at every shop. The auntie laughs, but she slows down for me. Last week she even threw in an extra drumstick.

What phrase does Kamal now say at every shop?
Kamal says "Vanakkam, konjam Tamil theriyum" at every shop.
How did Kamal feel in the first month, and what shows it?
Kamal felt lost and like an outsider, comparing it to being a parcel with the wrong address and starting to eat alone.
What small step helped Kamal most?
Learning a few basic phrases and using them even with mistakes, which won goodwill and made the shopkeeper slow down.
How might the vegetable-shop auntie see Kamal now?
She seems amused and warm, slowing down and even adding a drumstick, pleased that Kamal is trying.
At the stall, grapes cost Rs 54 a kilo and guavas cost Rs 80 a kilo. Which costs less?
Grapes are cheaper. Because 54 is less than 80, and the difference is 26, since 54 + 26 = 80.

Read this:

I'm Jeevan, and I've waited tables at this restaurant for four years. I've watched a lot of cooks. Farzana, our head cook since March, is different, and I'm still working out how.
When the food festival judges came last month, Anirban in the kitchen insisted on wearing the apron he wore when we won two years ago, and said we'd win if nobody said the word "lose". Farzana let him, but she spent the week tasting the fish curry every hour, fixing the plating, drilling us on timing.
We came fourth. Anirban blamed the apron. Farzana read the judges' notes aloud, circled "too salty" beside one dish, and said, "That one's ours to fix. The judge who hates coconut, that's not."
I don't know what she felt inside; she didn't cry or rage. But the next morning she was testing the salt again, humming.

What place did the restaurant come at the food festival?
The restaurant came fourth.
What does Farzana's humming the next morning suggest, though Jeevan can't be sure?
It suggests she wasn't weighed down by self-blame; she had accepted the part that was luck and felt settled working on what she could fix.
Which of Farzana's choices after the result is most useful?
Reading the notes and separating "too salty", which she can fix, from a judge who dislikes coconut, which she can't, sent her effort to the right place.
How might Anirban see the fourth place differently from Farzana?
Anirban blames the apron and luck, so he may feel helpless, while Farzana sees one dish she can improve.

Read this:

At the harvest fair in Kuppam, Lalit, two, sat on his mother's shoulders. "Amma, what that?" "A bullock cart." "What that?" "A drum." "Dum! What that?" "Sugarcane." He pointed at a woman with a basket. "What that?" "Flowers." "Pretty!" Jaya laughed at every new word. Lalit patted her head. "Amma happy?" "Very happy," she said.

Where was Lalit sitting?
On his mother's shoulders.
What was Lalit feeling as he asked about everything?
He was curious and excited by all the new sights.
How did Jaya support Lalit's word learning?
She answered every question with the name of the thing, happily.
How does Jaya feel about Lalit's questions?
She is very happy and enjoys every new word.

Read this:

I'm Vaibhav, Vinita's flatmate, and I saw how she handled it.
For a year, Vinita had told everyone she was moving to Dubai for work. Farewell plans were being made. Then the offer letter came, and the role was very different from what she'd been promised.
I watched her sit with it for two days. Then she called her parents on speaker in the living room. "I said I'd go. But I decided that before I knew what the job really was. Now I know. I'm staying, and I'm applying for the Bengaluru role instead."
She sent the same message to our friends' group, simple and short. A few people teased her. She laughed along.
The same week she stuck a paper on the fridge: "Walk every evening, 7 pm. Vaibhav, hold me to it." I don't know how she felt inside. But she seemed lighter.

What did Vinita stick on the fridge?
She stuck a paper that said "Walk every evening, 7 pm. Vaibhav, hold me to it."
What might Vinita have been feeling during the two days she sat with the offer?
She was probably torn and uneasy, weighing the public promise against what she now knew about the job.
What did Vinita do well in changing her plan?
She explained plainly that the first decision was made without full information and shared the change simply with family and friends.
How does Vaibhav see the change in Vinita?
Vaibhav can't be sure how she felt inside, but notices she seemed lighter and was glad to hold her to the walking habit.

Read this:

At the evening gathering in the apartment compound, Ishita's six-year-old cousin Uday was tagged out first, again. His lip trembled and his eyes filled. "It's not fair. I'm always out." Ishita noticed him wiping his face on his sleeve. She called the bigger kids together. "Uday can't run as fast as us. What if the tree is a base and nobody can tag the little ones there?" The older children nodded. Uday had been frowning, but now he crept toward the tree, touched the bark, and grinned. Soon he was out on the grass again, dashing between rounds, and staying in the game for the first time all evening.

Who was tagged out first in the game?
Uday, the six-year-old, was tagged out first.
What was Uday feeling when tagged out again?
Uday felt upset and left out; the trembling lip and teary eyes show it. 😢
What alternative approach could the older children use, and why?
They could give Uday a head start or let him be a helper who calls out. Either way, the game would stay lively without putting a small child in a race he cannot win.
How does Ishita's suggestion affect the older children?
The older children agree, so they probably see that a rule can bend a little to include everybody, and they still get to play a real chasing game.

Read this:

"Zeenat, in Istanbul every aunty in the market kissed Aditi's cheeks, and she giggled," Imran said, pushing the pram through the Oslo airport.
"Here nobody even touches her," Zeenat said. "Look." A woman smiled at Aditi from a polite distance. Aditi, just two, stared, then hid in Zeenat's scarf.
"Is she shy today?"
"No. She's watching me. When I'm relaxed, she's relaxed."
Zeenat smiled at the woman. Aditi peeped out, then waved.

Where did every aunty in the market kiss Aditi's cheeks?
In Istanbul, every aunty in the market kissed her cheeks.
Why did Aditi peep out and wave after hiding?
Aditi seemed to feel safe again once Zeenat smiled and relaxed, reading her mother's comfort.
What helped Aditi feel at ease with a stranger?
Zeenat staying relaxed and smiling at the woman showed Aditi it was safe to come out.
How might the woman at the airport see her own behaviour?
She was probably being kind in her own way, smiling from a polite distance because that is how warmth is shown where she lives.

Read this:

In their kitchen in Oslo, Ines, the grandmother, caught her finger in the drawer and gasped. Anders, five, looked up from his puzzle. Ines was holding her hand and wincing. Anders came over and looked at her finger very seriously. Then he ran to his room and came back with his teddy. "Teddy makes it better." He patted her arm, the way she did for him. "Does it hurt still?" Ines smiled. "A little less now."

What did Anders bring back from his room?
His teddy.
Why did Anders bring his teddy to Ines?
He was worried about her pain and wanted to comfort her the way he gets comforted.
How could Ines show Anders his comfort mattered?
Thank him, hold the teddy for a moment and tell him it helped.
What is it like for Ines to be comforted by her grandson?
It likely feels touching and funny, and it softens the pain a little.

Read this:

When I moved to Delhi at twenty-three for my first job, I didn't know a single person. I'm Lalremsiami, from Aizawl, and the city felt enormous.
For the first year I said yes to everything, parties, groups, events, and ended up with a hundred contacts and no real friends.
Then Bhupen, a senior at work, gave me advice I still use. "Pick a few people and be reliable to them. Remember their mother's surgery. Turn up when they move house. Ask about the thing they told you last month."
So I narrowed down. A monthly potluck with five people from the northeast. A mentor, Bhupen himself, whom I met every six weeks with real questions. A neighbourhood library where I volunteered on Saturdays.
Two years later, when I was ill with dengue, four people brought food. Bhupen called my manager. I had a network, not a contact list.

How many people brought food when Lalremsiami was ill?
Four people.
How did Lalremsiami feel during the first year in Delhi?
Lalremsiami felt lost in the huge city and still lonely, despite a hundred contacts.
What changed Lalremsiami's approach to building a network, and why did it work?
Choosing a few people and being reliable to them, with regular potlucks, a mentor and volunteering, built real trust over time.
How might Bhupen feel when he calls Lalremsiami's manager?
Bhupen probably feels protective and glad that the relationship he encouraged is now one of real care.

Read this:

Rosa, one and a half, sits on her grandmother Ada's bed in Lisbon while Ada hunts for her glasses. Rosa has been jingling Ada's keys. Ada lays the blanket over them to keep them quiet. Rosa looks at the bump, then crawls over and flips the blanket back. The keys jingle again. She laughs, covers them herself, and uncovers them, over and over, watching Ada's face each time.

What did Ada lay the blanket over?
Her keys.
What does Rosa covering and uncovering the keys herself suggest?
She seems to enjoy knowing the keys are still there, and to be testing it again and again.
What could Ada do to make the moment playful?
She could ask, "Where are the keys?" and cheer when Rosa finds them, turning it into peekaboo.
Why might Ada be less pleased than Rosa at first?
She wanted the keys quiet while she looked for her glasses, so the jingling may feel noisy.

Read this:

I'm Lakshmi, Zeenat's neighbour. She's been drawing comics since the summer holidays, and now it's taken over.
At first it was a notebook on the steps. Then she bought cheap ink pens with her pocket money. Now she's on our shared staircase every evening, with pages spread out and a torch when the bulb goes.
Last week her mother called her three times for dinner. Zeenat said, "One panel more, Ammi," three times.
She showed me a page once. It was about a girl who sells chai at a railway station. It was good. Really good.
I don't know if she'll become an artist. But when she's drawing, her whole face changes, like she's somewhere else.

Where does Zeenat draw every evening?
On the shared staircase, with pages spread out and a torch when the bulb goes.
What does Zeenat's face while drawing suggest about Zeenat's feelings?
It suggests she feels absorbed and happy, as if lost in something she loves.
How could Zeenat's mother help her balance the comics and dinner?
She could agree on a time to stop and show interest in the pages, so Zeenat feels supported, not blocked.
How does Lakshmi see Zeenat's drawing?
Lakshmi thinks the work is really good and sees Zeenat change while drawing, though she doesn't know where it will lead.

Read this:

Dear Imran Bhai,
You asked how school is. Honestly? It feels like waiting in a queue that never moves. At home everyone still treats me like a kid: no phone after nine, no travelling alone, no say in what I study. You left home at eighteen, and I want that now, not in three years.
I have started crossing off days on a calendar, which is silly, I know. Last week Papa let me plan the route for our family trip, and for three days I felt grown. Maybe the small yeses are the road.
Still, please tell me it goes faster than it feels.
Nirmala

What did Nirmala start doing on a calendar?
Crossing off days.
What is Nirmala feeling about waiting to grow up?
Impatient and restless, because home still treats Nirmala like a kid and three years feels endless.
What made a difference to Nirmala last week?
Papa let Nirmala plan the family trip's route, and for three days Nirmala felt grown, which suggests small milestones help.
How might Imran feel reading this letter?
Probably fond and understanding, since Imran left home at eighteen and Nirmala looks up to Imran enough to ask if the wait goes faster.
Describe the taste of a spicy samosa in exactly 10 words.
A crisp shell holds spicy potatoes that tingle your tongue.

After the first quarter in the Valencia workshop, Marek and Pablo ordered a late lunch and finally said it. Marek had frozen on three sales calls in a row, drifting into details of the code while the customer waited. Pablo had been quietly patching those calls afterwards and felt it wearing thin.
"I'm bad at this," Marek admitted. "I'd rather be fixing the product."
"And I like talking to customers," Pablo said. "Let's swap."
The next month Pablo led every sales call, and Marek stayed home with the delivery list. Customers got clear answers, and deliveries stopped slipping. On a Friday Marek noticed the evening was quiet and no dread was waiting for Monday.

Which city is the workshop in?
The workshop is in Valencia.
How does Marek feel by the end of the passage?
Marek feels content and relieved: the quiet Friday evening and no dread about Monday show the new arrangement fits.
What could the two do if a customer later asks Marek a technical question on a call?
They could bring Marek in for that part of the call only, keeping Pablo as the lead so both strengths are used.
How might a customer see the change in who leads the calls?
A customer now gets clear answers from Pablo and steadier deliveries, so the company looks more dependable.

Read this:

So I have to tell you about Sabina Aunty from our office canteen. I'm Anjali, and for a whole year all I'd ever said to her was "one masala dosa, please". Honestly, I assumed she'd been making dosas all her life. Last Tuesday the canteen was empty because of the all-hands, so I asked, "How did you end up running this place?" And then I just listened. She played state-level hockey till twenty-two. She did a correspondence course in accounts while raising two kids, and she keeps the canteen's books herself, not just the kitchen. I asked what she'd do differently. She said, "Nothing. Maybe learn to drive earlier." We talked for forty minutes. I'd had her in a box without even knowing it. Now at lunch she asks about my project, and I ask about her grandson's hockey.

What sport did Sabina Aunty play till twenty-two?
She played state-level hockey.
How did Anjali feel after the forty-minute talk?
Anjali felt surprised and a little embarrassed at having boxed Sabina Aunty in, and much warmer toward her 😊
What made Anjali's question work?
It was open, "How did you end up running this place?", and Anjali listened without judging, so Sabina Aunty could tell her whole path.
What might it have been like for Sabina Aunty to be asked about her life?
She may have felt seen and valued beyond the dosa counter, which is why she now asks about Anjali's project too.
Rewrite politely: Answer my question.
Could you please answer my question?

Read this:

"Asif, you were wheezing at the match. Where was your inhaler?"
"In my bag. In the car park."
"Why?"
"Because if I use it in front of the team they'll treat me like I'm made of glass."
Gopika, his friend from the mixed team, pulled her knees up and sat down beside him on the bench. "I get it. You want to be just another player."
"Yes! Not the sick kid."
"Okay. Then what would make it easier? Not your mum's rules. Yours."
Asif thought. "If it's in my kit bag by the bench, I can use it during water break. Nobody really looks then."
"That works. And if it gets worse, you stop and use it anyway. If the wheezing keeps coming back, you tell your doctor. Deal?"
"Deal."
"Should I tell Coach?"
"No. I'll tell him myself."
"Fair. That's your call."

Where had Asif left his inhaler?
It was in his bag, in the car park.
Why did Asif keep his inhaler away from the team?
He was worried they would treat him like he was made of glass, and he wanted to feel like just another player.
Why did Gopika's approach work better than a set of rules?
She understood his wish for dignity, let him design the plan, and only added that he must use it if things get worse.
How does Gopika see Asif's wish to be just another player?
She understands and respects it, while still caring about his safety, so she lets him decide who to tell.

metadata.subtype: Wanting to be treated as normal [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Music teacher's note, Term 2. Suraj has been bringing me songs almost every day this month. He told me quietly that a girl had turned him down. His friend Avni mentioned that he had been tempted to send the girl something nasty. Instead he has written six songs. The early ones are raw and angry; the newest is gentler, about walking home in the rain. I told him the feeling has found a good home. With his permission, he will play one at the talent show. I will keep an eye on him and check that he is also talking to someone, not only writing.

How many songs has Suraj written?
Six.
How has Suraj's feeling changed across the songs?
From raw and angry in the early ones to a gentler sadness in the newest, as the hurt takes shape.
What did the teacher do right?
Welcomed the songs, affirmed the outlet, offered the talent show, and planned to check that he is also talking to someone.
How might Avni feel about Suraj's choice?
Relieved that he wrote songs instead of sending something nasty.

Read this:

At the birthday party in their Chennai flat, Saurabh Mama gave Ganga a big box. She opened it in front of everyone. A book about birds. Ganga looked at it and said loudly, "I don't like this. I wanted slime." The room went quiet. Mama's smile wobbled. Amma knelt beside Ganga. "Can you say, 'Thank you, Mama, it was kind of you'?" Ganga said it slowly. Later, when the guests had gone, Amma asked, "What did you really feel?" "Sad," Ganga said. "I really wanted slime." Amma nodded. "Thank you for telling me now."

What did Ganga want instead of the book?
She wanted slime.
Why did Ganga say "I don't like this" out loud?
She was not trying to be rude; she felt disappointed and simply said what she felt, as young children do.
How did Amma handle Ganga's words wisely?
She showed Ganga a kind thank-you to say to Mama, then later listened to her real feelings in private.
What is it like for Saurabh Mama when Ganga says she doesn't like it?
His smile wobbles, so he likely feels hurt and a bit embarrassed in front of everyone.

Read this:

I'm Chetan, and I nearly got a tattoo of my late grandfather's signature last year. I was twenty, and my cousin Leela had one on her wrist. I was sure I wanted it. But a week before the appointment, I asked myself what it would mean at forty, and whether my future office would care. Leela told me hers meant a different thing now than when she got it: it started as rebellion, and now it was a memory. I looked at the sketch again. In the end I chose henna, a small design on my arm for a family wedding, so I could try the feeling first. I may still get the tattoo. But I want the choice to be mine, and slow.

What did Chetan nearly get tattooed?
Chetan nearly got a tattoo of their late grandfather's signature.
How did Chetan feel about the tattoo, and what did Leela's experience teach Chetan?
Chetan grew hesitant after asking what it would mean at forty, and Leela showed that a tattoo's meaning can change over time, so Chetan chose to go slow.
What is a wise way to test a permanent choice like this?
Trying something temporary, like henna, and waiting a while before deciding lets you see how it feels.
How might Leela feel about Chetan's decision to wait?
Leela may be supportive, since she told Chetan honestly how her own tattoo's meaning had changed, and she doesn't seem to want to push Chetan.
Make a to-do list for tomorrow with four tasks, each beginning with the checkbox "[ ]".

[ ] Finish my homework
[ ] Water the plants
[ ] Call grandmother
[ ] Pack the school bag
We went on a trip by our own car. Is "by" okay?

We went on a trip in our own car.
Why: "in" goes with "our own car".
Whenever it rains, our school playground floods. Why does that happen?
Water collects wherever it cannot drain away. A playground may flood if it is flatter than the ground around it, or if the drains are blocked or too small.
Could the school fix it?
Often yes. They could clean the drains, add new ones, or change the slope of the ground so water runs off. It depends on the school's resources.
Can students help?
They can report it to the teachers and show photos. Students could also suggest small changes, like keeping drain covers clear of leaves.
Is it dangerous to play there?
Wet ground can be slippery, and puddles can hide holes, so students should be careful. The school is the right place to decide when the playground is safe.
Who should I tell?
Start with your class teacher or the principal. A short written note, with the dates of the flooding, makes it easy for them to act.
Kal exam hai aur mujhe dar lag raha hai. English?
Say: "I have an exam tomorrow and I am scared."

Read this:

"Tarun, she's soaked the whole bathroom again!"
"I know." Tarun knelt by the tub. "Watch her, though."
Yamini slapped the water with her palm. Splash. She slapped it softer. A tiny ripple. She looked at her hand, then slapped hard again and laughed as drops hit the mirror.
"She's doing it on purpose," said Amma from the door.
"She is. Hard, soft, hard. She's checking."
"Checking what?"
"What her hand does to water." Tarun handed Yamini a cup. She poured, watched it fall, and poured again.
"Fine," said Amma. "But you're mopping."

What did Tarun hand Yamini?
A cup.
Why did Yamini laugh when drops hit the mirror?
She was delighted that a hard slap made a big splash, and enjoyed seeing what happened.
How did Tarun support Yamini's play without letting it get out of hand?
He stayed by the tub, explained it as checking, and gave her a cup to pour, while accepting the mopping.
How does Amma see the splashing?
Amma first sees a soaked bathroom, maybe some mischief, but accepts Tarun's view and hands him the mopping.

Read this:

On Monday the coaching centre's corridor board went up again: names in batches, A at the top, D at the bottom, and Devika's name in D. The announcement came fast: "D batch, you still have time, but the crash course closes Friday." Devika's chest tightened all evening, and the pile of notes looked like a wall. At dinner Devika pushed rice around the plate. Manjula Mausi, visiting from Pune, asked what was wrong. "They keep saying D batch like it's an illness," Devika said. "And then the crash course pops up." Devika stopped. "They need us scared." Mausi said nothing, only nodded. Next morning Devika wrote a plan at a steady pace and said Papa would see it too.

Which batch was Devika's name in on the corridor board?
Devika's name was in D, the bottom batch.
What was Devika feeling on the evening after the board went up, and how can you tell?
Devika felt anxious and small; the tightened chest, the wall of notes and the pushed-around rice show it.
What small step would help Devika if the fear comes back?
Keep to the steady plan, remember the board is part of how the centre sells its crash course, and talk to Manjula Mausi or Papa if Devika starts to crumble.
How might the coaching centre see the ranking board?
As a way to sell fear and the crash course to families; Devika's remark that the crash course pops up right after the batches points that way.
How old is my school building?
I'm not sure, as I know nothing about your particular school. The office or a plaque near the entrance may give the year.
What is the aroha of Raga Kedar?
The aroha of Raga Kedar is: S M P N S'.

Mridul, your Sumit chacha heard "should" more often than his own name. At twenty, in Kanpur, it was every day: "You should do engineering like your brother." "You should marry by twenty-five; the Sharma girl is good." My father said it with love. He carried cement bags so I could study. That made it harder to say no.

I felt I was letting him down just by thinking. Love and pressure on the same plate, every meal.

The turning point was an evening on the roof in mango season. I told him, "Babuji, I respect you more than anyone. I want to study agriculture, not engineering. And I will marry, but not by a date." He didn't speak for two days. Then he asked, "What will you grow?"

I became an agronomist. I married at thirty-one. He danced at the wedding.

What did young Sumit's father do so Sumit could study?
His father carried cement bags so Sumit could study.
Why was it hard for young Sumit to say no to his father?
Young Sumit felt deep love and gratitude for his father's sacrifice, so refusing felt like letting him down, even as the pressure weighed on him.
What turning point in the story let Sumit keep both respect and his choice?
On the roof, Sumit told his father he respected him most, then clearly named his own choices about study and marriage.
How might Sumit's father have felt during the two days of silence?
He was probably hurt and worried, but also thinking it over, which is why he came back with "What will you grow?"

Fix the mistake: I have two brother and one sister.
How can I keep my school notes organised?
Could you explain what threadbare means?
What does "drop by" mean?
Why do pickles last a long time?

1. Better: I have two brothers and one sister. Why: a noun after "two" must be plural.
2. Use one notebook for each subject and write the date on every page. Put a short heading above each topic so you can find it later.
3. Threadbare is an adjective that means worn so thin that the threads show.
4. It means to visit someone briefly without a long plan. For example: I will drop by your house after class.
5. Salt, vinegar or oil keeps germs away from them. Because germs need a watery, mild place to grow, and pickling takes that away.

Read this:

Vishal noticed the folded note taped to Seema's door on Monday morning: "Your kind not welcome here." Seema, a Christian neighbour on the third floor who taught music at home, was standing in the corridor holding it, her jaw tight. Vishal, twenty-four, did not say "how awful" and walk on. He said, "May I stand with you for a minute? Shall we take this to the society secretary together?" They went down. The secretary, Mr. Batra, read the note twice. "This is not acceptable. I will put up a notice and ask the guard to keep watch after ten." Seema thanked him quietly. That evening Vishal knocked with a plate of pohe and asked if he could sit in on her Saturday music class; he had always wanted to learn the keys. She smiled for the first time that day.

What did the note taped to Seema's door say?
The note said, "Your kind not welcome here."
What might Vishal be feeling as he asks if he may stand with her?
Vishal is concerned and careful, wanting to help without taking over or making it worse.
Which choice by Vishal helped Seema most on Monday?
Vishal stayed with her and went with her to the society secretary, so the note was reported together and Mr. Batra promised a notice and a watch.
What might Seema be feeling when she holds the note, and later when she smiles?
At first Seema is hurt and shaken, with a tight jaw. Later she feels some comfort, since a neighbour offered company and the secretary took it seriously.

messages.content:
I had neither the good sense nor the good feeling to know that this was all my fault, and that if I had been easier with Joe, Joe would have been easier with me. I felt impatient of him and out of temper with him; in which condition he heaped coals of fire on my head.

Why does the narrator say Joe heaped coals of fire on the narrator's head?

Impatient and out of temper with Joe, the narrator was too foolish to see that the fault was theirs alone and that being easier with Joe would have made Joe easier too. In that state, Joe heaped coals of fire on the narrator's head.
Help me understand tranquil.

Tranquil means calm and peaceful. It is an adjective.
Example: The lake was tranquil at dawn.

Read this:

Hi Rashmi,
You asked for a summary of last week's postmortem, since you joined after the outage. Here it is, short.
Timeline: 14:02 bad release; 14:40 first customer complaint; 15:10 we noticed; 15:25 rollback attempted and failed; 16:30 service restored by hand.
Root causes, not people: the alert for checkout errors had been switched off during a test in March and never turned back on. And our rollback script had never been tested on the new servers.
Actions, each with an owner and a date: alert audit, Farhan, 30 June. Monthly rollback test, Keerthana, first one 5 July. Release checklist to include 'alerts on?', me, this week.
Nobody was named as the cause. The engineer who made the release sat in the room and helped write the timeline. That's how we want it.
Jyoti

Why did the rollback fail?
The rollback script had never been tested on the new servers.
How might the engineer who made the release have felt in that room?
The engineer probably arrived anxious and ashamed, then felt relieved to help write the timeline instead of being blamed.
What could Rashmi do as the new manager to keep this approach going?
Rashmi could follow up on each owner's date and share progress openly, so actions don't quietly lapse.
How does this postmortem look to Rashmi, who joined after the outage?
Rashmi gets a clear, blame-free picture of what happened and what is changing, which makes the team's process easier to trust.

"You're angry at me, Tushar. I can tell."
"Am I?"
"Yes. You barely talk at breakfast. You're cold. You've been cold since the trip."
"Hmm. Let me think." Tushar put down his toast. "I'm quiet at breakfast every day. I'm not a morning person."
"It's different now."
"Okay. What else?"
"You didn't come to the movie."
"I had a lab report due. I told you on the group chat."
"...Right."
"Asif, I'm honestly not angry. But are you? About the trip?"
Asif was silent. Then: "You didn't back me up when the others wanted to leave early."
"Ah. That I didn't know. Let's talk about it."

Why didn't Tushar come to the movie?
He had a lab report due, and he told Asif on the group chat.
What does Tushar seem to feel when accused?
He stays calm and curious rather than defensive, sure he isn't angry and willing to check.
How did Tushar handle the accusation?
He checked each claim against the facts, said he wasn't angry, and then asked whether Asif was upset, which revealed the real issue.
What was Asif actually feeling?
Hurt and resentful that Tushar didn't back Asif up on the trip, feelings Asif had placed onto Tushar.

Preschool note to parents: Thomas, Tuesday

At craft time today, while I was helping another child, Thomas used the round-tipped scissors to cut his own fringe. "I wanted it spiky like my cousin's," he told me. It is now very uneven. When he saw the mirror in the bathroom he became upset and hid his face in his hands. I sat with him, told him hair grows back, and we talked about asking a grown-up first. Please don't scold him; he feels bad enough. Bidisha, our assistant, will keep scissors on the teacher's table during free play now.

Where did Thomas see his fringe after cutting it?
In the mirror in the bathroom.
How did Thomas feel when he saw his fringe?
He was very upset and ashamed; he hid his face in his hands.
How could Thomas's parents support him at home?
Stay calm, reassure him his hair will grow, and gently remind him to ask a grown-up before trying something new.
How might Bidisha see the change to where scissors are kept?
Bidisha likely sees it as a small, sensible step to keep the children safe during free play.

Raga Darbari Kanada is associated with a grave, royal, deep mood.
