In the lobby of the government office where he worked, Naveen, twenty-six, got the call from home: his mother had collapsed in the kitchen, and his younger brother Tanvir was alone with her. Naveen felt his chest tighten. He wanted to rush home, call the family doctor, think about the hospital bills and tell his aunts, all at once. He stopped himself. "Tanvir, listen. Hang up and call 108 now. Then call me back." Tanvir did. Naveen then called the neighbour to go and sit with Tanvir. Only then did he take an auto home. By the time he reached, the ambulance was there. He called his aunts from the hospital corridor.

Who was alone with Naveen's mother?
His younger brother Tanvir was alone with her.
What was Naveen feeling when he got the call?
He felt his chest tighten with panic, wanting to do everything at once.
Which order of steps did Naveen follow, and why was it right?
He had Tanvir call 108 first, sent a neighbour to help, then went home and informed relatives later, so emergency help came first.
How might Tanvir feel alone with his mother before the ambulance came?
Tanvir was likely very frightened, but steadier with clear instructions from Naveen and a neighbour arriving.

It was the night before exams, the power kept flickering, and Parul's phone had one bar of signal. She posted a photo of her notes with the caption 'wish me luck', then tapped a heart on Harish's post about his last revision session. Harish, at his desk with a candle beside him, saw her heart and felt lighter. She waited. Nobody reacted to hers for an hour. Her stomach dropped. Then she remembered what her grandfather had said and told herself: the network is bad and everybody is studying. She switched it off and went back to the chapter. In the morning, Harish sent, 'Good luck! I saw your post late, network was down.' She smiled and put her pen in her bag.

What did Parul tap on Harish's post?
She tapped a heart.
Why did Parul's stomach drop when nobody reacted?
She felt worried that people didn't care or that she was not supported, at a stressful time. Then she reminded herself that the network and studying could explain it.
What did Parul do that helped her cope?
She reminded herself of a likelier explanation and put the phone away to study.
How might Harish have felt when he saw Parul's heart?
He felt lighter, since the heart was a quick sign of support during a tense night.

Lalremsiami, you asked on the podcast why I kept learning Hindustani classical singing when everyone at school laughed. I'm Disha. In Class 9, when the others were into pop songs, I was practising ragas every morning. The boys called me 'Ustadji' and did fake alaaps when I walked past. It stung. There were weeks I thought of quitting just to be normal. But when I sang Yaman in the evening, something in me felt right, as if I was finally speaking my own language. My guru told me, 'You don't have to win them. You have to be true to the note.' So I kept going. Two years later, I sang at the school function. The same boys clapped. But honestly, by then it didn't matter much. The music was mine.

What did the boys call Disha?
'Ustadji'.
How did Disha feel singing Yaman in the evening?
Disha felt right and at home, as if speaking a true language, even though the teasing stung.
What does Disha's story suggest about following an inner interest?
That staying true to what feels right can matter more than fitting in, and support from a mentor can help.
How might Disha's guru have seen the teasing?
The guru seemed to see it as less important than Disha's connection to the music.
Cats are said to have nine lifes. Please check the plural.

Cats are said to have nine lives.
Why: "Life" becomes "lives".

Fix this: I am very good in chess.
How can I get my team to work well together?

1. Fixed: I am very good at chess. Why: We say "good at" a game.
2. Listen to everyone and give each person a part to play. Say well done when someone does well.

Read this:

Sand flew as Ganga swung the plastic spade, and it cracked against Usha's knuckles. Usha howled. The preschool teacher knelt between them in the sandpit. “Ganga, what do you say?” “Sorry,” Ganga muttered to the sand, already reaching for her bucket. The teacher gently turned her shoulders. “Look at Usha's hand. It's red, see? What could help it?” Ganga stared at the knuckle, then ran to the tap and came back with a dripping cloth. She pressed it on very carefully. “Sorry I hit it,” she said again, quieter, and handed Usha the spade first.

What did Ganga bring back from the tap?
Ganga came back with a dripping cloth and pressed it on Usha's hand.
What was Ganga feeling when she first muttered sorry to the sand?
She was most likely embarrassed and keen to get back to playing, since she looked away and reached for her bucket; she may also have felt a little scared of being in trouble.
How did the teacher help the sorry become real?
The teacher asked Ganga to look at the red knuckle and think of what could help, so Ganga saw the hurt and did something to repair it.
How might Usha feel about the second sorry compared with the first?
Usha probably felt more comforted by the second one, because it came with a cool cloth and the spade handed to her first.

Read this:

Teacher's note, Nursery B, Monday. At tidy-up, Deepika wanted more time with the clay. First she cried. When I said, "Tidy-up time now," she tried promising: "Just two minutes, I'll tidy everything, I promise!" Then she watched my face very carefully. When I said no again, she shouted, "You're mean!" and looked to see what I would do. Last week a helper gave in to her, and I think she remembers. Today I kept the same calm words and helped her put the clay away. Irfan, beside her, watched the whole thing. Tomorrow I'll give a five-minute warning before tidy-up.

What did Deepika want more time with?
She wanted more time with the clay.
Why did Deepika watch the teacher's face so carefully?
She was testing, hopeful that promising or shouting might move the limit, as it had when a helper gave in last week.
Why does keeping the same calm answer matter now?
If the limit moves after crying or shouting, Deepika learns that tantrums work; staying calm and consistent teaches her they don't.
What might Irfan be learning as he watches?
Irfan may feel curious and a bit unsettled, and he also sees that shouting did not change the rule.

Read this:

Monday: In the Dublin flat, Varun's roommate Ramesh answered his mother's call on speaker at seven in the morning, shouting cheerfully in Telugu. Varun saw their Irish flatmate, Aoife, freeze in the kitchen doorway, eyebrows up.
Wednesday: At work, Varun heard Ramesh ask a new colleague, "How much do they pay you? Married?" The colleague laughed awkwardly and changed the subject. Varun noticed his own head wobbling "yes" in a meeting, and the manager said, "Is that a yes or a no?"
Saturday: Over pizza, Varun told Aoife and Ramesh, "Back home these things are normal. Salary questions are just curiosity. Loud calls mean we're close." Aoife laughed with relief. "I thought something was wrong!" Ramesh agreed to take early calls on the balcony. Varun started adding a clear "yes". Aoife asked if she could learn the wobble.

What did Ramesh ask the new colleague?
"How much do they pay you? Married?"
What was Varun feeling as he noticed Aoife freeze in the doorway?
Varun felt surprised and a little embarrassed, seeing that a normal morning call from home startled their flatmate.
Which steps helped the flat, and why?
Varun explained kindly what the habits meant, and both adapted a little, with calls on the balcony and a clear yes, so neither side felt judged.
How did Aoife see the loud calls before Varun explained?
Aoife seemed worried that something was wrong, and was relieved to learn they were just a close family's normal chat.

Read this:

Dear Omkar,
You'll laugh, but I need to tell someone who doesn't go to my school.
Everyone in my class has started wearing their hair the same way, straightened and flat. I've always loved my curls. Last Friday a girl I like said, "You'd look so much older with it straight." On Saturday I stood in the salon for ten minutes and walked out without going in.
Part of me wanted to fit in so badly my chest hurt. Part of me was angry that I even wanted it.
On Monday I wore my curls with a new clip. Two girls said it looked nice. One rolled her eyes. I survived both.
I'm still not sure I made the "right" choice. But I'm glad it was mine.
Mehak

How long did Mehak stand in the salon?
Ten minutes, then walked out without going in.
What was Mehak feeling outside the salon?
Mehak felt torn: wanting to fit in so badly the chest hurt, and angry at wanting it.
What would you advise a friend in Mehak's place?
Take time, as Mehak did, and choose what feels like your own, knowing some people will like it and some won't.
How might Omkar feel reading this letter from outside her school?
Omkar may feel trusted and proud of Mehak, and able to see the pressure more calmly from outside that school.

Read this:

Okay, Kavitha, you asked why I'm now the family's official 'do not let them order' person. I'm Wasim, and here's what happened. Saturday, at the cinema snack counter, the board had three options. Small popcorn, no drink, 250. Medium popcorn with a cold drink, 280. Large combo, 420. And my brain went: the medium is only thirty more than the small, and I get a drink free! Total bargain! I felt so smart ordering it. I don't even like cold drinks. It sat there going flat through the whole film. On the way home my cousin laughed and said nobody ever buys that small popcorn; it's only there to make the medium look cheap. I was annoyed, then kind of impressed. It worked on me completely, and I'd been so proud.

How much was the medium popcorn with a cold drink?
The medium popcorn with a cold drink cost 280.
How did Wasim feel on hearing the cousin's explanation?
Wasim felt annoyed at first, then almost impressed, on realising the small popcorn had been placed there to steer the choice.
What could Wasim ask at the next snack counter?
Wasim could ask whether a drink is wanted at all and which size will actually be eaten, before looking at which deal seems cheapest.
What would change if the board had shown only the medium and large combos?
Without the small popcorn at 250, the medium would not look like a steal, so Wasim might have skipped the unwanted drink.

Read this:

Friday
We won again!!! Third match in a row. And yes, I wore the orange T-shirt under my jersey. Same one as the first win in July. Unwashed since Wednesday, don't judge.
Aditi said it's a coincidence. I said, then explain three wins. She said we also got a new coach in July. And Priyal came back from her injury. And we practise two extra days now.
Hmm.
Still not washing it.
Actually, if I'm honest, I'm scared to find out. What if I wear a different shirt and we lose, and it's MY fault? Easier to just keep wearing it.
Tomorrow is the semi-final.
– Aadhya

What did Aadhya wear under the jersey?
The orange T-shirt, the same one as the first win in July.
What is Aadhya worried about when thinking of changing the shirt?
Aadhya feels scared that a different shirt might cause a loss and make it Aadhya's fault.
What could Aadhya do to test the lucky shirt idea?
Aadhya could look at the other changes Aditi named, like the new coach and extra practice, and notice that the wins have many likelier causes than a shirt.
How does Aditi see the winning streak?
Aditi sees it as the result of real changes, like the new coach, Priyal's return and extra practice, not the shirt.

Read this:

Pankaj, you're asking whether to let the AI write all your reports. Let me tell you about me and the calculator.
When I started as an accountant, calculators were new in our office. Some young people used them for everything and forgot how to check numbers in their heads.
One day a colleague typed a wrong digit and sent a report showing profit instead of loss. Nobody noticed, because nobody could estimate anymore.
I decided then: use the machine, but always know roughly what the answer should be. That habit saved me many times.
So use the AI, beta. But keep your judgement sharp. That's what your Mehak aunty is telling you.

What did the wrong report show?
Profit instead of loss.
What was young Mehak feeling when seeing the colleague's mistake?
Mehak probably felt alarmed and wary about relying fully on machines.
What choice inside the story protected Mehak's work?
Deciding to always know roughly what the answer should be, even while using a calculator.
How might the colleague who sent the wrong report have felt?
The colleague probably felt embarrassed and worried once the error came out.
After the holidays the teacher said, "Back to the grindstone!" What does that mean?

It means to return to hard work, usually after a break.
Example: The festival is over, so it is back to the grindstone for everyone.

- What is the temperature outside my window now?
- what is the difference between "later" and "latter"?
- What's the meaning of the word apprehensive?
- Help me correct this: She was born at Monday.

1. I'm not sure. I can't see your location. Look at a thermometer or a weather website.
2. "Later" refers to time, as in "see you later". "Latter" is the second of two things already named.
3. "Apprehensive" is an adjective. It means worried that something bad may happen.
4. Corrected: She was born on Monday. Why: use "on" with days of the week.

The auditors were due at nine the next morning, and at six in the evening Hemant discovered that the vendor files were a mess. Half the contracts were unsigned. Two suppliers weren't even registered. He had given the whole vendor onboarding to Manoj, his sharpest junior, a month ago.

Hemant's first thought was bitter: never again. I'll just do everything myself. He stayed till midnight fixing the worst of it, alone, angry, and quietly doubting himself. Was he just bad at trusting people?

On the drive home he replayed the day he'd handed it over. A five-minute chat in the corridor. "Take care of onboarding, you'll figure it out." No checklist. No check-ins. He hadn't even told Manoj the audit date.

The next week he sat with Manoj. "I set you up badly. Let's try again, smaller." He gave him only the registration step, with a checklist and a Friday review. Manoj got it right. The week after, Hemant gave him the contracts too.

What did Hemant discover about the vendor files?
Half the contracts were unsigned and two suppliers weren't even registered.
What was Hemant feeling as he stayed till midnight?
Hemant felt bitter and angry, and quietly doubted his own ability to trust and delegate.
What did Hemant change when he delegated again?
He admitted his own unclear briefing, gave Manoj a smaller piece with a checklist and a Friday review, then added more once it went well.
How might Manoj have seen the task at the start?
Manoj probably felt he had been given a big job with little guidance, not even knowing the audit date.
How many time will the journey take?

How much time will the journey take?
Why: "time" is uncountable, so use "much"; "many" is for countable things.

Read this:

Class 3 teacher's note, Thursday.
Mehak is quick and neat, and loves finishing first. But she only picks worksheets she has done before. Today I put out a new kind of puzzle, number pyramids, where you guess and check. Mehak looked at it, went pale, and asked if she could do the old addition sheet instead. When I said everyone was trying pyramids, she wrote one number, rubbed it out so hard the paper tore, and sat still with her hands in her lap. She told me quietly, 'What if it's wrong?' I said wrong answers are how we find the right ones, and showed her my own crossed-out tries on the board. She tried one more number. Plan: next week I'll give her 'mistake-friendly' puzzles in pairs and praise her tries, not only her answers.
Indu

What new kind of puzzle did the teacher put out?
The teacher put out number pyramids.
Why did Mehak rub out her number so hard the paper tore?
She was anxious and afraid of being wrong, so she couldn't bear leaving a guess that might not be right.
What plan will help Mehak try new things?
Pairing her for 'mistake-friendly' puzzles and praising her tries, not only her answers.
How might Indu feel watching Mehak sit still?
Indu likely felt concerned and gentle, which is why the crossed-out tries on the board were shown to her.

Read this:

Pallavi, you told me yesterday your group only does banter. Let me tell you about the monsoon I turned fifteen, when your Dilnaz aunty thought the same.
There was a boy in our tuition class, Shiv, who stammered on his s's. Every day, when the rain kept us indoors, we copied him. "S-s-sir, s-s-sorry I'm late." The whole room laughing. When the tuition sir frowned, I said, "It's just banter. All of us joke like this. Shiv laughs too."
He did laugh. Then one evening I saw him at the bus stop in the rain, practising "sorry" under his breath again and again, so he wouldn't be copied the next day. His face looked nothing like laughing.
The next day I stopped, and I told the others why. Two of them stopped too. So, Pallavi, what does the one your group jokes about do when you're not looking?

What did Dilnaz say when the tuition sir frowned?
"It's just banter. All of us joke like this. Shiv laughs too."
Why did "banter" feel like the right word to young Dilnaz?
The word let young Dilnaz feel comfortable and blameless: it made the copying sound like shared fun, and Shiv's laugh seemed to prove nobody was hurt.
What turned things around in the story?
Seeing Shiv practising "sorry" alone at the bus stop showed what the label was hiding; Dilnaz stopped the next day and told the others why, and two of them followed.
How did the "banter" look from Shiv's side?
For Shiv it seems to have been daily mockery he had to prepare against, and his laugh in class probably covered how much it hurt.

You want to know if I'm still upset about the boards, Tushar? Not like before. Let me tell you why.

I'm Rekha. When I got 58 percent, I thought I'd let everyone down. I barely left my room for a week. Then, at my cousin's engagement in Indore, I ended up on the terrace with my older cousins, Pooja didi and Anshul bhaiya.

Pooja didi said she'd failed economics in Class 12 and had to take it again. She's an auditor now. Anshul bhaiya said he'd got a low rank in his entrance and went to a small college, then did a master's somewhere good.

They weren't lecturing. They were just telling stories. But I went home thinking, this is one stage, not the whole road.

A few weeks later I made one small goal: improve my maths basics before Class 12. And this time, when I got stuck in the first test, I asked for help in week one, not month three.

What percentage did Rekha get in the boards?
58 percent.
How did Rekha feel in the week after the result?
Rekha felt ashamed and low, thinking everyone had been let down, and barely left the room.
What else could Rekha do to keep this new view of setbacks?
Rekha could keep in touch with the cousins and share small wins with them, so the reminder that results are one stage stays close.
How might Pooja didi have felt sharing her own failure on the terrace?
She may have felt a bit exposed but glad to help, hoping her story would show Rekha that a setback does not decide a whole career.

Read this:

Hansa, I'm Santosh. You say you're going to the rally on Sunday and your mother is worried? Let me tell you what I saw at twenty-four. It was a festival procession, and the crowd was happy until two groups began shouting at each other. The chants got louder and faster, and people started pushing towards the front. My friend wanted to stay and film. My heart was thumping, but I kept my voice calm and said, "Let's go to the side lane now." We slipped out the way we had come in, walking, not running. A few minutes later a bottle was thrown. I never argued with the shouters or answered back. Know your exit before you need it.

Where did Santosh suggest they go?
To the side lane.
What was Santosh feeling while the chants got louder?
Santosh's heart was thumping, a sign of alarm, but Santosh kept a calm voice.
What could Hansa do before the rally?
Hansa can note the exits, stay near the edge, tell a family member where the rally is and leave if pushing starts.
How might Santosh's friend have felt about leaving?
Disappointed at missing the filming, since the friend wanted to stay, though leaving kept them safe.

The coffee machine on the fourth floor of the Copenhagen office had broken again, and when Emil walked into the small meeting room holding a mug of hot water, Layla laughed. "Brave choice." He laughed too. It helped; she had bad news. "The board turned down the recycling proposal," she said. "Not the idea itself. The budget, this year." Emil's smile went. He looked at the table. "I've put six months into it. Should I be worried about my job?" A reflex laugh rose in Layla's throat, the kind she used to soften things, and she swallowed it. This wasn't the moment. "No," she said steadily. "Your job isn't at risk. I'm sorry about the six months. I want to push it again next year, with you leading it." Emil breathed out. "Okay. Thank you for not laughing that off."

Why did the board turn down the proposal?
Because of the budget this year, not the idea itself.
What might Emil have been feeling when he asked about his job?
Emil felt disappointed and anxious, having put six months into the proposal and now worried about his position.
How did Layla handle laughter in this talk?
She shared a light laugh about the coffee to build rapport, then held back a reflex laugh when Emil voiced a real worry and answered steadily.
What would have changed if Layla had laughed when Emil asked about his job?
Emil would likely have felt his worry was being brushed aside, and the trust from the earlier shared laugh could have turned into hurt.

messages.content:
Read this:

Sunaina, you asked why your Tanvir mama never lets anyone at the shop talk about "those people". Let me tell you. I was twenty-five, waiting outside the maternity ward at the government hospital for your cousin Rubel to be born. The corridor was split: Bengali-speaking fathers on one bench, Hindi-speaking ones on the other, and I sat with my own without thinking. I even felt a little proud of our bench. Then the power went out at midnight. A Bihari man, Ramdeo, had the only torch. He walked it down the whole corridor so every nurse could see, then shared his flask of tea with our bench first. After that we weren't two benches. We were one row of frightened fathers. When I opened the shop, I hired Ramdeo's nephew. I still love our Bengali songs. I just don't need anyone else to be less.

Who had the only torch when the power went out?
Ramdeo, a Bihari man.
How did young Tanvir feel sitting on the Bengali bench at first?
He felt at home and a little proud of "our bench", sitting with his own people without thinking.
What choice in the story shows the us-them line loosening?
Tanvir later hired Ramdeo's nephew at his shop, treating an outsider fairly while still loving Bengali songs.
What might Ramdeo have felt, walking the torch down the corridor?
He probably felt anxious like every waiting father, and wanted every mother and baby to be safe, not just those from his side.

Read this:

The client in Gothenburg called Anders at 8:15, asking why they had never received the Friday update.
Anders turned to Hiroshi. "You said you sent it."
Hiroshi had. On Friday afternoon he'd said, "Done, sent." He'd meant to send it after the gym. He'd forgotten.
His first thought was the spam folder. His second was, you never reminded me. He could feel both on his tongue.
He swallowed them.
"I didn't send it. I told you I had because I wanted to leave on time, and I thought I'd do it in the evening. I forgot. That's on me."
Anders let out a breath. "The client thinks we're hiding something."
"I'll call them now, tell them it was my mistake and send it within the hour. And from now on, I'll forward you the sent email instead of just saying it's done."
Anders nodded. "Okay. It'll take a while before I stop checking."
"That's fair."

When did the client call Anders?
The client called Anders at 8:15.
Which excuses was Hiroshi tempted to use, and why did he hold them back?
Hiroshi was tempted to blame the spam folder or Anders for not reminding him, but he swallowed them because the lie was his own and blaming would delay repair.
What steps did Hiroshi offer to repair the damage?
He admitted exactly what was false and why, offered to call the client and send the update within the hour, and promised to forward sent emails in future.
How does Anders feel about trusting Hiroshi again?
Anders is willing to move on but honest that trust will take time, saying it will be a while before Anders stops checking.

Read this:

Vasudha rolled her eyes when Yash left his socks by the sofa again. "Of course. Genius at work." Yash went quiet. She felt superior and tired at once. Later she noticed what lay beneath: she felt alone with the housework. She said, "I mocked you, and I am sorry. What I need is help with the laundry on Sundays."

Two days later the row was about his sister Aadhya staying for a month. Vasudha's heart raced, and she wanted to say the cruellest true thing about his family. Instead she said, "I need ten minutes," went to the balcony, breathed, and came back. "I feel crowded, and I would like to talk about how long she stays." Yash listened fully. They chose Saturday for a proper talk and agreed on three weeks and a chores chart.

By Sunday they had bickered about the chart, and Yash burst out laughing at the colour-coding. Vasudha giggled and slid his favourite chai across. "Truce?" she said. "Truce," he said, and washed the cups. Then, quietly: "I should have told you sooner about Aadhya." They kept no score.

How many weeks did they agree Aadhya would stay?
They agreed on three weeks.
How did Vasudha's eye-rolling about the socks differ from how she handled the row over Aadhya's stay?

Rolling her eyes felt superior but tired, and she later named her hurt and asked for help on Sundays. Over Aadhya she paused for ten minutes to cool down, spoke about her feeling and request, and they chose a time and agreed on a plan.
What was Vasudha feeling when she wanted to say the cruellest true thing about his family?
She was flooded with anger, her heart racing.
What helped them repair things after bickering about the chart?
Humour and a small kindness did it: Yash laughed at the colour-coding, Vasudha slid over his favourite chai, and they called a truce.

"Kunal, take your finger out of your mouth."
"I'm not."
"You are, and you're picking your shirt."
"I'm waiting."
"For what?"
"For my turn on the trampoline." Kunal's shoulders were stiff.
Bhavna knelt. "Waiting is hard. Do you want the squishy star to squeeze while you wait?" Kunal took the star from her bag and squeezed it. "Better?" "A bit." "Let's count the bounces together." His fingers stayed out of his mouth.

What was Kunal waiting for?
He was waiting for his turn on the trampoline.
What does Kunal's biting and picking suggest he was feeling?
It suggests he was nervous or impatient about waiting for his turn, since his shoulders were stiff. He said only that he was waiting.
What worked in Bhavna's approach?
She didn't punish him and gave him a squishy star to squeeze and a counting game, which gave his fingers something else to do.
How might Kunal feel if Bhavna had just told him off?
He might feel ashamed and still be nervous, without a better way to cope.

Is it "milennium" or "millennium"?
Also, what does "lend a hand" mean?
Then, what is the meaning of tropical?

1. It is "millennium", with a double "l" and a double "n".
2. It means to help. For example: can you lend a hand with the heavy boxes?
3. "Tropical" is an adjective. It means belonging to the hot, wet regions near the equator.

The seed-saving camp in Morena village drew ninety farmers, triple what anyone expected. That evening, at the block office, the district officer shook Saroja's hand. "Your idea, your success." Saroja smiled but didn't let it end there. "The idea was mine, and I'm glad I pushed for holding it after harvest," she said. "But the rain stopped the day before, which was pure luck. And I printed the leaflets only in Hindi, when half the women speak mainly the local dialect. Asif translated for three hours without a break. Karthik fixed the loudspeaker when it died at noon." Asif looked up from his tea, surprised. The officer nodded slowly and wrote all three names in the report. On the jeep ride back, Karthik asked Saroja to plan the next camp with him.

How many farmers came to the seed-saving camp?
The camp in Morena village drew ninety farmers.
Why doesn't Saroja simply accept 'Your idea, your success'?
She seems to want an honest record, taking pride in her idea while admitting the luck and the help she had.
What could other team leads learn from Saroja's reply?
Name your own good choice and your mistake, say what was luck, and credit helpers by their task, like Asif's translating.
How does Asif react when Saroja names his work?
Asif looks up from his tea, surprised, which suggests he didn't expect his three hours of translating to be mentioned.

After the last bell, Farhan waited until the classroom was empty, then went up to Indu Ma'am's desk.
"Ma'am, can I keep my notebook in the class cupboard? The one with the lock?"
"Your homework notebook?"
"No, Ma'am. My own notebook. I draw things and write stories. My little brother keeps opening my bag at home and reading it out loud."
His ears were red. Indu Ma'am thought for a moment, then took a small key off her ring.
"There's one empty shelf. It's yours. Nobody will open it but you."
Farhan put the notebook on the shelf, locked it, and held the key tightly. "Thank you, Ma'am."
"Farhan," she said, as he reached the door, "wanting a private place is completely normal. It doesn't mean you're hiding anything bad."

Who keeps opening Farhan's bag at home?
His little brother keeps opening his bag at home and reading it out loud.
Why were Farhan's ears red when he asked?
Farhan felt shy and embarrassed, because his notebook of drawings and stories felt very personal.
How did Indu Ma'am support Farhan's need for privacy?
She gave him an empty locked shelf and told him that wanting a private place is normal, not a sign of hiding anything bad.
How might Farhan's little brother see the notebook?
His little brother probably sees it as a fun thing to read aloud, without realising it embarrasses Farhan.

Tejas, put the phone down and listen. I'm Vinita, and I want to tell you about the hair clips. When I was ten, a man I barely knew, older than my father, stopped me near the bus stop and gave me a pretty set of clips. "Our little secret, no need to tell your parents," he said. I liked the clips, but my stomach felt wrong, and the word secret sat on me like a stone. That evening I put them on the table and told my mother everything. She held my hand and said, "You did the right thing. None of this is your fault." That same evening my father called the school. I stayed away from that bus stop. Never blame yourself, Tejas. Telling is always right.

What did the man give Vinita?
A pretty set of clips.
How did Vinita feel about the secret even though she liked the clips?
Vinita felt uneasy and worried: her stomach felt wrong and the word secret sat on her like a stone, so a gift with a secret felt like a warning.
What should Tejas do if an older person gives Tejas presents and says to keep it secret?
Tell their parents right away and stay away from that person.
How might Vinita's mother have felt when Vinita told her?
Grateful and protective, since she held Vinita's hand, said it was not Vinita's fault, and the school was told that same evening.

Describe the stranger in this scene in your own words.

The stranger, with a comfortable kind of grunt over his pipe, put his legs up on the settle that he had to himself. He wore a flapping broad-brimmed traveller's hat, and under it a handkerchief tied over his head in the manner of a cap: so that he showed no hair. As he looked at the fire, I thought I saw a cunning expression, followed by a half-laugh, come into his face.
He sits comfortably with his legs up, smoking a pipe. He wears a broad hat with a handkerchief under it, so no hair shows, and his face seems sly as he half laughs.

The Professor was delighted. "Ah, that wonderful Madam Mina," he said, "pearl among women! She arrive, but I cannot stay. She must go to your house, friend John. You must meet her at the station. Telegraph her en route, so that she may be prepared."

Answer from the text. What does the Professor tell the listener to do about Madam Mina?
The Professor says Madam Mina has arrived but he cannot stay, so she must go to the listener's house. He tells the listener to meet her at the station and telegraph her en route so she is prepared.

In their Bengaluru flat, five-year-old Usha took a bite of banana and ran to put the rest on the little puja shelf for Ganesha. Ajji Nirmala caught her wrist gently. 'Not that one, kanda. Something you've bitten is jootha. God gets the first, fresh piece.'
Usha frowned. 'But I didn't bite much.'
Ajji smiled and gave her a whole banana to offer. At dinner, when Usha reached for Appa's steel tumbler, she stopped herself. 'Jootha,' she announced, and fetched her own. She still wasn't sure why. She only knew some things sat on one side of an invisible line.

What did Ajji give Usha to offer?
A whole banana.
What was Usha feeling when she frowned and said, 'But I didn't bite much'?
She felt confused and a little disappointed, not understanding why her bitten banana wasn't good enough.
How could Ajji help Usha understand the rule, not just follow it?
Explain simply, when Usha asks, that offering the first, fresh piece is a way of showing care and respect, and answer her questions kindly.
How might Ajji Nirmala feel seeing Usha fetch her own tumbler?
Ajji may feel pleased and a little amused that Usha is already following the family custom on her own.

When I started asking questions at our temple study circle, it went quiet fast. I'm Ojas, and I was nineteen. I asked, politely I thought, why women in our circle weren't allowed to read certain texts aloud. The uncle who led the circle said, 'This is not the place for arguments.' The next week, two boys I'd grown up with stopped saving me a seat. At the festival, people nodded at my parents and not at me. I felt so lonely I almost walked out for good, and I wrote a long angry post that I thankfully never sent. What saved it was Nandini-aunty, who ran the temple library. She found me sulking by the shoe stand and said, 'Your question is an old one. Come on Thursday; I'll show you three saints who asked it.' I did. I still go on Thursdays. I don't win every argument. I just have one person there I can ask anything.

Who ran the temple library?
Nandini-aunty ran the temple library.
What did Ojas feel when the boys stopped saving a seat?
Ojas felt lonely and rejected, close to walking out for good.
What turned things around for Ojas?
Finding one open-minded elder, Nandini-aunty, and going to her Thursday sessions instead of cutting all ties.
How might the uncle who led the circle have seen Ojas's question?
The uncle seems to have seen it as an argument that threatened the circle, not as an honest question.

I'm Ganga, and Tushar has been my lab partner since first year. For three weeks this term he rewrote his essay for the semester-abroad scholarship every night, reading it aloud to me between titrations.
On Thursday the list came out. His name wasn't on it.
By lunch he was telling everyone at our canteen table, "Honestly, I never really wanted it. That programme's overrated. It's just a nice brochure and expensive rent." He laughed a lot while saying it.
I don't know what was going on inside him. Maybe he truly changed his mind. But I remember him showing me that brochure in October, pointing at the lab photos. And when the coordinator emailed an offer of feedback on the essays, he deleted it in front of me without opening it. "Why would I need that?" he said.

How long did Tushar spend rewriting his scholarship essay?
For three weeks this term he rewrote it every night.
Why might calling the programme overrated feel reasonable to Tushar?
Believing he never wanted it softens the sting of being left off the list; if the prize was worthless, losing it hurts less.
What choice could have turned the rejection into something useful for Tushar?
Opening the coordinator's feedback email instead of deleting it, since it could show what to improve before a future try.
How does Ganga see Tushar's laughter at the canteen table?
Ganga isn't sure what Tushar feels, but notices the laughter doesn't match the weeks of rewriting or the excitement over the lab photos, so it looks like it might be covering disappointment.

Monday. Pradeep didn't get into the school band. He said, "It's fine," but his ears were red. Siddharth answered, "It's not a big deal, there's always next year." Pradeep looked away and said, "Yeah, right," and left early.

Wednesday. Siddharth couldn't stop thinking about Pradeep's face. He messaged, "That came out like your thing didn't matter. Sorry. Want to talk, or want me to just sit with you?" Pradeep replied, "Sit."

Saturday. They sat on the steps outside the music room. Pradeep talked about how much he'd practised. Siddharth said only, "That sounds really disappointing," and stayed. Pradeep leaned on the railing, breathing slowly, and finally said, "Thanks for staying."

What did Pradeep not get into?
He did not get into the school band.
Why did Pradeep say "Yeah, right" and leave early on Monday?
He was probably hurt and felt his disappointment was being brushed aside, since his ears were red and he looked away. He may also just have wanted to be alone.
What worked better for Siddharth on Saturday than on Monday?
Instead of offering a quick fix or calling it small, he listened, named the disappointment and stayed with Pradeep.
How might Siddharth have felt after Pradeep left early?
He may have felt worried and unsure, which is why he messaged to apologise on Wednesday.
When I wanted to ask about the old quarrel, my mother said "let sleeping dogs lie". Why?

It means do not stir up an old problem that is quiet now, because you may cause more trouble.
Example: The two neighbours have not argued for years, so let sleeping dogs lie.
Is line ko English mein batao: "Mujhe nahi lagta ki wo aayega."
It is: "I don't think he will come." In English we put the "not" in the first part: "I don't think", not "I think he will not come". Say "she" if you mean a woman.
What is the aroha of Raga Alhaiya Bilawal?
The aroha of Raga Alhaiya Bilawal is: S R G P D N S'.

How might Tanuja's parents see the limit of one trip home a month?

Together they sorted her notes: dates, amounts, emails, who knew what. He explained which protections might apply and what they wouldn't cover. She left with a folder and a plan.
June 24: Reena submitted her report to the regulator through its official portal, attaching only documents and dates. Then she called her mother and said, 'It's done.' Her hands were steady for the first time in months.

Where was Yusuf's office?
Yusuf's office was above a pharmacy.
What do Reena's steady hands on June 24 suggest?
They suggest she feels calmer and more certain, having finally acted through a proper channel after months of strain.

A report built on dates, amounts and documents is clearer and harder to dismiss, which strengthens her case with the regulator.
What might Reena's mother feel hearing 'It's done'?

The lizard in the bathroom and his new shoes.

Friday night

Suresh and I spent all evening with a calculator instead of watching the film we'd planned. Worth it.
Keerthana at work told me she chose her flat first and then found the EMI ate half her salary. She's stopped going out at all. I don't want that.
So we started from the other end. Our monthly income, both salaries together. We decided the EMI must remain below one-third of that, so there's room for savings, Amma's medicines and an actual life.
Then: what loan does that EMI allow over twenty years? Suresh used the bank's online calculator. Add what we've saved for the down payment. That gave us a top price.
It's lower than the flats on the ads Suresh keeps showing me. That hurt a bit. But now I know which listings to skip.
Next week we're meeting the bank to confirm it properly.
— Vandana

What did Suresh use to work out the loan?
The bank's online calculator.
How did Vandana feel seeing the top price?
Vandana felt a little disappointed that it was lower than the advertised flats, but also clearer and more settled about which listings to skip.
What else could Vandana and Suresh do after meeting the bank?
They could list their must-haves and only visit flats within the price range, so viewings stay focused.
How might Keerthana's experience have shaped Vandana's plan?
Keerthana's story of an EMI eating half her salary made Vandana wary, and pushed the couple to start from what they can afford.

Monday: At the recording studio, Aparna hears a faint buzz on the vocal track that nobody else notices. After six years at the desk, her hunch says it's the old cable, not the mic. She swaps the cable and records ten seconds. The buzz is gone.
Wednesday: The producer, Hrithik, asks her which of three album covers will sell best. Everyone expects a quick answer. "That's not my field," Aparna says. "My gut there is just taste. Ask the design team, or test them with listeners."
Friday: The cable hunch comes back on a different track. Before swapping anything, Aparna asks the junior engineer to listen too. He hears it. They check the cable together. Right again.

How long has Aparna been at the desk?
Six years.
Why did Aparna decline to pick an album cover?
She felt unsure and cautious outside her field; she knew her gut there was just taste, not trained judgment.
How does Aparna use her hunches wisely?
In her own field she trusts them but tests them quickly and checks with a colleague; outside it, she suggests asking experts or testing with listeners.
How might Hrithik feel when Aparna says it isn't her field?
Hrithik might be surprised at first, expecting a quick answer, but could come to respect the honesty and get better advice.

In their Delhi colony, Tenzin, ten, had organised a cricket team, a kite club and a treasure hunt, all in one summer. Everyone came to his door. But in class silent reading felt like torture; he tapped his pencil, whispered jokes and got shushed twice. At break he rushed up to Swati, who was sitting alone with a book. "Come on, we need a fielder!" She shook her head. He kept talking, about the match, the new ball, a funny video. Swati turned a page, her lips tight. Tenzin finally noticed. "You want to read, right?" She nodded. "Sorry. I'll save you a turn after lunch." Swati smiled for the first time that day.

How many activities did Tenzin organise that summer?
Three: a cricket team, a kite club and a treasure hunt.
How did Tenzin feel during silent reading?
He felt restless and bored, tapping his pencil and whispering jokes.
What did Tenzin learn to do with Swati?
He noticed her quiet cue, her tight lips, asked what she wanted and gave her space, offering a turn later.
How might Swati have felt while Tenzin kept talking?
Swati probably felt crowded and a bit irritated, wanting quiet time with her book.

She was booking a preventive health check-up. Her mother had diabetes, and a doctor had told her to keep an eye on it. She compared two clinics, asked which tests her insurance covered, and chose one nearer the metro.

Where did Jahnavi file the reports?
In a blue folder with her old records.
What might Jahnavi have been feeling while booking the check-up?
Jahnavi may have felt a little worried because of her mother's diabetes, but mainly calm and responsible.

Saurabh had switched the packaging supplier without telling Reena. The new one was cheaper, and it had felt so obvious that he'd skipped the conversation. For a week he had an uneasy stone in his stomach. He knew that "it saves us money" was not going to fix it. On Thursday he walked into the office early. "I changed the supplier without asking you, and I shouldn't have. I'll switch back until we decide together, and from now on anything over a small limit goes to both of us."

Reena blinked. She was not angry, exactly. Because on the investor call the week before, she had presented the new dashboard as her own work, and Saurabh had built most of it. She realised, sitting there, that she had wronged him too, and that he was hurt. The thought "but you hid something first" rose in her, and she set it aside. "You're right about the supplier. And I owe you something: I took credit for your dashboard on Monday. I'll email the investors today and correct it. If you want to change how we present things, I'll accept that."

Ritu, their advisor, saw them at the whiteboard later, sketching a decision list with both their names on it. She smiled, and left them to it.

What did Saurabh change without telling Reena?
He switched the packaging supplier.
How did Saurabh's coming clean and Reena's admission fit together?

Saurabh confessed the supplier change early, offered to switch back and set a shared rule. Reena set aside the thought that he had hidden something first, owned taking credit for the dashboard, and offered to correct it with the investors.
What was Saurabh feeling during the week before he told Reena?
He felt uneasy and guilty, like a stone in his stomach.
What could Reena do if Saurabh is still hurt about the investor call after her email?
She could accept the consequences without demanding forgiveness, and follow through on how they present work.

Week two. Mohit had been in Bengaluru for fourteen days and hadn't spoken to anyone beyond 'one tea'. Even small things felt heavy: the laundry bag sat in the corner for a week, and he missed a morning lecture because he couldn't make himself get up. His mother asked on the phone if he was eating. He said yes.
Week four. In the chemistry lab, Himani, who sat next to him, asked if he wanted to join three of them studying in the library on Thursdays. He almost said no. He said okay.
Week six. Thursdays had become the fixed point of Mohit's week. He did his laundry on Wednesdays so he'd have a clean shirt. He finished the problem sets early so he'd have questions for the group. On Sunday he called his mother and talked for forty minutes, mostly about Himani's terrible jokes.

When did the group study in the library?
They studied in the library on Thursdays.
Why did even small tasks feel heavy to Mohit in week two?
He felt lonely and disconnected in a new city, and without anyone around, his energy and motivation drained.
What helped Mohit's motivation return?
Saying yes to Himani's small study group gave him a fixed, connected point in the week that he wanted to prepare for.
How might Mohit's mother feel on the Sunday call?
She would likely feel relieved and happy hearing him talk for forty minutes about new friends.

Saurabh may feel hurt and shocked, but chooses calm support over anger.

messages.content:
He was away three weeks. The first day or two my charge sat in a corner of the library, too sad for either reading or playing: in that quiet state she caused me little trouble; but it was succeeded by an interval of impatient, fretful weariness; and being too busy, and too old then, to run up and down amusing her, I hit on a method by which she might entertain herself. I used to send her on her travels round the grounds—now on foot, and now on a pony; indulging her with a patient audience of all her real and imaginary adventures when she returned.

Could you recap this paragraph for me? Two sentences is enough.

A man is away for three weeks, and the narrator's charge first sits sadly in the library, then becomes restless and fretful. Too busy to play with her, the narrator sends her to explore the grounds and listens patiently to her adventures, real or imagined.

Read this:

The movers had packed every toy by noon, and rain kept Anirban indoors. He wandered, bored. Then he grabbed Seema's ladle. 'Hello, hello, mic testing!' He sang into it. A bedsheet over two chairs became his stage. A folded newspaper became a ticket. 'Didi, you're the audience.' Seema, wrapping plates, sighed, 'Two minutes only.' She clapped when he bowed, then took her ladle back.

What did Anirban use as a microphone?
He used Seema's ladle as a microphone.
How was Seema feeling when she said 'Two minutes only'?
She seemed tired and busy with packing, a bit impatient, but willing to join his game briefly.
How could Seema keep Anirban busy while she packs?
She could hand him a few safe objects, like an empty box or a cloth, and let his pretend show go on nearby.
What would change if Anirban's toys had not been packed?
He might have played with his usual toys and not needed to turn a ladle and bedsheet into a stage.

Read this:

The school trip bus to Mahabaleshwar left at six, and there was no time for breakfast. Charu noticed that Ankita didn't touch the sandwiches either at the stop or at lunch. "Not hungry," Ankita said, again, and hid her packed lunch in her bag.
It had been like this for weeks. Ankita talked constantly about "fixing" her shape and went quiet if anyone offered food.
Charu wanted to say, "You're fine, just eat." She didn't. At the viewpoint, away from the others, she said, "I've noticed you're skipping meals a lot. I'm not judging you. I just care about you and I'm worried."
Ankita's eyes filled. "Please don't tell anyone."
"I care too much to keep it secret. Let's tell Mrs Pinto together."
That evening on the bus back, Mrs Pinto sat with Ankita and called her mother to plan a doctor's visit.

Where did the school trip bus go?
To Mahabaleshwar.
What was Charu feeling when she chose her words at the viewpoint?
She felt worried and caring, and careful not to judge Ankita or comment on her body.
What did Charu do well, and why was it wiser than "just eat"?
She spoke privately with care and concern, avoided body comments or forcing food, and brought in a trusted teacher the same day so medical support could follow.
How might Ankita feel when Charu says she won't keep it secret?
She might feel scared and exposed at first, and also a little relieved that someone noticed and cared.

Read this:

'Farida Appi, can you check this before I delete it?'
'Delete it? It's the message to the museum curator. You wrote it in January.'
'She runs a whole wing. She'll think I'm some pest.'
'Nazia, it's three polite lines asking about one exhibit.'
'Exactly, one exhibit. She has hundreds.' Nazia scrolled. 'I have four more like it. The textile designer, the conservator...'
'Sent any?'
'...No.'
'Since January?'
'It's April, I know.' Nazia pulled her dupatta tight. 'Every time I hover over send, I picture her sighing at her screen.'
'And instead she never hears from you at all.'
'At least she's not annoyed.'
Farida put the phone down between them. 'She's not anything. That's the problem. No one's said no, but no one's said yes either. Five drafts, zero conversations.'
Nazia looked at the screen and didn't answer.

When did Nazia write the message to the museum curator?
She wrote it in January.
What does Nazia picture when hovering over send, and what does it show about her feelings?
She pictures the curator sighing at the screen, which shows she is afraid of being a bother and of being judged.
What could Farida suggest as a first step?
Send just the curator's message now, with Farida sitting beside her, and wait a week before deciding anything about the others.
How does the situation look to Farida?
Farida sees that avoiding annoyance has cost Nazia every chance of a yes, and is frustrated that five drafts led to nothing.

messages.content:
Read this:

It was 11 p.m., the night before the final exam, when the class group exploded. Someone had posted that Parveen had leaked the question paper. It wasn't true. Within minutes, forty messages: accusations, jokes, one person calling her a cheat and worse. Parveen's hands were shaking. She typed a furious reply, then stopped. Her friend Yamini called. "Don't reply in the group. Not angry. Not tonight." Parveen deleted her draft. Instead, she took screenshots of every message, especially the abusive one from a boy outside their class. She sent one calm line to the group: "That's false. I'll speak to the class teacher tomorrow." Then she muted it, reported the abusive account, and blocked him. At 11:30 she called her mother, then forwarded the screenshots to the class teacher. The teacher replied before midnight: "Thank you for telling me. I'll deal with this in the morning. Please rest."

What time did the class group explode?
At 11 p.m., the night before the final exam.
What was Parveen feeling as the messages poured in?
She was upset and furious, her hands shaking, and almost replied in anger.
Which steps helped Parveen handle the thread?
Not replying angrily, taking screenshots, posting one calm line, muting, reporting and blocking the abuser, and telling her mother and teacher that night.
How did the class teacher respond when Parveen forwarded the screenshots?
The teacher replied before midnight, thanked her, promised to deal with it in the morning and told her to rest.

Read this:

In the staff room of the government school at Rampura, Ishita suggested turning the empty storeroom into a reading corner. Sarita, who had taught there eleven years, didn't look up from her register. "Be realistic. The children won't come, the books will get stolen, and the headmaster won't sanction anything." Ishita had heard the same line about the kitchen garden in July and the morning radio quiz in August. Each time Sarita sounded wise. Each time nothing was tried. Ishita watched her thumb the edge of the register and remembered hearing that Sarita's own library plan had been scrapped years ago. That evening Ishita cleared one shelf herself and brought six books from home. By Friday, four children were reading there at lunch. Sarita paused in the doorway, then walked on without a word.

How long had Sarita taught at the school?
She had taught there eleven years.
What was Ishita feeling as Sarita called the idea unrealistic again?
Ishita felt frustrated but also curious, noticing that Sarita's "realism" always ended with nothing being tried.
What did Ishita's small test show?
Clearing one shelf with six books risked very little, and four children reading by Friday gave real evidence instead of predictions.
What might Sarita have felt pausing in the doorway?
She may have felt surprise mixed with an old sting, perhaps remembering her own library plan that was scrapped.
Change this into a wish with "I wish": It's a pity I can't sing well.
I wish I could sing well.

Read this:

On the girls' hostel notice board, lights-out was ten, even in exam week. Two girls had already argued with the warden, Kashish Ma'am, in the corridor. One had shouted, "Then we'll all fail and it'll be your fault." The door had shut in their faces.
Ira tried something else. She collected signatures from twenty-two girls in Block B who wanted to study late. Then she knocked on the office door after dinner.
"Ma'am, may I ask about exam week?" She laid down the list. "We're asking for eleven-thirty, only in the common study hall, not in rooms. Two seniors will sign everyone out at the end. And we'll keep it silent so the juniors can sleep."
Kashish Ma'am read the list slowly. "Who are the two seniors?"
Ira named them.
"Try it for three nights. If the hall stays quiet, we'll continue."

How many girls signed Ira's list?
Twenty-two girls in Block B signed the list.
What was Kashish Ma'am likely thinking as she read the list slowly?
She was probably cautious but interested, weighing whether the plan was safe, and she may have felt respected after the shouting in the corridor.
What made Ira's appeal succeed where the other girls failed?
Ira asked politely, brought evidence of support, and offered a clear, safe plan, while the others used threats that made the warden shut the door.
What is it like for Kashish Ma'am to be threatened in the corridor?
It probably felt disrespectful and stressful, making her less willing to bend the rule for the girls who shouted.

Read this:

Eco-club note, Saturday planting drive, Class 9 volunteers.
Ankita arrived early and planted more saplings than anyone, but she was quiet, not her usual self. During the water break she showed me a photo on her phone of a flooded town down the coast and asked, 'Will our trees ever matter to people there?' I explained, simply, how forests hold soil and slow rainwater, and that one drive is small but not nothing. She listened, then said she felt guilty having a dry bedroom. Her friend Nandini suggested a stall at the school fair for flood relief. Ankita brightened and started listing what they could sell. Action: on Monday I will connect them with the school's relief committee, and I will check in with Ankita, as her worry seemed heavy.

What did Nandini suggest during the break?
A stall at the school fair for flood relief.
What was Ankita feeling during the water break?
She was worried about the flooded town and guilty about having a dry bedroom, which is why she was so quiet.
Was the note-writer's plan to follow up a good one? Why?
Yes; linking Ankita and Nandini to the relief committee turns worry into action, and checking in makes sure Ankita doesn't carry the heavy feeling alone.
How might Nandini see Ankita's worry?
Nandini seems to see it as something they can act on together, which is why the stall idea came up and helped Ankita brighten.

Read this:

In the Mumbai flat, Vikas was revising the twelve steps of the nitrogen cycle for his biology test. He read the list from the top every time. The next day, in the test, he wrote steps one to four perfectly. Five to nine were blank. He got eleven and twelve half right. The same week, Jasleen joined his class from Chandigarh. Before she arrived, a boy had told Vikas she'd been "kicked out" of her old school. So when she was top in the test, Vikas thought she must have cheated. When she helped others, he thought she was sucking up. His mother, hearing all this at dinner, asked, "What's the first thing you heard about her?" He told her. "And what have you seen since?" He thought. Only good things. "Maybe the first thing was wrong," his mother said. "Like your middle steps."

Which steps of the nitrogen cycle were blank in Vikas's test?
Five to nine were blank.
Why did Vikas think Jasleen must have cheated?
He felt suspicious because the first thing he heard was that she'd been kicked out, and that first story coloured everything he saw.
What did Vikas's mother help him notice?
That the first thing he heard shaped his view of Jasleen, just as the first items of his list stuck while the middle faded.
How might Jasleen feel if she knew what Vikas thought?
Jasleen might feel hurt and unfairly judged, since she was only doing well and helping others.
Say what a wallet is in one sentence, using the words "cards" and "notes".
A wallet is a small case for carrying cards and notes.
What is the name of the person who sits behind me at work?
I don't know who sits behind you, because I know nothing about your office. A look at the seating chart or a friendly hello will do.

Read this:

Note from Nilesh, room teacher, Little Steps nursery, Tuesday:
At drop-off, Mia cried hard when her dad left. Tarun was stacking blocks happily nearby. He stopped, stared at Mia, and his face crumpled. Soon he was crying too, then two more children. None of them had any reason of their own. I sat on the mat, picked up Mia, and hummed our bus song. Tarun crawled over and leaned on my knee. Within a few minutes the room was quiet again 🙂

What was Tarun doing before Mia started crying?
Tarun was stacking blocks happily nearby.
What does Tarun's face crumpling as he stared at Mia suggest?
It suggests Mia's crying upset him and he began to feel the same distress, even though nothing had happened to him.
How did Nilesh help the room calm down, and why did it work?
Nilesh sat on the mat, held Mia and hummed the bus song, which calmed Mia and drew Tarun in, so the calm spread like the crying had.
What was drop-off like for the other children in the room?
Two more children started crying too, so for them it was a sudden sad moment that none of them could explain.

Read this:

Subject: Website move this Saturday: what you need to know (2-minute read)
Hi Vaibhav,
Short version first: the website will be down this Saturday from 10 pm to 2 am. Your team doesn't need to do anything, except avoid sending customer emails with website links during those hours.
Why: we're moving the site to new servers (the computers that store it and show it to visitors), so it loads faster.
What might go wrong: if something breaks, the site could stay down until Sunday morning. I'll message you by 3 am either way.
Details for anyone who wants them are in the attached plan. Last time I sent you four pages of tech notes, and you had to call me to ask what they meant for your campaign, so I'm trying the short version first this time!
Thanks for your patience,
Jomon

When will the website be down?
This Saturday from 10 pm to 2 am.
Why did Jomon decide to put the short version first?
Jomon likely felt a bit embarrassed that the four pages of tech notes last time left Vaibhav confused, and wanted this email to be easy to act on.
What makes this email clear for a mixed audience?
It starts with the one thing the reader must do, explains 'servers' in plain words, says what could go wrong, and puts the details in an attachment.
How might Vaibhav feel reading this email compared with the last one?
Vaibhav would likely feel relieved and prepared, knowing exactly what the team must avoid, instead of confused and needing to call.

Read this:

The night before the chemistry exam, a wedding band thundered two lanes away, and Varun gave up on sleep. "I'll just go through everything once more," he told himself, and when the power went too, he kept cramming by torchlight. By dawn the equations swam. On the way to the bus he couldn't recall the first flashcard, and his chest felt tight. His sister Indu stopped walking. "Breathe with me. In. Out. You've studied for weeks. You're not starting from zero." He breathed slowly and wrote what he could. That evening Indu helped him plan for the next paper: finish revising by dinner, then earplugs and lights out.

What was thundering the night before the chemistry exam?
A wedding band, two lanes away.
What was Varun feeling on the way to the bus?
He felt panicky; his chest was tight and he could not recall the first flashcard.
What is wiser about the plan for the next paper?
Finishing revision by dinner and then sleeping means he goes in rested instead of foggy and panicked.
How does Indu see Varun's panic?
She sees him as prepared but exhausted, so she calms his breathing and reminds him he has studied for weeks.

Read this:

Age two: Sabina hummed a wandering tune to no one while she stacked steel cups on the kitchen floor. Her grandfather, chopping onions, hummed the same tune back. She looked up, delighted, and made it longer.

Age nine: in assembly Santosh joined the morning chant, his voice rising with a hundred others until the hall seemed to hum and his shoulders loosened. Next to him a new girl kept her lips closed and stared at her shoes. The teacher noticed and did not scold. Afterwards they said quietly, 'You can join whenever you feel ready.'

Age twenty-five: Tenzin rocked the baby at three in the morning, dead tired, and sang the lullaby his own mother used to sing, flat and cracking on the high note. The baby's fists loosened. His partner murmured from the doorway, 'You're off-key.' Tenzin laughed softly. 'Nobody's complaining.' And he kept singing.

What did Sabina's grandfather do while chopping onions?
He hummed the same tune back.
How did music serve a similar purpose at two, nine and twenty-five?

Sabina hummed while stacking cups and her grandfather hummed back. Santosh joined the assembly chant with a hundred others until the hall seemed to hum, and Tenzin sang the lullaby flat and cracking at three in the morning while the baby's fists loosened. In each case the tune brought closeness and calm
What might the new girl have been feeling as she kept her lips closed?
Shy or unsure among a hundred voices rather than disrespectful, as her stare at her shoes suggests.
How did the teacher help the girl who stayed silent?
They did not scold her and quietly said she could join whenever she felt ready.

Make full sentences from these notes:

Exam on Monday. Syllabus chapters 4 to 6. Bring pen and ruler.
The exam is on Monday. The syllabus covers chapters 4 to 6. Bring a pen and a ruler.
For our anniversary, write a short message to my wife, Priyanka. About 60 words, warm but not too flowery.

Happy anniversary, Priyanka. Seven years ago, I married my best friend, and somehow you have become even more than that. Thank you for your patience on my grumpy mornings, your laughter on long drives and the way you make our home feel warm. I'm grateful for every year with you, and I'm looking forward to many more.
Love,
Mihir

I'm Rafiq, from 11B. Kashish has topped every exam since class eight, and some of the boys at the back call her "the machine". I used to laugh along. Then last Tuesday, after the chemistry test, I found her in the empty lab, redoing a question she'd already got right, lips moving. She'd scored 98. When I said, "Congrats," she flinched and said, "That's two marks gone." She didn't look happy at all. I don't really know what she feels. But I stopped laughing at the machine jokes. Yesterday I asked if she wanted to join our Saturday cricket, just to bowl badly with us. She said maybe.

What did Kashish score in the chemistry test?
She scored 98.
What did Rafiq seem to feel after finding Kashish in the empty lab?
Rafiq seems concerned for Kashish and sorry for laughing along, which is why the machine jokes stopped being funny and the cricket invitation came.
What choices did Rafiq make after seeing Kashish in the lab?
Rafiq stopped laughing at the "machine" jokes and invited Kashish to Saturday cricket, offering kindness and a way to relax.
How might Kashish feel being invited to bowl badly at Saturday cricket?
Kashish might feel surprised and a little lighter, since someone saw more than the marks; 'maybe' suggests cautious interest.

Week 1: Uma's first internship at the NGO office meant filing and tea orders. The coordinator barely learned her name. By Friday she was scrolling her phone at her desk by eleven.
Week 3: The coordinator left, and Jaya took over. She read Uma's college project on village water use and said, "This is good thinking. I want you on the survey report, and I'll give you honest notes." The notes came back covered in comments. Uma stayed late fixing every one.
Week 8: Uma presented the survey findings to the funders. Her voice shook for the first minute, then steadied. Afterwards she realised she hadn't looked at her phone all day.

What was Uma doing at her desk by eleven in week 1?
She was scrolling her phone.
Why did Uma stay late fixing every comment in week 3?
Jaya's belief that her thinking was good made the effort feel worthwhile, and she wanted to live up to it.
What was the turning point, and what made it work?
Jaya giving Uma a real report along with honest notes; the high expectation came with real work and feedback, not just praise. 🙂
How might the funders see Uma in week 8 compared with how the old coordinator saw her?
The funders see a capable intern presenting findings, while the old coordinator saw someone for filing and tea and never found out what she could do.

metadata.subtype: Boss expects excellence or expects nothing [Receiver]

Read this:

Sunday. Samuel, fourteen, sat down to learn the first twenty elements for Tuesday's chemistry test. Hydrogen, helium, lithium... he started from the top every time, and every time his mother Elizabeth called him for dinner somewhere around sodium.
Tuesday. In the test, the first eight poured out of his pen. After that the page stayed blank until the bell. "I knew them yesterday," he told his lab partner Salma, confused.
"You knew the start," Salma said. "I learn mine backwards, and from the middle too."
Friday. Samuel wrote the list on cards, shuffled them and began with calcium. On the retest he got seventeen. Still, when he closed his eyes, hydrogen and helium came first, loud and clear.

How many elements did Samuel get on the retest?
Seventeen.
Why was Samuel confused after Tuesday's test?
He felt sure he knew the list because the beginning came so easily, not realising he had practised the start far more than the end.
What changed in Samuel's studying, and why did it help?
He shuffled cards and began from the middle, so the later elements got as much practice as the first ones.
How does Salma see Samuel's problem?
Salma sees that Samuel only knew the start because he always began at the top, and shares a trick of learning backwards and from the middle.

Read this:

Ujjwal, you're squeezing that cushion like I used to squeeze myself. Let your Ayesha Khala tell you. When I was nine, a big storm knocked out the power in our Lucknow house. I sat on the stairs with my arms wrapped tight round my own body, rocking a little. My sister said, “She's cold, get her a shawl.” My father sat down beside me without a word. After a while he asked, very quietly, “Cold, or scared, or both?” I said, “Scared of the thunder.” He didn't laugh. He counted the seconds between flash and bang with me, and as they grew longer, my arms loosened.

What knocked out the power in the Lucknow house?
A big storm knocked out the power.
What was young Ayesha feeling as she hugged herself on the stairs?
She was scared of the thunder, as she told her father, though her sister thought she was just cold.
What choice did her father make, and why did it help?
He sat quietly and asked whether she was cold, scared or both, then counted the thunder with her, which soothed her without assuming.
How did Ayesha's sister read the self-hug?
Her sister thought Ayesha was cold and suggested a shawl, which shows the same hug could have more than one reason.

Read this:

At the school swap fair in Manchester, Wei set out his old comics on a blanket with a big sign: £5 EACH. Omar flipped through them. "These are good. I'll give you £1 each for the space ones." Wei looked shocked. "They're worth way more. I've read those twenty times." "That's why the corners are bent," Omar said. The comic stall next door had the same issues for 50p. By lunch Wei had sold nothing, and he told his mum the other kids were trying to rip him off. She held up one of the space comics. "Would you pay five pounds for this, if it was someone else's?" Wei looked at the bent corner for a long time.

What did the next-door stall charge for the same comics?
Why did Wei think the other kids were trying to rip him off?
He felt upset and insulted because the comics were his and read twenty times, so they felt worth far more than buyers offered.
Why is Wei's mum's question useful?
It makes Wei look at the comic as a buyer would, which shows the gap between what an owner feels and what others will pay.
How does Omar see the comics?
Omar likes them but sees bent corners and cheaper copies next door, so £1 seems a reasonable offer.
The shop's accounts are "in the red". What colour should I look for?

You do not need to see any colour. "In the red" means owing more money than you have, because losses are traditionally written in red ink.
Example: The small business was in the red for two years.

Read this:

Thursday

Fire alarm today at the bank. I was at the counter with Aditi. The siren started and the manager said, 'Probably a test.' Customers kept standing in line. Aditi looked at me. I looked at the clerk opposite, who kept counting notes. For almost three minutes nobody moved. I remember thinking, if it were real, surely someone would go. Then a security guard came running from the back, shouting to get out. Everyone left at once, bumping into each other. There was smoke from a short circuit in the server room, not big, but real. Outside, Aditi said, 'We were all waiting for each other.' She was right. I was waiting for someone to tell me what I already knew. Next time, I go first.

Joseph

Where was the short circuit?
In the server room.
What was Joseph thinking during those three minutes?
Joseph felt unsure and uneasy, thinking that if it were real someone would surely go, and waiting for a cue.
What does Joseph decide for next time, and why does it make sense?
To go first, because waiting for others' cues delays everyone, and one person moving helps the rest move.
How might Aditi have seen the moment?
Aditi noticed the whole group freezing and looking at each other, which is why she said they were all waiting.

metadata.subtype: Colleagues stay put when the alarm rings [Observer]
