Read this:

Crèche note, Christmas week.

Every evening at five, Pranav, two, stands by the gate watching for his grandmother. Today, when he saw her shawl, he dropped his toy and ran, shouting "Amma! Amma!"

He hugged her knees and wouldn't let go. When I tried to hand him his bag, he turned away and pressed his face into her sari.

His grandmother said he does the same at home. — Harsha

What did Pranav shout when he saw his grandmother?
He shouted "Amma! Amma!"
What was Pranav feeling when he hugged his grandmother's knees?
Pranav felt joyful and loving, happy to see the person he most wanted.
How can the crèche support Pranav's warm bond with his grandmother?
Let him greet her fully and give his bag to her, respecting his preference for her.
How might Harsha feel when Pranav turned away from her?
Harsha probably understood and felt warm about it, seeing it as a sign of his strong bond.

Read this:

Okay, so this was last term, in our class chat. Devika sent a long message about her science project, and it had one spelling mistake. Then a row of laughing faces started. Six, seven of them. Somebody wrote "typo queen".
I'm Urmila, and I read every reply and typed nothing. My thumb hovered. I thought, if I say something they will turn on me. So I put the phone down and ate my lunch, and my rice tasted of nothing.
That evening I messaged Devika alone: "That chat was unkind. I'm sorry I stayed quiet. Your project sounds great." She wrote back, "Thank you for saying that."

How many laughing faces did the class chat show after Devika's message?
A row of laughing faces started, six or seven of them.
Why did Urmila type nothing while the laughing faces piled up?
Urmila was afraid that the others would turn on her too. The hovering thumb and the tasteless lunch show she felt uneasy and guilty about staying quiet.
What did Urmila do that evening, and what else could a bystander try in the chat itself?
Urmila messaged Devika privately to say the chat was unkind and to apologise for staying quiet. In the chat a bystander could also change the subject or ask a plain question about the project.
How might Devika have felt when the laughing faces began and later when Urmila wrote privately?
Devika probably felt embarrassed and small at first, and then a little comforted by Urmila's private message. Saying "Thank you" shows the kindness reached her.

Read this:

I'm Sumit. Thirty applications through a single job site, six weeks, zero replies. Not even a rejection. I kept telling myself the thirty-first would be the one, because stopping felt like failing. Then I looked at my hours: about ten a week, going into a channel that never answered. So I stopped. Same ten hours, moved: five to alumni messages, three to the college placement cell, two to polishing my resume. Zubin, an alumnus at a mid-sized company, replied within two days and offered to refer me for a junior role. The placement cell also passed my resume to two recruiters. It's early. But for the first time, things are replying.

How many applications had Sumit sent on the portal?
Sumit had sent thirty applications through a single job site.
What was Sumit feeling before stopping?
Sumit was stubborn and worried, since stopping felt like failing.
What could Sumit measure to know when to cut a channel?
Sumit could track replies per hour spent, and shift time when a fair trial brings none.
How might Zubin see Sumit's message?
Zubin seems willing to help, since Zubin replied within two days and offered a referral.

metadata.subtype: Approach: cutting losses on a low-yield channel [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

The school picnic bus was delayed an hour by the rain, and everyone was stuck in the hot school hall. Binita saw Usha sitting alone by the window, and her stomach twisted. Last year they'd been inseparable, matching hairbands, the same seat on every trip. This year Binita had joined the football team, and her lunch table had changed. Usha had drifted to the art club. They hadn't argued. They just talked less, then barely. When the bus finally came, Binita sat with her new teammates and felt like a traitor all the way to the lake. That evening she told her mother, "I'm a bad friend." Her mother sat with her. "You're not bad. Friendships change sometimes. It's okay to feel sad about it." Binita cried a little. The next week, she waved to Usha in the corridor. Usha waved back, smiling.

What did Binita join this year?
The football team.
What was Binita feeling on the bus to the lake?
She felt sad and guilty, like a traitor, for sitting with her new friends instead of Usha.
How did Binita's mother help her?
She gave Binita space to feel sad and explained that friendships sometimes change, so Binita didn't have to feel bad about it.
How might Usha see the friendship now?
Usha seems to accept the change too, smiling and waving back when Binita greeted her.

Retell it in the first person, as Manoj, Siddharth's papa.

Monday: At the toy library, Siddharth, five, didn't even look at the wooden train. Manoj, his papa, picked it for him.
Wednesday: The train was his now. When his cousin asked to swap it for a fire truck, Siddharth shouted, "No! My train is special!" He slept with it that night.
Saturday: Time to return it. Siddharth cried. Papa said, "Take any other toy from the shelf." He shook his head hard. "I want MY train."

Monday: At the toy library, my son Siddharth, five, didn't even look at the wooden train. I picked it for him.
Wednesday: The train was his now. When his cousin asked to swap it for a fire truck, Siddharth shouted, "No! My train is special!" He slept with it that night.
Saturday: Time to return it. Siddharth cried. I said, "Take any other toy from the shelf." He shook his head hard. "I want MY train."

Read this:

Camila's robotics team in Valencia won the regional prize, and at lunch she heard herself say, "Honestly, I did most of the coding. Hana just did the wiring." Hana stopped eating. That night Camila couldn't sleep. She asked herself: am I proud because we built something good, or because I need to be the best one? The next morning she found Hana by the lockers. "What I said was unfair. Your wiring is why it didn't short out. We both did well." Hana crossed her arms, then pointed out that Camila's code had also crashed twice. Camila flushed, then laughed. "True. Fix it together for nationals?"

Where did Camila find Hana the next morning?
By the lockers.
What was Camila feeling the night after the lunch comment?
She felt uneasy and guilty, unable to sleep while questioning her pride.
What did Camila do that shows real pride?
She apologised, credited Hana's work and accepted Hana's correction about the code without collapsing.
How did Hana feel when Camila dismissed the wiring?
Hana was hurt, stopping eating, and later stood up for herself by pointing out the crashes.

Read this:

In his third week as a trainee site engineer, Karthik stood at the base of the scaffolding with a clipboard. Sabina Ma'am, the senior engineer with fifteen years on sites, pointed up. "Check the slab level on the third floor. Skip the harness, it takes too long. We finish today." Karthik knew the safety rule by heart; they had drilled it on day one. His mouth opened, then closed. She was his senior, older than his mother, and everyone greeted her with a little bow. Saying no felt like slapping her. So he climbed without the harness. On the third level a plank shifted under his boot, and he grabbed a pole just in time. He finished the check with his hands shaking. That night he couldn't eat, replaying the moment he had said nothing.

What did Sabina Ma'am tell Karthik to skip?
She told him to skip the harness because it takes too long.
Why did Karthik climb without the harness though he knew the rule?
Saying no to a senior everyone bows to felt as rude as slapping her, so respect for rank silenced what he knew.
What could Karthik have said at the base of the scaffolding?
He could have said politely, 'Ma'am, I'll be quick, but I'll wear the harness,' and if pushed, raised it with the site safety officer that day.
How might Karthik's family feel if they knew what happened on the third level?
They'd likely be frightened by how close he came, and want him to feel free to refuse unsafe orders.

Read this:

I'm Madhuri, Vandana's cousin, and I was doing homework at her dining table when her mother pulled a folded note out of the laundry. Auntie read it, and her eyebrows shot up. She laughed once, then stopped. "Who is this Rohit?" Vandana went pink to her ears and grabbed for the note. "Don't read it!" Auntie took a breath, sat down, and spoke in a much softer voice. "It's natural to like someone, Vandana. We can talk about it. I won't tell anyone." Vandana said nothing, but her shoulders came down. I couldn't tell whether she felt safe or just embarrassed.

Where did Vandana's mother find the note?
She found it in the laundry.
What might Vandana have been feeling when her mother read the note, and what tells you?
She was probably embarrassed and exposed, since she went pink to her ears and grabbed for the note, though Madhuri cannot be sure.
What did Vandana's mother do that helped after her first reaction?
She took a breath, sat down, said it was natural to like someone and promised not to tell anyone.
How might Vandana's mother feel on finding the note?
She was probably surprised and unsure, since she laughed once and stopped before softening her voice.

Read this:

Friday, late
Himani's admission letter came today. Pune! She screamed, Maa cried, and everyone looked at me, because I was the one who sat with her maths every night for two years. I felt proud enough to burst.
Then, while I was closing the dhaba's accounts, a strange heaviness came. I'm twenty-one. I left my own diploma after first year when Papa's back went bad. I cook, I do the accounts, I fix the tap, I take Maa to her check-ups. 'Hemant bhaiya will handle it' is practically our family motto.
I'm not sorry. I love them. But tonight I let myself write it: I want something that's just mine. Maybe a weekend course. Maybe just one day off a week.
Tomorrow I'll tell Maa about the day off. Small start.

Where did Himani get admission?
Pune.
What two feelings does Hemant have on the day of the letter?
He feels proud enough to burst about Himani, and later a heavy tiredness about all he carries and a wish for something of his own.
What small choice does Hemant plan for tomorrow?
To tell Maa he wants one day off a week, a small start toward something that's just his.
How might Himani feel if she knew how much her bhaiya carries?
Himani may feel grateful and perhaps a little guilty, and might want to support him having his own time.
Dost ka music bahut tez hai. Kaise bolun ki thoda kam karo?
Say: "Could you turn the music down a little, please?"

Read this:

Week 1: Joseph and his wife had just moved into their flat in Kochi. His cousin Mohit's family started dropping in without warning, three evenings in a row, expecting dinner. Joseph's wife said nothing, but her jaw tightened each time.
Week 2: Joseph noticed he was dreading the doorbell. He talked to his wife. "I love Mohit. But we need our evenings." They agreed Joseph would say it, since it was his family.
Week 3: On the phone, Joseph said, "Mohit, we'd love to have you over. But can you call before coming? And let's fix Sunday lunches, every other week?"
Mohit was quiet, then laughed awkwardly. "Our mother always said family doesn't need to call."
"I know. But we're new at this."
The next Sunday lunch, Mohit brought payasam and called ahead. Joseph's wife smiled properly for the first time in weeks.

What did Mohit bring to the Sunday lunch?
Payasam.
How did Joseph feel by the second week?
Joseph felt dread and tension, not wanting the doorbell to ring.
Why did it help that Joseph set the boundary himself?
Since it was his family, hearing it from him felt less like rejection from an outsider, and he could offer a warm alternative.
How might Mohit have felt when Joseph asked him to call first?
Mohit probably felt a bit hurt and awkward, since his mother taught that family doesn't need to call, but he accepted.

Read this:

January. Sabina's cousins had all done MBAs, and at the family lunch her uncle said, "You'll apply this year, of course." Her college friends were planning a Goa trip she couldn't afford and didn't want. She said yes to both and felt hollow on the bus home.
February. In the library, her friend Irawati slid over a blank page. "Write five things you'd still do if nobody clapped." Sabina wrote: teaching kids to read, honesty, time with Nani, learning Urdu, staying out of debt. The MBA wasn't on it. Neither was Goa.
April. She told her uncle she was applying for a two-year teaching fellowship instead. He frowned and said she would regret it. She told her friends she'd skip the trip and meet them for chai when they got back. Her hands shook both times. That night, filling in the fellowship form, she felt steady.

What did Irawati ask Sabina to write?
Five things she'd still do if nobody clapped.
How did Sabina's feelings change from the January bus ride to April?
In January Sabina felt hollow after saying yes to everyone; by April, though her hands shook, she felt steady acting on her own values.
Why was Irawati's question a useful tool?
It separated what Sabina valued from what earned approval, making it clear the MBA and the trip weren't really hers.
How might Sabina's uncle see her choice?
Her uncle frowns and predicts regret, so he probably sees it as a risky break from the family's path, perhaps out of worry for her.

I'm Irfan, the boy who sits at the back of 10B and watches. In our science project group there were six of us. On paper. In the first meeting, Ishita and a quiet boy from the front bench made a list. Everyone nodded. Then the four others, and honestly me too at first, just disappeared into cricket and phones. By the second week I saw Ishita in the library at lunch every day, charts spread out, eating with one hand. The front-bench boy stayed late to finish the model. On submission day, the four got the same marks. Ishita didn't say anything, but she didn't sit with us after that.

Briefly, in two sentences, what is this section about?

Irfan's science group had six members, but Ishita and a quiet boy did the work while the other four, at first including Irfan, drifted off. On submission day the other four got the same marks, and Ishita stopped sitting with them.

What does Ahab do after giving the usual orders to secure the whale for the night?

Darkness came on; but three lights up and down in the Pequod's main-rigging dimly guided our way; till drawing nearer we saw Ahab dropping one of several more lanterns over the bulwarks. Vacantly eyeing the heaving whale for a moment, he issued the usual orders for securing it for the night, and then handing his lantern to a seaman, went his way into the cabin, and did not come forward again until morning.
He hands his lantern to a seaman and goes into the cabin. He does not come forward again until morning.

Read this:

At the coaching centre in Kota, Farhan's day began at six with a test and ended at ten with doubt sessions. In between came school, lectures and a hostel study hour. By the second month he sat in the counsellor's room staring at the floor. 'I'm not sad exactly,' he told Alka Ma'am. 'I just feel nothing. And angry at everyone.' Alka Ma'am looked at his timetable. 'Where's your time to breathe?' There wasn't any. Together they found two gaps: Sunday morning off, and forty minutes after dinner for football or a walk. 'Your brain files away what you learnt while you rest,' she said. Farhan doubted it. Two weeks later he admitted his mock score had gone up.

What two gaps did Farhan and Alka Ma'am find?
Sunday morning off, and forty minutes after dinner for football or a walk.
What was Farhan feeling when he said 'I just feel nothing'?
He felt numb and resentful, worn down by a timetable with no space to rest.
How did Alka Ma'am support Farhan?
She looked at his timetable with him, built in real breaks and explained that rest helps the brain file away learning.
What would change if Farhan kept the old timetable?
He would likely keep feeling numb and angry, and his learning might suffer instead of improving.

metadata.subtype: Teen packed with classes and coaching [Actor]

messages.content: The branches of my neighbour's tree are blocking the light into my window. Write a friendly request, about 55 words, asking him to trim them.

Dear Neighbour,
I hope you are well. I wanted to mention that the branches of your tree have grown across my window and are blocking much of the light. Would you be willing to trim them when you have a moment? I would be very grateful. Please let me know if I can help in any way.
Warm regards
My photography guide says to lower the exposure. What does that mean?

In photography, exposure is the amount of light that reaches the camera sensor or film. It is a noun. The general meaning is being in a place or situation where you are not protected.
Example: Too much exposure made the photo of the white wall look washed out.
I want to buy a present for my grandparents' anniversary. They have everything.
People who have everything often appreciate something personal. Is there a memory you share with them?
I love making them laugh by dancing.
Then a handwritten card with a promise of a special dance, plus a small framed photo of all of you, would delight them.
A dance would be fun. They'd record it for sure.
It can become their favourite memory. Ask them about their favourite old song and dance to it.

Read this:

"Amma! Amma! AMMA!"
"Eshaan, I'm on the phone with Paati. What's our rule?"
"Touch your arm and wait." He touched her arm. Then: "AMMA!"
Kavitha smiled into the phone. "One minute, Amma." She crouched. "Your mouth was faster than your waiting. That happens. Let's try again."
Eshaan put his hand on her arm and held his breath.
"Good waiting. Now, what is it?"
"Can I have the green crayon? I grabbed it from Didi and she's crying."
"Ah. Then first give it back, and ask her."
He ran off. "Didi, can I please have the green?"
"Okay. After I finish the tree."

Who was Kavitha on the phone with?
Paati.
How was Eshaan feeling when he kept calling "AMMA"?
He was eager and impatient, wanting help right away.
What did Kavitha do that supported Eshaan's self-control?
She used a simple rule, stayed calm without shaming and let him practise waiting again.
How might Didi feel when Eshaan asks nicely?
Didi likely feels calmer and more willing to share after being asked instead of grabbed from.
What is the winning number in today's raffle at the fair? how can I carry heavy books to school comfortably?

1. I don't know that. I can't see the draw. Ask the organisers at the fair.
2. Use a bag with two straps and wear it on both shoulders. Keep the heavier items close to your back and carry only what you need.
In three innings a batter made 44, 34 and 39 runs. What is the total?
117. Because 44 + 34 = 78, and 78 + 39 = 117, so the total is 117 runs.

Read this:

Baljeet,
You're the only one I can tell, since you're in Delhi now.
Since Monday, everyone at school is saying I copied in the prelims. That I had answers on my wrist. I didn't. I scored 92 because I spent the whole Diwali break on past papers. You KNOW I did; you were on video call with me half the time.
I don't know who started it. Could be anyone. Now when someone looks at me in the corridor my face goes hot and I want to sink into the floor. Yesterday Ritu and Sameer stopped talking when I sat down. I keep practising what I'd say if someone asked me straight out. Nobody does. They just whisper.
Uday
PS: After writing this I showed it to Appa. He read it twice, said this is not my fault, and emailed my class teacher tonight to ask for a meeting tomorrow.

What did Uday score in the prelims?
Uday scored 92.
How does Uday feel walking through the corridor now?
Uday feels hot shame and fear of every glance, wishing to sink into the floor.
Why was showing the letter to Appa a good step?
An adult could act the same day, reassuring Uday and asking the school to deal with a rumour Uday can't fight alone.
How might Baljeet feel reading this from Delhi?
Baljeet may feel angry on Uday's behalf and helpless from far away, having seen the studying on video calls.

"The nurse is a foreigner, and Adela was born on the Continent; and, I believe, never left it till within six months ago. When she first came here she could speak no English; now she can make shift to talk it a little: I don't understand her, she mixes it so with French; but you will make out her meaning very well, I dare say."

What do we learn about Adela's English?
She knew none when she arrived about six months ago. Now she speaks a little, but mixes it with French, so she is hard to understand.

Read this:

Vishal, you're forwarding that earn-from-home link to the whole office? Sit. Your Aditi Didi has a story.
In my second year of college, my hostel roommate Pooja joined one of those groups. Rate a hotel, get Rs 100. The first week she got real money and bought everyone samosas. Then came "prepaid tasks": put in 3,000, get 4,000 back. Then 20,000 to unlock what she had already earned.
I noticed because she stopped eating dinner and started borrowing from girls down the corridor. One night I asked, "Pooja, can you withdraw anything right now?" She couldn't.
That was the turning point. Instead of calling her silly, I showed her the warning on the cyber police page and sat with her while she called the helpline. Then we pinned a notice on the hostel board.
Two other girls took it down to read. Both had just joined the same kind of group.
So, before you forward that link...

What did Pooja get for rating a hotel?
She got Rs 100 for rating a hotel.
What was young Aditi worried about when Pooja stopped eating dinner?
Aditi worried Pooja was in money trouble, especially as Pooja began borrowing from girls down the corridor.
Which choice inside the story was the turning point?
Asking whether Pooja could withdraw anything right now, then showing the cyber police warning instead of calling her silly, helped Pooja see the trap and report it.
How might Pooja have felt when she couldn't withdraw anything?
She likely felt shocked and scared, realising the earnings on her screen had never really been hers.

Pooja's mother, Neelam, wants this as her own diary entry. First person, past tense, please.

On the first cold morning of winter in their Lucknow flat, Pooja, six, did her routine without being told. Shoes. Sweater. Bag. Water bottle.
Her mother Neelam watched from the kitchen, holding her breath.
Pooja stopped at the door, looked at her hands, and said, "Tiffin!" She ran back for it.
"All by myself," she announced.
Neelam clapped. "All by yourself!"

On the first cold morning of winter in our Lucknow flat, Pooja, six, did her routine without being told. Shoes. Sweater. Bag. Water bottle. I watched from the kitchen, holding my breath. Pooja stopped at the door, looked at her hands, and said, "Tiffin!" She ran back for it. "All by myself," she announced. I clapped. "All by yourself!"

"And you," I interrupted, "cannot at all imagine the craving I have for fraternal and sisterly love. I never had a home, I never had brothers or sisters; I must and will have them now: you are not reluctant to admit me and own me, are you?"

Question: What does the speaker say about brothers and sisters?
The speaker has never had a home or brothers or sisters, craves that love, and says they must and will have it now. They ask whether the listener is reluctant to accept them.

Read this:

"Listen, Farida. 'The moon is a silver coin someone dropped in the sky.'"
"Nice! But why dropped?"
"Because it looks lonely up there." Anjali chewed her pencil.
"Is this about the moon or about you?"
Anjali shrugged. "Since Papa's transfer, our new flat is as quiet as a library at night. I didn't know how to say it, so I said the moon."
Farida read the line again, slowly. "Then add a line. Something that finds the coin."
"Like what?"
"A star that picks it up?"
Anjali grinned and wrote: 'A small star rolls over, as warm as a hand.'
"Ma'am will love it," said Farida.
"I don't mind about Ma'am. You got it. That's enough."

What did Anjali compare the moon to?
A silver coin someone dropped in the sky.
What does Anjali's line about the moon suggest she was feeling?
Anjali was probably feeling lonely since the move to a quiet new flat; the lonely moon gave words to a feeling that was hard to say directly.
How did Farida help Anjali's poem grow?
By asking what it was really about, listening, and suggesting a line that finds the coin, so Anjali could write some comfort into the poem 🙂
What is it like for Farida when Anjali explains the poem?
Farida gets to understand a friend's loneliness through the picture, and seems glad to help by offering the star.

Read this:

Monday, the first monsoon rain: Sharmila scolded Rajni for splashing the balcony bucket. Rajni scowled, then threw her rubber duck at little Pinky's head.

Wednesday, still raining: told off for tearing a book, Rajni grabbed Pinky's bottle and hurled it. Sharmila held Rajni's hands. "You're angry with me. Hit the pillow."

Saturday, rain drumming on the window: another "no". Rajni's fists clenched. She looked at Pinky, then thumped the pillow, hard.

What did Rajni throw at Pinky on Monday?
Rajni threw her rubber duck at little Pinky's head.
What does Rajni's scowl before throwing the duck suggest?
Rajni was angry at being scolded by Sharmila, and that anger went to Pinky, the smaller and safer target.
Which change helped by Saturday, and why?
Sharmila named Rajni's anger and offered the pillow, so by Saturday the anger had a safe place to go instead of Pinky.
How might Pinky be affected over these days?
Pinky gets hit by a duck and a bottle for no reason Pinky can understand, which may leave Pinky startled and wary of Rajni.

metadata.subtype: Hitting a sibling after being scolded [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

The third time that week was in the hostel dining hall. Raghav, new in Vidya's house, passed her the dal and asked, "So where are you actually from? Like, really?" "Here. This city. I was born two streets from the school." "No, but originally?" Vidya smiled the smile she had practised. That morning a substitute teacher had told her, "Your English is so good," as if it were a surprise. On Monday the librarian had asked whether she'd "come on the scholarship". Taken one at a time, none of it was anything. Raghav wasn't being unkind; he looked honestly curious. But Vidya ate the rest of her dinner in silence, feeling like a visitor in the only place she had ever lived.

Where was Vidya born?
Two streets from the school, in this city.
What was Vidya feeling as she ate the rest of her dinner in silence?
She felt out of place and alone, like a visitor in the only place she had ever lived, because Raghav's question was the third remark like it that week.
What could Vidya choose to say the next time someone asks "originally?"
She could calmly repeat that she is from here, or ask what makes them wonder, so she isn't swallowing it every time.
How might Raghav see his question, compared with how it landed for Vidya?
Raghav likely thought he was being friendly and curious, without knowing it was the third remark like that for her in one week.
Boss se bolna hai "Traffic ki wajah se main late ho gaya." English?
Say: "I am late because of the traffic."
Aur "Main kuch minute mein pahunchta hoon" kaise kahun?
Say: "I will be there in a few minutes."

Read this:

I'm Usha, and I was at the reception desk when Mariana, the new consultant from São Paulo, arrived at our Pune office. She walked straight up to Sarika, our team lead, put a hand on her arm and leaned in to kiss her cheek. Sarika went stiff and stepped back half a pace, hands coming together in a namaste almost by reflex. For a second both of them looked embarrassed. Mariana's smile faltered; I think she read the step back as coldness. I couldn't tell what Sarika was feeling, surprise or discomfort or both. Then Sarika laughed a little and said, "Sorry, I wasn't expecting that! Here we usually do namaste or a handshake. What do you do at home?" Mariana relaxed. "Kisses, always. But a handshake is good!" They shook hands. By the end of the week Mariana was greeting everyone with a namaste, slightly wrong, and nobody minded.

Where is Mariana from?
São Paulo.
What might Mariana have felt when Sarika stepped back?
Mariana probably felt embarrassed and a little rejected, reading the step back as coldness when she had meant warmth.
How did Sarika repair the awkward moment?
She laughed lightly, explained the local greetings and asked what Mariana does at home, then they shook hands, finding a middle way.
How did Usha read Sarika's reaction?
Usha couldn't tell whether Sarika felt surprise, discomfort or both, only that both women looked embarrassed for a moment.
The manager needs to "weigh up" both offers. Will she use scales?

No. "Weigh up" means to think carefully about the good and bad points of something before deciding.
Example: Weigh up the cost and the benefits before you choose.

Read this:

I'm Siddharth. When I joined the under-twelve football team, Coach Naveen asked if I understood the offside rule. I said, “Yes, Coach,” because everyone else was nodding and I didn't want to look stupid. In the first match I got caught offside four times. The other team's players laughed. After the game I finally told Coach, “I didn't really understand it. I just said I did.” I thought he'd be angry. Instead he said, “That's braver than scoring.” He showed me with bottle caps on the bench until I got it. Now when I'm not sure, I say so first. It saves a lot of running.

How many times was Siddharth caught offside in the first match?
Siddharth was caught offside four times.
What was Siddharth feeling when saying “Yes, Coach” at the start?
Siddharth felt worried about looking stupid while everyone else nodded, so pretended to understand.
What did Coach Naveen do that made admitting the gap feel safe?
He praised the admission as braver than scoring and patiently explained the rule with bottle caps.
How did the other team's players react to the offside calls?
They laughed at Siddharth for being caught offside again and again.

Read this:

Friday
Asif and I have been best friends since we were six. We walked to school together, shared tiffins, planned to open a cycle shop one day.
Since Class 10 started, he hangs out with the football boys. He still says hi. But it's like I'm furniture now. He laughs at their jokes, and when I say something he just nods and turns back.
Today at lunch I sat down and nobody moved over. I ate on the steps.
I felt hurt. I also realised friendships change, and Asif isn't a bad person for finding new people.
So after school, I told him, just once: "Hey, I miss you. It feels like I don't matter much now." He looked surprised and said, "Sorry, bhai. It's not like that." Maybe. Maybe not.
Either way, I'm going to join the robotics club Monday. Faizan asked me last week. I want friends who save me a seat too.
Wasim

Where did Wasim eat lunch today?
On the steps.
How does Wasim feel about Asif's change?
Wasim feels hurt and ignored, like furniture, but also understands that friendships can shift.
What did Wasim do wisely?
He told Asif once, honestly, how he felt, and then chose to invest in new friendships through the robotics club.
How might Asif see Wasim's comment?
Asif seems surprised and a little guilty, as if he hadn't noticed how left out Wasim felt.

Read this:

"Lalit, stay in the shallow end," said Francis, the swimming coach. Lalit, five, bobbed in the water, his goggles pushed up.
"If I stay, do I get a lollipop?"
"We'll see. Why should you stay there?"
"Because you'll be cross."
"And?"
"And no lollipop."
"What about the deep water?"
Lalit thought hard. "It's too deep?"
"Right. It keeps you safe."
"Okay. But I still get a lollipop?"
Francis laughed. "Stay there all lesson and we'll see."

Where did Francis tell Lalit to stay?
In the shallow end.
What does Lalit's question about the lollipop suggest about why he follows the rule?
He mainly wants the reward and is worried about Francis being cross, rather than thinking about safety.
What did Francis do to help Lalit think beyond rewards?
Francis asked why the rule mattered, so Lalit could start linking it to safety.
How might Francis see Lalit's answers?
Francis likely finds them funny and normal for a five-year-old, and uses them to teach a little more.

Read this:

Bidisha, I will tell you what my grandmother's hands taught me. Elder here, Lakshmi. When my own daughter was small and feverish, I stroked her back in slow circles and watched her face. If her breath softened and her shoulders dropped, I kept going. Once she flinched and pulled forward, so I stopped and asked her what she wanted, and she wanted a cool cloth instead. With my old aunt in the hospital, I held her hand and she squeezed back. Care is not what the giver intends; it is what the other person can take in. So watch the breath, watch the body. If they pull away, that is an answer.

What did Lakshmi hold in the hospital?
Lakshmi held the old aunt's hand.
What did the flinch by Lakshmi's daughter suggest, and how did Lakshmi respond?
It suggested the back stroking was not comforting at that moment, so Lakshmi stopped and asked. The flinch could also be discomfort from the fever, but asking found what she wanted.
What can a caregiver look for to know whether touch is helping?
A caregiver can watch for a softening breath and dropped shoulders, and stop if the person pulls away or flinches.
How might Lakshmi's daughter have felt when Lakshmi stopped and asked?
She probably felt listened to and in control, since her wish for a cool cloth was followed.
I wrote my plan in my dairy last night. What is wrong with the word?

I wrote my plan in my diary last night.
Why: "diary" is a daily notebook; "dairy" is milk products.

Read this:

Note from Aparna, nursery teacher. After his father left, Akash, two, sat on the mat, quiet, shoulders drooped, thumb near his mouth. He did not cry. At first I thought he was tired, but he had napped well. I sat next to him and said, "You miss Papa. You feel sad." He leaned into me and gave a small whimper. He later took a picture book and looked at it slowly.

What did Akash do after his father left?
He sat quietly on the mat with drooped shoulders and his thumb near his mouth.
What does Akash's quietness suggest about how he felt, and what else could explain it?
It suggests sadness at his father leaving, since he leaned in when Aparna named it. It could also have been some tiredness.
What could Aparna do at the next drop-off?
She can sit near him, name the feeling briefly, and offer a favourite book or quiet activity.
How might Akash's father feel to know about this?
He may feel a pang, but reassured that Akash was comforted and could show his sadness.

Read this:

In the school counsellor's room, Pradeep sat with his hands in his lap. "Everyone says I'll never be like my cousin Devika. She's in IIT. I'm just the average one."
The counsellor asked, "Who says that?"
"My father. My uncle. At every wedding."
"And what do you say?"
Pradeep shrugged. "I stopped trying for the science olympiad. What's the point?"
The counsellor was quiet, then asked, "What do you enjoy?"
"Designing posters for school events."
"Your posters are all over the corridor. People stop to read them." She paused. "I'll ask your father to come in next week."
Pradeep looked up, surprised.

Which exam did Devika clear?
She's in IIT.
What is Pradeep feeling as he sits with his hands in his lap?
He feels small and discouraged, having taken on the family's verdict that he is just average.
What steps did the counsellor take, and why might they help?
She asked what he enjoys, named his real strength and planned to talk with his father, which can change the message he hears at home.
How might Devika feel if she knew about the comparisons?
Devika might feel uncomfortable or sad, not wanting to be used to make her cousin feel small.

metadata.subtype: Family verdict about who they will become [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

It was harvest season, and half the village school had been helping in the fields. When the test papers came back, Noor and Nilesh had both failed the sums. Nilesh crumpled his paper and threw it in the ditch on the way home. "My head's made of mud. Baba says so too." Noor, walking beside him with her sister, looked at her own red marks. "We missed the whole week of division. We were cutting paddy." "So?" "So we just don't know division yet. We're not mud." Her sister said, "Master stays after school on Thursdays." On Thursday, Noor stayed. Nilesh walked past the classroom window, slowed down, then kept going.

What did Nilesh do with his paper?
He crumpled it and threw it in the ditch on the way home.
How was Nilesh feeling when he said his head was made of mud?
He felt hopeless and ashamed, believing he was permanently bad at sums.
What could help Nilesh try again, as Noor did?
He could see the failure as missing a week of division, not a mud head, and stay back for Master's Thursday help.
How does Noor's sister react to the failed sums?
She stays practical and encouraging, telling them about Master's Thursday help after school.

Read this:

Tushar, beta, you remind me of myself. At nine I loved my goat Moti so fiercely I slept in the shed. When the boys at school teased me about it, I cried so loudly the headmaster came out. I'd rage for hours, bang the door, refuse dinner. My father said, "Stop this drama." That only made it worse. But my mother would sit on the step and say, "Your heart is big, Akash. Big hearts feel big storms." She taught me to walk to the neem tree and count its branches until the storm got smaller. I, Akash, still feel everything strongly. But now I call it passion. It's why I became a vet.

What was the goat's name?
Moti.
How did young Akash feel when the boys teased Akash about Moti?
Akash felt crushed and furious, crying loudly and raging for hours.
What was the turning point in the story?
The mother naming Akash's big heart and teaching a way to count the neem tree's branches until the storm passed.
How did the father's "Stop this drama" affect young Akash?
It made the upset worse, because the feelings were dismissed instead of understood.

In the Chennai school canteen, every table had its group. Ayesha, new from Srinagar, stood with her tray.
The girls at the nearest table were chatting fast in Tamil. They glanced up, then back at each other. Ayesha didn't know one word. She walked to the end of the long table and sat alone.
For two weeks she noticed everything: who sat where, who laughed at whose jokes. Nobody noticed her. In class, when groups formed, she waited to be picked, and was picked last.
Then, on a Wednesday, Seema from her class waved from a crowded table. “Ayesha! Come, sit. I'll teach you one Tamil word a day. Today's is ‘saapadu’, food.”
Ayesha laughed for the first time in two weeks.

What word did Seema teach Ayesha?
She taught her "saapadu", food.
How did Ayesha feel during her first two weeks?
She felt lonely and invisible, watching everything but not being noticed, and picked last.
What made Seema's gesture so effective?
It was warm and specific: a seat and a Tamil word a day, which gave Ayesha a way in.
How might the girls at the nearest table have seen Ayesha?
They probably didn't think much about her, just continuing their own chat without meaning to shut her out.

metadata.subtype: Left out for being from elsewhere [Receiver]

messages.content: Where am I going on holiday this year?
I don't know your plans, as you haven't told me. Check with whoever is booking the trip.

Read this:

The breakup with Aparna happened on Sunday at the village tank, in four sentences. By Wednesday Kiran felt empty, as if someone had scooped out his chest.
He replayed it all day: her face, the way she said "I'm sorry," what he should have said instead. At night he lay on the charpai on the roof, phone in hand, typing messages to her and deleting them. He watched videos until two in the morning just to stop thinking.
On Thursday his friend Bhola found him skipping lunch behind the school pump. "You look like a ghost," Bhola said. He dragged Kiran home to eat his mother's kadhi.
That night, Kiran put his phone downstairs before bed. He made himself eat breakfast. On Saturday, he went to cricket with Bhola's brothers even though he didn't feel like it.
It still hurt. But he wasn't going to message her. He was just going to let it hurt, and wait.

Where did Kiran and Aparna break up?
At the village tank.
How did Kiran feel in the days after the breakup?
He felt hollow and empty, replaying the breakup constantly and struggling to stop thinking about it.
Which choices helped Kiran cope?
Eating with Bhola's family, putting his phone downstairs at night, keeping breakfast and cricket, and not messaging Aparna.
How does Bhola see Kiran after the breakup?
Bhola is worried, seeing Kiran looking like a ghost, and takes him home to eat so he is not alone.

Read this:

Thursday, late
New intern Alka started at the lab this week and I nearly broke her. On day one I walked her through the whole sample-tracking system, the safety sheets, the ordering process and the freezer map. Forty minutes, non-stop. She nodded and took notes. Today she labelled a whole rack with last year's codes and then apologised about eight times.
Not her fault. I remember my own first week; I cried in the washroom.
So this afternoon I slowed right down. Just labelling. I did two racks with her watching, gave her a checklist with a photo of a correct label, and let her do the third alone while I stayed nearby. Perfect.
Tomorrow: the freezer map, nothing else.
Bhupen

What did Alka label with last year's codes?
Alka labelled a whole rack with last year's codes.
Why did Alka apologise about eight times?
She probably felt embarrassed and worried about making a bad impression, not realising the mistake came from being given too much at once.
What did Bhupen's afternoon approach include?
Just one task, a demonstration on two racks, a checklist with a photo of a correct label, and a chance to practise alone with Bhupen nearby.
Why might Bhupen understand Alka so well?
Bhupen remembers crying in the washroom in a first week, so Alka's overwhelm feels familiar rather than annoying.

During lunch break at his school in Aliganj, Yusuf, ten, slid Abhinav's English worksheet under his own and copied the answers fast, pencil squeaking. His stomach gave a small twist.
That evening his cousin Rehana flipped through his bag and frowned. "These are exactly Abhinav's words."
"So?" Yusuf said, too quickly. "Everyone copies. Half the class copied from Abhinav. And Ma'am gives us four worksheets a day, it's crazy."
Rehana raised an eyebrow. Yusuf kept going. "I'm not a cheater. I'm top three in maths. I just didn't have time, that's all."
The more he explained, the better he felt. By dinner he had nearly convinced himself it was the only sensible thing to do. Still, when he packed his bag for school, he tucked the worksheet deep under his books.

Where did Yusuf copy Abhinav's worksheet?
During lunch break at his school in Aliganj, sliding it under his own.
Why did Yusuf feel better the more he explained?
Yusuf felt guilty after copying, and each reason he gave protected his picture of himself as a good student, so the guilt eased the more he explained.
What moment could have been a turning point for Yusuf?
When Rehana raised an eyebrow, Yusuf could have admitted copying and asked Ma'am for more time; instead he kept adding reasons.
How might Rehana see Yusuf's list of reasons?
Rehana probably notices that the reasons pile up only after being caught and come out too quickly, so they sound like a defence rather than the real story.

What does "lesson" mean?
What should I do if I am caught in a thunderstorm outside?

1. A lesson is a period of time in which a teacher teaches something.
2. Go inside a building or a car right away. Stay away from tall trees and open fields.

Read this:

Day one: Sunaina joined St. Anne's in Class 11. By lunch she understood the map: the science toppers by the lab, the dance girls by the stage, the hostellers at the far table. Nobody said the rules. Everyone knew them.
Two weeks later: Vishal, from the hosteller table, needed a partner for chemistry. She agreed. The dance girls stopped saving her seat. One of them said, too sweetly, "Oh, you're with them now?" Sunaina felt her face burn and said nothing.
A month in: She sat with Vishal's group on Mondays and with the dance girls on Thursdays, and when someone commented, she shrugged. "I eat where my friends are." Some of them still didn't like it. She decided she could live with that.

Where did the hostellers sit?
At the far table.
How did Sunaina feel when the dance girl said "Oh, you're with them now?"
She felt embarrassed and stung; her face burned and she said nothing.
What would you advise Sunaina if the comments kept coming?
Keep calmly eating with the friends she chooses and, if it turns into bullying, talk to a teacher or counsellor.
How might Vishal see Sunaina sitting with his group?
Vishal may feel pleased and a little surprised that someone from outside the hostel crowd chose to sit with them.

Akash's manager at the Bengaluru office said, "Is this the best you can do?" and something in Akash went cold. For three days he couldn't shake it. The words were his father's, from the day he failed his board exam. He had never talked about that day. On the third night, his wife Preeti found him sitting in the dark kitchen. Instead of saying "I'm fine", he said, "Can I tell you something from when I was sixteen?" He told her. His voice broke twice. She held his hand. The next week, because the heaviness kept coming back, he booked a session with a counsellor through his office's support line. "I'm tired of carrying it alone," he told Preeti.

What did the manager say?
"Is this the best you can do?"
Why did the manager's words make Akash go cold?
They were his father's words from the day he failed his board exam, and the old hurt and shame surfaced.
What did Akash do differently this time?
Instead of saying "I'm fine", he told Preeti the story, let himself feel it, and booked a counsellor because the heaviness kept returning.
What is it like for Preeti when Akash opens up?
She is probably moved and relieved to be let in, holding his hand as his voice breaks.

Read this:

Saturday. Tejas here. My drawer got stuck today and my maths set was inside. I pulled. Then I pulled harder. Then I put my foot on the wall and pulled with both hands. It went bang but it did not open. My fingers hurt a lot.
Mummy stood at the door with my bag and said we would be late for tuition. I pulled ten more times, maybe. Same thing. Nothing changed at all.
Now I am borrowing my sister's maths set, and it has a bent compass. I am still cross with the drawer. Tomorrow I will pull even harder.

How did Tejas try to open the stuck drawer?
Tejas pulled, then pulled harder, then put a foot on the wall and pulled with both hands.
What was Tejas feeling at the end of the diary entry?
Tejas felt cross with the drawer and still wanted to open it by pulling even harder.
What different thing could Tejas try, and why?
Tejas could lift the drawer a little or look inside to see what is stuck, since more pulling has not changed anything.
How might Mummy see the drawer struggle?
Mummy was waiting at the door with the bag, so may feel worried about being late and see the pulling as using up time.

A youngster is a young person, especially a child or teenager. It is a noun.

I'm Harish, and I was the child everybody praised. When relatives came for the weekend, Nana held up my drawing book and Mausi said, “Harish is the clever one.” My brother Pankaj went out to the terrace and threw a ball against the wall by himself. I felt proud for about a minute, then a knot in my stomach. I took him a glass of water and offered to share my sweets. “Don't bother,” he said. That night I lay awake thinking that if I stopped being clever, I would lose my place, and wondering whether Pankaj noticed how tightly I held on.

Where did Pankaj go while the relatives praised Harish?
Pankaj went out to the terrace and threw a ball against the wall by himself.
Why did Harish feel a knot in the stomach after feeling proud?
Harish seems to feel guilty about Pankaj's hurt and afraid that being less clever would cost the place. The sleepless night suggests pressure to keep earning it.
What could Harish try the next time relatives praise only one child?
Harish could steer the talk to something Pankaj is good at, or spend time with Pankaj afterwards and say the comparison feels unfair.
What might Pankaj be feeling on the terrace?
Pankaj may feel left out or hurt, which fits going off alone and saying “Don't bother” to Harish's kind offer.

Wed night, 11:40
Dear diary, today's score: chemistry 0, game 3 hours. 😅
The unit test that decides my term grade is two months away. Two months! My brain treats it like a rumour.
At 8 I opened the textbook. At 8:05 Shreya knocked: "New season's out, want to see my squad?" I said ten minutes.
Those ten minutes had music and fireworks and a rank-up. The chemistry chapter had moles.
Now it's late and I feel a bit sick, like I've borrowed time from some future Nazia who will have to pay it back.
Tomorrow: textbook first, one match after. Writing it here so I can't pretend I didn't.
Nazia

What time did Nazia open the textbook?
At 8, and at 8:05 Shreya knocked.
How can you tell that Nazia feels uneasy about the evening?
Nazia writes about feeling a bit sick and about borrowing time from a future Nazia who will have to pay it back.
What is Nazia's plan for tomorrow, and why might it work better?
Textbook first and one match after turns the game into a reward for studying, instead of something that eats the study time.
How might Shreya feel if Nazia answers the knock tomorrow with 'textbook first'?
Shreya might be a little let down at not showing the new squad straight away, but they could still enjoy one match together once Nazia's study time is done.

In the school hall in Toronto, the music swelled and Yael took her place for the group dance. Halfway through, her feet went left when everyone else went right. For one heartbeat the hall seemed to hold its breath. Yael smiled, listened for the drum, and slipped into the next move with the others as if it had been planned. Bilal, next to her, grinned. By the final pose, she was in step. Afterwards a parent told the teacher how beautiful it was, and Yael's mistake was never mentioned. Yael felt her face go warm, but it was from happiness now.

Where did the dance take place?
The dance took place in the school hall in Toronto.
What did Yael feel after the dance?
Yael felt relieved and happy, shown by the warm face and the fact that the slip went unnoticed. 😊
What alternative approach could Yael use if she loses her place again, and why?
Yael could watch a friend such as Bilal and follow the next move. Following a neighbour gets back into the flow quickly.
How might Bilal see Yael's slip?
Bilal grinned next to Yael, so Bilal probably saw a dancer recover gracefully and felt proud, not embarrassed on Yael's behalf.

Read this:

The clinic's waiting room was packed, the token number hadn't moved in an hour, and Nilesh's wrist throbbed in its sling. Beside him, his father, Chetan, let out a long, heavy sigh. Nilesh shrank. He's annoyed with me. I shouldn't have jumped off the wall. Another sigh, longer. Nilesh couldn't bear it. “Papa, are you angry I got hurt?” Chetan turned, surprised. “Angry? No. I was sighing because the doctor's message just came: the X-ray shows only a sprain, not a break.” He held up his phone. “That was a relief sigh. Two of them.” Nilesh let out his own breath. “I thought it was me.”

What did the X-ray show?
The X-ray showed only a sprain, not a break.
What was Nilesh feeling when his father sighed?
Nilesh felt guilty and worried, sure his father was annoyed with him for jumping off the wall.
What did asking achieve?
It showed the sighs were relief about the X-ray, so Nilesh stopped blaming himself.
What was the wait like for Chetan?
Chetan was worried about the wrist and tired of waiting, and then relieved when the X-ray message came.

At the bus stand in the small Kerala town, a bus blared its horn right beside them. Jomon screamed, arched his back and twisted away in Avni chechi's arms.
“Stop that noise!” snapped Ammachi.
Avni didn't scold. She held him close, walked to the far wall, and spoke low. “Loud horn. You're safe.” His screaming slowed.
Next time they waited, Avni stood away from the buses, and put her hands over his ears when one came in.

Where did Avni walk with Jomon after the horn?
She walked to the far wall.
What was Jomon feeling when he screamed and arched away?
He was frightened and overwhelmed by the sudden loud horn.
What did Avni do that helped, and what did she change next time?
She stayed calm, held him close and moved away from the noise; next time she noticed the trigger and stood away from the buses and covered his ears.
How did Ammachi react to Jomon's screaming?
She was irritated and snapped at him to stop the noise.

The block-level quiz final was held in the panchayat hall in Tirur, and Ayesha's team lost on the last question because she pressed the buzzer too early and said Kolkata instead of Chennai. The whole hall groaned. She kept her face still until she got home, then locked herself in the bathroom. For a week she didn't go near the school library, where the quiz team met. When the notice for the district quiz went up, her brother Jeevan brought it home. 'Your team's asking for you.' 'They're better off without me. I'm the one who lost it.' 'You also got them to the final.' Ayesha shook her head. It didn't feel like that. It felt as if the whole hall had seen who she really was: someone who panics and ruins things.

What did Ayesha say instead of Chennai?
She said Kolkata instead of Chennai.
Why does Ayesha avoid the quiz team for a week?
She feels deeply ashamed, as if one wrong answer showed the whole hall who she really is, so facing the team feels unbearable.
What could help Ayesha return to the quiz?
Remembering she got the team to the final, and talking with her teammates, who are asking for her, could show that one mistake isn't her worth.
How do Ayesha's teammates seem to see her?
They still want her for the district quiz, which suggests they value her far more than she believes.

Swimming coach's note, university team, February.
Simran asked this month to move from the intermediate lane to the advanced one. She knew she would be the slowest there. In her first week she missed the interval times on almost every set and once had to hold the wall to catch her breath. She looked frustrated, and a teammate, Reena, asked if she wanted to go back. Simran said, "No. In the old lane I was comfortable. Here I'm learning." By week three she was making half the intervals. I have kept her in the advanced lane and adjusted two sets so she can finish them with good form.

Which lane did Simran move to?
Simran moved to the advanced lane.
What was Simran feeling in her first week in the advanced lane?
She felt frustrated and exhausted, missing intervals, but still chose the difficulty because she knew it meant learning.
What did the coach do to support Simran's choice?
The coach kept her in the advanced lane and adjusted two sets so she could finish with good form.
How might Reena see Simran's decision to stay?
Reena, who offered her a way back, might be surprised and come to admire her willingness to struggle.

Her father is a doctor and she wants to become one too. Why: "She" is third person singular, so the verb "want" takes -s.

Class note, Friday, from Lakshmi

Two tongues today, two different meanings. At colouring time Swati's brother took the red crayon. Swati stuck her tongue out at him and said, "You're a baby." He looked hurt. I sat with Swati and asked what she felt. "Cross!" I showed her how to say, "I'm cross, give it back after." She said it, and he did.

Later, in the mirror game, the whole table stuck out their tongues and laughed. Swati laughed loudest. 😊

What did Swati's brother take at colouring time?
The red crayon.
What was Swati feeling when she stuck her tongue out at her brother?
She was most likely cross that he took the red crayon, and the tongue plus "You're a baby" were meant to tease him. Later in the mirror game the same gesture came from fun, not anger.
What kind alternative did Lakshmi teach Swati?
To say how she felt and what she wanted: "I'm cross, give it back after."
How does Swati's brother feel when she sticks her tongue out at him?
He looks hurt, because the tongue and the words are aimed at him as an insult, not as part of a game.

It was past bedtime, and Farhan, two, sat cross-legged on the bed rocking back and forth, one hand on his blanket, eyes half closed. He had cried when the lights went off, and now his rocking slowed to a gentle sway. Ganga sat in the chair by the door and watched. She did not stop him. She hummed the tune he liked and kept her voice low. After a little while the swaying stopped, his head tipped sideways onto the pillow and his breath deepened.

What was Farhan doing on the bed?
Rocking back and forth cross-legged with one hand on his blanket.
What do you think Farhan's rocking helped him feel?
It seemed to help him settle after the upset of the lights going off, as his rocking slowed into sleep. It could also just be a habit that comforts him.
What could Ganga do if the rocking ever seemed to worry her?
She could mention it to the doctor, especially if it goes on a lot or Farhan seems cut off from her.
How might Farhan feel with Ganga nearby?
He may feel safe because someone he loves is close and humming.

My name is Yusuf. In February I decided to be strict with my first salary: no eating out, no small treats, nothing that wasn't a bill. For three weeks it worked perfectly. Then on the last Saturday I walked past a shop, saw a pair of headphones, and bought them without thinking, for far more than a treat should cost. I felt bad within an hour. Trisha listened to me over the phone and said, "You weren't weak, you were starved." She was right. So in March I added a line to the plan: a fun allowance of eight hundred a month, spent on anything I like. I was surprised how much easier the rest of the plan became.

What did Yusuf buy on the last Saturday of the strict month?
Yusuf bought a pair of headphones for far more than a treat should cost.
How did Yusuf feel after buying the headphones?
Yusuf felt guilty within an hour, though Trisha said it came from being starved of treats and not from weakness.
What could Yusuf do if the fun allowance is spent in the first week, and why?
Yusuf could divide it into weekly parts, since smaller portions make the treat last through the month.
How might Trisha see the strict plan Yusuf started with?
Trisha thought it was too strict, and probably worried that cutting out all fun would lead to a binge.

messages.content: What is the usual time for Raga Bhairav?
Raga Bhairav is usually associated with Morning.
My friend wrote "changable weather". Is that correct?

The usual spelling is "changeable", keeping the e after "chang" so the g stays soft.

The sign said "Keep out". Can I read that as an invitation?

No. "Keep out" is a warning telling people not to enter a place.
Examples: The sign on the gate said "Keep out". Please keep out of my room.

Tuition centre note, Friday
Before class, one boy told a joke about Pooja's community, and several children laughed, Akash loudest. Pooja went quiet and stared at her book. I told the group firmly that jokes about anyone's religion or caste are not welcome here.
During the lesson Akash kept his head down and didn't finish his sums. Afterwards he waited till the others had gone. "I laughed," he said. "I don't even know why. Now I feel horrible."
I said that horrible feeling was his conscience working, and asked what he could do about it. He went straight to Pooja at the gate and said, "Sorry I laughed. It wasn't funny." She nodded. I also phoned the joking boy's parents that evening.

Who laughed loudest at the joke?
Akash.
What was Akash feeling during the lesson?
Guilty and horrible about laughing; he kept his head down and did not finish his sums.
What did Akash do to make amends?
He admitted it to the tuition teacher and apologised to Pooja at the gate.
How might Pooja have felt when the group laughed?
Hurt and alone; she went quiet and stared at her book.

I'm Nilesh, and I sit next to Ojas's highchair at family dinners. At first, Ojas, fifteen months, grabbed rice with his whole fist and most of it fell. Tonight I watched him pick up single peas between his thumb and one finger, slowly, tongue poking out. He dropped one, frowned, and picked it up again. Then he tried his spoon. It tipped halfway. He banged it on the tray and tried once more.

How did Ojas pick up the peas tonight?
He picked them up between his thumb and one finger.
What might Ojas's frown after dropping a pea suggest?
It might suggest he was a little frustrated, though he kept trying.
How could the family support Ojas's small hand skills?
They could keep giving him small, safe finger foods and let him try the spoon without rushing to help.
How does Nilesh see Ojas's progress?
Nilesh notices the change from grabbing with a whole fist to picking single peas carefully.

I'm Kunal, and last month I watched two colleagues face the same launch in very different ways. Three days before our app went live, the load tests were failing. Imran kept smiling. "Everything will be fine, yaar. Good vibes only." He skipped the risk meeting to order a cake.
Joyeeta was hopeful too; she kept saying we could make it. But she stayed back, listed the three likeliest failures and set up a simple waiting page in case traffic spiked.
Launch day, traffic spiked. The site slowed to a crawl, and Joyeeta's waiting page kept customers from seeing errors. Imran looked stunned.
What I took from watching them: hope isn't the problem. Hope with no plan is.

What did Joyeeta set up in case traffic spiked?
A simple waiting page.
How did Kunal feel watching the two colleagues before launch?
Kunal seems uneasy about Imran's breezy cheer and reassured by Joyeeta's careful hope, since only one of them was getting ready.
What could Imran learn from Joyeeta?
He can stay hopeful while also attending the risk meeting and planning for what might go wrong.
How might Joyeeta see Imran's "good vibes only"?
She might find it frustrating, since his cheer skipped the work that actually protected customers.

Society newsletter jotting, December. Gautam, secretary.
At the D'Costa family's Christmas open house, I noticed Simran from B-wing, twenty-four, arrive with a tray of pinnis she had made herself. She stood quietly during the grace before dinner, head slightly bowed, then helped Mrs. D'Costa hand out cake to the children. When little Joel asked if she believed in Santa, she laughed and said she believed in cake. In January the D'Costas turned up at Simran's family's Gurpurab langar with a basket of oranges. Next year I plan to put both dates on the society calendar, so everyone knows whose door is open when.

What did Simran bring to the Christmas open house?
A tray of pinnis she had made herself.
What does Simran's joke about believing in cake suggest about how she felt?
It suggests she felt relaxed and happy there, comfortable sharing the joy without needing to share the beliefs.
What is Gautam's plan, and why could it help the society?
Putting both families' festival dates on the society calendar, so neighbours know they are welcome and more visits across faiths happen.
How might the D'Costa family have felt about Simran's visit?
They likely felt respected and warmly connected, which is why they came to her family's Gurpurab langar in return.

Read this:

"So? How was she?" Suraj didn't even let Naveen get through the door.
"Keerthi? Nice. Really nice, actually."
"Nice-nice, or Amma's-friend's-daughter nice?"
"Nice-nice. She laughed at my bad joke about the traffic. And she's reading the same book I am."
"So it's fixed! I'll tell Amma."
"Don't you dare. She's doing her PhD in Bengaluru for three more years. My job is here in Chennai. And she said, straight out, that she won't move for someone she's known for a month."
"Fair."
"Very fair. That's what I liked. She asked what I want in five years. Nobody's asked me that."
"And what do you want?"
Naveen dropped onto the sofa. "I think... I want to see her again. And I also want to not get ahead of myself."
"Both?"
"Both."

How long will Keerthi be doing her PhD in Bengaluru?
Keerthi is doing her PhD in Bengaluru for three more years.
What mixed feelings does Naveen have after meeting Keerthi?
Naveen is excited and wants to see Keerthi again, but is also cautious about the distance and about getting ahead of things.
Why was Keerthi's question about five years a good sign?
It showed Keerthi was thinking about fit, not just the evening, which gives Naveen a chance to talk honestly about goals early on.
How does Suraj see the evening?
Suraj is eager to call it fixed and tell Amma, seeing the romance before the practical questions Naveen is weighing.
