Age two: Joseph pointed at the flowerpot, eyebrows up. 'Wha' that?' 'That's a marigold,' his grandmother said with a smile. 'Mari-gold,' Joseph repeated, and pointed at the next pot. 'Wha' that?' She smiled and answered again.

Age five: Pradeep's questions came like rain. 'Why is the moon following us? Why do we have to sleep? Why is the sea salty?' His father answered the first two briefly, then asked, 'What do you think?' Pradeep frowned, then said, 'Maybe the sea is crying?' and the two talked all the way home.

Age ten: Kavitha noticed that a girl named Sana, who usually chattered at lunch, was staring at her lunchbox. Kavitha sat down beside her. 'Are you okay?' Sana shrugged. 'Not really.' 'That's okay. I'm here if you want to talk.' Sana nodded slowly. 'Maybe later.' Kavitha stayed and shared her orange slices.

What did Joseph's grandmother say the flowerpot held?
A marigold.
How did the purpose of asking change from age two to age ten?

Joseph asked what-that with a pointing hand, wanting names and attention. Pradeep asked endless whys about the moon, sleep and the sea, and his father kept the talk alive by asking what he thought, and Kavitha asked a friend if she was okay, showing care without forcing an answer.
What was Sana probably feeling when she said, 'Maybe later'?
Sad and not yet ready to talk, though she appreciated the offer.
How could a parent keep Pradeep's questions going without getting worn out?
Give short honest answers and ask what he thinks, as his father did.

Read this:

Hostel tutor's note, 12 February — Mridul, Class 10
Mridul brought me his revision calendar to check. He had started from the end: all six exam dates circled, from 2 March to 21 March. Then he crossed out Sundays as rest days. Only after that did he fill in subjects, working backward, with the most blocks for Science and Maths. What I noticed most: the last two days ahead of every paper say only "light review, sleep by 10". When I asked, he said his brother had crammed new chapters the night before a paper and blanked in the exam. I suggested one change, a spare half-day in the middle for anything that slips, and he added it himself, on 10 March. I will check with him at the end of February.
— Gopika

Which days did Mridul cross out as rest days?
Sundays.
Why did Mridul protect the two days before each paper?
He was worried about blanking in the exam like his brother, who crammed new chapters the night before.
What does the spare half-day on 10 March add?
A buffer for anything that slips, so one bad day doesn't eat into rest or the light-review days.
How does Gopika see the calendar?
Gopika is impressed by how it was built, suggests just one change and plans a follow-up check.

metadata.subtype: Approach: backward calendar with buffer days [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

It was a winter birthday party in a Chandigarh flat. Ishita, four, was playing musical chairs when she wet her pants.

She froze, then ran to the bathroom and wouldn't come out. "I'm a bad girl," she said through the door.

Parul Masi knocked gently. "Ishita, accidents happen to everyone. You're not bad. I have spare clothes in my bag."

Ishita opened the door a little. Her face was red and wet.

What was Ishita playing when she wet her pants?
She was playing musical chairs.
How did Ishita feel about herself after the accident?
Ishita felt deeply ashamed, calling herself a bad girl and hiding.
How did Parul Masi help Ishita?
She spoke gently, told Ishita accidents happen and that she wasn't bad, and offered spare clothes.
How might Parul Masi feel hearing Ishita say she's bad?
Parul Masi likely felt sad and protective, wanting Ishita to feel safe.

Read this:

"Darshan-bhaiya, are you awake?" "Now I am. What is it, Jatin?" "If I tell you something, do you promise not to look at me differently?" "I promise." "I get these thoughts. Horrible ones. Things I'd never do. They just pop in, and then I can't stop thinking about why I thought them." "Like what?" "I can't say them. They're too awful. I'm scared it means I'm a bad person." Darshan sits up. "Jatin, listen. My friend in college had exactly this. The doctor told him these thoughts are really common, and they upset you because they go against who you are." "So I'm not... evil?" "You're my annoying little brother who cries at dog videos. That's who you are." Jatin laughs shakily. "Tomorrow we tell Mummy and Papa, together, and find someone to help. Okay?" "Okay."

Whose experience does Darshan mention to comfort Jatin?
His friend in college, who had exactly this.
What was Jatin scared his thoughts meant?
He was scared they meant he was a bad person.
What plan does Darshan suggest for the next day?
To tell Mummy and Papa together and find someone to help.
How does Darshan see his brother after hearing about the thoughts?
He still sees Jatin as his soft-hearted little brother, not as someone bad.
Why do some songs get stuck in my head?
Catchy tunes have simple, repeated patterns that the brain remembers easily. Repetition and a rhythm you can predict make a song easy to replay in your mind.
How do I get rid of one?
There is no sure method, but many people find that listening to the whole song, or humming a different tune, helps. Keeping your mind busy with a task also helps it fade.

Read this:

Creche note by Sudha, evening carer.
Damini's mother was late today, delayed by traffic. At six, Damini sat in the book corner, holding her teddy, and began to sing very softly: “Chanda mama door ke…” over and over, rocking. She wasn't crying. I didn't interrupt; it seemed to be helping her. After a while she held the teddy out to me and said, “Teddy wants you to sing too.” So I sang with them. When her mother arrived, Damini was humming and calm.

Why was Damini's mother late?
She was delayed by traffic.
What was Damini feeling as she sang to her teddy?
She was probably lonely and a little worried that her mother was late, and singing helped her feel calm.
Why was Sudha right not to interrupt?
Singing was Damini's own healthy way of coping, and Sudha joined in only when Damini invited her.
How might Damini's mother feel reading this note?
She would likely feel relieved and grateful that Damini found a way to stay calm and that Sudha supported her.

Read this:

'She still hasn't said a word,' Kiran said, turning the paper cup in her hands. The staff wellbeing room at the district hospital smelled of disinfectant and cardamom tea. Eight months ago Salma, the charge nurse, had blamed Kiran in front of the whole ward for a missed chart entry, and the entry had been Salma's own. The counsellor asked what holding on to it was giving her. Kiran thought. 'Every shift I check whether she's on the rota. I rehearse what I'd say. I'm the one losing sleep.' She was quiet for a while. 'I don't need her to admit it. I just want my shifts back.' She didn't text Salma or ask for a meeting. She walked back to Ward 4, took the handover sheet, and when she saw Salma's name on the rota she only nodded and started her rounds.

Who had actually made the missed chart entry?
The entry had been Salma's own.
What does Kiran's habit of checking the rota suggest about her state of mind?
It suggests the resentment had been ruling her working days; she was tense, rehearsing lines and losing sleep over it.
What helped Kiran decide to let the grudge go?
The counsellor's question about what holding on gave her showed Kiran that she was the one paying, so she chose release without waiting for Salma to admit anything.
How might Salma experience Kiran's calm nod on the ward?
Salma may be surprised or unsure what changed, since Kiran is no longer tense around her; the air between them is likely less charged.

metadata.subtype: Stage 5: Deciding to release the grudge [Response]

messages.content: Cieling or ceiling?

The correct spelling is "ceiling". It follows the rule "i before e, except after c": c-e-i.
Example: Papa painted the ceiling a soft cream colour.

Read this:

"Kavitha, you said yes to the concert on a school night?"

"Everyone was there, Tanuja. They all said yes, so I said yes."

"But you have your chemistry exam the next day."

"I know. I didn't think."

"When you're alone, you plan everything. You made a whole study timetable!"

"I know! It's like my brain works differently in the group."

"What will you do?"

Kavitha sat quietly for a moment. "If I think about it now, calmly, I don't want to go. I want to do well in chemistry."

"So?"

"So I'll tell them tonight. And next time, I'll say 'let me check' instead of yes."

What exam does Kavitha have the next day?
The chemistry exam.
Why did Kavitha say yes to the concert?
With everyone in the group saying yes, Kavitha felt excited and swept along and answered on a quick gut feeling.
What did Kavitha decide to say next time, and why will it help?
"Let me check," which gives Kavitha time to think calmly instead of deciding fast in the group.
How does Tanuja see Kavitha's two ways of thinking?
Tanuja notices that Kavitha plans carefully alone but decides fast in the group, and seems surprised by the difference.

Read this:

Warden's note, Thursday. Yusuf came to my office after dinner and stood at the door a while before sitting. Yusuf said a friend, Abhinav, has been skipping meals in the mess and keeping his door shut, and that Yusuf had stayed away for a week because "whatever I say will come out wrong." Yusuf's hands were tight together and the voice was low. I thought Yusuf looked more frightened than uninterested. I said plain, warm words are usually enough, and we wrote three short sentences on a card: I am here. I care. Let us get help. Yusuf took the card to Abhinav's room and I waited in the corridor. Afterwards Yusuf told me Abhinav opened the door and they sat quietly together. I have asked Abhinav to see the college counsellor tomorrow.

What three short sentences did Yusuf and the warden write on the card?
They wrote: I am here. I care. Let us get help.
What was Yusuf afraid of?
Saying the wrong thing, because Yusuf said "whatever I say will come out wrong" and stayed away for a week.
What could Yusuf do if Abhinav says little back?
Keep showing up quietly, repeat the simple words, and help Abhinav reach the counsellor.
How might Abhinav have experienced Yusuf's week of staying away?
Possibly as being left alone, which can feel like nobody cares, though the note only says Abhinav opened the door later and they sat together.
Why do players from opposing teams shake hands after a match?
They shake hands to show good sportsmanship. Because the game was a contest and not a quarrel, the handshake tells everyone that they respect each other whatever the result.
Three ideas for an evening with no electricity: a numbered list, each idea four words or fewer.

1. Play a board game.
2. Tell old stories.
3. Read by candlelight.

Read this:

Dear Sangeeta akka,
You asked how the new school is. Same as I said. The girls here have known each other since KG and they don't want a new girl in the group.
Last Saturday there was a class picnic at the lake. I sat on the steps with my book and my earphones in. No music. I just didn't want anyone thinking I was waiting to be asked.
Two girls did come over and said the samosas were in the blue box. I said 'okay' and went back to reading. After that they didn't come again. On the bus home I sat alone.
Amma says I should 'make an effort'. What effort, when they've already decided?
Maybe I look like I don't care. I do care, a bit. Don't tell Amma that part.
Love,
Lakshmi

What did the two girls tell Lakshmi at the picnic?
They said the samosas were in the blue box.
Why did Lakshmi wear earphones with no music at the picnic?
Lakshmi didn't want anyone thinking Lakshmi was waiting to be asked, which suggests a fear of looking hopeful and then being turned away.
When the two girls came over, what could Lakshmi have done differently?
Lakshmi could have taken the earphones out, thanked them and walked to the blue box with them, giving the conversation a chance to keep going.
How might the two girls have felt after Lakshmi said 'okay' and went back to the book?
They probably felt brushed off and decided Lakshmi preferred to be alone, which is why they didn't come again.

Read this:

So here's the thing I'm a bit embarrassed about. At the college fest committee, Ramesh was reading out the budget, and I laughed and said, "Say it again in your village accent, it sounds so cute." People giggled. After the meeting, Ramesh stopped me on the stairs, very quietly. "Zeenat, I know you didn't mean anything. But the accent jokes follow me everywhere. That one stung." My first feeling? Defensive. I wanted to say, "It was a compliment!" I wanted him to say it was fine. My ears were burning. But I made myself stop. I said, "You're right. I'm sorry it came across like that. I won't do it again." And then I left it there. I didn't make him reassure me. That part was hard.

Where did Ramesh stop Zeenat?
On the stairs.
What was Zeenat's first feeling when Ramesh spoke to her?
Zeenat felt defensive and embarrassed, wanting to insist it was a compliment and wanting Ramesh to say it was fine.
Which choice worked, and why?
Apologising for how it came across and not asking Ramesh for reassurance worked, because it respected his hurt instead of shifting attention to Zeenat's feelings.
How might Ramesh feel after Zeenat's apology?
Ramesh might feel relieved and respected, glad that speaking up quietly was heard without a fight.

metadata.subtype: Being told about an unintended slight [Actor]

messages.content: Our teacher asked us to not talk during the test. Is "to not talk" wrong?

It is acceptable as written.
Why: "To not talk" is widely used; "not to talk" is the careful form.

Read this:

At the Khalsa school in Amritsar, the hall was ready for the Dastar Bandi ceremony: twenty boys from Class 6 would have their first turbans tied before their families. Amandeep, eleven, stood at the back with the other girls, holding the tray of prasad.

Her classmate Nitin whispered, "Why aren't you up there? You wanted to."

Amandeep's throat tightened. "It's for boys."

Bhai-ji, the Gurmat teacher, overheard. After the ceremony he found her by the door. "You looked sad. Tell me."

She told him. He listened without interrupting. "Here this ceremony has always been for boys," he said. "But many Sikh women wear a dastar too. If you want one, I'll teach you, and we can ask the principal about including girls next year."

Amandeep nodded, still hurt. But she asked him for Thursday after class.

How many boys would have their first turbans tied?
Twenty boys from Class 6.
What was Amandeep feeling at the back of the hall?
Amandeep felt hurt and left out, her throat tightening because the rite was only for boys.
How did Bhai-ji respond to Amandeep's hurt?
He noticed, listened without interrupting, explained the tradition honestly, and offered to teach her and ask about including girls next year.
What might Nitin have felt when he asked his question?
Nitin was curious and a little puzzled, having seen that Amandeep wanted to be up there.

Read this:

Saturday: “Mummy, can I cycle to the market alone?” Jomon asked. Rehana shook her head. “Not yet. The main road has trucks, and you've never crossed it on your own. That's the reason, not that I don't trust you.” Jomon kicked the doorstep, but he understood about the trucks. Monday: They cycled the route together after school. Rehana showed him where to get off and walk the bike across, and where to wait. Wednesday: “Can I go to Joseph Uncle's shop for bread? It's before the main road.” Rehana thought. “Yes. Straight there, straight back, and ring the bell when you're home.” Jomon was back in twelve minutes, ringing the bell twice.

What was Jomon allowed to fetch on Wednesday?
He was allowed to go to Joseph Uncle's shop for bread.
What was Jomon feeling when he kicked the doorstep?
Jomon felt disappointed and frustrated at the no, though he understood the reason about the trucks.
Why did Rehana's clear reason help Jomon accept the no?
It showed the no was about safety on the main road, not distrust, and led to practice and a smaller yes.
What might Rehana have felt when Jomon rang the bell twice?
Rehana probably felt relieved and proud that he kept to the plan.

Read this:

"You came back," Dr Noor said, smiling. "I wasn't sure you would."

Hemant sat down without taking off his backpack. "I almost didn't. I slipped. Last Friday I played from nine till the sun came up. Missed my practical."

"Okay. What happened before you started?"

"My marks came out. I was ashamed. I thought, one game."

"And after?"

"I felt disgusting. I thought, what's the point of coming here if I'm going to fail anyway."

"But you're here."

"You told me slips happen and to return anyway."

"I did. And I meant it. A slip tells us something. Marks day is a trigger, so let's plan for the next one. Who could you be with that evening?"

Hemant thought. "My cousin. He lives two streets away."

"Good. Write that down." Hemant took his backpack off.

How long did Hemant play last Friday?
He played from nine till the sun came up.
How did Hemant feel after the slip, and what shows it?
Hemant felt ashamed and disgusted with himself, and nearly didn't come back because he thought he would fail anyway.
Why did coming back after the slip matter for Hemant's recovery?
Returning and being honest about the slip let the doctor turn it into a plan for his trigger, marks day.
How might Dr Noor see Hemant taking off his backpack at the end?
Dr Noor would likely read it as a sign he is settling in and starting to trust the process.
Can a gift displease someone?

Yes. To displease someone is to make them annoyed or unhappy. It is a verb.
Example: The loud music displeased the neighbours.

Read this:

In the office canteen in Bengaluru, Aditi scrolled through screenshots for Joseph: green numbers, big percentages, a trading group with thousands of members. "Forty percent in a month, Joseph. Guaranteed. The mentor picks everything."
Joseph was nearly twenty-five, still sharing a flat, watching everyone around him buy cars. His stomach did a nervous flip. What if everyone got rich and he didn't?
He joined the group that night and deposited ₹10,000 through the app. In a week, it showed ₹13,500. He withdrew ₹2,000, and it actually arrived in his bank. He felt a rush of relief. It was real.
The next message from the mentor came on Friday: "Special VIP round. Minimum ₹2 lakh. Only 24 hours. Don't miss this."
Joseph looked at his savings account. Two lakh was almost everything he had. His finger hovered over the transfer button. Something about "only 24 hours" made his chest tight.

How much did Joseph withdraw that actually arrived in his bank?
He withdrew ₹2,000, and it actually arrived in his bank.
What was Joseph feeling when Aditi showed him the screenshots?
Joseph felt nervous and afraid of missing out, worried everyone else would get rich except him.
What should Joseph do before transferring any more money?
Pause, not rush for the 24-hour deadline, check whether the scheme is registered with the official regulator, and talk to someone independent.
How might Aditi see the trading group?
Aditi seems to trust it fully, perhaps because she has also seen early gains, without noticing the warning signs.

Read this:

The Johannesburg winter term was cold. She had a rule she never said out loud: I must always come first. I must never cry at school. When the maths results came back, she was second, behind Bao, by one mark. Her throat went tight. You must not cry, she told herself. You should have checked question four. She bit the inside of her cheek so hard it hurt. At break, Bao came over, beaming. "We're both in the top two!" Lindiwe couldn't answer. She walked to the bathroom and cried, then felt even worse. Now she had broken two rules. On the bus home, her gran asked what was wrong. "I'm not first," she whispered. Gran said, "Who made that rule?" Lindiwe thought. Nobody had. "I did," she said.

By how many marks was Lindiwe behind Bao?
She was behind Bao by one mark.
Why did Lindiwe feel even worse after crying in the bathroom?
She felt ashamed because she had now broken two of her own strict rules, always first and never cry.
How could Lindiwe's gran help her further?
Gran could help her soften the rules, for example to "I try my best" and "Crying is allowed", and notice when they make her feel worse.
How might Bao see Lindiwe's silence at break?
Bao was happy about them both being top two, so Lindiwe's silence might confuse or hurt Bao.

Read this:

In their Lisbon flat, Beatriz, twenty-five, and Gabriel spread papers across the kitchen table. The baby was due in four months. Gabriel wanted to buy a bigger car now. Beatriz wanted to think about life insurance first. "What if something happens to one of us?" she said. Gabriel frowned. "Nothing's going to happen." "That's what everyone thinks." They argued, then stopped. "Neither of us knows enough," Beatriz admitted. They booked a meeting with an independent financial planner recommended by her sister. The planner listened to their goals for an hour: a home, the child's education, protection if one of them couldn't work. Afterwards, walking by the river, Gabriel said, "The car can wait." Beatriz squeezed his hand, relieved.

When was the baby due?
In four months.
What was Beatriz feeling when she said "What if something happens to one of us?"
She felt worried and protective about their future child.
How did Beatriz and Gabriel resolve their disagreement?
By admitting they didn't know enough and seeing an independent planner who asked about their goals.
How does Gabriel's view change after the meeting?
He decides the car can wait, seeing protection and long-term goals as more important.
Why does the clear part of an egg turn white and firm when it is fried?
Heat changes the protein in the egg white. Because heat makes the protein strands unfold and stick to each other, the runny clear liquid sets into a white solid.

Read this:

In the Class 3 play corner, Siddharth had built a small stretcher from rulers and laid a toy soldier on it. He walked it slowly across the mat while two friends hummed. 'This is Nana's funeral,' he told Manoj sir, quite matter-of-fact. At lunch he asked again, 'Sir, where do people go when they die? Where did Nana go?' He had asked the same thing on Monday and Wednesday. And every day at the gate, he looked for Nana's blue scooter before remembering. Manoj sir crouched down each time. 'People believe different things about where we go. What does your family say?' Siddharth thought. 'Ma says he's in our hearts.' 'Then that's a good place to keep him.'

What did Siddharth look for every day at the gate?
He looked for Nana's blue scooter.
What does Siddharth acting out Nana's funeral suggest he is doing inside?
He seems sad and to be grieving Nana, replaying the funeral in play so that the loss slowly becomes real to him.
Why is Manoj sir's answer about where people go a wise one?
He is honest that beliefs differ and lets Siddharth bring his family's words, which respects the home's beliefs and still answers patiently.
How might Siddharth's friends experience humming at the play funeral?
They may treat it as an ordinary game or feel a little unsure, but joining in helps Siddharth feel less alone.

Read this:

I'm Indu, and I share a lab bench with Binita in our second-year biotech course. Last month I started noticing things. Binita, who never makes mistakes, mislabelled two test tubes. She sighed every few minutes, a long tired sound. She skipped lunch three days in a row, saying she had to finish something. One afternoon her phone buzzed with a message from her tuition student's mother, then her hostel warden, then her project partner. I wanted to tell her to sleep more, or make a schedule. I didn't. I asked, "Is there anything I could take off your plate this week?" She stared at me, then laughed shakily. "Could you write up the lab report?"

How many days in a row did Binita skip lunch?
Binita skipped lunch three days in a row.
What was Indu feeling while noticing the changes in Binita?
Indu felt concerned and uneasy, seeing someone who never made mistakes mislabelling test tubes and sighing constantly.
Why was Indu's question better than advice?
Asking what could be taken off Binita's plate offered real relief, while advice about sleep or schedules would have added one more demand.
How might Binita feel when Indu asks the question?
Binita seems surprised and relieved, laughing shakily and quickly naming something Indu could take.
Rewrite this so it is in the future tense: The class goes to the park and plays games.
The class will go to the park and play games.

Read this:

The substitute teacher was trying to shout over the construction noise next door, and nobody could hear her anyway. Kiran turned in his seat. "Hey, Salma Samosa," he whispered, loud enough for the row. Two boys snorted. Salma kept her head down. Kiran watched her ears go red. At break he nudged her elbow so her juice spilled, then said "Oops" with a grin. More laughter. The substitute was busy with the register and didn't see. Before home time, Kiran hid Salma's bag behind the cupboard. She searched, her lip trembling. Nobody told her where it was. Kiran felt the whole row looking at him, and a warm, powerful feeling spread through his chest.

Where did Kiran hide Salma's bag?
He hid it behind the cupboard.
What was Kiran feeling when the row looked at him?
He felt a warm, powerful feeling, enjoying the attention and the laughter.
What turning point is available at this stage, and to whom?
Any classmate or the substitute could stop the small acts now, by telling Kiran to stop or reporting it, before he learns that teasing pays and moves to worse.
What is it like for Salma when nobody tells her where the bag is?
She likely feels alone and ashamed, as if the whole row is against her.

Read this:

Rain hammered the roof of the community hall so loudly that Sangeeta, the volunteer lawyer, had to shout over a microphone that kept cutting out. Water dripped near the front row. Noor, twenty, sat with wet sleeves and a soaked notebook, so she wrote on the back of her hand: "reason. call family. lawyer."
"Say it calmly," Sangeeta called. "You are not arguing. You are asking."
Someone at the back shouted, "What if they refuse?"
"Stay polite. Note the officer's name and the time. Reach your family or legal aid."
On the bus home, Noor typed the three points into her phone and sent them to her hostel group. Then she scrubbed the ink off her hand and did not forget a word.

What did Noor write on the back of her hand?
Noor wrote 'reason. call family. lawyer.'
What was Noor feeling as she sat with wet sleeves listening to Sangeeta?
Noor was focused and eager to learn, since she wrote the three points on her hand even though her notebook was soaked.
What did Noor do after the workshop that spread the learning?
She typed the three points into her phone and sent them to her hostel group on the bus home.
How does Sangeeta want people to behave if an officer refuses?
Sangeeta wants them to stay polite, note the officer's name and the time, and reach family or legal aid, because asking calmly is protective.

Read this:

Monday evening: After school, swimming and homework, Vikas stood in front of the fridge. "Mango juice or milk?" asked his father, Deepak. Vikas slammed the door. "Why do I have to choose everything?" and stomped off.
Wednesday evening: Same hour, and the question was which story to read. Vikas lay face-down on the carpet and would not answer. At dinner, Deepak noticed he had taken the plainest sandwich without even looking at the others.
Saturday morning: Rested, Vikas planned his whole weekend in five minutes, cheerfully. That night Deepak made a new rule: on school evenings he would set out two options before Vikas got home, or simply decide himself.

What did Deepak ask Vikas on Monday evening?
He asked, "Mango juice or milk?"
Why did Vikas feel so fed up on Monday evening?
After school, swimming and homework he had no energy left for choosing, so even a drink felt like one question too many.
Was Deepak's new rule a good turning point? Why?
Yes, because it removes small evening choices when Vikas is worn out, while Saturday shows he can decide well when rested.
What was it like for Deepak to watch the difference on Saturday?
Seeing Vikas plan the weekend cheerfully likely showed Deepak that the evening outbursts came from tiredness, not a difficult child.

Read this:

I'm Noor, Mehak's sister. On Sunday, Mehak drew our family: Ammi, me, her, Nani and the cat, but no Abbu. Ammi looked at it for a long time. Then she asked, “Tell me about your picture.” Mehak said, “This is us at home. Abbu is at work, so he's in the other picture.” She pulled out a second drawing of Abbu at his desk with a huge coffee cup. Ammi laughed with relief. I think Ammi was worried for a second, but I'm not sure.

What was on Abbu's desk in the second drawing?
A huge coffee cup.
What was Ammi feeling when she looked at the drawing for a long time?
She seemed worried about why Abbu was missing, and then felt relief when Mehak explained.
What did Ammi do instead of assuming something was wrong?
She asked Mehak to tell her about the picture, using the drawing to start a conversation.
How does Noor see Ammi's reaction?
Noor thinks Ammi was worried for a second but isn't sure, and noticed her laugh with relief.

Read this:

In Madrid, Bilal was in his last year of school and taking evening classes for the university entrance exam. Every week the teacher raced through more topics, and Bilal felt like he was always three chapters behind.

He stayed after class to talk to the tutor, Sofia. "Is this pace normal? I can't keep up."

Sofia smiled tiredly. "You're not the only one asking." She showed him the exam's past papers. "These four topics come up every single year. These three, almost never. Focus on the four."

The next morning, he also booked time with the school counsellor, who helped him turn Sofia's advice into a weekly plan: core topics on weekdays, one past paper on Saturday, and Sunday afternoon off.

For the first time in weeks, Bilal went to sleep without the sick feeling of being behind.

How many topics did Sofia say come up every single year?
Four topics.
How had Bilal been feeling before he spoke to Sofia?
Bilal felt anxious and overwhelmed, always three chapters behind, with a sick feeling of being behind.
What else could Bilal ask the counsellor at the next meeting?
He could ask how to adjust the plan if the Saturday past papers show new weak spots, so the focus stays on what matters.
How does Bilal's question look from Sofia's side?
Sofia seems tired but sympathetic, knowing many students feel the same and glad to point him to what matters most.

metadata.subtype: Approach: consulting a teacher or counsellor about pace [Action]

messages.content: Please give a call me when you reach home. Fix the order.

Please give me a call when you reach home.
Why: the person comes first: "give me a call".
Compose a paragraph of about 60 words on why we should respect elders.

Elders have lived long and learned many things. They have faced hard times and know what works and what does not. When we respect them, we listen to their advice and treat them politely. This does not mean we must agree with every word, but we should hear them with patience. Respect for elders makes our families and our communities warm and strong.

At midnight in the hostel common room, Dilnaz's phone buzzed nonstop. The group chat she'd joined in September, Real Talk, was in full flow: memes about "the parasites", a slur dressed up as a joke, voice notes of people mimicking accents. Dilnaz sent a laughing reply to each one. When she was funny, forty people reacted. It felt like being popular for the first time since school.
Damini, her roommate, looked over from the sofa. "Isn't Tenzin's dad one of those? You sat with Tenzin at lunch."
Dilnaz felt her face heat. "That's different. It's a joke."
In the chat, a boy had just written, "Some of them are okay, no?" Within a minute he was called a traitor and removed. Dilnaz didn't defend him. She typed, "Bye, soft boy," and got twenty likes.
Back in her room she scrolled past Tenzin's birthday photos and didn't like them.

What was the group chat called?
Real Talk.
What did Dilnaz feel when her face heated at Damini's question?
She felt embarrassed and a flicker of guilt, quickly covered by calling it a joke.
What could Dilnaz do before her empathy shrinks further?
Leave or mute the chat, message Tenzin, and talk honestly with Damini about why the jokes felt like belonging.
How might Damini see the change in Dilnaz?
Damini is worried and uneasy, watching her roommate laugh at people like her lunch friend's family.

metadata.subtype: Stage 4: Echo chamber and dehumanising talk [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Study chat, Tuesday night.
Harish: Rank list is up. Payal, you're third. Neel, ninth.
Neel: Payal, can you send the geometry notes you made?
Payal: I'll look for them tomorrow.
Harish: You found them in two minutes last term. I saw you tuck the notebook under your bag when Neel walked by 😅
Payal: Everyone's counting everyone's marks now. Whoever tops gets called up on stage.
Neel: Remember the science model? We swapped every single note for that. 🙂
Harish: Nobody hid anything, and we finished in three days.
Payal: ...okay. Give me till morning.

What did Harish see Payal do when Neel walked by?
Harish saw Payal tuck the notebook under the bag when Neel walked by.
What might Harish be feeling when pointing out the notebook tucked under the bag?
Harish seems a little frustrated by the hiding but keeps the tone light, wanting the easy sharing of the science model back.
What could Harish or Neel do to bring back the sharing they had during the science model?
They could suggest studying in a small group, as they did for the model, and offer their own notes first.
What might it be like for Payal, who used to share notes, to be asked for them now?
Payal may feel pulled between friendship and the rank list, which fits the late answer, “Give me till morning.”

Lakshmi, five, was threading beads at the table when her aunt Sangeeta came in with a cup of tea, eyebrows pulled low over her glasses as she read a bill. Lakshmi stopped mid-bead and went very still. "I'll clean up," she whispered. Sangeeta blinked. "Oh, my face! I'm just squinting at tiny numbers, Lakshmi, not cross. Thank you for telling me it looked scary." Lakshmi let out her breath and picked up the beads again.

What was Sangeeta reading when Lakshmi stopped threading?
She was reading a bill.
What did Lakshmi think Sangeeta's low eyebrows meant, and what did they really mean?
She seemed to think her aunt was cross, since she went still and offered to clean up. Sangeeta was actually squinting at tiny numbers.
What would you advise Sangeeta to do when her face looks stern while she concentrates?
She can name what she is doing, such as "I'm just squinting at tiny numbers," so Lakshmi doesn't have to guess.
What is it like for Lakshmi when an adult's face looks cross and nobody explains?
She may feel worried and try to be extra good or quiet, as Lakshmi did when she whispered "I'll clean up."

Rain forced the whole school into the noisy canteen on Manoj's first day in Nagpur. Steel plates clattered, and every bench was full of loud groups. Manoj held his tiffin tightly and stood by the door, his ears hot. Nobody looked up. He walked to the end of a bench and smiled at a boy with a ball-shaped eraser. "Can I sit here?" The boy, Siddharth, nodded without much talk. They ate quietly. Later Manoj heard Siddharth's group planning a card game and asked, "Can I play?" "Next time," one of them said. Manoj went home tired, but he told himself one lunch was only the start.

Why was the school crowded into the canteen on Manoj's first day?
Rain forced the whole school into the noisy canteen.
What was Manoj feeling as he stood by the door with his tiffin?
Lonely and unsure: he held his tiffin tightly and his ears were hot.
What small step could Manoj try next?
Sit near Siddharth again, smile, and ask to join a game.
How might Siddharth see the new boy?
Siddharth nodded without much talk, so he may be a bit shy himself, but he was willing to share a bench.
Which exercises strengthen your arms? And what does strengthen mean there?

To strengthen means to make something stronger. It is a verb.
Example: Swimming helps to strengthen the muscles in your arms and back.

Its disappearance, however, was but momentary. With a rending, tearing sound, one of the broad, white stones turned over upon its side and left a square, gaping hole, through which streamed the light of a lantern. Over the edge there peeped a clean-cut, boyish face, which looked keenly about it, and then, with a hand on either side of the aperture, drew itself shoulder-high and waist-high, until one knee rested upon the edge. In another instant he stood at the side of the hole and was hauling after him a companion, lithe and small like himself, with a pale face and a shock of very red hair.

Boil this extract down to under 55 words.

A broad white stone turns over with a rending sound, leaving a square hole lit by a lantern. A clean-cut, boyish face peeps out, and the young man climbs up and hauls out a small, lithe companion with a pale face and very red hair.

The power had gone out again in Saoner, and Jatin was sitting on the rooftop with his phone at eleven per cent. Ramesh's message came in: 'Bro can't come to the dam tomorrow. Papa needs me at the shop, sorry.' Jatin sighed. He'd fixed the chain on his cycle specially. He typed 'fine, whatever' and sent it, then switched the phone off to save the battery. In his head it was just a shrug, the way he'd say it with a half-smile if Ramesh were standing in front of him. Across town, Ramesh stared at the two words under the shop's flickering tube light. No emoji. No 'next time'. Just 'whatever'. He read it three times, and each time it sounded angrier.

What had Jatin fixed specially for the trip?
He'd fixed the chain on his cycle specially.
What did Jatin mean by 'fine, whatever'?
It was just a shrug of mild disappointment, the kind he'd say with a half-smile in person, not anger.
What small change could have kept Jatin's message from being misread?
Adding a friendly word or 'next time?' before switching off his phone would have carried the half-smile that the bare words lost.
What is Ramesh experiencing as he rereads the two words?
Without Jatin's voice or face, the message sounds angrier each time, and Ramesh likely feels guilty and worried that his friend is upset.
How much is the auto fare from the station to the market today?
I don't know the fare today, because I can't see local rates. Ask the driver for the price before you start, or check the fare chart at the stand.

"Rafiq, you've left the cricket group. And you walk home the long way now."
"It's nothing, Jeevan."
"It's been two weeks. Since the thing on the news."
"...Ammi said to be careful. Someone in your street shouted at my cousin."
"My street? Who?"
"Doesn't matter."
"It does. I'm sorry that happened. But I'm still me. We've been friends since Class 2."
"I know. But I got scared you'd think we're all like the men on TV."
"Rafiq. Did you do anything on TV?"
"No!"
"Then why would I blame you? I don't. Not for that, not ever."
"...Okay."
"Walk home with me today, bhai? The short way. I'll walk you to your gate."
"Your mother won't mind?"
"My mother asked where you've been. She misses your chatter."
"Fine. But I'm batting first on Saturday."

How long has Rafiq been walking home the long way?
It's been two weeks, since the thing on the news.
What was Rafiq afraid of?
Rafiq was scared that Jeevan would think Rafiq's family were all like the men on TV, and his cousin had been shouted at in Jeevan's street.
How did Jeevan help keep the friendship alive?
Jeevan asked honestly, apologised for what happened to Rafiq's cousin, said clearly he didn't blame Rafiq, and offered to walk him home.
How might Jeevan's mother see Rafiq's absence?
She seems to miss Rafiq and to feel no suspicion, asking where he has been.

Pankaj had pinned the councillor's photo above his tea stall in the kasba, next to the calendar. Ever since the councillor got the road to the bus stand laid, Pankaj felt part of something bigger, and he told every customer so. His sister Uma, stirring the pot, teased him. "You'd defend even a queue at the ration shop if they announced it." Then the notice came: the Sunday market would move outside town. Pankaj went quiet, wiping the same glass twice. "The road was right," he told Uma. "This isn't. Half these vendors will lose their customers." That evening he wrote a note to the party office, signed with his own name, the badge still on his shirt. Uma raised her eyebrows and poured him tea.

What did the councillor get done that made Pankaj feel part of something bigger?
The councillor got the road to the bus stand laid.
What was Pankaj feeling when he wiped the same glass twice after the notice came?
He seemed troubled and torn. He admires the councillor but thinks moving the market is wrong, and his sudden quiet shows the conflict.
How could Pankaj keep backing the councillor without becoming an uncritical follower?
By doing what he did: praising the road, objecting to the market move in a signed note, and continuing to judge each decision on its own.
How does Uma seem to see Pankaj's admiration at the start, and might that change?
She teases him as someone who would defend anything the councillor did. His note about the market, with the badge still on, may show her his support has room for disagreement.

Make this easy to read for a child.

The merchant purchased several metres of cloth and departed.
The shopkeeper bought a few metres of cloth and left.

Monday. Pankaj came down in his new shirt for the school photo. His elder brother Suraj looked up from his toast. "That colour makes you look ill." Pankaj changed shirts and said nothing all the way to school.
Wednesday. Pankaj showed Suraj his science model. "The wiring's messy. It'll short." Pankaj snatched it back and slammed his door.
Friday. The model had shorted in class, just as Suraj said. That evening Pankaj knocked on his brother's door. "You were right about the wiring. But when you say things like that, it sounds like you think I'm useless." Suraj stared. "I didn't mean it that way." "I know. Can you just tell me what's wrong and how to fix it, and skip the 'ill' part?" Suraj nodded slowly, then pulled out a screwdriver.

What did Suraj say about Pankaj's shirt colour?
"That colour makes you look ill."
How did Pankaj feel after the shirt comment, and how can you tell?
He felt hurt and criticised; he changed shirts and said nothing all the way to school.
What choice did Pankaj make on Friday, and what came of it?
He told Suraj how the words landed and asked for the fix without the harsh part; Suraj nodded and got a screwdriver.
How might Suraj have felt when Pankaj said his words sound like "you think I'm useless"?
He seems surprised, since he meant no harm, and may realise his honesty was landing as an attack.

messages.content:
Read this:

My name's Suraj, and last term I thought ₹200 a session for home maths tuition was good money. Then Elizabeth, who shares my table in the library, asked what I actually kept. I didn't know.
So I worked it out on the back of a lab sheet, half talking aloud. Auto both ways: ₹80. Mobile data for sending worksheets: roughly ₹20 a session. Printing: ₹10. That's ₹110 gone before I've taught anything. Each session is an hour, but with travel and preparing it's closer to two and a half. So I was earning about ₹36 an hour.
I stared at that number for a while. Elizabeth said, 'You're paying to teach.' Not quite, but close.
I've now asked the family to move two sessions a week online, and I'm working out what hourly rate would feel fair.

What did the auto cost both ways?
Auto both ways: ₹80.
How did Suraj feel on seeing the ₹36-an-hour figure?
Suraj was shocked and a bit embarrassed, staring at the number, and then determined to rethink the setup.
If you were Suraj, what would you change first?
Cutting the travel, as Suraj did by moving sessions online, is a sensible first step; counting all hours and costs before agreeing any new job would help too.
How does Elizabeth see Suraj's tuition work?
Elizabeth sees plainly what Suraj missed: after costs the job barely pays, so Elizabeth sums it up with a blunt joke.

Read this:

"Naveen, give me the truck!" Lokesh said.
"No."
"You never share."
Naveen looked at Lokesh's bag of cars. He thought out loud, "If I share the truck, then you share your cars?"
"Yes."
"All of them?"
"Five."
"Okay." Naveen handed over the truck, and Lokesh poured out five cars.

How many cars did Lokesh pour out?
Five cars.
What was Naveen thinking when he thought out loud?
He felt hopeful that sharing the truck would get him some cars too.
What else could Naveen try if Lokesh wouldn't trade?
He could suggest playing together so both toys are shared.
How does Naveen's rule look to Lokesh?
Lokesh finds it fair and agrees, since he gets the truck.

At five, Sunaina sat on the floor beside her grandmother Lakshmi while the evening puja began. The brass lamp was lit, the bell rang, and the smell of camphor drifted up. Sunaina watched the flame turn in circles. She clapped along with the aarti and asked, "Why do you swing the light, Nani?" Lakshmi smiled. "Because it's a way of saying thank you, and everyone joins in." Sunaina held up her palms to the warmth of the flame and copied her grandmother. At twenty, Sunaina stood on a street in the late afternoon as a wedding procession came down it. Drummers marched, dancers spun, and a groom sat on a decorated horse. Her friend Aditi, whose cousin was the groom, waved to her from the crowd. "Come, walk with us!" Sunaina stepped aside to let the drummers pass, and asked quietly, "What does the song they are playing mean? I don't want to do anything wrong." Aditi grinned. "It's the welcome song. Just clap along and smile." Sunaina clapped, happy to belong, and asked one more question when the music stopped.

What did Sunaina ask her grandmother about the light?
She asked why Lakshmi swings the light.
How does Sunaina's reading of ritual differ at five and at twenty?

At five she copied her grandmother's clapping and asked why the light is swung, learning that actions mark special moments. At twenty she read the wedding procession of drummers, dancers and a groom on a horse as joy, and asked Aditi what the song meant before joining.
What was Sunaina feeling when she asked about the song at the procession?
She felt respectful and a little unsure, wanting to join without doing anything wrong.
What could Sunaina do at another community's ceremony where she does not know the customs?
She could watch what others do and ask a friend like Aditi quietly what things mean and how to take part respectfully.

What English saying does the host quote, and what does he do after?

"You English have a saying which is close to my heart, for its spirit is that which rules our boyars: 'Welcome the coming; speed the parting guest.' Come with me, my dear young friend. Not an hour shall you wait in my house against your will, though sad am I at your going, and that you so suddenly desire it. Come!" With a stately gravity, he, with the lamp, preceded me down the stairs and along the hall. Suddenly he stopped.
"Welcome the coming; speed the parting guest." He says that spirit rules his boyars, promises not to keep the young man an hour against his will, and leads the way down the stairs with the lamp.

The nomination desk closed at four. Jaya, volunteering in the college office, had turned away two students at 4:05, one of them in tears. At 4:40 Gautam strolled in with his form. Professor Rane, in charge of the election, looked up and smiled. "Gautam! How is your father? Tell him Sunday lunch is on." The form went into the pile. Jaya's pen stopped. She knew the two families had holidayed together for years; she'd seen the photos on the office wall. Part of her understood: you look after your own, you don't shame them in public. But she had said no to a crying girl barely half an hour earlier. That evening she wrote a short, polite email to the student council, asking that late forms be handled the same way for everyone.

At what time did Gautam bring in his form?
Gautam strolled in at 4:40, after the desk had closed at four.
What was Jaya thinking when her pen stopped?
She partly understood the professor's loyalty to a family friend, but felt it was unfair after she had turned away a crying girl.
Jaya chose a polite email to the council over confronting the professor. What makes that a sensible choice?
It raises the fairness problem through the proper channel and asks for one rule for everyone, without a public scene.
How might the two students turned away at 4:05 feel if they learned about Gautam's form?
They would likely feel cheated, seeing the rule applied strictly to them but bent for someone with the right family connection.

I'm Sachin. Yesterday Amma gave my sister Chandrika a job while rushing to the office: "Take the clothes off the line, fold the towels, put Appa's shirts on the bed, water the tulsi, and switch the geyser on at six." Chandrika said yes to everything.
When I came home she had taken in the clothes and was sitting on the pile, looking confused. The shirts were still mixed with the towels. The tulsi was dry. I don't know exactly what was in her head, but she looked like she was trying to remember and couldn't.
I asked, "What did Amma say?" She said, "Clothes... and something about six?"
So I made it simple. "First, fold the towels. Then tell me." One thing at a time, she finished everything before Amma got back.

What was Chandrika doing when Sachin came home?
She was sitting on the pile of clothes, looking confused.
How was Chandrika feeling when she answered "Clothes... and something about six?"
Chandrika was confused and overwhelmed; she really tried to remember but could hold only a couple of the five jobs, not because she didn't care.
Which approach worked, and why?
Sachin's one-thing-at-a-time steps worked, because Chandrika only had to hold one small job in mind before checking back.
What would change if Amma had written the jobs down before leaving?
Chandrika could have looked at the list instead of relying on memory, and the tulsi and shirts might have been done before Sachin got home.

Three weeks before his Class 12 boards, Vikas stuck a timetable above his desk in their small Nagpur flat: physics in the mornings, chemistry after lunch, maths problems at night, and every Sunday afternoon a full mock paper with a timer. The hardest part wasn't the syllabus. It was his phone. Every buzz pulled him out of a derivation. So he started leaving it on the kitchen shelf with Aai while he studied, fifty minutes at a time, then a ten-minute break on the balcony. When Deepak called to go for chai at nine, Vikas hesitated. 'Saturday, after the mock,' he said. On the day of the physics paper his hands shook, so he did what he'd practised: read the whole paper, circled the easy questions and started there.

Where did Vikas leave his phone while studying?
On the kitchen shelf with Aai.
What might Vikas have been feeling when Deepak called?
He was tempted to go and a bit torn, since he wanted to see his friend but also wanted to protect his study time.
Which part of Vikas's exam strategy could help a nervous student most?
Reading the whole paper first and starting with the easy questions, which builds calm and momentum.
How might Deepak see the delayed chai plan?
Deepak might be disappointed at first but likely understands and respects Vikas's focus before boards.

Why do bees visit flowers?
What should I wear for a walk in the rain?
What is wrong with "The river flow very fast."?

1. They collect nectar. Because nectar is their food and they carry pollen from flower to flower.
2. Wear a raincoat or take an umbrella and shoes that grip. Keep your bag covered.
3. Fixed: The river flows very fast. Why: A singular subject needs the verb with s.

Saurabh's cousin's wedding filled the house in Kanpur for a whole week: relatives on every mattress, a dholak in the courtyard, and the pre-board maths exam ten days away. His phone never stopped. Family photos, dance videos, cousins tagging him.
On the first night he lost two hours to reels. On the second morning, he took a chit and wrote: If dinner is over, then maths book open, phone with Manoj bhaiya. He showed it to his older cousin Manoj. "You'll take it from me?"
"Every night," Manoj said. "Till the exam."
That evening the dholak started again, louder. After dinner, Saurabh didn't debate. He passed his phone to Manoj, took his book to the only quiet spot, the stairs to the roof, and did twelve sums while the courtyard sang below.

Where did Saurabh study after dinner?
He took his book to the stairs to the roof, the only quiet spot.
Why did Saurabh write the chit on the second morning?
He felt frustrated and worried after losing two hours to reels, and wanted a plan that would work even with the wedding noise.
Why did the if-then chit work even with the dholak playing?
It tied a clear cue, the end of dinner, to a clear action, handing the phone to Manoj and opening the book, so he didn't have to decide in the moment.
How might Manoj feel being given this job during the wedding?
Manoj might feel trusted and a bit proud to help, happy to hold the phone even while the celebrations go on.
Hana's book has 62 pages and Anita's book has 55 pages. Whose book is longer?
Hana's. Because 62 is more than 55, so her book has more pages.

I'm Madhuri's younger brother, and I've shared a flat with her and Jeevan since June. I've watched the same loop maybe ten times. Something small goes wrong, like Jeevan forgetting to call from a work trip. Madhuri asks what's wrong, then asks again, louder. Jeevan says "Nothing," and goes to the balcony. She follows. He puts his earphones in. She cries; he goes for a drive. Last Sunday something changed. Madhuri drew two arrows on the fridge whiteboard, one chasing, one running, making a circle. "This is us," she said. "Not you, not me. Us." Jeevan actually laughed. Then he stayed at the table. I don't know what they were feeling inside, but they talked for an hour.

What did Madhuri draw on the fridge whiteboard?
She drew two arrows, one chasing and one running, making a circle.
What might Madhuri be feeling when she asks again, louder?
She may feel anxious and shut out, needing reassurance that nothing is wrong between them.
What was the turning point on Sunday, and why did it help?
Madhuri showed the loop as "us", not one person's fault, which let Jeevan relax and stay to talk.
How might Jeevan see the whiteboard drawing?
He may feel relieved not to be blamed, which is why he laughs and stays at the table.

Thunder cracked, and everyone in the lane ran for cover. Salma, five, stood under the tin roof of the tea stall with her father. Across the road, Asif was crying, holding a kite that had turned into wet paper. Salma's face crumpled too. She tugged Abbu's kurta. "Asif's kite is dead." When the rain eased, she walked over, holding her father's hand, and stood close to Asif without saying anything. Then she patted his arm twice. "Poor kite," she said softly.

Where did Salma wait out the rain?
Under the tin roof of the tea stall with her father.
What does Salma's face crumpling suggest?
She felt sad along with Asif when she saw him crying over his ruined kite.
How could Abbu build on Salma's feeling?
He could name it, like "You feel sad for Asif," and ask what might help, such as making a paper kite together once it is dry. ❤️
How might Asif feel with Salma standing close and patting his arm?
He may feel less alone in his upset, even though the kite is still ruined.

Saurabh, you're making a science project? Let your Bhupen Dada tell you about mine. When I was in Class 6, I wanted to prove that bean plants needed sunlight. My first idea was: one plant on the roof, one plant in a dark room. Easy. But my teacher asked, "Is the pot the same? The soil? The water?" I thought about it and realised I was using a big clay pot for one and a tiny tin for the other. If one grew better, how would I know why? So I found two identical tins, filled each with the same soil, gave each the same half glass of water every day. Only the light was different. After a week, the difference was clear, and I could explain it.

What did young Bhupen first use for the two plants?
Young Bhupen used a big clay pot for one and a tiny tin for the other.
How did young Bhupen probably feel when the teacher asked about the pots?
Young Bhupen was probably surprised and a bit sheepish, realising the test was not fair yet.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
Switching to two identical tins with the same soil and water mattered, because it made light the only difference.
How might Bhupen's teacher have seen the final project?
The teacher would likely be pleased that the question made Bhupen rethink and produce a fair test.

"Swati, look! Snow!" Vishal said, crouching by the window of the Shimla cottage.
Swati, twenty months, turned toward his voice. He pointed outside. She followed his finger and gasped.
"Snow," he said again.
"No!" she said, which was her word for most things.
She pressed her hand to the cold glass and turned to him, eyes huge.
"Cold!" he laughed.
She pointed at a bird hopping on the white ground, then looked at him.
"Bird, yes!"

Where were Swati and Vishal?
At the window of the Shimla cottage.
How did Swati feel when she saw the snow?
She felt amazed and excited, gasping with huge eyes.
What is Vishal doing that supports Swati's learning?
He points, names what they see together, and answers when she points, sharing her focus.
What is it like for Vishal to share Swati's first snow?
He feels delighted and warm, laughing and naming things with her.

I was at the back of the hall when Uma gave her speech after the flood-relief drive, so I heard every word. We'd collected more supplies than any college in the district, and everyone expected her to take a bow. Instead she said, "Three things. I planned the collection points well; I'm proud of that. We were lucky: a local paper wrote about us on day two, and donations tripled. And I made a mistake: I forgot to arrange trucks, and Rehana's uncle lent us his for free." Then she thanked the volunteers by name, all thirty-one of them. I watched her face while she read the names. I can't say what she was feeling, but she didn't rush a single one.

How many volunteers did Uma thank by name?
All thirty-one.
What might Uma's slow reading of the names suggest?
She probably felt genuinely grateful to each volunteer, taking care not to rush anyone.
Why is Uma's three-part speech a good way to own a success?
She credited her planning, admitted the lucky newspaper story and her truck mistake, and thanked others, which builds trust.
How might Rehana feel hearing the uncle's truck mentioned?
Rehana would probably feel pleased and proud that the family's help was named in front of everyone.

Urmila: can we swap slots on friday? I'll take monday instead
Pradeep: okay.
Urmila: ...okay with a full stop? are you annoyed? 😬
Pradeep: no?? why
Urmila: in my group a full stop at the end is basically a door slam
Pradeep: lol I put full stops on everything. my dad taught me to text like I'm writing a letter
Urmila: ahh. that explains the "Good morning." every single day
Pradeep: exactly. if I'm ever annoyed you'll know, I'll write a whole paragraph
Urmila: noted. ok so friday is yours
Pradeep: OKAY!!! better?
Urmila: sooooo much better 😄
Pradeep: good. and thank you. monday was going to be a mess for me
