Aparna, you asked why I never took the manager's job at the mill. At twenty I was a weaver's apprentice in Chanderi, and all I wanted was to make a border so fine you couldn't see where one thread ended. My cousins got clerk jobs and laughed at me: "Still at the loom? No ambition." My mother worried too. But every day I sat with old Master Rehmat and redid the same paisley until my eyes watered. I, Usha, didn't tell anyone my goals. They were mine. Years later a buyer from Delhi picked up one of my saris and held it to the light without a word. That silence was the prize I had been working for.

Who did young Usha sit with every day?
Old Master Rehmat.
How did young Usha feel about those goals?
Usha felt determined and quietly private, caring about fine work more than status.
What was the turning point in the story?
The Delhi buyer silently holding the sari to the light showed that years of practice had reached true mastery.
How did Usha's cousins see that choice?
They laughed and thought Usha had no ambition because Usha stayed at the loom.

Read this:

Ramesh,
I'm writing this because when we talk, I lose my words.
On Saturday, when I said I wasn't ready to stay the night at your flat, you went quiet and then said, "If you really loved me, you wouldn't make me wait." I've heard some version of it three times now. Each time I feel guilty, then scared you'll leave, then angry that I feel scared.
So here it is, clearly. I do care about you. And I decide my own pace. Being ready is not a test of love. If you respect me, a "not yet" has to be okay without sulking or asking again the next day.
I told my friend Kokila about this yesterday. She asked whether I feel safe saying no to you. I want the answer to be yes. That part is up to you now.
Hansa

What did Ramesh say on Saturday?
"If you really loved me, you wouldn't make me wait."
What mix of feelings does Hansa describe each time Ramesh says it?
Hansa feels guilty, then scared that Ramesh will leave, then angry about feeling scared.
What else, besides the letter, can help Hansa if the pressure continues?
Keep talking with Kokila, the trusted friend who asked whether Hansa feels safe saying no, so Hansa isn't facing it alone.
How might Ramesh feel reading the letter?
Possibly defensive or embarrassed at first, but the letter gives Ramesh a clear choice: accept "not yet" or show that Hansa's pace isn't respected.

Summarize this croquet scene for a child.

The chief difficulty Alice found at first was in managing her flamingo: she succeeded in getting its body tucked away, comfortably enough, under her arm, with its legs hanging down, but generally, just as she had got its neck nicely straightened out, and was going to give the hedgehog a blow with its head, it would twist itself round and look up in her face, with such a puzzled expression that she could not help bursting out laughing: and when she had got its head down, and was going to begin again, it was very provoking to find that the hedgehog had unrolled itself, and was in the act of crawling away: besides all this, there was generally a ridge or furrow in the way wherever she wanted to send the hedgehog to, and, as the doubled-up soldiers were always getting up and walking off to other parts of the ground, Alice soon came to the conclusion that it was a very difficult game indeed.

Alice tries to play croquet using a flamingo as her bat and a hedgehog as the ball. The flamingo keeps twisting round to look at her, the hedgehog crawls away, and the soldiers keep walking off. Alice decides it is a very hard game.

Read this:

I'm Binita, Lakshmi's cousin, and this year I watched every milestone flow around her like water round a stone. At Pongal the whole family was at Paati's house; Lakshmi's place at the kolam was empty. In August Paati fell ill, and Lakshmi sat in the hospital corridor but left before her father arrived. Then in November her baby girl was born, and her parents didn't come. I brought her rasam in a flask. She said, "Every festival, every hospital visit, it opens again." Meanwhile the relatives were at me: Periamma saying, "Tell her to apologise and come home," and my uncle saying, "Tell her to stand firm, they'll come round." I didn't carry either message. I just held the baby while Lakshmi slept for an hour.

What did Binita bring Lakshmi after the baby was born?
Rasam in a flask.
What does holding the baby while Lakshmi slept suggest about how Binita feels?
Binita seems protective and tender, sad for Lakshmi and weary of the relatives pulling in opposite directions.
Why was Binita's choice not to carry either message wise?
Both messages push Lakshmi to one side; offering practical care instead gives her rest and support without adding pressure.
What is each milestone like for Lakshmi?
Each festival, illness and birth reopens the loss, a painful reminder that the family is not together.

metadata.subtype: Stage 3: Life events widen the gap [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

The whole gang in Samir's colony in Hyderabad got the same buzz cut the week before term started. 'Your turn tomorrow,' they told him at the gate. Samir, fifteen, had been growing his curls since summer; he liked tying them back when he played the tabla. That night he stood in front of the mirror, pulling the curls straight, trying to picture himself without them. His neighbour Kashish, sixteen, out walking her dog, saw him on the steps later. 'You look like someone going to a punishment.' 'They're all doing it.' 'Do you want to?' He took a long time to answer. 'I want them to stop calling me the different one.' Next morning he went to the barber, asked for just a trim, and walked to the gate with his heart thumping.

What instrument does Samir play?
He plays the tabla.
What did Samir's answer to Kashish show about what he wanted?
He didn't want the haircut itself; he wanted to stop being singled out, so he felt torn between belonging and staying himself.
What could help Samir if the group teases him about the trim?
He could answer lightly and confidently, and spend time with people like Kashish who accept him as he is.
What would change if Samir's friends had treated the haircut as optional?
He could keep his curls without feeling he was risking his place in the group.

Read this:

Playgroup note, rainy July week. Nazia had the block tub today. When Ojas came over, she tipped half the blocks toward him at once: "You gave me your red car yesterday." Then a boy who usually grabs and keeps things reached in. Nazia pulled the tub back. "No. You never give me." He started to cry. I sat with them both and said, "You remember who shares with you. That's fair thinking." Then I gave the boy a turn to share his puzzle with Nazia first. He did. Nazia passed him two blocks. Next: more take-turns games.

What did Ojas give Nazia yesterday?
His red car.
Why did Nazia pull the tub back from the other boy?
She felt it was unfair, because he never gives her things; she was annoyed and protective of her blocks.
What did the note-writer try next, and why could it help?
The boy got a turn to share his puzzle with Nazia first, so she saw him give and was willing to give back.
What is it like for the boy when Nazia says "You never give me"?
He feels hurt and left out, and cries, perhaps not yet understanding that his grabbing is why she won't share.

Read this:

You asked me for this interview how I noticed Afreen was burning out. I'm Deepika, and I run the home-care team for older patients here.
Afreen was our warmest carer. She'd sing to patients, remember their grandchildren's names. Then, last winter, three of her patients died in six weeks.
I started noticing small things. She stopped singing. She'd snap at the driver. Once I found her crying in the van, and when I asked, she said, "I'm fine, it's just the cold."
Another day she said, flat as a wall, "They all die anyway."
That's when I knew. I gave her a week off, paid. I sat with her for an hour and just listened. When she came back, I split her cases with two others and started a Friday tea where the whole team talks about hard days.
Caring people need someone caring for them too.

How many of Afreen's patients died in six weeks?
Three.
What was Deepika thinking when Afreen said "They all die anyway"?
Deepika felt alarmed and concerned, realising Afreen was burning out after too many hard losses.
Which of Deepika's steps helped, and why?
A paid week off, an hour of listening, shared cases and a Friday tea helped, because they gave Afreen rest, talk and a lighter load.
How might Afreen have felt when Deepika sat and listened?
She probably felt seen and relieved, having someone notice her pain instead of just the work.
I feel like my friend and I are drifting apart.
It happens when lives change. Sometimes it can be fixed with a little effort. Do you want to stay close?
Yes, but we talk less now.
Reach out with a simple message about something you shared, like a memory or a joke. Small, regular contact helps more than a big gesture.
What if they don't reply?
They may be busy. Wait a few days, and try once more. If the effort is one-sided for a long time, it may be worth accepting a different kind of friendship.
Should I suggest meeting up?
Yes, a specific idea works better than 'let's meet sometime'. Suggest a day and a place, like a walk or a cup of tea.
What if we have nothing in common any more?
You may still enjoy catching up on each other's lives. Ask about what they care about now. Friendships can change shape and still be real.

Read this:

Chandrika,
You told me to speak at least once in the design seminar this week. I didn't. Here's my defence.
On Tuesday I had a good point about the bridge model, a real one, written in my notebook. Then I imagined saying "tensile" wrong, or stumbling on the numbers, and Professor Rao's eyebrow going up, and the whole class remembering that eyebrow until the exams. So I stayed quiet.
Five minutes later someone else made my point, less clearly, and got a nod.
At dinner I asked my lab partner about the seminar. They had forgotten who even spoke. They remembered the samosas.
So maybe the audience in my head is bigger than the real one. I'll try on Thursday. Hold me to it.
Francis

What was Francis's point about?
Francis had a good point about the bridge model, written in a notebook.
What was Francis afraid would happen if the point came out wrong?
Francis was anxious that a mispronounced word would raise Professor Rao's eyebrow and the class would remember it until the exams.
What could Francis try on Thursday to make speaking easier?
Francis could read the point from the notebook early, before the fear grows, remembering that the lab partner only recalled the samosas.
How did the lab partner experience the seminar?
For the lab partner it was forgettable; they couldn't recall who spoke, only the samosas.

metadata.subtype: Speaking up in class or interviews [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the village school in Barmer, the midday meal came in big steel buckets. Irfan, nine, noticed that three children always sat by the far wall, away from the rest.
"Why do they sit there?" he asked his friend.
"My dadi says their family is different. We shouldn't sit with them."
Irfan didn't understand, but he stayed in his place.
The next day, Bidisha Madam noticed where Irfan was looking. At lunch, she carried her own plate to the far wall and sat down there. "Everyone eats together in my school," she said. "Nobody is less than anybody."
Irfan picked up his plate and went to sit beside her. One by one, others followed.

Where did the three children always sit?
They always sat by the far wall, away from the rest.
What was Irfan feeling when he stayed in his place?
He felt confused and unsure, because he didn't understand why his friend's dadi said the family was different.
How did Bidisha Madam handle it well?
She showed fairness through action, sitting with the separated children herself, and explained clearly that nobody is less than anybody.
How might the children by the wall feel when the others joined them?
They might feel included and relieved, no longer marked out as different at every meal.

Read this:

At the colony's inter-school debate practice, Parveen couldn't stop smiling at Nitin's speech. He had argued so clearly that even the coach clapped. Afterwards, she caught him at the gate. "You were amazing! Honestly, I'd never have guessed your father drives an auto, you speak so well." She meant it as the highest praise. Nitin's smile slipped. "Why wouldn't I speak well?" "No, I just meant..." She stopped. What had she meant? "You meant people like me usually don't," he said quietly, and got on his cycle. Parveen stood at the gate, stunned. She replayed her own words and heard them the way he had. That night she typed a message three times before sending: "I'm sorry. You're a great speaker. Full stop."

Where did Parveen catch Nitin after the speech?
At the gate.
What was Parveen feeling as she stood at the gate?
She felt stunned and ashamed, realising her compliment carried an assumption that hurt Nitin even though she meant it kindly.
Why is Parveen's final message a good repair?
It apologises and takes out the part that hurt, praising Nitin's speaking without linking it to his background.
How does Nitin see the compliment?
He hears it as saying that people from his background usually can't speak well, so the praise feels like a put-down.
I bought a "momento" of my trip. Is that spelled right?

The word is "memento", which starts with "mem-". It means an object kept to remember a person or a place.
Example: She kept a shell as a memento of the beach.

Read this:

Subject: Checking in after this morning

Hi Naveen,

I wanted to write properly, because at the stand-up I only managed a clumsy "you okay?"

When the director started going through the quarterly numbers, your face went grey and your hands were shaking so much the coffee cup rattled on the table. My first thought, honestly, was that you were scared of the review. I nearly said "relax, it's not that bad."

I'm glad I asked instead whether you'd eaten. When you said nothing since last night, I got the juice from the pantry and sat with you in the small room until your hands stopped trembling.

You said afterwards it was "probably both, the hunger and the nerves." Fair enough. I just didn't want to guess at the feeling before checking you were physically all right. If it keeps happening, please get it checked with a doctor.

Hafsa

What did Hafsa bring Naveen from the pantry?
Hafsa got the juice from the pantry and sat with Naveen in the small room until the trembling stopped.
What was Hafsa feeling on seeing Naveen's hands shaking, and how sure could Hafsa be of the reason?
Hafsa was worried and a little unsure: the first reading was that Naveen was scared of the review, but hunger or illness could look the same, so Hafsa checked on Naveen's health first.
Which choice worked here, and why?
Asking whether Naveen had eaten and staying with Naveen worked, because it dealt with a possible physical cause before anyone judged the mood.
How might Naveen have felt if Hafsa had said "relax, it's not that bad"?
Naveen might have felt misread and embarrassed, since part of the shaking came from not eating, and would still have been unwell.
Foreigner ko bola "It costs five lakh." Wo samjha nahi.
A "lakh" is used in India, and many people elsewhere do not know the word. Five lakh means five hundred thousand. You can say: "It costs five hundred thousand rupees."

Three bullet points for this, please.

But when the gentlemen entered, Jane was no longer the first object; Miss Bingley's eyes were instantly turned towards Darcy, and she had something to say to him before he had advanced many steps. He addressed himself directly to Miss Bennet with a polite congratulation; Mr. Hurst also made her a slight bow, and said he was "very glad;" but diffuseness and warmth remained for Bingley's salutation. He was full of joy and attention. The first half hour was spent in piling up the fire, lest she should suffer from the change of room; and she removed, at his desire, to the other side of the fireplace, that she might be farther from the door. He then sat down by her, and talked scarcely to anyone else. Elizabeth, at work in the opposite corner, saw it all with great delight.

- Miss Bingley turns to Darcy at once when the gentlemen enter.
- Bingley gives Jane warm attention, piling up the fire and moving her away from the door.
- He talks to hardly anyone else, and Elizabeth watches happily from her corner.
The bus to my college takes over an hour each way and I'm exhausted by the time I reach home.
That's a long day. The commute can use up a lot of energy. Can you use some of that time for something useful or restful?
I usually just look out of the window.
That's fine too, but you could listen to music, a podcast or an audiobook, or read notes for revision. Choose what helps you feel good.
I tried reading but it makes me feel unwell on the bus.
Then skip reading and use audio instead. Notes recorded in your own voice can be useful for revision.

"I forgot!" she exclaimed, shaking her beautiful curled head, as if shocked at herself. "I am so giddy and thoughtless! Do excuse me. It had slipped my memory that you have good reasons to be indisposed for joining in my chatter. Diana and Mary have left you, and Moor House is shut up, and you are so lonely. I am sure I pity you. Do come and see papa."

Question: Why does the speaker apologise to the listener?

She says she forgot that the listener has good reasons for not joining her chatter, since Diana and Mary have left, Moor House is shut up, and the listener is lonely. She then invites the listener to see papa.

Read this:

Simran, you asked why I still keep this tulsi mala in my pocket. Let me tell you about me at fourteen.
Every year, in the rains, my father and I walked with the wari to Pandharpur. Eighteen days on foot, with thousands of pilgrims singing abhangs, drums and cymbals, dust and mud. I didn't wonder whether Vitthal was listening. I didn't wonder anything. My feet hurt, my father's hand was on my shoulder, and an old woman from the next village fed me bhakri every evening as if I were her own grandson.
When we finally saw the temple spire, everyone wept and danced, and I did too, without knowing why. It was the happiest I have ever been.
Faith, for me then, was that crowd, my father's voice singing beside me, and that old woman's bhakri. That is what I still carry. I'm Nilesh; the questions came later, but that belonging never left.

How many days did the walk to Pandharpur take?
Eighteen days on foot.
What did young Nilesh feel when the temple spire came into view?
He felt overwhelming joy and belonging, weeping and dancing without needing to know why.
What choice inside the story shaped Nilesh's faith?
His father's choice to take him on the wari every year, which tied faith to walking together, singing and being fed by strangers.
How might the old woman who fed Nilesh have seen him?
She probably saw him as a young pilgrim to care for like her own grandson, sharing her bhakri out of kindness and devotion.

Read this:

I'm Jahnavi, Rafiq's younger sister. My brother is twenty-five, and he's the most careful person I know.
Last year his college friend offered him a place in a travel start-up. More excitement, maybe more money one day. Rafiq said no and took the clerk's post in the railway office. Steady salary, fixed hours, a pension.
On salary day, he sits at the table with a notebook and divides the money into envelopes: rent, Ammi's medicines, my college fees, and one marked 'emergencies.' He never touches that one.
When I asked if he regretted the start-up, he said, "When Abbu's shop shut down, we didn't know about rent for a year. I never want you or Ammi to feel that again."
Most days he seems calm, even content. But some nights I hear him awake, checking the envelopes again. I don't know if that's worry or just habit.

What is written on the envelope Rafiq never touches?
Emergencies.
What does Rafiq's answer about Abbu's shop suggest about why he chose the railway job?
It suggests the fear from that uncertain year still drives him, and he values safety for his family more than chances for himself.
What did Rafiq's choice give his family, and what might it cost him?
It gives them steady support for rent, medicines and fees; it may cost him some excitement and bring him restless nights of worry.
How does Jahnavi see her brother's careful ways?
She sees his care and calm and feels protected, but she also notices his late-night checking and wonders whether it is worry.

Read this:

Jana had fixed a dripping tap and a rattling shelf, so a faint gas smell behind the cooker seemed like the next small job. In her flat in Vienna she pulled the cooker forward, gripped the rubber hose and started to twist the clamp. "How hard can it be?" The smell grew stronger. Selin, her neighbour, knocked to borrow sugar and stopped. "That's gas. Stop. Don't touch any switch." Jana's hands were shaking. They opened the windows, turned off the gas at the wall valve, and left the flat. Selin phoned the gas company from the stairwell. The technician who came said the clamp had been loosened.

What did Selin come to borrow?
Selin came to borrow sugar.
What was Jana feeling after she heard Selin say "That's gas"?
Jana was frightened and shaken, and her overconfidence changed to alarm as her hands shook.
What safe steps did Jana and Selin take?
They opened the windows, turned off the gas at the wall valve, left the flat, avoided switches and phoned the gas company from the stairwell.
Why might Selin have said "Stop" so firmly?
Selin smelled gas and knew that a spark or another wrong move could be dangerous, so the firm tone came from concern for both of them.
It rained 6 millimetres each day for 6 days. How many millimetres fell in all? How can I help my mother in the kitchen? What does the word "lend" mean?

1. It is 36. Because 6 x 6 = 36.
2. Ask her what she needs and wash the vegetables or set the table. Stay away from the hot stove.
3. To lend is to let someone use your thing for a while. They will give it back.

Read this:

When the ordering system in the Lisbon office went dark at ten past two, the chat filled with people typing at once. Beatriz wrote, 'I'll be incident commander. Olga, you investigate. Mateus, you talk to customers and management.' Then she asked everyone else to stay quiet in the main thread unless called on. Olga opened the logs and posted findings every ten minutes. Mateus sent a short note to the support desk and another to the director, and promised the next one at three. Beatriz kept a running list of what had been tried. Nobody dug through the same log twice, and nobody talked over anyone. At ten to four the fix went in and the system came back. Beatriz thanked each role by name and set a review for the next morning.

Who did Beatriz tell to investigate?
Beatriz told Olga, 'you investigate'.
What did Beatriz want when she asked everyone else to stay quiet in the main thread?
Beatriz wanted calm and focus, so that the investigator and the person sending updates could work without being talked over.
What could the team add if an outage ran for many hours?
The team could rotate the roles after some hours so people stay rested, using the running list to hand over.
How might the director have felt about Mateus's updates?
The director would probably feel informed and calmer, since the notes came when promised.

Read this:

Diary, Thursday
The office is officially split. At lunch, Preeti's table was whispering about Karan "sabotaging" the launch. At the chai counter, Karan's friends were saying Preeti steals credit. I sat with neither group and ate my paratha standing up.
Then the chat group. Someone made a new one without Preeti in it. I left it after an hour. Felt sick reading it.
Our manager called me in today and asked, "Amandeep, what's going on with the team? Everyone's so tense." I said, "Just deadline stress, I think." Why did I say that? Because I didn't want to be the one who told. Now she's guessing, and the guesses are worse than the truth.

Where did Amandeep eat lunch?
Standing up, with neither group.
Why did Amandeep feel sick reading the new chat group?
Amandeep felt uncomfortable and uneasy, seeing colleagues ganging up and not wanting to be part of it.
What small step could Amandeep take now?
Go back to the manager and describe the actual disagreement between Preeti and Karan, without taking sides, so guesses stop multiplying.
What is the manager experiencing as she senses the tension?
She is likely worried and confused, feeling the strain but not knowing its real cause.

Read this:

I sit across from Eshaan's desk, so I watched this over a couple of months.
Eshaan had put Kunwar, our newest developer, on a six-week plan for the backend work. Every Friday they met. I'd hear bits of it: "the API is still failing," "this one's better."
Around week six I saw Eshaan staring at the whiteboard for a long time. He'd written two columns: "backend: patchy" and "testing: strong." Kunwar's test reports had been the best on the team for weeks. People had started forwarding them.
The next Monday, Eshaan went into our manager's office for half an hour. That afternoon, it was announced that Kunwar would move to the quality team.
I can't say what Eshaan was thinking at the whiteboard. But I saw Kunwar walk out of that meeting with his shoulders lighter than I'd seen in weeks. — Vinita

What were the two columns Eshaan wrote on the whiteboard?
"backend: patchy" and "testing: strong."
What does Eshaan staring at the whiteboard for a long time suggest?
It suggests he was thoughtful and perhaps uneasy, weighing whether the plan was fixing the wrong thing before changing course.
What else could Eshaan have done if the manager had said no to the move?
He could have kept Kunwar on backend but added testing tasks and support, adjusting the goals to build on his strengths.
How did the change look to Kunwar, as far as the observer could tell?
Kunwar seemed relieved; he walked out of the meeting with lighter shoulders, suggesting the new role felt like a better fit.

metadata.subtype: Approach: adjusting the plan when the fit is wrong [Revision]

messages.content: The boss told to me to finish the work.
The boss told me to finish the work. Why: "Tell" is followed directly by the person, with no "to".

Read this:

Nilesh, you look the way I did at twenty-one. Sit, drink your tea. I'm Sarita, yes, the boring one from accounts, but listen.
I was with a boy named Prakash for two years in Pune. When it ended, I cried in the ladies' hostel bathroom for weeks. My roommate declared, "That's it, no more love for me either," and she kept that vow for years.
About six months later, I was buying guavas at the market and heard a song we used to love. And I noticed: no stab. Just a small smile. That was the day I sat down and wrote two lists. What was good: he made me laugh, he believed in my exams. What I learned: I kept making myself smaller so he wouldn't be upset. That was my pattern, not only his fault.
I didn't give up on love. I just walked into the next one with my eyes open. You will too.

Where was Sarita when she noticed the song no longer hurt?
Buying guavas at the market.
What did Sarita feel when she heard the old song six months later?
Calm and a little warm: no stab of pain, just a small smile, a sign she had healed.
What was the turning point in Sarita's story, and what did she do with it?
Noticing the song didn't hurt; she then wrote two lists, the good parts and her own habit of making herself smaller, instead of calling the whole relationship bad.
How did Sarita's roommate respond to heartbreak differently?
She swore off love for years, protecting herself instead of learning, while Sarita kept her heart open with clearer eyes.
A shop opens at 9:30 a.m. and closes at 6:00 p.m. How many hours is it open?
It is open for 8 and a half hours. Because 9:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. is 8 hours, and 5:30 to 6:00 adds another half hour.

Read this:

Lakshmi, you asked what the philosophy club was like. I'm Anirban, and I went because of a free samosa, but I stayed because of one question.
The teacher asked: "If a friend asks if their drawing is good and it's terrible, do you lie?" We split into groups. One side argued the way some thinkers do: do whatever makes the most people happy, so be kind. Another side said lying is wrong in itself, no matter what. My friend Deepa brought up the Buddhist idea of right speech, truthful but also kind and timely. Our coach pointed out we'd found three different systems in one room.
What surprised me was nobody was stupid. Each view had a reason. I used to think religions and philosophies were just teams to support. Now I think they're tools, and you compare them fairly before you pick one up.

What question did the teacher ask the club?
"If a friend asks if their drawing is good and it's terrible, do you lie?"
Why did Anirban feel surprised by the discussion?
Anirban felt surprised and impressed that each view had a reason and nobody was stupid.
How could Anirban use what Anirban learned in a real disagreement?
Anirban could lay out each side's reasons fairly before judging, rather than treating views as teams.
How might Deepa have felt bringing a Buddhist idea to the group?
Deepa may have felt glad and valued that the group treated the idea as one serious option among others.
Why does a pot lid rattle when the water inside boils hard?
Steam pushes up on the lid. Because the steam needs somewhere to go, so it lifts the lid a little, and the lid drops back again and again.
What is a mastiff? Is it a kind of dog?

Yes. A mastiff is a very large, strong dog with a short coat and a broad head, often kept for guarding. It is a noun.
Example: The old farmer's mastiff slept by the gate and barked at every stranger.

Read this:

Faculty adviser's note, college cultural committee review, 18 February
The committee met to review the outdoor music night that was cancelled when the rain came. Most members said the risk was obvious and that Imran, who chose the open ground, should have known. Imran said little. Tanvir, the committee secretary, asked to see the notes from the planning meeting in January. He read out what the group had known then: the forecast showed clear skies, the indoor hall was booked by the exam cell, and every member had voted yes. He asked, "Given what we had that day, what would a better choice have been?" Nobody had an answer. The review turned to planning: a rain-backup clause for future bookings. I suggested we keep dated planning notes for every event.

What did the forecast show in January?
Clear skies.
Why did Tanvir ask to see the January notes?
He seemed uneasy that Imran was being blamed with hindsight, and wanted the review to be fair to what was known when the choice was made.
How did the review change after Tanvir's question, and why is that better?
It moved from blaming Imran to planning a rain-backup clause, which helps future events instead of punishing a reasonable choice.
What might it have been like for Imran before Tanvir spoke?
Imran probably felt blamed and ashamed, staying quiet while others called the risk obvious.
Friend said "I will ping you." Ping kya hota hai?
"To ping someone" means to send a short message to get their attention. "I will ping you" means "I will message you soon". It is casual, so use it with friends and coworkers, not in a formal letter.

Read this:

Note from Siddharth's aunt, who went along

Siddharth asked to join the students' silent march for a new school crossing on the Pune-Satara road. His parents were away, so I spoke with him first.

He had already checked: the march had police permission, the route was published, and the organisers were the parents' association. He had also read their rules: no blocking traffic, no slogans against anyone. I said I would come.

Before we left, he told his parents the location by phone. He packed water, a charged phone and a snack. We agreed with his friend Sarika and her father that the four of us would stay together, and that if any shouting began, we would leave by the side lane near the temple.

The march was calm and took forty minutes. We left at 6:15 as planned. On the way back, Siddharth asked how the association would follow up. I have asked them to send him the update.

Who were the organisers of the march?
The parents' association.
How might Siddharth have felt preparing so carefully for the march?
He probably felt responsible and a little nervous, wanting to take part while making sure it was safe.
What else could Siddharth do to stay involved after the march?

Okay, so you want to know how I handled Bidisha? I'm Leela, I work on the data team, and this went on for six months.
In meetings with the directors, Bidisha was warm and funny. Back at our desks, she'd say things like, "Leela's slides are cute, I'll fix them." Then she'd present my analysis as her own.

At 6 pm on a Thursday, three hours before Pune's biggest weekend food fair, Irawati, 26, the operations head at a packaged-meals start-up, got a message from the kitchen: the new label printer had dropped the "contains peanuts" line from two thousand boxes of curry.
Her co-founder, Ganga, was already calculating. "Reprinting costs us the fair. Most people read the menu board anyway."
Irawati paced the loading bay. She thought of the child with an allergy who might pick up a box, the city food inspector, the investors, the thirty staff paid from this weekend's sales.
"If one person gets hurt, there's no company left to save," she said. "And even if nobody does, we'd know."
She stopped the trucks, split the team into two lines to hand-sticker every box, called the fair organisers to delay their stall by a day, and posted an honest note online. Ganga argued, then picked up a sticker roll.

How many boxes were missing the "contains peanuts" line?
Two thousand boxes of curry were missing the line.
What was Ganga feeling when she started calculating?
Ganga felt anxious and under pressure about losing the fair and the money the staff depended on.
Which choice worked, and why?
Stopping the trucks and hand-stickering every box worked, because it protected customers with allergies and the company's trust while still saving most of the stock.
What would change if Irawati had followed Ganga's first idea?
The boxes would go out unlabelled, putting allergic customers at risk and exposing the start-up to legal trouble and a loss of trust.

This afternoon I found her sitting on the kitchen floor. I didn't ask what was wrong with her. I sat down too and said, "You've been carrying so much. I think we should both talk to the doctor, just to check you're okay. You're not doing anything wrong." She cried, then nodded. Her mother is coming tomorrow to sit with the baby while we go.
Tonight I've got the bottles and the night shift. Kavitha is asleep right now, properly asleep, for the first time in days. I'm scared I left it too long. But we've started.

Friday was also when he'd promised to help Varun, his friend since Class 6, revise for the same exam. Varun was struggling.

She wrote her talks full of easy words, "talk" instead of "presentation," "big" instead of "enormous," because P and E sounds got stuck. When a boy laughed at her last time, she wanted to disappear. Practice with a qualified speech therapist, and a teacher who let her go last and take all the time she needed.

Setting a daily limit, curating what she follows and stepping away when the reminder buzzed all cut down how much the feed can keep serving her.

Example: In winter the temperature decreases at night, so we wear sweaters at bedtime.

It helps them hide. Because a colour that blends into the ground, snow or trees makes it harder for hunters to spot them, or for their prey to see them coming.

I live across the corridor from Hansa and her mother, Vasudha aunty, so I noticed when their lights stopped going off before two in the morning last winter. Then the results came, and for weeks Hansa hardly left the flat. Vasudha aunty told me in the lift, "She failed the bar exam. She won't talk about it."
Around March something changed. Hansa began leaving at eight every morning with a small bag. I found out she'd taken a paralegal job at a two-person firm near the station. She set up a study table on the terrace too, one hour at seven every evening, a timer beside her.
Small things. She laughed with the watchman again. One day she held the lift for me, a file under her arm, and said, "First draft I wrote, they actually used it." I don't know what's in her head. But she walks faster now.

What job did Hansa take?
A paralegal job at a two-person firm near the station.
What might Hansa have felt when she said the firm used her first draft?
She likely felt proud and a little more confident, a small win after weeks of hiding.
Why do the paralegal job and the evening hour help Hansa more than waiting?
They give her small, real wins and steady practice, so confidence returns through doing rather than thinking.
How might Vasudha aunty feel watching Hansa change?
Vasudha aunty probably feels relieved and hopeful, seeing her daughter leave the flat and laugh again after weeks of silence.
Interviewer ko "Mujhe is job ki zaroorat hai" kaise bolun bina begging ke?
Say: "I am very interested in this role, and I believe my skills fit it well." This sounds confident and does not beg.
Aur "Mujhe kaam ka experience nahi" ke baare mein?
Say: "I do not have work experience yet, but I learn quickly. In college I did an internship and led a small project." Use only true facts about yourself.

In the architecture studio at the college, it was Wednesday, and the model for the housing project was due on Friday morning. Zainab had cut exactly four pieces of mountboard.
Keerthana, at the next desk, looked over. "Zainab. You said Monday you'd be done by today."
"I know. But this model is simpler. It's basically boxes."
"Your last model was 'basically a roof.' It took three nights."
Zainab laughed. She had even written an essay on the planning fallacy for her psychology elective last term. She knew every model she had ever made had taken twice as long as she planned. But this time felt different. This time she really could see it in her head.
At 11 p.m. on Thursday, the glue gun jammed. At 2 a.m., one wall wouldn't stand straight. At 6 a.m., she was painting windows with a toothpick.
She submitted at 8:55, eyes red.
"Different this time?" Keerthana asked gently.
"It felt different," Zainab said.

How many pieces of mountboard had Zainab cut by Wednesday?
Zainab had cut exactly four pieces of mountboard.
Why did Zainab believe this model would be different?
Zainab felt hopeful and sure, because this time she could picture it clearly and it seemed simpler.
What could Zainab do next time, given her own history?
Zainab could plan from how long her past models actually took, about twice her guess, instead of trusting the clear picture in her head.
How does Keerthana see Zainab's estimate?
Keerthana sees the pattern clearly and responds with gentle humour, remembering the "basically a roof" model.

I'm Reena, and I teach Class 4 in a school in Sydney. Samir's mother came for pickup today and Samir switched to Tamil mid-sentence, laughing, then looked around to see who was near and went quiet. In class Samir speaks careful English, and I have noticed a hand hovering before answering. I can't say for sure what is going on inside. Today at story time Samir said the Tamil word for moon, and a classmate asked, "Say it again!" Samir did, twice, smiling shyly. Afterwards Samir's mother told me they read one Tamil book and one English book every evening. Samir's shoulders looked lighter at the gate.

Which language did Samir switch to at pickup?
Samir switched to Tamil mid-sentence.
What might Samir feel when looking around before going quiet, and how sure is Reena?
Perhaps self-conscious about using Tamil near classmates, though Reena says there is no way to be sure what goes on inside.
How did the classmate's reaction help Samir?
Asking Say it again showed curiosity, which let Samir share the Tamil word proudly.
What might Samir's mother want for Samir?
For Samir to be at ease in both languages, keeping Tamil warmly while learning English, which the two evening books suggest.
What's a good way to study for a long exam?
Break the syllabus into small parts and give each part a day or session. Revising a little each day beats cramming at the end.
How do I know if I really understand a topic?
Try explaining it aloud in your own words without looking at the notes. If you get stuck, that is the part to review again.
Is it okay to study with music?
For some people, soft music without words helps, while others find any sound distracting. Try both and see which gives you better focus.
How many breaks should I take?
Short breaks, like five or ten minutes after each hour of study, help keep you alert. Stand up, stretch and drink some water.

At five, Rashmi knocked the milk glass off the table, saw the white pool spread and crawled behind the sofa. "I'm bad," came a small voice. Aparna, Rashmi's mother, knelt at the sofa's edge. "That was a slip, sweetheart. It doesn't make you bad. Come and help me with the cloth." Rashmi crept out and held one corner of the cloth.

At fifteen, Rashmi snapped at Sangeeta in the canteen, "Just leave me alone, you're so annoying," and Sangeeta went quiet. For four days Rashmi replayed the words at night, ate lunch on the stairs to avoid the canteen, and told herself it proved what kind of person she was. Nothing in that review helped Sangeeta, only kept the shame going.

At twenty-one, Rashmi looked back at a year lost to sleeping late and dropped courses. Every job listing felt like a reminder. One evening Rashmi wrote in the diary: the person who made those choices was doing the best she knew then. That night Rashmi began an application, one small paragraph at a time.

Where did Rashmi crawl after knocking over the milk glass?
Rashmi crawled behind the sofa.
How does Rashmi's way of judging her own mistakes change across five, fifteen and twenty-one?

At five Rashmi treats the spilled milk as identity, saying "I'm bad," until Aparna says the spill was a slip that does not make Rashmi bad. At fifteen Rashmi replays the harsh words for days and avoids the canteen, calling it accountability. At twenty-one Rashmi writes that the earlier self did the best it knew, and starts moving forward.
What was Rashmi feeling while eating lunch on the stairs after snapping at Sangeeta?
Rashmi felt ashamed and wanted to avoid Sangeeta, using harsh self-review as if it were making up for the remark.
What could Rashmi do at fifteen instead of replaying the words for days?
Rashmi could apologise to Sangeeta simply, without a long speech, and then let the matter rest, so that shame does not replace repair.

I need this in two sentences for my notes:

Mr. Pocket said he was glad to see me, and he hoped I was not sorry to see him. "For, I really am not," he added, with his son's smile, "an alarming personage." He was a young-looking man, in spite of his perplexities and his very grey hair, and his manner seemed quite natural. I use the word natural, in the sense of its being unaffected; there was something comic in his distraught way, as though it would have been downright ludicrous but for his own perception that it was very near being so. When he had talked with me a little, he said to Mrs. Pocket, with a rather anxious contraction of his eyebrows, which were black and handsome, "Belinda, I hope you have welcomed Mr. Pip?" And she looked up from her book, and said, "Yes." She then smiled upon me in an absent state of mind, and asked me if I liked the taste of orange-flower water? As the question had no bearing, near or remote, on any foregone or subsequent transaction, I consider it to have been thrown out, like her previous approaches, in general conversational condescension.

Mr. Pocket greets Pip warmly; he looks young despite his grey hair and has a natural, slightly comic manner. His wife, Belinda, is absent-minded and only asks Pip an odd question about orange-flower water.

"How was the presentation?" Simran asked, dropping her keys on the flat's counter.
"Not my best day," Maria said from the sofa. Her laptop had died mid-slide, the projector had shut off twice, and she'd spilled coffee on her professor's handout.
"That sounds a bit more than not your best."
"Well, the coffee did add some colour."
Simran snorted. "Did the professor say anything?"
"He said I 'recovered gracefully.' I think he was being kind." Maria pulled a cushion over her face. "I'm fine. Mostly."
Simran sat beside her. "Mostly is allowed. Do you want to keep joking, or talk properly?"
Maria peeked out. "Joking for ten more minutes, then talking."
"Deal."

What did the professor say about Maria's recovery?
He said she 'recovered gracefully'.
What does Maria's phrase 'not my best day' tell you about how she is coping, and what else could it mean?
It suggests she is using understatement to cope with an awful day, though she may also be hiding how upset she is, which her 'mostly' hints at.
What did Simran do that helped?
She played along with the joke, then gently asked if Maria wanted to keep joking or talk, so Maria could choose.
How might Simran see Maria's understatement?
Simran knows the presentation went badly, so she reads the understatement as coping but still checks, in case Maria needs more than a joke.

1) Explain the word "afford" in simple words.
2) Why do banks keep money safe for people?

1. To afford is to have enough money to pay for something. Example: We cannot afford a new bike.
2. It is safer than keeping it at home. Because the money is locked away and recorded.

At the municipal engineering office in Nagpur, Darshan's calendar had a new block every morning: 9:00 to 11:00, "Drainage report. No meetings." He had noticed his best thinking came before lunch; by four he was reading the same line three times.
Arnab leaned over the partition at 9:15. "Chai and gossip?"
"At eleven," Darshan said, not looking up. "This is my good-brain time."
"Your what?"
"For months I did emails in the morning and the report at night, then called myself lazy when it didn't get done. It wasn't laziness. I was doing the hardest thing when I was emptiest."
He had done the same with evenings: on Sundays he cooked three dinners and laid out his gym clothes, so after work there was nothing to decide.
At eleven the report section was done. He went for chai with Arnab and let himself enjoy it.

What was blocked on Darshan's calendar from 9:00 to 11:00?
"Drainage report. No meetings."
How does Darshan now feel about his past unfinished reports?
Darshan seems relieved of the old self-blame; he no longer sees himself as lazy, understanding he was doing the hardest work when he was emptiest.
Which two changes help Darshan most, and why?
Putting the hardest task in his best morning hours, and cooking and laying out gym clothes on Sunday so evenings need no decisions; both respect his energy limits instead of blaming his character.
How might Arnab react to "good-brain time"?
Arnab seems amused and puzzled at first, but still gets his chai at eleven with a friend who is actually relaxed. 😄

"Forgive me," I said: "I could not help it; but I had been thinking that it was of dear Lucy that you wished to ask, and so that you might not have time to wait--not on my account, but because I know your time must be precious--I have written it out on the typewriter for you."

Using only this passage: what has the speaker done, and why?
The speaker has typed it out so the other person need not wait, knowing their time is precious. The speaker had assumed the question would be about Lucy.

In the colony lane in Kochi, Gautam heard Thomas telling everyone the zoo trip was on Tuesday. Gautam knew it had moved to Thursday. He thought, Thomas doesn't know; he wasn't there when Ma'am said it. So he told him. Thomas thanked him. Gautam felt clever. Later, at the lane cricket match, Thomas asked to bowl first. Gautam wanted to bowl first too. He had been practising his spin all week. "No, you always bowl first!" Gautam shouted, though Thomas never did. Thomas walked off. That night Gautam lay in bed. He could see now that Thomas just wanted a turn, like him. Why hadn't he seen it at the time?

What day did the zoo trip move to?
Thursday.
Why did Gautam feel clever about telling Thomas the trip date?
He felt proud because he understood that Thomas believed something different since he hadn't heard the teacher.
What could Gautam do tomorrow to make things right with Thomas?
He could say sorry for shouting and suggest taking turns to bowl first.
If you were Thomas, what would you want Gautam to understand?
That he only wanted a turn at bowling, and it hurt to be told he always bowled first when he never did.

Rain drummed on the tin roof, and Reena, five, wanted to open the new jar of jam for her toast. She pulled the lid straight up. Nothing. She pushed it. Nothing. Then she stopped and thought of Amma with the pickle jar: Amma held the jar with one hand and turned the lid round and round. Reena held the jar against her tummy and turned. The lid gave a small squeak, then moved. 'Amma, I did it like the pickle jar!' she shouted over the rain. Amma laughed and handed her a spoon.

What did Reena want to open?
Reena wanted to open the new jar of jam.
How did Reena feel when the lid moved?
Reena felt proud and excited, shown by her shout over the rain. 😊
What could Reena do if the lid still would not move?
Reena could ask Amma to loosen it a little first, and then turn it herself.
How might Amma have felt hearing Reena's shout?
Amma was probably amused and proud, since Amma laughed and handed her a spoon.

Our hostel wing had a running joke in first year: "Parul's asking her gods for marks again." I fast on Tuesdays and keep a small Hanuman picture on my desk, and Rukmini, my roommate, would strike a match near it and ask if he'd blow it out. People laughed. I laughed too, which I regret. Inside I felt small, as if my whole family was being called foolish. One night in October I told her so, straight, without crying. Rukmini didn't apologise at once. She said, "I really don't get it. Explain it to me?" So I did: my Nani, the fasting, how the quiet helps me study. She told me why she stopped believing at fourteen. We didn't agree. We still don't. But she hasn't touched a matchbox near my desk since, and on Tuesdays she saves me fruit.

What did Rukmini say when Parul spoke to her in October?
She said, "I really don't get it. Explain it to me?"
How did Parul feel when the wing laughed at the jokes?
Parul felt small and hurt, as if the whole family was being called foolish, even while laughing along.
Why did Parul's way of speaking up work?
Parul told Rukmini plainly and calmly how it felt, which invited questions instead of a fight, so they could each explain their views.
How might Rukmini see Parul's faith now?
Rukmini still doesn't share it but seems to respect it, dropping the matchbox teasing and saving fruit for Parul on Tuesdays.

Hi Amandeep,
One month in, so I'm writing up how our plan is going, partly to thank you.
When we agreed at the office canteen to exercise together, I didn't think it would last a week. Here's what we actually did:
1. After every workout, we send each other one line in our chat: what we did and how long.
2. Every Tuesday and Saturday at 6:30, we meet at the park by the water tank and walk-jog together.
3. If one of us skips, the other just asks, "Tomorrow?" No lecture.
The log shows 22 sessions for me this month. Last year I managed about four. On the three mornings I wanted to stay in bed, what got me up was knowing you'd be standing at the water tank.
Also, the chats on our Saturday walks are the best part of my week.
Tushar

How many sessions did Tushar log this month?
Tushar logged 22 sessions.
What did Tushar feel on the mornings Tushar wanted to stay in bed?
Tushar felt tempted to skip but also responsible toward Amandeep, and knowing Amandeep would be waiting got Tushar up.
What else could Tushar and Amandeep do if one of them travels for work?
They could keep sending the one-line log from wherever they are, so the partnership still works even without the park meeting.
How might Amandeep feel reading this email?
Amandeep may feel appreciated and encouraged, learning that simply turning up at the water tank helped Tushar so much.

messages.content: Why might children feel sad when their favourite teacher leaves the school?
The children feel the loss of a person who mattered to them. Because they formed a bond with someone who encouraged them every day, they miss the support and the routine they shared.
What does the word "fanciful" mean? Also, is "make a decision" correct, or should I say "do a decision"?

1. Fanciful means imaginative or unreal, rather than based on facts. It is an adjective.
2. "Make a decision" is correct. We say "make" with decisions, plans and mistakes.

In the front room of their Pune flat, Shreya, two and a half, put the fourth block on her tower. It swayed and crashed. She stamped her foot. Nazia Khala knelt and rested one finger lightly against the side of the new tower. "Try again, jaan." Shreya placed block four, then five, tongue poking out. The tower wobbled but held. Shreya squealed and ran to the kitchen door. "Look! I made it big!" Khala quietly took her finger away.

What happened when Shreya first put the fourth block on her tower?
It swayed and crashed.
Why did Shreya run to the kitchen door shouting?
She was proud and excited, believing she had made the tall tower all by herself.
What choice did Nazia Khala make that helped, and why?
She rested one finger against the tower instead of building it for Shreya, so Shreya still placed every block.
Why might Khala have taken her finger away quietly?
Khala wanted Shreya to keep the joy of the win as her own, without being reminded of the help.

In the science lab, Sangeeta Ma'am rattled off the steps: "Two spoons of salt, stir, then add the vinegar, then the baking soda, and watch."
Everyone nodded. So did Parveen.
But when she started, she poured the vinegar first, then stared at the jar. She fidgeted with the spoon and glanced at her partner's table.
Sangeeta Ma'am came over. "Parveen, can you tell me the steps back, in order?"
Parveen opened her mouth. "Salt... then... baking soda?"
"Ah. That's where it got lost." Ma'am wrote the steps on a small card. "Now, read them to me."
Parveen read them aloud and nodded, and this time her nod looked sure.

What did Sangeeta Ma'am write the steps on?
A small card.
What does Parveen's staring and fidgeting suggest she felt?
It suggests she felt confused and unsure, even though she had nodded along with everyone.
Which choice of Sangeeta Ma'am's worked, and why?
Asking Parveen to say the steps back showed where the confusion was, and the written card fixed it.
How might Parveen's partner have seen her glancing at their table?
The partner might have thought Parveen was copying, when really she was confused and looking for clues.

Monday. Rehana, two weeks into the newsroom, told the desk she could write the budget story alone. "It's just numbers." Someone snorted, "Sure, genius," and Rehana crossed her arms and said it again, louder.
Tuesday. Rekha, the senior sub-editor, pulled a chair beside her. She didn't mention the snort. She showed Rehana last year's budget story and pointed to two lines: one where the reporter compared a figure with rising prices, and one where a farmer explained what the change meant for him. "Tell me, step by step, how you'd get from the budget document to lines like these." Rehana began confidently, then slowed. "I'd... read it. And then... I don't know who I'd call."
Thursday. Rehana came to Rekha's desk with a list of five people to phone and a question about prices she had written down herself.

What did Rehana bring to Rekha's desk on Thursday?
A list of five people to phone and a question about prices she had written down herself.
Why did Rehana cross her arms on Monday?
She felt mocked and defensive after the snort, so she dug in and repeated her claim more loudly.
Which response helped Rehana, and why?
Rekha's specific examples and step-by-step question helped, because Rehana found her own gap; the snort only hardened her claim.
How might Rekha see Rehana's list on Thursday?
Rekha probably feels pleased, since the gaps showed up through Rehana's own explanation and she is now filling them.

The bus depot was roaring with engines and Vidya had only a few minutes before her bus to Pune left. She called Raghav, pressing one finger to her other ear. The line kept breaking. "Raghav? Can you hear me? I want to say something before I lose you." She took a breath. "When you go out with your college group and I hear nothing, I feel insecure. I know that's mine to handle, not yours. I'd love a little reassurance sometimes. I'm not asking you to send photos or prove anything." The line crackled. Then his voice came back, soft. "Thank you for telling me like that. I'll message you when I get there, okay?" The conductor whistled. Vidya climbed on, lighter.

Where was Vidya going when she called Raghav?
Her bus was going to Pune.
How can you tell Vidya felt relieved after the call?
She climbed on the bus feeling lighter, after Raghav answered her softly and warmly. 😊
What made Vidya's way of speaking work even on a bad line?
She spoke about her own feeling, said it was hers to handle and asked for reassurance without demanding photos or proof, so Raghav did not have to defend himself.
What would change if Vidya had accused Raghav instead?
He might have argued or gone quiet, and the noisy, broken call would likely have ended in a fight instead of an offer to message her.

Monday. Neelam read the poem aloud and said “school” the way they said it back home in Muzaffarpur. Dhruv repeated it in a squeaky voice. The whole row laughed. Neelam finished the poem looking only at the page.
Thursday. She did not raise her hand once. At home she stood before the steel almirah mirror, saying “school, school, school” the way Dhruv's group did, until her mother asked who she was talking to.
The next Monday. Ms Kaur asked for a reader. Neelam kept her eyes down. When Dhruv read, badly, she said nothing, but pressed her pencil so hard the tip snapped.

Where did Neelam practise saying the word at home?
She practised in front of the steel almirah mirror.
What might Neelam be feeling when her pencil tip snapped?
She is likely resentful and hurt; she keeps silent while Dhruv reads badly, but her anger comes out through the pencil.
How could Ms Kaur support Neelam after the first Monday?
She could stop the mimicking straight away, tell the class accents are welcome, and quietly check in with Neelam so she feels safe to read again.
How might Dhruv see what he did?
Dhruv probably thought it was a harmless joke that made the row laugh, and has no idea Neelam now avoids reading.

The college fest committee met in the seminar hall, and Tanuja had to pick a head for the sponsorship team. Eshaan stood up and gave a speech about "vision" and "big brands" with perfect English and a smile. The room clapped. Tanuja felt sure: he was the one. Rukmini, from second year, sat at the back. Last year she had quietly got four local shops to sponsor the music night, but nobody remembered because she never talked about it. Tanuja chose Eshaan. By the second week, Eshaan had made three presentations and zero calls. Rukmini, on her own, had two shopkeepers ready to sign. Tanuja saw the list and felt her face go warm. She'd been dazzled by how Eshaan spoke, not by what either of them had done.

How many local shops had Rukmini got to sponsor the music night last year?
Four local shops.
Why did Eshaan feel like the right choice to Tanuja?
His fluent, confident speech felt like proof of ability, so Tanuja felt sure, and later embarrassed at being dazzled by style.
What would you advise Tanuja for choosing leads in future?
Look at past results, like Rukmini's sponsorships, before listening to speeches, and ask each person what they've actually done.
How might Rukmini feel about being overlooked?
Rukmini may feel unnoticed and a bit hurt, but she keeps working quietly.

Every night for a month before the trip to the Stockholm summer market, Emil and his father, Javier, sang the phone number to the tune of a silly birthday song. "Oh-seven-three, four-four-one..." Emil thought it was a joke. Then, on the Saturday, in the crowd between the fish stalls and the flower carts, he lost his father's hand. He found the information booth with the big blue i. His legs were shaking, his voice was shaking, but when the woman asked for a number, the song came out on its own: "Oh-seven-three, four-four-one..." She dialled. Javier answered on the first ring. In a minute he was there, lifting Emil off the ground.

What tune did they sing the phone number to?
A silly birthday song.
How was Emil feeling at the information booth?
He was frightened and shaking, but the practised song let him give the number anyway.
What else could Emil's family add to the plan, and why?
They could agree a meeting spot as well, in case the booth is closed or far away.
How does the song trick look to Javier now?
Javier probably feels deeply relieved and glad that the silly nightly song worked when it mattered.

Sunday, late

I checked the bank app four times today. Jasleen doesn't know. Or maybe she does.

It's been six weeks since I found out about the loan. She's told me everything, I think. She cries when she talks about it. And still I look at her face when her phone buzzes, trying to read it. When she said she'd be late from the office on Thursday, I felt my stomach drop, and I asked three questions in a row like a policeman.

She said quietly, "Jatin, I feel like I'm living with a detective." She's right. I hate it too.

It isn't that I want to punish her. I think my mind is trying to make sure nothing surprises me like that again. But I'm so tired. I'm her husband, not her guard.

Maybe it's time to talk to someone about this. Both of us.

How many times did Jatin check the bank app today?
He checked it four times.
What is Jatin feeling after six weeks of checking?
He is exhausted and anxious, afraid of another shock, and unhappy about acting like a guard.
What turning point is available to Jatin now?
He could tell Jasleen honestly about the checking and suggest they see a counsellor together, as he is already considering.
How does Jasleen experience Jatin's watchfulness?
Jasleen feels watched rather than forgiven, as if living with a detective.

It is a light frame or bed with handles used to carry a sick or injured person. It is a noun.

Couples counsellor's note, session 4, Saurabh and Rashmi.

Today Rashmi said, calmly, that Saurabh leaves all the planning of family events to her. Before she had finished, Saurabh was answering: "That's not true, I booked the cab for Diwali, and you never let me plan anyway, and your mother..." He spoke fast, leaning forward.

I asked him to stop and breathe. I asked what he felt when Rashmi spoke. After a pause: "Like I'm a failure. Like she's listing why I'm not good enough."

We practised again. Rashmi repeated her point. Saurabh breathed. Then he said, slowly, "Some of that's true. I leave most of it to you. I'm sorry." Rashmi's eyes filled.

Only after that did he add his side about wanting to be included in decisions. Rashmi listened properly this time.

Homework: when a complaint comes, first name one true thing in it.

- Noor

What did Saurabh say he booked for Diwali?
Saurabh said he booked the cab for Diwali.
What was Saurabh feeling when he answered so fast?
Saurabh felt like a failure, as if Rashmi were listing why he wasn't good enough, so he got defensive.
What did Noor teach Saurabh to do first when criticised?
Noor taught him to breathe, name what was true in the complaint and apologise before giving his own side.
How did Rashmi respond when Saurabh owned part of the complaint?
Rashmi's eyes filled, showing she felt heard, and she then listened properly to his side.

Harsha and Yusuf, both new teachers at the government school in Jhalawar, rented two rooms above a cloth shop. By the third week Harsha had a count in his head. Yusuf's tea glass on the window: washed it. Yusuf's dal pot with the burnt bottom: scrubbed it. Yusuf's plate under the charpai: found it, washed it. Nothing was said. But Harsha began banging the steel pots, sighing loudly, answering Yusuf's jokes with one word. One evening, scraping at the pot again, he nearly said something sharp. Instead he dried his hands, sat down across from Yusuf and said calmly, "Bhai, I've been washing your dishes for three weeks and getting annoyed without telling you. Can we split it? You wash on odd dates, I do even." Yusuf went red. "I thought you didn't mind. You never said." They wrote the rota on the back of a school timetable and stuck it by the tap. The banging stopped.

Where did Harsha and Yusuf rent their rooms?
Two rooms above a cloth shop in Jhalawar.
What was Harsha feeling during those three weeks, and how did it show?
He was growing resentful, and it came out as banging pots, loud sighs and one-word answers rather than words.
Which choice worked, and why?
Sitting down and saying calmly what was bothering him, with a simple odd-and-even rota, fixed the problem that weeks of silent anger had not.
How did Yusuf see the situation before Harsha spoke?
Yusuf honestly thought Harsha didn't mind, so he was embarrassed to learn about the three weeks, going red.

For a month Anders had been dragging himself through his job at the Oslo shipping office. He drank water constantly and was still thirsty, went to bed early and still woke up exhausted. He tried cutting sugar, walking at lunch, sleeping more. Nothing changed. 'Maybe I'm just lazy,' he told his sister Olga over dinner. Olga put down her fork. 'Lazy people aren't thirsty all day. That's your body saying something. Book a doctor.' Anders hesitated; he hated fuss. But the next morning he called the clinic, got an appointment for Thursday, and wrote down everything he'd noticed so he wouldn't forget.

When was Anders's appointment?
Thursday.
Why did Anders hesitate before booking the doctor?
He felt reluctant to make a fuss and half-believed he was just lazy.
What made Anders's response a sensible one?
When rest and small changes didn't help, he booked a doctor and wrote down what he'd noticed instead of guessing.
How did Olga see Anders's tiredness?
Olga felt concerned and saw it as a body signal, not laziness, so she urged a doctor.

Okay, so the podcast wants to know about our society rule? I'm Tushar, and last year our housing society banned kids from playing in the compound after six.
All of us were furious. Some boys wanted to put up angry posters. I said, let's go to the committee meeting instead.
My hands were sweating. I told Hafsa aunty, the secretary, “Aunty, I understand you're worried about the cars and the noise. But I don't think it's fair to stop all play after six, especially in winter when it gets dark at six.”
She raised her eyebrows. A couple of uncles muttered. But she said, “Fine, what do you suggest?”
We suggested the back lawn, till seven, no cricket balls near parked cars. They agreed to try it for a month. It's still the rule now.

What time did the society ban play after?
It banned kids from playing in the compound after six.
What was Tushar feeling as he spoke at the meeting?
Tushar felt nervous, with sweating hands, but determined to be heard respectfully instead of through angry posters.
Why did Tushar's approach work better than angry posters?
Tushar showed an understanding of the committee's worries and offered a clear compromise, so the adults could say yes without losing face.
How might Hafsa aunty have seen the kids' request?
She may have been surprised by the calm, respectful way Tushar spoke, which made her open to asking for his suggestion.

While I was making it I felt like I'd already done half of the studying. Calm and lucky and like I'm moving forward. Tomorrow I'll start Chapter 1. Well, tomorrow I'll make a revision-week chart so it's ready.
Actually the science book is still in the plastic cover and I haven't opened a single chapter. It's fine. The chart is so neat that studying will be easy once I begin.

Maths is pink on the chart.

"Does it get easier?" Baljeet asked. "Being around dying people every day?"

Vasudha, a nurse at the hospice for two years, stirred her tea in the canteen. "Easier isn't the word. Calmer, maybe."

"How?"

"When I started, I was scared all the time. Scared of saying the wrong thing. Scared of my own parents getting old." She paused. "Then I noticed what patients talk about at the end."

"Which is?"

"Almost nobody talks about their job title. They talk about who they forgave, who they didn't call. One man asked me to phone his brother, whom he hadn't spoken to in twenty years."

Baljeet put his cup down. "And did the brother come?"

"He came. They didn't say much. They held hands."

"So what did you change?"

"I call my sister even when we've fought. I'm doing my master's in palliative care so I can teach younger nurses." She smiled. "I think about death more than you. But I'm less afraid of it."

How long has Vasudha been a nurse at the hospice?
Vasudha has been a nurse at the hospice for two years.
How has Vasudha's feeling about death changed since she started?
She was scared all the time at first, but now she feels calmer and less afraid, even though she thinks about death often.
What did Vasudha change after listening to patients, and why?
She calls her sister even after fights and is studying to teach younger nurses, because patients showed her that relationships and passing on care matter most.
How might Baljeet see death differently after this conversation?
Baljeet started curious and perhaps uneasy, but may now see thinking about death as a way to focus on relationships.

Dear Pranav,

You asked how I am finding time for maths. Here is the trick I stumbled on. Last month I kept a little tally: at night my sums took forever and I made silly mistakes, but at six in the morning they came fast. So now I wake at 5:45, do maths for an hour with a cup of tea, and the hardest thing of my day is done. In the evening I only read my Hindi and history notes, or a novel for twenty minutes, because my brain is tired then and that is fine. I have done this for two weeks and I no longer dread Tuesday's maths class. Try tracking when you feel sharpest. See you at cricket on Sunday!

Imran

At what time does Imran wake up?
Imran wakes at 5:45.
How does Imran feel about maths class now?
Imran feels less afraid, since Tuesday's maths class is no longer dreaded.
What could Imran do if a family event stops the early mornings?
Imran could move the maths hour to another clear time and check whether the mistakes stay low.
How might Pranav see the advice?
Pranav might be curious and try tracking the hours that feel sharpest.

At eleven at night the birdwatchers' forum went down, and Varun, the volunteer moderator, sat at the kitchen table with cold tea and two hundred angry notifications. Vinita's post was the loudest: “Moderators are useless, my photo was removed for no reason!” Varun opened the written rules and read the third one again: no photos of nests. Her picture showed a nest. He replied politely, quoting the rule and offering to restore the photo with the nest hidden. Vinita answered with a complaint about favouritism. Another member asked why a similar photo had stayed. Varun took a breath, checked, found that it had been posted before the rule was added, and explained it the same way. By one o'clock the forum was up, and he was tired but steady.

Which rule did Varun read again?
Varun read the third rule again: no photos of nests.
What was Varun feeling as the notifications piled up at night?
Varun felt tired and under pressure, but wanted to be fair, so he went back to the written rules.
What choice helped Varun handle both complaints?
Varun replied politely by quoting the written rule, checked the other photo's date and explained it the same way, keeping consistent.
How might Vinita have felt when Vinita's photo was removed?
Vinita probably felt unfairly treated and embarrassed in front of others, which shows in the loud complaint and the accusation of favouritism.

Saturday night.
Finally quizzed three seniors, all hired last year, on how they actually got their jobs. Uma first. She said: not through the big job portal. She did a three-month internship at a small company, and the manager referred her. The second senior: a referral from an alumnus after one coffee call. The third: also a small company, found through a professor's contact. Not one of them got in through the portal I've been feeding for weeks. I had assumed portals were the main road. Now I'm rearranging: internship listings at small firms, a list of ten alumni to message, and one hour a week on the portal instead of every night. I feel lighter, and a bit silly for not asking sooner.
— Vidya

How did Uma get her job?
Uma did a three-month internship at a small company, and the manager referred her.
How does Vidya feel after talking to the seniors?
Vidya feels lighter and a bit silly for not asking sooner.
What could Vidya do next?
Vidya could message the ten alumni and look for internships at small firms, since those routes worked for the seniors.
How might the seniors have felt about being asked?
The seniors were probably happy to help, since all three gave clear answers about how they got in.

messages.content: Write a thank-you to a volunteer who planted trees, in exactly four sentences.
Thank you for planting trees in our neighbourhood. Your hard work will give us shade for years. The children enjoyed helping you dig. We hope to join you again.
My host said "make yourself at home". Can I sleep on his sofa?

The phrase means to relax and feel comfortable, but it does not mean you may do anything you like. Be considerate and ask if you are unsure.
Example: Please come in and make yourself at home.

Lights-out at the residential school in Pachmarhi was at ten, but Abhinav, thirteen, was still awake at midnight. The dorm smelled of phenyl and damp socks. At home, the pressure cooker would have whistled hours ago, Maa's dal-baati would be finished, and Papa would be locking the gate with the squeak he never oiled. Here there was only a dripping tap and eleven boys breathing. Abhinav pulled the blanket over his head and pressed his lips together hard. From the next bunk, Irfan whispered, "You awake?" Abhinav wiped his face quickly. "Mosquito," he said. "Keeps biting." He didn't want Irfan thinking he was a baby who missed his Maa. He lay still until Irfan's breathing slowed, then played the gate's squeak in his head until he slept.

What did the dorm smell of?
Phenyl and damp socks.
Why did Abhinav blame a mosquito?
He was afraid Irfan would think he was childish for missing home and Maa, so he hid his tears.
What could help Abhinav with homesickness at the hostel?
He could talk to a house parent or call home at a set time, and maybe find out that Irfan misses home too.
What might Irfan have been feeling when he whispered "You awake?"
Irfan might have been lonely or homesick himself, reaching out in the dark.

Sunday night
Went with Swati and her family to the Jain temple for Paryushan today. First time.
I was nervous. Swati had told me: no leather, no food inside, don't touch the idols, wash hands and feet first. I borrowed cloth shoes from my brother and kept my wallet at home.
Inside, it was quiet and white and smelled of sandalwood. Swati's grandmother was doing a long prayer, and I just sat at the back. I didn't understand the words, but I understood the stillness.
Afterwards I asked Swati's grandmother why they say sorry to everyone during Paryushan. She said, "Michchhami Dukkadam. We ask forgiveness for any hurt, even ones we don't know we caused." I found that beautiful.
I'm not becoming Jain. Swati knows that, and her family didn't ask me to. I just wanted to understand her better, and I think I do.
Vikas

What did Swati tell Vikas not to wear or bring?
Swati said no leather, no food inside, don't touch the idols, and wash hands and feet first.
How did Vikas feel sitting at the back during the prayer?
Vikas felt nervous at first and then calm and moved by the stillness, even without understanding the words.
Why is Vikas's approach a good model for visiting another faith?
Vikas prepared by learning the rules, stayed respectful and quiet, and asked a genuine question afterwards, all without any aim of changing belief.
How might Swati's grandmother see Vikas's question?
She probably felt pleased and warm that a young visitor wanted to understand the meaning of Paryushan.

"No-o-o!" muttered Dolokhov through his teeth, "no, it's not over." And after stumbling a few staggering steps right up to the saber, he sank on the snow beside it. His left hand was bloody; he wiped it on his coat and supported himself with it. His frowning face was pallid and quivered.

Is Dolokhov ready to give up the duel? How can you tell?
No. He mutters that it is not over, staggers forward and sinks into the snow, then leans on his bloody hand to hold himself up.

Thursday night.
I found out today. The lab data I shared with Sabina last week, three whole hours of readings, went into her report under her name alone, and she got the top mark in the practical. She never even said thanks. When I asked, she shrugged: 'Everyone shares data.' Except she's never shared anything with me. Ever. I feel so stupid. I've been the one who helps all year, and this is what it gets me. I want to lock my notebook and never help anyone again. But then I think of Akash, who stayed up with me before the viva, and Tenzin, who lends me his calculator every single class. If I shut everyone out because of Sabina, I lose them too. Tomorrow I'll talk to the lab instructor about the data, calmly. And I'll keep sharing with people who share back.
Santosh

Three whole hours of readings.

Santosh feels stupid and angry, used after being the helpful one all year.

To raise the data issue calmly with the lab instructor and keep sharing with people who share back, rather than shutting everyone out.
How might Akash and Tenzin be affected if Santosh stopped sharing?
