It had rained all night, so the assembly moved into the small hall, and the microphone died.
Harsha stood at the front with his poem. His heart was banging. His mouth felt like cotton. He said the first line. Then nothing. The second line had gone.
A boy giggled. Harsha's face burned. Gautam sir quietly walked up and said the first word of the line. Harsha finished, too fast and too soft, and ran back to his place.
That week Gautam sir asked him to say the poem only to him, in the empty classroom. Then to three friends at lunch. Then to his little sister at home. On Monday he said it to the class from his own desk. His hands still shook a little. He didn't forget a single line.

Why did the assembly move into the small school hall?
It had rained all night.
What was Harsha feeling when the second line went?
Harsha was frightened and ashamed; his heart was banging, his mouth was dry and his face burned when a boy giggled.
Which of Gautam sir's steps helped most, and why?
Having Harsha say the poem to one person, then three friends, then his sister, because small, safe practice made the class feel less scary.
How might Gautam sir have felt watching Harsha freeze?
Gautam sir was probably concerned and kind, stepping up quietly to give one word rather than letting Harsha struggle alone.

Dilnaz, you're wondering whether to forgive your friend. Let me tell you about Farhan.
When we were fifteen, Farhan told the whole class that I'd cried at my grandfather's funeral. I felt stripped bare. For two weeks I didn't speak to him.
Then he came to our door with his father. He didn't bring sweets or excuses. He said, "I did it because I wanted to seem important. It was cruel. I'm sorry." And he stood there, waiting, not demanding anything.
I didn't hug him. That was the turning point: I said, "Okay. Let's see."
I started small. I lent him my cricket bat. He returned it the next day. I told him something small, that I liked a girl in class. It stayed secret. Months of that.
By the next year, I told him bigger things. It wasn't the apology that rebuilt it, Dilnaz. It was the returning, again and again. That's your Mohit Mamu's advice.

What did Farhan tell the class about young Mohit?
That he had cried at his grandfather's funeral.
How did young Mohit feel after Farhan's apology?
He was cautious and still hurt, so he chose to trust Farhan slowly rather than hug him and pretend all was fine.
What was the turning point in how Mohit rebuilt trust?
He said 'Okay, let's see' and tested Farhan with small things like the bat and a small secret before sharing bigger ones.
How might Farhan have felt standing at the door waiting?
Farhan likely felt ashamed and nervous, hoping for forgiveness but accepting that he could not demand it.

Thursday night
Taught Dad the bank app again. Third time this month. He wrote everything in his little notebook last time and still got lost at the password screen.
I felt myself getting sharp. Then I noticed his hand shaking a little on the phone, and how he kept saying, "Sorry, son, I'm slow now." This is Kiran, the man the whole building used to call to fix every fuse and tap.
So I slowed down. One step, then wait. I let him type. When he got it wrong, I said, "That's fine, that screen confuses everyone." It took forty minutes. At the end he checked his balance himself and grinned.
He said, "Thank you for not making me feel old." That's the line I'm writing down.
Thomas

How long did the lesson take?
Forty minutes.
What made Thomas slow down?
Thomas felt tenderness and respect on noticing Kiran's shaking hand and apology, remembering him as the man who fixed everything.
What did Thomas do that made the lesson go well?
He went one step at a time, let Kiran type, and reassured him that the screen confuses everyone.
How did Kiran feel at the end?
Kiran felt grateful and pleased, grinning and thanking Thomas for not making him feel old.

At the hospital in Lucknow, Pranav led the operations team. Before each big change, he wrote a short entry in a register: the decision, the reasons, what could go wrong, and how sure the team was. When they moved the outpatient queue to a new token system, he wrote: "Should cut waiting by a lot. Seventy percent sure. Risk: older patients may struggle with tokens." A month later, waiting times had barely changed. At the review, some staff blamed Salma, who had designed the system. Pranav opened the register. "We expected risk with older patients. That's what happened. The design was sound; the help desk wasn't ready." Salma's shoulders dropped with relief. The team decided to add two volunteers at the token counter. Nobody was scolded. Everyone learned something.

What risk did Pranav write down before the token system?
Older patients may struggle with tokens.
How did Salma feel when Pranav opened the register?
Salma felt relieved, her shoulders dropping, because the record showed the problem was expected and not her fault.
What did the register allow the team to do?
It let them compare the decision with what happened, find the real gap at the help desk, and fix it without blaming anyone.
How might the staff who blamed Salma see the review afterward?
They might feel a little embarrassed, but also clearer about what really went wrong.

Beta, you want to know about best friends? When I was ten, in our lane in Lucknow, Naveen was mine. Only mine. People called me Farhan the shadow. We shared one bicycle, one tiffin and every secret. I told him I was scared of the dark and still slept holding Ammi's dupatta. He swore on his cricket bat he'd never tell. Two weeks later, in front of the whole class, he said it out loud, and everyone laughed. I went home and wouldn't eat. It felt as if the floor had gone. For a month I sat alone. Then Naveen came to our gate, red in the face, and said sorry. I forgave him slowly. Your Dadi says I still pick friends carefully. But I still pick them.

What secret did Farhan tell Naveen?
That Farhan was scared of the dark and still slept holding Ammi's dupatta.
How did Farhan feel after Naveen told the class?
Farhan felt devastated and betrayed, refused to eat at home and felt as if the floor had gone.
When Naveen came to the gate, what choice did Farhan face, and what came of it?
Farhan could stay shut off or forgive slowly. Forgiving slowly saved the friendship and led to careful trust instead of no trust.
Why might Naveen have come to the gate red in the face?

Okay, Varun, you want the truth about that ten-day silent course? Day one, I, Aparna, the girl who talks in her sleep, nearly left by lunch. No phone, no books, no talking. Just sitting and feeling air go in and out of my nose. My brain was like a railway station. Day four, I cried for no reason in the afternoon sitting, and the teacher only said, "Notice it, and come back to the breath." Day seven, I heard rain start on the tin roof and actually heard it, the whole thing, start to finish. Now? I'm no calm saint. I still check mail in meetings. But when I catch myself doing three things at once, I stop and take five breaths. That's it. Five breaths. My manager thinks I've become "very focused". Really I've just become slower at getting distracted.

What did Aparna hear on day seven?
Rain starting on the tin roof.
What might Aparna have been feeling when crying on day four?
Aparna was probably overwhelmed and unsettled as the silence let buried feelings rise, even without a clear reason.
Which habit from the course is most usable at work, and why?
Taking five breaths on noticing three things at once, because it is short enough to use anywhere and interrupts multitasking.
How does Aparna's manager see the change?
The manager sees a more focused employee, without knowing it comes from small pauses rather than a new personality.

Sunday
Today was the last day of the book fair and I couldn't buy the space encyclopedia. Why? Because two weeks ago Lavanya said, "Lend me your two hundred, I'll return it Monday, pakka." I gave it all. Monday came. Then another Monday. Every time I opened my mouth to ask, it felt like begging for a favour, not asking for my own money. Today at the fair I finally asked. Lavanya slapped her forehead. "Oh no, I totally forgot!" She wasn't lying, I think. She said she'd bring it on Tuesday. But the fair is over. New rule for me: small amounts only, and we say the day out loud before I hand anything over.
Pranav

The space encyclopedia.

It felt like begging for a favour, so Pranav felt uncomfortable and kept putting it off.
What other approach could help Pranav if Tuesday passes too?

It poured all Diwali evening, and the courtyard where Parul's family always made rangoli was a puddle. Parul, five, pressed her nose to the window.

"No rangoli this year?" she wailed.

Her big brother Ujjwal thought, then spread newspaper on the living room floor. "Our family always makes one. We'll just make it inside."

They used rice flour and turmeric. Parul pressed her small handprint in the middle, like Ma did every year.

"This is our Diwali way," she said, very proud.

What did they use to make the rangoli indoors?
They used rice flour and turmeric.
What was Parul feeling when she saw the courtyard?
She was upset and disappointed, pressing her nose to the window and wailing that there would be no rangoli.
What did Ujjwal do that helped keep the tradition?
He adapted the tradition by moving it indoors, showing that the family's way could continue despite the rain.
How might Ma feel seeing Parul's handprint in the rangoli?
She would probably feel touched that Parul copied her own yearly habit.
I am very afraid from dogs since my childhood. Two things are wrong, I think.

I have been very afraid of dogs since my childhood.
Why: "afraid of", not "from"; "since" needs the present perfect.
What is the fee for one month at the local swimming pool?
I can't check the fee, because fees change and I can't see them. The pool's front desk or website will list the rate.

Chinmay, you're saying your whole plan is just a list of don'ts. Let your Reena Masi tell you something.
When I was twenty-five and running my first clinic shift roster, I wrote rules for myself. No double shifts. No gaps at night. No nurse working three weekends running. It was a good list. Nobody could complain.
But after two months I felt like a traffic policewoman. Just stopping bad things. My roster was safe and my nurses were tired of it and so was I.
One evening I thought, where am I actually trying to go? So I added one aim each month. First month, every nurse gets one full weekend off. Next month, each senior teaches one junior a skill on shift.
Same don'ts, but now they were guarding something. That's what changed, beta.

What was Reena's aim for the first month?
Every nurse gets one full weekend off.
How was Reena feeling after two months of only following her rules?
Reena felt tired and flat, like a traffic policewoman just stopping bad things.
When Reena felt like a traffic policewoman, what else could she have done, and how might it have gone?
She could have kept only the don'ts, but the nurses would likely have stayed tired and the roster would have had no purpose.
How might the nurses have seen the new monthly aims?
They may have felt more cared for and more motivated, with full weekends off and chances to learn skills from seniors.

Pranav: what do YOU like writing about?
Pooja: rain. old houses. my nani's stories
Pranav: so write one of those. just for you. don't even show her
Pooja: hmm. ok i will
Pooja: still gonna frame the best-in-class comment though
Pranav: obviously

What did Menon ma'am do with Pooja's essay?
She read it out loud.
How did Pooja feel when Menon ma'am didn't comment on her essay?
She felt worthless and upset enough to cry in the bathroom, showing how much she depends on the teacher's approval.
What did Pranav suggest, and why is it wise?
To write something just for herself about what she loves, which helps build her own drive instead of depending on praise.
How might Menon ma'am see Pooja's writing?
Menon ma'am seems to admire Pooja's work, calling it the best in the class, likely without knowing how much Pooja relies on her praise.

Nicholas dismounted, and with Natasha and Petya, who had ridden up, stopped near the hounds, waiting to see how the matter would end. Out of the bushes came the huntsman who had been fighting and rode toward his young master, with the fox tied to his crupper. While still at a distance he took off his cap and tried to speak respectfully, but he was pale and breathless and his face was angry. One of his eyes was black, but he probably was not even aware of it.

What state is the huntsman in when he rides toward his young master?
The huntsman, who had been fighting, rides up with the fox tied behind his saddle. He is pale, breathless and angry in the face, and has a black eye that he is probably not even aware of.

In the one-room school outside Bhilwara, Usha Ma'am once said, "Vishal is weak at maths, let him copy from the board." She didn't say it again. She didn't need to. When she asked questions, her eyes moved past Vishal to the front row. If he started to answer, she waited only a moment before turning to someone else. Nobody asked him to come to the board anymore. By winter, Vishal kept his hand in his lap even when he knew the answer. He counted his father's goat money correctly every evening at home, but at school he left the sums blank. "I am weak," he told his little sister when she asked for help.

What did Vishal count correctly every evening at home?
His father's goat money.
Why did Vishal keep his hand in his lap even when he knew the answer?
After being called weak and passed over again and again, he felt discouraged and came to believe he was bad at maths, so trying seemed pointless.
What could Usha Ma'am change in how she asks questions?
She could wait as long for Vishal as for the front row and invite him to the board again, showing she expects him to be able to answer.
How might Vishal's little sister be affected when he says "I am weak"?
She loses a helper, and she may learn from her brother that a label means you stop trying. 😔

metadata.subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]

"Tanvir! Watch out!" Devika yanked his arm. A cyclist swerved past, bell ringing furiously, and shouted something rude.
"What? Where did he come from?"
"From right in front of you. You were looking straight at him."
"I was not. I was looking at... the road."
"You were looking at your phone, which was in front of the road."
Tanvir stared at the screen: a half-typed reply about the cricket match. "I swear I didn't see him."
"I know. That's the scary part. Your eyes were open. Your brain was in the group chat."
"Okay, okay."
"Not okay-okay. Phone in your pocket till we're home. I'm holding you to it."
He slid the phone into his pocket. His heart was still thumping. "Fine. And... thanks."

What was Tanvir typing when the cyclist swerved?
A half-typed reply about the cricket match.
Why does Tanvir insist he didn't see the cyclist?
Tanvir feels shocked and scared, genuinely unaware because his attention was in the group chat, even though his eyes were open.
What rule does Devika set, and why is it a good one?
Phone in the pocket till they're home, so Tanvir's attention stays on the road.
How does Devika see what happened?
Devika sees it as scary rather than silly: his eyes were open, but his mind was in the chat.

Read this:

I'm Aparna, the only woman in Pradeep sir's architecture studio, and for eight months I thought I was the lucky one.

He'd picked me as his mentee. "I'll teach you everything," he said. At first he did. Then the "learning" changed. I picked up his dry-cleaning. I booked his daughter's dance classes. I drew the full plans for the hospital wing, and at the client meeting he presented them as his, without my name.

I felt torn. He had opened doors for me. Maybe this was just how it worked? But every evening I went home angry, and I hadn't designed anything of my own in months.

One Monday I said it, as calmly as I could. "Sir, I'm grateful for your guidance. But I want the errands to stop, and I'd like my name on the hospital drawings. I'm here to learn design."

He looked offended. "Ungrateful." Two weeks later, nothing had changed. I applied elsewhere. I start at a new firm in June.

What did Aparna pick up for Pradeep sir?
She picked up his dry-cleaning.
How did Aparna feel about the errands and the lost credit?
Aparna felt torn between loyalty and unfairness, going home angry every evening.
Why was leaving the right step for Aparna after speaking up?
She had spoken up calmly and asked for fair learning and recognition, and when nothing changed, leaving stopped the exploitation.
How did Pradeep sir see Aparna's request?
Pradeep sir saw it as ingratitude, calling her "Ungrateful" instead of addressing the problem.

Read this:

Day 1: Darshan accepted the junior accountant offer in Coimbatore without a single question. Asking about pay felt like haggling at a temple, something decent people didn't do. His father had always said, 'Take what is given.'
Day 40: At lunch, Keerthana, who had joined the same week, mentioned she had asked for a small increase before signing and got it. Darshan smiled and said nothing. That night he lay awake, irritated at her, then at himself. The resentment sat in his chest for days.
Day 55: Keerthana noticed his cold replies and asked what was wrong. He told her. 'Asking isn't greedy,' she said. 'It's just a conversation. They can say no.' Darshan wrote down what he had taken on since joining, including two extra client files, and asked his manager for a meeting about the upcoming review. His voice shook at first. The manager listened, nodded and said she would note it for the review in March.

How many extra client files had Darshan taken on?
Darshan had taken on two extra client files.
What was Darshan feeling on Day 40 after lunch?
Darshan felt irritated and resentful, first at Keerthana and then at himself.
What did Darshan do on Day 55 instead of stewing?
He listed the extra work he had taken on and asked his manager for a meeting about the review.
How does Keerthana see asking about pay?
Keerthana sees it as an ordinary conversation where the answer can be no, not something greedy.

Question time:
My teacher used the word "rehearsal". What is it?
Meaning of "hit the nail on the head"?
Which is correct, "sandwhich" or "sandwich"?

1. As a noun, "rehearsal" means a practice of a play or show before the real performance.
2. It means to say or do exactly the right thing. For example: your answer hit the nail on the head.
3. It is "sandwich". There is no "h" after the "w".

People think this only happens with girlfriends. For me it was my best friend, Keerthana. I'm Wasim, Class 11, and last year if she didn't answer by lunch I'd assume she'd dropped me for the debate crowd. Message after message. One day I had three unanswered and was typing a fourth, something sarcastic, when my sister said, "Put it down. What are you actually scared of?" I said, "That she doesn't need me." Saying it out loud felt silly, and also lighter. So I asked Keerthana straight: "Are we okay? I get jumpy when you go quiet." She laughed and said her phone had been taken in class. Since then I've joined the photography club. It helps to have more than one person in my world.

What was Wasim typing when the sister spoke?
A fourth message, something sarcastic.
How did Wasim feel after saying the fear out loud?
Wasim felt silly but also lighter, because naming the fear took away some of its power.
What would you advise someone in Wasim's place, based on what worked?
Pause before the next message, name the fear and ask the friend directly, while also building other friendships and interests.
How does Keerthana seem to react to Wasim's direct question?
Keerthana takes it lightly and laughs, explaining her phone was taken, which suggests the friendship was never in danger.
Whom does Catherine Earnshaw marry?
She marries Edgar Linton of Thrushcross Grange. She tells Nelly she will accept him partly because he is handsome, rich and fond of her.

Dear Tenzin,
I’ve been meaning to write since Sunday’s listening party. When I moved into the hostel in a new city, I ate dinner alone for a month. Then I found our fan group online and you, Mira and Joel wrote to me.
Someone drew my favourite character. Someone else shared a playlist when I had a bad week. On Sundays we listen together and talk about anything. When a group from another band mocked us, you said, “Let them be. We’re here for the songs.”
It’s the first place here that felt like mine. Thank you for that. ❤️
Sabina

How long did Sabina eat dinner alone after moving to the hostel?
Sabina ate dinner alone for a month after moving into the hostel.
What was Sabina feeling before finding the fan group?
Sabina was lonely in a new city, which is why the group felt like the first place that was Sabina's own.
What did Tenzin's reply to the mocking group show about how the fan group works?
Tenzin answered the mockery calmly and said they were there for the songs. It shows connection here does not depend on hating anyone.
What might Joel or Mira have felt on hearing Sabina's message?
They may have felt glad and a little proud that the group made a lonely person feel welcome. The letter thanks Tenzin mainly, so their feelings are a guess.

In their Hyderabad flat, Gopika Aunty from next door was draining rice when Asif, five, asked for her old colander. She gave it to him. He put it on his head. "Astronaut helmet!" Then he held it up to the window. "Look, the sun has holes!" He poured water through it over his toy elephant. "Rain shower." Then he tapped it with a spoon. "Drum!" Gopika Aunty lost count of what it became. When she asked for it back, it was a boat full of marbles.

What did Asif first call the colander?
An astronaut helmet.
How was Asif feeling as he found use after use?
Asif felt excited and playful, delighted with each new idea.
How could Gopika Aunty encourage Asif's imaginative thinking?
Give him safe everyday objects and ask 'What else could it be?' instead of telling him.
How might Gopika Aunty feel asking for her colander back?
She probably felt amused and impressed that it had become a boat full of marbles.

What is Holmes saying here? Answer in one line.

"No; a client. It seems that a young lady has arrived in a considerable state of excitement, who insists upon seeing me. She is waiting now in the sitting-room. Now, when young ladies wander about the metropolis at this hour of the morning, and knock sleepy people up out of their beds, I presume that it is something very pressing which they have to communicate. Should it prove to be an interesting case, you would, I am sure, wish to follow it from the outset. I thought, at any rate, that I should call you and give you the chance."
Holmes tells a friend an excited young woman has come for help this early, so it must be urgent, and invites the friend along.

"They closed it," Pranav said, dropping the letter on the hostel bed. "The anti-ragging committee. 'Insufficient evidence.'"

Dhruv picked it up. "After what those seniors did to you?"

"And now they're saying I'm a troublemaker. My warden told me to 'let it go for my own good.'"

Dhruv sat down next to him. "Pranav, this isn't your fault. The college failed you."

"It feels like they're punishing me for speaking."

"They are. That's on them." Dhruv opened his laptop. "Do you still have the messages they sent?"

"Screenshots. And the date I went to the clinic."

"Good. Keep everything. There's a national anti-ragging helpline, outside the college. And the legal aid clinic at the law college does free advice on Saturdays."

Pranav stared at the screen. "You think anyone will listen?"

"I'm listening. Your parents will. Call them tonight." Dhruv pushed the phone toward him. "Then we call the helpline together tomorrow morning."

What reason did the committee give for closing the complaint?
"Insufficient evidence."
What was Pranav feeling after the complaint was closed?
He felt betrayed and punished, as if the college was blaming him for speaking up.
What steps did Dhruv suggest, and why are they useful?
Keeping all screenshots and clinic dates, calling the national anti-ragging helpline, using free legal aid, and telling his parents, which moves the complaint outside the college that failed him.
How does Dhruv see the college's response?
Dhruv sees it as the college failing Pranav, not Pranav's fault, and stands by him.
The dog snarled at the stranger. I need snarled explained.

Snarled means growled in a fierce, angry way, usually showing the teeth. It is a verb, the past tense of snarl.
Example: The stray dog snarled when the boy came too close to its food.

After Lalremsiami's father lost his job in March, the flat in Aizawl went quiet in a heavy way. Her parents talked in low voices. Lalremsiami, fifteen, felt like the ground had gone soft under her.
She stopped doing homework. What was the point, if everything was falling apart?
The school counsellor, Mr Darshan, didn't give her advice. He gave her a sheet of paper with a line down the middle. “Left side: things you can influence. Right side: things you can't.”
Right side came fast: Papa's job. Money. Whether we move.
Left side was slower: Study for one hour after school. Help Mama with dinner. Talk to Mr Darshan on Thursdays. Tell Papa I love him.
She stuck the sheet inside her cupboard. That night she did one hour of history. It didn't fix anything. But for an hour, she felt a little less helpless.

What was on the right side of Lalremsiami's list first?
Papa's job, money and whether they move.
How did Lalremsiami feel after doing an hour of history that night?
She felt a little less helpless, even though nothing at home was fixed.
Why did the two-column list help?
It separated what she could influence from what she couldn't, and acting on the first list gave her back some sense of power.
How might Lalremsiami's father feel if she tells him she loves him?
He would likely feel touched and comforted during a hard time.

Counsellor's note, session three. Santosh came in again with a folder: printed articles on the stages of grief, a timeline of his grandmother's illness, questions about "what the research says". His mind is sharp, and it helps him. Today I asked, "After you understand it, where does the feeling go?" He was quiet, then said he hadn't cried once. We agreed he would keep the folder, and also try twenty minutes each evening just for remembering her, no reading. His friend Elizabeth has offered to sit with him on Sundays. Next week we will talk about how that went.

What was in Santosh's folder?
Printed articles on the stages of grief and a timeline of his grandmother's illness.
How might Santosh have felt when he admitted he hadn't cried?
Quiet and perhaps a little surprised or uneasy, realising his understanding had kept the sadness away.
What plan did they agree on?
Keep the folder, add twenty minutes each evening just for remembering her, and let Elizabeth sit with him on Sundays.
How might Elizabeth feel offering to sit with him?
Caring and supportive, glad to help him feel less alone.

metadata.subtype: Letting thinking and feeling share the table [Response]

Back from the zoo in Mysuru, Shankar, five, burst through the flat door. "Amma! Th-th-th-the elephant, it, it, it squirted water on a man!" His eyes squeezed tight on the "th," his cheeks tense. He didn't seem to notice; the story kept pouring out. Payal, his mother, knelt to his height and kept looking at him, not rushing. She didn't finish his sentence, though she could guess it. "Really? On a man? What did the man do?" "He, he, he jumped!" Shankar shouted, laughing, and hopped across the room to show her. She laughed with him.

What did the elephant do at the zoo?
The elephant squirted water on a man.
How was Shankar feeling as he told the story?
He was excited and happy, so eager to share that he did not seem to notice the repeated sounds.
What did Payal do that helped Shankar keep talking?
She knelt, kept looking at him, waited calmly and did not finish his sentence, then asked about his story.
How might Payal feel listening to Shankar's elephant story?
She seems amused and happy, laughing with him and enjoying his excitement rather than worrying about his words.

At the students’ union meeting in the small college hall, Pankaj stood up and proposed a shared cycle stand and a bicycle-lending scheme for students who travel from distant villages. Someone laughed. “Cycles? We want a canteen!” More laughter came from the back, and Pankaj sat down, red-faced.
I’m Kavitha, and I was near the front. I didn’t laugh. I raised my hand and asked, “How many students come from that far, and how do they get here now?”
Pankaj stood up again and said, “Almost forty. Many walk an hour.” The hall went silent. The chair wrote the number down.

What did Pankaj propose at the meeting?
Pankaj proposed a shared cycle stand and a bicycle-lending scheme for students who travel from distant villages.
What might Kavitha have been feeling when the hall laughed at Pankaj?
Kavitha probably felt uncomfortable with the laughter and curious about the idea, which is why Kavitha did not laugh and asked a real question instead.
Why was Kavitha's follow-up question useful?
It gave Pankaj a chance to explain with a real number and it showed respect for the idea. The answer changed how the hall reacted.
What might Pankaj have thought when the chair wrote the number down?
Pankaj might have felt relieved and heard for the first time, though the passage does not say what Pankaj thought.

Sana washed 13 cups and 20 plates. How many things did she wash?
And one more: Why do farmers want rain in the season for planting?
One more thing. Meaning of "curtain"?

1. It is 33. Because 13 + 20 = 33.
2. Seeds need water to sprout. Because rain gives the soil the water that plants use to grow.
3. A curtain is a piece of cloth that hangs over a window or door.

At the park near their flat in Lagos, Chidi ran straight to the sandpit where two older girls were digging, sat down beside them and shouted, 'Me dig!' When one girl laughed, he laughed louder and flung sand in the air. Then he tried to hug the smaller girl, who shrank back. His father Daniel knelt. 'She's shy. High five, not hug.' Chidi slapped her palm gently. On the walk home, alone in his pushchair, he went quiet and heavy-eyed.

What did Chidi shout at the sandpit?
'Me dig!'
Why did Chidi laugh louder and fling sand?
Being with the other children made him excited and full of energy.
Why was 'High five, not hug' a good limit?
It kept Chidi friendly while respecting the shy girl, giving him another way to connect.
How might the smaller girl feel when Chidi tries to hug her?
She probably felt startled and uncomfortable, shrinking back from a stranger's hug.

At the Thursday haat near their village, Chandrika bargained for mustard oil while Bidisha, her little sister, wandered to the bangle stall.
Three older boys started calling after Bidisha: "Look at her slippers, all stitched up! Beggar's girl!"
Chandrika was there before she even decided to go. "Say it again," she said, standing between them, voice low. "Go on." The boys backed off, muttering.
On the walk home along the paddy, Chandrika held Bidisha's wrist hard. "You don't wander off. You don't talk to anyone. You carry the oil. Walk faster."
Bidisha pulled her hand free. "You're not Maa."
Chandrika stopped. She thought of how she'd snapped at Bidisha that morning for using her comb, and yesterday for singing too loudly.
"Sorry," she said. "I was scared for you. And I'm always cross at home." She took the heavy oil can back and let Bidisha choose the path.

What did the boys tease Bidisha about?
Her stitched-up slippers.
What was Chandrika feeling when she stood between Bidisha and the boys?
She felt angry and fiercely protective of her little sister.
What went wrong on the walk home, and what fixed it?
Chandrika turned her protection into bossing Bidisha; apologising, admitting her fear, and letting Bidisha choose the path softened it.
How does Bidisha see Chandrika's bossiness on the walk home?
Bidisha feels controlled and hurt, which is why she pulls away and says Chandrika is not their mother.

Before the Rath Yatra crowd, Salma Phuppo had squeezed Pranav's shoulder. "If we get separated, meet me at the temple gate. The big one with the elephants." An hour later, in the pushing, singing crowd, Pranav lost her. Then the rain started, sheets of it, and everyone ran for cover. Pranav couldn't see the temple at all. His stomach flipped. But he knew exactly where he needed to be. He went into a sweet shop with its shutters half down and asked the owner, "Which way is the temple gate with the elephants?" The man pointed. "Straight, then left at the post box." Pranav walked, soaked, counting streets. At the gate, under the stone elephants, Phuppo was waiting, dripping and smiling.

What did the temple gate have on it?
Stone elephants.
How did Pranav feel when he couldn't see the temple in the rain?
He felt a flash of fear, his stomach flipping, but steadier once he remembered the meeting point.
What else could the family add to the plan for next time?
They could add a phone number for Pranav to give a shopkeeper, in case he can't reach the gate.
How does the meeting point look to Salma Phuppo?
Phuppo knows exactly where to wait, so she can stay calm even in the rain until Pranav arrives.

metadata.subtype: Approach: fixed meeting point agreed in advance [Action]

messages.content: The article calls him an inveterate reader. Is that good?

It can be. Inveterate means having a habit for a long time and not likely to change it. It is an adjective.
Example: Grandmother is an inveterate reader and finishes a book every week.
Rahul said the facts in the story do not "add up". Is he talking about sums?

Not here. When facts do not "add up", they do not make sense together, so something may be missing or wrong. It can also mean to total numbers.
Examples: His excuse does not add up, because the shop was closed. Add up the marks for all four sections.

At the vegetable market Jomon spotted a jar of orange sweets and asked for one. "Not today," said his father, Naveen, calmly. Jomon's face crumpled. He screamed, dropped flat on the wet floor and kicked off his sandals. His body felt huge and hot. Naveen crouched beside him, kept his voice low and said, "We are not buying sweets. Breathe with me. In, and out." Jomon gulped air until the screaming shrank to hiccups. Then he saw people watching and hid his face in his father's shirt. "You were upset, it's done now, and we'll sort out your sandals together," Naveen said, and they did. Next morning at school, Ujjwal threw his crayon box and shrieked when a puzzle piece would not fit. Jomon's tummy went tight. He backed away to the shelf, unsure what to do, then walked to the teacher and said, "Ujjwal is really loud." The teacher went to him gently. At snack time Jomon put a spare biscuit beside Ujjwal's cup and said nothing else.

What did Jomon spot at the market?
Jomon spotted a jar of orange sweets.
How was Jomon's own tantrum at the market different from the way he acted when Ujjwal had one at school?
At the market Jomon was the one overwhelmed and needed his father to stay calm and help him breathe, while at school he stepped back, told the teacher and was kind to Ujjwal later at snack time.
What was Jomon feeling when he hid his face in his father's shirt?
He felt embarrassed and sorry, because people were watching after his screaming.
What did Naveen do that helped Jomon, and what might have kept the shame stuck?
Naveen kept the limit, stayed calm and said it was over, so Jomon could fix things with him; calling Jomon bad would probably have left the shame stuck.

I live in the room next to Baljeet and Meenal, so I heard the whole thing last Sunday, Arohi here. First there was a week of slammed drawers. Then, Sunday afternoon, both of them at the table with a pad. I could hear pieces: "You take Monday and Thursday for the floor." "Then I get the kitchen on weekends." Later I saw a chart pinned up, with names rotating. On the same page they had written that lights and music go down at eleven on weeknights. And they agreed to put a small amount each into a jar for soap and cleaning things. I do not know if they were both happy. But they laughed twice, and the drawers stopped slamming. — Arohi

Who lives in the room next to Arohi?
Baljeet and Meenal live in the room next door.
What might Baljeet and Meenal have felt during the talk, judging by what Arohi saw?
They may have felt relief and some goodwill, since they laughed twice, though Arohi says the actual feeling is unknown.
What alternative approach could they use if the chart stops working, and why?
They could hold a short check-in after a month, because plans made in a hurry often need a small adjustment.
What is it like for Arohi to overhear this from the next room?
Arohi hears only pieces and can see the chart and the calmer drawers, so Arohi reports what was heard and avoids claiming to know their hearts.

Emil found Chidi on the stairwell of their building in Utrecht, holding the landlord's letter. The top-floor flat was free: a balcony facing the canal, the same rent, but twenty minutes further from the hospital where she worked. "So? Swap?" Emil asked. "My gut says no," Chidi said. "I'd lose my short ride." She sat on the step and tried something. Suppose she already lived upstairs. Would she give up the balcony, the morning light, the herbs she kept meaning to grow, just to save twenty minutes of cycling along the water? She laughed. "No. I wouldn't trade it back." "Then your gut was just scared of moving," Emil said. Chidi folded the letter carefully. "Maybe. Let me sleep on it, with both sides written down in front of me."

What did the top-floor flat offer?
A balcony facing the canal at the same rent, but twenty minutes further from the hospital.
Why did Chidi's first reaction lean towards saying no?
Losing the short ride felt heavier than gaining the balcony, so staying put felt safe and comfortable before she had weighed both sides.
Which trick helped Chidi, and why?
She imagined already living upstairs and asked whether she would give up the balcony for a shorter ride; flipping the frame made the gain feel as real as the loss.
How does Emil see Chidi's first reaction?
Emil sees it as nerves about moving rather than a real preference, and gently nudges Chidi to look at both sides.

Who stops Nicholas before he says something cruel to his mother?

Exploding at the word intriguer, Nicholas, raising his voice, told his mother he had never expected her to try to force him to sell his feelings, but if that were so, he would say for the last time.... But he had no time to utter the decisive word which the expression of his face caused his mother to await with terror, and which would perhaps have forever remained a cruel memory to them both. He had not time to say it, for Natasha, with a pale and set face, entered the room from the door at which she had been listening.
Natasha. She walks in, pale and serious, from the door where she had been listening, so he never finishes his sentence.

Sunday night
First real fight with Adil. Not a sulky one, a real one.
It was about his parents. He'd told them we'd come for lunch every Sunday "from now on", without asking me. I said I also need Sundays for my own family and, honestly, for sleep. He said, "But that's how it's always been in our house." I said, "It's not only your house any more."
He went quiet and walked to the window. I thought, here we go, the silent treatment. But after a few minutes he came back and said, "You're right that I should have asked. I'm upset, but I'm not going anywhere. Can we work out a schedule?"
I'd braced for him to storm off. Instead he stayed in the room while being angry. Nandini always says the first fight tells you more than the first date. I think she's right.
Farida

What had Adil told his parents without asking?
Adil had told them they'd come for lunch every Sunday 'from now on'.
What did Farida expect when Adil walked to the window, and how did that change?
Farida braced for the silent treatment, then felt reassured when Adil came back, admitted he should have asked and stayed in the conversation.
What did Adil's response show that matters for the future?
He could be upset and still stay, own his part and move to problem-solving, which suggests they can handle later disagreements together.
How might Adil's parents experience the new schedule talk?
Adil's parents may feel disappointed at fewer Sunday lunches, since weekly lunches are how it has always been in their house.

Indu had moved to Hyderabad for a hospital job with rotating night shifts, and after three months she knew exactly one person outside work: the man who sold idlis near her gate.

The shifts made everything harder. The book club met on Thursday evenings, which she usually worked. The residents' group planned outings for Sunday mornings, when she was asleep.

So she chose smaller things. She joined the building's group chat and answered questions about fevers with "please check with a doctor" and a kind word. She fixed a standing Saturday lunch with Simran, a nurse from her ward, and turned up every time, even when tired. When the elderly couple on the second floor needed someone to collect a parcel, she did it on her way back from a shift.

In the fourth month, she got flu. By noon there was khichdi from the second floor, a message from the idli man, and Simran at the door with soup.

What made it hard for Indu to join the book club?
The book club met on Thursday evenings, which she usually worked.
How might Indu have felt when people arrived with food during her flu?
Indu probably felt touched and comforted, seeing that her small efforts had built real support in a lonely city.
What could someone with an unusual schedule copy from Indu?
Choose small, regular commitments that fit the schedule, turn up reliably, and offer practical help to neighbours.
How do the elderly couple on the second floor see Indu?
They see her as a helpful, trustworthy neighbour, which is why they send khichdi when she is ill.
Is toothache one word? What does it mean?

Yes, one word. Toothache is a pain in a tooth. It is a noun.
Example: Maya stayed home from school because of a bad toothache.
I'm comparing two pairs of shoes, one cheaper and one sturdier. How do I choose?
Think about how often you will wear them and for what. For daily use or walking, a sturdy pair usually lasts longer, so it can cost less over time.
The cheaper pair looks nicer.
Looks matter, but fit and comfort matter more. Try both on and walk around the shop. Uncomfortable shoes tend to stay in the cupboard, however nice they look.
What if my feet are still growing?
Then a cheaper pair may be the sensible option, since you will outgrow either pair soon. Leave a little space at the toe, and check the fit again after a few months.

Read this:

On Sunday afternoon in her Hyderabad flat, Rashmi finally decided to pay for music. The app showed three plans: Solo ₹119, one device. Duo ₹229, two devices, no downloads. Family ₹239, six devices, downloads, lyrics.
"Family is only ten rupees more than Duo," she told her brother Tarun, who was lying on the sofa. "It's the obvious choice."
"Who else is using it?"
"Nobody. But look how much more you get."
Tarun sat up. "Would you have picked Family if Duo wasn't there?"
Rashmi paused. Without Duo, it was Solo against Family, and Solo was all she needed. She laughed. "That Duo plan is weird, isn't it? Who would ever pick it?"
"Nobody. That's its job."

How much was the Family plan?
Family was ₹239.
What was Rashmi feeling when she called Family the obvious choice?
She felt confident and pleased, sure she was getting great value because Duo made Family look like a bargain.
What question helped Rashmi see the decoy, and why?
Tarun asked if she would pick Family without Duo, which made her compare only the real options and see Solo was enough.
How does Tarun see the Duo plan?
Tarun sees it as a plan nobody would pick, there only to make Family look like value.

Read this:

Kunal slid into the debate room at 4:02, breathless from the stairs. Ankita, sitting with her usual group of four by the window, didn't look up from her notes. "Some people treat practice like a hobby," one of them said, loud enough.
Kunal sat at the far end and opened his folder. His cheeks burned.
At 4:15 the door banged again. Ankita's closest friend walked in, hair wet from the rain, laughing.
"Poor thing, the buses are terrible today," Ankita said, moving her bag so a chair was ready.
Nobody said anything about hobbies.
In the practice round, Kunal made a sharp point about school timings. The window group exchanged looks. When Ankita's friend repeated almost the same point ten minutes later, they clapped.
Kunal stared at his pen and counted the ceiling fan's turns until the bell.

At what time did Kunal reach the debate room?
Kunal slid into the debate room at 4:02, breathless from the stairs.
What was Kunal feeling when the group clapped for the repeated point?
Kunal felt hurt and humiliated, because the same point earned him looks but earned the group's friend applause, as if the rules depended on who you were.
How could the debate teacher make practice fairer for someone like Kunal?
The teacher could treat lateness the same way for everyone and credit each point to whoever made it first, perhaps by writing names on the board.
How might Ankita see her own reactions to the two late arrivals?
Ankita probably doesn't notice any unfairness: her friend's lateness looks like bad luck, while Kunal's looks like a lack of commitment, because she already trusts her friend.

Read this:

At the Durga Puja cultural programme, Kalyani, five, went on stage for her group dance. The drums were so loud she couldn't hear the music clearly.

She forgot the steps and stood still while the others danced.

When she came off, she hid her face in Chaitanya's kurta. "I'm bad. I'm the worst dancer."

Chaitanya knelt. "You're not bad. The music was hard to hear. You were brave to go up."

Why couldn't Kalyani hear the music clearly?
The drums were so loud she couldn't hear the music clearly.
How did Kalyani feel about herself after forgetting the steps?
Kalyani felt ashamed, believing she was bad and the worst dancer.
How did Chaitanya help Kalyani with her shame?
He told her she wasn't bad, explained the noise problem, and praised her bravery.
How might Chaitanya feel seeing Kalyani hide her face?
Chaitanya was likely worried and caring, wanting her to feel better about herself.

1) Is "triumphant" a hard word? What does it mean?
2) Quick one: why do we say "thank you" to someone who helps us?
3) who called me while I was asleep

1. Triumphant means joyful because you have won. It is an adjective.
2. Thank you shows the helper that you noticed and value what they did. Because people feel respected when their effort is recognised.
3. I don't know that. I can't see your phone. Check your call list to see which numbers called you.

Read this:

'Reena, since when do you care about insurance?' That's what you asked me, Anjali. Okay, so last Sunday I made a list on the back of an electricity bill. At the top I wrote: who eats if my salary stops? Mummy, obviously, since Papa's pension barely covers the rent. My younger brother, who's in his second year of college. Then I asked, what would hurt them first? If I died, his fees and the loan on the flat would land on Mummy. So that's a term life policy, purely for protection. Then I thought, what if I'm alive but Papa falls ill? My office health plan covers only me. So Papa and Mummy need their own health cover, apart from mine. I'm not buying anything yet. I'm meeting an adviser on Friday with this list, and it feels like I finally know what questions to ask.

What did Reena write at the top of the list?
Reena wrote: who eats if my salary stops?
How does Reena feel about insurance after making the list?
Reena feels steadier and more confident, because the list turned a vague worry into clear questions to ask.
Which other approach could suit Reena at the Friday meeting, and why?
Reena could turn the list into a short checklist of gaps in order of priority, so the meeting stays on the family's needs rather than on products.
How might Reena's mother see this plan?
Reena's mother might feel relieved and cared for, since the plan asks what would fall on her if Reena's income stopped.

Read this:

Kamal, you already said no to your friend once, and now you feel you must say yes to the smaller thing? Your Minakshi athai knows that feeling. When I was twenty, in my first year of work in Chennai, a distant cousin asked if he could live in my tiny room for a whole year while he looked for a job. A year! I said no, and he said, very gently, "Of course, I understand."
Then he asked, "Just one month, then?" I felt I owed him something for taking my no so kindly. I said yes. The month became three, and I slept on a mat.
What I learned: his first request made the second one look small. It wasn't small.

How long did the cousin first ask to stay?
A whole year.
Why did young Minakshi agree to the one month?
She felt she owed him something for accepting her no so kindly, a pull of guilt and affection.
What choice in the story could have changed how it turned out?
Judging the one-month request on its own, as if it were the first ask, before saying yes.
How might the cousin have seen the arrangement?
The cousin probably felt relieved and grateful, maybe not noticing that the month stretched into three.

metadata.subtype: Refusing a huge favour, then feeling bound by a smaller one [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Thursday. Vaibhav came in late again and got a warning, and I whispered to Riya, loud enough, "Some people never learn." I felt tall inside. I have not been late once this whole term, and I have never used the back door. At lunch, though, the others sat together laughing and I sat alone, because I had said something about Vaibhav's shoes to everyone. Nobody asked me to join. I still think rules matter. But I could have said, "Vaibhav, you should come on time," without the sneer. Tomorrow I will try. Yamini.

How many times has Yamini been late this term?
Yamini has not been late once this whole term.
What did Yamini feel on whispering, "Some people never learn"?
Yamini felt superior and proud of always following the rules, which led to looking down on Vaibhav.
What could Yamini do tomorrow to stay firm about rules but kinder?
Yamini can tell Vaibhav plainly to come on time, without the sneer, and sit with the others at lunch.
How might Vaibhav have felt hearing Yamini's whisper?
Vaibhav probably felt embarrassed and judged, especially after the warning, which could make Vaibhav less willing to listen.

Read this:

It was pouring on the school trip, and forty children were packed into one hall at the science museum, waiting for the rain to stop. Vasudha, ten, had spent the whole bus ride whispering to her group: "Don't sit with the new girl, Rhea. She thinks she's so smart." Now, in the hall, Rhea tried to join them on the mat. Vasudha shook her head, and the others turned their backs. Vasudha felt a little rush: they'd listened to her. Rhea sat alone near the door. Anand, from their class, looked at Vasudha. "Why are you doing this?" "She's a show-off," Vasudha said quickly. But the truth was, since Rhea came, Vasudha's best friend had started sitting with Rhea at lunch. Vasudha was afraid of being the one left out. The class teacher noticed Rhea alone and walked over.

How many children were packed into the hall?
Forty children were packed into one hall.
What was Vasudha really afraid of?
Vasudha was afraid of losing her best friend to Rhea and being the one left out herself.
What could Vasudha do instead of freezing Rhea out?
Vasudha could talk to her best friend about feeling left out, and include Rhea rather than turning others against her.
What is it like for Rhea sitting alone near the door?
Rhea likely feels hurt and lonely, shut out on a trip where everyone else has a group.

Read this:

The engagement was in a rented hall in Aliganj, marigolds everywhere, and Indu's younger cousin Abhinav was beaming on the stage.

"Now it's your turn, Indu," said Chhoti Bua, patting her cheek. "Twenty-six already. After twenty-eight, the good boys are gone."

Indu smiled the smile she'd practised. Another aunt asked about her salary; a third asked why she'd moved to Gurgaon alone.

In the washroom she stared at her face under the tube light. She had a job she mostly liked. She'd paid off her scooter. Six months ago she'd felt fine. Now, counting on her fingers, she felt like she was already late for a train everyone else had boarded.

Abhinav found her by the snacks table. "Didi, ignore them. Mummy used to say this to me when I was twenty-two."

Indu laughed, but her hands were still cold.

Where was the engagement held?
The engagement was in a rented hall in Aliganj.
What was Indu feeling in the washroom?
She felt anxious and suddenly behind, as if time was running out, even though six months earlier she had felt fine about her life.
How could someone support Indu at this stage?
A trusted cousin or friend could remind her that the 'deadline' is the family's clock, not a real rule, and help her name what she wants on her own timeline.
How does Abhinav see what is happening to Indu?
Abhinav sees the aunties' pressure as unfair and familiar, and wants to reassure her, though he may not realise how deeply it has shaken her.

Read this:

Early December. Omkar, two, runs for the gate whenever it opens. "Wait!" Preeti calls. He keeps running, laughing.
Two weeks later, on a foggy morning. At "Wait!", Omkar stops, looks back at his mother, then waits, bouncing on his toes, until she takes his hand.
Makar Sankranti. His Aaji arrives with tilgul. Omkar waits at the gate as told, then runs to hug her knees and presses a sticky sweet into her palm.

What does Aaji bring on Makar Sankranti?
Tilgul.
What does Omkar looking back at his mother before waiting suggest?
Omkar was checking and trusting her guidance, still eager but willing to wait.
What helped Omkar learn to stop at the gate?
Preeti using the same clear word, 'Wait!', every time and taking his hand when he stopped.
How might Aaji feel receiving the sticky sweet?
Aaji would likely feel delighted and loved by Omkar's affectionate gift.

Read this:

The rain had flooded the road outside the school, and the buses were an hour late. Raghav and Ira waited in the empty staff room with Mrs Bose, the debate coach.
Raghav's grandfather had died on Sunday. When Mrs Bose asked how he was, Raghav said, "Fine, ma'am. Boys don't make a fuss." His jaw was clenched.
Ira had the form for school captain folded in her bag. She hadn't filled it in. "My aunt says girls who push too much look proud," she mumbled.
Mrs Bose put down her tea. "In this room, crying is allowed, Raghav. And Ira, wanting to lead isn't pride."
Raghav's eyes filled, and for once he didn't wipe them away. Ira pulled out the form. By the time the bus horn sounded through the rain, her name was on it.

Why were Raghav and Ira waiting in the staff room?
The rain had flooded the road outside the school, and the buses were an hour late.
What did Raghav's clenched jaw suggest about how he was feeling?
It suggested he was holding back deep sadness about his grandfather because he believed boys shouldn't make a fuss.
What did Mrs Bose do that could help other teenagers?
She gave clear permission for both a boy's tears and a girl's ambition, widening what each of them felt safe to show.
How might Ira see Raghav crying in front of her?
She may feel moved and trusted, and it might make her braver about showing her own hidden wish to lead.
My little sister Pari is learning to swim. Write her an encouraging note under 20 words, without the word "afraid".
Every swimmer started by splashing, Pari. Keep kicking, and soon the water will feel like your friend.
The thief looked shamefaced. What is the look?

Shamefaced means showing that you feel ashamed or embarrassed about something you did. It is an adjective.
Example: He came home shamefaced after breaking the neighbour's window.

Dear Ma'am, I'd value your advice on something I've been watching since I promoted Suraj to team lead three weeks ago. He was everyone's favourite colleague. Now, I notice, the team has quietly pulled back. Nobody is rude. But they reply to his messages hours later, "forget" to copy him on client emails, and go to lunch without him. At Friday's review, when Suraj asked for ideas, the room went silent; the same people had plenty to say to me afterwards. Suraj hasn't complained, but he looks tired. I think the group was comfortable when everyone was equal, and his rise has unsettled that. I plan to talk to the team about how we support leads, and to meet Suraj weekly. Is there anything else I should do? Damini

Boil this letter down to three sentences.

Damini asks Ma'am for advice because the team has quietly pulled back from Suraj since he became team lead. They reply late, leave him off client emails and go silent when he asks for ideas. Damini plans to talk to the team and meet Suraj weekly, and asks what else to do.

Read this:

Clara, two, saw the ducks at the pond in Leeds and shrieked with joy, flapping her arms.
When her dad said it was time to go, she dropped flat on the wet path, kicking and wailing. Wei did not shout. He crouched beside her. "You loved those ducks. It's hard to leave."
He waited, one hand near her back. Slowly her kicks stopped. She crawled onto his knee and waved. "Bye, ducks."

What did Clara do when it was time to go?
She dropped flat on the wet path, kicking and wailing.
How was Clara feeling when she lay on the path?
She was angry and upset about leaving the ducks, and too small to calm down on her own.
What helped Clara settle, and why might it work?
Wei stayed close and calm, named her feeling and waited, so she could borrow his calm until her body slowed.
How might Wei feel while Clara kicks and wails on the path?
He may feel tired or tense, but he chooses to stay calm and close so she can learn to settle.

metadata.subtype: Big feelings in a small body [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

I sit across from Tejas, our team lead, so I saw how it played out, though I can only guess what went on in his head.
For weeks Sharmila did the client calls, the reports and the invoices. Gaurav mostly forwarded emails. The rest of us noticed, of course. We didn't say anything.
Then one Tuesday I saw Tejas looking at the task board for a long time, frowning. He looked at Sharmila, who was eating lunch at her desk again, then at Gaurav, who was out for his third tea.
That afternoon he took Gaurav into the small room. The door was closed for twenty minutes. The next day he did the same with Sharmila.
By Friday, Gaurav had his own client calls. Sharmila went home at six.

Where was Sharmila eating lunch?
She was eating lunch at her desk again.
What did Tejas's long frown at the task board suggest?
It suggested he felt concerned and troubled by the uneven effort, noticing that Sharmila was overloaded.
What did Tejas do that worked?
He spoke to Gaurav and Sharmila privately, one at a time, and then shared the work more fairly.
How might Sharmila have felt going home at six on Friday?
She likely felt relieved and valued, finally not carrying Gaurav's share.

Read this:

Friday, 9 pm
Today was the district science fair and it was a disaster.
Nilesh built our whole solar tracker himself over the last month. Whenever I offered to help, he said, "It's faster if I do it, Lakshmi." It was faster. So Farhan and I made the poster, and that's all.
This morning his mother called: Nilesh had a high fever and wasn't coming. Farhan and I stood next to a machine we had never switched on. The first judge asked why the panel turns toward the light. I said, "Because of the sensors?" She asked, "Which sensors?" I didn't know. Farhan tried to start it and pressed the wrong switch. The panel just sat there.
I'm not even angry at Nilesh. I'm angry at us for letting it happen. Next project, everyone learns everything, at least once.
Lakshmi

What did Nilesh say when offered help?
It's faster if I do it, Lakshmi.
How does Lakshmi feel at the end of the day?
Lakshmi feels frustrated, angry at the team more than at Nilesh for letting one person hold all the knowledge.
What would you change first for the next project?
Have each member build, run and explain every part at least once, with the builder teaching as they go.
How might Nilesh feel hearing about the fair?
Nilesh, stuck at home with fever, may feel guilty and helpless that the project he built couldn't be shown without him.

metadata.subtype: Approach: one strong member doing everything [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Don't talk to me." Kunal threw his muddy boots at the door. Rain was still hammering the tin roof.
"You lost one match," Shreya said. "In a flood."
"We lost 4–0! I missed the penalty!"
"You also saved two before that. I saw."
"Nobody remembers saves."
"I do." She tossed him a towel. "Did you shake their hands?"
Kunal went quiet. "No. I walked off."
"Hmm."
"Their goalie was really good, okay?"
"So tell him that. You'll see him at practice on Saturday."
Kunal rubbed his hair. "Can we do penalties in the lane tomorrow? You take them, I'll dive."
"In the mud?"
"It's the monsoon, Didi. It's always mud."
Shreya laughed. "Fine. Twenty each."

What was the final score of Kunal's match?
They lost 4–0.
How can you tell Kunal felt ashamed about walking off?
He went quiet when Shreya asked about the handshake and then admitted it, which suggests he felt ashamed and regretful.
What small step would help Kunal after this match?
Telling the other goalie on Saturday that he played well, and practising penalties with Shreya, would help with both grace and skill.
What is it like for Shreya when Kunal comes home angry?
Shreya probably feels patient but firm; she stays calm, notices his saves and nudges him toward sportsmanship without lecturing.
Grandma says "a leopard cannot change its spots" about my cousin who is always late. Is she being unkind?

It can sound a little unkind. The saying means that a person's basic character does not change, so people who behave in a certain way will probably keep doing so. Use it carefully, because it can sound hopeless about someone.
Example: He promised to stop forgetting things, but a leopard cannot change its spots.

Read this:

Monday: In the office canteen, Jagdish showed Ankita a group on his phone. "Double your money in thirty days. Crypto signals. Everyone's making lakhs."
Ankita, in her first job, felt the pull. Her salary felt small.
Wednesday: Her company held a free session by a registered financial adviser. He drew one line that grew slowly, then steeply: compounding. "Small amounts, over long time, spread across different things, beat big promises," he said. "If someone promises to double your money fast, walk away."
Friday: Jagdish's group had disappeared, along with the admin. Jagdish had lost what he'd put in. He sat with his head in his hands.
Ankita didn't say "I told you". She bought him chai. That evening she called her mother and made an appointment to talk to the adviser properly before deciding anything.

What did the group on Jagdish's phone promise?
"Double your money in thirty days."
How did Ankita feel when Jagdish showed her the group?
Ankita felt tempted, since her new salary felt small.
Why was Ankita's plan to talk to the adviser before deciding a sound choice?
It relies on a qualified person and time rather than a get-rich-quick promise, which is exactly the kind of offer the adviser warned about.
How might Jagdish feel when Ankita buys him chai instead of saying "I told you"?
Jagdish probably feels ashamed but grateful for the kindness.

Read this:

I noticed it at the school canteen. Mehak held up her phone and tapped, tapped again for a snack, and again for a drink, without looking at what it said. By Friday she had paid for two game top-ups and three snack rounds. On Saturday she opened her payment app and stared. "Where did it go?" she whispered. The balance was almost nothing, and her pocket money was for the month. I showed her the list of payments, one by one. Her face went pink. "It didn't feel like money." She took a small notebook out of her bag and wrote the date and the amounts. Ujjwal

How many game top-ups had Mehak paid for by Friday?
Mehak had paid for two game top-ups by Friday.
What was Mehak feeling when she stared at the balance and whispered "Where did it go?"
Mehak felt shocked and embarrassed, and her face went pink when the payments were listed.
What habit did Mehak start after seeing the payment list?
Mehak began writing the date and the amount of each payment in a small notebook, so spending could be tracked.
What might Ujjwal have been thinking while showing Mehak the list?
Ujjwal was probably careful and kind, showing the payments one by one without making a fuss, since Mehak was already upset.

Read this:

By second period, half of Class 10 in their Kolkata school knew that Minakshi's parents were separating. She had told only one person: Alka. Minakshi's hands shook as she typed in the class group: "Want to know Alka's secret? She copied her whole science project from her cousin." Her thumb hovered over send. She hated Alka right then. She wanted her to feel exactly this. Instead she deleted it, walked twice around the basketball court, and sat on the steps until her breathing slowed. After school she caught Alka alone near the cycle stand. "I told you that because I trusted you. Why?" Alka's face crumpled. "I told Nisha, and she told everyone. I'm so sorry." Minakshi didn't forgive her yet. "I need time to decide if I can trust you again."

Who had Minakshi told about her parents?
Minakshi had told only one person: Alka.
What was Minakshi feeling as her thumb hovered over send?
Minakshi felt betrayed and full of hatred, wanting Alka to feel the same exposure.
Which steps made Minakshi's path wiser than exposing Alka?
She deleted the post, walked to cool down, confronted Alka privately and took time to decide about trust.
How does Alka see Minakshi's question at the cycle stand?
Alka feels ashamed and sorry, knowing her slip to Nisha hurt her best friend badly.

Read this:

Dear Anand sir,
You'll laugh: I am now teaching someone to swim. Farida from my office never learned as a child, and after seeing my lake photos she asked me, very shyly, if I would help.
In the first lesson she asked why her legs drop when she breathes out. I opened my mouth and nothing useful came. Two years of swimming, and I couldn't explain the thing you drilled into me every Sunday. I went back to the pool alone and paid attention to my own breathing for a whole session. My exhale is still too short. You were right, and I had simply stopped noticing.
I swim three mornings a week now, only thirty minutes, just to keep it. Farida floated for ten seconds on Saturday. I think I was happier than she was.
Thank you for your patience with me back then. I understand it better now.
Kiran

What did Farida ask in the first lesson?
Why her legs drop when she breathes out.
What was Kiran feeling when no useful answer came?
Kiran felt embarrassed and humbled, discovering a gap after two years of swimming.
Which choice helped Kiran most after the awkward lesson?
Going back to the pool alone and paying close attention to breathing, which uncovered the short exhale and made the teaching better.
How might Anand feel reading this letter?
Anand would likely feel touched and proud that the Sunday lessons are being passed on, and amused at the gap Kiran found 🙂
Write a three-line poem about a river. Every line must begin with "Down".

Down the hill the river runs,
Down past fields and sleepy towns,
Down to meet the waiting sea.

Read this:

I was staying with Neelam's family over Diwali when she got two offers, one in Pune near home and one in Bengaluru. One night she sat at the dining table with a notebook and drew a line down the middle of two pages. Her father, Pradeep uncle, watched over his reading glasses. She wrote fast on the Bengaluru side: better name, bigger team, more learning, "exciting". The Pune side got: near home, smaller, "safe". Then she stopped and laughed. "This list is just saying what I already feel." Pradeep uncle asked, "And what would the move cost?" She frowned, then added under Bengaluru: deposit for a flat, first month's rent, travel home. She added it up on her phone and went quiet. I can't say which way she's leaning now, but the Bengaluru page had a new line circled twice.

Where were Neelam's two offers?
One in Pune near home and one in Bengaluru.
What might Neelam have felt after adding up the moving costs?
Neelam likely felt sobered and unsure, going quiet after the list had seemed to confirm her excitement.
What else could Neelam do with the new cost line?
Neelam could ask the Bengaluru company about any joining or relocation support and talk the total over with her parents before deciding.
How does Pradeep uncle see the list?
Pradeep uncle quietly steers her to the missing piece by asking about the cost of moving, which the list had left out.
I'm in a hurry. Turn this into a short message to Dad: Tell Dad that I have reached school safely and that the bus was on time today.
Dad, I reached school safely. The bus was on time today!

Read this:

Gopika called Arnab at eleven at night from outside the group's hostel in Salt Lake. She had one bag. 'Can I come to you? Just for tonight.'
He was there in forty minutes in a borrowed car. He didn't ask why. He didn't say I told you so.
On the drive she talked in pieces. The promised job at the group's school had never come, after three years. She was so tired she'd fallen asleep standing in the prayer hall. And Arnab had kept sending her cricket scores every Sunday, no matter what.
The next weeks were practical. He cleared the spare room. He helped her write a CV that didn't have a three-year hole in it, and forwarded two openings from his office. When she couldn't decide what to eat without asking someone, he found a counsellor who worked with people leaving such groups and went with her to the first appointment.
He never once said the group's name with a sneer.

How long did it take Arnab to arrive?
He was there in forty minutes in a borrowed car.
What does Gopika's trouble deciding what to eat suggest about her state?
It suggests the group had taken over her choices for so long that she has lost confidence in her own judgement.
Which kinds of support from Arnab made leaving possible and safe?
No blame, patient listening, a room to stay in, help with her CV and job openings, and going with her to a counsellor.
How might Arnab have felt, sending cricket scores every Sunday with no reply for years?
He may have felt worried and sometimes hopeless, but kept going because he wanted her to know someone outside still cared.

Read this:

Friday night: Karthik hadn't turned up at the wedding of Uday's sister. No call, no message, after promising to handle the baraat music. At 1 am, still in his sherwani, Uday typed: "You're the worst friend I've ever had. Don't bother calling." He didn't send it. He saved it and went to sleep.
Saturday: He read the draft aloud in the empty kitchen. It sounded like a door slamming. He rewrote it: "I was really hurt you didn't come or call. What happened?" Better. But still a message about something that mattered a lot.
Sunday: He called instead. Karthik answered on the first ring, voice rough. "Uday, I'm so sorry. My father was admitted to hospital on Friday evening. I was in casualty all night, and my phone died." Uday sat down on the bed. "Why didn't you tell me?" "I was going to call today. I'm sorry, yaar." Uday looked at the saved draft and deleted it.

What had Karthik promised to handle at the wedding?
The baraat music.
How was Uday feeling when he typed the first message?
Uday felt hurt and furious, let down by his friend on an important day.
What steps helped Uday avoid a damaging message?
He saved the draft, reread it aloud the next day, softened it, then chose a phone call for such an important matter.
What had actually happened to Karthik?
Karthik's father was admitted to hospital on Friday evening; he spent the night in casualty and his phone died.

Read this:

3 February
Healthier this year. That's what I wrote on 1 January in big letters on the first page of this diary. I, Indu, twenty-four, was going to be a new person.
Let's see. Week one I walked twice in the morning. Week two it was cold. Week three there was the audit, and Darshan kept bringing samosas to the office at four, and I kept eating them. By week four I had forgotten the resolution existed until I opened this diary today.
Healthier how? When? I never wrote any of that. Every morning I woke up and decided depending on how I felt, and most mornings I felt sleepy.
It's annoying that the page still looks so confident. I feel a bit silly. I think "healthier" needs a time and a place, or it's just a nice word.

What did Darshan keep bringing to the office at four?
Darshan kept bringing samosas.
How does Indu feel reading the resolution page on 3 February?
Indu feels a bit silly and annoyed, because the confident page contrasts with a month of drifting back to old habits.
What could Indu change to make the resolution work?
Indu could turn it into something specific with a when and where, like walking at seven on weekday mornings, instead of deciding by mood each day.
How might Darshan see the samosa habit?
Darshan probably sees it as a friendly office treat and has no idea it is undoing Indu's resolution.

Jaya's first month of Saturday tutoring brought in twelve hundred rupees, and the festival sale began in two days. Her brother Lokesh waved a flyer. “Spend half now, you've earned it!” Jaya took her school notebook and ruled three columns: Home, Laptop, Mine. Four hundred for Amma's household jar, five hundred toward the laptop, three hundred to spend. She wrote each amount and the date. “Only three hundred?” Lokesh groaned. “Three hundred, and I choose how,” Jaya said, and bought a sketch pad for two hundred and fifty, putting fifty back. At night she totted up the columns again. The laptop column looked tiny beside the price she'd seen online, but next to last month's zero it was a start.

How much did Jaya set aside toward the laptop?
Five hundred rupees.
How did Jaya feel looking at the laptop column that night?
A little proud but slightly disappointed: it looked small beside the laptop's price yet bigger than last month's nothing.
What else could Jaya add to the notebook, and why?
A target amount and month for the laptop, since knowing how many months it will take makes the saving feel real and planned.
How does the split look to Amma?
Amma sees that Jaya's contribution to the household comes first, and may feel proud that Jaya is planning with real money.

A message pinged Elizabeth's phone at sixteen. "Your account will be blocked. Send the OTP now to keep it." The tone was urgent and the request came with a countdown. Her thumb hovered. Then she remembered her mother Charu's words at the kitchen table and put the phone down. She found Charu folding laundry and held the phone out. "Someone wants my OTP, and there's a collect request too. I didn't ask for anything." Charu read it, sat down beside her and they blocked the sender together. "You didn't pay or reply," Charu said. "That was the right pause." Nine years later Elizabeth's brother-in-law Kamal asked how she never seemed short at month-end. She showed him her phone. Rent and electricity were set to leave her account on the third; on payday, before anything else, a fixed amount went into savings. A small reserve sat beside it for emergencies. On the last Sunday of each month she scrolled through her spending. "I don't rely on willpower," she said. "I set it up so I can't forget."

What did the message ask Elizabeth to send?
It asked her to send the OTP.
How does Elizabeth's response to the message at sixteen relate to her money habits at twenty-five?

At sixteen she paused and checked with her mother instead of obeying an urgent message that asked for the OTP. At twenty-five she made her money habits automatic, with bills on fixed dates, savings first and a small reserve, so urgency and forgetting have little room to work.
What was Elizabeth probably feeling when her thumb hovered over the message?
She felt uneasy and pressured by the countdown, unsure whether to obey until she remembered what her mother had told her.
How could Charu support Elizabeth after she showed her the message?
She can stay calm, praise the pause, block the sender with her and keep the door open for Elizabeth to bring the next odd message.
Excercise or exercise?

The correct spelling is "exercise". There is no c after the x: ex-er-cise.
Example: Nani does gentle exercise, like a short walk after dinner.

Sunaina, you're asking whether to go outside the company. Let me tell you what Ujjwal did at twenty-six, when the internal route failed.
I was a site engineer at a housing project in Ranchi. The steel in the columns wasn't what the drawings said. I wrote to my manager, then to the head office quality team, with photos and test certificates. Nothing. Then I was taken off the site.
I was frightened, but people were going to live in those buildings. So I didn't write angry posts. I went first to a lawyer at a legal aid centre, a patient woman who explained what protections existed. She told me: facts, not opinions. Dates, documents, photographs.
With her help I sent a formal complaint to the state building authority. Inspectors came within a month and stopped work on two towers.
It cost me that job. But the columns were rebuilt. That choice, to get proper advice before acting, is the one I'm proudest of.

Who did young Ujjwal go to first after being taken off the site?
A lawyer at a legal aid centre.
What did young Ujjwal feel before going outside the company?
Ujjwal felt frightened of the cost, but deeply concerned for the people who would live in those buildings.
What choice inside the story made the external report strong?
Getting proper legal advice first, then documenting facts rather than opinions before complaining to the building authority.
How might the lawyer at the legal aid centre have seen young Ujjwal?
She likely saw a frightened but serious young engineer and felt it important to explain protections and the careful way to proceed.

messages.content: A group of lions are called a pride. Is the verb right?

A group of lions is called a pride.
Why: The subject "a group" is singular (is).
