Gautam's father ran the fertiliser shop on the main road of Sehore, and every customer knew Gautam was supposed to top Class 10. When the half-yearly results came, he had come ninth.

"Just keep the card in your bag," his cousin Abhinav said on the bus home. "Tell Chacha the school is sending it next week. By then the finals will fix it."

Gautam watched the fields go by. His throat felt thick. Hiding it would buy a week. It would also mean lying every evening at the shop.

He got off at the stop and walked straight into the shop, past the sacks. "Papa, my result." His father read it standing at the counter, slowly.

"Ninth." Papa let out a long breath. "I expected more."

"Me too, Papa. I didn't understand accounts at all. Can Sharma Sir's evening class take me?"

Papa was silent, then said, "Ninth is not the end. We'll ask him tomorrow."

Where did Gautam's father run his shop?
Gautam's father ran the fertiliser shop on the main road of Sehore.
How can you tell Gautam felt anxious on the bus?
His throat felt thick as he stared at the fields, showing how afraid he was of disappointing his father.
What went right when Gautam reached the shop?
He showed the card straight away, owned the result and asked for help with accounts, instead of hiding it as Abhinav suggested.
Why might Abhinav have suggested hiding the card?
Abhinav probably wanted to protect Gautam from his father's disappointment, without thinking about the week of lying it would take.

Rafiq had two days before the hostel closed for summer, and the Mumbai monsoon had started. The fourth landlord that week said it most plainly. On the phone the rent was agreed; at the door, the man looked at Rafiq's face, then at his name on the Aadhaar card. "Sorry, society doesn't allow Muslims."

Rafiq walked back through the rain, fists tight, wanting to shout. Worse was the small voice asking what was wrong with him.

Jomon was waiting at the hostel with two cups of chai. "Fourth one?" Rafiq nodded.

"Write it down," Jomon said. "Name, address, what he said, time." They did. Jomon's sister worked with a tenants' help group that knew the rules and could advise on options. That evening they called her. She also shared a list of landlords who didn't care about religion.

By Sunday Rafiq had a room in Kurla.

How many days did Rafiq have before the hostel closed?
Rafiq had two days.
What was Rafiq feeling as he walked back through the rain?
Rafiq felt angry, with tight fists, and also hurt and small, with a voice asking what was wrong with him.
Which steps helped Rafiq, and why?
Writing down what happened, contacting a tenants' help group, and using a list of fair landlords helped, because Rafiq had evidence, options and allies.
How does Jomon see what the landlords did?
Jomon sees it as the landlords' prejudice, not Rafiq's fault, and responds with practical help instead of just sympathy.

On the village bus the morning after Bohag Bihu, Simran realised her maths notebook was still at home, under the pile of new gamosas. Her chest went tight. Ma'am will shout, she thought. Then she'll hit my hand with the ruler. Then she'll call Deuta. Then they'll throw me out of school, and everyone in the village will know, forever.
"Simran, why are you crying?" asked Binita, her friend from the next seat.
"I forgot my homework and now my whole life is finished."
Binita blinked. "Last week Rupam forgot his. Ma'am just said bring it tomorrow."
Simran wiped her nose. It didn't feel like it could be that simple.

Where was Simran's maths notebook?
At home, under the pile of new gamosas.
Why did Simran say her whole life was finished?
She felt panicky and ashamed 😰, and her mind leapt from a forgotten notebook to the worst possible ending, each step feeling real.
What could help Simran when her mind races like this?
Stop and ask what really happened last time someone forgot, as with Rupam, and plan one small step, such as telling Ma'am and bringing it tomorrow.
How does Binita see Simran's worry?
Binita is surprised, because she has seen Ma'am calmly say "bring it tomorrow", so the disaster seems far bigger than the problem.

In their village kitchen, Manjula Ajji poured buttermilk from a tall steel glass into a wide brass bowl for Arohi. 'Ajji, you gave me less!' Arohi said, pointing at how low it sat. Ajji smiled. 'Did I pour any out?' Arohi frowned. 'No...' 'Then pour it back.' Arohi carefully tipped it into the glass. It came right up to the same mark. She stared. 'It's the same! The bowl is just fat.' She drank it straight from the bowl, giggling.

What did Ajji pour the buttermilk into?
She poured it from a tall steel glass into a wide brass bowl.
Why did Arohi stare when the buttermilk reached the same mark?
She was surprised to discover the amount hadn't changed, only the shape of the container.
What made Ajji's approach effective?
She asked a question and let Arohi test it herself, so Arohi reached the answer on her own.
How might Manjula Ajji have felt watching Arohi pour the buttermilk back?
Ajji probably enjoyed it, since she smiled and let Arohi discover for herself that the amount had not changed.

At five, Avni stopped at a party door and pressed her face into Papa Yogesh's legs. Papa did not hurry her. He kept a hand on her head until she looked around at the balloons.
At fifteen, Avni stood in the corridor after class as Vishal, in front of some others, mimicked the way she had stumbled over a word in the debate. The others laughed. Her face felt hot, and she could feel her voice going high and shaky. She took a breath. "Give me a moment out. I'll be back to talk." Then she turned and walked to the end of the hall, sat on a bench and counted her breath until her hands stopped trembling. From a distance the others thought she was running away. After ten minutes she walked back to Vishal and said calmly, "That didn't feel good. Please stop." Vishal shrugged, then muttered "Sorry." That evening Avni told Papa Yogesh about it. He listened without interrupting and said he would come with her to talk to the class teacher if it happened again.

Where did Avni go when she said she needed a break?
She went to the end of the hall and sat on a bench.
How is Avni's walking away at fifteen different from her hiding at five?

At five, hiding behind Papa gave relief from what scared her. At fifteen she walked away too, but she said she needed a moment out and would be back, then did return to speak calmly, so her leaving was a pause and not just avoidance.
What was Avni feeling when her face went hot and her voice went shaky?
She felt embarrassed and hurt, with the taunt making her upset.
What could Avni and Papa Yogesh do if Vishal mimics her again?
They can speak to the class teacher together, and Avni can keep using her moment-out words.

"Rajni, you ask how I stay cheerful at seventy. I'll tell you what I learned at twenty-five.
I, Bhupen, your grandfather, was working in the tea gardens near Jorhat. My friends and I spent every payday at the town fair, eating, gambling on card games, drinking till late. I thought that was joy. By Monday I was sick and broke.
Then an old supervisor invited me to his house. His wife served simple rice and fish. He ate slowly, laughed at every story, then went to bed early. 'Enjoy things, boy,' he said, 'but don't let them chase you.'
After that, I kept one good meal every Sunday with friends, a song in the evening, a nap after lunch. I still do. I've enjoyed more that way."

Where was Bhupen working at twenty-five?
He was working in the tea gardens near Jorhat.
How did young Bhupen feel on Mondays after the payday fairs?
He felt sick and unhappy, worn out from overdoing the pleasures of payday.
What turning point changed how Bhupen enjoyed life?
Watching the old supervisor eat slowly and go to bed early, and hearing 'don't let them chase you', led him to keep simpler, steady pleasures.
How might the old supervisor have seen young Bhupen?
The supervisor probably saw a young man chasing fun too hard and wanted to show him a gentler way to enjoy life.

In the small village school, results day was loud with children crowding the noticeboard. Usha had topped the district, and Ramesh Sir asked her to say a few words to the class.
She stood up. "Thank you, Sir. Next year I'll be going to a school in the city..." Her voice caught. She cleared her throat, clipped the rest of the words short. "So. Thank you."
She sat down quickly, staring at her desk.
Ramesh Sir didn't ask her to continue. After class, he waited by the door. "Usha, would you like to sit in the staff room for a minute? It's quiet there."
She nodded. In the empty room, she finally said, "I'll miss everyone. I'll miss this school."
Sir nodded. "We'll miss you too. That's why it's hard to say."

What had Usha achieved in the results?
She had topped the district.
What was Usha feeling when her voice caught?
Usha felt sad and emotional about leaving her village school and friends.
What did Ramesh Sir do that helped?
He didn't press her to finish in public and offered a private, quiet moment in the staff room.
How might the class have seen Usha's short speech?
They might have thought she was shy or in a hurry, not realising she was holding back tears.

"Lavanya, why are you on the phone at midnight again?"
"Office work."
"Office work doesn't make you cry."
Lavanya put the phone face down. "It's the loan. The business loan I told you about."
"You said you'd dropped that idea."
"I paid the processing fee in March. Ten thousand. Then they said tax, then insurance, then a stamp charge. It's fifty-five thousand now, Lalit."
"Fifty-five? And the loan?"
"It's approved! They just need one final release fee. After that it all comes back with the loan."
"Lavanya..."
"Don't. If I stop now, fifty-five thousand is simply gone. I can't tell Amma I lost that. I can't tell anyone." She wiped her eyes. "One more payment and it's over."
Lalit sat down slowly beside her. "Show me the messages."

How much has Lavanya paid so far?
Fifty-five thousand now.
What is Lavanya feeling when she says she can't tell Amma?
She feels ashamed and trapped, so desperate not to admit the loss that paying more seems easier.
What could Lalit do now that he will see the messages?
Stay calm and blame-free, help stop the payments, save screenshots, and report to the bank and cyber-crime helpline together.
What is it like for Lalit to hear the amount?
Lalit is shocked and worried, but chooses to sit beside Lavanya rather than shout.

messages.content: On a form I saw "Mr / Ms / Mx". What is "Mx"?

"Mx" is a title, pronounced "mix" or "mux", that people who do not wish to use Mr or Ms can choose. It is used mostly in Britain and some other places, and is not found in every form.
Example: Mx Taylor will give the talk.

Neelam ma'am closed her laptop when the young founder said he wanted two more months to polish before showing anyone. "Sit. Let me tell you about Divyansh. Years ago he came to me with savings for eight months and a lovely idea: an app for booking home cooks. He was twenty-four and terrified of looking amateur.
So he polished. New colours, new icons, smoother animations. Every time I asked, 'Has any customer used it?' he said, 'Not yet, it's not ready.' Five months went. His designer cost money. His rent cost money. When he finally showed it to real families, they said the booking steps were confusing and they wanted to pay in cash. Everything he had perfected was the wrong thing.
He had three months left by then. He didn't make it. He's fine now, a good product lead, but he tells everyone: show it rough, show it early."

How many months of savings did Divyansh start with?
Eight months.
What was young Divyansh afraid of?
He was terrified of looking amateur, which is why he kept polishing.
Which choice in the story could have changed the ending?
Showing the rough app to real families in the first month, so he would have learned early about the confusing booking steps and cash payments.
How did the families who finally tried the app see it?
They found the booking steps confusing and wanted to pay in cash, so the polish meant little to them.

Make it formal.

Hi everyone, we're starting now. Please take your seats and be quiet.
Hello, everyone. We are beginning now. Please take your seats and be silent.
Our captain, he is a very brave player. What is wrong?

Our captain is a very brave player.
Why: "our captain" is the subject; do not repeat it with "he".

Wanjiru used to be the one who organised Friday football on the estate behind her school in Nairobi. Since March, when her best friend moved to Mombasa and the group chat seemed to carry on without her, she had stopped messaging first.
Valentina, the exchange student from Argentina, asked her to art club three times. Wanjiru said she was busy three times.
You don't have to be nice to me because I'm alone, she wanted to say. Instead she said, "I'm more of a lone person. I like my own company."
In truth, she ate lunch in the library so no one could see she had nobody to sit with. On Saturday she heard laughter from the football pitch and closed her window.
It felt safe. If she didn't join, no one could leave her out again. But the weekends were getting very long.

Where does Wanjiru eat lunch?
In the library.
Why does Wanjiru close her window when she hears laughter?
She feels lonely and afraid of being left out again, so shutting it out feels safer.
What small step could Wanjiru try?
Accept Valentina's next invitation to art club just once, instead of saying she's busy.
What might Valentina feel after being turned down three times?
Valentina may feel discouraged and unsure whether Wanjiru likes her, even as she keeps trying.
What is a "biscuit"? My American cousin means something different.

In British English, a biscuit is a small, crisp, baked snack, which Americans call a cookie. In American English, a biscuit is a soft, bread-like roll. In India, "biscuit" usually has the British meaning.
Example: Dad dipped a biscuit in his tea.
The streetlight in our lane has not worked for two weeks, and it is dark at night. Write a letter, about 65 words, to the municipal office asking them to repair it.

Dear Sir or Madam,
I am writing to report that the streetlight in our lane has not worked for two weeks. The lane is very dark at night, and it is hard to walk there safely. I request you to send someone to repair the light as soon as possible. Thank you for your attention.
Yours faithfully
11 fours and 8 sixes were hit in the innings. How many runs is that?
Simplify for an English learner: Despite the fact that he had studied diligently, he was unable to complete the paper within the allotted time.
He had studied hard, but he could not finish the paper in time.
I'm joining a new school in the middle of the year and I don't know anyone.
That's a big change, and it's normal to feel nervous. The first days are the hardest. What are you most worried about?
Eating alone at lunch.
Try to introduce yourself to one or two classmates on the first day. A simple 'Hi, I'm new. Can I sit here?' works. Most children are kind to new students.
What if no one talks to me?
Give it a few days. People take time to warm up. Join an activity like a club or sports period, where you can meet others with the same interests.
I like drawing.
Then look for an art club or ask the art teacher. Sharing a hobby is a natural way to make friends.
That gives me something to look forward to.
Good. Bring a small sketchbook on the first day, and it might start a conversation.

What treat does Miss Temple give the girls?

Having invited Helen and me to approach the table, and placed before each of us a cup of tea with one delicious but thin morsel of toast, she got up, unlocked a drawer, and taking from it a parcel wrapped in paper, disclosed presently to our eyes a good-sized seed-cake.
After tea and a thin slice of toast, she takes a good-sized seed-cake from a locked drawer.

I'm Kiran, and here's what I used to do every time. Uday would say something like, "You were on your phone the whole dinner with my parents." And before he'd finished, I'd be talking. "I had a work message. You were on your phone last week. Why do you always attack me?" Explain, deny, blame. In about four seconds.

It felt like survival. Any criticism landed like: you are unlovable.

Last Sunday it happened again. He said I never ask about his day. I felt my mouth open, the defence ready.

I breathed instead. One long breath. Then I said, "That's true. I haven't been asking. I'm sorry." Just that.

Uday looked shocked, then his face softened. "Thank you. That's all I wanted."

Later I said, "I get defensive because criticism feels like you don't love me." He said, "It's the opposite. I say it because I want us close."

What did Uday say Kiran never asks about?
Uday said Kiran never asks about his day.
Why did Kiran react so quickly with explanations and blame?
Kiran felt that any criticism meant being unlovable, so defensiveness felt like survival, driven by fear and hurt.
What did Kiran do differently last Sunday?
Kiran took a breath, admitted what was true in the complaint, and apologised before explaining anything.
How does Uday see his own criticism?
Uday sees it as a way to stay close, not an attack, saying he raises things because he wants them close.

In the car park of the community pool in Vancouver, Soo-ah climbed into the back seat with wet hair and a face ready for bad news. She had come fifth out of six in the 50-metre freestyle.
Her father, Chen, started the engine but didn't pull out. "What was the best part?"
"The dive. I didn't belly-flop this time."
"I saw. Clean. What would you change?"
"I breathed every two strokes. Coach said every three. I got tired."
"Want to practise that on Saturday?"
"Okay." She paused. "Aren't you going to ask where I came?"
"Where did you come?"
"Fifth."
"Fifth," he repeated, as if it were the weather. "Dumplings or noodles?"
Soo-ah laughed for the first time since the race.

How did Soo-ah finish in the 50-metre freestyle?
Fifth out of six.
What does Soo-ah's face show when she climbs into the car?
She was nervous and braced for disappointment about coming fifth.
Which choice by Chen helped most, and why?
Asking about the best part and one change before the result, so Soo-ah could look at her swim calmly instead of only the placing.
What would change if Chen had asked the placing first?
Soo-ah might have felt judged and shut down, missing the chance to notice her clean dive and breathing plan.

At the family's ancestor-remembrance meal in Kuala Lumpur, Wanjiru stood with her husband's relatives before a small table of photographs, food and lit incense. She had been raised in a different tradition and did not share the belief that the dead would come to eat. Xin, the eldest aunt, handed her three sticks of incense. Wanjiru took them, bowed her head as the others did and stayed silent, neither pretending nor pulling away. Xin's hands trembled as she set out her late husband's favourite dish. Wanjiru noticed the aunt's lips moving, telling him something quietly. Across the room a teenage cousin studied his phone. Afterwards Xin squeezed Wanjiru's arm without a word.

How many sticks of incense did Xin hand to Wanjiru?
Xin handed Wanjiru three sticks of incense.
What might Wanjiru have been feeling as Wanjiru stood there without sharing the belief?
Wanjiru probably felt respectful and a little outside the belief, wanting to take part honestly without pretending.
What choice did Wanjiru make that let her join honestly?
Wanjiru took the incense, bowed her head as the others did and stayed silent, neither pretending to believe nor pulling away.
What might the ritual have meant for Xin as her hands trembled?
Xin was probably feeling love and loss for her late husband, and the ritual gave her a way to tell him something quietly.

Put this section into three bullet points.

I held the little printed slip to the light. "Missing," it said, "on the morning of the fourteenth, a gentleman named Hosmer Angel. About five ft. seven in. in height; strongly built, sallow complexion, black hair, a little bald in the centre, bushy, black side-whiskers and moustache; tinted glasses, slight infirmity of speech. Was dressed, when last seen, in black frock-coat faced with silk, black waistcoat, gold Albert chain, and grey Harris tweed trousers, with brown gaiters over elastic-sided boots. Known to have been employed in an office in Leadenhall Street. Anybody bringing," &c, &c.

- A printed notice reports that a gentleman named Hosmer Angel went missing on the fourteenth.
- He is about five feet seven, strongly built, with black hair thinning in the middle, black whiskers and tinted glasses.
- He was last seen in a black coat and grey tweed trousers, and worked in an office in Leadenhall Street.
"Mujhe ek minute do." Polite aur casual dono mein bolo.
Polite: "Could you give me a minute, please?" Casual: "Hold on a sec."

After the Friday lecture on signals, Yamini waited at the front of the lecture room until the others left. "Professor, I didn't understand anything today." The professor asked which part. "All of it, honestly. I feel lost." So the professor turned to the board and went through the first ten minutes of the lecture again, slowly, with the same examples. Yamini nodded at each step and said "okay" but kept looking at the clock. Afreen, waiting at the door for a lift home, saw the professor sigh quietly and Yamini leave with the same blank look. Neither had got what they hoped for. In the corridor Yamini muttered, "That did not help at all."

What did Yamini say to the professor at the front of the room?
Yamini said, Professor, I didn't understand anything today.
What was Yamini feeling while nodding and looking at the clock?
Yamini felt lost and frustrated, since repeating the whole lecture did not touch the actual confusion.
What could Yamini say next time to get a better answer, and why?
Yamini could name the one step or example that stopped making sense, because a precise question lets the professor explain exactly that part.
How might the professor feel when the only request is that nothing made sense?
The professor may feel stuck and a little frustrated, since there is no clue where the trouble is and repeating the lecture is the only option.

metadata.subtype: Approach: vague requests that get vague answers [Pitfall]

Lindiwe had paid the whole fee for the private animation academy in Cape Town in one go, using savings from two years of weekend work. By October the classes were half empty, two tutors had left, and the software licences still hadn't arrived.

"It's still the best course in the country," Lindiwe told her friend Rania over coffee. "The self-study is actually good for discipline. And the certificate will look great."

"You said you haven't touched the software in six weeks."
"That's temporary. Everyone says it'll be fixed."
"Who's everyone?"

Lindiwe stirred her coffee harder. "Look, I'm not dropping it. I put everything into this."

Rania didn't push. But she noticed that every time Lindiwe listed the course's strengths, the list got longer and her voice got higher.

How long had Lindiwe not touched the software?
Lindiwe hadn't touched it in six weeks.
Why does Lindiwe insist the course is still the best?
Lindiwe feels disappointed but has put two years of savings in, so admitting doubt feels too painful, and defending it eases that tension.
What could help Lindiwe look at the choice honestly?
Lindiwe could list what the course has actually delivered and talk options through with a college counsellor or trusted adult before deciding.
How does Rania see Lindiwe's list of strengths?
Rania notices the list getting longer and Lindiwe's voice getting higher, a sign of doubt underneath.

Tuesday

Worst day ever. In the spelling test I wrote "becaus" without the e. ONE word. Ma'am put a red circle on it. So the whole test is ruined. I got 19 out of 20, but that doesn't count because it isn't 20.

I am stupid at spelling. I'm probably stupid at everything.

Yogesh got 17 and he was happy! He said, "You got nineteen, you're mad." I didn't answer.

At dinner Baba asked about the test and I said "bad". He saw the paper and said, "Nineteen right, one wrong. Which one was wrong?" I said "because". He said, "Then practise because. Not the other nineteen."

Maybe. I still feel bad.

Anirban

What score did Anirban get?
Anirban got 19 out of 20.
Why does one red circle make Anirban feel the whole test is ruined?
Anirban feels disappointed and ashamed; to Anirban anything short of 20 counts as total failure, which leads to the word "stupid".
What did Baba suggest, and why is it a good countermeasure?
Practise just "because", not the other nineteen, which shows that one mistake is one thing to fix, not a whole disaster.
How might Yogesh see Anirban's reaction?
Yogesh is puzzled, happy with 17 himself, and thinks Anirban is being silly about 19.

Every Sunday at Gogo's house in Soweto, Thabo, ten, heard the same story. When Grandpa was young, he had walked forty kilometres to his first job with only one pair of shoes, carrying them in his hands so they wouldn't wear out. Thabo's cousin Gabriel rolled his eyes. "We know, Gogo." But Thabo never minded. He liked hearing how Grandpa put the shoes on only at the factory gate. At school, when a teacher asked the class to write about someone they admired, Thabo wrote about Grandpa's shoes. He read it aloud. His voice shook a little at the end. That evening, he told Gogo about it. She squeezed his hand. "You carry him too, now." Thabo felt taller all week.

How far did Grandpa walk to his first job?
Forty kilometres.
How did Thabo feel after Gogo said 'You carry him too, now'?
He felt proud and connected, feeling taller all week.
How could a teacher use Thabo's story to help other children?
The teacher could invite others to share a family story, helping them feel a sense of belonging too.
How does Gabriel see the repeated story?
Gabriel seems bored by it, rolling his eyes, while Thabo finds it meaningful.
A science article talks about how to harness the power of the sun. Is a harness not the strap on a horse?

As a verb, to harness means to control and use a natural force or resource for a purpose. The noun is a set of straps, for example for a horse or a climber.
Example: The village built a small dam to harness the river's energy.

What trick does Denisov use in his replies to the two generals?

"No, bwother, I have gwown mustaches myself," said Denisov on reading these documents, and he wrote to the German that, despite his heartfelt desire to serve under so valiant and renowned a general, he had to forgo that pleasure because he was already under the command of the Polish general. To the Polish general he replied to the same effect, informing him that he was already under the command of the German.
He politely refuses both. He tells the German general that he already serves under the Polish general, and tells the Polish general that he serves under the German, so he ends up serving neither.

Saturday: Jeevan was on his way to Uday's birthday dinner when a college friend texted: "Rooftop party, the whole batch is here, come!" He messaged Uday, "Sorry, not feeling well, next time for sure." He went to the rooftop.
Sunday: Jeevan woke late. Uday had replied: "Get well soon. I saw the photos." Jeevan's stomach dropped. He read it three times.
Monday: He opened the chat to apologise. His fingers typed, "Actually, it's not like you invited me early." He deleted it. He typed, "I'm sorry." He deleted that too. The guilt and the urge to defend himself sat side by side.

What did Uday's reply say?
"Get well soon. I saw the photos."
What was Jeevan feeling when he read Uday's reply?
He felt a sharp pang of guilt, his stomach dropping, mixed with an urge to defend himself.
What turning point is available to Jeevan on Monday?
He could send a simple, honest apology that admits he went to the party, without adding a defence about the invitation.
What is Uday experiencing after seeing the photos?
He likely feels hurt and let down, knowing Jeevan lied and chose the party over his birthday.

Rain drummed on the tin roof, and the playroom was so loud that Teacher could not hear small voices. Yamini was holding the red toy train when Vinita grabbed the other end. "Mine now," said Vinita, and pulled. Yamini's hands went stiff, her lip shook, and she let go. She crept under the table and cried there while the noise rolled on. Next morning Vinita reached again. Yamini's chest thumped, but she pressed her feet to the floor and shouted, "Stop!" Vinita jumped. Then Yamini walked, still shaking, to Teacher and said, "Vinita pulled my train." She held the train against her tummy.

What did Yamini do when Vinita first pulled the train?
She went stiff, let go of the train and hid under the table crying.
What was Yamini feeling as she shouted "Stop!" the second morning?
She was still frightened, since her chest thumped and she was shaking, but she pushed through it anyway. Her fear and her courage were there together.
Why did Yamini need to shout and then go to Teacher, and what might help her next time?
The room was too loud for a quiet voice to be heard, so a loud "Stop!" and telling Teacher made sure an adult knew. Practising the word with a grown-up beforehand could help her. 🙂
How might Vinita have felt when Yamini shouted?
Vinita was startled, since she jumped, and may have realised Yamini would not simply hand over toys. She might have been surprised that a quiet child could be that loud.

Read this:

The caller said he was from Avni's bank and that her card would be blocked in ten minutes unless she read out the code that had just arrived. His voice was warm and hurried. Avni's heart raced, and she nearly read it out. Instead she said, "I'll call the number on the back of my card," and hung up. Later at work Pranav looked grey. A recruiter had asked him for an upfront fee for a job, and he had paid. He could not bring himself to tell a soul. Avni sat beside him and said, "Scammers count on shame. Let's report it now." They rang his bank and filed on the cyber portal within the hour. Pranav, furious, wanted to hunt the fraudster down; Avni said, "Put that into the complaint instead." He gathered screenshots and the transaction ID and posted a warning for his friends. That weekend her uncle Chaitanya phoned, shaky: he had sent money to a fake courier. Avni did not scold him or remind him of any warnings. She helped him stop the next payment and report it, and they agreed a habit: call her before paying anyone new.

What did the caller say would happen in ten minutes?
He said her card would be blocked.
How did Avni's response to the caller differ from what happened to Pranav, and what did she then do for him?

Avni nearly read out the code but hung up and planned to call the number on her card, while Pranav paid an upfront fee to a fake recruiter and hid it; Avni sat beside him and got him to report to his bank and the cyber portal within the hour.
What was Pranav feeling when he looked grey at work?
He felt embarrassed and ashamed, too much to tell anyone that he had been scammed.
What could Avni do next to help her uncle Chaitanya feel safe?
She could keep supporting his safety habit of calling her before paying anyone new, and stay kind without blaming him.
Party mein pati ka parichay dena hai. "Ye mere pati hain." English?
Say: "This is my husband, Raj." Replace "Raj" with his name.

Kindergarten note, Christmas craft day.

Gargi took Asha's gold crayon while Asha was washing her hands. When Asha came back and started looking for it, Gargi went red and looked down.

After a few minutes, Gargi gave it back. "I took it. Sorry." Asha said, "Okay."

I told Gargi it was a good thing to give it back. — Madhuri

What did Gargi take?
She took Asha's gold crayon.
How did Gargi feel when Asha started looking for the crayon?
Gargi felt guilty, going red and looking down.
How did Madhuri respond to Gargi's apology?
She told Gargi it was a good thing to give it back, encouraging her honesty.
How might Asha feel when Gargi returned the crayon?
Asha seemed relieved and ready to forgive, saying "Okay".

"I'm bored of kabaddi."
"I'm bored of tag."
"So let's make a new game," said Sangeeta.
"From scratch? That'll take forever," Anand said.
"Not scratch. Take bits. Kabaddi: two teams, a middle line, one raider goes over."
"And from tag?"
"The raider tags, and whoever's tagged has to freeze. Like freeze tag."
"How do they unfreeze?"
"A teammate crawls under their legs."
Anand counted the terrace tiles. "Middle line here. Teams of four."
"And the raider has to keep saying 'chaka-chak' instead of 'kabaddi'."
Everyone laughed. "Chaka-chak! Okay. First raid, Anand!"

What does the raider have to keep saying?
'Chaka-chak', instead of 'kabaddi'.
How did Anand feel about making a new game at first?
Anand felt doubtful and a bit impatient, thinking it would take forever from scratch.
Which part of Sangeeta's thinking made the game quick to start?
Taking pieces from games everyone already knew, kabaddi's teams and raider and tag's freezing, so nobody had to learn everything new.
How do the others seem to feel about 'chaka-chak'?
Everyone laughs, so they seem amused and excited to start.

metadata.subtype: Approach: copying rules from a game they already know [Thinking]

messages.content: Why does a girl feel left out when two friends whisper near her?
A whisper feels like being shut out. Because it suggests there is a secret she is not allowed to share, she feels pushed out of the group.

Okay, Gurpreet, I know what you're going to say. I'm Nilesh, I've heard it before. "Test yourself, don't just read." But listen. Rereading is how I've always studied. Since Class 6. I sit with my notes, highlighter, three hours, and I go through every page two or three times. It feels like it's going in. Yes, I got 41 in chemistry. Yes, 38 in physics. But that's because the papers were tricky, not because of my method. You want me to cover my notes and write answers from memory? That feels like wasting time when I could be reading more pages. I'll just read more this time. Four hours instead of three. You'll see. Okay, I'm not totally sure. But it's my way.

What marks did Nilesh get in chemistry and physics?
41 in chemistry and 38 in physics.
What does 'Okay, I'm not totally sure' suggest about Nilesh's feelings?
It hints that under the confident talk, Nilesh feels uneasy and doubtful about the method, but is afraid to change it.
What other approach could Nilesh try, and why?
Covering the notes and answering from memory, as Gurpreet suggests, because it shows what isn't learned yet instead of just feeling familiar.
How might Gurpreet feel listening to this?
Gurpreet is probably frustrated and worried, seeing a friend repeat what isn't working.

metadata.subtype: Approach: keeps studying the same way despite poor results [Pitfall]

The email from the architecture firm in Bengaluru sat in Tenzin's inbox for nine days before he declined the internship. It would mean presenting to clients, and just picturing that made his hands go cold. In the hostel mess, his classmate Vandana waved her phone. "Did you accept? I got the Chennai office! We can compare notes!" Tenzin said he'd decided to stay back and focus on his portfolio. He hadn't opened the portfolio in weeks. He had also skipped two studio reviews this term, and his grades showed it. That evening, walking past the chai stall, he watched the same group of juniors he used to mentor laughing about their site visit. A heavy, sour feeling sat in his chest. A year ago he had wanted to be the one presenting. Now he couldn't even explain to Vandana why he'd said no.

How long did the email from the firm sit in Tenzin's inbox?
It sat in Tenzin's inbox for nine days before he declined.
What is the heavy, sour feeling in Tenzin's chest?
It is shame and disappointment in himself, because he gave up something he once wanted and cannot explain why.
What turning point is still open to Tenzin?
He could tell Vandana or a college counsellor honestly that fear of presenting is behind the refusals, and seek help before more opportunities slip away.
How might Vandana see Tenzin's answer about his portfolio?
Vandana may feel puzzled and a little let down, having expected to share the excitement, and may not guess that fear is behind it.

Read this:

I'm Binita, and when I joined the firm I watched two ways of getting ahead. Divyansh worked the corridors: favours, flattery, a quiet word against whoever stood in his way. I kept my promises, even the small ones, like sending the minutes the same evening. I put people's names on their work in every deck and left the gossip alone. For a year it seemed slow. Divyansh was invited to more lunches. Then the company restructured, and the partners asked around about who could be trusted with the big account. Several people said my name, and one said, “When Binita says Thursday, it's Thursday.” Divyansh's favours had mostly dried up. Looking back, I never felt clever. I just felt steady.

What small promise did Binita keep every time?
Binita sent the minutes the same evening.
How did Binita feel during the first year when Divyansh was invited to more lunches?
Binita probably felt overlooked and a little doubtful while Divyansh got the lunches, yet kept a quiet patience.
What choice did Binita keep making during the slow first year, and why did it matter?
Binita kept small promises, credited others and stayed out of gossip, and that reliability showed when the company restructured and people said, “When Binita says Thursday, it's Thursday.”
How might Divyansh have felt when the partners asked around and his favours had mostly dried up?
Divyansh may have felt surprised and uneasy, since the corridor alliances he built did not help when people were asked who could be trusted.
Is bridegroom the old word for groom? I read it in a wedding story.

Yes, it is another word for the groom, the man who is getting married. It is a noun, and a rather formal one.
Example: The bridegroom arrived on a white horse with his family and friends.

On Sankranti morning in the village, Divyansh and his friend Elizabeth flew kites from the flat roof. "You want the high wind, I want the low," Divyansh said, proud he had noticed. "Different wants." Then Elizabeth's kite cut his string, and his red kite drifted away over the fields. His face went hot. "You did that on purpose! You wanted my kite gone!" Elizabeth stared. "I didn't even see it." Somewhere inside, Divyansh knew she was telling the truth. But the angry feeling was so big that it drowned out the knowing. He stomped downstairs, then stopped on the last step.

What colour was Divyansh's kite?
Red.
Why did Divyansh accuse Elizabeth though part of him knew she was honest?
He felt hot, angry and upset about losing his kite, and the big feeling drowned out his understanding that she had her own view.
What could Divyansh do next?
Take a breath on the step, go back and say he knows she didn't mean it, and perhaps fly a kite together.
How might Elizabeth feel when accused?
Shocked and hurt, since she hadn't even seen his kite.

Diego, five, told his babysitter Ulla that a dragon had visited kindergarten and eaten all the sandwiches. "It was green, bigger than the school, and it breathed on Mateo's hat." Ulla smiled. "Wow. Was it a pretend dragon or a real one?" Diego thought. "Pretend. Mateo was the dragon." "And who really ate the sandwiches?" "We did. At snack." He grinned and roared quietly at the sofa.

What did Diego say the dragon breathed on?
Mateo's hat.
What was Diego feeling as he told the dragon story?
Excited and playful, shown by the details and his grin. He was not necessarily trying to fool anyone, since he happily said Mateo was the dragon.
How did Ulla help separate pretend from real?
She played along first, then asked a friendly question about pretend or real, without calling him a liar.
How might Ulla see Diego's dragon tale?
As imaginative play. She smiles and stays curious, so she does not treat it as lying. 😊
Can you "ring up" the plumber? Is it the same as "call"?

Yes. "Ring up" is British and Indian English for to telephone someone. Americans more often say "call".
Example: I will ring up the plumber in the morning.

Childminder's note, Tuesday. In the garden, Rashmi ran off toward the hedge, then stopped and looked back at me with a huge grin. I took the hint and chased her, slowly, saying "I'm going to catch you!" She shrieked. After a few rounds, she stopped, turned round and ran after me instead. We took turns until snack time. She is starting to understand the game goes both ways. Nirmala, childminder

What did Rashmi do after a few rounds?
She stopped, turned round and ran after Nirmala instead.
What was Rashmi feeling when she looked back with a grin?
She felt playful and excited, and was inviting Nirmala to chase her.
What did Nirmala's joining in help Rashmi learn?
Turn-taking, since the chasing game went both ways.
How might Rashmi's parents feel reading the note?
They would likely feel happy to hear she had such fun and is learning to take turns.
How do I decide whether to repair or replace something?
Compare the repair cost with the price of a new one, and consider how old the item is. If the repair is a small part of the price and the item is otherwise sound, repairing makes sense.
What about the environment?
Repairing usually creates less waste, since you keep the item in use longer. Making new products takes materials and energy.
What if the item is very old?
Older items may have more problems soon, so ask the repairer if other parts are close to failing. A new, more efficient model may serve you better in some cases.
Where do I find a reliable repairer?
Ask friends and neighbours, and check local reviews. Get the price in writing, or ask for an estimate before work starts.
Do repaired items come with a guarantee?
Some repairers offer a short guarantee on their work. Ask before you agree, and keep the receipt.
Sunil is paid ₹120 an hour. He worked 6 hours on Monday and 4.5 hours on Tuesday. What did he earn?
He earned ₹1,260. Because 6 plus 4.5 is 10.5 hours, and 10.5 times 120 is 1,260.

Dear Jatin,

You asked how I'm feeling about moving to Bengaluru next month, so here is the honest answer: excited and scared, taking turns. The excited part imagines the new job and my own flat. The scared part keeps asking, what if I can't manage? Last night I got tired of both and made a list instead. Find a room near the office, ask Uncle Rao about the first week, save the number for the landlord, pack the winter jacket. Then I emailed my new manager to ask what the first day looks like. She wrote back kindly within the hour. I still feel the dread, but now it has steps.

Come visit when I've a sofa.

Amandeep

Where is Amandeep moving?
Amandeep is moving to Bengaluru.
What do the two feelings Amandeep describes look like, and what shifted them?
Amandeep alternates between excitement about the new job and flat and fear of not managing, and making a list and emailing the new manager gave the dread steps.
What could Amandeep do if the dread stayed strong?
Amandeep could keep breaking it into small steps and talk to someone trusted, such as Uncle Rao or a mentor.
How might Jatin feel reading the letter?
Jatin may feel touched that Amandeep answered honestly, and possibly glad to be asked to visit.

metadata.subtype: Hopeful and apprehensive about the future [Regulating]

In class ten, geometry was my monster. My cousin Dolma, two years older, noticed me circling the desk the way you circle a dog you don't trust. “Don't do the chapter,” Dolma said. “Do five minutes. Lay out the compass, the ruler and the pencil, and open the book to the first theorem. Then, if you want, close it.” I laughed, because it sounded too small to matter. But when the geometry box was open and the pencil sharpened, drawing the first triangle seemed only natural. I didn't close the book that day, or the next. I still lay out my tools before any dreaded job. — Manoj

Who suggested the five-minute start?
Manoj's cousin Dolma suggested it.
How did Manoj feel about geometry in class ten?
Manoj felt wary and dreading it, like circling a dog one doesn't trust, and laughed at first because five minutes sounded too small to matter.
What did Dolma suggest laying out, and what was the effect?
Dolma suggested laying out the compass, the ruler and the pencil and opening the first theorem; with the tools ready, drawing the first triangle felt natural.
How might Dolma have felt suggesting such a small step?
Dolma was probably gentle and understanding, since Dolma noticed the circling and gave permission to close the book afterwards.

Self-help group facilitator's note, Nashik, quarterly review (Chetan)
Leela, 25, joined the group in January wanting to buy her own sewing machine by December. In the first months she saved almost nothing; she said the money "just melted" on market day.
In April she made three changes on her own. She asked the bank to move a fixed amount into a separate account every salary day, before she saw it. She stopped carrying her card to the Sunday market and took only cash for vegetables. And she stuck a photo of the exact machine she wants, with its price, on the door of her cupboard.
She admitted she felt irritated at first. "I don't like my own rules some days." But since April she hasn't missed a month.
Next: I've asked her to show the group her cupboard photo idea at our next meeting.

What did Leela stick on her cupboard door?
A photo of the exact machine she wants, with its price.
How did Leela feel about her new rules at first, and what shows it?
She felt irritated, admitting, "I don't like my own rules some days", though she kept following them.
Which of Leela's changes do the most to help her future self, and why?
Moving money automatically on salary day and leaving the card at home remove the choice in tempting moments, while the photo makes December's reward concrete.
How might the other group members see Leela's cupboard photo idea?
They may find it simple and encouraging, a way to keep their own goals in sight, since Leela went from saving almost nothing to not missing a month.

Kishore, you and your roommate are fighting about the room? Let me, Tanvir, your old hostel senior, tell you how I solved it back in my own hostel days.
My roommate Prakash was a night owl and messy. I was an early riser and tidy. For a month we snapped at each other. Then one Sunday we sat down with a notebook and each wrote what we wanted most. He wanted quiet after he came in; I wanted the floor clear.
So we made a trade. A chore chart on the door, bin and sweeping rotating every week. Quiet hours after eleven, Monday to Thursday, so I could sleep and he could read. And a small biscuit tin where we each put in money for soap and phenyl, so nobody felt he was paying for the other.
We didn't become best friends. But we stopped fighting, and we shared that room for three years. Now, what does your roommate want most?

What did Tanvir and Prakash keep in the biscuit tin?
Money for soap and phenyl.
How did Tanvir feel during that first month?
Tanvir felt irritated and tense, snapping at a roommate whose habits were the opposite.
Which choice in the story made the trade possible?
Each writing down what they wanted most, which showed that both wants could be met at once.
How might the plan have looked to Prakash?
Prakash got quiet after coming in and a fair share of costs, so the rules felt like a deal, not a punishment.

metadata.subtype: Approach: negotiating a win-win chore and quiet-hours plan [Action]

messages.content: How does a rubber slipper grip a wet floor better than a smooth leather sole?
Rubber holds on to the floor better. Because rubber is soft and rough enough to grip, there is more friction to stop the foot from sliding.

Beatriz had moved to Cape Town from São Paulo two years ago, and Lindiwe had been the first person to sit with her at lunch. They'd been together since March. By September, Beatriz knew her feelings had changed.
She didn't want to do it by text. On Sunday evening she called.
"Lindi, I have to say something, and I'm going to say it straight because you deserve that," she said, sitting on her bedroom floor. "I care about you a lot. But I don't feel the way I did, and I won't keep you hoping for something I can't give."
There was a long silence. Then Lindiwe's voice, small: "Was it something I did?"
"No. Honestly, no. You've been nothing but good to me."
"Okay." A shaky breath. "I'm glad you called instead of just going quiet."
After they hung up, Beatriz cried for a while. It still felt like the right kind of hard.

When did Beatriz call Lindiwe?
Beatriz called on Sunday evening.
Why did Beatriz cry after the call even though it felt right?
Beatriz still cared about Lindiwe, so ending it was sad, even though she knew being clear was the kind thing.
What choices made Beatriz's ending clear and kind?
Beatriz called instead of texting, spoke briefly and honestly, avoided blame and didn't leave false hope.
What did Lindiwe value about how the ending happened?
Lindiwe was hurt but glad Beatriz called rather than going quiet, because clarity showed respect.
Tighten this sentence: The movie that we watched last night was a movie about animals.
The movie we watched last night was about animals.

Monday. Seema whispered that Kunal's shirt looked like his grandfather's, and Pranav laughed along. Kunal heard. He pulled his jumper over the shirt.
Tuesday. Pranav couldn't eat his lunch. He kept picturing Kunal's hands tugging the jumper down. He felt a little sick. Part of him wanted to say, "It was only a joke," but that didn't feel honest.
Wednesday. Pranav sat next to Kunal at break. "I'm sorry I laughed about your shirt. It wasn't fair."
Kunal shrugged, but his shoulders loosened.
Later, Seema started another joke about someone's shoes. Pranav shook his head. "Not funny, Seema." He walked off to play football.

What did Seema say about Kunal's shirt?
That it looked like his grandfather's.
What does Pranav not eating his lunch suggest?
It suggests he felt guilty and uneasy about laughing at Kunal.
What did Pranav choose instead of defending himself as "only a joke"?
He apologised to Kunal and, when Seema joked again, refused to join in.
How might Kunal see Pranav's apology?
Kunal seems cautious but a little relieved, since his shoulders loosen even though he only shrugs.

Sudha's right shoe had gone missing, so she went back through the day in order: the bedroom, then the verandah, then the gate where she had been playing. It was not in the bedroom or on the verandah, so she went to the gate, and there it was under the bench. Thomas walked to the kitchen and said, "Mummy, I can't find my shoe." His mother asked, "Where did you last have it?" and the question gave him a place to start. Anaya sat by the front door with her arms round her knees. "My shoe ran away," she said. "If I wait here, it will come home." She waited, and the shoe did not come. Varun couldn't find his shoe either, and he was wandering from room to room without a plan. A friend, Ritu, said, "Check the last place you played." Varun thought a moment, ran to the balcony, and there it was, next to a toy car.

Where did Varun find his shoe?
Varun found his shoe on the balcony, next to a toy car.
How does Thomas's way of searching differ from Anaya's, and what came from each?
Thomas asked his mother, whose question about the last place he had it gave him a starting point. Anaya waited by the door for the shoe to come home, so no searching happened.
What might Anaya be feeling as she sat waiting with her arms round her knees?
She may be sad and hopeful at once; she wants the shoe back and believes waiting will bring it, which is comforting but does nothing.
What could an adult say to help Anaya begin searching?
An adult could ask where she last wore the shoe and offer to look with her, one room at a time. That turns waiting into a plan. 🙂

Supervisor's note, programme meeting, Thursday. The team discussed moving our village health camps from Sundays to Saturdays. Everyone agreed except Sonali. She explained that many women in two of our villages work in the fields on Saturdays and would miss the camp. She added that she understood the team's reason: our doctors are more available on Saturdays. Chinmay pushed back hard. Sonali didn't argue louder. She asked, 'Could we try Saturday in three villages and keep Sunday in the two where women work?' Chinmay said that would complicate the schedule. She said, 'Fair. I'll go with the group if we review attendance after a month.' We agreed. I noted how calm the room stayed throughout.

Why did Sonali think some women would miss a Saturday camp?
Many women in two of the villages work in the fields on Saturdays.
How might Chinmay have felt when Sonali stayed calm and offered a compromise?
Probably less defensive, since she acknowledged the team's reasons and didn't argue louder.
What made Sonali's disagreement constructive?
She explained her reasoning, acknowledged the doctors' availability, offered a trial, and agreed to go with the group if attendance was reviewed.
How did the supervisor experience the meeting?
The supervisor noticed and valued how calm the room stayed throughout the disagreement.

In the clinic waiting room, Yash kicked the chair leg and wailed, "I want to go home!" Earlier, in the long queue, Payal had snapped, "Stop whining!" and his lip had trembled.
Now she knelt in front of him. "You're scared about the injection, and you're tired of waiting. That's a lot."
He nodded, sniffing.
"And Mumma was sharp with you in the queue. I'm sorry. I was tired too, but I shouldn't have shouted."
Yash climbed into her lap. When the nurse called his name, he held her finger tight and walked in.

What had Payal snapped at Yash in the queue?
She had snapped, "Stop whining!"
What was Yash feeling in the waiting room?
He was scared about the injection and tired of waiting; he kicked the chair and wailed that he wanted to go home.
What did Payal do that helped Yash feel safe again?
She knelt down calmly, named his fear and tiredness, and said sorry for shouting, which repaired the moment.
What would change if Payal had never apologised for snapping?
Yash might still feel hurt and unsure of her, and be less likely to lean on her when he walked in to the nurse.
What is the over-by-over score of the club cricket final in our town?
I don't know the over-by-over score, as I can't see local matches. Ask the club organiser or someone watching at the ground.
