Supervisor's note, summer internship, week 6
In week 2, I put Madhav in charge of two first-year trainees, Charu and another student. He did well at first: checked in, explained tasks.
Since week 4 I've noticed changes. He now leaves early on Fridays, "because leads can." He didn't notice when Charu stayed till eight fixing his slides. When she asked for help with a spreadsheet, he said, "Figure it out, that's how I learned."
Yesterday I asked him how his team was doing. "Great," he said. "I'm the same as I was, just busier."
Next week I'll ask Charu and the other trainee to fill in a short anonymous feedback form, and I'll go through it with Madhav.

When did the supervisor put Madhav in charge of the trainees?
Madhav was put in charge in week 2.
What does Madhav's answer "I'm the same as I was" suggest?
He feels confident and a bit self-satisfied, not noticing how he has changed toward his juniors.
Why could the feedback form help?
It lets Charu and the other trainee say how they feel without fear, so Madhav can see what he isn't noticing.
What is it like for Charu when Madhav tells her to figure it out?
Charu feels unsupported and a little hurt, having stayed till eight fixing his slides.

Lokesh ran a mobile repair shop in a small town and thought he knew phones. One day his sister Jaya got a message: "Your electricity will be cut tonight. Call this number." Lokesh laughed at first, then paused. Their neighbour had lost money to a message like this. Jaya almost called. Lokesh took the phone and checked the number; it wasn't the electricity board. "It's a trick," he said. "They want you to panic." That evening he helped her set a strong password on her email, turn on two-step login, and check which apps could see her contacts. Jaya was surprised how many had access. "I never agreed to this," she said. "You did," he said, "when you clicked 'allow' without reading."

What did the message to Jaya say?
It said her electricity would be cut tonight and to call a number.
Why did Lokesh pause after laughing?
He remembered their neighbour losing money to a similar message, which made him take it seriously.
What steps did Lokesh take to protect Jaya's accounts?
He set a strong password, turned on two-step login, and checked which apps could access her contacts.
How might Jaya feel about her phone's permissions now?
She was surprised and perhaps uneasy to learn she had allowed access without reading, and may be more careful next time.

Note on the fridge for Mumma, from Joseph (Papa), Tuesday.
Arohi woke at six with a stomach ache, holding her tummy and saying the school trip would be ruined. No fever, no vomiting, she'd eaten normally last night.
I sat with her and said, "I know it hurts. Let's try Papa's trip-day mint." I gave her one of the plain mints from the tin and told her it usually helps tummies settle. She sucked it slowly while I rubbed her back and we talked about the zoo.
Within twenty minutes she was laughing and eating toast. She went on the trip.
I asked her class teacher to call if it came back. If it keeps coming on trip days, let's talk to her and see the doctor together.

What did Papa give Arohi from the tin?
He gave her one of the plain mints from the tin.
What was Arohi feeling when she woke at six?
She felt hurt and worried, holding her tummy and afraid the school trip would be ruined.
Which parts of Papa's response show good care beyond the mint?
He sat with her, rubbed her back, talked about the zoo, asked the teacher to call if the ache returned and planned a doctor visit if it keeps happening.
How might Mumma feel reading the note?
Mumma may feel reassured that Arohi was cared for calmly, and thoughtful about whether trip days bring on the ache.
Each starting with the word "The" and each on its own line, write three sentences about a vegetable market.

The vegetable sellers call out their prices.
The air smells of coriander and ripe guavas.
The crowd moves slowly between the stalls.

Squeeze this piece into three sentences.

Vaishampayana continued, "Hearing these words, the high-souled Vasudeva, addressing the venerable Gandhari, said unto her these words, with a faint smile, 'There is none in the world, save myself, that is capable of exterminating the Vrishnis. I know this well. I am endeavouring to bring it about. In uttering this curse, O thou of excellent vows, thou hast aided me in the accomplishment of that task. The Vrishnis are incapable of being slain by others, be they human beings or gods or Danavas. The Yadavas, therefore shall fall by one another's hand.' After he of Dasharha's race had said these words, the Pandavas became stupefied. Filled with anxiety all of them became hopeless of life!"

Vasudeva tells Gandhari with a faint smile that only he can destroy the Vrishnis, and he is already trying to bring it about. He says her curse has helped, since nobody else can kill them, so they will fall by one another's hands. The Pandavas are stunned and lose hope of life.

Note from the class teacher, Class 7, Tuesday.
This morning Gurleen came to me before assembly with her mother's phone. The night before, Ramesh had posted a photo of her asleep on the bus during the school trip, mouth open. Twenty classmates had reacted with laughing faces.
Gurleen's voice was steady, but her eyes were red. She said she had wanted to reply with something rude but had taken screenshots instead.
I told her she had done exactly the right thing and that none of this was her fault. I spoke to Ramesh and his parents at lunch. The photo was deleted and Ramesh apologised to Gurleen. I will talk to the whole class about the group chat tomorrow.

How many classmates reacted with laughing faces?
Twenty classmates.
How did Gurleen seem to feel when she came to the teacher?
She seemed hurt and embarrassed, with red eyes, though she kept her voice steady.
What did Gurleen do that helped stop the mockery?
She didn't reply in anger; she took screenshots and brought them to the teacher, who acted that same day.
How might Ramesh see the photo after talking to the teacher and his parents?
Ramesh may now see that what felt like a joke was public humiliation for Gurleen, which is why he deleted it and apologised.
Instructions should be commands, not passive: The mixture should be stirred and then left to cool.
Stir the mixture, then leave it to cool.

Naveen: ok. are u ok? where are u exactly

Naveen: u did great. wait 2 mins, drink water, then ride home slowly

Where was the insurance copy?
It was in the glovebox, in the blue folder.
How did Rukmini feel while the police checked her papers?
Rukmini felt scared and anxious, her hands shaking.
What helped Rukmini handle the stop well?
Naveen reminded her to breathe and stay polite, told her where the papers were, and called Papa, so she stayed calm and showed every document.
How does Naveen seem to feel during the chat?
Naveen seems worried but steady, keeping calm to help Rukmini and proud of how she handled it.
A shopkeeper sells 10 pens at Rs 4 each and 3 pencils at Rs 6 each. How much does he get?
Rs 58. Because 10 x 4 = 40 and 3 x 6 = 18, so 40 + 18 = 58.

In their kitchen in Enugu, Chidi, four, wailed when his older sister Paulo took the last biscuit. His face was red and tears rolled. "It's mine!" Paulo froze. Their father knelt down. "You're really upset." Chidi kept crying, then said, wetly, "She always... gets the big one." "So you feel it's unfair," said their father. "We can fix it. You're going to choose which biscuit you'd like tomorrow, first." Chidi sniffed. "Promise?" Their father nodded.

What did Paulo take?
Paulo took the last biscuit.
What was Chidi feeling when he said "She always... gets the big one"?
He felt it was unfair and was hurt and angry. The words came out while he was still crying, so he was probably still very upset.
What could their father do next to help both children?
He can keep his promise about choosing first and make sure Paulo also feels heard.
How might Paulo feel after freezing and hearing Chidi?
She may feel surprised and a little guilty, and may want to make it right.

Subject: Congratulations on your new baby

First day of Ganesh festival: Damini holds a banana to her ear. "Hello, Ganpati Bappa?" Manoj laughs.

Three days later: she puts a shoebox on the table, drapes a dupatta on it, and says, "This is the mandap." She sits her doll inside.

Last day of the festival: she waves a stick with a marigold on top. "This is my aarti," she sings, walking round the shoebox.

What did Damini put her doll inside?
She sat her doll inside the shoebox mandap.
How was Damini feeling when she waved the marigold stick?
Damini was happy and absorbed in her pretend festival, singing as she walked around.
How can Manoj encourage Damini's pretend play?
He can join in, pretend with her, and give her more everyday things like boxes and cloth.
How might Manoj feel watching Damini's play grow?
Manoj was amused at first and likely delighted to see her imagination grow.
Why is it a good habit to put things back where they belong?
Putting things back saves time. Because we will know where to look the next time we need them, and nobody else has to search either, little things do not get lost.

How many pages did I read today?
What does "rain on someone's parade" mean?
Tell me the meaning of "persevering".

1. I'm not sure. I can't see what you read. Check where your bookmark is now and where it was this morning.
2. It means to spoil someone's plans or happy moment. For example: I did not want to rain on her parade by pointing out the small error.
3. It is the -ing form of "persevere", a verb meaning to keep trying in spite of difficulty.

The week after Papa's knee operation, everyone said the same thing: "Now Lokesh will run the shop."

I'm Lokesh, and I was in the final year of architecture in Nagpur. I loved it. But every time I looked at Papa's bandaged leg, I felt like a selfish person for even wanting to go back.

For a few days I did nothing. I didn't answer my classmates and I didn't tell my parents what I was thinking. My elder sister Seema noticed. "You're sulking in the hardware aisle," she said. "Talk to them."

So one evening I sat with both of them and said it straight: "I'm grateful for this shop. It paid for my studies. I want to finish my degree. Here's what I can do: come home every weekend, train Raju bhaiya to handle the counter, and check the stock lists every Sunday."

Papa was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "Show me the schedule."

Where was Lokesh studying architecture?
Lokesh was in the final year of architecture in Nagpur.
What was Lokesh feeling in the days after Papa's operation?
Lokesh felt guilty and torn, like a selfish person for wanting to go back to studies while Papa was hurt.
What did Lokesh do that turned the situation around?
Lokesh stopped avoiding it, thanked the parents honestly and offered a concrete plan: weekends at home, training Raju bhaiya and Sunday stock checks.
How does Seema see Lokesh during those first few days?
Seema sees Lokesh sulking and stuck, and believes an honest talk with the parents is the way out.

On his fourteenth month in Mumbai, Sumit noticed he'd stopped calling the flat in Andheri "the room" and started calling it home.

It happened the day Hansa joined his team from Jaipur. She sat at her desk with a stiff smile and the same lost look he remembered in his own mirror.

At lunch he took her to the Gujarati thali place he'd found after weeks of searching. He told her which local train to avoid at nine. He gave her the number of his building's cook.

"Do you still miss Patna?" Hansa asked.

"On Chhath, a lot," Sumit said. "I go home for it every year. But when I land back here, I feel relieved too."

That night he messaged his mother a photo of the monsoon from his window: "Thank you for letting me go." And then, to Hansa: "Monsoon tip: carry two umbrellas."

Which month in Mumbai was Sumit in when he started calling the flat home?
It was his fourteenth month in Mumbai.
What was Sumit feeling when he messaged his mother?
He felt grateful, both for Mumbai and for his mother letting him leave Patna.
How could Sumit keep helping Hansa over the next weeks?
He could keep sharing small practical tips and invite her to regular lunches, since he remembers how lost the first months feel.
How might Hansa see Sumit on her first days?
Hansa probably sees him as a relief, a colleague who understands being new and makes the city less overwhelming.

Sachin sat at the tea stall near Sagar bus stand, watching his phone light up with Chandrika's messages. He had let three of them sit unanswered. She wanted to move to Bengaluru after her degree and never look back at the town. He wanted to stay near his parents and teach at the government school. Every conversation lately circled back to that, and he felt guilty just for wanting his own life.

He knew what he was doing. He had gone quiet, hoping that she'd give up first, and it made him feel like a coward.

That evening he called her. "Can we talk properly? I don't think our plans fit any more, and I'd rather say it than disappear."

She was silent, then said, "I've been feeling it too."

They talked till the shop's lights went out.

Which town is Sachin sitting in when he watches his phone?
He is at the tea stall near the bus stand in Sagar.
What was Sachin feeling as he let Chandrika's messages sit unanswered?
Guilt and a sense of cowardice: he was hoping she would give up first, and he felt bad about wanting a life different from hers.
What made Sachin's call kinder than continuing to disappear?
He named that their plans no longer fit and chose honesty, so Chandrika did not have to guess or wait for him to fade away.
How might Chandrika have felt when Sachin said their plans no longer fit?
She may have felt sad, but also relieved to hear it plainly, since she says she had been feeling it too.

"Himani! The scholarship list is up!"
Aparna grabbed her arm and pulled her to the notice board. Himani looked. Then looked again.
Her name. Top of the list. Full scholarship.
She didn't scream. She didn't move. Her hand went to her mouth and stayed there.
"Himani? Say something!"
Nothing. Just staring.
Aparna was about to shake her. Then she stopped. She stood beside her and said nothing at all.
A full minute passed. Other students pushed past to look.
Finally Himani whispered, "That's my name."
"It is."
"I applied because Ma'am told me to. I didn't think... we can't afford college. We can now?"
"You can now."
Himani's eyes filled. Then she laughed, a shaky, astonished laugh, and hugged Aparna so hard they both nearly fell over.
"Give me one more minute," she said, "before I call Amma."

Where was Himani's name on the list?
Top of the list.
What was Himani feeling as she stood frozen at the notice board?
Himani was astonished and overwhelmed, unable to believe the news, which later turned into joy and relief.
Which of Aparna's choices helped most?
Stopping herself from shaking Himani and simply standing beside her in silence, giving her a moment of quiet space.
How might Himani's Amma feel when she gets the call?
She would probably be astonished and overjoyed, since the family thought college was out of reach.

I'm Hrithik. Two years ago, a junior named Jasleen joined my team at the Gurgaon consulting firm. Within six months, she was presenting to clients I'd spent three years winning over. The partners loved her.

I noticed the sting at a team dinner, when the senior partner said, "Jasleen's going places." I smiled and felt sick.

For a few weeks, I did small, ugly things. I didn't forward her an email about a big project. I let her struggle with a spreadsheet I could have fixed in five minutes.

Then I caught myself. That wasn't who I wanted to be. And honestly, it was hurting the team.

So I did the opposite. I recommended her for the project. I credited her work by name in a partner meeting. And I signed up for a course on the financial modelling I'd been avoiding.

We work well together now. And I've grown too. Her speed pushed me.

How long did it take Jasleen to present to clients Hrithik had spent years winning?
Within six months.
What did Hrithik feel when the senior partner praised Jasleen?
Hrithik felt a sting of envy, smiling while feeling sick inside.
What did Hrithik change once he noticed his envy?
Hrithik stopped holding Jasleen back, recommended her for the project, credited her by name, and worked on Hrithik's own skills.
How might Jasleen have been affected by Hrithik's early behaviour?
Jasleen may have felt frustrated and unsupported, missing an important email and struggling alone with the spreadsheet.

Vaibhav wanted the mehendi on the riverside lawn in Guwahati, in the middle of June. I remember thinking, in June, it's not if it rains, it's when.
So I didn't argue about the lawn. I just asked myself: what would we do at four in the afternoon if the sky opened? The answer was the community hall two streets away. We booked it for the same evening and paid a small deposit. We also set aside a bit of money in an envelope, labelled "surprises", for things like extra umbrellas or a second auto.
My friends thought I was being gloomy.
At three-thirty that day, black clouds came over the river. Vaibhav looked at me and said, "Hall?" I said, "Hall."
By four-thirty, the mehendi artists were set up indoors, and the music was playing again. The envelope paid for plastic sheets and a lot of chai.
— Jaya

Where was the backup hall?
The community hall two streets away.
How did Jaya feel when friends called the plan gloomy, and later when the rain came?
Jaya may have felt a little doubted at first, but calm and quietly vindicated when the rain came and the move took only an hour.
What else could Jaya and Vaibhav have done to make the switch even smoother?
They could have assigned specific people to carry things and tell guests, so everyone knew their job the moment the clouds came.
How might Vaibhav have felt on asking "Hall?"
Vaibhav was probably relieved and grateful that a backup already existed, turning a possible disaster into a quick decision.

Neelam had run every morning for forty-one days, and her phone app showed the unbroken line of dots. On day forty-two her right knee began to ache on the stairs. She told herself it was just stiffness.

Her friend Vishal, running beside her, said, "You're limping. Stop for today." She shook her head. "I'm not losing the streak." She ran the full loop, her jaw set.

By the weekend she could not bend the knee without wincing. The doctor told her to rest completely. Neelam missed the weeks she had been so afraid to miss, and stared at the app's blank squares, thinking how the streak she protected had cost her the running itself.

On which day did Neelam's knee begin to ache?
On day forty-two.
What was Neelam feeling when she shook her head at Vishal?
Neelam was determined and afraid of losing the streak, so pride and fear pushed her to ignore the pain.
What could Neelam do when she can run again, and why?
Neelam could allow rest days and stop at the first sign of pain, because the aim is running for the long term and not a perfect chain of dots.
How might Vishal have felt watching Neelam run on?
Vishal was probably worried and frustrated, having said clearly that she was limping, and felt helpless as she carried on.

metadata.subtype: Approach: push through pain to keep the streak [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Friday night
Launch day for the booking page. At 10 a.m. a client from the Pune office emailed our whole team: "Page is confusing. Who approved this?" My chest went tight and for an hour it was the only thing in my head.
Then I did the thing Joseph and I agreed on after last year's burnout: before deciding how a day went, write the wins next to the hits.
Wins: 412 bookings in the first day. Two emails from users saying it was easier than the old form. My lead said "clean work" in the stand-up. Mobile loading fixed after a week of fighting it. Joseph brought the good biscuits.
Hits: one angry client. One button label that honestly is confusing; I'll fix it Monday.
Looking at the page, it was a good day with one bad email in it. Not a bad day. I'm going to bed.
— Anjali

How many bookings came in on the first day?
412 bookings in the first day.
What was Anjali feeling after the angry email, and what shows it?
Anjali felt shaken and worried, with a tight chest and the email being the only thing on Anjali's mind for an hour.
Which habit helped Anjali decide how the day really went?
Writing the wins next to the hits, which let the bookings, the users' thanks and the lead's praise count as much as one angry email, while still fixing the confusing button.
What would change if Anjali had judged the day only by the client's email?
Anjali might have gone to bed thinking the launch failed, missed the real good news, and slid back towards the burnout of last year.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, Holi week, Class 9B. Sabina
Vijay has changed a lot since June. In term one he sat with the cricket boys and talked only scores. By August he was with the art-club group, nails painted black. Last month he was loudly arguing politics with the debate crowd; this week he sits alone at lunch. Today, at the Holi celebration, he refused colour, then later joined in, then snapped at a friend who asked which group he's with now.
He stayed back and said, "Ma'am, I don't know who I'm supposed to be." He looked genuinely unsettled.
I told him that trying things on is normal at his age and that he does not have to choose today. I will mention to his parents that he seems unsettled, and I have booked him a chat with the school counsellor next week, only to talk.

Which group was Vijay with by August?
The art-club group, nails painted black.
What is Vijay feeling when he says "I don't know who I'm supposed to be"?
He feels unsettled and confused, which also shows in snapping at a friend and sitting alone at lunch.
What did the teacher do next, and why does it help?
The teacher told him trying things on is normal, took away the pressure to choose, and arranged a counsellor chat and a word with his parents, so he has support while exploring.
How might Vijay's friend feel when snapped at?
The friend was likely hurt and puzzled, asking a simple question and getting an angry answer.

Simplify the language for a learner of English.

Rain moved assembly indoors, and snack time was forty minutes late. Jagdish, the kindergarten teacher, was finishing the colours lesson with twenty restless children.
Tanuja, five, would not sit. She kicked her chair, and when Jagdish said her name, her eyes filled with tears.
Jagdish nearly sent her to the corner. Then he checked the clock. 11:20. She usually ate at 10:40.
"Snack now, everyone," he said.
Tanuja ate her poha slowly. By the last spoon she was calm, humming, sorting crayons without being asked.

Rain moved the assembly indoors, and snack time was forty minutes late. Jagdish, the kindergarten teacher, was finishing the colours lesson with twenty restless children. Tanuja, five, would not sit. She kicked her chair. When Jagdish said her name, her eyes filled with tears. He almost sent her to the corner. Then he looked at the clock. It was 11:20. She usually ate at 10:40. "Snack now, everyone," he said. Tanuja ate her poha slowly. By the last spoon she was calm. She hummed and sorted crayons without being asked.

Read this:

I'm Naveen, Kashish's brother, and I watched from the veranda. Kashish and five friends had named themselves “the Lightning Six” and drawn rules on a chart: a secret handshake, a bottle-cap badge, no talking to anyone who wasn't in. Kashish was glowing, holding the chart like a trophy.

Leena, from next door, stood at the gate. “Can I join?” “We're already six,” said Kashish, and everyone nodded. I couldn't tell if Kashish enjoyed saying no or only the feeling of being chosen. Leena held a cap she'd found for a badge, looked at it, and put it in her pocket.

What name had the group given themselves?
Kashish and five friends had named themselves “the Lightning Six.”
What might Kashish have been feeling while holding the chart like a trophy?
Kashish was probably thrilled and proud to be chosen and to belong, though Naveen cannot tell what else crossed Kashish's mind.
What could Kashish try on seeing Leena at the gate?
Kashish could ask the group whether a seventh member could join or find a role for Leena.
What might Leena have felt, putting the bottle cap in a pocket?
Leena probably felt hurt and embarrassed, having hoped to join with a badge of her own.

Read this:

Warden's note, Room 214. Disha, second year, is fiercely independent: fixes her own fan, never asks for anything, eats early to avoid the crowd. Tonight her boyfriend waited at the gate for an hour. The guard said he wanted to "talk about where this is going". Disha sent word she was busy, then sat in the common room with a book she never turned a page of. When I asked if she was all right, she said, "I just don't do the needy stuff." Later I heard her on the phone to her mother, voice thick, saying she felt alone in a full hostel. I've left a note under her door with the counselling centre's evening hours, and I'll check in at breakfast.
Elizabeth

How long did Disha's boyfriend wait at the gate?
For an hour.
What was Disha feeling as she held a book without turning a page?
She seemed tense and lonely, avoiding a deep talk while feeling alone in a full hostel.
How is Elizabeth supporting Disha?
By leaving the counselling centre's hours under her door and planning a breakfast check-in, without pushing.
What is it like for the boyfriend to wait an hour and get "busy"?
He probably feels hurt and shut out, wanting to talk about the relationship and getting no answer.
Why should a stranger not be told where you live?
The stranger may not mean well. Because you cannot know a person's real purpose from a short meeting, and an address could be used to find you.
Why does a snake keep flicking its tongue in and out?

The snake flicks its tongue to smell its surroundings. Because the tongue picks up tiny particles from the air and the ground and brings them to special organs in the mouth, the snake can find food and sense danger.

Read this:

During garden time at the kindergarten, Manjula crouched by the neem tree and stopped moving. A line of ants was carrying tiny white crumbs into a crack in the ground.
"Sudha Ma'am! Look! Where are they going? Do they have a house? Is there a mummy ant?"
Sudha knelt down beside her in the dust. "Let's watch and see."
They watched together. An ant dropped its crumb, and another picked it up. Manjula gasped. "They're helping!" Two more children came to look, then three.
Soon half the class was lying on their tummies in a row, whispering, and Sudha was whispering too.

What were the ants carrying?
Tiny white crumbs.
What does Manjula's gasp suggest?
It suggests she was amazed and delighted to see one ant help another.
How did Sudha deepen Manjula's wonder?
She knelt in the dust and watched with her, saying "Let's watch and see" instead of answering everything.
Why might the other children have come over?
They were probably curious, drawn by Manjula's excitement and the teacher kneeling in the dust.

Read this:

Gargi sat on her bed at night, sure she had no gift of any kind. Manjula could sing like a bird, and her cousin Nikhil won every quiz. At dinner Papa said, "Look at your cousin Nikhil, he plays the flute so well." Gargi's chest crumpled and she put down her spoon. "I do try, just differently from him," she said. "Can you notice something I did today?" Papa paused. "You fed the neighbour's cat every day this week."

At school Manjula sang the morning song and the whole hall went still. Gargi's mouth fell open. Instead of deciding she could never, she asked after class, "How do you practise?" Manjula grinned. "Every morning, with my grandmother's harmonium." She sang the tune again slowly so Gargi could try.

Over the term Gargi tried drums, chess and clay. She was slow at chess, dropped the drums, and loved clay. In March she took a small clay owl to the district fair and won a prize. The applause made her cheeks glow. Afterwards she thanked Aditi Ma'am, who had taught her to knead, and stayed behind to show two younger children how to roll a coil.

What did Gargi make that won a prize?
She made a small clay owl.
How did Gargi's reaction to Manjula's singing differ from her reaction to Papa's comparison, and what changed by March?

Papa's comparison crushed her, though she spoke up for herself. Manjula's singing amazed her, and she asked how to practise instead of giving up. By March, after trying drums, chess and clay, she loved clay and won a prize.
What was Gargi feeling when Papa praised Nikhil's flute playing?
She felt crushed. Her chest crumpled and she put down her spoon.
How did Gargi stay humble after winning the prize?
She thanked Aditi Ma'am, who had taught her to knead, and stayed behind to show two younger children how to roll a coil.

Read this:

On Monday morning Jatin clutched his stomach by the cowshed. 'Kaka, it hurts. I can't go.' Monday was reading-aloud day in Class 4, and last time the words had jumbled in his mouth while everyone laughed.
Ramesh Kaka felt his forehead, frowned and said, 'Then come with me to the field.'
By the time they reached the cotton rows, the pain was gone. Jatin chased a mongoose, ate a guava and felt light as a kite.
But the next Sunday, while the pressure cooker whistled for dinner, his stomach began to twist again. Tomorrow was Monday. He hadn't even thought about school yet, and already his body was saying no.

What did Jatin do in the field once the pain was gone?
He chased a mongoose and ate a guava.
Why did Jatin's stomach start twisting on Sunday evening?
Staying home had brought such quick relief that his body now linked Monday with danger, so the fear started a day early, before he even thought about school.
What might help at this stage before the pattern grows?
Ramesh Kaka could talk with Jatin about the reading-aloud worry and ask the teacher about a gentler way to practise, so Jatin goes to school instead of avoiding it.
What might Ramesh Kaka be thinking as Jatin runs about the field?
Kaka may start to wonder whether the stomach ache was really about school, since Jatin seemed perfectly well among the cotton rows.

Read this:

On Saturday afternoon in their Lucknow flat, the power went, and so did the internet. Ayesha sat on the sofa staring at the black TV screen. "I'll wait," she said. Her brother Harish dragged out a box of old comics. Her father suggested finishing the jigsaw puzzle on the dining table. "It's too dark," she said, though the window was wide open and bright. Harish read three comics, laughing out loud. Her father fitted the whole sky of the puzzle. Ayesha kept pressing her dead tablet's button, as if it might come alive. At five the power came back and the TV came on. Ayesha had been bored for three hours and hadn't done a single thing.

How many comics did Harish read?
Three.
How was Ayesha feeling during the three hours?
Bored and restless, stuck waiting for the power.
What else could Ayesha have tried?
Joining the puzzle by the bright window or reading a comic with Harish.
What was the afternoon like for her father?
He enjoyed fitting the whole sky of the puzzle.

metadata.subtype: Approach: waiting passively for things to return to normal [Pitfall]

Read this:

"Papa! A dog chased me today. It was as big as a bus!"
"As big as a bus?" Kamal put down his newspaper. "Did it have wheels?"
"No! It had six legs and red eyes!"
"Wow. What did you do?"
"I flew! Up to the water tank."
Kamal laughed. "Brilliant story. Now tell me the true part. Was there a real dog?"
Charu twisted her frock. "A brown dog by the gate. It barked. I ran to Dadi."
"Good thing you ran to Dadi. And the flying?"
"...That was a story part."
"Best story part," Kamal said. "Draw me the six-legged one?"

Where did Charu run when the brown dog barked?
She ran to Dadi.
What might Charu have been feeling when the real dog barked?
She was probably scared, which may be why her story made the dog huge and let her fly away.
How did Kamal keep a gentle line on the facts?
He enjoyed the story, then asked for "the true part", so Charu could tell what really happened without being called a liar.
How did Kamal seem to feel about Charu's tall tale?
He seemed amused and delighted, calling it a brilliant story and asking for a drawing.

Read this:

I've shared a desk cluster with Nirmala at the design studio in Bengaluru for a year, and I still can't fully explain her. I'm Elizabeth. From nine to eleven every morning, Nirmala puts on her big headphones, closes her mail, and props up a little card that says 'Deep work till 11'. Her phone goes face down. We learned not to disturb her. At eleven she opens everything at once and answers all the messages in about twenty minutes. Then she takes a walk outside. Afternoons are the same: one more block. I used to think she was being antisocial. Then I noticed her designs were always done first, with fewer revisions than anyone's. I don't know how it feels inside her head. But last month I made my own card.

What does Nirmala's little card say?
'Deep work till 11'.
What might Nirmala feel during her morning block, as far as Elizabeth can tell?
Nirmala seems calm and absorbed in one task, though Elizabeth admits not knowing how it feels inside her head.
Which parts of Nirmala's routine make her work faster?
Single-task blocks with notifications off, answering all messages together at eleven, and a walk to rest.
How did Elizabeth's view of Nirmala change over the year?
Elizabeth went from thinking Nirmala was antisocial to admiring her results and making a card of her own.

Read this:

"I sent the client the old figures," Indu said, staring into her cold coffee. "The old ones. To the whole mailing list."
Manoj leaned on the pantry counter. "Okay. And?"
"And I'm the most careless person alive. Sir will think I'm useless. I think I'm useless."
"Stop. What actually happened?"
"I had two files with the same name. I picked the wrong one."
"So, one mistake with a clear cause."
"One mistake the whole client saw."
"And what did you do after?"
Indu sighed. "Sent a correction in ten minutes. Told Sir before he found out."
"That's what a responsible person does. Not a useless one."
"It doesn't feel like it."
"It won't, for a day. So what changes?"
She sat up slightly. "Date in every file name. And I check the attachment before anything goes to a client."
"See? That's the useful voice. The other one just shouts."
Indu almost smiled.

Why did Indu pick the wrong file?
She had two files with the same name.
What was Indu feeling as she stared into her cold coffee?
Indu felt ashamed and was harsh with herself, calling herself useless after the client saw the mistake.
Which of Manoj's questions helped most, and why?
'What actually happened?' and 'So what changes?' moved Indu from self-attack to a clear cause and a fix, like dates in file names.
How might Sir see Indu's handling of the mistake?
Sir would likely see responsibility in a correction within ten minutes and being told before he found out, not carelessness.

Read this:

The other boys on the football field in Toronto laughed at Chen's lunch box and called his dumplings smelly. Chen's face went hot. He said nothing, and at recess the next day he sat behind the bookshelf in the library. He began saying his stomach hurt so he could skip football. On Thursday his classmate Oskar found him alone and sat down beside him. Chen told him, in a small voice, what had been said. Oskar said he should tell the teacher. The next time the boys started, Chen said calmly, "I like my lunch," and walked to the library door where Oskar was waiting. The teacher spoke with the boys later that week.

Where did Chen sit at recess after the teasing?
He sat behind the bookshelf in the library.
Why did Chen say his stomach hurt?
He felt ashamed and wanted to avoid the boys, so he made an excuse to skip football.
What did Chen try that was better than fighting?
He answered calmly, walked away and told a teacher with Oskar's support.
What was it like for Oskar to find Chen alone?
Oskar probably noticed that Chen was hurting and wanted to help, and sitting down beside Chen made it easier for Chen to speak.

Say what this is about in one short line.

When tea was over Mr. Hurst reminded his sister-in-law of the card-table--but in vain. She had obtained private intelligence that Mr. Darcy did not wish for cards, and Mr. Hurst soon found even his open petition rejected. She assured him that no one intended to play, and the silence of the whole party on the subject seemed to justify her. Mr. Hurst had, therefore, nothing to do but to stretch himself on one of the sofas and go to sleep. Darcy took up a book. Miss Bingley did the same; and Mrs. Hurst, principally occupied in playing with her bracelets and rings, joined now and then in her brother's conversation with Miss Bennet.
Mr. Hurst wants cards, but his sister-in-law has learned that Mr. Darcy does not, so he sleeps while the others read or chat.

At the school council meeting, Samir and Trisha were arguing about the annual day budget. It started calm, but soon they were both shouting across the table.
"You always take the sports side!" Trisha yelled.
"And you only care about the dance!" Samir shouted back.
Other members went quiet. The teacher in charge, Mr Kulkarni, raised a hand. "Let's take a five-minute break."
Samir walked out to the corridor and leaned against the wall, breathing hard. Trisha stayed in the room, arms crossed.
When they came back, Samir spoke first, quietly. "Sorry. I got loud. Can we split it and try both?"
Trisha let out a breath. "Okay. I was loud too."
They worked it out in fifteen minutes.

How long a break did Mr Kulkarni call?
A five-minute break.
What was Samir feeling when he shouted across the table?
Samir felt frustrated and unheard, believing Trisha only cared about the dance.
How did the break help the argument?
It gave both of them time to calm down, so they could return with lower voices and find a compromise.
How might the other members have felt during the shouting?
They probably felt uncomfortable and tense, which is why they went quiet.

Read this:

The tax letter arrived the same week Sunaina was packing to move from Jaipur to Pune for her new job. She saw the department's name on the envelope, felt a cold drop in her stomach and slid it into the box marked 'papers, later'. Her flatmate, Himani, asked about it once. 'Probably a mistake,' Sunaina said, taping the box shut.
In Pune, the box sat unopened under her bed for three months. Then an email came with the heading 'penalty order'. She tore the box open at midnight. The first letter had asked her to explain a mismatch: one freelance payment of twenty thousand that the department's records showed but her return did not. The reply date was long gone. Now there was interest, a penalty and a much longer form to fill.

What was the box marked?
The box was marked 'papers, later'.
What did Sunaina feel when she first saw the department's name?
She felt a cold drop of fear and wanted to avoid it, telling herself it was probably a mistake.
What other approach could have fit Sunaina's busy moving week?
She could have opened the letter, put the reply date in her phone and asked a chartered accountant for help, which takes minutes even in a busy week.
How might Himani feel on hearing about the penalty?
Himani might feel a pang of regret for not pushing harder after asking about the envelope.

metadata.subtype: Approach: ignoring the notice from fear [Pitfall]

messages.content:
In the library I found, to my great delight, a vast number of English books, whole shelves full of them, and bound volumes of magazines and newspapers. A table in the centre was littered with English magazines and newspapers, though none of them were of very recent date. The books were of the most varied kind--history, geography, politics, political economy, botany, geology, law--all relating to England and English life and customs and manners. There were even such books of reference as the London Directory, the "Red" and "Blue" books, Whitaker's Almanac, the Army and Navy Lists, and--it somehow gladdened my heart to see it--the Law List.

What does the narrator find in the library, and what does it suggest?
He finds shelves of English books and magazines about history, law, geography and daily life, plus directories and almanacs. It suggests the owner has been studying England carefully.

Read this:

Saturday, late
Got the fourth internship rejection today. I turned it into a bit at dinner: "At this rate I'll be interning in my own bedroom." Everyone laughed. I did three more jokes on the walk back, one about framing the rejection emails. Sangeeta laughed at the first two, then went quiet. In our room she sat on the end of my bed and said, "You've been funny all day. How are you actually?" My throat closed up. I said, "Fine, obviously, I'm a comedian now," and she didn't laugh. She just waited. Then I cried for the first time since the first rejection. Turns out the jokes were holding the door shut. We talked for an hour. She said her cousin had found the careers cell useful, and I've booked a slot for Monday. I still think the bedroom-internship line was good. But I'm glad someone didn't laugh.
Aadhya

When did Aadhya first joke about interning in a bedroom?
At dinner.
What was Aadhya feeling beneath the jokes?
Aadhya felt hurt and discouraged by four rejections; the jokes eased the tension but held back distress that came out as tears once Sangeeta asked.
What did Sangeeta's approach get right?
She stopped laughing, asked a direct and serious question, waited through the deflecting joke, then listened and pointed toward the careers cell.
How might the friends at dinner have seen Aadhya?
As cheerful and coping well, since the jokes made them laugh, without realising how discouraged Aadhya felt.
Make this sentence shorter: The reason why I was late is that I missed the bus.
I was late because I missed the bus.
Our teacher said, "Please correct your answers." Is correct only a word for right?

Correct is also a verb meaning to find mistakes in something and fix them. As an adjective it means right or true.
Example: My sister corrects the spelling in my notes before every exam.

Read this:

Manjula: how's the conference talk coming?
Kalyani: haven't opened the laptop yet
Manjula: ?? it's in 4 days
Kalyani: I'm drawing it first. 8 boxes on paper, one per slide
Kalyani: each box has a job. problem, method, result or next step. if it has no job it's gone
Manjula: what got cut?
Kalyani: the 'about me' slide. the history of the lake. two graphs that say the same thing
Manjula: brave. the lake history was pretty
Kalyani: pretty, but it doesn't help anyone understand why the fish are dying 🐟
Kalyani: photo of the paper plan coming
Manjula: ok that's actually clear. I can follow it without you talking
Kalyani: that's the test 🙂

How many boxes did Kalyani draw?
8 boxes on paper, one per slide.
What does 'that's the test' suggest about how Kalyani feels?
Kalyani feels confident and pleased, seeing that the paper plan makes sense even to someone reading it alone.
What else could Kalyani do with the paper plan before building slides?
Time a rough run-through from the boxes, to check the talk fits before any design work.
How does the plan look to Manjula?
Manjula is doubtful at first, but finds the paper plan clear enough to follow without Kalyani explaining it.

Read this:

The ferry to Almada was nearly empty on a wet Thursday. Gabriel had been rehearsing the sentence since the morning stand-up.
"Tomas, can I tell you something stupid?" He watched the river instead of his mentor. "I think I'm a fraud. Every sprint I'm waiting for someone to notice I don't know what I'm doing."
Tomas laughed, not unkindly. "Stupid? I felt that for my first four years. Some weeks I still do." He counted on his fingers. "Ana felt it. Our CTO told me she felt it after her second promotion."
Gabriel turned. "Seriously?"
"Seriously. It usually means you care and you can see how much there is to know. It doesn't mean you're bad."
Gabriel let out a long breath. The sentence he had carried all day seemed lighter now, just something people said on ferries.

Where were Gabriel and Tomas when Gabriel told his secret?
They were on the ferry to Almada on a wet Thursday.
Why does Gabriel watch the river instead of his mentor as he speaks?
He feels ashamed and nervous about admitting he feels like a fraud, so looking away makes the confession easier.
What went well in how Tomas responded?
Tomas shared his own experience and named others who felt the same, which made the feeling normal and eased Gabriel's shame.
How might Tomas see Gabriel after the ferry talk?
Tomas probably sees Gabriel as someone who cares and is growing, not as a fraud, and may feel glad he was trusted with it.

Read this:

The rain had flooded the bus stop outside the college, and the last bus to Thrissur was forty minutes late. Elizabeth had been awake since four for her practical exam; she leaned on the pole with her eyes half closed. Anjali was scrolling through homestay photos. 'Three days in Wayanad after results. Look at this one, it has a swing.' Elizabeth nodded. 'Mm.' 'Fine,' Anjali said, locking the phone. 'You clearly hate the plan. You could just say so.' Elizabeth felt the words land wrong, like a coat on the wrong shoulders. She opened her eyes. 'I don't hate it. I'm so tired I can't feel my face. Show me the swing again tomorrow, when I'm a person?' Anjali looked at her properly, then laughed. 'Okay. Tomorrow.'

How late was the last bus to Thrissur?
The last bus to Thrissur was forty minutes late.
What did Elizabeth feel when Anjali said 'You clearly hate the plan'?
Elizabeth felt misread, as if a feeling that wasn't hers had been put on her, because the 'Mm' came from exhaustion, not dislike.
What choice did Elizabeth make that turned the moment, and why did it work?
Elizabeth opened her eyes and calmly named the real feeling, tiredness, and asked to see the swing tomorrow, which corrected the guess without starting a fight.
How might the moment have looked from Anjali's side before Elizabeth explained?
Anjali was excited and got only 'Mm' back in the rain, so the flat reply felt like rejection; hearing the real reason let Anjali see Elizabeth clearly again.
"Hamare gaon mein bijli kam aati hai" kaise kahun?
Say: "We do not get much electricity in our village." Another way: "The power supply in our village is not good."

Read this:

The school's winter picnic at Lodhi Garden was noisy, and Elizabeth Ma'am was busy counting heads when a bee stung Rimjhim on the hand. She wailed. Vasudha, five, heard her and dropped her sandwich. She sat beside Rimjhim, held her other hand, and blew on the sting. "I'll get Ma'am." She pushed through the crowd, tugged Elizabeth Ma'am's sleeve, and pointed. When Ma'am came with the first-aid bag, Vasudha stayed close, stroking Rimjhim's hair.

What stung Rimjhim?
A bee.
What was Vasudha feeling when she dropped her sandwich?
Vasudha felt worried and concerned for Rimjhim.
How did Vasudha comfort Rimjhim and get help?
She held her hand, blew on the sting, fetched Elizabeth Ma'am, and stayed beside her.
How might Elizabeth Ma'am feel about Vasudha's help?
Elizabeth Ma'am likely felt grateful and proud that Vasudha fetched her quickly and stayed kind.

Read this:

At the hostel committee meeting, twenty-three residents wanted to turn the reading room into a music room at night. Minakshi was the only one who disagreed. 'Some of us have no quiet place to study after ten,' she said. Lokesh, the committee secretary, sighed. 'Minakshi, it's twenty-three to one.' She nodded. 'I know. I'm not trying to stop the music. I'm only asking where the night readers should go.' She said it again, just as politely, at the next two meetings, and brought a list of fourteen residents who studied there late but hadn't come to the meetings. Nobody could laugh that off. At the fourth meeting, Lokesh proposed using the common hall for music instead. It passed easily.

How many residents did Minakshi list who studied late?
Fourteen residents.
What does Minakshi's calm nod at 'twenty-three to one' suggest?
She felt steady and confident, not shaken by being outnumbered.
What made Minakshi's lone view persuasive?
She stayed polite and consistent, made clear she wasn't against music, and brought evidence of the fourteen late readers.
How did Lokesh's position change?
From sighing at a lone objector to proposing the common hall as the solution.

Read this:

"Urmila, your banana's going brown," her Dadaji, Jagdish, called.
"Mm."
"What are you drawing?"
"The whole road to school. This is the bakery. This is the dog."
Jagdish came and looked at the chalk lines spreading across the courtyard. "Shall we call Mummy to see?"
"No, not yet. The river isn't done." Urmila bent lower, tongue between her teeth, adding wiggly blue lines.
"It's been an hour, beti."
"Has it?" She didn't look up. "Now the bridge. The bridge is hard."
Jagdish sat on the step and peeled the banana for himself, smiling.

What had Urmila drawn along the road to school?
The bakery, the dog, and a river of wiggly blue lines.
Why did Urmila say "No, not yet" to calling Mummy?
She was so absorbed in the river that showing it off didn't matter yet; she was eager to get the hard bridge right.
What did Jagdish do that let Urmila keep going?
He didn't insist on the snack or on showing Mummy; he sat on the step and let her work.
How might Jagdish feel watching Urmila draw?
Jagdish seems amused and fond, smiling as he eats the banana himself.

Supervisor's note, final-year seminar series, week 6.
Sudha presented her project on rainwater harvesting today. It was well organised. About four minutes in, she said "catchment" wrongly, paused, corrected it and went on. The rest was confident.
Afterwards she came to my desk looking close to tears. "Everyone heard that. They'll remember it as the girl who can't say 'catchment.'"
I asked her to wait. When the class returned from the break, I asked them, without naming anyone, to write down one thing they remembered from each talk. On Sudha's, eleven of fourteen wrote about the rooftop tank photo. Nobody mentioned the word. Rekha, who presented after her, wrote only "I was too nervous about mine to notice much."
I showed Sudha the slips. She read them twice and let out a long breath.
I will repeat this exercise with the next group; it helps.
— Seminar supervisor

What did most of the class remember about Sudha's talk?
Eleven of fourteen wrote about the rooftop tank photo.
What was Sudha feeling when she came to the desk?
Sudha was upset and ashamed, close to tears and sure everyone had noticed and would remember the mistake.
Which choice by the supervisor worked, and why?
Asking the class to write what they remembered, because it showed Sudha real evidence that the stumble went unnoticed.
What was the seminar like for Rekha?
Rekha was too nervous about her own talk to notice much about Sudha's.

Pranav, you asked if anyone ever teased me for being Hindu. Sit. I was fifteen, the only brown boy in my class in Leicester. One morning Gary held his nose when I opened my lunch and said my lot prayed to monkeys. The whole row laughed. I went hot, then silent. I wanted to disappear into my collar. Then Colin, a quiet boy who kept pigeons, said, "That's rubbish, Gary. You don't know a thing about it." At lunch Colin told Mr. Hughes, our teacher. That afternoon Mr. Hughes stopped the lesson and said plainly that what Gary had said was false and unkind, and asked if I'd like to tell the class about Diwali. I said no that day. The next year I said yes. Your Karthik Thatha still remembers Colin's pigeons, beta.

Where was Karthik the only brown boy in his class?
He was the only brown boy in his class in Leicester.
What did young Karthik feel when the whole row laughed?
He felt ashamed and silenced; he went hot, then quiet, and wanted to disappear into his collar.
At the turning point in the story, why did Colin's choice matter?
Colin spoke up in the moment and then told the teacher the same day, so Karthik was not alone and an adult could name the stereotype as false.
How might Colin have seen what Gary did?
Colin clearly saw it as ignorant and unfair, and though quiet, felt strongly enough to call it rubbish in front of everyone.

You asked about that time at the factory? Okay. I'm Chaitanya, and I was a line supervisor then.
Ruchir, from payroll, sat next to me. One Friday I saw him changing the contract workers' overtime sheets, cutting everyone's hours by two. Manager's orders, the whole payroll room knew. Nobody said a word. The workers were outside at the gate, waiting for their slips.
I didn't want to make a scene. So I just leaned over and asked, “Ruchir, is this okay?”
He went red. “Sir told me.”
“I know. I'm only asking.”
He sat there for maybe a minute. Then he said, “It's not, is it.” He saved the original sheets, and on Monday we both walked into HR together. It started with one small question.

By how many hours were the workers' overtime cut?
Everyone's hours were cut by two.
How did Chaitanya feel when he asked Ruchir the question?
Chaitanya felt uneasy about the change but careful and calm, not wanting to make a scene or accuse Ruchir.
What followed from Chaitanya's question, and why did it work?
Ruchir saved the original sheets and they went to HR together, because the question let him decide for himself rather than defend himself.
How might the contract workers at the gate be affected?
They would have lost pay for hours they really worked, so the question protected people who had no voice in that room.
Either the cat or the dog ate the biscuit, not both. The dog was out of the house when it vanished. Who ate it?
The cat ate it. Because it was the cat or the dog and the dog was not in the house, the dog could not have eaten it.

I'm Sahil, in Class 6. Last month I had a science project on circuits. My tuition teacher, Sharmila Ma'am, just did it for me. She connected all the wires in five minutes while I watched. It worked. But when the class asked me how, I couldn't explain. I felt so small.
Then my class teacher gave us a new project and said, "No help at all." I opened the kit and nothing made sense. I gave up after ten minutes.
Finally my uncle, who's an electrician, sat with me. He asked what I thought each wire did. He only told me one thing: "Follow the path of the current." I figured the rest out.
It was hard. But I understood it.

How long did Sharmila Ma'am take to connect the wires?
She connected them in five minutes while Sahil watched.
How did Sahil feel when the class asked how the circuit worked?
Sahil felt small and embarrassed, unable to explain something done for him.
Why did the uncle's help work better than the other two ways?
He asked what Sahil thought and gave one hint, so the task stayed hard but possible.
How might Sharmila Ma'am have seen her help?
She may have thought finishing the project quickly was helpful, not realising Sahil learned nothing.

Thursday. My report is due Friday noon, and today Parveen asked if I could tidy the slides for the team outing. It would take an hour, and I said, “I can't today, Friday's report has to go first. Ask me next week?” My face went warm. Parveen said “okay” in a flat voice, and my chest felt tight for a while. Then I put on headphones and worked from ten to twelve without opening chat. The results section is done, with the numbers checked. I still feel a little rude and I keep replaying the flat “okay”. But the report will not be crowded out by slides. I'll bring biscuits next week, and do the slides then. — Ira

What hours did Ira work with headphones on?
Ira worked from ten to twelve with headphones on and chat closed.
Why does Ira keep replaying Parveen's flat “okay”?
Ira feels guilty and a little rude for refusing, and worries the request has left Parveen upset.
What did Ira gain by saying no, and what did it cost?
The results section got finished and checked, which protects the Friday deadline; the cost was a moment of awkwardness and some guilt.
How might Parveen have felt when asking for the slide help?
Parveen probably felt hopeful that a quick favour would be granted, then a bit let down, though “next week” leaves the door open.

Mehak asked two of us who had raised money before to tear her pitch apart before her real investor meetings. Varun and I sat on her sofa with coffee and did exactly that.
I asked, "Who else does this, and why won't they crush you?" She talked for four minutes. Varun asked, "What does it cost you to get one customer, and what do they pay you over a year?" She guessed, then admitted she had guessed. I asked, "Why now? Why not five years ago?" Silence.
She didn't argue. She wrote every question on a card. Three evenings later we did it again. The competition answer was now three sentences. The customer numbers were real, from her sheet, including one she didn't like. For "why now" she said, "I'm not sure it's perfect timing; here's what changed last year."
I don't know how nervous she was at the real meetings. But her answers were short and honest.
— Leela

Which question met silence the first time?
"Why now? Why not five years ago?"
What might Mehak have felt when she admitted she had guessed?
She may have felt embarrassed and exposed, but she didn't argue; Leela can only see her writing the questions down.
What else could Mehak do before the real meetings?
Practise once more with someone who doesn't know the business, to check that the short answers make sense to outsiders.
How does Leela see Mehak's second attempt?
Leela sees real improvement: shorter answers, real numbers even when unflattering, and honesty about why now.

The week before Diwali, Miss Joshi handed out orange and purple bibs for the relay, straight out of the box. Reena got orange, Zeenat purple. At snacks Reena spread her mat and said, 'Only oranges sit here.' Zeenat, who sat with her every single day, stood holding her tiffin. 'But I'm your friend.' 'You're purple,' Reena said, as if it were a rule. Miss Joshi knelt down. 'Who decided who got which colour?' Reena thought. 'You did. From the box.' 'So is purple worse?' Reena looked at Zeenat's bib, then moved over. 'Purples can sit too.'

What colours were the bibs?
Orange and purple.
What was Reena feeling when she said 'Only oranges sit here'?
Reena felt proud of her orange team and sure it came first, as if belonging made a rule.
What did Miss Joshi's questions help Reena notice?
That the colours came at random from a box, so purple wasn't worse and the new rule made no sense.
What is it like for Zeenat to be told 'You're purple'?
Zeenat feels hurt and confused, shut out by a friend over a colour she didn't choose.

March. Pema's aunt sent three thousand rupees for Pema's sixteenth birthday. That weekend it all went: a gaming headset, a hoodie, and treats for Tushar and the others. "Birthday money is for fun," Pema said.
April. Pema started weekend shifts at the cafe near the bus stand, washing cups for three hundred rupees a day. By the end of the month there were two thousand four hundred rupees in the tin, and Pema wouldn't touch a coin. When Tushar suggested splitting a pizza, Pema refused. "That's work money."
May. Pema's phone screen cracked. The repair cost two thousand. Pema stared at the tin. "If I'd kept even half the birthday money..."
Tushar shrugged. "Money's money. The headset doesn't know where it came from."
Pema paid for the screen from the tin, wincing, and stuck a note on it: all money counts.

How much did Pema earn per day at the cafe?
Pema earned three hundred rupees a day washing cups.
Why did Pema refuse to split a pizza in April?
Pema felt protective of the work money, which felt hard-earned, while the birthday money had felt free to spend.
What does Pema's note, 'all money counts', suggest for next time?
Treating a gift like earned money, so a surprise cost like a cracked screen can be met from either.
How does Tushar see Pema's two kinds of money?
Tushar sees them as the same, saying money is money and the headset doesn't know where it came from.
Which title does the third chapter in my class textbook have?
I can't see your textbook, so I don't know. Open the contents page at the front of the book.
What is the phone number printed on the back of this notebook?
I can't see the notebook, so I don't know. Turn it over and read the number there.
Why is it wise to charge a phone before a long journey?
A charged phone will not run out when needed. Because a journey may bring delays and we may need maps or calls, a full battery avoids being stranded.

Please write this old verse as an easy modern paragraph.

The vulture monarch having wrought
A hard and glorious feat,
Honoured by Rama sage in thought,
Soared to his blissful seat.
The brothers, when each rite was paid
To him of birds supreme,
Their hearts with new-found comfort stayed,
And turned them from the stream.
Like sovereigns of celestial race
Within the wood they came,
Each pondering the means to trace,
The captor of the dame.

The vulture king had done a hard and glorious deed, and after Rama, wise in thought, honoured him, he soared up to his blessed home. When the brothers had performed every rite for the chief of birds, their hearts were steadied with new comfort, and they turned away from the stream. Like kings of the race of gods they came into the wood, each wondering how to find the one who had captured the lady.

When the class birthday trip was planned without them, both Kiran and Bhavna found out from the same chat thread. Neither said anything at school.

Bhavna spent the next Saturday at the library, where a poster asked for people to help build a model bridge. Four others turned up, they argued about glue for an hour, and by the end of the month she felt she belonged there, staying after school because the small group needed a hand with the beams.

Kiran went home. After that he stopped texting first, said no to the football game, and told his aunt he liked being on his own. It felt safer that way, because there was no rejection from people you did not ask.

In the corridor Reena laughed at something on her phone as Kiran passed, and his shoulders went up: she was laughing at him. Two days earlier he had sent her a message and gotten no reply until evening. He took that as dislike, when Reena's phone had simply died in the school bag. Next time she said hello, Kiran answered so stiffly that she blinked and walked on, and he added it to the list of things that proved it.

What did the poster in the library ask for?
It asked for people to help build a model bridge.
How did Bhavna and Kiran respond differently to being left out, and what happened to their sense of connection as a result?

Bhavna joined a small group around building a bridge and came to belong, while Kiran pulled back to avoid rejection and took a late reply and a laugh as dislike, which made him stiff and confirmed his fear.
What was Kiran feeling when he saw Reena laughing at her phone?
He felt hurt and on guard, assuming she was laughing at him, though the passage shows she was reading something on her phone.
What could Kiran try next to test his belief that Reena dislikes him?
He could send a simple, low-stakes message about something shared, like the homework, and see what actually comes back, before deciding what her silence meant.
How long will the next train to Chennai take today with delays?
I don't know how long the train will take with delays, as I can't see live railway data. The railway's tracking app shows delays.

Sum up Van Helsing's instructions to his friend in this passage.

Van Helsing returned in a couple of hours, and presently said to me: "Now you go home, and eat much and drink enough. Make yourself strong. I stay here to-night, and I shall sit up with little miss myself. You and I must watch the case, and we must have none other to know. I have grave reasons. No, do not ask them; think what you will. Do not fear to think even the most not-probable. Good-night."
Go home, eat and drink well, and build up strength. Van Helsing will sit up with the patient himself, and no one else must know about the case.

Help Amma with the kolam instead of sleeping.
What was Shankar feeling when describing Sankranti at home?
Shankar felt joyful and connected, part of something older than any one person.

Shankar keeps the festival with devotion but questions unfair rules, choosing to share work like the kolam.

Vaibhav values the festival too, but is annoyed by rules like only men sitting for the main puja.

Tuesday night. Dear diary, it's me, Nazia. Today at lunch I told Ankita I'd finished the whole mystery book. She squinted at me. “You're blinking loads. You're lying.” I WASN'T. My eyes have been itchy since swimming yesterday, and then she stared, and I got nervous, and they blinked even more. I said, “Ask me the ending, then.” I told her the ending. She went quiet and said, “Okay, sorry, my cousin says blinking means lying.” I said her cousin should get itchy eyes one day. We laughed. But it felt bad for a minute, being called a liar because of my eyelids 😔

Why had Nazia's eyes been itchy?
Nazia's eyes had been itchy since swimming yesterday.
What was Nazia feeling when Ankita called the blinking lying?
Nazia felt nervous and hurt at being called a liar, and the nerves made the itchy eyes blink even more.
What worked in how Nazia answered?
Offering to tell the ending gave real evidence instead of arguing about blinking, and it cleared things up calmly.
Where did Ankita's idea come from, and how might she feel now?
Ankita got it from her cousin, and after hearing the ending she probably felt a bit embarrassed for the accusation.

The print shop in Andheri had its big press break down on Monday, and by Wednesday Elizabeth knew the conference catalogues would be four days late.
She drove to Farhan's office in Lower Parel rather than emailing. Over a cup of cutting chai, she laid it out: a cracked roller, a spare part coming from Pune, the new delivery date of the twenty-second.
"I'm sorry. This one is on us for relying on one press."
Then she slid across a single printed page. Days one and two, proofs approved at a second shop, owner Elizabeth. Day three, printing, owner Mr. Joshi. Day four, delivery to the venue. Update calls every Monday and Thursday until the event.
Farhan read it twice. "At least I can tell my director something real."
He circled day three and asked for a photo of the first printed sheet.

Why were the conference catalogues going to be late?
The print shop's big press broke down with a cracked roller, and the spare part was coming from Pune, so the catalogues would be four days late.
What does Farhan's comment about telling his director suggest he was feeling?
He sounds relieved but still under pressure; he was worried about facing his director and felt steadier once he had a concrete plan to pass on.
Which other approach could suit Elizabeth if Farhan had been angry and unwilling to meet?
She could ask a colleague Farhan already trusts to share the news and the plan with her, because a familiar voice may keep him open to the recovery steps.
How would Farhan's day look different if Elizabeth had only emailed that the catalogues were late?
He would have a problem with no dates or owners to pass up the chain, so he would likely feel more anxious and have to chase her for answers.

Note for Vidya's file, from Gautam (Class 6 teacher), Wednesday

In the group discussion on banning weekend homework, Priyanka said weekends are for rest. Last term Vidya would have shouted "That's rubbish!" and sulked. Today she put up her hand and said, "I see it differently. If there's no weekend homework, Monday gets too heavy. That's why." Priyanka nodded and argued back, and they both kept smiling.

Later Vidya argued that Class 6 should get two extra PE periods. I told her, "I disagree, and here's why: exams are close," and she said, "Okay, but can we have one?" I think the phrase is sticking. I'll put her in charge of the next discussion.

What was the group discussion about?
Banning weekend homework.
How did Priyanka likely feel when Vidya said, "I see it differently"?
Respected rather than attacked, which is why she nodded, argued back and kept smiling.
What phrase helped Vidya disagree without shouting?
"I see it differently… That's why," giving a reason instead of calling the other idea rubbish.
How did Gautam model respectful disagreement for Vidya?
Gautam said, "I disagree, and here's why: exams are close," showing that disagreeing is about the idea, not the person.

The goats had eaten half the okra plants by the time Madhuri came out of the house. “Avni! You left the gate open again!” Avni stood by the broken fence, eyes on the ground, saying nothing. Her silence made Madhuri crosser. “Don't you care? Say something!” Avni's lips pressed tight, but still nothing came. Madhuri stopped. She remembered her own father's shouting, and how she had gone silent too, not because she didn't care, but because the words wouldn't come. She took a breath. “Okay. The plants are gone. Let's fix the gate so it closes by itself.” Together they tied a stone to a rope as a weight. Avni finally whispered, “Sorry, Amma.”

What did the goats eat?
The goats ate half the okra plants.
What was Avni likely feeling as she stood silent?
Avni was likely ashamed and upset, too overwhelmed to find words, not uncaring.
What did Madhuri change that helped?
She stopped demanding words and focused on the fix, weighting the gate together, which let Avni say sorry.
Why did Madhuri recognise Avni's silence?
Madhuri remembered going silent under her own father's shouting, not because she didn't care but because the words wouldn't come.

I'm Leela, and I live one floor below Seema in our Goa housing society. In March, half the building started going to the Sunday beach cleanup. Photos everywhere, matching caps. Seema, twenty-five, didn't join at first. She told me, "I don't want to go just because it's the thing everyone's posting."
I noticed she went down to the beach alone one weekday evening and walked the whole stretch, looking at the plastic by the rocks. The next week she asked the organiser what happened to the waste after they bagged it. She also asked me, half joking, "Would I go if no one ever took a photo?"
I can't tell you what she decided inside. But the following Sunday she was there at seven, no cap, sorting bottles from wrappers by herself. When someone lifted a phone for a group photo, she smiled, waved, and kept sorting.

What did Seema ask the organiser?
She asked what happened to the waste after they bagged it.
What does Seema's question, 'Would I go if no one ever took a photo?', suggest she wanted to know?
It suggests she wanted to be sure she cared about the beach itself, not just about joining what everyone was posting.
What did Seema do before joining, and why does that make the choice more her own?
She walked the beach alone, asked where the waste went, and questioned her own reasons, so when she joined it was a deliberate choice.
How does Leela see Seema's decision to join?
Leela noticed the difference between Seema and the crowd, careful not to claim to know her mind, but seeing her work without a cap and keep sorting during the photo.

Tuition teacher's note, end of term
I have taught Kamal and Manoj together for two years. This term Manoj's school test scores rose sharply, into the top five of his class, while his work here stayed the same. Kamal's stayed steady.
Each time results came out, I noticed Kamal went quiet, staring at his notebook, while Manoj celebrated. After the final test Kamal stayed back. He said he had seen Manoj using a cheat sheet in every school test since August. “I told myself it wasn't my business,” he said. “But every time the marks come, I feel sick. Two people who actually studied got pushed below him.”
I told him that feeling uneasy was a signal worth listening to, and that it is not too late to talk to Manoj or a teacher. He has agreed to speak to his class teacher on Monday. I will ask him how it went.

Since when had Kamal seen Manoj using a cheat sheet?
In every school test since August.
How did Kamal feel each time the marks came out?
Kamal felt uneasy and sick, knowing honest classmates were being pushed below Manoj.
What would have been a better choice back in August?
Talking to Manoj privately after the first test, and to a teacher if it continued, before months of unfair marks built up.
How are the honest classmates affected by the silence?
Two of them who actually studied were pushed below Manoj in rank, losing places they had earned.

The meeting with her manager had run until seven, and the office lights in the Gurugram tower were switching off floor by floor. Indu had one more thing to do before the cab came in fifteen minutes.
They had agreed a lot in that hour. The core payment flow would ship on the 30th. Refunds and reports would move to next month because the bank's test system wasn't ready. Indu's team would get one extra tester for two weeks.
Her colleague Reena, packing up, asked, "Aren't you going home?"
"In a minute. If I don't write this down tonight, in a month everyone will remember it differently."
She typed quickly: "Hi Vikram, thanks for today. Summary of what we agreed: 1. Core payment flow ships 30th. 2. Refunds and reports deferred to next month, because the bank test system is unavailable. 3. One extra tester for two weeks from Monday. Please correct me if I've missed anything."
She hit send as the cab pulled up.

When will the core payment flow ship?
The core payment flow will ship on the 30th.
Why did Indu stay to write the email, and how did she feel?
She was worried that everyone would remember the agreement differently later, so she felt it was worth staying even though she was tired.
What else could Indu do if Vikram replies with a correction?
She could update the summary and resend it, so the final written version is the one everyone agrees on.
How might Reena see Indu's late email?
Reena may think it's extra effort at the end of a long day, but could see why a written record avoids arguments later.

Durga Puja drums were still thudding from the pandal across the lane when Suraj lay back on his bed in the Salt Lake flat, chemistry notes beside him. "Tomorrow," he told the ceiling. "Tomorrow I'll wake at six and do all three chapters. Tomorrow-me will be fresh."
He picked up his phone to check one video. Then another. A dhunuchi dance, a cooking clip, a friend's pandal selfies.
At half past midnight his elder brother Jeevan leaned in the doorway. "Six a.m., right?"
"Totally," Suraj said, eyes on the screen.
Jeevan smiled. "You said that on Saptami too."
The chemistry notes slid off the bed. Suraj didn't pick them up.

What time does Suraj plan to wake tomorrow?
He plans to wake at six.
Why does putting chemistry off feel reasonable to Suraj?
He feels tired tonight and hopeful that tomorrow-me will be fresh and keen, so the scrolling feels harmless rather than a choice against his own plan.
What small step could Suraj take tonight instead of waiting for tomorrow?
He could put the phone in another room and read one page of one chapter now, so tomorrow starts with something already done.
How does Jeevan see Suraj's six a.m. promise?
Jeevan seems amused and doubtful, because he heard the same promise on Saptami.

Jatin, sit. Your Sumit Mama is going to tell you something I never told your mother properly. At twenty-one I was seeing a girl from my typing class, Rekha. If I said I was tired, she said I was bored of her. If I said I wasn't bored, she said I was calling her a liar. I went home feeling guilty for things I hadn't done. One evening my friend Iqbal asked, 'Why do you always say sorry after meeting her?' That question stuck in me. I began writing in a small notebook what I had actually said each day. After a month I read it back and saw the same trick on every page. I trusted that notebook more than the fog in my head, and I ended it. So when your friends say something feels off, listen to them, Jatin.

Where did Sumit meet Rekha?
Sumit met Rekha in the typing class.
How did young Sumit feel after meeting Rekha?
Sumit felt guilty and confused, going home sorry for things he had not done.
What turning point in the story helped Sumit see the pattern?
Writing down what he had actually said each day and reading a month of it back, which let him trust the record over his confusion.
What was it like for Iqbal watching Sumit back then?
Iqbal noticed Sumit apologising after every meeting and was concerned enough to ask why, which gave Sumit the first push.

Jomon came home from the city for a weekend to help his father Manoj update the pension form at the bank in the small town. Manoj held the pen like a proud teacher, and Jomon wanted to grab it and finish the lines himself. Instead he said, "You read out the field, Appa, and I'll point." They went slowly: name as on the passbook, account number, mobile number. When Manoj mixed up two lines, Jomon did not snatch the form. He asked, "Which one is your birth date?" and Manoj tapped it himself. At the counter the clerk asked a question, and Manoj answered before Jomon could open his mouth. On the bus home Manoj said, "Next time I'll fill the whole thing and you just check it."

Which form did Jomon help his father fill in at the bank?
Jomon helped his father Manoj update the pension form.
What did Jomon want to do at first, and what does his holding back show about his feelings?
Jomon felt impatient and wanted to grab the pen, but held back out of respect for his father's dignity.
What did Jomon do instead of taking over when his father mixed up two lines?
He asked "Which one is your birth date?" so that Manoj could tap it himself.
How does Manoj likely feel about being asked to read out the fields himself?
Respected and proud, since he keeps the pen, taps the answers himself, and says he will fill the whole form next time.

Tell this from Nkechi's point of view, in the first person.

Yara, four, drew on the wall with a crayon. Her mother Nkechi walked in and her face went hard. "Yara! No! The wall is not for crayons!" Yara froze. Nkechi breathed in, crouched and spoke quietly. "Crayons go on paper. Let's clean the wall." Yara's shoulders eased and she fetched a cloth. Nkechi added, "I still love you."

Yara, four, drew on the wall with a crayon. When I walked in, my face went hard. "Yara! No! The wall is not for crayons!" Yara froze. I breathed in, crouched and spoke quietly. "Crayons go on paper. Let's clean the wall." Yara's shoulders eased and she fetched a cloth. I added, "I still love you."
