Friday night

Tarun posted his study log again today. "14 hours ✅". Every single day. And every single day I look at mine, eight hours on a good day, and feel sick.

I'm Santosh, and I have a rule that I'm behind. It doesn't matter what I do. Today I did two full mock papers and my score went up by six marks. But then I saw Tarun's post and it didn't feel like anything.

Mom says, "You're a different boy from Tarun." He reads twice as fast as me, and he doesn't take the bus for an hour each way like I do. And last year he pushed so hard he fell ill and missed a month. I know all that. But when I see "14 hours", my brain deletes it.

I'm tired of feeling like a failure even on days I do well. Maybe I should stop looking at his posts. Maybe I should look at my own graph instead.

How many hours does Tarun post that he studies every day?
14 hours.
How does Santosh feel when looking at Tarun's posts?
Santosh feels sick and inadequate, like a failure, even on good days.
What would you advise Santosh to try first?
Stop checking Tarun's log for a while and track progress against Santosh's own past scores, since speed, travel and health differ so much.
How might Santosh's mom see the comparison?
She probably feels worried and frustrated, knowing the differences between the two boys and wishing Santosh could see them too.

metadata.subtype: Approach: comparing with others without context [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Damini, Maria's colleague at the school, so I heard most of this over lunch breaks.
For months Maria and her husband, Anil, had struggled with his parents turning up in Goa for weeks at a time, without much notice. Maria tried talking. Anil tried talking. Every conversation ended with his mother crying.
Then Maria mentioned his aunt, Tia Rosa, who everyone in both families respects. She's fair, and she's never taken sides. Maria and Anil asked her to help.
I don't know exactly what Tia Rosa said. Maria only told me it was over coffee after Sunday Mass, and that she suggested the parents come for two weeks at Christmas and two in May, planned in advance, so the house would be ready for them.
Anil's mother agreed that same afternoon.
The next Monday, Maria walked into the staff room looking lighter than I'd seen her all term.

When did Tia Rosa suggest the parents come to stay?
Two weeks at Christmas and two in May, planned in advance.
How did Maria seem to feel the Monday after, as far as Damini could tell?
Maria seemed relieved and lighter, as if a long strain had eased.
What else could Maria and Anil do if the plan started slipping?
They could thank Tia Rosa and, if needed, ask her gently to remind everyone of the plan, rather than going back to tense talks.
How might Anil's mother have seen the suggestion from Tia Rosa?
Coming from a respected, fair elder, the idea felt like good sense rather than rejection, so she accepted it the same afternoon.

metadata.subtype: Approach: asking a trusted elder to mediate [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Every day at the government school in Rampur, Vikas watched his best friend Naveen take the tiffin of a small Class 6 boy, Gopal, and eat the parathas behind the water tank. Gopal had started crying on the way to school. Vikas felt sick about it, but Naveen was the one who'd stood up for him back in Class 5. Telling felt like betrayal. On Monday, walking home past the sugarcane fields, Vikas said, 'Leave Gopal alone, yaar. He's tiny. It's not funny.' Naveen shrugged. 'Just parathas.' On Wednesday it happened again, and this time Gopal had a scraped knee from being pushed. Vikas went to Master ji after the prayer bell and told him everything. Master ji thanked him, sat with Gopal that same morning, and called Naveen's father to school after lunch. Naveen didn't talk to Vikas for a week. Then, at the handpump, he muttered, 'You were right.'

Where did Naveen eat Gopal's parathas?
Behind the water tank.
Why did Vikas feel torn about reporting Naveen?
He felt sick about the bullying, but guilty at the idea of betraying the friend who once stood up for him.
Which steps did Vikas take, and why was that order wise?
He talked to Naveen first, and when Gopal got hurt he told Master ji, because the harm kept going.
How might Gopal have felt before Vikas spoke up?
Scared and helpless, crying on the way to school and then hurt as well.

Read this:

For three years I introduced Vidya the same way: 'She's the shy one.' At the park, when an aunty asked her name, I answered for her. On her fourth birthday I told the other parents she wouldn't want to cut the cake in front of everyone, so I cut it. She hid behind my knees and I thought, see, shy. Last month her playschool teacher showed me a video on her phone: Vidya on a little stage, singing loudly, grinning. 'She volunteered,' the teacher said. 'Sumit, let her try more.' I sat in the car afterwards feeling I had been wrong about my own daughter. Now I bite my tongue. Yesterday the shopkeeper asked her which pencil she wanted, and I counted to five in my head. Vidya answered. Quietly, but she answered, and then looked up at me, pleased.

What did the playschool teacher's video show?
It showed Vidya on a little stage, singing loudly and grinning.
How did Sumit feel sitting in the car after seeing the video?
Sumit felt shaken and guilty, realising the 'shy one' label had been wrong about Vidya.
What small step is Sumit trying now, and why might it help?
Sumit counts to five before answering for Vidya, which leaves her room to speak for herself, as she did with the shopkeeper.
How might Vidya have experienced being called 'the shy one' for three years?
She probably learned to hide and let the adult speak, since her name was answered for her and her cake was cut for her; being given room lets her try.

metadata.subtype: Parent who is sure of what the child is [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Their landlord in Bengaluru had given notice with just three weeks to go, and Tanvir and Salma had shortlisted three flats in a hurry. On Friday night, with the packing boxes around them, Salma opened a spreadsheet: rent, size, commute, balcony, floor.
"Let's weight them," Tanvir said. They tried equal weights. Flat B won. Then Salma, who loved cooking, doubled the weight on size. Still B. Tanvir doubled rent. Still B.
Salma frowned. "Why does B always win?"
Tanvir scrolled across. "Look. B is twenty minutes from both our offices. The others are over an hour for one of us. Commute swamps everything else."
They sat quietly for a second.
"So what we actually care about," Salma said slowly, "is not being stuck in traffic every evening."
"And having dinner together," Tanvir said.
They booked B the next morning.

How far is flat B from both offices?
B is twenty minutes from both their offices.
How did Salma feel on realising that commute decided every result?
Salma was surprised and then thoughtful, realising what they truly cared about was not being stuck in traffic every evening.
What else could Tanvir and Salma try to double-check their choice?
They could each drive or ride the route to B at rush hour once, since commute is the criterion that decides everything.
How might the choice look to Tanvir?
Tanvir sees the commute swamping everything else and ties it to what matters to Tanvir, having dinner together.

metadata.subtype: Approach: uses the matrix to expose which criterion truly drives a choice [Thinking]

messages.content:
(1) why is the sky dark at night
(2) how can I learn to swim safely

1. Our side of the Earth faces away from the sun at night. Because direct sunlight cannot reach us then, the sky is dark.
2. Learn at a pool with a trained instructor and never swim alone. Start in shallow water and follow the pool's rules.

Read this:

Maria, seventeen, had spent six weeks organising the school's first charity food stall at the Bandra street fair. She'd made the rota, talked the canteen uncle into lending a stove, and kept seven tired classmates going with voice notes and jokes. On the day, the batter ran out at four, right when the crowd arrived. Simran had placed the order with the supplier, and some of the team were already whispering her name. When the principal walked up and asked what happened, Simran's face went white. Maria stepped forward. 'I checked the order list and missed it. It's on me.' Afterwards, in the empty stall, she told the team, 'Next year we make a stock checklist. Together.' Simran squeezed her hand.

What ran out at four o'clock?
The batter ran out at four, just as the crowd arrived.
What might Simran have been feeling when the principal walked up?
She was probably scared and ashamed, since she had placed the order and people were whispering her name.
What does Maria's response show about leading a team?
A leader takes responsibility for failures, protects teammates from blame and turns the mistake into a shared fix.
How might the rest of the team see Maria after this?
They'd likely trust her more and be willing to work with her again next year. 🤍
This books are mine, and that one are yours. Please check.

These books are mine, and that one is yours.
Why: "These" is plural; "that one" takes "is".
Why do some flowers close up at night?

Many flowers close to protect their delicate parts. Because shutting the petals helps keep the pollen and the inner parts shielded from cold and damp, the flower is ready to open again when pollinators return in the daylight.

Read this:

At 3 a.m. in her Pune flat, Chandrika walked the hallway with her crying baby and thought of her own father, Amandeep, who had done this with three children and a long bus commute. She remembered him falling asleep over his tea, and her fury when he missed her school recital. Now the fury had a crack in it. In the morning Amandeep arrived with a steel tiffin of poha. "You look tired, beta," he said. She nearly cried. "Papa, how did you manage us?" He laughed. "Badly, some days." She said quietly, "I'm going to be home for my child's recitals, Papa, even if I have to move a meeting." He nodded, said nothing, and pressed the tiffin into her hands. Her respect for him had grown. So had the ache.

What did Amandeep bring in the morning?
Amandeep arrived with a steel tiffin of poha.
What is Chandrika feeling toward her father as she walks the hallway at 3 a.m.?
New tenderness mixed with old hurt: the fury 'had a crack in it', and she nearly cried when he called her tired.
What does Chandrika decide to do differently from her father?
She resolves to be home for her child's recitals, even if she has to move a meeting.
How might Amandeep have felt hearing Chandrika ask how he managed?
Amandeep may have felt seen but a little exposed; he laughed and admitted 'Badly, some days,' then pressed the tiffin into her hands without a word.

Keep the future tense and turn this verse into modern prose.

In vain the captive will be wooed
With proffered love and dainty food,
She will not hear, she will not taste:
But, lest her beauty wane and waste,
Lord Indra's self will come to her
With heavenly food, and minister.
Then envoys of the Vanar race
By Rama sent will seek this place.
To them, O roamer of the air,
The lady's fate shalt thou declare.

It will be useless to woo the captive with offers of love and dainty food. She will not listen and she will not eat. But so that her beauty will not fade and waste away, Lord Indra himself will come to her with heavenly food and serve her. Then messengers of the Vanar race, sent by Rama, will come to this place. To them, O roamer of the air, you shall tell the lady's fate.
Write the sentence again without repeating "and": We went to the fair and we ate candyfloss and we rode the giant wheel and we came home late.
At the fair, we ate candyfloss and rode the giant wheel, then came home late.

Read this:

Ritu wrote to Sahil, an urban planner whose article on bus lanes she had quoted in her project, on the first Monday of exam season. Before sending, she wrote a line in her planner: 'No reply by next Monday? Send one polite follow-up. Still nothing? Move on, no hard feelings.'
Exams swallowed the week. Twice she caught herself checking her inbox between papers and made herself put the phone away. The plan was already made.
Next Monday: nothing. At 9 a.m., as written, she sent two lines: 'Just bringing this to the top of your inbox in case it got buried. Completely understand if you're busy.'
Another week passed. Silence. Ritu crossed out Sahil's name, put a small tick beside it, and felt surprisingly light. She added the next name to the list, a transport researcher in Kolkata, and turned back to her revision.

What did Ritu write in her planner before sending?
No reply by next Monday? Send one polite follow-up. Still nothing? Move on, no hard feelings.
How did Ritu feel after crossing out Sahil's name, and why?
She felt surprisingly light, because the plan had already decided the next step, so the silence did not turn into resentment.
What else could Ritu do with the next contact?
Use the same if-then plan and keep the first message short with one clear question, so each attempt costs little.
How might Sahil see the follow-up if the first message was buried?
Sahil would likely find it polite and easy to handle, since it offers an easy way to say no and adds no pressure.

Read this:

Mum: Physics result? 🤔
Sachin: 92
Mum: What happened to the other 8? Riya's son got 99. You're capable of more.
Sachin: ok
Mum: We'll add Sunday tuition.
Sachin: Mum can I ask something
Mum: Yes
Sachin: Would you still be proud of me if I was just normal? Like 70s?
Sachin: Sometimes it feels like you only like me when I top.
Mum: ...
Mum: Sachin, that's not true. But I can see why it feels that way.
Mum: I'm sorry. I love you for you. Your jokes, how you help Nani with her phone, all of it.
Sachin: really?
Mum: Really. 92 is great. No Sunday tuition. Let's get chaat tonight.
Sachin: ok. thanks Mum

Whose son got 99, according to Mum?
Riya's son.
How was Sachin feeling when asking if Mum would still be proud with marks in the 70s?
Sachin felt hurt and anxious, as if Mum's love depended on being brilliant.
What went wrong, and what did Mum do to fix it?
Her pressure made Sachin feel loved only for marks; she apologised, named things she loves about Sachin beyond ability and dropped the extra tuition.
How might Mum be feeling after reading Sachin's question?
She seems shocked and guilty, then tender, realising her pride had come across as conditional love.

Read this:

In the school staffroom, Nilesh was waving a printout. "Since I started the five-minute brain-gym claps before class, my Class 7 scores have gone up. We should do it school-wide." Hemant, who taught maths next door, read the numbers. "Up from the first test, which was the hardest of the year," he said. "What would your scores have done without the claps?" Nilesh blinked. "Gone up anyway, maybe?" "Maybe. Let's find out. You do the claps in 7A, I'll skip them in 7B. Same tests, whole term." Nilesh agreed, grinning. By March the two sections were almost level. Nilesh kept the claps because the children liked them, and quietly dropped the plan to make them compulsory for the whole school.

Which section did Hemant say would skip the claps?
Hemant said he would skip them in 7B.
Why did Hemant feel doubtful about the rise in scores?
Hemant felt cautious because the first test was the hardest of the year, so the scores might have risen anyway without the claps.
Why was the 7A and 7B plan a good test?
With the same tests over a whole term and only one section doing the claps, it shows what happens without them, instead of just before and after.
How might Nilesh have felt when the two sections came out almost level?
Nilesh may have felt a little disappointed, but kept the claps for the children's enjoyment and let go of making them compulsory.

Read this:

The panchayat office in Rajpur had closed for the evening, but Ankita waited under the neem tree outside until Sudha came out with her files.

Everyone in the village had heard by now that Sudha had told the block officer that Ankita's self-help group accounts were "not in order." Ankita had heard it from the tea-stall owner.

She could have shouted in the market. Half the women wanted her to.

Instead she said, "Sudha, walk with me to the bus stand."

On the way, she spoke evenly. "You told the officer my accounts were messy. You never asked me. I heard it from the tea stall. I felt ashamed in front of the whole village, and I thought you were my friend."

Sudha stopped walking. "I was worried you'd get the new scheme and not me."

"Thank you for saying it," Ankita said. "Now I know where we stand. I can work with honesty. I can't work with that again."

Where did Ankita wait for Sudha?
Under the neem tree outside the panchayat office.
How did Ankita feel when she heard the news from the tea-stall owner?
She felt ashamed in front of the whole village and betrayed by someone she thought was a friend.
Why was walking to the bus stand better than shouting in the market?
A private talk let Ankita describe what happened and how she felt, so Sudha could answer honestly instead of defending herself in public.
What might Sudha be feeling when she admits her worry about the scheme?
She is probably ashamed and exposed, but perhaps relieved to say the truth.
"Usne mujhe galat samjha" English?
In English: "He misunderstood me." Or: "He got me wrong." Use "misunderstood" when writing and "got me wrong" when chatting. Say "she" if you mean a woman.

Read this:

At the kitchen table in Lagos, Nkechi pressed a jigsaw piece into a gap. It didn't fit. "It wants to go here," she said, and pushed harder. Her friend Sofia said, "It's the wrong shape." "No, it likes this spot." Nkechi pressed with both thumbs. The piece bent. She held it up, crumpled at the corner, and her lip trembled.

What did Sofia say about the piece?
"It's the wrong shape."
What was Nkechi feeling when her lip trembled?
She was upset and sorry to see the piece bent.
What would you change first in Nkechi's approach?
Listen to the shape, as Sofia said, and try the piece in other gaps.
How does the pushing look to Sofia?
Sofia is frustrated that Nkechi won't listen.

Read this:

When I heard Kunal had been cut from the state drama auditions, I was on the bus home, and I smiled so wide the auntie next to me smiled back. I'm Tejas, and Kunal had spent a year telling everyone I was 'too stiff' to act. He'd bragged he'd go straight to the finals. And he didn't. For about a minute I felt like justice had happened. Then I pictured him telling his parents, who had driven him four hours for the audition. The smile went away. I felt small, like I'd been caught doing something I shouldn't. I didn't message anyone about it. I still don't like him much. But I didn't like myself much in that minute either.

How far had Kunal's parents driven for the audition?
Four hours.
What did Tejas feel after picturing Kunal telling his parents?
Tejas felt small and ashamed, as if caught enjoying something wrong.
What choice did Tejas make that was wise, and why?
Not messaging anyone about it, which kept a private flash of glee from turning into gossip that could hurt Kunal.
How might Kunal's parents feel about the result?
They would probably feel disappointed for him, especially after the long drive.

metadata.subtype: Rival's failure feels good and bad [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

On the wall above Suraj's bed in the Dharwad hostel hung a sheet of chart paper with thirty boxes. Every morning he coloured one in: green if he had slept by eleven and studied two hours, red if not. In the first week there were three reds. Harsha, his roommate, laughed at it. "Like a school kid's star chart." Suraj shrugged and kept colouring. By the third week, the greens ran in a line. He wasn't yawning in the morning lecture. The accounts problems that used to take him an hour now took twenty minutes. When the mid-term marks went up on the notice board, he stood in front of his name for a long time. Back in the room he looked at the chart, the long line of green. "I did that," he said quietly, and he felt taller. Harsha didn't laugh this time.

What colour did Suraj use for a day he slept by eleven and studied two hours?
Green.
How did Suraj feel looking at the chart after the mid-term marks?
He felt proud and taller, confident that the improvement came from his own steady choices.
What made the chart useful rather than just a 'star chart'?
It made his progress visible every day, so he could see the link between his actions and the better marks.
How does Harsha's reaction change over the weeks?
At first Harsha mocks the chart, but later stays quiet, seeming impressed by the results.
Which chapters will be in my exam?
I don't know, because only your teacher knows what the paper will cover. Ask your teacher or read the exam notice.

Read this:

Wednesday night
Chinmay called again at eleven. Forty minutes. His landlord is cheating him. His boss is jealous of him. His sister never calls. And tonight, somehow, it was also my fault, because I "never really help."
I listened. I do care about him. Some of it is real. His boss does sound difficult.
But I've noticed I end every call feeling guilty for things that aren't mine.
So tonight, near the end, I asked him something new. "Chinmay, what do you want to do about the landlord? Is there a step you want to take?" He went quiet. Then he said, "I don't know. Maybe look for a new flat."
Then I said, kindly, "I want to keep being your friend. But I can't take calls after ten on weeknights anymore. I'm exhausted. Sundays are good."
He sighed. I didn't apologise. I said goodnight.
Salma

What time did Chinmay call?
At eleven.
How does Salma feel at the end of Chinmay's calls?
Salma feels guilty and exhausted, taking on blame for things that don't belong to Salma.
What did Salma do that shows compassion with boundaries?
She listened, asked what Chinmay wanted to do about the landlord, and kindly set a limit of no calls after ten on weeknights.
How might Chinmay feel when Salma sets the limit?
Chinmay may feel a little hurt or disappointed, which is why he sighs, but he was also given a real question to think about.

Read this:

Aparna, ten, came home from her Delhi school and threw her bag on the sofa harder than usual. Noor had come to school on a shiny red bicycle with gears, and at lunch she'd shown everyone her new phone. Aparna had a bicycle too, a blue one from her cousin, with a squeaky bell. At home there was dal, rice and the mango pickle she loved. Her mother had just bought her new sandals. But none of it felt like enough. "Why can't we have nice things?" she said at dinner. Her father looked up, surprised. Her mother said nothing, just passed the pickle. Later, lying in bed, Aparna thought about it. Her bicycle worked fine. Yesterday she'd loved it. It was only after seeing Noor's that it felt old.

What colour was Noor's new bicycle?
Noor had come to school on a shiny red bicycle with gears.
What was Aparna feeling when she threw her bag on the sofa?
Aparna felt sad and hurt, comparing her things with Noor's and feeling they weren't enough.
What could Aparna's parents say to help her?
They could gently ask how she felt about her bicycle yesterday, helping her see that the hurt came from comparing, not from lacking anything.
How might Aparna's mother feel hearing "Why can't we have nice things?"
Aparna's mother might feel hurt or worried, having just bought new sandals, and unsure how to answer.

metadata.subtype: Feeling poor next to a friend [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Supervisor's notebook, Ramesh, Thursday.
During the vendor review, Jatin's phone kept buzzing face down. At the break he asked to step out for five minutes. I was in the corridor and heard him call his wife, Mitali. His voice was low and steady: 'I was rushed and my message sounded harsh. Farooq is in hospital; I was trying to arrange things between slides. I'm sorry.' A pause. Then he laughed a little and said, 'Yes, I'll eat something.' He came back in looking lighter.
What I did next: told him to leave at four and go to the hospital; I'd cover the last agenda item. Also noted for myself: explaining the context and owning the tone ended it in under two minutes. Worth remembering at home.

Who is in hospital, according to Jatin?
Farooq is in hospital.
What does Jatin coming back 'looking lighter' suggest?
He felt relieved after clearing things up with Mitali, no longer carrying the tension of a harsh message left unexplained.
What made Jatin's call end the loop so quickly?
He owned his harsh tone, gave the real context of a friend in hospital, and apologised, so Mitali didn't have to guess his intention.
How might Mitali have felt hearing the call?
She likely felt relieved and softened once she knew why the message was harsh, which may be why she told him to eat something.

Read this:

College in Nagpur had no bells. Darshan, nineteen, had two free days a week and a project due Friday. On Wednesday, the hostel internet went down, and his roommate Ojas groaned, "Holiday!" Darshan was tempted: movies, sleep, cricket in the corridor. But he'd already wasted Monday. He took his laptop to the library, which had working internet, and wrote three time blocks on a paper: 10 to 12, research; 1 to 3, draft; 4 to 5, references. At noon his phone buzzed with memes; he flipped it face down. By five, the draft was done. He walked back to the hostel and joined the cricket without guilt. "How are you so calm?" Ojas asked. "I did the boring part first," Darshan said.

What were Darshan's time blocks from 1 to 3?
Draft.
How did Darshan feel when he joined the cricket?
He felt relaxed and free of guilt, having finished the draft.
What worked in how Darshan planned his day?
Moving to the library, setting clear time blocks and putting his phone face down.
How might Ojas see Darshan's calm?
Ojas seems surprised and perhaps a little envious of how relaxed Darshan is.

Read this:

Friday lunch at the design studio, and the team had ordered in. Vinita had left at four again to pick up her son. "Part-time Vinita," someone joked. "Must be nice." A couple of people laughed. Nirmala put down her roll. "Actually, Vinita logs on again at nine every night. The client deck we're all proud of was mostly hers." Her tone was calm, almost casual. "Just saying." The joker shrugged. "I didn't know." "Most people don't." The conversation moved on. Nirmala didn't mention it to Vinita. The next Monday, when the manager praised the deck, Nirmala said, "Vinita built most of it," in the same calm voice. It wasn't a big moment. She did it every time.

What time does Vinita log on again at night?
At nine every night.
What seems to be going through Nirmala's mind when she puts down her roll?
Nirmala seems quietly annoyed at the unfair joke and determined to correct it calmly, not angrily.
How can small acts like Nirmala's make a difference over time?
Calmly correcting jokes and crediting Vinita's work every time slowly changes how the team sees her.
If you were Vinita, what would you want from colleagues when you're not in the room?
You would want someone to state the facts about your work and give you credit, as Nirmala did.

metadata.subtype: Speaking up in rooms the target is not in [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

I sit two benches behind Harshita at lunch, so I saw it. She carried her tiffin to the table by the window where a group of girls from our class sat, and one of them said, "There is no space here," though there were two empty seats. She stood there a moment, then went and sat on the steps outside. I could not tell how she felt; her face was very still. The next day I told her I liked her drawing of the train, and she sat with me. She joined the art club after that. Later, I saw her talking to the class teacher quietly, so maybe she mentioned it. I am Tejas, from Class 6.

Where did Harshita sit after she was turned away from the table?
She sat on the steps outside.
What might Harshita have been feeling on the steps, and why can Tejas not be sure?
She may have felt hurt, but her face was very still, so Tejas cannot tell for certain whether it was hurt or just holding it in.
What small step did Tejas take that helped?
Tejas complimented Harshita's drawing of the train and made room for her, giving her one kind classmate to be near. Joining a club also gave her a place.
What is it like for Tejas to watch this from two benches behind?
Tejas sees the empty seats and the refusal clearly but cannot read Harshita's still face, so Tejas is left unsure, and that uncertainty turns into a kind word the next day.

Read this:

I'm Bidisha, and I sit behind Mohit and Arvind. Mohit had been angry with Arvind for a week, ever since he saw him copying in the maths test. I heard him say, “I'm telling Sir if you do it again.”
Then on Friday something changed. They were talking by the water cooler, and Arvind was crying, which I'd never seen. I caught bits: his father had said that if he failed maths again, he'd be sent to his uncle's town for school. He'd been failing since August and was too scared to say.
Mohit didn't back down about the copying. I heard him say, “You still have to stop. But you need help, not a cheat sheet.” After school he went with Arvind to Sir, not to report him, but to ask about the free remedial classes on Tuesdays.
On Tuesday I saw them both in the remedial room. Arvind had his notebook open. Mohit was there too, doing his own homework, just keeping him company.

What did Mohit and Arvind ask Sir about?
The free remedial classes on Tuesdays.
What might Mohit have been feeling when Arvind cried?
Mohit was probably surprised and sympathetic, his anger softening into concern, though he still felt the copying had to stop.
What else could help Arvind besides the remedial classes?
Talking with a teacher or counsellor about the pressure at home, so an adult can help his father understand.
How does the change look to Bidisha?
Bidisha sees a friendship shift from anger to support, with Mohit even sitting in the remedial room for company.

metadata.subtype: Approach: reconsidering after seeing the friend's reasons [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

On Pongal morning, Trisha sat in the courtyard while the grown-ups broke coconuts for the puja. Suddenly she pointed and squealed. "Face! Face!"
Farida Aunty looked. The coconut had three dark dots, like two eyes and a round mouth. "Oh-oh!" Trisha said, copying its surprised look, her own mouth round. She patted the coconut's cheek and laughed so hard she fell over. Farida laughed too, and drew a smile on another coconut with kumkum.

What did the coconut have?
Three dark dots, like two eyes and a round mouth.
What was Trisha feeling when she saw the coconut face?
She felt delighted and excited, laughing so hard she fell over.
How could Farida Aunty make a game of it?
Point out more faces around the courtyard, as she began to by drawing a smile on another coconut.
How might Farida Aunty feel watching Trisha?
She likely feels amused and charmed, joining in the laughter.

Read this:

"Anirban, how are you already done with the budget sheet?"

"Started at nine. Stopped at ten-thirty."

"I started at nine too," Nitin said. "But the team chat, the emails, two calls..."

"I turned all that off. Put a note on my status: back at ten-thirty."

"And if something's urgent?"

"They can call. Nobody did."

"Then what?"

"Then I replied to everything in one go. Took fifteen minutes. Then I got coffee and walked around the block."

"You walked? In the middle of the day?"

"That's why I'm not fried by three."

Nitin looked at his own screen, twelve tabs open, and closed eleven.

What did Anirban put on his status?
Back at ten-thirty.
How does Anirban seem to feel about his way of working?
He seems relaxed and confident, not fried by three, because fewer switches make work easier.
What could Nitin try, based on Anirban's routine?
He could block time for one task, turn off chat and email, answer messages in one batch, and take a short walk.
How does Nitin react after hearing Anirban's method?
Nitin seems curious and a bit envious, and closes eleven tabs to try it.

Read this:

The lab's fire alarm rang during Harish's second week as a research assistant. He looked around. Ojas, the senior student, kept pipetting. Two others at the bench exchanged a look, then went back to their samples. Harish half stood, then sat again. If they weren't worried, maybe he shouldn't be. For four long minutes the alarm shrieked and six adults pretended it wasn't there, each sneaking glances at the others. Then the security guard pushed open the door. "Everybody out, now, smoke on the second floor!" They filed down the stairs fast, faces red. Outside, by the bicycle stand, Harish quietly asked Ojas, "Why didn't you move?" Ojas rubbed his neck. "I was waiting for someone else to go first. I thought you'd know if it was real. You were closest to the door."

What did the security guard shout?
"Everybody out, now, smoke on the second floor!"
Why did Harish sit back down after half standing?
Harish read the others' calm as a sign it wasn't serious and didn't want to be the only one reacting.
What went wrong in the lab, and what could any single person have done about it?
Everyone waited for someone else to move, so nobody moved for four minutes. Any one person standing and heading out would probably have got the rest to follow.
How did Ojas see the situation from the bench?
Ojas was also waiting for a cue and assumed Harish, closest to the door, would know if it was real, so each of them was leaning on the other.

metadata.subtype: Colleagues stay put when the alarm rings [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

Wednesday
Disaster, then not a disaster. My tower of cardboard tubes for the school stall was nine tubes tall this morning. At lunch Tanuja slammed the door and the whole thing toppled onto the carpet. I wanted to scream. Then I looked at how it fell. It tipped from the bottom, like a person standing on one leg. The base was only one tube wide. So I cut four strips of cardboard, made a square frame, taped it round the bottom three tubes and rebuilt the rest on top. Tonight Tanuja slammed the door again, on purpose, to test it. It wobbled. It stood. We both cheered.
Jasleen

What made the tower topple at lunch?
Tanuja slammed the door.
How did Jasleen feel when the tower toppled?
Jasleen was frustrated enough to want to scream, before calming down to study how it fell.
What other approach could help before the stall day?
Building a small test tower to try base shapes, so the big one is not the first to be tested.
What was it like for Tanuja?
Tanuja caused the first fall, then became a helpful tester, and they cheered together. 🎉

metadata.subtype: Approach: model collapses and is redesigned [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

You asked, Vandana, why my notebooks look so strange. Every line has a little letter in the margin. I'm Alka, and I collect oral histories in the villages around Bhuj. In my first year, I wrote up a story about a well that saved a whole village in the great drought. I was sure an old man had told me he had seen it. When my editor asked for his name, I went back to my notes and found nothing. I had heard it from three different people, each of whom had heard it from someone else. None of them had seen it. That scared me. So now: S means I saw it, T means I was told it, and by whom, I means I'm inferring. Before I write any sentence, I ask myself: how do I actually know this? It's slow. It's also why people trust my work.

What do the letters S, T and I mean in Alka's notebook?
S means seen, T means told (and by whom), and I means inferred.
Why did the well story scare Alka?
Alka felt shaken on finding that a story believed to come from an eyewitness had only been passed along by people who hadn't seen it.
What question does Alka ask before writing, and why does it help?
'How do I actually know this?', which separates what was seen, told and inferred before anything is written as fact.
Why does the editor matter to the story?
The editor's request for the old man's name made Alka check the notes and discover the gap.
How should a library book be treated? Give two rules, one per line, each beginning with "Do not".

Do not write inside the pages.
Do not bend or tear the covers.

Read this:

“Tanu Di, look.” Yusuf pushed his phone across the bed. His hands were shaking.
Tanuja read the class group. A photo of him asleep at last week's sleepover, mouth open, in his old cartoon pyjamas. Under it, a caption about babies and forty-one laughing reactions.
“Who posted it?”
“Some account I don't know. But it was taken at Faisal's house.” His voice rose. “I'm going to write something so bad that they'll—”
“What would you write?”
He stopped. Typed. Deleted. “If I reply angry, they get a second show. They'll screenshot my reply and laugh at that too.”
“So what's the first step?”
“Not fighting. Getting help.” He breathed out slowly. “Screenshots first. Then Ammi and Abbu, tonight.”
“Ammi's in the kitchen right now. Come. I'll stand with you.”
Ammi read the screenshots twice, then put an arm round him. “You were right not to answer. Tonight we report the account, and tomorrow I call your class teacher first thing.”

How many laughing reactions were under the photo?
Forty-one laughing reactions.
What was Yusuf feeling when he started to type a reply?
Yusuf felt humiliated and furious, hands shaking and voice rising, wanting to hit back with words.
What else could Yusuf do instead of replying, and why is it better?
Save screenshots and let adults report the account and speak to the school, because a reply only gives the group a second show.
How might Ammi see Yusuf coming to her that night?
Ammi is likely hurt for him but relieved he came straight to her, and ready to back him with the report and the school.

metadata.subtype: Approach: staying calm and not replying in anger [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Saturday night
Today at Ganga's birthday I told everyone I ate a thousand gulab jamuns, my stomach turned into a hot-air balloon, and I floated over the whole building. Ganga laughed so hard her juice came out of her nose. Then she said she ate two thousand and flew to the moon, and the moon was made of rasmalai 😆 We kept going till her Nani said the ceiling fan would chop us if we floated any higher.
But little Tinku, who is four, asked me very seriously if my tummy still hurt. So I told him, "No, it's a pretend story. I only ate three." He looked relieved and went back to his cake.
Irfan

How many gulab jamuns did Irfan really eat?
Only three.
Why did Irfan tell Tinku it was a pretend story?
Irfan felt concerned when Tinku looked worried, and wanted Tinku to know the truth; the tale was only fun while everyone knew it was a joke.
What made Irfan's exaggeration play rather than a lie?
Everyone at the party knew it was silly and joined in, and when Tinku didn't share the joke, Irfan cleared it up at once.
How was the tall tale different for Ganga than for Tinku?
Ganga was in on the joke and delighted, adding her own moon story; Tinku didn't share it, so it felt like a real worry until Irfan explained.

Reduce this passage to a single line.

Dolma had one week to finish her school project on migration, and the only person she could interview was Yash, the new boy whose family had moved from a town in Nepal. The problem: Yash barely spoke, and the library's internet was down. Dolma waited after class. "Can I ask you some questions? For the project?" Yash looked wary. "Why?" "Because I only know what's in the textbook," she said honestly. He hesitated, then shrugged. For three lunch breaks they sat on the steps. He told her about the long bus journey, missing his grandmother, learning Hindi from cartoons. Dolma realised some classmates' jokes about him were plain cruel. In her presentation, she used his words, with his permission, and the class went quiet.
Dolma interviews the new boy Yash for her migration project, and his words, used with his permission, make the class go quiet.

Read this:

Monday. At the corner shop, Sumit saw the orange ice lollies and yelled, "Want!" His cousin Salma said, "After lunch." He cried all the way home.
Wednesday. Same shop, same lollies, same crying.
Friday. Before they reached the shop, Salma started singing the train song and made Sumit the engine. "Choo choo, to lunch!" He chugged past the lollies, still singing. After lunch, Salma gave him one. He licked it slowly, beaming.

What did Sumit want at the corner shop?
Sumit wanted the orange ice lollies.
Why did Sumit cry on Monday and Wednesday?
Sumit felt upset and frustrated, because 'after lunch' meant nothing and he wanted the lolly right then.
What did Salma try on Friday, and why did it work?
Salma sang the train song and made Sumit the engine, so he was busy and happy walking past the lollies.
How might Salma feel on Friday after lunch?
Salma probably felt relieved and pleased that the song worked and Sumit was beaming.

Read this:

Himani, two years old, sat on the sofa with the phone propped in front of her, her face gone still and her mouth a little open as bright colours flashed. Her father, Yash, was chopping onions and had handed it over so she would stay quiet. She did not look up when he spoke to her, or when the pan hissed. When Yash gently lifted the phone away, she screamed and reached for it with both hands. Her uncle Eshaan, visiting, saw the screen go dark and Himani fling herself flat on the floor, heels drumming. He sat beside her and kept his voice low. "You're sad. The phone is finished now." He did not give it back. He opened his arms, and she sobbed into his shoulder for a minute. Then he rattled a tin of wooden spoons and small pots and said, "Shall we make soup?" Himani gave a hiccup and stirred with a spoon. Afterwards Yash sat cross-legged with her on the floor and named the pots as she banged them. That evening they watched one short video together, and Yash talked about the animals on the screen and asked her to point to the cow.

What did Eshaan rattle to get Himani's attention?
He rattled a tin of wooden spoons and small pots.
How was the phone different when Yash handed it over to keep Himani quiet and when they watched the video at the end?

When it was handed over to keep her quiet, Himani got bright colours but no person and screamed when it was taken; in the evening Yash watched one short video with her, talked about the animals and asked her to point to the cow, so the screen became a shared tool.
What was Himani feeling when she flung herself on the floor?
She felt sad and frustrated, not naughty, which showed in her drumming heels and her sobbing into Eshaan's shoulder.
What could Yash do next time he needs to cook while Himani is nearby?
He could give her a tin of spoons and small pots to play with beside him and keep the phone for shared moments.
Tell a tiny story of about 120 words about a grandfather teaching his granddaughter to ride a bicycle.

Every evening, Dadu held the back of Anya's blue bicycle and jogged beside her down the colony lane. "Look ahead, not at your feet," he kept saying. Anya wobbled, squealed and fell into the hedge twice. On the fifth evening, she was pedalling hard and chatting about her school play when she noticed that Dadu's voice sounded far away. She turned her head. He was standing at the gate, waving both hands in the air. Anya had ridden all the way to the corner by herself. She was so surprised that she almost fell again. Instead, she rang her bell three times, turned carefully and rode back to him, grinning. Dadu pretended he wasn't out of breath.
I got a low mark in science today and I feel awful.
I'm sorry. That feels bad, especially when you studied. Did you expect a different result?
Yes, I thought I did well.
That is disappointing. Look at the paper to see where you lost marks. Sometimes it's a misread question rather than not knowing the topic.
What if my parents get upset?
Tell them yourself and show that you're ready to improve. Parents often respond better when they see you take it seriously.
I feel better. I'll ask my teacher about it.
Good. Asking the teacher shows you care about learning, and she can point out what to improve.
Thanks for listening.
Anytime. One test doesn't decide how you do in the long run.
Write a four-line rhyme for children about a bus that is always late.

The bus is late, the bus is late,
We stand and wait beside the gate.
It finally comes, with a honk and a sigh,
And off we go, as the clouds float by.

Read this:

In the small back office of the travel agency where she had worked for three months, Avni, twenty-two, waited while her supervisor Mehak finished a call. Avni's part-time MBA exams fell on four Saturdays next month, and Saturday was their busiest day. She had rehearsed on the bus: ask, don't demand. 'Ma'am, I need those four Saturdays. I know it's peak. I can cover Sundays and two late shifts on Wednesdays, when the group bookings come in.' Mehak frowned. 'Sundays are dead. Wednesdays help, though.' 'Then three Wednesday late shifts?' Mehak tapped her pen. 'And you train the new intern on refunds before you go.' Avni hesitated; that was extra work. 'Done, if the training happens during my Wednesday shifts, not on top of them.' Mehak laughed. 'Fair. Write it down before either of us forgets.'

How many Saturdays did Avni need off?
Four Saturdays.
Why did Avni hesitate before agreeing to train the intern?
She saw it as extra work on top of what she had offered and wanted the deal to stay fair to her.
What made Avni's approach to the request work?
She came with specific offers instead of demands, listened to what Mehak valued, and protected her own interest with a small condition.
How might Mehak see Avni after this conversation?
As a reasonable, reliable employee who solves problems rather than just asking for favours.

Read this:

Monday: Baljeet's new cycle was stolen from outside the library. Disha rushed over. “Oh no, I'm so sorry for you! My cousin's got stolen too, and he cried for days, and…” Baljeet stared at the empty stand and said nothing. Disha kept talking. He walked off alone. Tuesday: Disha thought about it all night. She'd felt sorry for him, but she hadn't asked what he felt. At break she found him. “I talked too much yesterday. Do you want company walking home, now you're on foot?” Baljeet nodded. Wednesday: On the long walk, Baljeet finally said, “I saved for two years for that cycle.” Disha just listened. This time she didn't guess.

Where was Baljeet's cycle stolen from?
It was stolen from outside the library.
What was Baljeet feeling as he stared at the empty stand?
Baljeet was shocked and upset, too stunned to talk about the cycle he had saved for.
What did Disha change on Tuesday, and why did it help?
She admitted talking too much and simply offered company on the walk home, which let Baljeet share his feelings when ready.
What was Monday like for Baljeet with Disha talking?
Baljeet likely felt unheard, as Disha's stories about her cousin filled the space where his own feelings should have been.

Read this:

I'm Vishal, and I'm ten. This happened last month in games period.

We were playing kho-kho, and two captains picked teams. They picked and picked, and I was the last one standing by the wall. My face went hot. When I sat down, I told my sister Usha, who's in the same class, "Nobody ever picks me. I never win anything. Never."

Usha looked at me like I was crazy. "Bhai, you were captain in July. You picked me first."

"That was different."

"And your team won the relay on Sports Day."

I didn't want to hear it. It felt like one time was the real truth and all the other times didn't count.

The next week I got picked third. I didn't say anything to Usha. But I stopped saying "never" so much.

When had Vishal been captain?
He was captain in July.
Why did being picked last once feel like "nobody ever picks me" to Vishal?
Vishal felt embarrassed, and the hot feeling made that one moment seem like the whole truth. The good times, like being captain, felt as if they didn't count.
What could Vishal try the next time he hears himself say "never"?
He could stop and remember one time it wasn't true, like the relay on Sports Day. Checking for one counter-example stops one bad day from becoming a rule.
How might Usha feel hearing Vishal say nobody ever picks him?
Usha might feel confused or even a bit hurt, since Vishal picked Usha first in July. Usha seems to want to remind him of what really happened.

metadata.subtype: Always and never after one event [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

"Ammi, everyone in my class has a spinning top with lights. Everyone!"
Zeenat looked up from the sewing machine. "Faraz, last month you said spinning tops were for babies."
"That was before. Now Mohit and Varun and the whole back bench have them. They have battles at lunch."
"And you want to battle?"
"I want to be in the battles."
"Do you like spinning tops?"
Faraz thought about it. "Not really. My kite is better. But nobody flies kites now."
"So you want a toy you don't like?"
"I want the toy they like. If I have it, I can sit with them."
Zeenat stopped the machine. "Tell me about lunch these days, beta."
Faraz looked at his feet. "I sit with my kite book."

What does Faraz say is better than a spinning top?
Faraz says his kite is better.
Why does Faraz want a toy he doesn't even like?
He wants to be in the lunch battles and sit with the others, so being included matters more to him than his own taste. 🥺
How could Zeenat support Faraz beyond buying the top?
She could keep asking about lunch, help him find one friend to share his kite with, and talk about joining in without pretending.
What is Zeenat noticing when she stops the sewing machine?
Zeenat notices this isn't really about a toy; Faraz seems lonely at lunch and wants a way in.

Read this:

In Accra, Chidi, twenty-five, had been a junior engineer at the construction firm for a year. He'd learned to stay quiet in meetings; the old director hated being questioned.
The new director, Mr. Kofi Mensah, started differently. At his first review, he put his design on the screen and said, "Please, find the problems. I'd rather hear them now than on site."
A young woman from the drawing team said, carefully, "Sir, the beam spacing on level three may be too wide." Everyone froze.
Mr. Mensah studied it. "You're right. Thank you, Abena. That could have cost us." He shook her hand in front of everyone.
Chidi felt something loosen in his chest. At the next meeting, he pointed out a drainage issue. Kofi thanked him too.
Years later, Chidi still told junior engineers about that director.

What did Abena point out?
She said the beam spacing on level three may be too wide.
What was Chidi feeling when something loosened in his chest?
Chidi felt relieved and safe, seeing that disagreement was welcomed rather than punished.
What did Mr. Mensah do that built an honest team?
He invited people to find problems, thanked Abena publicly and shook her hand, which made others like Chidi willing to speak.
How might Abena have felt when Mr. Mensah thanked her?
Abena was probably relieved and proud, after taking a risk to question the director's design.

Read this:

"Sonali, you're welcome, by the way."
"Anjali, I need to tell you something about the canteen."
"I defended you! That guy made the comment about your weight, and I told him off in front of everyone."
"I know. Thank you. Really."
"But?"
"But you stood on the bench. Everyone turned. You talked about me for ten minutes. You said I was 'too shy to speak for myself.'"
"You are shy."
"I would have said something. Or not. It was my call."
"I was trying to help."
"You did help. I also felt smaller than when he said it."
Anjali was quiet. "So what should I do next time?"
"Ask me. Or stand next to me. And let me speak."

Where did Anjali stand while defending Sonali?
Anjali stood on the bench.
How did Sonali feel about Anjali's defence?
Sonali felt grateful but also smaller, as Anjali spoke for Sonali and made a scene.
What does Sonali ask for instead, and why does it help?
Sonali asks Anjali to ask first or stand alongside and let Sonali speak, so support follows Sonali's lead.
How does Anjali feel when Sonali explains?
Anjali feels a bit hurt and surprised at first, having only tried to help, but then asks what to do next time.
Is it wise to say yes to everything a new friend asks?
No, it is better to think first. Because some requests may not suit you or may be unfair, and a good friend will accept a polite no without getting upset.

Read this:

Rain drummed on the school's tin roof, and lunch was indoors, noisy and crowded. Manoj, five, did not eat. He sat by the window, holding Amma's yellow hair clip.
Amma worked the night shift at the hospital. She had been asleep when he left.
He pressed his nose to the glass and watched the blurry gate.
Aditi, the teacher, noticed his tiffin was still full. She crouched beside him. "Is that Amma's?"
He nodded, very small.
"You're missing her."
He nodded again. His lip wobbled.
Aditi ate her lunch next to him. After a while, Manoj opened his tiffin too.

What was Manoj holding?
Amma's yellow hair clip.
What was Manoj feeling as he pressed his nose to the glass?
He felt a deep longing for Amma, showing it by going quiet rather than crying.
How did Aditi support Manoj, and why did it work?
She noticed his full tiffin, named his missing gently and sat with him, so he felt less alone and began to eat.
What is it like for Amma working night shifts?
She might miss seeing Manoj in the mornings and would want to know someone comforted him at school.

Read this:

The night before, Pema and Nilesh had argued until midnight about the transfer to Shillong. They'd agreed on one thing only: stop, sleep, and talk tomorrow.
The next day they met in the hospital canteen where they both worked, she in radiology, he in pharmacy, during the three o'clock lull.
Nilesh had slept badly, but he looked calmer. "There's something I didn't say last night," he said. "It's not the job. I'm scared about my father. If we go, and something happens to him here, I won't forgive myself."
Pema put down her tea. "Why didn't you say that?"
"I didn't know it myself till this morning."
Suddenly the choice wasn't "go or stay". Pema said, "What if I take the transfer for a year, and you ask for a position here, near him? Or we both go and plan monthly visits?"
For the first time, there were more than two options on the table.

Where did Pema and Nilesh meet the next day?
In the hospital canteen where they both worked.
What was Nilesh afraid of, as he admitted the next day?
Nilesh was scared that if they moved and something happened to his father, he wouldn't forgive himself.
What else could Pema and Nilesh do to decide among the new options?
They could list what matters to each of them and look at how each option protects Nilesh's father and Pema's career.
How did Pema react to Nilesh's fear?
Pema was surprised but understanding, and immediately widened the options instead of arguing.

metadata.subtype: Approach: sleeping on it before deciding [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

I share the flat with Jatin, so I was on the sofa when Sarita came round on Friday with plans for the new café and a big grin. Jatin had been quiet all evening after a long shift at the hospital pharmacy; he'd eaten standing up and gone to his room. When she called him out and told him the plan, he rubbed his face and said calmly, "I'm really glad you thought of it. But I need some time alone tonight. Can we go tomorrow instead?" There was a pause. Sarita's grin slipped for a second, and I braced for a sulk; my last flatmate would have hinted for an hour and then slammed a door. But she said, "Okay. Tomorrow, seven?" and he said, "Seven. I'd like that." She left and he went back to his room. I can't say exactly how either of them felt. But the next evening they went out laughing, and nobody had to guess anything.

Where had Jatin worked his long shift?
At the hospital pharmacy.
What do Jatin's quiet evening and rubbed face suggest about his state?
He was likely tired and drained after the long shift and needed rest more than an outing, though he still seemed glad Sarita had thought of him.
Why did Jatin's way of saying it work?
He stated a clear, calm, specific need, thanked her, and offered another time, so Sarita didn't have to guess.
What was the moment like for Sarita?
She was briefly disappointed, her grin slipping, but the clear request made it easy to agree to seven the next day.

Read this:

In Johannesburg, Lindiwe, seventeen, was reading two news sites about the city council's vote to raise water tariffs. One headline said, 'Council Robs Residents!' The other said, 'Council Approves Tariff Change After Drought Warnings.' She frowned and messaged Sami from civics class: 'Same story, totally different vibe.' Sami replied, 'Check the actual council minutes. They're public.' That evening she found them online. Forty councillors had voted; the reasons were listed, and some had objected. She also found out her ward councillor's name for the first time. Lindiwe turns eighteen next year. She added a reminder on her phone: 'Register to vote.' Then she emailed her councillor a question about the drought plan.

What were the two headlines Lindiwe read about the council?
'Council Robs Residents!' and 'Council Approves Tariff Change After Drought Warnings.'
How did Lindiwe feel reading the two different headlines?
She was puzzled and a bit suspicious, noticing the same story was told with very different emotion.
Which of Lindiwe's steps could any young reader copy?
Comparing sources, reading the original public record and contacting their representative with a question.
How might Lindiwe's councillor see an email from a young resident?
The councillor might be pleased, or at least reminded that young future voters are paying attention.

Read this:

Shalini: ugh. I think I upset Harish today
Keerthana: what happened?
Shalini: he asked me to redo the chart for the third time and I let out this huge sigh. like a whole balloon deflating
Shalini: didn't say a word. just the sigh
Keerthana: 😬 from his side that probably sounded like "you're wasting my time"
Shalini: I was just tired!! the sigh wasn't at him
Keerthana: he doesn't know that though
Shalini: true. his face kind of closed after
Keerthana: try the slow kind next time. breathe out long through your nose, no sound, then say "give me ten minutes"
Shalini: the secret sigh 😅
Keerthana: exactly. same calm, no audience
Shalini: okay. messaging him now to say sorry, it was the day, not him
Keerthana: 👍 good call

How many times had Harish asked for the chart to be redone?
Three times; this was the third.
What was Shalini feeling when the sigh came out?
Shalini was tired and frustrated with the day rather than annoyed at Harish, though from his side it could sound dismissive.
What did Keerthana suggest for next time?
A silent, slow breath out through the nose followed by words like "give me ten minutes", so the calming works without an audience.
How did the sigh probably land with Harish?
It likely sounded like "you're wasting my time"; his face closed, so he may have felt dismissed.

metadata.subtype: Sighing to hide or show stress [Regulating]

messages.content:
Read this:

Tuesday
Coach Sir says I'm his favourite in the whole swimming club. He gives me the good lane and juice from his bag, only me. He says, "Don't tell the others, Jasleen." I feel so special!
But today he said I should stay after practice when everyone goes, and not tell Mumma because she'll worry for nothing.
My tummy felt weird. I like Coach Sir. So why can't Mumma know?
When Manjula Masi picked me up, I told her. She stopped the scooter and listened to all of it. "Thank you for telling me. You did the right thing, and you're not in trouble."
Masi called Mumma right away. Tonight they went to the club office together to tell the manager. I'll practise in the other batch now.

What did Coach Sir give Jasleen after practice?
Juice from his bag, only for Jasleen.
How did Jasleen feel when told to stay back and not tell Mumma?
Jasleen felt confused and uneasy, with a weird tummy feeling, because she liked the coach but didn't understand why Mumma couldn't know.
What did Manjula Masi do that was right?
She stopped to listen fully, thanked Jasleen, said Jasleen wasn't in trouble, called Mumma at once, and went with Mumma to the club office that night.
How might Mumma feel when Masi called?
Mumma would likely feel frightened and protective, and relieved that Jasleen told Masi.

Read this:

The teacher put Rajni next to Varun, and for the first week they said nothing to each other. Then Varun's pencil case fell open and a stack of cricket cards slid across the floor. Rajni gasped. "You have the Mumbai captain!" she whispered. By break they were trading behind the water cooler, and by Friday the bench felt like theirs.

On Monday Rajni gave Varun half her tiffin's puri and told him, very quietly, that she was scared of the dark. She watched his face. If he laughed, that would be the end. Varun only nodded. "I hate lifts," he said. Every day they offered each other something a bit bigger and each time checked what happened next.

Soon they walked home together, invented a code of knocks on the desk, and Rajni announced, "You are my best friend." Varun grinned so wide his ears moved.

At the next recess Aditi asked Rajni to skip rope. Rajni went, laughing. Varun stood by the wall with his cards, chewing his lip. When Rajni came back he said, "I'm not trading with you anymore," and turned his back. Rajni stared at his shoulders, confused and a little cross.

What did Varun's cards do that first made Rajni speak to him?
They slid out of his pencil case onto the floor, and Rajni noticed the Mumbai captain.
How did the first week differ from the days that followed, and what test did Rajni give the friendship along the way?

At first they sat together silently, but shared cards and a bench started the friendship, and then Rajni shared puri and her fear of the dark while watching Varun's face to see whether he would laugh.
What was Varun feeling as he stood by the wall while Rajni skipped rope?
He felt hurt and left out, and possessive of his best friend, which is why he turned his back and refused to trade.
What could Rajni do to repair the moment with Varun?
She could tell him she still counts him as her best friend and suggest a plan for them both, such as trading cards after school.

Kindergarten teacher's note, Wednesday.
During free play, Raghav and two friends were building a block tower. Ujjwal, five, came to join. Raghav said, "No, you can't play. Only us." Ujjwal froze, then came to me holding his stomach: "My tummy is paining." His eyes were full. I sat him on my lap and told him being left out can hurt inside, and it wasn't his fault. Then I helped Raghav's group make space for one more builder. Ujjwal placed the top block. I'll tell his mother at pickup today.

What were Raghav and his friends building?
They were building a block tower.
What was Ujjwal feeling when he held his stomach?
Ujjwal felt hurt and upset at being left out, and it felt like a real stomach pain.
What did the teacher do that helped?
The teacher comforted Ujjwal, told him it wasn't his fault, helped the group include him, and planned to tell his mother at pickup that same day.
How might Raghav feel when the teacher asked the group to make space?
Raghav might feel a little reluctant at first, but seeing Ujjwal place the top block could help him feel good about including him.

Kishore: salary is great on paper

90 minutes each way.

Kishore feels disappointed and sad, missing time with the family more than expected now that the higher salary barely helps.
What would you change first about how Kishore made the decision?
Before saying yes, compare the full picture: rent, commute time and family time, not only the salary figure.

"Jaya, my hands are shaking," Uma whispered in the corridor.
"It's only Ma'am."
"She looks at me and I forget everything, even 5 times 6."
"You could ask her a question after class. Just one small one."
"What if she gets angry?"
"Try."
After the bell, Uma stood at the teacher's desk. "Ma'am, can you tell me again how to do long division?"
The teacher took off her spectacles. "Of course, beti. Sit here." She drew the steps slowly and even smiled. "You should have asked earlier."
Outside, Uma told Jaya, "She is still strict, but she is kind."

What did Uma forget when the teacher looked at her?
She forgot everything, even 5 times 6.
Why was Uma afraid to ask the teacher a question?
She feared the teacher would get angry, and her fear of getting things wrong made her hands shake.
What small step helped Uma see the teacher differently?
She asked one small question after class, when it was quiet, and saw the teacher's softer side.
How might the teacher have felt when Uma asked about long division?
The teacher probably felt glad that a student came for help, as her smile and "You should have asked earlier" suggest. 😊

Beatriz was wiping tables at the café in Lisbon when Daniel came in for his first date, the one he had been nervous about all week. She watched from behind the counter. He arrived early, which was good, but when his date walked in he stood up too fast and knocked his coffee into the sugar bowl. From then on, Beatriz could see it: the date checked her phone, answered in short sentences, sat back. Daniel kept apologising. Then, twenty minutes in, they found they both hated the same football team, and the date laughed properly for the first time. By the end they were leaning in. Later, while closing up, Beatriz told him, "The first two minutes nearly sank you. Next time, sit down, breathe, and say one easy thing before you do anything with your hands." Daniel grinned. "But she stayed."

What did Daniel knock his coffee into?
He knocked it into the sugar bowl.
What was Beatriz thinking as she watched the date check her phone?
Beatriz felt a pang of worry for Daniel, seeing how one clumsy first moment was colouring the date's whole reaction.
What advice did Beatriz give, and why does it make sense?
Sit down, breathe and say one easy thing before moving, because a calm opening shapes the rest of a first meeting.
How did the date's view of Daniel change over the evening?
The date started distant after the spill, then warmed up once they found a shared joke, showing a first impression can update.
Make this first person singular: The boy said that he was late and that his bag was heavy.
I said that I was late and that my bag was heavy.

I've lived next door to Jagdish Uncle and his son Asif for fifteen years, so I heard most of it through the open window on Sunday.
Asif had got a job offer in Hyderabad. His father wanted him to stay and join the family shop. Voices rose. Jagdish Uncle said, "If you go, don't come back asking for anything."
Then Asif spoke, and I remember how calm he sounded. "Abbu, I love you. I'm taking the job. I'll come home every month, and I'll call you every evening after the shop closes. I'm not leaving the family. I'm just choosing my work."
There was a long silence. I couldn't see their faces.
A month later, I saw Asif get out of an auto with a box of sweets and walk straight into the shop. His father didn't smile, exactly. But he took the box.
I don't know what either of them felt. But I know Asif kept coming.

Where was Asif's job offer?
In Hyderabad.
How did Asif seem to feel when he answered his father?
Asif seemed calm and loving, though probably nervous, firm about his decision while trying to keep the family close.
What did Asif do that set a boundary without cutting off?
He calmly said he would take the job, promised monthly visits and evening calls, and then kept coming home.
How does the neighbour see the relationship a month later?
The neighbour notices Asif returning with sweets and his father taking the box, though they can't know what either felt.

The bad-weather delay had made it worse. Rehana had walked into the clinic waiting room an hour early for her job interview, and now the rain drummed the window and the receptionist said the panel was running behind. She got up and began pacing the corridor, up to the window, back to the poster of vaccination dates, up again. A stranger on the bench, Zainab, watched her. "Looks like you are burning off a lot," she said. Rehana laughed shakily. "Nerves." "Step outside under the porch for a minute," Zainab suggested. "Fresh air. Breathe slowly." Rehana did, and when she came back her shoulders had dropped a little.

Why was Rehana at the clinic?
She was there for her job interview, an hour early.
What did Rehana's pacing suggest about how she felt, and how might others have read it?
It suggested nerves about the interview, which she confirmed. Others might have read it as impatience about the delay, but Zainab guessed it was nervous energy.
What small step helped Rehana?
She stepped under the porch for fresh air and slow breathing, and her shoulders dropped.
How might Zainab have felt watching Rehana pace?
She likely felt kind concern and wanted to help, since she spoke gently and gave a practical suggestion.

Tuesday. Keerthana found Jatin in the hostel common room, staring at nothing, a bandage on his wrist. "I've been hurting myself," he said, very quietly. "When everything piles up, it's the only thing that makes it stop for a minute. Then I feel disgusting." Keerthana sat down next to him. "Thank you for telling me. You're not disgusting. You're in a lot of pain. I'm staying with you and we're going to the campus counsellor now." She walked with him there, and the counsellor saw him straight away and helped him make a safety plan.
Friday. In the counsellor's room, Jatin said the relief never lasted. "Then I just feel numb and ashamed." The counsellor nodded. "That's pain asking for care, not punishment."
Three weeks later. On a bad night, Jatin called Keerthana instead, and together they used his plan.

What did Keerthana notice on Jatin's wrist?
A bandage.
How did Jatin feel after hurting himself?
He felt brief relief, then numb, ashamed and disgusted with himself.
What made Keerthana's response the right one?
She stayed calm, showed care without judgment, stayed with him and took him to a professional immediately, which led to a safety plan.
How might Keerthana feel on the night Jatin calls her instead?
She probably feels worried but also relieved and trusted, glad he reached out.

I share a hostel room with Yamini, so I heard both of her calls with the online reader. The first one was free. The man's voice was soft: "You carry an old hurt you rarely mention, beta." Yamini went very quiet and pressed the phone to her ear. Afterwards she said, "He understood me in two minutes, Ramesh." The second call cost money. This time he said her new friendship with the girl from the dance club "would bring confusion." Since then she has skipped two dance practices and hardly replies to that girl's messages. On Sunday she paid for a third call. I don't know what she feels exactly. I only know she keeps her phone face-up now, waiting for him.

How much did the first call with the online reader cost?
The first call was free.
What does Yamini saying "He understood me in two minutes" suggest about how she feels?
She feels deeply seen by the line about an old hurt, and that warmth has quickly turned into trust in the reader.
What could Ramesh do when Yamini starts skipping dance practice?
Ramesh could gently ask what Yamini actually knows about her friend, apart from what the reader said, and point out that the "old hurt" line would fit almost anyone.
How might the girl from the dance club be affected by the readings?
She is getting fewer replies and seeing Yamini miss practice, with nothing to explain it, so she may feel pushed away and confused.

"I'm the fastest in the whole building. I'll beat you to the gate by a mile."
"Mridul, I'm twelve. You're eight."
"So? I beat Chintu yesterday. And Chintu's fast."
"Chintu is five."
"Doesn't matter. I'm definitely winning. One hundred percent."
Kiran didi tied her laces. "Okay. Ready, steady..."
"GO!" Mridul shot off before she finished.
Halfway across the compound, Kiran passed him easily. She was leaning on the gate when he arrived, red-faced.
"You... you started early!"
"You started early, Mridul."
He stood there panting, mouth open. "But I was sure. I was so sure."
"Being sure isn't the same as being fast," Kiran said, and ruffled his hair. "Want to practise tomorrow?"
He kicked a pebble. "...Maybe."

Who did Mridul beat the day before?
He beat Chintu, who is five.
Why was Mridul so stunned at the gate?
He felt shocked and embarrassed, because he had been completely sure he would win and his loud confidence had never been tested against someone faster.
How does Kiran help Mridul after the race?
She gently says being sure isn't the same as being fast and offers to practise with him, turning the loss into a chance to get better.
What is it like for Kiran when Mridul says she started early?
Kiran seems amused rather than upset, calmly pointing out that he was the one who started early and staying kind.

The family counselling centre in Nagpur had one small room with a ceiling fan that clicked on every turn. Kalyani, the counsellor, let the silence go on after Sameer said, "I keep finding things."

Rekha took a breath. "Then I'll say all of it now, in front of someone, so it can't change later."

She went through it: the loan she took for her brother's shop, the gold she used as security, the time she deleted the bank's messages from the family phone, and the second amount her brother asked for in the summer, which she also paid.

"I didn't tell you about the summer one even when you found the first," she said. "That was wrong. Hiding any of it was wrong. I kept thinking the next piece would be the last one you had to hear."

Kalyani asked, "Is there anything else, Rekha?"

"No. Some dates might be off. But no."

Where does this conversation take place?
In a small room at the family counselling centre in Nagpur, with a ceiling fan that clicks.
What did Rekha hope for each time she kept back another piece?
She hoped each piece would be the last one Sameer had to hear; she felt ashamed and afraid of hurting him more, so she kept delaying.
What does Rekha do at this stage that makes rebuilding possible?
She tells everything in one go, including the parts Sameer had not found, and says plainly that hiding any of it was wrong, so he stops finding new things.
What would change for Sameer if Rekha had again told only part of it?
He would go on finding things, and every new piece would reopen the wound and make him trust nothing she said.

In Stockholm, Astrid and Ivan had been together since their first year of university, four years now. Lately they spent evenings in separate rooms. When Ivan talked about moving to his hometown after graduation, Astrid felt her stomach drop. She wanted to go abroad.
She told her friend Maja, "We just need to get through this phase."
"How long has the phase been?"
Astrid thought. "Since last spring."
"And why are you staying?"
"Four years, Maja. We've been through so much. His family is like mine. I can't just throw all that away."
"You're not throwing it away. It happened. It was good. The question is whether the next four years would be good."
Astrid didn't answer. That night, she sat with Ivan in the kitchen and said, "Can we talk honestly? Not about the past. About what we both want next." Ivan nodded slowly. It was the first real conversation in months.

How long had Astrid and Ivan been together?
Four years now, since their first year of university.
How did Astrid feel when Ivan talked about moving to his hometown?
Astrid felt a sinking dread, because she wanted to go abroad and their futures didn't match.
What choice does Astrid make at the end, and why is it wise?
She asks Ivan to talk honestly about what they both want next, shifting the decision from past investment to the future.
How might Ivan feel when Astrid asks to talk?
Ivan might feel nervous but also relieved, since it was their first real conversation in months.
Put this into modern English: Prithee, good sir, wouldst thou tell me where the market lies?
Please, sir, could you tell me where the market is?

Crèche note, Christmas week, by the room caregiver.

Today Abhinav's mother Kavitha visited during our decorating time. When I said, "Abhinav, don't pull the tinsel," he walked straight to the tree and yanked it, looking back at me. He laughed when I came near.

I stopped saying no. I gave him his own piece of tinsel to shake and moved the glass baubles higher. He played happily for a while.

Tomorrow I'll try telling him what he can do, not only what he can't. 🎄

What did Abhinav yank?
He walked straight to the tree and yanked the tinsel.
Why did Abhinav look back and laugh when he pulled the tinsel?
He seemed excited and pleased with himself, as the no made the tinsel more tempting and let him show his own will.
What worked better than saying no again?
Giving Abhinav his own tinsel to shake and moving the glass baubles higher kept him safe and happy.
How might Kavitha feel watching Abhinav pull the tinsel?
Kavitha might feel a little embarrassed, then relieved when the caregiver calmly redirected him.

On Friday, Uma ma'am gathered the class in a circle for the safety drill. Each child stood and said a name, a home address and two phone numbers from a card. Ujjwal's knees felt wobbly, but he read in a steady voice: his flat number, the lane, Papa's number and Kaur aunty's number from next door. "And what do you do if your grandmother falls and nobody else is home?" Uma ma'am asked. "Call 112," said Ujjwal. "I say my address and stay on the line. Then I call Kaur aunty." The girl beside him forgot her lane, and Uma ma'am gave her time to try again. Ujjwal put the card back in his bag pocket.

Whose number besides Papa's did Ujjwal read from the card?
Ujjwal read Kaur aunty's number from next door.
What might Ujjwal be feeling as he stands up with wobbly knees?
He is nervous but determined, and his steady voice shows the practice is helping.
What should the girl beside Ujjwal do to be ready like him?
She could practise her address and numbers until she can say them without stopping, using the card for support.
How does Uma ma'am help the girl who forgot her lane?
Uma ma'am gives her time to try again, so she does not feel judged while she is learning.
