Monday: Arnab came home from the hospital IT desk at ten, ate standing up, and fell asleep with his phone on his chest. Gopika covered him with a sheet and told herself it was just a bad week.
Thursday: She'd made his favourite fish curry. He ate it, said "good", and went to sit on the balcony in the dark. She washed up alone, wondering when she had turned into furniture.
The next Tuesday: Gopika didn't cook. She didn't wait up either. When Arnab came in and asked, "Where's dinner?", she said, "Didn't think you'd notice." He looked confused, almost hurt. He had only wanted quiet. He hadn't known she was counting the empty evenings.

What did Gopika make on Thursday?
She made his favourite fish curry.
What was Gopika feeling as she washed up alone?
She felt invisible, wondering when she had turned into furniture.
What could each of them do at this stage to stop the distance growing?
Gopika could say "I miss you in the evenings" before resentment sets in, and Arnab could name his tiredness and offer a small window of time.
How does Arnab experience the "Didn't think you'd notice" reply?
He is confused and almost hurt, because he only wanted quiet and never meant to reject her.

The radio was playing in the Jalandhar flat and Gurleen couldn't sit still. She jumped off the sofa and started dancing, arms like wings, spinning, then stamping. Vaibhav, her big brother, laughed. She paused, cheeks pink. But then he picked up two steel spoons and drummed on a plate. "Do the bird again!" Gurleen flapped and twirled, making up new moves with each beat, until they both fell on the carpet laughing.

What did Vaibhav use to drum on a plate?
He picked up two steel spoons to drum on a plate.
What might Gurleen have felt when Vaibhav first laughed?
She may have felt embarrassed, since she paused and her cheeks went pink.
What turned the moment around for Gurleen?
Vaibhav joined in with a drum and asked for her bird move, which showed he enjoyed her dance.
How does Vaibhav's joining in change things?
It shows his laugh was fun, not mockery, so Gurleen feels safe to keep creating.
Grace buys a bottle of oil for Rs 8 and a water bottle for Rs 17. How much does she spend in all?
Rs 25. Because 8 + 17 = 25, so both cost Rs 25.
I get nervous when I have to speak in a group.
Many people do. A little preparation helps: know your first sentence well, breathe slowly before you start, and speak a bit slower than feels natural.
What if my mind goes blank halfway?
Pause for a moment and take a breath. Silence feels longer to you than to listeners. You can glance at your notes or say, 'Let me gather my thoughts,' and then carry on.

The hostel study hall at eight p.m. was silent except for pages turning. Pankaj sat at the corner desk with his chemistry notes, but his pen hadn't moved in forty minutes.
In his head: the exam could have questions from the part he didn't understand. He could blank out. His handwriting could be too slow. His rank could drop, and his parents had paid for coaching. If his rank dropped, the college would be worse, the job would be worse...
Vandana didi, the evening warden, noticed his blank page on her round. She crouched beside him. "You've been very still."
"I'm thinking about the exam. All the ways it could go wrong."
"And how much chemistry have you done?"
He looked at the page. "None."
"Worry is pretending to be work," she said gently. "Pick one topic. Just one. I'll check back at nine."
Pankaj opened to equilibrium and, slowly, started writing.

How long had Pankaj's pen not moved?
His pen hadn't moved in forty minutes.
How was Pankaj feeling as he sat at the corner desk?
He felt anxious, his mind jumping from one possible failure to the next, all the way to a worse job.
What did Vandana didi do well here?
She noticed his stillness, named worry as pretending to be work, and gave him one small topic with a check-back at nine, which turned worry into action.
How might Vandana didi see Pankaj's still silence on her round?
She seems to recognise it as worry rather than laziness, and responds with a gentle push instead of a scolding.

I'm Omkar, and last winter at the college fest I learned something about myself. The last act was over and the crowd rushed the gate to the backstage lane. Ankita, my friend from the dance club, caught my sleeve and said, “Don't.” I went anyway. Hundreds of us pushed at the steel barricade, and someone shouted to lift it. I put both hands on it and heaved. The guard's face was frightened. Alone in a quiet hallway I would never have done that. In the crowd my courage felt huge and nobody's fault, least of all mine.

On the walk home Ankita said nothing. Finally I said, “That wasn't me.” Ankita answered, “It was you, though.” I've been thinking about that ever since.

What did Ankita say when catching Omkar's sleeve?
Ankita caught Omkar's sleeve and said, “Don't.”
Why did Omkar's courage feel like nobody's fault, least of all Omkar's?
In the crowd Omkar felt bold and hidden among hundreds, so responsibility seemed to spread out until it almost disappeared.
What could Omkar try the next time a crowd starts pushing at a barricade?
Omkar could listen to a friend's warning like Ankita's and step out of the surge before touching the barricade.
What might the guard have felt while the crowd heaved at the barricade?
The guard was probably frightened and outnumbered, worried about being hurt or unable to control the crowd.

In the children's dental clinic in Pune, the receptionist, Swati, held out a sheet of dinosaur stickers. "Yogesh, you can have one sticker now, or two after the doctor checks your teeth."
Yogesh, five, didn't even look at the doctor's door. "Now!" He peeled one and stuck it on his shirt.

He folded his arms and wouldn't look at anyone all the way to the car.

Where did Yogesh stick his sticker?
He stuck it on his shirt.
How did Yogesh feel about the sticker at first, and what shows it?
Yogesh felt eager for the sticker right away, saying "Now!" without even looking at the doctor's door and sticking it on his shirt.
What could Swati try with the next child, to make waiting easier?

Subject: The launch timeline, and a question I should have asked
Hi Leela,
In our planning meeting on the 3rd, you agreed to the new launch date, and I moved on quickly. Since then the design review has slipped, the copy deadline has passed, and your updates say "nearly done". You're one of the most reliable people on this team, so I've been wondering what's going on.
I think I may have missed something. Looking back, I announced the date more than I discussed it. If you disagreed, I didn't make it easy to say.
So I'm asking now, with no penalty: do you think the date is realistic? What would you change? A straight "no" is welcome. I'd rather hear it now than find out at the next missed milestone.
Can we talk tomorrow at 11, just the two of us?
Chetan

When was the planning meeting where Leela agreed to the launch date?
On the 3rd.
Why does Chetan think Leela might have kept quiet in the meeting?
Chetan realises the date was announced rather than discussed, so disagreeing may not have felt easy or safe.
What makes Chetan's email a good way to invite honesty?
It admits Chetan's own part, promises no penalty, asks direct questions and welcomes a straight 'no', then offers a private talk.
How might Leela feel reading 'A straight no is welcome'?
Probably relieved and a bit nervous, finally allowed to say the date isn't realistic without it looking like failure.

Tuesday, 1 July. Joseph and Sahil have argued about the price of their tuition app for a week: ₹199 or ₹349 a month. Sahil slams his laptop shut. "We're going in circles." Joseph says, "Then let's stop guessing. Test both."
Wednesday, 2 July. They write the rules together. For three weeks, parents who sign up on odd dates see ₹199; parents on even dates see ₹349. The winner is whichever brings more paying parents who are still active after their first week. "Whatever it says, we follow it, even if it's you," Sahil says. They shake on it.
Wednesday, 23 July. The numbers: ₹349 brought fewer signups but nearly as many active parents, and more money. Joseph, who had wanted ₹199, winces, then laughs. "Fine. You win. The spreadsheet wins."

How were the two groups of parents split?
Parents signing up on odd dates saw ₹199; parents on even dates saw ₹349.
How did Joseph feel when the numbers came in?
Joseph winced with disappointment, then laughed, accepting the result with good humour.
What made this test fair to both founders?
They wrote the rules together, chose the winning measure in advance and promised to follow it.
What was it like for Sahil before the test?
Sahil felt frustrated by going in circles, which is why he slammed the laptop shut.

Thursday.
Interviewed Tenzin for the college magazine today, about the Tibetan food stall he runs outside the hostel. I'd prepared questions. Bad ones, it turns out. My first was, "Isn't it hard to study and run a stall?" He said, "Yes." That was it. Then I asked, "Don't your grades suffer?" and his face closed. He said, "Why, did someone say they did?" I felt awful. I sounded like a teacher catching him out.
So I put my list down. I said, "Sorry, let me try again. How did the stall start?" And he smiled and told me about his grandmother's momo recipe and the first night he sold twelve plates. I just kept asking, "And then?" and "What was that like?" By the end I had four pages.
Lesson: ask so the other person can tell a story, not so they have to defend themselves.
— Nandini

What did Tenzin sell on the first night?
Twelve plates.
What was Nandini feeling after Tenzin asked, "Why, did someone say they did?"
Nandini felt awful and guilty, realising the question sounded like a teacher catching Tenzin out.
What did Nandini change, and why did it help?
Nandini put the list down and asked open questions like "How did the stall start?" and "And then?", which let Tenzin tell his story instead of defending himself.
If you were Tenzin, what kind of interviewer would you want?
One who is curious rather than suspicious, asking open questions about the stall's story instead of hinting that something is wrong.

Counsellor's note, Thursday. Swati (Class 9) came to my room looking pale. She told me a message had promised a free phone if she paid a small delivery fee. She had imagined the phone in her hand all evening. She paid two hundred rupees using a wallet, and then a second message asked for more. When she ignored it, the messages stopped and the phone never came. “I feel so stupid,” she said. I told her scammers depend on excitement, not on people being foolish, and that it was not her fault. We rang her parents that afternoon, and they reported it to the bank. Swati asked me to help her write a short rule: free things never need payment first. — Jasleen

How did Swati pay the fee?
Using a wallet.
What was Swati feeling after the messages stopped?
Embarrassed and upset: she said she felt stupid and blamed herself.
What could Swati do next time, and why?
Treat any prize that asks for money first as a warning, and check with an adult before paying, since real prizes do not need a payment up front.
How does the situation look to the counsellor?
Jasleen sees a student tricked through excitement instead of foolishness, and wants her to feel supported and not blamed.

Saturday, first week of the summer holidays: Tanvir's team won the gully match by six runs. "That's because I batted like a pro," he told Ira, twirling his bat. "Nobody can bowl to me."
Tuesday: Hot wind blew dust down the lane. Tanvir was out on the second ball, and his team lost. He threw the bat down. "The bat's cracked. And the umpire's blind. That was never out!" Ira, who had been umpiring, crossed her arms.
Friday: Ira drew a chalk line down the wall and wrote two columns, WINS and LOSSES. "So whose fault?" she asked. Tanvir looked at the wall, then at his dusty sandals. "Maybe I swing too early," he mumbled. "Sometimes." He picked up the same bat and asked her to bowl.

By how many runs did Tanvir's team win on Saturday?
By six runs.
Why did Tanvir blame the bat and the umpire on Tuesday?
Losing made him feel embarrassed and angry, and blaming the bat and the umpire protected his idea of himself as the best batter.
What helped Tanvir look at his own part?
Ira's two chalk columns, which made him look at wins and losses the same way and ask whose part each one was.
How might Ira feel when Tanvir calls the umpire blind?
Ira, who was umpiring, likely feels annoyed and unfairly blamed for his loss.

The monsoon had turned the paddy fields into mirrors. Joseph squatted at the edge of the bund, listening to the frogs.
"Vinita aunty, why do frogs shout when it rains?"
Vinita, carrying a basket of tapioca, stopped. "They're calling each other."
"Why do they call only in rain?"
"The water is back, so it's their time to meet."
"Why do they need water to meet?"
"Their eggs need water."
Joseph was quiet for a moment. "So the rain is like their school bell?"
Vinita laughed. "Something like that."

What was Vinita carrying?
A basket of tapioca.
What does Joseph's question about the school bell suggest?
Joseph feels curious and pleased to connect the new idea to something he already knows.
How could Vinita support Joseph's questions next time?
Vinita could take him to see frog eggs in the water, so he can watch the answer for himself.
How might Vinita see Joseph's many questions?
Vinita seems amused and patient, and she enjoys his clever comparison.

At the IT company's training centre in Mysuru, the eight trainees were split into teams for the final demo. Chetan, the team lead, kept the presentation, gave the slides to two friends, and handed Gopika the testing. "Your English, no? Clients won't get it." He said it lightly. The others smiled.
Gopika said nothing and ran tests till nine every night.
On demo day, the client's engineer asked a hard question about a failing case. Chetan froze. Gopika stood up and explained it slowly, simply, precise down to the line number. The engineer nodded.
That night Chetan couldn't sleep. Since joining, he had been scared that his own college wasn't good enough; mocking Gopika's English had made him feel less small. It hadn't made him better.
Next morning he went to her desk. "I was wrong about you, and about why I said it. Will you present the testing section next week?" Gopika considered him for a long moment. "Yes. And you'll check your own slides for once."

Which task did Chetan hand Gopika?
The testing.
What feeling was really behind Chetan's remark about Gopika's English?
His own fear that his college wasn't good enough; mocking her made him feel less small, a hidden insecurity.
What did Chetan do to put things right?
He admitted he was wrong about Gopika and about his reason, and asked her to present the testing section next week.
How might Gopika have felt during the weeks before the demo?
Belittled and left out, yet determined, working on the tests till nine every night.

On the first day of term at the Deaf school in Bristol, a new girl stood by the classroom door, holding her bag straps tight. Chidi walked up, signed a question, and pointed at her.
She fingerspelled slowly: F-R-E-Y-A.
Chidi copied it letter by letter, grinning. Then he spelled his own name back, fast, the way he had done a hundred times.
At break the class argued about what Freya's name sign should be. Someone suggested a sign near the head, because of her springy curls. Freya laughed and shook her curls. Chidi nodded hard.
In science, Mr Owens fingerspelled a new word, V-O-L-C-A-N-O. The class had no shared sign for it yet, so everybody spelled it out until Chidi made up one with a bursting hand. Freya used it straight away.

What new word did Mr Owens fingerspell in science?
V-O-L-C-A-N-O, the word volcano.
How can you tell Freya's mood changed during the day?

She held her bag straps tight at the door, which suggests she felt nervous, but at break she laughed and shook her curls, which suggests she felt pleased and included. She may also simply have found the argument funny.
What did the class do when a word had no shared sign yet?
They fingerspelled it until Chidi made up a sign, which shows fingerspelling filling a gap inside a full language rather than replacing it.
What would change for Freya if the class never gave her a name sign?
Everyone would have to spell her name letter by letter each time, which is slower and might leave her feeling less like part of the group.

In my first month in Amsterdam, a colleague, Sanne, invited me home for dinner. When she asked, "More soup?" I said, "No, thank you, I'm fine," exactly as my Amma taught me. In Chennai, that's the first line of a polite little dance; the host insists, you give in. Sanne just said, "Okay!" and cleared the table. I cycled home starving and laughing at myself. I realised that here, if I needed something, I'd have to say it plainly, even if it felt rude. It took practice: "Yes, please, I'd love more." Then last winter Lakshmi Aunty from our Tamil association came to stay with me. When I offered her more rice, she said, "Enough, enough, ma." And I heard my old self in it. So I offered again, and on the third time I just served a spoonful. She ate every grain and smiled at me. I'm Madhuri, and I switch dances now depending on who's at the table.

What did Sanne offer Madhuri?
More soup.
How did Madhuri feel cycling home after Sanne's dinner?
Madhuri felt hungry but amused, laughing at having followed a politeness script Sanne didn't know.
How does Madhuri now handle offers and needs in different settings?
Madhuri states needs plainly with Dutch hosts, but with Lakshmi Aunty offers more than once and serves a little, reading the polite refusal cautiously.
How did Lakshmi Aunty respond when served on the third offer?
She ate every grain and smiled, showing her 'enough, enough' had been politeness rather than a real no.

Bao got his first bank card at sixteen in Hanoi and used it to buy snacks, games, and bus fares. By the end of the month, the money from his part-time job at his uncle's shop was almost gone. He couldn't remember where it went. His friend Paulo, whose family had moved from Brazil, showed him a notebook. "I write everything down. Every coin." Bao laughed, but that evening he checked his account. Twenty small payments for games he had forgotten. His face went hot. He made a simple table: needs, wants, savings. He also set a spending alert. The next month, he still bought one game, but he knew exactly how much was left.

How many small payments for games did Bao find?
He found twenty small payments for games.
Why did Bao's face go hot when he checked his account?
He was embarrassed to see how many forgotten game payments had eaten up his earnings.
What made Bao's new system work?
Sorting spending into needs, wants and savings and setting an alert helped him see his money clearly without banning all fun.
How might Paulo feel seeing Bao adopt Paulo's idea?
Paulo might feel pleased that the notebook habit from home helped a friend. 👍

I'm Abhinav, and last year I spent two months managing a rumour that wasn't even true.
I'd taken four Fridays off, one each week, to take my father for physiotherapy after his fall. I didn't tell anyone why. Raghav, from the next desk, finally said, “Bro, the whole floor thinks you're interviewing with the competitor.”
Suddenly I was performing loyalty. I posted about how much I loved the company. I stayed late on Thursdays so nobody would think I was slacking. I laughed extra loud at my manager's jokes. Every time I walked into the pantry and conversation stopped, my chest tightened.
Then my manager asked me straight, and I told her about my father. She said, “Why didn't you just say?” It was over in a minute.

Why had Abhinav taken four Fridays off?
To take the father for physiotherapy after a fall.
How did Abhinav feel walking into the pantry during those months?
Abhinav felt exposed and anxious, chest tightening whenever conversation stopped.
What finally ended the rumour, and what does that suggest?
The manager asked directly and Abhinav explained; a short, honest word early might have saved two months of image-managing.
How might Raghav have felt telling Abhinav about the rumour?
Raghav was probably concerned and a bit awkward, wanting to warn a colleague.

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Bhupen Chacha,

I wanted to tell you before you hear it from the family. I turned down the offer from the bank in Mumbai. Yes, the big one, with the salary Papa told everyone about. I've taken a job at a small school for children with hearing difficulties in Hubli. The pay is much less. Papa is upset. Honestly, I'm scared. But when I visited the school last month and a little boy signed 'thank you' to me, I felt something I've never felt in an interview. Calm. Like I fit. You once told me that the best work is where you forget to check the clock. I think this is that. Please be on my side at Diwali.

With love,
Manjula

Where is Manjula's new job?
At a small school for children with hearing difficulties in Hubli.
What is Manjula feeling about the decision?
Manjula feels scared about the lower pay and Papa's reaction, but calm, as if the school is the right fit.
What could Bhupen Chacha do to support Manjula?
He could stand by Manjula at Diwali and help Papa understand why the work matters to Manjula.
How might Papa feel about the decision?
Papa is upset, perhaps worried about Manjula's future and disappointed after telling everyone about the bank.

Sahil had been a junior analyst in Mumbai for three months when he used an AI tool to draft his first market report. It looked polished: charts, confident sentences, a neat summary.
His manager, Bhavna, read it and asked one question. "Why did sales in the east drop in March?"
Sahil opened his mouth and closed it. The report said "seasonal factors". He didn't know what that meant for this product.
Bhavna didn't scold him. "Use the tool. It's fast. But you're the analyst, not it."
That evening Sahil went back to the raw data. The drop was actually because two big stores had closed. The AI had guessed.
He rewrote the section himself, using the tool only to tidy the language. Next time Bhavna asked a question, he answered without opening the file.

What did the report say caused the drop in the east?
It said "seasonal factors".
How did Sahil feel when he couldn't answer Bhavna's question?
Sahil felt embarrassed and exposed, realising he didn't understand his own report.
How can Sahil use AI at work while keeping his own skill growing?
Let the tool speed up drafting and tidying, but do the analysis himself and check claims against the raw data.
How might Bhavna see Sahil after the rewrite?
Bhavna would likely trust him more, seeing he now understands the numbers rather than relying on the tool's guesses.

why do we use sunscreen outdoors
why do we get a headache from staring at a screen for hours
Could you explain what irrational means?

1. Sunscreen shields the skin from sunburn. Because it blocks or absorbs part of the sun's harmful rays.
2. Long screen time can cause tired eyes and headaches. Because the eyes work hard to focus and we blink less, so they get dry and strained.
3. Irrational is an adjective that means not based on clear thought.

At the family dinner in their Delhi flat, the radio played an old film song, and Pooja masi sighed. "They don't make music like this any more. Every song from our time was a gem. Today it's all noise." Varun, twenty-four, smiled and pulled up a list on his phone: every film song released in 1975. There were hundreds. He read a few titles aloud. Nobody at the table recognised them. "Masi, these are from your time too," he said. "We only hear the ones that were so good people kept playing them for fifty years. The rest disappeared." Pooja masi laughed and swatted his arm. "So you're saying my generation also made noise?" "Some. Just like mine. In fifty years, only our best will be left."

Which year's film songs did Varun look up?
What does Varun's smile suggest as he pulls up the list?
He felt amused and curious rather than annoyed, wanting to show Pooja masi the full picture gently.
What point does Varun make, and why is it fair?
That only the best old songs are still played while the forgotten ones vanished, so the old era sounds better than it was.
How does Pooja masi take Varun's point?
She laughs and swats his arm, taking it in good humour.
Why do we see stars at night but not in the daytime?
They are still there in the day. Because sunlight scatters in the air and makes the sky so bright that the faint stars cannot be seen against it.

It was the monsoon holiday, the power had gone out, and the whole building was dark. Ganga, ten, had a pencil stub and the back of an old calendar. By candlelight, she began drawing the view from her window: the rain, the tangle of wires, the neem tree. Her cousin Vandana called her for a card game. 'In a minute.' An hour later, Vandana came again. 'The power's back! Didn't you notice?' Ganga looked up, surprised. The candle had burned down. Her drawing covered the whole calendar, even the corners. 'Is it for a competition?' Vandana asked. 'No,' said Ganga. 'I just wanted to see if I could draw the rain.'

What did Ganga draw on?
The back of an old calendar.
How did Ganga feel while drawing?
Ganga felt absorbed and happy, so lost in the drawing she didn't notice the power come back.
How could adults encourage Ganga's absorption?
They could give her time and materials to draw for its own sake, without turning it into a competition.
How might Vandana feel seeing the finished drawing?
Vandana is probably surprised and impressed, asking if it's for a competition.

I'm Aadhya, and I sit behind Tenzin. Last week, a girl pinched his cheek and said, "Look at these round cheeks! Like a momo!"
Everyone laughed, and I laughed too, for a second. Tenzin didn't.
He was quiet the whole lesson. At lunch, he didn't eat his tiffin.
Then, the next morning, when the same girl said it again, Tenzin looked at her and said, "Please stop. I don't like jokes about my face."
She said, "It was just a joke." He said, "Not to me," and turned back to his book.
I felt bad that I'd laughed. I told him sorry at break.

What did the girl compare Tenzin's cheeks to?
A momo.
What might Tenzin have been feeling when he didn't eat his tiffin?
Tenzin probably felt hurt and self-conscious after being laughed at.
What did Tenzin do that kept his self-respect?
He calmly asked her to stop and said it wasn't funny to him, without insulting her back.
How does Aadhya see her own laugh?
Aadhya feels guilty about laughing and chooses to apologise to Tenzin.
We have a six-hour bus ride tomorrow, and my little sister gets restless after an hour.
Plan a few small surprises. Pack a snack, a short story to read aloud, and some paper for drawing or word games.
She likes guessing games.
Then you're in luck. You can play 'I spy' out of the window, or twenty questions, where she thinks of an animal and you guess it. These need no equipment at all.
What if she gets bored of those too?

Take turns picking a song to hum, and the other person guesses it. Short breaks to stretch at a rest stop help too. Between games, let her look outside quietly, since travelling can tire a person out.
We'll try them all. Thank you!
You're welcome. I hope the bus ride goes smoothly, and maybe she'll even doze off.

Lights-out in the girls' hostel was at ten, but at nine-forty Vasudha was still cross-legged on her bed, a small brass diya unlit in her hand. Her roommate Damini looked up from her notes. 'You've stopped lighting it.' 'I'm not sure what I'm doing when I light it,' Vasudha said. 'At home Amma does it and I just copied.' For weeks she had been borrowing library books, one on the Gita, one on Buddhist ideas, one by a scientist who believed in no god at all, and arguing with all of them in the margins of her notebook. 'So what do you believe?' Damini asked, not unkindly. Vasudha turned the diya over. 'That I want five quiet minutes every morning. The words, I'm still choosing.' She set the diya back on the shelf, facing the window.

What time was lights-out in the hostel?
Lights-out was at ten.
Why had Vasudha stopped lighting the diya?
She was unsure what it meant to her, since she had only copied Amma, and she wanted her practice to be her own choice.
How could a warden or teacher support Vasudha's exploring?
They could keep different books and views available and let her talk it through without pushing her toward any answer.
How does Damini seem to see Vasudha's questioning?
She notices the change and asks directly but kindly, which suggests curiosity rather than judgement.

Last Tuesday, in the middle of the winter prelims, I did something I'm still a bit ashamed of. I had spent six hours on physics numericals at the dining table while fog pressed against the window. By eight my brain felt like wet paper.
Payal, my little sister, asked, "Ganga Didi, roti or the khichdi Mumma left?" I couldn't decide, so I tore open a family packet of chips and ate it standing at the fridge.
Then my friend Tanvi sent three photos of dresses for her cousin's wedding. "Which one?? Help!!" I typed "whatever u like" and turned the phone face down.
In the morning, after sleep and a proper breakfast, I saw her reply: "ok 🙁". It wasn't that I didn't care. I had simply run out of choosing.

What did Ganga eat instead of choosing between roti and khichdi?
She tore open a family packet of chips and ate it standing at the fridge.
Why did the chips and the quick reply feel like the only choices Ganga could make that evening?
After six hours of numericals Ganga felt drained, with a brain "like wet paper", so anything that needed a decision felt too heavy and the easiest option won.
What could Ganga try on the next long study day?
She could settle dinner and reply to friends during an afternoon break, or tell friends she'll answer properly after sleep.
How might Tanvi have felt reading "whatever u like"?
Tanvi may have felt brushed off and a little hurt, since she was excited about the dresses and wanted Ganga's help 🙁

At the end of her night shift at the Delhi hospital, Dolma sat in the nurses' changing room with her phone. Another message from her father: the homestay in Sikkim was busy, her mother's back was bad, when was she coming home for good? She loved this work, the quiet steadiness she felt at 3 a.m. beside a frightened patient. She loved her family too. For a year she had felt split in two, a nurse in Delhi and a guilty daughter on the phone. Anand, the charge nurse, found her there. "Still deciding between two lives?" "It feels like choosing who I am." "Or maybe you're building one life that has both." He mentioned that the district hospital in Gangtok was hiring. Dolma sat very still. Nursing near home, weekends at the homestay. Not everything, but all of her in one place. She opened the application before her bus came.

Where was the district hospital that was hiring?
It was in Gangtok.
What had Dolma been feeling for the past year?
She felt torn and guilty, split between being a nurse in Delhi and a daughter far from home.
What shift in thinking helped Dolma move forward?
Seeing it not as a choice between two lives but as building one life that holds both, then taking a concrete step by applying.
How might Dolma's father feel about the Gangtok plan?
He would likely feel relieved to have her close and able to help at weekends, even if it isn't everything he asked for.

They had forty-eight hours to sign the lease on the Kochi flat, and Tanvir and Raghav still hadn't agreed on how to split anything. The broker kept calling. That evening the power went out in Raghav's building, so they sat on the stairs with a torch and a notebook. "I earn more," Raghav said. "I should pay more rent." Tanvir shook his head. "Then I'll feel like a guest." They tried another way: rent in proportion to income, a shared account for groceries and bills, each keeping their own savings. Cooking went to Raghav, who loved it; Tanvir took the laundry and the monthly paperwork. The harder question came last. "Your parents still think I'm your flatmate," Tanvir said quietly. Raghav was silent a while. "I'll tell them before we move. Together, if you'll come." Tanvir squeezed his hand. They signed the next morning.

Which chore did Raghav take on?
Cooking went to Raghav, who loved it.
Why did Tanvir refuse to let Raghav simply pay more rent?
Tanvir worried about feeling like a guest instead of an equal partner in their home.
What helped them reach a fair arrangement under pressure?
They tried a proportional split, a shared account for bills and separate savings, divided chores by preference, and faced the family question openly.
What would change if Raghav kept the relationship hidden from his parents?
Tanvir would likely keep feeling hurt and unseen in their shared life, and the secret could strain the partnership.

Sit, beta. Your grandmother Reena has a story about a bean plant. When I was ten, we grew beans for the school fair. I put one pot in the dark cupboard and wrote on my paper that it would stay green. It grew, but pale as chalk. My classmate Ganga whispered, "Change it, write green." I nearly did. Then I thought, the plant did not lie, so why should I? At the fair I stood by my board and said, "I guessed green, and it turned pale, and that surprised me." The old teacher judging asked why. I said I did not know yet. He gave me a ribbon, but I remember his smile more.

What colour was the plant that grew in the cupboard?
It was pale as chalk.
What was Reena feeling when Ganga whispered to change the paper?
She felt tempted and uneasy, since she nearly did it and then reasoned that the plant had not lied.
What choice did young Reena make at the fair, and why did it work out?
She chose to show the pale plant and say she was surprised, and the judge valued her honesty enough to give her a ribbon.
How did the judging teacher see Reena's answer that she did not know yet?
The teacher seems to have taken it as honest work, giving her a ribbon and a smile.

In the staff room of the city hospital pharmacy, Deepika and Nilesh had a running joke: whoever lost the lunchtime crossword bought the evening tea. They had been close since induction.
Then the chief pharmacist asked Deepika to draw up the Diwali-week roster. Nilesh leaned over her shoulder. "You'll give me the day shift, na? My sister's coming."
Deepika laughed but covered the sheet with her hand. "Put in a request like everyone else. I'm going by the dates they came in."
He went quiet for the rest of lunch. That evening she found him at the tea stall.
"I'm not being cold. If I bend it for you, Rinku and the others will notice, and then we're the pair who get favours."
Nilesh sighed, then grinned. "Fine. But you're buying the tea."

What did the chief pharmacist ask Deepika to do?
Draw up the Diwali-week roster.
What does Deepika covering the sheet with her hand suggest?
It suggests she feels awkward and protective, wanting to keep the friendship warm without letting it bend the roster.
Why did Deepika go to find Nilesh at the tea stall?
To explain her reason calmly so the quiet lunch did not harden into resentment; clearing it up quickly helped the friendship survive the disagreement.
How might Nilesh see Deepika's refusal at first?
He probably feels hurt and let down, since they are close, until her point about fairness makes sense and he can joke again.

Sangeeta, you asked how I came to my beliefs. It wasn't one moment. Let me tell you about Sudha at twenty-four.
I had a job in Chennai and a head full of questions. So I made the search serious. Every Saturday I read: the Upanishads, the Gospels, the Dhammapada, and a thick book by a scientist who believed in nothing. I wrote in the margins until the pages curled.
I went to talk to people too. A Carnatic singer who prayed through her music. A Jesuit priest who ran a night school. My neighbour, a retired professor who called himself a cheerful sceptic. I asked each of them the hardest thing I could think of, and none of them got angry.
Then I tested what I read against life: against my father's illness, against the kindness of a stranger on a bus. Some ideas held. Some didn't.
It took four years. I didn't get certainty. I got a faith I could live with, full of question marks.

How long did Sudha's seeking take?
Four years.
What does Sudha feel about ending with a faith full of question marks?
Sudha feels at peace and content, accepting uncertainty as part of a faith that can be lived with.
What choice inside the story made young Sudha's seeking serious?
Setting aside every Saturday to read many traditions, talking with believers and a sceptic, and testing ideas against real life.
How might the cheerful sceptic neighbour have felt about Sudha's questions?
He likely enjoyed them and felt respected, glad to talk honestly with a young seeker.

"Captain Peleg," said Bildad steadily, "thy conscience may be drawing ten inches of water, or ten fathoms, I can't tell; but as thou art still an impenitent man, Captain Peleg, I greatly fear lest thy conscience be but a leaky one; and will in the end sink thee foundering down to the fiery pit, Captain Peleg."

What does Bildad fear about Captain Peleg's conscience?
He fears it may be a leaky one. Since Peleg still has not repented, Bildad worries it will sink him in the end, down to the fiery pit.

Monday: Rashmi watched Hansa say yes three times before lunch: an extra report, a colleague's shift, organising the office farewell. Hansa laughed, but her hands were shaking as she poured tea.
Thursday: Hansa was at her desk at 8 p.m. when Rashmi left. On Friday morning, Hansa had dark circles and had forgotten her own deadline. The manager frowned. Rashmi felt a pang of worry.
The next Monday: When a senior asked Hansa to cover yet another client meeting, Rashmi spoke first. “Hansa's with me on the vendor review this week. I can check if someone else is free.”
Later she whispered to Hansa, “You can say you're with me anytime. Practise.”
On Wednesday, Hansa said it herself. “I'm on the vendor review with Rashmi. Can we look at next week?” The senior nodded. Hansa sat back, stunned, and smiled.

What three things did Hansa say yes to on Monday before lunch?
An extra report, a colleague's shift, and organising the office farewell.
How did Rashmi feel when Hansa forgot her own deadline?
Rashmi felt a pang of worry, seeing Hansa burning out quietly.
What did Rashmi offer that let Hansa practise saying no?
She offered a line, being “with Rashmi on the vendor review,” and backed it up so Hansa could decline without losing standing.
How did Hansa feel when the senior nodded on Wednesday?
Hansa felt stunned and relieved, surprised that saying no was accepted.

What did Vaibhav love at school, according to Indu?
The geography olympiad.
What does Vaibhav's line 'it's decided, so I don't have to think about it' reveal?
It shows the certainty comes from following the family plan, and that underneath Vaibhav feels unsure and a bit flat.
What makes Indu's offer to send the form 'just to look' a wise move?
It doesn't fight the family plan but opens a small door for Vaibhav to explore before committing.
How might Indu see the uncles calling Vaibhav 'the boss'?
Indu may see it as pressure dressed up as praise, making it harder for Vaibhav to question the plan.

metadata.subtype: Foreclosure under family or community pressure [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Thursday night
Signed nothing yet, but I saw the flat. One room, a window over a neem tree, twenty minutes from the office instead of ninety. Irfan, who found it, kept saying, 'Just tell them.' Easy for Irfan. At dinner Papa asked about my day and I talked about traffic, nothing else. Mummy's knee has been bad; who will take her to physio on Saturdays? If I leave, will the aunties say I abandoned them? I keep picturing announcing it all at once and Papa going silent. Maybe instead: sit with them on Sunday, tell them why, promise Saturdays and Sunday dinner, and actually mean it.
Ishita

How far is the flat from the office?
Twenty minutes from the office, instead of ninety.
What is Ishita worried about when thinking of telling Mummy and Papa?
Ishita feels guilty and afraid, worried about who will take Mummy to physio and that the aunties will call it abandoning the family.
Which plan is better for Ishita, and why?
Sitting with them on Sunday to explain and promising Saturdays and Sunday dinners, because an honest talk about visits and duties hurts less than a sudden announcement.
How might Papa react if Ishita announced the move all at once?
Papa might go silent and feel rejected or blindsided, which could turn a practical move into a wound.

Read this:

"Harsha, forward this to your sisters," Samir said, holding out his phone. "A gang is drugging people in malls with perfume samples. It's all over the family groups."
"Where's it from?"
"Doesn't matter. I've got it from eight people. Eight! It has to be real."
"Did any news site report it?"
"Why are you being like this? It's about safety. Do you want your sisters to get hurt?"
"No. But I don't want to scare them over nothing either."
"You're so careless sometimes." Samir sent it to four more groups right there.
Harsha typed the first line into a search bar. The top result was a fact-check from two years ago.
"Samir…"
But Samir was already reading the next forward.

How many people had Samir got the message from?
He'd got it from eight people.
Why does Samir call Harsha careless?
Samir feels anxious and protective, and because so many people sent the message, doubting it feels careless about safety.
What could Samir do before forwarding a safety message?
He could search the message or check a trusted news source, as Harsha did, before sending it to more groups.
How might Harsha feel when Samir ignores the fact-check?
Harsha may feel frustrated and worried that fear is spreading faster than the truth.

Read this:

Dear Asif bhaiya,

Thank you for your advice about the scholarship application. I didn't listen, and I want to tell you what happened.

You said to start a month early. I thought, it's just forms and one essay. Two evenings, maybe three.

I started last Monday. The deadline was Friday.

The essay took three drafts. My professor needed four days to write the reference letter. The online form crashed twice. My mark sheets needed to be attested at the college office, which is only open till two.

On Thursday night I was in tears, with the reference letter still not in.

It arrived Friday at eleven, an hour before the deadline. I submitted with fifty minutes to spare.

I made it, but barely. Next time, I'll ask how long it took you, and I'll believe the answer.

Ishita

When did Ishita submit the application?
I submitted with fifty minutes to spare.
How was Ishita feeling on Thursday night?
Ishita was in tears, panicked because the reference letter still wasn't in.
What will Ishita do differently next time, and why?
Ishita will ask how long it took Asif and believe the answer, planning from real experience rather than a best-case guess.
How might Asif feel reading this letter?
Asif might feel relieved Ishita made it and glad the advice will be taken next time.
Put together a to-do list for tomorrow with exactly four items, each starting with a capital letter and with no punctuation at all.

Wash the car
Call Aunt Rekha
Buy notebooks
Tidy the desk
Moon goes around Earth once a month. Does it need articles?

The Moon goes around the Earth once a month.
Why: "The Moon" and "the Earth" need "the".

Read this:

Irawati's diary. Bengaluru. Late.

Papa fell in the bathroom in Indore this morning. He's fine, only a bruise, but I heard it from Kamal-uncle next door, not from Papa. Papa said on the phone, "Why worry you for nothing?"

I sat at my desk after the call and cried. I'm six hundred kilometres away building a career while my parents get older without me. Should I quit and go home? I love this job. I love them more. It feels like choosing.

But crying at my desk isn't helping them.

So tonight I made a list. Video call every evening at eight, not just Sundays. Book a trip home for Diwali now, not "sometime." Ask Kamal-uncle if he'd check on them each morning, and pay a local helper to come in daily. Tell Papa honestly that I'd rather know about small falls than find out later.

Love can travel, I think. It just needs a timetable.

Who told Irawati about Papa's fall?
Kamal-uncle next door.
What was Irawati feeling after the call with Papa?
Irawati felt guilty and torn between loving the job and loving the parents more, crying at the desk.
What did Irawati decide to do, and why is it wise?
Irawati planned daily calls, booked a Diwali trip, arranged a morning check and a helper, and asked Papa for honesty, turning guilt into action.
How might Papa see Irawati's request to hear about small falls?
Papa may have hidden it to protect Irawati from worry, so the request could feel both loving and a little uncomfortable.
Write a short note to a friend about our day out. It must end with the words "See you soon."
I enjoyed the day with you so much. See you soon.

Read this:

Kalyani, listen to your Uday uncle's story before you go off to that job in the city. When I was twenty-one, I rode my cycle to the night shift at the sugar factory. One night a constable stopped me at the crossing. He said my cycle had no light, and it didn't, that part was true. Then he said, "Two hundred rupees, or I take you to the station and you'll lose your job."

My legs shook. Two hundred was half my week. I nearly paid.

But I remembered my father's words: never pay or sign in a panic. I said, "Sir, I'll come to the station. Please let me call my father first." I read his name badge aloud, slowly, so he knew I'd seen it.

He looked at me for a long moment. Then he said, "Get a light by tomorrow," and walked off. I bought the light. And I wrote his name in my diary.

What was missing from young Uday's cycle?
His cycle had no light.
How did young Uday feel when the constable demanded money?
Young Uday felt frightened, with shaking legs, and nearly paid out of panic.
What choice in the story changed the outcome?
Uday refused to pay in a panic, asked to call his father, and read the constable's name aloud, so the constable backed off.
How might the constable have seen Uday after he read the name badge?
The constable probably realised Uday was not easy to pressure and might report him, so he let him go.

Read this:

In the government school at Nandgaon, Madam asked Tanuja to read the Hindi lesson aloud. Tanuja stood up, and the words on the page seemed to jump. "The farmer... the far... the fra..." Someone giggled. Tanuja crossed her eyes, puffed out her cheeks and said in a deep voice, "The farmer has lost his reading glasses!" The whole class burst out laughing, and so did she. Madam smiled but didn't move on to the next reader.
After the bell, Madam called her over. "You made them laugh very well. Was the reading hard today?" Tanuja shrugged and pulled another face. Her friend Zeenat, waiting by the door, noticed Tanuja's fingers twisting the end of her plait.

What did Tanuja say in a deep voice?
"The farmer has lost his reading glasses!"
Why did Tanuja pull a funny face instead of trying the word again?
She was embarrassed as the words jumped and someone giggled; the joke let her take charge so the class laughed with her, not at her.
What choice did Madam make after the bell, and why is it wise?
She praised the joke but gently asked if the reading was hard, which looks past the clowning to the worry underneath.
What might Zeenat have understood from Tanuja's twisting fingers?
Zeenat may have sensed that Tanuja was more worried than her funny faces showed.

Read this:

Teacher note, Class UKG. Written by Deepika.
A new boy joined us this week. He speaks Malayalam at home and very little Hindi. At lunch one child laughed at his words. Nirmala (5) frowned and said, "He's not wrong, it's a different language." Then she asked him how to say "water" and repeated "vellam" carefully. They shared her tiffin.
Next: we'll learn a greeting in each child's home language during circle time. 😊

What word did Nirmala learn from the new boy?
She asked him how to say "water" and repeated "vellam."
What might Nirmala have been feeling when she frowned at the laughter?
She probably felt annoyed and protective, since she frowned and told the child the new boy was not wrong.
What is Deepika's plan to support kindness about languages?
She plans to have the class learn a greeting in each child's home language.
How might the new boy feel after Nirmala's reaction?
He likely feels relieved and included when she stands up for him and shares her tiffin.

Read this:

Monday. Zeenat opened the plan for the app update and deleted the cushions from each task. "Honest numbers only," she told the team. At the bottom she added one bar labelled Buffer, six days, just before the client date. Tarun frowned. "What if my task runs over?" "Then tell me, and we look together," said Zeenat.

Thursday, week three. Tarun's login task took two days longer than planned because the test server crashed. He said so at stand-up. The team took two days from the buffer, and every other task kept its date.

Friday, week five. The update went out with four days of buffer left. Zeenat wrote in the notes: buffer used once, for a real delay.

How many days of buffer were left when the update went out?
Four days of buffer were left when the update went out.
What was Tarun feeling on Monday when he asked what if his task runs over?
Tarun felt uneasy about being caught short or blamed for an overrun, now that the padding was gone.
What could the team do if the buffer were used up early?
They could talk to the client about scope or dates as soon as possible and drop the least important item, instead of hiding the delay.
How might the client see the update going out with buffer left?
The client might see the team as reliable, having received the update before the agreed date.

metadata.subtype: Approach: keeps one shared buffer at the end of the project [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Class 5 teacher's note, after the "My Holiday" talks
Chaitanya described the family trip to the salt desert in detail: flamingos, a camel that sat on the car, getting lost at night. Chaitanya's older brothers were in my class in earlier years and gave nearly the same talk, camel included.
When I asked, Chaitanya said firmly, "I remember it, sir. I was there." I believe Chaitanya means it; there was no sign of making things up. Chaitanya's mother later told me the camel story is the eldest brother's favourite, told at every family dinner.
I didn't mark it wrong. Next week, the class will draw one thing they remember from a trip and then check it with a photo or a family member, just to see what changes.
Lalit

What did Chaitanya say about the camel when asked?
Chaitanya said firmly, "I remember it, sir. I was there."
Why is Chaitanya so sure the camel sat on the car?
Chaitanya feels confident and sincere, because the camel story told at every family dinner has become part of Chaitanya's own memory and feels completely real.
What activity did Lalit plan, and why is it a kind approach?
The class will draw a trip memory and check it against a photo or a family member, which shows memories change without accusing anyone of lying.
How might Chaitanya's older brothers react to hearing their camel story from Chaitanya?
They might laugh or feel proud that their story is so memorable, or insist Chaitanya was too small to remember it.

Read this:

Keerthana, you think your school friends will vanish now that you're all in different cities? Let me tell you about Latha and me.
We met at college in Madurai when we were eighteen. Then I married and moved to Delhi, and she went to the Gulf with her husband. No phones then, only letters and expensive trunk calls.
For the first year I wrote every month, and she didn't reply for four months. I was so hurt I nearly stopped. Then her letter came: her baby had been ill. She had read mine every night. I decided then: I would keep writing, even if replies were slow.
Thirty-two years, Keerthana. Letters, then emails, then video calls. She came to your mother's wedding.
So write to your friends even when they're slow. That's what your Sarita Athai learned.

Where did Latha move with her husband?
Latha went to the Gulf with her husband.
How did young Sarita feel when Latha didn't reply for four months?
Young Sarita felt hurt and nearly gave up writing.
What was the turning point in the friendship, and why did it matter?
Latha's letter explaining her baby's illness showed that silence wasn't rejection, so Sarita chose to keep writing even when replies were slow.
How might Latha have felt reading Sarita's letters during her baby's illness?
Latha probably felt comforted and less alone, reading them every night even though she couldn't reply.

Read this:

At the hospital where they both worked, Yamini sometimes saw Baljeet step into the empty staff room to take long calls, speaking softly in Punjabi.
"Your husband has a lot of private calls," a nurse from the next ward said one lunchtime, with a meaningful smile.
Yamini felt the sting of it. She could ask him who it was. She could look at the call list at home.
But she and Baljeet had made an agreement when they married: each keeps their own friendships and thoughts, and anything that changes their life together gets said. He had told her about the transfer offer the day it came. He had told her when his brother borrowed money.
That evening, he mentioned it himself. "Those calls are with my old school friend. He's going through a bad time. I can't share his story, but I wanted you to know."
Yamini smiled. "Thank you. That's all I need."

Where did Baljeet go to take long calls?
He stepped into the empty staff room.
How did Yamini feel when the nurse made her comment?
Yamini felt stung and briefly suspicious, tempted to ask or look at the call list, before remembering their agreement.
What agreement helped Yamini respect Baljeet's boundaries?
They agreed that each keeps their own friendships and thoughts, while anything that changes their life together gets said.
How does Baljeet see his friend's calls?
Baljeet sees them as his friend's private story to protect, while still wanting Yamini to know nothing is being hidden from her.

Read this:

Omkar: presentation done!! I think it went ok? 🙂
Elizabeth: it was good info
Omkar: but?
Elizabeth: honest answer?
Omkar: yes
Elizabeth: you read every slide. like word for word. and you never looked at us
Omkar: I was so nervous. if I look at the slide I don't forget anything
Elizabeth: I get that. but half the class was on their phones by slide 4
Elizabeth: we could read it ourselves, it was right there
Omkar: 😔
Omkar: I thought it looked professional
Elizabeth: the part where you told the story about your grandad's farm was the best bit. you weren't reading then
Omkar: that was the only slide I forgot to write
Elizabeth: exactly 😅
Omkar: ok. next time fewer words on slides and I talk?
Elizabeth: yes. practise with me on Saturday if you want
Omkar: deal

By which slide was half the class on their phones?
Half the class was on their phones by slide 4.
Why did Omkar read every slide word for word?
Omkar was nervous and felt safe reading, afraid of forgetting anything without the slide in view.
What could Omkar try next time?
Omkar could put fewer words on the slides and talk to the class, practising first with Elizabeth on Saturday.
How did the presentation feel from Elizabeth's side?
Elizabeth found most of it dull because the class could read the slides themselves, but Elizabeth enjoyed the farm story when Omkar stopped reading.
Write Mira's diary entry for today, 40 words: she baked her first cake in the afternoon, it sank in the middle, and she laughed and ate it anyway with her mother.

Dear Diary,
This afternoon I baked my first cake. It sank in the middle, but I laughed and ate it anyway with my mother. It was not perfect, but I enjoyed every bite, and I want to bake again.
Mira

Read this:

Coach's note, hockey trials. Parveen, school coach.
Today I announced the state squad. Jasleen missed out by one place; her best friend Harleen made it. I was worried about how Jasleen would take it. She ran across the field and lifted Harleen off her feet, shouting.
Later, packing the sticks, she was very quiet, and I saw her wipe her eyes behind the storeroom. When I sat with her, she said, "I'm really happy for her. I'm also really sad. Is that weird?" I told her it wasn't weird at all; both feelings can be true together.
Next step: I've asked her to train with the squad as a reserve, and I'll talk with her again after the first week.

By how many places did Jasleen miss out?
By one place.
What was Jasleen feeling behind the storeroom?
She felt sad and disappointed, though she was truly happy for Harleen.
What did the coach do that helped?
Sat with Jasleen, said both feelings can be true, and offered a reserve place with a check-in after a week.
How might Harleen feel when Jasleen lifts her off her feet?
Harleen would likely feel joyful and loved, sharing the moment with her best friend.

metadata.subtype: Happy for the friend chosen instead of self [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Pallavi,
You asked how I stopped panicking about everything, so here is my boring secret. On the first Sunday of every month, at ten, I make coffee and sit at the table with three things: my bank app, my little health notebook, and my work targets sheet. One hour. No other plans.
I used to open the bank app only when I felt rich, and I pushed the dentist visit off for a year. Then everything came as a big, late shock.
Now I look when nothing is wrong. Last month my spending on taxis had crept up, and my blood test reminder was due. Two small things, caught early. Neither ruined my day.
Would you like to join me next month on a video call? You bring your sheets, I'll bring mine. It's calmer with company.
Love,
Himani

When does Himani sit down to look at the numbers?
On the first Sunday of every month, at ten.
Why does Himani feel calmer now than before?
Looking when nothing is wrong means problems show up small and early, like the taxi spending, instead of as big, late shocks that used to cause panic.
What does Himani's approach do that the old habits did not?
It sets a regular time for money, health and work, so checking isn't left to mood; adding a calm friend on a call makes it easier to keep up.
How might Pallavi feel about the invitation?
Pallavi might feel relieved and supported 🙂, since the scary task becomes a shared, ordinary hour instead of something faced alone.
Why do babies cry? How old is my pet? Is this sentence right? She is afraid to dogs.

1. A baby cannot speak yet. Because crying is the way a baby tells us it needs something.
2. I don't know, because I can't see your pet. Check with the person who gave it to you.
3. Fixed: She is afraid of dogs. Why: We say "afraid of".
Describe your favourite season in two sentences. Use the word "because" exactly once.
My favourite season is the monsoon because the air smells fresh. Everyone slows down to listen to the rain.

Read this:

Toddler room note, Monday. Baljeet, almost two, clapped his hands the moment we began the morning song, first watching me, then laughing when the other children joined. Later, when Meher finished her puzzle, Baljeet clapped for her, even though he had not done it himself. He looked at me to see whether I was clapping too. I was. We ended up with a room full of clapping toddlers. 🙂 Lokesh

What did Baljeet clap for after the morning song?
He clapped for Meher when she finished her puzzle.
What might Baljeet be feeling as he claps, and how can you tell?
He seems happy and part of the group, shown by his laughing and his look to Lokesh to check that Lokesh was clapping too. He might partly be copying the others.
How could Lokesh keep this happy routine going?
Lokesh could make clapping a regular part of songs and successes so that children share joy together.
What might Meher feel when Baljeet claps for her?
She may feel proud and noticed, because a friend shared her success.
Why should we pull a plug out by the plug itself and not by tugging the wire?
Pulling by the plug is safer. Because tugging the wire strains the thin wires inside and can loosen or break them, the cable can get damaged and later cause sparks or a shock.

Read this:

Thursday night
Told Rekha today that I'm not doing the Pune MBA after all. Six months ago I told everyone I would, and I'd even paid the form fee. But back then I didn't know Papa would need me here, or that my team would offer me the analytics role. I said it plainly: "I decided with less information than I have now. The new information points the other way." She just said, "Makes sense." I had imagined a big scene. Then I did something on purpose: I told her I'll do the online statistics course and send her my weekly quiz scores every Sunday. A promise I want to be held to. Old promise released, new one chosen.
Simran

What will Simran send Rekha every Sunday?
The weekly quiz scores from the online statistics course.
How did Simran feel about telling Rekha, and what happened?
Simran had imagined a big scene and seemed nervous, but Rekha just said "Makes sense", which probably brought relief. 😌
Which two choices did Simran make well?
Explaining the change plainly as a decision made with less information, and then deliberately making a new public commitment to the statistics course to build a good habit.
How might Rekha see Simran's change of plan?
Rekha seems to find it reasonable, since Simran explained what had changed; to Rekha it looks like good sense, not failure.
Why do we use oven gloves to lift a hot dish?
The thick cloth keeps heat off the skin. Because thick cloth carries heat poorly, the heat of the dish does not reach the skin quickly enough to burn.

Read this:

Monday: Bhavna was in the bathroom when her little brother barged in looking for his toy boat. “GET OUT!” she screamed. He cried. Rekha came running. Tuesday: At bedtime Bhavna said, quietly this time, “Amma, I need the bathroom to be private. Can there be a knocking rule?” Rekha nodded. “That's fair. You're growing up. Everyone knocks, even me. But don't slide the top bolt, so if you ever slip, I can get in.” Thursday: A tiny knock came at the bathroom door. “Didi? Is my boat in there?” Bhavna laughed. “Wait two minutes!” She handed it out, dripping, through the gap.

What was Bhavna's brother looking for?
He was looking for his toy boat.
What was Bhavna feeling when she screamed “GET OUT”?
Bhavna felt shocked and embarrassed at her privacy being broken.
How did Rekha honour Bhavna's request and keep a safety limit?
She made a knocking rule for everyone but asked Bhavna not to slide the top bolt, so Rekha could get in if she ever slipped.
What was Thursday like for Bhavna's little brother?
He remembered to knock and got his boat back without any shouting.
Give me a gender-neutral version: Every student must bring his own lunch.
All students must bring their own lunch.

Read this:

"Sumit, can you tidy the blocks after you play?"
"Yes, Papa! I promise!"
"And Abhinav, you'll help your brother?"
"I promise too!"
Later, blocks everywhere. Sumit lay on the sofa.
"Sumit, you promised."
"I'm tired, Papa."
"But you said you would."
"That was before. I wasn't tired before." Sumit's eyes filled with tears.
Abhinav picked up two blocks. "I promised too."
Papa knelt down. "When you promise, it's also for later-you. Tired Sumit has to do what happy Sumit said."
Sumit sniffed. "Can tired Sumit do only the red ones?"
Papa smiled. "Tired Sumit can start with the red ones."

What did Sumit promise to do after playing?
He promised to tidy the blocks.
Why did Sumit's eyes fill with tears?
Sumit felt tired and sad, and confused that the promise he meant earlier now felt too hard.
How did Papa help Sumit understand promises?
Papa explained kindly that a promise is also for "later-you" and let him start small with the red ones.
What is it like for Abhinav when Sumit won't tidy?
Abhinav wants to keep that promise too and feels a little proud picking up blocks, even when Sumit lies on the sofa.

Read this:

"So you'll recommend me?" Jeevan asked, leaning into the manager's cabin.

"The team lead post is between you and Uday," said Mr Kulkarni. "Uday's strong."

Jeevan felt the old fear rise: another year stuck while Uday moved up. Uday, who'd covered for him during his father's surgery. Uday, who'd told him, over beer last month, that he thought Kulkarni's targets were unrealistic.

"Sir," Jeevan heard himself say, "I just think the lead should believe in the targets. Uday's said privately he thinks they're... unrealistic."

Kulkarni's eyebrows went up. "Did he."

That evening, Jeevan's flatmate asked why he was so quiet.

"Just work."

"Did something happen?"

"Nothing. It's business. Everyone looks out for themselves." He turned the TV up. He didn't want to hear the word his mind kept offering him.

What had Uday said privately about the targets?
Uday had said he thought Kulkarni's targets were unrealistic.
What was Jeevan afraid of when he spoke to Mr Kulkarni?
He was afraid of being left behind, stuck another year while Uday moved up, and that fear overrode his loyalty.
What turning point is still available to Jeevan?
He could go back to Kulkarni and correct himself, and tell Uday honestly what he did, rather than calling it business.
How might Uday feel if he learns what Jeevan said?
Uday would likely feel shocked and betrayed, since he had supported Jeevan and shared the complaint in trust.

Read this:

"Say 'water' again, Noor. Wah-tar!" Jiten's voice carried down the corridor, and two boys laughed.
Noor's ears burned. "My name is Noor, and it's not funny."
"Relax, it's a joke."
Thomas looked up from the steps, where he was eating his lunch. "It didn't sound like one."
Later, by the water tank, Noor said quietly, "Part of me wants to talk flat, like everyone else."
"Why would you? I like how you say things," said Thomas. "If he keeps doing it, tell Mrs. Bhatt. And sit with us tomorrow, we keep the corner bench." 🙂
Noor nodded slowly. "Okay. If it happens again, I'll tell her on Monday."

Which word did Jiten ask Noor to say again?
He asked Noor to say 'water' again, mocking the way Noor pronounces it.
What was Noor feeling by the water tank, and how can you tell?
Noor felt hurt and self-conscious: the burning ears and the wish to talk flat, like everyone else, show the teasing stung.
What could Noor do if the teasing keeps going?
Noor could tell Mrs. Bhatt, as planned, and keep sitting on the corner bench with people who like how Noor talks. There is no need to change the accent.
How might Thomas have seen the moment in the corridor?
Thomas thought the remark did not sound like a joke and saw that Noor was hurt, so Thomas offered a seat on the bench and some backup. 🙂

Read this:

Trisha, you asked me for a story where a plan didn't work out the way I expected. Here's one.
Last year I had a junior, Sunil, struggling on backend work. I'm Pankaj, I lead the platform team, and I did everything by the book: a six-week plan, goals, weekly check-ins.
At the six-week review, the backend goals were patchy. One done, two half done. But I noticed something in my notes. Every week, the thing he did best was testing. He'd found bugs nobody else caught. He wrote test cases like he enjoyed it.
So I asked myself, am I trying to fix the wrong thing? I spoke to my manager, and she agreed to try him in the QA team.
Three months later he's the one people ask when a release looks risky. That plan failing was the best thing that happened.

How many of the backend goals were fully done at the six-week review?
One done, two half done.
How might Sunil have felt doing testing work, according to Pankaj?
Pankaj says Sunil wrote test cases like he enjoyed them, which suggests Sunil felt more engaged and confident in testing than in backend work.
What was the key signal Pankaj noticed, and what did it change?
Pankaj noticed from the notes that testing was Sunil's strongest work every week, which changed the plan from fixing backend skills to moving him to a quality role.
How did the move look to Pankaj's manager?
The manager agreed to try it, likely seeing a sensible way to keep a capable person in a role that matched his strengths.

metadata.subtype: Approach: adjusting the plan when the fit is wrong [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

Lars had decided in the first week of term that Daniel was fake. Now, on the tram home through the grey Oslo drizzle, he scrolled back through the class group chat, hunting. Daniel had written "great goal, man" to the new boy: obviously sucking up. Daniel had put a heart under the teacher's post: trying too hard. Lars screenshotted both. He thumbed past Daniel's message from Tuesday offering everyone his notes for the chemistry test, and past the one wishing Lars luck at his handball match. Those didn't count; anyone could type nice words. His feed kept suggesting a video called "Signs someone is two-faced." He watched it twice, nodding along.

What did Daniel offer everyone in his Tuesday message?
Daniel offered everyone his notes for the chemistry test.
Why does it feel reasonable to Lars to screenshot some messages and skip others?

Lars already believes Daniel is fake, so he feels suspicious of every friendly message and quietly satisfied by any sign of effort he can call proof. Because he is so certain, collecting only those screenshots feels like fair evidence to him.
What could Lars do to test his view more fairly?

He could read the whole chat and sort every message from Daniel, including the notes offer and the good-luck wish, before judging. He could also ask what Daniel would have to do for Lars to see him as genuine.
How might Daniel feel if he knew his kind messages were being read as fake?
Daniel would probably feel hurt and confused, since even his offers of help were being turned into evidence against him.

The application closed at midnight, the hostel wifi kept dropping, and Bhupen had just asked Uma, a senior now working at an analytics firm, to look at his portfolio over a crackly call.
'Your descriptions are all tools,' Uma said. 'Python, SQL, charts, cloud. I read three and I still don't know what any of it did.'
Bhupen scrolled. She was right. The canteen project said: 'Built using Python and SQL with interactive charts.'
'Then what do I write?'
'What was wrong before, what you made, what got better.'
The call dropped. Bhupen didn't wait for it to come back. By 10:30 the canteen project read: 'Lunch queues ran twenty minutes. I built a pre-order sheet for the canteen. Average wait fell to eight minutes over one month.' By 11:40 the other two were rewritten the same way. He submitted at 11:52, on his phone's hotspot.

What did the canteen project description say before the rewrite?
'Built using Python and SQL with interactive charts.'
What was Bhupen likely feeling when he scrolled and saw Uma was right?
He likely felt a sting of embarrassment, then determination, since the deadline left no time to argue.
What else could Bhupen do before the next application?
Send the rewritten descriptions to Uma or another senior to check the results are clear, instead of rushing at night again.
How does the old portfolio look to Uma?
To Uma it is a list of tools that says nothing about what the work achieved, which is exactly what a recruiter would miss.

On the Delhi metro last month, I got a seat at Rajiv Chowk after a long day. I'm Rehana, and my feet ached. At the next station, an elderly man got on with a walking stick. Lalit Uncle, I found out later.
Nobody moved. People looked at their phones. He held the pole with both hands, swaying.
I stood up and said, "Uncle, please sit." He smiled and sat. That was it.
But then something happened. At the next station, a young man got up for a pregnant woman. Two stops later, a college girl gave her seat to a man with a crutch. It spread down the coach like a wave.
Lalit Uncle said, "In my day we did this without thinking. Nice to see it."
I stood the rest of the way. My feet still ached. But I felt lighter.

Where did Rehana get a seat?
She got a seat at Rajiv Chowk.
How did Rehana feel standing the rest of the way?
Rehana's feet still ached, but Rehana felt lighter and happy after offering the seat.
What happened after Rehana gave up the seat?
Others copied her: a young man got up for a pregnant woman and a college girl gave her seat to a man with a crutch, showing kindness spreads.
How might Lalit Uncle have felt when he sat down?
Lalit Uncle probably felt relieved and pleased, glad to see young people offer seats.

Our lane's little Pallavi, about two, sits on her doorstep every evening waiting. I watch from my window. When her father Uday rounds the corner on his bicycle, she beams, kicks both feet and calls “Papa!” She does it the same way for her grandfather and, I noticed, for the milk-delivery man once, who happened to wave. I can't tell exactly what she thinks. To me it looks like plain gladness at a friendly, familiar face, nothing sly about it.

Where does Pallavi sit each evening?
On her doorstep, waiting for her father to come around the corner.
What does the narrator think Pallavi's beam means, and what is left uncertain?
The narrator thinks it is plain gladness at a friendly, familiar face, seen in the kicking feet and the call of “Papa”. She admits she cannot know exactly what Pallavi is thinking.
What could Uday do when he sees the smile?
He could get off the bicycle, smile back and greet her by name so the happy moment is shared. 😊
What might the milk-delivery man feel when Pallavi beams at him?
He may feel pleasantly surprised and welcomed, since a toddler's smile is easy to take as a small greeting even from a passer-by.

In the small college town of Dharwad, Ganga and Pranav shared a rented room above a tailoring shop. On Wednesday evening, Pranav came in and saw the lights still on and the fan running. "You always leave everything on. You never think about anyone else." Ganga felt her face go hot. Always? Never? She'd switched everything off on Monday and Tuesday. "That's not true," she snapped. "I switched off yesterday. And the day before." "You know what I mean." "No, I don't. You said never." They went back and forth about the words for ten minutes. Then Ganga stopped. "Okay. We're fighting about always and never. What's actually the problem?" Pranav sighed. "The electricity bill came. It's high. I'm worried." "Ah," said Ganga. "Then let's look at it together."

What did Pranav find still running?
The lights and the fan.
Why did Ganga's face go hot when Pranav said "always" and "never"?
Ganga felt unfairly accused and defensive, because those words erased the days she had switched everything off.
What helped Ganga and Pranav move past arguing?
Ganga noticed they were fighting over the words and asked what the real problem was, which revealed the worry about the bill.
What might Pranav have been feeling behind the harsh words?
Pranav seems to have felt worried about the high electricity bill, and it came out as blame.

It's been a month, and I still remember the heat in my ears. Our sociology group had to run a survey. We got eighty-seven responses. Jatin wanted to write "over two hundred" on the slide. "Nobody checks," he said, and the other three laughed and agreed. I said, "I'm not presenting a number we made up." Four people looked at me like I'd switched off the wifi. For two days the group chat went silent whenever I posted. I lay awake thinking maybe I was being a goody-goody, maybe everyone rounds up. Then the professor asked every group to upload raw data. Jatin messaged me: "ok fine, 87." No thanks, no sorry. Being right didn't feel like winning. It felt like paying a small bill, one I'd pay again.
Amandeep

How many survey responses did the group actually get?
They got eighty-seven responses.
What was Amandeep worried about while lying awake after the meeting?
Amandeep wondered about being a goody-goody, thinking that maybe everyone rounds up numbers.
Looking back, which moment was the real choice, and what did it cost?
Saying "I'm not presenting a number we made up" to four laughing teammates was the choice; it cost two days of a silent group chat.
How might Jatin feel typing "ok fine, 87"?
Jatin may feel embarrassed at being caught by the raw-data rule, which could explain why there is no thanks or sorry.
What is a "torch" in British English?

In British English, a "torch" is a small hand-held light that runs on batteries. Americans call it a "flashlight". In American English, "torch" refers to a burning stick or a blowtorch.
Example: Take a torch because the power cuts are frequent.

On the balcony of their rented flat in Pune, Rekha set down two glasses of cutting chai and a sheet of paper. "Before we say forever, let's be boring and honest," she said. Shreya laughed, but she took the pen. They had been together two years. Shreya had seen Rekha snap at everyone during her father's surgery, then go back and apologise to each nurse by name. Rekha had seen Shreya lose her job and spend a week in pyjamas before sending out forty applications. They had also danced badly at three weddings. On the paper they wrote: Rekha wants to study abroad in two years. Shreya wants to stay near her mother. How we share rent. Who calls whom first after a fight. They circled the abroad question twice and agreed to decide it together by spring. Then Shreya put the pen down. "I'm choosing you, knowing all of this." Rekha squeezed her hand. "Same. Eyes open."

How long had Shreya and Rekha been together?
They had been together two years.
What does Rekha's suggestion to be 'boring and honest' suggest she wants?
She wants their promise to rest on clear, shared facts rather than on the joy of the moment, and she seems calm and secure enough to face hard topics.
What makes this a strong moment to commit rather than an impulsive one?
They have already seen each other at their worst, during the surgery and the job loss, and they name real goals, even the clash over studying abroad, before deciding.
What would change if Shreya had said 'forever' without talking about Rekha's plan to study abroad?
The clash with Shreya's wish to stay near her mother would likely surface later as a painful surprise, instead of being something they agreed to work on together.
