In the Kothrud flat, the argument had been circling since breakfast. Pradeep's mother wanted the puja for the new flat on Saturday, when the priest was free. Swati had already promised that Saturday to her parents, who were coming from Nagpur. Pradeep's father kept repeating, "The priest decides, not us." Pradeep scrolled his phone. For two days he had said nothing, and both women had noticed. Swati slept facing the wall. His mother told him he had "changed after marriage". On Thursday evening he put the phone face down on the dining table. "Aai, Swati's parents booked their tickets first. Swati, Aai has waited years for this puja. Can we ask the priest about Sunday morning? I'll call him myself." His mother sighed, then nodded slowly. Under the table, Swati squeezed his hand.

In the Kothrud flat, Pradeep's mother wants the puja for the new flat on Saturday, but Swati has promised that day to her parents. After two silent days, Pradeep says Swati's parents booked first and his mother has waited years, and suggests asking the priest about Sunday morning. His mother nods slowly, and under the table Swati squeezes his hand.
Write a paragraph on the importance of teamwork, 35 words: tasks get done faster, ideas are shared, people support one another, and the work feels lighter. Say the team feels strong.

Teamwork is important because tasks get done faster when many people help. Ideas are shared, and people support one another. When we work together as a team, the work feels lighter, and the team feels strong.

On Pola day in their village near Wardha, the decorated bullocks came down the lane with bells and a drum. Tanuja, eighteen months, sat on the step with her Aaji, Kalyani. The drum boomed. Tanuja jerked, her face crumpled, and she buried it in Aaji's sari, clutching hard. Aaji held her close and hummed. "Big noise. Aaji is here." After a while Tanuja peeked out at a painted horn, then hid again.

What came down the lane on Pola day?
The decorated bullocks, with bells and a drum.
What was Tanuja feeling when she buried her face in Aaji's sari?
Tanuja felt frightened by the sudden boom of the drum.
How did Aaji help Tanuja cope with the fear?
She held her close, hummed, and named the noise calmly, letting Tanuja peek out when ready.
How might Kalyani feel as Tanuja peeks at the painted horn?
Kalyani probably feels tender and reassured, seeing Tanuja's curiosity start to return.

The email from HR reached Gurpreet at 4:10, and by 5:00 his desk was in a cardboard box. Six years of late launches, and the same director who thanked him at the anniversary dinner had signed the letter. He sat in the car park with his hands shaking, feeling lied to. Then he opened his laptop, and instead of the angry draft he wanted, he wrote to HR asking for the terms in writing and to his old manager asking for a reference.

Hansa, laid off in the same round, went home and said nothing. She kept leaving the house at nine in a work shirt and sitting in a cafe, sure that this said something rotten about her. On the fourth day she called her cousin and told her.

Gurpreet's parents took the news quietly at dinner, then his mother asked about the rent. He laid out his savings and his plan on paper. Darshan, his father, stayed silent, then pushed the roti toward him.

The next week, still furious about the party photos from the record quarter, Gurpreet sent HR three exact questions about notice, severance and his rights. He posted nothing online.

How many years had Gurpreet worked at the company?
He had worked there for six years.
How did Gurpreet's and Hansa's first reactions to the layoff differ, and what did each eventually do?

Gurpreet felt lied to and turned his anger into written terms, a reference and exact questions to HR. Hansa felt ashamed and hid the layoff in the cafe until she told her cousin on the fourth day. Both then took a step involving someone else.
What was Hansa feeling when she kept leaving the house in a work shirt?
She was ashamed, treating the layoff as a judgement on her worth and not wanting anyone to know.
What could Hansa do now to steady her days while she searches for work?
She could keep the trusted person close, build a simple daily routine and treat the job search as her new work, remembering the layoff came from a company round rather than her worth.

Thursday, late.
Forgot how to run the month-end reconciliation today. Sat at my desk with the spreadsheet open and my mind completely blank, even though I did it perfectly in March. Old me would have spiralled: "I'm losing it, I'm useless." Instead I opened my "How I did it" notes file, found the eight steps I'd written after last quarter, and was done in forty minutes. Alka from accounts peeked over and said, "You remember all that?" I laughed. "Nope. I remember where I wrote it." Brains aren't meant to hold every quarterly task; they drop what isn't used. I've set a reminder to skim the steps every six weeks so it's less of a shock. Honestly felt calm, which is new.
Dhruv

How many steps were in Dhruv's notes?
Eight steps.
How did Dhruv feel after finishing the reconciliation?
Dhruv felt calm, which is new; instead of spiralling into "I'm useless", Dhruv treated the blank as normal and trusted the notes.
What habit is Dhruv adding, and why is it sensible?
Skimming the steps every six weeks, so a rarely used task stays fresh and forgetting it is not a shock.
How might Alka see Dhruv's approach?
Alka seems impressed at first, assuming Dhruv remembered everything, and may learn that good notes matter more than a perfect memory.

Day one. Jahnavi, twenty, from Manipur, called about a flat near her new internship in Gurugram. The broker's voice changed when he heard her name. "Owner prefers north Indians. Family types," he said, and hung up.
Day three. She went to see another flat with her office friend Tarun. The owner asked Jahnavi, "Do you cook smelly food? Your people eat dogs?" Tarun stiffened. Jahnavi said calmly, "I'm here for the flat, sir." They left. On the stairs, her hands were trembling. Tarun said, "That's discrimination. Let's write it all down."
Day six. At her office's HR desk, Jahnavi and Tarun showed a notebook: dates, names, the broker's number, the exact questions. HR connected her with a legal-aid group and a list of owners who had signed a fair-housing pledge. Jahnavi moved into one of those flats the next week.

Where is Jahnavi's new internship?
Her new internship is in Gurugram.
What was Jahnavi feeling on the stairs?
She felt shaken and humiliated, her hands trembling after staying calm in front of the owner.
How did Jahnavi and Tarun respond wisely?
They named it as discrimination, wrote down dates, names and questions, and took the notes to HR, which connected her with legal aid and fair owners.
How might Tarun have felt watching the owner's questions?
Tarun stiffened, which suggests he felt angry and embarrassed on Jahnavi's behalf, and it pushed him to support her.

Subject: About the list Dear Varun, I have been thinking since Sunday's planning call, and I would rather write than argue on the phone. The list sent to the bride's family, with the car, the cash "for the function" and the jewellery, is dowry, even if nobody says the word. I know you didn't write it, and I know they mean well. I'm not angry with anyone. But I don't want Meera's parents to borrow for us, and I don't want your marriage to begin with a price. I spoke to Dadi, and she said quietly that she never liked the custom either. She is willing to talk to Chachaji this week. Will you say something too? One more voice will make it easier for everyone. With love, Disha

Who did Disha speak to about the list?
Disha spoke to Dadi, who said she never liked the custom either.
What is Disha feeling as she writes this email?
Disha feels concerned but calm. Disha says nobody is being blamed and chose to write rather than argue on the phone.
Which choice did Disha make that might help the change happen?
Disha wrote calmly at the planning stage, spoke to Dadi first to find an ally and asked Varun to add a voice too.
How might Varun feel on reading the email?
Probably caught between family and conscience. Disha writes that she knows Varun did not write the list, which lets Varun listen without feeling attacked.

'Just sign the calibration sheet,' Lokesh said, not looking up. 'We'll do the check tomorrow.'
Shalini held the pen. 'You said that last week.'
'And nothing happened, right? The machine's fine.'
'We signed it as done on the fourteenth. It wasn't.'
'Everyone signs it. The audit only looks for signatures.' He finally looked at her. 'You want the whole lab in trouble for one missed check?'
She signed. Her hand felt heavy.
The next Friday, Lokesh didn't even ask. He just left the sheet on her bench with a sticky note: 'Usual.'
Shalini stared at it. 'Usual,' she said aloud. Three weeks ago she'd never have signed. Now there was a 'usual'.
She peeled off the note and went to find the calibration kit.

What did Lokesh's sticky note say?
'Usual.'
What does Shalini's heavy hand when signing suggest?
She felt guilty and uneasy, knowing she was signing for a check that hadn't happened.
What did Shalini do at the end, and why does it matter?
She went to find the calibration kit and do the check, breaking the slide before it became normal.
How does Lokesh seem to see the skipped checks?
As harmless paperwork, telling himself the audit only looks for signatures and that it protects the lab.

Last Navratri I had a big dance competition, and I did all my lucky things. I wore my red vest under my kurta, the one from when I won the sack race. I tapped the door frame three times. I didn't step on any lines on the way to the pandal. My little sister Gargi asked, "Tarun bhaiya, will the vest make you dance better?" I said, "No," but I kept it on. It's funny. I knew it was just a vest. But when I touched it before going on stage, my heart slowed down a bit. We came second. I still have the vest. Next time I think I'll practise more and tap less.

What did Tarun wear under his kurta?
His red vest from when he won the sack race.
Why did Tarun keep the vest on after saying it wouldn't help?
It made him feel calmer; touching it slowed his heart a bit, even though he knew it was just a vest.
What is Tarun planning for next time, and why is it sensible?
Practise more and tap less, so the ritual stays a comfort and doesn't replace effort.
How might Gargi see her brother's rituals?
She is curious and maybe puzzled, asking honestly whether the vest helps him dance.

Saturday, 11 pm
Watched another video tonight: a guy who dropped out of college at nineteen and now owns a whole company. Three different toppers on the news said they only studied four hours a day. And that streamer everyone follows quit school in Class 11. So clearly school is optional if you're good.
I told Asif I might skip the coaching classes and just build my baking page instead. He said, "You only hear about the ones who made it." Classic Asif, always the wet blanket.
But... I tried to think of one person I actually know who left school and got famous. I couldn't. I only know them from videos.
Anyway. Sleeping on it.
Irawati

What did Irawati tell Asif about the coaching classes?
Irawati told Asif about maybe skipping the coaching classes to build a baking page instead.
Why does school seem optional to Irawati tonight?
Irawati feels hopeful and excited because every story on screen is someone who dropped out and succeeded, so the path looks easy and the many who failed never appear.
What could Irawati do before deciding about the coaching classes?
Irawati could look for people who tried the same path and didn't make it, and keep the classes while testing the baking page on the side.
How does Asif see the videos Irawati is watching?
Asif thinks they only show the ones who made it, so they give a false picture of how easy the path is.

In second year I thought I was generous. I'm Anand, and I'd send my lab reports to anyone who asked. Bhupen asked the most. He never sent anything back, but I told myself that was fine.
Then the final list for the research project came out. Bhupen was selected. I wasn't. His report used my graphs, almost line for line.
I felt so foolish that I couldn't eat that evening. For months after that I stopped helping anyone. When my lab partner asked for my readings, I said I'd lost them. She stopped asking.
Looking back, I punished the wrong people. Bhupen never noticed. My partner did.

What did Bhupen's report use?
His report used Anand's graphs, almost line for line.
What did Anand feel when the final list came out?
Anand felt foolish and angry, so much that eating that evening was impossible.
What could Anand have done instead of refusing everyone?
Anand could have stopped sharing with Bhupen while still trading notes with partners who gave back.
How does Anand's lab partner seem to have been affected?
She stopped asking, likely feeling shut out and puzzled, since she had done nothing wrong.

Last week our teacher asked me what a noun is, and I said, “Hmm… uh… a noun is… um…” Some kids giggled. My hands went cold. I thought they believed I didn't know. But I did know, I just needed a moment to pick the right words. Miss waited, and I said, “A noun is the name of a person, place or thing.” She smiled and nodded. Later I told Aparna I say hmm when my brain is looking through its drawers. She said hers does too. Now I don't mind so much when the sounds slip out. I'm Rukmini and I like thinking time.

What did the teacher ask Rukmini?
What a noun is.
How did Rukmini feel when some kids giggled at the hmm and um?
Rukmini felt nervous, with cold hands and the worry that the class thought the answer was unknown. In fact Rukmini knew it and just needed a moment to pick the words.
What could a teacher do to help a child who uses these sounds?
She could wait a few seconds, like Miss did, so the child can finish the thought.
How might the giggling classmates have seen Rukmini's hmm and um?
They may have taken the sounds as not knowing, which is one way to read them, though the correct answer shows otherwise.

You asked what the new job's like. Okay, one story. Last month Joseph walked in twenty minutes late, and our manager, Sarika, said in front of everyone, "This is an attitude problem, Joseph." He just nodded and sat down. What got me was that the Monday before, Sarika herself had come in half an hour late, laughing, "The traffic at that flyover is impossible!" Nobody called that attitude. I sat on it for two days. Then, over lunch, I said, "Sarika, can I say something awkward? When you were late, it was the flyover. When Joseph was late, it was attitude." She went quiet. Then she said, "Mridul, that's fair." The next week she asked Joseph, privately, what his mornings were like. Turns out he drops his little sister at a school across town. They moved his start time by fifteen minutes.

What did Sarika say when Joseph was twenty minutes late?
"This is an attitude problem, Joseph."
What was Mridul feeling during the two days before speaking up?
Mridul felt uneasy and torn, bothered by the double standard but nervous about saying something awkward to the manager.
Why did Mridul's comment lead to fairer feedback?
It set Sarika's own excuse beside Joseph's case, so she noticed the double standard and got curious, asking Joseph privately about his mornings.
How might Joseph have felt being called out in front of everyone?
Joseph probably felt embarrassed and misjudged, since the lateness came from dropping his little sister across town, not from his attitude.

The storm had knocked out the office internet, so Vaibhav joined the sprint call from his phone, camera off to save data. When Aparna, two weeks into the team, said the release would slip a day, he drawled, "Oh, brilliant. My weekend was getting far too relaxing anyway." In person his tongue would have been in his cheek and everyone would have known. On the crackly line there was only silence. Then Aparna's small voice: "Sorry. I can try to finish tonight." Vaibhav winced. Without his face, the joke had landed as a complaint. He unmuted quickly. "No, no, that was me being dry. The slip is fine." Then he typed in the chat: "Joke, promise 😅 Thanks for flagging it early." Aparna replied with a 👍 and, after a moment, a 🙂.

Why did Vaibhav keep his camera off?
To save data, because the storm had knocked out the office internet and he joined from his phone.
What might Aparna have felt when she offered to finish tonight?
She likely felt anxious and guilty, hearing the dry line as a complaint about her delay; being new, she had no way of knowing his joking style.
What did Vaibhav do to repair the misread joke?
He unmuted to say he was being dry and typed a clear message with a 😅 and thanks, adding the signal his hidden face couldn't give.
What would have changed if Vaibhav's camera had been on?
Aparna might have seen his tongue-in-cheek face and read the joke correctly, though as a newcomer she might still have needed a smile to be sure.

Dear Kishore mama,
The Class Twelve results came out yesterday. I failed physics.
Everyone in our building knew I wanted engineering. Aunty from the second floor asked Amma, "So, which college?" and Amma just said, "Let's see." I heard it from my room. I felt like the whole building was looking at our door.
Last night I kept thinking my whole future was gone. That all my friends would move ahead and I'd be stuck. I told Amma I felt like that, and she sat with me till I slept. Today she took me to the school counsellor, who said I can take the compartment exam in July and still join college this year.
It still hurts. I'm writing because you once told me you failed your first year of college, and I never believed you. Was it true? Can I call you on Sunday?
Chinmay

Which subject did Chinmay fail?
I failed physics.
How did Chinmay feel when the neighbour asked Amma about college?
Chinmay felt ashamed and exposed, as if the whole building was looking at their door.
What steps have already helped Chinmay, and what is the next one?
Telling Amma, who sat with Chinmay that night, and seeing the school counsellor about the July exam; the next step is talking to Kishore mama on Sunday.
How might Kishore mama feel reading this letter?
Kishore mama would probably feel touched and protective, glad Chinmay reached out and ready to share his own story.

The Nagpur wedding hall was deafening, and the only way to follow the match was Vidya's phone, which kept losing signal. Her cousin Raghav, nine, pressed against her elbow. "He'll hit a fifty. He always does." The score froze, then jumped: his favourite all-rounder, out for four. Raghav didn't blink. "That ball was unplayable. Plus the umpire is from the other side." "The replay showed it was a normal ball," Vidya said, shouting over the band. "No, remember last month? Eighty-two against the same team." "And the two ducks before that?" Raghav frowned as if she'd spoken another language. "Those were bad luck." The dhol started again. Vidya gave up, but noticed he never mentioned the ducks when he told his uncles the story at dinner.

How many runs did Raghav's favourite all-rounder score before getting out?
He was out for four.
Why does Raghav blame the ball and the umpire instead of his hero?
To him the all-rounder is simply the best, so a low score must have an outside cause. Holding on to the eighty-two feels like proof, while the ducks feel like accidents.
Vidya gave up arguing over the band. What could she try at a quieter moment instead?

She could make a game of writing down every score for the next few matches, good and bad, and look at the list with Raghav. Seeing all the numbers together is harder to explain away than one argument.
What might the uncles at dinner believe after hearing Raghav's version?
They would only hear about the eighty-two and the unplayable ball, so they might think the all-rounder is doing better than he really is.

Dear Imran,

Thank you for the lovely lunch last Sunday. Your daughter and I have been talking about how to make our visits easier for everyone, because with our shifts we often arrive tired and hurried. Could we try something for two months? We would come on the first and third Sundays and stay properly, with our phones put away. At the end of the two months the three of us can sit down and say what worked and what did not, and change it if it isn't right. It is only an experiment, not a new rule, and you are very welcome to suggest changes now. We love these lunches and want to keep them good.

With warm regards,
Tushar 🙂

On which Sundays did Tushar suggest coming for lunch?
On the first and third Sundays.
What does Tushar hope Imran will feel about the proposal?
Tushar hopes Imran will feel reassured that this is not a rejection, since the letter calls it "only an experiment, not a new rule".
What could Tushar and Imran's daughter do if the trial turns out to be too few visits?
At the end of the two months they could add a lunch or a short evening visit, because a trial can be adjusted without anyone losing face.
How might Imran read the letter?
Imran may feel valued at being asked and invited to suggest changes, though there could be a little sadness about fewer lunches.

Three times.

Neelam had a shiny brochure from a consultancy and a lot of questions it did not answer. On a Sunday in her Mumbai flat, she wrote a short message and sent it to five professionals she found through an alumni group who lived in Toronto.
"I'm thinking of moving. Could you tell me what rent really costs, what tax takes, how long your job hunt took, and whether it gets lonely?"
By Wednesday four had replied. Rent was higher than the brochure said. One had needed five months to find a job. Abhinav wrote the longest note: the first winter was the hardest, and he had called home every night.
Neelam read them at the kitchen table, unsettled and grateful in equal measure, and made a fresh list of questions.

Neelam messaged five professionals.

Neelam was unsettled and grateful at once, learning things the brochure had left out.

Abhinav was probably remembering his hard first winter and wanted to be honest so that Neelam would be prepared.

In Sikar, the coaching institute for government exams had a big glass front and a banner of smiling toppers. Akash's father had sold a piece of farmland to pay the fee: one full year, paid in advance.

Four months in, classes were packed with two hundred students, the good teacher had left, and the new one read from the book. Akash's mock test scores had gone down.

His sister Jahnavi, home for Holi, looked through his notes. "Akash, you said last month that the doubt sessions were cancelled. And the teacher who you liked left. Why not try the free online lectures and the library instead?"

"No," Akash said sharply. "It's the best institute in Sikar. Everyone says so. The system just takes time."

"Your scores went down."

"That's me, not them. The institute is excellent."

He didn't say what he was thinking: Papa sold the land for this. It has to be worth it.

What did Akash's father sell to pay the fee?
A piece of farmland.
Why does Akash insist the institute is excellent, even as his scores go down?
His father sold land to pay for it, so admitting it's disappointing would feel like wasting that sacrifice. The more that was invested, the harder it is to doubt.
What could help Akash look at the choice more honestly without feeling he has failed Papa?
He could list what is and isn't working and talk with Jahnavi or Papa about adding the library and free lectures. Changing course to do better isn't wasting the land.
How might Jahnavi feel when Akash blames himself instead of the institute?
Jahnavi may feel worried and frustrated, since she can see the cancelled sessions and the teacher leaving. She wants to help, but his defensiveness makes it hard.

In the small meeting room of the city library, Charu opened the folder she had kept since January before Joseph's yearly review.
Joseph came in tense. The last month had been rough: he had mixed up two event dates, and a school group had turned up to a locked hall. He expected that to be the whole review.
"Let's go month by month," Charu said. She had a page for each. February: he set up the children's reading corner. April: he cleared the late-return backlog. July: three thank-you letters from readers. September: he helped train the new assistant. November: the date mix-up.
"I'd forgotten half of this," Joseph said.
"So had I, until I read my notes this morning," Charu admitted. "That's why I keep them."
They spent five minutes on November: what went wrong and what would help. The rest of the hour was about the other months.

What happened in November?
Joseph mixed up two event dates, and a school group turned up to a locked hall.
Why does Charu admit she had forgotten half of it too?
Charu feels honest and a little humble, knowing her own memory favours the latest month, which is why she trusts the notes.
How does Charu's folder make the review fairer?
A page for each month means the whole year counts, so one bad November doesn't outweigh the reading corner or July's letters.
What is the review like for Joseph?
Joseph goes from tense to relieved, seeing his whole year counted and not just the mix-up.

People always ask me, "Why are you so quiet? Are you okay?" And honestly, I'm fine. I'm Dilnaz, second-year botany, and this is just how I am.
At the orientation party I stood near the wall and didn't talk to many people. Someone told me I should "come out of my shell," and I was annoyed, to be honest. I don't live in a shell.
What I like is three or four people, a table, chai, a proper conversation. My friend Maria and I have been talking every Sunday since first year. She knows about my father's shop, my exams, the plant I killed. I know about her sisters. That's worth more to me than fifty people who know my name.
Strangers? I'll warm up, slowly. And if I don't, that's okay too. Quiet isn't the same as unhappy.

How often have Dilnaz and Maria been talking since first year?
Every Sunday.
How did Dilnaz feel when told to "come out of my shell"?
Dilnaz felt annoyed, because Dilnaz is fine and does not see being quiet as something wrong.
What would you advise someone who wants to help a quiet friend like Dilnaz?
Accept that being reserved isn't a problem, and invite them to small, calm meetups rather than pushing them to be more outgoing.
How might Maria see Dilnaz's quietness?
Maria knows Dilnaz deeply through their Sunday talks, so she likely sees the quiet as part of a loyal, thoughtful friend, not as a problem.

"Who keeps ringing at this hour?" Ritu's mother asked, looking at the buzzing phone.
"Zubin. Twelve messages today. He waited outside tuition again."
"You told him it was over?"
"Twice. He says I owe him another chance."
"Do you?"
Ritu looked down at her hands. "No. But I feel guilty, Mummy. Like I'm being cruel."
"Guilt isn't a debt, beta. You have said no. That is enough."
"What do I do?"
"One clear message, then we stop replying. And tomorrow your father and I will speak to your class teacher."
Ritu typed: "No. It's over. Please stop contacting me." She pressed send, then blocked the number. Her hands were shaking, but her mother held them until they stopped.

Where had Zubin waited for Ritu?
He had waited outside tuition.
Why does Ritu feel guilty, and what does her mother say about it?
Ritu feels she is being cruel by refusing Zubin. Her mother tells her guilt is not a debt and that she has already said no, which is enough.
What steps do Ritu and her mother take?
Ritu sends one clear final no and blocks the number, and her parents plan to speak to her class teacher the next day.
How might Zubin be seeing the situation?
He may feel hurt and refuse to accept the ending. He says she owes him another chance, but she owes him nothing. 🤍

For two days Marek and Santiago had been trading short, cold messages about a missed football practice. At 9 p.m., sitting on his bed in Warsaw with the heater ticking, Marek typed and deleted three angry replies. Then he wrote: 'Can I call you? I think we misunderstood each other.' The reply came fast: 'ok.' The phone rang. For a second neither spoke. Then Santiago said, 'So when you wrote "fine, whatever"...' and Marek groaned. 'I meant, like, oh well! Not I hate you!' 'It read like you hated me!' 'And you wrote "I have a life too"!' 'Because I thought you hated me!' There was a pause, then both burst out laughing. Five minutes in, two days of hurt felt ridiculous.

How many angry replies did Marek type and delete?
He typed and deleted three angry replies.
What does the burst of laughter show about how both felt once they heard each other?
It shows relief; hearing each other's voices made the hurt feel silly, as each realised the other had never meant to attack.
Why was Marek's message a good turning point?
Instead of another cold text, he suggested a call and named the likely misunderstanding, which invited Santiago in without blame.
What might Santiago have felt when the phone rang?
Probably nervous and a bit defensive at first, then relieved once Santiago could hear Marek's real tone 😊.

After Ms. Rao scolded the class, Leela pulled out her headphones and hummed under her breath at her desk. I'm Chetan and I sit next to her. Her face was tight at first, her fingers tapping. Slowly her jaw loosened. I couldn't tell what she was thinking. At the break I asked if she was okay, and she said, "I needed to reset. I was angry and didn't want to snap at anyone." Later that day I saw her talking to the counsellor in the corridor, so I guess the humming was step one. She looked calmer.

What did Leela pull out after the scolding?
She pulled out her headphones.
What was Leela probably feeling when she hummed with a tight face?
She was angry and trying not to snap at anyone. She said she needed to reset.
What could Leela do alongside humming?
Talk to a trusted person, like the counsellor, as she did later. Humming calms her, and talking helps more.
How does Chetan see Leela's humming?
Chetan isn't sure what she was thinking but later sees it as a first step, then sees her talk to the counsellor. Chetan notices her calmer face.

I thought they'd want to be my friends. Instead, when I sat down at lunch, Urmila said, "Oh no, not the planetarium again," and the others laughed. Then they talked about some song I don't know, and I just ate. On the way home I told Amma they're all boring. She asked, "Did you ask them anything about themselves, beti?" I didn't answer. I'm still annoyed. But also, my stomach feels heavy.

Urmila said, "Oh no, not the planetarium again."

I'm Afreen, and for a month I watched my older sister Zeenat collect opinions like stamps. She called Khala, who once left Lucknow to teach in a mountain village. She met a man from her old college who had done the same two-year teaching fellowship and quit after one. She even asked our neighbour, who has never left the colony, and actually listened. Every night she wrote in a green notebook. I couldn't tell if she was scared or excited; maybe both. The man's story seemed to shake her, because she went quiet for two days. Then on Sunday she showed Ammi a page with three lines: "I want to teach. I want to be nearer home by thirty. Two years fits." She signed the form that evening. Nobody had told her to.

Where did Khala once go to teach?
She once left Lucknow to teach in a mountain village.
What might Zeenat have been feeling after hearing from the man who quit?
She may have felt shaken and unsure, since she went quiet for two days after hearing his story.
What did Zeenat's way of deciding get right?
She asked people with different experiences, including someone who quit, then checked their views against her own three lines before deciding herself.
How might Ammi see the page Zeenat showed her?
Ammi may feel reassured that the choice was thought through and tied to being nearer home by thirty, even if two years away will be hard.

I'm Nazia, and I watched my little sister Shreya, five, at a birthday party. A man I had only just met tried to lift her up. "Stop, I don't want that," Shreya said, loud and clear, stepping back. He laughed it off and reached again. She ran across the room to our mother. "He won't stop." Mum went straight over, calm, took Shreya onto her lap and said, "Thank you for telling me." I don't know exactly what Shreya felt, but she did what she had been taught.

Who did Shreya run to when he reached again?
Their mother, across the room.
How might Shreya have felt when the man reached for her again?
Uncomfortable and perhaps scared, shown by stepping back and running to her mother. The man may have meant it as playful.
What did Nazia's mother do that supported Shreya?
She went straight over calmly, took Shreya onto her lap and thanked her for telling.
How does Nazia see Shreya's reaction?
She is unsure exactly what Shreya felt but sees that Shreya spoke up and went to a trusted adult, as she had been taught.
I wanted to go, however it was raining. Please correct the punctuation.

I wanted to go; however, it was raining.
Why: "however" needs a semicolon before it and a comma after.

By eleven o'clock the next day we were well upon our way to the old English capital. Holmes had been buried in the morning papers all the way down, but after we had passed the Hampshire border he threw them down and began to admire the scenery. It was an ideal spring day, a light blue sky, flecked with little fleecy white clouds drifting across from west to east. The sun was shining very brightly, and yet there was an exhilarating nip in the air, which set an edge to a man's energy. All over the countryside, away to the rolling hills around Aldershot, the little red and grey roofs of the farm-steadings peeped out from amid the light green of the new foliage.

Shrink this excerpt to two sentences.

On the train the next day, Holmes stops reading the morning papers after the Hampshire border and starts admiring the scenery. It is a bright spring day with a light blue sky, a crisp nip in the air, and farm roofs among fresh green leaves.

So you want to know about the insurance claim? I'm Seema. My father had surgery last year.
I thought insurance meant you just show a card. It didn't. The hospital asked for the policy number, ID, pre-authorisation forms, doctor's notes. I was running between counters while he was in the ward.
My friend Disha, who works in a hospital billing office, came and helped. She said, "Keep copies of everything. Get every bill itemised. Ask for the claim status in writing."
The first claim was partly rejected because a form was missing. We resubmitted with the doctor's letter. It went through.
Now I keep a folder for my parents' health papers. And I read the policy before we need it.

Disha.

Seema felt stressed and overwhelmed, worried about her father.
What choice inside the story got the claim approved?
Resubmitting with the doctor's letter after the first partial rejection.
How might Disha have felt helping Seema?
Disha probably felt glad she could use her experience to help a friend.

Grandma tells us a story and we listen quietly.

Hansa here. Reena asked me today why I haven't booked the counsellor she recommended. Honest answer: I'm scared it means something's badly wrong with me.
She said, "It's like a gym. You don't wait for a heart attack." Then she explained what she'd learned: a counsellor for talking things through; a psychologist for deeper work and assessments; a psychiatrist, a medical doctor, if medicine might help; and peer groups for people who've been through the same thing.
I think what I need is talking things through. The move, the breakup, work. Nothing dramatic. Just heavy.
I looked up the clinic. They have evening slots and a sliding fee. I filled the form, then deleted it, then filled it again and pressed send.
Appointment Thursday, 7 p.m. I feel nervous and a bit proud.

Thursday, 7 p.m.

Hansa feels nervous and a bit proud.

I'm Santosh, and last month I nearly failed my biology project because of one claim. It said goldfish have a three-second memory. I saw it on a science-facts page, then on a quiz account, then in a video, then Swati sent it to me as a sticker. Four places! I wrote it in my project as a proper fact. The night before submission, Swati said, 'Did you check where it started?' I hadn't. I looked, and every post pointed back to the same old meme, with no study behind it at all. When I finally searched a real science site, it said goldfish can remember things for months. I had to rewrite a whole page at midnight. What still bothers me is how sure I felt, just because I'd seen it so many times.

What did the claim say about goldfish memory?
That goldfish have a three-second memory.
How does Santosh feel about having been so sure of the goldfish claim?
Santosh feels uneasy and a bit embarrassed about how sure the claim felt, just from seeing it many times.
What did Swati's question show, and how could Santosh use it?
It showed all the posts led back to one meme; Santosh can ask 'where did it start?' before treating anything as fact.
How might Swati feel after that question saved the project?
Swati probably feels relieved and a little proud that one question helped Santosh catch the mistake in time.

When the board results were read out at the village school in Bihar, Arnab's name was at the top of the list. He stood at the back of the crowd, wide-eyed but silent. Gopika, his friend since childhood, felt like leaping and shouting. She nearly did. But she noticed his hands trembling and how he kept looking at the ground. She walked over, put her hand lightly on his arm and said, "I saw the hours you put in. I'm really proud of you." Arnab let out a long breath, and his eyes filled. "Thank you," he said. Gopika left the loud celebration to the others for now, and stayed beside him.

Where was Arnab's name on the list?
Arnab's name was at the top of the list.
What was Arnab feeling at the back of the crowd?
Arnab was overwhelmed and probably relieved, shown by the wide eyes, silence, trembling hands and filling eyes. He might also have felt the pressure of the result, so joy was not the only feeling.
What did Gopika do that fit Arnab's mood?
She held back her shouting and gave a short, specific note of pride, staying beside Arnab.
How might the loud celebrating crowd have looked to Arnab?
It may have felt too much for Arnab right then, so Gopika's quiet way suited him better.

Notes on Arohi, Saturday junior batch
For two months Arohi has done the home practice sheet every day, as I asked. This month I noticed her feet were correct but her face was flat, and twice she asked if class could end early. On Thursday she stayed back and said, "I love dancing, but practice every day feels like homework." We made a change together: home practice on Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Sunday, and on the other days she can dance however she likes, to any music, or rest. Today, for the first time in weeks, she was smiling through the adavus, and she asked to show me a few steps she had made up to a film song. I will check in again at the end of the month.
— Nirmala, dance teacher

Which days are home practice now?
Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Sunday.
What did Arohi's flat face and wish to end class early suggest?
They suggested she felt bored and weighed down, with the joy of dancing squeezed out by practice every day.
Why might four practice days work better for Arohi than seven?
Free days bring back choice and play, so dancing feels like hers again, while four days is still enough to keep improving.
How does Nirmala seem to see the change?
Nirmala seems glad to see Arohi smiling again, but plans to check in at the end of the month rather than assume it is fixed.

In their flat in Nairobi, Wanjiru sang the tidy-up song and held open the toy basket. Her son Hiroshi, two and a half, threw one wooden car in, then lay flat on his back and kicked. "No tidy!" One wooden car.
What does Hiroshi lying on his back and kicking suggest?
He was frustrated and unwilling to stop playing just to tidy up.

Ritu, you asked for the college radio what it's like being hostel secretary. I'm Zainab, and I'll be honest.
I stood because I wanted a say. The mess food was awful, the Wi-Fi died every night, and nobody listened to us. I wanted to be the person who could fix things. And yes, I liked the idea of people respecting me.
First month, it was great. I got the Wi-Fi fixed. People thanked me in the corridor. I felt tall.
Then I started deciding things alone. The movie night date. The rules for guests. I stopped calling committee meetings because they were slow.
One day Meenal, on my committee, said, "You're acting like the warden." That stung. She was right.
Now I have a rule: no decision without the committee. It's slower. But it's ours, not mine.

What did Zainab get fixed in the first month?
The Wi-Fi.
What was Zainab feeling when Meenal said "You're acting like the warden"?
Zainab felt stung and ashamed, realising the wish to fix things had turned into control.
What rule did Zainab make, and why is it wise?
No decision without the committee, because it keeps influence serving the group instead of becoming control.
How might the committee members have felt when meetings stopped?
They probably felt ignored and frustrated, left out of decisions they were elected to share.
Has the budget speech finished yet?
I can't tell if the speech is over, because I can't see live broadcasts. A news channel or the parliament's page will show it.
Quick question: how do you use maintain, and what does it mean?

Maintain means to keep something in good condition, or to keep it going at the same level. It is a verb.
Example: You must brush your teeth twice a day to maintain good dental habits.
What disguise did Arjuna choose for the year at King Virata's palace?
He chose to live as Vrihannala, one of the third sex, wearing bangles to hide the bowstring marks on his arms. He would teach the palace women singing, dancing and music.
Has the new metro line in our city opened yet?
I'm not sure, as I can't see recent city updates. The metro company's official website will say whether it is open.

"Yes, that is what makes it amusing. Had they fixed on any other man it would have been nothing; but his perfect indifference and your pointed dislike make it so delightfully absurd! The offsite had been moved at the last minute to a cramped room above a Chandigarh restaurant, with eight chairs for eleven people and a smell of frying from the kitchen. The director took the head of the table, and the senior leads filled the chairs beside him. Salma, the most senior of them all, stayed standing at the back by the door. Gurleen, three months into the job, watched her all morning. Everyone knew Salma had argued against the reorganisation. Was this a protest? A way of saying "not my plan"? At the tea break Gurleen almost repeated the theory to a colleague, then stopped herself and went over to Salma instead. "Would you like my chair? I'm happy to stand." Salma smiled. "Kind of you, but no. My mother's in hospital, and I may need to step out for calls. By the door is easier."

How many chairs were there for how many people?
Eight chairs for eleven people.
What was Gurleen feeling as Salma stood at the back?
Gurleen felt curious and a little uneasy, wondering whether Salma was protesting against the reorganisation she had argued against.
What did Gurleen do instead of spreading her theory?
She stopped herself and offered Salma her chair, which opened a kind conversation and revealed the practical reason.
How might Salma have felt if people assumed she was protesting?
Salma might have felt misjudged and more stressed, already worried about her mother and standing by the door only for calls.
My mother, not my brothers, are going to the wedding. Which verb is right?

My mother, not my brothers, is going to the wedding.
Why: In "X, not Y", the verb matches the first subject (is).

On Tuesday evening Asif and Irshad from Room 7 got into a shouting match in the common room, over a borrowed phone charger, though it clearly wasn't about the charger. Other boys started gathering, so I asked them both to go to their rooms and cool off. On Wednesday morning, before breakfast, Asif showed me his phone, a bit sheepish. He had sent Irshad a message: "Yesterday got out of hand. My fault too. Walk to the tea stall after classes? Just us." Irshad replied, "ok". I saw them walking back from the tea stall at five, talking quietly, Asif carrying both cups. The common room was the wrong place for it. They found a better one themselves.

A borrowed phone charger.
How did Asif seem to feel showing the warden his phone?
He seemed a bit sheepish, embarrassed about the shouting but hopeful about his message.
Why might a walk to the tea stall help more than another talk in the common room?
It removes the audience and the heat of the moment, giving a calmer setting where they can talk quietly.
How does Chaitanya see the way the boys fixed it?
Chaitanya is pleased the boys found a better place themselves, after the common room proved the wrong setting.

messages.content: I've lost my place in the book because the bookmark fell out.
That's annoying. Do you remember the last scene?
Roughly. A character was on a train.
Flip through to find the train scene and read from there. It's fine to reread a page or two, and you'll be back in the story soon.

The computer lab closed at nine, Tarun's data pack had almost run out, and the problem set was due at midnight. Tarun worked through question after question by hand, erasing and trying again, hunched over one desk in a noisy corridor.

Across the room, Anand finished the whole set in ten minutes with an AI tool, closed the laptop and left for tea. Next week the marks came back: Anand scored higher. Tarun felt foolish, as if hours of effort had bought nothing.

A month later, at a mock interview, the panel asked Anand to explain one solution on the whiteboard. Anand's marker stayed still.

Tarun, on the other hand, had used the AI as a tutor that night, asking it to explain the one step that didn't click, and could walk through every line.

What time did the computer lab close?
The computer lab closed at nine.
How did Tarun feel when the marks came back, and why?
Tarun felt foolish, as if hours of effort had bought nothing, because Anand scored higher after finishing in ten minutes.
What did Tarun do with the AI that helped later?
Tarun used it as a tutor to explain the one step that didn't click, so Tarun could walk through every line, while Anand copied without understanding.
How might Anand feel at the mock interview?
Anand probably felt exposed and stuck, with the marker staying still, because the shortcut left no understanding to explain.

On my first day at the logistics software company, I wore the new shirt Amma had ironed twice. The office had bean bags and a coffee machine I didn't know how to use. By ten I was in a stand-up meeting where people said "sprint velocity", "blockers" and "push to staging" as if everyone was born knowing them. I nodded. I wrote the words in my notebook to search later. Abhinav, my buddy for the week, asked, "Yogesh, anything blocking you?" I said, "No, all good," though I couldn't even log into the laptop. At lunch I kept thinking, maybe HR mixed up two CVs. Maybe the real Yogesh is sitting at home. Then I'd remember the offer email, and a small, fizzy excitement would come back. I went home both terrified and thrilled.

What did Yogesh write in the notebook?
The unfamiliar words, to search later.
What mix of feelings did Yogesh go home with?
Yogesh went home both terrified and thrilled, worried the selection was a mistake yet excited about the job.
What small step could help Yogesh on day two?
Telling Abhinav honestly about the laptop login and asking what one or two of the terms mean.
How might Abhinav see Yogesh on day one?
Abhinav likely sees a new joiner who says all is good, not knowing Yogesh could not even log in.

Monday, winter holidays. Jatin opened a new 1000-piece jigsaw of a boring grey bridge. He found it dull after ten minutes. But he'd spent his whole birthday money on it.

Wednesday. Jatin had done the edges. His back hurt. Imran came to call him for cricket. "Two more hours," Jatin said. "I've already done so much."

Saturday. Jatin was still hunched over the grey bridge. Imran came again. "Are you even having fun?"

"No. But if I stop now, all those hours are wasted."

"They're gone anyway," Imran said. "Are the next hours going to be fun?"

Jatin looked at the grey pieces, then out of the window at the sunny street. He slowly put the lid on the box and went to get his bat.

What was the jigsaw a picture of?
A boring grey bridge.
Why did Jatin keep doing the jigsaw even though it was dull?
Jatin felt that stopping would waste the birthday money and hours already spent, so continuing felt necessary even though he was bored.
What question from Imran helped Jatin decide, and why?
Imran asked whether the next hours would be fun, which turned Jatin's thinking toward what comes next rather than what was already spent.
How might Imran have felt when Jatin kept saying no to cricket?
Imran probably felt disappointed and a bit puzzled, missing his friend during the holidays.

Paula spread a sheet of paper on the kitchen table in Valencia and wrote at the top: What do I wonder about? Ten questions followed: Do plants grow towards light? Why do ice cubes melt faster in salt water? How high does a paper plane fly? She put a tick next to those she could test with things at home, and a cross beside the ones needing special tools. Her brother Alejandro peered over. "Which will you choose?" Paula tapped the plants. "I have beans, cups and a windowsill. And I have three weeks." She circled the question and drew a little sun beside it.

How many questions did Paula write?
Paula wrote ten questions.
What did Paula think when tapping the plant question?
Paula thought the plant question could be tested with beans, cups and a windowsill within three weeks, so it felt possible and exciting.
What alternative approach could Paula use to choose, and why?
Paula could ask her teacher which questions are safe and interesting, or talk to a friend. Another view might spot a hidden problem.
How might Alejandro see Paula's list?
Alejandro peered over and asked which she would choose, so Alejandro seems curious and interested in the plan.

messages.content: Online order galat aaya. Email mein likha: 'I ordered blue shirt but you have sended red.' Fix karo.

Corrected: "I ordered a blue shirt, but I received a red one." The past of "send" is "sent", not "sended". Saying what you received also sounds more polite than "you sent". Add your order number so they can help you quickly.

Urmila had moved to the city in June, and by July some classmates mocked how she said "water" and wrinkled their noses at her lunch. One remarked that people from her region and "her sort of family" did not belong at this school. Urmila felt small and angry. She told the class teacher, who took it seriously, and she kept eating with the two girls who asked about her hometown. Gurpreet, one of them, had frozen when the remark was made and felt uncomfortable afterwards. The next day she said to the classmate, "That isn't okay," and later checked on Urmila. "I should have said it sooner." "It helped," Urmila said. Madhuri, at the next desk, had always looked down on scholarship students and rolled her eyes at their old bags. Seeing how Urmila was treated, she caught herself. "I have had things easy," she thought. She asked Urmila to teach her a phrase in her language and to bring lunch to share. Urmila kept her roots and learned the local ways slowly.

How did Gurpreet respond the day after the remark?
She told the classmate, "That isn't okay," and later checked on Urmila.
How did Gurpreet's small stand differ from Madhuri's change, and what did each do for Urmila?
Gurpreet, after freezing, said it was not okay and checked on Urmila, while Madhuri noticed her own contempt for scholarship students and asked Urmila to teach her a phrase and share lunch.
What was Urmila feeling after the remark about her region and family?
She felt small and angry.
What could Urmila do to keep her roots in the new city?
She could keep sharing her language and food with friends who are curious, keep her allies close, and learn local ways gradually.

Kalyani, you ask why I don't let your little brother play games at night? Let me tell you about me during one summer vacation, when I was eleven.
I, Jahnavi, got a hand-held game from my uncle. I played it day and night. I stopped going to the river with my friends. I got headaches. I became cranky with everyone.
One evening my grandmother took the game and put it in her cupboard. I cried and cried.
The next day, bored, I went to the river. My friends had built a raft. I'd missed it.
After that, I played the game one hour after lunch, and spent evenings outside. Summers are too short for screens only.

What had Jahnavi's friends built?
A raft.
How did Jahnavi feel when the grandmother took the game?
Jahnavi felt upset and angry, crying and crying.
What was the turning point in Jahnavi's story?
Going to the river the next day and seeing what had been missed, then choosing one hour of games and evenings outside.
How might the grandmother have felt taking the game?
She likely felt worried about the headaches and firm but caring.

The village fair was loud with drums. Shankar kaka held Madhav's hand near the sweet stall.
"A small peppermint now," kaka said, "or the big jalebi after the bullock race. Your choice."
Madhav looked at the peppermint jar. The race had not even started. The jalebi pan was far away, behind a crowd of people.
"Peppermint!" he said, and held out his hand.
He sucked it hard while the carts thundered past. Walking home, he saw another boy with a huge orange jalebi and tugged kaka's sleeve, his lip wobbling.

Which two treats did Shankar kaka offer Madhav?
A small peppermint now, or the big jalebi after the bullock race.
What made the peppermint feel like the better deal to Madhav in that moment?
The jar was right in front of him, while the race had not started and the jalebi pan was hidden behind a crowd, so later felt too far away to matter.
What could Shankar kaka try at the next fair so Madhav can wait?
Kaka could walk him to watch the jalebis frying and make cheering for the race the waiting game, so the big treat feels close and the time passes.
What might Shankar kaka feel when Madhav tugs his sleeve on the way home?
Kaka may feel tender and a little sorry, seeing Madhav wish for the jalebi he gave up, and may not want to scold a small child for it.

Read this:

I sit next to Jahnavi at our study group. For two weeks I saw her turn her phone face down whenever Tara's messages came in. She didn't look angry, more tense, like someone holding her breath. Tara asked me twice if I knew what she had done wrong. I said I didn't. I don't know what was in Jahnavi's mind. Maybe the talk felt too hard to start. Yesterday Jahnavi typed something short and sent it. She showed me: "I'm sorry I went quiet. It was hard to say I want to work alone this time. Can we talk on Friday?" Her shoulders dropped after. Tara sent a thumbs-up within a minute. Rafiq

How long did Rafiq see Jahnavi turn her phone face down?
Rafiq saw it for two weeks.
What might Jahnavi have been feeling, according to Rafiq's account?
She seemed tense rather than angry, and Rafiq thinks the talk may have felt too hard to start, though Rafiq cannot be sure.
Why was Jahnavi's short message kinder than more silence?
It told Tara that the quiet was not about Tara's mistakes and offered a talk, so Tara no longer had to guess. 🙂
How might Tara have felt during the two weeks?
Tara asked twice what she had done wrong, so Tara was probably worried and confused.

Rekha had been with Charu for eight months, and his friends at their Chennai college had still never met her. She kept him in neat compartments: Tuesday dinners, Saturday walks along the beach road, nothing else. When he invited her to his sister's birthday, she said she had a class.
Then her internship interview went badly, and she sat alone on the hostel stairs for an hour instead of calling him. He found out from her roommate. On the phone that night his voice was quiet. "I don't know if I know you, Rekha. You tell me about films, never about you."
She almost said she was fine. Instead she said, "I thought if you saw me upset, you'd leave." A long silence. "I'm still here," he said.
She went to the birthday the next Sunday. She also kept her Friday painting class, just for her.

What reason did Rekha give for not going to his sister's birthday?
She said she had a class.
Why did Rekha keep Charu in neat compartments?
She was afraid that if he saw her upset he would leave, so keeping him at a distance felt safer.
What was the turning point, and what did Rekha choose?
When Charu said he didn't know her; instead of saying she was fine, she told him her fear, which let them actually get closer.
How did it feel for Charu to hear about the bad interview from Rekha's roommate?
He likely felt hurt and shut out, wondering whether he really knew the person he had been with for eight months.

Every evening in their Nagpur flat, Vikas asked his mother the same question. "Aai, where did Aaji go?"
Irawati would stop cooking and answer. "Aaji died, Vikas. Her body stopped working. She isn't anywhere we can visit."
"But where?"
In the day he played with his cars, lining them up like the cars outside the crematorium. He made the cars go slowly. He made them stop. Then he started again.
On Sunday, when the doorbell rang, he ran to it shouting, "Aaji!" It was the milkman. Vikas stood very still.
Irawati knelt and held him. "You were hoping it was Aaji." He nodded into her shoulder.

Who was at the door on Sunday?
The milkman.
What was Vikas feeling when he stood very still at the door?
He felt disappointed and sad, having hoped Aaji had come back.
What small thing did Irawati do that helped at this stage?
She knelt, held him and named his hope, rather than dismissing it or distracting him.
What is it like for Irawati to answer the same question every evening?
She is likely grieving herself and tired, yet chooses to stop cooking and answer patiently each time.
Would you mind if I open the window? It is very warm in here. Please polish the request.

Would you mind if I opened the window? It is very warm in here.
Why: "Would you mind if" takes the past simple (opened).

"I can't do another night," Hansa whispered in the corridor. "Mummyji called for water six times."
Sangeeta, her sister-in-law, leaned against the wall. "I know. I heard. I thought you wanted to do it all."
"I thought I had to. You work, and she's my husband's mother."
"She's my husband's mother too." Sangeeta rubbed her eyes. "Why didn't you ask?"
"Because everyone would say I'm not managing."
"You're not managing. Neither am I. Nobody could."
Hansa laughed, close to tears. "So what do we do?"
"A rota. You Monday, Wednesday, Friday nights. Me Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday. Sunday, the brothers."
"The brothers?" Hansa's eyebrows shot up. "Both of them?"
"They're her sons. They can hold a glass of water."
"And the physiotherapy bills?"
"All four of us sit down on Sunday and split them properly. No more one person paying and sulking."
Hansa hugged her, hard.

How many times did Mummyji call for water?
Six times.
What was Hansa worried about that stopped her asking for help?
Hansa was afraid everyone would judge her as not managing, so she felt she had to do it all alone.
What makes Sangeeta's plan fairer and more sustainable?
A night rota that includes the brothers, and a Sunday talk to split the physiotherapy bills openly, so no one carries it alone.
How does Sangeeta see the situation?
Sangeeta is exhausted too and sees that nobody could manage alone, so she wants the care shared, including by the sons.

The metro broke down, it was pouring, and Usha got home an hour late, still hearing her supervisor's words: "Maybe this job is too much for you." Her flatmate Parveen had cooked, and asked cheerfully, "Rajma okay?" Usha heard herself snap, "Does it matter?" Parveen's smile dropped. Usha stopped. That sharpness wasn't about rajma. She put her bag down. "Sorry. That was my supervisor, not you. I need twenty minutes." She walked round the block under an umbrella, then sat on the stairs and wrote in her phone what had been said and what she wanted to say. When she came back, she ate the rajma and thanked Parveen properly. On Monday she asked the supervisor for a proper review.

What did the supervisor say to Usha?
"Maybe this job is too much for you."
What made Usha stop after snapping?
She saw Parveen's smile drop and realised, with a flash of guilt, that her anger belonged to the supervisor, not to Parveen.
What did Usha do before replying to anyone?
Apologised to Parveen, took twenty minutes to walk, wrote down what was said and what she wanted to say, and later asked for a proper review.
How might Parveen have felt when snapped at?
Hurt and surprised after cooking kindly, with the smile dropping from Parveen's face.

At the municipal disaster-management office in Chennai, Naveen, twenty-six, had to recommend by 6 p.m. whether to evacuate a low-lying settlement. The forecast said heavy rain was "likely", but the models disagreed on how heavy.
His senior, Siddharth, asked, "What happens if we evacuate and it doesn't flood? What happens if we don't and it does?"
Naveen wrote it out. Evacuating: families lose a night's sleep and some wages, and trust drops if it's a false alarm. Not evacuating: people might drown. The costs weren't equal.
At 4 p.m., a new update raised the rain estimate. Naveen updated his view. He recommended evacuation.
The rain came, but less than feared. Some residents grumbled. Siddharth said, "We'd make the same call again. Explain it to them honestly." Naveen went to the relief centre the next morning and explained the forecast to anyone who asked.

By what time did Naveen have to make his recommendation?
By 6 p.m.
How might Naveen have felt when some residents grumbled?
Naveen probably felt uncomfortable and a bit defensive, but reassured by Siddharth that the decision was right.
What made Naveen's decision sound even though the flood was smaller?
He compared the unequal costs of each mistake, updated his view with the new forecast, and explained the reasoning openly afterwards.
How might the residents see the evacuation after Naveen explained the forecast?
Some might still be annoyed, but many could understand and trust the office more for being honest.

Subject: Thinking it through, and could you check my sums?

Dear Naveen,

You are the one person outside the office I trust to think this through with me. I have decided to report what I saw, but first I want to be clear about what it might cost.

Risks: my next promotion could stall, and if things turn ugly, my job could be at risk. I have read the protection section in our policy for people who report, and I will ask a lawyer to explain what the law says, since I don't want to guess.

Meanwhile I have set aside four months of costs and updated my CV, in case I need to look elsewhere.

Does that sound sensible to you?

Ishita

How many months of costs has Ishita set aside?
Ishita has set aside four months of costs.
How does Ishita feel about reporting?
Ishita is determined but careful, having decided to report while wanting to face the costs honestly, and asking a friend to check the plan.
What could Ishita do if the lawyer says the protections are weaker than expected?
Ishita could rethink the timing and the route of the report, and strengthen the savings and job search before going ahead.
How might Naveen feel on receiving this email?
Naveen probably feels trusted and a bit worried, and would likely reply thoughtfully since Ishita asked for a check.

Read this:

Class 4 diary, Monday
Yusuf came in today holding a small telescope as if it were made of glass. He told the class his Abba bought it on Saturday. "I asked in March. He said wait till my birthday. I waited six months!"
Deepika asked if he wasn't angry about waiting. Yusuf thought and said, "At first. But now it feels more special. Abba saved for it. He works nights at the bakery."
At break he let every child have one careful look through it.
During art period I asked Yusuf to make a thank-you card for his Abba. He drew the moon and wrote, "Worth the wait." I have tucked it into his bag to take home.

When did Yusuf first ask for the telescope?
In March.
How does Yusuf feel about the telescope after waiting?
He feels grateful and proud, and says it feels more special because he waited.
How did the class teacher help Yusuf show his gratitude?
They asked him to make a thank-you card in art period and tucked it into his bag to take home.
How might Abba feel when he reads "Worth the wait"?
He would probably feel touched and proud, knowing his effort was noticed.

At the chess club in the community centre, Reena, twelve, had been practising openings every evening for three weeks. She had them written in a notebook.
In the final, she played Minakshi. For twenty minutes it was even. Then Reena made a mistake and lost her queen. She lost the game.
She stared at the board. Her throat tightened.
Then she held out her hand. “Well played. How did you see that move?”
Minakshi showed her. Reena wrote it in her notebook.
The club coach said, “That's how champions learn.”

How long had Reena been practising openings?
Every evening for three weeks.
How did Reena feel after losing her queen and the game?
She felt upset and disappointed, her throat tightening.
What did Reena do after losing that shows good sportsmanship and learning?
She shook hands, praised Minakshi and asked how she saw the move, then wrote it down.
How might Minakshi feel when Reena asks about her move?
She probably feels proud and respected, happy to share.

Read this:

My grandson Hrithik asked me how to help a friend who was upset, so I told him about my school friend Tejas. I was your age then, Hrithik, and Tejas failed his board mathematics paper. I said all the clever things: "It's only one paper. You'll pass the supplementary." Tejas's jaw went hard and he stopped speaking to me for two days. I had answered the problem, not the person. So I went to his house with a small packet of jalebis and said, "I'm sorry. I'm here. You don't have to say anything." We sat on his verandah for an hour. He talked a little. Sometimes that's all it takes, just showing up and listening.

What did Tejas fail?
He failed his board mathematics paper.
Why did Tejas stop speaking to his friend for two days?
He felt brushed aside by clever comments, since his jaw went hard after hearing that it was only one paper. He probably wanted to feel understood first.
What did the narrator change on the second visit?
The narrator apologised, stayed with Tejas and did not push him to talk, which let Tejas open up a little.
How might the narrator have felt on seeing Tejas's jaw go hard?
The narrator probably came to feel regretful, seeing that the clever words answered the problem and not the person, which is why they went to apologise with jalebis.

Sabina had been in the 'Inner Light' group for eighteen months when she noticed Hansa at a café near Bandra station. Hansa had left the group a year ago; the leader said she had 'fallen'. Sabina nearly walked past. Instead she sat down. Hansa didn't lecture. She talked about her first months out: the nightmares, the guilt, the relief of reading any book she wanted. 'I was scared of exactly what you're scared of,' she said. 'That I'd be nothing without them.' Sabina felt her throat close. For the first time in months she felt less alone. 'So what should I do?' Hansa shook her head. 'I'm not going to be your new leader. Don't swap one person telling you what to do for another. But if you want, come to the Tuesday meeting for former members. Just listen.' Sabina didn't promise. But she saved the address, and on the way home she called her mother for the first time in weeks.

Where did Sabina see Hansa?
Sabina saw Hansa at a café near Bandra station.
What did Sabina feel as Hansa spoke?
Sabina felt less alone for the first time in months, her throat closing with emotion.
Why does Hansa refuse to tell Sabina what to do?
So Sabina doesn't swap one authority for another, and can take her own steps at her own pace.
How does Hansa describe her time since leaving?
Hansa describes nightmares and guilt at first, then relief, like reading any book she wants.

My name is Keerthana, and last year I joined Class 6 in the middle of term. Shreya was the first person to share her pencil box with me. But her old friend Bhoomi went silent every time I sat down near them. She'd turn her back and talk only to Shreya.
I felt like an intruder. Once I almost said, "Bhoomi always copies you, you know," just to make her look bad. I stopped myself. I knew Shreya would hate being pushed to pick.
So I kept saying good morning to Bhoomi, even when she didn't answer. I asked about her drawings. By the winter holidays, she was saving both of us a seat.

Who was the first person to share a pencil box with Keerthana?
Shreya was the first.
What was Keerthana feeling when Bhoomi turned her back?
Keerthana felt like an intruder, unwanted and insecure, sensing that Bhoomi disliked the newcomer.
Why was Keerthana's patient approach wiser than the remark she almost made?
Making Bhoomi look bad would have pushed Shreya to choose, while staying friendly and giving it time let Bhoomi warm up.
How might Bhoomi have seen Keerthana at first?
Bhoomi may have felt threatened, as if the newcomer could take Shreya away, which explains her silence.

Every Sunday Swati wrote the whole month on a slate at the village dairy collection centre: which routes, which days, which cans. And every week it cracked. Rain washed out the lane to the far hamlet, the chilling machine stopped for a day, a helper fell ill.
By the third Sunday she was rubbing out more than she kept. "Why do you rewrite it every week?" asked Zeenat, who helped with the cans.
"Because it only holds till Tuesday," said Swati. She wiped the slate and this time wrote the coming week in detail, and across the remaining weeks just two rough goals: keep the far hamlet route, cut spoilage.
The next Sunday the slate barely needed a change.

What did Swati write for the rest of the month?
Swati wrote two rough goals: keep the far hamlet route, cut spoilage.
What did Swati notice about her monthly plan that made her change it?
Swati noticed she was rubbing out more than she kept and felt frustrated that the plan only holds till Tuesday.
What else could Swati try if even the weekly plan started cracking?
Swati could plan only the next two days in detail, since shorter plans are less likely to be broken by rain or machines.
How might Zeenat see the new way of planning?
Zeenat, who helps with the cans, may find the slate steadier and the week easier, since it no longer changes each day.

metadata.subtype: Approach: plans the next step in detail and leaves later steps loose [Revision]

messages.content: My chess tournament is tomorrow and my hands are shaking from nerves.
Nerves mean you care. Before the game, take a few slow breaths and drink some water. A short walk can calm the body.
What if I lose in the first round?
Then you'll have learned from it, and there may be more rounds or another event. Play one move at a time and don't think about the result.
What do I do if my opponent is very confident?
Ignore how they look and focus on the board. Confidence doesn't win games, good moves do.
I'll try to focus on the board.
That's the right idea. After the match, review the game, whether you win or lose.
I waited a long time for my food at a restaurant and the dal arrived cold. Write a polite complaint to the manager, about 60 words. I'm Farah Khan.

Dear Manager,
I visited your restaurant and was disappointed. I had to wait a long time for my food, and when the dal finally arrived, it was cold. I understand that restaurants get busy, but I hope you can look into this and improve the service. Thank you for your attention.
Sincerely,
Farah Khan

At the civil engineering firm in Chennai, Uday had a habit: whenever a problem came up on the site drawings, he walked to Sudha ma'am's desk. "Ma'am, what should I do?" In three months he had asked her about beam sizes, email wording, and once, where to eat lunch.
On Thursday she didn't look up from her screen. "Uday, before you ask me anything today, bring me two options and which one you'd choose."
He went back to his desk, irritated, and stared at the drainage problem. Slowly he sketched one fix, then another. The second was cheaper but meant rerouting a pipe. He wrote down why he'd pick it.
At four he returned. "Option A, option B. I'd go with B because..."
She listened, asked one question he hadn't thought of, and nodded. "Good. Adjust for that and send it."
Walking back, he felt taller than he had in weeks. The next morning he solved a smaller problem without going to her at all.

What had Uday asked Sudha ma'am about in three months?
Beam sizes, email wording, and once, where to eat lunch.
How did Uday feel when Sudha ma'am asked for two options?
Irritated at first, then, after presenting his own choice, proud and taller than he had felt in weeks.
What habit did Sudha ma'am's request build?
Bringing his own options and a recommendation, which grew his judgement until he solved the next problem alone.
Why might Sudha ma'am have stopped answering directly?
She could see him handing her every decision and wanted him to build independent judgement.

Read this:

During wet break in their Kraków classroom, Olga tossed a rubber ball to Thabo and it hit the globe on the teacher's desk. The globe rolled off, and a crack split right across the Atlantic.
Pan Nowak came back and stared at it. "Who did this?"
Olga's stomach went tight. Last month he had made Kuba stand in the corridor the whole afternoon for spilling paint. "It was already cracked," she said. "It was like that this morning."
Thabo looked at the floor and said nothing.
Pan Nowak frowned but moved on to spelling. Olga didn't hear a single word of the lesson. On the bus home, Thabo said quietly, "You didn't have to say that." Olga pressed her forehead against the cold window and didn't answer.

What happened to the globe?
It rolled off the desk and a crack split right across the Atlantic.
Why did Olga say the globe was already cracked?
Olga was scared of being punished, remembering that Pan Nowak made Kuba stand in the corridor all afternoon for spilling paint.
What could make it easier for Olga to tell the truth next time?
If Pan Nowak met accidents calmly, for example by asking who could help fix things rather than punishing, Olga might feel safe enough to own up.
What is it like for Thabo when Olga blames the globe's crack on the morning?
Thabo seems uncomfortable and torn, staring at the floor in class and later saying quietly, "You didn't have to say that."
In science class we talk about elements. What does the word mean there?

In science an element is a basic substance, such as oxygen, iron or gold, that cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical means. The plural of this noun is Elements.
Example: Oxygen and hydrogen are both elements, but water is not.
