I'm Kavitha, and last term I learned this the hard way. Mrs Rao kept picking the same four students for the debate team, even when Ira and I had higher scores in the trials. For a month I said nothing and just sulked. Nothing changed. Then one day I snapped in class: "You only pick your favourites!" The room went silent, and I got sent out. That didn't help either. Ira suggested another way. We collected the trial score sheets, wrote a short, polite letter asking how selection worked, and took it to the English coordinator. Two weeks later the school put up clear selection rules on the notice board. I made the team in the next round. I still cringe about snapping, though.

Who kept picking the same four students?
Mrs Rao kept picking the same four students for the debate team.
What was Kavitha feeling during the month of saying nothing?
Kavitha felt resentful and unfairly treated, sulking because the higher trial scores seemed ignored.
Which approach finally worked, and why?
Collecting the score sheets and taking a polite letter to the English coordinator used evidence and a proper channel, so the rules became clear.
How might Mrs Rao have felt when Kavitha snapped in class?
Mrs Rao probably felt accused and embarrassed in front of everyone, which made her less open to the complaint.

Switch "I" to "you".

I am sure I closed the door, and I locked it.
You are sure you closed the door, and you locked it.

"Amandeep, you watch your science teacher's hands closely. Good. I, your Gautam Tauji, learned that the hard way. Our teacher in Class 6, Mr Bhatt, loved big gestures. One day he talked about dropping a stone and a feather. For the stone, his hand shot down like lightning. For the feather, his fingers floated side to side, slow as a leaf. So I wrote in my notebook: heavy things always fall faster. Something bothered me, though, and after class I asked, 'Sir, would a heavy stone and a small stone land together?' He stopped, then laughed. 'Yes! My hands made the feather too dramatic. It's the air that slows it.' Always ask, beta."

Two sentences, please: what is this short passage about?

Gautam Tauji tells Amandeep that in Class 6 his teacher's gestures made him think heavy things fall faster, so he asked about two stones. The teacher laughed and said it is the air that slows a feather, and Gautam says to always ask.

Read this:

I'm Pallavi, and in my second year of teaching I learned to shut my own mouth. A flower vase fell off the reading-corner shelf during lunch, and Damini was the only child nearby. My first instinct was to ask whether one of the rough boys had pushed it. I stopped myself. Instead I knelt and said, "Tell me what happened."
Damini said the fan blew the curtain, and the curtain knocked the vase. I wrote it down right away in my diary, with the time, before anyone else could talk to her. By home time other children had theories, and by the next day Damini was half-repeating them. But I had her first words on paper: the curtain and the fan.
The fan is now set lower.

What did Damini say knocked the vase?
The curtain; the fan blew the curtain.
What was Pallavi feeling when tempted to ask about the rough boys?
Pallavi felt a quick pull of suspicion, then caution, not wanting to plant an idea in Damini's memory.
Why did writing it down right away matter?
Damini's first account was saved before other children's theories could reshape it.
How might Damini feel being asked "Tell me what happened"?
Damini may feel calm and trusted, free to describe what she saw without being steered.

metadata.subtype: Asking open questions and noting memory early [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the Johannesburg flat, Zanele held a banana to her ear. “Hello! Hello, Gogo!”
Marek, her father, laughed. “Tell Gogo I said hi.”
Then he put on music. “Hop like a bunny!” Zanele hopped, giggling, hands up like ears.
Rain started hammering the window. “Wow, it's raining cats and dogs,” said Marek.
Zanele ran to the window and pressed her nose to the glass, searching. “Where doggy?”
Marek crouched beside her. “No doggies. Just lots of rain."

What did Zanele hold to her ear as a phone?
She held a banana to her ear.
What was Zanele feeling when she ran to the window looking for the dogs?
She was excited and curious, taking the words literally and expecting to see real dogs, which shows the saying meant nothing to her yet.
How did Marek respond well when Zanele took the idiom literally?
He crouched beside her and explained simply, "No doggies. Just lots of rain," without laughing at her.
How might Marek feel watching Zanele search the window?
He would likely feel amused and tender, realising she heard his words exactly as spoken.

Read this:

At 11:05 the message showed two ticks, both blue. Sarita had asked Sunaina, two desks away in the design studio, whether the client notes were ready. By one o'clock there was still nothing. Sarita's mind started running: Sunaina was annoyed at being chased, or thought the question was silly, or had found a mistake and did not want to say so. Sarita stopped drawing and stared at the phone.
At two, a door opened. Sunaina walked out of the meeting room with a client, phone in hand, face down against a folder. Sunaina caught Sarita's eye and mouthed, "Notes in ten minutes!"
Sarita smiled at the screen, a bit embarrassed, and picked up the pencil again.

How many ticks appeared on the message, and what colour were they?
The message showed two ticks, both blue.
What was Sarita worried about while waiting for a reply?
Sarita was anxious and wondered if Sunaina was annoyed, thought the question was silly, or had found a mistake. The waiting made every possible reason feel worse.
What could Sarita do next time the message is read but not answered?
Sarita could give Sunaina the benefit of the doubt and get on with work, or walk over and ask briefly. Delays usually mean busyness, as the client meeting showed.
What was Sunaina dealing with while the message sat unanswered?
Sunaina was in a meeting room with a client, phone face down against a folder. The unanswered message came from being busy, not from ignoring Sarita.

Read this:

In Toronto, the day after his grandfather's funeral, Sami sat with his friend Nour in the school library and talked about heart disease. "It's the leading cause of death worldwide," he said. "About a third of all deaths. His arteries were eighty percent blocked. The surgery had a ten percent risk at his age, so they didn't do it." Nour watched him. His voice was completely flat, like a news reader. "Sami, are you okay?" "I'm fine. It makes sense, statistically." That weekend, Sami went to his grandfather's apartment to help pack. On the table was the chessboard, the pieces still set up from their last game, Sami's move. He picked up his knight. Then he sat down on the floor, and the tears came all at once.

What was still set up on the table?
The chessboard, the pieces from their last game.
Why did Sami talk about statistics so flatly in the library?
The facts gave him a way to think about the death without feeling it, keeping the grief and hurt at a distance.
What could Nour do to support Sami after the weekend?
Nour could check in, listen if Sami wants to talk about his grandfather or the chess games, and suggest talking to a trusted adult if the sadness gets heavy.
How might Nour have felt listening to the numbers?
Nour seemed concerned, noticing that the flat voice didn't match what Sami must be feeling.

Read this:

Month one: At her school in Aizawl, Lalremsiami sat the maths test with a hot water bottle pressed under her desk, too sore and foggy to finish. When Akash asked why she was pale, she muttered, "Stomach." A girl behind her giggled, "Being dramatic again."
Month two: The pain came back, worse. She missed two days of school and cried from tiredness as much as from pain. Her mother didn't say "just bear it". She sat on the bed and said, "This much pain needs a doctor."
Month three: After the doctor's check and a plan, Lalremsiami got through the week. When Akash asked again, she said, "Period pain. I'm seeing a doctor about it." He just nodded and slid across his notes for the days she had missed.

What did Lalremsiami press under her desk?
A hot water bottle.
How was Lalremsiami feeling in month two?
She was exhausted and in pain, crying from tiredness as much as from the pain itself.
What was her mother's key step?
She believed her instead of saying "just bear it", and took her to a doctor for a plan.
How does Akash respond when she says it's period pain?
Akash simply nods and shares his notes, treating it as ordinary.
My cousin Asha used the word confirm at dinner. What does it mean?

To confirm means to say or show that something is true or certain. It is a verb.
Example: Please call the restaurant to confirm our table for Friday.

Read this:

With five minutes left before the bell, Jahnavi Ma'am called Akash into the corridor and asked him quietly what had happened at the tap with Nikhil. She did not shout. Akash's first thought was to say Nikhil had bumped him. The words were ready. But her calm, waiting face made the lie feel heavy in his mouth. "I pushed him," he said. "I was annoyed about the cricket team." She asked what was really bothering him, and he admitted he had been feeling left out. "Thank you for telling me the truth," she said. They agreed he would talk to Nikhil before the bell and ask what he needed. Akash's chest felt lighter than he expected.

What did Akash say when the teacher asked what had happened at the tap?
He said, "I pushed him."
Why did the lie feel heavy in Akash's mouth?
The teacher's calm, waiting face made lying feel worse than owning up, so he chose to be honest and it felt lighter.
What steps in this scene helped Akash repair the harm?
He admitted the push, agreed to talk to Nikhil and ask what he needed, and looked at what he had really been feeling.
How might Nikhil see Akash coming to talk to him?
Nikhil may be surprised or wary at first, but an honest apology that asks what he needs gives him a chance to feel respected.

Read this:

Dear Uday Mama,
You missed it! I know you were on night duty, so let me tell you. Our school team was playing the district cricket final and I was in the stands with the whole of Class 11.
Last over, eight runs needed. I honestly could not breathe. My legs were shaking like I was the one batting. Somebody's aunty next to me was praying out loud.
Then our Rehan hit a six. A SIX. 🎉 Everyone screamed. I hugged people I don't even talk to in class. My throat still hurts.
The funny thing is, I didn't score a single run and I've never felt prouder. It felt like it was all of ours.
Come for the celebration on Sunday, please.
Love,
Seema

How many runs were needed in the last over?
Eight runs were needed in the last over.
What was Seema feeling while the last over was bowled?
Seema was so tense and excited that breathing was hard, legs shaking as if Seema were the one batting.
Why was it good for Seema to be in the stands with the class?
Cheering together let Seema share the win and feel proud and connected, even hugging classmates Seema doesn't usually talk to.
What might Uday Mama feel reading this letter after night duty?
Uday Mama might feel sorry to have missed the match but warmed and happy to share Seema's excitement through the letter.

metadata.subtype: Thrill at a team's win or a character's fate [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Shreya: hey you weren't at the fest. everything ok?
Deepak: yeah. no. idk
Shreya: ?
Deepak: I've been alone every weekend since the group stopped inviting me. I tell myself I like it but I don't
Shreya: that sounds really lonely
Deepak: it is. I just watch stuff all day and feel worse
Shreya: I'm going to the library cafe with Rukhsar and Mohan on Saturday. come
Deepak: they don't even know me
Shreya: they will. they're nice. and if it's awkward we'll leave together
Deepak: ok. maybe
Shreya: not maybe. I'll pick you up at 4 🙂
Deepak: ok. thanks for asking

Where is Shreya going on Saturday?
To the library cafe with Rukhsar and Mohan.
What was Deepak feeling on admitting the weekends alone weren't a choice?
Deepak felt lonely and low, cut off from the group.
What did Shreya do that helped Deepak act on the loneliness?
Shreya named Deepak's feeling, gave a specific invitation and offered a pick-up, making it easy to say yes.
What would change if Shreya had only said "hope you feel better"?
Deepak would probably stay home alone, since a concrete invitation was what Deepak needed to take the first step.

Read this:

"Vikas, look at this." Damini spread a row of cloth scraps on the table.
"Pink, yellow, brown… so?"
"Onion skins, turmeric, tea. From our kitchen bin."
"You dyed cloth with rubbish?"
"With biology." Damini, twenty-one, grinned. "Remember my microbiology class? Some bacteria fix colour better than salt does. And fashion is drowning in chemical dyes."
"So you're mixing lab stuff with clothes."
"And food waste. That's the idea. A dye kit for small tailors."
"Does it wash out?"
"The tea one does. The turmeric doesn't. I'm testing."
Vikas picked up the yellow scrap. "Can you make this blue?"
"Not yet," she said. "Give me a month."

What did Damini use to dye the cloth?
Onion skins, turmeric and tea from the kitchen bin.
What was Damini feeling as she showed Vikas the scraps?
She felt excited and proud of an idea that combined her different interests.
What would help Damini develop the idea further?
Keep testing which dyes last, and talk to small tailors about what they actually need.
How does Vikas see Damini's project?
He's sceptical at first, then curious enough to ask for a new colour.

Read this:

Age ten: Ishita and Bidisha called each other "Professor Pencil" and "Captain Crumbs" and doubled over laughing. Then a third girl joined in and joked about the way Bidisha stammered on a word. Bidisha went quiet and stared at her shoes. Ishita stopped laughing, walked over and said, "Sorry, that wasn't okay. Are you all right?"

Age fifteen: Anand's school trip was cancelled because of rain. "Great, just great," he said flatly, tapping his pen. His friend Ishita looked up from her phone and asked, "Are you joking, or actually upset?" Anand exhaled. "Upset. I'd saved up for it."

Age twenty-four: Bidisha joined a team overseas and cracked a dry joke about her own hopeless cooking. Two colleagues smiled politely; one looked puzzled. She noticed the silence, gently added, "That was meant to be funny, not a complaint," and afterwards kept to lighter, kinder jokes until she knew the group better.

What did Ishita say to Bidisha after the third girl joked about the stammer?
Ishita said, "Sorry, that wasn't okay. Are you all right?"
How do the three scenes show humour being read differently as people grow up?

At ten a joke turns hurtful when Bidisha goes quiet, at fifteen sarcasm hides real upset until Ishita asks whether Anand is joking, and at twenty-four Bidisha finds that a dry joke travels badly to a new team and watches reactions before joking again.
What was Anand probably feeling when he said, "Great, just great"?
Anand was disappointed and frustrated about the cancelled trip, and his flat voice covered how upset he really was.
What did Bidisha do well when her joke met a polite silence?
She noticed the reaction, clarified her intent gently, and switched to lighter jokes until she knew the group.
What does "convince" mean in English?

To convince means to make someone believe something or agree to do it. It is a verb.
Example: Aditi convinced her friends to join the clean-up.

Read this:

"Yogesh, you're doing civil too, right? All four of us together!"
"I… I guess, Sachin. Everyone is."
"You don't sound sure."
"I'm sure. It's safe. We'll help each other."
Eight months later, in the hostel corridor.
"Yogesh, surveying lab starts in ten minutes."
"I'm not going."
"What? Why?"
"Sachin, I don't like any of it. Soil, concrete, load. I sit there and feel nothing."
"Then why did you pick it?"
"Because you all did. I thought being with friends would be enough."
"What do you actually like?"
Yogesh looked at the floor. "Writing. I used to write stories. I never even checked if there was a course for that."
Sachin sat down next to him, quiet.

What does Yogesh say he used to do?
"Writing. I used to write stories."
How does Yogesh feel about the civil engineering subjects?
He feels flat and unhappy, saying he sits there and feels nothing.
What could Yogesh do now?
Talk to a college counsellor about his interest in writing and what options exist, rather than just skipping labs.
How might Sachin feel hearing this?
Sachin seems shocked and sad, sitting quietly, perhaps realising the group's choice didn't suit everyone.

metadata.subtype: Approach: follows friends into the same course without checking his own interest [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Final-year exams, part-time job, a project that wouldn't end. I'm Disha, and last winter I forgot how to laugh.
My flatmate Ira noticed first. "You used to sing in the shower. Now you just shower like a robot."
She dragged me to an open-mic comedy night at a café. I didn't want to go. I sat at the back with my arms crossed. Then a nervous boy did five minutes about his grandmother's forwarded good-morning messages, and I laughed so hard I snorted.
Something unlocked. I started drawing silly cartoons again on Sunday mornings, just for me.
My marks didn't drop. If anything, I focused better. I now think fun isn't a reward for finishing work. It's part of how I keep going.

Where did Ira take Disha?
To an open-mic comedy night at a café.
How was Disha feeling before the comedy night?
Disha felt worn out and flat, reluctant to go and sitting with crossed arms.
What did Disha learn about balancing work and fun?
That play isn't just a reward after work but part of what keeps a person going, so it needs a regular place.
How might Ira feel seeing Disha laugh again?
Ira would likely feel relieved and happy that her flatmate came back to life a little.

Read this:

Tuesday night

The Chandigarh offer came today and my heart did a little dance. New city, bigger title, mountains on weekends. I wanted to reply YES before dinner.

Then I remembered what I promised myself after the last rushed move: feelings first, then facts, then decide.

Feeling: excited, with a tiny knot of worry underneath.
Facts for: a better role, and a team lead who answered all my questions honestly.
Facts against: rent there is higher, and the raise barely covers it. And the knot? It's Nirmala Aunty, my landlady here, who has called me "beti" and sent up parathas since the day I moved in.

So the excitement is real, and so is the knot. Tomorrow I'll ask about a better salary and call two people who work there. Then I'll decide.
Gurpreet

What does Nirmala Aunty send up?
Parathas.
What does the 'tiny knot of worry' tell Gurpreet?
It points to real facts, the higher rent and leaving Nirmala Aunty, so the excitement isn't the whole picture.
What steps is Gurpreet taking before deciding?
Asking about a better salary and calling two people who work there, so the choice rests on facts as well as feelings.
How might Nirmala Aunty feel if Gurpreet moves?
She would probably miss her a lot, while still being glad for her new role. 🤍

Read this:

Daniel had just found the chorus on his electric guitar when the knock came. Mr Chidi Eze from downstairs stood there in his security-guard uniform, eyes red. "Son, I work nights. Every afternoon, it comes through my ceiling." Daniel's face went hot. Every afternoon? He practised one hour. Other flats had dogs, babies, a man who drilled on Sundays. Why was it always him? He almost shut the door. Instead his mum, drying a pan, asked what times Mr Eze slept. Nine till three, he said. Daniel stared at the floor. "I could play after four," he muttered. "And with headphones before that." Mr Eze's shoulders dropped. "That would help me a lot." Next week Daniel left a note under his door: amp off till four. It came back with a smiley face drawn on it and the word thanks.

What hours did Mr Eze sleep?
He slept from nine till three.
Why did Daniel almost shut the door on Mr Eze?
He felt unfairly singled out and defensive, because other flats made noise too and he only practised for an hour.
What made the compromise work?
Asking about Mr Eze's sleep hours turned the complaint into facts, and a clear time plus headphones respected both Daniel's practice and the neighbour's rest.
What is it like for Mr Eze when the guitar comes through his ceiling?
After working nights he is exhausted, so noise during his sleep feels hard to bear, and Daniel's offer brings him real relief.

Read this:

Snow had turned the path outside Fernhill Primary into grey glass. On Monday, Layla came in with her arm in a sling, and the violin she had practised for the winter concert stayed in its case.
"She's always running," Nkechi whispered to her table. "That's what happens." It felt true the moment she said it. Careful people didn't get hurt. Nkechi was careful. So Nkechi was fine.
At break, Layla's gran came to the gate with a flask of cocoa. "We were walking so slowly," she told the teacher. "Holding hands, even. The ice didn't care."
Nkechi pulled her scarf higher. She thought of her own careful feet on the same path that morning, and of how much she had wanted to be right.

What happened to the violin Layla had practised for the concert?
The violin stayed in its case because Layla came in with her arm in a sling.
Why did it feel good to Nkechi to say Layla was always running?
It made Nkechi feel safe and in control: if only careless people get hurt, then careful Nkechi is protected.
What might help Nkechi the next time someone gets hurt?
Nkechi could ask what happened before deciding whose fault it was, and offer help, like carrying Layla's bag.
How might Layla feel if she heard the whisper?
Layla would likely feel hurt and blamed, already sad about missing the concert and now judged for an accident on the ice.

He had already locked up his safe, and made preparations for going home. He had left his desk, brought out his two greasy office candlesticks and stood them in line with the snuffers on a slab near the door, ready to be extinguished; he had raked his fire low, put his hat and great-coat ready, and was beating himself all over the chest with his safe-key, as an athletic exercise after business.

How did the man prepare to go home?
He locked up his safe, left his desk, set two greasy candlesticks and the snuffers in line near the door, raked his fire low and put his hat and great-coat ready.

Read this:

You asked what I'd do if it happened in our group, Indu. It already did, last month, so I'll just tell you. I'm Vidya, and I was scared the whole time, just so you know.
Someone posted a photo of Mariam asleep on the bus with a cruel caption, and then everyone added stickers. I felt sick. I didn't add anything, and I didn't forward it, even when someone asked, “Did you see?”
That evening I messaged Mariam alone: “I saw. Are you okay?” She said she was fine. Ten minutes later: “Not really.”
I took screenshots of the whole thread, names and times showing, and showed Amma before bed. She messaged Mehta Ma'am right then. Next morning I told Mariam, “Let's go to Ma'am together. You don't have to talk, I'll start.” She came. Ma'am read everything, called Mariam's mother from the staffroom, and by lunch the posts were gone.
Mariam sits with me at lunch now.

What did Mariam reply ten minutes later?
Not really.
How was Vidya feeling while all this happened?
Vidya felt scared the whole time and sick at the stickers, but still acted.
What else could Vidya have done when someone asked "Did you see?"
Simply not respond, or say privately that it isn't funny, staying out of the pile-on while adults handled it.
What was it like for Mariam to get a message from Vidya alone?
It let Mariam admit to not being fine and gave her company going to the teacher, which made asking for help possible.

metadata.subtype: Approach: helping a friend who is being targeted [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the girls' hostel, Madhuri had the only alarm clock in Room 12, and three times she had promised to wake Ayesha for early swimming practice. Three times she had slept through it, and Ayesha had been scolded by the coach for coming late. The fourth night, Madhuri said, 'Tomorrow for sure. Trust me.' Ayesha felt a small, sad hardness in her chest. She smiled and said, 'Thanks, but I'll manage.' Then she asked the warden to lend her a wind-up clock and set it herself. It rang in the dark. Madhuri was snoring. Ayesha tucked Madhuri's blanket back over her foot and went to practice on time. At lunch they still shared pickle and giggled over comics. Ayesha just didn't trust Madhuri with her mornings any more.

Which room were they in?
Room 12.
What was Ayesha feeling when Madhuri said 'Trust me'?
Sad and wary; after being let down three times, she no longer believed the promise.
How did Ayesha protect herself while staying kind?
She borrowed a clock and woke herself, but still shared lunch and jokes with Madhuri.
How might Madhuri feel if she noticed Ayesha's new clock?
Perhaps a bit embarrassed, realising her broken promises had cost Ayesha's trust.
The festival of lights is marked by lighting lamps, bursting crackers and exchange sweets. Check the list.

The festival of lights is marked by lighting lamps, bursting crackers and exchanging sweets.
Why: List items after "by" need the same form (exchanging).
"Jab main chhota tha, tab hum gaon mein rehte the." English mein kya hoga?
It is: "When I was small, we lived in a village."
Isme "used to live" bhi chalega kya?
Yes. "We used to live in a village" is also correct. It shows that this was true in the past but is not true now.

Read this:

The school van would honk in five minutes. Abhinav buttoned his shirt fast, but one side hung lower. His brother Farhan, putting on shoes, pointed. "You're crooked." Abhinav looked down, groaned, undid every button and started from the bottom. The van honked just as he did the top. "Straight!" he said, running out.

How long until the van honked?
Five minutes.
What was Abhinav feeling when he groaned?
He was frustrated and worried about being late.
What else could Abhinav do when time is short?
Start from the bottom button every time, so he gets it right the first time.
How does Abhinav's fix look to Farhan?
Farhan sees his brother fix it quickly and make the van in time.
My new cooker has a "hob". Is that the same as a "stovetop"?

Yes. It is the flat top part where you put pots to cook. "Hob" is British, and "stovetop" is American.
Examples: Put the pan on the hob. Put the pan on the stovetop.

Read this:

You look sad that your friends are all online tonight, beta. Let me tell you about when I was eleven. I'm Anjali, your aunt. My friends, Joseph and the others, had started playing one online game every evening, and if I didn't join I felt lonely, like a chair nobody sat in. So I joined, for hours. Afterwards my head felt heavy and I was grumpy with everyone at home. I noticed that. So one Sunday I said, "Joseph, come play tag outside, just for an hour." He grumbled, but he came, and two others followed. We were sweaty and loud, and I felt lighter. We still played online sometimes, but not every evening.

Who did Anjali ask to come and play tag outside?
She asked Joseph to come and play tag outside.
How did Anjali feel when she was not part of the online game?
Lonely, like a chair nobody sat in.
What did Anjali try instead of joining every evening?
She noticed how she felt after long screen time and invited her friends to play outside.
How might Joseph have seen Anjali's invitation to play tag?
He grumbled at first, so he may have been reluctant, but he came, which suggests he was willing to be asked.

Read this:

Sahil: made my first cake in the hostel kitchen 🎂
Binita: without a recipe??
Sahil: didn't need one, I just felt it. looked golden, smelled right, took it out
Binita: did you do the toothpick test
Sahil: the what
Binita: poke the middle. if it comes out wet, it's not done
Sahil: ...
Sahil: it's soup inside
Binita: 😅 okay I've baked every weekend for six years and I still check
Sahil: but you always know just by looking
Binita: because I've been wrong about two hundred times and checked every single time
Sahil: so my gut is useless
Binita: your gut is new. bake every Sunday, check every time, note what you got wrong. by summer it'll be better
Sahil: ok. sunday cake club
Binita: bring me a slice

How long has Binita baked every weekend?
For six years.
Why did Sahil feel no need for a recipe?
Sahil felt sure and a bit proud because the cake looked golden and smelled right, and without experience that feeling seemed like enough.
What would you advise Sahil for the Sunday baking?
Keep checking every cake with the toothpick and write down what went wrong, so each try gives honest feedback.
What is it like for Binita when Sahil says Binita knows just by looking?
Binita seems amused and wants Sahil to understand that a quick sense like Binita's comes from being wrong many times and checking every time.

How can I make my handwriting neater?
I saw "equanimity" in a story. What does it mean?
What is wrong with this sentence? "Their going to win the match."

1. Write slowly and keep your letters the same size. Use lined paper and practise a few lines each day.
2. Equanimity means calmness of mind in a difficult moment. It is a noun.
3. Corrected: They're going to win the match. Why: "they're" means "they are", while "their" shows ownership.

Read this:

I'm Vasudha. I sat across from Tejas the morning the promotion email came. The team lead post went to Kunal, who had joined a year after Tejas. I watched Tejas read the email, go very still, and close his laptop. He walked out for twenty minutes. When he came back he was red around the eyes, but he went straight to Kunal's desk and said, "Congratulations. You'll be good at it." I couldn't tell you what he felt. In the team meeting that afternoon, when Kunal presented the new plan, Tejas asked two sharp questions, and I tensed. But they were fair questions, and then he offered to take the hardest client. A week later he booked a meeting with our manager; I heard he asked, "What would I have needed to show?" He didn't sulk in the pantry the way some of us would have. I'm still not sure how he did it.

Who got the team lead post?
Kunal.
What might Tejas have been feeling when he went very still and walked out?
Tejas was probably hurt and envious, maybe angry, and stepped away to calm down before reacting.
Which of Tejas's actions turned envy into something useful?
Taking time out, congratulating Kunal, asking fair questions, volunteering for the hardest client, and asking the manager what he would need to show.
How might Kunal have felt when Tejas congratulated him?
Kunal was probably relieved and grateful, perhaps a little awkward, knowing Tejas had wanted the role.

The mobile tower on the water tank gave Kamal two bars if he stood by the fertiliser sacks, so that was where he read Rhea's messages every night.
Four months of good-mornings. Voice notes in a soft accent from abroad. She called him her gentle farmer.
Tonight the message was different. "Kamal, I'm in hospital after an accident, my cards are blocked. I need 60,000 by morning or they won't treat me. I have no one else."
His hands went cold. He pictured her alone and hurt. The money in the shop account was meant for the monsoon stock. He sent it anyway, at 1 a.m., before he could think.
By morning her number no longer existed.
When Manjula Bhabhi asked at breakfast why he looked ill, he said it was the heat. He couldn't say it aloud, that the gentle voice had never been real. So he reported nothing, and the silence sat on him all day.

Where did Kamal stand to get a signal?
He stood by the fertiliser sacks, where the tower gave two bars.
What was Kamal feeling when the emergency message arrived?
He felt cold with fear for her, picturing her alone and hurt, which pushed him to act before thinking.
What could Kamal still do the morning after?
He could tell Manjula Bhabhi, report the fraud quickly to the cybercrime helpline and his bank, and remember that being fooled by professionals is not a personal failure.
What would change if Kamal had told Manjula Bhabhi at breakfast?
He would have support instead of carrying the shame alone, and reporting quickly might give a better chance of help.

Sarika, you asked how I stayed sane after failing stats. Okay, so, I'm Lavanya, second-year psych, and the funny part is we'd literally studied explanatory style that semester. Didn't stop my brain. The result came, 38, and my head went: you're stupid, you'll never do research, everyone knew but you. I cried in the library washroom, honestly. Then that night I thought, fine, I'd tell a client to check the evidence, so check it. I opened the paper. Lost marks on regression, all of them, and I'd missed both regression classes for my cousin's wedding. The descriptive stats section? Full marks. So, other explanation: not 'stupid', just two missed classes. And one change: I booked the professor's office hours for Tuesday and asked for the regression notes. I wasn't happy, Sarika. I was still upset. But I was upset about something real and small, not something huge and made up.

Why did Lavanya miss both regression classes?
Lavanya missed both regression classes for a cousin's wedding.
What was Lavanya feeling right after the result came?
Lavanya felt crushed and ashamed, with thoughts like 'you're stupid' and 'you'll never do research', and cried in the library washroom.
What would you advise Sarika to take from Lavanya's approach if Sarika fails an exam?
Look at the actual paper to see where the marks were lost, find the real cause and choose one step, like booking office hours, instead of believing the harsh first story.
How might the professor see Lavanya coming to office hours for regression notes?
The professor would likely see a student taking the failure seriously and working on a specific gap, not someone who has given up.
Help me invite my relatives to a surprise dinner for my parents' 30th wedding anniversary. It is at our house on Saturday at 7 pm. Keep it to about 40 words, and ask guests to keep the secret.

Dear all,
You are warmly invited to a surprise dinner for my parents' 30th wedding anniversary. It will be at our house this Saturday at 7 pm. Most importantly, please keep it a secret! We hope to see you there.

Kunal, you're asking me how to know if you're ready to marry Leena. Your Hemant mama can't tell you that. But I can tell you what Asha and I did.

Before we said yes to the families, we went for a long walk on Juhu beach, every Sunday for a month. Each week, one topic. Where we'd live. Whether she'd keep working. Children, and when. My parents, and hers, and who we'd look after when they got old.

The third week, we fought. She wanted to live near her mother, and I wanted to go wherever my job took me. We walked the whole beach in silence.

But we came back the next Sunday. We found a middle: two years in my city, then we'd decide again.

Better to fight on a beach, Kunal, than across a dining table with two children watching. That month was the turning point.

Where did Hemant and Asha walk every Sunday?
On Juhu beach.
How did Hemant feel during the silent walk after their fight?
He was probably tense and worried, unsure whether they could agree about where to live.
What turning point in the story does Hemant point to?
That month of Sunday talks, especially coming back after the fight and finding a middle path about where to live.
How might Asha have felt about her wish to live near her mother?
She likely felt strongly about it and anxious at first, but respected when they found a compromise.

When Ma'am said, "Spelling test after the break," Rashmi's stomach twisted into a tight knot. Her heart thumped so hard she could feel it in her ears.
She looked at Aadhya, who was humming and swinging her legs. How could she be so calm? Something bad must be coming. Rashmi's hands went cold and sweaty at the same time.
At break she didn't eat her paratha. She sat on the bench and whispered the words again and again: necessary, necessary. The letters kept jumbling.
"Are you sick?" Aadhya asked.
"I think so," Rashmi said. Her tummy hurt so much, it must mean the test was dangerous somehow. That's what it felt like. Like a dog about to bite.

What did Rashmi not eat at break?
Her paratha.
Why did Rashmi think the test must be dangerous?
She felt so scared, with a knotted stomach and thumping heart, that her body's alarm seemed like proof of danger.
What could help Rashmi in this moment?
A teacher or parent could explain that the knot is her body's alarm, not a sign of danger, and help her take slow breaths.
What might Aadhya think when Rashmi says she might be sick?
Aadhya may be puzzled and a little worried, not knowing how frightened Rashmi feels about the test.

So, Meghna, you want to know why I'm at the gym at seven? It's a long story, but I'm Kalyani and you're my oldest friend, so sit. When Pankaj left for his internship in Hyderabad in May, I fell apart. Not heartbreak; nothing happened between us. I just realised I didn't know what to do with myself. For a year he'd chosen our films, our food, even whether I should cut my hair. When he didn't reply for four hours, my whole mood dropped. On day three I cried because I couldn't decide what to have for dinner. That's when I thought: this isn't love, this is leaning so hard I've forgotten how to stand. So I started small. Joined the gym. Called you. Picked up the sketching I'd dropped in second year. When Pankaj came back, I told him all of it. He said, 'You seem more you.' I think that's the best thing he's ever said.

Where did Pankaj go for his internship?
To Hyderabad, in May.
What did Kalyani feel on day three of Pankaj's internship?
Kalyani felt lost and helpless, crying over not being able to decide what to have for dinner.
What small steps helped Kalyani stop depending so heavily on Pankaj?
Joining the gym, calling Meghna, and picking up sketching again.
How does Pankaj see Kalyani when he returns?
He says Kalyani seems 'more you', noticing a fuller, more independent self.

Read this:

In the school hall, Bidisha, nine, recited the poem for the class competition perfectly on Friday. She had learnt it the night before, all twelve lines, repeating them until midnight.

On Monday, her teacher Naveen sir asked her to recite it again for the parents' visit.

Bidisha stood up. "The river runs... the river runs..." She couldn't remember the second line. Her face went hot.

Naveen sir smiled kindly. "You learnt it all in one night, didn't you?"

She nodded, eyes stinging.

"Try five minutes a day for a week next time. It'll stay."

That week she practised the new poem a little each day. The next month, she could still say every line.

How many lines did the poem have?
Twelve lines.
How did Bidisha feel when she forgot the second line?
She felt embarrassed and upset, with her face hot and her eyes stinging.
What did Naveen sir suggest, and why did it help?
He suggested five minutes a day for a week, which helped the poem stay in her memory much longer.
How might Naveen sir have felt when Bidisha forgot the line?
Naveen sir likely felt sympathetic and wanted to help her learn a better way.

Read this:

Monday. Sunaina realised she had attached last year's price list to a client's quote. She told nobody, hoping the client would not notice.
Wednesday. The client asked why the prices looked old. Vikas, her manager, asked what had happened, and Sunaina said, "The template must have changed." Vikas looked at her for a moment and said nothing more, and the client call was tense.
Next Monday. Sunaina caught another slip, a wrong date on a quote. Within an hour she went to Vikas: "I put the wrong date on the quote. I've fixed it, I've called the client, and I'll resend by noon." Vikas said, "Thanks for telling me right away," and went back to his screen. Her stomach was tight, but it eased.

What did Sunaina attach to the client's quote on the first Monday?
Last year's price list.
What was Sunaina likely feeling when she said "The template must have changed"?
She was probably anxious about being blamed and wanted to avoid it, though she may also have been trying to buy time.
What did Sunaina change the second time, and why does it help?
She reported the slip within an hour with the fix and a time, so Vikas could trust her and plan.
How might Vikas have seen her Wednesday answer?
Vikas may have doubted it, since he looked at her and said nothing more, though he may simply have been waiting for more.

How does the narrator get food here, and what does the man think of her?

"Will you give me a piece of bread? for I am very hungry." He cast on me a glance of surprise; but without answering, he cut a thick slice from his loaf, and gave it to me. I imagine he did not think I was a beggar, but only an eccentric sort of lady, who had taken a fancy to his brown loaf. As soon as I was out of sight of his house, I sat down and ate it.
She simply asks him for bread, and he cuts her a thick slice. She thinks he took her for an odd lady, not a beggar.

Read this:

I was on the other bed pretending to do my maths when Didi called Ritu. I'm not sure what Damini was feeling; her hand kept smoothing the bedsheet flat. She didn't text it, which I thought she would. She said, "Ritu, I need to tell you something properly. I don't feel the same any more, and I don't want to mislead you."
There was a long quiet on the other end. Didi didn't say "maybe later" or "it's not you, it's me", or anything about Ritu being clingy, which she had grumbled to me about before. She just said, "You were good to me. I'm sorry this hurts." Then she listened.
After the call she sat with her face in her hands. I brought her a glass of water. She said, "That was the hardest ten minutes of my life," and I believed her.

What was the narrator pretending to do during the call?
The narrator was on the other bed pretending to do maths.
What might the narrator have been feeling while watching Damini make the call?
The narrator seems tense and protective, noticing her hand smoothing the sheet, and caring enough to bring water afterwards.
Which parts of Damini's call made the ending clear and kind?
She called instead of texting, said plainly that she didn't feel the same, left out excuses, blame and 'maybe later', and then listened.
What is Ritu likely experiencing on the other end of the call?
Ritu is probably hurt and stunned, hence the long quiet, but is spared false hope and insults, which may make healing easier later.

"Timer's done, Ramesh," Kishore said, holding out his hand for the tablet.

"Just one more video!"

"Tomorrow. That was the deal."

Ramesh, five, stamped, then gave it back. "Papa, in the ad, the boy drank juice and flew. Can I fly?"

Kishore sat down. "Can people fly?"

Ramesh thought. "No. Only birds and planes."

"So the ad is pretend. They want you to buy juice."

"Tricky ad," Ramesh said, frowning. Then he went to play with his blocks.

What did the boy in the ad do after drinking juice?
He flew, according to Ramesh.
How did Ramesh feel when the timer ended?
He felt frustrated and wanted more, stamping his foot before handing the tablet back.
What did Kishore do that helped Ramesh understand the ad?
He asked Ramesh whether people can fly and let him reason it out, then explained the ad simply.
How might Kishore have felt when Ramesh handed back the tablet and worked out the ad?
Kishore probably felt pleased and relieved that Ramesh kept the deal and figured out for himself that the ad was pretend.

I'm Rashmi, and I play on our college's women's cricket team, so I saw the men's selection from the next net. Samir had been the best opening batsman in the trials all week; he hit the ball cleanly and never lost his wicket cheaply. On Friday the list went up. Samir wasn't on it. Instead there was Karan, who had got out for nothing twice. Everyone knew Karan's uncle and the coach had grown up in the same village and still went to each other's weddings. I don't know what the coach was thinking. Maybe he felt he owed that family. I can even understand that; my own father would do almost anything for his cousins. But I saw Samir's face when he read the list, and then I saw him quietly pack his kit and leave before practice.

Who was the best opening batsman in the trials?
Samir had been the best opening batsman in the trials all week.
What does Samir quietly packing his kit suggest about how he feels?
It suggests he is hurt and discouraged, feeling his good performance did not count against a family connection.
What could the college do to keep selection fair?
It could publish trial scores and have more than one person on the selection panel, so a single coach's family ties cannot decide.
How might Karan feel knowing the reason for the selection?
Karan might feel uneasy or less proud of the place in the team, knowing others think it came from family ties rather than batting.

At the birthday party in the Kochi apartment clubhouse, two-year-old Jomon had been fine all afternoon. By seven he was clinging to his uncle Sumit's leg, crying at the balloons, and throwing himself on the floor when offered cake. A woman at the next table tutted. Sumit knelt. Jomon's eyes were red and heavy, and he kept rubbing them with his fists. "You're sleepy, aren't you?" Sumit picked him up and walked out to the quiet corridor. Within five minutes Jomon was asleep on his shoulder.

Where did Sumit carry Jomon?
Out to the quiet corridor.
What does Jomon rubbing his eyes suggest?
It suggests he was exhausted, and the crying came from tiredness, not naughtiness.
What did Sumit do instead of scolding?
He noticed the tired signs, picked Jomon up and took him somewhere quiet to sleep.
How might the woman who tutted see Jomon?
She may have seen a badly behaved child rather than an overtired one.

What do the count and Simon see when they gallop out of the wood?

The count and Simon galloped out of the wood and saw on their left a wolf which, softly swaying from side to side, was coming at a quiet lope farther to the left to the very place where they were standing. The angry borzois whined and getting free of the leash rushed past the horses' feet at the wolf.
They see a wolf on their left, swaying softly as it lopes toward the place where they stand. The angry borzois break free of the leash and rush at it.

Counsellor's note from Usha, after sessions with Sarita, 24.

Sarita came in months after her grandmother died. She had meant to visit that weekend but stayed back for an office deadline. She spoke of it as if it were a crime. "I chose work over her," she kept saying.

Over several sessions, we talked about what she knew at the time: her grandmother had seemed well, and the deadline had felt urgent. I asked her what she would say to a friend in the same place. She was quiet, then said, "I'd tell her it wasn't her fault."

Last week she brought a photo of her grandmother and said she'd started writing her letters. She said, "I'm trying to forgive myself. Some days I can."

Next step: continue, and ask about her support at home. — Usha

Why had Sarita stayed back instead of visiting her grandmother?
For an office deadline.
What does Sarita's statement 'I chose work over her' reveal about her feelings?
She blamed herself harshly, feeling guilt and resentment toward herself for missing the visit.
How did Usha's question about a friend help Sarita?
It helped her see her situation with the same kindness she'd offer someone else, easing her self-blame.
How might Sarita's grandmother have seen the missed visit, if she could have?
She'd likely understand and not want her granddaughter to carry such guilt. 🤍

Sunday night

Eleven months of flat-hunting. Shalini and I were both exhausted, and last night we snapped at each other over a parking space in a flat we hadn't even bought.
Today my brother Lokesh came for lunch and asked, "What exactly are you looking for?" We rattled off the list: near Shalini's office, two bedrooms, a school nearby, a lift, within budget.
"And have you seen flats with all of that?"
"Yes, maybe five."
"Then why are you still looking?"
We had no answer. So we made a rule, right there at the table: from now on, the first flat that meets every must-have and is within budget, we take. No "one more viewing".
Next Saturday we'll go back to the list and look at what's open.
Writing this, I feel lighter than I have in months.
— Yogesh

What did Lokesh ask at lunch?
He asked, "What exactly are you looking for?"
How does Yogesh feel after making the rule?
Yogesh feels lighter and relieved after months of exhausting searching.
What else could Yogesh and Shalini add to their rule?
They could set a deadline, such as deciding within a month, so the rule is backed by a clear end point.
How might Shalini be affected by the new rule?
Shalini may feel relieved too, since fewer viewings mean less tension and fewer arguments.

Pranav: whoa. did you tell your parents?

Ishita thought of working at the phone repair counter.

Ishita is worried about the fees while Papa's shop is slow, and wants to help the family.

Asif did his homework at the back of the waiting room of his father's small clinic, as he did every weekday. Yash's sleepover was on Saturday, and the question had been sitting in his throat all afternoon. At five the room was full: a crying baby, an old man coughing, the phone ringing. His father came out twice, rubbing his forehead, and took a call standing in the corridor. "Not now," Asif thought. "If I ask now, I'll get the tired answer." He waited. At home after dinner, his father leaned back with his tea and started talking about a cricket match. Asif slid in beside him. "Abbu, Yash has invited me to sleep over on Saturday. His parents will be home. Can I go?"

Where did Asif do his homework?
At the back of the waiting room of his father's clinic.
What was Asif thinking when he decided 'Not now'?
He was worried that a tired, busy father would say no, so he chose to wait for a calmer mood.
What else could Asif add when he asks?
The details Abbu might want, such as Yash's parents' number, so the decision is easy.
How might Abbu feel being asked after dinner?
Relaxed and more ready to listen than he was in the rush of the clinic.

Joseph, you're struggling with your wife and your mother in the kitchen? Let me, Vinita, your grandmother, tell you what I learned as a new bride in Kottayam.
My mother-in-law cooked everything. Every meal, every day. If I tried to make even the fish curry, she would take the spoon from my hand. At first I thought she didn't trust me.
Then one evening I saw her sitting alone after dinner, when everyone had praised the fish. Her face was so happy. And I understood: it wasn't about me. After her husband died, the kitchen was where she still mattered.
So I stopped trying to take it over. I asked her to teach me her fish curry. Then I asked her to plan the Sunday lunches, while I did the weekday cooking.
She became my best friend in that house, Joseph. Look for what the demand is protecting.

Where was Vinita a new bride?
In Kottayam.
What did Vinita realise about her mother-in-law's feelings after seeing her sit alone after dinner?
Vinita realised the mother-in-law felt happy and valued when cooking; after being widowed, the kitchen was where she still felt needed.
What was the turning point in Vinita's story, and what choice followed?
The turning point was seeing the mother-in-law's happy face after dinner; Vinita chose to ask to learn her recipes and let her plan Sunday lunches instead of resisting.
How might the mother-in-law have felt when asked to teach the fish curry?
She likely felt respected and needed, which is why she later became like a best friend.

On Sunday afternoon in their village near Nalgonda, Kamal spread his building blocks on the mat. His cousin had given him the set, and he wanted to make a tractor like his uncle's. The wheels kept falling off. He tried a longer axle. Still wobbly. He tried two small blocks instead. Better. His tongue poked out at the corner of his mouth. The hen pecked outside. His mother Lakshmi called, "Kamal, lunch!" He didn't hear. She called again, then came and stood behind him. The tractor had a trailer now, and a tiny driver. "You forgot to eat," she said, smiling. Kamal looked up, surprised. The sun had moved across the whole courtyard.

What did Kamal want to build?
A tractor like his uncle's.
What does Kamal's surprise when he looked up suggest about how he felt while building?
It suggests he was completely absorbed and happy, so focused on solving the wobbly wheels that he lost track of time and food.
Why did the tractor keep Kamal so focused?
The problem was just hard enough; each fix, like the longer axle or two small blocks, needed thought but was within his skill.
How does Lakshmi seem to feel seeing Kamal so absorbed?
Lakshmi seems amused and fond, smiling rather than scolding, as she sees how deeply he was playing.

Short breaks absorb delays and keep a tired mind working well. Because tasks often take longer than expected and a tired mind works badly, gaps keep delays from piling up and help us do better work.

Sit down, Eshaan. Your Chinmay Chacha has lost more than one pitch, you know.
When I was twenty-four I failed the state services prelims. I didn't leave my room for three days. Then, for weeks, I swung between two stories. Story one: I'm just not smart enough. Story two: the paper was unfair, the questions changed, bad luck.
My old teacher, Joshi-ma'am, made me write a list. Three questions. What was in my hands? I never did full mock tests with a timer. I read, but I didn't practise. What was luck? Yes, the pattern changed that year. Everyone got the same luck, though. What would I change? Timed tests, every Sunday.
That list was the most useful thing I wrote that whole year, Eshaan. Not because it made me feel better. Because it told me what to do.
So. Your pitch. Get a paper.

How many days did Chacha not leave his room after failing the prelims?
He didn't leave his room for three days.
How did Chacha feel during the weeks he swung between two stories?
He felt stuck and discouraged, thinking either he wasn't smart enough or it was all bad luck, and neither story let him move forward.
What is Chacha advising Eshaan to do about the lost pitch?
He wants Eshaan to write down what was in his hands, what was luck and what to change, so the failure turns into clear next steps.
What might Eshaan be feeling as his Chacha tells this story?
Eshaan may feel comforted that an elder he respects also failed, and ready to look at the pitch honestly instead of just feeling bad.
I'm making a pookalam for Onam this year, but I'm not sure how to start.
What a cheerful tradition. Which flowers do you have?
Yellow marigolds, white jasmine and some red ones.
Sketch a circle with chalk on the floor, divide it into rings and fill each ring with a colour. Start from the centre and work outwards, pressing petals gently so they stay.
Can I make a pattern, like a star?
Yes. Mark the points of the star first with chalk, then fill the shape with one colour and the background with another. Keep the lines neat by using small petals along the edges.
The star came out lopsided.
That's easy to fix. Brush the petals aside gently and redraw the guide lines with chalk, using a ruler or string for straight edges.

Daycare note, Holi week.

We set out bowls of dry colour for a hand-printing activity. Anand, two, reached for the pink bowl before his turn. I said, "Wait, Anand. My turn first." He pulled his hand back and watched.

Later he stroked our rabbit, Motu, with one finger, very softly, saying "Nice."

At snack time he told me "Potty!" in time. Great week. — Deepika

What did Anand say while stroking the rabbit?
He said "Nice."
How might Anand have felt waiting for his turn?
Anand was probably eager and impatient, but he managed to pull his hand back and wait.
How could Deepika keep supporting Anand's gentle, patient behaviour?
Keep giving short, clear instructions and praise him when he waits or handles animals softly.
How might Motu the rabbit be affected by Anand's soft stroking?
Motu would likely stay calm and comfortable being touched so gently.
I will meat you at the station at six. Is that the right word?

I will meet you at the station at six.
Why: "meet" means come together; "meat" is food.
Rain is the only thing that makes the water tank overflow here. The tank is overflowing. Did it rain?
Yes, it must have rained. Because rain is the only thing that makes the tank overflow here and the tank is overflowing, the rain is the cause.

It was the Saturday before Diwali, and the whole flat was upside down for cleaning. I was on the sofa with my board-exam sample papers when Papa asked me, for the third time, to take down the curtains. I shouted, "Can't you see I'm studying? I'm so stressed!" He shouted back, and I stormed off. Later I texted Irfan: "My dad is so controlling. He just loves yelling." Irfan wrote back, "Didn't you yell first?" I typed, "That was different, I was under pressure." That night I heard Papa tell Mummy, "The boy has become so rude, Lalit never listens. And I'm only tense because the painters come on Monday." I lay awake thinking: he says I'm rude and he's tense. I say I'm tense and he's rude. We were both describing the same afternoon.

What did Papa ask Lalit to take down?
The curtains.
Why did Lalit think his own shouting was fine but Papa's was controlling?
Lalit felt the stress of the sample papers from the inside, so his own shouting seemed justified and angry Papa seemed controlling by nature.
What could Lalit try the next time an argument starts?
He could pause and ask what pressure Papa might be under, like the painters coming on Monday, and say his own stress calmly instead of shouting.
How does Papa see the same afternoon?
Papa sees his own shouting as tension about the painters and sees Lalit as having become rude, the mirror image of Lalit's view.

I'm Gurleen, Kishore's cousin, and we grew up in the same building in Ludhiana. This year he applied to exactly one master's programme, in Milan. "Why waste fees on backups?" he said. "They'll take me." When his mother suggested two more colleges, he laughed. He even told his manager he'd be leaving in August and sold his old bike to a neighbour. I didn't say much. He sounded so sure, and I don't really know how admissions work. The email came on a Tuesday. Rejected. He didn't come down for dinner for two days. When I finally knocked, he said, "I never even thought about this happening." I don't know what he's planning now.

How many master's programmes did Kishore apply to?
Kishore applied to exactly one master's programme, in Milan.
Why does the rejection hurt Kishore so much?
He never allowed any doubt and had already told his manager and sold his bike, so the rejection lands with no plan and nothing to cushion it.
What could Kishore do differently when planning the next round?
He could keep his hopes but add a margin: apply to a few programmes, keep his job until an offer comes, and ask what he'd do if the first choice says no.
How does Gurleen feel watching this happen?
Gurleen seems sad and a little guilty for staying quiet, and unsure how to help now that Kishore is shaken. 🤍

Monday. Kavitha, twenty-five, took the 8:10 metro, sat at desk 42, and updated the same three spreadsheets. At lunch Thomas asked about her weekend. "Fine," she said. It was. Nothing was wrong. Everything was just grey.
Two Mondays later. Same metro, same desk. She noticed she couldn't remember a single thing from the week before. That night she watched five episodes of a show she didn't like, eating chips from the packet, until the laptop went hot on her knees.
A month later. She scrolled until two most nights now. It was easier than thinking. Thomas mentioned a pottery class near the office. "Maybe," she said, and knew she wouldn't go. Monday was waiting. Monday was always waiting.

What seat number was Kavitha's desk?
Desk 42.
How was Kavitha feeling by two Mondays later?
She felt dull and tired of the sameness, not sad, just grey, and numbed herself with shows.
What could Kavitha try instead of scrolling until two?
She could take one small step to break the pattern, like trying the pottery class Thomas mentioned, or talking with someone about how flat things feel.
How might Thomas see Kavitha over the month?
Thomas might notice she seems distant and flat, and mentioning the pottery class could be a way of trying to help.

My name is Nikita. In Class Five I got a low mark in the maths test, and I put the paper at the bottom of my bag. The paper needed my mother Arohi's signature. Every evening I told myself, "Tomorrow." At dinner I talked very loudly about anything else. The paper felt heavier each day, like a stone I had to carry to school and home again. On the fifth day, my mother stopped stirring the dal and said, "You've been quiet in a strange way. Is something on your mind?" My voice shook. I took out the paper. She said, "Thank you for showing me. Let's look at it together," and I cried a little.

Where did Nikita put the maths paper?
At the bottom of the bag.
What was Nikita feeling every evening while saying "Tomorrow"?
Afraid and burdened. The paper felt heavier each day, like a stone Nikita had to carry.
What made the first admission easier for Nikita?
Arohi stopped stirring, asked calmly what was on Nikita's mind, and then said "Thank you for showing me. Let's look at it together."
How might Arohi have felt watching Nikita talk loudly about anything else?
Concerned and puzzled. Arohi noticed the strange quiet and gave Nikita a calm chance to say what was wrong.
Use the passive and leave out who did it: Someone cleaned the classroom before the inspection.
The classroom was cleaned before the inspection.

Nikita's left arm was in a sling and her phone had shattered in the collision, but the insurer's leaflet on the hospital table said to inform them within a set time. Her brother Anand read it aloud twice.
"We need to do this properly," she said, "even from this bed."
First, the police report. The traffic police had come to the scene; Anand went to the station that afternoon with her licence, the car papers and her statement, and brought back a copy of the report.
Second, the insurer. From Anand's phone, Nikita called the helpline, gave the policy number from the glovebox papers and the report number, and wrote the claim number on her hand with a pen because there was no paper.
Third, the records. Anand saved every hospital bill in a folder and she asked him to photograph each receipt as well. The photos from the scene were on his phone already.
By evening the claim was registered, well within the time.

Where did Nikita write the claim number?
She wrote it on her hand with a pen because there was no paper.
How was Nikita likely feeling in the hospital bed, and what shows her determination?
She was likely in pain and worried, yet determined, saying they needed to do it properly even from the bed.
What else could Nikita do to keep the claim smooth?
She could keep a simple list of every call and document sent, with dates, so any follow-up questions are easy to answer.
How might Anand feel being Nikita's hands for the day?
Anand probably feels useful but stretched, running to the police station and handling bills while worried about his sister.

Incubator mentor's note: Siddharth and Mohit, month four

Their start-up has three employees and very little money. They want to hire one sales person. Siddharth showed me their process: five rounds, a psychometric test, a case study, a presentation to "the leadership team", and reference checks. He told me it was copied from a large consulting firm he admired. In practice, the leadership team is Siddharth and Mohit. They have spent three weeks on it; the two strongest candidates accepted other offers while waiting. Mohit looked tired and said he had written the case study twice. I asked them what their company actually needs from this hire, and suggested they design a process that fits three people, not three thousand.

How many rounds did their hiring process have?
Five rounds.
What does Mohit's tiredness suggest about how he feels?
He seems worn out and frustrated, having written the case study twice for a process that isn't working.
What else could Siddharth and Mohit do to hire faster?
Hold one real conversation about the sales role and a short paid trial, focusing on what their company needs.
How might the two strong candidates have seen the process?
They likely felt it was slow and oversized for a tiny start-up, so they accepted other offers.

List the key points of this diary entry as three bullets.

Diary, Sunday 9 June. Did it. Told Ma and Papa I'm taking the Bengaluru job and moving out in August. I'd been waiting for the right time for a month. Last Saturday was Papa's cousin's engagement: impossible, the whole family there. On weekdays Papa comes home wrecked from the site and just wants dinner and the news. Tanuja said, "Dhruv, do it after Diwali," but that's months away, and festivals are worse. So I picked today. After lunch, Tanuja out at her class, the house quiet, phones on the table, fan on. Just the three of us with chai. I asked if we could switch the TV off for a bit. Papa looked surprised, then did. Ma cried a little. Papa asked a lot about rent. But nobody shouted, and nobody had to put on a show for guests. They had room to actually listen.

- Dhruv told Ma and Papa about taking a Bengaluru job and moving out in August.
- Dhruv chose a quiet Sunday afternoon, when Tanuja was out, because other times seemed worse.
- Ma cried a little and Papa asked about rent, but nobody shouted, and they had room to listen.

The wedding hall in Hyderabad was noisy, and Hemant was at a table of strangers when the conversation turned to family. He began to describe his sister's hospital stay in detail, then his father's debts, his own doubts, and the fight with his cousin. Ganga, next to him, listened but saw the others' polite smiles going stiff. She touched her plate and said gently, "Hemant, we could talk about this outside later, if you like." Hemant stopped, cheeks warm. Outside, on the steps, he said, "I think I said too much." Ganga said, "You needed to talk. Just not with everyone at once." She stayed until he felt steadier.

Where did Hemant start telling his family story?
Hemant was at a table of strangers at the wedding hall in Hyderabad.
What did Hemant feel outside on the steps, and what does it suggest?
Hemant felt embarrassed and said he thought he had said too much, and his warm cheeks suggest he was flustered. It also suggests he needed to talk to someone.
What did Ganga do that helped?
Ganga gently suggested talking outside later, listened on the steps and stayed until Hemant felt steadier.
How might the strangers at the table have felt as Hemant told the details?
They may have felt uncomfortable or unsure how to respond, since their polite smiles went stiff.
Arjun has Rs 60. A pair of sandals costs Rs 32. Does he have enough?
Yes, he does. Because 60 is more than 32, so he would have 28 left, since 60 - 32 = 28.

When Mr Duarte announced that each class in their Lisbon school would pick a mentor for the fifth graders' reading club, Beatriz ruled Jamal out at once. Tall, hood always up, earphones in, slang in every sentence: the type who ends up outside the head's office. "He'll scare them," she told her friend, and volunteered herself instead. On Thursday Jamal came along only because the library was warm. Within ten minutes, Beatriz's group of ten-year-olds was fidgeting, and Jamal's was silent, leaning in, as he did the voices of three pirates. One small girl wouldn't let go of his sleeve at the end. "I read to my little brothers every night," he said, shrugging, when Beatriz stared. She walked home turning it over, slightly embarrassed.

What did Jamal do to hold the children's attention?
He did the voices of three pirates.
Why was Beatriz so surprised by Jamal in the library?
She was surprised, and a little embarrassed, because his hood, earphones and slang had seemed like proof he was trouble, yet he was the best reader there.
What could Beatriz try before ruling someone out next time?
Give the person a chance to show what they can do, or ask them, instead of deciding from clothes and slang.
How might Jamal feel if he knew why Beatriz ruled him out?
He might feel hurt and judged, since he reads to his little brothers every night and was dismissed for his hood and slang.

The maths test was in five minutes, and the fan in Class 4B had stopped with the power cut. On the board, Sir had written the last example: 7 × 8 = 54. Tenzin stared at it. He knew his tables. Seven eights were fifty-six. But Sir was Sir. Sir had been teaching for thirty years. Tenzin's hand half rose, then dropped. What if he was wrong and everyone laughed? What if Sir got angry? Omkar, beside him, whispered, "Is that right?" Tenzin shrugged. When the test came, question six was 7 × 8. Tenzin's pencil hovered. He wrote 54. At the end of the day, the marked papers came back. Tenzin had a red cross on question six.

What had Sir written on the board?
Why did Tenzin write 54 even though he knew the answer was 56?
He felt afraid to question Sir, mixing respect and fear, and worried that everyone would laugh or Sir would get angry.
What small step could Tenzin try next time a teacher's answer looks wrong?
He could quietly ask after class, "Sir, I thought seven eights are fifty-six, can you check?", which respects the teacher and still checks the fact.
How might Sir feel on finding the red crosses came from his own mistake?
Sir might feel embarrassed and sorry, and wish a child had pointed out the slip before the test.

Read this:

Thursday, late.

Had a fight at lunch today. My friend said Santosh was rude to that reporter in the clip, and that his last film was boring. I said the reporter must have deserved it and the film was a masterpiece, and I didn't speak to my friend for the whole break. Everything Santosh does is right, I told myself.

But at home I watched the clip again, and he really did snap at her for no reason. Something in my stomach turned. I felt like a traitor for even thinking it. Maybe I can love his songs and still think that was wrong. Maybe he's a person and not a god. I'll say sorry to my friend tomorrow.

- Lalit

What did Lalit say about the reporter at lunch?
Lalit said the reporter must have deserved it.
Why did Lalit feel like a traitor when watching the clip again?
Lalit felt guilty and torn: Lalit had always defended Santosh, so admitting that Santosh snapped for no reason felt like disloyalty, even though it was clearly wrong.
How can Lalit keep admiring Santosh's songs in a healthy way?
Lalit can enjoy the songs while allowing disagreement, and remember that Santosh is a person who can be wrong.
How might Lalit's friend have felt at lunch?
The friend was probably annoyed or hurt at being ignored for the whole break, having only shared a fair point.

Sahil: bro you awake
Mridul: ya. exam stress?
Sahil: no. career stress 😩
Sahil: dad wants me to do CA like him
Mridul: and you?
Sahil: i want to be a chef. i know it sounds silly
Mridul: it doesn't. you made that biryani for my bday. everyone still talks about it
Sahil: but chef is long hours, low pay at first
Mridul: so is CA at first
Sahil: true 😅
Mridul: what are you actually good at?
Sahil: cooking. numbers too tbh. managing stuff
Mridul: restaurant owner then? 🤔
Sahil: …ok that's actually not bad
Sahil: i'll ask the hotel school about their open day

What did Sahil make for Mridul's birthday?
That biryani.
What was Sahil feeling when he called being a chef "silly"?
Sahil felt unsure and a bit embarrassed, worried the dream wouldn't be taken seriously.
What helped Sahil think more clearly?
Mridul's question about Sahil's real strengths, which led to an idea combining cooking and numbers.
How might Sahil's father react to the restaurant idea?
He might be doubtful at first, but could see that Sahil's number skills still matter.
What do you call a baby cow, a baby dog and a baby cat? Answer on one line with commas.
calf, puppy, kitten

The peer-rating portal closed at 11:59 p.m., and Santosh opened it at 11:48, the hostel Wi-Fi crawling. One question per teammate: "Rate their overall contribution, 1 to 5."
For Hansa, his finger went straight to 2. She had missed the last two meetings and replied late on the group chat all of last week. The final presentation had felt like it was all on his shoulders.
The page buffered. While it spun, Santosh's eye fell on the project folder. Hansa's name was on the survey design, the first three chapters and the data cleaning in August. All of it before October.
The clock said 11:55. Santosh's finger hovered. "She checked out at the end," he muttered, and clicked 2 anyway. The page loaded: Submitted.

What was Hansa's name on in the project folder?
The survey design, the first three chapters and the data cleaning in August.
Why does Santosh still click 2 after seeing the folder?
The missed meetings and late replies are the freshest memories and still sting, so they feel like the real picture, and with the clock running out he doesn't stop to weigh August.
What could Santosh do before rating next time?
Open the form early, list what each teammate did month by month, and then give a score that covers the whole semester.
How might Hansa feel when she sees a 2 for the semester?
She might feel it's unfair, since she built the survey, three chapters and the data cleaning, and only slipped near the end.

Note to Nazia's parents, Class 3
I've noticed a pattern on the days Nazia buys sweets from the canteen at break. For about half an hour she is very excitable: running in the corridor, talking over others, unable to sit. Then, by the last period, she is tired, tearful and irritable, and she struggled with her reading today. On days she has her lunch box from home, she seems steadier. I'm not suggesting a ban on treats; she enjoys them, and that's fine. Perhaps a filling breakfast and a packed snack like chana or fruit, with the canteen sweet saved for Fridays, might help her energy last the day. Happy to talk.
Anand, class teacher

What does Nazia buy from the canteen at break?
Sweets.
How does Nazia seem to feel by the last period on sweet days?
She seems tired, tearful and irritable.
What does Anand suggest instead of a ban?
A filling breakfast, a packed snack like chana or fruit, and saving the canteen sweet for Fridays.
How might Nazia's parents feel reading this note?
They may feel grateful for the observation and relieved that the teacher is not asking them to ban treats.

How does Tanvir Ma'am help Sudha learn?

In her second week at the marketing firm, Sudha sat beside Tanvir Kaur for forty minutes over a spreadsheet. "Try it first, then I'll show you," Tanvir Ma'am said. It was the first real task Sudha had been given: the client's monthly report. When the numbers came out wrong, Tanvir Ma'am did not sigh. She circled one cell and asked, "What do you think happened here?" Sudha found the slip herself. On her last Friday, Sudha asked shyly for a reference and for feedback, and Tanvir Ma'am listed two things to work on. That evening Sudha texted a friend that she wanted to be exactly like her manager, then paused and wrote her own plan: message every month, prepare for the other interview, finish her own project.
She lets Sudha try the task first and, when the numbers are wrong, asks what she thinks happened instead of sighing. She also gives honest feedback, listing two things to work on.

I'm Vikas, twenty-two, the eldest of four, and I don't remember a time I wasn't in charge. When Papa's shop closed, I was sixteen. I started tutoring kids after school so my brothers' fees got paid. I learned to fix the pump, fill in forms, talk to the bank. Everyone says, "Vikas is so responsible, just like his father." My father, Ramesh, pats my back. And I am proud of it. But last month a friend asked me what I want to do, just me, and I couldn't answer. I stood in the shower for ages that night, so tired I couldn't think. I think somewhere I stopped wanting things. I'd like to find out what they were.

How old was Vikas when Papa's shop closed?
Sixteen.
How did Vikas feel when asked about wanting something just for Vikas?
Vikas felt lost and very tired, unable to answer because those wants had faded.
What could Vikas try next to reconnect with those wishes?
Set aside a little time each week just for Vikas, and talk honestly with the family about sharing some duties.
How does Ramesh seem to see Vikas?
Ramesh seems proud, patting Vikas on the back for being so responsible.

The night before Makar Sankranti, kites were stacked in the corner of the small-town house. Ujjwal, five, wouldn't go to sleep.

"Mummy, the kite demon will cut my kite tomorrow."

His mother Swati sat on the bed. "The kite demon? Tell me about him."

"He's in the sky. He has a big knife."

Swati nodded. "That sounds scary. Do you know what really cuts kites?"

Ujjwal shook his head.

"Other people's kite strings. That's the game. There's no demon. And if your kite gets cut, we'll have more."

Ujjwal thought about it. "So the demon is just a string?"

"Just a string," Swati said, and tucked him in.

What does Swati say really cuts kites?
Other people's kite strings.
Why couldn't Ujjwal go to sleep?
He felt scared that a kite demon would cut his kite the next day.
Why did Swati's answer calm Ujjwal down?
She listened, didn't mock him, and gave a simple true explanation, plus a reassurance about having more kites.
How might Swati feel tucking Ujjwal in?
Swati probably feels tender and relieved that he's calmer.

So you want the story of me and Eshaan? Okay. I'm Trisha, and this is not a happy ending, just an honest one. Second year, my birthday dinner. Eshaan said he'd come. At nine he texted, "Sorry, stuck," and I saw on the group story that he was at another friend's party. It hurt. A lot. And did I tell him? No. I just got a little quieter. I didn't join the Diwali trip. I said I had assignments when they went for chai. I kept thinking, it'll wear off, I don't want to be dramatic. And every time I skipped a plan, I felt this little rush of relief. No awkward talk. No crying in front of him. But the relief was the trap. By the end of the year, we were just people who liked each other's posts. Last month, he messaged, "Did something happen between us?" I still don't know what to say.

What did Eshaan text at nine on Trisha's birthday?
He texted, "Sorry, stuck."
Why did each skipped plan give Trisha a rush of relief?
Skipping meant no awkward talk and no crying in front of Eshaan, so avoiding the hurt felt easier than facing it.
What could Trisha do now that Eshaan has asked what happened?
Trisha could answer honestly and name the birthday dinner, since Eshaan's question is an opening to repair things.
How might Eshaan see the way the friendship faded?
Eshaan may feel puzzled and sad, noticing the distance but not knowing what caused it until now.
