Read this:

Sunday night
I've felt weird for weeks. Not sad exactly, just heavy, and my chest gets tight before school every morning. Today I skipped Binita's birthday because I couldn't face people. That's not me. I used to love parties.
I searched online about it, and the pages said a lot of scary things that made me feel worse. So I stopped.
Binita texted: "Missed u. U ok?" I almost wrote "yes" but I wrote "not really." She said to talk to someone older.
So I'm going to tell Bade Papa tomorrow. He's calm and doesn't make things into a drama. My hands shake just writing this. But I think I need someone to help me work out what's happening.
Harish

Whose birthday did Harish skip?
Harish skipped Binita's birthday.
How is Harish feeling while writing this entry?
Harish feels heavy and anxious, with a tight chest before school, and scared enough to shake at the thought of telling someone.
Why is telling Bade Papa a better step than searching online?
The online pages made Harish feel worse, while a calm trusted adult can listen and help Harish reach proper help.
What might Binita be feeling when Harish replies "not really"?
She is probably worried but also glad Harish was honest, which is why she encourages Harish to talk to someone older.
Write an invitation, about 60 words, for my daughter Ishita's 7th birthday party. It is on Sunday at 4 pm at Green Park Club, and the theme is jungle animals. It is from Sunita and Prakash.

You are invited!
Ishita is turning seven, and we are having a jungle animals party. Come dressed as your favourite animal and join us for a fun afternoon.
Date: Sunday
Time: 4 pm
Place: Green Park Club
Please let us know if you can join us. We can't wait to see you!
Warm regards,
Sunita and Prakash
Write a description, around 90 words, of a night market in a city that never sleeps.

By ten at night, the old part of the city should be asleep, but the night market is just warming up. Bright bulbs hang over rows of stalls selling kebabs, falooda, fried fish and steaming bowls of noodles. Smoke from the grills drifts over the crowd. College students share plates of chaat, while taxi drivers sip tea between rides. A man sells glowing toys that spin in the air. Music plays from somewhere. Even at midnight, the lanes are full, as if the whole city is too hungry to sleep.
There are 3 apples on the table and you take away 2. How many apples do you have?
You have 2 apples. Because the question asks how many you have, and you took 2; the 1 left on the table is not yours.
Who laid the first brick of our town's old clock tower?
I'm not sure, as that is a very specific local fact. The town museum or library may have records.

What does the speaker tell Jane to do whenever she imagines Mr. Rochester thinks well of her?

"Whenever, in future, you should chance to fancy Mr. Rochester thinks well of you, take out these two pictures and compare them: say, 'Mr. Rochester might probably win that noble lady's love, if he chose to strive for it; is it likely he would waste a serious thought on this indigent and insignificant plebeian?'"
He tells her to compare the two pictures and remind herself that he could win a noble lady's love. So he would hardly think seriously about a poor, unimportant girl like her.

At dusk the village hens were scattered all over the lane. Chaitanya saw the coop door swinging open. His daughter Deepika, five, stood by the neem tree with her hands behind her back.
He did not ask, "Who opened it?" He crouched and said, "The hens are out. The truth matters more to me than hens. What happened?"
Deepika's lip shook. "I wanted to hold the brown one. I forgot to close it."
"Thank you for telling me," he said. "Now let's catch them before dark." They chased the hens together, Deepika laughing.

Where was Deepika standing when Chaitanya saw the open coop?
She stood by the neem tree with her hands behind her back.
What does Deepika's shaking lip show?
It shows she was scared of being scolded for letting the hens out.
What made it easy for Deepika to confess?
Chaitanya avoided asking who opened it, said the truth mattered more than hens, thanked her, and then fixed the problem with her.
How might Deepika feel about her father after the evening?
She would likely feel relieved and close to him, laughing as they chased the hens, and safer telling the truth next time.

In their Nashik flat the tap water came only from six to seven, and every morning Jatin needed Nilesh up to fill the drums. "Nilesh! Six o'clock! Get up!" A grunt. At 6:20 Jatin banged on the door. "Useless boy!" Nilesh stumbled out, filled one drum in silence, and slammed the bathroom door so hard a bucket toppled. That night, after a colleague mentioned how teenagers' sleep runs late, Jatin knocked softly. "Can we make a deal? You're up at 6:15, and no shouting from me. Your phone goes to the hall at 10:30." Nilesh looked at him for a long second. "And no 'useless'?" "No 'useless'." The next morning at 6:15, Nilesh was at the tap, yawning, but talking.

When did the tap water come?
From six to seven.
What does Nilesh's question, "And no 'useless'?", reveal?
He had been hurt by the word more than by being woken, and he wanted to feel respected as part of the deal.
Why did the deal work better than banging on the door?
It set a steady wake time and a phone cut-off both could agree on, and dropping the insult protected their relationship.
How does Jatin see the morning fights after talking to his colleague?
He begins to see Nilesh's grunts as partly sleepiness rather than laziness, and chooses a deal over shouting.

Bao and Diego had shared a lab bench in Melbourne for a year before Diego asked.

"You pray before every exam. Every single one. Don't take this the wrong way, but why? You know the answers."

Bao felt the old urge to defend, to list reasons. He let it pass.

"It isn't really about the answers. My grandmother taught me. When I pray, I stop panicking and remember that I'm more than my marks. And I feel less alone."

"I don't believe in any of that," Diego said. "No offence."

"None taken. What calms you down?"

Diego grinned. "Running. Very badly."

They talked through the rest of the lunch break, about grandmothers, about fear, about the odd comfort of routines. Neither tried to change the other. Walking back to the lab, Bao realised he knew Diego better than he had in a whole year.

What does Diego do to calm down?
He runs, "very badly".
What was Bao feeling when Diego first asked his question?
Bao felt a flash of defensiveness, an urge to argue, which he chose to let pass.
What made Bao's answer work well?
He shared what praying means to him personally and asked about Diego in return, listening instead of trying to win or convert.
How does Diego likely see the conversation?
Diego seems relaxed and curious, able to say he doesn't believe without offence and ending up sharing his own ways to cope.

The shop would shut in fifteen minutes, rain was hammering the awning, and Papa had money for exactly one new school bag. "Vidya, take the blue one. You've earned it." Her brother Raghav, standing beside her with his torn strap knotted at the corner, said nothing. Vidya felt a warm glow, and then a twist in her stomach. That same afternoon Papa had proudly told the shopkeeper about her science fair prize. She turned to the shopkeeper. "Actually, Raghav built half the model. He did the wiring." Papa blinked. "Did he? Then Raghav, choose one too," he said, counting again. "We'll check for a smaller one." Raghav looked up, surprised and shy. Vidya let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding.

How much time was left before the shop shut?
Fifteen minutes were left before the shop shut.
What was Vidya feeling as she held the blue bag while Raghav stood beside her?
She felt warm about being valued but uneasy, because she noticed that Raghav's strap was knotted and he said nothing.
What did Vidya do that used her favoured position kindly?
She shared credit by telling her father and the shopkeeper that Raghav built half the model, instead of enjoying all the praise. 😊
How might Raghav have felt when Vidya spoke up?
Probably surprised and shy, and maybe relieved, since his work was finally mentioned and his father offered him a bag too.

Hi Tejas bhaiya,
Quick question, but first my big discovery. I checked the class result list with Riddhi. Of the nine people in our section who scored above 90 in science, seven go to Sharma Sir's coaching. SEVEN. So I've decided coaching is the secret, and I need to join from next month. Can you help me convince Papa? He says it's expensive and I should try harder on my own first.
I know Riddhi said those seven also sit in the front row, finish homework on the bus, and have parents who come to every PTM. But they all have coaching in common, right? That has to be what does it.
Please reply before Sunday, because that's when I'm asking Papa.
Your favourite cousin,
Vinita

How many of the top science scorers go to Sharma Sir's coaching?
Seven of the nine people who scored above 90.
Why does Vinita feel so sure that coaching is "the secret"?

Vinita feels excited because seven out of nine sounds striking and coaching is the shared thing Vinita was looking for, so it feels like the answer while the front row and homework habits fade into the background.
What could Tejas bhaiya suggest in reply?
He could point out that those seven also study hard and have involved parents, and suggest Vinita try their habits for a while before asking Papa to pay.
How might Papa see this request?
Papa is thinking about the cost and wants Vinita to try harder first, so he may feel the 'seven out of nine' argument skips over effort.

Shalini had walked into Indu Amma's evening satsang in the middle of a dark year, with her marks slipping and her sleep gone. The teacher's steady kindness helped her through, and she felt deep thanks. She found peace and direction in the chanting, yet she watched for demands for money or pressure to drop family. She also noticed a habit: she rang Indu Amma before choosing a bus route, a college elective, even a shirt, and without an answer she felt lost. One day Indu Amma said, "You choose this one, and tell me how it went." Shalini picked her elective alone, and it felt strange and good.

Her friend Kamal had moved into another ashram and stopped answering his mother's calls. When Shalini visited, she saw peace on his face. She also heard that questions were not welcome there and that a large donation would help him grow. She felt afraid for him. At tea she did not attack his teacher. "I have missed you," she said. "What do you love about it?" He talked for an hour. Before leaving she said, "My door is open whenever you want to talk." Kamal said nothing, but he saved her number in his phone.

Whom did Shalini ring before choosing a bus route?
She rang Indu Amma before choosing a bus route.
How was Shalini's relationship with Indu Amma different from Kamal's with his ashram, and what did Shalini watch for?

Shalini's thanks sat alongside clear eyes, and Indu Amma encouraged her to choose alone. Kamal's ashram discouraged questions, hinted at a large donation and left him cut off from his mother, the signs Shalini watched for.
What was Shalini feeling when she heard that questions were not welcome at Kamal's ashram?
She felt afraid for Kamal and worried about where it could lead.
What did Shalini do that helped keep the door open with Kamal?
She stayed warm, asked what he loved about the ashram without attacking his teacher, and told him her door was open.

Monday. Dhruv says the big gulmohar by the society pond is "only for brave people". Kishore says he'll climb it tomorrow. He can't stop thinking about it all through maths.
Tuesday. After school the whole gang waits. "Scared?" Dhruv asks. Kishore climbs past the fork, onto the thin branch over the water, and hears it crack. He can't go forward or back. The watchman props up a ladder and talks him down while everyone goes quiet. His shin is scraped from knee to ankle, and his new school shoes are full of pond mud.
Saturday. Kishore sits out the cricket match with a bandaged shin. When Dhruv mentions the tree again, Kishore shakes his head. "I wanted you lot to stop calling me scared. Now I'm just scraped."

Who helped Kishore down from the tree?
The watchman propped up a ladder and talked him down.
What might Kishore have been worried about during maths on Monday?
He was probably anxious about the climb and about looking scared in front of Dhruv and the gang if he backed out.
What would you change first if you were Kishore on Monday?
I would not promise to climb at all, and say the branch looks too thin; backing out before the gang gathers is much easier than on the day.
What was it like for Dhruv and the gang when the branch cracked?
They went quiet, which suggests they were frightened once the dare turned into real danger.

metadata.subtype: Approach: accepting the dare to prove courage [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Last term my friend Shankar went quiet for almost three weeks. He stopped coming to the canteen and muted the class group chat. I was certain I'd caused it. The week before, I'd missed his street play because of an internal exam, and I'd sent a thumbs-up instead of a proper message. Every time I saw him, a wave of guilt came so heavy it felt like a confession. I wrote apologies in my notes and never sent them. When I finally sat next to him on the library steps and said I was sorry about the play, he frowned. 'Sarika, you messaged. That was fine.' His father had lost his job, and he'd been working evenings. My guilt hadn't been evidence of anything. Looking back, it was a sign of how much the friendship mattered to me, which is a much better thing to act on.

Why had Sarika missed Shankar's street play?
Sarika missed it because of an internal exam.
Why did the guilt feel like a confession to Sarika?
Sarika felt heavy with guilt over the thumbs-up, and because the feeling was so strong it seemed to prove wrongdoing, even without any evidence from Shankar.
What could Sarika do sooner next time?
Sarika could ask the friend how things are going early on, and treat guilt as a question to check rather than proof to apologise for.
What were those three weeks like for Shankar?
Shankar was dealing with his father losing his job and working evenings, so his silence had nothing to do with the missed play.

metadata.subtype: Feeling guilty so must be guilty [Actor]

messages.content:

At the agricultural training centre in a small town near Thrissur, Shankar, twenty, had avoided writing the soil report for a week. Words slipped around on the page. His classmates typed fast. That evening, under the tamarind tree, he spoke his whole report into a voice-to-text tool on his phone, sentence by sentence, about the red soil, the paddy, the drainage. Next morning he knocked on Jomon Sir's door, his heart thumping. "Sir, I have a reading difficulty. I did it by voice. Is that allowed?" Jomon read it twice. "Allowed? This is the best drainage plan in the batch." Shankar walked back to the fields with his shoulders straight.

What was Shankar's report about?
It was about the red soil, the paddy and the drainage.
How was Shankar feeling as he knocked on Jomon Sir's door?
He felt nervous and embarrassed, his heart thumping, worried that the voice tool might not be allowed.
What did Shankar do that others with similar difficulties could learn from?
He used a voice tool to show his thinking and then honestly told his teacher about his difficulty and asked about it.
How does Jomon Sir see Shankar's work?
Jomon Sir sees it as excellent, calling it the best drainage plan in the batch and fully accepting the method.

In the course of the tale I had mentioned Mr. Lloyd as having come to see me after the fit: for I never forgot the, to me, frightful episode of the red-room: in detailing which, my excitement was sure, in some degree, to break bounds; for nothing could soften in my recollection the spasm of agony which clutched my heart when Mrs. Reed spurned my wild supplication for pardon, and locked me a second time in the dark and haunted chamber.

Why does the narrator's excitement break its bounds when telling about the red-room?

The narrator never forgot that terrible episode. Nothing could soften the memory of the sharp agony felt when Mrs. Reed refused the plea for forgiveness and locked the child a second time in the dark, haunted room.

In the clinic waiting room, Pooja was bored. The queue was long. Lalremsiami, her mother, handed her an empty paper cup from the water cooler. Pooja held it to her ear. 'Hello, Nani?' Then she put it on her finger. 'This is a tiny hat.' She turned it upside down on the chair. 'A cake! Happy birthday, Mumma.' A boy nearby watched, so she made it a trumpet and tooted.

What did Lalremsiami hand Pooja?
She handed her an empty paper cup from the water cooler.
What was Pooja feeling at the start, and how did it change?
She started bored by the long queue, then became playful and absorbed as she invented new uses for the cup.
Why was giving Pooja a plain cup a clever idea?
A simple object leaves room for imagination, so Pooja could turn it into a phone, hat, cake and trumpet.
What might the boy nearby be thinking as he watches?
He may be curious and amused, and perhaps wish he could join her game. 🙂

At the warehouse, our team got a bonus for every month with 'zero incidents'. The first near-miss I didn't report was small: a pallet slipped off the forklift and missed Pallavi's foot by a hand's width. Our supervisor said, 'Nobody's hurt. Don't spoil the record for the whole team.' I told myself he was right. The second time a shelf wobbled, I said nothing without even being asked. By the fourth, I was the one telling new people, 'We sort these things ourselves.' Then Pallavi fractured her wrist when that same shelf finally came down. She reported everything, including the earlier near-misses, and the shelves were all checked that week. I'm Vishal, and I still can't forgive myself for how easy each silence got.

What was the team's bonus for?
Every month with 'zero incidents'.
How does Vishal feel looking back?
Vishal feels deep guilt and regret, unable to forgive how easy each silence became.
What could Vishal have done at the first near-miss?
Reported it despite the supervisor's words, so the shelf could have been checked before anyone was hurt.
What was it like for Pallavi to report everything after her injury?
Painful and probably lonely, going against the team's record, but necessary to stop further harm.

"Santosh, you asked what a new teacher should do when a child comes for help. Let me tell you two stories. My first year as a teacher, a girl named Rekha came to me crying. 'Ma'am, I can't cope.' I said, 'Everyone is stressed, study harder.' She never came to me again. I think about her still. Years later, a boy named Imtiaz knocked on my staff room door. I remembered Rekha. I put down my pen. I said, 'Thank you for telling me.' I let him speak without interrupting. Then I walked him to the counsellor myself, and we called his mother together. He finished school and still sends me a card each Diwali. That first answer, Santosh, decides everything." Kavitha folded her hands.

What did Kavitha tell Rekha?
'Everyone is stressed, study harder.'
How does Kavitha feel about what happened with Rekha?
She feels regretful and still troubled, thinking about Rekha years later.
What choice in the second story made the difference?
Kavitha stayed calm, thanked Imtiaz, listened without interrupting and walked him to the counsellor, calling his mother.
How might Rekha have felt after Kavitha's reply?
Rekha likely felt dismissed and alone, which is why she never came back.

metadata.subtype: Adult receiving a request for help [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

The clinic waiting room in Lucknow was packed, and the wait had stretched to two hours. Sumit, whose father sat grey-faced on a bench, came to the reception counter and slammed down his token. "Two hours! Is this a hospital or a joke? Do you people even care?" His voice cracked on the last word. Abhinav felt his own heart speed up and a sharp reply rise, but he dropped his voice instead, slow and low. "You've been waiting a long time, and your father doesn't look well. I understand you're worried." Sumit was still loud. "Then do something!" Abhinav kept his tone steady. "I'll ask the duty nurse to check on him right now, before his turn. She'll come to the bench." He picked up the phone. Sumit's shoulders dropped a little. "Okay," he said, quieter. "Thank you." The nurse arrived two minutes later.

How long had the wait stretched to?
Two hours.
What was Sumit feeling when he slammed down the token?
Sumit was angry and frustrated, but his cracking voice suggests fear for his grey-faced father underneath.
How did Abhinav calm the exchange?
He lowered and slowed his voice, acknowledged the long wait and Sumit's worry, and took a concrete step by calling the duty nurse.
What would have changed if Abhinav had matched Sumit's volume?
The shouting would likely have escalated, others in the waiting room might have joined in, and Sumit's father would not have been checked any sooner.

In the first week of the polytechnic course, I was the only one who put a hand up and asked what "earthing" actually meant. I'm Indu, by the way, and I remember the lab going silent. Someone at the back muttered, "Didn't you do Class 10?" My face burned. But Mr Pillai drew a stick figure touching a wire, explained it slowly, and for the first time it clicked. Ganga, on the stool beside me, had nodded all through that lecture. That night she messaged me: "Can you explain earthing? I didn't get it either." Looking back, that question cost me thirty seconds of embarrassment. By the practical exam I had asked maybe forty more like it. Ganga later told me she spent the term copying my notes and hoping nobody noticed the gaps. I don't think I was cleverer. I was just less busy pretending.

What did Indu ask in the first week of the course?
Indu asked what "earthing" actually meant.
How did Indu feel right after someone muttered about Class 10?
Indu felt embarrassed, with a burning face, but kept listening and soon felt the relief of the idea finally clicking.
What could Ganga have tried during that lecture instead of nodding?
She could have raised her hand too, or caught Mr Pillai after class, rather than hoping nobody noticed the gaps.
How might Ganga look back on that term?
Ganga might feel some regret that hiding her confusion left her copying notes, and some gratitude that Indu's questions helped her as well.

The monthly meeting at the block development office in Kalol ran the way it always did. The BDO spoke for twenty minutes, the senior engineer for fifteen, the accountant for ten more. Sudha, a year into her job as a junior assistant, watched Trisha beside her lean forward three times with her notebook open, then sit back each time as another senior voice filled the pause. Trisha had the only data on which village handpumps had failed. Sudha had seen this at every meeting. Nobody was rude; there just never was a gap. When the accountant finally paused, Sudha raised her hand and said to the BDO, "Sir, could Trisha have two minutes? She has the handpump data." The BDO blinked, then nodded. Trisha's voice shook on the first sentence, then steadied.

How long did the senior engineer speak?
The senior engineer spoke for fifteen minutes.
What was Sudha feeling as she watched Trisha lean forward and sit back?
Sudha felt frustrated for Trisha and a little anxious, knowing the gap Trisha was waiting for would never come.
What made Sudha's request work?
She asked the person chairing, named exactly how much time was needed and gave a reason, so it was easy for him to say yes.
What was it like for Trisha to finally speak?
She was nervous at first, her voice shaking, then steadied, probably relieved that her data was finally being heard.
Why can good friends disagree even when they like each other very much?

Liking someone does not make people think alike, so even good friends disagree. Because each person has different wishes and opinions, disagreements will happen, and talking about them calmly can even make a friendship stronger.
The scientist did many researches on bees in the garden. Please correct.

The scientist did a lot of research on bees in the garden.
Why: "Research" is uncountable; use "a lot of".

January: Six months after his father's death from a long lung illness, Manoj quits his sales job and enrols in a nursing course. "I learned so much in those hospital nights," he tells his friend Tenzin. "I want to use it."
April: Manoj is top of his class in patient care. He works double shifts on the training ward and never talks about his father. Tenzin notices he hasn't taken a day off since January.
July: On the anniversary of his father's death, Manoj freezes by a patient's bed when the man coughs the same way. He goes into the staff room and sobs. His supervisor sits with him. That evening he calls Tenzin: "I think I've been working instead of grieving." They light a lamp together for his father.

What course did Manoj enrol in?
A nursing course.
What did Manoj feel when the patient coughed like his father?
He froze and then sobbed; the grief he had been working through instead of feeling came flooding back.
What does Manoj realise, and what might help?
That he has been working instead of grieving; keeping the nursing purpose while taking time off and marking the loss, as with the lamp, gives grief its own space.
What had Tenzin noticed by April?
That Manoj hadn't taken a day off since January, which worried Tenzin.

Read this:

This is kind of embarrassing, but here goes, since you asked on the podcast. I'm Santosh, seventeen. Last year I was going out with Hansa, and I thought I was a great boyfriend. I texted her all day. If she didn't reply in ten minutes, I'd get this burning feeling and send more. I got annoyed when she hung out with her cousin's friends. Then one day she said, 'It feels like a leash, Santosh.' I was so offended. I sulked for two days. Then I read our chats from start to finish. I sounded like a guard, not a friend. I apologised. We're not together now, but we're good friends. I learned trust means not checking.

What did Hansa say the relationship felt like?
She said it felt like a leash.
Why did Santosh feel a 'burning feeling' when Hansa didn't reply quickly?
He felt anxious and jealous, and he treated her silence as something to control.
What helped Santosh see the problem in his behaviour?
Reading their chats from start to finish let him see that he sounded like a guard, not a caring friend.
How might Hansa have felt during the months of constant texts?
She probably felt watched and pressured, less free to see friends without explaining herself.

From my flat across the corridor I've watched Dilnaz tutor for months. It started with Dolma, a Class 4 girl, twice a week. By January there were five children, every evening from five to eight, and I'd hear Dilnaz's own books opening at eleven. She looked pale in the lift. Once she fell asleep sitting on the stairs with a notebook on her knees. Then her pre-board marks came, and I heard her mother's voice through the wall, not angry, just worried. A few days later the schedule changed: only Dolma and one other child, only at weekends. Her father went to the school office to ask about the fee concession, and her mother told mine, "Her studies come first. We'll manage the rest another way." I can't say how Dilnaz felt. But the light in her room went off by ten after that.

How many children was Dilnaz tutoring by January?
Five children.
What does Dilnaz falling asleep on the stairs suggest?
It suggests she was exhausted and overstretched, with tutoring eating into her sleep.
Why was cutting the sessions and asking about the fee concession a wise balance?
It protected Dilnaz's sleep and revision while still looking for help, keeping education as the long-term priority.
How did the narrator see the change?
The narrator noticed the lighter schedule and the light going off by ten, while not knowing how Dilnaz felt inside.

Monday: Sumit glared at the fraction problems, eyebrows crunched together, pencil tapping. Vikas, his desk partner, had just borrowed his eraser. He slid it back quietly and shifted to the far end of the bench.

Tuesday: "Ma'am, Sumit's angry with me. He keeps giving me that look." Mrs Pillai watched Sumit frown at a word problem. "Sumit, what are you thinking about?" "Whether it's three-fourths or four-thirds." She turned to Vikas. "That's his working-it-out face. Sumit, maybe tell Vikas that."

Thursday: Sumit's brow knotted over long division. Vikas leaned in. "Thinking face or angry face?"
"Thinking face. Help me?"

What was Sumit trying to decide on Tuesday?
Whether it's three-fourths or four-thirds.
What was Vikas feeling when he slid the eraser back and moved to the far end of the bench?
Vikas felt worried and a bit hurt, believing Sumit was angry about the borrowed eraser.
What helped clear up the misunderstanding?
Mrs Pillai asked Sumit what he was thinking and explained that the face meant working it out, so Vikas could ask instead of guessing.
What would change if no one had asked Sumit about the frown?
Vikas might keep avoiding the desk, and Sumit could lose a partner without ever knowing why.

For a long time Pierre could not understand, but when he did, he jumped up from the sofa, seized Boris under the elbow in his quick, clumsy way, and, blushing far more than Boris, began to speak with a feeling of mingled shame and vexation.

How does Pierre react once he finally understands what Boris means?
Pierre jumps up from the sofa, seizes Boris under the elbow in his quick, clumsy way, and blushes even more than Boris. Then Pierre begins to speak with a mix of shame and annoyance.
A farm has 6 hens and each lays 2 eggs in a week. How many eggs is that?
12. Because 2 x 6 = 12, so they lay 12 eggs.

On the second Sunday of the month Usha took the train from her Pune flat to her parents' house. Over lunch her aunt said, "Why live alone when there's a room here?" Usha smiled and passed the salad. "Because I like my own place. But look at our whiteboard." On it, in Usha's handwriting: Usha pays the monthly grocery order and calls on odd days. Her brother Chaitanya handles the society meetings and bank visits and calls on even days. Wednesday evenings were Usha's pottery class, and nobody phoned then unless it mattered.
"We agreed this in March," Usha said. "If it gets heavy for anyone, we change it." Her father tapped the board and nodded, as if it were a contract everyone had signed.

What day of the month did Usha visit her parents' house?
Usha visited on the second Sunday of the month.
What was Usha feeling when her aunt asked why she lived alone?
She felt calm and sure of herself, shown by her smile and her explaining plainly that she likes her own place.
What made Usha's arrangement fair to the whole family?
The duties were agreed openly and split between Usha and her brother Chaitanya, with free evenings kept for Usha and a promise to change the plan if it gets heavy.
How might Chaitanya see the whiteboard plan?
Chaitanya likely finds it fair, since his tasks are written next to Usha's and the calls alternate on odd and even days.

Rain hammered the tin roof, so lunch was inside the classroom instead of under the neem tree. Forty tiffins opened at once in the damp air.
Zeenat lifted the lid on her ammi's dried-fish rice. The smell spread fast. Aadhya pinched her nose. “Eww, who brought fish?” Three boys at the back made gagging sounds and pointed.
Zeenat snapped the lid shut. She ate two biscuits from her bag instead and said she wasn't hungry.
The next morning she told Ammi she wanted bread and jam, like everyone else. Ammi looked at her for a long moment and packed it. Zeenat carried the tiffin to school feeling lighter and emptier at the same time.

Why was lunch inside the classroom?
Rain hammered the tin roof, so lunch was inside instead of under the neem tree.
What was Zeenat feeling as she carried the bread-and-jam tiffin?
She felt mixed: lighter because no one would tease her, but empty and a bit sad at giving up her ammi's food.
How could the teacher respond to the teasing at lunch?
The teacher could stop the gagging at once, say that every home cooks differently, and make sure Zeenat can eat her lunch in peace.
What might Ammi be thinking when she looked at Zeenat for a long moment?
Ammi probably guessed something had happened at school and felt sad, but chose to pack the bread and wait for Zeenat to tell her.

The night bus from Manali broke down near a dhaba at 2 a.m., in pouring rain, and the driver said it would take an hour. Lokesh, twenty, got off and stood under the tin roof. A young woman with a shaved head, tattoos up both arms and a heavy leather jacket stood nearby. Lokesh moved a step away without thinking. He expected her to be rude or trouble. Then an old man slipped on the wet steps. She was there first, holding his elbow, then asked the dhaba owner for a dry chair. "I'm Pema," she said later, handing Lokesh a cup of tea. "Nurse in Delhi." Lokesh took the tea and felt uneasy about that step he'd taken. He didn't make a big speech to himself. He just noticed it: tattoos, rude. Where did that come from? The bus coughed back to life.

What was Pema's job?
A nurse in Delhi.
How did Lokesh feel when Pema handed him tea?
Lokesh felt uneasy and a little embarrassed about the step he had taken away from her.
What did Lokesh do with his mistake that was healthy?
He noticed the assumption honestly and asked where it came from, without punishing himself or making a big speech.
What might it be like for Pema when strangers step away from her?
It may feel tiring and a bit hurtful, being judged by her tattoos and jacket before she has said anything.

I'm Raghav, Dhruv's neighbour in Dehradun. Dhruv's twenty-six. For the past year, I've seen him juggle everything. Every morning he helps his grandmother to the balcony, sets her tea and pills, and checks her blood pressure with the machine the doctor gave them. Then he goes to work, where he runs a solar project for mountain schools. On Sundays, three college juniors come to his flat, and he teaches them how to write project proposals. He also started a tree-planting group for our lane. I don't know how he doesn't collapse. Once I asked. He said, "Nani looked after me. The mountains looked after us. I'm just returning it." He laughed, but his eyes were tired.

What does Dhruv run at work?
A solar project for mountain schools.
What might Dhruv be feeling behind his laugh?
He may feel tired and stretched, but also committed and purposeful.
How could Raghav or others support Dhruv so he doesn't burn out?
They could share some tasks, like sitting with his grandmother or joining the tree planting.
How does Raghav see Dhruv's efforts?
Raghav is impressed and a little worried, noticing his tired eyes.

I'm Chandrika, and last March I typed my resignation in eleven minutes. Bhupen, my manager, had cut me off in the client meeting and taken credit for the design I'd spent three weeks on. I was shaking with anger at my desk. The email was ready, cursor on Send. Then I saw my reflection in the dark monitor, jaw tight, face red, and I thought: this isn't a decision, this is a temperature. I saved the draft and walked round the block twice. I didn't answer Bhupen's "all good?" message either. Next morning, calm, I read the draft again. Half of it was true. Half was just heat. Instead of resigning, I asked Bhupen for twenty minutes and told him, plainly, that I needed my name on my work. He agreed. I still have the draft. It reminds me to wait.

How long did the narrator spend on the design Bhupen took credit for?
Three weeks.
What was Chandrika feeling when she saw her reflection in the monitor?
Chandrika was still furious, but seeing the tight jaw and red face made her wary of acting in that heat, so she felt the need to pause.
Which choice worked, and why?
Saving the draft and rereading it the next morning worked, because calm let Chandrika separate the true complaint from the anger and ask Bhupen directly for credit.
How might Bhupen have seen things if the resignation had been sent that afternoon?
Bhupen might have been shocked and defensive, never learning the real issue about credit, and the chance to fix it would have been lost.

I remember the Ganpati aarti in our building courtyard when I was in Class 3. Everyone stood in a circle with little brass lamps, and Kaka banged the drum.
I didn't know all the words. So I just clapped and sang the "Jai Dev" part really loudly. My arms had goosebumps. I felt like I was part of something much bigger than me.
Tanuja, from the flat opposite, stood beside me. She kept giggling and nudging me. At first I thought she was making fun. Later she told me she loved the drum so much she wanted to dance, but everyone was standing still.
We both came every evening that week. Tanuja for the drum, me for the singing.
- Shankar

What part of the aarti did Shankar sing loudly?
The "Jai Dev" part.
What did Shankar first think Tanuja's giggling meant, and what was the real reason?
Shankar first worried she was making fun, but she was actually excited because she loved the drum and wanted to dance.
What does this memory teach about joining group rituals?
Children can join in their own way, singing, clapping or enjoying the drum, and still feel part of the group.
How did Tanuja experience the aarti differently from Shankar?
Tanuja was drawn to the drum and felt like dancing, while Shankar felt goosebumps from singing with everyone.

Every month, in the week before her period, Sarika's life in their Kochi flat seemed to fall apart. She cried through meetings, snapped at Joseph over nothing, and one month called in sick three days running because she couldn't face anyone. Her mother said, 'All women go through it. Bear it.' Sarika had borne it for years. One evening, after a week of barely sleeping, she told Joseph, 'It feels like I disappear for a week and a stranger lives here.' Joseph held her hand. 'This isn't something you just tolerate. Let's see a doctor.' He found a women's health clinic, went with her, and helped her write down her monthly notes. The doctor took her seriously and made a plan with her.

What did Sarika's mother say?
'All women go through it. Bear it.'
What was Sarika feeling when she said a stranger lives there?
She felt overwhelmed and lost, as if she disappeared for a week every month.
What steps did Joseph take?
He refused to treat it as something to tolerate, found a clinic, went with her and helped write down her monthly notes.
How might Joseph have experienced the snapping over nothing?
Joseph may have felt hurt at times, yet he saw a real problem rather than a character flaw.

Amara's phone lit up again during dinner in their small London flat: her mother, then her uncle, then the family group. Her brother's fees were due. Her cousin's wedding in Enugu needed "something from the London one". The roof at home was leaking again. Amara loved them; she was the first to go abroad, and sending money home felt like carrying them with her. But the course she wanted, the one to become a midwife, had been "next year" for three years now. "You went quiet," Alejandro said. "I'm angry," she said, surprised to hear it. "And I feel terrible for being angry." That Sunday she called her mother and said it plainly: she would keep helping with the fees and the roof, not the wedding, and some of her pay would stay in London for the course and for emergencies. There was a long silence on the line. Then her mother said, "You should have told us sooner, my daughter."

What did Amara want to train to become?
A midwife.
What mix of feelings does Amara have about the requests from home?
She feels real love and duty towards her family, but also anger about her own plans slipping, and then guilt for being angry.
Which of Amara's choices is most likely to keep the goodwill alive, and why?
Telling her mother openly what she could and couldn't cover, rather than quietly giving until she was bitter, so the family knew where they stood.
How might Amara's mother feel after the call?
Her mother may be surprised and a little hurt at first, but her words suggest she understands and wishes Amara had spoken earlier.

Read this:

In their Pune classroom, Tarun leaned over Bhavna's desk. “Wow, your drawing is amazing. You're the best artist in the class.” Bhavna felt her cheeks warm. Then he added, “Can I borrow your gold pen?” She lent it. The next day: “Your handwriting is so neat.” Then: “Can I copy your homework?” Bhavna frowned. Every compliment came with a request. On Friday, her friend Sana said, “I love how you did the sky,” and then just went back to her own work. That one felt different. Bhavna kept it in her head all day. When Tarun started his next compliment, she said, “Thanks. What do you need?” He laughed, caught out.

What did Tarun ask to borrow after the first compliment?
Tarun asked to borrow her gold pen.
What was Bhavna feeling when she noticed every compliment came with a request?
Bhavna felt uneasy and a bit let down, sensing Tarun's praise was a way to get favours.
How did Bhavna respond to Tarun's next compliment, and why was it fair?
She thanked him and asked what he needed, calmly naming the pattern without being rude.
What made Sana's compliment feel different?
Sana praised something specific and asked for nothing in return, so it felt sincere.

Read this:

Dear Mummy,

I'm writing this because I get tongue-tied when we talk. I know you check my phone each night, and that you started after the group chat mess. I understand you were scared. But it makes me feel watched, and I've started deleting messages just to feel private, which I don't like doing.

Can you tell me exactly what you're worried about? I'll show you my chats myself on Sunday evenings for now, and I promise I won't make secret accounts. Could we look at it again in a couple of months, and if I've been open, you check less?

Thanks for reading this. 🙂

Sarika

P.S. I'll be in the kitchen. Irawati Auntie next door says hi.

On which evenings does Sarika offer to show the chats?
Sarika offers to show them on Sunday evenings.
What is Sarika feeling about the nightly phone checks, and how does it show?
Sarika feels watched and uneasy, and it shows in how Sarika has started deleting messages just to feel private.
What is Sarika doing that could help build trust with Mummy?
Sarika asks for a clear reason, promises no secret accounts, shares the chats openly and suggests a review in a couple of months, so constant checking becomes less needed.
How might Sarika's mother feel when she reads the letter?
Probably relieved that Sarika is talking openly, and maybe a little sad to hear the checking hurt, while still worried about what caused it.

Read this:

Dear Zubin,

I've written this four times. Here's the plain version.

When I told you about the diagnosis in March, you hugged me hard and said, "Anything you need." Then you went quiet. No calls. You didn't come to the hospital. I heard from Aman you were at the match on the day of my surgery.

It hurt, more than I'll admit. At first I thought you'd stopped caring.

But I know you. You were the one who couldn't go to your grandfather's funeral because you didn't know what to do with your face. I think this is the same. You don't know what to say.

So I'll tell you. You don't have to say anything wise. Send me a stupid meme on Tuesdays. Come on Saturday and watch cricket with me, even if we just shout at the screen.

I miss you. That's all.

Lokesh

What did Zubin say when Lokesh first shared the diagnosis?
"Anything you need."
What did Lokesh feel when Zubin went quiet?
Lokesh felt hurt and at first feared Zubin had stopped caring.
What did Lokesh do that could bring Zubin back?
Lokesh named the hurt gently and told Zubin exactly how to help, a meme on Tuesdays and a cricket visit on Saturday.
Why might Zubin have disappeared?
Zubin probably felt uncomfortable and helpless, not knowing what to say, as at the grandfather's funeral Zubin couldn't face.

Read this:

People ask if I hate Yusuf. I'm Kalyani, by the way, and no, I don't. I did for a while.

We started the tuition centre together at twenty-three. By year three, he was taking the classes he liked and leaving me the accounts, the parents' complaints, everything. When I raised it, he said I was "too controlling". That stung for months.

Last year we decided to end it. We sat down with a friend who's a chartered accountant and wrote everything out: who keeps the name, who keeps which batches, how the savings are split. We signed it. No shouting.

The day he moved his last box out, I made him tea. It felt strange, but also light.

What I kept is the lesson, not the bitterness. My new partner and I wrote our roles on paper before we opened. And when I see Yusuf at the market, I say hello and mean it.

Who helped Kalyani and Yusuf write out the terms?
A friend who's a chartered accountant helped them.
What was Kalyani feeling on the day Yusuf moved his last box out?
Kalyani felt it was strange but also light, a sense of relief and letting go.
Which choices helped Kalyani let go of bitterness?
Ending the partnership with clear written terms, making tea on the last day, and keeping only the lesson by defining roles with a new partner.
How might Yusuf see Kalyani's hello at the market?
Yusuf might feel relieved and respected, since there is no hostility left between them.

Stockholm's winter was at its darkest, and Oskar was walking to his accounting evening class again. He hated it. He'd hated it since October. But he had paid for the full year, and he'd told his whole family, and his friend Diego, that he was going to be an accountant. At the class, he stared at spreadsheets and daydreamed about the carpentry workshop he passed every morning. "Why don't you just stop?" Diego asked over coffee. "I've done five months. And everyone knows." "So?" "So quitting means I was wrong." Diego shrugged. "You were wrong. So what?" Oskar felt a flash of annoyance. Walking home in the snow, he resented the course, the fee, and most of all himself for starting it.

Where does Oskar walk past every morning?
The carpentry workshop.
What is Oskar feeling as he walks home in the snow?
He feels resentful toward the course, the fee and himself, and stuck because quitting would mean admitting he was wrong.
What question could help Oskar decide about the course?
He could ask: knowing what I know now, would I sign up today? If not, the months already spent shouldn't decide the rest.
How does Diego see Oskar's reason for staying?
Diego sees it as unimportant; being wrong once is normal and shouldn't keep Oskar in a course he hates.

Jatin's alarm rang at six. He turned it off. At six-thirty his mother, Nikita, shook him. "The bus is at seven!" He leapt up and stuffed things in his bag: tiffin, a jumper, a comic. He couldn't find his socks, then his shoes. At six-fifty-five he ran down the stairs of their building in Thane. The bus was at the gate. He was halfway up the steps when the teacher asked, "Permission slip?" Jatin's stomach dropped. It was on the fridge. And his water bottle was on the kitchen counter. His mother came flying down the stairs in her nightdress and slippers, the slip in one hand, the bottle in the other.

What time was the bus due?
The bus was due at seven.
How did Jatin feel when the teacher asked for the permission slip?
He felt a sinking panic, his stomach dropping, as he remembered it was on the fridge.
Which approach would have suited Jatin better, and why?
Packing the night before with a list, because checking calmly catches things like the slip and the bottle.
How does the morning look to Nikita?
Nikita has to run downstairs in her nightdress, so she is probably flustered and a little annoyed.

Read this:

Coach's notes, 14 March.
Vidya and Kiran, founders of the solar-pump rental startup. Third session. They came in after a bad week: two farmer cooperatives had cancelled. Within five minutes they were arguing about who should have followed up. Vidya said Kiran "always drops things"; Kiran said Vidya "never lets anything go".
I stopped them and asked when these fights usually happen. They looked at each other. Kiran said, "Late, after a bad day." Vidya nodded. "On the phone, at 11 pm, when a deal falls through."
Before leaving, they set a new rule themselves: no business arguments after 8 pm or on the day of a lost sale. Anything serious gets written down and discussed on Saturday morning over tea, once they have both slept. I'll ask at the next session whether it held.

When did Vidya say the fights usually happened?
"On the phone, at 11 pm, when a deal falls through."
What was Kiran feeling when accused of always dropping things?
Kiran likely felt stung and defensive, which is why the reply was that Vidya never lets anything go.
Why is a Saturday morning over tea a better time?
Both are rested and not raw from a lost sale, so they are less defensive and can actually solve the problem.
How does the coach see the change in the pair?
The coach sees them spot their own pattern and set the rule themselves, and plans to check next session whether it held.

messages.content:
Read this:

The form for the Class 11 trip to Rishikesh was due tomorrow, and Nikita's parents had already said no. Since her seizures started two years ago, they had decided everything for her: no cycling, no sleepovers, no trips. 'It's for your safety, beta,' her mother said. Nikita, sixteen, went to her room and cried with rage. She loved them. She also felt like she was suffocating. Her elder brother Divyansh knocked. 'Want me to try?' At dinner he said, 'What if Nikita helps make the plan instead of us deciding for her?' Nikita spoke up, voice shaking. She'd carry her medicines, the teacher would be told what to do, she'd share a room with Tanvi, who knew, and she'd call home every night. Her father was quiet a long time. Then he signed the form.

When was the form for the Rishikesh trip due?
Tomorrow.
How did Nikita feel when her parents said no?
She felt furious and smothered, as if she was suffocating, even though she loved them.
What did Divyansh suggest, and why did it work?
He suggested Nikita help make the plan, which respected her autonomy and gave her parents a safe plan to trust.
How might Nikita's parents have been feeling before signing?
They were probably frightened for her safety, torn between protecting her and letting her grow up.

Read this:

Noor read Pranav's answer aloud in English class in a wobbly voice, and Lakshmi snorted. The laugh rolled through the back rows, and Noor felt something warm: they were all looking at her. By Friday she had a name for him, and the name got laughs too.

Soon it moved to phones. Noor cut Pranav's face from the sports-day photo and pasted it on a cartoon pig. Lakshmi set up a spare account to post it, and nobody put his name on the weekend plan. Typing it was easy; she never saw his face when he opened the message.

Pranav stopped raising his hand. At lunch he took his tray to the far step by the water tank. His notebook margins filled with doodles, and he yawned through first period, eyes red.

"All okay, Pranav?" asked Mr Iyer, pausing at his desk.

"Fine, sir." He smiled a small, quick smile.

The teacher did not take that as the whole story. Before the bell he told the class mentor what he had noticed and asked the counsellor to look in on Pranav that same afternoon. On the step, Pranav kept thinking that if he told anyone, they would say it was only a joke.

Where did Pranav take his lunch tray after the mocking began?
He took it to the far step by the water tank.
How did the mocking change between the first week and the later weeks, and how did it feel different to Noor and to Pranav?

It began as spoken nicknames that won laughs in class, then moved to an edited photo, a spare account and being left out of the weekend plan; typing felt easy to Noor because she never saw Pranav's face, while it felt much heavier to him.
What was Pranav thinking on the step at the end?
He was afraid nobody would believe him and that anyone he told would call it only a joke, which is why he answered Mr Iyer with a quick smile and said he was fine.
How could a teacher respond when a student says he is fine but shows changes like these?
They can pass what they noticed to the mentor and counsellor the same day, as Mr Iyer did, instead of accepting the smile at face value.

Read this:

"Hi, I'm Francis. Were you in the maths session?"
Zainab stared at her orientation badge. "Yes."
"It was long, huh."
"...Yes."
Francis tried again. "Where are you from?"
"Bhopal." Silence. Zainab's mind was screaming: this is so fake, why are we doing this?
Francis shrugged. "I'm from Kochi. It's so hot there, I thought Delhi would be cooler. It isn't."
Zainab almost laughed. "Bhopal's the same. My mother packed three sweaters anyway."
"Mine packed an umbrella. In April."
Now Zainab did laugh. "Mothers."
"Mothers," Francis agreed. "Are you doing the chemistry elective?"
"Yes. I'm scared of it, actually."
"Same. Want to sit together tomorrow?"
Zainab nodded. It hadn't felt fake at all.

Where is Francis from?
Kochi.
What was Zainab feeling when she answered in one word?
She felt uncomfortable and stuck, thinking the small talk was fake.
What turned the small talk into a real conversation?
Light shared details about hot cities and packing mothers built friendliness, which led to admitting a real fear about chemistry.
How might Francis have felt as Zainab kept giving one-word answers?
Francis probably felt a bit awkward but kept trying, and was pleased when she finally laughed.

'Thirty-one out of eighty?' Pradeep held the physics paper at arm's length. 'Siddharth, you told me on Sunday you were fully ready.'
'I was! I went through every chapter, Papa. Twice.' Siddharth dropped onto the divan. 'When I looked at the notes, I knew all of it. I swear.'
'Okay. Tell me why a pencil looks bent in a glass of water.'
'It's refraction. The light... bends. Because of the... hang on.' Siddharth frowned. 'I know the diagram. It's on page forty-two, bottom left.'
'You know where it lives,' Pradeep said, not unkindly. 'Do you know what it says?'
A long silence.
'I thought seeing it meant I knew it,' Siddharth said slowly. 'It felt exactly the same.'
'Then let's find a way to check. Tomorrow you explain one page to me without looking. I'll make the chai.'

What did Pradeep ask Siddharth to explain?
Why a pencil looks bent in a glass of water.
Why was Siddharth so shocked by the mark?
Looking at the notes, Siddharth felt everything was known; recognising the page, down to 'page forty-two, bottom left', felt exactly like understanding it.
Which choice at the end helps Siddharth most, and why?
Agreeing to explain one page tomorrow without looking; saying it aloud tests real understanding instead of the feeling of familiarity.
How does Pradeep react to the low mark, and why might that help Siddharth?
Pradeep is surprised but asks questions 'not unkindly' and offers chai; calm curiosity lets Siddharth find the gap instead of getting defensive.
The news about the exam results were shocking. Is the verb right?

The news about the exam results was shocking.
Why: "news" is singular, so "was".

During the wheat harvest in Moga, the polytechnic office was half-staffed, and the clerk never looked up. "Roll 117, form incomplete. You people always come late." Nitin had come from Darbhanga two months ago, and by now he answered to 117 faster than to his own name. In the workshop the instructor pointed at him with a spanner: "You, the outsider at the back." On the bus a man grumbled about "these fellows" taking all the seats.
That evening Nitin sat on the hostel roof, scrolling to his mother's number without calling.
Gurpreet climbed up with two glasses of lassi from the Baisakhi stall. "Nitin! You missed the bhangra. My chachi keeps asking where the boy who fixed her pump went."
Nitin laughed for the first time that day. He called his mother after that, and on Sunday he went to the fair in Gurpreet's village.

What did the clerk call Nitin?
"Roll 117", telling him the form was incomplete.
What does Nitin scrolling to his mother's number without calling suggest?
Nitin seems lonely and low, worn down by a day of being treated as a number and a burden, perhaps not wanting to worry his mother.
What helped Nitin, and what else could help?

Gurpreet using his name and pulling him into family and the fair helped; keeping close to people like his mother and Gurpreet, and raising the office's treatment with the hostel warden, could help more.
How does Gurpreet see Nitin?
To Gurpreet, Nitin is a person with a name and a place, the one who fixed the chachi's pump and was missed at the bhangra. 😊

Madhav worked at the cooperative dairy in the taluka town, and after the doctor advised a scan and possibly a small operation, he sat on the office verandah with his policy booklet during the tea break. He read every line about waiting periods and which procedures were covered, tapping a pen against a paragraph he did not follow.

Then he walked to the HR window where Yamini kept the registers. She showed him the leave rules on a printed sheet and explained how medical leave was recorded. Madhav copied the two phone numbers of the insurer's helpdesk into his diary. Nothing was decided yet, but on the bus home he was no longer afraid of surprises in the paperwork.

Where did Madhav read his policy booklet?
On the office verandah, during the tea break.
What was Madhav feeling as he tapped his pen on a paragraph he did not follow?
He was puzzled and a little anxious about the fine print, wanting to understand it before treatment began.
If the printed leave sheet had been unclear, what could Madhav try next, and why?
He could ask Yamini to walk him through an example or call the insurer's helpdesk, because someone who handles the rules daily can clear up doubts quickly.
How might Yamini see Madhav coming with questions early?
Yamini would probably find it easier to help, since she could explain the rules before any leave was needed rather than in a rush.

Dear Swati,
You asked about the new job. The strangest thing is watching two people on my team react to the same news. Our biggest client might leave next quarter. My manager keeps saying, "It'll be fine, they love us," and changes the subject. No plan, nothing. Then there's Kavin, who's my age. He said, "I think we can keep them, but not by hoping." He called the client, asked what was bothering them, and made a list of fixes. He's cheerful too, but his cheer comes with a spreadsheet. I trust his version more. I've started helping him with the list. I'll tell you how it turns out.
Neelam

What might happen with the biggest client next quarter?
The client might leave.
How does Neelam feel about the two reactions?
Neelam feels uneasy with the manager's "It'll be fine" and more trusting and hopeful about Kavin's approach.
Why is Kavin's approach wiser than the manager's?
He combines hope with action, calling the client to find out what's wrong and listing fixes.
How might Swati read this letter?
Swati might see that Neelam is learning to tell empty reassurance from real, prepared hope.
A farmer picked 56 oranges and sold 14 of them. How many does he have left?
42. Because 56 - 14 = 42, so 42 are left.

Dear Imran,
You asked why I didn't reply all week. I didn't get into the music academy. The result came on Sunday, and I spent three days in bed with the curtains shut. I didn't want to talk to anyone, not even Ammi. All I wanted was the sweet vermicelli she made when I was small, and old cartoons. I felt like a little kid again. On Thursday Ammi just sat on my bed with a bowl and stroked my hair. She didn't say "try again" or "it's fine". That helped more than anything. Today I opened the curtains and played the piano for ten minutes. Not well. But I played.
Sharmila

What did Sharmila want to eat?
The sweet vermicelli Ammi made when Sharmila was small.
How did Sharmila feel after the result?
Deeply disappointed and small, like a little kid again, wanting only comfort food, cartoons and the curtains shut.
What helped Sharmila most?
Ammi sitting with a bowl and stroking Sharmila's hair without saying "try again" or "it's fine".
How might Ammi have felt during those three days?
Worried but patient, choosing quiet comfort over advice.

"Didi, I got the job!" Preeti burst into the café. "Senior designer at the studio in Bengaluru!"

Ankita jumped up and hugged her. "I knew it!"

"And the salary is more than yours," Preeti added, then clapped a hand over her mouth. "Sorry, that came out wrong."

Ankita laughed. There was a tiny sting there, she noticed. She'd trained Preeti from her first internship. Now Preeti was going further, faster.

"Don't be sorry. That's the best news."

"I couldn't have done it without you."

"You did the portfolio. You did the interviews. I just told you to stop apologising in presentations."

"You were the one who—"

"Preeti. Take the credit. It's yours."

Preeti looked at her. "Will you still help me if I get stuck?"

"Of course. But I don't think you'll need me much." Ankita smiled. "That's the whole point."

What job did Preeti get?
Senior designer at the studio in Bengaluru.
What did Ankita feel when Preeti said the salary was higher?
Ankita felt a tiny sting of wistfulness, mixed with real joy and pride for Preeti.
How did Ankita handle Preeti's success?
She celebrated warmly, refused to take credit, and saw Preeti not needing her much as the goal of mentoring.
How does Preeti see Ankita's role in her success?
Preeti believes she couldn't have done it without Ankita and still wants her help if she gets stuck.

The Friday of the funeral. Afreen stood at the back of the crowded hall while person after person spoke about Urmila Ma'am, the professor who had supervised her master's. Nobody mentioned her publications. They talked about how she answered every student's email by midnight, and taught the watchman's daughter maths on Saturdays. Afreen went home and couldn't sleep. What would people say about her?
Two weeks later. The dread had turned into questions. She wrote in her notebook: What would I want to have done, if I had ten years? Twenty? The answers surprised her. Not the promotion. Teaching. Her sister's children. Her father's stories, recorded before they were lost.
Three months later. Afreen was tutoring two girls from her building on Sundays and recording her father's village stories every Friday evening. She still thought about death sometimes, but now with a calmer, almost practical feeling: then let me use the time.

What did Urmila Ma'am teach the watchman's daughter?
Maths, on Saturdays.
How did Afreen's feelings change from the funeral to three months later?
At first Afreen felt restless dread and couldn't sleep; later she felt calmer and practical, letting the thought of death guide how she used her time.
What did Afreen's notebook questions help her do?
Imagining ten or twenty years left showed what mattered, teaching, family and her father's stories, so she acted on them.
How might Afreen's father feel being recorded every Friday?
Her father would probably feel valued and touched that his village stories are being kept.

Read this:

At the baby song hour in a library in Oslo, Mei, thirteen months, sits on Ingrid's lap. She has no words yet. When the leader sings, "Touch your nose," Mei's finger lands on her cheek, then slides to her nose. At "Clap, clap, clap," she bangs her palms together. As they leave, Ingrid whispers, "Wave bye-bye," and Mei flaps her hand at the leader.

Where does Mei's finger land first?
On her cheek, before sliding to her nose.
What does Mei's finger sliding to her nose suggest she understood?
She seemed to understand the word "nose" and corrected her aim to match it.
How could Ingrid build on this at home?
She could sing the same action songs and use short everyday requests, giving Mei time to respond.
How might the song leader see Mei's wave?
As a sweet sign that Mei understood "bye-bye" even though she can't say it yet. 🙂
Tell me what Holi is in one sentence, without using the words "colour", "colours" or "coloured".
Holi is a spring festival in India when friends and families throw bright powders and splash water at each other to celebrate the end of winter.
How is "water under the bridge" used after a quarrel?

It means that something unpleasant happened in the past and is no longer important, so there is no need to be upset about it.
Example: Forget the old argument, Vimal; it is water under the bridge.
How would you describe applause to a younger child?

Applause is the sound people make by clapping their hands to show they enjoyed something. It is a noun.
Example: The whole hall broke into applause when Meera finished her song.

Summarize this in a few short bullet points.

"He investigated the case with great care, for Dr. Roylott's conduct had long been notorious in the county, but he was unable to find any satisfactory cause of death. My evidence showed that the door had been fastened upon the inner side, and the windows were blocked by old-fashioned shutters with broad iron bars, which were secured every night. The walls were carefully sounded, and were shown to be quite solid all round, and the flooring was also thoroughly examined, with the same result. The chimney is wide, but is barred up by four large staples. It is certain, therefore, that my sister was quite alone when she met her end. Besides, there were no marks of any violence upon her."

- The investigator found no clear cause of death.
- The door was locked from inside, and the windows had shutters and iron bars.
- The walls, floor and chimney were checked, and nothing was found.
- The sister had no marks of violence and was alone when she died.

The hospital reception was packed at 11 a.m. A man pushed to the front of the queue and slammed his palm on the desk. "My father has been waiting two hours! What kind of place is this?" Deepika, twenty-four, the receptionist, felt her jaw tighten. A year ago she'd have snapped: Everyone is waiting, sir. She paused. Counted her breath. Looked at his red eyes and shaking hands. "I'm sorry it's taking long," she said quietly. "Let me check where your father is in the list." She called the ward, found he was next, and told him. The man's shoulders dropped. "Sorry for shouting," he muttered. Her colleague Farida leaned over after he left. "How do you stay that calm?" Deepika laughed. "I don't. I just wait before I open my mouth."

How long had the man's father been waiting?
Two hours.
What did Deepika realise the man was feeling, and how did that help her stay calm?
His red eyes and shaking hands suggested he was scared for his father, not just rude, so she answered his worry instead of his tone.
What is the key skill Deepika describes, and how could others practise it?
Waiting before speaking; others could practise noticing their tight jaw or breath as a signal to pause.
How might the man have felt after Deepika's calm reply?
He likely felt heard and a bit ashamed of shouting, which is why he apologised.
What is invisible in a story, and is it the same as hidden?

Invisible means that cannot be seen. It is an adjective. It is not exactly hidden, since something hidden is out of sight on purpose and could still be seen.
Example: The gas is invisible, but you can smell it.

Read this:

Dhruv was minding his father's fertiliser shop in the village after school when the phone buzzed. A man said he was a trader from the next taluka. "I'm sending payment for ten bags. Just approve the request on your app, quickly, my tempo is leaving." A request popped up. Dhruv looked closer. It didn't say receive. It said Pay, and it wanted his PIN. "If you're paying me, why do I enter my PIN?" The man's voice went hard. "Don't waste my time! Approve it now." The hurry made Dhruv's neck prickle. He declined the request and said, "My father will call you back." Then he phoned Tanvir chacha at the mandi. His uncle listened and said, "Good. That was a trap. Nobody sends you money by asking for your PIN. Block the number." When his father came home, Dhruv showed him the screenshot, and his father patted his shoulder twice.

What did the request on the app actually say?
It said Pay, and it wanted his PIN.
What was Dhruv feeling when the caller's voice went hard?
He was suspicious and uneasy, his neck prickling at the pressure to hurry.
Which of Dhruv's steps defeated the trap, and why?
He paused to read the request, refused to enter his PIN, declined it and checked with his uncle, because the scam depended on him acting in a rush.
How might Dhruv's father feel seeing the screenshot?
He is probably relieved and proud, patting Dhruv's shoulder for handling the shop's money carefully.

Read this:

At Kamal's nephew's birthday party in their Kolkata building, his sister Rupa announced to the room, "Ira's still at that NGO? Must be nice, having a husband who earns properly."

Ira smiled politely and went to help cut the cake. Her hands were steady, but her chest felt tight. She could name five things wrong with Rupa's comment and one hurtful thing Rupa had said at their wedding.

She said none of them. She played musical chairs with the children, thanked Kamal's mother for the food and left with everyone else.

At home, Ira made two cups of tea and sat on the bed next to Kamal. "Can I tell you something that upset me tonight, just between us?"

He listened. Then he said, "She's been like that with me too. I'm sorry. What would help?"

"I don't need you to fight her. I just need you to know, and not laugh along next time."

"I won't," Kamal said.

Where does Ira work?
Ira works at an NGO.
What was Ira feeling during the party, and how can you tell?
Ira felt hurt and tense; her chest felt tight though she smiled and kept her hands steady.
What did Ira do that protected her marriage and the family peace?
She didn't confront Rupa in public, and instead raised it with Kamal privately and asked for a specific kind of support.
How does Kamal see his sister's behaviour?
Kamal recognises it, saying Rupa has been like that with him too, and wants to support Ira.
Why do people clap at the end of a performance?
Clapping is a way to say well done. Because the performers worked hard and want to know the audience enjoyed it, and a shared sound lets everyone show thanks together.

Read this:

Subject: accountability partners? (no pressure, just a message)
Hi Dolma,
We met at the mock test centre last Sunday, the one with the broken fan. You said you keep skipping days, and honestly, so do I. I have an idea.
Every morning by 8, we each send the other one message: today's targets, three at most. Every night by 10, we send what got done. That's it. No advice unless asked, no judging, and we don't involve our families. My parents already ask enough!
I think it works because someone simply knows. When nobody knows I've skipped, skipping is easy. If you're waiting for my message, it's harder.
If we both miss twice in a week, we meet for tea and fix the plan, not blame each other.
Want to try it for two weeks, starting Monday?
Uma

Where did Uma and Dolma meet?
At the mock test centre, the one with the broken fan.
Why does Uma think the idea will work?
Uma admits skipping days too and hopes that having Dolma expect a message will make skipping harder.
What else could they agree before starting?
They could agree what counts as a fair target, so neither sets impossible lists and feels bad every night.
How might Dolma feel receiving the email?
Dolma, who also keeps skipping days, may feel relieved to find someone in the same spot offering support without pressure.

metadata.subtype: Approach: a study partner as accountability [Action]

Read this:

Friday: Papa Hemant folds Zainab's small hands together in front of Dadi. 'Pranaam, Dadi.' Zainab, twenty months old, squeals and claps instead. Dadi claps back.
Saturday: Zainab toddles to Dadi's chair on her own, bends at the waist until her curls brush the floor, and looks up. Dadi laughs and kisses her forehead. 'Khush raho, meri gudiya.'
Monday: The moment Dadi comes in from the market, Zainab drops her spoon, folds her hands, bends, and waits, beaming, for the kiss.

What does Zainab do on Friday instead of folding her hands?
She squeals and claps.
What was Zainab feeling on Monday when she dropped her spoon to greet Dadi?
She felt excited and happy, expecting Dadi's kiss, so the bow had become a joyful little ritual.
What helps a toddler like Zainab link the gesture to warmth?
Gentle guidance from Papa without pressure, and Dadi answering every try with claps, laughter and kisses.
How does Dadi seem to feel as Zainab learns to bow?
Dadi seems delighted and affectionate, clapping, laughing and blessing her 'gudiya'.

Every Saturday in Durban, Sami, eight, went to the public library with his big sister Lindiwe, sat at the same corner table by the fish tank, and ate the same jam sandwich at noon. This week, things had moved. The fish tank was now near the windows, and a reading nook with beanbags filled the old corner. Sami froze in the doorway. "Where's my table?" "Look, beanbags!" Lindiwe said. "I want MY table." He sat stiffly at another desk, arms folded, not reading. At noon he refused a new sandwich from the café and ate his jam one. After a while, he crept over to the beanbags, just to look. He sat on one. "It's… okay," he said. Then, quieter, "It's actually squishy."

Where had the fish tank been moved to?
The fish tank was now near the windows.
Why did Sami refuse to enjoy the new beanbags at first?
His usual table and routine felt safe and known, so any change felt risky, even though the new nook was fine.
What small step helped Sami try the change?
He crept over to the beanbags just to look, and then sat on one. Trying a tiny piece of the change let him discover it was okay.
How might Lindiwe feel when Sami says the beanbag is squishy?
She is probably relieved and amused after his stubborn start, and glad he tried it on his own.
When a list of chores is long, what should be done first?
The important chores should come first. Because time or energy can run out before the list is finished, doing the key tasks early means the things that matter most are done.

Mahima here, from the QA desk. I'll tell you what I saw after the payments launch failed. Kamal, our newest engineer, had merged one small change that week. By Monday the project channel had turned strangely tidy: people wrote “the change that broke it” and never used his name. The lead kept saying, “Let's not point fingers,” while looking at Kamal's chair. Tasnim, who had reviewed that same change, went very quiet. In the pantry, talk stopped when Kamal walked in.

I can't know what he felt. But he began eating lunch at his desk and staying late to re-check everything. I raised it with the lead and asked for a full timeline before anyone was named. The timeline showed a config gap nobody owned.

Kamal merged one small change that week.

Mahima asked for a full timeline before anyone was named, so the facts could show what failed instead of guessing at a person.

Tasnim may feel guilty and afraid of being blamed too, so silence feels safer, even though it leaves Kamal alone with the blame.

In the placement cell's waiting room, Yogesh sat with his rejection email open. Dhruv, who'd been placed a week earlier, sat beside him. "The interviewer asked that graph question nobody could solve," Yogesh said. "Three of us got it. All three failed." "Bad luck," Dhruv agreed. Yogesh was quiet. "Yeah. But the first two questions were basic arrays, and I fumbled those too. I haven't practised since June." He opened his notes and typed two lists. "Not mine: which interviewer, which question." "Mine: one hour of practice daily, two mock interviews with the cell before the next company." He showed Dhruv. "This feels less like I'm cursed and less like I'm useless." Dhruv nodded. "Mock tomorrow at four?"

What did Yogesh put on the "Mine" list?
One hour of practice daily and two mock interviews with the cell before the next company.
What does Yogesh mean by feeling "less like I'm cursed and less like I'm useless"?
Splitting the result into luck and his own share frees him from blaming fate or himself entirely, which feels lighter and more hopeful.
Which choice by Yogesh shows a balanced response to the rejection?
Admitting the unlucky graph question while owning the fumbled array questions, then planning practice and mock interviews.
How might Dhruv feel being shown the two lists?
Dhruv may feel relieved his friend isn't sinking, and glad to help by offering a mock interview the next day.

Age nine: Chaitanya slid his reading book under the bench when the teacher began calling names to read aloud. Letters flipped and jumped, and he stumbled over 'was' and 'saw'. Quietly he told himself, 'I'm stupid.' The teacher noticed the book under the bench and sat beside him after class. 'You explained the story to me beautifully yesterday. Reading seems hard for you. Let's find some help.' Chaitanya's shoulders dropped.

Age fifteen: Francis told the best stories in class and thought in pictures, but spelling tests and timed papers made his mind go white. The school arranged an assessment, and afterwards he had extra time and a reader in exams. On the first paper he finished every question, and his marks matched what he knew.

Age twenty: Maria used audio books and voice typing and asked for extra time in her first year. She blushed when she asked the professor. 'Thank you for telling me,' the professor said. 'It helps me support you.' Her grades rose, and she began telling new tutors early.

What did Francis's school arrange for him?
An assessment, and afterwards extra time and a reader in exams.
How did understanding and support change the experience of reading difficulty at nine, fifteen and twenty?

At nine Chaitanya hid his book and thought he was stupid until the teacher offered help. At fifteen an assessment and extra time showed Francis's real knowledge, and at twenty Maria used audio books, voice typing and extra time and told tutors early, earning understanding.
What did Chaitanya believe about himself when the letters jumped?
That he was stupid, though the teacher had seen him explain the story beautifully.
What could Maria do when she meets a new tutor?
Tell them early what helps her, since sharing usually earns understanding.
