Monday: Lokesh didn't wait for Rehana at the bus stop, and didn't reply to her "where are u??" message. She thought he was just late.
Wednesday: He walked right past her in the corridor. Rehana went home and scrolled up through six months of their chats, looking for a clue. Was it the joke about his handwriting? The science project? She made a list of every possible mistake in her notebook.
Friday: She couldn't eat dinner. Her stomach was in knots. She typed a long apology for all of it, then deleted it, because she didn't even know what she was sorry for. She lay awake thinking that if he'd just shouted, it would be easier.

What did Rehana make a list of in her notebook?
Every possible mistake she might have made.
What was Rehana feeling by Friday?
She was anxious and confused, with her stomach in knots, unable to eat and not even sure what to apologise for.
What turning point is available to Rehana now?
Instead of a long apology for everything, she could send one calm message asking Lokesh what's wrong and saying she'd rather know.
What might Lokesh be experiencing during the week?
He may be holding onto a hurt he hasn't spoken about, not realising how anxious his silence is making Rehana.

So the podcast theme is group projects? Okay. I'm Varun, and I'll be honest. I hated them.
In Class 9 our group had to make a documentary about our neighbourhood. Yamini said she'd do the interviews. She didn't. Aman said he'd edit. He didn't. So I did the interviews, the filming, the editing, three nights till one.
I never said anything. I was scared they'd call me bossy, the one who ruins the mood. Instead I just went quieter and quieter. I'd answer them in one word.
At the screening, everyone clapped for our team. Yamini hugged me. I smiled and wanted to scream.
Now I know: it wasn't them I was angry at most. It was me, for never saying a word.

How many nights did Varun work till one?
Three nights.
What was Varun feeling when Yamini hugged him at the screening?
Varun felt angry and resentful, smiling on the outside while wanting to scream inside.
What could Varun have said early on without sounding bossy?
Varun could have calmly reminded the group of the tasks each had agreed to, with a clear date, before doing everything alone.
How might Yamini have seen the project?
Yamini may have thought everything was fine, since Varun said nothing, and hugged him without seeing the resentment.

Creche note, Diwali week. Kavitha, room caregiver.
A cracker burst outside during snack time. Avni jumped and began to cry. Within a minute three other toddlers were crying or staring at her with worried faces; none of them had looked at the window.
I sat on the mat, took Avni on my lap and hummed our tidy-up song. The others crawled close. Soon they were quiet again.
This week we will draw the curtains and play soft music during cracker hours.

What happened outside during snack time?
A cracker burst outside.
What were the other toddlers feeling when Avni began to cry?
They felt worried and upset, catching Avni's distress though none of them had noticed the noise.
What could help the room during cracker hours this week?
Drawing the curtains and playing soft music, as Kavitha planned, and staying calm and close when one child cries.
What was it like for Avni when the cracker burst?
It was sudden and frightening; being held and hearing a familiar song helped her feel safe again.

"Third time unlucky," Anand announced at dinner, dropping into his chair. "The examiners have now seen my handwriting more often than my own mother has."
Amma laughed. Usha didn't, quite. "You failed the accounts exam again?"
"By four marks. Four! I'm going to frame the result. 'Almost.'"
Usha studied him across the table. "Anand. Honestly. Is this funny-funny, or funny so you don't have to talk about it?"
He paused with a chapati halfway to his mouth. "Hm. Fair question." He chewed. "Honestly? It stung this morning. I sulked on the bus. But I've already booked the next attempt, and I know exactly which paper let me down. So... mostly funny-funny now."
"Okay." Usha passed the dal. "If it turns into the other kind, tell me."
"You'll be the first." He grinned. "After the frame shop."

By how many marks did Anand fail?
By four marks.
How was Anand really feeling about failing again?
Anand admitted it stung in the morning and he sulked, but by dinner he felt mostly okay and determined, having booked the next attempt; the jokes were largely genuine resilience.
Why was Usha's question a good one?
It named both possibilities without assuming, letting Anand check honestly and share both the sting and the recovery.
How might Usha feel after Anand's answer?
Usha probably felt reassured, since he was honest about the sting and seemed genuinely okay, while the door stayed open if that changed.

Every evening after closing her mother's tailoring shop in Barabanki, Sabina walked to the cyber café by the bus stand with a notebook and a little saved data on her phone. She was teaching herself spreadsheet basics from a free online course, the skill every job listing in Lucknow seemed to ask for. The videos went too fast. So she changed her method: watch one lesson, pause, redo it herself on the café computer, then explain it in the notebook as if teaching someone. Her friend Yamini, who ran the café counter, became her test student. "Okay, show me this formula thing," Yamini said one night, arms folded. Sabina got it wrong, fixed it, and got it right. By the end of two months she had built an order tracker for the shop, which her mother now actually used.

What did Sabina build by the end of two months?
She built an order tracker for the shop.
How might Sabina have felt when she got the formula wrong in front of Yamini, then fixed it?
She likely felt a flash of embarrassment, then satisfaction and growing confidence when she corrected it herself 😅
What change in method helped Sabina learn?
Pausing after each lesson to redo it herself and explaining it in writing, which turned passive watching into practice.
What is it like for Sabina's mother to use the order tracker?
She likely feels proud and practically helped, since a skill Sabina built on her own now keeps the shop organised.

Week 1: At the start-up meet, Irfan, a mentor who advises café owners in the big city, looked at Aparna's price list for her home-baked cakes. "Too cheap," he said. "Double everything. People pay for premium." Aparna nodded and wrote it down. She didn't ask why.

Week 3: She printed new cards with the doubled prices. Her regulars in the small town, mostly teachers and shop owners ordering for birthdays, went quiet. Only two orders came that week instead of the usual nine.

Week 5: A neighbour said gently, "Beta, we loved your cakes, but this is city money." Aparna sat with the order book and realised Irfan's clients were office crowds in the city, not her street. She had never asked what his advice was based on.

How many orders came in week 3, compared with usual?
Only two orders instead of the usual nine.
How did Aparna feel when she sat with the order book in week 5?
She probably felt dismayed and a bit foolish, realising she had followed Irfan's advice without asking what it was based on.
What could Aparna have asked Irfan in week 1?
She could have asked why he suggested doubling, and who his clients were, then tested one new price with a few regulars before changing everything.
How did the change look to Aparna's regular customers?
To her regulars it felt like the cakes were suddenly priced for the city, not for them, so they quietly stopped ordering.

Dear Diary,
Today I baked my first cake. I followed every step carefully, but when I took it out of the oven, it had sunk in the middle! I felt disappointed at first. Then my family tasted it, and everyone said it was delicious. We ate it all by the evening. Next time, I will try to make it rise properly.

The power had gone again in the lanes of the small town, so Damini sat in the cyber café running on the inverter, a new online form tool open on screen. Her uncle's milk cooperative wanted its collection records moved online, and Damini, the only one in the family studying computers, had promised to do it in a week.
It was now day five. She had read the official manual twice, all sixty pages, and still did not understand what a 'schema' was; the manual used the word on page one as if everyone knew. Nandini, who ran the café, pointed to a short local-language video playing on the next screen for another customer. 'Ten minutes, didi. It shows the whole thing.'
'Videos make people lazy,' Damini said, and turned back to page thirty-one.
On day seven the cooperative secretary came by. There was nothing to show.

How many pages was the official manual?
Sixty pages.
Why did Damini turn back to page thirty-one, and what was she likely feeling?
She felt stubborn and proud about doing it the proper way, and perhaps anxious about the week's promise, so she dismissed the video as making people lazy.
Which approach would suit Damini better on day five?
Watching the short video for the big picture, then using the manual for details like the schema, would likely have saved days.
How might the cooperative secretary see day seven?
The secretary likely feels let down, since a week was promised and there was nothing to show.

Yosef had been sleeping four hours a night since he took over his father's bakery in Haifa. Orders were late, he'd shouted at a supplier, and last Tuesday he'd sat in the cold store for twenty minutes because he couldn't face the counter. On Friday evening, washing trays, he said to his sister Noa, "I'm not managing. It's not just tired." Noa turned off the tap. "Thank you for saying it." That weekend he told his mother and uncle too, and they worked out who could cover mornings. On Monday he booked an appointment with a psychologist a friend had recommended. He felt embarrassed in the waiting room. But when he came out, he texted Noa: "Next appointment's Thursday. I think I did something right." She sent back a heart.

Where did Yosef sit for twenty minutes last Tuesday?
He sat in the cold store because he couldn't face the counter.
How did Yosef feel in the waiting room, and why?
He felt embarrassed, perhaps because asking for professional help felt like admitting weakness after trying to cope alone.
What was the turning point for Yosef, and what did it lead to?
Telling Noa "I'm not managing" while washing trays. It led to telling his family, sharing the mornings and booking a psychologist.
How might Noa have felt when Yosef texted after his first appointment?
She was probably relieved and proud of her brother, since his words showed he felt he had done something right.

After the meeting where Manoj sir corrected my table in front of everyone, the other interns said, "Come, let's go for chai and vent." I nearly did. It would have felt good for maybe ten minutes.
But I sat at my desk and thought, what do I actually want? I wanted to get better. And I wanted to not feel like that again.
So I went to his cabin and said, "Sir, do you have five minutes? I want to do this well. Could you tell me what I should improve? And, if possible, could feedback be given privately?"
He looked surprised. Then he said, "Fair. Sit." We talked for twenty minutes. Honestly, I'm Mahima, the youngest girl on that floor, and that was the most grown-up I've ever felt.

What did the other interns suggest after the meeting?
Going for chai to vent.
What was Mahima feeling when she decided not to vent?
She felt hurt but determined, wanting to improve and not feel that way again.
Why was going to Manoj sir directly a better choice than venting?
It was calm and professional, got real feedback, and gave him a clear, fair request about private correction.
What might Manoj sir experience when Mahima asks for five minutes?
He is likely surprised and then respectful, seeing an intern who wants to improve and speaks clearly.

"Deepak! It's Kalyani, obviously. Day four in Pune and I have to tell you everything. The hostel room is tiny but it has a window with a tree, and a crow that visits every morning. I've already been to three cafés, a bookshop that stays open till ten, and a street where they sell vada pav for fifteen rupees. Kalyani has already been to three cafés.

The meeting room at the engineering firm in Haifa went quiet when Daniel, the senior architect, tapped the drawing. "This beam is fine. I've designed a hundred like it." Noa, two years out of university, had run the load numbers the night before. They didn't look fine to her. She felt her pulse in her ears. "Daniel, can I ask how you checked it? I'd like to learn your method." He frowned, then explained. It was a rule of thumb from older buildings, with lighter roofs. "That makes sense for those," Noa said. "This roof has the solar panels, though. I ran it last night, and I got a much higher load. Could I show you? I might have made a mistake." Daniel studied her laptop for a long minute. Then he sighed. "No. You didn't. Good catch." He turned to the others. "Deeper beam."

What was different about this roof, according to Noa?
This roof has the solar panels.
What was Noa feeling before she spoke up?
She felt nervous, her pulse in her ears, because she was challenging a very experienced senior in a quiet room.
Which part of Noa's approach worked well, and why?
She asked how he had checked it and offered her numbers while allowing she might be wrong, which kept respect while testing the claim.
How might Daniel feel after admitting "Good catch"?
Daniel probably felt a mix of discomfort and respect, embarrassed about the rule of thumb but grateful the error was caught.

At the panchayat meeting in a village near Wardha, the seed company's leaflet said the new cotton variety "reduces crop loss by 50 percent!" Everyone murmured. Madhav, the young agriculture officer, stood up with the leaflet. "Let's say it three ways before anyone decides. Fifty percent less loss sounds big. But on our fields, loss has been about four quintals out of a hundred. So this seed saves around two quintals. And the seed costs more, so some of you could still end up with less in hand if prices fall." Tarun, who farmed six acres, scratched his head. "So it's good, but not magic." "Good for some fields, magic for none," Madhav said. "I'll show my working to anyone who wants it. You decide."

How much has loss been on their fields, according to Madhav?
About four quintals out of a hundred.
Why did Madhav stand up with the leaflet?
He felt concerned that "50 percent less loss" would sound bigger than it was, and wanted the farmers to decide from fair numbers.
How did Madhav frame the choice fairly?
He restated it as a percentage, as actual quintals saved and as a possible downside if prices fall, then left the choice to the farmers.
How does Tarun see the seed after Madhav speaks?
Tarun sees it as good but not magic, a clearer picture than the leaflet gave.

A balloon.

'Who were you playing with downstairs?' Parul Bua asked.
'Salim. From the third floor. He's my best friend.'
Bua's mouth tightened. 'Stay away from those people. They're not like us. They're bad.'
Omkar's stomach went funny. 'But... Salim shared his lunch with me every day when I broke my arm. And his Ammi fixed my kite.'
'That's how they fool you.'
Omkar looked at the floor. He didn't want to be rude to Bua. 'Bua, which people are bad? All of them? Have you met Salim?'

'Can I bring him to say hello tomorrow?'
Bua sniffed. 'We'll see.'

His kite.
Why did Omkar's stomach go funny?
He felt confused and uneasy, because Bua called Salim's people bad while Salim had been so kind.
How did Omkar stay polite while holding on to what he knew?
He shared his own experience of Salim and asked calm questions instead of arguing rudely.
What might Bua have felt when Omkar asked if she had met Salim?

Before the maths olympiad, I told everyone I wasn't going to study. “It's just for fun,” I said. “I won't even open the practice book.”
I didn't. I watched cartoons. When Usha Miss asked if I had done the sample paper, I shrugged.
The truth is, I was scared. Last year Kamal from 5B came first and everyone said I was the clever one in our class. What if I studied hard and still came nowhere?
I got 34 out of 100. I told people, “I didn't even try, so it doesn't count.” It sort of worked. Nobody said I wasn't clever.
But at night I kept thinking about question 12. I knew how to start it. If I had practised, maybe I could have finished.
Next year, I think I'll try properly. I'm still scared, though.

The narrator got 34 out of 100.

The narrator was scared of trying hard and still doing badly, which would threaten being called the clever one.

Sunaina Apa,
You told me to write when it was done, so here it is. Last night I told Ammi and Abbu I'm leaving the bank job to train as a chef.
I had the speech ready. But when I got to "I've been unhappy for two years," my lips started trembling like a kid's and my voice cracked. Abbu looked alarmed. I think he thought I was ill or in some trouble.
I remembered what you did before your own big talk: stop, breathe slowly, let the silence sit. So I did. Three slow breaths. Ammi just waited, her hand on the table near mine.
Then I finished properly. They didn't say yes. Abbu said, "Let us think." But they listened to all of it, and that's more than I'd hoped for.
Your nervous cousin,

Monday. At the Goa day-care, Francis, two, heard Chetan cry at drop-off. Francis stared, then cried too.

Wednesday. Chetan cried when his juice spilled. Francis's lip wobbled. His big sister, waiting at the gate, called, 'Francis, you're okay!' He cried anyway.

A loud drum.

Francis caught Chetan's distress and felt upset too, even though nothing had happened to him.

Sunday
Dear diary, today I swept the whole hall for the pooja guests. It took forever and my arm ached. Then Bhupen walked across in his white socks and held his feet up at me. Grey. I nearly cried. I was so fed up of doing it wrong that I went to the kitchen and asked Ammamma to show me properly. She took the broom and swept in short strokes from the walls into one corner, keeping it low, and then pushed the little heap into the dustpan in one go. "Your turn, good girl, Kiran," she said. I did the bedroom her way. It was done in about half the time and my arm didn't hurt. After lunch Bhupen checked his socks again. White!
- Kiran

What colour were Bhupen's socks after Kiran first swept the hall?
They were grey.
How was Kiran feeling when Bhupen held up his grey socks?
Kiran felt upset and fed up, close to crying, because all that effort still left the hall dusty.

Gurpreet had his milk at two. As he drank, his forehead smoothed, his hands went loose on the bottle, and his eyelids drooped. By the end his whole face was soft and he was asleep on my arm.
Woke at three-thirty, babbling and reaching for the ball, bright as usual.
What I watch for: if his face ever stays very still and he doesn't respond while awake, I'll tell his parents straight away.

When did Gurpreet have his milk?
Gurpreet had his milk at two.
What does Gurpreet's soft, relaxed face while drinking suggest he felt?
It suggests he felt comfortable, safe and content, relaxed enough to drift off to sleep in Urmila's arms.
What is sensible about what Urmila watches for?
Urmila knows a relaxed face in sleep is a good sign, but a very still, unresponsive face while awake needs attention, so Urmila would tell his parents straight away.
How might Gurpreet's parents feel reading this note?
They would probably feel reassured that he is comfortable with Urmila and that she is watching closely.

messages.content: Anil has seen only white swans, so he says all swans are white. Is he right?
He cannot be sure. Because he has seen only some swans and not all of them, there may be swans of other colours, and black swans do exist.

At the milk cooperative office in a small town near Erode, the clock showed 8 p.m., and Karthik was still sorting the farmers' payment slips for the third village. He'd already covered the morning collection for a colleague and agreed to fix the manager's nephew's computer.
Asif, packing his tiffin, watched him. Karthik said yes to everyone. Last week he'd dozed off at the weighing scale.
'Karthik, go home.'
'Manager asked me. How can I say no?'
Asif sat down beside him. 'Tomorrow, when he asks for the next thing, say you're finishing the slips first. I'll be right there. I'll take the computer.'
Karthik rubbed his eyes. 'He won't think I'm lazy?'
'You? Nobody in this office thinks that.'
Next morning, when the manager came over, Karthik said it, voice shaking a little. The manager just nodded. 'Okay. Finish the slips.'

What was Karthik sorting at 8 p.m.?
The farmers' payment slips for the third village.
Why did Karthik ask 'He won't think I'm lazy?'
Karthik worries that saying no would cost him the manager's good opinion; that fear keeps him agreeing to everything.
What backup did Asif offer, and why did it help Karthik say no?
Being there when the manager asked and taking the computer job; with that support, Karthik could set a limit without fearing he would look lazy.
How might the manager see Karthik's first no?
The manager simply nodded and told him to finish the slips, suggesting the refusal cost Karthik nothing; the manager may not have known how much Karthik was carrying.

(1) How do I prepare for a class presentation?
(2) My teacher used the word "taciturn". What is it?
(3) What does "barking dogs seldom bite" mean?

1. Make a few short points on cards and practise aloud with a friend or a mirror. Speak slowly and look at your audience.
2. As an adjective, "taciturn" means speaking very little.
3. It means people who make a lot of noise or threats are often not dangerous. For example: do not worry about his shouting, as barking dogs seldom bite.

After my father's long illness and the project that swallowed that whole winter, I stopped being someone people could reach. I'm Gargi, the loud one from college, and suddenly I ate lunch at my desk, answered in single words, jumped when a door slammed. Some colleagues decided I'd become arrogant after the promotion.
Vandana didn't decide anything. She kept leaving a second cup of tea on my desk at four, no questions. Once she said, "You don't have to talk. I just want you to know I'm around." Another day she slipped me the number for the counselling service our office offers and said, "Only if and when you want."
It took me three weeks to call. I still don't fully know what that winter was: grief, tiredness, something else. But I remember who didn't push.

What did Vandana leave on Gargi's desk at four?
A second cup of tea, with no questions.
What might Gargi's startling and single-word answers have shown?
Most likely Gargi was worn out and grieving after the father's illness and a hard project; it could also have been exhaustion alone, which is why Gargi still isn't sure.
What made Vandana's support helpful?
She stayed present through small, steady gestures, didn't push Gargi to talk, and offered the counselling number for whenever Gargi was ready.
How did some colleagues read Gargi's withdrawal?
They decided Gargi had become arrogant after the promotion, misreading the pulling back as pride.

"Three weeks, tops," said Xin, the lead developer, leaning back. The clinic's booking system in Durban had to move to new servers, and Lindiwe had to give the board a date by Friday. Three weeks already sounded like a fact. That evening she wrote at the top of a page: If nobody had said three, what would I guess? She didn't fully trust her answer, so she gathered comparisons. The pharmacy team's move last year took seven weeks. A friend at another clinic said theirs took six. The vendor's own case notes said five to eight. On Friday she told the board six to eight weeks and explained where each number came from. Xin grumbled, then admitted, "I was thinking of the easy part."

How long did the pharmacy team's move take last year?
Seven weeks.
Why did Lindiwe not trust her own first guess?
She felt uneasy that Xin's three weeks was already sitting in her head like a fact, so she wanted numbers that did not start from it.
What makes Lindiwe's method worth copying?
She asked what she would judge without the first figure, then checked three separate sources before giving the board a range.
How does Xin react to the six-to-eight-week estimate?
Xin grumbles at first but then admits the three weeks only covered the easy part.
Colleague ko bolna hai "Yeh kaam meri zimmedari nahi hai". Rude na lage.
Say: "I think this task belongs to the accounts team. Shall I tell you who to ask?" It explains clearly and does not blame anyone.
Aur agar boss ne diya ho wahi kaam?
Say: "Sir, I am already handling two tasks. Could we decide which one comes first?" This shows you are willing to help, but it makes the load clear.

Nandini found '#partner' at the end of the caption.
How did the reel's opening line make Nandini feel?
It made Nandini feel uneasy, as if Nandini's own flat were dirty, which was the need the ad was trying to create.
Which checks did Dhruv suggest, and why do they help?
Checking whether the post is paid, reading independent reviews and looking at the yearly filter cost; together they show what the reel left out.

It was pouring, the power was out, and the teacher had gone to fetch the register. Mridul, five, and Imran were at the block corner.
Imran knocked down Mridul's tower. Mridul's fists clenched.
"Hit him," someone whispered. "No one's looking."
Mridul raised his hand. Then he stopped and looked at the door. "Ma'am will know," he said.
"She's not here."
"She'll know," Mridul said, very sure. "Then I'll get the corner."
He put his hand down. Imran, surprised, began rebuilding.
When the teacher came back, Mridul told her at once. "I didn't hit. So no corner, right?"

What did Imran knock down?
Mridul's tower.
What was Mridul feeling when he looked at the door?
He felt worried about punishment, sure the teacher would somehow know and put him in the corner.
How could the teacher build on Mridul's choice?
She could praise him for not hitting and gently add that hitting hurts Imran, so he starts to think about feelings as well as punishment.
How might Imran see Mridul putting his hand down?
Imran seemed surprised and relieved, enough to start rebuilding the tower.

Mentoring notes, 12 February
Yamini came to my flat this evening, the first time since her college days. She works in quality at a pharma plant now. She asked if she could speak in confidence, and I said of course.
She has found batch records that don't match the lab results. She was frightened: of losing the job, of her younger brother's fees, of being wrong. She had not slept properly in a week.
We did three things. We wrote down only the facts she had seen, with dates. We listed what her family would need if the job went for a while. And I gave her the name of a lawyer I trust, for advice before she acts.
She said she felt like a coward for not reporting it today. I told her that getting ready properly is not the same as being afraid; a report built this way is much harder to brush aside. She left calmer.
- Ramesh

What had Yamini found at the plant?
She had found batch records that don't match the lab results.
What was Yamini afraid of?
She was afraid of losing her job, of not covering her younger brother's fees, and of being wrong.
Why is the careful plan in the note a wise step at this stage?
Recording only dated facts, planning for her family's needs and getting a lawyer's advice first protect her and make any report she makes stronger.
How might Ramesh feel seeing Yamini leave calmer?
Ramesh probably feels relieved and glad the trust from her college days still holds, and ready to keep supporting her.
Why do people light oil lamps on a windowsill during Diwali rather than only inside the house?
Lamps in the window show the glow to everyone outside. Because light placed at the edge of the home can be seen from the street, it welcomes visitors and shares the festival mood with the neighbours.
Describe a school playground during the break, 35 words: swings creaking, children running, a teacher's whistle, a vendor selling ice candy.

The playground is busy during the break. The swings creak, and children run in every direction. A teacher blows a whistle, and a vendor at the gate sells ice candy to the children, who gather around him.

At the taluka science exhibition in Sangamner, Anand's solar dryer for onions won first place. Back in the village, the men at the tea stall slapped his back, and his cousin said, "Now go tell Ganesh his windmill was rubbish." Anand almost laughed along. Then he pictured Ganesh's face at the exhibition and stopped. Did his prize only feel big if Ganesh felt small? "His windmill actually turned," he said. "Mine won because of the chart." The next day Parul ma'am pointed out a mistake in his temperature readings. His ears burned. "Show me where," he said, and fixed the numbers that evening by lantern light, still proud of his dryer.

What did Anand's project dry?
It was a solar dryer for onions.
What made Anand stop laughing along with his cousin?
He pictured Ganesh's face and asked himself whether his prize only felt big if Ganesh felt small, and he didn't want that.
How did Anand handle Parul ma'am's correction, and why was it wise?
His ears burned, but he asked her to show him and fixed the numbers that evening, accepting the correction without losing his pride.
How might Ganesh feel if he heard Anand praise his windmill?
He would probably feel respected and less bruised by losing.

At five, Tanvir slid off his chair and announced, "I'm bored. What can I do? Can I have the tablet?" His mother handed him a roll of masking tape and some cardboard tubes. "Build something." He grumbled, then taped a very long telescope and spent the afternoon spotting imaginary ships.

At nine, Tanvir sat at the back of the classroom with his chin in his hand and his body sunk low in the chair. The teacher, also named Payal, saw it and thought, "He looks bored." She stopped beside his desk. "Tanvir, are you with us? Tell me what you're working on." He straightened a little. "I stayed up late finishing my model. And I was thinking about the answer. I think it's twelve." He was right.

His friend Hrithik whispered after class, "I thought you were asleep." Tanvir grinned. "I think better slumped." The teacher smiled and added, "Next time I'll ask first and assume later."

What did Tanvir's mother give him when he said he was bored at five?
She gave him a roll of masking tape and some cardboard tubes.
How do Tanvir's boredom at five and his slouching at nine differ in what they show?

At five Tanvir's boredom is real and settled by simple materials, while at nine his slumped posture looks like boredom to the teacher but actually comes from tiredness and thinking, so posture is a clue and not proof.
What was Tanvir probably feeling when he said he was thinking about the answer?
Tanvir felt sleepy but engaged, comfortable slumped in a way that helped him think.
What did the teacher do that was wiser than assuming?
The teacher stopped at his desk and asked him about his work instead of deciding from his posture that he was bored.
I put "current" in my cake recipe and my sister laughed. Why?

For a dried berry in cakes, the word is "currant". "Current" means happening now, or a flow of water or electricity.
Examples: Add a handful of currants to the dough. The current news is about the match. The river has a strong current.

Nikita, you worry that questioning your teacher means you're ungrateful. Let your Tejas-kaka tell you about Swami Anandji. I was twenty, and my father had just died. I couldn't eat or study. Anandji ran a small ashram school near Nashik, and he let me sit in the library every afternoon, no questions asked, and fed me khichdi. He saved that year for me. I'd have done anything for him. Two years later he told us all to vote for a certain candidate, because 'the ashram needs it'. Something in me said no. I was ashamed of even thinking it. I went to him and said, 'Swamiji, I owe you my life. But my vote I must decide myself.' He was quiet for a long time. Then he laughed and said, 'Good. I didn't teach you to be a sheep.' Not every teacher would say that. But thanks and thinking can live together, Nikita.

What did Anandji feed Tejas?
Anandji fed him khichdi.
How did young Tejas feel when Anandji told them how to vote?
Tejas felt uneasy and ashamed, torn between deep gratitude and his own judgement.
What turning point in the story shows gratitude and clear thinking together?
Tejas telling Anandji he owed him his life but would decide his vote himself.
How did Anandji react to Tejas's refusal?
Anandji was quiet, then laughed and said he hadn't taught Tejas to be a sheep, accepting the independence.

Counsellor's note, Class 10. Written by Neelam Joshi.
Dolma met me today about choosing a stream. Her parents want science with biology so she can study medicine. Her results show she scores well in biology, but her strongest marks and her real excitement are in art and design. When she talks about sketching buildings, she sits up and speaks fast. When she talks about medicine, she looks at the floor.
We did an interest and aptitude activity. It pointed to architecture, which needs maths and physics as well as drawing.
Dolma was nervous: "Papa will be disappointed." I invited her parents in for a meeting next Friday. Her father came today to pick her up; I told him briefly and he agreed to come.
Next: at Friday's meeting, share both options and let Dolma explain in her own words.

Which career did the activity point to?
It pointed to architecture.
What does Dolma looking at the floor when talking about medicine suggest?
It suggests Dolma feels reluctant and unexcited about medicine, and maybe anxious about letting her parents down.
How could the Friday meeting help Dolma and her family decide?
If the counsellor lays out both paths and Dolma explains her interests herself, the family can weigh her strengths and their hopes together.
How might Dolma's father see her choice after the meeting?
He may start to see architecture as a serious path that still uses her maths and science, which could ease his worries.

Present this as a short note from Miss Joyce to Francis's parents.

In the colony playground, Francis snatched the ball from Jeevan and ran off laughing. Jeevan sat down in the dust and cried.
Miss Joyce, who ran the evening play group, walked over to Francis and crouched down so their eyes were level.
"Francis, look at Jeevan," she said softly. "Look at his face. It's all wet. He's sad."
Francis looked. Jeevan's cheeks were shiny with tears.
"What happened just before he started crying?" Miss Joyce asked.
Francis looked at the ball in his hands. "I took it," he said, very quietly.

Note for Francis's parents

In the colony playground, Francis snatched the ball from Jeevan and ran off laughing. Jeevan sat down in the dust and cried. I walked over, crouched down so that our eyes were level, and said softly, "Francis, look at Jeevan. Look at his face. It's all wet. He's sad." Francis looked. Jeevan's cheeks were shiny with tears. I asked, "What happened just before he started crying?" Francis looked at the ball in his hands and said, very quietly, "I took it."

The power went out at the recording studio at 4:50, ten minutes before the choir from Reena's school was due. The generator kicked in, but the big mixing desk reset to factory settings. Payal stared at it. She had last patched a twelve-voice choir in March, and now the order of the cables was simply gone. Her phone was at two percent, so the notes app was no help. For a second her chest tightened. Then she remembered the laminated card taped inside the second drawer, the one she rewrote every few weeks. She pulled it out, traced each line with her finger, and began plugging in. "Of course I forgot," she muttered. "I haven't touched this since March." When Reena walked in with the children, the first microphone was already live.

Where did Payal keep the backup steps for patching the choir?
On a laminated card taped inside the second drawer.
How can you tell Payal was scared at first, and what calmed her?
Her chest tightened and she stared at the desk, feeling panicky; the memory of her card steadied her, and she felt calmer once she saw forgetting a March setup as normal.
What small habit helped Payal most, and how could she make it stronger?
Rewriting the card every few weeks kept it ready; she could also keep a paper copy near the generator in case both power and phone fail.
What would change for Reena and the children if Payal had blamed herself instead?
Payal might have frozen or rushed, and Reena would have walked in to a studio that was not ready, with nervous children waiting.

Mitul, you told your friend to stop being such a baby about the boys teasing him. I said the same thing once, at fifteen, and I've never forgotten it.
At my school in Nagpur, the older girls called my friend Sushmita 'Moti' every day at the water cooler and made pig noises. She came to me with red eyes. And I, Irawati, her best friend, said, 'Arre, you're too touchy. Toughen up and ignore them.'
It was easier for me. If the trouble was her softness, then I didn't have to face those girls.
Sushmita stopped telling me things after that. All that summer she went to the water cooler alone, or not at all.
Years later she said, 'I didn't need to be tougher. I needed you next to me.'
So, Mitul. Tomorrow, stand next to him.

What did the older girls call Sushmita at the water cooler?
They called her 'Moti' and made pig noises.
Why did telling Sushmita to toughen up feel easier to young Irawati?
If the problem was Sushmita's softness, Irawati did not have to face the older girls; blaming Sushmita's sensitivity let Irawati dodge a frightening confrontation.
What choice does Irawati hope Mitul will make tomorrow, and why?
To stand next to the friend being teased; Sushmita's words show that a bullied person needs company, not advice to be tougher.
What was that summer like for Sushmita after Irawati's reply?
Sushmita stopped confiding and went to the cooler alone or not at all, left to face the teasing without the friend she had counted on.

Read this:

Bidisha was nine when she got stuck on the word "enormous" in front of the whole class. Her ears went hot. Instead of trying again, she crossed her eyes, puffed out her cheeks and read the next line in a squeaky voice. The class burst out laughing, and Asif Sir hid a smile before asking her to read properly. Bidisha grinned around at everyone, but her hands were shaking against the book.
At fifteen she still reached for a joke when her stomach dropped. After a group project went missing, she texted her friend Uday: "Great, just great 🙂". Uday stared at the screen. Was she angry, or being funny? Her flat voice in class the next day gave him no clue either. He nudged her at lunch. "Are you joking, or are you actually upset?" Bidisha let out a breath. "Upset. I was hoping you'd ask." She pushed her tray aside and told him about the lost files.

What did Bidisha do after she got stuck on the word "enormous"?
She crossed her eyes, puffed out her cheeks and read the next line in a squeaky voice.
How are Bidisha's squeaky reading at nine and her "Great, just great" text at fifteen alike, and how do they differ in how others take them?

Both are jokes she uses to cover worry. At nine the class saw a silly face and laughed, but at fifteen the sarcasm was flat and in text, so Uday could not tell whether she was angry or being funny until he asked.
What was Bidisha feeling when she grinned at the class with shaking hands?
She was embarrassed and anxious. The grin showed she wanted to stay in charge of the moment, while the trembling hands showed the worry underneath.
What could Uday do when someone's sarcastic message leaves him unsure?
He can ask a plain, kind question, like "Are you joking, or are you actually upset?", and then really listen to the answer.

Tuesday. At the bus stop Madhav saw Sanya share her earphones with Kunal from their class. They were laughing at something on her phone. Madhav got on the bus and said nothing. He replayed it all the way home.

Wednesday. He scrolled through Sanya's tagged photos until midnight. Kunal was in four of them. In one, from the dance practice, Kunal's hand was on her shoulder. Everyone's hands were on everyone's shoulders; it was a group dance. Madhav saw only Kunal's.

Friday, three days after the bus stop. He asked Sanya, "Do you like Kunal?" She laughed. "What? No! He's just funny." Madhav felt relieved. For one evening.

Saturday. He asked again, in a different way. "Why do you always sit near him?" Sanya's smile faded. "I don't. Why are you asking me this again?"

That night Madhav realised the answers weren't helping. The fear just waited, and came back.

What did Sanya share with Kunal at the bus stop?
Her earphones.
How can you tell Madhav feels afraid again after each answer?
He feels relieved for one evening after Sanya's answer, then anxious again the next day, asking in a different way.
What turning point is open to Madhav at this stage?
Noticing that asking again doesn't help, and turning to look at his own fear, perhaps with a trusted adult, instead of seeking more reassurance.
What is it like for Sanya to be asked again on Saturday?
She feels confused and a bit hurt, her smile fading, as the repeated questions start to feel like distrust.

On Thursday Mrs. Rao said we needed seven things for Friday's craft class: glue, scissors, chart paper, crayons, cotton, ribbon and glitter. I didn't have a pencil, so I made them into a chant. Glue-scissors-chart-crayons-cotton-ribbon-glitter. I chanted it through the school gate and down the lane, over and over, like a song on a bus. It worked, until our front door. My little brother Mohit jumped out shouting, "Trisha didi, look, I lost a tooth!" I looked. I admired the tooth. When I opened my mouth to tell Amma the list, only five things came out. Ribbon and cotton had run away. On Friday I sat with a cotton-less, ribbon-less cloud picture.

Which two items did Trisha forget?
Trisha forgot the ribbon and the cotton.
How did Trisha feel when only five things came out?
Trisha probably felt annoyed and a bit embarrassed, since the chant had worked all the way home.
What other approach could have kept all seven items safe, and why?
Trisha could have borrowed a pencil and written the list, because writing does not vanish when someone interrupts.
How might Mohit see the lost list?
Mohit was just excited about his tooth and probably had no idea his news chased two items out of Trisha's head.

Dear Diary,
It rained so hard today that the school sent us home early. Water filled the playground like a pond, and we jumped in the puddles on the way out. My shoes were soaked, but I didn't mind. It felt like a surprise holiday.

Dear Payal ma'am,
I wanted to tell you where things stand, since you asked me to write even if the news was bad. It was: twelve applications since graduation, nine silences, three rejections. The last one was the design studio I really wanted. I read the email on the bus and got off two stops early so no one would see my face.
I took your advice anyway. I asked them for feedback, politely, and they actually replied: strong visuals, but no explanation of my process. That stung, but it was fair. I've added short case notes to three projects and applied to four more places this week.
Some days I still wonder if I'm good enough. But I'm treating each no as information, not a verdict.
Thank you for not letting me hide.
Lavanya

What feedback did the design studio give?
Strong visuals, but no explanation of the process.
Why did Lavanya get off the bus two stops early?
Lavanya felt hurt and embarrassed after the rejection and didn't want anyone to see that disappointment.
What did Lavanya do after the rejection that others could copy?
Asked politely for feedback, fixed the specific gap with case notes, and kept applying.
How might Payal feel reading this email?
Payal might feel moved and proud that the advice was used, and glad Lavanya wrote even with bad news 🤍

Monday: Darshan, Jatin's cousin, called from the hostel office. 'You're on the allotment committee. Just put me on the ground-floor list. Nobody will notice.' Jatin said he'd think about it, then lay awake counting: forty-two first-years waiting, some from far-off districts with no relatives in the city.
Wednesday: he walked past the notice board, found Darshan's name at thirty-one on the queue list, and felt sick. Darshan's family had lent him their scooter all last year. Saying no felt like betrayal; saying yes felt like cheating strangers.
Friday: he met Darshan at the tea stall. 'I can't move you up. It wouldn't be fair to the others. But I'll help you find a paying-guest room nearby till your turn comes, and I'll move your stuff myself.' Darshan sulked, then asked which lanes were quietest.

Where was Darshan's name on the queue list?
At thirty-one on the queue list.
What was Jatin feeling on Wednesday?
Jatin felt torn and sick: refusing seemed like betraying family who had helped him, while agreeing seemed like cheating strangers.
Why is Jatin's Friday answer better than a plain yes or no?
It keeps the list fair for the other first-years but still shows loyalty, because Jatin offers real help with a room and the move.
How might the first-years from far-off districts be affected if Jatin had said yes?
One of them could have lost a ground-floor place to someone with connections, and learned that the list does not really count.

I'm Abhinav. Last semester Zainab submitted our joint project under her name only, and I lost the internship it could have got me. For months I called her a thief in my head. Then, last week, at the college canteen, her roommate told me something I didn't know. Zainab's scholarship depended on that grade; if she lost it, she'd have to leave college and go back home. She had panicked the night before the deadline. Hearing that didn't make what she did okay. It was still wrong, and I still lost something real. But I noticed something change in me. She stopped being a villain and became a scared person who did a bad thing. The bitterness I'd been carrying loosened a little, like a knot finally let go. I don't know if I'll talk to her yet. I just don't hate her the way I did.

What did Zainab's scholarship depend on, according to her roommate?
Zainab's scholarship depended on that grade.
How did Abhinav feel after hearing about Zainab's scholarship?
Abhinav still felt wronged, but his bitterness loosened, as if Zainab had become a frightened person instead of a villain.
What is Abhinav's next possible step now that the bitterness has eased?
Abhinav could decide calmly whether to talk to Zainab, naming what her act cost while understanding her fear, without pretending it was okay.
How might Zainab have felt the night before the deadline?
Zainab was probably panicked and desperate, terrified of losing the scholarship and being sent home.

Read this:

At the Dussehra fair in their village near Nashik, Siddharth, nine, bought a big plate of jalebis with his pocket money. After two bites he didn't like them. Too sticky, too sweet. But he kept eating. "I paid ten rupees," he told his cousin Yash. "I have to finish." His stomach started to hurt. Yash offered to throw the rest away. "No! Then my money is wasted." Siddharth ate another one, slowly, frowning. Then another. By the last one, he felt sick. He sat on the steps of the temple while the other children ran to the giant wheel. He had no money left for the ride, and his stomach ached. "At least I didn't waste the jalebis," he said weakly.

How much did Siddharth pay for the jalebis?
Ten rupees.
Why did Siddharth keep eating jalebis he didn't like?
He felt reluctant to waste the ten rupees, so the money already spent felt like a reason to continue, even though he was miserable and sick.
What could Siddharth do next time he doesn't like something he paid for?
He could stop when he dislikes it, since the money is already spent either way, and save his stomach for something he enjoys.
How might Yash see Siddharth's choice?
Yash probably thinks it's silly and a bit worrying, since he offered to throw the rest away.
I enjoyed to watch the match last night.

I enjoyed watching the match last night.
Why: The verb "enjoy" is followed by the -ing form, not "to" plus a verb.
Aur "I like to watch" bhi sahi hai?

The electricity bill arrived the same morning as the third reminder from the credit card company, and Siddharth put both, unopened, under the fruit bowl. Rent was due in four days. His salary was due in six.
It'll sort itself out, he told himself. Next month's bonus. Or the side project. He had been saying it since March.
His phone buzzed with an unknown number. He turned it face down.
At lunch his sister Sunaina called. "You sound tired. Everything okay?"
"All good. Just busy." He laughed. He always laughed.
That night he couldn't sleep. At 2 am he lifted the fruit bowl and looked at the envelopes, then put the bowl back on top. Opening them would mean knowing the number. Knowing the number would mean doing something.
He lay in the dark, heart racing, telling himself one more time that it would all work out.

Where did Siddharth put the envelopes?
Under the fruit bowl, unopened.
Why did Siddharth put the fruit bowl back on the envelopes at 2 am?
Siddharth felt frightened; opening them would mean knowing the number and having to act, which he wasn't ready for.
What could Siddharth do instead of waiting for it to sort itself out?
Open the envelopes in daylight, tell Sunaina the truth when she calls, and speak to a qualified debt adviser about the options.
What would change if Sunaina knew what was under the fruit bowl?
Sunaina could offer support and help him find proper advice, instead of hearing 'all good' while he lies awake.

Dear Kishore,
You asked why I cancelled my trip to Rishikesh after that rafting accident video and then un-cancelled it. Honestly, I watched it five times and my stomach dropped every time. I was ready to swear off rivers forever. Then I made myself stop and ask: how often does this actually happen? I found the state tourism report and a rafting association's safety data. Thousands of people raft there every season; serious accidents are rare, and most involve groups without licensed guides or life jackets. So I've rebooked, with a licensed company, and I'll wear the jacket they give me. It still feels a bit scary, but now it's a fear I've checked.
Your sister,
Sunaina

What did Sunaina find to check the risk?
Sunaina found the state tourism report and a rafting association's safety data.
Why was Sunaina ready to swear off rivers forever?
Watching the accident video five times made the danger feel vivid and close, so for a while one dramatic case felt like what usually happens.
What in Sunaina's approach can others copy when a scary story shakes them?
Pause, ask how often it truly happens, look at reliable figures, and then adjust the plan sensibly, like choosing a licensed company and wearing the life jacket.
How might Kishore feel reading this letter?
Kishore would probably feel reassured that Sunaina's decision rests on checked facts, not on one frightening clip.

Tuesday night
Had a fight with Varun today. He said, "You always take the bigger piece of cake." And before he even finished I was saying, "No I don't! Last week YOU took the bigger piece!"
Then he said, "I'm not talking about cake, I mean you never let me choose anything." And I said, "That's not true, I let you choose the movie on Sunday!"
Then he went quiet and went to his room.
Now I'm lying here thinking. I heard every word he said, but I was only listening for the bits I could argue with. I didn't really hear what he meant. I think he meant he feels left out.
Tomorrow I'll ask him what he meant, and just listen.
Ankita

What did Varun say Ankita always takes?
The bigger piece of cake.
What was Ankita feeling while lying in bed thinking about the fight?
Ankita felt sorry and a bit guilty, realising the listening was only to argue and missing that Varun felt left out.
What small step does Ankita plan for tomorrow?
To ask Varun what he meant and simply listen, without arguing back.
How might Varun have felt when Ankita kept arguing?
He probably felt unheard and frustrated, which is why he went quiet and left.

Two thieves were caught near the station last night.
Why: "Thief" becomes "thieves".
Explain what causes tides in two sentences, and use the word "moon" in the first one.
Tides are caused mainly by the pull of the moon's gravity on the oceans. The sun adds a smaller pull, so the highest and lowest tides change through the month.
What do people do during Eid?

Celebrations vary, but many families start the day with special prayers, then wear new clothes and visit relatives and friends. Sweet dishes like sheer khurma are common, and elders often give children small gifts of money called eidi.
My neighbour invited us over. What should I say when I arrive?
"Eid Mubarak" is the usual greeting, and it means "blessed Eid." Smile, say it to each family member you meet, and accept the food they offer. A small box of sweets is a kind thing to bring along.

Swati slid in from the other side and grabbed the rope.
"That's mine!" Chaitanya shouted, so loud that the boys by the handpump looked up. His ears burned. She had seen him waiting, he was certain. She always found a way to be first.

Where did the tyre swing hang?
It hung from the neem tree behind the panchayat school.

One afternoon, his old classmate Kishore, now working in the city, stopped by. He wore a crisp shirt and talked about his office, the traffic and his big salary. "Don't you want more?" he asked. At seven.

You think your manager will eat you alive over one slide, beta? Listen to your old Arnab mama. When I was twenty-five I shared a flat with Vinita, who did designs for a printing press. Clever girl, sharper than me.

That winter she stopped coming to our Sunday cricket and stopped eating dinner with us. I would wake at two and see her lamp still on, and her rubbing out a line she'd drawn ten times.

One night I asked to see it. It was a poster for a school fair. It was beautiful. She said the border was uneven. I said, "Vinita, show me the version you'd give if the press opened in one hour." She laughed, but she handed it over, and I told her the two things I'd really change.

Nitin joined the chess club.

By gently explaining the drift isn't rejection, encouraging a Saturday invite to Nitin, and helping Jagdish find his own new activity.

He hit two fours and even laughed when the ball smacked the umpire's shoe. Then, walking off, a horrible thought hit harder than any ball: what kind of grandson laughs two days after his Dadi dies?
He sat alone behind the pavilion. Coach Gautam Sir found him there. "You played well. What's wrong?"
Yash blurted it out. "I didn't cry. Now I'm laughing. I think I'm broken."
Gautam Sir sat beside him. "You're not broken. People grieve differently. Sometimes the tears come later, sometimes in small bits. Tell your parents what you told me, tonight. And if it comes during practice, you can sit out, no questions."
Yash nodded, and his shoulders came down a little.

What did Yash hit in the final?
Two fours.
What was Yash worried about behind the pavilion?
He felt guilty and scared that something was wrong with him because he felt nothing and even laughed.
What did Gautam Sir advise?
That Yash is not broken, people grieve differently, he should tell his parents tonight, and he can sit out practice if feelings come.
How might Gautam Sir have seen Yash sitting alone?
As a boy carrying a heavy worry after his Dadi's death, needing reassurance more than cricket talk.

This Sunday she brought him to the meeting too, holding his elbow over the uneven ground. When the talk turned to the broken handpump near the school, most of the young people stayed at the edges, scrolling. Kavitha stood up and read out the complaint her father had dictated to her, plus her own count of how many children fetched water from far away. Her neighbour Sarika, who had come only to watch, stepped forward. 'I'll collect signatures from our lane.' Her father squeezed Kavitha's hand, hard.

Where did the gram sabha meet?
Under the neem tree.
What does her father squeezing Kavitha's hand hard suggest?
It suggests he felt proud and moved that she was speaking up and carrying his concern.
How could Kavitha keep balancing care for her father with community work?
She can keep involving him, as she did at the meeting, and share tasks with neighbours like Sarika so she isn't carrying it alone.
How might Sarika's view of the meeting have changed?
She came only to watch, but seeing Kavitha speak made her want to take part herself.

Yash's plan for the Darjeeling trip looked almost boring. Tenzin, reading it over his shoulder at the station, pointed at one line: "Spare: 450 (10% of 4,500)." "Why keep money doing nothing?" "Because something always goes wrong," Yash said. "And every day has one empty hour. See, after lunch." Tenzin shrugged. Then the announcement came: their train from Siliguri was running ninety minutes late. Rain had slowed everything on the line. Tenzin groaned. Yash was already recounting. "We lose today's empty hour, plus a bit. So we skip the tea shop and still reach the homestay before dark." In Darjeeling, the shared jeep to the monastery cost more than the website had said. Yash paid the difference from the spare. By day three, the plan had bent twice and nothing had broken.

How late was the train from Siliguri?
The train from Siliguri was running ninety minutes late.
What does Yash's quick recounting suggest about how he felt when the delay was announced?
Yash stayed calm rather than panicked, because the spare hour meant a delay was a problem he had already expected.
What else could Yash try if a delay ran much longer than the spare hour?
He could decide in advance which stop is first to drop each day, so a big delay means one quick cut instead of a scramble.
How might Tenzin see the boring spare line by day three?
Tenzin, who shrugged it off at first, likely sees its worth after the delay and the costlier jeep, since the empty hour and the spare money kept the trip on track.

Saturday night. Rain! It came at ten, just as we were leaving for the ground. Samir's cousin and I stood at the window for five minutes looking sad. Then Samir said, "What if today is a carrom day?" So it was. Three of us on the floor around the board, and after lunch Nani's ludo box came out, and the fight over the yellow tokens was louder than any cricket match. I lost three games and won one. Pakoras at four while the rain drummed on the tin roof. Cricket next week. Honestly, this felt like a different kind of good day, not a wasted one. Aditi

What games did the children play after the rain started?
They played carrom on the floor and later ludo.
How did Aditi feel by the end of the day?
Content, since Aditi calls it a different kind of good day and not a wasted one. 😊
What other approach could turn a rained-off day into something good, and why?
They could cook something together, like pakoras, or plan the match for next week, because a shared activity keeps spirits up.
How might Samir's idea of a carrom day have felt to the others at the window?
Probably like a relief, since they were looking sad and Samir gave them something to do straight away.

messages.content:
Miss Havisham is talking to her relatives. What does she picture happening when she dies?

"Matthew will come and see me at last," said Miss Havisham, sternly, "when I am laid on that table. That will be his place,—there," striking the table with her stick, "at my head! And yours will be there! And your husband's there! And Sarah Pocket's there! And Georgiana's there! Now you all know where to take your stations when you come to feast upon me. And now go!"
She imagines her body laid on the table, with each relative standing in a fixed place around it. She says they will come to feast on her.
Why is the ground cooler under a big tree in summer?

The tree's shade and cool leaves keep the ground below cooler. Because the leaves block much of the sunlight and the tree also gives off water vapour from its leaves, which cools the air around them, the spot stays pleasant.

On a Tuesday in the woodwork room of a school in Leeds, Emeka, the design teacher, noticed something: Wei, sixteen, hadn't called him over once. Two months ago Wei had asked about every mark of the dovetail joint: where to saw, how deep, which chisel. Last month the questions had shrunk to "Is this line okay?"
Emeka stayed at his desk, pretending to mark books, and watched Wei scribe, saw and pare the joint alone. It went together tight on the second try.
Across the corridor, a colleague still stood over every student's shoulder, and those students still waited, hands in laps, for the next instruction. Emeka had once taught the same way.
He carried his stool to the far bench and started on his own project. When Wei looked up for him, Emeka only raised a thumb.

What joint was Wei making?
Wei was making a dovetail joint.
How does Emeka seem to feel as he watches Wei work alone from his desk?
He seems pleased and confident in Wei, holding back on purpose and only raising a thumb when Wei looks up.
What choice did Emeka make after the joint fit, and why does it help?
He moved to the far bench and only raised a thumb, so Wei learns to trust their own judgement while help is still in the room.
What is it like for the students across the corridor, whose teacher still stands over every shoulder?
They sit waiting for the next instruction with hands in their laps, because help that is never withdrawn keeps them from building confidence.

Monday: Arnab's history project was due on Friday. At nine he lay on his bed with his phone. "Tomorrow I'll be fresh," he told his sister Kalyani when she asked. "Tuesday me is way more serious." He watched videos until midnight.
Wednesday: Tuesday had gone the same way. Now he scrolled with a small knot in his stomach, the empty project file open on the laptop behind the phone. "Tomorrow, full focus," he muttered. Kalyani raised an eyebrow and said nothing.
Friday, 6 a.m.: Arnab sat at the dining table, eyes red, gluing pictures onto chart paper and scribbling captions. He handed it in half-finished. That evening he asked Kalyani to keep his phone until eight.

When was Arnab's history project due?
Arnab's history project was due on Friday.
Why did 'Tuesday me is way more serious' feel true to Arnab on Monday night?
Tonight he felt tired and the videos were easy, so he imagined a fresher, more serious self tomorrow who would happily do the hard part.
What turning point does Arnab reach, and why might it help?
He asks Kalyani to keep his phone until eight, which removes the scrolling at the moment he usually gives in instead of trusting tomorrow's mood.
How might Kalyani feel when Arnab hands her the phone on Friday evening?
She may feel quietly glad, having watched the week unfold without lecturing, and pleased he chose the fix himself.
I introduce myself as "Myself Ravi." My teacher said change it.
The standard form is: "I am Ravi." Or: "My name is Ravi." The word "myself" is not used as the subject of a sentence.
Aur phone pe kaise introduce karun?
Say: "Hello, this is Ravi." It is clear and polite on a call.

"Look, ants!" Pranav lifted his foot.
"Stop!" Farhan grabbed his arm. "Don't squash them."
"Why? They're tiny."
"They're carrying food. See? That one has a crumb bigger than him."
Pranav crouched. "He's strong."
"And they're going home. Their family's waiting."
Pranav put his foot down slowly, away from the line. "Let's give them a biscuit."

What did Farhan say the ants were carrying?
Farhan said they were carrying food, one with a crumb bigger than itself.
Why did Farhan grab Pranav's arm?
Farhan didn't want the ants to be hurt and felt they mattered.
How did Farhan change Pranav's mind without fighting?
Farhan showed him something interesting about the ants so Pranav could see them as living creatures.
How does Pranav's view of the ants change?
He goes from thinking they're tiny and unimportant to admiring them and wanting to help.

Monday. At a loud birthday party Uma pushed both children onto the dance floor. Nakul whooped; Pooja, five, hid behind the curtain and cried.
Wednesday. Worn out by Nakul's chatter, Uma declared quiet time for both. Nakul, four, kicked the sofa and wailed. Pooja finally smiled.
Saturday. Uma sent Nakul to the park with the neighbour's boys and sat alone with Pooja, rolling dough in silence. When Nakul burst back full of stories, she listened to every one. That night she felt tired, but less torn.

Where did Pooja hide at the party?
Behind the curtain.
How did Uma feel on Saturday night, and why?
She felt tired but less torn, because each child had got the kind of attention they needed.
What did Uma learn from Monday and Wednesday?
Forcing both children into the same thing upset one of them each time; giving each a different kind of time worked better.
What was Wednesday's quiet time like for Nakul?
Nakul felt frustrated and trapped, kicking the sofa and wailing, because quiet suits Pooja, not him.

The Christmas holidays power cut came right in the middle of the card game. Francis, Ayesha and two cousins sat around a candle, trying to finish before it burned down. In the flicker, Francis could see Ayesha's cards reflected in the steel plate. He could win easily. He looked away. "Your turn," he said. One cousin, though, kept peeking and pretended he wasn't. Everyone noticed. The candle guttered and died just as Ayesha won. The next evening, Ayesha knocked on Francis's door. "Cards again? Just you and me and Chotu." "What about the other cousin?" Ayesha shrugged. "He peeks." Francis felt a warm little glow of pride.

What did Francis see Ayesha's cards reflected in?
The steel plate.
What did Francis feel when Ayesha invited him but not the cousin?
He felt a warm glow of pride, knowing that playing fairly made him someone she wanted to play with.
What does the story show about how a reputation forms?
It forms quickly from small acts: one evening of peeking or playing fair decided who was invited back.
How might the cousin who peeked feel when he isn't invited?
He may feel left out and confused, not realising everyone noticed his peeking.

Class teacher's note, Class 10-A, civics project
For the unit on local government, Joseph and Nazia chose to track how complaints reach the municipal office. They filed a real complaint about a broken streetlight near school and followed it.
Joseph was frustrated when nothing happened for two weeks. He wanted to post angry comments online. Nazia said her father would be upset if the family name appeared in a public fight.
They argued, then chose a middle path: a polite follow-up letter, signed by both families, and a visit to the ward office. The light was fixed in the fourth week.
In their presentation, Joseph said, "I thought respecting rules meant staying quiet. It means using them properly." I have shared their letter as a model with the other sections.

What did Joseph and Nazia complain about?
A broken streetlight near school.
What was Joseph feeling when nothing happened for two weeks?
He felt frustrated and impatient, wanting to post angry comments online.
Which choice worked, and why?
The polite letter signed by both families and a ward office visit worked, because it used the proper system and respected both families.
How might Nazia's father see the way they handled it?
He would likely feel relieved and proud that the complaint was made respectfully without a public fight.

In the career guidance room at a training institute, a poster about "new skills" hung crooked on the wall. Avni, three weeks after the layoff, sat across from the counsellor Baljeet and said, "I'm not sure what I should do." Baljeet asked one question: "What is the market paying for right now?" Avni pulled out the phone and looked at job listings. Cloud skills appeared everywhere. "Then start there," Baljeet said. Avni signed up for an entry-level cloud course and, in the same meeting, planned two evenings of freelance work to keep some income going. Avni still felt anxious, but the anxiety now had somewhere to go. The poster still hung crooked, though it looked less mocking.

What did Baljeet ask about the market?
Baljeet asked what the market is paying for right now.
How did Avni feel at the end of the meeting?
Avni still felt anxious, but the anxiety now had somewhere to go, which made it easier to bear.
What could Avni do if the course turns out to be too hard, and why?
Avni could ask the counsellor about a smaller first step, since a manageable course keeps the plan alive.
How might Baljeet see the start of the meeting?
Baljeet probably sees a worried person who needs a direction, and uses a single question to help.

"Madhuri! The alarm! Madhuri, come!"
"Harsha bhaiya... I can't..."
"What do you mean, you can't? You know the rules!"
"I know them. My legs won't go."
"Give me your hand. Low, like this. Door. Stairs. Go."
Outside, on the pavement, their mother wrapped Madhuri in a shawl. It had only been smoke from burnt toast, and Papa had already opened every window.
"I knew what to do," Madhuri sobbed. "I said it in class. But I just stood there."
"Knowing it isn't the same as doing it," Harsha said. "You've only ever heard it. Tomorrow we'll do it for real. Ten times, if you want."

What had caused the smoke?
Burnt toast.
How did Madhuri feel when she said her legs wouldn't go?
She felt frozen with fear and later upset and ashamed that she knew the rules but couldn't act.
What else could help Madhuri besides practising at home?
She could ask her school to include a surprise drill, so she practises moving when she isn't expecting it.
How does the moment look to Harsha?
Harsha is scared and impatient at first, then understanding, offering to practise with her as many times as she wants.

Elizabeth, you've got your first offer letter? Wonderful. Sit, I'll tell you what happened with mine, in Delhi, when I was a young woman of twenty-two. The company offered a figure. Before that, I had no idea what a fair salary was. So their number became my world. I asked for a tiny bit more, felt brave, and signed. Two years later, my manager showed me the salary survey for our role. I was well below the middle. Not because I was worse. Because I'd started from their number and moved a few steps. My friend Sudha, who joined the same month, had asked a senior first, and she started from the survey. We did the same job. So before you reply to them, talk to people in the field and the college careers office. That's what Parul learned the hard way.

Who showed Parul the salary survey?
Her manager, two years later.
How did young Parul feel after asking for a tiny bit more?
Parul felt brave and satisfied, because the company's number had become the only reference, so a small increase felt like a win.
What choice in the story made the difference between Parul and Sudha?
Sudha asked a senior and started from the salary survey, while Parul started from the company's number and moved only a little.
How might Sudha have seen the offer when she joined?
Sudha likely felt more confident and informed, knowing what the role usually paid before she replied.

The maths test in the Mexico City school started right after recess. Javier slid into his seat, shirt stuck to his back, drops of sweat running down his temples.
Wei, at the next desk, whispered, "Are you okay? You look really nervous."
Javier grinned and wiped his forehead with his sleeve. "Nervous? I just ran the whole yard six times. We won the race!"
Wei looked again. Javier's face was red, not pale, and he was breathing hard but smiling. His pencil was steady.
"Oh," Wei said. "I thought it was the test."
"The test is easy," Javier said, fanning himself with the question paper. "The race was hard."
By the second question, his breathing had slowed and the sweat had dried.

How many times did Javier run the yard?
Six times.
What was Wei thinking when seeing Javier's sweat?
Wei felt concerned and assumed Javier was nervous about the test, reading the sweat as worry.
How could Wei have read the situation more accurately?
By noticing the setting, right after recess, and other signs like a red face, a smile and a steady pencil, which point to exercise, not nerves.
How might Javier see Wei's question?
Javier seemed amused and a bit surprised, since he felt happy from the race, not worried.

"Arjuna said, 'Sikhandin, O Krishna, will certainly be the cause of Bhishma's death, for Bhishma, as soon as he beholds the prince of the Panchalas, abstains from striking. Therefore, keeping Sikhandin before him and at our head, we will, by that means, overthrow the son of Ganga. Even this is what I think. I will hold in check other great bowmen with my shafts. As regards Sikhandin, he will fight with Bhishma alone, that foremost of all warriors. I have heard from that chief of the Kurus that he would not strike Sikhandin, for having been born before as a woman he subsequently became a male person.'"

Why does Arjuna want Sikhandin placed in front of Bhishma?
Arjuna says Bhishma will not strike him, because Sikhandin was born a woman before becoming a man. So Sikhandin can face Bhishma while Arjuna holds back the other great bowmen.
Soften this rejection, please: No, you can't join our team. You're not good enough.
Thank you for wanting to join the team. We can't offer you a place this time, but we would be glad to see you try again next season.
Society secretary ko likhna hai ki paani ka tanker kal nahi aaya.
You can write: "The water tanker did not come yesterday." Use "did not come" because it is about a finished day.

In the courtyard of the house in a small town near Nashik, Sharmila's mother-in-law Minakshi was oiling her own hair when she looked up and said, "Come here, sit. I'll do yours as well. My own girl is far away, so you are my girl now." Sharmila felt warmth and a shy flutter. Nobody had done this since childhood. While Minakshi's fingers worked, she said, "Don't take the night shift job, it will tire you." Sharmila smiled. "Thank you, Amma. I'll think about it, I promise." Later, on the porch, Sharmila called home and told the mother about the courtyard and the oil. "Being loved here doesn't take anything away from you," Sharmila said. The mother laughed, delighted.

Where was Minakshi sitting when she invited Sharmila to sit?
In the courtyard of the house in a small town near Nashik.
What did Sharmila feel when Minakshi offered to oil Sharmila's hair?
Warmth and a shy flutter, since nobody had done this since childhood.
How did Sharmila handle Minakshi's advice about the night shift job?
Sharmila thanked Minakshi and promised to think about it, taking the advice as care while keeping the choice to Sharmila.
How might Sharmila's own mother have felt hearing about the courtyard?
She was delighted and laughed, so she seems glad that Sharmila is cared for, especially since Sharmila reassured her that being loved there takes nothing away.

1) I keep seeing "coverlet" in my reading. Meaning?
2) Please correct: Both of them was happy.

1. "Coverlet" is a noun. It means a bedspread.
2. Say it this way: Both of them were happy. Why: "both" means two, so it is plural and takes "were".

On Monday Leela stood by the fence at playtime and watched the skipping rope go round. Nobody looked her way. She counted the bricks in the wall until the bell rang. At home her mother asked about school, and Leela shrugged, so her mother taught her a line to try, "Can I play too?", and asked Mridul's mum whether he could come over on Saturday.

On Tuesday Leela walked up to the ball game and said the line. A girl said, "You can't play with us." Something heavy sat in Leela's tummy like a stone, and her eyes filled. She sat down on the bench with her chin tucked in.

The teacher crossed the yard and sat beside her, saying very little. After a while the teacher fetched a bag of beanbags and called, "Anyone want to try beanbags with Leela and me?" Two children ran over. Leela felt less alone, though her cheeks were still warm.

On Saturday Mridul came to play, and by Monday he was waving at her from the goal. "Come, you can be the goalkeeper!" Leela ran over, warm all through, and remembered who had asked her. At the fence she saw Jagdish standing alone with his hands in his pockets. "Do you want to play with us?" she called.

What did the teacher fetch after sitting beside Leela?
The teacher fetched a bag of beanbags.
What changed for Leela between the Tuesday bench and the Monday game, and what did the teacher and Mridul each add?

On Tuesday she was told she could not play and sat alone with a stone in her tummy. The teacher sat beside her and invited others to the beanbags, and later Mridul called her to be goalkeeper, so she felt she belonged and then invited Jagdish.
What was Leela feeling when she stood by the fence on Monday?
She likely felt invisible and lonely, since nobody noticed her and she counted bricks to pass the time.
How could a parent help a child who often stands alone at playtime?
They could practise a friendly line like Can I play too, and arrange a small play date, as Leela's mother did.

Playgroup note, Holi week. We used gentle flower colours. I blew a puff of yellow powder off my palm. Rafiq (2) jumped, blinked, and stared at the yellow dust on his arm. His eyebrows shot up, and his mouth opened with no sound. Then he looked at me, as if checking whether this was allowed. I laughed, he laughed too, and he patted his arm to make more puffs. Next time I'll warn the children first with a countdown. — Vinita

What colour powder did Vinita blow?
Yellow.
What did Rafiq's raised eyebrows and silent open mouth show?
Rafiq felt surprised by the sudden puff of colour.
Why is Vinita planning a countdown next time?
A warning gives children a moment to prepare, so the surprise stays fun rather than scary.
How might Rafiq's parents feel seeing yellow on his arm?
They would likely be amused and happy that he enjoyed his first gentle Holi colours.
