Teacher's note. Kavitha, Class 9 class teacher.
Nandini has been very quiet this week. She usually argues with me about everything. Today she put her head down in the free period. When I asked quietly, she said her dog, Bruno, died on Sunday. He was fourteen, older than her.
She said, "It's silly, he's just a dog," and her eyes filled up.
I told her it wasn't silly at all; he'd been part of her family her whole life. I offered her some paper and suggested she write to him, or about him, if she wanted. She wrote for the whole period and asked to keep it.
I've informed her parents about how she's doing, and let her know the counsellor is there on Thursdays if she'd like to talk. I'll check in with her again on Monday.

How old was Bruno when he died?
Bruno was fourteen, older than Nandini.
What does Nandini calling it "silly" while her eyes filled up suggest?
It suggests Nandini felt deep grief but also embarrassed about feeling so sad over a pet.
What did Kavitha do that other teachers could learn from?
She took the loss seriously, offered a simple way to express it, told the parents and pointed to the counsellor, with a planned check-in.
How might Nandini's parents feel when Kavitha tells them how she is doing?
They may feel worried for their daughter but grateful that her teacher noticed her grief and took it seriously.

Himani, you asked on your podcast how I decide big things. Let Karthik give you a real example from March.
I got an offer from a startup in Bengaluru. Bigger role, more money, exciting product. On the call I almost said yes right there. My heart was racing.
But I told them, "Give me until tomorrow evening."
That night I made two columns on a sheet of paper. On one side: the role, the money, the learning. On the other: they had raised funding only for a year, the team was tiny, and I'd have to move from Chennai away from my partner. I also messaged two people who had worked there before.
Then I slept. In the morning the excitement was still there, but it was calmer. I saw that the one-year funding worried me more than I'd admitted.
I asked them one more question about funding before I said yes. That question mattered.

How long did Karthik ask the startup to wait?
Karthik asked them to wait until tomorrow evening.
How was Karthik feeling on the call?
Karthik felt excited, with a racing heart, and almost said yes right away.
What else could Karthik have done during that night, and why?
Karthik could have talked it over with the partner in Chennai, since moving away was one of the main points against.
How might the startup see Karthik's question about funding?
The startup may see Karthik as careful and serious about the role, not just chasing a bigger title.

The water tanker was late again in the Hyderabad colony, and every bucket counted. Dilnaz, eleven, had been given one bucket to wash the floor. She used half, then carried the rest to the small neem tree near the gate, which had drooping leaves, and to the dog's bowl by the watchman's cabin. Ramesh Uncle, the watchman, raised his eyebrows. "Your mother gave you that for the floor." "I used half. The floor's clean," Dilnaz said. "The tree and Moti needed some." Ramesh Uncle nodded, patting the dog. "Good thinking, beti."

Where was the dog's bowl?
By the watchman's cabin.
What was Dilnaz feeling when she carried water to the tree and the dog?
She felt concerned and caring for the tree and the dog during the water shortage.
What could Dilnaz do to check her choice was okay?
She could tell her mother how she split the water, so the family agrees on it.
How might Ramesh Uncle see Dilnaz's choice?
He seems impressed and pleased that she cared for the tree and dog without wasting water.

Subject: Day two, and the end of my plan
Hi Seema,
You asked how the new routine is going, so: it isn't. On the first of January I woke at five, ran three laps of the campus ground, did two hours of revision and ticked every box on a chart. On day two my alarm rang and I slept through it. I looked at the empty box and thought, that's it, the streak is dead. By evening I had peeled the chart off the wall, skipped the run, the revision and dinner in the mess, and eaten biscuits in bed. It has been ten days. One bad morning should not have wiped out everything, but at the time it felt like all or nothing. Maybe I'll try again on Monday with a smaller plan. Tell me I'm not hopeless. 🙂
Wasim

What did Wasim do on the first of January before revising?
Wasim woke at five and ran three laps of the campus ground.
What was Wasim thinking when looking at the empty box on the chart?
That the streak was dead and the whole plan was ruined, a discouraged all-or-nothing thought.
What could Wasim change in the plan for Monday?
Make it smaller and allow one missed morning without dropping everything else, so a slip stays a slip.
How might Seema read the line asking to be told Wasim is not hopeless?
As a request for reassurance. Seema would likely see someone discouraged rather than lazy and may reply kindly. 😊

At the school stationery counter before exams, Yogesh needed one gel pen. The board said: 1 pen ₹10. Pack of 3: ₹28. Pack of 5: ₹30.
Yogesh stared. "Two more pens for two rupees? Who buys the pack of 3?"
Shankar, behind him, said, "Nobody. That's the point."
Yogesh laughed and bought the five-pack anyway, feeling very sharp. By the end of the week, two pens had rolled under benches, one had been borrowed for good, and one he had never opened.
"Still a great deal," he told Shankar. Shankar just clicked his single pen.

How much was the pack of 5?
What was Yogesh feeling when he bought the five-pack?
He felt clever and pleased, sure the pack was a smart bargain.
What question could Yogesh have asked at the counter?
How many pens he actually needed, which was one, before comparing the packs.
What does Shankar understand about the pack of 3?
Shankar sees it is there so nobody buys it, only to make the five-pack look like a bargain.

The shared jeep to Champhai school bumped along the hill road. Mawii slid next to Lalremsiami and whispered, "Chinmay told me you're boring now. That's why he sits with the Class 6 boys."
Lalremsiami's throat tightened. She stared out at the terraced fields. All morning she didn't look at Chinmay once.
But at lunch she remembered how Mawii had once tried to split two other friends. So she walked up to Chinmay at the water tap. "Did you say I'm boring?"
Chinmay's mouth fell open. "What? No! I sit with them because they're teaching me football. Come watch tomorrow."
Lalremsiami let out a long breath and grinned.

Why did Chinmay say he sits with the Class 6 boys?
Because they are teaching him football.
What was Lalremsiami feeling after Mawii's whisper in the jeep?
She felt hurt and anxious; her throat tightened and she avoided looking at Chinmay all morning.
What did Lalremsiami do that was wise?
She checked directly with Chinmay instead of trusting Mawii, which cleared up the lie in one question.
How might Chinmay feel when he hears what Mawii said?
Chinmay seems shocked and maybe a little hurt that his friend believed it, and quickly reassures her with an invitation.

'You look tired, Gopu.' 'I played teacher-teacher with Rinku again. I'm always the student who gets scolded.' 'Do you like being the student?' 'No. I like drawing.' Gopika picked at the sofa. 'But Rinku gets upset if I say no. Then she won't talk to me.' 'For how long?' Gopika thought. 'Last time, till lunch.' 'And then?' 'Then she wanted to sit with me.' 'So a no costs you one morning, and she still comes back.' Vidya grinned. 'Let's practise. I'm Rinku. Gopika, come play teacher-teacher!' Gopika giggled, then took a breath. 'Not today. I want to draw. Tomorrow I'll play.' 'Hmph,' said Vidya-as-Rinku. 'Okay. Can I watch you draw?' 'Rinku wouldn't say that.' 'Try it and see.'

Why does Gopika play teacher-teacher with Rinku even though she does not like being the student?
Rinku gets upset if she says no and will not talk to her. Vidya points out that last time it lasted only till lunch and Rinku came back to sit with her, so she practises saying no.

Read this:

Pranav, you're laughing about the kids from the other school. Let me tell you something. I'm your Vandana bua, and at your age I was worse.
In our town there was the railway colony, near the tracks. My friends and I called all those kids “rowdies”. If anything got broken, it was the railway kids. If a boy whistled, it was the railway kids. We said it and laughed, and each time the laugh made us closer.
I never actually knew one of them.
Years later, at college, my closest friend, Shobha, told me she grew up in that colony. She had heard us, she said, all those years ago, walking past our gate.
I still feel a heaviness in my chest when I think of it.

What did young Vandana and her friends call the railway colony kids?
They called them "rowdies".
How does Vandana feel remembering it now?
She feels sad and ashamed, with a heaviness in her chest.
At what point in the story could young Vandana have made a different choice?
Any time the group laughed, she could have asked if they actually knew any railway kids, instead of repeating the label.
How might Shobha have felt as a child walking past their gate?
She probably felt hurt and small, hearing girls label all the children of her colony as rowdies.

Project log, site 14. Written by Vidya Kulkarni, project head. On Tuesday the contractor wanted the night crew up on the scaffolds during the storm warning. It was within the permit, and the crew leader said his men needed the overtime. Pranav, our junior site engineer, refused to sign the shift sheet. He said, "The permit allows it, but I won't send people up where I wouldn't go myself. Their lives aren't worth less because they are paid by the day." The contractor complained to head office, and Pranav lost his quarterly bonus for delaying the pour. He knew that would happen and did not argue the penalty. I don't think Pranav is some kind of saint; last month he rushed his paperwork like everyone else. But on Tuesday he held a line on principle. I have asked head office to review storm permits.

What did the contractor want the night crew to do on Tuesday?
To be up on the scaffolds during the storm warning.
What did Pranav feel about the day-paid workers, and how can you tell?
He felt protective of them, believing their lives were worth no less than anyone's; he said he wouldn't send people up where he wouldn't go himself.
What choice did Vidya make after Tuesday, and why does it matter?
Vidya asked head office to review storm permits, which could turn one person's stand into a safer rule for every crew.
How might the crew leader see Pranav's refusal?
The crew leader may be torn: relieved the men stayed safe, yet frustrated that they lost overtime they needed.

In the hospital family room, the morning after Sachin's father died, three people grieved in three directions. Sachin's younger brother, Nikhil, was on the phone nonstop: the crematorium, the priest, the relatives in Indore, a list growing on his palm in blue ink. Nazia, Sachin's wife, kept trying to talk. "Remember how he sang in the car?" she said, twice. Sachin sat by the window and said nothing. Inside, he was furious with both of them. How could Nikhil think about timings? Why did Nazia need words? Around noon Nikhil snapped, "Could you at least help, bhaiya?" Sachin nearly shouted back. Then he saw his brother's hands shaking over the list. He took the phone. "You call the family. I'll call the priest." Later, in the corridor, he told Nazia, "I can't talk yet. Stay close anyway?" She nodded and held his arm.

What was Nikhil writing on his palm?
A list of calls, the crematorium, the priest and the relatives in Indore, growing on his palm in blue ink.
What was Sachin feeling as he sat by the window?
He was grieving silently and also angry, judging Nikhil for thinking about timings and Nazia for needing words.
What helped the three of them grieve side by side?
Sachin noticed Nikhil's shaking hands and shared the calls, and told Nazia plainly that he couldn't talk yet but wanted her close.
How might Nazia have seen Sachin's silence?
She may have felt shut out and worried that he was not grieving at all, until he explained and asked her to stay close.

Read this:

Three weeks into her first term in Edinburgh, Astrid had done everything herself: opened a bank account, found the cheapest supermarket, fixed the radiator in her room with an online video and a butter knife. She was proud of it. She texted her mother in Uppsala photos of her tidy shelf. Then on Sunday, walking past a bakery, she smelled cardamom buns exactly like her grandmother's and had to stop on the pavement because her eyes filled. Back at the flat, her flatmate Sofia, from Lisbon, found her sitting on the kitchen floor. 'Home?' Sofia asked. Astrid nodded. 'I thought I was fine.' 'You are fine,' Sofia said, sitting down beside her. 'I cried over sardines last week.' That night Astrid called her grandmother and asked for the bun recipe.

What did Astrid fix with an online video and a butter knife?
The radiator in her room.
What did Astrid feel when she smelled the cardamom buns?
Astrid felt a sudden, aching homesickness, her eyes filling for her grandmother's baking.
What was a good response to the homesickness?
Calling her grandmother for the bun recipe kept the bond alive while Astrid stayed and managed on her own.
How does Sofia see Astrid's tears?
Sofia sees them as normal, sharing that she cried over sardines, so missing home doesn't mean Astrid isn't fine.

Read this:

I'm Salma, the neighbour. Last month Joseph's best friend, Kiran, moved to another city. Joseph is five.
For days after, Joseph sat on the stairs where they used to play marbles. He didn't want to play with anyone else.
One evening he asked me, “Aunty, how far is Chennai?”
“Very far.”
He went quiet. Then he said, “I'll draw Kiran a picture so he doesn't forget me.”
Yesterday I saw his mother posting it.

Where did Joseph sit after Kiran moved?
He sat on the stairs where they used to play marbles.
How did Joseph feel after Kiran moved away?
He felt sad and lonely, missing his best friend.
How could Joseph's family help him with missing Kiran?
They could help him send pictures or talk on the phone, and gently invite him to play with other children.
How does Salma see Joseph's feelings?
Salma notices his sadness and is touched by how he wants Kiran not to forget him.

Monday: Rehana, five, couldn't fit the last puzzle piece and swept the whole puzzle onto the floor, screaming for ten minutes. Her mother Manjula sat nearby. Wednesday: the piece didn't fit again. Rehana threw it, then cried, then came to sit in Manjula's lap. Saturday: she got stuck again. She put the piece down, hugged her cushion, and said, "I'm cross." After a minute she turned the piece round and it clicked in.

How long did Rehana scream on Monday?
For ten minutes.
What does Rehana hugging her cushion and saying "I'm cross" suggest?
She felt angry but was learning to soothe herself and name the feeling instead of melting down.
Which choice by Manjula helped over the week?
Sitting nearby calmly each time, so Rehana felt safe enough to learn to settle herself.
How might Manjula feel on Saturday?
Relieved and proud to see Rehana handle her frustration on her own.
Say this in an informal way: Unfortunately, I will be unable to attend your birthday celebration on Sunday.
Sorry, I can't make it to your birthday on Sunday.

Vishal's friend Zainab tapped his shoulder before the fractions test and mouthed, "Answers?" Vishal's pencil hovered. It would be easy. Two minutes, and she would get her marks. But then what? If she copies, the teacher thinks she knows fractions. Next chapter is ratios, and fractions sit inside ratios. She will be lost, and I will have helped her get lost. Marks would come today; learning would not. He turned his paper a little, shook his head and whispered, "I will help you learn it after school. Copying will not help you." Zainab sighed but nodded. Vishal felt his hands go steady.

Which chapter did Vishal think would come after fractions?
Vishal thought the next chapter would be ratios.
How was Vishal feeling while his pencil hovered, and what made him decide?
Whether giving Zainab the answers truly helps her, and he realised it would give marks without learning, so he felt torn but chose to refuse. 😅
What other approach could Vishal use to help Zainab?
Offer to study together after school, because then she learns the method she needs for the next chapter.
How might Zainab see Vishal's refusal?
Disappointed at first, since she sighed, but she nodded, so she may come to see that he wants her to understand.

metadata.subtype: Approach: thinking of what the test is for [Thinking]

Read this:

Tuesday
Nitin asked me today when the annual report would be ready. My mouth wanted to say "two weeks." It always wants to say two weeks. Instead I said, "Let me check and tell you tomorrow."
So tonight I opened my old calendar. Last year's report: started 3 Feb, finished 19 March. Six and a half weeks. The year before: seven. Both times I had promised two.
Broke it into pieces: data from four departments (always late, so a week), writing (two weeks), charts (a week), two rounds of edits (a week each, because Nitin always adds a section). That's six weeks, plus one for surprises.
Tomorrow I'll tell him seven weeks. He won't love it. But I'd rather disappoint him once on Wednesday than every Friday after.
Minakshi

How long did last year's report take?
Six and a half weeks, from 3 Feb to 19 March.
Why did Minakshi hold back from saying two weeks?
Minakshi felt wary of the old habit of promising two weeks and missing it, so checking real past timings felt safer.
How did Minakshi build the seven-week estimate?
By checking how long the last two reports took, breaking the job into parts with realistic times, and adding a week for surprises.
How might Nitin react to hearing seven weeks?
Nitin may be disappointed at first, but later relieved if the date holds instead of slipping every Friday.
What is my neighbour's phone number? Why do we breathe faster after running? What does "cub" mean?

1. I don't know, because I can't see private details. Ask your neighbour or someone in your family.
2. The muscles need more air when we run. Because breathing faster brings in more air.
3. A cub is a young lion, tiger or bear.

Saurabh here, the neighbour. I had come to drop off a parcel and the door was open. Toys covered Jaya's floor: blocks, dolls, crayons, a small drum. Jaya stood in the doorway a long moment. Then she walked to the middle, sat down and picked up a doll. She combed its hair, hummed to it and tried a dress on it. When I left, nothing had gone into the box. I could not tell whether she was tired, bored, or simply did not know where to begin.

Where did Jaya sit down?
Jaya walked to the middle and sat down.
What might Jaya be feeling as she stood in the doorway?
She may feel overwhelmed by how much there is to put away. Saurabh cannot be sure, but Jaya stood still a long moment and then chose to play.
What alternative approach could help Jaya start, and why?
She could pick one kind, like the blocks, and put only those away first. A small first step makes the job feel finishable.
What does Saurabh see, and what can Saurabh not know?
Saurabh sees Jaya play and nothing go into the box. Saurabh cannot know if Jaya is tired, bored or lost about where to begin.

“Me first! Me first!” Nkechi shot up from the reading mat, arm stretched so high her shoulder shook. The teacher held up a paper star. “The star goes round the circle. When it reaches you, it's your turn.” Nkechi sat, hands squeezed between her knees, bouncing. Hana had the star first and passed it on. Nkechi watched each pair of hands it went through, lips pressed together. When it finally reached her, she took a big breath and began, “My dog...”

What object went round the circle?
A paper star went round the circle.
What was Nkechi feeling while she waited for the star?
Eager and excited to share, with some impatience: she bounced and pressed her lips together with her hands squeezed between her knees. She may also have worried her idea would be forgotten.
How did the star rule help Nkechi?
It gave a clear, fair signal for when her turn would come, so she had something concrete to watch while she waited.
How might Hana see Nkechi's jumping up?
Hana had the star first and may have felt watched or a little rushed by an eager friend, or she may simply have been excited too. Nothing in the scene says which.

For the final-year project, Dhruv had written a first draft proposal: a water-quality sensor for the college lake. He'd spent a week on it. He loved it.

In the group meeting, his teammate Omkar shared a different idea: a sensor for measuring air quality in classrooms, with a clear plan, a smaller budget, and a professor already interested.

Dhruv felt his chest tighten. "Mine's more original."

"It needs equipment we don't have," Omkar said gently. "And no professor has agreed to guide it."

"We can work it out."

The other two teammates looked at each other.

That night, Dhruv read both proposals side by side. If someone else had written his, and he'd written Omkar's, which would he pick?

Omkar's. Easily.

It stung. His draft was his. But the next morning, he sent the group a message: "Let's go with Omkar's. I'll bring my lake ideas as a side test."

What was Dhruv's first draft proposal about?
A water-quality sensor for the college lake.
Why did Dhruv feel his chest tighten when Omkar shared his idea?
Dhruv felt defensive because his own draft felt precious simply because he wrote it and loved it.
What did Dhruv do that helped him judge fairly?
Dhruv imagined the proposals had swapped authors and asked which he'd pick, which showed Omkar's was better.
How might Omkar feel when Dhruv agrees to Omkar's idea?
Omkar might feel relieved and grateful, and appreciate Dhruv bringing the lake ideas as a side test.

After the evening prayer at the village temple, Shalini pulled Sarika behind the flower stall.
"My cousin from Nashik wants your number. He saw you at the fair. Just give it, na? And don't tell your Amma, she'll make a big thing."
Sarika's fingers tightened on her dupatta. "I'm not comfortable giving my number to someone I don't know."
"Don't be so boring. He's nice. I promised him."
"Then that's your promise. Not mine. No."
Shalini rolled her eyes and walked off in a huff.
Walking home along the canal, Sarika kept thinking about "don't tell your Amma." That was the part that felt wrong.
At dinner she told Amma everything. Amma listened, put a hand on her head and said, "You did right. Both times." That same night she went next door and spoke to Shalini's mother, calmly, about the cousin.

Where did Shalini pull Sarika after the evening prayer?
She pulled Sarika behind the flower stall at the village temple.
What was Sarika feeling as she walked home along the canal?
She felt uneasy and troubled, because Shalini's "don't tell your Amma" felt wrong even after she had refused.
How did Amma support Sarika well?
Amma listened, praised Sarika for saying no and for telling, and spoke to Shalini's mother that same night instead of waiting.
How might Shalini see the refusal compared with Sarika?
Shalini seems to see it as Sarika being boring and making her break a promise, while Sarika sees a stranger asking for her number in secret.

I'm Chinmay, and I'm eleven. This is about the card game in our building's stairwell. Last month I peeked at Eshaan's cards when he went to drink water. I won three games in a row. I felt clever. The next Sunday, I came down with my cards and everyone was already playing. Nobody had called me. Eshaan had been called. He always gives back the cards he borrows and says sorry if he drops one. I asked, 'Can I play?' Rinku said, 'Maybe later.' Later never came. Now I know people remember. It only took one peek.

What did Chinmay do when Eshaan went to drink water?
Chinmay peeked at Eshaan's cards.
How did Chinmay feel after winning three games, and how did that change?
Chinmay felt clever at first, but later felt left out and understood that people remember, when nobody called Chinmay to play.
What could Chinmay try now to get back into the game?
Chinmay could tell the others about the peek and say sorry, then play fairly every time so they slowly trust Chinmay again.
Why might Rinku and the others call Eshaan but not Chinmay?
They know Eshaan always gives back borrowed cards and says sorry, so he feels safe to play with, while Chinmay's peek made them unsure.

Our luggage is very heavy, we need a trolley.
Why: "luggage" has no plural and takes a singular verb.

I'm Ritu, and I'm nine. On Diwali my little sister Gargi wanted to touch the diyas on the steps. Papa picked her up and moved her away.

Gargi screamed and kicked. She threw her sparkly clip on the floor. Her face went all red.

I don't know if she was angry or scared. Maybe both.

Papa put her down near the rangoli and gave her a bowl of flower petals. She threw some, then started sprinkling them, still hiccupping.

What did Gargi throw on the floor?
She threw her sparkly clip on the floor.
What might Gargi have been feeling when she screamed and kicked?
Ritu wasn't sure, but Gargi was likely angry and frustrated at being moved away from the diyas, and maybe a bit scared.
How did Papa handle Gargi's frustration safely?
He kept her away from the diyas and gave her something safe to do with the petals.
How does Ritu see Gargi's tantrum?
Ritu watches closely and wonders what Gargi felt, understanding it might be more than one feeling.

Beatriz's spreadsheet for their school's two-day London trip had eight rows and neat colour codes. Soo-ah had asked about walking times, but Beatriz waved it off: "It's all close on the map." They pre-booked timed tickets for the tower at two o'clock and a river cruise at five. By eleven on day one, they were still stuck in the bag queue at the second museum. The underground was packed, and one line was suspended. They reached the tower at quarter to three, and the gate staff said their slot had passed. The cruise went the same way. On day two, Soo-ah sat on a bench outside the fourth place and refused to walk another step. "We saw four," she said quietly, rubbing her heels. "And we paid for two we never saw."

What time was the tower slot?
The tower tickets were for two o'clock.
What was Soo-ah feeling when she refused to walk another step?
Soo-ah was exhausted and quietly frustrated, since her question about walking times had been waved off and now they had paid for tickets they never used.
Which approach would suit this group better next time?
Planning fewer places a day with honest travel and queue times, and booking timed tickets only after that, would leave room for delays.
How might Beatriz see the spreadsheet after day two?
Beatriz may feel embarrassed that the colour-coded plan ignored how slow queues and trains can be, and sorry that Soo-ah's early question was brushed aside.

Read this:

Arnab, you asked why I get upset when people say "these migrants." Let me tell you about Zainab. When I was your age, she joined our school in Kolkata. Her family had come from across the border after floods took their fields. The other kids called her names. I didn't join in, but I didn't stop them either. One day we had a geography project on rivers, and she was put in my group. She knew everything about how the delta shifts, how floods move people. She told us about her grandfather's boat. I realised I'd been scared of her without knowing anything. After that I asked her questions. We're still friends. So when you hear "these migrants," ask who they are first.

What had taken Zainab's family's fields?
Floods had taken their fields.
How did the speaker feel about Zainab before the geography project?
They were scared of her without really knowing her, and felt uneasy about not stopping the name-calling.
What advice does the speaker give Arnab, and why is it useful?
To ask who migrants are before judging, because curiosity replaces fear and stereotypes with real people's stories.
How might Zainab have felt when her classmate started asking questions?
She probably felt seen and less alone, after being called names by others.

Hi Abhinav,
I've been thinking about Sunday's meeting. You said the clean-river campaign only moves because of the rallies, and that the 'office people' don't count. I got angry and said nothing, so here goes.
I've watched this group for a year. Meher does the accounts every night so our donations stay clean. Sanjay drives the old van to every site. Pritam dadi has written seventy letters to the council by hand. Laila designs the posters you hold up. None of them ever speaks on the mic.
You're a great speaker. The rallies matter. But when you say only speeches count, the quiet ones feel invisible, and some have stopped coming.
Can we thank them properly at the next meeting? Together?
Amandeep

How many letters has Pritam dadi written to the council?
Seventy letters, by hand.
How did Amandeep feel when Abhinav dismissed the 'office people'?
Amandeep felt angry but stayed silent at the meeting, then felt the need to speak up in writing.
What does Amandeep suggest, and why would it help?
Thanking the quiet contributors together at the next meeting, so they feel valued and the group's resentment eases.
How might Meher feel hearing that only speeches count?
Invisible and unappreciated, despite doing the accounts every night.

At the university residence in Uppsala, Ingrid and Yosef were made hall assistants in their second year. They got keys, a clipboard and the right to write warnings.
First-years were loud. By October, Ingrid was writing warnings for a laugh after ten. Yosef took a first-year's speaker away for a week because the student argued.
"They're children," Ingrid said. "They have to learn."
One evening Yosef saw a first-year crying in the kitchen over a warning letter. The student was homesick and had only been playing music from home.
Yosef stood in the doorway, clipboard in hand. Last year that had been him.

What did Yosef take away from a first-year?
He took a first-year's speaker away for a week.
What does Yosef feel, standing in the doorway with the clipboard?
He feels shaken and guilty, remembering that last year he was the homesick first-year.
What could Ingrid and Yosef change?
They could talk to first-years before writing warnings, ask a hall supervisor to review hard cases, and treat them as people, not problems.
How does Ingrid see the first-years?
Ingrid sees them as children who deserve harsh rules, not as people with reasons like homesickness.
Airport par bolna hai "Meri flight ka gate kahan hai?" English?
Ask: "Where is the gate for my flight?"

In the kasba post office, Madhav slammed his receipt on the counter. "Twenty days! My son's university papers were sent twenty days ago and you people have lost them!"
The queue went quiet. Sunaina, the clerk, felt her heart speed up. She wanted to say the delay wasn't at her branch.
She lowered her voice instead. "Twenty days is a long time, and those papers matter. I understand why you're angry."
Madhav blinked. "Of course I'm angry."
"What would help most today? A tracking update, or a written complaint to the head office?"
"Both."
"Let me check." She found the parcel stuck at the district sorting centre, called them on the office phone while he watched, and wrote the complaint with him.
Madhav's shoulders came down. "They said it will move tomorrow?"
"Tomorrow. I'll call you when it does."

How long ago were the papers sent?
They were sent twenty days ago.
What was Sunaina feeling when Madhav slammed his receipt?
Sunaina felt her heart speed up, tense and tempted to defend herself because the delay wasn't at her branch.
Which of Sunaina's choices helped most, and why?
She kept her voice low, acknowledged his frustration, and asked what outcome would help, so Madhav felt heard and could work with her.
How did Madhav experience the conversation?
Madhav went from furious to calmer, his shoulders coming down once he felt heard and saw real action.

Read this:

Last month our volcano model at the inter-school science fair collapsed right in front of the judges. The papier-mâché cone sagged sideways, and the baking-soda lava ran all over the table. Somebody at the next stall laughed.
I'm Rehana, and normally I'd have said "It's fine, whatever" and gone quiet for days. When Zainab found me by the water cooler and asked, "You okay?", I nearly did. Instead I said, "No. I'm really disappointed. We worked three weekends on it. And I'm embarrassed. Everyone saw."
Zainab said, "Yeah. I'd feel like that too." That was all. But something in my chest loosened. We went back, wiped the table, and I even explained our idea to the next judge. By evening I was laughing about the lava. Pretending would have taken me days to get over.

Where did Zainab find Rehana?
By the water cooler.
What was Rehana tempted to say, and why might that have felt safer?
Rehana was tempted to say "It's fine, whatever," because hiding the hurt after people laughed felt less exposing than admitting it 😔
What choice at the water cooler made the rest of the day go better for Rehana?
Saying "I'm really disappointed" and "I'm embarrassed" instead of "fine" let the feelings ease, so Rehana could go back and explain the idea to the next judge.
How did Rehana's honesty make it easier for Zainab to help?
Because the feelings were named, Zainab knew exactly what to respond to and could simply say "I'd feel like that too" instead of guessing.

The bus broke down on the way to the zoo trip, and the teacher went to phone the school. Gopika and Arnab, waiting by the roadside with their class, argued about whether to play word games or sing songs until help arrived. “Songs are boring!” said Arnab loudly. Gopika bit back what she wanted to say. Then she took a breath. “I see it differently. Songs help us all join in, and word games only work for some of us. What do you think?” Arnab folded his arms, then unfolded them. “Okay, maybe one of each,” he said. They started with a song.

Where were the children waiting?
By the roadside, after the bus broke down.
What was Gopika feeling when she bit back what she wanted to say, and how did she handle it?
She felt annoyed at being called boring, but she took a breath and calmly explained her view.
What did Gopika say that helped, compared with shouting or sulking?
She said “I see it differently,” gave a reason and asked Arnab what he thought.
How might Arnab have felt when Gopika asked what he thought?
He probably felt listened to, which may be why he unfolded his arms and offered a compromise.
How much does a new cricket bat cost at the sports shop this month?
I don't know the shop's current prices, as I can't see them. Ask the shop or look at its website.

The tree-planting drive started at seven, but by ten the sun was brutal and there were only forty saplings for sixty volunteers. Vijay, sixteen, wiped his face with his T-shirt. On his phone that morning he'd seen photos of a coastal town in another country, houses gone, people sleeping on a school roof. He'd felt sick and angry. What was the point of a few trees here? He said so to Sarita, the volunteer coordinator. She handed him a sapling. "Mangroves on coasts, forests on hills, all the same story. Less heat, fewer floods. Every place connected." Vijay dug slowly, thinking about that. Then he asked for her number: the school holidays were coming, and he wanted to join the mangrove drive.

How many saplings were there for sixty volunteers?
Only forty saplings.
How did Vijay feel after seeing the photos of the coastal town?
He felt sick and angry, and wondered if his few trees here could make any difference.
What turning point changed Vijay's view of his work?
Sarita explained how forests and mangroves everywhere reduce heat and floods, so Vijay saw the connection and chose to join the mangrove drive too.
How might Sarita see Vijay's frustrated question?
Sarita probably sees it as real concern, not laziness, and uses it as a chance to explain how places are linked.

Read this:

At the state sports hostel, the senior athletes had been mocking Parul's running videos in the hostel group: slow-motion clips, silly music. When Parul told Karthik in the mess, he said, "Well, you shouldn't post your training videos if you can't take it. You should have known better." Parul put down her plate. "So it's my fault?" Karthik opened his mouth, then closed it. It wasn't her fault. He just didn't want to be the one who had a problem with the seniors. "No," he said slowly. "It's theirs. I said that because I didn't want to deal with it." Parul's eyes were wet. "I just wanted to share my progress." "I know. Come. Let's show the warden now." They took the phone to the warden's office before evening practice. The warden scrolled through the clips, frowned, and said, "This stops tonight. I'm calling the seniors in after practice, and I'll inform the coach."

What were the seniors mocking?
They were mocking Parul's running videos in the hostel group.
Why did Karthik first say Parul should have known better?
Karthik felt uncomfortable and didn't want trouble with the seniors, so blaming Parul let him avoid taking a stand.
What made Karthik's second response better?
He admitted the blame was the seniors', owned why he'd said it, and went with Parul to the warden that same evening.
What was it like for Parul to hear "you should have known better"?
Parul felt hurt and blamed, as if sharing her progress had caused the mocking.

messages.content: What does "barking up the wrong tree" mean?

It means to look for something in the wrong place, or to blame the wrong person.
Example: If you think I took your pen, you are barking up the wrong tree; I do not even use that colour.
What colour is chestnut, and is it also a nut?

Both. A chestnut is a kind of nut that grows in a prickly case and is often roasted. It is also a reddish-brown colour, like the nut's skin. It is a noun, and as a colour it can also be an adjective.
Example: The girl brushed her chestnut hair before the photo.

Yamini ran the girls' group chat at the coaching centre hostel in Kota. Every night she posted a voice note imitating Nazia's careful English: "Excuse me, sir, may I please ask a doubt?" Everyone sent laughing faces. Yamini called it "the Nazia show".

When Nazia texted her privately, "Please stop," Yamini replied, "Relax yaar, it's banter. We roast everyone." But nobody else had been roasted every night for three weeks.

On Tuesday Nazia didn't come to morning class. The warden, Mrs Kulkarni, found her crying in her room and heard the whole story. That afternoon she called Yamini in and played one of the voice notes. "Tell me who laughs at this, and who doesn't."

Yamini's face went red. "It was just a joke."

"Not to Nazia. It stops today. Delete them, and we'll call your parents and Nazia's this evening."

What did Yamini call her voice notes?
Yamini called them "the Nazia show".
Why did Yamini call it banter?
The word banter let Yamini feel it was harmless fun, hiding how hurt and humiliated Nazia felt.
What did Mrs Kulkarni do that same day?
She listened to Nazia, called Yamini in, played a voice note, stopped it and required deletion, and arranged calls to both families that evening.
How did Nazia feel after three weeks?
Nazia felt so hurt and humiliated that she skipped class and cried in her room.

Lindiwe had been a nurse at a small clinic outside Durban for three years. The pay was modest; the queues were long. Her cousin in London kept sending job links.
On a Tuesday morning, a woman came in with a baby on her back. "You don't remember me," she said. "You helped me when I was pregnant and scared. This is Themba."
Lindiwe held the baby, who grabbed her badge. Her colleague Rafael, the pharmacist, grinned from the counter.
That evening she walked home past the football field where kids she'd vaccinated were playing. She thought about the job links. She would answer her cousin kindly, but no.
She didn't feel heroic. She felt like she was exactly where she was supposed to be.

What was the baby's name?
Themba.
How did Lindiwe feel walking home that evening?
She felt a deep, quiet fulfilment, sure she was where she was supposed to be.
What would you say to Lindiwe about the London job links?
Her choice to stay seems based on real purpose; she can keep weighing it, but the meaning she feels is a real reason.
How might the mother of Themba feel returning to the clinic?
She likely feels grateful and warm, wanting Lindiwe to see the baby she helped.

"He said he just wasn't feeling it any more. What does that even mean?" Vasudha's voice cracked.

"I don't know," Parul said, and put the kettle down. "It's a rubbish thing to say."

"I keep going over the last month. Was it my laugh? The way I hugged too long?"

"Vasu."

"I've drafted six messages. I could say I'll change. I could just ask for one more talk."

Parul held out her hand for the phone, and Vasudha, after a moment, gave it up.

"Cry. It's allowed. You're not going to find the perfect reason tonight."

"I feel worthless," Vasudha said. "And stupid, for feeling worthless."

"Then be worthless and stupid on my sofa. I've got biryani and a terrible film." 

Vasudha laughed, wet-eyed. Then she cried again, properly.

How many messages had Vasudha drafted?
She had drafted six messages.
What might Vasudha be feeling as she goes over the last month, asking about her laugh and her hugs?
She is confused and doubting her worth, searching for a reason she did something wrong that would explain the ending.
What did Parul do that helped Vasudha on that evening?
She took the phone so Vasudha would not send a begging message, told her crying is allowed, and offered company and food.
How might Parul see the moment when Vasudha hands over the phone?
Parul probably feels protective and a bit anxious, wanting to keep her friend from a message she would regret, while staying kind.
The recipe says add a liberal amount of butter. Doesn't liberal belong to politics?

As an adjective, liberal can also mean generous or plentiful. In politics it describes a person who supports more freedom and change.
Example: Grandmother gave us a liberal helping of rice and dal.

In a busy café in Istanbul, Yosef was telling Elif about the internship he'd been offered in Ankara. At first she sat square to him, knees pointing his way, nodding. Halfway through, she shifted in her chair, her body turning toward the door, her bag pulled onto her lap. Yosef slowed down. Was she upset he might move? He didn't want to guess. "Elif, you've turned toward the door. Should I stop?" Elif looked startled, then sheepish. "Sorry, my sister's supposed to pick me up at four and she hates waiting. I didn't mean to look like I was leaving you." She turned her chair back a little. "But I also feel strange about you going to Ankara. That's true too." Yosef nodded. "Can we finish this tomorrow, properly?" Elif smiled. "Yes. Same table."

Where was Yosef's internship?
In Ankara.
What was Elif feeling when she turned toward the door?
She was mainly anxious about keeping her sister waiting, but she also admits she feels strange about Yosef moving, so the turn carried more than one feeling.
What small step did Yosef take instead of guessing?
He named what he saw and asked if he should stop, which let Elif explain both reasons.
What would change if Yosef had assumed Elif was uninterested?
He might have felt hurt and cut the talk short, never hearing that she had to leave and also felt strange about him going.

Gargi had fetched water past the old peepal by the village pond a hundred times. Then, on the walk home from school, Neelam said her cousin had seen a lantern moving in its branches at night. The next day the milkman's son said the lantern floated. By Saturday, women at the hand pump were saying a spirit swung from the lowest branch and tugged at dupattas. Gargi's Dadi clicked her tongue, but even she walked a little faster past it. That evening Amma asked Gargi to bring water. Gargi stood at the door, pot on her hip, staring at the dark tree. "Everyone says it," she whispered. "Everyone." She waited until her brother could come along.

Who said the lantern floated?
The milkman's son.
What was Gargi feeling while standing at the door with the pot?
Gargi was afraid of a tree that had never scared her before, because so many people now repeated the spirit story. 😟
When Gargi hesitated at the door, what could Amma have done?
Amma could ask who had actually seen anything and walk to the pond with Gargi, showing that the story grew by retelling, not by new sightings.
Why might Dadi walking faster matter to Gargi?
When even a grown-up seemed uneasy, Gargi took it as more proof, so Dadi's small reaction made the story feel even more real.

metadata.subtype: Playground story grows with each telling [Actor]

By nine in the evening, Mateo had been at his desk in Valencia since lunch: three past chemistry papers, a history timeline, forty small decisions about what to revise next. When his mother called him for dinner, he said he wasn't hungry and grabbed a bag of crisps and a fizzy drink from the cupboard instead. Then his phone buzzed. Liam had sent a long message about splitting the biology project: who does the poster, who does the talk, which days to meet. Mateo stared at it. His brain felt like wet cardboard. He typed "whatever u want" and threw the phone on the bed. An hour later, Liam replied: "ok, u do the talk then." Mateo groaned. He hated giving talks. On any other evening, he'd have said so.

What did Liam's long message ask about?
It was about splitting the biology project: who does the poster, who does the talk, and which days to meet.
Why did Mateo reply 'whatever u want'?
Mateo felt drained and foggy after hours of choosing what to revise, so one more decision felt too heavy and the easiest reply won.
What could Mateo do the next time a big choice arrives at the end of a long study day?
He could reply that he will answer in the morning, and eat a proper meal before deciding anything.
How might Liam read 'whatever u want'?
Liam might take it as real agreement, or feel brushed off, not knowing Mateo was simply exhausted.

In my second year of college in Nashik, I joined the "business opportunity" because all eleven boys on my hostel floor had joined. I'm Jatin, and I'm usually careful, but that week I wasn't. The meetings were full of cheering, and everyone I knew was there. If so many smart people were in, how could it be a trick? My cousin Salma didi asked me on the phone, "Bhai, what do they actually sell?" I didn't really know. "Everyone's making money," I said, which wasn't true either. I paid the joining fee from my scholarship money. Three months later the organisers stopped answering calls. The eleven of us sat in one room, staring at each other. We had all joined because the others had. Now I ask my father or a teacher I trust before I sign anything, however many friends are already in.

How many boys on Jatin's hostel floor had joined?
All eleven boys on my hostel floor had joined.
Why did joining feel safe to Jatin at the time?
Jatin felt reassured and swept along by the cheering crowd, believing that so many smart people couldn't all be wrong.
What does Jatin do now, and why is it a good habit?
Jatin asks his father or a trusted teacher before signing anything, however many friends are already in, so popularity doesn't replace real checking.
How might Salma didi have felt when Jatin couldn't say what they sold?
She was probably worried, sensing that Jatin was trusting the crowd rather than understanding the scheme.

I was sitting on the bench in the school yard when I heard Jasleen tell Rajni, “You should drop that game and play with us instead.” Rajni shook his head and clutched the ball. Jasleen tried again: “I just think it would be better.” Rajni walked away. I don't think Jasleen meant to be bossy. She looked hurt. She probably wanted to help. After a few minutes, Jasleen went over and said, “Would you like some ideas for how to share the ball?” Rajni turned around. “Okay,” he said. I couldn't tell if he really wanted ideas or only wanted not to argue.

What did Rajni clutch when Jasleen advised him?
The ball.
What did Jasleen probably want when she gave her advice?
She probably wanted to help and include Rajni, since she looked hurt when he walked away and did not seem to mean to be bossy.
What changed Rajni's reaction?
Jasleen asked if he would like ideas, which left the choice to him, and he turned around.
What might Rajni have been feeling when he first shook his head?
He may have felt pushed and wanted to keep playing his own game, though the observer cannot be sure.

In the small town, Devika, sixteen, practised Bharatanatyam every morning before school on the flat roof, while the rest of the house slept. Her teacher Shalini had said she had the steps but not yet the feeling. So Devika watched old performances in the evenings and cried at one of them without knowing why. She started practising the facial expressions in front of the steel almirah's mirror. Her feet bled once. She didn't stop. When Shalini finally said, "Now you're telling the story," Devika felt her whole chest open. She wanted this more than anything.

Where did Devika practise every morning?
On the flat roof.
How did Devika feel when Shalini said she was telling the story?
She felt overjoyed and moved, as if her whole chest opened.
What would you advise Devika about her bleeding feet?
Rest and have them looked at by an adult, since passion lasts longer when the body is cared for.
How might Shalini see Devika's progress?
With pride, seeing a student who went beyond steps to real feeling.

Gautam's family trip to the hills had one problem: the guest house had no network except on one rock behind the kitchen. On day two his streak with Ganga broke at 47 days.
Ganga noticed at breakfast in Delhi. Then she saw his only message, sent from the rock at dawn: "all good here 🙂".
In her group, a plain 🙂 meant "I'm annoyed but whatever." She read it five times. Had she done something? Was he bored of her?
She almost sent a cold reply. Instead, she waited.
When Gautam got back on Sunday, she met him at the colony gate. "Can I ask what the 🙂 meant? And the streak?"
He looked baffled. "The smile meant smile! And I had one bar on a rock, Ganga. I climbed it at six just to message you."
She laughed, embarrassed and oddly touched.

At how many days did the streak break?
The streak broke at 47 days.
What was Ganga feeling as she read Gautam's message five times?
She felt anxious and hurt, worried the plain smile meant he was annoyed or bored of her.
Which choice of Ganga's worked, and why?
Waiting and then asking directly worked, because the smile meant something different to Gautam and the broken streak was about network, not feelings.
What was it like for Gautam to find out how his message was read?
He was baffled, since for him a smile meant a smile and he had climbed a rock at dawn just to send it.
Dost ko bolna hai "Tune toh kamaal kar diya!" Casual English mein?
Say: "You did a great job!" Or even more casual: "That was amazing!"

I used to lecture my daughter Rekha about manners, and it never stuck. Then one Saturday at the vegetable market, I realised she wasn't listening to my words at all; she was watching me. I'd snapped at the vendor about the price of tomatoes, and five minutes later Rekha snapped at her little cousin for taking her ball. Same tone. So I tried something. I started thanking the auto driver, waiting behind the old man at the cash machine without sighing, apologising when my bag bumped someone. I didn't point any of it out. Three weeks later, in the temple queue, Rekha stepped aside for a woman with a baby and said, 'You go first, aunty.' I'm Chetan, and that's the best lesson I never taught.

What did Rekha say to the woman with a baby?
'You go first, aunty.'
How did Chetan feel after hearing Rekha snap in the same tone?
Chetan felt uncomfortable and a bit ashamed, realising Rekha was copying Chetan's behaviour, not the lectures.
What changed in Chetan's way of teaching manners?
Chetan stopped lecturing and started modelling: thanking the driver, waiting patiently and apologising, without pointing it out.
How might the woman with the baby see Rekha?
As a kind, thoughtful child, and she was likely grateful to be let ahead in the queue.
A storm warning must be polite and clear: Do not go out in the storm.
Please stay indoors during the storm.

The records office in the district hospital basement smelled of paper and phenyl, and Saurabh had never pictured himself working there. After nine weeks without a single offer for fintech roles, his savings were down to a month and a half. Thomas, who ran the hospital's IT and had studied with Saurabh's older brother, offered a four-month contract: move twenty years of appointment records into the new system.
It wasn't what he wanted. But it paid the rent, and Thomas agreed he could leave early on interview days.
So every morning Saurabh wrote data scripts in the basement, and on Wednesdays he took recruiters' calls in the corridor by the canteen. Handling messy real-world data made his interview answers sharper. In month three, a payments company offered him a role starting after the contract ended.

What was the contract for?
To move twenty years of appointment records into the new system.
How did Saurabh feel about working in the records office?
He was reluctant and a bit disappointed, since it wasn't the fintech role he wanted.
What arrangement made the contract work alongside job hunting?
Thomas let him leave early on interview days, and he kept Wednesdays for recruiters' calls.
How does the hospital benefit from Saurabh's contract?
The hospital gets its old records moved into the new system by someone skilled with data.

Counsellor's note, women's college, 3 February
Afreen, final-year B.Com, came in upset. Her family has been sharing biodatas every weekend and arranged two "just tea" visits this month. She said she had been agreeing to each meeting "to end the conversation", then feeling trapped. She wants two years of work first.
We practised what she might say. She wrote it in her own words: "I'm not refusing marriage. I want to work for two years first, and I want someone who respects that. What are you most worried about?" She practised the last question three times; it mattered to her to listen too.
Today she came back. She had spoken to her parents on Sunday. Her father worried about her "getting too old"; her mother worried about what relatives say. They agreed to pause visits until after her exams and talk again then. She looked tired, and much lighter.
Disha, counsellor

How many "just tea" visits were arranged this month?
Two.
How had Afreen been feeling after agreeing to each meeting?
Trapped and upset, because she agreed only to end the conversation.
What made Afreen's prepared words a wise approach?
They stated her timeline and values calmly and ended with a real question about her parents' worries, so she listened as well as spoke.
What worries did Afreen's parents share?
Her father worried about her "getting too old" and her mother about what relatives say.
Why is it dangerous to touch an electric switch with wet hands?
It can give you a shock. Because water carries electricity well, so wet skin lets current pass through your body more easily.

'You saw it, Pooja? The accident near the college gate?'
'I was right there, Shalini. An auto hit the scooter at the signal.'
'The auto jumped the red light, na? That's what everyone's saying.'
'Yes, definitely jumped the red. And the auto driver was on his phone.'
'Was he? The news said the scooter was speeding.'
'No, no. Auto on the phone. I'm sure.'
'The video in the class group shows the scooter coming fast.'
Pooja paused. 'I was looking at my own phone when I heard the crash.'
'So how did you see the light?'
Pooja opened her mouth and closed it. 'I don't know. It feels like I saw it. I've read it ten times since yesterday.'
'Maybe you saw the crash, and the rest came later?'
'Maybe,' Pooja said slowly. 'But it feels so real.'

Where was the accident?
Near the college gate, at the signal.
What is Pooja feeling when she says 'But it feels so real'?
Pooja feels unsettled and unsure, noticing her certainty came partly from messages she read later.
What could Pooja do before telling anyone else what happened?
She could separate what she actually saw, the crash, from what she read later, and say 'I heard' for the rest.
How does Shalini's questioning help?
Shalini's calm questions let Pooja notice she was looking at her phone, which exposes how later reports filled the gaps.

metadata.subtype: Witnessing an event and then reading reports [Actor]

messages.content: Shut the window, there is a draught! I only know draughts as a board game.

A draught is a current of cold air in a room. It is a noun, and it is the British spelling; Americans write draft. Draughts is also the name of a board game.
Example: A draught from the door made the candle flicker.

Rehana, you asked what the first step was, and honestly it was the meeting with the advisor. I had avoided it for a week. Then on Wednesday I took my marksheet, printed, folded in a file, and knocked. I said, "I failed two subjects because I missed weeks after a family illness. I want to know what to do now." The advisor listened, did not sigh, and pulled up my record. They told me the dates for the backlog exams, how the credit counts work, and that I could take fewer courses next term. I wrote it all down. I walked out with a page of dates and a twenty-minute appointment for the following month. It felt smaller than I had feared. — Kavitha

On which day did Kavitha meet the advisor?
Kavitha went on Wednesday.
What was Kavitha feeling before knocking on the advisor's door?
Kavitha was nervous and reluctant, having avoided the meeting for a week and carrying the marksheet in a folded file.
What alternative approach could Kavitha add after the meeting, and why?
Kavitha could form a small study group for the backlog subjects, because the advisor sorted the rules and dates but a group helps with the actual studying.
How might the advisor have seen Kavitha's visit?
The advisor listened, did not sigh and pulled up the record, so the advisor met a student with a clear question and gave practical details.

In the staff room of a Jaipur secondary school, Kashish clicked to her Class 8 attendance chart and the projector showed a recipe for aloo paratha instead. Twelve teachers stared at it. Kashish burst out laughing, too loud and too long. "Oh my god, I'm such a disaster, ha ha, don't mind me, I'm hopeless with laptops!" She kept laughing while she scrolled, cheeks burning, and people began to shift in their chairs. Vinita, the vice principal, waited quietly. Kashish caught her calm look and took a breath. "Sorry, my mistake, wrong file. Here's the right one." She opened the chart. "Attendance dropped on Mondays in October. I'd like to try a Monday morning quiz to pull it back up." Two teachers nodded and started writing. Afterwards, Vinita stopped by her chair. "That second minute was much stronger than the first." Kashish let out a shaky breath and smiled.

What appeared on the projector instead of the Class 8 attendance chart?
A recipe for aloo paratha appeared instead.
What does Kashish's loud, long laugh suggest she was feeling?
Mostly embarrassment, shown by her burning cheeks, mixed with hope that laughing would ease the tension; it could also have been nervous surprise at the wrong file.
What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
Laughing it off and calling herself hopeless kept the attention on the mistake; owning it briefly with "wrong file" and moving on to the Monday quiz got the meeting back on track.
How might the other teachers have felt during the long laugh?
They were likely uncomfortable, shifting in their chairs and unsure whether to laugh along or look away, until Kashish moved on 😅
This is the most easiest question in the paper. Is it fine?
No. Say: "This is the easiest question in the paper." "Easiest" already means "most easy", so "most" is not needed.
Tiny story, about 35 words: a thirsty crow finds a jug with a little water, cannot reach it, drops pebbles in one by one, and drinks.
A thirsty crow found a jug with a little water in it. He could not reach the water. So he dropped pebbles into the jug, one by one. The water rose, and the crow drank.

At the village fair, the swing had a long line of children. Kalyani, five, ran straight to the front.
"Kalyani, no," said her cousin Aadhya, who was nine. "See? We stand at the back."
Kalyani stamped her foot. "But I want it!"
Aadhya took her hand and walked her to the end of the line. "I'll wait with you. We'll count the swings."
They counted together. When Kalyani's turn came, the swing man said, "Good girl, you waited." Aadhya pushed her high. Kalyani laughed.

Who took Kalyani to the end of the line?
Her cousin Aadhya took her hand and walked her to the end of the line.
How was Kalyani feeling when she stamped her foot?
Kalyani felt impatient and cross, wanting the swing right away.
What made Aadhya's help work?
She showed Kalyani where to stand, waited with her and made counting a game, and the swing man's praise rewarded her.
How might the other children have felt if Kalyani had stayed at the front?
They might have felt it was unfair and upset, having waited their turn.

I'm Nandini. Last year, when I was eleven, Trisha and I were the only girls in the mental-maths round at the inter-school fest. At home I could add big numbers in my head faster than my dad.
Just before we went up, a boy from the other team said loudly, "Girls always freeze in speed rounds." His friends giggled. The quizmaster read the first question, and my stomach twisted into a knot. All I could hear was his voice. I got the first three wrong, even the easy one.
Trisha squeezed my hand under the table. On the fourth question I shut my eyes and pictured our kitchen table. I got it.
Now I know the numbers never left me. The worry was just sitting on top of them.

What did the boy from the other team say?
He said, 'Girls always freeze in speed rounds.'
Why did Nandini get the first three questions wrong, even the easy one?
Her stomach knotted and all she could hear was the boy's voice, so the fear of proving him right crowded out the numbers.
What helped Nandini get the fourth question right?
Trisha's squeeze and picturing the kitchen table at home calmed her enough for her real skill to come back.
How might Trisha have felt watching Nandini miss easy questions?
Trisha may have felt worried and protective, knowing how good Nandini is, which is why she squeezed her hand.

metadata.subtype: Feeling watched for a group label [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

At recess Tushar tripped on the edge of the sandpit and sat down hard, his lip wobbling. Zainab dropped her skipping rope, ran over, held out her hand and asked, "Are you okay?" She felt a warm ache in her tummy as he sniffled and stood up. The teacher, watching, said, "That was kind, Zainab." After school she could not find her left shoe in the cubby, until Tushar looked under the bench and pulled it out from behind a bag. Zainab's shoulders dropped in relief. "Thanks!" she said, and she decided she would help him back tomorrow with his stubborn water bottle lid. At home she set out four spoons on the table, one by one, while her father, Jagdish, stirred the dal. He noticed and said, "Thanks, Zainab. You made dinner much easier." Zainab stood up straight and felt important, and she carried the plates next. Nobody offered her a sweet in exchange, and she did not ask. Helping just felt good.

What did Zainab set out on the table at home?
She set out four spoons on the table.
How did Zainab's helping Tushar differ from Tushar's helping her, and what did her father's thanks add?

She helped Tushar up when he fell and asked if he was okay, and later Tushar found her lost shoe, so each looked out for the other; her father's thanks for the spoons made her feel important without turning help into payment.
What was Zainab feeling when Tushar pulled her shoe out from behind the bag?
She felt relieved and happy, and wanted to help him back.
How could a grown-up keep building Zainab's kindness?
They could keep noticing and naming her kind acts and thank her for real help, without paying her for it.
Reading in English is my new goal, but difficult words keep stopping me.
Don't stop at every word. Try to follow the story, and underline only the words that come up more than once. Those are the ones worth learning.
What kind of book should I start with?
A short story collection or a book for younger readers can be a good start. Pick something about a topic you already enjoy, so you can guess the missing words from the story.
I like animal stories.
Then you have a clear direction. Animal stories use plain language and lots of repeated words, so reading one will feel easier than you expect.
I'll ask my school librarian. Is it okay to read the same book twice?
Yes. A second reading helps you notice words you missed and lets you enjoy the story at a relaxed pace. Many readers do it on purpose.

Shankar: essay due friday. starting tonight
Uday: tonight tonight or "tonight" 😅

Uday: bro the last essay you said 3 hrs and it was 2 days

Shankar: ok maybe I'll start at 8 instead of 10
Uday: or start now
Shankar: can't, match on tv
Uday: lol
Uday (next day, 1 am): how's the 3 hrs
Shankar: 600 words
Shankar: don't

How many words was Shankar's essay?
The essay was 2000 words.
Why did Shankar believe this essay would be quick?
Shankar felt hopeful and sure this one was easier, treating each earlier delay as a special exception.
What would you advise Shankar to do next time?
Look at how long the last two essays really took, about two days, and start that much earlier instead of trusting the feeling.
How does Uday see Shankar's plan?
Uday is amused and doubtful, having watched the same promise fail before, and teases Shankar to start now.

Tuan had set up the robotics club chat for their Melbourne school at the start of the year, which made him admin. He hadn't expected to like it so much. He could pin messages, mute people, remove them with one tap. On Thursday, Rafael, the loudest boy in the club, messaged him privately: "Kick Oliver. His code crashed our robot at the demo. Everyone's annoyed." Tuan looked at the member list. Oliver was quiet, new, and the only Year 8. Removing him would make Rafael happy. It would also humiliate Oliver in front of everyone. Tuan felt the pull of it: the power to decide, the approval of the loud ones. He wrote back: "Not removing anyone for a bug. That's what debugging is for." Then, in the main chat: "Team session on Friday to fix the code together. Oliver, want to walk us through it?" Rafael sent an eye-roll. Oliver sent: "Yes!"

Three sentences, please: what is this excerpt about?

Rafael privately tells Tuan, the robotics chat admin, to remove Oliver, whose code crashed the robot at the demo. Tuan says no one should be removed for a bug, and suggests a Friday session to fix the code together. Oliver, the quiet new Year 8, agrees to walk everyone through it.

Week one: Pankaj, twenty-four, laughed when his sister Aadhya told him to get a check-up. "I play football. I'm fine."

Week three: At the family lunch, their uncle spoke about his kidney problem, found late. Aadhya caught Pankaj's eye across the table. He looked away, uncomfortable.

Week six: Pankaj went to the clinic near his office. The doctor asked about family history, which he didn't know. He called his mother from the waiting room. The doctor explained which tests made sense for him and said to come back if anything worried him. The results were mostly fine; one number was worth watching. Pankaj started keeping his reports in a folder. He texted Aadhya: 'Okay. You were right. Don't gloat.'

Where did Pankaj go for his check-up?
He went to the clinic near his office.
Why did Pankaj look away when Aadhya caught his eye?
He felt uncomfortable, realising his uncle's late-found illness made her point hard to ignore.
What helped Pankaj move from dismissing check-ups to getting one?
Hearing about his uncle's illness made the risk feel real, and his sister's steady nudging kept him thinking.
How might Aadhya feel reading Pankaj's text?
She might feel relieved and quietly pleased that he took care of himself. 😊
Suggest a title for a picture book about a shy robot. Use title case and keep it to four words.
The Shy Little Robot

Shorten this excerpt to under 70 words.

Elizabeth listened in silence, but was not convinced: their behaviour at the assembly had not been calculated to please in general; and with more quickness of observation and less pliancy of temper than her sister, and with a judgment, too, unassailed by any attention to herself, she was very little disposed to approve them. They were, in fact, very fine ladies; not deficient in good-humour when they were pleased, nor in the power of being agreeable where they chose it; but proud and conceited. They were rather handsome; had been educated in one of the first private seminaries in town; had a fortune of twenty thousand pounds; were in the habit of spending more than they ought, and of associating with people of rank; and were, therefore, in every respect entitled to think well of themselves and meanly of others. They were of a respectable family in the north of England; a circumstance more deeply impressed on their memories than that their brother's fortune and their own had been acquired by trade.

Elizabeth listens in silence but is not convinced, judging the sisters by their behaviour at the assembly. She sees handsome, educated, wealthy ladies who can be agreeable when they choose, but are proud and conceited.

Read this:

"Shreya, what's wrong with him today? He threw his banana at me!"
"I don't know, Mummy. He bit my shoulder, and now he won't eat."
"Look at the drool. Chin all red, fist in his mouth."
"Ramesh, come here, baby. Let me see. There. Feel that, Mummy? A new tooth at the back."
"Ah. So that's the grumpy prince."
"No wonder he didn't sleep. His gums must hurt."
"Give him the cold teething ring from the fridge."
"Good idea. And if he's still this miserable tomorrow, I'll ask the doctor."

What did Shreya feel at the back of Ramesh's mouth?
A new tooth at the back.
What was Ramesh feeling when he threw his banana?
He was in pain and cranky from his sore gums, and too little to say so.
What was sensible about Shreya's plan?
She eased the pain with the cold teething ring and planned to ask the doctor if he stayed this miserable.
How did Mummy first see Ramesh's mood?
At first she saw only a grumpy child throwing food, until the drool and red chin pointed to teething.

Akash sir said the legs of my cow were too short. I had worked on that cow all morning. My face went hot and I said, "Then the whole drawing is bad." I put my head on the desk. He did not get cross. He said, "I did not say the drawing is bad. I said the legs are short." Then he gave me an eraser and asked me to measure the legs against the body with my pencil. I did not want to, but I did it. The legs got longer. The cow stood up better. I still felt a little bit sad. Sarita

What did Akash sir say was wrong with the cow?
Akash sir said the legs of the cow were too short.
Why did Sarita say the whole drawing was bad?
Sarita felt hurt and ashamed, as if the correction about the legs meant the whole cow and the morning's work were judged.
What helped Sarita move from putting the head down to fixing the drawing?
Akash sir stayed calm, said only the legs were short, and gave an eraser and a way to measure the legs against the body.
How does Akash sir see the short legs?
Akash sir sees them as one part of the drawing to fix and not a judgment of the drawing or of Sarita.

Read this:

Pallavi, you want to train two hours every day from tomorrow? I did that once. Listen.
I was fifteen, Sahil the skinny one. A new gym opened near our house. I decided to become strong in a month. First week, I lifted every day, skipped rest, ate only eggs. By day nine my shoulder hurt so badly I couldn't lift my school bag. The doctor said to rest, and I sat out for three weeks, angry and sulking.
My coach at the time said, "Strong is built like a wall. One brick a day, not all at once."
So I started again, slowly. Three days a week. Dal, rice, vegetables, not just eggs. Sleep. It took a year. But I never stopped again.
That's why your Sahil Mama will make you start with twenty minutes.

What happened to young Sahil's shoulder by day nine?
It hurt so badly that young Sahil couldn't lift the school bag.
How did young Sahil feel sitting out for three weeks?
Young Sahil felt angry and frustrated, sulking about the lost time.
What was the turning point in Sahil's story, and why?
Starting again slowly, three days a week with balanced meals, because steady habits lasted where rushing had failed.
How might the coach have felt watching young Sahil come back?
The coach was probably relieved and pleased that the boy had learned patience rather than quitting.

Read this:

Dear Ma'am,
I'd value your advice on something I've been watching since I promoted Suraj to team lead three weeks ago. He was everyone's favourite colleague. Now, I notice, the team has quietly pulled back. Nobody is rude. But they reply to his messages hours later, "forget" to copy him on client emails, and go to lunch without him. At Friday's review, when Suraj asked for ideas, the room went silent; the same people had plenty to say to me afterwards.
Suraj hasn't complained, but he looks tired. I think the group was comfortable when everyone was equal, and his rise has unsettled that.
I plan to talk to the team about how we support leads, and to meet Suraj weekly. Is there anything else I should do?
Damini

How long ago was Suraj promoted?
Three weeks ago.
What is Damini feeling while watching the team?
Damini feels concerned and uneasy, seeing polite silence and exclusion undermine Suraj.
Which of Damini's planned steps could help most?
Talking to the team about supporting leads and meeting Suraj weekly, so the pulling back is named and he isn't left alone.
What might these weeks feel like for Suraj?
He likely feels lonely and tired, cut off from colleagues who used to be his friends.

metadata.subtype: Team sniping at the promoted colleague [Observer]

messages.content:
Read this:

Every Monday, Jeevan's tummy hurt. He lay on the sofa of their Chennai flat, holding his belly, while Urmila packed his bag. Last week she had snapped, 'You're fine, it's just school.' This Monday she sat beside him instead and rubbed his back. 'Where does it hurt, kanna?' He pointed. 'Does anything at school feel scary?' Jeevan was quiet. Then: 'The new teacher shouts. What if she shouts at me?' Urmila held him close. 'That sounds worrying. Your tummy is telling us you're worried.' She promised to meet the teacher that afternoon. Jeevan sat up and ate half his idli.

What did Jeevan eat after talking to Urmila?
Half his idli.
What was Jeevan really worried about?
He was scared that the new teacher, who shouts, would shout at him.
What worked better than last week's approach?
Sitting with him, asking gently about school and treating his tummy ache as real, instead of saying he was fine.
How might Urmila feel about last week's snapping now?
She may feel a little sorry, now that she understands the tummy ache was carrying a real fear.

Read this:

The heavy rain warning came on the news the night before Raghav's interview for the state science scholarship. The office was in the city centre, two buses and a walk away.
He lay in bed and went through the day in his head. Seven-thirty bus from the corner. Change at the depot. Walk from the bus stand to the office, maybe ten minutes. Wait in the hall. Hand over the file with his certificates.
He stopped. Ten minutes walking. In this rain. And the file was a cardboard folder.
He sat up. His mother Usha was still awake in the kitchen. "Amma, do we have a plastic cover? Big enough for this file?"
She found one from an old calendar. He slid the folder inside, taped the edge, and put the whole thing in his school bag.
The next morning the rain was so heavy that his shoes squelched. The certificates arrived dry.

What did Raghav's mother find for the file?
She found a plastic cover from an old calendar.
How might Raghav have felt when he realised the file would get wet?
He probably felt a jolt of worry, which is why he sat up in bed and went to ask his mother at once.
What else could Raghav have walked through in his head, and why?
He could picture what to do if a bus was late, like leaving earlier or knowing another route, since rain often delays buses.
How does Usha experience Raghav's late-night question?
Usha is still awake and helps at once, perhaps glad he thought ahead before the big day.

metadata.subtype: Approach: imagines the route and timings of an event day [Thinking]
