Read this:

In a Pune supermarket queue, Uma watched the mother ahead of her. The toddler was on the floor, screaming for chocolate.

People stared. The mother, Anjali, had flushed cheeks and shaking hands. Uma saw her open her mouth as if to shout, then close it.

Anjali put down her basket, knelt beside the child, and said quietly, "I'm here." She didn't buy the chocolate. She didn't yell.

Uma caught her eye and gave a small smile. Anjali looked close to tears, but kept breathing.

What was the toddler screaming for?
Chocolate.
What was Anjali feeling as people stared?
She felt embarrassed and stressed, her cheeks flushed and hands shaking, close to tears.
Which choice did Anjali make, and why was it the most useful?
She stayed calm and close without shouting or giving in, which is hardest but keeps the child safe and teaches that limits hold.
How might Uma's small smile help Anjali?
It may make Anjali feel less judged and more supported in a hard moment.

metadata.subtype: Stage 3: Caregiver's stress and choice point [Observer]

messages.content:
"I intended to reason. This passion is detrimental to me, for you do not reflect that you are the cause of its excess. If any being felt emotions of benevolence towards me, I should return them a hundred and a hundredfold; for that one creature's sake I would make peace with the whole kind! But I now indulge in dreams of bliss that cannot be realised. What I ask of you is reasonable and moderate; I demand a creature of another sex, but as hideous as myself; the gratification is small, but it is all that I can receive, and it shall content me. It is true, we shall be monsters, cut off from all the world; but on that account we shall be more attached to one another. Our lives will not be happy, but they will be harmless and free from the misery I now feel. Oh! My creator, make me happy; let me feel gratitude towards you for one benefit! Let me see that I excite the sympathy of some existing thing; do not deny me my request!"

In three sentences, what is the main idea of this section?

The speaker says the creator caused the speaker's anger, and that any kindness would be returned a hundredfold. The speaker asks for a creature of another sex, as hideous as the speaker, and calls this request reasonable. Two such outcasts would be attached and harmless, so the speaker begs not to be refused.

Read this:

Gurleen, you asked how your baby will ever learn Punjabi here, with both grandmothers so far away. Let your Aparna Dida tell you something. When my son's family lived with me in Kolkata, I said my evening prayers aloud and told stories while shelling peas. I thought nobody listened. Then one afternoon I heard my grandson Tuhin, nine, telling his little sister, 'Slowly, slowly, the river fills the sea,' in my exact sing-song, finger raised like mine. Another day he corrected his father's Bangla. I sat on the steps and cried a little, happy. Nobody had given me that job. It came from simply being there every day.

What saying did Tuhin tell his little sister?
'Slowly, slowly, the river fills the sea.'
What was Aparna feeling when she sat on the steps and cried a little?
Aparna felt happy and moved, realising her prayers, stories and sayings had been passing to Tuhin just through everyday life.
Which moment in the story changed how Aparna saw the daily prayers and stories, and why?
Hearing Tuhin repeat her saying in her exact sing-song; it showed that simply being present every day was already teaching him.
How might Tuhin have seen Aparna's everyday stories at the time?
To Tuhin they were probably just part of home, so natural that he copied them, gesture and all, without thinking of them as lessons.

Read this:

Looking back, I, Wasim, can see how fast it spread. It started as a quarrel between Rehana and Tushar about who owned the vendor project. Within two weeks the lunch table had split: Rehana's side by the window, Tushar's by the fridge. Someone made a chat group without Tushar in it, then another without Rehana. I was in both, and said different things in each. Shameful, honestly. Devika, our manager, clearly felt something was off. She asked in a meeting, 'Is everything okay with the team?' Nobody said a word. So the guesses started: that Rehana wanted Devika's job, that Tushar was leaving, that Devika played favourites. None of it was true. The one true thing, the project quarrel, nobody ever told her.

Where did Rehana's side sit at the lunch table?
Rehana's side sat by the window.
Why does Wasim now call being in both chat groups 'shameful'?
Looking back, he feels guilty for saying different things to each side and feeding the split instead of calming it.
What could have stopped the rumours from multiplying?
If someone had told Devika the real cause, the quarrel over project ownership, she could have dealt with it directly instead of everyone guessing.
What was it like for Devika to sense tension but hear nothing when she asked?
She was probably frustrated and anxious, left to guess while rumours even pulled her own fairness into question.

Read this:

Kalyani, sit, you're making me nervous with all that pacing. Let me tell you something from when I was your age.

My final-year project was a model bridge. I wanted every joint perfect. Two weeks before the deadline, I still had not glued the deck, because the railings were a millimetre off. My guide, an old professor with chalk on her sleeves, looked at it and said, "Lokesh, you have until Friday evening. Whatever stands on Friday, you submit."

I was furious. But on Friday at five I stopped. The railings were still a little off. The bridge held the test weight anyway, and I passed well. That night I wrote in the back of my file: next time, cut all the parts first, then fix details.

I still have that file. So, how long are you giving your thesis chapter?

What did young Lokesh write in the back of the file on Friday night?
Lokesh wrote: next time, cut all the parts first, then fix details.
What was young Lokesh feeling when the professor set the Friday deadline?
Young Lokesh felt furious, because the railings were still a millimetre off and stopping felt like accepting a flaw.
Which turning point in the story made the difference, and why?
The choice to stop at five on Friday mattered most: the bridge held the test weight anyway, which showed the small flaw did not matter.
How might the professor have seen young Lokesh's railings?
The professor probably saw a nearly finished bridge being held back by tiny details and felt a deadline would help more than more polishing.

Read this:

"Hansa Ba, can I have some more dhokla?"
Hansa Ba wobbled her head side to side.
Ojas paused, plate in hand. "Is that a yes or a no?"
"It's a yes, beta! Take!"
"But in Chicago, shaking your head means no."
"This isn't shaking. This is..." She wobbled again. "Like 'Okay, go ahead.'"
"What if you just nod?"
"Nodding is too stiff. The wobble is friendlier." She laughed.
Ojas tried it. His head went side to side, a bit jerky.
"Not bad! Now you're a real Gujarati boy."
He grinned and took three pieces of dhokla. "I'll ask next time if I'm not sure."

What food did Ojas want more of?
Dhokla.
What was Ojas feeling when Hansa Ba wobbled her head?
Ojas felt confused and unsure, since in Chicago head shaking means no.
What did Ojas decide to do if he's unsure next time?
He decided to ask if he doesn't understand the head wobble.
How does Hansa Ba see the head wobble?
She sees it as a friendly way to say "okay, go ahead", warmer than a stiff nod.

Read this:

I'm Vidya, and I've volunteered at the community centre with Mohit for a year. Last month he rebuilt the centre's whole website on his own, evenings and weekends. At the volunteers' meeting, the coordinator thanked him in front of everyone. Mohit laughed and said, "It's just a simple template, nothing special." Later a senior member told him the new donation page had doubled the online forms. He shrugged. "Luck, probably." I can't know what goes on inside him. But I noticed how fast he looks away whenever someone thanks him. After the meeting, I walked with him to the bus stop. I said, "Mohit, I watched you work on that site till eleven, three nights in a row. You fixed the forms twice. That took real effort, and it's helping people." He started to say, "It's nothing." Then he stopped, and after a long pause said, "Thanks, Vidya." We waited for the bus in silence. It felt like a good silence.

What did the new donation page do, according to the senior member?
It had doubled the online forms.
What was Vidya feeling as Mohit kept brushing off the thanks?
Vidya felt concerned and a bit frustrated, noticing how quickly Mohit looked away from every thank-you.
Why did Vidya's words at the bus stop work better than the public praise?
Vidya named concrete effort seen first-hand, the late nights and fixing the forms twice, which was harder for Mohit to wave away.
What might it have been like for Mohit to hear Vidya's words?
Mohit was probably uncomfortable at first, then touched, since he stopped himself from deflecting and said thanks.
I'm on a school trip to Jaipur. Write a short message to my parents, about 50 words, telling them we reached safely and what we did on day one.

Hi Ma and Papa,
We reached Jaipur safely this morning. The train was late, but nobody minded because we played antakshari the whole way. Today we visited Amber Fort and climbed so many steps! The hotel food is good. I'm tired but very happy. I'll call you tomorrow night.
Love,
Tanvi
Why do people who play a sport together often become good friends?
They share time, goals and effort. Because training, winning and losing together gives them many shared moments, and working as a team builds trust.

Read this:

Tuesday. Sofia has been full of surprises. This morning I asked the baker if she had seeded bread, and she shook her head side to side and said "Da." I froze. In my head, a head shake meant no, but she seemed to be saying yes. She handed me the loaf, so it was yes. My classmate Sangeeta, who's lived here two years, laughed for a full minute. She told me that in Bulgaria the meanings of nodding and shaking are the reverse of what I'm used to. She also said back home some people nod to show they're listening, not that they agree. Lesson learned: when in doubt, use words. I'll say "yes" and "no" out loud, and show my palms. - Lakshmi

What did Lakshmi ask the baker for?
She asked if she had seeded bread.
What was Lakshmi feeling when the baker shook her head and said 'Da'?
She was confused and frozen, because the head shake she knew as no came with a word that meant yes.
What did Lakshmi decide to do in cross-cultural situations?
She decided to use words, saying yes and no out loud, since gestures can mean different things.
How might the baker have seen Lakshmi's reaction?
She may have found it puzzling that a customer froze, since to her a head shake and 'Da' both meant yes.

At the gram sabha meeting in their village near Madurai, the panchayat hall was full of older men. Lakshmi, sixteen, stood up with a sheet of paper in her shaking hand.
Her brother Hrithik had helped her practise all week under the neem tree. “Say what's wrong, why it matters, what you want,” he'd said.
She began. “The girls' toilet at our school has been broken for four months.” A few men muttered. She looked at the back wall, as she'd practised, and kept going. “Twelve girls stopped coming to school. I'm asking the panchayat to fix it before the exams.”
The hall went quiet. The sarpanch nodded slowly and asked for a quote from the mason.
Outside, Hrithik slapped her on the back. Her legs were still trembling.

How long had the girls' toilet been broken?
It had been broken for four months.
How did Lakshmi feel as she stood up to speak?
She felt nervous and scared, her hand shaking and her legs trembling.
What helped Lakshmi hold the audience's attention?
A clear structure of problem, reason and request, and looking at the back wall to stay steady.
How might the sarpanch have seen Lakshmi's speech?
He probably saw it as clear and serious, which is why he asked for a quote from the mason.
The word for what "time" and "lime" share: is it rhime?

The correct spelling is "rhyme", beginning with rh and with a y before the m and a silent e at the end.
Example: "Cat" and "hat" rhyme.
Why does Raga Marwa sound so restless?
Marwa leaves out Pa and leans on komal Re and tivra Ma, which creates tension. Its mood is linked to sunset.

Subject: Shift pilot proposal for Floor 2

Dear Joseph,

Before we change the roster for the whole floor, I would like to test it with one team first. Here is my plan. Team B, nine people, moves to the new pattern from the first of next month for four weeks. Team A stays as it is. Every week I will count absences and handover errors, meaning forms filled in wrongly or tasks missed at shift change, for both teams, and ask Team B one short question. At the end of the month I will bring you the numbers side by side, and we can decide whether to extend, adjust or drop the change. I would rather learn on nine people than on ninety.

Regards,
Minakshi

How many people are in Team B?
Team B has nine people.
What does Minakshi hope to gain by running a pilot?
Minakshi wants to learn from a small group first, so that any problems affect fewer people.
What could Minakshi do if Team B's numbers improve only slightly?
Minakshi could extend the pilot or ask Team B which part helped, before deciding about the whole floor.
How might a Team B member feel about being in the pilot?
A Team B member might feel curious or nervous about the new pattern, but the weekly question gives them a voice.

metadata.subtype: Approach: runs a pilot with a small group before a full rollout [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Sumit, you asked how I lasted thirty years on the wards. I'll tell you. At twenty-four I was a young nurse in Goa: work, then collapse in front of the television, then work again. I thought rest was a treat you had to earn. I snapped at patients' families. One evening my friend Lourdes, from the same ward, said, 'Maria, when did you last swim?' I had loved the sea as a girl. That Sunday I swam at dawn and came back hungry and laughing. So I made a rule: Tuesday and Sunday mornings, the sea, whatever happened. Some weeks the matron grumbled. I went anyway, the way you oil a machine. I was a kinder nurse for it. Now tell me, Sumit, what is your sea?

What did young Maria do at twenty-four?
Maria worked as a young nurse in Goa.
How did young Maria feel after swimming at dawn that Sunday?
Maria felt refreshed and happy, coming back hungry and laughing.
What choice turned things around for young Maria?
Making a rule to swim on Tuesday and Sunday mornings whatever happened, treating it as upkeep rather than a treat to be earned.
How might Lourdes have seen Maria before that Sunday swim?
Lourdes probably saw a worn-out friend who snapped at families and had lost touch with what Maria loved, which is why Lourdes asked about swimming.
How do I know my dog is happy?
A happy dog often has a loose, relaxed body, a wagging tail, bright eyes and a soft mouth. It plays and comes to you readily.
What does a growl mean?
A growl is a warning. It may mean the dog is scared, in pain, or guarding something. Back away calmly, and do not punish it. A vet or trainer can help find the reason.
And a wagging tail?
Usually friendly, but not always. A stiff, high, fast wag can show tension. Look at the whole body, not only the tail.

Read this:

You asked what changed with Yamini? I'm Siddharth, and honestly, nothing dramatic. We just started seeing each other a lot.

At first she seemed perfect. Clever, funny, always up for a late-night walk. Then we went on a weekend trip with friends, and I saw her in a bad mood for the first time. She snapped at the driver, then went quiet for an hour. Later she apologised, but it surprised me.

I started noticing other things too. She wants to live in a big city forever; I want to go back to my hometown someday. She's very close to her family; mine is distant.

None of it is a deal-breaker. But the question in my head has shifted. It used to be, "Do I like how she makes me feel?" Now it's, "Do I like who she is, on the bad days too?" And that's a harder question.

Where did Siddharth first see Yamini in a bad mood?
On a weekend trip with friends.
How did Siddharth feel when Yamini snapped at the driver?
He felt surprised and a little unsettled, seeing a side of her he had not seen before.
What would help Siddharth at this stage?
Talking honestly with Yamini about the differences, like where they want to live, and seeing how they handle it together.
How might Yamini see the weekend trip?
She might have been embarrassed about snapping and worried about how Siddharth saw her, which may be why she apologised.

metadata.subtype: Stage 3: Getting to know the real person [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the engineering college library, Anand noticed his lab partner Lalremsiami had changed. She used to be the first to answer; now she stared at her screen for an hour without typing. She was always tired, even after weekends. She stopped eating in the mess with the group. One afternoon he asked quietly, "Are you okay?" She laughed, a thin laugh. "Just burned out. I'll push through." But then she said, "Some mornings I can't get out of bed." Anand remembered a poster about the campus wellness centre. He said, "I'll walk with you there, if you want." She hesitated for two days, then texted him: "Okay." After her first session, she told him the counsellor suggested also seeing a doctor. She was going next week.

Where did Anand offer to walk with Lalremsiami?
He offered to walk with her to the campus wellness centre.
What does Lalremsiami's thin laugh suggest?
It suggests she felt low and worn out but was trying to brush it off, hiding how much she was struggling.
What did Anand do well in this situation?
He noticed the changes, asked gently, and offered practical support by walking with her to get professional help.
How might Lalremsiami feel about Anand's offer?
She may have felt embarrassed at first, which is why she hesitated, but also relieved that someone noticed and cared.

metadata.subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help

messages.content:
"Yes; she's in the kitchen, sir," I answered. "She's sadly put out by Mr. Heathcliff's behaviour: and, indeed, I do think it's time to arrange his visits on another footing. There's harm in being too soft, and now it's come to this—." And I related the scene in the court, and, as near as I dared, the whole subsequent dispute. I fancied it could not be very prejudicial to Mrs. Linton; unless she made it so afterwards, by assuming the defensive for her guest. Edgar Linton had difficulty in hearing me to the close. His first words revealed that he did not clear his wife of blame.

Shorten this text to under 55 words.

The narrator says Mrs. Linton is in the kitchen, upset by Mr. Heathcliff's behaviour, and that his visits should be put on another footing. Edgar Linton hears the whole account only with difficulty, and his first words show he does not clear his wife of blame.
Two sentences about a night train journey, please. The second sentence should start with "Outside".
The train rocked gently as we ate dinner. Outside, dark fields passed by the window.

Read this:

In the canteen Nilesh, a first-year, pulled out a chair. “Keerthana, you did Prof. Verma's course. Is he fair with marks?”

Keerthana set down her samosa. “Honestly, yes, from what I saw. He gives the rubric on day one and sticks to it. But he's slow to reply to emails, so ask early.”

“What about the internal exam?”

“Two people in my batch said it was hard. I only know my batch, so check with others too.”

Priya, at the end of the table, grinned. “And he wears the same tie every Monday, ha!”

Keerthana shook her head. “That's not useful, Priya. He's fair. That's what Nilesh needs to know.”

When does Prof. Verma give the rubric?
Prof. Verma gives the rubric on day one and sticks to it.
Why did Keerthana add, “I only know my batch”?
Keerthana wanted to be accurate and not present a small sample as the whole truth.
What choice did Keerthana make when Priya joked about the tie?
Keerthana said the joke was not useful and steered back to what Nilesh needed: that the professor is fair.
What might Nilesh, a first-year, gain from Keerthana's answer?
Nilesh gets practical, honest information to plan with, and may feel welcomed by a senior who took the question seriously.

Read this:

Sahil: update. I called the electricity board today 🎉
Sumit: WHAT. the one you've been avoiding for 3 months?
Sahil: well no. I started with the easiest one. the gas agency, to change the address
Sumit: and?
Sahil: 4 minutes. the lady was nice. I didn't die
Sumit: haha
Sumit: ok sorry. proud of you
Sahil: tomorrow is the bank. then electricity. then the passport office on friday, that's the scary one
Sumit: one a day?
Sahil: one a day. short. easiest first. I write down what to say before
Sumit: this is actually genius
Sahil: honestly, the dread was worse than the calls. every time I finish one, the next one feels smaller
Sumit: call me after the passport one
Sahil: deal

Which call did Sahil make first?
The gas agency, to change the address.
Why does each finished call make the next feel smaller to Sahil?
Each call shows Sahil the feared thing is bearable, so the dread shrinks and confidence grows.
What makes Sahil's plan work?
One short call a day, easiest first, with notes prepared, so each step is manageable.
How does Sumit feel about Sahil's progress?
Sumit is surprised and proud, and wants to hear how the scariest call goes.

metadata.subtype: Approaching the fear in small steps [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Rain hammered the bus shelter, and the last bus was forty minutes late. Asif sat with his elbows on his knees. He had been cut from the school football squad that afternoon. "I'm done. I'll never make anything of it."
Neelam didn't say it would be fine. She sat down next to him and let the rain fill the quiet. After a while she said, "That's really rough. You practised all term."
He nodded, jaw tight.
"There's another trial in January, isn't there?"
"Yeah."
"We could run drills on Sunday mornings. Ten laps, then see what the coach says."
"You'd do that?"
"I've got nothing on Sundays."
The bus lights appeared down the road, and for a moment neither of them moved.

How late was the last bus?
The last bus was forty minutes late.
How might Neelam have been feeling as she sat in the rain with Asif?
Neelam was probably worried and caring, choosing to stay and listen. Her offer of Sundays suggests she wanted to be useful.
What did Neelam do that offered hope without empty promises?
Neelam stayed beside him without saying it would be fine, acknowledged the effort, and pointed to the January trial with a small plan of Sunday drills.
How might Asif have seen Neelam sitting beside him without saying it would be fine?
As real support. Asif was crushed after being cut from the squad, with a tight jaw, and Neelam's company and small plan gave him something to hold on to.

Read this:

In the town of Tiruppur, Karthik had turned down a job in Chennai to stay near his ageing parents. But he'd also refused to join his father's textile shop. Instead, he started a small graphic design business from home. His friend Vaibhav asked, 'Isn't that just defying them?' 'No,' Karthik said. 'I'm here for them. I take Appa to the doctor every Thursday. I do the shop's accounts on Sunday. But the design work is mine.' He had explained it to his father over many evenings: why he loved design, how it could grow, what he'd do if it failed. His father still grumbled. But he'd started showing Karthik's posters to his customers. 'My son made this,' he said.

On which day does Karthik take Appa to the doctor?
Every Thursday.
How does Karthik seem to feel about his choices?
Karthik seems calm and settled, sure that he can keep both his freedom and his duties.
What does Karthik do that balances independence and duty?
He stays near his parents, helps with the doctor visits and accounts, and explains his reasons patiently, while still running his own design business.
How does Karthik's father's view seem to be changing?
His father still grumbles, but proudly shows Karthik's posters to customers.

Read this:

The hailstorm lasted twenty minutes and flattened Akash's whole wheat field outside the village near Bhopal. Next morning, at the tea stall, someone said, "His father fought with the temple committee. What goes around comes around." Others nodded.
Aparna, twenty-six, the agriculture extension worker, put down her glass. "The hail fell on his field and on the Rathores' field too. Did they fight with anyone?" Nobody answered.
She walked to Akash's house. He was sitting in the yard, not speaking. She didn't say it was destiny or a lesson. She said, "This was bad luck, and it's heavy. I'm here." She sat with him for an hour, then helped him photograph the damage and fill the relief form at the block office.
Back at the office, she pushed for the hailstorm survey to cover every farm in the area, not just the big ones.

How long did the hailstorm last?
The hailstorm lasted twenty minutes.
What did Aparna seem to feel when she heard the tea-stall talk?
Aparna seemed troubled and unwilling to accept the blame, which is why she put down her glass and pointed out that the hail also fell on the Rathores' field.
What did Aparna do for Akash, and what did she do for fairness more widely?
She sat with him and helped him photograph the damage and fill the relief form, then pushed for the survey to cover every farm, not just the big ones.
How might Akash have experienced Aparna's visit?
Akash, sitting silently in the yard, may have felt less alone and less judged when she called it bad luck instead of a punishment.

Ishita managed the only bank branch in Barhi, and by five she had signed forty forms, calmed two angry farmers and decided on three loan files. Walking home past the chai stall, she bought two samosas and a jalebi without thinking about it.
Her walking shoes waited by the door, where she had left them that morning. She looked at them and lay down on the charpai instead.
Her husband Lalit came in from the shop. "No walk?"
"I can't choose anything else today. Not even which road."
"Tired, or just bored of the same road?"
She thought. "Maybe both. Maybe I just stopped caring by evening."
Lalit sat down. "Then walk in the morning, before the bank. And I'll pick the road."
Ishita laughed. The shoes stayed by the door, one day closer to being used.

How many forms had Ishita signed by five?
She had signed forty forms by five.
How does Ishita feel when she looks at the walking shoes?
She feels drained and a bit fed up, saying she cannot choose anything else today, not even which road.
What does Lalit suggest, and why could it work?
He suggests walking in the morning before the bank and offers to pick the road, which moves the effort earlier and removes one choice from her evening.
How might Lalit feel seeing Ishita on the charpai?
Lalit might feel concerned but understanding, curious whether she is tired or bored, and keen to help rather than scold.

The hackathon ended at 6 pm, and at 1 pm Ujjwal was still drawing boxes on the whiteboard: screens, buttons, database tables, a colour scheme. Hrithik, his teammate, looked at the clock and groaned. "Five hours left and we have zero code." Ujjwal kept drawing. Then the power flickered and the whiteboard marker died. In the sudden quiet, Ujjwal put it down. "Okay. New plan. We build the ugliest version possible in the next two hours. Just one screen that works." They hacked it together, no colours, no logo. At three they tested it. The login part broke constantly; the list screen was fine. "So login needs real planning," Ujjwal said. "The rest doesn't." They spent the last hours on login and submitted at 5:52.

When did the team submit?
How did Ujjwal seem to feel when the marker died?
He seemed to snap out of it, suddenly clear-headed and a bit relieved to stop planning.
Why did the rough version help the team?
It showed that only the login needed careful planning, so they spent their last hours where it mattered.
How did Hrithik feel at 1 pm?
Hrithik felt anxious and frustrated, seeing five hours left and no code.

metadata.subtype: Approach: starts a rough version early to learn what matters [Revision]

messages.content:
What does Disha do differently the second time she corrects Sharma Sir?

In Class 10 geography, Sharma Sir wrote that the Tropic of Cancer passes through Kerala. Disha's hand shot up. 'Sir, that's wrong! It goes through Madhya Pradesh. It's in our textbook!' The class went 'Ooooh.' Sir's ears turned red. 'Sit down. Don't teach me my subject.' At break Disha fumed to Pema. 'Why can't we correct them when they're wrong? It's just facts.' Pema shrugged. 'You're right about the map. But you said it like a quiz-show buzzer.' After the last bell Disha went to the staffroom, textbook open. 'Sir, I think page 42 says otherwise. Could you check?' Sir looked, sighed, and nodded. The next morning he corrected the board himself.
She waits until after the last bell, goes to the staffroom with her textbook open and politely asks him to check page 42. The next morning he corrects the board himself.

Sum this up in one sentence.

Anxiety on Jane's behalf was another prevailing concern; and Mr. Darcy's explanation, by restoring Bingley to all her former good opinion, heightened the sense of what Jane had lost. His affection was proved to have been sincere, and his conduct cleared of all blame, unless any could attach to the implicitness of his confidence in his friend. How grievous then was the thought that, of a situation so desirable in every respect, so replete with advantage, so promising for happiness, Jane had been deprived, by the folly and indecorum of her own family!
Darcy's explanation shows Bingley truly cared, so it hurts to think Jane lost such a chance through her family's foolish behaviour.

Read this:

'Ojas, beta, why are you walking like a question mark?'
'I'm not.'
Rashmi Maasi raised an eyebrow. Ojas had grown nearly a hand's width since summer, and now he hunched everywhere, backpack clutched to his chest.
'Everyone keeps saying how tall I've got. I feel like a giraffe. My arms don't fit anywhere.'
'Ah. The awkward growing year. I had it at thirteen too. I used to hide behind my hair.'
'Did it stop?'
'It did. You'll grow into yourself.' She paused. 'Want to play badminton with me on Sunday? Tall people are amazing at the net.'
Ojas almost smiled. 'I'll probably trip.'
'Then we'll trip together.'
On Sunday he did trip, twice. He also smashed a shot past her and whooped, standing straight up without thinking.

What was Ojas clutching to his chest?
His backpack.
How was Ojas feeling about his growing body?
He felt awkward and self-conscious, like a giraffe whose arms did not fit anywhere.
What helped Ojas start to feel at home in his body?
Rashmi Maasi's kind reassurance and inviting him to enjoy badminton, where his height was an advantage.
How might Rashmi Maasi have felt watching him whoop on Sunday?
She was probably pleased and warm, seeing him forget to hunch for a moment.

Read this:

Class 5 teacher's note, Deepika, 12 August
Trisha got 9 out of 25 in the science test again. When I gave the paper back, she said, "You always give me low marks, ma'am. Riddhi is lucky, you like her." I asked how she had studied. She said she hadn't, because "it doesn't matter, it depends on your mood". She says this after almost every test. On the one test she did revise for, the plants chapter in July, she got 21, but when I reminded her, she said the questions were "just easy that day". I am worried she has stopped trying.
What I did next: I asked her to revise one short topic with me on Wednesday, and we will put the two marks side by side to see what changed.

What did Trisha get on the plants chapter test she revised for?
Why does Trisha say the marks depend on the teacher's mood?
Believing results come from outside feels easier than linking them to her own preparation; it also spares her the worry that revising might not help.
What choice by Deepika could help Trisha see the link to effort?
Revising one short topic together and putting the marks side by side, so Trisha sees for herself what preparation changes.
How might Riddhi feel if she heard she was only "lucky"?
Riddhi might feel her own hard work had been dismissed, and a little hurt at being called the teacher's favourite.

metadata.subtype: Everything is luck or teacher's mood [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Bhavna stopped Minakshi outside the Class 5 door in Pune with a loud whisper. "Is it true you go to the special reading class because you can't read properly?" A few heads turned. Minakshi's cheeks burned, and for a second she wanted to run to the toilets. It was partly true: on Tuesdays and Fridays she did go for extra help with reading. She took a slow breath. "Yes, I go for extra reading help," she said evenly. "It's private, though, so let's not talk about it." Bhavna shrugged. "Oh. Okay." The little crowd drifted off toward the swings. Minakshi's hands still trembled, but her shoulders felt lighter than they had all morning.

On which days does Minakshi go for extra help with reading?
On Tuesdays and Fridays.
What was Minakshi feeling when her cheeks burned, and what changed after she answered?
She felt shame and wanted to run away; after saying it calmly, her shoulders felt lighter.
What could Minakshi do if the talk starts again?
She can say calmly that yes, it is true but private, and tell a teacher if the teasing keeps going.
How might Bhavna see Minakshi's calm answer?
Bhavna shrugged and said "Oh. Okay," which suggests the calm answer left Bhavna with nothing more to whisper about.

Read this:

Last year I used to take Reena's gel pens from her desk every morning before she came in. I called it borrowing. I'd tell myself, She has so many, she won't mind, and I'll put them back. I usually didn't. Sometimes they stayed in my bag for a week. One day I saw her looking into her empty pencil pouch with her lip pressed tight, and I still told myself it was only borrowing. Then Mummy found six of Reena's pens in my bag and asked, 'Pallavi, did Reena say you could?' The word stopped working. She hadn't. I'd never asked. I gave them all back the next day and said sorry. Reena didn't say anything for a while. Then she lent me the purple one, properly.

How many of Reena's pens did Mummy find?
Mummy found six of Reena's pens.
Why did Pallavi call taking the pens 'borrowing'?
Pallavi felt a little guilty, and the softer word made taking them without asking feel harmless.
What did Mummy's question do?
Asking whether Reena said yes made Pallavi see that taking without asking wasn't borrowing, which led to returning the pens and apologising.
How did Reena feel finding her pouch empty?
She seemed upset and tense, pressing her lip tight, even though she didn't say anything.

Read this:

Every night Nitin watched the corner of his room where the dressing gown hung, sure it was turning into a shape. His stomach fluttered. At school he told Karthik, who laughed. "Scaredy-cat!" Nitin's ears burned. He took a breath. "Everyone is scared of something. You hate spiders." Karthik went quiet, then said, "Yeah, I do."

One night he woke from a bad dream, heart hammering, and called out. His mother, Yamini, came and sat on the edge of his bed. "You are safe. I am right here." Her hand on his back was steady, and his heartbeat slowed. He told her about the dream in a whisper, and it seemed smaller in the telling.

The next evening they bought a small night-lamp shaped like a moon and left the door ajar. He explained which part scared him most, the corner. Yamini moved the dressing gown to the hook behind the door. Over the weeks the corner became just a corner. When Karthik slept over, Nitin showed off the lamp, and nobody made a joke.

What shape was the night-lamp?
The night-lamp was shaped like a moon.
How did Karthik's laugh and Yamini's calm affect Nitin's fear differently?
Karthik's laugh stung until Nitin said everyone is scared of something. Yamini's calm slowed his heartbeat and made the dream smaller in the telling.
What was Nitin feeling when Karthik called him a scaredy-cat?
He felt stung and embarrassed. His ears burned.
What helped Nitin with his fear of the dark corner?
He talked about it with Yamini, they bought a small night-lamp and left the door ajar, and she moved the dressing gown behind the door.

Read this:

Supervisor's note, new trainee check-in Ira joined our Pune office three weeks ago from a small town. Her work is careful and quick. But I've noticed a few things. She often takes long breaks in the stairwell. Twice in meetings her breathing looked fast and shallow, and her hands were gripping the table. When I ask how she is, she says "All good!" too brightly. What I did next: I asked her for a quiet word in an empty meeting room. I said I wasn't worried about her work, only about her. After a long pause she said her thoughts race at night and her chest goes tight, and she's scared she won't cope here. I thanked her for telling me. I gave her the number for the company's counselling service and suggested a check-up with a doctor too. She booked both before she left. - Darshan

Where does Ira often take long breaks?
In the stairwell.
What was Ira scared of, according to what she finally shared?
She was scared she won't cope in the new place, with racing thoughts at night and a tight chest.
Which of Darshan's choices made it easier for Ira to open up?
Darshan spoke to her privately and made clear the concern was about her, not her work.
How might Darshan have seen Ira's bright 'All good!' before the quiet word?
Darshan likely sensed it was too bright to match the fast breathing and gripped table, and worried that Ira was struggling.

Read this:

In a Manchester cafe, Jamal listened to his new classmate Bilal, who had grown up in Lagos and Karachi, speak at an astonishing speed, the words rolling up and down like music. Jamal felt lost and a bit annoyed. He'd assumed Bilal was rushing to impress him or was not listening. But when Bilal paused and asked about Jamal's own hometown, his questions were sharp and kind. Jamal realised the rhythm was simply how Bilal talked, in a tune shaped by two homes. Jamal asked Bilal to slow down a touch and Bilal laughed and did. Jamal also decided never to guess someone's attitude from their speech rhythm alone.

Where did Bilal grow up?
Bilal grew up in Lagos and Karachi.
What did Jamal feel while listening to Bilal at first?
Jamal felt lost and a bit annoyed, assuming Bilal was rushing or not listening. Bilal's sharp, kind questions showed the assumption was wrong.
What could Jamal do when someone's speech rhythm is hard to follow?
Ask politely for a slower pace and listen to the content, not just the rhythm.
How might Bilal have felt when asked to slow down?
Bilal laughed and slowed down, which suggests he took it kindly, though he may have felt a touch self-conscious about his accent.

Read this:

Since Babuji's death in the monsoon, Amma had barely left the back room of their house in Sitapur. She sat by his photo with the lamp burning, and when Charu brought her tea, she nodded without seeing her. Charu cooked the rice, packed her brother's tiffin and walked to school alone. At night she lay awake missing Babuji and, somehow, missing Amma too, though she was right there. One Sunday at the handpump, Aditi Chachi asked, 'How are you, beti?' and Charu surprised herself by saying, 'Chachi, I need someone. Amma can't see me.' Chachi put down her bucket and hugged her hard. From then on Charu ate dinner at Chachi's twice a week, and Chachi sat with Amma in the afternoons. 'Your Amma loves you the same,' Chachi said. 'Her grief is just very loud right now.' Charu held on to that.

Where did Amma sit most of the time after Babuji's death?
In the back room, by his photo, with the lamp burning.
What was Charu feeling as she lay awake at night?
She felt doubly alone and sad, missing Babuji and missing Amma too, though Amma was right there.
What did Charu do that helped?
She named her need to Aditi Chachi, reaching a trusted adult who fed her and sat with Amma.
How does Aditi Chachi explain Amma's distance?
She says Amma loves Charu the same; her grief is just very loud right now 🤍

Read this:

The children's ward lights dimmed at eight. Arohi, in the bed by the window after a small operation on her ear, sat up at once. 'Papa, I need water.' Vikas gave her a sip. 'Papa, one more story.' He told a very short one about a sleepy owl. 'Papa, one more hug.' He hugged her. Then she whispered, 'What if you go home when I'm asleep?' So that was it. 'I'm sleeping right here in this chair all night,' Vikas said calmly, resting his hand on her blanket. Arohi held his finger, and her eyes closed.

Where did Vikas say he would sleep?
Right here in this chair all night.
What was Arohi worried about behind all her requests?
She was scared that Papa would go home while she was asleep in the dark ward.
What worked to settle Arohi?
Vikas gave short, calm answers and reassured her he would stay, with his hand on her blanket.
How might Vikas have felt as the requests kept coming?
He may have felt tired or a little impatient at first, then tender once he understood she was afraid.

Read this:

Subject: The launch delay, and my part in it
Hi all,
I want to put this in writing. The two-week delay on the billing launch was my call. Lavanya warned me in the planning meeting that we hadn't tested with real invoices, and I overruled her because I wanted to hit the date I'd promised the directors. I was wrong, and I made it worse by suggesting in Monday's meeting that testing had been slow. It hadn't. I'm sorry.
Lavanya, thank you for speaking up, and for continuing to after I brushed you off. The rest of you: I need you to do what she did. If you think I'm making a bad call, tell me, in the meeting or privately.
I've set up a short anonymous form for feedback on how I lead. I'll share what comes in, uncomfortable parts included, on Friday.
Madhav

Who warned Madhav in the planning meeting?
Lavanya.
What might Madhav be feeling as he writes 'I was wrong'?
Madhav likely feels humbled and a bit nervous, but also relieved to own the error openly instead of hiding it.
Which part of the email is likely to earn the team's respect, and why?
Publicly thanking Lavanya and admitting the false blame shows honesty, making it safer for others to speak up.
How might Lavanya feel reading the email?
Lavanya would probably feel respected and vindicated, and more willing to keep warning Madhav in future.

Read this:

Every morning at the village school near Sehore, Jaya waited at Anjali-teacher's elbow instead of joining the line. She followed Anjali to the staff room, to the water pot, to the hand pump. The headmaster muttered, "That one just wants attention. Send her off." Anjali watched Jaya's eyes flick to the gate whenever a motorbike passed; her father had gone to work in the city in June. So Anjali gave her a job, ringing the bell for recess, and a promise: "After you ring it, come and tell me." Each week she asked Jaya to carry the register a little farther, first to the next classroom, then alone to the office.

What job did Anjali give Jaya?
Ringing the bell for recess.
What does Anjali seem to think about Jaya's clinginess?
She is concerned rather than irritated, seeing Jaya's worry about the gate and her absent father instead of attention-seeking.
How could Anjali keep helping Jaya grow more independent?
Keep giving small tasks that take her a little farther away, with a steady promise to check back in.
What is it like for Jaya when the headmaster wants her sent off?
Jaya might feel unwanted and more anxious, since what she needs is steady warmth while her father is away.

Read this:

"Did you see Preeti's handover notes again? Half empty," Kunal said by the printer. "Everyone's talking about it."
"I saw," Darshan said. "I'm going to talk to her."
"To her? Just mention it to Ma'am in the review."
"That's talking about her. I'd rather talk to her."
Later, in the small meeting room: "Preeti, got five minutes? It's about the night-shift handovers."
Preeti's face tightened. "What about them?"
"Twice this week I came in and didn't know which client tickets were still open. I lost an hour each time. I wanted to tell you first, not anyone else. Is something going on?"
Preeti was quiet. Then: "My mother's been in and out of hospital. I've been leaving in a rush."
"I'm sorry. Could we do a two-minute voice note instead of written notes, just for this month?"
"Yes. Thank you for coming to me. I'd heard people were talking."

How much time did Darshan lose each time?
An hour each time.
What does Preeti's face tightening suggest?
Preeti felt wary and defensive, bracing for criticism, especially since she had heard people were talking.
What made Darshan's conversation with Preeti work?
Darshan spoke privately, described the effect plainly, asked what was going on and offered a small fix instead of blame.
How might Kunal see Darshan's choice?
Kunal probably finds it odd or awkward, since chatting about Preeti or telling the manager felt easier than facing her.

Read this:

Dear Mumma (yes, Sarita Tiwari, strictest mother in Lucknow),
I'm writing because when I talk I just shout. Yes, I came home at 9:40 when you said 9. Yes, I said I was at Kritika's when we were actually at the mall food court. I'm sorry about the lie. I'm not sorry for wanting to be out with my friends. They get me in a way that's different from you. That's not an insult. I know I roll my eyes and shut my door and don't tell you things. It's not because I don't love you. I think I'm trying to figure out who I am when you're not in the room. But I still listened for your footsteps last night, to know you weren't too angry. Can we talk about 9:30 instead of 9? I'll text every time.
Vidya

What time did Vidya get home?
At 9:40, when Mumma said 9.
What was Vidya feeling while listening for Mumma's footsteps?
Vidya felt anxious and still attached, wanting to know home was safe and Mumma wasn't too angry.
What does Vidya offer to make the curfew fairer?
A 9:30 curfew with a text every time, trading more freedom for more honesty.
How might Sarita feel reading the letter?
Sarita may feel hurt about the lie but touched by the honesty and relieved to hear she is still loved.

Read this:

Parul had the slides ready: car-free Sunday mornings on the lake road in Kukatpally. She was sure. But on Friday evening, in the noisy municipal office, she turned to Ojas and asked, "Who will hate this most?" "The shop owners," he said. "Harish from their association wrote us a long letter." Parul printed all six pages and read them on the bus home, pen in hand. Some points were weak. One was not: the vegetable vendors' delivery vans came only on Sunday mornings. In her notebook she wrote, "If deliveries can't work, I rethink this." On Saturday she called Harish. "What would make this workable for you?" By Monday her plan had a delivery lane until nine.

How many pages was the association's letter?
The letter from Harish's association was six pages long.
Why did Parul ask Ojas who would hate the plan most?
Parul felt confident in the plan but was eager to find its weak spot before committing, so she treated the strongest opposition as useful information rather than a threat.
What could other planners learn from Parul's weekend?
They could read the opposing letter in full, call its writer with an open question, and let the one strong point reshape the plan instead of defending the original.
How might Harish see the municipal office after Parul's call?
Harish would probably feel heard, since the association's letter led to a real change, and may trust the office more in future talks.

Read this:

Outside the district hospital in the small town, Rekha sat on a bench with a paper cup of tea going cold in her hands. Her sister Charu had been taken in for tests an hour ago. Rekha kept wringing her fingers, then pressing them together, then wringing again. A woman from the tea stall, who sat nearby, saw it and said nothing for a while. Then she handed Rekha a folded steel cup of water and sat beside her. "You want me to call your husband?" she asked gently. Rekha nodded. "Please," she said, and her hands finally rested on her knees.

Where was Rekha sitting?
She was sitting on a bench outside the district hospital.
What might Rekha's wringing hands have meant, and what else could explain them?
They most likely showed worry about her sister Charu's tests, and the way her hands rested after help arrived supports this. They could partly be cold hands or restlessness.
What did the woman from the tea stall do that helped?
She sat beside Rekha quietly, gave her water and gently offered to call her husband.
How might the woman from the tea stall have felt seeing Rekha's hands?
She probably felt concern and wanted to help, since she waited a while, offered water and sat down beside her.

metadata.subtype: Wringing hands and grief or anxiety [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

The power had been out in the school office since noon, and the district's reporting portal closed at five. Salma sat by the window with three files and her phone. For a month she had noticed that the scholarship list for girls in Class 9 included four names she couldn't match to any register. The payments had gone to accounts handled by Mridul, the accountant. It would have been easy to march into the staffroom and say Mridul was a thief. Half the staff already muttered about his new bike. Instead, on Sunday she had called her cousin, a lawyer, who said: facts only, no guesses about people, use the official route. So her complaint listed what she could show: four names, the registers checked, the payment dates, copies attached. Nothing about Mridul's character, nothing about the bike. At 4:40 her phone's hotspot finally connected. She submitted it to the district grievance portal and saved the receipt number.

How many names on the scholarship list could Salma not match?
Four.
What was Salma feeling as the deadline neared?
Salma felt pressured by the deadline and tempted, like the muttering staff, to accuse Mridul outright, but stayed steady and careful.
What made Salma's report careful?
It listed only facts she could show, followed her cousin's legal advice, went through the official district portal, and left out guesses about Mridul's character.
How might Mridul be affected by a report that sticks to facts?
Mridul faces an inquiry into the payments rather than public gossip, so any innocent explanation can come out fairly.

Read this:

Last summer in Seville, cousin Ulla had won hide-and-seek by squeezing into Grandma's big wardrobe. This year Pablo remembered. When his friend Mateo began counting, Pablo ran straight to the wardrobe, pulled the door almost shut and crouched among the coats. Mateo, who hadn't been there last summer, searched the kitchen and the garden. Ulla walked past and winked. Pablo stayed hidden until Mateo gave up.

Where did Pablo crouch?
He crouched among the coats in the wardrobe.
What was Pablo feeling as he stayed hidden?
He was probably excited and pleased that Ulla's trick was working for him.
What else could Pablo try when playing with Ulla?
He would need a new spot, because Ulla knows the wardrobe trick and would look there first.
How does the wardrobe trick look to Ulla?
Ulla recognises her own trick and is amused, winking because she knows Mateo won't guess.

Read this:

Her team lead's message came on Friday at 7 p.m., just as Pallavi was packing for the overnight bus home for Ganesh Chaturthi: 'Need you Sat and Sun. No OT, but your growth depends on commitment. Don't discuss with the team.' It was the third weekend in six. The one senior she trusted was on leave, and her bus left at ten. Her fingers hovered over a resignation email. Instead she called her college friend Ishita, who worked in HR at another company. 'Don't quit tonight,' Ishita said. 'Screenshot that message. Find your offer letter and see what it says about working hours. On Monday we'll work out who you can talk to, your HR or the labour department's helpline.' Pallavi saved everything into a folder named 'weekends', replied, 'I'm travelling for the festival, will discuss Monday,' and caught her bus with four minutes to spare.

At what time did the team lead's message come?
The message came on Friday at 7 p.m.
What was Pallavi feeling as her fingers hovered over the resignation email?
Pallavi felt angry and cornered, and afraid of being pushed into another unpaid weekend.
Why was Ishita's advice better than quitting that night?
Keeping screenshots, checking the offer letter and finding the right person to talk to builds a record and support, while quitting in anger would lose both.
How does the team lead seem to see weekend work?
The team lead treats it as a test of commitment and wants it kept quiet, which suggests they know it may not be fair.
My colleague is used to wake up at five every day. Can you correct it?

My colleague is used to waking up at five every day.
Why: "be used to" takes -ing (waking).

Read this:

"...and the report's attached," Farhan said, his voice flat and muffled through the laptop speaker.
Disha paused. "Farhan, can I ask something? You sound really low today. Everything okay?"
"Low?" A crackle. "Do I?"
"Flat. Like you've had a terrible week."
"Hang on." Rustling. His voice suddenly came through clearer. "Better?"
"Much. What happened?"
"My headset was stuffed in my hoodie pocket. And I've had a cold, so I sound like I'm talking through a pillow." He laughed. "But my week's been fine. Good, even. The report finally balanced."
"Oh, thank goodness. I was about to message your manager to go easy on you."
"Please don't! He'll give me a pep talk."
"Noted. Cold, pocket, good week."
"Exactly. Now, slide three?"

Where was Farhan's headset?
Stuffed in his hoodie pocket.
What did Disha think Farhan's flat voice meant?
Disha felt concerned, reading the flat, muffled voice as a sign he was low and having a terrible week.
Why was asking better than messaging Farhan's manager?
Asking directly revealed that the headset and a cold were behind the flat sound, so Disha avoided a worried message about a problem that didn't exist.
How was Farhan's week really going?
It was fine, even good, since the report finally balanced; only the headset and his cold made him sound low.

Read this:

"Sahil, you've taken Arjun a gift three weekends in a row since he got that job. Sit. Let your Mehreen phuppo tell you something.
When I was twenty-five, teaching at a girls' school in Hyderabad, my colleague Asma was given the senior post I had wanted badly. From the next week I baked for her every Friday. I praised her lessons in the staff room. I told the principal she was a gift to the school.
One day old Mrs Rao, who taught Urdu, said quietly, 'You praise her like you're paying off a debt.' I was furious. At home I sat on the step and finally said it to myself: I'm jealous, and I'm glad for her. Both are true.
The next Monday I told Asma, 'I wanted that post too. And I'm glad it's you.' She held my hand. Later she asked me to run the debate club with her, and I stopped baking for her. We've been friends for forty years."

What did Mrs Rao say about young Mehreen's praise of Asma?
"You praise her like you're paying off a debt."
Why was young Mehreen baking for Asma every Friday?
The extra sweetness covered envy about the senior post that Mehreen didn't want to feel, so being very nice made the resentment seem to vanish.
What turning point let Mehreen's kindness become real?
Admitting on the step at home that she was both jealous and glad, then telling Asma, "I wanted that post too. And I'm glad it's you."
What might Asma have felt on hearing Mehreen's honest words?
Asma probably felt trusted and relieved, since an honest mix was easier to believe than weekly baking, and it opened the way to working together.

Read this:

In the Powai colony, the boys with cycles rode round the park every evening. Saurabh had watched for months from his balcony. When he finally got a second-hand cycle, he rode slowly near the gate. Francis, the oldest, circled back. "You're the one on the fourth floor, right? Come." By the third round they were calling him "Speedy," because he'd almost crashed into a bench. Saurabh laughed louder than anyone. At home he couldn't stop talking about it. "They gave me a name, Mummy. A real one." He went to bed smiling.

What did the boys start calling Saurabh?
"Speedy."
How did Saurabh feel about getting a nickname?
He felt thrilled and accepted, as though he was truly part of the group.
What could Saurabh's mother say to support him?
She could share his happiness and ask about the new friends, while encouraging him to keep his other friendships too.
How might Francis see the new boy?
Francis likely sees Saurabh as a friendly addition and enjoys welcoming him.

Read this:

Gopika: Did you sign the flat lease?
Arnab: Not yet. The landlord wants an answer today.
Gopika: Send me the agreement, I'll read it with you.
Arnab: I can read it myself, Gopika.
Gopika: I know. Sorry. I keep wanting to fix it for you 😅
Arnab: I'm the one who has to live there.
Gopika: True. What do you want me to do, if anything?
Arnab: Just be around if I get stuck. And tell me if the deposit sounds normal.
Gopika: That I can do. And whichever you pick, I'm behind you, even if I'd have chosen the other flat.
Arnab: Thanks. That actually helps 🙂

What does the landlord want from Arnab today?
The landlord wants an answer today about the flat.
What does Gopika mean by 'I keep wanting to fix it for you'?
Gopika feels a protective urge to take over and recognises it as steering rather than support.
What could Gopika do to support Arnab without taking control?
Stay around in case Arnab gets stuck and answer the questions Arnab asks, while accepting the choice belongs to Arnab even if Gopika would have picked the other flat.
How might Arnab feel when Gopika offers to read the agreement?
Arnab may feel treated as unable to cope, which explains 'I can read it myself'; Gopika's apology lets Arnab ask for help on Arnab's own terms. 🙂

Sachin: hey, sorry I walked out of the review just now
Sachin: not ignoring you. I was about to say something really rude about the budget cuts and didn't want to
Ankita: ok. honestly it looked like you stormed off on me 😕
Sachin: I get that. I should've said "give me a minute" before leaving
Sachin: I'm on the stairs, breathing. back in 10?
Ankita: ok. I was pretty heated too tbh
(15 minutes later)
Sachin: I'm outside the room. can we start again from the timeline?
Ankita: yes. come in
Ankita: and thanks for texting. if you'd just vanished I'd have assumed the worst
Sachin: next time I'll say it out loud before I go 🙏

Where was Sachin while texting?
On the stairs, breathing.
What did Ankita feel when Sachin walked out?
Ankita felt hurt and uneasy, reading it as Sachin storming off, and admits to being heated too.
What made Sachin's walk-out turn into de-escalation?
Sachin quickly explained why, said when to expect a return, came back and suggested starting again calmly from the timeline.
What would have changed if Sachin had left without texting?
Ankita says the worst would have been assumed, so the walk-out would have read as disrespect and the argument could have hardened.

Honeybees visit flowers and collect something called nectar. They turn it into honey.

Read this:

Thursday
Experiment update. Two weeks ago I told Dilnaz something small: that I can't ride a cycle, at fifteen. Not a huge secret. But if it got round, the boys in our class would never let it go.
I waited. Nothing. On Monday Rohit made cycle jokes about someone else, and Dilnaz just looked at me and said nothing. Not a wink, not a hint. Nothing!
So today in the library I told her the real one: about Papa losing his job, and why I've stopped going to the canteen. She listened, then asked if I wanted to share her tiffin, and didn't make it weird.
I know it's strange to test a friend. But last year Megha told the whole class about my braces photo within a day, and I still think about it. This time I went slowly. It worked.
Sharmila

What small secret did Sharmila tell Dilnaz first?
That Sharmila can't ride a cycle, at fifteen.
Why did Sharmila want to test Dilnaz with a small secret first?
Sharmila was still hurt by Megha spreading the braces photo last year, and wanted proof Dilnaz could keep something private before trusting more.
What was the turning point in the library, and why did it feel safe?
After two weeks of silence about the cycle, Sharmila shared the real worry about Papa's job; Dilnaz had already shown she could keep quiet, so the bigger step felt safe.
How might Dilnaz feel on learning she had been tested?
Dilnaz might be a little surprised but could understand, given how Sharmila had been hurt before, and might feel glad to have earned the trust.

Read this:

Monday. At the bus stop Deepak rolled up his sleeve and showed Shalini the purple marks. "The lodger at home grabs me when he's drunk. Promise you won't tell. Promise." Shalini hooked his little finger with hers. "Promise."
Wednesday. In science, Mr Iyer lifted his hand to point at the board, and Deepak flinched so hard his pencil box fell. Shalini hardly slept that night. A promise was a promise. But the marks.
Thursday. At lunch Shalini went to the counsellor's room. "I promised not to tell, but I think someone is hurting Deepak." Mrs Rao put her pen down and listened to all of it. "Thank you. You were right to bring this to me. A promise can't cover someone getting hurt." She called Deepak in before the last bell and phoned the school safeguarding lead that same afternoon. At the gate Shalini said, "I broke it because I care." Deepak said nothing, but he didn't walk away.

What did Deepak show Shalini at the bus stop?
Deepak rolled up his sleeve and showed Shalini the purple marks.
What was Shalini feeling on Wednesday night?
Shalini felt torn and worried: loyal to the promise, but frightened for Deepak after the flinch and the marks, which is why she hardly slept.
What did Mrs Rao do that helped?
Mrs Rao listened fully, thanked Shalini, said a promise can't cover someone getting hurt, saw Deepak before the last bell and phoned the safeguarding lead that same afternoon.
How might Deepak feel about the broken promise?
Deepak may feel scared or let down at first, which could explain the silence, but not walking away hints at some relief that an adult now knows.
We visited Taj Mahal on our school trip. Is an article missing?

We visited the Taj Mahal on our school trip.
Why: famous monuments usually take "the".

Read this:

Subject: Thank you for the honest feedback

Dear Minakshi,

Thank you for taking the time to reply. After my third final round, I decided to ask instead of guessing, and your answer was clear: my answers on designing large systems were hazy, and I jumped to tools before explaining the problem.

I was disappointed for a day or two, to be honest. Then I started working on it. Every Saturday I sit with a friend who plays interviewer. I draw the problem, say what could go wrong, and only then choose parts. My friend stops me whenever I get fuzzy. It is slower than I expected, but my answers are changing.

I would like to apply again in the next cycle. Thank you again.

Asif

What did Minakshi say was wrong with Asif's answers?
Minakshi said the answers on designing large systems were hazy.
How does Asif feel now compared with right after the feedback?
Asif was disappointed for a day or two, and now is determined and grateful, as the email describes the practice and thanks Minakshi twice.
What could Asif do to check that the practice is working before applying?
Asif could ask the friend to give a score on clarity for each mock interview and watch whether it improves over several Saturdays.
Why might Minakshi have chosen to reply with honest feedback?
Minakshi may have seen that Asif asked sincerely and would use it, since Asif thanks Minakshi for taking the time.

Read this:

Rain hammered the auto's canopy, and Parveen's train to Nagpur left in forty minutes. Imran gripped the seat in front. "Let me come with you. I'll sit in another compartment."

"Bhaiya, it's a two-hour interview. Alone."

He listed the problems: the crowded station, the ticket checker, her phone battery. She laughed a little, then didn't. "You said the same before I went to hostel. I lived."

Imran wanted to shout, "Because I called you every night." He swallowed it. "Take my power bank. Message me when you board and when you arrive. Take the ladies' coach if it feels better. But you decide."

"That I can do," Parveen said.

At the platform he handed her a packet of biscuits, not another warning. When the train pulled out, his hands were shaking, and he let them.

How long until Parveen's train left?
Forty minutes.
What was Imran feeling in the auto, and how can you tell?
Anxious. He gripped the seat, listed one problem after another and wanted to shout.
Which choice helped, and why?
Offering the power bank and messages while leaving the decisions to Parveen. It gave guidance without taking over.
How might Parveen see Imran's worry?
As too much at first, since she has managed before. But she accepts his help once it stops being control and lets her decide.

Read this:

"Yamini, you've been at that laptop since lunch. How's the essay?"
"Look, Sabina!" Yamini turned the screen. "A timeline. Research in green, outline in blue, drafts in purple. Every day till the deadline, in fifteen-minute slots."
"It's beautiful. How many words have you written?"
"Of the essay? Well… none yet. But the plan's ready."
"You said the plan was ready yesterday."
"Yesterday I didn't have the colours."
Sabina sat on the bed. "What's the first sentence going to be about?"
Yamini went quiet. "That's the problem. It's about why I want the scholarship. And every time I start, it sounds stupid."
"So the timeline is safer."
"…Maybe."
"Close the timeline. Write one bad sentence about why you want it. Just one. I'll wait."
Yamini opened a blank page. Her fingers hovered. She typed: "I want this because my mother never got to study." She stared at it.
"That's not stupid," Sabina said softly.

How many words of the essay had Yamini written?
None yet.
Why did Yamini keep working on the timeline instead of the essay?
Yamini was afraid the first sentence would sound stupid, so planning felt safer than starting.
What did Sabina suggest, and why did it work?
Sabina suggested closing the timeline and writing one bad sentence, which made the frightening first step small enough to take.
How did Sabina feel reading Yamini's first sentence?
Sabina felt moved and gentle, telling Yamini softly that it was not stupid.

Read this:

Sahil had fifteen minutes to finish a peace poster for the school hallway, and all the markers except blue and black had dried out.
He drew a dove in the middle with the blue marker. Elizabeth, who had come from London for a term, looked over. "In my old school, we'd draw a rainbow for peace."
Sahil frowned at his dove. It looked lonely with only blue and black.
"Maybe make the sky light blue and leave white space around the bird," Elizabeth said. "It'll look calm."
Sahil tried it, pressing lightly. The poster looked peaceful and quiet, not sad.
When Ma'am pinned it up, a younger girl asked, "Why a bird?" Sahil explained what a dove stands for. She nodded slowly.

How many minutes did Sahil have to finish the poster?
Fifteen minutes.
How did Sahil feel when he frowned at his dove?
He felt worried and disappointed that the dove looked lonely with only blue and black.
How did Sahil solve the problem of having only two colours?
He took Elizabeth's advice to press lightly and leave white space, which made the poster look calm instead of sad.
How might the younger girl see the dove at first?
She didn't know what a dove means, showing that symbols need explaining for people unfamiliar with them.
I am learning to draw. Give two tips for a beginner, as a numbered list with no more than eight words per tip.

1. Practise drawing simple shapes every day.
2. Look closely at what you are drawing.

Read this:

I'm Tenzin, Dhruv's big sister. At tea time Mummy cut the cake, and Dhruv shouted, “It's not fair! My piece is smaller!” He banged the table. Mummy didn't tell him to stop complaining. She said, “You think it's not fair. What do you want?” Dhruv thought, still cross. “The same size as Didi.” Mummy put both pieces side by side. Mine was a bit bigger. She cut a sliver off mine and gave it to him. I didn't mind much. Dhruv stopped banging and ate.

What did Dhruv bang?
The table.
What was Dhruv feeling when he shouted “It's not fair!”?
He felt cross and hard done by, believing his piece was smaller. Tenzin could see the complaint was really a call for help.
How did Mummy help Dhruv object in a better way?
She listened and asked what he wanted, so he could say “the same size as Didi” instead of just shouting.
How did Tenzin feel about giving up a sliver?
Tenzin didn't mind much, seeing it made things fair.

Read this:

"How did you know you were ready?" Jasleen asked, rocking Arohi's three-month-old while Arohi finally ate.
Arohi snorted. "I didn't. Nobody does."
"Then how did you decide?"
"We asked ourselves boring questions. Can we manage a year on less money? Who gets up at 3 a.m.? What do we do if we disagree about smacking, screens, God?"
"And?"
"Vikram and I disagreed about half of it." Arohi grinned. "We fought for a month. Then we wrote down what we agreed on. Night feeds split. No hitting, ever. Grandparents advise, they don't decide."
Jasleen looked down at the sleeping baby. "Manpreet wants a baby next year. I'm not sure I want one at all."
"Then that's your first boring question." Arohi put down her plate. "Don't let anyone rush you. Not Manpreet. Not me."
The baby stirred, and Jasleen didn't hand her back.

How old is Arohi's baby?
Three months old.
What might Jasleen be feeling about Manpreet wanting a baby next year?
Jasleen feels unsure and torn, not certain about wanting a child at all.
Which of Arohi's 'boring questions' are most useful for Jasleen, and why?
The questions about money, night feeds and parenting values, because they turn a vague wish into concrete choices and show where partners disagree.
How does Arohi see Jasleen's uncertainty?
Arohi respects it, treats it as a valid first question, and warns against anyone rushing the decision.

Read this:

In the courtyard of their house in Satara, Jaya, just two, held up her empty cup to Aaji. "More doodh, please! Pani nako!" Aaji laughed and poured milk. Rukmini, her mother, heard it from the well: Hindi, Marathi and English in one breath. A neighbour frowned. "She'll get confused." Rukmini shook her head. "She's sorting it out." Jaya pointed at the hen. "Kombdi! Chicken!" and toddled after it, calling both words at once.

What did Jaya ask Aaji for?
Jaya asked Aaji for more doodh.
What does Jaya's toddling after the hen suggest she is feeling?
She seems excited and happy, delighting in the hen and in naming it with both words.
What was wise about Rukmini's reply to the neighbour?
Rukmini calmly treated the mixing as normal sorting, not confusion, so Jaya can keep enjoying all her languages.
Why might the neighbour see Jaya's mixing differently?
The neighbour worries three languages will confuse her, not seeing that small children mix words while they learn to separate them.

And he overwhelmed those sons of Pandu with clouds of arrows. Then Sahadeva, beholding his maternal uncle, engaged in battle (with him), covered him with arrows like the clouds covering the maker of day. Covered with those clouds of arrows, the ruler of the Madras wore a delighted expression, and the twins also felt great delight for the sake of their mother.

Why are the twins pleased to fight the ruler of the Madras?
He is their maternal uncle, so they feel delight for their mother's sake. He also looks pleased when Sahadeva covers him with arrows.

Why does Pierre only pretend to attend to the business?

Pierre had none of the practical persistence that would have enabled him to attend to the business himself and so he disliked it and only tried to pretend to the steward that he was attending to it. The steward for his part tried to pretend to the count that he considered these consultations very valuable for the proprietor and troublesome to himself.
He has none of the practical persistence needed to do it himself, so he dislikes it and only pretends to the steward that he is dealing with it.

Read this:

I teach Class 10 here, so I see the lunch hour every day. Since the term began, Naveen has been opening his tiffin, rearranging the chapati and closing it again. He carries a small notebook that he snaps shut when anyone passes. On Monday a boy joked loudly about Naveen's "new skinny look" and a few laughed. I didn't know what was going on inside him, and I still don't. But I stopped the joke on the spot, without making Naveen the topic, and later asked him to help me carry books to the staffroom. There I said only that I had noticed lunch seemed hard lately and that I cared. He shrugged, eyes wet. That evening I phoned his parents, gently, and suggested a visit to their family doctor.
Irawati, class teacher

What does Naveen do with his tiffin at lunch?
He has been opening his tiffin, rearranging the chapati and closing it again.
What was Irawati feeling after the joke at lunch, and how can you tell?
Irawati was worried and protective; the teacher stopped the joke at once and then made a private chance to show care.
Why was the teacher's private approach wiser than raising it in class?
A quiet word and a call to the parents avoided shaming Naveen in public, and the doctor's visit brings in the right help.
How might Naveen have experienced the teacher's words in the staffroom?
He may have felt exposed but also noticed and cared for; he shrugged, but his eyes were wet.

Naveen: FORWARDED: "Sector 9 boys broke our cricket nets last night, saw them running!! share so everyone knows"
Naveen: told you they're like this
Sabina: who saw them?
Naveen: it says "saw them running"
Sabina: who is "saw". there's no name
Naveen: why are you defending them
Sabina: not defending. asking
Sabina: I just asked Joshi uncle at the gate. he says a branch fell on the nets in the storm
Naveen: ...seriously?
Sabina: sending you the photo he took this morning
Naveen: ok that's a branch
Naveen: I already sent it to 4 groups 😬
Sabina: then send the photo to the same 4
Naveen: feels like I'm letting our side down
Sabina: our side is the side with the branch

What did Joshi uncle say broke the nets?
He said a branch fell on the nets in the storm.
What does 'feels like I'm letting our side down' show about Naveen?
Naveen feels torn and a bit ashamed: forwarding felt like loyalty to the colony, so correcting it feels disloyal.
What small step can Naveen take now?
Send the gate photo to the same four groups, as Sabina said, and ask for a name or source before forwarding next time.
How might the Sector 9 boys see the forwarded message?
They would feel blamed for something a storm did, and bad feeling between the colonies could grow before anyone checks.

Read this:

During free time at the preschool, Dhruv sat on the floor and sighed loudly. "Manoj sir, I'm bored. Can I play on the computer?" "Not today," said Manoj sir, and put a basket beside him: leaves from the garden, some clay and two lids. "What can these become?" Dhruv pushed the basket away and lay on his back, staring at the fan. Manoj sir didn't hurry him. A few minutes later Dhruv sat up, pressed a leaf into the clay and looked at the print. Then another. By snack time he had a "leaf zoo" with a lid for a pond, and he was telling everyone who passed about each animal.

What was in the basket Manoj sir put beside Dhruv?
Leaves from the garden, some clay and two lids.
What does Dhruv lying on his back and staring at the fan suggest?
He was fed up and restless, not ready to play yet; the boredom felt unpleasant before an idea arrived.
Which choice by Manoj sir let Dhruv's idea grow?
Giving simple materials and then not hurrying him, so Dhruv had time to move from boredom to making something.
How might the other children experience Dhruv's leaf zoo?
They get a proud guide telling them about each animal, and may want to make prints of their own.
