The movers came at seven. Nikita, two, watched her toys vanish into cartons and started to wail. She clung to Salma Didi, the nanny, and wouldn't let go.
In the new flat in Delhi, nothing was familiar. Nikita refused her food and followed Mumma from room to room.
That night, Salma Didi unpacked the small plastic plate with ducks and the orange cup first, and hummed the usual bath song. Nikita ate every bite from the duck plate.

What did Salma Didi unpack first?
She unpacked the small plastic plate with ducks and the orange cup first.
How was Nikita feeling when she followed Mumma from room to room?
Nikita felt insecure and anxious in the strange new flat, wanting to stay close.
Why did the duck plate and the bath song help?
Familiar objects and routines made the new place feel safer, so Nikita could relax and eat.
How might Salma Didi feel when Nikita eats every bite?
Salma Didi would probably feel relieved and pleased that the familiar things worked.

Kindergarten note, Monday

This morning Tejas knocked down Jasleen's sand castle by accident. Jasleen cried, and turned her back on him.
Tejas stood still for a moment. Then he knelt and started piling sand back up, patting it with his hands. He looked at Jasleen.
Jasleen watched him for a little while. Then she knelt down too. She added a shell on top.
Within five minutes they were building a new castle together, bigger than the first. 🙂 I told them both I was proud of how they fixed it together.

What did Jasleen add on top of the new castle?
A shell.
What was Jasleen feeling when she turned her back on Tejas?
She felt hurt and sad that her castle was knocked down.
What helped Jasleen go back to playing with Tejas?
Tejas started rebuilding the castle, a real repair that showed he cared, so Jasleen could forgive quickly.
What was Tejas experiencing as he piled the sand back up?
He likely felt sorry and hopeful, looking at Jasleen to see if she would join him.

I'm Payal, and I sit next to Farhan in the final-year lab. In June he told me his portfolio would go live 'this weekend'. I saw it that weekend: clean, three projects, looked good to me.
Then the fonts changed. Then they changed back. In July he spent a week on an animation where the project cards flip over when you hover. Every few days he'd turn his screen toward me: 'Better, or was the old one better?' I honestly couldn't tell the difference.
In August the placement cell asked everyone to submit portfolio links. Farhan submitted his old college profile page instead. I watched him close the laptop harder than usual.
The portfolio is still sitting on his machine, now with a loading animation, and as far as I know no recruiter has seen it.

What did Farhan submit to the placement cell instead of the portfolio?
His old college profile page.
What might Farhan have been feeling when he closed the laptop harder than usual?
He may have felt frustrated with himself and embarrassed, since two months of polishing still left nothing to submit.
What would you change first in Farhan's approach?
Publish the June version as it was and improve the fonts and animations after it is live, so recruiters see something while it gets better.
What is it like for Payal to be asked 'Better, or was the old one better?'
Payal can't tell the difference and may feel helpless, watching a friend polish something that already looked good.
Is my teacher's daughter older than I am?
I can't check that, as I know nothing about her family. You could ask your teacher politely.

The school safety committee had one small budget for the term, and Chinmay, the student representative, had to choose between two plans.
Plan A: remove the old wall clock in the lab that had once fallen. Zero chance of that ever happening again.
Plan B: put anti-slip strips on the main staircase, where three students had slipped this year. It wouldn't stop every fall, but it would cut most of them.
"Plan A," Chinmay said at once. "Then that danger is gone. Completely."
Thomas, the Class 12 rep, frowned. "The clock fell once, in ten years. The stairs had three falls in six months."
"But strips don't make it zero. People will still slip sometimes."
"Fewer people, though. Far fewer."
Chinmay looked at the two plans. Getting one thing to zero felt so clean. Cutting a big risk to a smaller one felt messy and unfinished. But the stairs were where people actually fell.

How many students had slipped on the main staircase this year?
Three students had slipped on the main staircase this year.
Why did Plan A feel better to Chinmay?
Chinmay felt relieved at the idea of getting one danger to zero, which felt clean and complete, while cutting a bigger risk felt messy.
What should Chinmay compare before choosing?
How much total risk each plan removes: the clock fell once in ten years, while the stairs had three falls in six months.
How does Thomas see the choice?
Thomas sees the stairs as the bigger danger and thinks cutting far more falls matters more than one perfect zero.

By four o'clock Ines had sent the report, but in the Lisbon open-plan office jackets still hung over chairs like little flags. Emil ate a sandwich at his desk and murmured, "One more thing," though his screen was blank. Marta, the team head, was on a long call with her door open. At five Tomas quietly packed his bag and left, and two people glanced at his empty chair. Ines opened an old spreadsheet and scrolled without reading. She wondered whether anyone truly needed her at seven, and whether anyone would say so if she asked.

What hung over the chairs in the Lisbon office?
Jackets hung over the chairs like little flags.
What is Ines worried about while scrolling the old spreadsheet?
Ines worries about looking less committed than the others, and doubts whether staying is needed at all.
What could Ines ask or try instead of scrolling through an old spreadsheet?
Ines could ask Marta which work really needs evening hours, or leave on time once and see what actually happens.
How might Tomas have felt when leaving at five while two people glanced at his chair?
Tomas may have felt a little self-conscious but settled enough to go; packing quietly and leaving suggests he had decided the work was done.

Last week in GK period, Ma'am asked, "What is the capital of Australia?" My hand shot up so fast my elbow hit Lokesh. "Sydney!" I said, loud, like it was obvious. I was so sure I didn't even think. Ma'am said, "Not quite. Anyone else?" Lokesh said, very softly, "Canberra?" and he was right. My ears went hot. I kept thinking, but I KNEW it. I had seen Sydney in a cartoon with the big white building by the water, so it just felt like the answer. Now I think knowing something feels different from just seeing it a lot. Next time Ma'am asks, I'm going to count to three first. Maybe Saurabh can be loud and right, not only loud.

What answer did Lokesh give?
Canberra, and he was right.
Why did Saurabh feel so sure the answer was Sydney?
Saurabh had seen Sydney in a cartoon, so it felt familiar and certain; being wrong in front of everyone left Saurabh embarrassed, with hot ears.
What does Saurabh plan to try next time, and why might it help?
Counting to three before answering, which gives time to check whether the answer is really known or just familiar.
How might Lokesh have felt answering softly after Saurabh's loud guess?
Lokesh may have felt shy or unsure, speaking quietly after such a confident answer, and then pleased to be right.

Every Friday Yamini posted the Sirsi town news on the local community page: rainfall, market prices, school results, who needed blood donors. Four thousand people followed it.

On Saturday morning, Pallavi-teacher, retired from the girls' school, stopped Yamini outside the vegetable shop. "Your post said the dam gates open Monday. The notice at the taluk office says Wednesday. Farmers downstream might move their cattle too early."

Yamini's cheeks went hot. She had rushed that post at midnight.

"Are you sure?" slipped out, sharper than she meant.

Pallavi-teacher just held out her phone with a photo of the notice.

Yamini looked, then breathed out. "You're right. Thank you, really."

She posted the correction before she even reached home: "Correction: dam gates open WEDNESDAY, not Monday. My mistake. Thanks to a reader for pointing it out." By evening, more people had shared the correction than the original.

According to the taluk office notice, when would the dam gates open?
On Wednesday.
What was Yamini feeling when Pallavi-teacher pointed out the error?
Yamini felt embarrassed and a bit defensive, her cheeks going hot and "Are you sure?" slipping out sharply.
What did Yamini get right after checking the notice?
She thanked Pallavi-teacher and posted a clear correction right away, owning the mistake openly.
How might Pallavi-teacher see Yamini's quick correction?
Pallavi-teacher may feel respected and reassured that the farmers would get the right date, and trust the page more.

Monday. Mr Thomas held up Amandeep's pencil sketch of the school banyan tree in art class. 'Look at the shading here.' Amandeep stared at the desk. 'It was a fluke, sir. The pencil was new.'
Wednesday. Jomon leaned over during a free period. 'Can you show me how you did the leaves? Mine look like broccoli.' Amandeep shrugged. 'Anyone can do it. You just scribble.' Jomon tried scribbling. It still looked like broccoli.
Friday. The notice for the inter-school art contest went up with Mr Thomas's handwritten note: Amandeep, please apply. Amandeep read it twice, then walked past to the canteen. Real artists apply to contests, Amandeep thought. Not people who got lucky with a new pencil.

What did Amandeep sketch?
Amandeep sketched the school banyan tree in pencil.
Why did Amandeep walk past the contest notice?
Amandeep felt uneasy and unworthy, believing the good sketch was only luck with a new pencil, so applying felt like pretending.
What could help Amandeep take the praise seriously?
Noticing that Jomon couldn't copy the leaves by scribbling, and asking Mr Thomas what he saw in the shading, would show the skill is real.
What might Mr Thomas think when Amandeep doesn't apply?
He might feel disappointed and puzzled, since he singled out the shading and wrote a personal note asking Amandeep to apply.

Mohit, you're about to rent your first place, so I'll tell you what I did at your age. I'm Radhika. I had found a flat I liked, and I was ready to say yes, my list ticked: bed, tap, near a bus stop. Then the landlord mentioned that the lease ran eleven months, and something clicked: this wasn't a phone case, it was where I'd wake up every day for a year. I went home and added lines to my list: noise at night, whether water comes all day, and what earlier tenants say about the landlord. The landlord didn't mind my questions and gave me two tenants' numbers. I visited two more flats. One had a wedding hall next door; another had water for only two hours a day. So I took the first one after all, and slept easy.

How many months did the lease run?
The lease ran eleven months.
What was Radhika thinking when 'something clicked'?
Radhika realised the flat was a big commitment and not a small purchase, and felt a new seriousness about choosing.
Which turning point changed Radhika's approach, and how?
Hearing that the lease ran eleven months changed it, since Radhika then added noise, water and the landlord's record to the list and looked at more flats.
How did the landlord seem to see Radhika's questions?
The landlord didn't mind them and gave two tenants' numbers, which suggests openness to being checked.

metadata.subtype: Approach: raises the threshold after noticing the stakes and rechecks options [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

The notice board in the nursing college hostel in Mangaluru had a new sheet pinned beside the mess timings: Sangeeta's chart. Two columns, "Lights out by 11" and "Two hours of study before dinner", with a tick or a cross for every day of September. In August she'd been sleeping at two, dozing through anatomy, and blaming the hostel noise. Now the chart showed twenty-two ticks in the first column and nineteen in the second. Her roommate Gopika stopped to read it on the way to breakfast. "You put it where everyone can see?" "That's the point," Sangeeta said. "If I cross it, it's me who crossed it." That week her anatomy quiz mark jumped from eleven to seventeen. She drew a small star next to it and stood a little straighter at assembly.

How many ticks did the chart show in the first column?
The chart showed twenty-two ticks in the first column.
What does 'If I cross it, it's me who crossed it' show about Sangeeta's thinking?
She now sees herself as responsible for her results instead of the hostel noise, and that ownership feels motivating rather than heavy 🙂
What choice made Sangeeta's progress visible, and why did that matter?
Pinning the chart on the notice board and marking the quiz score beside it; the ticks and the jump from eleven to seventeen gave her proof that her own changes worked.
How might Gopika see the chart on the notice board?
Gopika seems surprised that Sangeeta would make it public, and may be impressed, perhaps even tempted to try a chart of Gopika's own.

Read this:

Xin and Priscila were partners for fractions in their Sydney classroom. Priscila suggested cutting the pizza drawing into eighths. Xin went silent, brows pulled down hard, pencil tapping. Priscila's stomach sank. She's annoyed with me. I said something silly. She scooted her chair a little away and stopped talking. After a minute Xin looked up. “Eighths works! I was checking if sixths would too.” Priscila blinked. “You looked so cross.” Xin laughed. “That's my thinking face. My brother says I look like I want to fight the page.” “Maybe warn me next time?” “Deal. I'll say ‘thinking’.”

What did Priscila suggest cutting the pizza drawing into?
Priscila suggested cutting it into eighths.
What was Priscila feeling when Xin's brows pulled down?
She felt anxious and embarrassed, believing Xin was annoyed at her suggestion, so she moved away and went quiet.
What small step did the girls agree on?
Xin would say “thinking” when frowning over work, so Priscila wouldn't mistake the face for anger 👍
How does Xin see her own frown?
Xin sees it as a normal thinking face, even joking about it, and hadn't realised it looked cross to others.

Read this:

Sunday, late. Aadhya, you nearly said sorry again. Three weeks ago Chaitanya booked a surprise weekend in Lonavala, wrote me a song, called me 'the best thing in my life' in front of everyone at the canteen. Tonight I said I couldn't skip my cousin's engagement for another trip he'd planned. And just like that, nothing. Read, no reply. Saw my story, no reply. It's the same swing as after I said no to moving in with him. Huge warmth, then ice the moment I have a limit. Didi read the chats and said, 'Watch what he does on a boring Tuesday, not on a Lonavala weekend.' Didi's right. Boring Tuesdays with Chaitanya are mostly silence. Tomorrow I'm not chasing, and I'm going to that engagement with a clear head.

Where did Chaitanya book the surprise weekend?
Chaitanya booked a surprise weekend in Lonavala.
What was Aadhya feeling when the messages went unanswered?
Aadhya felt hurt and confused by the sudden silence, and guilty enough to nearly apologise.
What would help Aadhya judge the relationship more clearly?
Doing what Didi suggested: watching Chaitanya's behaviour on ordinary days rather than on grand gestures like the Lonavala trip.
How might Chaitanya see Aadhya's limit about the engagement?
Chaitanya seems to take the no as rejection and pulls back warmth, perhaps expecting the silence to bring Aadhya back.
What happens if you do not drink enough water on a hot day?
You may feel tired and get a headache. Because the body loses water through sweat, and without enough of it the body cannot work well.

What are the match timings for tomorrow's game? One more thing: why do we use a net in badminton? Then, how many people watched the cricket match last night? Plus, I don't understand "objection". Can you help?

1. I don't know; I can't see the schedule. Check the tournament's official page.
2. A net divides the two sides. Because the players must send the shuttle over it, which makes the game fair and sets the rules for each point.
3. I don't know that. I can't see recent figures. Check a sports news site that reports the official numbers.
4. Objection means a reason or statement against something. It is a noun.
What is one teaching note for Raga Mishra Khamaj?
Mishra means mixed; extra notes are allowed.

Read this:

Rekha, you're worried because your friend got promoted and has stopped listening. Let me tell you about Joginder. We joined the textile mill in Ludhiana together at twenty-four and shared a tiffin for three years. Then he became shift manager. Within months he interrupted everyone, walked past our old lunch spot and expected his tea brought to his desk. The others gossiped about him in the dyeing shed. I nearly joined in. Instead, one evening, I waited for him at the gate and said, 'Joginder, you've stopped letting people finish their sentences. Even me.' He was angry at first. Then he admitted the owners were pressing him hard every day and he felt he had to look strong. We walked home together like old times. The next week he came back to the lunch spot. Vaibhav's advice, beta: say it to his face, kindly, and remember the pressure on him too.

How long did Vaibhav and Joginder share a tiffin?
For three years.
What did Vaibhav feel watching Joginder change?
Vaibhav felt hurt and was tempted to gossip, missing his old friend.
Vaibhav chose to speak to Joginder at the gate instead of gossiping. Why was that the right turning point?
It named the change honestly and kindly, gave Joginder a chance to explain the pressure, and brought him back to his old friends.
How did Joginder feel when Vaibhav spoke to him?
Joginder was angry at first, then honest, admitting the owners' pressure made him feel he had to look strong.

Read this:

At the community centre ground, Nirmal held the handlebars of a small red cycle. No training wheels, only Damini the coach nearby with folded arms. "Ready?" Nirmal pushed off, wobbled twice and toppled onto the grass. Up again. This time he went four pedals before the front wheel twisted. Again. Six pedals. Damini said nothing but nodded. After an hour his knees were scuffed and his shirt was green with grass, but he was smiling. "I think I felt it," he said. "The falling part isn't so scary now." The last try took him almost to the far fence.

How many pedals did Nirmal manage on the second try?
Nirmal managed four pedals.
What might Nirmal feel when saying the falling part is not so scary?
Nirmal probably feels growing confidence and a little pride, because the scuffed knees did not stop the smile. 😊
What alternative approach could Nirmal use to learn faster, and why?
Nirmal could ask Damini to hold the seat for the first pedals or glide without pedals first. That would give balance practice with less fear.
How might Damini see Nirmal's tries?
Damini stood with folded arms and only nodded, so Damini seems to trust the practice and probably sees steady improvement.

messages.content: Our plan depends of the weather tomorrow.

Our plan depends on the weather tomorrow.
Why: The verb "depend" is followed by "on", not "of".

Read this:

At the district sports club, the junior swimmers lined up for medals. Madhuri got bronze in freestyle. She held it up, beaming, until she saw Sarita's gold.
For the rest of the evening, she kept counting: Sarita, two golds. The girl from the other club, one silver. Me, one bronze. Every time someone passed with a medal, she checked its colour.
In the changing room, the coach asked, "Madhuri, how was your turn at the wall?"
"Slow. I only got bronze."
"Your turn was the best I've seen from you. Two seconds faster than last month."
Madhuri looked at the bronze again. It suddenly felt a little heavier, in a good way.

What medal did Madhuri get in freestyle?
She got bronze in freestyle.
What was Madhuri feeling when she saw Sarita's gold?
She felt her pride drop and felt smaller, comparing her bronze with Sarita's gold.
How did the coach help Madhuri see her swim differently?
The coach pointed to her own improvement, two seconds faster than last month, instead of the medal colours.
How might Sarita see the evening?
Sarita may simply be enjoying her golds, not knowing Madhuri is measuring herself against them.

Read this:

It was the week of the half-yearly exams, the power kept cutting out, and at home in Hyderabad nobody seemed to see Yusuf at all. His baby sister had colic; his parents moved around the flat like ghosts, holding her.

But every night, on his phone's last bit of battery, the online group for the young preacher was there. "Yusuf! Brother, how was your day?" Thirty people knew his name. They sent voice notes. They prayed for his exams. He felt warm for the first time in weeks.

On Wednesday, a group admin wrote, "The people around you don't understand you like we do." Yusuf paused. They were kind. But was kindness the same as being right?

At school the next day, Siddharth, who sat behind him, asked if he wanted to come to chess club after exams. Yusuf almost said no. Then he said yes.

That weekend, with the lights finally back on, he played three games and lost all of them. He laughed anyway.

What did the group admin write on Wednesday?
The admin wrote, "The people around you don't understand you like we do."
What did Yusuf feel when the group greeted him every night?
Yusuf felt warm and seen for the first time in weeks, because at home he felt invisible.
Why was saying yes to chess club a good choice?
It gave Yusuf real, offline friends, so the online group was not his only source of warmth and belonging.
How might Yusuf's parents feel if they knew how unseen he felt?
They would probably feel sad and a bit guilty, since they love him but were exhausted caring for the baby.
Make one sentence out of these three, using a suitable connecting word: The shop was crowded. The queue was long. We waited anyway.
The shop was crowded and the queue was long, but we waited anyway.
What was the name of the bus driver who drove my cousin's school bus in 2015?
I can't tell, because a school's old staff details are private. The school transport office keeps staff records.

Read this:

"Francis, you didn't reply for six hours yesterday."
"I know, I know."
"I thought you were angry about the match. I kept checking my phone."
"Tenzin, my phone died at my grandmother's. She doesn't have a charger that fits."
"Six hours!"
"I'm sorry. Were you worried?"
"I was sure you were upset with me. I even typed a long apology."
"For what?"
"For the missed pass."
Francis laughed. "I forgot about the pass!"
Tenzin groaned. "I wasted my whole evening worrying."
"Next time just call me. Or ask straight away. Don't spiral."
"Okay. But charge your phone."
"Deal."

Why didn't Francis reply for six hours?
His phone died at his grandmother's.
What was Tenzin feeling while waiting for a reply?
Tenzin felt anxious and worried, sure that Francis was upset about the missed pass.
What does Francis suggest for next time?
Francis suggests calling or asking straight away instead of spiralling over a delayed reply.
How did Francis see the delayed reply?
Francis didn't think it meant anything, since his phone had died and he had forgotten the pass.

Read this:

Lalit sat on the step, crying. His ice cream lay melting on the ground.

Shreya ran over and patted his back hard. "Don't cry, I'm here! You can have my car. Look, it's red!"

"Go away," Lalit sobbed, turning his shoulder.

Shreya looked hurt. "But I'm helping!"

Her mother, sitting nearby, called softly, "Shreya, come here a sec." She whispered, "You were so kind. Sometimes people want a little space first. Shall we wait here, and you can offer the car later?"

Shreya sat with her mother, watching Lalit. After a while, he looked over. "Can I see the car?"

What lay melting on the ground?
His ice cream.
What was Shreya feeling when Lalit said "Go away"?
She felt hurt and confused, because she was sincerely trying to help and he pushed her away. Her "But I'm helping!" shows she didn't yet understand he wanted space.
How did Shreya's mother help her?
She praised Shreya's kindness and explained that people sometimes want space first, suggesting she wait and offer the car later.
If you were Lalit, what might you want right after dropping the ice cream?
A little time to be sad without someone patting you, and then maybe some company, as Lalit shows when he asks to see the car.

The project review at the Pune office had been tough: forty minutes of missed deadlines, a client complaint, two people defending their work. Nilesh, twenty-six and leading the team for the first time, could feel the room sagging.
With five minutes left, he closed the laptop. "Before we go. Three clear next steps." He wrote them on the whiteboard, each with a name and a date. Then he turned around. "And one more thing. Tarun, the way you stayed with the client on that last call saved the account. Shreya, your testing caught the bug before it reached users. Thank you, all of you."
People sat up a little. Tarun smiled for the first time that morning. On the way out, someone said, "That wasn't as bad as I thought."

How many next steps did Nilesh write on the whiteboard?
Three, each with a name and a date.
Why did Nilesh close the laptop with five minutes left?
He could feel the room sagging after a tough review and wanted people to leave with clear steps and a warm memory, not only the complaints.
What two things did Nilesh do to end the meeting well?
He gave clear next steps with names and dates, then thanked people for specific things, so the finish people remember is clear and warm.
What was the meeting like for Tarun?
After a tough morning, Tarun heard specific thanks for saving the account and smiled for the first time that day.

In the paediatric ward at nine at night, Shreya, a nurse on her first year, watched her colleague Parveen try to calm a boy with a cut hand. Parveen was kind, but kept saying, "Oh no, oh no, does it hurt a lot? Tell me if it hurts!" The boy's crying got louder with every question.
Shreya stepped in to hold the dressing tray. She knelt and spoke slowly. "Hi. I'm Shreya. We're going to clean this and it'll sting for a moment. Then you can choose a sticker. Ready?"
The boy hiccupped, watched her face, and held still. The sting came; he winced but didn't scream.
Afterwards, Parveen said quietly, "I was scaring him, wasn't I?" Shreya shook her head. "You care a lot. It just shows in your voice."

What could the boy choose after the dressing?
He could choose a sticker.
What was Shreya feeling as Parveen kept asking if it hurt?
Shreya felt concerned, noticing that the boy's crying got louder with each anxious question.
What could any caregiver learn from what Shreya did?
A slow, confident voice, a clear warning about the sting and a small choice can settle a frightened child during care.
How might Parveen feel after asking "I was scaring him, wasn't I?"
Parveen may feel embarrassed but grateful, since Shreya answered kindly and helped explain what happened.
Why do we put a date on the pages of a notebook?
The date helps us find things later. Because it records when the work was done, we can look up a lesson or see how our writing has improved.

At last, passage paid, and luggage safe, we stood on board the schooner. Hoisting sail, it glided down the Acushnet river. On one side, New Bedford rose in terraces of streets, their ice-covered trees all glittering in the clear, cold air. Huge hills and mountains of casks on casks were piled upon her wharves, and side by side the world-wandering whale ships lay silent and safely moored at last; while from others came a sound of carpenters and coopers, with blended noises of fires and forges to melt the pitch, all betokening that new cruises were on the start; that one most perilous and long voyage ended, only begins a second; and a second ended, only begins a third, and so on, for ever and for aye. Such is the endlessness, yea, the intolerableness of all earthly effort.

What does the writer think the busy scene at the wharves shows?
He sees ships and workshops getting ready for new voyages, so that one finished journey only begins another. He calls this the endlessness of all earthly effort.

Read this:

Gurleen, you think I don't understand because I'm old? Listen.
When I was a girl of sixteen, my best friend Harjot suddenly started sitting with other girls. No fight, nothing. Just gone. I, Dilnaz, felt like someone had pulled the floor away. I went to school and came home and cried in the bathroom so my mother wouldn't hear. I didn't eat my lunch for weeks.
My Nani noticed. She didn't lecture. She took me to the market every evening to help her carry vegetables, and on the walk she let me talk or not talk.
It didn't make Harjot come back. But slowly the ache got smaller than my day.
So, beta, cry if you need to. And come to the market with me this evening.

Where did Dilnaz cry so her mother wouldn't hear?
In the bathroom.
How did Dilnaz feel when Harjot started sitting with other girls?
She felt heartbroken and lost, as if someone had pulled the floor away.
What choice inside the story helped Dilnaz most?
Going to the market each evening with Nani, where she could talk or stay quiet, slowly made the ache smaller.
How might Nani have felt watching Dilnaz stop eating lunch?
Nani probably felt concerned and protective, which is why she found a gentle way to be near her.

Sunday. Vasudha told Nani about their trip to Ooty: the toy train, the rose garden, the cold.

Wednesday. At dinner, her brother Omkar told the story too, adding a monkey that stole his sandwich on the train. Vasudha laughed with everyone.

The next Sunday, telling her friend on the phone, Vasudha said, "And a monkey grabbed my brother's sandwich right out of his hand on the toy train!" She could almost see it.

Later, Mummy looked at the photos. "Omkar, wasn't the monkey at the lake? After the train?"

Omkar shrugged. Vasudha frowned. She was sure it had been the train. She'd seen it, hadn't she? Or had she just heard it so many times?

What did Omkar add to the story at dinner?
A monkey that stole his sandwich on the train.
How did Vasudha feel when Mummy said the monkey was at the lake?
She felt confused and unsure, because the train version felt so real to her.
What could Vasudha's family do to check memories of the trip?
They could look at the photos together and talk about who remembers what, without deciding anyone is lying.
How might Omkar see the confusion?
Omkar just shrugs, so he may not care much or may not be sure himself.

Read this:

Monday, first week of Class 9: Urmila ma'am split the class into 'A group' and 'support group' by last year's marks. Darshan saw his name on the support list and felt his face burn. His friend Mehul was in A group. Two weeks later, Thursday: Darshan had stopped doing homework. 'Support group doesn't get the hard questions anyway,' he told Mehul. Mehul, for his part, had cried in the washroom after getting a B, terrified of dropping out of A group. A month later, Friday: after the parents' meeting, Urmila ma'am mixed the groups and gave everyone the same worksheet. Darshan finished the first three sums and hesitated over the fourth. He didn't hand it in blank.

How did Urmila ma'am split the class in the first week?
Into 'A group' and 'support group' by last year's marks.
Why had Darshan stopped doing homework by the second week?
He felt discouraged and ashamed of the 'support' label, believing the hard questions weren't meant for him anyway.
What change did Urmila ma'am make, and why might it help?
She mixed the groups and gave everyone the same worksheet, removing the label so Darshan could try again.
How did the label affect Mehul, who was in A group?
He was terrified of dropping out of A group and cried after getting a B, so the 'clever' label brought him fear too.
Should "ingredient" end in "ant" or "ent"?

It ends in "-ent": "ingredient". The letters "ie" come before the "nt".
Example: Salt is an important ingredient in most recipes.

Cut this paragraph down to two sentences.

At school in Sydney, Mrs Hughes handed back the spelling tests with a sticker. "Chen, eight out of ten right! Well done." Chen grinned all the way to the bus. At home, his older brother looked at the sheet. "Two wrong? Which ones?" Chen's grin dropped. Suddenly the sticker looked silly. He went to his room and lay on the bed. "I'm bad at spelling," he told his mum at dinner. She looked at the sheet. "Eight right, two wrong. It's the same paper you were happy about at three o'clock." Chen frowned at it. It was the same paper, with the same ticks and the same two crosses. It just felt completely different.

Chen is proud of eight out of ten on a spelling test until his brother asks about the two wrong ones. At dinner he says he is bad at spelling, and his mum points out it is the same paper he was happy about earlier.

At the community-centre chess club, Yash moved his queen and sat back, pleased. Coach Manoj studied the board, pushed his tongue into his cheek so it bulged, and said, “Brilliant move, grandmaster.” The older kids snorted. Yash beamed. Then the girl opposite took his queen with a pawn, and the snorting got louder. Yash's face crumpled; he looked from the board to the coach's bulging cheek. Manoj stopped smiling and pulled a chair over. “Sorry, Yash. That face is my joke face; the older ones know it. It wasn't fair when you didn't. Let's look at what the pawn could do.”

What took Yash's queen?
The girl opposite took his queen with a pawn.
What was Yash feeling when he looked from the board to the coach's cheek?
He felt confused and embarrassed, realising the praise may have been a joke that everyone else understood.
What did Manoj do to repair things?
He apologised, explained that the bulging cheek was his joke face that only the older kids knew, and helped Yash look at the pawn's move.
How did the older kids read the coach's bulging cheek?
They knew from shared experience that it meant a joke, so they snorted instead of taking the praise seriously.
I want to plan a surprise for my grandmother's birthday.
A small surprise can be lovely. Start by deciding the budget, the guests and the day. Do you know what she enjoys?
She likes old film songs and sweets.
Then you could ask a few relatives to gather, play her favourite songs and bring one special sweet. Something she loves will matter more than anything big.
How do I keep it secret?
Tell only the people who need to know, and agree on a story for why everyone is coming. Ask them not to mention it in any group chat she can see.

Read this:

From her first week at the ad agency in Bandra, Sangeeta felt it: her manager, Sabina, smiled at everyone else's ideas and frowned at hers. In the Monday meeting, Sabina cut her off twice.
At lunch a colleague whispered, "She's like that with anyone from a Hindi-medium school." Sangeeta wanted to believe it, and to join in. It would feel good for five minutes.
She didn't. That evening she started a simple file: date, task, what she submitted, what feedback came back. After two weeks she asked Sabina for fifteen minutes.
"I'd like concrete feedback. What should I be doing differently on the campaign drafts?"
Sabina looked surprised. "Honestly? Your ideas are good, but you send them without checking the client brief. I have to redo half." She showed an example.
It stung, but it was specific. Sangeeta changed her process. She also started having coffee with Imran, a senior copywriter who happily reviewed her drafts. By the next month, Sabina had stopped cutting her off.

How many times did Sabina cut Sangeeta off in the Monday meeting?
Twice.
Why did Sangeeta want to believe the colleague's whisper?
She felt hurt and unwanted, and blaming a bias would have felt good for five minutes.
What did Sangeeta do instead of gossiping?
Kept a file of tasks and feedback, asked Sabina for concrete feedback, changed her process, and found another mentor in Imran.
How did Sabina see Sangeeta's work?
Good ideas that weren't checked against the client brief, so half had to be redone.

Read this:

Thursday
The barber cut my hair way too short today. I looked in the mirror and wanted to cry. I pulled my hood up and kept my head down all the way home.
Nazia saw me at the gate. I covered my face with my hands. "Don't look."
She laughed a little, then said, "Abhinav, it's just hair. You're still you."
She didn't make fun. She just walked with me to the shop and bought us both samosas.
By the end, I took my hood off. I still feel weird, but less.
- Abhinav

What did Abhinav pull up after the haircut?
The hood.
What was Abhinav feeling when covering the face?
Abhinav felt embarrassed and self-conscious about the short haircut.
What did Nazia do that helped?
Nazia gave steady acceptance, saying it's just hair, and treated Abhinav normally.
How might Nazia have seen Abhinav hiding?
Nazia understood Abhinav was embarrassed and chose to be kind and accepting.

metadata.subtype: Shielding the body and avoiding notice [Mismatch]

messages.content: Why do travellers keep a spare copy of their tickets in a different place?
The spare copy protects against loss. Because a bag with the original might be stolen or misplaced, a spare set lets the traveller carry on.

Read this:

"Akash, your father's asking again when you'll move back to Ludhiana."
"Mum, I've told him. My job is here."
"He says you could find a job there."
"I could. But Jasleen and I have built a life in Pune. We just bought furniture."
"Jasleen can come too."
"She has her career here. It's not only my decision."
"So you're choosing her over us?"
"No, Mum. I'm choosing to live where we both can work. I'll visit every Diwali, and call every Sunday. That's a promise."
"Your father will be upset."
"I know. I'll call him tonight myself, and tell him the same thing kindly. I don't want him hearing it from you."
"...Okay. Call him."

Which city do Akash and Jasleen live in?
They live in Pune.
How does Akash's mother seem to feel when she says 'So you're choosing her over us?'
She seems hurt and afraid of losing her son, which makes her see his decision as rejection.
What does Akash do to keep respect while holding his boundary?
He explains his reasons calmly, promises regular visits and calls, and chooses to speak to his father directly.
How might Akash's father see the situation?
He may feel disappointed that his son won't move back, but hearing it kindly from Akash himself may soften it.

In the small Accra office, the hiring panel had just finished its fourth interview of the day. Mr Boateng, who had run recruitment for fifteen years, closed his folder. "That one's a no. I can tell in five minutes."
Kwame, the team lead and newest on the panel, had noticed something. Two of Mr Boateng's "tell in five minutes" hires from last year were now among the best on the team; two others had left within months. Nobody had ever tracked which was which.
"I don't doubt your read," he said carefully. "But could we also score each candidate on the same five questions, and look back in a year?"
Rania from HR nodded. "We've never checked how our gut calls turned out."
Mr Boateng grunted, then picked up the score sheet.

How many years had Mr Boateng run recruitment?
Fifteen years.
Why did Kwame speak 'carefully' to Mr Boateng?
He respected the man's experience and didn't want to insult him, while still believing gut calls in hiring needed checking.
What did Kwame suggest, and why does it suit hiring?
Scoring every candidate on the same five questions and looking back in a year, because hiring gives slow, mixed feedback that experience alone doesn't sharpen.
How might Mr Boateng feel about the score sheet?
He may feel his skill is being doubted at first, but could also be curious to see how his calls actually turn out.

Read this:

Debate club mentor's note, Thursday. Sangeeta has always been one of our sharpest speakers, and fair to opponents. Since she started a short-video channel about campus issues, her tone has changed. Her early videos explained both sides of the library-hours debate. The newer ones have titles like 'Admin HUMILIATED' and get ten times the views. In today's practice debate, she mocked Gurleen's accent instead of the argument. The room laughed, then went quiet. Gurleen sat down without finishing. I spoke to Sangeeta afterwards. She said, 'The angry ones do better. People expect it now.' I asked whether the audience was shaping her or she was shaping it. She was silent for a while. I have asked her to apologise to Gurleen, and she agreed to make one calm video next week and compare how it feels.

What kind of title did Sangeeta's newer videos have?
Titles like 'Admin HUMILIATED'.
What does Sangeeta's silence after the mentor's question suggest?
She was probably uncomfortable and thoughtful, starting to see that her audience was shaping her tone.
What steps did the mentor take, and why do they help?
Asked her to apologise to Gurleen and to try one calm video, so she can repair the harm and notice the difference for herself.
What was it like for Gurleen in today's practice?
Gurleen was mocked for an accent instead of an argument, felt humiliated in front of the room and sat down without finishing.

Read this:

Sit, Shalini. You asked why I never laugh at your debate club. When I was about your age, in our small school in Madurai, a teacher, Mr. Joseph, ran a Saturday circle. Each week one of us had to explain a belief that wasn't our own: the middle path of the Buddhists, Jain non-violence, the duty taught in the Gita, even an atheist's argument from a thin library book. I, Usha, a temple priest's granddaughter, got the atheist. I was furious. I thought it was a trap. But I read it, found one point I could not answer, and said so in front of everyone. Mr. Joseph only nodded and asked, "Now which of your own beliefs will you test the same way?" I went home and argued with my father till midnight, respectfully. I still go to the temple, kanna. I just know why now.

Which belief was Usha given to explain in the Saturday circle?
Usha got the atheist's argument from a thin library book.
What did Usha feel when she was given the atheist's view, and how did that change?
Usha was furious and suspicious at first, thinking it was a trap, but after reading honestly Usha felt humbled enough to admit a point she could not answer.
What choice in the story turned the exercise into real learning?
Usha chose to admit in front of everyone that she couldn't answer one point, instead of pretending, and then to test her own beliefs the same way.
How might Mr. Joseph have seen Usha's honest admission?
Mr. Joseph was probably pleased that the circle was working, since he answered with a deeper question rather than praise or a verdict.

Read this:

Mahima: it's 6pm and already dark here, and I just stood in the grocery aisle almost crying over a packet of poha 🥺
Sharmila: aww that's so relatable. did you buy it?
Mahima: yes. the shop guy looked confused
Mahima: nobody here laughs at my jokes. they smile politely 😅
Sharmila: give it time. the first stretch is hardest for everyone
Mahima: I signed up for the Thursday walking club and asked two colleagues to lunch
Sharmila: !!! and a call home every week?
Mahima: Sundays, video. Mummy shows me the whole kitchen 🙂
Sharmila: belonging takes a while, no rush
Mahima: ok. small steps.

Which day is the walking club that Mahima signed up for?
It is the Thursday walking club.
What was Mahima feeling in the grocery aisle?
Mahima felt homesick and lonely, shown by almost crying over a packet of poha.
What else could Mahima do to feel settled over time?
Keep going to the walking club, keep meeting colleagues for lunch, keep the Sunday video calls with home and be patient while belonging builds.
How does Sharmila see the first stretch in a new place?
As hard for everyone and normal, with belonging taking a while and no need to rush.
Is it "accross" or "across"? How can I get along with a classmate I do not like? What is wrong with this: Raju and Mohan is best friends.

1. It is "across", with one "c" and one "r".
2. Be polite, find one thing you both enjoy and keep a little distance if you need it. You do not have to be best friends.
3. Raju and Mohan are best friends. Why: Two names joined by "and" make a plural subject, so use "are".

Read this:

Lakshmi Paati set the rice on the table and folded her hands. "Before we eat, let's say thank you."

Lalit folded his hands too, eyes squeezed shut, and said the short prayer with her, word for word.

Then he opened one eye. "Paati, who are we saying thank you to?"

"To God, who gives us everything. To the farmer who grew the rice. And to your Amma, who cooked it."

Lalit thought. "And to the cow? For the curd?"

Paati laughed. "And to the cow."

"Thank you, cow," Lalit said seriously, and reached for the curd.

What did Lakshmi Paati set on the table?
The rice.
What was Lalit feeling when he opened one eye and asked who they were thanking?
He was most likely curious about what the prayer meant, and comfortable enough with Paati to ask. Adding the cow shows he was thinking hard and felt grateful in his own way.
How did Lakshmi Paati help Lalit learn what the prayer means?
She answered his question simply and warmly, naming who they were thankful to, and welcomed his own idea about the cow.
What would change if Paati had told Lalit to be quiet and just pray?
He might keep saying the words by routine without learning what they mean, and feel his questions were not welcome.

Read this:

Hi Imran,
Remember the forwarded post about the new water policy that had the whole hostel furious? I nearly shared it too. Instead I tried something I'd been meaning to do.
I checked it against two news sites and the actual government notice. The notice said something much duller and less scary. Half the post was simply wrong.
So I've made a small habit: three people I follow now disagree with me on most things. One is a farmer in Bathinda who writes long, careful threads. I don't enjoy reading him. Some nights I'm annoyed, some nights I'm honestly unsure who's right, and that feeling is uncomfortable in a way I didn't expect.
But I argue better now. In our group chat last week, when Rhea and Joy were raging about the policy, I could explain what it actually said.
Try it for a month?
Gurleen

What did Gurleen check the forwarded post against?
Two news sites and the actual government notice.
How does Gurleen feel while reading people who disagree?
Gurleen feels annoyed on some nights and uncomfortably unsure on others, but keeps reading anyway.
What habits could Imran copy from Gurleen?
Check a claim against the original source and more than one site before sharing, and follow a few thoughtful people who disagree.
How might Rhea and Joy have reacted when Gurleen explained what the policy said?
They may have felt surprised or even irritated at first, but it gave the group chat facts instead of only anger.
Rewrite these two sentences as one using "who": I met a girl. She can speak five languages.
I met a girl who can speak five languages.

Read this:

Swati, you're sulking over that one comment from your art teacher? Sit with your Yogesh Nana. When I was nine, in a small school in Jhansi, my report card came home with ten remarks from ten teachers. Nine said things like "bright", "helpful", "lovely handwriting". One, from the drawing master, said "careless with colours". Do you know which one I remember, seventy years later? "Careless with colours." I didn't show Amma the card for two days. I hid it under my mattress. When she finally read it, she read all nine good ones out loud to me, twice. I still remember the bad one best. But now I know it was one out of ten.

How many remarks were on Nana's report card?
Ten remarks from ten teachers.
Why did Nana hide the report card under his mattress?
The one remark, 'careless with colours', hurt so much that it seemed to be what the whole card said, so he felt ashamed to show it.
What did Nana's Amma do that helped, and what could Swati try?
She read all nine good remarks out loud twice; Swati could read all her own comments, count the kind ones, and see the unkind one as one of many.
What would change if Nana had shown the card on the first day?
Amma could have read out the good remarks sooner, and he might not have spent two days feeling ashamed.

Read this:

At nine, Simran stumbled while reading about the water cycle and ended up with the word "evaporation" in a knot. She crossed her eyes and made a hissing kettle noise. The class roared and the teacher, Yamini, sighed with a laugh. Simran bowed, then sat still, biting her thumbnail.

At fifteen, in the corridor, Simran gave her friend Jomon a mock salute. "Captain of the lost-and-found," she said, because he had found her missing lunchbox. Jomon saluted back, grinning. A minute later another boy passed and said to Jomon, with a flat voice and air quotes around the word, "Your 'project' was really something." Jomon's grin dropped and he looked at the floor.

Simran recognised that feeling. She stepped between them, said, "That wasn't funny, and you know it," and walked Jomon away. "Same gesture as mine," she said quietly on the stairs, "but not the same tone, was it?" Jomon breathed out and nodded.

What noise did Simran make after crossing her eyes at nine?
She made a hissing kettle noise.
How do the two gestures at fifteen differ, and how does this link back to Simran's joke at nine?

Simran's mock salute is friendly teasing that Jomon returns, while the boy's air quotes carry a put-down that makes Jomon look at the floor; the tone decides it, and Simran, who once used humour to cover her own embarrassment, recognises that feeling.
What was Jomon probably feeling after the boy's remark about his project?
Jomon felt hurt and embarrassed, so his grin disappeared and he looked at the floor.
What did Simran do that helped Jomon?
Simran told the boy the comment was not funny, walked Jomon away, and talked with him about how the same gesture can feel different with a different tone.

Read this:

“Seema, you're in for the Navratri decorations, right? Everyone brings one string of lights,” said Mrs Kulkarni at the society committee meeting.
“Of course. I'll bring two.”
“Good. Now,” Gargi leaned in, “has anyone seen the new tenants in B-wing? Not married, I hear. Coming home at midnight.”
A few heads turned to Seema. She smiled. “I haven't met them yet. I'll probably just say hello at the garba.”
“But don't you think—”
“Honestly, Gargi, I'd rather not decide anything about them. Should we fix the rangoli roster?”
Mrs Kulkarni laughed. “Yes, the rangoli. Seema, you take Saturday.”
“Done,” Seema said, writing it down.

How many strings of lights did Seema offer to bring?
She offered to bring two.
What was Gargi feeling while leaning in about the tenants?
Gargi seemed curious and eager for gossip, keen to share the rumour.
Which choice by Seema worked, and why?
She happily joined the shared decorations but politely stepped away from the gossip and moved to the rangoli roster, so nobody was insulted.
How might the new tenants be affected by the way this meeting went?
Because Seema refused to judge them, they may get a friendly hello at the garba instead of arriving to rumours.

Read this:

Registration day. Vidya's cursor hovered over Marine Biology for a full minute. The seniors said the professor failed a third of the class. She clicked Environmental Awareness instead: guaranteed A, no fieldwork. Her CGPA would stay above 9.
Mid-semester. Her friend Deepak came back from the marine biology field trip to Karwar sunburnt and glowing, with photos of starfish in rock pools. 'You would have loved this,' he said. 'I know,' Vidya said, smiling, and felt something twist inside.
End of semester. Vidya got her A. Deepak got a B-minus and talked about octopuses all evening. Vidya looked at her grade card, then at his photos, and couldn't work out which of them had actually won.

Where did the marine biology field trip go?
It went to Karwar.
Why did something 'twist' inside Vidya when Deepak showed his photos?
She felt regret and longing, knowing she loved marine biology but had let fear of a lower grade choose for her.
What could Vidya do next semester?
She could choose the course she loves and accept the risk to her grades, perhaps asking the professor what the course demands.
How does Deepak experience his B-minus?
Deepak seems happy despite the grade, glowing with what he learned and talking about octopuses all evening.

Read this:

Dear Ujjwal,
You said on the phone that current electricity makes no sense. It didn't for me either, until Sunday. So here's what worked for me, before Thursday's test.
I was staring at the circuit diagrams and then I looked out at the water tank on our roof. And I thought: what if the wire is a pipe and the current is water flowing through it?
Then the rest fell into place. Voltage is like the pressure, how hard the water is pushed from the tank. Resistance is a narrow bit of pipe that slows the flow. So if you add more narrow bits one after another, less water gets through. That's why bulbs in a row get dimmer!
I solved six questions from the exercise after that, and I got five right.
Try it with the tank picture and tell me if it works for you too.
Noor

How many questions did Noor get right after using the tank picture?
Noor solved six questions from the exercise and got five right.
How can you tell Noor felt excited about the idea?
Noor writes that the rest fell into place and ends the explanation with an exclamation about bulbs in a row getting dimmer. 😊
What else could Ujjwal try if the pipe picture doesn't help?
Ujjwal could try a different comparison, like traffic on a road, or ask the teacher for one worked example, since the aim is a picture that makes the rules make sense.
How might Ujjwal feel reading this letter before the test?
Ujjwal may feel relieved and encouraged, since a friend who was just as stuck found a simple way in.

Arohi had worn her green frock since morning. The mela in the next village! Then Saurabh bhaiya came back from the field shaking his head. "The tractor's broken, Arohi. No mela today."

Arohi's shoulders dropped. She kicked the charpai leg and shouted, "You promised!" Then she sat on the step with her face in her knees. Bhaiya sat down beside her. "You're really disappointed. Me too." He said nothing else. After a while she leaned on his arm, and together they watched the goats.

Arohi had worn her green frock since morning. The mela in the next village! Then I came back from the field shaking my head. "The tractor's broken, Arohi. No mela today."
Arohi's shoulders dropped. She kicked the charpai leg and shouted, "You promised!" Then she sat on the step with her face in her knees. I sat down beside her. "You're really disappointed. Me too." I said nothing else. After a while she leaned on my arm, and together we watched the goats.
How do I write this with British spelling? The color of the theater curtains is gray.
The colour of the theatre curtains is grey.

Dhruv: Before we sign on Saturday, can we do the thing from last night? Imagine it's a year from now and buying this flat went badly. Why?
Bhupen: Gloomy, but ok 😅 1. The builder never gets the completion certificate.
Dhruv: 2. The land title has some old family claim we missed.
Bhupen: 3. One of us loses a job and the EMI starts to hurt.
Dhruv: Right, we can't undo this like a rental. For 1 and 2, the lawyer your cousin suggested checks every paper first.
Bhupen: Booked her for Thursday, 4 pm. I'll scan the sale deed and the society papers tonight.
Dhruv: For 3, we don't put everything into the down payment. We keep a reserve untouched and ask the bank's advisor what size suits us.
Bhupen: Agreed. And if the lawyer finds a problem?
Dhruv: Then we walk away. Annoyed beats trapped.
Bhupen: Ok. Feeling less scared now 🙂

When is the appointment with the lawyer?
It is on Thursday, 4 pm.
How did Bhupen feel after they listed what could go wrong?
Bhupen felt less scared, because each risk now had a check or a backup; naming the bad endings made them feel handled rather than hidden.
Which other approach would suit a smaller, easy-to-undo choice better, and why?
For something easy to reverse, like picking a rental, a quick checklist or simply trying it would be enough, because a mistake there can be fixed later.
How might the lawyer see the pair's list of worries?
The lawyer would likely find it useful, since it points straight to the papers that matter, such as the sale deed and the society papers.

Read this:

A dog barked hard behind the mud wall, and Vikas, two, froze in the yard. His shoulders shot up towards his ears and his fists tightened, eyes on the wall. Sunaina scooped him up. “It's only Motu next door.” She walked around the yard, patting his back. Slowly his shoulders dropped, his hands opened and his head rested in the crook of her neck. When the dog barked again, Vikas only sighed and stayed loose in her arms.

Where did Vikas's shoulders go when the dog barked?
They shot up towards his ears.
What does the change in Vikas's shoulders show he feels?
The tight shoulders show fear, and the loose ones in Sunaina's arms show he feels safe. Tense shoulders might also mean pain, but the barking makes fear more likely.
What could Sunaina do to help him with barking dogs?
She could stay close when they bark, keep a calm voice and let him look at the dog from a safe distance.
What might Sunaina feel while carrying him?
She may feel protective and glad he trusts her arms to calm him.

Read this:

Karthik's father, Yogesh, called him into the living room of their Chennai flat. "Look, the city water supply is poisoned! Everyone in my walking group sent it."
Karthik read it. No name, no date, just capital letters. He searched the Chennai water board website. There was a normal notice about a pipeline repair, nothing about poison. He checked two newspapers. Nothing.
"Appa, how often have you heard of a whole city's water being poisoned?"
"Never. But all twenty people sent it."
"And they all got it from each other. The water board says it's just a pipe repair." Karthik showed him the notice. "I'm not forwarding it. Can you tell your group what the notice says?"
Yogesh read it twice, then slowly typed a message to his walking group.

What did the Chennai water board website say?
There was a normal notice about a pipeline repair, nothing about poison.
What was Yogesh feeling when he called Karthik in?
Yogesh felt alarmed and worried, trusting the message because twenty people in his walking group sent it.
What steps did Karthik take to stop the chain?
He checked the water board website and two newspapers, asked how often such a thing happens, and chose not to forward it.
How might the walking group react to Yogesh's message?
They might feel relieved to learn it was just a pipe repair, and maybe a bit sheepish for spreading the scare.

Read this:

I was third in the line at the bakery counter when I saw it. A man walked up and stood at the front, right beside the register. A woman in a green scarf, Gargi, turned to him with a smile and said, “Sorry to jump in, but the queue begins over by the door.”
He frowned. “I’m only buying one thing.”
“Of course,” she said, still pleasant. “Most of us are, though. It’s just past the door.”
For a second I thought he would snap. Instead he shrugged, muttered something, and walked to the end. Gargi turned back to the counter and did not look smug. I’m Sharmila, and I’m not sure whether she was nervous, but her voice never rose.

What did Gargi say to the man at the front?
Gargi said, “Sorry to jump in, but the queue begins over by the door.”
What might Gargi have been feeling as she spoke to the man?
Gargi may have felt a little nervous but determined to be fair, though Sharmila cannot know for sure; the passage only shows a pleasant, steady voice that never rose.
What helped Gargi's request work, according to what Sharmila saw?
Gargi smiled, stayed pleasant and repeated the point with no heat. She also did not gloat once the man had walked to the end.
How might the man have experienced being sent to the end of the queue?
He may have felt embarrassed or defensive at being pointed out, which fits his frown and excuse, but the pleasant tone let him shrug and walk to the end without a scene.

Read this:

After the breakup last year, I became an expert. I read about attachment styles, love languages, the psychology of rejection. When my friend Joseph asked how I was, I gave him a twenty-minute talk with hand gestures. I even made a spreadsheet of what went wrong, colour-coded. Everyone said I was handling it so maturely. I thought so too. Then, three months later, I heard her favourite song in a shop and had to leave, because my throat closed. I sat on a bench and cried for the first time. That's when I understood: the analysis was true, but it was also a wall. I'm Farhan, and I still like understanding things. I just let myself feel them now too.

How was Farhan's spreadsheet organised?
Colour-coded, listing what went wrong.
What did Farhan feel in the shop?
Farhan's throat closed; the grief finally broke through, and Farhan sat on a bench and cried for the first time.
What did Farhan learn?
That analysis can be true and still be a wall against feeling; now Farhan lets the feelings in as well.
How might Joseph have experienced the twenty-minute talk?
Probably impressed but also uneasy, sensing Farhan was explaining rather than feeling.

Please write the sentence on the board.
Why: "Sentence" ends in "-ence".

Read this:

In an office in Dublin, Clara, twenty-five, watched the online booking system for the city's swimming pools crash at seven in the morning, just as hundreds of people tried to book. Her manager stood behind her. Two more people joined the call. Her chest tightened, and the error messages on the screen blurred into one grey block. She started typing three fixes at once. Her colleague Esther put a hand on her desk. "Clara. One at a time. What's the first error in the log?" Clara scrolled up, breathing slowly. The first error pointed to a full disk. She cleared the old files. The system came back. Only later did she realise how close she'd come to making it worse.

What time did the booking system crash?
At seven in the morning.
How did Clara feel as the manager stood behind her?
She felt panicked, her chest tightening and the error messages blurring, which pushed her toward three fixes at once.
What did Esther's question do for Clara?
It slowed her down to one step, reading the first error in the log, which pointed straight to the full disk.
How might Clara's manager have felt watching the crisis?
The manager was likely tense and worried, and relieved when the system came back after one clear fix.

Read this:

The final meeting of the six-month project was supposed to be a relaxed hour. Instead, the office power went out, the client moved the handover to that same evening, and Uday had twenty minutes in a dim conference room with a team that looked exhausted. He could have read out the remaining tasks and sent everyone back to their desks. He didn't. He spent five minutes on logistics, clearly: who sends what to the client, and by when. Then he used the rest to go round the table. "Farhan, the night you rebuilt the database, you saved the whole thing." "Meena, your calls kept the client on our side." Each person got one specific line. He ended with, "Tomorrow, we sleep. Friday, lunch is on me." Farhan walked out tired but grinning. Months later, that dim room was what people talked about.

How long did Uday have for the final meeting?
He had twenty minutes in a dim conference room.
Why did Uday choose to spend most of the twenty minutes on thanks rather than tasks?
Uday cared about his tired team and was determined the project would end on a warm note, knowing the finish shapes how people remember six months.
What made Uday's ending work even under pressure?
He kept logistics short and clear, gave each person one specific line of thanks, and closed with a simple plan for rest and lunch.
How did Farhan leave the meeting feeling?
Farhan left tired but grinning, recognised for rebuilding the database.

Read this:

I've shared a flat with Elizabeth in Leeds for two years, and there's a small ritual I've watched without ever quite asking about. Every night she brushes her teeth with the door open, then sets the brush down and immediately leans into the doorframe, one arm up, then the other. Calves against the bath edge next. Maybe two minutes. The first few weeks I assumed it was a phase. It wasn't. Last Saturday we came back from a friend's birthday dinner near midnight, both yawning. I went straight to bed. Through the wall I heard the tap run, the brush clink in the glass, then the soft creak of the doorframe. I don't know if she enjoys it or just does it. When I asked once, she only said, "I don't think about it, Darshan, it just comes after the brushing." I've started trying the same with my morning water glass.

What does Elizabeth lean into after setting her brush down?
She leans into the doorframe, one arm up, then the other.
What does Darshan seem to feel about Elizabeth's ritual after the late dinner?
Darshan seems quietly impressed and curious, not sure whether Elizabeth enjoys it, but struck that it happened even when they were both tired.
What could Darshan do to make the morning water glass habit stick?
Darshan could decide exactly what follows the water glass, for example one stretch at the sink, every single morning, the way Elizabeth's stretch follows brushing.
How does Elizabeth seem to experience the stretch herself?
From what she says, it feels automatic and effortless to her; she doesn't have to think about it because brushing reminds her.

In the student centre in Nairobi, Wanjiru held the gym leaflet out to Valentina, her exchange-student roommate. 'Look. Basic is gym only, 2,500 shillings a month. Standard is gym plus one class a week, 5,800. Premium is gym, unlimited classes and the pool, 6,000.' 'So?' 'So Standard is ridiculous. Two hundred more gets everything. Premium is obviously the smart one.' She signed up at the desk before Valentina could answer, grinning at her own good sense. Three weeks later, Valentina found her on the treadmill at seven in the morning, as always. 'Been to the pool yet?' Wanjiru laughed. 'I haven't swum since primary school.' 'Classes?' 'I hate classes.' Valentina raised an eyebrow. Wanjiru slowed the belt and went quiet. 'Nobody ever buys Standard, do they? It was only there to make Premium look good.'

What does the Premium plan include?
Gym, unlimited classes and the pool, for 6,000 shillings a month.
How did Wanjiru feel while signing up for Premium?
Wanjiru felt pleased and proud, grinning at her own good sense because Standard made Premium look like obvious value.
What could Wanjiru have asked before signing up?
Wanjiru could have asked which parts she would really use, like the treadmill before lectures, instead of which plan looked like the best deal.
How might Valentina have seen the choice differently from the start?
Valentina was not caught up in the gap between Standard and Premium, so she could notice that Wanjiru never swims or goes to classes.

Pema's father, Hemant, refused the walking frame and said his tablets tasted bad, so he sometimes skipped them. Pema, who lived in another city for work, felt frustrated and worried. On the phone she said, "Would you rather use the frame or the stick? It's your choice," and rang his doctor's office with him to ask about the taste. She felt guilty for living far away, so she called every evening at eight, arranged a home nurse for two mornings a week and travelled home one weekend a month. She and her brother Hrithik made a list: he took the Tuesday clinic visits, she paid the nurse and handled the forms, and her husband agreed to cover her chores at home while she was away. Hemant's dignity mattered to her; she knocked before going in and let him pick his own shirt. When she helped him with his bath, she remembered how harshly he had spoken about her exam results as a child, and old hurt stirred beside the care. She said calmly, "I have to leave at six, and I'll see you on Sunday," and later talked about the past with a counsellor.

What did Hemant refuse to use?
Hemant refused the walking frame.
How did Pema's approach to her father's refusals differ from how she dealt with her guilt about living far away?

For his refusals she offered choices and involved his doctor instead of arguing, while for her guilt she turned it into action with evening calls, a home nurse, monthly visits and a task list shared with Hrithik.
What was Pema feeling when she helped her father with his bath and remembered his harsh words?
She felt old hurt and resentment stirring alongside her care.
How could Pema keep caring for Hemant while holding her boundaries?
She could keep giving care within limits like her leaving time and keep talking with the counsellor about the past.

Read this:

Santosh, let me, Harsha, tell you how I got through my exam year. Before I started, I drew the day on a sheet: 6 to 9 study, tea, 10 to 1 second block, lunch, a nap, 3 to 6 third block, then a walk, then dinner, and lights out at 10:30. Sunday evening was for one review of the week. Simple. The trouble came in week three. One morning I woke up with no wish to open a book. I thought, what is the point? My mother did not say a word. She left tea on the desk at six. I looked at the sheet and sat down. Not because I felt like it, but because the sheet said so. Half an hour later the wish came back.

What time was lights out on Harsha's schedule?
Lights out was at 10:30.
What was Harsha feeling on the morning of week three?
Harsha felt flat and unmotivated, wondering what the point was and having no wish to open a book.
What choice inside the story turned that morning around, and why?
Harsha sat down because the sheet said so, not because Harsha felt like it, and starting anyway brought the wish back after half an hour.
How might Harsha's mother have seen that morning?
Harsha's mother said nothing and left tea on the desk at six, so she seems to have trusted the routine and offered quiet support instead of pressure.
