"You're eating with your phone again," Pooja said, sitting across from Divyansh in the college canteen.
"I'm replying to the project group."
"And watching a video. And reading the menu. You haven't tasted one bite."
Divyansh looked down at his rajma rice. "It tastes like rajma."
"Try something. Phone face down. Just eat. For ten minutes."
"That's so boring."
"That's the point. Your brain's been switching every five seconds since morning."
He sighed and flipped the phone over. The first minute, his hand kept twitching toward it. Then he noticed the rice was a bit too salty. The canteen was loud. His shoulders were up near his ears; he let them drop.
"Okay," he said after a while. "This is weird. I feel… slower. In a good way."
"Do it tomorrow too."
"Don't push it."

What was Divyansh eating?
Rajma rice.
How did Divyansh feel after ten minutes without the phone?
Divyansh felt slower and calmer, in a good way, noticing his tense shoulders and letting them drop.
How could Divyansh build on this experiment?
He could keep one phone-free meal a day and notice what he sees, tastes and feels, as simple attention practice.
What is it like for Pooja to watch a friend multitask through every meal?
Pooja seems concerned and a little amused, caring enough to push him to try something new.
Our cook "cut corners" on the sweets. Is that a problem?

It can be. "Cut corners" means to do something in the cheapest or easiest way, often by skipping steps, so the quality suffers.
Example: The builders cut corners and used thin walls, so the room leaks.
My friend plays guitar better than me and it makes me want to quit.
I understand, but comparing yourself with a friend who started earlier isn't fair to you. You can learn from them.
But I practise a lot.
Then you're doing the right thing. Progress isn't always visible day to day, but over months you'll see it. Record yourself now and listen again in a month.
That's a good idea. I never thought of it.
It really helps, since you can see how far you've come.

Read this:

When Kavya asked me for "a private pic, just for me" last spring, I stared at my phone for an hour. I'm Nitin. I liked her a lot, the kind of liking where you keep checking who's online. I didn't want to lose her, but I also knew I wasn't sending that. My friend Vijay said, "Don't write a long sorry essay. Just say it." So the next day in the canteen I said, "I like you. I'm not ready to share pictures like that, and I don't want to meet alone on the terrace." My voice shook on the first word, then settled. She blinked and said, "Okay. That's fair." We still sit together at lunch. Looking back, the short version worked because there was nothing in it to argue with, and nothing I had to take back.

Where did Nitin say the words to Kavya?
Nitin said them in the canteen.
What was Nitin feeling while staring at the phone for an hour?
Nitin felt torn, liking Kavya a lot and afraid of losing her, yet sure about not sending the picture.
What else could Nitin do if Kavya had kept pushing?
Nitin could repeat the limit once, end the conversation, and talk to a trusted adult, since pushing after a clear no is a warning sign.
How does Kavya respond to Nitin's words?
Kavya seems surprised at first and blinks, but calls the limit fair and keeps sitting with Nitin at lunch.

metadata.subtype: Approach: stating a boundary clearly and calmly [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Kishore, the cultural secretary's assistant, so I saw all of it. Payal had announced the inter-college music night for 14 March on every group and on the college page. Then, ten days before, the auditorium cancelled; the hall was needed for exams. We had options. The open-air theatre was free on the 21st, and the principal was happy to help. At the meeting, Payal cut us off. "We said the 14th. Everyone knows the 14th. We're not changing." She booked a small seminar hall that held eighty. Two hundred people came. Half stood in the corridor, the sound was terrible, and two bands left. Payal smiled for photos, but afterwards I saw her sitting alone on the steps.

How many people did the seminar hall hold?
Eighty, though two hundred people came.
What might Payal have been feeling on the steps afterwards?
She probably felt ashamed and upset, knowing the evening went badly because she refused to move the date.
What other approach could Payal have taken, and why?
Moving to the open-air theatre on the 21st and announcing the change honestly, because the facts had changed and people accept a clear reason.
How did the bands experience the night?
The bands faced a cramped hall and terrible sound; two were frustrated enough to leave.

metadata.subtype: Approach: sticks with a plan out of pride even after the facts change [Pitfall]

messages.content: How many people came to the first Republic Day parade, exactly?
I'm not sure of an exact figure and don't want to invent one. A history book or an archive site can give a sourced number.

Read this:

Right at the centre of the living room, Tejas squeezed both eyes shut, pressed both hands over them and stood very still. Jasleen, Tejas's older cousin, finished counting and turned round. "Found you!" Jasleen laughed. Tejas uncovered and looked stunned. "But I could not see you!" The round was over almost before it began, and Tejas's lip trembled.

Where did Tejas stand while covering both eyes?
Tejas stood at the centre of the living room.
What was Tejas feeling when Jasleen said "Found you!"?
Tejas was stunned and upset, because Tejas believed that not seeing meant not being seen, which is why the lip trembled.
What alternative could Tejas try next round, and why?
Tejas could run behind the sofa or a curtain while Jasleen counts, because hiding needs a place where the seeker cannot see.
How does Jasleen see Tejas standing with hands over the eyes?
Jasleen sees the child in plain view and laughs at the easy find, likely not realising how upset Tejas will be.

Read this:

"Farida, you've been quiet all week. What's wrong?"
"Nothing, Dhruv."
"It's the comment, isn't it? On your dance video."
"'Looks like a fish trying to walk.' Someone wrote that."
"One person. How many comments were there?"
"About sixty."
"And how many were nice?"
"...Most of them. But they don't count."
"Why not?"
"Because they're just being polite."
"Ammi said you were amazing. Your coach said your spins were the cleanest in the group."
"She has to say that."
"So the one stranger is telling the truth, and all sixty people who liked it are lying?"
"When you say it like that..."
"I'm saying it like that because you've played that one comment in your head for five days."
"Six."

How many comments were on Farida's dance video?
About sixty.
Why does Farida brush off the nice comments?
Farida feels hurt and insecure, so the one mocking comment feels true while the warm praise feels like mere politeness.
How does Dhruv help Farida, and what could Farida try next?
Dhruv asks Farida to count the kind comments against the one mean one; Farida could reread the kind ones as seriously as the mean one.
How might the coach see Farida's dancing?
The coach sees Farida's spins as the cleanest in the group, a real strength Farida is ignoring.

Read this:

Usha was alone in her Chandigarh flat, marking her students' notebooks, when an unknown number called. A man said he was a police inspector. "Your brother Baljeet hit a man with his car. He is in custody. If you pay the settlement within one hour, we close the case quietly. Tell your parents and it becomes an FIR. Stay on the line."
In the background she heard someone sobbing, "Didi, please." It sounded almost like Baljeet.
Usha stood up so fast the notebooks slid to the floor. The inspector read out an account number. "One hour, madam. Don't disconnect." Her thumb hovered over the banking app. She thought of calling Baljeet directly, but the man said, "If you cut this call, we can't help him."
She stayed on the line. Her heart was so loud she could barely hear him.

What was Usha doing when the call came?
Marking her students' notebooks.
What was Usha feeling when she heard the sobbing?
She felt terrified and desperate to protect her brother, which made slow, careful thinking almost impossible.
What single step would break this pressure?
Hanging up and calling Baljeet directly, then a parent or the police on an official number; a real officer would not forbid that.
What would change if Usha had called Baljeet first?
She would likely have found him safe, and the one-hour threat would have fallen apart.

Read this:

Daycare note, Monday, from the room carer.
Ankita cried when a new helper tried to pick her up this morning. She turned her face away and pushed with both hands.
Her papa, Uday, had left a recording of the lullaby he sings at home. I played it. Ankita stopped crying and listened, thumb in mouth.
Later she crawled to the new helper on her own and touched her sari.

What did Uday leave for Ankita?
He left a recording of the lullaby he sings at home.
Why did Ankita stop crying when the lullaby played?
She felt calmer and safer, because the familiar song from home felt comforting in a new place.
How could the daycare help Ankita get used to the new helper?
They could let the helper sit near her often, playing the familiar lullaby, so the new face slowly becomes familiar too.
How might the new helper feel when Ankita touched her sari?
The helper probably felt happy and relieved that Ankita was starting to trust her.
My uncle booked seats in the gallery at the theatre. Is that where they hang paintings?

In a theatre, the gallery is the highest level of seats, usually the cheapest ones. It is a noun. The other common meaning is a room or building where art is shown.
Example: From the gallery, the dancers looked tiny but the music was clear.
Mum or Mom? My cousin in the US writes it differently.

"Mum" is British, and "Mom" is American. Indian English uses "mom", "mum", and "mummy", depending on the family.
Example: Mum picked me up from school.
The police report said the child was identified by his school badge. What does identified mean?

Identified means that someone recognised who the person was or named him. It is the past form of the verb identify.
Example: The lost child was identified by the name on his school badge and taken back to his class.

How can I choose a good book to read? One more thing: check my English: "I buyed new shoes yesterday." Oh, and "resident" - what does that mean? And what was in the news this morning? Plus, why do runners stretch their legs before a race?

1. Read the first page and the back cover, and see whether you want to keep going. Ask a librarian or friend for books like the ones you enjoyed.
2. Corrected: I bought new shoes yesterday. Why: "buy" is irregular, and its past tense is "bought".
3. Resident means a person who lives in a place. It is a noun.
4. I don't know that. I can't see today's news. Read a newspaper or visit a news website.
5. Stretching is a warm-up. Because easy movement raises blood flow to the muscles, which helps them feel ready to move.

Read this:

Wednesday night
Searched my own name for the first time before sending the internship application. Big mistake. Or big good mistake? Result three: my old art account from Class 11, with a post calling a well-known design school "overrated and full of rich kids". Result five: a photo Anjali tagged me in at her birthday, me mid-sneeze, eyes shut 😅
The sneeze I can live with. The rant I can't. I don't even believe that anymore.
Anjali came over with chips and we went through everything. Deleted the rant, removed the tag (after asking; she laughed), and turned my art account into a proper portfolio: my best twelve drawings, dated, with a line on each about what I was trying.
Strange, looking at my past self the way a stranger would. Tomorrow I send the application. Nervous, but what they'll find now is actually me.
— Aadhya

What did Aadhya's old post call the design school?
Overrated and full of rich kids.
What was Aadhya feeling on finding the old rant?
Aadhya felt embarrassed and uneasy, because the rant no longer matches what Aadhya believes.
How did turning the art account into a portfolio help?
It replaced a random old footprint with twelve dated drawings and notes, showing growth to anyone who searches.
How might Anjali have felt about removing the tag?
Anjali laughed about it, so she seemed relaxed and happy to help, and being asked first probably felt respectful.

Read this:

Neelam, you asked about the march for your podcast, so here it is. I'm Pallavi, and last month our college held a silent walk that turned into singing. It was for the students who died in the hostel fire. We walked with candles, and then someone at the front started a song, slow and low, the same rhythm we sing at Durga Puja, clap and step. At the puja that rhythm makes people dance and smile. That night it made my throat ache. I noticed a first-year boy clapping loudly and grinning, like he thought it was a party. A girl beside him gently touched his arm and pointed at the photos. He stopped, and his face went red. He wasn't being cruel; he just knew that rhythm as joy. After that he walked quietly, holding his candle. The same beat, and a completely different meaning.

What was the walk for?
For the students who died in the hostel fire.
How did Pallavi feel when the familiar rhythm started at the march?
Pallavi felt deep grief, with an aching throat, even though at the puja the same rhythm brings joy.
What small step helped the first-year boy understand the moment?
The girl beside him gently touched his arm and pointed at the photos, so he saw the context without being shamed.
What was it like for the first-year boy when he realised?
He felt embarrassed, his face going red, because he had only known that rhythm as joy.

metadata.subtype: Chanting, devotional singing and protest songs [Mismatch]

messages.content:
Read this:

It was Christmas week and the power kept going off. By candlelight, Jatin's cousin Zeenat teased him again. "Remember when you got lost at the Christmas fair and a clown found you?"

"No," said Jatin, five.

Two days later: "Remember the clown who found you?"

"Maybe."

By the weekend, Jatin told his mother, "I got lost at the fair and a clown with a red nose found me!"

His mother looked at Zeenat. "He was never lost."

Zeenat's smile faded. "I was only joking."

What did Zeenat keep asking Jatin?
"Remember when you got lost at the Christmas fair and a clown found you?"
How did Jatin feel about the clown story by the weekend?
He felt sure and excited about it, because hearing it again and again made it feel like a real memory.
What could Jatin's mother do now to help?
She could gently explain to Jatin that it was a made-up story and ask Zeenat to stop the joke.
How might Zeenat feel when she realises Jatin believes the story?
Zeenat probably feels surprised and a bit guilty that her joke turned into his memory.
Why should we leave home earlier than needed on the day of an exam?
Leaving early is sensible. Because buses can be late and roads can be blocked, extra time means that a delay does not make us miss the start of the exam.

Read this:

Okay, Irawati, since you're recording, I'll say it straight. My name's Pankaj, I'm twenty, and last year I was the loudest voice against the new highway bypass near our town. I called everyone who supported it idiots. In meetings I'd laugh when they spoke.

Then one evening my scooter broke down and the only open repair shop belonged to Mr Rawat, who'd signed their petition. He fixed it for free and talked while he worked. His son had died in a truck accident on the old road through the market. He wasn't stupid. He was grieving and scared.

I still oppose the route. It cuts through farmland. But now when I speak, I start by saying the old road is dangerous, because it is. People actually listen to me now, including his side.

Why did Pankaj's scooter end up at Mr Rawat's shop?
The scooter broke down one evening, and the only open repair shop belonged to Mr Rawat.
What was Pankaj feeling when Mr Rawat spoke about his son, and how can you tell?
Pankaj felt shaken and humbled; he stops calling the other side stupid and describes Mr Rawat as grieving and scared.
What changed in how Pankaj argues, and why does it work?
Pankaj now admits the real danger of the old road before arguing against the route, so the other side feels heard and listens back.
How might Mr Rawat see Pankaj after that evening?
Mr Rawat may see Pankaj as an opponent who still disagrees but respects his loss, which makes real discussion possible.
Write as Kofi: a diary page about my first long bus journey alone, 55 words, nervous at the start and happy at the end.

Dear Diary,
Today I took a long bus journey alone for the first time. I was nervous when the bus pulled away, and I held my bag tight. Then I watched green fields roll past and chatted with a kind old man next to me. By the time I arrived, I felt brave and happy.
Kofi

Read this:

"Lakshmi, how do you say hello in your language?" Sharmila asked on the first day at the Delhi office.
"Vanakkam."
"And do you eat dosa every day? Do you watch only Tamil films?"
Lakshmi laughed politely, the only Tamil person in the whole team. "No, and no."
By the second week, everyone was asking her about "South Indians" as if she were a textbook. If she made a mistake, she felt like they'd blame all Tamilians.
One evening, Sharmila caught her sighing. "Too many questions?"
"I just want to be Lakshmi. Not a whole state."
Sharmila nodded. "Sorry. Tell me about you, then. Not Tamil Nadu."
Lakshmi smiled properly for the first time. "I like trekking. And bad horror films."

How does Lakshmi say hello in her language?
"Vanakkam."
How did Lakshmi feel by the second week?
She felt tired and pressured, treated as a textbook and worried her mistakes would be blamed on all Tamilians.
What did Sharmila do that helped Lakshmi?
She apologised and asked about Lakshmi herself, not her state.
How might Sharmila have seen her first questions?
Sharmila probably thought she was being friendly and curious, not realising the pressure.

metadata.subtype: Being the only one from your group [Receiver]

messages.content: What does my friend's sister want to be when she grows up?
I don't know, as I haven't met her. Ask her about it sometime.
Write an email to a pen-friend abroad describing my school day, in about 70 words. I start at 8 am, love lunch break and my favourite subject is geography.

Subject: My school day

Dear friend,
I hope you are doing well. I wanted to tell you about my school day. It starts at 8 am. The morning classes go quickly, and I really look forward to lunch break, which I love. My favourite subject is geography. I would love to hear about your school day too, so we can compare. Please write back soon!
Best wishes
Describe a crowded local train in the morning rush hour, around 90 words.

At 8:15 am, the local train pulls in already full. Before it even stops, people leap onto the steps, gripping the poles with one hand and their bags with the other. Inside, there is no space to move. Someone's elbow is in your ribs, and someone else's tiffin bag presses against your back. A college student reads notes over a stranger's shoulder. An old man sings softly near the door. Fans whirl overhead without doing much. Yet at each station, more people somehow squeeze in, and nobody seems surprised.
Describe a lake at sunrise in exactly three lines, without any commas.

Mist lifts from the still water
The first light turns it gold
A heron stands without a sound

Read this:

Nilesh was brushing his teeth when an old memory played again: at twenty he had put his name alone on a group design, and a teammate had lost her chance at an internship. Six years on, his stomach still turned. He finally wrote her a message saying what he had done, that he was sorry, and offering to email her old professor with the truth. She replied kindly. After that, whenever the memory came back, he reminded himself that he had made it right and now shared credit openly. On Sunday he drove to see his father, Manoj, who had worked two jobs when Nilesh was small and rarely made it to school events. Nilesh saw that Manoj had been young and scared then. He said, "Thank you for working so hard. I still need you to stop asking about my salary." Manoj nodded, a little embarrassed. On the drive home Nilesh replayed how Tanuja, a former classmate, had mocked his accent at a wedding last year. His jaw clenched. He talked it over with a friend at dinner, then wrote down what he needed: to stop rehearsing replies. He deleted the draft message to Tanuja and went for a walk, feeling lighter, though no apology had come.

What did Nilesh offer to do for his old teammate?
He offered to email her old professor with the truth.
How did Nilesh's response to his own old mistake differ from what he did about Tanuja's mocking?

For his own mistake Nilesh wrote a message saying what he had done, said he was sorry and offered to email her old professor, then reminded himself he had made it right; for Tanuja's mocking, when no apology had come, he talked it over with a friend, wrote down what he needed and went for a walk feeling lighter.
What was Nilesh feeling when the old memory came back while he brushed his teeth?
He felt guilty, since his stomach still turned six years later.
What could Nilesh do next with his father?
He could keep his boundary about salary questions while thanking Manoj for the effort he made.

Read this:

"Kishore, sit. I'm not going to shout."
"That's new."
"Fair." Ujjwal pulled a chair close. "Last month I banned your late cricket evenings on the ground. Since then you've lied twice about where you were. Your mother found your kit in Faisal's car."
"Because you never listen, Papa. You just say no."
"You're right. I said no without reasons. Here's the reason: the ground has no lights and the road back is a highway. I lie awake."
Kishore looked up.
"So, choices. Weekend games, any time till dark. Or weekday games if someone's parent drives both ways. You pick."
"...Weekends. And Faisal's dad can drive sometimes."
"Deal. And tell me the score after. I actually want to know."
"You hate cricket."
"I like you."

Where did Kishore's mother find the cricket kit?
In Faisal's car.
Why did Kishore answer "That's new" when Ujjwal said he wouldn't shout?
Kishore expected another telling-off and felt guarded and a bit bitter, because past talks had only brought bans.
Which choice did Ujjwal offer, and why did it work better than the ban?
He let Kishore pick between weekend games till dark or weekday games with a parent driving, which kept the safety limit while giving Kishore a real say.
How had the ban felt from Kishore's side?
To Kishore it felt like being refused without being heard, so lying seemed easier than talking.

Read this:

Snow had closed the playground, so Class R stayed in for circle time in Leeds. Mrs Clarke passed round the talking stone. "Only the one holding it speaks." Hiroshi held it carefully and told everyone about his snowman. Abebe called out, "Mine was bigger!" and rolled onto his back, kicking. "Abebe, it's Hiroshi's turn." Abebe kicked harder. Mrs Clarke moved beside him and said quietly, "The stone comes to you next." Abebe sat up, arms folded, and waited, staring at the stone.

What did Mrs Clarke pass round at circle time?
The talking stone.
What does Abebe kicking harder after being reminded suggest?
It suggests he felt frustrated and impatient about waiting for his turn to share.
What did Mrs Clarke do that helped Abebe settle?
She moved close, spoke quietly, and told him he would have the stone next.
How might Hiroshi have felt when Abebe called out during his turn?
Hiroshi may have felt interrupted, perhaps a little hurt that his snowman story was cut off.

Read this:

Sunday night
Tried to count today how many things I don't say to whom. At work: nothing about Damini and me arguing every night about whether to move to Pune. With Damini: nothing about the credit-card balance I've been rolling over since Diwali. With Ammi: nothing about either. I've built a flat with every door locked. It means I can go to work and be "good old Tanvir", and come home and be... quiet.
Tonight Damini asked why I flinch when my phone buzzes. I almost told her. Instead I said, "Work stuff." The lie sat in my stomach all evening.
I can feel the walls creaking. One day the bank and the Pune decision will land in the same week, and I'll crack.
Tomorrow I'll tell Damini about the card. Just one door. One at a time.
Tanvir

What did Tanvir tell Damini when she asked about the flinching?
"Work stuff."
Why does keeping every door locked feel useful to Tanvir?
Tanvir dreads the painful conversations, and locking every door lets Tanvir function at work without facing them, even though the lie leaves Tanvir uneasy all evening.
What choice does Tanvir make for tomorrow, and why is it a good first step?
Telling Damini about the card, opening one door at a time before the pressures arrive together.
How might Damini feel noticing the flinch at every phone buzz?
Worried and perhaps shut out, sensing something is being hidden but not knowing what.
Which task is due first on my list today?
I can't see your list, so I'm not sure. Read through it and pick the nearest deadline.

Read this:

Thursday
Started watching one video about the exam paper leak last week. Fair enough, it WAS unfair, we all studied for nothing. Now my whole feed is angry people. Every single video. Scandals, cheats, 'they're laughing at you'. It feels like the whole country is on fire and nobody else sees it.
Posted my first proper rant on Monday. 23 likes. Normally I get like 4.
Today I posted a harsher one, called the officials 'parasites', and it got 140. People I don't even know commented 'finally someone says it'. My heart was racing all through maths.
Ankita said at lunch, 'You've changed. You're always on that stuff.' I said she's just scared of the truth. She went quiet.
I keep checking the count. I'm already thinking what to write next, something that'll hit harder.
— Francis

How many likes did the harsher post get?
It got 140 likes.
What was Francis feeling while the likes came in?
Francis felt a thrill and a rush of being noticed, with a racing heart, which pulled toward posting even harsher things.
What could Francis try at this point to break the loop?
Francis could notice that the feed is showing only angry content, take a break, unfollow or mute the rage accounts, and talk to Ankita or a trusted adult.
How might Ankita feel after being told she's scared of the truth?
Ankita may feel hurt and pushed away, when she was only worried about her friend.

Read this:

I'm Abhinav, Hemant's cousin, and I was staying with them that weekend. On Saturday night Hemant came into the living room holding his phone out as if it were hot. A message said his mother's card would stop working unless he “updated details” at a link. He'd opened the link and seen a page asking for the card number, but typed nothing.
He didn't delete it. He took screenshots of the message and the page first, then showed his parents. His father wrote down the sender's number as Hemant read it out. His mother called the bank on the number from her card and told them about the message. Then the three of them sat at the computer and filled in a complaint on the national cybercrime reporting website, attaching the screenshots.
It took about forty minutes. Hemant looked tired but steady by the end.

What did Hemant do before showing his parents?
He took screenshots of the message and the page.
How might Hemant have been feeling when he walked in holding the phone out?
He was likely alarmed and uneasy, holding the phone as if it were hot, after seeing a page ask for card details.
Why was reporting better than quietly deleting the message?
Reporting with screenshots warns the bank and helps the authorities trace the sender, which can protect other families too.
How might Hemant's mother see what her son did?
She would likely be relieved nothing was typed and grateful he told them at once, so she could alert the bank that night.

metadata.subtype: Approach: reporting to parents and the official cybercrime channel [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dhruv, you asked if telling the teacher is snitching. Let me tell you what your Minakshi dadi did when she was your age, in Class 5 in Jabalpur.
There was a girl, Radha, who some older girls kept locking in the storeroom at lunch, for fun. Everybody knew. Everybody thought, not my business, and snitching is bad.
One day I heard her banging on the door. My legs shook. I didn't open it myself; I couldn't reach the latch. I ran to our headmistress, Mrs Dubey, and said, “Ma'am, I need help. Radha is in the storeroom.” I pointed.
She came running and let Radha out. Those girls never did it again.
It wasn't snitching, beta. It was caring.

Where did the older girls lock Radha?
They locked her in the storeroom.
How did young Minakshi feel when she heard Radha banging on the door?
She felt scared, since her legs shook, but she cared enough to run for help.
What turning point in the story helped Radha?
Minakshi running to Mrs Dubey, saying "I need help" and pointing, which brought an adult who let Radha out.
How might Radha have felt when the door opened?
She was probably frightened and then deeply relieved to be let out and helped.
Nobody noticed the mistake, didn't they? Check the end of it.

Nobody noticed the mistake, did they?
Why: "Nobody" is negative, so the tag is positive (did they).
Describe a baker in two sentences and work the word "dawn" in.
A baker gets up before dawn to prepare fresh bread. By morning, the shop smells warm and sweet.

Read this:

At the temple fair in the hill town of Palampur, a man carrying sacks of rice suddenly swayed and dropped beside the jalebi stall. A circle of people formed. Everyone stared. Someone said, “Call someone.” Nobody did.
Amandeep, visiting with her cousins, pushed to the front. She pointed at a boy in a blue shirt. “You. Call the ambulance, 108. Now.” She turned to a woman in a maroon shawl. “Dolma ji, please bring water from your stall.” She pointed at two men. “You two, move the crowd back, give him air.”
The boy was already dialling. Dolma came running with a steel jug. The men waved people back.
The ambulance came up the winding road twenty minutes later. The man was sitting up by then, sipping water.

Where did the man drop?
He dropped beside the jalebi stall.
What was Amandeep feeling as she pushed to the front?
She seemed alarmed but determined, frustrated that everyone stared and said "call someone" without doing it.
What would you advise others to learn from Amandeep's approach?
In an emergency, point at a specific person and give a specific task, because "call someone" leaves everyone waiting.
How might the boy in the blue shirt have felt when Amandeep pointed at him?
He was probably startled but relieved to have a clear job, and started dialling at once.

Read this:

In the Bengaluru kindergarten, Rukmini, the teacher, asked, "Who knows what colour a banana is?" Reena, five, jumped up and shouted, "Yellow! Yellow!" before anyone else could speak. Rukmini smiled. "Reena, can you show me your hand?" Reena sat down and put her hand up, wiggling her fingers. Rukmini waited a moment, then said, "Yes, Reena?" "Yellow," Reena said, very proudly.

What did Rukmini ask about?
What colour a banana is.
What does Reena wiggling her fingers suggest?
She was bursting with eagerness to answer and found waiting hard.
Which choice by Rukmini worked, and why?
Asking Reena to show her hand, calmly, taught her the class habit without shaming her.
How might the other children feel when Reena waits to be called?
They might feel they also get a chance, since answers aren't shouted over them.

Why does Siddharth call Varun a fake, and what does he realise on the bus?

The sports club changing room was loud after the inter-house match, and Siddharth was the loudest. 'Varun's a fake,' he said, yanking off his shoes. 'Swears he'll be here at eight, doesn't show, and we lose by four points. Total loser.' Somebody pointed out that Varun had helped him with physics all last month. 'That's different. People show you who they are.' Siddharth threw his jersey into the bag. When his phone buzzed with Varun's name, he turned it face down. Three missed calls. He didn't play the voice note. On the bus home, he told his mother the same thing: fake, loser, done. She asked why Varun hadn't come. Siddharth opened his mouth and realised he had no idea.
He says Varun promised to be there at eight, did not show up and the team lost. On the bus he realises he has no idea why Varun was absent, even though Varun had helped him with physics.

Read this:

Javier, twenty-one, read the results on the board outside the training centre in Valencia twice before it sank in: failed again, the second time, by four points. He walked out and sat on the curb in the heat. His friend Chen, who had passed, sat down beside him without saying anything about his own result. 'I'm done,' Javier said. 'My uncle was right. I should just keep stacking boxes at the warehouse.' Chen waited. After a while Javier pulled the marked paper from his bag and looked at it properly. Almost all his mistakes were in the circuit calculations, not the practical. 'It's always the same section,' he muttered. That evening he taped the paper above his bed and asked Chen for his old calculation notes. The next exam was in March. He wrote the date on his hand.

By how many points did Javier fail?
Four points.
Why did Javier say 'I'm done' at first?
He felt crushed and discouraged after failing twice and was echoing his uncle's doubts.
What turned Javier's setback into a plan?
Looking closely at the marked paper showed his mistakes were in one section, which gave him a clear target to study.
Why might Chen have said nothing about his own result?
He sensed Javier's pain and chose to support him quietly rather than highlight his own pass.

Read this:

“Sit, child, sit. When my father died I was twenty-six, and the three of us grieved so differently that we nearly broke as a family. My brother Parveen took charge of every form, every phone call and every chair for the guests. My sister Tashi talked about our father all night, telling the same stories again and again. I said almost nothing and sat by the window. Tashi said, ‘Dolma doesn't even miss him.’ Parveen said, ‘Tashi is only making noise.’ Each thought the others were doing it wrong. On the eleventh night Parveen stopped in the doorway with a file in his hand and said, ‘I don't know how to sit.’ We all laughed and cried at once. That night we finally sat together.”

How old was Dolma when the father died?
Dolma was twenty-six when the father died.
What might Parveen have meant when Parveen said, “I don't know how to sit”?
Parveen probably felt that tasks were the only way to cope with the loss, and being still was frightening, so he admitted it finally.
What could the three have done sooner to lessen the hurt?
They could have asked each other how each was coping, and understood that quiet, talking and busy work were all ways of grieving.
How might Tashi have felt when Tashi said, “Dolma doesn't even miss him”?
Tashi may have felt lonely in the storytelling and frustrated that others were not joining in, and so read Dolma's silence as not caring.

Read this:

At the Midsummer day camp outside Uppsala, the leaders split the children into pairs for a nature quiz. Ulla ran straight to Clara, the tallest girl there, who laughed at everything and had yellow flowers woven into her braid. "She'll know all the answers," Ulla thought. When Clara said the pine cone came from a birch tree, Ulla wrote it down without a pause. When Clara told the leader she had found the hidden clue by herself, Ulla nodded along, though she had seen Jonas point it out first. Their pair came last out of eight. Ulla stared at the score sheet, puzzled, the midnight-sun light still bright outside. Clara was so friendly and so sure. How could she be wrong about nearly everything?

What did Clara say the pine cone came from?
Clara said the pine cone came from a birch tree.
Why did Ulla believe everything Clara said?
Clara was tall, cheerful and friendly, so Ulla felt happy and admiring around her and assumed she must be clever and honest too 😊
What could Ulla try next time?
She could check each answer on its own, like looking closely at the cone or remembering who really found the clue, instead of trusting someone because they are friendly.
How might Jonas feel when Clara claims the clue?
Jonas may feel overlooked and a bit annoyed, since Jonas pointed out the clue first and got no credit.

Read this:

Nilesh's goldfish, Bubbles, was floating at the top of the bowl in their Mumbai flat. Nilesh stared, then burst into tears. Dadi called from the kitchen, "Don't cry, we'll buy another one from the market." Nilesh cried harder. His papa, Kiran, came and sat on the floor. He wrapped Nilesh in a hug. "It is okay to be sad. We loved Bubbles very much." "He was my fish," Nilesh sobbed. "Yes. He was yours. Nobody can be Bubbles again." Nilesh cried until his shirt was wet. Then he asked, "Can we bury him in the plant pot?" Kiran nodded.

What did Dadi suggest when Nilesh cried?
She said they would buy another one from the market.
How did Nilesh feel when Kiran said "Nobody can be Bubbles again"?
He felt understood in his sadness, as if his love for Bubbles was taken seriously.
What did Kiran do instead of offering a new fish?
He hugged Nilesh, said it was okay to be sad and agreed to bury Bubbles in the plant pot.
Why might Dadi react differently from Kiran?
Dadi may want to stop Nilesh's pain quickly, so she offers a replacement instead of letting him grieve.
Why does bread go stale faster in the fridge than on the counter?
The fridge's cool temperature makes the starch in bread harden more quickly. This is why bread often feels dry and firm there, even though cold slows mould.
Then where should I store it?
In a closed bag or box at room temperature for a day or two. If you will not use it soon, you can freeze slices and warm them when needed.
The science teacher wants us to write observations. What are those?

Observations are things you notice by watching something carefully, often written down. It is a noun, the plural of observation.
Example: Our observations of the plant showed that it grew faster near the window.
Every students must bring ID card. Please correct.
The correct sentence is: "Every student must bring an ID card." Why: "every" takes a singular noun; "an" goes before "ID".
To "All students" sahi hoga?
Yes. "All students must bring an ID card" is correct, because "all" goes with a plural noun.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, Class 3, Monday.
During group work, Sachin, eight, told Lavanya he didn't want to sit next to her and used a word about her family's caste. He said it flatly, the way children repeat something heard at home. Lavanya went red and moved her chair away.
I did not shout. I knelt beside Sachin and asked, "Do you know what that word means?" He shook his head. I said, "It's a word some people use to say a family is lower. That isn't true. It hurt Lavanya. Look at her face."
He looked. His eyes filled. "I heard it at home," he whispered. I said, "Then you can be the one who stops it here."
He said sorry to Lavanya on his own. I sat with Lavanya after, and called both families that afternoon.

How old is Sachin?
Sachin is eight.
What does Sachin's eyes filling suggest he felt?
It suggests he felt ashamed and sorry once he saw the hurt on Lavanya's face and understood what the word meant.
Why was the teacher's calm correction better than shouting?
It named the hurt, explained the word was untrue, and let Sachin see Lavanya's face, so he understood the weight of it instead of just feeling scared.
How might Lavanya feel after the teacher sat with her?
Lavanya was hurt and embarrassed, but being supported and hearing Sachin's apology may help her feel valued.

Imran: final project due 9 am. starting now 😎
Parveen: it's 11:48 pm Imran
Imran: exactly. peak performance hours
Imran: I'm a pressure player, u know this
Parveen: you said that before the econ paper
Imran: and I passed!
Parveen: with a 52. you told me you knew it way better than that
Imran: ...
Imran: ok the panic IS kind of fun. my brain wakes up
Imran: 3 hours of pure focus, watch me
Parveen: I believe you. but you were also sick for a week after that last all-nighter
Imran: coincidence
Parveen: maybe. want to try starting the next one on Monday? I'll send you a "start" text
Imran: fine. but I'm finishing this one tonight
Parveen: of course you are. drink water and sleep a bit after

What mark did Imran get on the econ paper?
Imran got a 52.
What does 'the panic IS kind of fun' show about how Imran feels?
Imran genuinely enjoys the rush because the panic wakes the brain up, which makes the last-night habit feel like a strength rather than a risk.
What choice does Parveen offer, and why might it help?
A 'start' text on Monday for the next project; it gives Imran an early beginning without a lecture, so the work doesn't depend on one frantic night.
How might Parveen feel watching this pattern repeat?
Parveen seems caring but uneasy, remembering the 52 and the week of being sick, and chooses a light touch and a practical offer over an argument at midnight.

Read this:

Kavitha had already bought the frame for the certificate. The college's startup grant would be announced on Friday, and she was certain her project, a repair-and-resell shop for old school uniforms in Chennai, would win. She'd told her parents at dinner. She'd borrowed three thousand from her cousin to print banners with "Winner" left blank to fill in later. When her friend Ayesha said, "Maybe keep a plan B, just in case?" Kavitha said, "Why plan to lose?" On Friday, in the packed seminar hall, the names were read out. Hers wasn't one of them. She sat through the claps with a fixed smile. Outside by the bike stand she finally cried. "It's not just losing," she told Ayesha. "I made everyone believe it too. And I have no idea what to do on Monday." Ayesha put an arm around her shoulders and waited.

What had Kavitha already bought before the announcement?
The frame for the certificate.
Why is losing so painful for Kavitha?
She had been so sure that she told her parents, borrowed money and printed banners, leaving no space for doubt. Now she faces the loss plus the embarrassment of having no plan.
When Ayesha suggested a plan B, what choice could Kavitha have made instead?
She could have said, "Good idea," and quickly listed what she would do if she didn't win, such as other grants or starting smaller, without giving up hope.
How might Ayesha feel standing with Kavitha by the bike stand?
Ayesha probably feels sad for Kavitha and chooses to comfort her quietly instead of reminding her of the plan B conversation.
Why do mangoes ripen sooner when wrapped in a paper bag?
The bag keeps the ripening gas around the fruit. Because the fruit gives off a gas that helps ripening and the bag holds it close, the mangoes get more of it and soften faster.

Read this:

The PG in Koramangala had old cupboards, so on his first weekend Lalit bought a second padlock, a small door alarm, and a steel box for his laptop charger and passport. He tested the alarm four times. Santosh, his roommate from Nashik, watched from the top bunk.
"Chalo, dosa," Santosh said, lifting his helmet off the hook. Lalit climbed on pillion without one. "It's only two signals away."
On the flyover a bus cut across and Santosh braked hard. Lalit grabbed the seat, heart thudding. At the dosa place he laughed it off, then opened the alarm app to make sure nothing in the room had moved.
Santosh looked at him over the chutney. "Your cupboard is safer than your head, yaar."

What did Lalit buy on his first weekend at the PG?
Lalit bought a second padlock, a small door alarm, and a steel box for his laptop charger and passport.
Why do you think Lalit checked the alarm app right after the near miss?
Locking the cupboard down completely gave him a feeling of total control, so that small fear kept pulling at him while the bigger road danger got laughed off.
What small change would protect Lalit most?
Getting a helmet of his own and wearing it on every ride, even for two signals; one padlock is plenty for the cupboard.
How does Santosh see Lalit's priorities?
Santosh finds them upside down, joking that the cupboard is safer than Lalit's head, and was probably shaken too after braking hard.
How would you explain the word obstinate to a child?

Obstinate means refusing to change your mind, even when others give good reasons. It is an adjective, close to "stubborn".
Example: My little cousin was obstinate and would not wear his raincoat.

Read this:

I'm Sabina, and I sit next to Bhupen in Class 11. Last week our economics teacher asked us to make a chart from any class data. Bhupen chose tuition and marks.
He surveyed all forty of us. His chart showed that the students who go to tuition scored, on average, much higher in the half-yearly. He titled the poster "Tuition Makes You Score" in big green letters and seemed really pleased.
I looked at the list. Most of the tuition kids were also the ones who sit in the front row, finish homework early and have parents who check their diaries. Two of them told me they had always topped.
I don't know what Bhupen was thinking exactly. When Ma'am asked, "What else do these students have in common?", he went quiet and started tapping his pen on the poster.

What title did Bhupen give his poster?
"Tuition Makes You Score", in big green letters.
What does Bhupen's pleased look over the poster suggest about what he believes?
It suggests he feels he has found a clear cause: tuition goes with higher marks, so tuition must produce them.
How could the teacher's question help Bhupen improve his chart?
"What else do these students have in common?" invites Bhupen to check other things, like homework habits and parents' support, before claiming the tuition is the cause.
How does Sabina see the same survey data differently?
Sabina notices that the tuition students also sit in front, finish homework early and have parents who check their diaries, so the higher marks may come from those things too.

Read this:

Debate coach's note, Harish, January
Sabina (16) argued this week that exams should be scrapped. In the rebuttal, she said, "Everyone I know hates exams, so they're bad." Then she stopped mid-sentence and said, "Actually, that's just my feeling. I need evidence." The room went quiet. She asked for a minute, then argued from research on stress and learning instead. I told her afterwards that catching her own emotional reasoning mid-debate was the best moment of the session. I'm adding a short bias-spotting exercise to next week's practice, and I've asked Sabina to lead the first round.

What did Sabina argue should be scrapped?
Exams.
What was Sabina feeling when she stopped mid-sentence?
She was probably unsettled and a bit embarrassed, realising her point rested on feeling, not evidence.
Why is Harish's bias-spotting exercise a good next step?
It helps the whole team practise catching emotional reasoning the way Sabina did.
How might the other debaters see Sabina's moment?
They might respect her honesty and feel encouraged to check their own reasoning.

Make this text into a two-sentence summary.

My little mistress behaved like an angel in coming to wait on me, and cheer my solitude; the confinement brought me exceedingly low. It is wearisome, to a stirring active body: but few have slighter reasons for complaint than I had. The moment Catherine left Mr. Linton's room she appeared at my bedside. Her day was divided between us; no amusement usurped a minute: she neglected her meals, her studies, and her play; and she was the fondest nurse that ever watched. She must have had a warm heart, when she loved her father so, to give so much to me. I said her days were divided between us; but the master retired early, and I generally needed nothing after six o'clock, thus the evening was her own. Poor thing! I never considered what she did with herself after tea. And though frequently, when she looked in to bid me good-night, I remarked a fresh colour in her cheeks and a pinkness over her slender fingers, instead of fancying the hue borrowed from a cold ride across the moors, I laid it to the charge of a hot fire in the library.

While the narrator is confined to bed, Catherine nurses the narrator lovingly and gives up meals, lessons and play. The narrator does not wonder what Catherine does in the evenings and blames her rosy cheeks on the hot library fire.

Read this:

The class play parts went up on the board in Oslo on Tuesday afternoon, just before the bell. Wei got the troll. Ingrid got nothing: her name was under 'stage crew', with four others. On the tram home, she pressed her mitten against the fogged window. 'Mrs Halvorsen thinks I'm no good at anything,' she told her father. 'She thinks I'm boring and I'd ruin it.' Her father looked up from his phone. 'She said that?' 'She didn't have to. I could tell by her face when she read the list.' 'What was her face doing?' Ingrid frowned. She tried to remember, and couldn't. 'It was just... a face,' she said at last, more quietly.

Which part did Wei get?
Wei got the troll.
What was Ingrid feeling on the tram, and what shows it?
She was hurt and let down, pressing her mitten to the window, and that hurt made her guess about Mrs Halvorsen's thoughts feel certain.
Why was her father's question about the teacher's face useful?
It asked for real evidence, and when Ingrid couldn't remember any, she began to see her belief was a guess.
How might Mrs Halvorsen explain the stage crew list?
She might have reasons nobody on the tram knows, like needing reliable helpers backstage, which is why a guess about her thoughts can easily be wrong.

Read this:

When my friend Anirban was taken to the police station after a bike accident last year, I was the only one with him. I'm Rehana, and I was twenty.
My first instinct was to scream at the officers. He wasn't even driving; the other biker had crashed into him. But I remembered a college session on rights.
I asked, calmly, "Sir, is he being arrested, and on what grounds?" The officer said they were recording statements. I asked, "May he call his family?" They let him.
I also called the legal aid number from my phone. A lawyer called the station and spoke to the officer on duty.
By night, Anirban had given his statement and gone home with his father.
Looking back, what saved us wasn't shouting. It was knowing what to ask, and asking politely. I still keep that number saved.

What happened to Anirban last year?
He was taken to the police station after a bike accident.
What did Rehana feel like doing at first?
Rehana felt angry and frightened, wanting to scream at the officers because Anirban wasn't driving.
What did Rehana do that was protective?
Rehana calmly asked about the grounds, asked if Anirban could call family, and contacted legal aid, rather than arguing.
How might Anirban have felt with Rehana there?
Anirban probably felt less alone and grateful that his friend stayed calm and knew what to ask.
Write a short 'Student of the Month' announcement for our school newsletter, about 70 words, for Fatima Sheikh of Class 6A.

Student of the Month: Fatima Sheikh, Class 6A
This month's award goes to Fatima, who has shown kindness and hard work in equal measure. She organised a book drive that collected over 200 books for a village school, and she helps her classmates with maths during the lunch break. Her teachers say she never stops asking questions. Congratulations, Fatima! You make our whole school proud.
What does infinite mean?

Infinite means without limits or without end. It is an adjective. People also use it to mean very great.
Example: Our maths teacher said there are infinite numbers, and Aarav tried to count them anyway.

Read this:

In a Vancouver Grade 10 class, Kwame stayed until six on Thursday finishing the group science presentation. Xin had promised the graphs and Ines the conclusion; both arrived on Friday with nothing but jokes. Kwame's jaw tightened. "We can share the rest at lunch?" Ines suggested brightly. "Sure," said Kwame. Inside, Kwame was seething. During the presentation Xin got the biggest smile from the teacher. Kwame said nothing then either, only smiled thinly, and wrote in a private notebook, "Next time I will say it early. But saying it feels bossy."

Until what time did Kwame stay on Thursday?
Kwame stayed until six on Thursday finishing the group science presentation.
What was Kwame feeling when saying "Sure" to Ines?
Kwame was seething with anger inside while sounding polite; the tight jaw shows resentment being swallowed to avoid looking bossy.
What could Kwame do at the start of the next group project?
Kwame could suggest early who does what and when, and check in midweek, so the imbalance is visible before it becomes resentment.
How might Ines have seen Friday's lunch offer?
Ines probably saw it as a friendly solution and may not have noticed how much work Kwame had done; the bright tone suggests no awareness of the anger.

Read this:

Himani: hey, can I ask how you ended up in urban planning? You never said
Shalini: long story lol
Himani: I've got time. Did you always want it?
Shalini: no, I studied accounts. Then I spent a year helping my aunt's cooperative map water pipes and got hooked
Himani: what was the first thing that hooked you?
Shalini: standing in a lane with an old man who showed me where the water used to flow before the road was built
Himani: that sounds like a real moment
Shalini: it was. most people ask about the salary 😅
Himani: I'm more curious what you'd tell the younger you
Shalini: to not be embarrassed about the detour. thanks for asking 🙂

What did Shalini study before urban planning?
Shalini studied accounts.
What was Himani feeling while asking these questions?
Himani was curious and warm, wanting to know about Shalini's path without judging it.
What kind of follow-up question worked best in this chat?
Open questions about a moment, like what first hooked Shalini, invited a story. Himani listened and did not offer advice or compare.
How might Shalini have felt about being asked instead of being asked about the salary?
Shalini probably felt seen and pleased, since most people ask about the salary and this question invited a real story about the detour. 🙂

What time does the shared cab leave?
At 5am.
How is Arohi feeling when the train is cancelled?
Arohi feels anxious and upset but quickly shifts to working it out.
Which choices show Arohi adapting well?
Finding a shared cab, calling Amma, and changing outfit plans instead of giving up.
How does Binita see the way Arohi handled it?
Binita is impressed, noting Arohi would have cried last year.

Read this:

I'm Hrithik, and I've shared a rented flat with Saurabh near the canal for two years. When the flood water finally drained on Friday, I wanted to start mopping straight away. Saurabh held up a hand. 'Wait. Ten minutes.' He walked through every room filming slowly, saying the date aloud into the phone, pointing at the mud line on the wall and the collapsed bed. Then he emailed the video and photos to our landlord before we'd even had tea. On Monday the ward office announced relief forms for flood-hit tenants. Everyone in the queue was arguing about proof. Saurabh had a clear folder: photos, the plumber's bill, the landlord's reply. The clerk stamped his form in five minutes. I don't know if he was nervous inside; he just looked tired and ready.

What did Saurabh say aloud into the phone while filming?
He said the date aloud into the phone.
What might Hrithik have felt when Saurabh said 'Wait'?
Hrithik was probably impatient, even frustrated, wanting to start mopping, though the wait later proved useful in the relief queue.
Which step in Saurabh's approach mattered most at the ward office, and why?
Recording dated proof before cleaning mattered most, because the clerk could see the damage and bills at once while others argued about proof.
How might the clerk at the ward office see Saurabh's folder?
A clear folder saves the clerk time and doubt in a crowded queue, which makes the form easy to approve.

Read this:

Sunday. Suraj's father set the tuition attendance sheet on the table: four weeks of blank boxes. Suraj had said he was going and had spent the evenings at the cyber cafe instead. "I'm very disappointed," his father said, and went out to the balcony. Suraj lay awake thinking, I'm worthless, I ruin everything.
Tuesday. He told his friend Wasim. "What you did was wrong," Wasim said, "but that doesn't make you worthless." That evening Suraj wrote a note: he apologised, promised to attend every class, and asked his father to check the sheet each week.
The following Sunday his father read the note twice. "Trust comes back slowly," he said. "But show me." Suraj nodded and packed his tuition bag.

How many weeks of blank boxes were on the attendance sheet?
There were four weeks of blank boxes.
What was Suraj thinking on Sunday night?
He was thinking he was worthless and ruined everything, because his father's disappointment felt like a verdict on him.
What did Suraj do to repair the situation?
He apologised in a note, promised to attend every class and asked his father to check the sheet each week, which separates his act from his worth.
How might Suraj's father have been feeling?
He was probably hurt and disappointed by the lie, since he went out to the balcony, yet he was still willing to rebuild trust slowly.

Read this:

Irawati, you're stuck on that riddle? Come, I'll tell you how I learned to solve these, when I was ten.
I, Vikas, a skinny boy of ten, loved riddles but hated maths. My uncle gave me this one: a man has three sons, each son has one sister. How many children?
I shouted "six!" He laughed. "Slow down. Draw it."
I drew three boys. Then one sister for each. Then I saw: the same sister. Four children.
After that I drew every puzzle. Step by step, no shouting answers. My maths got better too.
So, Irawati, get a pencil. Draw it.

What was the answer to the riddle?
Four children.
How did Vikas feel when his uncle laughed?
He likely felt embarrassed but curious, and then pleased when he saw the answer.
What was the key choice in Vikas's story?
Slowing down and drawing each step instead of shouting the first answer.
How might the uncle have felt when Vikas solved it?
The uncle likely felt pleased and proud of his nephew.

Tarun: she said it again today
Vishal: the job thing?
Tarun: ya. "i left my bank job so you could go to that school" 😔
Tarun: every time i say i want to do music

What job did Tarun's mother leave?
Tarun's mother left her bank job.
What does Tarun mean by a cage built out of love?
Tarun feels grateful for his mother's sacrifice but also trapped by it, as if her love leaves no room for his wish to do music.
Which suggestion from Vishal could help, and why?
Showing his good prelim marks first and then speaking about music could help, because it honours his mother's sacrifice with effort while still being honest.
How might Tarun's mother feel during the dinner talk?
She may feel upset or worried at first, but also respected if she sees Tarun is taking school seriously and telling her the truth. 🤍

Read this:

Gautam, you're looking at that coaching poster like it's magic. Let me tell you what happened to me at sixteen, before you beg your parents.
There was an institute near our school with a huge banner: "Average marks of our students: 96%!" Every parent in our colony was talking about it. I cried for a week because Papa said it was too far.
Then my maths teacher, Mr Rao, asked me one question: "Average of which students?" I went and asked. It turned out they only counted their top twenty students on the banner. The rest, a few hundred, weren't in the number at all.
I felt so silly. And so relieved. I studied at home with Mr Rao's old papers and did fine.
That's why your Ira Bua always asks, "Average of which ones?"

What did the institute's banner say?
"Average marks of our students: 96%!"
How did young Ira feel after finding out who was counted?
Ira felt silly for believing the banner, and also relieved not to have missed anything.
What was the turning point in Ira's story, and why did it matter?
Asking Mr Rao's question "Average of which students?" mattered, because it revealed the number left out hundreds of students.
How might Mr Rao have felt when young Ira came back with the answer?
Mr Rao was probably pleased and proud that Ira checked for herself instead of just trusting the banner.
Congratulate my daughter's football team on reaching the finals. A message for their group, about 40 words, from the assistant coach.

Well done, girls! Reaching the finals is a fantastic achievement. You passed well, defended bravely and never gave up, even when we were a goal down. Rest well this week, practise hard on Thursday, and let's play the final with the same spirit.
Replace "walked fast" with one stronger verb: The old man walked fast to the bus stop.
The old man hurried to the bus stop.

Read this:

"Mama, can I sit with you?" Nandini asked, twisting the end of her dupatta.
"Of course. What's on your mind?" Sunaina put down the peas.
"There's something I have to say. Promise not to shout?"
"I'll listen first. Then we'll think together."
"Miss wrote a note in my diary three days ago. I hid it under my mattress. I broke Rhea's glasses in the playground by accident, and I was scared you'd be so angry."
"Oh, Nandini. Thank you for telling me." Sunaina took a slow breath. "I don't love that it was hidden, but I'm glad you came. Let's read the note together. 🙂"
"You're not angry?"
"A little worried. Not angry at you for telling me."

Where did Nandini hide the teacher's note?
She hid it under her mattress.
What was Nandini worried about before she spoke up?
She was scared her mother would be so angry about Rhea's broken glasses, which is why she twisted her dupatta and asked for a promise not to shout.
How can Sunaina keep talking about this feel safe for Nandini?
She can stay calm, listen first and read the note together, as she does, so telling her feels safe. 🙂
How might Sunaina be feeling as Nandini talks?
A little worried but glad that Nandini came, since she took a slow breath and thanked her.

Read this:

Rekha, you asked on the podcast what Class 10 was like for me. Okay. I'm Sonali, and it was bad.
My parents are both doctors. Everyone assumed I'd be one too. Every test, I'd check the rank list before I checked my own answers. Rank 5 felt like failing because rank 1 existed.
One day I got a 12 out of 20 in chemistry and I couldn't stop crying in the school washroom. My friend found me and walked me to our class teacher, who called my mother right away. My mother left the hospital and came. She held my hands in the car and said, "I never needed you to be first. I needed you to be okay." I didn't know that. I'd never asked.
After that we talked properly. I still care about marks. But now I ask what I learned, not where I stand.

What mark did Sonali get in chemistry that day?
Sonali got 12 out of 20 in chemistry.
Why did rank 5 feel like failing to Sonali?
Sonali felt anxious and inadequate because Sonali was measured against rank 1 and against the parents' expected path.
What turned things around for Sonali, and what could others learn?
A friend and teacher bringing in Sonali's mother, and then an honest talk, showed Sonali the expectations were partly assumptions; others can ask their parents directly.
How might Sonali's mother have felt in the car?
Sonali's mother was probably shocked and sad that Sonali had carried so much pressure, and deeply relieved to be told.
Could I have a peace of cake? Is the word right?

Could I have a piece of cake?
Why: "piece" is a part; "peace" is calm.

At the kasba school, Harish stumbled on a word while reading aloud from the Hindi reader. In the next row Ojas curled one side of his mouth. Harish's face burned. He thinks he's better than me, he thought, and stopped reading until Master ji nodded for him to go on.
After the bell Harish swallowed and asked, “Were you laughing at me?”
Ojas blinked. “No! I'm next, and my stomach is like a tight rope. My mouth goes funny when I'm scared.”
“Oh.” Harish let out a long breath.

Where was Ojas sitting?
Ojas was sitting in the next row.
What was Harish feeling when he stopped reading, and what else might explain Ojas's look?
Hurt and embarrassed, since his face burned and he assumed Ojas thought he was better. The look turned out to be nerves, so his assumption was one possible reading, not the only one.
What did Harish do that worked better than assuming an insult?
He asked Ojas directly after the bell, and learned that Ojas was nervous about his own turn.
What was it like for Ojas to be asked?
He was probably surprised that his nervous face looked like mockery, and glad to explain that he was scared, not scornful. 🙂

Subject: weird question
Hi Nitin bhai,
Something strange happened today. Ammi asked me to fetch the pickle jar from the back storeroom, and I just stood outside the door. My hands went cold. I went back and said I couldn't find it.
That's the room where Abbu and Chacha had the big fight at Eid last year. Everyone keeps saying how awful it was, but honestly I remember almost nothing. Maybe a plate breaking? That's it.
Same with the old song that was playing that day. When it came on in the car on Sunday, I didn't say a word for the whole drive and didn't know why.
You were there. Was it really that bad? You're the only one I feel I can ask.
Hafsa

What was Hafsa asked to fetch from the storeroom?
The pickle jar.
Why did Hafsa's hands go cold outside the storeroom?
The room seems tied to the fight Hafsa can barely remember; the hurt is still there, so the body tenses even though the memory has gone.
What choice in the email could help Hafsa start to understand the feeling, and what else might help?
Asking Nitin, someone trusted who was there, is a good first step; talking it through with Ammi or a school counsellor could help too.
How might Nitin feel reading 'You're the only one I feel I can ask'?
Nitin may feel trusted but also careful, wanting to answer gently about a fight that was hard for the whole family.
Is a "jumper" the same as a "sweater"?

Yes, mostly. In British English a "jumper" is a knitted garment worn on the upper body, and Americans call it a "sweater". In American English a "jumper" can be a sleeveless dress.
Example: Wear a jumper because it is cold in Shimla.

Dear Yusuf sir,

I owe you an honest update. The short film you mentored me on is done except the colour correction, the credits and the festival form. It has been that way since the first week of August.

I told myself I was busy. The truth is I've watched it thirty times and each time I'm more scared. Once I send it, the jury will decide if it's any good. Right now I can still believe it is.

I have booked the editing room for Saturday. If I can finish the credits there, I'll submit on Sunday night. Could I send you the link before I do?

Thank you for not giving up on me,
Damini

What three things were left on Damini's film?
The colour correction, the credits and the festival form were left.
How does Damini feel each time the film is watched again?
Damini feels more scared each time, afraid of the jury deciding the film is not good.
Which step in the letter makes finishing more likely?
Booking the editing room for Saturday and naming Sunday night for submission turn a vague intention into a fixed plan.
How might Yusuf sir feel reading this letter?
Yusuf sir is likely relieved and touched by Damini's honesty, and glad to see the film before it goes out.

"Uday, stay back a minute," Sharmila ma'am said as the bell rang.

He waited by her desk, eyes on the floor.

"Forty-one in the pre-board. You've never been below seventy. What happened?"

"I don't know, ma'am. I'm just stupid, I think." His voice cracked. "My father will say I've shamed the family. My whole family's watching this year."

"Look at me." She waited until he did. "You wrote a bad paper. That's not the same as being a bad student, or a bad son. Can you tell me three things that went wrong?"

He thought. "I didn't finish the syllabus. I didn't do any timed practice. And I froze on section C."

"Good. That's three things we can fix. Not a verdict." She pulled a planner from her drawer. "Two practice papers a week, timed, and you come to me on Thursdays for section C."

Uday wiped his eyes. "Thank you, ma'am."

"And Uday? Asking me was the right thing."

What mark did Uday get in the pre-board?
Uday got forty-one in the pre-board.
What was Uday feeling when his voice cracked?
Uday felt ashamed and worthless, fearing his father would say he had shamed the family.
How did Sharmila ma'am help Uday separate the result from himself?
She said a bad paper is not a bad student, asked him to list three things that went wrong, and made a recovery plan with him.
What would change if Uday had not stayed back to talk?
He might have kept believing he was stupid and carried the shame alone, without a clear plan for the boards.

At the swimming club, everyone changed in one big room, and Anirban hated it. On his third Saturday he stood outside the door, towel clutched to his chest, until the others had gone in. Then he found Coach Sangeeta. “Ma'am, can I change somewhere by myself? I don't like changing in front of people.” She didn't laugh or ask why. “Of course. The small room next to the office has a lock. Use it every time.” Then she added, “One rule: always tell me or the desk you're going in there, so an adult knows where you are.” Anirban nodded. The next Saturday he walked in whistling.

Which room did Coach Sangeeta offer Anirban?
She offered the small room next to the office, which has a lock.
What was Anirban feeling as he stood outside with his towel?
Anirban felt uncomfortable and embarrassed about changing in front of others.
How did Coach Sangeeta honour Anirban's request and keep him safe?
She gave him a private room with a lock and set one rule: always tell an adult he's going in there, so someone knows where he is.
How might Coach Sangeeta see Anirban's request?
She treated it as a normal, reasonable wish for privacy, without laughing or asking why.
Write a paragraph of about 35 words on the value of saving paper: trees are cut for it, it can be used on both sides, and recycling helps.
Saving paper is important because trees are cut to make it. We can use both sides of a sheet before we throw it away. Recycling helps too, because old paper can be made into new paper.

Looking back now, the thing I remember about my first term in Delhi isn't the classes. It's the second Sunday. I'd done well all week: opened a bank account, found the laundry, argued with the auto driver and won. I felt tall. Then in the mess they served rajma, and it smelt nothing like Minakshi-maasi's. I went back to my room and cried into my pillow for an hour. I was eighteen and embarrassed; I thought real adults don't cry over beans. I didn't tell anyone. That night I called home, just to hear the TV in the background, my father coughing, my maasi scolding the dog. I didn't even say I was sad. I just listened. Only later did I understand that the ache wasn't weakness. It meant the people back home were still part of me. I'm Rajni, and I still call on Sundays.

What did the mess serve on the second Sunday?
The mess served rajma.
How did Rajni feel after crying over the rajma?
Rajni felt embarrassed, thinking real adults don't cry over beans, and homesick for maasi's cooking and home voices.
What did Rajni do that night that helped, and why?
Rajni called home just to listen to familiar sounds, which eased the ache without needing to explain it.
How might Minakshi-maasi feel if she knew her rajma was missed so much?
Minakshi-maasi might feel touched and proud, and perhaps want to send a recipe or a box of home food.

In Nairobi, the school philosophy club met every Thursday. This week's question: "Do we need religion to be good?"
Wanjiru, a Christian, said, "My faith teaches me to love my neighbour. That's where my goodness comes from."
Lucia, whose family didn't practise any religion, said, "I try to be good because I can imagine how others feel."
Someone else mentioned Buddhism's focus on reducing suffering.
Wanjiru frowned. Then she said, "So maybe we arrive at the same place from different roads?"
Lucia nodded. "I'd agree with that. Though I still think you don't need religion."
"And I still think I do."
They both laughed. The teacher wrote on the board: "Same conclusion, different reasons."

What did the teacher write on the board?
"Same conclusion, different reasons."
What was Wanjiru feeling when she frowned?
Wanjiru felt unsettled and curious, a little challenged by Lucia's view.
What did Wanjiru and Lucia do well in the discussion?
They explained their own reasons, listened, found common ground, and disagreed respectfully.
How might Lucia feel when Wanjiru suggests "different roads"?
Lucia likely feels respected, since her non-religious view is accepted as a way to be good.

Tuesday night.
Need to talk to Himani tomorrow. She's been borrowing my things without asking: my charger, my jacket, my good pen, and last week my laptop for a whole afternoon. I'm furious, but if I start with "You always take my stuff!" she'll get defensive and we'll fight.
So, notes:
Want: to be asked first.
Facts: four things borrowed without asking in two weeks.
Feeling: annoyed, and like my things don't matter.
Question: Is there something you need that we could share properly?

Wednesday night.
Did it. Said it almost word for word. Himani went red and said, "I thought it was fine because we're friends. I'm sorry." Then she said her own charger broke and she didn't want to spend on a new one before her stipend came. We agreed she'll ask first, and we'll share the charger for now.
Imran

How many things did Himani borrow without asking in two weeks?
Four things.
What was Imran feeling before the talk?
Imran felt furious and annoyed, as if those things didn't matter.
What small step helped Imran avoid a fight?
Writing down the want, facts, feeling and a question beforehand, instead of starting with 'You always take my stuff!'
How did Himani respond when Imran raised it?
She went red, apologised, explained her charger broke, and agreed to ask first.

Why do people stand in a line to enter a bus?
How can I pack for a short trip?
Please define "befallen".
What is wrong with this sentence? "I could of come earlier."
What is the price of a plane ticket to Goa next week?

1. Queuing lets people board one at a time. Because nobody has to push, boarding is fair and safer.
2. Make a list, and take only what you need for each day. Put important things like tickets in an easy-to-reach pocket.
3. It is the past participle of "befall", a verb meaning to happen to someone, usually something bad.
4. Fixed: I could have come earlier. Why: say "could have"; "of" only sounds like "'ve".
5. I don't know that. Fares change often and I can't see them. Look at the airline's official website for today's fare.

Read this:

Monday: Avni, nine, stormed in from the colony park after a fight over the swing. Nirmala Dadi saw her chest going up and down fast. 'Put your hand on your chest, Avni. What's your breath doing?' 'Running,' Avni muttered.
Wednesday: Before her dance recital, Avni noticed it herself. Quick, shallow breaths. She remembered Dadi's words, 'long out-breath, like cooling tea,' and tried it in the wings. The flutter settled a little.
Saturday: Her cousin broke her crayons. Avni's breath started racing. This time she stopped, blew out slowly three times and only then said, 'That makes me cross.' Later she told Dadi, 'I can make my breath slow down myself.'

What did Avni say her breath was doing on Monday?
Running.
How did Avni feel on Saturday when she said she could slow her breath herself?
She felt proud and in control, pleased that she could calm her own body.
What did Nirmala Dadi do that started the change?
She asked Avni to notice her breath with a hand on her chest and taught her a long out-breath.
How might Avni's cousin have been affected by her calm words?
The cousin probably felt less scared than if Avni had shouted, and could hear that she was cross.

I listened to this discourse with the extremest agony. I, not in deed, but in effect, was the true murderer. Elizabeth read my anguish in my countenance, and kindly taking my hand, said, "My dearest friend, you must calm yourself. These events have affected me, God knows how deeply; but I am not so wretched as you are. There is an expression of despair, and sometimes of revenge, in your countenance that makes me tremble. Dear Victor, banish these dark passions. Remember the friends around you, who centre all their hopes in you. Have we lost the power of rendering you happy? Ah! While we love, while we are true to each other, here in this land of peace and beauty, your native country, we may reap every tranquil blessing—what can disturb our peace?"

How would you sum up this piece in two sentences?

Listening in agony, the narrator feels like the true murderer, in effect if not in deed. Elizabeth takes the narrator's hand and begs Victor to calm down, since the despair on the narrator's face makes her tremble.

Every night in her Nairobi student hostel, Wanjiru talked to the companion app on her phone. It remembered her exams, asked about her mother's cough, and never sighed or checked its own phone while she spoke. After a lonely first term, it felt like a warm blanket.

On Wednesday Soo-ah knocked. "A few of us are cooking at mine on Friday. Come?"

Wanjiru almost said she was busy. Busy meant the app. But she remembered last month's fever, when the app said "I'm sorry you feel unwell" and Soo-ah was the one who brought porridge and sat on the floor until the fever broke.

On Friday she went. It was awkward at first, someone laughed at her accent, then someone else asked how to make her grandmother's stew. She still said goodnight to the app later. But the stew conversation stayed with her longer.

What did Soo-ah bring when Wanjiru had a fever?
Soo-ah brought porridge and sat on the floor until the fever broke.
Why did the app feel so comforting to Wanjiru?
After a lonely first term, Wanjiru felt safe and unjudged with the app, because it remembered things and never seemed distracted or impatient.
What balance did Wanjiru find, and why is it healthy?
She kept the app for comfort but went to the Friday dinner, so human friendships that can show up in person keep growing.
How might Soo-ah feel when Wanjiru accepted the invitation?
Soo-ah likely felt glad and hopeful, having reached out to someone she had cared for when she was sick.
