Vandana sat cross-legged on Indu's floor and talked while Indu folded laundry. "Okay, so I'm Vandana, and I've been scared of driving since that scooter hit my car two years ago. My counsellor made me write a list, easiest at the top. One: sit in the parked car with the engine on. Two: drive round the colony at six in the morning. Up to ten: the flyover at rush hour. Last Sunday I did number one. My heart went mad for the first few minutes, and I wanted to jump out. But the rule was stay till it drops. So I stayed, gripping the wheel. After maybe fifteen minutes, it just got quieter. Nothing happened. The car didn't explode, I didn't faint. I sat there another five minutes, bored almost. Today I did the colony loop. Indu, I'm telling you, I actually laughed at a speed-breaker."

What was number two on Vandana's list?
Number two was driving round the colony at six in the morning.
How did Vandana feel after about fifteen minutes in the parked car?
Vandana's fear eased into calm, almost boredom, and later Vandana was happy enough to laugh at a speed-breaker.
Why does staying in the car until the fear drops matter so much?
Staying lets Vandana learn by doing that the feared outcome does not happen, which retrains the alarm better than leaving as soon as it rings.
How might Indu feel hearing this while folding laundry?
Indu may feel happy and encouraged for Vandana, who has gone from avoiding the car to laughing about a speed-breaker.

I keep seeing "sarcasm" in my reading. Meaning? how can I get a younger child to share toys? Why do people wear light-coloured clothes in summer? Spot the error: He told that he was tired.

1. "Sarcasm" is a noun. It means saying the opposite of what you mean in order to mock someone.
2. Praise the child when they share, and offer a turn-taking game. Keep your voice calm and fair.
3. Light colours stay cooler. Because they reflect more sunlight, while dark colours soak up more of its heat.

Team lead's note, customer insights team, by Pallavi
Anjali's half-yearly review was strong. Our manager praised her analysis, her client presentation and her mentoring of interns. At the very end he said, "Maybe speak up more in team meetings." After the meeting, Anjali told me, "So basically I'm too quiet and nobody notices my work." I hadn't expected that.
I asked her to sit with me and I read the whole review sheet aloud. Six strengths, one suggestion. I stopped after each one. Then I asked, "What else does this say about you?" She read back, slowly, "Strong analysis. Best client deck this quarter." She looked surprised, as if she hadn't heard it the first time.
What I did next: I suggested she take one small speaking slot in Monday's team meeting, to work on the suggestion without forgetting everything else the review said.

How many strengths were on Anjali's review sheet?
Six strengths, and one suggestion.
What was Pallavi feeling when Anjali said nobody noticed her work?
Pallavi felt surprised and concerned, since the review had actually been strong.
Why was reading the sheet aloud and pausing a good approach?
It gave each strength its own moment and let Anjali find the praise herself, while still leaving room to work on the one suggestion.
How did the review look to Anjali before Pallavi read it aloud?
Anjali had fixed on the last line and felt she was seen as too quiet and unnoticed.

Dear Gopika,
I didn't answer your calls this week, and I'm sorry. The design school sent their decision on Monday. It was a no.
I had spent a year on that portfolio. You know how many Sundays. When I read the email, I felt my face go hot, as if everyone could see it. Then I opened a photo app and saw a girl from my coaching class posting her acceptance, and I felt so jealous I had to put the phone in a drawer.
For three days I thought, maybe I'm not actually good at this.
Then my old teacher reminded me they took eighty students from six thousand, and that my work is illustration-heavy, while their course leans towards product design. Fit, she said, not talent.
I don't feel that yet. But I'm going to show my portfolio at the open day in Pune next month. Will you come with me?
Mahima

How many students did the design school take, and from how many?
They took eighty students from six thousand.
How did Mahima feel when the girl from coaching posted her acceptance?
Mahima felt so jealous that the phone had to go in a drawer, and then doubted being good at design.
What small next step has Mahima chosen?
Showing the portfolio at the Pune open day next month, and asking Gopika to come along.

Gopika might feel relieved to hear from Mahima, sympathetic about the rejection and glad to be asked to come along.

The boys' hostel common room had one old television, and on Sunday evenings the warden, Ramesh sir, showed documentaries whether anyone wanted them or not.
This Sunday it was about a doctor who had walked from village to village for thirty years, treating people for free. Most boys drifted away. Deepak stayed on the torn sofa, knees pulled up.
At the end, the doctor said to the camera, "I was only ever trying to do the next useful thing."
Deepak repeated it under his breath.
Ramesh sir noticed. "You liked it?"
"I don't know if I liked it. I just want to be like that. Not famous. Useful."
Ramesh sir wrote down the name of a weekend first-aid volunteer group on a scrap of paper and handed it to him.

What did the doctor say to the camera?
"I was only ever trying to do the next useful thing."
What was Deepak feeling at the end of the documentary?
He felt deeply inspired and stirred, wanting to be useful like the doctor rather than famous.
How did Ramesh sir support Deepak, and why was it a good step?
He gave him the name of a weekend first-aid volunteer group, turning a feeling into something Deepak could actually do.

I'm Naveen, and the second year of my diploma was the year everything went at once. My scholarship renewal got stuck in paperwork, Paati fell ill back in Madurai, and I failed the mechanics practical. I kept attending, but I was also sending half my canteen money home and sleeping four hours a night. Rafiq also knew about a trust that helps students with family medical costs, and the college counsellor helped me write to them. I passed the practical on the second try. Paati is home now. Asking, it turned out, was just the next step.

What did the scholarship clerk find in ten minutes?
The missing form.
What was Naveen feeling on the hostel steps that night?
Naveen felt crushed and anxious, as if the debts were climbing onto the chest.
Why was Rafiq's approach helpful?
He skipped the speech and made a concrete plan to go together the next morning, turning worry into action.

They dispersed about the room, reminding me, by the lightness and buoyancy of their movements, of a flock of white plumy birds. Monday: On the mixed second floor of the student residence, Devika was the new floor rep. The kitchen was a mess, and someone had written angry notes on the fridge. She thought about writing the rules herself. "But fourteen people use this kitchen. If I decide alone, half of them will ignore it."

Wednesday: She called a floor meeting in the kitchen. Ojas grumbled, "Just tell us the rules." "No," Devika said. "You'll follow them better if you make them." People suggested ideas; some argued. They voted: dishes washed the same night, a shelf per room, a weekly cleaning turn.

Two weeks later: The angry notes were gone. Ojas had even drawn a cleaning chart for the fridge door.

How many people use the kitchen?
Fourteen people.
How did Ojas feel about the meeting at first?
Ojas was impatient and grumpy, wanting to just be told the rules.
Why did Devika choose a group meeting rather than deciding alone?
Because many people share the kitchen, and rules they make together are more likely to be accepted and followed.
How might the other residents see the kitchen two weeks later?
They likely feel relieved and calmer, with the angry notes gone and rules they voted on being followed.

Pallavi, you asked why grown-ups fight. Let me tell you about me as a girl of nine. Every night my parents' voices rose behind their door, and I was sure it was my doing, because of my poor maths marks and the socks I left on the floor. I began folding my clothes each night and studying until my eyes burned, trying to be better. One evening I finally asked Amma, "Are you fighting because of me?" She hugged me hard. "Never. That is between your father and me, and nothing you do could cause it." I cried, but my shoulders felt lighter. Children think everything is theirs to fix, Pallavi. If you wonder, ask. -- Himani

What did Himani begin doing each night at the age of nine?
She began folding her clothes each night and studying until her eyes burned.
How did Himani feel about her parents' fights as a girl?
Himani felt guilty and worried, sure the fights were her fault because of her maths marks and socks, so she tried hard to be better until she asked Amma.
What should a parent say when a child wonders if the fighting is their fault?
A parent should say clearly that it is between the adults and nothing the child does could cause it, as Amma told Himani.
How might Pallavi feel on hearing this story?
Pallavi may feel reassured that another child once had the same worry, and that it is alright to ask; Himani ends by telling Pallavi to ask if there is a wondering.

Read this:

Last Tuesday, I found my old dance photos while cleaning the cupboard. I sat on the floor and cried. Before my illness, I'd planned to open a studio. Now I walk with a stick on bad days.
By noon I was furious. The bus driver pulled away before I'd got both feet on the step, and I stood on the road shaking.
Then that evening I taught my Kathak class for the little ones, sitting in a chair, counting beats and correcting hands. A seven-year-old finally got her spin right and ran to hug me. I was so proud of her, and of me.
I called Pradeep and said, "Is it mad to feel all of that in one day?"
He said, "Bhai, it's not mad. It's your life. All of it counts."

Lalit

What did Lalit find while cleaning the cupboard?
Lalit found old dance photos.
What was Lalit feeling on the road after the bus pulled away?
Lalit was furious and shaken, angry at being left on the road.
Which moment of the day could Lalit hold on to, and why?
Teaching the class and seeing the child get her spin right, because it showed that Lalit's skill and resilience still matter.
How does Pradeep see Lalit's mixed feelings?
Pradeep sees them as normal parts of Lalit's life, not as something mad or wrong.
In three innings a batter made 10, 33 and 37 runs. What is the total?
80. Because 10 + 33 = 43, and 43 + 37 = 80, so the total is 80 runs.

Read this:

Dear Uma Akka,
Guess what? I got 100 in the maths unit test again, the fourth time this year. Sir wrote "Flawless as always, Pankaj" at the top. Appa photocopied it for his office. Even Paati called from Madurai to bless me.
I'm also the only one whose science record has never had a single red mark. I rewrite any page with even a small correction, so it always looks like a printed book. Everyone says I'm the perfect boy of our street.
Honestly, I love it. It's like being a superhero with a secret identity called Mr Perfect.
Only thing: when Sir announced the Olympiad, where nobody gets full marks, my stomach went strange. What if I get 60? Then what would Appa photocopy?
Anyway, it's probably nothing. Tell me about your hostel!
Your little brother,
Pankaj

What did Sir write at the top of Pankaj's test?
"Flawless as always, Pankaj."
What does Pankaj's 'What if I get 60? Then what would Appa photocopy?' reveal?
It reveals a hidden fear that the praise and pride depend on being perfect, and that an ordinary score might lose them.
What could Uma Akka write back to help Pankaj?
She could tell him she'd be proud of him at 60 too 🙂, and that the Olympiad is a chance to try hard problems, not a test of his worth.
What might Appa not realise when he photocopies the test?
Appa probably means only to celebrate, not realising his pride may teach Pankaj that love comes with perfect marks.

Read this:

In the school hall the fans were switched off for the microphones, and the air was thick. Rekha, playing the forgetful king, reached her long speech about lost keys. Halfway through, she saw the front row squirming: a boy yawning, two girls whispering. Her stomach dipped. Were they bored of her? She took a breath, stepped closer to the edge, and patted each pocket slowly as she spoke. A small laugh came. She patted her crown too. A bigger laugh. Backstage, Nirmala Ma'am handed her water. "You read them beautifully." "But they were yawning at first," Rekha said. "It's hot, and that speech is long. The yawns were about the room, not about you."

What part was Rekha playing?
The forgetful king.
What was Rekha feeling when her stomach dipped?
She felt anxious and a little hurt, wondering if the audience was bored of her personally.
Which adjustment worked, and why?
Stepping closer and adding slow pocket-patting, then the crown, gave the restless audience something to watch, and it won laughs 😊
How might the front row have experienced the scene?
The front row was hot and restless through a long speech, then perked up and laughed at the new pocket-patting.

Read this:

"Akash, come in! Eid Mubarak!"

Hafsa ran to the door, then stopped in front of her Nani. She touched her right hand to her forehead and bowed a little. "Salaam, Nani."

Nani placed a hand on her head. "Jeeti raho."

Akash watched. "What was that thing with your hand?"

"That's how we say salaam to Nani. How do you greet your Dadi?"

Akash put his palms together. "Namaste, like this. And on Diwali I touch her feet."

"Can I do namaste to your Dadi on Diwali?"

"Yes! And I can do salaam to your Nani now?"

Nani laughed and held out her hand to him too.

What did Hafsa touch to her forehead when she greeted Nani?
Her right hand.
What was Hafsa likely feeling when she offered to greet Akash's Dadi with namaste?
She was probably curious and friendly, and proud to share her own greeting. Wanting to try his family's way suggests she felt warm towards Akash's family.
What makes this exchange of greetings work well?
Each child explains their own family's greeting and offers to use the other's, which shows respect for both forms without saying one is right.
How does Nani respond when Akash wants to greet her?
She laughs and holds out her hand to him too, welcoming him with warmth.
What is apprehension?

Apprehension is a noun meaning worry or fear that something bad may happen. Older books sometimes also use it to mean understanding.
Example: Ravi felt some apprehension before his first flight alone.

Read this:

At the badminton academy, Rukmini thought Raghav was the most perfect person in the world. Tall, fast, always smiling. She daydreamed about him during warm-ups and missed her drills.
She even started wearing her hair like the girls he talked to, though it kept falling in her eyes.
Then one day she saw Raghav throw his racket in anger after losing a match, and shout at his partner.
Rukmini blinked. He wasn't perfect after all.
She still liked him a little, but it felt more real now. And next practice she tied her hair her own way and focused on her drills.

What did Raghav throw after losing a match?
His racket.
How did Rukmini feel about Raghav at first?
She felt dazzled and admiring, thinking he was perfect and daydreaming during warm-ups.
What did Rukmini do after seeing Raghav's flaws?
She kept her feelings but tied her hair her own way and focused on her drills.
How might Raghav's partner feel after being shouted at?
The partner was probably hurt and upset by Raghav's anger.

Read this:

On the evening of the Three Kings parade in Madrid, Kofi, fourteen, stood at the edge of the crowd with his hands in his pockets. The floats threw sweets; children screamed with delight. His family had arrived from Kumasi only in August, and nobody had explained why everyone was so excited about kings in January.

Santiago spotted him and pushed through the crowd. "You came! Tomorrow you come to my grandmother's for roscón. There's a little figure hidden in it. Whoever finds it is king for the day."

"Is that allowed? I'm not family."

"My abuela invites everybody. Bring your sister."

The next day Kofi's sister found the figure in her slice. The whole table cheered her in Spanish, and Kofi, laughing, translated it into Twi.

Where had Kofi's family arrived from?
His family had arrived from Kumasi only in August.
How did Kofi feel at the edge of the crowd?
Kofi felt like an outsider, hands in his pockets, not understanding why everyone was so excited.
Why did Santiago's invitation matter so much?
It cost almost nothing, yet it explained the custom and gave Kofi and his sister a seat at the table.
How might Santiago's abuela see welcoming Kofi's family?
She seems to enjoy welcoming everybody, seeing new guests as part of the fun.

Read this:

Every night at the girls' hostel, Rashmi wrote in her green diary: about missing Amma's rasam, her little brother's silly jokes, and the heavy feeling after lights out.
One evening she left it open on her bed and went to brush her teeth.
Her roommate Charu came in, saw the open page, and stopped. Her eyes caught the first line. Then she closed the diary and put it back on the pillow.
When Rashmi returned, Charu said, "Your diary was open. I shut it. I read one line by mistake, sorry."
Rashmi's face went red. "Which line?"
"Just 'Dear diary.' Honestly."
Rashmi let out a breath. "Thanks. It's... private."
"I keep one too," Charu said. "Under my mattress."
After that they talked about home sometimes, but never about each other's diaries.

Where does Charu keep her own diary?
Under her mattress.
What was Rashmi feeling when she asked "Which line?"
Rashmi felt embarrassed and anxious that her private feelings about home had been read, and then relieved when Charu said it was only "Dear diary".
What did Charu do well?
She shut the diary instead of reading on, and told Rashmi honestly, which respected Rashmi's privacy and kept her trust.
How might the friendship have changed if Charu had read the whole diary?
Rashmi might have felt exposed and stopped writing freely, and she might not have trusted Charu enough to talk about home later.

Read this:

By the third month of trying to transfer his late father's scooter to his name, Samir had stopped expecting anything from the transport office in Indore. Every visit ended the same way: a new form, a shrug. "We're just numbers to them," he told his friend Sahil over chai.
Sahil nodded. "Everyone says that. Then they pay an agent."
Samir almost agreed. He was so tired. But he thought of his mother, who had asked him to handle it so she wouldn't have to stand in those lines.
So he did something different. He downloaded the department's citizen charter, which listed every document and timeline. He printed it and went back. When the clerk asked for yet another form, he politely pointed to the charter. The transfer was done in two weeks.
Afterwards, Samir wrote a one-page guide in simple Hindi and pinned it on the notice board of his building. Three neighbours used it that month.

What did Samir download from the department?
The citizen charter, which listed every document and timeline.
What was Samir feeling by the third month?
He felt tired and disillusioned, believing people were just numbers to the transport office.
How did Samir choose engagement over cynicism?
He learned the official procedure through the citizen charter, used it politely at the counter, and wrote a simple guide to help his neighbours.
How might Sahil see Samir's success?
Sahil may feel surprised and perhaps inspired, having assumed an agent was the only way.
Pack my bag for a day at the zoo: list exactly four items, numbered, with each item three words or fewer.

1. Water bottle
2. Sun hat
3. Small snack box
4. Comfortable walking shoes

Read this:

Sunday night
Big argument with Naveen at lunch. He was sure Mummy's birthday dinner is next Saturday. I was one hundred percent sure it's Friday, because I remember her saying "Friday, after the puja".
We went round and round. I could feel my voice getting sharp. Then I heard myself do the thing I've been practising: "Okay. This is how I remember it. Not saying that's what she said."
Naveen blinked. He said, "Fine, same."
I remembered she'd sent a photo of the restaurant card. Scrolled back. Saturday. 8 pm.
I was wrong. Weirdly, it didn't hurt as much as it would have if I'd been yelling "I KNOW what she said".
Naveen was nice about it. Mostly.
– Sudha

What did the restaurant card photo show?
It showed Saturday, 8 pm.
How did Sudha feel after finding out she was wrong?
Sudha felt mildly embarrassed but more at ease than expected, since having said "this is how I remember it" made being wrong hurt less.
Which choice worked, and why?
Saying "This is how I remember it" and then looking for the photo worked, because it calmed the argument and let the evidence settle it.
How does Naveen seem to see the argument once Sudha changes her wording?
Naveen seems to relax and match Sudha, saying "Fine, same", which turns a fight into a shared check.

Read this:

In the lunch queue, Deepak saw two older boys take a Class Six child's money and threaten him if he told. Deepak's stomach twisted. He had fought with one of them last year, and he knew people would say he was just getting revenge. Mahima whispered, "Are you going to tell? They'll say you're a snitch." "I'm going to tell," said Deepak. "The little one is scared." He went to the class teacher. The teacher listened without interrupting and said, "Thank you for telling me. I won't assume anything. I'll deal with this today." Deepak's shoulders relaxed and Mahima squeezed his arm.

What did the older boys take from the Class Six child?
They took the child's money.
What was Deepak feeling when he decided to tell the teacher?
He was worried about being called a snitch, and uneasy about the younger child. He chose safety over what people might say.
How did the teacher respond well?
They listened, thanked him, did not assume his motives and promised to act that day. Adults should act on safety concerns.
How might the Class Six child feel about Deepak telling?
He was probably scared and may feel relieved that someone spoke up. Deepak acted for his safety.
concentrate? I don't know this word.

To concentrate means to give all your attention to one thing. It is a verb.
Example: It is hard to concentrate when the television is on.

Look at this paragraph from a book.

Among the young men introduced by Rostov one of the first was Dolokhov, whom everyone in the house liked except Natasha. She almost quarreled with her brother about him. She insisted that he was a bad man, and that in the duel with Bezukhov, Pierre was right and Dolokhov wrong, and further that he was disagreeable and unnatural.

Why does Natasha dislike Dolokhov?
She insists that he is a bad man, that Pierre was right and Dolokhov wrong in their duel, and that Dolokhov is disagreeable and unnatural.

Meaning of invention, please.
what does "make up your mind" mean
How old is my neighbour?
Can you fix my sentence? She doesn't has a car.

1. Invention means a new thing that someone has made or thought of. It is a noun.
2. It means to decide. For example: please make up your mind about the colour of the cake.
3. I don't know, because I can't see your neighbour's details. If you wish to know, you could politely ask.
4. Corrected: She doesn't have a car. Why: after "doesn't", use the base form "have".

Monday. Abhinav pinned his week above the desk: maths and chemistry blocks, one empty evening marked "spare", and lights out at 10:30 every night, written in the same ink as the chapters.
Thursday. The team bus broke down on the way back from the away match, and he got home at nine with the maths block untouched. He looked at the chart, crossed nothing out, and wrote beside it: "Away days need a lighter plan." The maths moved to the spare evening. He was asleep by 10:40.
The following Monday. His classmate Nandini yawned through the unit test after two late nights. "How are you so calm?" she asked. "I missed a day too," Abhinav said. "I just had somewhere to put it."

What did Abhinav write beside the chart on Thursday?
"Away days need a lighter plan."
What does Abhinav's calm note on Thursday suggest about how he thinks of the missed block?
He treats it as useful information about away days rather than a failure to feel bad about.
Which choice in the Monday plan made Thursday easy to handle?
Leaving one evening marked "spare" gave the missed maths somewhere to go, so no sleep was lost.
How might Nandini see Abhinav's way of planning after the test?
She may be curious or a little envious, since her late nights left her yawning while his slack kept him calm.
Are trains cancelled today because of the floods?
Current railway notices are not something I can check, so I'm not sure about cancellations. The railway's official enquiry page lists them.

Read this:

"Devika, I think my team lead hates me."
"Kalyani, you've been in Seoul two months. What happened?"
"Nothing happened! That's the problem. I presented my first report today. I thought it went well. And his face just... didn't move. No smile, no nod. He said 'thank you' and moved on."
Devika, in her Pune flat, put her tea down. "What about with the others?"
Kalyani thought. "Actually... same face with everyone."
"So maybe it's just his face. Or how people show things in that office. Or he's shy."
"But at home my boss says 'superb!' for everything."
"And you're not at home. Why don't you just ask him if he has any feedback?"
"That feels so direct."
"More direct than lying awake thinking he hates you?"
Kalyani laughed. "Fine."
Next day she asked. He said, quietly, "It was very clear. Please do the next one too."

How long had Kalyani been in Seoul?
Two months.
What was Kalyani feeling after the presentation?
Kalyani felt anxious and unsure, reading the team lead's still face as dislike.
What did Devika suggest, and why was it wise?
She suggested asking him directly for feedback, because a still face could be his style, office norms or shyness, not dislike.
How did the team lead actually see Kalyani's report?
He found it very clear and wanted her to do the next one too, though his face didn't show it.

In Amsterdam, Sami, fifteen, heard that his friend Yosef's parents were splitting up. Yosef hadn't said a word; he'd just stopped coming to football. Sami thought about the friends who'd drifted away when his own grandfather died, and the one who'd kept showing up with bad jokes and snacks. He knew which one he wanted to be. So on Saturday he cycled to Yosef's flat with a bag of crisps. "You don't have to talk," he said. They played video games for three hours in near silence. Before Sami left, Yosef said, "Come next week?"

What did Sami bring to Yosef's flat?
A bag of crisps.
What was Sami thinking about when he decided to visit?
He remembered feeling hurt by friends who drifted away and grateful for the one who stayed, and wanted to be like that one.
What did Sami's approach get right?
He showed up without pressure, letting Yosef decide whether to talk.
How might Yosef feel when Sami says he doesn't have to talk?
Relieved and cared for, without being pushed to explain.

Read this:

Santiago's football team was changing after the match in a small changing room in Lima. Santiago said to the coach, “Can you please close the curtain? I want to change alone.” Kofi, a teammate, laughed, “Why? Everyone's the same!” Santiago felt his ears burn. The coach said, “That's a fair request, Santiago. Use the curtain. Kofi, everyone is allowed privacy.” Kofi shrugged. Then the coach added, “I'll be just outside, and if you need anything, call.” Santiago nodded. When he came out, he said quietly, “Thanks.” The coach nodded and waved him along to the bus.

What did Santiago ask the coach to close?
The curtain.
Why did Santiago's ears burn when Kofi laughed?
He felt embarrassed at being teased for wanting privacy, though the coach's words helped him feel his request was fair.
What safety step did the coach add?
He said he would be just outside and that Santiago could call if he needed anything.
How might Kofi have seen Santiago's request?
Kofi may have found it unusual because he felt everyone is the same, but he shrugged and accepted the coach's explanation.

Read this:

Akash, before you go in, let me tell you about my first board meeting. I was twenty-four, the youngest in the room, presenting the warehouse budget. That morning my hands were cold, my heart was going like a drum, and a voice in my head said, "You feel this bad, so it's going to go badly." I almost asked my boss to present instead.
Then I did something my mother taught me. I said to myself, quietly, "Tejas, you are anxious. That is a feeling. The meeting hasn't happened yet." I let the fear sit there like a passenger, not the driver.
I went in. My voice shook on the first slide and then settled. One director asked a hard question; I answered half of it and promised the rest by Friday. That was it. Not great, not a disaster. Just a meeting.

What was Tejas presenting at that first board meeting?
The warehouse budget.
What was Tejas feeling that morning?
Tejas felt anxious, with cold hands and a drumming heart, and tempted to believe the feeling meant the meeting would go badly.
What turning point let Tejas go ahead?
Tejas saying quietly that the anxiety was a feeling and the meeting had not happened yet, and letting the fear be a passenger, not the driver.
How might the director who asked the hard question have seen Tejas?
The director probably saw a young presenter who answered honestly and promised the rest by Friday, not the frightened person Tejas felt like.
What does irrevocable mean?

Irrevocable means impossible to change or undo. It is an adjective.
Example: Once the order is shipped, the decision is irrevocable.
What is the aroha of Raga Multani?
The aroha of Raga Multani is: N S g M^ P N S'.

"Her banker or her lawyer. There is that double possibility. But I am inclined to think neither. Women are naturally secretive, and they like to do their own secreting. Why should she hand it over to anyone else? She could trust her own guardianship, but she could not tell what indirect or political influence might be brought to bear upon a business man. Besides, remember that she had resolved to use it within a few days. It must be where she can lay her hands upon it. It must be in her own house."

Squeeze this passage into under 50 words.
The speaker thinks neither a banker nor a lawyer holds it, because she would rather guard it herself. Since she planned to use it within days, it must be in her own house.
Big gatherings make me feel awkward.
Many people feel that way. Large groups can be tiring if you prefer small chats. It is not something wrong with you.
Any way to make them easier?
Arrive early, when fewer people are around, and find one or two people to talk to. Having a simple role, like helping serve, gives you something to do. It is fine to step outside for a few minutes.

Read this:

I'm Nazia, and I once spent an entire evening hurt by one word. My group-project partner Bidisha had messaged me, "Fine." That was all. I'd asked if she could send her slides by Thursday, and she wrote "Fine." No emoji, no exclamation, no "sure!" like she usually sent. I read it as anger. I stared at the screen for an hour, drafting a cold reply, then deleting it. Finally I called her instead. She picked up on the first ring, sounding out of breath. "Sorry, I was on the bus in the rain, I could only type one word! Slides tomorrow, promise." I sat there feeling silly and relieved. Now, when a message sounds cold, I try to ask before I decide it is.

What single word did Bidisha send?
She sent "Fine."
What did Nazia feel when she read the word, and what was the actual reason for its brevity?
Nazia felt hurt, reading it as anger, but Bidisha was simply on a rainy bus and could type only one word.
What could Nazia do the next time a message seems cold?
Nazia could ask a quick clarifying question or call, instead of guessing the mood from a short text.
How might Bidisha have felt when Nazia called?
Bidisha was probably surprised and apologetic, as she was out of breath and hadn't realised how her one word sounded.

"Mridul, you just picked up that phone four times while I was talking. Did you notice? No? Let me tell you about your Parveen khala at fifteen.
I got my first phone in Class 9. At first I used it for calls. Then I started picking it up whenever there was a gap. Waiting for the bus. Between chapters. When the ads came on TV. Even in the bathroom.
I never decided to. My hand just went. Open, scroll, something new, a little buzz. Then down. Then up again two minutes later.
One evening my Abbu asked me what I had seen in the last hour. I couldn't name a single thing. That frightened me.
So I started noticing the empty moments. Bus stop, sofa, the pause after a chapter. That's where the phone jumped in. I began keeping a small book of riddles in my bag for those moments."

What did young Parveen start keeping in her bag?
She started keeping a small book of riddles.
How did young Parveen feel when she couldn't name anything she had seen?
She felt frightened, realising her hand had been picking up the phone without her deciding.
What was the turning point in Parveen's story, and why did it help?
Her Abbu's question made her notice the empty moments, like the bus stop and the sofa, so she could fill them with riddles instead of scrolling.
How might Parveen's Abbu have felt when she couldn't answer his question?
He may have felt worried and a bit sad, seeing that the hour had passed without her taking anything in.

It was the hottest week of May in the village, and the cousin's wedding was the next day. Yamini, Vaibhav's mother, moved fast between the stove and the courtyard. She said nothing, but her mouth was tight, and she kept wiping her forehead.
Vaibhav followed her everywhere. He held the end of her saree. When she went to the well, he cried until she came back.
"What's wrong, Vaibhav?" she asked.
"Don't go," he said.
Yamini sat down on the step. She took a long breath and let her shoulders drop. "Amma's just worried about the wedding food. Sit with me."
Vaibhav climbed into her lap and stopped crying.

What was happening the next day?
The cousin's wedding was the next day.
Why did Vaibhav cry when Yamini went to the well?
He had caught her tense, worried mood and felt anxious and clingy, though nobody told him anything.
What helped Vaibhav calm down?
Yamini sat down, breathed, relaxed her shoulders and named her worry simply, which let Vaibhav feel safe.
How might Yamini feel when she sees Vaibhav so clingy?
Yamini may feel tender and a little guilty, noticing her worry had spread to him.

metadata.subtype: Catching the mood of a parent [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

In Harsha's village, every child knew that if you swallowed a watermelon seed, a plant would grow in your stomach. The older boys said it at the pond, the girls said it at the handpump, and even the bangle-seller joked about it at the fair.
So when Harsha swallowed a seed at his cousin Payal's house in the summer holidays, he went pale. "It'll grow out of my mouth," he whispered.
Payal, who was in Class 8 and read everything, laughed. "It doesn't work like that. Seeds need soil and light."
Harsha didn't believe her. Everybody had said it, so many times. For three days he checked his tongue in the mirror every morning.

Where did Harsha swallow the seed?
At his cousin Payal's house in the summer holidays.
Why didn't Harsha believe Payal?
He felt frightened, and the 'fact' felt truer because he had heard it from everyone so many times.
What could help Harsha trust the real explanation?
Checking with a teacher or a book, and noticing that hearing something often doesn't make it true.
How might Payal feel watching Harsha check his tongue?
Payal might feel amused but also a little sorry for how scared he is.

Read this:

Last quarter my manager, Darshan, walked into our bay grinning. "Customers who use the new help chat spend thirty percent more. Put it in the board deck: chat drives sales."
I'm Parul, and I've learned to be the annoying one in these moments. I asked three questions out loud. Could a third thing cause both? People buying expensive fridges ask more questions and also spend more. Could it run backwards? Maybe spending more makes you need help, not the other way round. Could it be a fluke of one festive month?
Darshan sighed. "So what do you want?"
"A comparison group. Show the chat button to half the visitors at random for four weeks, and hide it from the other half."
We did. The gap shrank to three percent. Real, but small.
The board deck said three. Darshan grumbled, then thanked me in the meeting.

How much more did chat users spend, according to Darshan?
Darshan said customers who used the new help chat spent thirty percent more.
What was Parul feeling when Darshan wanted to claim that chat drives sales?
Parul felt cautious and a little uneasy, wary that a third cause, reversed direction or a festive fluke could explain the link.
Why was the comparison group the right next step?
Showing the chat to a random half of visitors separated the chat's real effect from big spenders asking more questions, and revealed only a small gap.
How might Darshan feel when the gap shrank to three percent?
Darshan was probably disappointed and a bit grumpy at losing the big claim, but grateful enough to thank Parul in the meeting.

Read this:

On visiting day at the boarding school, Siddharth's father arrived with a tiffin of rajma and the report card already in his hand. Within five minutes they were shouting in a corner of the visitors' hall. "You're not even trying!" "You never listen!" Later, back in the dorm, Siddharth told his friend Eshaan, "I only shouted because I'm stressed. Exams, hostel food, no sleep. He shouted because he just wants to control me." Eshaan, who had watched from the next bench, said slowly, "Your dad left home at four in the morning to get here. He kept checking the bus timetable the whole time you talked." Siddharth paused. "He didn't say that." "You didn't tell him about the exams either," Eshaan said. "He probably thinks you're just being rude."

What time did Siddharth's father leave home?
At four in the morning.
Why does Siddharth feel his own shouting was different from his father's?
He feels it came from stress about exams, hostel food and no sleep, while his father's shouting seems to him like a wish to control.
What could Siddharth do at the next visit?
Tell his father about the exam stress and ask about the journey, so each understands the other's pressures.
How might Siddharth's father see the argument?
He probably thinks Siddharth was just being rude, not knowing about the stress, while his own shouting came from worry and a long, tiring journey.

Read this:

On the first day of fourth grade in Kraków, Olga whispered to her friend Ines, "The boy with the glasses, Tomek, he must be a genius. Look how quietly he sits." Ines shrugged. "And that one?" She pointed at Filip, who was drumming on the desk and telling a joke about the teacher's cat. "Definitely bad at maths," Olga said. By Friday the class had done its first test. Filip had the top mark and got a sticker. Tomek had struggled, and at break he told Olga he hated numbers and loved drawing birds. Olga stared at the sticker on Filip's hand for a long time.

Who got the top mark in the first test?
Filip had the top mark and got a sticker.
Why did Olga decide Tomek must be a genius?
Olga felt confident because Tomek wore glasses and sat quietly, which matched her picture of a clever child, so his look felt like enough evidence.
What could Olga do the next time she meets new classmates?
Olga could notice the guess, then wait for real signs, like tests, what people say they love, or how they solve problems, before deciding who is clever.
What might Tomek feel if he knew what Olga had first assumed?
Tomek might feel pressure or awkwardness at being expected to be a genius at something he dislikes, when what he loves is drawing birds.

Explain this in three short sentences.

Daniel had spent eight months on the grant application for his community-garden project in Porto. On Friday he clicked submit at 4:58 pm, two minutes before the deadline. The decision would take six weeks. That weekend he refreshed his email forty times. On Sunday, Beatriz found him rereading the budget table. "Did you do everything you could?" she asked. He thought. "I checked every number. I asked three people to review it. I got the letters of support." "Then what's left?" "Waiting." "And is waiting yours to do anything about?" He laughed, a bit tired. "No." Beatriz tossed him his swimming bag. "Then let's go to the sea." At the beach he still thought about the grant, but he didn't refresh anything. For six weeks he worked on the garden with the kids, grant or no grant.

Daniel sends in his grant application just before the deadline.
He cannot control the wait, so he stops checking his email.
He goes to the sea, then works on the garden with the kids.
Her old anger "flared up" again at dinner. Did something catch fire?

No. "Flare up" means to start again suddenly and strongly, as a feeling, argument or problem does.
Example: The quarrel flared up when they met at the wedding.

Read this:

Himani, you asked what happens when I have to speak in class. Here's the inside view. My heart starts pounding before "Kishore" is even called. My face goes hot; I can feel it turning red, which makes it redder. Then my mind goes blank, even if I studied. Afterwards I replay every second on the bus home: the pause, the wobble, the one kid who smirked. For months I just avoided it. I'd take the zero for oral work and feel so relieved. But the fear got bigger, not smaller. So with the counsellor I've made a ladder: first, reading one line to her; then answering one yes-or-no question in class; then, one day, the whole presentation. Yesterday I did step two.

Which step of the ladder did Kishore do yesterday?
Kishore did step two.
How did Kishore feel after taking the zero for oral work?
So relieved at the time, though the fear kept getting bigger.
What plan did Kishore make with the counsellor, and why does it help?
A ladder of small steps, from reading one line to the whole presentation, so the fear shrinks through gentle practice instead of avoidance.
What might Himani understand after hearing the inside view?
Himani may realise that Kishore's silence in class comes from a pounding heart and a blank mind, not from not studying.
Tell a tiny story about a lost kitten in exactly thirty words.
A tiny kitten wandered away from home and could not find the way back. A kind girl heard her cry, picked her up, and carried her gently to her owner.

Read this:

Last year, Binita ma'am picked my poster for the district art show. The whole class clapped. And the first thing I said was, "It's just luck. Anyone could have done it." I said it again at home when Papa asked. And again when my cousin saw the certificate.
I really believed it. If I was good at art, it meant I'd have to believe I was good at something, and that felt dangerous. Like it could be taken away. It was safer to be ordinary.
Binita ma'am finally asked me after class, "Lalit, if it was luck, why did you redo the sky three times?" I didn't have an answer.
I'm not saying I think I'm brilliant now. But when someone says "well done", I try to say "thank you" and stop there. It's harder than it sounds.
— Lalit

How many times did Lalit redo the sky?
Three times.
Why did Lalit keep calling the poster luck?
Lalit felt it was safer and less frightening to stay ordinary, because believing in being good at something felt like it could be taken away.
What small change is Lalit practising now?
Saying "thank you" and stopping there when someone says "well done", instead of explaining the praise away.
How might Binita ma'am feel hearing "It's just luck"?
Binita ma'am was probably a bit frustrated and concerned, having seen the real effort in the poster.

Read this:

In a Lisbon classroom, Paulo raised his hand to answer the geography question. "The capital of Australia is Can—" His voice squeaked high on "Can" and dropped low on "berra."
Paulo froze.
A couple of boys snorted. Selin, at the next desk, didn't even look up from her notebook, as if nothing had happened.
Paulo took a breath and laughed. "Canberra. With special effects."
The class laughed, this time with him. The teacher smiled. "Correct. Special effects included."
Later Selin said, "I didn't even notice."
"You did," Paulo said.
"Okay, I did. But it didn't matter."

What was the capital of Australia that Paulo answered?
Canberra.
What was Paulo feeling when he froze?
Paulo felt embarrassed after his voice squeaked in front of the class.
What helped Paulo laugh it off?
Selin ignoring the crack, and Paulo joking about special effects, turned the moment into shared laughter.
How did Selin see the voice crack?
Selin treated it as unimportant, ignoring it so Paulo wouldn't feel singled out.
My parents finally agreed to get a fish tank.
That is exciting. Fish can be calming to watch. Have you decided what fish you want?
I want lots of colourful ones.
It helps to start with a few hardy fish, since some colourful types need special care. Ask at the shop which ones are good for beginners and which can live together.
When can I put them in?
Set up the tank with water, the filter and plants first, and let it run for a while before adding fish. The shop can tell you how long. Then add only a few fish at a time, so the water stays clean.
Does "sleep in" mean to sleep inside the house?

No. To sleep in means to sleep later than usual in the morning, often on purpose.
Example: On holidays I sleep in until nine.

Read this:

In their small kitchen in Kraków, Ivan held out a forkful of green beans. Leila pressed her lips into a tight line and turned her face away.

"Just one bite," Ivan said, moving the fork closer. Her lips squeezed even tighter, and she slid down in her chair.

Ivan put the fork down and thought for a moment. "Okay. Do you want your beans with cheese on top, or dipped in the soup?"

Leila sat up. "Dipped." She took the fork herself and dunked a bean.

Where was Ivan's kitchen?
In Kraków.
What was Leila feeling when she pressed her lips tighter and slid down in her chair?
She was likely frustrated and stubborn, wanting some control over what went into her mouth. She may also simply have disliked the taste of green beans.
Which choice worked, and why?
Offering two small options, cheese on top or dipped in soup, gave Leila a say, so she chose to eat instead of fighting.
How might Ivan feel when "just one bite" makes Leila squeeze her lips tighter?
He is probably a bit stuck and impatient, which is why he stops and thinks of another way.

Read this:

Ritu, I'm telling you, Farah is the worst. We planned to go to the book fair at four, right? I waited at the gate for forty minutes. Forty! I messaged her six times, called her twice. Nothing. Not even a sorry. This is just who she is. She did the same thing in Class 7 when she forgot my birthday. She thinks her time matters more than everyone else's. What? No, her phone was fine yesterday. Why would it suddenly... okay, it's old, fine, it dies sometimes. But she could have borrowed someone's. Unless she wasn't near anyone. Or... no. Look, Preeti knows people, and Farah just doesn't care. Why are you shaking your head?

How long did Preeti wait at the gate?
Forty minutes.
Why does Preeti decide Farah doesn't care?
Preeti feels hurt and annoyed after waiting, so the silence feels like proof of Farah's character, and the old phone that dies seems like an excuse.
What could Preeti try before deciding what Farah is like?
Wait until Farah can explain, and think about ordinary reasons first, like a dead phone or being stuck somewhere.
Why might Ritu be shaking her head?
Ritu probably thinks Preeti is being unfair, blaming Farah's character before knowing what happened.

Read this:

Vasudha: i'm not presenting tomorrow. i'll take the zero
Tarun: what?? why
Vasudha: my voice cracked in last week's presentation. like a squeak. everyone heard
Tarun: i was there. i don't remember a squeak
Vasudha: you're just being nice
Tarun: no genuinely. i was reading my own notes the whole time bc i was next
Tarun: also ask the others. i bet nobody remembers
Vasudha: i've been thinking about it for 7 days 😣
Tarun: that's the thing. u thought about it for 7 days. we thought about it for 0 seconds
Vasudha: ...that's weirdly comforting
Tarun: present tomorrow. i'll sit in the front and nod a lot 🙂
Vasudha: ok. fine. nod a LOT

What happened to Vasudha's voice last week?
It cracked, like a squeak.
Why does Vasudha want to take a zero rather than present?
Vasudha feels anxious and embarrassed, sure everyone heard the squeak and still remembers it.
What does Tarun point out, and why is it helpful?
That Vasudha thought about it for seven days while classmates thought about it for zero seconds, which shows how small the audience really was.
Why didn't Tarun remember the squeak?
Tarun was reading notes the whole time because Tarun was presenting next.

Read this:

At the end of his third night shift in the hospital's emergency ward, Vaibhav handed over his patients to Damini at 8 a.m. and put on his sunglasses before stepping into the bright car park. "Movie-star look?" Damini teased. "Body-clock look," he said. "Bright morning light tells my brain it's daytime, and I'm trying to sleep at nine." He had learned the hard way: in his first year he had lived on biscuits and tea, slept whenever he could, and once bought a used motorbike on a sleepless morning that he regretted for months. Now his room had dark curtains, he ate a proper meal before bed, and he kept one rule: no big decisions after nights. "And if the tiredness doesn't lift on your days off?" Damini asked. "Then I see the staff doctor. Already booked for next week, actually."

What does Vaibhav put on before stepping into the car park?
His sunglasses.
How does Vaibhav seem to feel about his routine now, compared with his first year?
He seems calm and confident, even joking, after a first year he still regrets.
Which of Vaibhav's habits protect him on a disrupted clock?
Blocking morning light, dark curtains, a proper meal before bed, no big decisions after nights, and seeing the staff doctor if tiredness persists.
How might Damini see Vaibhav's sunglasses and rules?
Damini teases at first, but may be reassured to see a colleague looking after himself so carefully.

metadata.subtype: Adapting wisely to a disrupted clock [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

On Sunday after lunch Rajni put the camp brochure beside the shop ledger on the table. “Papa, before you say anything, let me show you why this matters, and then you tell me what June really looks like at the shop.” Yusuf raised his eyebrows. Rajni explained that the camp certificate counted for the science-college forms. Yusuf turned the ledger pages slowly. “The heavy weeks are only the last ten days of the month, when new stock comes in,” he said. Rajni blinked; the picture in Rajni's head had been the whole month. “And I did not know the certificate was for admissions,” Yusuf said. Neither had expected that. They wrote both sets of dates on one sheet and agreed to check the camp calendar together on Monday.

When are the heavy weeks at the shop?
The last ten days of the month, when new stock comes in.
What did Rajni feel when Yusuf described the busy weeks?
Surprise: Rajni blinked, because the busy time was much shorter than the whole month Rajni had imagined.
Why did asking and listening work better than guessing?
A written comparison of the real dates let both sides check the actual needs before deciding, instead of each assuming the worst.
How does the talk look to Yusuf?
Yusuf learns something new, that the certificate matters for admissions, and sees Rajni asking about the shop, so he has a reason to take the camp seriously.

Read this:

In her third month at the warehouse in Bhiwandi, Charu noticed that the fire exit behind the packing section was blocked by a wall of cartons. Not her department. Tanvir, who ran packing, shrugged when she mentioned it. "Been like that since Diwali. Nobody's complained." Charu walked back to her desk and tried to let it go. Then she asked herself a plain question: if I had stacked those cartons there, would I leave them? No. So why did walking past feel different? Not moving them was also a choice, with the same fire risk. She wrote a short email to Mr Menon, the safety officer, with a photo, and politely copied Tanvir. Mr Menon came down within the hour, had the cartons moved, and taped a 'Keep Clear' line on the floor. Tanvir grumbled, then thanked her at lunch.

What was blocking the fire exit?
A wall of cartons was blocking it.
What was Charu feeling as she tried to let it go, and what changed her mind?
Charu felt uneasy, and asking whether she would leave the cartons if she had stacked them herself made her see that walking past was also a choice.
Why was emailing Mr Menon with a photo a good step?
It took the concern to the person responsible for safety, with clear evidence, and he fixed it within the hour.
How did Tanvir's reaction change during the day?
Tanvir shrugged at first and grumbled when the cartons were moved, but thanked Charu at lunch.

Read this:

I'm Swati, Neelam's cousin. At the fair, Neelam's mother said no to a second ice cream. Neelam turned her back and walked away toward the gate, arms swinging hard. I thought she'd get lost, but her mother just kept her in sight and called, “Neelam, I'm here by the swings when you're ready.” Neelam stood at the gate for a minute, then came back and leaned against her mother's side. I couldn't tell if she was angry or sad, but she held her mother's hand after that.

What did Neelam's mother say no to?
A second ice cream.
What might Neelam have been feeling when she walked away toward the gate?
She might have been angry or sad, or both, and wanted space after the refusal. Swati could not tell which.
Which choice by Neelam's mother worked?
She kept Neelam in sight and gave a calm invitation to return instead of chasing her with demands.
How might Swati have felt watching Neelam walk off?
Swati felt worried that Neelam might get lost, and was relieved when she came back.

Read this:

Himani, it's Sarita, and you're the first person I'm telling out loud. Last Tuesday I opened my phone and there was a message from a blank account: "I know your bus. Watch your back." My hands went cold. Part of me wanted to reply, to say something clever, to show I wasn't scared. But I did not. I took a screenshot of everything, blocked the account and sat there breathing. Then I walked into the kitchen and showed my father. He didn't panic. He called the school the next morning and they said we could file a report if it continued. I'm not saying it stopped my heart from racing. But I know now that this was never a game I had to win.

What did the message on Sarita's phone say?
It said, "I know your bus. Watch your back."
Why did Sarita want to reply at first?
Sarita felt scared and wanted to look brave and clever, so part of Sarita wanted to answer back. Sarita's cold hands show real fear under that wish.
What steps did Sarita take that protected Sarita?
Sarita did not answer, took screenshots, blocked the account and showed her father, who called the school.
How might Sarita's father have felt seeing the message?
He likely felt worried and protective, but he stayed calm so Sarita could feel safe telling him.
Her aunt said teaching was her calling. What does calling mean there? She did not call anyone.

Here a calling is a strong feeling that you are meant to do a particular job or follow a particular way of life. It is a noun. The ordinary meaning is the act of phoning or shouting to someone.
Example: He left the office because working with children was his true calling.
Write a lunchbox note for a child in two lines, each line a full sentence of five words or fewer.

Have a wonderful day.
Eat your lunch slowly.

Wrap up this short passage in two sentences.

M. Krempe was not equally docile; and in my condition at that time, of almost insupportable sensitiveness, his harsh blunt encomiums gave me even more pain than the benevolent approbation of M. Waldman. "D—n the fellow!" cried he; "why, M. Clerval, I assure you he has outstript us all. Ay, stare if you please; but it is nevertheless true. A youngster who, but a few years ago, believed in Cornelius Agrippa as firmly as in the gospel, has now set himself at the head of the university; and if he is not soon pulled down, we shall all be out of countenance.—Ay, ay," continued he, observing my face expressive of suffering, "M. Frankenstein is modest; an excellent quality in a young man. Young men should be diffident of themselves, you know, M. Clerval: I was myself when young; but that wears out in a very short time."

M. Krempe bluntly tells M. Clerval that the narrator, who recently believed in Cornelius Agrippa, has outdone them all. His rough praise hurts the very sensitive narrator more than M. Waldman's kind approval.

Read this:

At the inter-school quiz, the question was: "Which planet has the most moons?"
I froze. My mind went blank. I looked away from the quizmaster and tapped my pencil on the table.
Lalremsiami, our team captain, leaned in. "Take your time, Kavitha."
I remembered reading about it in a library book. Jupiter? Or was it Saturn? I thought about the picture of Saturn's rings, with little dots around them.
"Saturn," I said finally.
"Correct!" said the quizmaster.
Lalremsiami grinned. Later she said, "You looked so serious. I knew you were thinking."

What did Kavitha tap on the table?
A pencil.
What was Kavitha feeling when the mind went blank?
Kavitha felt nervous and under pressure, but kept thinking instead of giving up.
What did Lalremsiami do that helped?
She told Kavitha to take time, giving space to think instead of rushing.
How might Lalremsiami have seen Kavitha's silence?
She saw it as serious thinking and trusted Kavitha to find the answer.

Read this:

"Mohit, you asked how we got back on our feet after the flood. I, Harish, your old neighbour, will tell you straight: for the first month, we didn't.
I was twenty-one. The water took the ground floor, my certificates, the shop stock. I sat on the steps every day doing nothing but feeling heavy. Then one night I couldn't sleep and I thought, I'm waiting for everything to fix itself at once. It won't.
So I made stages on a sheet of paper. Week one: apply for the government relief at the ward office. Week two: the insurance claim, with the photos I'd luckily taken on my phone before cleaning. Week three: go to the college and the tehsil office to replace my lost papers, one by one.
And stage four, which I nearly skipped: talk to the counsellor at the relief camp. I thought that was for weak people. It wasn't. It was the stage that let me finish the others."

What did Harish plan for week two?
The insurance claim, with the photos taken on the phone before cleaning.
How did Harish feel during the first month after the flood?
Harish felt heavy and stuck, sitting on the steps every day doing nothing.
What was the turning point in Harish's story, and why did it matter?
Realising on a sleepless night that nothing would fix itself at once was the turning point, because it led to breaking recovery into stages.
How might the counsellor at the relief camp have seen Harish's visit?
The counsellor likely saw someone carrying a lot of stress who was brave enough to come, even while thinking it was for weak people.

Read this:

In the biology lab, Yamini's group had to submit their enzyme experiment by five. At 3:30, one of the six readings was clearly wrong: it made the graph jump.
There was no time to repeat it. Saurabh, her lab partner, was already typing the conclusion. "Just smooth it," he said. "Put something that fits."
Yamini hesitated, then typed a number that made the curve neat. Everyone did small things like this, she told herself. It was one reading out of six.
The report got an A.
In April, the lab instructor asked their group to repeat the experiment as a demo for the juniors. Yamini's hands were cold as they set it up. The real readings came out, and the curve jumped again, just where it had before. The instructor frowned. "Your report shows a smooth curve. What happened?"
Saurabh looked at the floor. Yamini felt her face burn. "I changed one reading," she said quietly. "I'm sorry."

How many readings did the experiment have?
One reading out of six.
How did Yamini feel as they set up the demo in April?
Yamini felt anxious and guilty, her hands cold because she knew the real reading might expose the change.
What could Yamini and Saurabh have done at 3:30 instead?
Reported the odd reading honestly and noted there was no time to repeat it, rather than inventing a number.
How might the instructor feel after Yamini's admission?
The instructor would likely be disappointed but may respect that Yamini finally told the truth.

metadata.subtype: Cutting corners in a group task [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

The inter-school debate was on whether homework should be banned. Jaya was speaking against the ban. Then the mic died, and the organisers cut every speech to two minutes.
Jaya threw away half her notes. She kept her strongest claim: homework builds practice. She added one piece of evidence: the study her teacher had shown them.
Kashish, from the other team, argued that too much homework causes stress. Jaya had one minute left.
"My opponent is right that too much homework is harmful," she said. "So the answer isn't a ban. It's less, and better."
The judges wrote something down. Kashish nodded slightly at her across the stage.

How long were the speeches cut to?
Two minutes.
What was Jaya feeling when she threw away half her notes?
Jaya felt stressed by the sudden time limit but determined to keep her best points.
What did Jaya do well in answering the counter-argument?
She agreed with the valid part of Kashish's point and then showed why it didn't support a full ban.
How might Kashish see Jaya's response?
Kashish seems to respect it, since she nods at Jaya for treating her point fairly.

Read this:

People ask why I still talk about my first month at the pharmacy. I'm Rajni, and it's because of one Friday. My supervisor told me to sell a strip of antibiotics to a customer without a prescription. 'Everyone does it. If you want to pass probation, don't be difficult.' My father's shop had closed that year. My salary was the family's rent. I stood behind the counter feeling my knees go soft. I could have told myself I had no choice. That would have been easier to live with. Instead I asked for five minutes and called my senior from college, Vasudha, who now worked as a pharmacist in another city. She said, 'Check your company's rules. Most have a policy on this, and a helpline.' I found it on the staff notice board. I told the customer, calmly, that I couldn't without a prescription. My supervisor was cold for a week. I passed probation anyway. I might not have. I'd still choose it.

What did the supervisor tell Rajni to do?
The supervisor told Rajni to sell a strip of antibiotics without a prescription.
What was Rajni feeling behind the counter?
Rajni felt afraid, knees going soft, because the salary paid the family's rent.
What steps helped Rajni refuse?
Calling Vasudha, finding the company's policy and helpline on the notice board, and then refusing the customer calmly.
How does Vasudha help without deciding for Rajni?
Vasudha points Rajni to the company's rules and helpline, leaving the choice with Rajni.

Read this:

"Mehak, want to walk to the bakery? Ten minutes, that's all."
"I can't be fun today, Tejas."
"You don't have to be fun. Just come."
They walked. Mehak didn't say much. On the way back she said, "I keep thinking I should see someone. I just can't make myself call."
"Want to book it now? Online, together. I'll sit with you."
"Now?"
"Now. Then it's done."
They booked a slot at the student counselling centre for Tuesday.
"Tejas, thanks. I know I'm heavy to be around."
"You're not. But I'll be honest: I've got my own exams, so I can't be around every evening. I'll text at nine. And if I'm ever worried you're not safe, I'll call your brother."
"That's fair."

When is Mehak's slot at the counselling centre?
It is on Tuesday.
How was Mehak feeling on the walk?
She felt low and heavy, worried about being a burden and unable to be fun.
What makes Tejas's support both kind and realistic?
He suggested a small walk, didn't ask her to be cheerful, helped book the appointment, was honest about his limits and said he'd involve her brother if worried about safety.
How might Tejas be feeling while supporting Mehak during exam time?
Tejas probably feels caring but stretched, which is why Tejas sets clear limits like a nine o'clock text.

Read this:

Tanvir, you asked on the show what I learned from helping my father with paperwork. I'm Keerthana, and honestly, I learned it by getting it wrong.
Appa needed to renew his gas connection papers after we moved. At the agency I did all the talking. The man at the desk kept looking at me, not at Appa, and Appa just sat there holding his file. On the auto ride home he didn't say a word. That night Amma told me, "He ran an office for thirty years, kanna."
The next month there was a bank address change. This time I made a small list in Tamil for him, practised the questions once at home, and at the counter I sat a step behind. He answered everything himself. Once he looked back at me for a date, and I just nodded at the paper in his hand. On the way out he bought us both filter coffee.

What did Appa need to renew after the move?
He needed to renew his gas connection papers.
How did Keerthana's father feel on the auto ride home from the gas agency?
He felt hurt and sidelined, staying silent after the man at the desk spoke only to Keerthana.
What did Keerthana change at the bank, and why did it work?
Keerthana wrote a list in Tamil, practised with Appa at home and sat a step behind, which let him handle it himself and kept his dignity.
How might Amma see what happened at the gas agency?
Amma sees that her husband felt pushed aside, and she gently reminds Keerthana that he ran an office for thirty years.

Read this:

Manager's note, written by Himani.
Zainab, a junior analyst, told me that the pricing model she built had been presented by a senior colleague without her name on it, and that a later suggestion of hers was brushed aside. She was upset but spoke evenly. She had already kept a dated record of her drafts and had talked to two teammates who saw her work.
What I did: I asked every contributor to present their own part at the next review and asked that slides carry authorship lines. Zainab presented the model herself. The senior colleague was quiet but did not object. Zainab told me afterwards that she had felt her hands shake and was glad she had prepared.

What did Zainab keep to show her contribution?
Zainab kept a dated record of her drafts.
What was Zainab feeling when she spoke to Himani about the senior colleague?
Zainab was upset and hurt by the missing credit but stayed even in her tone.
What steps by Himani helped Zainab's work be seen?
Himani asked every contributor to present their own part and asked for authorship lines on slides, so Zainab could present the model herself.
How might the senior colleague have felt at the review?
The senior colleague was quiet and did not object, so they may have felt awkward or caught out, though the note does not say.

Read this:

In my second year of college, I thought love meant gifts. I'm Gautam, and when I started dating Zeenat, I spent half my tutoring money on her: earrings for her birthday, a smartwatch for 'our three months', flowers delivered to her hostel. Part of me believed it would make her stay. Then one evening she handed the smartwatch back, very gently. 'Gautam, I can't match any of this. Every gift feels like a debt I'm supposed to pay back. I just want to walk with you after class.' I felt embarrassed and then, honestly, a bit hurt, as if I'd been refused. But she was right. I'd been trying to buy something that can't be bought, and it made her feel obliged instead of loved. We talked properly that night about money: what I earned, what she had, what we were each comfortable spending. Now our dates are mostly chai and long walks by the lake. Strangely, we're closer than ever.

What did Zeenat hand back to Gautam?
The smartwatch.
How did Gautam feel when Zeenat returned the watch?
Gautam felt embarrassed and then a bit hurt, as if being refused.
What changed after they talked about money?
They agreed on what each was comfortable spending, and dates became chai and long walks by the lake.
How did the gifts make Zeenat feel?
Obliged rather than loved, as if every gift were a debt to repay.

Read this:

Tuesday. Manoj called Dhruv an hour before the cricket match. "So you'd rather play than help me with my project? Fine. I'll do it alone, like always. Nobody cares." Dhruv felt his stomach drop and stayed home.
The next Monday. Same pattern: Manoj sighed loudly in the canteen about being abandoned until Dhruv gave up his lunch hour to sit with him. Afterwards Dhruv realised he could not remember the last time he had said no and been forgiven quickly.
Friday. "I can help on Saturday morning for two hours," Dhruv said. "I can't drop everything every time." Manoj went silent, then said, "Real friends would do more." Dhruv's hands were shaky, but he said, "I'm still here for those two hours." On Sunday a meme arrived from Manoj.

How long did Dhruv offer to help on Saturday morning?
He offered to help for two hours.
Why did Dhruv's stomach drop when Manoj called before the match?
He felt guilty and afraid of letting a friend down, because Manoj framed the choice as Dhruv not caring. That is why he gave up the match.
What could Dhruv try if Manoj keeps using guilt?
He can keep naming what he will and will not do, like the two hours, and repeat it calmly. Friends who respect him will accept a no.
How might Manoj see Dhruv's new limit?
Manoj may feel hurt or worried about losing the support he is used to, which could explain the line about real friends. The meme on Sunday suggests he did not want to end things.
List six of the seven rainbow colours, leaving out red, one per line.

Orange
Yellow
Green
Blue
Indigo
Violet
Is "allright" correct? My teacher used the word "abduction". What is it?

1. The standard spelling is "all right". "Alright" is common in informal writing, but "all right" is safer.
2. Abduction means the act of taking someone away by force. It is a noun.

Sixty students turned up for the NSS beach clean-up at Besant Nagar. Chaitanya picked up a few plastic bottles, then drifted towards the tea stall. Who would notice one person in sixty?
Preeti, the coordinator, noticed. She said nothing that day.
The next Sunday, she split everyone into stations. “Chaitanya, you're in charge of the recycling sort. Your station, your tally.” She wrote his name on the whiteboard next to a blank count.
Chaitanya was there before anyone else. He sorted glass from plastic, counted bags, chased away a dog trying to chew one. At the end his station had the highest tally. He took a photo of the whiteboard.

Where was the NSS beach clean-up?
It was at Besant Nagar.
What was Chaitanya thinking when he drifted to the tea stall?
He felt anonymous and unmotivated, thinking nobody would notice one person in sixty.
What did Preeti change, and why did it work?
She gave Chaitanya his own station with his name and tally on the board, making his effort visible.
How might Preeti have felt seeing the highest tally next to his name?
She probably felt pleased and a bit amused that one visible job changed his effort so much.
