Read this:

Neelam: quick question for my project. how does photosynthesis work again?
Sangeeta: we did that in March. I got 48/50
Neelam: great, explain it to me
Sangeeta: uh
Sangeeta: sunlight... chlorophyll... something with glucose
Neelam: that's it?
Sangeeta: I learnt it for the test. I don't remember it now
Neelam: you topped the class!
Sangeeta: yeah. rank 1. Papa put it on the family group
Neelam: but you don't actually know it
Sangeeta: I know how to write it in an exam
Neelam: isn't that kind of sad?
Sangeeta: ...kind of. I never wonder about anything. I just learn what's coming in the test
Neelam: remember in Class 6 you wanted to grow a plant in a dark cupboard to see what happens?
Sangeeta: omg yes
Neelam: want to try it for real this time?
Sangeeta: yes. actually yes

What did Sangeeta get in the March test?
Sangeeta got 48/50.
How does Sangeeta feel when she can't explain photosynthesis?
Sangeeta feels a bit sad and uneasy, realising the learning was only for rank and approval, with no curiosity left.
What did Neelam suggest that could bring back curiosity?
Trying the old experiment of growing a plant in a dark cupboard, learning for the joy of finding out.
How might Papa see Sangeeta's rank 1?
Papa is proud, sharing it on the family group, probably not knowing Sangeeta has forgotten what was learnt.

Read this:

The message came from Nilesh's school friend on a Thursday night: a "trading group" where members "doubled their money in ninety days, guaranteed." Nilesh, three months into his first job in Pune, felt the pull. He had some savings sitting idle, and everyone at the office seemed to be talking about markets. At lunch he showed the screenshots to Sangeeta, a senior on his team. She scrolled, then put the phone down. "Guaranteed and doubled in the same sentence? That's the red flag. Real investments go up and down." She told him how she had started years ago: small, regular amounts spread across different kinds of funds, after sitting down with a registered adviser. "Boring. Slow. Mine still has bad months." Nilesh muted the group that evening. He booked a session at his bank's advisory desk for Saturday, and wrote his questions down first.

What did the trading group claim?
That members doubled their money in ninety days, guaranteed.
What was Nilesh feeling when he first saw the message?
He felt tempted and a little left out, with idle savings and colleagues all talking about markets.
What did Nilesh do that others could learn from?
He showed the offer to someone experienced before acting, muted the group, and booked time with a qualified adviser, questions written down.
How does Sangeeta see the trading group?
She sees it as a warning sign, because real investments go up and down, while the group promises a guaranteed double.

Read this:

The shipment labels for the Busan warehouse had gone out with the wrong postcodes, and two pallets came back. Soo-ah, the logistics lead, found Leila's initials on the label file. By lunch she had half-typed a message moving Leila off the Friday export run.
She stopped before sending it. The thought had come too fast, she noticed, and it came with a picture of Leila as "the careless one," though Leila had been on the team for fourteen months.
She opened the full record instead. Leila had handled over two hundred shipments without a returned pallet. Then she checked the day of the error: the postcode template had been changed that morning by another department, and no one had told the team.
Soo-ah deleted her draft. She called Leila, explained what went wrong, and asked her to help write a checklist for template changes.

How many pallets came back because of the wrong postcodes?
Two pallets came back.
Why did Soo-ah stop before sending the message about Leila?
She noticed the thought had come too fast and brought a picture of Leila as 'the careless one', which made her doubt that one error should decide things.
What steps did Soo-ah take before deciding, and what did they show?
She looked at Leila's full record of over two hundred shipments and checked the day's context, finding the postcode template had been changed without warning.
How might Leila feel being asked to write the checklist instead of being moved off the export run?
Leila would likely feel trusted and fairly treated, since her long record counted and the real cause was fixed rather than blamed on her.

Read this:

Wednesday
Today Kamal told me a secret behind the library. He wants to join the kathak class, but he's scared his cousins will laugh. "You're the only one who knows," he said.
I felt special. Also like I was holding something that could break.
At lunch Sonam asked why Kamal was so quiet. I just said, "Dunno."
I've decided: I'll keep it. It's his to tell. If it were something that could hurt him, like someone being mean to him at home, I'd tell a teacher and explain to him why. But this is just his dream.
Maybe I'll go with him to watch the class.
Tenzin

Which class does Kamal want to join?
The kathak class.
How did Tenzin feel when Kamal shared the secret?
Tenzin felt special and trusted, but also responsible, as if holding something that could break.
When would Tenzin tell an adult instead of keeping the secret?
If the secret meant Kamal could be hurt, Tenzin would tell a teacher and explain why.
How might Kamal feel knowing Tenzin kept his secret?
Kamal would likely feel safe and trust Tenzin more.
Make a poster line about covering your mouth when you cough. All capital letters, fewer than eight words.
COVER YOUR MOUTH WHEN YOU COUGH

Read this:

'Lavanya, a word before you pick your shifts.'
'Sure, Sarika.'
'Take Dr Menon's night shifts if you can. She actually explains.'
'I haven't met her yet.'
'Nobody needs to meet her. Ask any intern.'
'And Dr Rao?'
'Nice man. But double-check everything he signs. Twice.'
'Has he done something wrong?'
'Not big. Small things. A missed dose chart, a late handover. Everyone knows.'
'That's... a lot to know about someone I've never seen.'
'Welcome to the hospital. By next month, people will be saying things about you too.'
'Like what?'
'Like whether you finish your notes before handover. Whether you answer the ward phone.'
Lavanya looked down at her clipboard, at the notes she hadn't finished yet. 'Okay. Then I'd better finish these.'
Sarika laughed. 'See? You're learning faster than Rao.'

Whose night shifts does Sarika tell Lavanya to take?
Sarika tells her to take Dr Menon's night shifts because she actually explains.
What did Lavanya realise when she looked at her unfinished notes?
She realised that people would soon judge her by small things like finishing notes before handover, just as they judged Dr Rao.
What choice did Lavanya make after the conversation, and why does it matter?
She decided to finish her notes, because small, consistent habits like that are what the ward will remember and pass on about her.
How might Dr Rao feel if he knew what interns were told about him?
He might feel upset or unfairly labelled, since his reputation came from small slips and was spread before new interns ever met him.
I have drank two glasses of water already.

I have drunk two glasses of water already.
Why: after "have", use the past participle "drunk", not "drank".
When did I reach home last night?
I don't know when you reached home last night, as I can't see your movements. Your own memory or a family member might help.

Read this:

I'm Nandini, and I live next door to Bidisha. I was at her fifth birthday. Before the cake, her grandfather sat in his chair, and Bidisha bent to touch his feet. “Aashirwad,” she announced, though she said it as “ashi-wat,” and he tapped her head, chuckling. She ran to fetch a plate of sweets for the old aunt. Then she stood on tiptoe by the cake, eyes squeezed shut, for the family's little wish. I can't know what she felt inside. But afterwards she looked around at every face, as if to check she'd done it right.

What did Bidisha do before the cake in front of her grandfather?
Bidisha bent to touch his feet.
Why might Bidisha have looked at every face after the wish?
Bidisha seems to care whether she did the family's custom right, and wants to see that people are pleased and that she belongs.
How could a relative respond to Bidisha's checking looks?
A relative could smile and say, “You did it just like us,” so that Bidisha's pride in belonging is confirmed.
How might Bidisha's grandfather see her mispronounced “ashi-wat”?
Bidisha's grandfather seems touched and amused, since he tapped her head and chuckled instead of correcting her.
Maine dost se kaha "I'll give you a missed call." Foreigner samajh nahi paya. Kya bolun?

A "missed call" is a call that rings and is not answered. In India people use it as a signal, but many foreigners do not know this habit. You can say: "I'll ring once and hang up, then you can call me back."

Note from the class teacher, Thursday.
Vaibhav has been quiet and edgy since the start of term. When the class made Father's Day cards, he said he'd "lost his pencil" and sat looking out of the window. I later learned from his mother that his parents have separated.
Today I noticed him talking quietly with Joseph at the back of the class during break. Joseph just nodded and listened. Vaibhav looked lighter afterwards and joined in the cricket match.
I spoke to Vaibhav briefly after school and told him he could always talk to me as well. He didn't say much, but he smiled.

What did the class make that Vaibhav avoided?
Father's Day cards.
How had Vaibhav seemed since the start of term?
He seemed quiet, edgy and embarrassed, avoiding anything that might reveal his parents' separation.
What helped Vaibhav start to feel lighter?
Telling one trusted friend, Joseph, who listened, and knowing the teacher was also there to talk to.
How might Joseph see his role in helping Vaibhav?
Joseph seems to understand that listening quietly was enough, without making it a big deal.

Lalit: had to pick what actually matters. Ended up with 9 formulas. Before I'd have copied 30

How many formulas did Lalit end up with on the chapter 5 sheet?
Lalit ended up with 9 formulas.
How did Lalit feel about the two hours spent on the chapter 5 sheet?
Lalit was worn out but satisfied; the tired emoji shows the effort, and cutting 30 formulas to 9 shows why it felt worth it.
What could Saurabh add to check whether the sheets are working, and why?
Saurabh could write a timed mock from memory and mark it, because the scores show whether the sheets hold the essentials.
How might Saurabh see Lalit's advice to make their own sheet?

Monday night
Today in the review Mehak told the whole room the launch slipped because "Ojas never sent the test results." I sent them on the 3rd. I have the email.
The reply in my head was pure poison: "Maybe try opening your inbox, Mehak." My jaw actually hurt from holding it in. I said only, "I'll check the timeline and follow up," and wrote down her exact words.
After the meeting I did three things. Found the email from the 3rd, with the attachment and her reply, "thanks, got it." Wrote a short, dated note of what was said in the room. Sent both to our manager with one line: "Could we correct the record, and agree on how test results are handed over?"
No sarcasm. No group chat. Still furious, honestly. But tomorrow I'll be the one with the facts, not the one who started a fight.

When were the test results sent?
The test results were sent on the 3rd.
What was Ojas feeling when Mehak shifted the blame in the review?
Ojas felt furious and wronged, with a sarcastic reply ready and a jaw that hurt from holding it in.
What three steps did Ojas take after the meeting?
Found the email from the 3rd with Mehak's "thanks, got it" reply, wrote a dated note of what was said, and sent both to the manager asking to correct the record and agree on handovers.
What would change if Ojas had answered with sarcasm in the room?
The review would have turned into a public fight, and Ojas might have looked like the aggressor instead of the one with the facts.

I'm Vinita, I'm in the science club, and I noticed something at Tuesday's meeting that I keep thinking about.
Lokesh, our captain, didn't let anyone speak at the start. He gave each of us a sticky note and said, "Five minutes, write your idea for our open day event. Alone."
Usually Aryan talks first and we all go along. This time the room was silent except for pens.
Then Lokesh stuck all the notes on the board. Some were poster shows, some a magic-science demo. One note said: "A quiz where visitors play against club members, with torches as buzzers."
It was from Meera, who never talks in meetings.
When the class voted, the torch quiz won by a lot. Meera was looking down at her desk, but she was smiling. I don't know what Lokesh was thinking, but he looked very pleased.

What did Lokesh give each member at the start?
He gave each of us a sticky note.
What might Meera looking down but smiling suggest?
It suggests Meera felt shy but happy and proud that the idea won, though Vinita can only guess.
What else could Lokesh try to keep quieter members involved?
He could keep the silent writing for every meeting and let quieter members present their own notes, if they want to.
How might Aryan experience this new way of starting meetings?
Aryan may feel a bit held back from speaking first, but still gets to share an idea on a note like everyone else.

The wedding hall was loud with drums, and the ceremony was taking forever. Aditi's Masi held up a plate. "One laddoo now, or two when the pheras finish?" Aditi, five, looked at the golden laddoo right there. The pheras felt as far away as next year. She grabbed the one and stuffed it in. Her cousin Suraj, six, sat on his hands and chose two. When the pheras ended, Masi gave Suraj his two. Aditi's lip trembled. "Not fair!" she wailed, and hid her face in Masi's sari.

What did Masi offer Aditi?
One laddoo now, or two when the pheras finish.
Why did Aditi grab the one laddoo?
Aditi felt so eager for the laddoo right in front of her that the end of the pheras seemed impossibly far away, so waiting felt unbearable.
How could Masi help Aditi wait next time?
Masi could hide the plate, give Aditi something to do like counting the drums, and tell her how many rounds are left.
How might Suraj have felt sitting on his hands?
Suraj probably found the waiting hard too, and felt proud and pleased when the two laddoos came.

Preschool note, Eid week

The yard was decorated with paper lanterns for the Eid party. Jeevan tripped on the steps and scraped his knee, and he cried out.
Yusuf was right next to him. He did not move. He stood with his arms stiff, screamed and cried even louder than Jeevan, eyes squeezed shut. He did not look at Jeevan's knee at all.
I cleaned Jeevan's knee while a helper held Yusuf. Once both were calm, Yusuf asked, "Is Jeevan broken?" and gave him the lantern he had made.

What did Jeevan trip on?
Jeevan tripped on the steps.
Why did Yusuf stand stiff and cry louder than Jeevan?
Yusuf was so frightened and upset by Jeevan's fall that his own distress took over, so he could not move to help.
What was a wise way for the adults to handle both children?
One adult cared for Jeevan's knee while a helper held Yusuf, so both got comfort, and later Yusuf could show his caring.
How might Jeevan feel when Yusuf gives him his lantern?
Jeevan might feel cared for and cheered up, seeing that his friend was worried about him.

Last year on the trip to the science park, my small bottle was empty by noon. My mouth felt like paper and I had to ask Hemant for sips, which made me feel bad. So this time I packed the big steel bottle. Amma said it was heavy, but I said I would rather be heavy than thirsty. I also told Hemant, "Bring a big one too, it gets really hot there." He laughed but agreed. At noon we sat in the shade, both bottles still half full, and I remembered last year and smiled. - Sonali

Why did Sonali have to ask Hemant for sips last year?
Sonali's small bottle was empty by noon.
How did Sonali feel about asking Hemant for sips last year?
Sonali felt bad and uncomfortable about it, and that memory pushed the change to a bigger bottle.
What other approach could Sonali use to make sure water lasts through a hot day, and why?
Sonali could ask the teacher where taps are on the route and top up there, so the day does not depend on one bottle.
How might Hemant see Sonali's advice to bring a big bottle?
He laughed, so it may seem a bit fussy at first, but at noon his bottle is half full too, which suggests the advice was sensible.

Read this:

I'm Aadhya and I'm eleven now. When I was eight, I thought I was lazy and dumb, because reading took me forever. The others finished the chapter and I was still on the first page, sounding words in my head.

So I stopped. If I was dumb, why try? I hid the reader in my school bag and said I'd forgotten it.

My friend Ira didn't believe it. One day she brought comics to my house. "Read me the bubbles," she said. "Only the bubbles." The bubbles were short, so I could. We read the whole comic. It took ages, but we laughed a lot.

We did that every Saturday. Slowly, my eyes got faster.

Now I know I wasn't dumb or lazy. I was just slow at reading, and slow can be practised. I still read slower than Ira. But I read.

What did Ira ask Aadhya to read in the comics?
"Read me the bubbles. Only the bubbles."
Why did Aadhya stop trying to read at eight?
Aadhya believed the words dumb and lazy, so trying felt pointless. The label made reading seem like something impossible, not something that could be practised.
Which choice of Ira's worked, and why?
Starting with short speech bubbles in a fun comic let Aadhya succeed and enjoy reading. Practising every Saturday built the actual skill that the label had hidden.
What might Ira have noticed that made her not believe the label?
Ira probably saw that Aadhya could read, just slowly, and was hiding the reader rather than being unable. Ira seemed to see a friend who needed practice, not a dumb person.

Read this:

The Mumbai airport terminal was chaos: three flights cancelled because of fog in Delhi, and the airline desk had two staff for four hundred passengers. Eshaan, twenty-five, was one of them. A woman, Reena, pushed to the front, shouting. "My mother is having surgery tomorrow morning! I need to be there!" People muttered at her for cutting the line. Eshaan saw her shaking hands, her phone clutched tight. Under the anger, she was terrified. He didn't take the shouting personally. "Ma'am, I understand. You're scared you won't reach her in time. Let me check every option." He found a seat on a train-and-flight route through Jaipur, arriving by six a.m. Reena's shoulders dropped. "Thank you," she whispered. Eshaan took a breath and turned to the next passenger.

Why were the flights cancelled?
Because of fog in Delhi.
What was Reena feeling under her anger?
She was terrified of not reaching her mother before surgery.
What helped Eshaan respond well without being swept up in her emotion?
He read the fear behind her shouting, named it calmly and focused on solving the problem.
How might the other passengers have seen Reena at first?
They likely saw her as rude for cutting the line, not knowing her mother's situation.

Read this:

Afreen wore her grandmother's hand-stitched jacket to school and did not care who stared. She liked being the odd one out, and when Nandini smiled and waved her over to the lunch bench, Afreen said, "I don't need a table," and walked on. Alone, it sometimes felt colder than she admitted.

Sarita had a different plan. She handed out compliments like coins and passed along who said what about whom. By March the popular table saved her a seat. Then she saw a group chat where her new friends called Afreen weird and poor, with a photo of the jacket attached. Sarita had supplied the joke that started it. Her stomach turned hollow, and she wondered what they would say about her once she left the room.

Nandini, meanwhile, noticed how quickly praise for her haircut came from people who had never spoken to her in June. She thanked them warmly but kept her weekends for two friends who had known her since Class 6.

A classmate showed Afreen the chat. Her cheeks burned. It was not her fault, she told herself, and next morning she took screenshots to the school counsellor, who listened, said so too, and went to the year head that same day. On Thursday Afreen joined the robotics club. A week later Sarita deleted the joke, sat at the club table, and apologised.

What did Afreen wear to school that people stared at?
She wore her grandmother's hand-stitched jacket.
How did Afreen's way of standing apart differ from Sarita's way of belonging, and what did each cost?

Afreen kept everyone at a distance with "I don't need a table" and sometimes felt colder than she admitted. Sarita won a seat with compliments and gossip, but it left her stomach hollow and cost her trust once the joke was aimed at Afreen.
What was Sarita feeling when she saw the group chat about Afreen?
She felt hollow and uneasy. Her stomach turned and she wondered what those friends would say about her.
What helped Afreen after she saw the chat?
She took screenshots to the school counsellor, who acted the same day, and she joined the robotics club, a place where she fitted in.

Read this:

Grandparents' Day at school fell in the last week of December, with a heater in the hall and tea in paper cups. Salma had practised a speech about her Dadi. Her little brother, from Class 2, kept grabbing the microphone and saying "My Dadi!" before her.
"He's ruining it," Salma hissed to her friend Gargi.
Dadi pulled Salma close. "When your Abbu was small, he did the same to his sister. She let him say one line, and then she said the rest. Everyone remembers her speech."
So Salma knelt, let her brother say "My Dadi makes the best sheer khurma," and then stood up and gave hers. The hall laughed at his line and clapped at hers. Gargi gave her a thumbs up.

What line did Salma's little brother say into the microphone?
He said, "My Dadi makes the best sheer khurma."
What was Salma feeling when she hissed to Gargi?
Salma felt frustrated and annoyed that her brother kept grabbing the microphone and, she thought, ruining her speech.
Which idea from Dadi worked, and why?
Letting her brother say one line first worked, because he got his turn and stopped competing, and Salma still gave her speech.
How might Dadi feel watching both grandchildren speak about her?
Dadi probably feels proud and loved, and pleased that her story helped Salma choose patience over a fight.

Read this:

In the art room of a Chandigarh school, Payal scribbled a big black line across Meher's sunflower because Meher had taken the yellow crayon. Meher burst into tears. Baljeet Ma'am came over and knelt. "Payal, I can see you wanted the yellow. Scribbling on Meher's work isn't okay. How can we help her?" Payal stared at her shoes, then looked up. "Sorry, Meher. I'll help fix it." Together they turned the black line into a stem. When Baljeet Ma'am patted her shoulder, Payal leaned into her side for a moment.

Why did Payal scribble on Meher's sunflower?
Because Meher had taken the yellow crayon.
Why did Payal lean into Baljeet Ma'am's side at the end?
Payal felt comforted and cared for, not rejected, after being corrected kindly, and trusted her teacher.
How could a teacher keep correction feeling like care?
Name what the child wanted, say clearly what isn't okay, and invite them to fix it, as Baljeet Ma'am did.
How does Meher see Payal helping turn the line into a stem?
Meher likely feels her hurt was taken seriously and is pleased her sunflower got fixed.
Please rewrite as an announcement for the school assembly: no school tomorrow, rain.
Good morning, everyone. Because of the heavy rain, school will remain closed tomorrow. Please stay safe and look out for updates.

Read this:

At the KG library corner, Vishal knocked his water bottle over the big picture book. The pages went soggy. He froze, then looked around. Nobody had seen. He walked up to Pallavi Ma'am, his face red. “Ma'am, I spilled water on the dinosaur book.” Pallavi put down her pen. “Thank you for telling me, Vishal. That's very honest.” She showed him how to stand the book open by the window so the pages could dry. “Bottles stay closed near books.” Vishal nodded, relieved.

Which book did Vishal spill water on?
The dinosaur book.
What was Vishal feeling when he walked up to Pallavi Ma'am with a red face?
He was nervous and embarrassed, but chose honesty even though no one had seen, and felt relieved afterwards.
What did Pallavi Ma'am do that encourages future truth-telling?
She thanked and praised his honesty, showed him how to dry the book and gave a clear rule about bottles.
How might Pallavi Ma'am see Vishal's confession, given that no one saw the spill?
She likely values it highly, since he chose honesty when he could have hidden it, which is why she thanks and praises him.

Read this:

"Ankita, it's two in the morning. Still on the lab report?"
"Just checking the formatting, Ma."
Jyoti sat on the bed. "You checked it at dinner too."
"There might be a mistake."
"And if there is?"
Ankita's hands stopped on the keyboard. "Then they'll see."
"See what?"
"That I'm normal. Everyone's always said I'm the one who never makes mistakes. Since school. You, Papa, my teachers."
Jyoti was quiet. "We said that because we were proud."
"I know. But now if I get one thing wrong, I'm just ordinary."
"Do you even like chemistry anymore?"
Ankita laughed shakily. "I don't know. I don't have time to think about liking it. I'm too busy not failing."
Jyoti closed the laptop gently. "Ordinary is allowed in this house."

What was Ankita still checking at two in the morning?
The formatting of the lab report.
What is Ankita afraid a single mistake would show?
That Ankita is ordinary; the family's pride in never making mistakes has become something to protect, so fear drives the checking more than love of chemistry.
What choice by Jyoti helps, and why?
Closing the laptop and saying ordinary is allowed, which separates Ankita's worth at home from flawless work.
How does Jyoti feel on hearing "too busy not failing"?
Jyoti seems saddened to realise the family's proud praise became a weight, and wants to lift it.
What does "balcony" mean? Why do we feel hungry before lunch?

1. A balcony is a small platform with a railing that sticks out from an upper floor.
2. The stomach is empty after several hours. Because the body needs food for energy.

Read this:

Subject: Science exhibition project

Dear Jomon Sir,

I'm sorry the project isn't ready. I know you asked for the first draft on Monday and it's now Thursday.

I want to be honest, because you've been kind to me.

I haven't been lazy. I've opened the file almost every evening. But each time, I think: what if my water-filter model doesn't work? What if everyone sees it and thinks I'm not as good as they thought? So I close it and do something else, and tell myself I'll start fresh tomorrow.

Now I have less time than ever, and the model will probably be worse than if I'd started last week. I can see that.

Could I show you what I have tomorrow, even if it's rough? I think it would help to have someone look at it early.

Gargi

What is Gargi's science exhibition project?
Gargi's project is a water-filter model.
Why does Gargi keep closing the file?
Gargi feels anxious that a model that fails would reveal weakness, so putting it off protects Gargi's self-image.
What step does Gargi propose, and why might it help?
Showing Jomon Sir the rough work tomorrow; early feedback makes the task less scary and gives time to fix it.
How might Jomon Sir feel reading this email?
Jomon Sir might feel concerned but touched by the honesty, and glad to help early.

Hemant, ten, had moved from the municipal school to the big school across the flyover in Thane in June. On the first day Omkar told him cheerfully, "Municipal kids are always weak in English, na? Don't feel bad." Hemant had read three storybooks that month. But on Friday, when the teacher said, "Dictation, twenty words," a knot formed in his stomach. He felt Omkar's eyes on his notebook. 'Receive.' Was it ie or ei? He knew this. He wrote it, rubbed it out, wrote it again. By the time he looked up, the teacher was on word nine. He had missed three. Walking home, he spelled 'receive' perfectly in his head, which made it worse.

How many storybooks had Hemant read that month?
Three storybooks.
Why did Hemant keep rubbing out 'receive'?
Feeling Omkar's eyes and remembering the remark about municipal kids, he was so afraid of proving it true that he doubted a word he knew.
What small step could Hemant try before the next dictation?
He could remind himself of the three books he read and focus on one word at a time instead of on who might be watching.
How might Omkar read Hemant's dictation mark, and why would that be misleading?
Omkar might think the low mark proves the remark, not realising the fear of being judged is what made Hemant miss the words.

"The Holy One said, 'Behold, O son of Pritha, my forms by hundreds and thousands, various, divine, diverse in hue and shape. Behold the Adityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Aswins, and the Maruts. Behold, O Bharata, innumerable marvels unseen before (by thee). Behold, O thou of curly hair, the entire universe of mobiles and immobiles, collected together in this body of mine, whatever else thou mayst wish to see. Thou art, however, not competent to behold me with this eye of thine. I give thee celestial sight. Behold my sovereign mystic nature.'"

Answer from the text. What does the Holy One give, and why?

The Holy One says the listener cannot see the divine forms with ordinary eyes, so the Holy One gives heavenly sight. The listener can then see the many forms, the gods and the whole universe gathered in the Holy One's body.

The courtyard floor was wet from washing. Anjali ran, slipped, and sat down hard on her bottom. For a second she was silent. Then she looked up at Mohit, her father, and burst out laughing.
"No shame, laughing when she falls!" said her aunt.
Mohit stayed calm, crouched, and checked her hands and back. "Bump! Up you get." Anjali held out her arms, still giggling.

Why was the courtyard floor wet?
It was wet from washing.
What might Anjali's laugh after falling have meant?
It might have been relief that she wasn't badly hurt, or confusion after the surprise; looking at Mohit shows she was checking how he felt.
What did Mohit do that was wise?
He stayed calm, checked her hands and back, and named the bump lightly, showing her the moment was safe.
How does the aunt see Anjali's laugh?
The aunt sees it as shameless, as if Anjali should be crying, not as a small child's relief or confusion.

Karthik, you say you can't leave engineering because you've done two years. Listen to your Zeenat aunty for a minute. At nineteen I started a pharmacy degree because my father liked the idea. By second year I knew I hated it; I was happiest editing the college magazine. But I thought, two years, all those fees, all those nights. So I stayed. Third year, fourth year. I passed, just, and worked in a medicine shop for a year feeling like a ghost. At twenty-three I finally started journalism, older than everyone in my class. The two extra years didn't save the first two. They only added two more I didn't want. The day I left, I cried, and then I slept better than I had in years.

What was young Zeenat happiest doing in college?
Editing the college magazine.
Why did young Zeenat stay in the pharmacy degree?
She felt she couldn't waste two years of fees and nights, so the fear of losing them outweighed how unhappy she was.
Which choice in the story could have come earlier, and what might have helped?
Leaving after second year; asking whether she would start the degree today could have shown that the extra years wouldn't rescue the first two.
How might Zeenat's father have felt about her staying in pharmacy?
He was probably pleased, since he liked the idea, and may not have known how unhappy she was.

Lalit walked home along the canal path with Chetan after the evening class at the town institute. It was the accounts course, twice a week, and Lalit had done six months of it and disliked every session.

"Six months gone," said Chetan. "If you leave now, all that is wasted."

Lalit kicked a stone. "That's the wrong question. Those six months are gone whether I stay or not. The question is the next six." He counted on his fingers. "Six more months, Tuesdays and Saturdays, four hours each. Would I rather spend those on this, or on the drawing class that starts in June?"

He was quiet for a minute. "The drawing class. I keep what I learned about spreadsheets. I don't need the certificate."

How many months of the course had Lalit already done?
Lalit had done six months of the course.
How did Lalit feel about the accounts course?
Lalit disliked every session and was reluctant to spend more time on it.
What could Lalit do before leaving the course?
Lalit could talk with the institute and family, and check whether part of the course can be kept, so that the decision rests on facts about what lies ahead.
How might Chetan see Lalit's reasoning?
Chetan may feel surprised, having thought that leaving meant wasting the six months, and may be persuaded by the new question.

In the small town of Wardha, Nandini was preparing for her nursing entrance exam. Her cousin Jagdish, who had cleared it last year, came over one evening.

"Don't read the whole book every night," he said. "Do one chapter a day. Then close it and tell me what you remember."

It felt terrible at first. Nandini would sit on the charpai, eyes shut, trying to recall the parts of the heart, and only get half. "This is so much harder than reading," she said.

"Harder is the point," Jagdish said.

Every few days, he'd ask her about an old chapter, just as it began to fade. By the exam, even the earliest chapters came back quickly. Nandini walked out of the hall smiling.

Where did Nandini sit when trying to recall the parts of the heart?
On the charpai.
How did Nandini feel about testing herself at first?
She felt frustrated and discouraged, finding it much harder than just reading.
Why did Jagdish's method work, even though it felt harder?
Recalling without looking and revisiting old chapters just as they faded made the memories stronger.
How might Jagdish feel seeing Nandini smile after the exam?
Jagdish probably feels proud and glad his advice helped.
Report what she asked: Ananya asked the teacher, "Can I submit the file tomorrow?"
Ananya asked the teacher whether she could submit the file the next day.

The power went out at school just as the rain started, and the van was late, so Kiran had to walk home. That meant passing the old peepal tree by the water tank. A lady in white sat there at dusk. Salma had said so, and Rafi, and the big boys in Class 7, and even the canteen uncle had laughed and said, "Don't stop there." Kiran had heard it maybe a hundred times. It felt as solid as the tank itself. Now Kiran stood at the corner, stomach tight. "Has anyone actually seen her?" Salma asked, sharing the umbrella. Kiran started to answer, then stopped. Nobody had. Everyone had only heard. They walked past together, fast, and saw only wet leaves and a stray dog.

Who had told Kiran about the lady in white?
Salma, Rafi, the big boys in Class 7, and even the canteen uncle.
What does Kiran's tight stomach at the corner show?
Kiran was truly scared 😰 because the story had been heard so many times that it felt as solid as the tank itself.
Which question became the turning point, and how could Kiran use it again?
Salma's "Has anyone actually seen her?" Kiran could ask it whenever a story feels true only because everyone keeps saying it.
Why might Salma ask that question even though Salma had helped spread the story?
Standing near the real tree in the rain, Salma may have begun to doubt it, and asking aloud helped both friends feel brave enough to walk past.
We have approve in our word list this week. What does it mean?

To approve means to agree to something officially, or to think that something is good. It is a verb.
Example: The teacher approved our plan for the science project.

Last month I posted in our class group about Mridul's surprise birthday: a plan, a time, a shared cost. I'm Sunaina. The message showed "Seen by 23". Replies: zero. For two hours nothing. I kept checking. I felt stupid, like everyone thought my plan was silly, or worse, that they didn't care about me. I almost deleted it. Then Mridul, who wasn't in the group, called me about something else, and I blurted it out. He laughed. "It's exam week! Half of them read everything at the library and forget to reply. And people hate committing to money in a group." That evening, replies trickled in: "sorry, lab all day", "count me in", "can I pay later?" By night eighteen people had said yes. Looking back, I'd read the silence as a feeling about me. It was mostly just people being busy.

How many people had said yes by night?
Eighteen people.
What was Sunaina feeling during the two hours of silence?
Sunaina felt stupid and hurt, worried everyone thought the plan was silly or didn't care.
What did Sunaina learn about reading group chat silence?
That slow replies usually reflect busyness or hesitation about money, not feelings about the sender.
How did Mridul explain the silence?
He said it was exam week, people read at the library and forget to reply, and many avoid committing to money in a group.

I'm Ojas, Binita's big brother, and I was the judge of the staring game on our balcony.

Binita and our little cousin sat nose to nose. No blinking, no smiling. Binita's lips kept twitching, and she pressed them together hard, cheeks shaking. I thought she would burst.

Then our cousin's eyes went watery and the chin started to wobble. Binita noticed straight away. "Stop, stop, game over!" She patted the cousin's hand. "You were really good."

After that, she finally let her giggle out.

Where did the staring game happen?
On the balcony.
What does Binita's twitching lips and shaking cheeks suggest she was feeling?
She was probably full of giggles and working hard to hold them in to win the game. She may also have felt a little nervous about losing in front of her brother.
Which choice worked, and why?
Binita stopped the game as soon as the cousin's chin wobbled, which kept it fun and safe instead of pushing on to win.
How does the little cousin experience the game?
The cousin finds it hard and gets close to tears, and is comforted when Binita ends the game and praises them.

It was raining, so all twenty-five children were stuck indoors, and lunch was in five minutes. In the noise, Sachin snatched the green crayon from Ayaan, and Ayaan began to cry. Chandrika Miss had a stack of plates in her hands. She put them down anyway and crouched to Sachin's height. "Sachin, look. See Ayaan's eyes? They're wet. His face is all crumpled. Ayaan is sad." Sachin looked at Ayaan for a long moment, the crayon still in his fist. His own face went quiet. Slowly, he opened his hand.

How many children were stuck indoors?
All twenty-five children were stuck indoors.
What does Sachin's face going quiet suggest?
It suggests he was noticing Ayaan's sadness and starting to feel it himself.
Why was it worth Chandrika Miss putting down the plates, even with lunch so close?
Taking a moment at Sachin's level to point out Ayaan's wet eyes helped him link the snatch to the tears, which a quick telling-off would miss.
What would change if Chandrika Miss had just taken the crayon back herself?
Ayaan would have the crayon, but Sachin would miss seeing Ayaan's sadness and learning why his action mattered.

In the church in Beirut, Sami, eight, stood in the line of children in white, his new shoes pinching. His grandmother had pressed his shirt twice. His cousin Tariq, who had made his first communion the year before, winked from the pew.

Sami's stomach fluttered. Everyone was watching: his parents, both grandmothers, the neighbours from the third floor.

When his turn came he remembered to fold his hands, and he didn't trip. Afterwards the family took eleven photos on the steps.

At lunch he whispered to Tariq, "What was supposed to feel different?"

Tariq shrugged. "Teta says it means you're bigger now in church. You take part properly."

Sami chewed on that with his almond cake. He felt proud. He also still didn't quite know what had changed.

How many photos did the family take on the steps?
The family took eleven photos on the steps.
What mixed feelings did Sami have after the ceremony?
Sami felt proud of doing it right, yet confused about what was supposed to feel different.
What would help Sami understand the rite?
An adult, perhaps Teta or the priest, sitting with him to explain what the step means and what he now takes part in.
How might Tariq see Sami's question?
Tariq takes it lightly, sharing Teta's simple explanation, maybe because he wondered the same last year.

When Neelam started leaving Yamini's messages on 'seen', Yamini knew. For three months her cousin had been her only lifeline through the low weeks at the teacher-training hostel in Sirsi: every tearful call, every sleepless night. Last Sunday Neelam finally said it: 'I love you, but I'm drained. I have my own exams.'
Yamini spent a day feeling ashamed. Then she took a sheet of paper and made a plan with more than one name on it.
The district hospital's counsellor, Wednesdays, booked through the hostel warden. A fixed call with Amma and Appa every Friday at eight, where she would actually tell them how she was. The women who walk around the temple tank at six every morning, whom the mess cook introduced her to.
With each one she said what she hoped for: listening on Wednesdays, just talking on Fridays, company in the mornings. And to Neelam she wrote: 'You're still my favourite person. Just not my only one.'

When does the fixed call with Amma and Appa happen?
Every Friday at eight.
How did Yamini feel after Neelam said she was drained?
Ashamed for a day, then determined to build a plan with more than one person in it.
Why is telling each person what she hopes for a good step?
It keeps each role clear and small, so no one is overwhelmed and Yamini knows whom to turn to for what.
How might Neelam feel reading Yamini's message?
Relieved and touched, freed from carrying everything while knowing she is still loved. 🤍

The monsoon had flooded the hostel basement again, and Vishal's placement books were stacked on his bed to keep them dry. Still, at 2 pm on Saturday he pulled on his raincoat. "Coding club?" asked Abhinav from the top bunk. "They don't even give you a certificate." "I know." At the municipal school down the road, nine children in damp uniforms waited around two old laptops. Last month they had made a program that printed their names in stars. Today Vishal showed them how to save it on a pen drive and teach the next batch. "So when you're gone, we can still do it?" asked Salma, eleven. "That's the idea." He walked back through the puddles, already planning Monday's mock interview, and felt oddly steady.

How many children waited around the laptops?
Nine children.
Why did Vishal keep going to the coding club without a certificate?
He felt a quiet satisfaction in building something that would outlast him, like the children being able to teach the next batch.
How can Vishal balance the club with his placement goals?
He can keep the club to a fixed Saturday slot and train the children to run it themselves, so both his ambition and the project have room.
What does Salma's question suggest about how the children see the club?
Salma seems worried the club might end when Vishal leaves, and is relieved to hear it is meant to carry on.

In the waiting room of the children's clinic in Aizawl, Lalremsiami sat with the baby asleep on her shoulder and dark circles under her eyes.
Disha, the clinic nurse, sat next to her while they waited. "How are nights?"
"Our plan was that I'd do all the nights, since I'm on leave and my husband, Mapuia, works. It seemed fair on paper."
"And now?"
"One month in, I'm so tired I cried over a spilled cup of tea."
Disha nodded. "That happens a lot. What does Mapuia say?"
"We talked last night. We're changing it. He'll take alternate nights. And his cousin knows a woman who helps part-time in the mornings."
"That sounds wise. And keep asking each other how you're coping, not just the baby."
"And if I keep feeling this low?"
"Then tell the doctor at your check-up. That's what we're here for."

What is Lalremsiami's husband's name?
Mapuia.
How was Lalremsiami feeling after the first month of doing all the nights?
Lalremsiami was exhausted and low, so tired she cried over a spilled cup of tea.
What else could Lalremsiami and Mapuia do to keep the new plan working?
They could set a regular time each week to ask each other how they're coping and adjust nights or help as needed.
How might Mapuia be affected by the change?
Mapuia takes on alternate nights, so he will be more tired at work but more involved and able to support Lalremsiami.

By March, Tariq was answering emails from the London office at midnight and waking at five with his heart racing. When he asked his manager, Nour, for a lighter week after three months of overtime, Nour didn't look up from the screen. "Everyone's tired. Can you have the forecast by Thursday?"

On the bus home Tariq realised he had forgotten to eat lunch for four days.

That night he did three things. He opened a document and wrote down every late night and weekend, with dates. He read the company's leave policy, which he had never opened. And he emailed HR asking about the wellbeing programme.

On Monday he booked five days of leave. Nour frowned but approved it. Tariq spent the first two days sleeping and the third walking by the river, noticing he could taste food again.

How many days had Tariq forgotten to eat lunch?
Tariq had forgotten to eat lunch for four days.
What was Tariq feeling when Nour asked for the forecast?
Tariq felt unseen and exhausted, with a racing heart, as his request for a lighter week was ignored.
Which steps protected Tariq, and why?
Recording his hours, reading the leave policy, contacting HR and taking leave put his recovery first instead of pushing until he collapsed.
How might Nour see Tariq's leave?
Nour seemed focused on deadlines and may see the leave as inconvenient, even though it prevents a bigger breakdown.

Why does he want Jane to sleep in the nursery?

"And there is room enough in Adele's little bed for you. You must share it with her to-night, Jane: it is no wonder that the incident you have related should make you nervous, and I would rather you did not sleep alone: promise me to go to the nursery."
The incident she described would naturally make her nervous, and he would rather she did not sleep alone. So he asks her to share Adele's little bed.

Two days before the school sports day, Hafsa found Nikita in the staffroom with a list split into two columns.
"Why is 'banner' in the right column?" Hafsa asked. "You redid it three times last year."
"Exactly," Nikita said. "Nobody remembered the banner. The left column is what must be perfect. First-aid table staffed all day, water every hundred metres, the long-jump pit raked and checked for stones. And the engraved medals: once a name is cut into metal, we can't undo it, so the list gets checked twice, by two people."
"And the right column?"
"Certificates, decorations, the music list. Good enough is fine. If a certificate prints off-centre, we reprint one."
Hafsa read the medal list slowly while Nikita checked the first-aid box. They found one misspelled name, Tejaswini with an 'i' missing.
On the day, the banner sagged a little. Nobody got hurt, and every medal was right.

What mistake did Hafsa find on the medal list?
A misspelled name: Tejaswini with an 'i' missing.
Why might Hafsa be puzzled about where the banner is listed?
Hafsa seems surprised and puzzled, since Nikita redid the banner three times last year yet now puts it in the good-enough column.
How did Nikita decide which things got extra care?
Nikita gave extra care to what affects safety or can't be undone, like first aid, water, the pit and the engraved names, and let decorations be good enough.
What would change if the medal list had not been checked twice?
A student might have been handed a medal with a misspelled name cut into the metal, a mistake that cannot be undone.

Sabina had grown up in London and came back to her grandmother's village near Malappuram for the first time in ten years. The cousins called her "the English one." In London, people had asked where she was really from.

At the well, the older women spoke too fast for her rusty Malayalam. She smiled, understood half, and felt like a visitor in her own family.

Her cousin Varun found her sitting alone on the veranda. "You're sad."

"I'm not from here and I'm not from there. I don't know what I am."

Varun shrugged. "The kids at the tuition centre want to practise English for their exams. You're the only one who can help them and still understand their Malayalam jokes."

The next afternoon she taught twelve children. When she got a word wrong in Malayalam, they corrected her, laughing. She kept a notebook of new words.

That evening she felt, for once, useful to both halves of herself.

How many children did Sabina teach?
Twelve children.
How did Sabina feel at the well with the older women?
She felt like an outsider and a visitor in her own family, sad and unsure where she belonged.
What turned Sabina's in-between identity into a strength?
Teaching the children English while learning their Malayalam, which let her act as a bridge between both cultures.
How might the tuition children see Sabina?
The children likely enjoyed having a teacher who helps with English and laughs with them when she gets Malayalam wrong.

I'm Dhruv, and in my third year I learned the smartest thing I know from a two-minute walk. I'd been stuck on a statistics assignment for two hours. The same formula, the same wrong answer. I was tense and staring so hard my eyes ached. My friend Mehak came in and said, "Explain it to me." I started talking. "First I take the mean, then I subtract..." And halfway through the sentence, I heard it. I'd subtracted from the wrong column. Two hours, and the error showed up as soon as I said it aloud. Now, when I'm stuck for more than twenty minutes, I walk to the canteen and back, or I explain it to someone. It's not giving up. It's a tool.

What did Dhruv realise halfway through the explanation?
Dhruv had subtracted from the wrong column.
How was Dhruv feeling before Mehak came in?
Dhruv felt tense and frustrated, staring so hard that the eyes ached after two hours on the same error.
What does Dhruv now do when stuck, and why does it work?
Dhruv takes a short walk or explains the problem aloud, which breaks tunnel vision and often reveals the error.
How might Mehak feel when Dhruv finds the error mid-sentence?
Mehak might feel amused and pleased, having helped just by listening.

Behind her house in a village near Dharwad, Malti had spent two years and most of her savings on a mushroom shed. Her brother Hrithik had helped build it, and her friend Pankaj from the agriculture office had brought the spawn. But every summer the humidity went wrong and the crop rotted. This July, standing in the stink of another failed batch, Malti asked herself a question Pankaj had once asked her: "If you had never built this shed, would you start it today, knowing what you know?" She sat on an upturned bucket for a long time. The answer was no. She cried a little, for the money, the early mornings, the hope. Then she wrote down what she'd learned: check water, check buyers first, start small. The next week she and Hrithik turned the shed into a shelter for her goats. "Not a waste," Hrithik said. "It's a good roof."

How long had Malti spent on the mushroom shed?
Two years and most of her savings.
Why did Malti cry after deciding to stop?
She was grieving the money, the early mornings and the hope she had put in. Stopping was right, but the loss still hurt.
What question helped Malti decide, and what did she do after answering it?
Whether she would start the shed today, knowing what she knows now. When the answer was no, she wrote down her lessons and turned the shed into a goat shelter.
How might Hrithik see the end of the mushroom project?
He seems to see it without shame, calling the shed "a good roof," which helps Malti feel the effort wasn't wasted.

Tuesday.
Counted today: I checked the news eleven times, refilled my water bottle six times, reorganised my desktop folders, and read half an article about octopuses. Actual work: maybe ninety minutes.
It's not that there's too much. There's too little. Same reconciliation sheets I've done for two years. I could do them half asleep, and mostly I do.
I feel guilty about it all day. Uday, at the next desk, is always busy and slightly stressed. I'm neither.
Tonight I tried to work out what the boredom is asking for. It isn't rest. I sleep fine. It isn't fun, exactly. I think it's difficulty. Something I can't already do.
Tomorrow I'll ask my manager if I can help with the new vendor audit. It's messy and nobody wants it. That might be exactly why I do.
— Jaya

How many times did Jaya check the news today?
Jaya checked the news eleven times.
How does Jaya feel about the small distractions?
Jaya feels bored, restless and vaguely guilty, especially next to a busy colleague.
What does Jaya decide the boredom is asking for, and what step follows?
Difficulty, something new to master, so Jaya plans to ask to help with the messy vendor audit.
How might Uday see Jaya's workday?
Uday, busy and slightly stressed, might not notice Jaya's boredom, or might envy what looks like an easy day.

In a dorm room in Warsaw, Emil and Wei opened the order log again. Their delivery service for student errands had been slow all autumn: a parcel here, a shopping run there. But tonight, sorting by date, Wei pointed. "Look at these bunches. December, January, June. Nearly everything is print jobs, and always the week before exams." Emil scrolled. "Lecture notes. In the next exam period, orders tripled. Wei laughed at the counter. "We did not lose the idea. We just found the part people wanted."

Madhuri: Ishita, people say lab work is all brilliant ideas. What is it really like?

Ishita: A lot of it is a laminated card. Before every experiment I follow the same eleven lines: clean the bench, check the balance reads zero, label the tubes, then buffers, then samples, in that order. Last week I had been up till two with a deadline and my head was cotton. I ran the card anyway. Halfway down I caught myself skipping "label the tubes" because I was in a hurry. The card was right there, so I went back, labelled everything, and the run worked. From memory I would have mixed up two samples.

Madhuri: Does it get boring?

Ishita: Sometimes. But tired me and hurried me do not trust my memory, so I trust the card.

How many lines does the card have?
Ishita follows the same eleven lines before every experiment.
How was Ishita feeling when the head was like cotton, and why use the card anyway?
Ishita was very tired and in a hurry, and did not trust memory in that state, so the card was the safer guide.
What could a new lab assistant do to keep such a card useful?
They could tick each line as it is done and tell the supervisor if a step seems missing or out of date, so the card can be improved.
How might someone relying on Ishita's results see this habit?
They might feel reassured that the samples are labelled and not mixed up, since Ishita follows every step even when tired.

Read this:

By evening on the last day of the Pongal fair, Leela had made a hundred choices: which ride, which sweet, which game, which friend to sit with on the bullock cart.
At the bangle stall, Ishita said, "Pick any one pair. Take your time."
There were red ones, green ones, glass ones with gold dots. Leela stared at them. Her eyes filled with tears.
"I don't know! You pick!" She grabbed the nearest pair, plain brown, without looking.
On the walk home she looked at them and sniffed. "I didn't even want brown."
Ishita put an arm round her. "Tomorrow morning, after sleep, we'll come back and swap them. Morning Leela chooses better."

Which bangles did Leela grab?
Leela grabbed the nearest pair, plain brown.
Why did Leela cry at the bangle stall?
Leela felt overwhelmed and tired after a hundred choices all day, so even picking bangles felt too much.
What does Ishita suggest, and why is it sensible?
Coming back the next morning after sleep to swap, because a rested Leela will choose better.
How does Ishita see Leela's tears?
Ishita sees a tired child rather than a fussy one, and responds gently with an arm round her.

Read this:

On Sunday morning, in their Pune flat, Tarun spread paper and crayons across the floor. "Shalini, remember yesterday at the sweet shop?"
Shalini nodded, not looking up.
"You were angry. I was angry too, and I shouted. That wasn't okay. I'm sorry."
Shalini looked up then, surprised.
"Let's make a plan for angry times," Tarun said. They drew three pictures together: feet stomping softly, a crayon scribbling hard, two arms asking for a hug. Shalini stuck them on the fridge herself, the hug picture lowest, where she could reach it.

Where did Shalini stick the pictures?
On the fridge, with the hug picture lowest where she could reach it.
What did Shalini's surprised look suggest when Tarun said sorry?
She seemed surprised and perhaps relieved that her father admitted shouting too, so she did not carry all the blame.
Which part of Tarun's plan works well for a young child, and why?
Drawing the choices as pictures, because Shalini can see and point to them when she is too angry for words.
How might Tarun feel after apologising to Shalini?
He may feel lighter and hopeful, having modelled repair instead of pretending he did nothing wrong.

What does Joe worry about while the clock works up to strike eight?

"However," said Joe, rising to replenish the fire; "here's the Dutch-clock a-working himself up to being equal to strike Eight of 'em, and she's not come home yet! I hope Uncle Pumblechook's mare mayn't have set a forefoot on a piece o' ice, and gone down."
Joe worries that Uncle Pumblechook's mare may have set a forefoot on a piece of ice and gone down, since 'she' has not come home yet.

Read this:

Week one, a Monday. In the reading room, Pallavi pushed her thesis folder away. "I'll start the literature review tomorrow, properly." Madhuri nodded and kept working, but noticed Pallavi's jaw was tight.

Week two, a Thursday. Same words, softer. "Tomorrow, promise." This time Pallavi left early, and later sent Madhuri a message: "I'm useless." Madhuri read it three times, a knot in her stomach, and replied with a heart.

Week three, a Tuesday. Madhuri waited by the library steps. "Sit with me for twenty minutes," she said. "Just twenty. What's the easiest piece?" Pallavi thought. "Listing the papers I've already read." They sat side by side, Madhuri on her own work, Pallavi typing titles. When the timer went off, Pallavi had a list of eleven and didn't stop. Madhuri pretended not to notice the smile.

How many papers did Pallavi list when the timer went off?
She had a list of eleven.
How did Madhuri feel after reading Pallavi's 'I'm useless' message?
Madhuri felt worried, with a knot in her stomach, unsure how to help beyond sending a heart.
Which choice worked for Madhuri, and why?
Offering to sit together for just twenty minutes and start with the easiest piece worked, because it made starting small and less lonely.
What is it like for Pallavi to keep promising 'tomorrow'?
Each broken promise leaves Pallavi feeling worse about herself, with a tight jaw and eventually calling herself useless.

Read this:

Elif had been in Hamburg for four months, long enough to learn that nobody at school said her name right and that her parents stopped talking when she walked into the kitchen. The divorce papers sat on the fridge under a magnet.
Then Emil, the quiet boy from maths, said, "Come to the Circle on Friday. It's just people who get it."
The room above the bakery was warm and smelled of tea. Twelve people, mostly older teens and a few adults, sat on cushions. A woman named Marta said Elif's name perfectly on the first try. Everyone clapped when Elif said where she came from. They asked about her drawings and wanted to see them.
Marta said, "Here, you're never alone. The world outside doesn't understand people like us."
Walking home under the streetlights, Elif realised she hadn't felt this light since Izmir. She wished Friday would come again tomorrow.

Where was the Circle's room?
Above the bakery.
What does Elif wishing for Friday again reveal about her feelings?
She feels lonely and unsettled at home and school, so the group's warmth makes her feel light and wanted for the first time in months.
What warning sign could a trusted adult help Elif notice?
The line that the outside world doesn't understand 'people like us'; talking with a parent or school counsellor about the group would help her see it clearly.
What might Elif's parents be missing right now?
Caught up in the divorce, they may not notice how lonely Elif feels or where she spends Friday evenings.

Read this:

Jaya: he said no again
Asif: the manager? about the transfer?
Jaya: yes. third time. i keep thinking why. is it me, is it my work, did i say something wrong in the review
Asif: we talked about this on sunday
Jaya: i know. and monday. and last night
Jaya: i just keep going over it
Asif: does talking about it help? like after, do you feel better?
Jaya: ...no. worse actually
Asif: ok. i'm here and i'll listen. but maybe we try something different
Asif: what's one small thing you could do this week? not fix everything. one step
Jaya: ask him what i'd need to do to be considered next time?
Asif: that's a real step
Jaya: ok. i'll email tomorrow
Asif: 🤍

How many times had the manager said no to Jaya's transfer?
Three times.
What did Asif seem to feel on hearing that the talks left Jaya worse?
Asif noticed the talks brought no relief and left Jaya feeling worse, which suggests Asif felt concerned and wanted to change the pattern.
Why is Asif's question about one small step helpful?
It gently moves Jaya from going over the same questions to a concrete action, like emailing the manager.
How does Jaya seem to feel after deciding to email?
Jaya seems a bit steadier and hopeful, having a clear step instead of the same questions.

Read this:

Dear Diary,
Today in moral science Sir said God is watching everything. At home, Papa says he isn't sure if God exists at all. Mumma prays every night. So who is right?
I asked Papa at dinner. He didn't laugh. He said, "Seema, I don't know for sure. Mumma believes, and I respect that. Some people believe, some don't, and some keep wondering, like me."
Mumma said, "And you can decide for yourself when you're older. You can ask me anything."
Chaitanya, my little brother, said, "I think God is a big cat." Everyone laughed, even Papa.
I felt better. I thought it was bad that my parents think different things, but it isn't. They still hold hands on the balcony.
I will keep wondering. That's allowed.
Seema

What did Chaitanya say he thinks God is?
Chaitanya said, "I think God is a big cat."
How did Seema feel after talking with her parents?
Seema felt relieved and calmer, realising it wasn't bad that Seema's parents think different things.
What did Papa and Mumma do that protected Seema's trust?
They answered honestly and calmly, each respecting the other's view, and told Seema she could keep asking and decide for herself.
How might Seema's teacher's words look different after the family talk?
Seema may now see the teacher's words as one belief among many, rather than a fact that makes her father wrong.

Friday. I was so nervous I nearly did not go, but I told myself: just walk up. At lunch I found a group with a football, and I stood near them until there was a gap. "Hi, I'm Rehan. I just moved here from Kanpur. Can I play?" One boy, Vidya, grinned and said, "Sure, you're on my team!" Another asked about my old school, and I told him about the cricket ground behind it. By the end of lunch my knees were muddy and my heart was light. It was one small sentence, and it worked. I'll do it again on Monday with someone else.

Where did Rehan say the move was from?
Rehan said the move was from Kanpur.
How did Rehan feel after the friendly answer?
Rehan felt welcome and happy, shown by the light heart and the plan to try again on Monday. 😊
What alternative approach could Rehan use if a group says no, and why?
Rehan could try another group or ask the teacher who might like to play. A refusal is only one group's answer, and many others may say yes.
How did Vidya's reply affect the new boy?
Vidya grinned and put Rehan on the team straight away, so Rehan felt included at once and the nerves eased.

messages.content: Dost ne kaha "I need to hit the books." Matlab kya hai?
It means he needs to study hard.
The man maintains that he was at home all evening. Does maintain mean to repair something?

Here, to maintain means to say firmly that something is true. It is a verb. The other meaning is to keep something in good condition.
Example: She maintains that the song was written by her grandfather.

Read this:

Rosa was convinced the number 14 bus in Nairobi was late every time she left the flat exactly on time, and early every time she ran late.
"It's cursed," she told Wanjiru over breakfast. "Or it knows."
Wanjiru raised an eyebrow. "How many times have you actually counted?"
"Enough." Rosa paused. "Well. I remember the bad ones."
"So if it was pure chance, what would you expect?"
Rosa thought. "Sometimes late, sometimes early, whenever I leave."
For two weeks she wrote it down on a card in her bag: when she left, when the bus came. Twenty trips.
Late when she was on time: five. Late when she was late: five. Early and on time, all mixed.
"It's just a bus," she said, laughing, handing Wanjiru the card.
"A bus that doesn't know you," Wanjiru said.

How many trips did Rosa record?
Twenty trips.
What was Rosa feeling when she said "I remember the bad ones"?
She felt a little unsure, realising her sense of a curse came from remembering only the frustrating days.
What could someone else learn from Rosa's card?
Writing down every case, not just memorable ones, shows whether a pattern is real or just chance.
How might Wanjiru feel when Rosa hands over the card?
Wanjiru probably feels amused and pleased, since her question led Rosa to test the idea herself.

messages.content:
Read this:

Mehak, thanks for having me on. You asked what it's like being Christian in my town. Mostly fine. But I'll tell you about Class 10.
A rumour went round that Christians "pay people to convert." One boy asked, loudly, "So how much did your family get?" People laughed. I laughed too, which I hate now. Then I went home and didn't eat.
The next day, my friend Ruksana stood up in the canteen and said, "Devika's family has been Christian for five generations. She's my friend, and that rumour is rubbish." Our teacher, Mrs. Pillai, heard it and took the whole class through what stereotypes do. She said clearly the rumour was false.
I stopped laughing along after that. That's what I'd tell teenagers now: find the one friend and the one adult. It was the two of them that protected me. I'm Devika, by the way, if anyone's listening.

How long has Devika's family been Christian?
Devika's family has been Christian for five generations.
Why did Devika laugh along and then not eat?
Devika laughed to hide shame and hurt, and then felt so upset at home that she didn't eat.
What made the difference for Devika?
Ruksana spoke up publicly and Mrs. Pillai named the rumour as a false stereotype in front of the class, giving real protection.
How might Ruksana have felt standing up in the canteen?
Ruksana may have felt nervous but determined, angry at the rumour and protective of Devika.
Begin a letter to my grandfather with "Dear Dada" and keep the opening line to twelve words or fewer.
Dear Dada, I hope the garden is blooming beautifully this month.

Read this:

Shankar: TOPPER!! 95 in the anatomy practical!!!
Amandeep: it was an easy practical
Shankar: the average was 62
Amandeep: I got lucky with the specimen
Shankar: you've said "lucky" three times this year
Amandeep: because it's true
Shankar: and when you got 58 in physiology?
Amandeep: that was because I'm not good enough
Shankar: so the 58 is you and the 95 is luck?
Amandeep: ...when you put it like that
Shankar: I'm just saying. you can't only count the bad ones
Amandeep: it feels safer to count the bad ones
Shankar: safer how
Amandeep: if I think I'm good and then I fail, it'll hurt more
Shankar: ok. but you're failing to enjoy a 95 right now
Amandeep: 😅
Amandeep: ok. 95. I studied. it wasn't luck
Shankar: louder
Amandeep: IT WASN'T LUCK 🎉
Shankar: better

What was the average in the anatomy practical?
The average was 62.
Why does counting only the bad marks feel safer to Amandeep?
Amandeep is afraid that believing in success will hurt more after a later failure, so dismissing the 95 feels protective.
What did Shankar do that helped?
Shankar pointed out the double standard, the 58 counting while the 95 was luck, and nudged Amandeep to say the result was earned.
How might Shankar feel seeing "IT WASN'T LUCK"?
Shankar would likely feel pleased and warm, glad Amandeep finally owned the success.

Read this:

Sunday: In the church in Aizawl, Lalremsiami squeezed her eyes shut during the prayers. "Lord, if I pass science, I'll sing in the choir every week and never skip Sunday school." She peeked to see if anyone had heard.
Thursday: Science results. Sixty-one, a pass. She hugged her friend Ishita, who had drilled her on the parts of a flower all week. "God kept the deal!" she laughed.
The next Sunday: She stood in the choir as promised. During the silent prayer she didn't ask for anything. She just thought of Ishita's flower drawings and her mother's late-night cocoa, and whispered, "Thank you."

What did Lalremsiami promise if she passed science?
She promised to sing in the choir every week and never skip Sunday school.
What was Lalremsiami feeling during the silent prayer the next Sunday?
Lalremsiami felt grateful rather than hopeful for a deal, thinking of Ishita's help and her mother's cocoa.
What does the change across the week suggest for adults who notice bargaining prayers?
Bargaining is normal at this age, and gratitude can grow naturally when a child notices the people who helped.
How might Ishita see Lalremsiami saying "God kept the deal"?
Ishita may be amused, and perhaps a little proud of the flower drills that helped.

Read this:

Sunday
Diary, today we went to Sarojini market, which is like a sea of people. Before we went in, Vidya Masi held my shoulders and said, "Divyansh, if you lose us, what's the plan?" I said it out loud like a poem: "Stop. Find a shop. Say Mummy's number. Don't go anywhere." She made me say the number twice. I felt silly, but also a bit safer. We didn't get lost. But once, at a shoe stall, I turned round and couldn't see Masi for a second, and my brain said STOP before my feet moved. Then I saw her waving. I think practising made my brain do it by itself. Going to teach my little sister tomorrow.
- Divyansh

What did Vidya Masi make Divyansh say twice?
She made Divyansh say the number twice.
How did Divyansh feel after saying the plan aloud?
Divyansh felt a bit silly but also safer, knowing what to do.
What else could Divyansh practise with the little sister, and why?
They could act it out at home, pretending a room is the market, so the steps feel automatic for her too.
How does the rehearsal look to Vidya Masi?
Vidya Masi wants Divyansh ready for the crowd, and is probably reassured to hear the plan said clearly.

Read this:

Rashmi came home from her college hostel on Friday and noticed the change within an hour. At dinner in their Pune flat, Papa told the whole internship story again, then turned to Abhinav. "See what didi managed? You could too, if you tried."
Abhinav only said, "Hmm," and kept eating. No argument, no slammed door. Later Rashmi found his tuition notes still sealed in their plastic cover.
"You've stopped going," she said.
"What's the point? He compares anyway. I don't care now."
"Do you actually not care, or is it just easier not to feel it?"
Abhinav picked at the plastic for a long time. "It's easier," he admitted. "It still stings."
That night he knocked on Papa's door. "When you compare me with didi, I don't try harder. I stop trying," he said, voice shaking. Papa put down his newspaper and, for once, did not answer quickly.

Where did Rashmi find Abhinav's tuition notes?
Still sealed in their plastic cover.
What was Abhinav feeling when he said he didn't care?
He was hurt; he had gone numb because not feeling was easier than the sting of being compared with his sister.
What went wrong, and what helped fix it?
Abhinav had quietly given up on tuition; talking honestly with Papa once, instead of staying numb, started to fix it.
How might Papa see the moment when Abhinav knocks on his door?
Papa seems caught off guard and thoughtful; he had not realised his comparisons were making his son stop trying, so he pauses instead of answering quickly.
Which one is about weather: "climatic" or "climactic"?

"Climatic" is about climate. "Climactic" is about a climax, the most exciting point of a story or event.
Examples: Climatic changes affect farming. The climactic scene of the film was exciting.

"Mohit, your handwriting is SO bad. Did a chicken write this?"
The group round Kashish's desk laughed.
"Very funny, Kashish."
"And why do you always wear that same blue jacket? Don't you own anything else?"
More laughter. Mohit shrugged and went back to his seat.
Anjali leaned over. "Why are you always on his case?"
"Because he's annoying."
"He's not, though."
"He is! Everything about him is annoying." Kashish's face was hot.
Anjali narrowed her eyes. "Wait. Do you like him?"
"Eww! No! Are you mad?"
"You've talked about his jacket three times this week."
"Because it's ugly!"
Kashish stared at her book, heart pounding, and did not look at the blue jacket for the rest of the period.

What did Kashish say about Mohit's jacket?
"Why do you always wear that same blue jacket? Don't you own anything else?"
Why did Kashish's face go hot when Anjali asked if she liked Mohit?
Kashish felt exposed and panicked, because the teasing had been hiding a crush she didn't want anyone to see.
What could Kashish try instead of teasing Mohit?
She could simply be friendly or stay neutral, which is less hurtful to Mohit even if she isn't ready to share her feelings.
How might Mohit feel about Kashish's comments?
Mohit probably feels puzzled and a little hurt, picked on for his handwriting and jacket without knowing why.

messages.content:
Read this:

Jyoti here, the neighbour whose balcony looks over the courtyard. I was watering my plants when I saw little Reena lose at ludo to her big cousin. She stamped once. Then she stopped, lower lip pushed out, looked at the sky, took a big breath and shook the cousin's hand. "Good game," she said, not quite smiling. Then, "Again?"
I can't say what she was feeling; her chin was wobbling. But she didn't throw the board, and she didn't say it was unfair.

What game did Reena lose?
Ludo, to her big cousin.
What might Reena be feeling as she loses?
Upset and disappointed. She stamps, pushes her lip out and her chin wobbles, though she stays in control.
What choice by Reena stands out?
She took a big breath, shook the cousin's hand, said 'Good game' and asked to play again instead of throwing the board or crying unfair.
What does Jyoti say about how much Jyoti can know?
Jyoti admits not knowing exactly what Reena was feeling, only what the wobbling chin and stamping suggested.
Near the horizon the moon looks huge. Is it actually bigger there?
It is mostly an illusion created by the brain. The moon is the same size in the sky all night, but near the horizon it sits beside buildings and trees, which makes it seem larger.
Can I test that somehow?
Yes. Photograph the moon low in the sky and again when it is high, using the same camera and zoom. The two pictures will show it at nearly the same size.

Read this:

The school van would honk in five minutes. Indu was plaiting Zainab's hair when she spotted a big blue ink stain on the clean uniform.

"Zainab, what happened here?"

"No! I didn't do it!" Zainab stepped back, eyes wide.

Indu took a slow breath. She knelt so their faces were level. "Ink spills happen. You're not in trouble. I just need to know, so we can fix it."

Zainab's lip trembled. "The pen leaked. I was drawing."

"Thank you for telling me. Let's find the other shirt, quickly!"

They were at the gate when the van came.

What did Indu spot on the clean uniform?
A big blue ink stain.
Why did Zainab say "No! I didn't do it!"?
She was most likely scared of getting into trouble, especially with the van coming; stepping back with wide eyes shows fear. She may also have felt embarrassed about spoiling the clean uniform.
How did Indu separate Zainab from the mistake?
She stayed calm, knelt at Zainab's level, said spills happen and that Zainab was not in trouble, so it felt safe to tell the truth.
What would change if Indu had shouted about the stain?
Zainab would probably have kept denying it out of fear, and they might have missed the van as well.
I need a polite note to her teacher about my daughter: Riya has dance class on Tuesday so she will leave 20 minutes early. Please excuse.
Dear Ma'am, Riya has a dance class on Tuesday, so she will need to leave twenty minutes early. Kindly excuse her. Thank you.

"You told Arjun I still see a speech therapist?"
"Vaibhav, wait—"
"Now the whole cricket team's doing the voice. You know what I could tell them about you? About your dad's shop?"
"..."
"I'm not going to. I thought about it all through maths. I wanted to. But that's not me."
"I'm sorry. Arjun asked why you leave early on Thursdays and I just... said it. I didn't think."
"You didn't think, and now I hear the voice every practice."
"I'll tell Arjun it's not funny. I'll tell the whole team."
"Do that first. Then we'll see."
"Are we still friends?"
"I don't know yet, Noor. Ask me next week."

Who did Noor tell about the speech therapist?
Noor told Arjun.
What was Vaibhav feeling all through maths?
Vaibhav felt betrayed and angry, and was tempted to expose Noor back by telling the team about the dad's shop.
What did Vaibhav do instead of exposing Noor, and why was it wiser?
He confronted Noor privately, asked for the harm to be fixed first and gave himself a week to decide about trust, so he didn't add more hurt.
How might Noor feel hearing "Ask me next week"?
Noor probably feels anxious and ashamed, but also has a clear chance to rebuild trust by fixing things with the team.
