"It's impossible!" Tarun glared at the triangle in his notebook. "Twenty minutes and it still doesn't work!"
"Then close the book," said his mother Neelam. "Go and play."
"But it's homework."
"It will be here when you come back."
Tarun kicked the ball around the courtyard for half an hour. When he came in, red-faced and thirsty, he picked up his pencil and looked at the figure again.
"Oh!" he said. "I wrote AB where it should be BC. I mislabelled the sides!"
He fixed them and finished the problem in five minutes.
"Ma, it was that easy."

How long did Tarun stare at the triangle before he stopped?
He had worked on it for twenty minutes.
What was Tarun feeling when he said "It's impossible!"?
He was frustrated and stuck. He glared at the notebook and thought twenty minutes should have been enough.
What alternative approach could Tarun use the next time he is stuck, and why?
He could check the labels on his figure and read the question again before quitting. Small slips in labelling can hide behind a problem that seems impossible.
How does Neelam see Tarun's stuck problem?
Neelam sees a boy who is tired and wound up, so she sends him to play, trusting the problem will look different afterwards. 😊

Read this:

Honestly, Mitra? My father's friend runs the press. I'm Hansa, twenty-four, and I won't pretend my English-medium school and that one phone call didn't help. They did. So when the press asked me to find two more translators for the children's series, I didn't just ring my college friends, who all sound like me. I put up a notice in the district library and sent it to a teachers' group. That's how I found Vasudha, who teaches at a town school and translates better than I do. At our first meeting she said our glossary used city words no village child would know. I wanted to defend it. I wrote her point down instead. We changed forty words. I don't wake up guilty about the head start every morning, and I don't hide it either. I just try to hold the door open the way someone held it for me.

Where did Hansa put up the notice for translators?
In the district library, and it went to a teachers' group too.
When Vasudha criticised the glossary, what did Hansa feel, and what does writing the point down show?
Hansa's first urge was to defend the glossary, but writing the point down shows a real wish to listen to someone who sees what Hansa can't.
Which choice at the hiring stage made the biggest difference?
Instead of ringing college friends who all sound alike, Hansa widened the search, which brought in Vasudha, the better translator.
How might Vasudha see this way of working?
Vasudha probably felt taken seriously: invited on merit, then heard about the city words, which could make the partnership feel equal.

Read this:

Saturday: at Dadi's flat in Kanpur, Saurabh watched her water her tulsi, hum an old film song and tell the milkman a joke. She had lost Dadaji two years ago and her knees were bad, but she said, 'I've had a full life, beta. Now I'm just enjoying the extras.'
Wednesday: at Nanaji's house across town, everything was a complaint: the government, the neighbours, the sons who never visited. He said life had cheated him. Saurabh's cousin Leela rolled her eyes behind his back.
The following Sunday: on the terrace, Saurabh asked Leela, 'Why is Dadi like that and Nanaji like this? Same age, both lost people.' Leela shrugged. 'Luck?' Saurabh wasn't sure. He lay back watching the kites and wondered, uneasily, which one he was already becoming.

What did Dadi say about her life?
'I've had a full life, beta. Now I'm just enjoying the extras.'
What was Saurabh feeling as he watched the kites?
Saurabh felt curious and a bit uneasy, wondering which path he might already be on.
What could Saurabh do to explore his question?
He could ask Dadi and Nanaji about their lives and what they would do differently, listening for what shaped each one.
How does Leela see Nanaji?
Leela seems irritated by Nanaji's complaints, rolling her eyes, and thinks the difference is just luck.
Write it in fewer words: At this point in time, we are not in a position to accept any new members into the club.
We cannot accept new members right now.
Write a text, about 35 words, to my friend Joel saying sorry that I could not come to his concert because my train was cancelled. I'm Mira.

Hi Joel,
I'm so sorry I missed your concert. My train was cancelled, and I could not reach in time. I really wanted to be there. Please tell me how it went, and I'll make it up to you!
Mira

I'm Nilesh, and when my parents separated in Class 6, I told no one. When friends asked why my dad didn't come to sports day, I said he was busy.
Every lie made my stomach tight. I was sure everyone would think our family was broken.
Then one day Leela, who sat next to me, said her parents had separated two years earlier. She said it so simply.
After school I walked with her and told her everything. She just nodded. "It gets less weird."
I didn't tell the whole class. Just Leela. But for the first time in months, I didn't feel like I was hiding.

What did Nilesh say when friends asked why Dad didn't come to sports day?
That he was busy.
What was Nilesh afraid of?
Nilesh felt ashamed and afraid that everyone would think the family was broken.
Why was telling Leela a good choice?
Leela had been through the same thing and was kind, so sharing with one trusted friend ended the lonely feeling of hiding.
How might Leela feel when Nilesh tells her?
Leela may feel understanding and glad to help, since she had been through it herself.
Why does a rumour spread so fast?

People pass surprising news on before checking it. Because people like to share surprising news, each person who hears it passes it on without checking whether it is true, and the story is often made more exciting on the way.
A teacher criticised my drawing in front of the class and I still feel bad.
Being criticised in front of others is hard, and it is fine to feel bad about it. A teacher may mean to help, but the way it was said can still hurt.
Should I tell someone?
You could tell a parent or a trusted adult how it felt. If you want, you can later ask the teacher privately what to improve. Asking calmly often leads to useful, kinder feedback.

The photocopy shop near the bus stand in Malerkotla was where the college seniors sat in the evenings. Three days before the cost accounting exam, Hafsa finally went there, her file clutched to her chest. She had missed most of October helping in her family's bangle shop during the wedding rush, and every week since, she had meant to catch up. Every week the pile looked more embarrassing. When classmates asked, she said, "Almost done revising." Nilesh, the senior who tutored, flipped through her half-empty notebook. "Hafsa, six chapters? In three days?" She stared at the floor. "I know." He was kind about it, but honest. "I can take you through two properly. Marginal costing and budgets carry the most marks. The rest you'll have to skim." Walking home past the closed shutters, she worked it out herself: back in early November, one hour a week would have been enough.

How many chapters had Hafsa fallen behind on?
Six chapters.
Why did Hafsa wait until three days before the exam to ask?
She felt ashamed as the pile grew, so she kept saying she was almost done revising instead of admitting she was behind.
What could Hafsa have done in early November?
She could have told Nilesh or a teacher right after the wedding rush that she had missed October, when an hour a week would have been enough.
How might Nilesh feel about only being able to cover two chapters?
Nilesh is probably sorry and a little frustrated, wanting to help properly but knowing three days leave room for only the chapters with the most marks.

messages.content:
Can you help with these? Why do some trees lose their leaves in autumn?
What does "mean business" mean?
My book uses the word "throttle". What does it mean?
How can I keep calm when I am in a hurry?
Is this sentence correct? I have two brother.

1. They get ready for the cold months. Because bare branches use less water and energy.
2. It means to be serious about what you say you will do.
3. As a verb, "throttle" means to choke someone, or to stop something from growing or working freely.
4. Take a slow breath and do one thing at a time. A short pause helps you think better than rushing.
5. I have two brothers. Why: After "two", the noun needs a plural "-s".

The Copenhagen product team had argued for forty minutes about the launch date, and four voices had filled the room. Bao, the newest engineer, sat with his notebook closed, the way he had for three meetings.
Freya, who chaired, stopped the talk. “Bao, you’ve been checking the test results all week. What do you see?”
Bao hesitated. “The payment step fails on older phones. If we launch Friday, a lot of people will get stuck.”
“Thank you,” said Freya. “Nobody had that. Let’s move the date and put Bao’s test list on the board.”
Two colleagues nodded slowly. Bao opened his notebook.

How many meetings had Bao sat with his notebook closed?
Bao had sat with his notebook closed for three meetings.
What might Bao have felt when Freya turned to him in the middle of the argument?
Bao probably felt nervous at being put on the spot, since he hesitated before speaking. Opening his notebook at the end shows he felt more at ease once heard.
What did Freya do that gave the quiet member a real chance to be heard?
Freya paused the argument, named what Bao had been checking and asked directly for his view. Freya then credited his test list and changed the date.
How might the two colleagues who nodded slowly have felt?
They were probably surprised that a quiet colleague had found something the loud discussion missed. Nodding slowly suggests they were rethinking.

The dorm in Vancouver was quiet at eleven, which was morning in Seoul, so Jin called home. He told his mother about the lab report, the grocery list, even which bus he took. "Good choice," she said to each, and he smiled at the screen.
Then he mentioned the summer. The design studio downtown had offered him an internship. It was the thing he had been sketching toward all year.
His mother paused. "Your father thought you would come home and help at the restaurant. Your aunt is getting older."
"I know. I was only saying they offered."
After the call, his roommate Marek found him staring at the offer email. "You look like you lost."
"I feel like a bad son for even wanting it," Jin said. "And I still want it."

What had the design studio offered Jin?
The design studio downtown had offered him a summer internship.
Why does Jin say he feels like a bad son?
He feels guilty because his wish for the internship clashes with his parents' hope that he will help at the restaurant, and he loves them and wants their approval.
What would you advise Jin?
He could tell his parents honestly what the internship means to him and look for a middle path, like helping at the restaurant for part of the summer.
How might Marek see Jin's situation from the outside?
Marek sees a friend looking defeated over good news and may not understand how much family duty weighs on Jin, so he is likely to be concerned and curious.

At the school gate Thomas gripped Mummy's dress and cried. She crouched and said, "I'm going now. I'll come back after lunch, when the bell rings. Ma'am will look after you." She kissed his forehead, waved, and walked out through the gate without sneaking. Thomas howled. The teacher took his hand and led him to a shelf of toy trains. "Which is your favourite? Let's find the blue one." He sniffed, scared but a little bit safe. He looked around the room at the other children, curious and shy: a boy chewing his sleeve, a girl arranging blocks. The teacher said, "Tejas and Farhan, Thomas, would you build a bridge together for the trains?" The three of them stacked blocks. Farhan handed Thomas a long block, Tejas laughed when the tower fell, and Thomas laughed too, forgetting to cry. When the bell rang after lunch, Mummy was at the gate, and Thomas ran to her. "I built a bridge!"

What did the teacher lead Thomas to?
The teacher led Thomas to a shelf of toy trains.
How did Mummy's goodbye and the teacher's steps each help Thomas on his first day?

Mummy said a short kind goodbye, told him when she would come back and did not sneak away; the teacher took his hand, showed him the trains and paired him with Tejas and Farhan to build a bridge, so a friendship could begin.
What was Thomas feeling as he looked around at the other children?
He felt shy and curious, wondering who might be his friend.
What could Mummy do at the gate tomorrow?
She could keep the same short kind goodbye and the same return time, without lingering. 🙂

In the small town of Sultanpur, word travels by the tea stall. So when the Siddiqui family from the next mohalla came asking about Sabina's younger brother Akash for their daughter, Sabina, as the eldest, was sent to meet them.
She sat in their courtyard with a plate of biscuits and spoke about Akash's gentle nature, his job at the district office, the way he looked after Ammi. All true. She did not say that the district office job was a contract that ended in March, and that Akash had not found anything after it yet.
The girl's father nodded warmly. "A government job. That's a relief for us."
Sabina's biscuit turned to dust in her mouth. She had not told a lie. But she could see exactly what belief she had let grow in his mind, and she had let it grow on purpose.
On the walk home, she stopped at the gate and turned back.

When does Akash's district office job end?
It was a contract that ended in March.
What was Sabina feeling when the father said "A government job"?
Sabina felt guilty and uneasy, realising that her silence about the contract had deliberately shaped a false belief.
What could Sabina say when she goes back to the gate?
She could tell the family plainly that Akash's job is a contract ending in March, so they can decide with the full picture.
What would change for the girl's family if they learned about the contract only after the wedding?
They would likely feel deceived and lose trust in Sabina's family, even though no false word was spoken.
Teasing that seems harmless to one person can hurt another. Why?
People feel things differently. Because a joke may touch something the other person is sensitive about, and the one teasing cannot see how it lands inside them.

At the village school's handpump, Kashish held the tin cup and looked at Leela, who had just come from the next village and knew nobody. Kashish wanted Leela's friendship. “I'll tell you a secret,” Kashish whispered. “Kishore practises singing in the cowshed. He's too scared to sing in class.”

Leela's eyes lit up. “Really? Say it again!” Kashish felt warm, as if giving a present. Two other girls leaned in, then giggled.

That afternoon, when the teacher asked who would sing for annual day, Kishore shook his head fast and kept his eyes on the floor. The giggles started again at the back. Kashish smiled at Leela and did not look at Kishore.

Where does Kishore practise singing?
Kishore practises singing in the cowshed.
How did Kashish feel when Leela's eyes lit up at the secret?
Kashish felt warm and pleased, as if giving a present, because Kashish wanted Leela's friendship.
What could Kashish do after seeing Kishore refuse to sing?
Kashish could tell Kishore sorry for sharing the secret and ask the girls to stop giggling.
What might Kishore have felt when the giggles started at the back?
Kishore probably felt exposed and hurt, realising a private fear had been passed around.

Hrithik, come, put your phone down a minute. You've been quiet all week, and it reminds your old grandpa of something.

When I was fifteen, the year the mill shut and your great-grandfather lost his job, I stopped doing homework. I sat at the back. I told everyone at home I was fine, because they had enough troubles.

Our English teacher, Mrs D'Souza, kept me back one day. She didn't scold. She said, "Joseph, you used to write the best essays in this class. What's happening?" I meant to say nothing. Instead, the whole thing came out, the mill, the shouting at home, how I couldn't sleep.

She listened. She told me I wasn't the only one carrying things like that. That same day she spoke to my mother, gently, and after that she let me stay after school to study where it was quiet.

I've never forgotten it. So, Hrithik, is there someone you could tell?

What happened the year young Joseph turned fifteen?
The mill shut and Joseph's father, Hrithik's great-grandfather, lost his job.
Why did young Joseph tell everyone at home he was fine?
Joseph felt worried and didn't want to add to his family's troubles, so hiding his struggle felt kinder at the time.
What was the turning point in Joseph's story, and why did it matter?
When Mrs D'Souza asked what was happening and Joseph told the whole thing instead of saying nothing, it brought help at home and a quiet place to study.
How might Mrs D'Souza have seen Joseph before he opened up?
Mrs D'Souza likely noticed a strong writer slipping to the back and worried something was wrong, which is why she kept him back kindly.

Sunday 14 May
Kalyani: Papa, I'm sorry the talk got so tense yesterday. I know you worry. I'm not shutting you out. Can we talk again when we're both calm?

Kalyani shared that the internship offer at the design firm had come, with a stipend that covers rent.
What did Ujjwal feel about the messages, by the end?

Kalyani may feel encouraged, since Papa agrees to talk tomorrow and gives thanks for the messages after the earlier 'Let's see.'

In her first month at the design studio in Manchester, Amara was everyone's favourite: coffee for the team, compliments on every sketch, stories that made the manager laugh. By month four, things were different. She expected the corner desk by the window, and got it. She presented Soo-ah's packaging idea to the client as "something I've been developing". When Soo-ah mentioned her mother was in hospital, Amara said, "Oh no," then asked if Soo-ah could still finish the mock-ups by Friday. Amara was warm when the director was around and bored when she wasn't. She told herself she was simply more ambitious than the others. The team had stopped inviting her to lunch; she hadn't noticed yet.

Whose packaging idea did Amara present as her own?
Soo-ah's.
How does Amara seem to feel about her own behaviour?
She seems pleased and self-satisfied, telling herself she is simply more ambitious, with no sign of guilt.
What could Amara do if she wanted to repair things with the team?
Credit Soo-ah openly, ask how Soo-ah's mother is and stop expecting special treatment.
How might Soo-ah feel when Amara asks about the mock-ups right after hearing about the hospital?
Soo-ah likely feels hurt and used, as her worry is brushed aside for deadlines.

I'm Pema. I teach at the same school as Kalyani, and I've shared the staff room with her for three years.
Kalyani used to be the loudest laugh in there. She ran the science club and stayed late to help students with projects. This year she took on exam duty, two extra classes and the annual day.
By December she always seemed to have a cold. She'd rub her lower back and sit with her eyes closed at lunch. When students came with project questions, she answered politely but flatly.
After the winter break she came back looking the same, pale and tired.
In January I saw her go into the principal's office. Afterwards her name was off the annual day list and one of the extra classes. I don't know everything she said. But last week she laughed in the staff room again, and it sounded like her.

What extra work did Kalyani take on this year?
She took on exam duty, two extra classes and the annual day.
What might Kalyani have been feeling by December?
She may have been exhausted and detached, though Pema can't be sure; she seemed tired, often ill and flat with students.
What change seems to have helped Kalyani most?
Talking to the principal and dropping the annual day and an extra class, since the break alone had not helped.
How might Kalyani's students have experienced her in December?
They probably noticed she was polite but flat, and may have missed her old warmth and energy.
Why do bees keep visiting flowers?
Bees eat the sweet nectar. Because they brush against pollen while feeding and carry it from flower to flower, the plants can make seeds as a result.

At the residential school in Shillong, evening study hour was nearly over when Rekha, fifteen, slid a folded note across the hostel common room to her cousin Charu. It said: "Can we talk? I'm not okay."
They sat on the back steps. Rekha's words came slowly. She hadn't been sleeping, she'd stopped calling home, and most nights she cried in the bathroom because she felt she didn't belong here. "I didn't want anyone to know," she said.
Charu squeezed her hand. "I'm really glad you told me. Let's tell Mrs Lyngdoh too, tonight."
Mrs Lyngdoh, the housemother, was still in her office. She put down her pen, listened to all of it and said, "Thank you for trusting us. This is not something you should hold alone." She rang Rekha's parents while the cousins sat beside her, and booked Rekha in with the school counsellor for the next morning.

What did Rekha's note to Charu say?
"Can we talk? I'm not okay."
What was Rekha feeling that made her cry in the bathroom most nights?
She felt she didn't belong at the school and was lonely and worn out, and she didn't want anyone to know.
What did Charu choose to do after listening, and why was it a good step?
Charu suggested telling Mrs Lyngdoh that same night, which brought in an adult who called Rekha's parents and arranged the counsellor.
How might Rekha's parents feel after Mrs Lyngdoh's call?
They would likely be worried to hear she had been struggling, but relieved that she reached out and that the school was already supporting her.

His grandmother practises it with him.
What does Asif starting a second poem suggest about how he feels?
It suggests he enjoys reciting and feels confident after mastering the first one.
What helped Asif remember the middle part?
His grandmother clapped the rhythm with him, which helped his memory.
How does Tenzin see Asif's practice?
Tenzin thinks Asif loves saying the words, though Tenzin isn't sure Asif understands them all.

Supervisor's note, community centre, Wednesday.
A young woman, Bidisha, came in this afternoon very distressed; her landlord had told her to leave by the weekend. She was shaking and talking fast.
Manjula, our new caseworker, met her in the front room. I watched from the door. I saw Manjula's own face tighten for a moment. Then she sat down, put both feet on the floor, and took two slow breaths before speaking.
She kept her voice low. "That sounds frightening. What would help most today?" Bidisha said a place to stay for two nights. Manjula made two calls and found a hostel bed.
At six, when Manjula would usually stay late, I saw her pack up. She said, "I'll be better for her tomorrow if I sleep tonight."
What I did next: I gave Manjula the follow-up slot tomorrow morning and told her I'd noticed how steady she was.

What did Bidisha say would help most?
A place to stay for two nights.
What was Manjula feeling when her face tightened?
She felt Bidisha's fear catch in her, and then steadied herself with slow breaths.
What did Manjula do well, and why does it matter for her work?
She settled first, asked what would help, found a hostel bed and went home to rest, so her care stays steady and lasts.
How might Bidisha have felt with Manjula speaking calmly?
She probably felt less panicked and more hopeful as someone steady focused on what would help.
Why does honey last so long without going bad? Any idea what "warehouse" means? Is it "I have been to Jaipur" or "I have gone to Jaipur"?

1. It is very sweet and has little water. Because germs find it hard to grow in such food.
2. It is a noun. It means a large building where goods are stored.
3. "I have been to Jaipur" means you visited and came back. "I have gone to Jaipur" means you are still there or on the way.

On the auto ride to school in Pune, Pradeep went over it in his head. Yesterday Sarita had hinted she'd ask to copy his English homework today, like last week. Last week he'd said, "That's cheating," and she'd sulked for two days. "That made it about her," he thought. "As if I was calling her a cheat." What if he made it about himself instead? He practised under his breath: "Sorry, I can't. Ma'am compared my book with Rohan's last time, and I really don't want any trouble." It was true, and it didn't point at her at all. At the gate Sarita came up. "Pradeep, English?" He said his line. She shrugged. "Okay, fair." And she walked with him to class, chatting about cricket.

How long did Sarita sulk last week?
Two days.
What was Pradeep thinking as he rehearsed?
He was worried about hurting Sarita again and wanted a refusal that didn't sound like judging her.
What else could Pradeep offer Sarita?
To go over the English homework with her at lunch, so she isn't left stuck.
How does Sarita react this time?
Sarita shrugs, says 'Okay, fair', and walks with him chatting about cricket.

messages.content: The factory in our town "shut down". What does that phrase mean?

To shut down means to stop operating, either for a time or for ever. It is also used for computers and machines.
Examples: The factory shut down last year. Please shut down the computer before you leave.

At sixteen, Trisha sat in the school canteen when a classmate, Chaitanya, laughed and said, "People from your state are all loud and dramatic, right?" A few others chuckled. Trisha felt her chest tighten, as if she had been turned into a sticker on somebody's notebook. She put down her sandwich and said calmly, "I'm Trisha, and I'm not either of those. Ask me about myself." Chaitanya shrugged, a little embarrassed. Later her friend Pallavi caught up with her and said, "That wasn't fair to you. Come sit with us."

At twenty, in her engineering lab, someone told Trisha, "You'll top the maths paper. People from your community always do." She smiled but felt a weight settle on her shoulders. If she slipped even a little, would that prove something? After class she said to the person, "Thanks, but I still find calculus hard some days. Please don't expect me to be perfect."

What did Trisha say when Chaitanya made the remark about her state?
Trisha said, "I'm Trisha, and I'm not either of those. Ask me about myself."
How are the two remarks to Trisha alike, and how do they feel different?

Trisha is treated as a label: at sixteen, "loud and dramatic", she feels her chest tighten; at twenty, one who will always top the paper, she feels a weight settle and worries about any slip. Both times she says who she really is.
What was Trisha feeling as her shoulders grew heavy in the lab?
Trisha felt pressure and worry, as if any slip would prove something and she was not allowed to fail.
What did Pallavi do that helped Trisha?
Pallavi caught up with Trisha, said the remark had not been fair to Trisha, and invited Trisha to sit with them.

Monday. Siddharth's landlady pinned a notice: no guests after ten. He felt his face go hot and almost called a friend over that night just to test her.

Wednesday. Walking home, he asked himself why it bothered him so much. His friend Simran had said on a call, "Are you angry about the rule or about her telling you?" He realised he rarely had guests after ten anyway. It was the tone that stung.

Saturday. Siddharth knocked on the landlady's door. "I'm fine with ten most days. Could I have a later guest now and then, if I tell you first?" She agreed. He felt calmer, and for once didn't need to prove anything.

What did the landlady's notice say?
No guests after ten.
Why did Siddharth feel his face go hot on Monday?
He felt angry at being told what to do, so the rule stung even though it barely affected him.
What small step did Siddharth take on Saturday, and why was it wise?
He asked for occasional later guests with notice, which dealt with his real need instead of testing the rule out of irritation.
How might the landlady see Siddharth's request?
She would probably feel respected and willing to agree, since he came to her calmly and politely.

"Can I tell you something?" Dhruv said, sitting down on the bench by the bus stop next to Shalini, a friend since Class Five.
"Sure." Shalini was texting, but quickly slid the phone into a pocket. "Go on."
"I'm scared I'll freeze at the audition for the school play. My hands go cold even thinking about it."
"Cold hands. Wait, is it the first line that scares you most?"
"Yeah. Just the first line. After that I think I'd be okay."
"Then that's a really specific thing. Tell me more about the first line."
Dhruv laughed shakily. "You didn't tell me what to do."
"Did you want me to?"

What is Dhruv scared of?
Freezing at the audition for the school play, especially on the first line.
What was Dhruv feeling when saying "Thanks for the pocket thing"?
Grateful and relieved. Dhruv noticed Shalini put the phone away and felt that mattered more than advice.
What did Shalini do that made Dhruv feel heard?
Shalini slid the phone into a pocket, asked a follow-up about the first line, and did not offer advice unless it was wanted.
What is it like for Shalini to hear "You didn't tell me what to do"?
It may be a small surprise. Shalini can see that listening and asking counted for more than solutions, so asking "Did you want me to?" was the right move.

Dear Kunal,
You caught me yesterday, and you were right, so I'm writing this properly instead of mumbling at breakfast.
I told you I couldn't come to your football final because of a work meeting. There was no meeting. I was at home, tired after the week, and I didn't want to stand in the sun for two hours. When you came home early with your knee scraped and found me on the sofa, your face said everything.
And then I made it worse by saying, "The meeting got cancelled." That was a second lie. You knew it, and I knew you knew.
The truth is simple: I was tired, and I chose rest over your match, and I was embarrassed to say so. I should have just told you.
I'll be at the next match, and if I can't come, I'll tell you the real reason.
Love,
Mumma
Kiran

Where was Kiran really during the football final?
Kiran was at home, tired after the week.
What was Kiran feeling after being caught by Kunal?
Kiran felt exposed and embarrassed, especially after adding a second lie that both of them knew was false.
Why is Kiran's letter a good way to repair things?
It admits both lies simply, explains the real reason without excuses, and promises honesty next time, showing Kunal what owning a mistake looks like.
How might Kunal have felt finding Mumma on the sofa?
Kunal likely felt hurt and let down, coming home with a scraped knee to find the meeting excuse was not true.

What one change did Jasleen choose, and why does it fit?

How might Vinita feel watching Jasleen argue with the inner critic?
Vinita probably feels relieved and impressed, seeing Jasleen move from "too dumb" to a clear plan 🙂

'You know, when I was eight,' he said, 'the milkman in our lane kept a big brown dog tied at his gate. Every morning I had to pass it to fetch milk. The moment I turned the corner, my heart went dhak-dhak-dhak and my stomach went tight like a knot in a kite string.

Where was the big brown dog tied?
The dog was tied at the milkman's gate.
How did young Vijay feel when his heart went dhak-dhak-dhak?
He felt so frightened that he believed the dog must be about to eat him, because his body was shouting and he took that as proof.
What could Nana do next to help Sarita at this stage?

The metro was stuck between stations, lights flickering, and Kashish was already late for a client call. Then her phone buzzed: Uma, her batchmate, had been promoted to team lead. Congratulations poured in on the group.

The lights came back on. She typed to Uma: "Well deserved. Coffee this week?"
She was still a little jealous. But the mood was hers again.

Preeti, you want to know why I write letters to the newspaper? It started when I was eleven, during the Pongal holidays.
I, Yogesh, was angry that the colony park was locked. My father said, "Write it down. But give reasons, not just anger."
I wrote: the park should open because children need to play, old people need to walk, and it's our park. I ended: please open it before the holidays end.
The colony committee read it at the meeting. They opened it for evenings.
That's when I learned: an opinion with reasons can change things. So, Preeti, write yours.

To open the park before the holidays end.

Sumit, you tell me your internship is just photocopies and you've stopped caring. Let your Mridul Chacha tell you about 1998. From then on he gave me site drawings to check, real ones, and every Friday he sat with me and marked my mistakes in red. Some Fridays I went home embarrassed. He gave him site drawings to check, real ones, and marked his mistakes in red every Friday.

For seven months I compared paths. UX, cloud, data science, product management. I made a spreadsheet with twelve columns: salary, course cost, demand, how much coding, how much talking to people. I read every article. I watched every "day in the life" video.
Every week I added rows. Every week the answer changed.
My friend Pankaj finally asked, "Have you tried any of them? Even for a weekend?"
I hadn't. Not one tutorial, not one project. I was scared that trying one meant closing the others, so I kept comparing.
Meanwhile, two people from my batch who'd simply started a UX course had portfolios. I had a very beautiful spreadsheet.
I'm Jaya, and I've learned that comparing only helps when you have something real to compare. Next weekend I'm trying one UX exercise and one data exercise. Then the spreadsheet can have actual data.

How many columns did Jaya's spreadsheet have?
Jaya's spreadsheet had twelve columns.
Why did Jaya keep comparing instead of trying?
Jaya felt scared that trying one path meant closing the others, so comparing felt safer.
What would you change first in Jaya's approach, and why?
I would try one small exercise from each path early on, because real experience adds information that more research cannot.
How might Pankaj feel after asking that question?
Pankaj may feel a little worried for a friend but relieved that the question finally pushed Jaya toward trying something.

Dear Shankar,
You asked what it was like to go to the gurdwara with Jasmeet's family for her grandfather's anniversary. I want to tell you properly, because I nearly got it wrong.
When the kirtan began, the whole hall started singing together, slowly, eyes half closed. I didn't know the words. I wasn't sure if I, a guest from a Muslim family, should sing along or stay quiet. So I covered my head like everyone, sat on the floor at the back, and watched. Some aunties were smiling, some had tears. I couldn't tell if it was grief for her grandfather or joy in the singing, maybe both.
After a while Jasmeet's mother leaned over and whispered that I was welcome to join the refrain. So I did, softly. I felt calmer than I had in weeks.
With love,
Salma

Why did Salma go to the gurdwara with Jasmeet's family?
For her grandfather's anniversary.
What was Salma feeling when the kirtan began?
Salma felt unsure and a bit nervous, not knowing whether a guest should sing along; later, after being invited, Salma felt calm.
What did Salma do that showed respect for the group?
Salma covered the head like everyone, sat at the back and watched, and joined the refrain only after being invited.
How did Jasmeet's mother seem to see Salma's quiet watching?
She seemed to appreciate it, and warmly invited Salma to join the refrain softly.

Ujjwal, you want to drag your friend out of that group? Let your Farhan-chacha tell you what I did wrong. In 1995 my friend Suresh joined a 'brotherhood' in Aligarh that made him wear white and stop eating with us. I was furious and scared for him. So I made a plan with two others: we'd tell him his mother was ill, bring him home, and not let him go back. It worked for one night. The next morning he found out, walked back, and told the group, 'You were right, my friends are against me.' He didn't speak to me for two years. The second time, I did it differently. I wrote him a letter every month, just news from the mohalla. When he came to a wedding, I sat with him and asked what he found there. Once, only once, I shared an article about the group's leader. Five years later he came home by himself. So, Ujjwal: no tricks. Keep the door open.

What did the group make Suresh wear?
The group made Suresh wear white.
How did young Farhan feel when Suresh joined the brotherhood?
Farhan felt furious and scared for Suresh.

Seeing the trick backfire and prove the group right, after which he wrote monthly letters, asked open questions and shared information only once.
How did Suresh see the plot to keep him home?

Last term I nearly punished Swati for sleeping in my maths class. She was the girl who hummed while doing sums, always first to laugh at my terrible jokes. For a week she yawned, put her head down, and once kicked her chair when I called on her. I had the detention slip half written. Then I remembered my own bad months as a student, and after class I asked her, softly, how she was sleeping. Her family had moved in with relatives, she said, and she slept in the hall, where the TV ran till one. I phoned her mother that evening, and they moved her mattress into the small storeroom. Two weeks later Swati was humming again. I, Ganga, still keep that unfinished detention slip in my drawer.

Till what time did the TV run in the hall?
Till one.

Ganga seems relieved and a little ashamed at how close that punishment came, and keeps the slip as a reminder to ask first.
What made asking gently work better than detention?
It uncovered the late TV in the hall, and a call to her mother led to a quieter place for Swati to sleep.
What was that week like for Swati?
She was exhausted and irritable, too tired to hum or laugh, and possibly worried about being in trouble.

Monday: Urmila found out at lunch that Darshan had told the whole cricket group she still sleeps with a night lamp and hid in the storeroom during the last thunderstorm. By evening she had typed a message to the class group about Darshan's report card, the one his father tore up. Her thumb hovered over send.
Tuesday: She hadn't sent it. Her cousin Manu had said, "Sleep on it. If it's still right tomorrow, it'll still be right." In class she moved to the front bench and didn't look back once when Darshan said "Urmi". She felt cold, as if a door had slammed shut inside her.
Friday: The anger had cooled into something heavier. She deleted the draft. She still wasn't talking to Darshan. But she was glad the story about the report card was still his to tell.

Darshan told them she still sleeps with a night lamp and hid in the storeroom during the last thunderstorm.

Sleeping on it let the anger cool, so Urmila deleted the draft instead of exposing Darshan's secret and becoming the one in the wrong.

Darshan's private pain about the report card would have been exposed, and the story would shift from what Darshan did to what Urmila did.

In the Class 12 counselling room, Aparna slid the two course forms across the desk. "The last date is the fifteenth. Have you picked?"

Santosh shrugged. "I'll sleep on it."

A week later he said it again, and the week after that. Each time Aparna asked what he had found out, he said, "Nothing new, I'm still thinking." He had not opened either college website or asked a senior about the hostel. On the sixteenth he came in with the forms still unsigned and read the notice on the board.

"It closed yesterday." He stared at the paper. "I thought more time would just make it clear."

Aparna pulled a chair up beside him and asked what he wanted to do about it now.

The forms closed on the fifteenth, the day before Santosh read the notice.

Finally did the adult thing. I've had this cough on and off for weeks and kept buying lozenges from the chemist. Lokesh, my roommate, got fed up: 'Stop guessing, Shankar, go to a proper doctor.' Problem: I didn't know a single doctor in this city. At home Amma just took me to the family doctor down the road. Lokesh helped me look up clinics near us, check which doctors were general physicians, and read a few patient comments, not just the stars. Picked a clinic ten minutes away. The doctor listened properly, asked a lot of questions, and said it didn't look serious but to come back if it kept going or worried me. I also made a folder on my phone for prescriptions and reports so I stop losing papers. Felt oddly grown-up. Also slightly proud.

Probably worried and a bit annoyed by the guessing, which is why Lokesh pushed Shankar to see a proper doctor.

Subject: A plan so you can rest

Dear Devika,

Last night I saw you fall asleep at Amma's bedside with the phone in your hand. I have been thinking about it all day. For two months you have done every night and every visit, and I let it happen because you never complained. That was wrong of me.

One person cannot hold this up for the long run, so here is a plan. You take nights on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. I take the other nights and weekends. We hire a helper from ten to two on weekdays. And Thursday is your day off, no phone.

If it does not work, we change it. But please say yes.

Jasleen

Which day is Devika's day off?
Thursday is Devika's day off.

Jasleen feels guilty and worried, admitting that letting Devika carry everything was wrong.

Ayesha, beti, you're sulking because your new friend won't hug you back? Let your Devika Khala tell you something. When I was your age, I had a friend at work called Farzana. Whenever I hugged her, she went stiff as a board. I was hurt. I thought she didn't like me. For months I kept hugging her, thinking she'd warm up. Then one day she told me, very quietly, that in her home touching was rare, and that some old things made hugs frightening for her. I felt terrible. I had never asked. After that I always asked, 'Hug or no?' Mostly she said no. So instead I brought her cutting chai every morning and saved her a seat. She came to my wedding and cried. We're still friends, forty years later.

Pema's mother had promised both children one drink each at the juice bar in their Mumbai market after swimming class. Pema chose mango in a second. Varun stood under a board of forty juices and shakes: kiwi-mint, chikoo, watermelon-basil, cold coffee, pineapple-ginger... He read from top to bottom, then back up again. Pema had finished half her glass. "Chikoo," he said at last. Then, "No, wait, watermelon-basil." The juice-wala sighed and made it. Varun sipped, frowned and looked at Pema's orange glass. "Yours looks nicer," he said. "Maybe I should've picked mango. Or the kiwi one." He drank slowly, still reading the board.

How many juices and shakes were on the board?
There were forty juices and shakes.

Varun felt unsure and a bit disappointed with his choice, frowning at his watermelon-basil, saying Pema's looked nicer and still reading the board.
What small step would help Varun choose faster and enjoy his drink more next time?
He could choose from just two or three he already likes instead of reading all forty, so there are fewer what-ifs afterwards.
What might Pema's mother be thinking as Varun read the board up and down?
She might be amused but also a bit impatient, and puzzled that a simple treat turned into so much worry for him.

I share the room with my brother Chetan this year, so I saw the whole thing.
The results came in on his phone at dinner. He'd failed Engineering Mechanics. He went very still, pushed his plate away and went to the balcony. I didn't follow.
About an hour later he came back in. "Kalyani, I'm really gutted," he said. "I'm not going to pretend I'm not." Then he got out the question paper from his bag and sat on the floor with it.
I watched him go through each question and mark it: knew it, rushed it, never studied it. Most of the red marks were in the last two units. He muttered, "So I didn't run out of brain. I ran out of weeks."
I can't say what he was thinking out there. But he came back with a plan, not an excuse.

What subject had Chetan failed?
He'd failed Engineering Mechanics.

He felt deeply disappointed and was honest about it, but he also seemed determined to find out what went wrong.

Kalyani can't be sure what Chetan felt on the balcony but notices, with some respect, that he came back with a plan, not an excuse.

At the block office in Chhindwara district, the notice came by email at noon: the new primary health centre for Lalit's village had finally been approved. Disha watched Lalit read it. His eyes went wide, he let out a long breath, and when he spoke, his voice was tight and strange. "It's approved." Then he went out onto the verandah and stood very still with his back to everyone. Disha couldn't read it. Was he worried about the land it would take? Upset about something she didn't know? She gave him a few minutes, then went out with two cups of tea and stood beside him. "You looked surprised in there. Are you okay?" He took the tea, eyes wet. "Relieved. My mother had to travel forty kilometres for every check-up last year. Now the village won't have to." Disha nodded and said nothing more, letting him have the quiet. After a while he laughed shakily. "Don't tell anyone I cried at a notice."

How far did Lalit's mother have to travel for check-ups?
Forty kilometres.
What was Lalit feeling after reading the notice?
Lalit felt surprised and deeply relieved, even tearful, because his mother and village would no longer travel so far for care.
How did Disha check in well?
She gave him a few minutes, joined him with tea, named what she saw and asked if he was okay, then let him have quiet.
What would have changed if Disha had assumed Lalit was upset about the land?
She might have offered the wrong comfort or asked awkward questions, missing that he was actually relieved.

I'm Francis, from next door. Sumit, who's eleven, has two little twin brothers, and I used to hear him shouting at them through the wall. Last summer his grandmother came from Kerala for three months. Every evening I'd see her on their porch teaching Sumit how to peel mangoes in one long strip. The twins would try to grab the knife, and she'd hand them the seeds to suck instead. Sumit started doing the same thing when she wasn't there. Once I saw him split his biscuit into three. I don't know what he felt, but the shouting got less. When his grandmother left, he stood at the gate for a long time after the taxi turned.

She taught him how to peel mangoes in one long strip.

Minakshi, come, sit by your Pooja Dadi. I know you haven't slept since your classmate's funeral. Let me tell you something.
When I was sixteen, my best friend Shobha died of a fever. One week she was laughing with me by the well, and the next she was gone. I stopped talking. I wouldn't eat.
My mother didn't tell me to be brave. She gave me a notebook and said, “Write to her.”
So I did. Every night for a year. I told Shobha everything: exams, a boy I liked, my fights with my sister.
On the first anniversary I went to Shobha's mother, gave her the notebook and helped her cook for the prayer. She held me for a long time. Grief doesn't vanish, beti. It just finds a place to live.

A notebook.
How did young Pooja feel after Shobha died?
She felt deep grief and shock, so heavy she stopped talking and eating.

Writing to Shobha every night and later going to help Shobha's mother on the anniversary.
How might Shobha's mother have felt when Pooja gave her the notebook?
She probably felt moved and comforted to know how much her daughter was loved.

"Watch, Francis mama," Bhupen's mother said. "Bhupen, show him."
Bhupen marched to the sofa, planted a knee on the seat's edge and pushed. Up.
"Wah!" said Francis mama. "How did he learn that?"
"Last week the knee worked once. Now it's always the knee."
"Down, and again!" Bhupen slid off, knee up, push. Up. Faster than before.
"He's timing himself," Francis mama laughed.

He planted a knee on the seat's edge.

He was proud and excited, eager to show off his fast climb.
What else could Bhupen's mother try to keep him learning?
She could offer a different sofa or a higher chair with her nearby, so he tests whether the knee trick works elsewhere.
How does Francis mama see the climbing?
He is impressed and amused, laughing that Bhupen seems to be timing himself.

The inter-school chess tournament in Chennai was held in a crowded hall with fans that barely worked. Karthik, eight, lost his second game in twelve moves. He walked out to the corridor, face hot, and started crying behind a pillar. His mother Disha was supposed to be there, but she was stuck in traffic. A volunteer sat near him. Twenty minutes later Disha rushed in, breathless, and found him. She knelt and hugged him. "You lost. That hurts." Karthik sobbed into her shoulder. She waited, rubbing his back. When he was calm, she gave him a banana and said, "Round three starts in ten minutes. Do you want to play?" He sniffed. "What if I lose again?" "Then I'll hug you again." Karthik laughed a little, wiped his nose, and walked back to the board.

How many moves did Karthik's second game last?
Twelve moves.
How did Karthik feel after his mother's hug?
Karthik felt comforted and calm enough to laugh a little, safe to try again because his mother would be there either way.
What did Disha's response get right?
She named his hurt, let him cry without rushing, and then offered the next round with the promise of support, not pressure.
How might the volunteer have felt waiting near Karthik?
The volunteer may have felt concerned and relieved when his mother finally arrived.

“Jasleen, you've been staring at the wall for ten minutes.”
“Nani's in hospital again, Asif. Mum's there all day, Dad's travelling. I can't do anything.”
“You can't fix Nani, true.”
“So what's the point of anything?”
Asif pulled out a notebook. “My cousin did this when her parents were splitting up. Two lists. Stuff you control, stuff you don't.”
“That's so… school counsellor.”
“Humour me.”
Jasleen sighed. “Don't control: Nani getting better. Dad's work. Mum being tired.”
“And control?”
“I guess… I can make dinner so Mum doesn't have to. I can visit Nani after school. I can keep up with maths so I'm not failing on top of everything. I can call Dad at night.”
Asif underlined the second list. “So do those.”
Jasleen looked at it for a while. “Okay. Dinner tonight. I'll make khichdi.”

Where is Jasleen's Nani?
Nani is in hospital again.
How did Jasleen feel before making the lists?
Jasleen felt helpless and stuck, asking what the point of anything was.
Why does acting on the “control” list help Jasleen?
It turns Jasleen's attention to real actions like making dinner and visiting Nani, which restores a sense of power in a hard situation.
How does Asif see Jasleen's situation?
Asif accepts that Jasleen can't fix Nani, but believes there are still things to do, and wants to help Jasleen find them.

Pradeep: where are you? your mum called me
Nilesh: I hit someone with the bike near the bus stand
Pradeep: WHAT. is he ok??
Nilesh: I don't know. people were running at me. I got scared and rode off
Pradeep: Nilesh you have to go back
Nilesh: they'll beat me. I saw them shouting
Pradeep: then go to the police station. not back to the crowd. the station
Nilesh: I'll get arrested
Pradeep: leaving is worse. and the man might still be lying there
Nilesh: ...
Pradeep: I'm calling your mama. he'll come with you
A little later Nilesh's uncle messaged Pradeep: "Found him at the tea shop. We're at the police station now. The man was taken to hospital by an auto driver. He's hurt but awake."
Nilesh: I should have stopped. I keep seeing him on the road

Who took the injured man to hospital?
An auto driver took him to hospital.
Why did Nilesh ride off, and how does Nilesh feel afterwards?
Nilesh was frightened of being beaten by the crowd, and afterwards feels guilty, unable to stop seeing the man on the road.
What would have been a safer choice than riding off?
Nilesh could have stopped at a safe distance, called 112 and waited for the police, so the man got help without Nilesh facing the crowd alone.
How does Pradeep respond to Nilesh's panic?
Pradeep is shocked but firm, pushing Nilesh toward the police station and calling his uncle to go with him.

Read this:

After two slow rounds of the mustard field on Chacha's motorbike, Anand announced at dinner that he could ride to the Thursday haat himself. "It's easy. Clutch, gear, go." His cousin Afreen raised an eyebrow. "In the field, with Chacha holding the back?" "That was just the first time." On Thursday morning he wheeled the bike into the lane while everyone was at the well. The lane had a bullock cart, three goats and a curve by the pond that the field did not. At the curve he braked too hard, the bike wobbled, and his foot went into the ditch. Afreen, who had followed on foot, grabbed the handlebar. "Keys," she said. Anand handed them over, shaking. That evening Chacha put the keys on the high shelf.

What did the lane have that the field did not?
A bullock cart, three goats and a curve by the pond.
Why did Anand feel ready to ride to the haat?
He felt confident because two slow rounds in the field felt easy, so he mistook a little practice for real skill.
What would have been a wiser next step for Anand?
Keep practising in the field with Chacha and wait until an adult agrees he is ready, instead of taking the bike onto the lane alone.
What was it like for Afreen to follow Anand on foot?
Afreen was probably worried about him, which is why she followed and grabbed the handlebar the moment he wobbled.

Read this:

The community centre's Wednesday reading circle met in a room that smelled of floor polish and chai. Lalit had come for six weeks now. Tonight's reading was from the Book of Job, and the circle held a Sikh schoolteacher, two Catholic nurses, a retired engineer who called himself an atheist, and Lalit, who no longer knew what to call himself.
'Why would a good God allow this?' Lalit asked, tapping the photocopy.
Santosh, the retired engineer, shrugged. 'I've decided there's no God. Doesn't make the question go away, though.'
One of the nurses said she asked it every night shift.
Lalit wrote in his notebook: Nobody here has solved it. Everyone is still showing up.
He stayed behind to stack chairs, turning the question over like a smooth stone. He wasn't in a hurry anymore.

What was the reading at tonight's circle?
Tonight's reading was from the Book of Job.
What does Lalit's note 'Everyone is still showing up' suggest he is realising?
He is realising that hard questions don't need quick answers to be worth sitting with, and he feels less alone in them.
What about the reading circle supports Lalit's seeking?
It brings believers of several faiths and an atheist together around one text, so he can test ideas against real experience without anyone pushing a conclusion.
How might the nurse who asks the question every night shift experience the circle?
She might find comfort in hearing others wrestle with the same question she faces at work.

On the coach back from the zoo, the back row belonged to Felix's class. When Aiko, three rows ahead, laughed her high, hiccuping laugh, Jonas squeaked it back. Then five boys squeaked it, then eight. Felix pulled his hood up and squeaked loudest of all. Under the hood he was just part of the noise, one of many grey sweatshirts, and the coach rocked with laughter. At the rest stop, though, Felix ended up alone at the hand dryer beside Aiko. She was quiet, drying her hands for much longer than she needed to. He opened his mouth and realised he could not make that sound to her face, not in a million years. "Nice penguins today," he mumbled instead, and felt his ears burn.

Where did Felix end up alone beside Aiko?
At the rest stop, Felix ended up alone at the hand dryer beside Aiko.
What do Felix's burning ears suggest he is feeling?
Felix seems embarrassed and guilty, because alone with Aiko he knows he could never make that sound to her face.
What could Felix choose to do now that the hood is off?
Felix could say sorry to Aiko for the squeaking and refuse to join in on the ride home, even if the back row carries on.
Why might Aiko have dried her hands for much longer than she needed to?
Aiko may have been hurt and putting off going back to the coach, where so many voices had been copying her laugh.

"So if I go to the camp, who handles the flower orders for the Navratri weddings?" Bhavna's mother asked.

"Kamal bhaiya," Bhavna said. "I called him. He'll come from Nashik for four days."

Her elder cousin Kamal, on speakerphone, said, "Only four, though. After that I have exams."

"The camp's six days," her father pointed out.

"I know. So before I go, I'll work Monday and Tuesday evenings, and I'll make all the garlands for the first two weddings in advance. And every night from the camp I'll update the orders sheet on the phone."

Her mother crossed her arms. "And the last two days?"

"Can Masi help? She offered at Diwali."

Her mother thought. "She did."

Her father smiled for the first time that evening. "It's not perfect. But it might work."

How many days can Kamal come from Nashik?
Four days.
What does her father's first smile of the evening suggest?
It suggests he felt relieved and reassured, seeing that Bhavna had thought through how the shop would manage.
What could the family do if Masi can't help after all?
They could reduce the number of orders taken for those two days, so no one is overwhelmed while Bhavna is away.
How might Bhavna's mother see the plan?
Her mother seemed sceptical at first, arms crossed, but she softened on remembering Masi's offer, which suggests growing trust in the plan.

Monday. Sabina's mother Leela stood at the kitchen door shouting, "Sabina, it is time for your bath, and we have to go early tomorrow and the water is getting cold and if you don't come now..." Sabina kept stacking blocks and did not look up.
Tuesday. Leela knelt beside the tower, eyes level with Sabina's. "Bath time. Two more blocks, then we go." Sabina placed two blocks and took Leela's hand.
Friday. Leela only had to crouch and say, "Bath time." Sabina put down the last block by herself and reached up to be carried, still holding one block in a fist.

Which day did Leela kneel beside the tower of blocks?
Leela knelt beside the tower on Tuesday.
What might Leela have been feeling on Monday while shouting from the kitchen door?
Leela was probably hurried and frustrated, since the long list of reasons ran on and Sabina did not look up. The kneeling on Tuesday shows a calmer try.
What did Leela change on Tuesday, and how did it help?
Leela knelt to Sabina's eye level and gave one short instruction with a small choice of two more blocks. Sabina placed them and took Leela's hand.
How might Sabina see the difference between Monday and Tuesday?
On Monday Sabina heard a long, rushed stream of words and kept stacking. On Tuesday Sabina saw a face and heard one clear idea, so listening was easy.

Wed, 11 pm
Jatin's first week at the station. Tonight he had to cut a ten-minute interview into a three-minute clip for the morning show, and I could have done it in fifteen minutes. My fingers actually hovered over his keyboard.
Instead I asked what he'd tried. He'd cut from the start and run out of time before the good part. One hint: find the best thirty seconds first, then build around it. Then I made myself go and refill the water jug.
He took nearly an hour. We missed the eleven o'clock handover, and the producer gave me a look.
But the clip was good. Better than mine would have been, honestly, because he kept the bit where the fisherman laughs.
Next week he'll do it in twenty minutes, and I'll have a colleague, not a trainee. Worth one look from the producer.
Amandeep

What hint did Amandeep give Jatin?
Find the best thirty seconds first, then build around it.
Why did Amandeep go and refill the water jug?
Amandeep wanted to get away from the urge to take over, so that Jatin would finish the clip alone.
Was the slower route worth the missed handover, and why?
Yes: the producer's look cost little, while Jatin made a better clip and will soon be a colleague who can do it fast.
How might the producer have seen the missed handover differently from Amandeep?
The producer probably saw only a delay, not the training that Amandeep was putting in for next week's shows.

On Saturday morning, three rooms needed tidying.

Tushar looked around and said, "Books first." He put the books on the shelf. "Then toys." They went in the box. "Then clothes," and the clothes went into the basket. Each kind went by itself, and the floor came back.

Zainab had a rule her mother helped her make: "If it has wheels, it goes in the blue box." She picked up a car, a truck and her scooter, and put them in the blue box without asking anyone whether each one belonged.

Jagdish stood at the door and saw toys on the floor, on the bed, under the chair. He walked into the middle of the room, sat down, and picked up a wooden train. Chug, chug. By lunchtime the train had crossed the carpet twice, and nothing had gone into a box.

What went in the blue box?
Things with wheels went in the blue box: a car, a truck and a scooter.
How did Jagdish's way of facing the mess differ from Tushar's and Zainab's?
Tushar and Zainab used an order or a rule that made each next step clear, while Jagdish sat down to play with one toy and nothing got put away.
What might Jagdish be feeling when he sees toys everywhere?
Overwhelmed and unsure where to begin, so he turns to something familiar.
How could an adult help Jagdish?
An adult could start with him on one small kind of thing, like the wheeled toys, and let him finish it.

At sixteen, Hrithik told the host's grandmother at a birthday party that her sweets were "a bit dry" and then laughed too loudly. The grandmother blinked. Hrithik stared at the floor for the rest of the party and spent the next three nights replaying the sentence from every angle. What if I'd said "lovely"? Everyone must still be talking about it. On Monday Lalit, a friend, said, "Honestly, I forgot it before we got home." Hrithik nodded, then replayed it again that night.

At twenty, Hrithik failed the thermodynamics paper. Why did this happen? Too little sleep? The wrong notes? Am I just not clever enough? The same questions circled in the hostel room, on the walk to the canteen and under the shower, and after a week none had turned into a single step. Manoj, a roommate, put down his tea. "You've asked why nine times. What's one thing you could do tomorrow?" Hrithik looked at the wall and had no answer yet.

What did Hrithik say about the grandmother's sweets?
Hrithik said her sweets were "a bit dry."
How are Hrithik's thoughts after the party and after the failed paper alike, and why do they not help?

After the party Hrithik replays the dry-sweets sentence and imagines everyone still talking; after the paper Hrithik asks why it happened, with the same questions circling and no single step. Going over and over feels like solving something, but without any action it deepens the sting and keeps the mood low.
What was Hrithik feeling while staring at the floor during the party?
Hrithik felt embarrassed and ashamed, sure that the remark had been heard by everyone.
What small step could Hrithik take in response to Manoj's question?
Hrithik could look through the marked paper, note one topic to revisit and ask the lecturer or a classmate about it, turning the why into a plan.

The school ground in the kasba was dusty and loud. Jahnavi and Afreen crouched at the chalk line for the sack race. Jahnavi wanted to beat Afreen more than anything. Before the teacher shouted "go", she jumped. The whistle blew. "Jahnavi, come back." Jahnavi's face burned. The teacher, Sunita Ma'am, bent down. "I know you want to win. You can be proud if you try your best, whatever happens." On the restart, Jahnavi waited for "go". Afreen beat her by a hop. Jahnavi fell over laughing and still felt proud.

What race were Jahnavi and Afreen in?
They were in the sack race.
How did Jahnavi feel when the whistle blew?
She felt embarrassed, her face burning, after starting early because she wanted to win so badly.
Which part of Sunita Ma'am's response helped Jahnavi?
She named Jahnavi's wish to win and told her she can be proud of her best effort, so Jahnavi waited properly.
What is it like for Afreen when Jahnavi starts early?
Afreen may feel it is unfair and upset at first, then pleased to win the fair restart. 😊

So you want to know how the whole mess started? I'm Kalyani, and honestly, it started with me.

It was the day of the science fair. I was setting up our volcano when Tarun and Mitali walked in together, forty minutes late, carrying the same box.

My brain just went: they're a couple. They came together. They're late. They're giggling. Obviously.

I didn't stop to think. I wanted to be the first to know. I wanted everyone to crowd around me and say, "What? No way!" So I texted two friends right there, under the table.

Later I found out Tarun's project partner had fallen ill and Mitali had helped him carry the box from his house. That's it. That was the whole thing.

But by then my guess had already become everyone's fact.

Why were Tarun and Mitali carrying the same box?
Tarun's project partner had fallen ill and Mitali helped him carry it from his house.
What was Kalyani feeling when she texted her friends under the table?
Kalyani felt excited and eager to be the first with news, wanting everyone to crowd around.
What went wrong, and what could Kalyani have done instead?
Kalyani shared a guess as if it were fact; waiting, or simply asking Tarun or Mitali why they were late, would have stopped it.
What was it like for Mitali when the guess became everyone's fact?
She probably felt embarrassed and unfairly talked about, just for helping a classmate.
My friend Dev just got his first job. Write him a happy congratulations message, about 45 words.

Dear Dev,
Congratulations on your first job! You deserve this, and I am delighted for you. I am sure you will do very well. Let us celebrate soon, and the first round is on you! Well done, my friend.
Cheers

Computer club log, Thursday
During free play, Chinmay joined an online kart race. Another racer began sending insults in the open chat, calling him slow and stupid. I watched his ears turn red and his hands press hard on the keys. He typed a long reply in capitals. Elizabeth, sitting next to him, whispered, "Don't send it." He held his finger over Enter for a moment, then deleted the message.
He came to my desk, still breathing fast. Together we muted, blocked and reported the racer. I told Chinmay that stopping was the harder and smarter move. I also emailed his mother so they could talk it through at home.
He spent the rest of the session building a track with Elizabeth.

What did the other racer call Chinmay?
Slow and stupid.
What do Chinmay's red ears and hard key presses suggest he was feeling?
He was furious and humiliated and wanted to hit back with insults of his own.
What did the club supervisor do next that helped?
They muted, blocked and reported the racer with Chinmay, praised him for stopping, and emailed his mother.
How did Elizabeth see Chinmay's long reply?
Elizabeth could see it would only make things worse, so she quietly urged him not to send it.
Why does a firecracker make such a sudden loud bang?
The bang comes from a quick burst of gas. Because the burning powder makes a lot of hot gas in a flash and the gas shoves the air outward sharply, we hear a loud crack.

"How are you so calm, Kiran? You teach five classes and run the science club."
"I'm not calm by nature. I just stopped trusting my head to hold everything."
"Meaning?"
Kiran opened a small notebook. "Everything goes in here. Marking, parent calls, club stuff. If it's written, I don't have to keep remembering it."
"And the huge things? Like the annual exhibition?"
"Broken into bits. This week it's only 'book the hall'. Next week, 'list the projects'."
"My phone buzzes all day with school groups."
"Mine too. I turned them off. I check them twice a day, at lunch and at four."
Anjali sighed. "And breaks?"
"Ten minutes after every two classes. I sit outside. No phone."
"That sounds too simple."
"It is simple. That's why it works."

When does Kiran check the school groups?
Twice a day, at lunch and at four.
Why did Kiran stop 'trusting my head to hold everything'?
Kiran felt overwhelmed trying to remember everything, and found calm by moving tasks into a notebook.
Which of Kiran's habits could help Anjali most, and why?
Writing everything down and breaking big projects into weekly bits, because it frees the mind to focus on one thing at a time.
How does Anjali seem to feel during the conversation?
Anjali seems overwhelmed and a little doubtful, sighing and finding it all too simple.

Baljeet arrived at the Pune hostel in the middle of the monsoon, knowing nobody, with a phone that barely held a charge and his family three states away. By the second week he was up till three every night, because that's when Wing C came alive: card games, loud debates, instant noodles on a smuggled heater. The seniors drank on Saturdays, and Baljeet, who had never touched alcohol, held a glass he didn't drink so he'd fit in. He began repeating their opinions on everything from cricket to politics. Mid-term exams were ten days away. One night his roommate Omkar, who went to bed at eleven, said, 'You don't even like cards.' Baljeet laughed it off, but lying awake later, he couldn't remember the last opinion he'd had that was really his.

Until what time was Baljeet up every night?
Till three.
What did Baljeet feel lying awake at the end?
Uneasy and a bit lost, unable to remember the last opinion that was truly his.
What could Baljeet try to find himself again?
Set a bedtime before the exams, keep one or two of his own habits, and spend time with people like Omkar who notice who he really is.
How might Omkar see Baljeet's first weeks?
Omkar seems to notice Baljeet changing to fit Wing C and is quietly concerned, pointing out he doesn't even like cards.

At Sunday lunch in Teta's flat in Marseille, Aunt Samira passed the couscous and said, "Rosa got the highest maths mark in her class again. Twenty out of twenty!"

Everyone clapped. Nour's cousin Rosa went pink.

Nour, ten, looked at her plate. Her own test, fourteen out of twenty, was folded in her school bag. On Friday she had been proud of it.

"And Nour?" someone asked.

"Fourteen," she said quietly.

"Good, good," said Teta, and reached for the bread.

On the bus home Nour unfolded the test and studied the two questions she'd got wrong. Part of her wanted to beat Rosa next time. Part of her just wanted Friday's feeling back.

What mark did Nour get on her test?
Nour got fourteen out of twenty.
What mixed feelings did Nour have on the bus home?
Nour felt hurt that her proud Friday feeling had faded, and also motivated, wanting to beat Rosa next time.
What small step would help Nour hold on to her pride?
Keep her own progress in view, like the fourteen she was proud of on Friday, and fix the two wrong questions for herself rather than only to beat Rosa.
How might Rosa feel when everyone claps?
Rosa went pink, so she may feel pleased and embarrassed at once, and perhaps awkward next to Nour.

At fifteen, Indu felt her cheeks flame every time the teacher called on her. She was sure the whole class was staring, so she looked at the floor and mumbled. One day Tenzin, her music teacher, paused the lesson and said, "Look at the window and tell me one thing you can see." Indu breathed out slowly, looked at a crow on the ledge, and answered in a steadier voice. Nobody had turned to stare; most of them were looking at their own notebooks.

At twenty-one, on the morning of her viva, Indu's hands shook and her palms were damp. She had rehearsed her answers with her friend Baljeet the night before. Now she pressed her feet into the floor, counted five breaths and told herself, "My body is getting ready." When the first question came, she began speaking, and the shaking eased. She had decided that if it ever grew into panic that stayed, she would go to the college counsellor.

What did Indu see when Tenzin asked her to look at the window?
Indu saw a crow on the ledge.
What did Indu learn about handling her body's signals between fifteen and twenty-one?

At fifteen she used a slow breath and looked outward, discovering that few people had noticed her blush; at twenty-one she added preparation, feet on the floor and counted breaths, and read the shaking as her body getting ready.
What was Indu feeling when her cheeks flamed at fifteen?
Indu was anxious and self-conscious, sure that everyone was staring at her.
Why did Indu rehearse with Baljeet before the viva?
Preparation calms nerves, and answering aloud to a friend meant she had practised her responses before the shaky, high-stakes moment.
Change to direct speech: Mother asked me if I had eaten lunch.
Mother asked me, "Have you eaten lunch?"

By lunchtime the class had decided, over the long canteen table of a Kolkata college: Jaya had leaked the tutorial answers. "She's always in the professor's cabin," someone said. "Obviously." Heads nodded. Jaya sat at the far end, eating very slowly, not looking up.
Urmila put down her glass. "What's the evidence?"
"Everyone's saying it."
"That's not evidence. The answers came from a photo of the key, right? The key was pinned on the notice board on Monday for ten minutes. Anyone walking past could have taken it." Her voice stayed level. "And Jaya was at the dentist on Monday. She posted about it."
A pause. Tanmay said, "Oh. Yeah, she did."
"I'm not joining this," Urmila said, and moved to sit next to Jaya.
Two others picked up their trays and followed.

How long was the answer key pinned on the notice board?
For ten minutes on Monday.
What does Jaya eating slowly without looking up suggest?
Jaya felt hurt, humiliated and alone, wishing to disappear while the table accused her.
Which of Urmila's steps broke the spiral?
Asking for evidence, calmly laying out the facts, refusing to join, and physically sitting with Jaya, which gave others a way to follow.
How might Tanmay see things after Urmila spoke?
Tanmay seemed surprised and a bit sheepish, realising he had nodded along without checking 😅

Yamini, sit. Your Ujjwal chacha has an interview story for you. I was twenty-four, applying to the cooperative bank in Indore. Three weeks before, I had already decided I would fail. "Those boys from the city colleges will walk in," I told my mother. So why prepare? I played carrom every evening instead.
On the day, my collar was wet with sweat before I even sat down. The manager asked me something simple about interest, and my mind went white. I stammered and looked at the floor. When the no came, I said, "See, Amma, I told you."
She said, "You told yourself, and then you listened."
The next year I sat with the books every night. Same bank, same manager. That time, I got it. So, what are you doing this evening?

What did Ujjwal do every evening instead of preparing?
He played carrom every evening.
What was young Ujjwal feeling when he sat down for the interview?
He was very anxious, sweating before he sat and going blank, because he had expected failure for weeks.
What choice turned things around for Ujjwal the next year?
He sat with the books every night instead of assuming he would lose, so he walked in prepared.
What did Ujjwal's mother see that he missed?
She saw that his own prediction shaped his lack of effort: he had told himself he would fail and then acted on it.

When the hall clapped and someone shouted "Irfan!", I walked up for the regional sales award holding a trophy that felt heavier than it looked. Looking back, I nearly did what I always used to: smile, say "it was a team effort", and sit down. But that quarter, Pooja had rebuilt our customer list at night, Manoj had driven six hours to close the Nashik order, and Sameera had fixed every invoice error before it reached the client. So I named them, one by one, on stage. On Monday I sent the director an email listing what each of them had done, and split the bonus pool evenly. Pooja later said no leader had ever done that. I didn't do it to be liked. I just knew the trophy had many hands behind it.

Who drove six hours to close the Nashik order?
Manoj did.
What was Irfan aware of as the trophy felt heavier than it looked?
Irfan was aware that the success had many hands behind it, so the credit was not Irfan's alone.
What did Irfan do on Monday, and why does it matter?
Irfan emailed the director a list of what each person had done and split the bonus pool evenly, so the team's work was seen by senior leaders and shared fairly.
What might Pooja have felt when Irfan named the team?
Probably valued and trusted, given that Pooja later remarked that no leader had done this before. 😊

I'm Jyoti, I sit next to Tejas's team in the lab, and the week before the hackathon they were strange to watch.
On Monday they stood at the whiteboard and Tejas wrote in big letters: WE LOST. WHY? I thought it was a joke. Then they started filling it. "Network dies." "Laptop crashes." "Only Tejas knows the backend."
By Wednesday each line had a name and a fix next to it. Someone had a pocket hotspot on the desk. The backend was split into three parts with three different people's names on sticky notes, and Tejas was teaching the other two how the database worked.
On the day of the hackathon, their laptop froze during setup, and they carried on from a second one with the same code. I don't know if Tejas was calm inside. He looked calm.

What did Tejas write on the whiteboard on Monday?
Tejas wrote WE LOST. WHY? in big letters.
What does Tejas looking calm on the hackathon day suggest?
It suggests Tejas felt prepared and fairly confident, though Jyoti admits not knowing what was going on inside.
What else could Tejas's team add to their list, and why?
They could add a timed rehearsal of the pitch, since running out of time while presenting is another common way hackathon teams lose.
How does Jyoti see the team's week of planning?
Jyoti first thinks the whiteboard is a joke, then watches the fixes appear and sees the team handle the frozen laptop smoothly.
