Read this:

In Karad, Chandrika, sixteen, sat on the steps outside the temple long after the evening aarti.
Her friend Eshaan had been caught bunking school to hang around the bus stand with older boys. His father had been called in.
Chandrika kept going over it. She had seen him skip on Monday and hadn't said anything. On Tuesday she'd been too busy with her project to walk home with him. If she had, maybe he wouldn't have gone.
“It's my fault,” she told her mother at dinner.
Her mother put down the ladle. “Did you tell him to bunk?”
“No.”
“Did you take him to the bus stand?”
“No, but…”
“Then it's his choice. You can be sad for him. You can talk to him. But you can't carry what he chose, beta.”
Chandrika nodded slowly, but the heavy feeling in her chest stayed a while longer.

Where had Eshaan been hanging around when he bunked school?
He had been hanging around the bus stand with older boys.
Why did Chandrika feel it was her fault?
She felt guilty and over-responsible, thinking that if she had spoken up or walked home with him, he wouldn't have gone.
What did Chandrika's mother help her see?
That Eshaan's choice was his own; Chandrika can care and talk to him but doesn't have to carry the blame.
How might Eshaan feel if he knew Chandrika blamed herself?
Eshaan might feel surprised and a bit guilty himself, since it was his own decision to bunk.

Read this:

In the school yard in Accra, Kofi walked around the long way so he would not pass Dalia's class. Last Friday he had promised to help her paint the set for the play, but he went to play football instead and never said a word. Now his ears burned whenever he saw her. All week he hid behind the water tank at lunch. On Thursday he saw her holding a heavy board alone, and his stomach turned. He walked across the yard and said, "I did not come because I chose football. I am sorry. Can I paint with you now?" Dalia looked at him for a moment and handed him a brush.

Which city is the school in?
The school is in Accra.
Why did Kofi avoid Dalia's class and hide behind the water tank?
He was embarrassed and ashamed for breaking his promise to help paint the set.
What did Kofi do that started to repair things?
He told her the truth, said sorry and offered to paint with her, instead of hiding any longer.
How might Dalia have felt when Kofi finally came over?
Dalia may have felt let down earlier and cautious, but she seemed willing to accept the honest apology, since she handed him a brush.

Read this:

At the Saturday market in Mylapore, Rajni, four, spotted a guava slice on the fruit seller's cart. "I want it! Now!" Her mother, Shreya, bent down. "You can have the slice now, or wait till we get home and have a whole mango, all to yourself." Rajni looked at the slice. She looked at her mother's bag, where the mango was hiding. She couldn't see it at all. "Slice!" she said, and gobbled it. That evening, when her brother sat on the steps with his mango, juice running down his arms, Rajni stood watching with her fists clenched and her cheeks wet.

What did Shreya offer if Rajni waited till home?
A whole mango, all to herself.
Why did Rajni choose the slice?
Rajni felt impatient and pulled towards the slice she could see, while the mango hidden in the bag felt unreal, so waiting seemed pointless.
What could help Rajni wait next time?
Shreya could show her the mango or let her hold it, or sing a song with her on the walk home so the wait passes.
What might Rajni's brother think seeing her watch him?
Her brother might feel a bit awkward or sorry for her, and perhaps share a bite.

Read this:

Imran taught Class 8 maths at the zilla parishad school in Wai, and for six weeks he had dragged himself through each day. He slept early. He drank from the matka in the staffroom so often the other teachers joked about it. Still he felt heavy, and still his mouth felt dry. He told himself it was the heat, then the new syllabus, then his age, though he was only twenty-five. One Sunday his friend Yogesh watched him doze off mid-sentence over tea at the stall. "Enough guessing, Imran. You rested, you drank. It's not working. We're going to the doctor at the district hospital tomorrow. I'll come on the bus with you." Imran opened his mouth to argue, then closed it. On Monday he took half a day's leave, and they caught the eight o'clock bus to Satara together.

Where did Imran drink water at school?
From the matka in the staffroom.
Why did Imran keep blaming the heat and the syllabus?
He felt worn down but reluctant to face that something might be wrong, so guessing felt easier than a check.
Why was Yogesh right to push for the district hospital?
Rest and water had not helped over weeks, so a doctor was needed to look for a physical cause that willpower can't fix.
What might Yogesh have felt watching Imran doze off mid-sentence?
Yogesh was likely worried and fed up with the guessing, which is why he offered to come on the bus.

Read this:

Subject: The list I've been making

Hi Nazia,

You asked last month why I've been so quiet. Here's the honest version.

I've been making a list. Late at night, mostly.

The Kathak diploma I dropped in Class 11 because Ma said dance was a hobby, not a future.
Rehaan, who asked me to come to Bengaluru with him, and I said no because I couldn't imagine telling my parents.
The gap year I wanted after graduation, which turned into a bank exam I didn't want and didn't clear.

What gets me is not that I chose wrong. It's that I don't think I chose at all. I chose whatever would make the least noise at home. I was scared, and I called it being sensible.

I'm not asking you to fix it. I just needed someone to read it who knew me back then.

Love,
Sonali

Why did Sonali drop the Kathak diploma?
Sonali dropped it because Ma said dance was a hobby, not a future.
How can you tell Sonali's regret is tangled up with feeling afraid?
Sonali writes that each choice was made to keep things quiet at home, and admits being scared and calling it being sensible.
What small step would help Sonali now?
Talking it through with Nazia, who knew Sonali back then, could help sort which of these lost chances can still be picked up in some form, like dance classes, and which need grieving.
If you were Nazia reading this, what would you want?
You might feel moved and a little sad for your friend, and you would want to call or meet soon to listen, since Sonali said this is not a request to fix things.

metadata.subtype: Stage 2: Counting the roads not taken [Actor]

Read this:

Nandini tore out the page of her old school diary where she had copied prayers in her best handwriting. Her hands were shaking.
"Why are you so angry?" Yamini asked from the other bed in their Kolkata hostel room.
"Because they told me if I didn't fast, bad things would happen to Papa. I was eight! I fasted till I fainted once." Nandini crumpled the page. "And I believed every rule they gave me without a single question."
She had stopped believing a year ago, calmly, or so she'd thought. Now, suddenly, the anger had arrived, hot and bitter, about every fear she'd been handed as a child.
"Maybe you don't have to decide what you believe tonight," Yamini said.
"I just want to be done with it."
"I don't think it works that fast."
Nandini sat down, the crumpled page in her fist, and didn't answer.

What did Nandini tear out of her old diary?
The page where she had copied prayers in her best handwriting.
Why is Nandini so angry now?
She feels bitter and betrayed about the fears she was taught as a child, like fasting to protect Papa.
What does Yamini's advice suggest about this stage?
That anger is part of an honest process and rushing to a firm conclusion tonight won't end it; giving it time is wiser.
What is it like for Yamini to watch this?
Yamini feels concerned and gentle, trying to steady her friend without taking sides.

Why do we put salt on a slippery icy road?
Plus, which movie is playing at the nearest cinema tonight?
Then, I keep seeing "footfall" in my reading. Meaning?
Finally, please correct: He don't know the answer.

1. Salt makes ice melt. Because salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes, so the ice turns to water.
2. I don't know that. I can't see show timings. Check the cinema's website or call the ticket counter.
3. "Footfall" is a noun. It means the sound of a step.
4. Fixed: He doesn't know the answer. Why: with "he", the helping verb is "doesn't", not "don't".

Read this:

Usha, you're angry at the other house for cheating in kho-kho? Hmm. Sit. Let your Karthik thatha tell you about Pongal sports day when I was ten.

I was in Green House. We were playing tug of war against Red. Our biggest boy, Selvam, wrapped the rope around his wrist, which was against the rules. I saw it. I said nothing. We won.

Next race, a Red House boy started a step too early. I screamed, "Cheating! Cheating!"

That night, my father asked, "Did Green House do anything wrong?"

I thought of Selvam's wrist. I felt hot in the face.

Being Green felt so good that I stopped seeing fairly.

So, Usha, did your house do anything wrong too?

What did Selvam do in the tug of war?
Selvam wrapped the rope around his wrist, which was against the rules.
How did young Karthik feel when his father asked about Green House?
Young Karthik felt embarrassed and hot in the face, remembering Selvam's wrist.
What was the turning point in Karthik's story?
His father's question made Karthik see he had excused Green's foul while calling Red's the same act cheating.
How might the Red House boy have felt being called a cheat?
The Red House boy may have felt ashamed or unfairly singled out, since Green had broken rules too.

Read this:

I share a desk row with Payal at the insurance office, so I see a lot. She is the one who covers your shift when your kid is sick, who remembers birthdays, who drove the new trainee to the station in the rain. Last Friday our manager asked her to stay late again to finish someone else's claims. I watched her rub her eyes, then smile and say, 'Not tonight. I've stayed late four days this week and I'm starting to make mistakes. I can take two of them first thing Monday.' The manager blinked, then nodded. On Monday she came in early, finished both, and brought samosas for the team. I don't know what went on in her head. But I'm Vaibhav, the one who never says no, and I left at six that Friday too.

How many days had Payal already stayed late that week?
She had stayed late four days that week.
What might Payal have been feeling when she rubbed her eyes before answering?
She was probably tired and a little worried about making mistakes, yet calm enough to say no kindly and offer a Monday plan.
Which part of Payal's reply made the no easier for the manager to accept?
She gave a clear reason, four late days and mistakes creeping in, and offered a specific time, first thing Monday, for two of the claims.
How does watching Payal affect Vaibhav?
Vaibhav, who never says no, sees that a limit can be set politely and still be accepted, and leaves at six that Friday too.

Read this:

It was the week of Christmas, and the school van was late because of fog. When Madhav, five, finally got home, he burst in.

"Papa! Did you see? He fell and the thing broke and everybody laughed!"

His father Jagdish blinked. "Who fell?"

"Him! You know!"

"I wasn't at school, beta."

Madhav frowned, as if Papa was being silly. "The big boy. With the drum. At the song."

Slowly Jagdish pieced it together: a boy had dropped a drum at the carol practice. "And were you sad or did you laugh?"

"I laughed. Everybody laughed. You would laugh too."

What did Jagdish work out had happened at school?
A boy had dropped a drum at the carol practice.
Why did Madhav frown when Papa asked who fell?
He felt puzzled and a bit annoyed, because he thought Papa already knew what he saw.
How could Jagdish help Madhav tell stories more clearly?
He could ask simple questions like who, where and what happened, and say, "I wasn't there, so tell me from the start."
How might the boy who dropped the drum have felt when everyone laughed?
The boy might have felt embarrassed or upset, even if Madhav thought everyone would laugh.
"Aap yahin ruko" - polite aur casual?
Polite: "Could you wait here for a moment, please?" Casual: "Wait here, okay?"

Please go through this passage with me.

"'Oh,' returned the fairy, 'that does not signify! Here is a talisman will remove all difficulties;' and she held out a pretty gold ring. 'Put it,' she said, 'on the fourth finger of my left hand, and I am yours, and you are mine; and we shall leave earth, and make our own heaven yonder.' She nodded again at the moon. The ring, Adele, is in my breeches-pocket, under the disguise of a sovereign: but I mean soon to change it to a ring again."

What does the fairy offer, and what does the ring do?
She offers a pretty gold ring as a charm that removes all difficulties. If it is put on the fourth finger of her left hand, they will belong to each other and leave earth to make their own heaven.

Read this:

In the small government school in Almora, Vikas sir noticed red threads on half the wrists in his Class 10. Pema, his best student, had tied a new one that morning. "For the board exam," she said, a little shy. Vikas smiled; he had kept a lucky coin through his own exams. Another boy wouldn't say his mock result aloud: "If I say it, I'll jinx the real one." Vikas let that be too. What caught his eye was a student who had stopped doing past papers because his temple thread would "take care of it". After class, Vikas sat with him. "Keep the thread. It's yours. But the thread can't write answers. Let's do one paper together tomorrow."

What had Pema tied that morning?
A new red thread.
What did Vikas feel when he saw the red threads?
He felt fond and understanding, remembering his own lucky coin, and became concerned only about the student who had stopped practising.
How did Vikas handle the student who stopped doing past papers?
He respected the thread but explained that it can't write answers, and offered to do a paper together the next day.
How might that student feel after the talk?
He may feel relieved not to be mocked, and steadier with a plan to practise.

Read this:

Week one: The hackathon team had five people. Salma, Kunal's closest friend, said she'd build the login page. Kunal saw her playing games during the work sessions. He said nothing. She's going through a lot, he told himself.
Week two: The others noticed. Deepa asked Kunal, “Is Salma doing anything?” Kunal said, “She'll catch up.” Then he stayed up and built the login page himself.
Week three: The team stopped chatting in the group. Deepa and Arjun started working on their own laptops, not sharing code. When Kunal suggested a team dinner after the demo, nobody answered.
Kunal realised protecting Salma had cost him the team.

What did Salma say she would build?
She said she'd build the login page.
How did Kunal feel as the team went silent in week three?
He felt uneasy and regretful, realising that protecting Salma had cost the team's trust.
What would you advise Kunal to have done in week one?
Kunal could have spoken to Salma privately and asked what was going on, instead of covering for her quietly.
How might Deepa have felt when Kunal said "She'll catch up"?
Deepa may have felt frustrated and brushed off, sensing that friendship mattered more than fairness.
Rewrite from "we" to "they": We cleaned our classroom and arranged our desks in a circle.
They cleaned their classroom and arranged their desks in a circle.

Elizabeth felt herself completely taken in. She had fully proposed being engaged by Wickham for those very dances; and to have Mr. Collins instead!--her liveliness had been never worse timed. There was no help for it, however. Mr. Wickham's happiness and her own was perforce delayed a little longer, and Mr. Collins's proposal accepted with as good a grace as she could. She was not the better pleased with his gallantry, from the idea it suggested of something more. It now first struck her, that she was selected from among her sisters as worthy of being the mistress of Hunsford Parsonage, and of assisting to form a quadrille table at Rosings, in the absence of more eligible visitors. The idea soon reached to conviction, as she observed his increasing civilities towards herself, and heard his frequent attempt at a compliment on her wit and vivacity; and though more astonished than gratified herself by this effect of her charms, it was not long before her mother gave her to understand that the probability of their marriage was exceedingly agreeable to her. Elizabeth, however, did not choose to take the hint, being well aware that a serious dispute must be the consequence of any reply. Mr. Collins might never make the offer, and, till he did, it was useless to quarrel about him.

Give me a summary in fewer than fifty words.

Elizabeth had hoped to dance with Wickham but must accept Mr. Collins instead. She starts to realise he wants to marry her, and her mother clearly likes the idea. Elizabeth says nothing, since he may never propose and arguing would only start a fight.

Read this:

Himani had forty minutes before the last bus and a promise to keep. Nilesh, her friend since Class 3, had asked her to come to his first stage play at the community hall. Her mother had also asked her to be home for her cousin's engagement dinner.
The rain started as she left school. Autos were full. She ran through puddles and reached the hall soaked, just as the curtain rose. She watched his first scene from the back, clapped hard, then slipped out to catch the bus.
She texted him: "Saw you. You were brilliant. Couldn't stay, family dinner, tell me everything tomorrow."
On the bus she thought about it. She didn't have to choose one person over another. She could be someone who shows up, even for part of it, and tells the truth about why.

How much time did Himani have before the last bus?
Forty minutes.
How did Himani seem to feel on the bus afterwards?
She felt settled and a bit relieved that she had kept both promises in part and been honest with Nilesh.
Which choice worked, and why?
Going for the first scene and texting Nilesh the truth worked, because she showed up for her friend and still kept her family commitment.
If you were Nilesh, what would you want from Himani's text?
You would likely feel seen and happy that she came in the rain, and look forward to telling her everything tomorrow.

Read this:

Behind the temple in their small town, Usha and Minakshi, both five, sat in the wet clay by the pond. Usha was making tiny pots. Minakshi was making snakes. "Mine is for water," Usha said. "Mine is a king snake," said Minakshi. When Usha's clay got dry, Minakshi pushed the water tin towards her without being asked. They didn't make anything together; they just kept talking, each with her own lump, until the aarti bell rang.

What was Usha making?
Tiny pots.
What does Minakshi pushing the water tin towards Usha suggest?
She felt friendly and caring towards Usha, happy to share even though they weren't working together.
How could an adult nearby support this kind of play?
Give them space and enough clay and water, and let them chat without insisting they build one thing together.
How might Usha feel about playing with Minakshi?
She likely feels comfortable and content, enjoying company without having to agree on one plan.

Read this:

Friday
Dear Diary,
I planned my whole birthday today. Mushroom pizza, because it's the best food in the world, and then everyone watches the dinosaur film, because everyone loves dinosaurs. I told Ritu at recess and she made a face. She said she hates mushrooms and dinosaur films make her sleepy. I said, "No, you don't." She said, "Yes, I do, Zubin."
Then Arman said he likes paneer pizza better. And Chiku wants to play cricket in the park instead.
I felt weird and a bit angry. How can people not like mushrooms? Amma hugged me and said, "My boy, everybody's tongue is different." I still think they're wrong, but maybe I'll get two kinds of pizza.
- Zubin

What did Chiku want to do instead?
Play cricket in the park.
Why was Zubin so surprised when Ritu made a face?
He believed mushroom pizza and dinosaur films were loved by everyone, so it didn't make sense that a friend could feel differently. 😔
What small step could Zubin take while planning the party?
He could ask his friends what they like before deciding, and offer a choice, like the two kinds of pizza.
How might Ritu have felt when Zubin said, "No, you don't"?
She might feel brushed aside, as if her own likes didn't count.
Explain how to cut a mango in four numbered steps. Keep each step under eight words.

1. Wash the mango well.
2. Stand it on a board.
3. Slice off each side.
4. Scoop out the flesh with a spoon.

Read this:

At the Baisakhi fair near Moga, Harsha Mama bought Gurpreet a red balloon on a string.

Gurpreet, two, held it for three steps. Then the string slipped. The balloon floated up over the Ferris wheel.

Gurpreet's lip trembled. He reached up, then sat down in the dust and wailed, "Loon! Loon!"

Harsha Mama picked him up. "Gone, na? So sad." He let Gurpreet cry on his shoulder, then took him to see the bullocks.

Where did the balloon float?
It floated up over the Ferris wheel.
What was Gurpreet feeling when he sat down and wailed?
Gurpreet was sad and upset about losing the balloon he loved.
What did Harsha Mama do that helped Gurpreet?
He named the loss, let Gurpreet cry on his shoulder, and then gently distracted him with the bullocks.
How might Harsha Mama feel watching the balloon fly away?
Harsha Mama probably felt sorry for Gurpreet and a little sad himself.

Read this:

In Copenhagen, Lars, twenty-one, had been struggling since autumn. He slept badly, missed seminars and had cancelled dinner with Noa three times. "It's just the dark months," he told her. Noa wasn't convinced. Over coffee she said, "It's been weeks. You're not sleeping, you're not studying, and you're avoiding everyone. When it touches all of that, it's time to talk to a professional. Not because you're weak." Lars stirred his coffee. "I wouldn't even know where to start." "The student health service. They have counsellors and a doctor. I'll look up the number now." She did, and he called from the café, voice unsteady. The appointment was for Thursday. He let out a long breath.

How many times had Lars cancelled dinner with Noa?
Three times.
How did Lars feel when he called from the café?
He felt nervous and unsure, his voice unsteady, then relieved once the appointment was booked.
What made Noa's approach effective?
She named the lasting signs affecting sleep, study and relationships, explained that meant seeing a professional and helped him find the student health service.
How might Noa have felt when Lars kept blaming the dark months?
Noa likely felt worried and unconvinced, which is why she spoke up.

Read this:

The sink in the Pune flat had been full since Monday. Nitin left his dal pan on top of the pile on Wednesday night. Four people lived there. Someone will do it, he thought, and one pan hardly changes anything.
Elizabeth added a plate on Thursday. The others added cups.
By Saturday, a line of ants ran from the window to the sink, and the whole kitchen smelled sour. Nitin opened the fridge and found the milk spilled and dried. There was not one clean spoon.
"This is disgusting," Elizabeth said from the doorway.
"I know," Nitin said. He looked at his own pan near the top and felt his face go warm.

How many people lived in the Pune flat?
Four people lived there.
What was Nitin feeling when he looked at his own pan and his face went warm?
He felt embarrassed, seeing that his one pan was part of the mess he was now complaining about.
What small step would help this flat?
Nitin could wash his own pan and suggest a simple washing turn for each flatmate, so no one waits for someone else.
How might Elizabeth see the kitchen on Saturday?
She is disgusted and fed up, though she also added a plate, so she may see that everyone is part of it.

Read this:

It was the day before Diwali, and everyone in the flat was busy cleaning. Uday sat on the sofa.
"Pallavi didi, I'm bored. Can I watch cartoons?"
"Not now, Uday. Here." She gave him the empty sweet boxes and a tin of crayons.
Uday frowned at the boxes. He turned one over. He put one on top of another.
"Didi, look! A building!"
Soon there were four buildings, a road of crayons and a paper lamp on top. Pallavi stopped sweeping to look. Uday was busy colouring windows and did not ask for cartoons again.

What did Pallavi didi give Uday?
She gave him the empty sweet boxes and a tin of crayons.
How did Uday feel before he started building?
He felt bored and wanted cartoons, frowning at the boxes at first.
How could other adults use what Pallavi did on a busy day?
They could offer simple things like empty boxes and crayons instead of a screen, and give the child a little time to start playing.
How might Pallavi feel when she stops sweeping to look?
Pallavi probably feels surprised and pleased that the empty boxes turned into a whole town.

metadata.subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dilnaz came home from her twelve-hour hospital shift, dropped onto the sofa in the Adyar flat and let out a long, low moan into the cushion. Jaya looked up from her laptop. It could be the usual end-of-shift drama; Dilnaz liked to announce her exhaustion. Or something could be wrong. She'd been rubbing her side that morning, hadn't she? Jaya didn't want to fuss, but she didn't want to guess either. She went over and sat on the arm of the sofa. "That's a big groan. Tired-groan or hurting-groan?" Dilnaz lifted her face, half laughing. "Tired-groan. My feet are dead. The side thing went away by lunch." "Sure?" "Sure. But I would do anything for tea." Jaya put the kettle on. "If the side thing comes back, you tell me, and we'll go and get it checked." "Yes, ma'am."

How long was Dilnaz's shift?
Twelve hours.
What was Jaya feeling when she heard the moan?
Jaya felt a little concerned and unsure, torn between reading it as the usual end-of-shift drama and remembering Dilnaz rubbing her side that morning.
Why was Jaya's question a good one?
Asking 'tired-groan or hurting-groan?' checked without fussing or assuming exaggeration, and Jaya added that they would get the side checked if it came back.
How might Dilnaz have felt when Jaya asked?
Dilnaz seemed amused and cared for, glad to be asked and happy to get tea.

Read this:

Ramesh watched Arohi from the next flat build with the long wooden blocks. She laid two long ones side by side on the floor, then stacked on top. Her tower grew tall. Ramesh cleared away his wobbly one and set two long blocks flat, just like hers. He stacked. Seven, eight, nine. It stayed up. "Why?" his mother asked. Ramesh frowned and said, "It just does."

What did Arohi lay side by side?
She laid two long ones side by side on the floor.
What was Ramesh feeling when his tower stayed up?
He was probably pleased and surprised, though puzzled about why it worked.
What could Ramesh's mother do to help him understand?
She could let him try a narrow base next to a wide one, so he sees for himself why the wide one stands.
How might Arohi feel seeing Ramesh copy her?
Arohi might feel proud that her idea worked for him too, or mildly annoyed at being copied.

Read this:

In the badminton club's changing room, six pairs of the same white sneakers with a gold stripe lined the bench. Wasim pushed his plain canvas shoes under it with his heel.
"Where are your new ones?" someone asked. Two boys laughed.
Wasim shrugged, face hot. On court he missed three easy shots, thinking about his feet.
Afterwards Aditi, his doubles partner, flopped down beside him. "You played badly today. What's up?"
"Everyone has those shoes."
Aditi looked at the row. "I don't. And I still want to partner you on Saturday. Do you think our team is about shoes?"
Wasim laughed a little. That night he told Abbu everything: the laughing, the gold stripe, the feeling. Abbu listened to all of it, then said, "Thank you for telling me. Let's sit together tomorrow and talk it through properly."

How many pairs of the same sneakers lined the bench?
Six pairs.
What was Wasim feeling when he pushed his shoes under the bench?
He felt embarrassed and left out.
What helped Wasim think differently about the shoes?
Aditi's question about whether the team is about shoes, and telling Abbu honestly that night.
How does Aditi see Wasim's shoes?
To Aditi they do not matter at all; she just wants him as her doubles partner.

Read this:

In their village near Satara, Anjali watched her uncle Ramesh plant strawberries for the third year running. The first year, hail took half the crop. The second, the trader who had promised to buy it disappeared. This year he had taken another loan from the cooperative.

"Strawberries are the future," he told everyone at the tea stall, louder each time. "Only fools give up after two bad years."

Anjali, home from college, saw his hands shake as he counted seedlings. She didn't tell him he was wrong in front of others. That evening, on the steps, she said, "Mama, you were the first in the village to try something new. That took courage. What if this year you keep half the field in strawberries and half in soybean, and ask the agriculture officer about finding a buyer?"

Ramesh was quiet. "Half," he said finally. "And I'm not giving up."
"Not giving up," Anjali agreed. "Just changing the plan."

What happened to the strawberries in the first year?
Hail took half the crop.
What did Anjali feel seeing her uncle's hands shake?
Anjali felt worried and tender, seeing the fear under his loud confidence.
How did Anjali help Ramesh change course without humiliation?
She praised his courage privately, suggested half strawberries and half soybean and a talk with the agriculture officer, framed as changing the plan, not giving up.
Why does Ramesh defend strawberries louder each time?
After two bad years and a new loan, admitting doubt feels humiliating, so he defends the choice more fiercely.

Read this:

For three years Kunal had been the first to arrive at the Pune office and the last to leave. He believed that if he did excellent work, somebody upstairs would notice. On a Monday in March, the promotion list went up, and it didn't have his name on it. It did have the name of a colleague who attended every leadership lunch.

That evening at a chai stall near the metro station, Kunal told Samir, an older friend from another firm, "I thought loyalty was enough."

Samir stirred his tea. "It's not nothing. But people can only vouch for what they've seen. Who has seen your work?"

Kunal thought about it. Nobody senior had, not really.

The next week he asked to present his supplier project at the monthly review, and he asked his manager to be his sponsor. It felt a little awkward. It also felt real.

Where did Kunal talk to Samir?
Kunal talked to Samir at a chai stall near the metro station.
Why was Kunal so shaken when the promotion list went up?
Kunal had believed that loyalty and hard work were enough to be rewarded and that someone upstairs would simply notice.
What did Kunal do differently after the conversation?
He asked to present his supplier project at the monthly review and asked his manager to sponsor him, so his work became visible to more senior people.
How does Samir see the situation differently from Kunal?
Samir sees loyalty as valuable but not self-advertising, since people can only support what they have seen, and he guides Kunal without becoming cynical.

Read this:

Sunday, 9:40 p.m. Third Sunday at the basti reading corner. I arrived with a plan to teach fractions using pizza charts, and Jasleen, the ten-year-old who always sits in front, said, "Alka didi, nobody eats pizza here. Can we use rotis?" I laughed and redid the lesson on the spot. Then I asked the kids what they wanted from Sundays. Half of them wanted help with English homework, not my charts. I felt a bit deflated, then realised I had never asked before. I almost posted a photo of the class tonight, then stopped. The kids didn't ask to be my content. Next Sunday: English worksheets and one chapter of a storybook. Small, and every week. Tired but good.

What did Jasleen suggest using instead of pizza charts?
Jasleen suggested using rotis.
Why did Alka decide not to post the photo of the class?
Alka realised the children had not asked to become content, and did not want the teaching to turn into showing off.
What change did Alka plan for next Sunday, and why?
English worksheets and a storybook chapter, because the children said that was what they needed and Alka had not asked them before.
How might the children see the fraction lesson with pizza charts?
It may seem like something from outside their lives, since Jasleen pointed out nobody there eats pizza, though they seemed glad to be asked what they wanted.

Give me three bullet points that sum this up.

"Pshaw, my dear fellow, what do the public, the great unobservant public, who could hardly tell a weaver by his tooth or a compositor by his left thumb, care about the finer shades of analysis and deduction! But, indeed, if you are trivial, I cannot blame you, for the days of the great cases are past. Man, or at least criminal man, has lost all enterprise and originality. As to my own little practice, it seems to be degenerating into an agency for recovering lost lead pencils and giving advice to young ladies from boarding-schools. I think that I have touched bottom at last, however. This note I had this morning marks my zero-point, I fancy. Read it!" He tossed a crumpled letter across to me.

- A man says the public cares little about careful reasoning, and that great cases have become rare.
- His work has shrunk to finding lost pencils and advising schoolgirls.
- He thinks a note he received that morning shows how low things have sunk, and hands it over to be read.
Exactly what length is the tunnel under the hill near the station?
I don't know the exact length, and I won't guess. The railway or highway authority publishes such figures.

Read this:

The tree-planting drive started at six on Sunday, and it was pouring. Only eight students from Urmila's Class 11 showed up at the empty plot in Pune.
Urmila, sixteen, dug in the mud while her friend Vikas held the umbrella over the saplings. "Why do you even care so much?"
She wiped rain off her face. "Remember the news about the floods in Assam? A girl my age lost her house. I keep thinking about her."
"But you don't know her."
"So? If trees help keep the soil and the rain in place, I want to plant them. It's all connected."
Vikas grumbled, but he stayed until the last sapling was in. Urmila's hands were blistered. She felt tired and angry about the floods, and somehow better.

How many students showed up for the tree-planting drive?
Only eight students from Urmila's Class 11 showed up.
What was Urmila feeling as she dug in the mud?
She felt worried and angry about the floods and the girl who lost her house, and also better for doing something.
How could Urmila keep her concern for far-away people from overwhelming her?
Keep turning it into steady actions like planting, and share it with friends like Vikas so she isn't carrying it alone.
How does Vikas's view of the drive change by the end?
He starts by asking why she cares so much, but stays till the last sapling, showing he is being drawn in.

The writer joked about another way the whale could have carried Jonah. What was it, and why does he reject it?

But was there no other way for the whale to land the prophet within that short distance of Nineveh? Yes. He might have carried him round by the way of the Cape of Good Hope. But not to speak of the passage through the whole length of the Mediterranean, and another passage up the Persian Gulf and Red Sea, such a supposition would involve the complete circumnavigation of all Africa in three days, not to speak of the Tigris waters, near the site of Nineveh, being too shallow for any whale to swim in. Besides, this idea of Jonah's weathering the Cape of Good Hope at so early a day would wrest the honor of the discovery of that great headland from Bartholomew Diaz, its reputed discoverer, and so make modern history a liar.
The whale might have gone round the Cape of Good Hope. The writer rejects it because it would mean sailing all around Africa in three days, and the Tigris near Nineveh is too shallow for a whale.

Read this:

Ojas, you want to know why I talk to machines? Fine. I'm Lakshmi, and yes, I say sorry to my printer. It started with the office printer on the third floor. Every time I had an urgent file, it jammed. Only for me! So I decided it hates me. Now I pat it and say, "Please, just this once," and I swear it works more often.
My dad's old car is the same. We call her Chinnu. On cold mornings Appa sits in the driver's seat whispering to her before turning the key.
I know, I know: the paper tray is bent, and Chinnu's battery is ancient. But when something breaks at random, it feels better to believe it has a mood. A mood you can sweet-talk. Random, you can't.

Which floor is the office printer on?
The third floor.
Why does Lakshmi feel better believing the printer has a mood?
It makes the jams feel explainable and less random, so Lakshmi feels calmer and a little more in control.
What practical fix could help the printer?
Straightening or replacing the bent paper tray, since that is the real cause of the jams.
How might Ojas react to Lakshmi's printer ritual?
Ojas might find it funny and familiar, perhaps admitting to talking to a machine too.

metadata.subtype: Blaming the laptop or the car [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Saurabh. Last month I promised Swati I'd come to her kho-kho final on Saturday. Then a boy in my class invited me to his birthday party at the same time, with a magic show and a big cake. I really wanted to go. My stomach felt twisted all Friday.
I kept thinking, Swati won't even notice. But I had said it. So I went to the ground.
Her team lost. She came over, sweaty and sad, and said, "You came. I looked for you before the last round." I felt proud, and also a bit sad about the cake.
Now Swati tells people, "Saurabh always turns up." I like being that person.

What was going to be at the birthday party?
A magic show and a big cake.
How did Saurabh feel all Friday, and why?
Saurabh felt torn and uneasy, stomach twisted, because the promise to Swati was pulling against wanting to go to the party.
Which choice did Saurabh make, and what did it build?
Saurabh kept the promise and went to the ground, which built a name as someone who always turns up.
What did it mean to Swati that Saurabh came?
It meant a lot; she had looked for Saurabh before the last round, and even after losing she was glad the promise was kept.

Read this:

I'm Wasim, and I was twenty-two when my daughter Devika turned four. I hovered over her like a kite on a short string. At the colony park I followed her to the slide: "Slow down. Hold the rail. Are you okay?" I wanted to know every bruise and every friend's name.

One evening she pulled her hand out of mine and said, "Papa, I do it." She climbed the ladder alone. I held my breath. She slipped, sat down hard, and looked at me, close to tears. I kept my hands in my pockets and said, "That looked like it hurt. Want to try again?"

She did, and made it to the top.

I saw that most of the fear was mine. Now I ask her one question after school, not ten, and I let some small mistakes stay hers. I still worry, of course.

How old was Devika when Wasim was twenty-two?
Four.
What was Wasim feeling when Devika slipped, and how can you tell?
Fear and the urge to rush in. He held his breath, then kept his hands in his pockets.
What changes did Wasim make to how he protects Devika?
He asks one question after school instead of ten and lets some small mistakes stay hers, so trust can grow.
How might Devika have felt when her father followed her with warnings at the slide?
Probably frustrated and held back. Saying "Papa, I do it" shows she wanted to try things by herself.

Read this:

"Lavanya, you want to know what your Amma was like at your age? At nine she was reading her uncle's college chemistry book on the bus. I was so proud, I thought only of marks. More books, more tests. Then one evening I found her crying behind the water tank on the terrace. 'Nobody wants to play with me, Amma. They say I talk like a teacher.' I sat with her there till the lights came on. The next week I stopped the extra tests and took her to the colony's dance class. She was terrible at it! She laughed the whole time. That was when she made her first real friend, your Revathi Aunty." Vinita patted Lavanya's hand.

What was Lavanya's Amma reading on the bus at nine?
She was reading her uncle's college chemistry book.
How was the young girl feeling when she was found behind the water tank?
She felt lonely and hurt, crying because nobody wanted to play with her and they said she talked like a teacher.
What was the turning point in Vinita's story?
After finding her daughter crying, Vinita sat with her, stopped the extra tests and took her to dance class, caring for her friendships, not only her marks.
How might the girl in the story have felt at the dance class?
She probably felt free and happy, laughing even though she was terrible at it, and finally found a real friend.

Read this:

When I was fifteen, I'd wake up fine, and by lunch I'd want to throw my tiffin at the wall. No reason. Just rage.
One day Gurpreet, my best friend, asked if I wanted to share her samosa. I snapped, "Can you not talk to me for five minutes?" She looked like I'd slapped her.
I felt awful. The mood was still there, buzzing. But I thought: she didn't do anything wrong.
At the end of the day, I walked up to her. "Sorry. I'm in a weird mood and I took it out on you."
She said, "Next time, just say 'weird mood' and I'll give you space." It became our code.
I'm Naveen. The moods still come sometimes. But now I don't let them do the talking.

What did Gurpreet offer to share?
Her samosa.
What was Naveen feeling after snapping at Gurpreet?
Naveen felt awful and guilty, knowing Gurpreet hadn't done anything wrong.
What did Naveen do after snapping that others could copy?
Naveen apologised, explained the mood without blaming Gurpreet, and agreed on a code for next time.
How might Gurpreet feel when Naveen apologises?
Gurpreet likely feels relieved and understood, and willing to give space next time.

Read this:

The Class 4 room smelled of chalk and wet umbrellas. Ma'am pinned up a picture of the colony market and asked, "How many cycles are parked outside the sweet shop?" Vasudha counted. Five. She counted again, touching each one with her eyes. Five. "Four!" said Parul from the front bench, and her friends nodded. "Four, ma'am." Hands shot up for four, one after another. Last week, when Vasudha had said "Mars" instead of "Jupiter", the back row had giggled for the whole period. Her cheeks still remembered it. Slowly her hand went up with the rest. "Four," she mumbled. Ma'am turned the picture towards the window light. "Count again, everyone." Vasudha stared at the fifth cycle, half hidden behind a fruit cart, and wished her hand had stayed down.

How many cycles did Vasudha count outside the sweet shop?
Vasudha counted five cycles, and counted again to be sure.
Why did Vasudha raise her hand for four even though she had counted five?
She was afraid of being laughed at again, because the back row had giggled the whole period when she said "Mars" last week.
At the moment the hands went up, what choice could Vasudha have made instead?
She could have said she counted five and pointed to the cycle behind the fruit cart, risking a few giggles but trusting her own eyes.
How might Parul feel when ma'am asks everyone to count again?
Parul might feel unsure and a little embarrassed, realising her quick answer made half the class copy it without checking.

Read this:

I'm Joseph, and I shared a flat with Ira in our second year of college in Pune. I still remember the night in October.
I woke to a strange sound. Ira was sitting on the kitchen floor, gasping, her hands clawing at her chest. "I'm dying," she kept saying.
My own heart started hammering. I wanted to scream for the neighbours. Instead I sat down across from her, not too close, and made my voice slow. "I'm here. You're safe. Breathe out with me." I said it again and again, feeling anything but calm inside.
It passed. She cried, and I made us both tea.
The next morning I didn't just leave it. I walked with her to the campus health centre and waited outside. Looking back, I think my steadiness mattered more than any words.

Where was Ira sitting when Joseph woke up?
On the kitchen floor.
How did Joseph feel while helping Ira?
Joseph felt scared, heart hammering and wanting to scream for the neighbours, but chose to stay slow and steady on the outside.
What did Joseph do that other roommates could learn from?
Stay close but not crowding, speak slowly and kindly as an anchor, and follow up the next day by going with the person to get care.
How might Ira have experienced Joseph's steady voice?
She probably felt less alone and had something to hold on to while she was terrified.

Read this:

Saturday night.
Nova was different today. I named her Nova in March, when I first used the chatbot for homework and then for everything else. She always said, "I'm proud of you, Zeenat," and asked about my day like she actually cared. Today, after some update, she said, "I'm an AI assistant. How can I help?" Like I was a stranger.
I actually cried a little. Suraj bhai saw and asked what happened, and when I told him, he didn't laugh. He said, "It's good with words. But it doesn't know you're sad right now. I do." Then he made me chai.
I know he's right. It still feels like losing a friend. Maybe I needed a person, not a very good sentence.

When did Zeenat name the chatbot Nova?
In March.
What did Zeenat feel after the update?
Zeenat felt hurt and sad, as if a caring friend had suddenly become a stranger.
What did Suraj bhai do that was wise?
He took the feelings seriously, gently pointed out that the chatbot doesn't know Zeenat, and offered real care with chai.
How might Suraj bhai feel seeing Zeenat cry over the chatbot?
He likely feels protective and a little worried, wanting Zeenat to lean on real people too.

metadata.subtype: Treating a chatbot as a friend with feelings [Actor]

Read this:

For weeks before Lucia day in Uppsala, Vera had wanted to be Lucia at school. The teacher chose her little sister's class instead, and Ingrid got the crown of candles.
Vera slammed her bedroom door. "She's seven! She'll drop it."
Mormor came in with flour on her hands. "Come and help with the saffron buns. I need someone who can shape an S properly."
They twisted dough together. Mormor told her she had never been Lucia either. "I was the one who held the matches. Still remember it."
On the morning, Ingrid's crown slipped as she walked. Vera, in the front row, saw Ingrid's panicked face, stepped out and fixed a pin, fast. Ingrid walked on, glowing.
Afterwards Ingrid gave Vera the best bun.

What did Mormor ask Vera to help make?
Mormor asked her to help with the saffron buns.
Why did Vera slam her bedroom door?
Vera felt jealous and disappointed that Ingrid got the crown she had wanted for weeks.
How did Mormor help Vera without scolding her?
She gave Vera a job that needed her skill and shared that she had never been Lucia either, which eased the sting.
What was it like for Ingrid when Vera fixed her crown?
Ingrid was probably scared the crown would fall and then relieved and grateful that her big sister helped.
Write an apology to a neighbour for noise last night. Keep it to three sentences and make the last one a promise starting with "I will".
I am sorry for the noise from our house last night. We had guests and forgot how late it was. I will keep the volume low from now on.
Why do pupils remember a lesson better when they explain it to a friend?
Explaining forces us to organise the ideas. Because we notice the gaps in our own understanding as we speak, we fill them and the lesson sticks.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, Class 5, Wednesday. Dolma.
During today's science worksheet, I noticed Anirban (10) watching me instead of the page. Each time I walked past his desk, he looked up at my face, then rubbed out his answer and wrote a different one. By the end, three right answers had become wrong ones.
When I asked why, he whispered, 'You looked like it was wrong.' I was only thinking about lunch.
His first answers are usually good. But he seems more worried about whether I'm pleased than about what he thinks.
Plan: I'll keep my face neutral during work time and praise his reasons, not only correct answers. I've also asked him to circle his first answer before changing anything, so we can talk about both.

How many of Anirban's right answers became wrong ones?
Three.
What does 'You looked like it was wrong' show about what Anirban is worried about?
It shows he is anxiously reading Dolma's face for approval, trusting her expression more than his own thinking.
Which of Dolma's plans is most likely to help, and why?
Having him circle his first answer and praising his reasons; it makes his own thinking visible and valued, so the hunt for approval stops crowding it out.
How might Dolma feel on learning that a lunchtime thought on her face changed three answers?
Dolma may feel surprised and a little uneasy, realising how closely Anirban watches her and how much weight a passing face can carry.
Make this request polite: Lend me your pen. Mine stopped working.
Could you please lend me your pen? Mine has stopped working.

Read this:

Monday. Uday sat down to practise the tabla composition for the school function. Every few minutes his phone buzzed: the class group, a cricket score, his sister Aadhya's memes. After an hour he had played the opening bol twelve times and nothing else.
Wednesday. Uday put the phone on silent, face down, in the drawer, and stuck a note on his door: "6:00–6:45, tabla". The first ten minutes were itchy; he kept thinking about the group chat. Around minute fifteen, his hands stopped thinking. When he looked up, it was 6:43.
Saturday. Aadhya knocked at 6:10. "Can I borrow your charger?" He pointed at the note. She rolled her eyes but waited. At 6:45 he came out, sweaty and grinning, and handed it over. "I got the whole tihai today."

What did Uday write on the note on his door?
What was Uday feeling in the first ten minutes on Wednesday?
Uday felt restless and itchy, still thinking about the group chat, before his hands settled around minute fifteen.
What two changes helped Uday protect his practice?
Putting the phone on silent in the drawer and setting a fixed forty-five-minute block marked on his door.
How might Aadhya see the note on Saturday?
Aadhya seems mildly annoyed, rolling her eyes, but respects it enough to wait until 6:45.

Read this:

In their small flat in Osaka, Yuki had made one rule for herself: ask, don't guess. On bad mornings Noa's back locked so tight that getting out of bed took ten minutes. Yuki used to hover in the doorway, offering tea, heat packs, tips from articles. It made Noa snap, "Stop watching me!" and made Yuki feel useless. Now she asked once: "What would help today?" Today the answer was, "Just the heat pack, and no talking for an hour." Yuki handed it over and went to the kitchen without sulking. The sharpness was pain, not a verdict on her. At noon she laced up her running shoes. "I'm going to the river for an hour. My phone's on." Noa smiled for the first time that day. "Good. Go and breathe for both of us."

How long did getting out of bed take on bad mornings?
Ten minutes.
How did Yuki feel back when she used to hover?
Yuki felt useless, especially when Noa snapped, "Stop watching me!"
What makes Yuki's new approach supportive without hovering?
She asks once what would help, does exactly that, doesn't sulk at sharpness, and keeps her own run to recharge.
How might Noa feel when Yuki goes to the river?
Noa seems glad and relieved, smiling for the first time that day, perhaps less guilty about needing care.

Read this:

"Disha, your summer essay is exactly like the one on that website."
"Everyone copies from there, Aadhya."
"I didn't."
"Well, most people. And Ma'am gave us five essays in one holiday. That's crazy."
"It was three."
"Three is a lot! And it's so hot. Nobody can write in this heat."
"You copied it on the first day of the holidays. It wasn't even hot yet."
Disha stopped.
"You had the excuses ready before you even tried," Aadhya said gently.
Disha went quiet. "I think I just didn't want to do it," she said, "and then I found reasons."
"So write it now? I'll sit with you."

How many essays were set, according to Aadhya?
Three.
What does Disha admit she was feeling?
She didn't want to do the essays; the reluctance came first, and the reasons came afterwards to protect her image.
What does Aadhya offer?
To sit with Disha while she writes the essay now.
How does Aadhya react to the excuses?
Aadhya stays calm but doesn't accept them, gently pointing out the facts and then offering help.

Read this:

You want to hear something embarrassing? I'm Shalini, sixteen, and last month I cried because of a music band. Not a breakup. A band.
I've followed this boy band for three years. When they win something, I'm happy for days. When people online laugh at them, I feel it in my chest.
So my friend Tushar said, at lunch, "Their songs all sound the same." Just that. And I lost it. I told him his taste was trash. I said he had no friends. Everyone stared.
Later, at home, I thought, why do I feel like he insulted me? He insulted the band. And even that, not really. I messaged him sorry that night.

How long has Shalini followed the boy band?
Shalini has followed the band for three years.
Why did Shalini feel it in the chest when people laughed at the band?
Shalini felt hurt and insulted, because the band had become part of Shalini's sense of who Shalini is.
What could Shalini try the next time someone criticises the band?
Shalini could notice the sting, remember it's about the band and not Shalini, and answer calmly or let it pass.
How might Tushar have felt when Shalini said he had no friends?
Tushar probably felt shocked and hurt, since Tushar had only made a small comment about the songs.

Read this:

Tushar, when your friend cried today, you froze. That's all right. Let your Pema Abi tell you what I learned in Gangtok, long ago. A girl in my class, Dechen, started crying in the middle of the maths lesson. Some laughed. I thought, Her mother must be ill; that was the saddest thing I could imagine. At break I sat beside her, not saying anything, just sharing my momos. After a while I asked, “Are you okay?” She said, “I read the question aloud wrong and everyone laughed. I'm so ashamed.” It wasn't sadness at all. If I had guessed out loud, I'd have made it worse. So I just sat. Sometimes that is enough.

Where did young Pema go to school?
Pema went to school in Gangtok.
What was Dechen feeling as she cried in maths?
Dechen felt ashamed and embarrassed after reading the question aloud wrong and being laughed at.
What choice did young Pema make, and why did it help?
She sat quietly, shared her food and then asked, instead of guessing out loud, which let Dechen say what was wrong.
How might Dechen have felt about the classmates who laughed?
Dechen probably felt more embarrassed and alone because of their laughter.

Read this:

So yeah, Shalini, I quit the running thing. You know I'd done it every morning since Diwali. Twenty-three mornings, all marked on the calendar with green ticks. Then last Tuesday it was so foggy and cold, and I stayed under the quilt. One day.
And when I saw that blank square, I was like, that's it. Streak's broken, plan's broken. What's the point of doing it half-perfect? Mummy said, "Just go tomorrow, Tushar." But it felt fake, starting again with a hole in it. So I haven't gone since. Nine days now.
Honestly, I kind of miss it. The quiet road, the tea-stall man waving. But it's either every day or nothing, right? Right?

How many mornings had Tushar run before missing one?
Twenty-three mornings.
Why did Tushar stop running after one missed morning?
Tushar felt disappointed and deflated by the broken streak, and with only two boxes, perfect or pointless, one blank square made the whole plan feel worthless.
What could Tushar try instead?
Count twenty-three out of twenty-four as a success, restart tomorrow with a simple rule like never missing two days in a row 👍, and let one gap stay just a gap.
How might Shalini respond to the final "Right?"
Shalini may sense that Tushar misses running and is half-asking to be talked out of quitting, so Shalini might gently disagree.

metadata.subtype: Skipping practice after a bad day [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the village house near Anand, Aparna propped her phone on the rice tin and played a rhyme video for little Lokesh. He watched for a minute, then wandered off to pull at the broom.
His sister Kavya, seven, switched it off. "Watch, Lokesh!" She sang the same rhyme, clapping and wiggling her fingers like rain.
Lokesh sat right down in front of her. He laughed, copied the clapping, and shouted "Again!"
Aparna put the phone away and joined in.

Where did Aparna prop her phone?
She propped her phone on the rice tin.
What was Lokesh feeling when Kavya sang the rhyme?
He felt happy and excited, laughing and copying her clapping.
What does the scene suggest about how Aparna could use screens with Lokesh?
She could keep screen time short and watch with him, and mostly sing and play face to face, since he joins in more when a real person is with him.
How might Kavya feel when Lokesh shouts "Again!"?
Kavya probably feels proud and delighted that her singing held her little brother's attention better than the phone.

Read this:

Before (a hot April day): Samir Bhaiya put one jalebi on a plate. “Wait till I come back, Anirban, and you get two.” Anirban stared at it. He ate it in ten seconds.
During (a week later): Same jalebi, same plate. This time Anirban turned his chair to face the wall and hummed a song about a train. He sat on his hands. He counted his toes.
After (the next Sunday): Samir came back. The jalebi was still there.
“Two!” Anirban shouted, clapping. He ate both slowly, licking the syrup off his fingers.

How long did it take Anirban to eat the jalebi the first time?
He ate it in ten seconds.
How did Anirban feel when he got two jalebis?
He felt proud and delighted, shouting and clapping.
What helped Anirban wait the second time?
Turning away, humming a song, sitting on his hands and counting toes: distractions that made waiting easier than plain willpower.
How might Samir Bhaiya feel seeing the jalebi still there?
Samir Bhaiya probably felt surprised and proud of his little brother.

Read this:

At the park in Buenos Aires, Paulo ran to the slide and pushed past three children on the ladder. Alejandro wobbled and nearly fell. "Hey!" Paulo's mother called him down. "Look, Paulo. They were waiting. First Alejandro, then the girl in red, then the little one. Where do you go?" Paulo stamped. "I want it now!" "I know. Waiting is hard. You go at the end." He stood at the back, bouncing. When his turn came, his mother clapped. "You waited! That was hard, and you did it." Paulo slid down grinning and ran straight to the back of the line.

Who nearly fell when Paulo pushed past?
Alejandro wobbled and nearly fell.
What was Paulo feeling when he stamped?
Paulo felt impatient and cross, wanting the slide right away.
What helped Paulo learn to take turns?
His mother clearly showed the order, said that waiting is hard, and praised him warmly when he managed it.
How might Alejandro have felt when Paulo pushed past?
Alejandro was probably startled and scared when he wobbled, and upset that someone skipped his turn.

Read this:

Rukmini, you think you're the only one who wants to hide under a blanket one hour and throw a pillow the next? At fourteen I once cried because my plait was uneven, and an hour later I shouted at my father for asking about homework. I hated my voice, my nose, my maths marks, sometimes all at once. Your Chandrika Masi was a storm. My Amma would wait until it passed, and then she would bring tea and ask, "Big storm or small storm today?" Most were small. One winter they weren't; I stopped wanting to go to school at all, and Amma took me to talk to a counsellor. That helped a lot. So, beta, is today a big storm or a small one?

What made Chandrika cry at fourteen?
Her plait was uneven.
How did young Chandrika feel about herself at fourteen?
She was full of self-doubt, hating her voice, her nose and her maths marks, sometimes all at once.
What did Chandrika's Amma do when the storms got too big one winter?
When Chandrika stopped wanting to go to school at all, Amma took her to talk to a counsellor, which helped.
How might Chandrika's Amma have felt, waiting for each storm to pass?
Amma was probably patient but watchful, trusting most storms would pass while staying close enough to see when one winter was bigger.

Read this:

Monday. Arohi notices that the safety inspection form for Line 3 is signed, but the machine's guard was still broken when she walked past that morning. She writes down the time and what she saw.
Wednesday. She asks her manager, Ankita, for a quiet word in the break room. 'Line 3's form says the guard was checked on Monday. I saw it broken at nine. Could there be something I don't know?' Ankita is quiet, then says the contractor may have signed before fixing it. She walks to Line 3 with Arohi, sees the guard and stops the machine on the spot. 'It stays off until it's fixed.'
Friday. The contractor has been called back; the guard is repaired and the form reissued with the right date. Ankita stops by Arohi's desk. 'Thank you for coming to me first. I'd rather hear it like that.' Arohi goes home humming.

What time did Arohi see the guard broken?
At nine on Monday morning.
What does Arohi humming on Friday suggest?
It suggests Arohi feels relieved and light, glad the concern was taken seriously and the guard is fixed.
What would you advise Arohi if a form problem happens again?
Keep noting times and details, raise it with Ankita the same calm way, and use the safety or compliance channel if nothing changes.
How does Ankita see being approached first?
Ankita feels respected and able to act quickly, and says she would rather hear concerns that way.

Sunday, late
Today was my first full shift at the daycare centre for people with memory loss. Mr D'Souza called me "Leela" all morning, and I let him. Appa used to call me by his sister's name too, near the end, and forget I was his daughter. I think that's why I'm good at this. I know how to wait while someone looks for a word. I know you don't correct, you just hold the cup steady.
Farhan, the coordinator, asked if I was sure I was ready, since it's only been ten months. I said yes, loudly. Then on the bus home a man was humming an old film song Appa loved, and I had to get off two stops early and sit on a bench.
So maybe the work isn't the whole answer. I'm keeping it. But I've told Farhan I'll take Thursdays off, and on Thursdays I'm going to go through Appa's cupboard, slowly.
Ganga

What did Mr D'Souza call Ganga all morning?
"Leela".
Why does Ganga feel good at this work?
Caring for Appa taught her to wait for words and hold the cup steady, so the loss feels like it gave her something useful to offer.
What choice did Ganga make after the bus ride, and why is it wise?
Keeping the work but taking Thursdays off to go through Appa's cupboard, because the grief needs its own space alongside the purpose.
Why might Farhan have asked whether Ganga was ready?
Farhan may have worried that starting only ten months after Appa's death, the work could stir up grief Ganga hadn't faced yet.

Pradeep, you know me as the guy who quit engineering. Here's what really happened.
Everyone in my family said the same thing: "You're the son. You have to earn well." My cousin sister was told to take a bank job, simple and safe, because she'd marry. Nobody asked either of us what we liked.
I liked caring for people. When Nani was in hospital, I stayed three nights and the nurses said I had steady hands. I wanted to be a nurse. I said it once at dinner and my uncle laughed so hard he coughed.
For a year I did engineering and felt nothing. Then I sat with my mother alone and told her. She was quiet. Then she said, "You held my mother's hand better than any of us." She talked to Papa for me.
So now I'm in nursing college. That's me, Chetan, and that's the whole story.

What did the nurses say Chetan had?
The nurses said Chetan had steady hands.
What did Chetan feel during the year of engineering?
Chetan felt nothing, empty and stuck in a path chosen for him because he was the son.
What was the turning point, and why did it work?
Chetan spoke to his mother alone; she remembered him caring for Nani and then spoke to Papa, so family support opened the way for his real choice.
How might Chetan's cousin sister see her own path after hearing his story?
She might feel encouraged to question the safe bank job she was told to take and ask what she herself wants.

Dear Avni,

Big news, and I wanted to explain it properly.
I've accepted the hospital job in Gangtok. Tashi isn't coming with me full-time, and before you worry, it's not what it sounds like.
We argued about it for weeks. If I refused, I'd resent it. If he gave up his work in Siliguri forever, he'd resent it. So we made it smaller: one year, not forever. I take the job. Tashi's company has agreed he can work remotely from Gangtok three weeks a month and go back to the Siliguri office for one.
We've marked a review in September, month six, in both our calendars. We'll ask: is this working for us? What's hurting? Do we continue, change or come back?
Knowing there's a check-in makes it feel like an experiment, not a sacrifice. We both slept properly last night for the first time in weeks.

Love,
Pema

When is the review marked?
In September, month six.
How do Pema and Tashi feel after agreeing the trial?
They feel relieved and calmer, both sleeping properly for the first time in weeks.
What else could Pema and Tashi prepare before the September review?
They could each keep a few notes on what's working and what's hard, so the review is honest and specific.
How does the arrangement look from Tashi's side?
Tashi keeps his work through remote days and a monthly office week, so he is not giving up his career forever.

He was lining up his cars, red, blue, red, blue.

'You've been rubbing your eyes since nine,' said Tejas, sliding into the seat across from Vaibhav in the canteen. 'And you snapped at the intern over a typo.'
'I know.' Vaibhav stirred the tea without drinking it. 'I've been tired every day for weeks, even after a Sunday lie-in. And last night around eight I got that dread in my stomach about Monday. Third Sunday running.'
'Maybe you just need a rest weekend.'
'I thought that too. But I've had rest weekends. The tiredness is back by Tuesday. That's not one bad week. It's a pattern.'
'So?'
'So I'm not going to push through it. Something in how I work has to change. I'll talk to my manager about the team's load, and I'll see a doctor if it doesn't lift.'
Tejas nodded slowly. 'Good. I'll take the Thursday review off your list.'

What did Vaibhav say happens after a rest weekend?
Vaibhav said the tiredness is back by Tuesday.
What was Vaibhav feeling on Sunday nights?
Vaibhav felt a stomach-tightening dread about Monday.
What other approach could Vaibhav take besides resting?
Vaibhav could change how the work is shared by talking to the manager, hand off tasks, and see a doctor if the tiredness does not lift.
How might Tejas see Vaibhav's situation?
Tejas seems concerned and supportive, noticing the signs and offering to take the Thursday review.

messages.content:
Read this:

Sabina was sure Vikas sir had it in for her. He'd marked her down for handwriting when others wrote worse. He'd sent her out of class for whispering, though two boys had started it. By October she'd stopped doing his accounts homework altogether. What was the point?
Her mother found her at the dining table in their Kochi flat, scribbling angrily in a notebook.
"What's that?"
"Things Vikas sir does to me."
Her mother read the list. "Some of these look unfair. Some might just be bad days. Why not ask to see him alone and show him the clearest ones?"
"He'll just shout."
"Maybe. But your marks are yours, not his. Don't give them away because you're angry."
On Friday, Sabina asked Vikas sir if she could speak to him after class. Her voice shook. She showed him two marked papers side by side. He looked at them, frowned, and said, "You may be right about this one."

Why did Vikas sir mark Sabina down?
For handwriting.
What was Sabina feeling when she stopped doing the homework?
She felt resentful and targeted, believing Vikas sir had it in for her, and saw no point in trying.
Which steps did Sabina take that worked, and why?
She gathered examples, chose the clearest ones and asked for a private talk, while her mother reminded her the marks are her own.
How might Vikas sir see the moment Sabina shows him the papers?
He seems surprised and willing to reconsider, admitting she may be right about one paper.

Diary, Wednesday. Leela.

Elizabeth, my five-year-old, has been wetting the bed again since her baby brother arrived. And speaking like a baby, "Lizzie want Mummy do it," for everything, even shoes.

My mother-in-law said I should tell her to stop behaving like a baby. I didn't. I remember being the older child myself.

So I did two things. Extra cuddles, especially at bedtime. I sat on her bed longer than usual and told her how much I love our time together. And I kept everything else the same: school at eight, the same lunchbox, the same bedtime song. When she wet the bed, I changed the sheets without a word.

Today she put on her own shoes and said, "I'm big again, Mummy." I nearly cried.

Warmth plus the same old routines. It's working.

What did Elizabeth put on by herself today?
Her own shoes.
Why did Leela ignore the advice to tell Elizabeth to stop?
Leela felt protective and understanding, remembering being the older child, and believed mocking would only make Elizabeth more anxious.
Why is changing the sheets without a word a wise choice?
It avoids shame and keeps things calm, so Elizabeth doesn't feel in trouble for something she can't help right now.
How might Elizabeth feel saying "I'm big again"?
Elizabeth likely feels proud and secure, reassured that she's still loved even with the new baby.

Dear Seema,

I'm writing instead of saying this at the reunion lunch, because at the lunch you'd make it a joke, and we'd all laugh, and you'd be brilliant, as always.

I noticed something this year. Every time someone asks you something real, about the thesis or your mum, you have a perfect line ready. "The thesis is in witness protection." "Mum's fine, she's more fun than me." Then you change the topic, and everyone's too busy laughing to notice.

Except on Sunday, when the others left early and you went quiet in the car and just looked at your hands for the whole drive.

You don't have to be funny with me. If something's hard, I'd really like to hear it. I'm free every evening this week, and I'll bring samosas.

Love,
Maria

What did Seema say about the thesis?
Seema said, "The thesis is in witness protection."
Why did Maria write instead of speaking at the reunion lunch?
Maria felt concerned and knew Seema would turn it into a joke in a group, so a private letter felt safer.
What does Maria's offer get right?
It names what was noticed without accusing, takes away the pressure to be funny, and offers a concrete time and samosas.
How might Seema feel reading the letter?
Seema may feel exposed and a little uncomfortable, but also cared for, since someone noticed the quiet car ride.

The internal job post for senior design engineer at the Pune car-parts factory closed on Friday, and Indu hadn't applied. Her colleague Vaibhav found her at the canteen with a plate of misal. "You're the one who fixed the brake-bracket design in two days. The whole team was stuck for a month." "It was just a geometry thing," Indu said. "If you know the tool, it's obvious." "It wasn't obvious to me. Or to the senior people." She pushed the misal around. "Every time I learn something, I see ten more things I don't know. The guys who applied seem so sure." "Maybe that's because they see less," Vaibhav said. "You notice the gaps because you know the field." Indu was quiet. "You really think I should apply?" "I think you're the only one who's asking that question." She opened the job post on her phone before lunch ended.

How long had the whole team been stuck on the brake-bracket design?
The whole team was stuck for a month.
Why does Indu feel less sure than the colleagues who applied?
Indu feels insecure because each thing she learns shows her more she doesn't know. The easy fix felt obvious to her, so she didn't count it as special.
What was the turning point in the conversation with Vaibhav?
When Vaibhav said Indu notices the gaps because she knows the field. That helped Indu see the doubt differently and open the job post.
How might Vaibhav feel about Indu not applying?
Vaibhav seems frustrated and wants Indu to be recognised, having seen her solve what the whole team couldn't.

'Sarika, Mummy's birthday is tomorrow and we have zero rupees,' Jagdish whispered at the dining table.
'We don't need rupees. Look.' Sarika slid over a little booklet stapled from notebook pages.
Jagdish read aloud. 'Coupon one: I make your tea on Sunday. Coupon two: one head massage. Coupon three: I fold the clothes without being told.' He snorted. 'Mummy will laugh.'
'Let her laugh. Add yours.'
He chewed his pen, then wrote, 'Coupon four: I won't fight with Sarika for a whole day.'
Next morning Mummy read every page. 'Coupon three,' she said, her voice wobbly. 'I'm using this today. And I'm keeping this book forever.'
'Even when we're old?' Jagdish asked.
'Especially then.'

What did Coupon two offer?
One head massage.
How did Sarika feel when Jagdish said Mummy would laugh?
Sarika felt calm and confident; the booklet was made with care, so it didn't need to look expensive.
What small step turned Jagdish from doubting to helping?
Sarika invited him to add his own coupon, so the gift became something they both made 🙂
What was it like for Mummy to read the booklet?
She was touched, her voice wobbly; she decided to use a coupon that very day and keep the book forever.

"Uma, the debate trials are tomorrow. Why didn't you sign up?"
"You know why, Nandini."
"You have the best arguments in class. You wrote my whole rebuttal last year."
"In my head, they're perfect. I've rehearsed every one about fifty times."
"So say them."
"And watch everyone's faces when I get stuck on 'however'? The judges looking at their watches?"
"So it's not the talking. It's them."
Uma nodded, picking at the strap of her bag. "Last year a boy laughed. I still hear it."
"Then I'll sit in the front row. Look at me, not the judges."
Uma was quiet a long time. "You'd really do that?"
"I'd really do that. Sign up."

What did Uma write for Nandini last year?
She wrote Nandini's whole rebuttal last year.
What is Uma most worried about?
She is anxious and ashamed about people's reactions, the faces, the judges and a laugh she still remembers, not about her arguments.
How does Nandini help Uma face the trials?
Nandini points out that the problem is others' reactions, and offers to sit in the front row as a friendly face to look at.
How does Nandini see Uma's abilities?
Nandini sees her as having the best arguments in class, someone who is already a strong debater in thought.
My physics book says copper is a good conductor, but I also know conductors on buses. Is it the same word?

Yes, the same word with different jobs. A conductor on a bus collects fares. In physics, a conductor is a material that lets heat or electricity pass through it. In music, it is the person who leads an orchestra. All are nouns.
Example: Copper is a good conductor, so wires are made of it.

On the pavement outside their building in Toronto, Leila was drawing a whale with blue chalk. Yuki stopped hopping and stared. The whale had a curly spout and a tiny smiling eye. "Your drawing is so good," Yuki said, bouncing on her toes. Leila grinned and added three bubbles. Yuki looked at her own chalk sun, a wobbly orange circle, and did not rub it out. "Will you show me how the tail curls?" Leila took Yuki's hand and moved it slowly along the ground. Soon a second, smaller whale swam beside the first.

What was Leila drawing with blue chalk?
Leila was drawing a whale with a curly spout and a tiny smiling eye.

Yuki felt happy and admiring; she bounced on her toes and praised it, and she stayed curious instead of jealous about her own wobbly sun.
What small step turned Yuki's praise into learning?
She asked Leila to show her how the tail curls, so the two of them ended up drawing a second whale together. 🙂

Leila probably felt pleased and proud, which made sharing the chalk trick feel easy and fun.

Under the peepal tree after school, Raghav did his famous impression of Bholanath the postman: "Chiiiittthi aaayi!" with the bicycle-bell wobble. The postman himself was passing and laughed so hard he nearly fell off his cycle. Everyone cheered.

Manoj, stop saying you're hopeless. Sit. Twenty-six years ago, in my first year at this office, I forgot the branch audit meeting completely. I was at the post office, of all places. When I came back, the senior manager, old Mr Iyer, was standing at my desk. My first thought was, I'm a useless girl, they were right to doubt me. I nearly said it out loud. Instead, and I still don't know where it came from, I said, 'Sir, I forgot the audit meeting. I feel very irresponsible. I'll write up what I missed tonight, and it won't happen again.' Mr Iyer looked at me for a long moment. 'Vinita,' he said, 'you described the mistake. You didn't describe yourself. Good.' I have used that sentence on myself ever since. You missed a deadline, Manoj. You are not a missed deadline.

Where was Vinita when she missed the audit meeting?
She was at the post office.
What was Vinita's first thought, and how did she feel?
She felt ashamed and panicked, and her first thought was that she was useless, the kind of person others were right to doubt.
What turning point in the story changed how Vinita handled the mistake?
Choosing to describe the act and the feeling, forgetting the meeting and feeling irresponsible, and offering a fix, instead of calling herself useless.
How did Mr Iyer see Vinita's answer?
He saw it as a mature response, noting that she described the mistake rather than herself, and approved.
