Half past eleven at night, and the phone buzzed on the shelf among the rice sacks in the family shop near Kolhapur where Pranav worked from home while on call. Payments were failing. Every minute, someone at a counter is failing to pay, he thought. I don't need the reason yet. The release went out two hours ago; rolling it back takes five minutes, and I know how. Hunting the bug could take hours. He typed the rollback, watched the dashboard, and saw the failures thin out and stop. Then he wrote in the team channel, 'Rolled back the latest release, payments recovering, will look at the cause in daylight,' and asked Charu, who owned that release, to check the logs when she woke.

What did Pranav roll back?
Pranav rolled back the release that had gone out two hours earlier.
What was Pranav worried about when he chose to act before finding the cause?
Pranav was worried that every minute someone at a counter failed to pay, which pushed him to stop the damage first.
What could Pranav do if the rollback had not fixed the payments?
Pranav could ask a second person to investigate while he keeps watching the dashboard, so diagnosis carries on with shared work.
How might Charu see the rollback of the release?
Charu might feel a little disappointed, but also relieved that customers recovered and the cause can be checked calmly in daylight.

Tuesday night

The Pune offer came through today. Better role, same pay. I should be thrilled. Instead I feel sick.

I spent all evening listing what I'd lose: my flat, my Thursday dance class, being near Bidisha, knowing the city. The list got longer and longer.

Then I noticed I hadn't written a single thing I'd gain.

So I did an experiment. I imagined losing the dance class. How bad? Honestly, a 6. Then I imagined gaining a role where I'd lead a small team, which I've wanted for two years. How good? An 8.

I did it for each thing. Loss of the flat: 5. Gain of new people, new projects: 7.

When I put them side by side, Pune looked better. But my gut still wanted to stay. Losses just shout louder.

I'm going to sleep on it. But I feel calmer. I'm weighing things now, not just panicking.

Rashmi

What did Rashmi score losing the dance class?
Honestly, a 6.
How did Rashmi feel before doing the experiment?
Rashmi felt sick and anxious, focused only on the growing list of losses.
What did Rashmi's experiment do well?
Scoring each loss and gain of similar size side by side eased the automatic pull toward staying, so Rashmi could weigh the choice fairly.
How might Bidisha feel if Rashmi moves to Pune?
Bidisha might feel sad to lose having Rashmi nearby, but also happy for Rashmi's new role.

Sunday, 10 pm
Friday night I made the Great Weekend Plan: ten History and Geography chapters, five on Saturday, five today. I even drew little clocks next to each one. I figured if I just sat down and nothing went wrong, it would work. Things went wrong. On Saturday the chapter on nationalism took four hours on its own. Three chapters out of ten.
How does Hansa feel on Sunday night?

Monday: During story time, Dhruv crossed his eyes at Lokesh. Lokesh burst out laughing, and the teacher stopped reading. Lokesh's face went hot.
Wednesday: Dhruv crossed his eyes again. Lokesh pressed both hands over his mouth, looked down at his shoes, and his whole body shook, but not a sound came out. The teacher caught his eye and whispered, “Hold it, tell me after.”
Friday: At break, Lokesh told the teacher, “Dhruv did the eyes!” and laughed until he hiccupped.

What did Dhruv do to make Lokesh laugh?
He crossed his eyes at him.
What was Lokesh feeling on Wednesday as his body shook?
He was amused but determined not to laugh out loud, remembering how embarrassed he felt on Monday. The effort shows he knew the quiet rule.
What did the teacher's whisper do?
It showed Lokesh she saw his effort and gave him a later time to let the laugh out.
How might Dhruv see Lokesh holding in the laugh?

Office manager's note, Tuesday
At about 3 pm a man in a blue uniform with a lanyard came to reception and told Anand he was from the building's fire-safety contractor, there to check the server room extinguishers. He was confident and in a hurry. The badge looked real enough.
Anand told me later his first instinct was to wave him through. Instead he said, politely, "Sure, one moment, I just need to confirm with facilities," and called the number on our own contractor list, not the number on the man's card. Facilities had no visit booked.
When Anand turned back, the man had already walked out.
Ankita, at the next desk, pointed out that the lanyard's logo was slightly wrong. We have reported it to building security and the police, and shared his description with the other offices in the building.
Anand did exactly what we trained for: a uniform tells you someone wants to look official, not that they are.

What did the man say he was there to check?
The server room extinguishers.
What does Anand's first instinct suggest about how he felt?
Wanting to wave the man through suggests Anand felt reassured, and perhaps a little pressured, by the confident manner, uniform and hurry.
How did Anand check the visitor?
He politely said he needed to confirm, and called facilities on the number from the office's own contractor list, not the man's card.
What did Ankita notice that others might have missed?
Ankita noticed that the lanyard's logo was slightly wrong.

Wasim, you asked how I got through end-sems last year. Okay, here's Rashmi's version. My grandmother died on the second day of exams. Nani, who basically raised me. My mother called at seven in the morning and I had a paper at ten. I remember thinking, very clearly: I'm going to put this in a box. Not now. And I did. I went to the exam. I studied every night. I didn't cry once. I got my best marks ever. But here's the thing I want you to hear. The day after the last paper, I took the train home, sat in Nani's room, and opened the box. I cried for two days straight. My mother held me. If I'd never opened it, I think I'd still be carrying it. The box helped. The opening mattered more.

What time did Rashmi's mother call?
At seven in the morning.
Why did Rashmi decide to put the grief in a box?
Rashmi felt the grief was too much to face with a paper at ten, so setting it aside made it possible to study and sit the exams.
What made Rashmi's way of coping healthy in the end?
Rashmi opened the box after the last paper, going home to grieve with the family instead of keeping it shut.
How might Rashmi's mother have felt holding Rashmi after the exams?
She likely felt sad and tender, grieving her own mother and comforting her child at the same time.

Every one knows that by the peculiar cunning of their gills, the finny tribes in general breathe the air which at all times is combined with the element in which they swim; hence, a herring or a cod might live a century, and never once raise its head above the surface. But owing to his marked internal structure which gives him regular lungs, like a human being's, the whale can only live by inhaling the disengaged air in the open atmosphere.

Why must a whale come up to the surface when a fish need not?
A fish breathes through gills, taking air from the water. A whale has lungs like a person, so it can only breathe the open air above the sea.

Sofia had grown up in Cape Town and wanted to give something back to the small town in the Eastern Cape where her grandmother had taught. Her first idea was a library with new books. But before ordering anything, she spent two weeks there, sitting in on classes and visiting families after school.
Lindiwe, a teacher at the primary school, walked her through the township at dusk. 'Look,' she said. Windows were dark; many homes had no electricity once the prepaid meter ran out. 'The children have books from school. What they don't have is light and a quiet table.'
Sofia rewrote her plan on the drive back. First, a room at the community hall with solar lamps and tables, open every weekday evening, with a volunteer to keep it safe. Books would follow, chosen with the teachers.

Where had Sofia's grandmother taught?
In a small town in the Eastern Cape.
How might Sofia have felt walking with Lindiwe at dusk?
Sofia may have felt humbled and a little uneasy, seeing that her first idea didn't match what the children most needed.
What else could Sofia do before opening the room?
She could check with parents about the best evening hours and safe routes home, so the room fits family life.
How might Lindiwe see Sofia's changed plan?
Lindiwe would likely feel respected and hopeful, seeing that her observation shaped the plan.

By Tuesday, Jaya and Raghav had each spent an evening comparing the same three bus companies. They found out only in the hostel common room, when they held up identical screenshots. "That's two hours each, gone," Raghav groaned. Kabir and Meera looked up from the carrom board. Jaya pulled a chart paper off the notice board. "Okay. Four jobs, four people." Raghav kept transport, since he'd already started. Jaya took the stay near Rishikesh, Meera took food, and Kabir took safety: the warden's permission slips, a first-aid kit, emergency contacts. They made one shared sheet with a tab for each job and pinned the link in the hostel group. "All quotes by Sunday night," Jaya said. "Monday after assembly, we choose." The warden, passing by, read the chart and initialled the corner.

What did Jaya pull off the notice board?
Jaya pulled a chart paper off the notice board.
How did Raghav feel when he saw the identical screenshots?
Raghav felt frustrated about the wasted effort, groaning that two hours each were gone.
What would you change first if the Sunday deadline slipped?
They could still meet on Monday and decide with whatever quotes are in, filling any gap with the simplest safe choice rather than delaying everything.

Kabir may feel trusted with an important part, and keeping slips, first aid and contacts in one place means the others need not worry about them.

"You keep saying 'I should have'," Salma said. They were sitting on the bench outside the college counselling room, where she volunteered.

"Because I should have," Uday said. "Imran told me he was tired all the time. I said, 'Everyone's tired, yaar.' Two weeks later his heart just stopped. On the football field."

"Did anyone know he had a heart problem?"

"No. Not even his parents."

"So how could you?"

Uday was quiet. "I just wish I'd said something better."

"I think that wish is love, Uday. It just doesn't have anywhere to go now."

He pressed his palms against his eyes.

"What would you want to say to him?"

"That he was the funniest person I knew. That I'm sorry."

"Write it down. And come to the memorial circle on Friday. His other friends will be there."

Where did Imran's heart stop?
It stopped on the football field.
What was Uday feeling when he kept saying "I should have"?
Uday felt guilty and full of regret, blaming himself for missing something nobody knew.
What did Salma suggest, and why could it help?
Salma suggested writing to Imran and going to the memorial circle, which gives Uday's love and sorrow a place to go instead of self-punishment.
How might Salma see Uday's guilt?
Salma sees it as love with no outlet, not as proof Uday did something wrong, since nobody knew about Imran's heart problem.

Thursday. Today I finally asked Jatin why he never looks at me when we talk. I had been reading it as him not caring, or even hiding something. It made me a bit annoyed. I asked it quietly at the water cooler, and I said I was not angry, only curious. He looked at the floor and said, "Amandeep, when I look at faces I cannot listen properly. Looking away helps me hear you." I did not know that. I said thanks and asked if it was okay for me not to expect eye contact. He said yes and looked relieved. Now I watch how he listens: he nods and repeats what I said. I was wrong to assume.

Where did Amandeep ask Jatin about his gaze?
Amandeep asked at the water cooler.
What had Amandeep first thought about Jatin's averted gaze?
Amandeep read it as not caring or hiding something, which was annoying. Jatin's explanation showed that looking away helps him listen, so the first reading was wrong.
What did Amandeep do that worked better than assuming?
Amandeep asked gently, said there was no anger and accepted Jatin's answer without demanding eye contact.
How might Jatin have felt being asked about his gaze?
He looked relieved after the explanation, so he probably appreciated the gentle question, though he may have felt a little nervous at first.

And "torrent" - what does that mean?
How do I plan a day out with friends on a school holiday?
Plus, is it "beleive" or "believe"?

1. Bright lights confuse them. Because many night insects steer by the moon, and a lamp makes them circle it by mistake.

Friday
Still shaky. After school, at the bus stop on Canal Road, a car hit a boy on a cycle. He was lying on the road holding his leg. Everyone just stared. Ojas started running toward him, into the traffic, and I grabbed his bag and pulled him back. “Cars!”
Then I called the emergency number. I made myself say it the way we learnt in the safety class: where, how many, what happened. “Bus stop on Canal Road, opposite the petrol pump. One boy hurt, he was on a cycle, hit by a car. He's awake, holding his leg.” The woman on the phone asked me to stay on the line and tell her if anything changed. I did, from the footpath.
The ambulance came in about ten minutes. A shopkeeper stood with the boy until it did.
I only realised afterwards how hard my heart was beating.

Where exactly did Vijay say the accident was?
Bus stop on Canal Road, opposite the petrol pump.
What was Vijay feeling during and after the call?
Vijay stayed focused during the call, but afterwards felt shaky, heart pounding, as the fear caught up.
What else could Vijay have done while staying on the line?
Ask an adult nearby, like the shopkeeper, to stay with the boy and keep people from crowding, while Vijay kept giving updates.

Ojas might be annoyed in the moment, but later glad to have been stopped from running into the traffic.

It was raining hard outside the tuition centre when a man stepped up to Vinita. "Your mother has had an accident. Come with me quickly." Vinita's stomach lurched. Her grandmother's rule rang in her ears: always listen to elders, never be rude. She followed him two lanes, her shoes soaked, though a small voice said, wait. At the corner, Vikas, the paan-shop owner who knew her family, called, "Vinita! Where are you going?" The man walked off fast. Vikas phoned her mother, who answered from home, perfectly well. Vinita was shaking. Later, drying her hair, she wondered why no one had told her that saying no was allowed too.

Who called out to Vinita at the corner?
Vikas, the paan-shop owner who knew her family, called out.
What was Vinita feeling as she followed the man?
Frightened for her mother, and torn between the rule to obey elders and a small voice saying wait.
What could Vinita do instead if a stranger says her mother is hurt, and why?
She could refuse to go, stay near people and ask a trusted adult to phone her mother, because a real emergency can be checked without following a stranger.
How does Vikas see the situation at the corner?
Vikas sees a child from a family Vikas knows walking off with a stranger, so Vikas steps in and phones her mother.

In the school canteen, Vinita saw two boys pour salt into Suraj's juice while he fetched a spoon. They sniggered. Suraj came back, took a sip and spat it out, red-faced.
Vinita turned back to her sandwich. Not my problem, she told herself. Someone else will say something.
But nobody did. Everyone was busy. Suraj sat alone, staring at his cup.
Vinita chewed slowly. The sandwich felt like cardboard. If everyone waits for someone else, then no one helps.
She got up and bought Suraj a fresh juice. "Here. I saw what they did." Then she told the canteen supervisor, who went to talk to the two boys.

What did the boys pour into Suraj's juice?
Salt.

She felt uneasy and guilty; the sandwich felt like cardboard as she realised no one was helping.

She bought Suraj a fresh juice, told him she had seen it, and reported it to the canteen supervisor.

On the bench outside the tea shop in the small town, after Class 10 tuition, Anand held up his phone. “Everyone's using AI for the essays. Half of 10-B. So it's fine.”
Ishita frowned. “Sir said the assignment has to be your own.”
“Sir doesn't know how many do it. If everybody does, that's basically the rule.” He liked that sentence and repeated it in his head all the way home. He pasted the prompt, submitted the answer and felt good. Then Ishita's essay, stumbling and honest, got 7 marks and his got 9 for no effort of his own, and he felt a small, unpleasant pinch. He shrugged it off. Later, when the teacher asked him to write two lines on the topic in class, he found he couldn't.

What did Anand say about the rest of the class?
Anand said everyone is using AI for the essays, half of 10-B.
What might Anand's small pinch mean?
Anand may feel uneasy and a little guilty, sensing it is not fair that his effortless answer beat Ishita's honest one.
What could Anand do differently?
Anand could follow the school's rule, use AI only to explain ideas and write the essay himself, since a crowd's habit does not change fairness or his own learning.
How might Ishita feel about the marks?
Ishita may feel frustrated or unfairly treated, since Ishita's honest work earned fewer marks than an answer with no effort.

Tejas, you asked me why your grandfather made the tea every morning of his life. Sit. I'll tell you.
When we married in 1986, I was a bride of twenty-four and teaching at the girls' college, and he worked shifts at the post office. My mother-in-law expected me to do everything at home as well. For three months I tried. I was so tired I fell asleep marking papers.
One Sunday he found me like that. He said, "Sarita, this isn't fair. Let's divide it by who's home and who's better at what." He was better at tea and markets. I was better at accounts. We made a list, and every Sunday we checked it.
His mother was shocked for a year. We were patient. By the end she was telling the neighbours her son made the best tea on the street.
So, Tejas, when you marry, talk every week.

What year did Sarita marry?
Sarita married in 1986.
How was Sarita feeling in the first three months of marriage?
She was exhausted and overwhelmed, so tired she fell asleep marking papers while trying to do all the housework alone.
What was the turning point in Sarita's story?
It came when her husband found her asleep and suggested dividing work by who was home and who was better at what, with a weekly check.
How did the mother-in-law's view change over time?
She was shocked for a year, but with the couple's patience she came to boast that her son made the best tea on the street.

Arnab, you ask why I'm smiling at this old photo? That's Bimal. I was engaged to him at twenty-three. Your Ishita dida has a story.

Three months before the wedding, he broke it off by letter. No reason. My father had already printed the cards. For years I couldn't hear his name without my hands going cold. I told myself I'd forgive him only when he apologised.

He never did.

When I was twenty-six, I saw him at the Durga puja pandal with his wife and a small boy. I expected rage. Instead I felt tired of the weight. That night was my turning point. I decided I would forgive him, for my sake, not his. No letter, no apology needed.

The next year I saw him again, by the sweet stall. I said, "Bimal, I hold nothing against you. Be well." He looked stunned. I walked away and bought rosogolla for your grandfather.

I never went back to that story again.

How did Bimal break off the engagement?
He broke it off by letter, with no reason.
How did young Ishita feel for years after the engagement ended?
She felt hurt and resentful, her hands going cold at his name, waiting for an apology.
What was the turning point in Ishita's story?
Seeing Bimal at the pandal made her feel tired of the weight, and she chose to forgive him for her own peace without needing his apology.
How might Bimal have felt when Ishita spoke to him?
Bimal was stunned, perhaps surprised and relieved by her calm forgiveness.

Quick one: why does cold water make a glass look wet on the outside on a hot day?

2. The outside of the glass gets covered with tiny drops of water. Because water vapour in the warm air turns into liquid when it touches the cold surface.

The inter-college debate was in twenty minutes, and the auditorium in Patna was so packed the fans barely helped. Umesh paced backstage. A year ago, he'd have been in the principal's office instead. His temper had got him suspended once for shouting down a lecturer. Then Jatin, the debate captain, had seen him argue in the canteen and said, "You'd be terrifying on stage. With rules." Now Umesh had rules: three minutes, no personal attacks, rebuttals only on points. The opposing speaker went first and made a cheap jab about his college. Umesh felt the old heat rise. His hands clenched. Jatin caught his eye and tapped his watch. Umesh breathed, wrote the jab on his card, and turned it into his opening line, sharp but clean. The audience roared. He'd kept every bit of the fire and used it inside the lines.

How long did each speaker have?
Three minutes.
What did Umesh feel when the opponent made the cheap jab?
He felt the old anger rising, hands clenching, but he held it and turned it into a sharp, clean argument.
How did the rules help Umesh use his intensity well?
Clear limits like no personal attacks and a time limit gave his fierce energy a shape, so it became skill instead of trouble.
How might Jatin feel watching Umesh's opening line?
Jatin probably felt proud and relieved, seeing that his faith in Umesh's fire had been right.

"Papa, I'm a Star!" Usha waved her hand. A shiny sticker sat on it. "A star? What for?" "For the Stars team. We're the best team." "Best at what?" "Everything." Usha climbed onto her chair. "The Moons are silly." Papa passed the dal. "Is Imran a Moon?" "Yes." "But you sit with Imran every day." Usha frowned. "Not today. Stars sit with Stars." "How did you become a Star?" "Miss gave stickers from a box. I got a star." "So if you got a moon?" Usha looked at her sticker. "Then... Moons are the best?" She did not sound sure.

What was on Usha's hand when she came to the table?
A shiny star sticker was on her hand.
Why does Usha frown when Papa says she sits with Imran every day?
She feels torn, because she likes Imran but now believes Stars should only sit with Stars.

Imran might have felt left out and puzzled, since they sit together every day and nothing changed except a sticker.

Coach's note, Saturday, junior athletics, Jodhpur.
Uday, ten, arrived today red-eyed and silent. His aunt, Damini, who dropped him off, told me quietly that there had been a big quarrel at home last night between his parents. Uday didn't want to talk. He asked if he could run. I let him. He ran lap after lap around the ground, much faster than usual, fists clenched at first, then loosening. After eight laps he slowed down and lay on the grass. When I sat next to him, he said, "I feel better now. Still sad, but not angry." What I did next: I told him running is a good way to let anger out, and that I'm always here if he wants to talk. I also mentioned to Damini that he might want someone to listen at home.

How many laps did Uday run before slowing down?
Eight laps.
Why did Uday ask to run instead of talking?
He felt angry and upset after the quarrel, and running gave the anger a safe place to go before he could put it into words.
What did the coach do after the run that was wise?
The coach praised running as a healthy outlet, offered to listen, and told Damini he might need someone at home to talk to.
How might Damini feel after hearing from the coach?
Damini might feel relieved that Uday found a safe way to cope, and ready to listen to him at home.
Maine apni teacher ko ghar bulaya. "I invited my teacher at my home" theek hai?
Say: "I invited my teacher to my home." Why: We use "to" for inviting someone to a place.

On Lohri night, after too many peanuts and rewri, Preeti curled up on the sofa. "My tummy hurts." Her big brother Ujjwal sat beside her and rubbed her back. Papa came from the kitchen with a tiny white mishri sweet. "Here. This will help settle it." Preeti sucked it slowly while Papa put a warm cloth on her tummy and told her about the bonfire songs. "Better?" he asked after a while. "A bit," she said, and it was true. The ache had softened. "If it keeps hurting or you feel worse, tell me, and we'll call the doctor," Papa said. Ujjwal whispered, "That's just sugar." Papa smiled. "Sugar and care."

What did Papa give Preeti?
A tiny white mishri sweet.
How did Preeti feel after Papa's sweet and the warm cloth?
She felt comforted and a little better, as the ache softened with Papa's care and reassurance.
What did Papa do wisely besides giving the sweet?
He stayed with her, used a warm cloth, and said they would call the doctor if it kept hurting or she felt worse.
How does Ujjwal see the mishri?
Ujjwal thinks it's "just sugar" and doesn't realise how much the reassurance itself helps.

Sit, Jyoti. You asked why I light a lamp for my own thatha every Deepavali. I was fifteen when he died, just like that, at his shop counter in Salem. That evening everyone told me, "Rukmini, don't cry, your amma needs you strong." So I didn't. I made coffee, I swept, I kept my face like stone. On the third day my Periamma found me behind the well, shaking. She didn't scold. She sat down in the dirt beside me and said, "Cry, kanna. He was your thatha too." And I cried until my throat hurt. After that I sat with the family through every ritual, and I cried whenever it came. Grief is not a guest you can hurry out of the house, Jyoti. I learned that behind a well, and it has stayed with me all these years.

Where did Rukmini's thatha die?
He died at his shop counter in Salem.
What was Rukmini feeling while keeping a face like stone?
Rukmini was grieving but felt pressured to be strong, holding the sadness in until it came out as shaking behind the well.
What turning point changed how Rukmini grieved?
When Periamma sat in the dirt and said to cry, Rukmini stopped hiding the tears and sat with the family through the rituals, crying whenever it came.
How did Periamma see Rukmini behind the well?
Periamma saw someone hiding grief and chose not to scold, sitting close and saying that he was Rukmini's thatha too.

Give me this verse in plain modern prose.

No change of hue, no pose of limb
Gave sign that aught was false in him.
Concise, unfaltering, sweet and clear,
Without a word to pain the ear,
From chest to throat, nor high nor low,
His accents came in measured flow.

No change of colour and no pose of his limbs gave any sign that anything about him was false. His words came in a measured flow, concise, unfaltering, sweet and clear, without a word to pain the ear, from chest to throat, neither high nor low.

"Papa, I'm wearing my sparkly sandals!"
"Not today, Trisha. It's raining. Wellies."
"But sparkly!"
"I know you are upset. The answer is still no."
"You're not fair!" Trisha threw herself on the stairs and cried.
Joseph sat one step below her. "Big feeling, hmm? I'll wait."
"Can the sandals come in my bag?"
"They can come in the bag. Wellies on the feet."
Trisha sniffed. She pulled on one welly, then the other. "Can I jump in the puddles?"

What did Joseph say could go in the bag?
Joseph said the sparkly sandals could come in the bag, but wellies had to go on her feet.
How was Trisha feeling when she threw herself on the stairs?
She was upset and cross that her father would not let her wear the sparkly sandals in the rain.
What small step helped Trisha move on from her big feeling?
Joseph waited calmly and let the sandals come in her bag, which gave her something to hold onto while the rule stayed firm. 😊
How does Joseph see Trisha's crying on the stairs?
He sees it as a big feeling that will pass, so he waits nearby instead of shouting or giving in.
Can I use exclamation marks in a formal email?

You can, but sparingly. One may be fine in a warm greeting or thanks, but too many make an email look unprofessional.
Example: Thank you for your quick reply! I will send the form today.

At his cousin's wedding in Seville, Alejandro, twenty-six, watched the bride dance with her father, and something old cracked open. His own father had left when he was ten and never came to his graduation. He'd told himself for years that it didn't matter. Now his throat locked and he walked out to the car park. His first instinct was to go back in, smile, and have another drink. Instead he called Zanele, his closest friend from university. "It's stupid," he said. "It was sixteen years ago." "It's not stupid," Zanele said. "Tell me." He talked for twenty minutes and cried twice. Afterward he felt emptied, but lighter. Over the next month the feeling kept coming back at odd moments, so he booked an appointment with a counsellor at the clinic near work. "Good," Zanele texted. "I'm proud of you."

How old was Alejandro when his father left?
He was ten.
Why did Alejandro say "It's stupid" on the phone?
Part of him still felt he shouldn't be hurting after sixteen years, as if the old pain didn't deserve attention.
Which choices did Alejandro make instead of shoving the feeling down?
He called a trusted friend and let himself talk and cry, and when the feeling kept returning, he booked a counsellor.
How might Zanele feel hearing Alejandro finally talk about his father?
Zanele seemed warm and glad he reached out, and proud of him for booking the counsellor.
Text my parents that I reached home safely. Lowercase and no punctuation at all, please.
reached home safe and sound see you soon

As she said this she looked down at her hands, and was surprised to see that she had put on one of the Rabbit's little white kid gloves while she was talking. "How can I have done that?" she thought. "I must be growing small again." She got up and went to the table to measure herself by it, and found that, as nearly as she could guess, she was now about two feet high, and was going on shrinking rapidly: she soon found out that the cause of this was the fan she was holding, and she dropped it hastily, just in time to avoid shrinking away altogether.

Can you explain this in simple words for a child?

Alice sees that she is wearing one of the Rabbit's tiny gloves, so she thinks she is shrinking again. She checks her height at the table and learns that the fan in her hand is making her smaller. She drops it just in time, before she shrinks away to nothing.

Why does Jane cry while she studies?

One day I had come to my studies in lower spirits than usual; the ebb was occasioned by a poignantly felt disappointment. Hannah had told me in the morning there was a letter for me, and when I went down to take it, almost certain that the long-looked for tidings were vouchsafed me at last, I found only an unimportant note from Mr. Briggs on business. The bitter check had wrung from me some tears; and now, as I sat poring over the crabbed characters and flourishing tropes of an Indian scribe, my eyes filled again.
She had hoped a letter would bring news she had waited a long time for. It was only an unimportant business note from Mr. Briggs, and the disappointment made her cry.

Read this:

"When my Thatha died, Seema, I was a girl about your age. For thirteen days our house was full: relatives sleeping on mats, the lamp always burning, Amma's cousins singing low songs at dusk. I didn't understand why nobody cooked anything sweet. I asked Amma, 'Where did Thatha go?' She didn't say he was sleeping. She said, 'His body stopped working, Vasudha. He won't come back, but we will keep remembering him.' I cried hard that night. And the next afternoon I was playing hopscotch with my cousins in the backyard, laughing. I felt guilty and stopped. My Periamma saw and said, 'Play, kanna. Thatha loved your laughing.' Crying and playing both came and went for weeks."

How many days was the house full after Thatha died?
Thirteen days.
What was young Vasudha feeling when she stopped playing hopscotch?
She felt guilty, as if laughing was wrong while the family was grieving.
What choice inside the story helped Vasudha?
Her Periamma chose to tell her it was all right to play, saying Thatha loved her laughing, which eased her guilt.
How might Amma have felt when Vasudha asked where Thatha went?
Amma was grieving herself but chose to answer with simple honest words, likely wanting her daughter to understand without being frightened.

Avni, let me tell you something about your Leela Didi. When she was fifteen, she wanted to write a whole novel. Everyone laughed. "A novel? You can't even finish your homework." She wrote one page every night. Some nights it was just half a page, and she complained it was rubbish. After three months, she was bored and wanted to stop. I told her, "Then write boring pages. Just write." She laughed, but she kept going. Around the sixth month she lost a whole chapter when her notebook got wet in the monsoon. She cried for a day. Then she started it again, and she said the new one was better. She finished in a year. It's still on my shelf. Your turn now, beta.

What happened to Leela Didi's chapter around the sixth month?
She lost a whole chapter when her notebook got wet in the monsoon.
How did Leela feel when she lost the chapter?
She was heartbroken and cried for a day, but then found the resolve to start again.
What can Avni learn from Leela's approach?
Small daily effort, even on boring days, and restarting after a setback can carry a long project to the end.
How might Leela's family see her finished novel now?
They likely feel proud and a bit sheepish about laughing, seeing it on the shelf as proof of her persistence.
Make an acrostic from the word RAIN, one line for each letter.

Rooftops shine and gutters sing
All the puddles start to grow
Inside, we sip hot tea
Now the clouds drift slowly on

Dear Diary, Tanvir here, and I have made a BIG discovery. Every time Nani comes from Lucknow, it rains. Last July she came: rain. In September: rain. Today she got off the train and the clouds opened right over the station! So Nani makes it rain. I told my friend Lakshmi from next door, and we planned to ask Nani to visit in May, when the tank at school is dry. Lakshmi said maybe Nani just comes in the rainy months because that's when the holidays are. I said no, it is Nani. Then Abbu reminded me that Nani came in December too, and it didn't rain once. Hmm. I am still keeping a chart at the back of this diary. Nani laughed and said she only brings pickles. 🙂

Where did it rain when Nani arrived today?
The clouds opened right over the station.
Why does Tanvir feel sure that Nani makes it rain?
Tanvir feels excited and proud of the discovery, because the visits Tanvir remembers came with rain, so the two things seem joined.
What could Tanvir's chart help check?
The chart could list every visit, rainy or dry, including December, so Tanvir can see whether rain follows Nani or just the rainy months.
How does Lakshmi explain the rain differently?
Lakshmi thinks Nani probably visits in the rainy months because the holidays fall then, so the season brings both.

When I was eleven, I had a huge pile of animal cards. Chinmay and I kept swapping them, and they were a mess.

One Sunday I decided to sort them. First into animals and birds. Then the animals into wild and pet. Then the wild ones into cats, dogs, bears. I made little boxes with labels.

Chinmay laughed. "Why is the tiger in two boxes?"

"It's not. It's in 'cats', and 'cats' is inside 'wild'."

He didn't get it at first. I drew a big circle with smaller circles inside.

I'm Samir, and that was the first time I understood that one group can live inside another.

How did Samir first sort the cards?
First into animals and birds.
How did Samir feel explaining the circles to Chinmay?
Samir felt proud and determined to make Chinmay understand.
How could a teacher build on Samir's sorting?
A teacher could give him more things to sort into groups and subgroups and ask him to draw them.
How might Chinmay see the sorting at first?
Chinmay found it confusing and funny at first, asking why the tiger was in two boxes.

Cut this to about half its length.

Tushar, since your podcast is about being twenty-two and lost, here's mine. I'm Reena. For about a year I called myself lazy every morning. Lazy, useless, wasted my best years. I dropped out of my MBA prep, I slept till eleven, I watched my college friends post about jobs. I thought if I was harsh enough, I'd shock myself into working.

Tushar, your podcast is about being twenty-two and lost, so here is my story. I'm Reena. For a year, I called myself lazy every morning. I dropped my MBA prep, slept till eleven and watched my friends post about jobs. I thought being harsh with myself would make me work.

The school bus had broken down in the rain, and twenty children were waiting in the porch of a closed shop in Aizawl. Lalremsiami, who had snatched Minakshi's pencil box every day for a month, stood apart with a phone to her ear. "Pa, please don't go. Mum is crying." Her voice cracked. Minakshi pretended not to listen, but her anger wobbled. When the replacement bus came, Lalremsiami grabbed the pencil box again. Minakshi held on. "I'm sorry things are hard at home. But you still can't take my things. Give it back." Lalremsiami stared, then let go. The next morning Minakshi told Miss Zote about the snatching. Miss Zote thanked her, spoke to Lalremsiami that day, and asked the counsellor to check in with her too.

What did Lalremsiami say on the phone?
Lalremsiami said, "Pa, please don't go. Mum is crying."
Why did Minakshi's anger wobble in the shop porch?
Hearing the call, Minakshi felt sympathy and sensed that Lalremsiami might be hurting at home.
How did Minakshi balance understanding with a boundary?
She said she was sorry things were hard but still refused to let the box go, and told Miss Zote about the snatching.
How might Lalremsiami see Minakshi's words about home?
Lalremsiami may feel exposed and surprised that Minakshi knew, but also seen, which may be why she let go.
After a hard test is over, why do we feel relieved?
Relief comes once the pressure of the test is gone. Because the mind has been tense while waiting and the worry has ended, the body relaxes.

Having descended the hill the general after whom Pierre was galloping turned sharply to the left, and Pierre, losing sight of him, galloped in among some ranks of infantry marching ahead of him. He tried to pass either in front of them or to the right or left, but there were soldiers everywhere, all with the same preoccupied expression and busy with some unseen but evidently important task. They all gazed with the same dissatisfied and inquiring expression at this stout man in a white hat, who for some unknown reason threatened to trample them under his horse's hoofs.

What does Pierre try to do after he loses sight of the general, and how do the soldiers look at him?
He gallops in among the infantry and tries to pass in front of them or to the right or left, but there are soldiers everywhere. They all gaze at him with a dissatisfied, inquiring look.
Present perfect, please: Meena finished her homework.
Meena has finished her homework.

Arnab had been on the call with the Mumbai client for forty minutes when it happened. "Frankly, this is amateur work," the client said, and hung up. Arnab stared at the black screen. His throat closed, and to his horror his eyes filled. In his first job a senior had told him, "Men don't cry in office." He blinked hard and gripped the desk, but a tear slid down anyway. Baljeet, at the next desk, saw. She didn't comment, and she didn't make a show of looking away. She just said, "Terrace? Five minutes?" Up there, among the water tanks and the neighbouring building's laundry, Arnab let his breath shudder out and wiped his face with his sleeve. "Sorry," he said. "Nothing to be sorry for," Baljeet said. When he had steadied, he said, "Okay. I'll ask for a list of exactly what they want changed, and do it by Friday." They went back down.

How long had Arnab been on the call?
Forty minutes.
What was Arnab feeling when his eyes filled?
Arnab felt hurt by the harsh words and horrified at crying, remembering a senior saying men don't cry in office.
What helped Arnab recover and move forward?
A short break on the terrace to breathe and wipe his face, then a plan to ask exactly what the client wanted changed and deliver by Friday.
How did Baljeet respond, and why was it kind?
Baljeet didn't comment or stare, just offered five quiet minutes on the terrace and said there was nothing to be sorry for, letting him recover with dignity.

messages.content:
Read this:

Kindergarten note, Thursday.
While I was talking with Gurpreet's mother at pickup, Avni (5) ran up and tugged my sleeve. "Ma'am! Ma'am! My tooth is wobbly! Look!" She did it three times. When I said, "Wait, Avni," her face crumpled and she said, "But I'll forget!"
I knelt and showed her a signal: put your hand on my arm, and I'll put mine on yours, which means "I know, your turn is next." She tried it. She held my arm, jiggling, for about a minute. Then I turned to her. "Now, tell me." She showed me the tooth, beaming.
I'll teach the hand signal to the whole class tomorrow.

What did Avni want to show the teacher?
Her wobbly tooth.
Why did Avni keep interrupting?
She was excited and worried she'd forget what she wanted to say if she waited.
Why did the hand signal work better than just saying 'wait'?
It promised Avni a turn and gave her something to do while waiting, so she didn't feel ignored or scolded.
How might Gurpreet's mother have felt during the interruptions?
She was probably a little distracted but likely amused, seeing how excited Avni was.

My name is Simran, and I live next door to Maria's parents. I only know what I saw over the wall on Sunday.

Maria's mother had been telling everyone at the temple that Maria was about to be made a manager. That evening Maria arrived, still in her work shoes, and sat down at the table under the veranda light. Her parents stopped talking when she came in.

I couldn't hear all of it, but I heard Maria say, "I didn't get it. Someone else did. I should have told you last week." Her father stared at his tea. Her mother reached over and held Maria's wrist for a moment.

Later the mother came to water the plants, humming. I don't know how she really felt. But Maria was laughing at something by the time I went inside.

Where did Simran see Maria sit with her parents?
Simran saw Maria sit at the table under the veranda light.
What does the mother's touch on Maria's wrist suggest, and how sure can Simran be?
Holding Maria's wrist suggests warmth and support, but Simran admits not knowing how the mother really felt, so the inner state is uncertain.
What did Maria do that helped with the awkwardness?
Maria told her parents plainly that she did not get the role and that she should have said so sooner, instead of letting them hear it from others.
How might the parents have felt after telling relatives that Maria was rising?
They may have felt awkward or embarrassed in front of the relatives, though their quiet reaction and the later humming suggest they were not blaming Maria.

Mentor's note, 12 January.
I asked Lakshmi, who joined us two years ago, to talk to the new graduates about their first salaries, since hers is the calmest desk in the office. Pooja, one of the new joiners, said she keeps her bonus in a 'fun' account and her salary in a 'serious' one. Lakshmi smiled. "I used to do that too. Then I'd pinch every rupee on lunch while blowing the bonus on shoes." She showed them her single sheet: all accounts added together, debts taken away, money in and money out for the month. "The labels are still there," she said. "Rent, emergencies, my sister's wedding. But it's all one pool. I just look at the whole thing once a month." Pooja asked for a blank copy. I've asked HR to arrange a session with a certified financial adviser next month for anyone who wants it.

What does Pooja keep in a 'fun' account?
Pooja keeps her bonus in a 'fun' account.
Why does Lakshmi smile when Pooja describes her two accounts?
Lakshmi feels amused and understanding, recognising her own old habit of pinching on lunch while spending the bonus on shoes.
What does Lakshmi's single sheet do that separate accounts don't?
It adds all accounts together and takes away debts, showing the whole pool and the month's flow, while labels remain as tools for goals.
What might Pooja be feeling when she asks for a blank copy?
Pooja seems curious and a little relieved to find a simpler way to see her first salary clearly.

Sunday: Uma asked Mummy, "Can I teach the Class 5 kids in our lane after school? Their parents offered a small fee." Alka thought for a moment. "One hour, four days a week, and only after your own homework. I will talk to their parents first."

Two weeks later, Wednesday: Uma sat on the veranda with three children, a slate and a bag of chalk. She noted their trouble spots: fractions, spellings. By evening she was tired, but proud.

End of the month: Uma counted the fees on the table: six hundred rupees. She put half in Mummy's hand, "for the house," and half into a tin labelled Exam Fee. Alka pressed her hand and said nothing.

How many days a week and how long each day did Alka allow Uma to teach?
Alka allowed one hour, four days a week.
How did Uma feel on the first Wednesday evening?
Uma felt tired but proud after teaching three children.
What else could Uma do to keep the earning study-safe, and why?
Uma could set a fixed stopping time and skip the sessions in exam week, because study time protects the longer-term goal that the fee is meant for.
How might Alka feel when Uma puts half the fees in her hand?
Alka is probably moved and proud, which is why she presses Uma's hand and says nothing.
Which months have exactly 30 days? List them in calendar order, separated by commas.
April, June, September, November

I'm Harish, Ojas's big brother. On Sunday night Dadi told us about the hairy monster that lives in the old tamarind tree. Ojas, five, listened with the blanket up to his nose. On Tuesday we went to the colony park, and he just played on the slide. But yesterday he told his nursery class, "I saw a hairy monster in the tamarind tree at the park! It waved at me!" His teacher phoned Mummy. I don't think he was fibbing; he told it the way he tells about the slide. He knows the monster well. He just forgot it came from Dadi's story, not the park.

Where did Dadi say the hairy monster lives?
In the old tamarind tree.
Why did Ojas tell the class about the monster so confidently?
He knew the monster well from Dadi's story and had lost track of where it came from, so to him it felt like something seen at the park.
What could Mummy ask Ojas to help sort out the story?
She could gently ask, "Did you see it at the park, or hear about it from Dadi?", letting him find the source without calling it a lie.
How might Ojas's teacher have felt hearing about the monster?
The teacher was probably puzzled and a little concerned, unsure whether something had really frightened him at the park.

"Mumma, Jaggu wants the baby bottle," said Jagdish in a squeaky voice.
"You are five, Jagdish." Preeti rubbed her eyes, the baby fussing on her shoulder. Then she stopped. "Sorry. I am tired, and it is not your fault."
"Am I a baby too?"
"You are my big boy and I love you." She kissed his hair. "When she sleeps, it will be you and me, no phone. What shall we do?"
He thought. "Cards!"
"Cards it is."

What did Jagdish ask for in a squeaky voice?
He said Jaggu wants the baby bottle.
Why did Jagdish talk like a baby?
He probably feels left out while Mummy is busy with the baby, and baby talk is a way of getting close to her again.
What did Preeti do to reassure him?
She admitted she was tired and said it was not his fault, told him he is her big boy, and promised time for just the two of them when the baby sleeps.
How might Preeti be feeling as she holds the fussing baby and talks to Jagdish?
She is tired and stretched, and probably a little guilty about snapping. Her apology and her promise show she wants to be there for both children.

Teacher's note, Class 4, Thursday.
Since Aparna joined last week, Usha has been following her everywhere. She holds Aparna's hand in the line, fetches her water, and tells me three times a day, "Aparna is SO nice, Ma'am! She's my best friend!" It's very loud. But I notice that when I praised Aparna's drawing today, Usha's smile stayed fixed and her hands squeezed together under the desk. Usha was the class's best drawer until last week. I think she may feel pushed aside and can't say it. What I did next: I asked Usha to help me put up the art wall, and I told her quietly that it's normal to feel a bit funny when someone new is good at the same thing. She stared at me, then nodded, very slowly.

What was Usha known for until last week?
Being the class's best drawer.
What do Usha's fixed smile and squeezed hands suggest?
They suggest Usha feels jealous and pushed aside, hiding it behind loud friendliness towards Aparna.
Why was the teacher's quiet comment a good step?
It told Usha that her feeling is normal without accusing her, making it easier to admit.
How might Aparna see Usha's attention?
Aparna may feel welcomed but perhaps a little overwhelmed by being followed everywhere.

The power went out at the Nagpur office at seven, two hours before the tender documents were due. Darshan moved to the stairwell where the backup light still worked, laptop balanced on one knee, battery at forty percent. By eight his shoulders had crept up almost to his ears. When Akash came to ask about the annexure, Darshan snapped, "It's in the folder," without looking up. Akash went quiet. "Sorry I asked," he said, and turned to go. Darshan caught the hurt in it. He put the laptop down, rolled his shoulders back three times and stretched his arms over his head until something in his neck clicked. "Wait. I'm not annoyed with you. My shoulders are just locked from this deadline. The annexure is the third file. Sit, we'll check it together." Akash sat. They submitted at 8:52.

How much battery did Darshan's laptop have in the stairwell?
The battery was at forty percent.
What was Akash feeling when he said 'Sorry I asked'?
Akash felt hurt and a bit rejected, reading Darshan's raised shoulders and short reply as irritation with him, when it was really deadline strain.
How did Darshan repair the moment?
He put the laptop down, rolled and stretched his shoulders, explained the tension came from the deadline, and invited Akash to check the file together.
What would have changed if Darshan hadn't caught the hurt in Akash's voice?
Akash might have walked away believing Darshan was angry with him, and the annexure might not have been checked before the deadline.

Kishore here, from the desk next to Ujjwal's. During yesterday's client call the lead kept saying, "We'll sync the schema and push it by Friday." Ujjwal didn't nod along. He unmuted and said, "I follow the Friday deadline. I don't follow which schema, the old one or the new one. Could someone write down which, and who owns it?" Nobody spoke for a second, and he looked down at his notebook, tapping his pen. I couldn't tell whether he was embarrassed or just impatient. The lead typed the answer into the chat, and it turned out I had assumed the wrong schema, and so had another colleague. Ujjwal wrote something down and said thanks.

Which two things did Ujjwal say he did and did not follow?
He followed the Friday deadline but did not follow which schema, the old one or the new one.
What might Ujjwal have been feeling as he tapped his pen after the silence?
Most likely he was a little embarrassed at being the only one to ask, but Kishore admits it could also be impatience to get the answer.
What could the lead do so that questions like this come up earlier?
The lead could name the schema and its owner from the start, and ask the group what is still unclear before ending the call.
How did Kishore's own understanding change after Ujjwal's question?
Kishore found out that Kishore and another colleague had assumed the wrong schema, so Ujjwal's question stopped them building on a wrong guess.

The community centre's back room was empty on a Tuesday evening, which was why Tarun had suggested it. Tanvir sat across from his old college mentor with a folder on his knees. "I haven't told anyone at work. Not yet." Tarun nodded. "Good. Start with what you saw, not what you think it means." Tanvir opened the folder: a dated list of ration-supply deliveries that the NGO had recorded but the villages never received, with copies of the delivery slips. "I'm scared," he admitted. "My father's surgery is next month, and I'm the only earner." Tarun didn't tell him to be brave. "Then plan around that. Keep your notes at home, not on the office laptop. Talk to the lawyer from the legal-aid clinic I mentioned, in confidence, before you file anything." Tanvir let out a long breath. "So waiting a week isn't cowardice?" "It's preparation. It'll make your report stronger."

What did Tanvir's folder contain?
It held a dated list of ration-supply deliveries the NGO had recorded but the villages never received, with copies of the delivery slips.
How does Tanvir feel when he says waiting a week might be cowardice?
Tanvir feels scared and a bit ashamed, worried about his father's surgery and about seeming weak for not acting at once.
What makes Tarun's guidance a strong turning point?
Tarun helps Tanvir record facts, protect his notes, plan around family needs and speak to a lawyer in confidence, so any report is careful and stronger.
How might Tarun see his role as a mentor here?
Tarun likely sees himself as a steady, private sounding board, helping Tanvir think clearly without pushing him into risk.

The district match was the next morning, and training ran late in the heat. Coach Farida blew her whistle. "No water breaks today. Real athletes train through thirst. It makes you tough."

Vikas's head was pounding. He knew from science class that the body needs water in heat. His cousin, a nurse, had said the same.

But Coach Farida had played for the state. Everyone said she knew everything. And she sounded so sure.

He looked at his bottle on the bench. If he drank, would he look weak? Would she drop him?

After fifteen more minutes he felt dizzy. He walked to the bench, drank, and said, awkwardly, "Sorry, Coach. My cousin's a nurse. She says we need water in the heat."

The team went silent. Farida frowned. Then, slowly, she said, "Everyone, water. Two minutes."

Vikas's face burned. But his head started to clear.

What had Coach Farida played for?
Coach Farida had played for the state.
Why did Vikas hesitate to drink water?
Vikas felt afraid of looking weak and being dropped, because the coach seemed so sure and had played for the state.
What did Vikas do that was wise, even if awkward?
Vikas drank water and politely mentioned his cousin's advice, looking after his health while respecting the coach.
How might Coach Farida have felt when Vikas spoke up?
Coach Farida may have felt surprised and a little challenged, but her call for a water break suggests she reconsidered.
What is a wise saying about patience? Make it one sentence of exactly eight words.
Patience turns many small steps into long journeys.

Reena: Shankar, I did it. I'm at the art camp 🎨
Shankar: wait WHAT. your parents said yes??
Reena: no. I told them I'm at Priti's for a group project
Shankar: Reena. your dad needed you at the shop this week
Reena: they'll manage. it's MY summer
Shankar: ok...

Two days later
Reena: my dad called Priti's mom
Reena: they know
Shankar: oh no
Reena: he's not even shouting. just said "we trusted you"

Shankar: 😬

Where did Reena tell her parents she was?
At Priti's, for a group project.
How does Reena feel after her parents find out?
Reena feels sick and guilty, and afraid her parents won't believe anything now.
What would have been a better approach than going secretly?
Telling the parents how much the art camp mattered and looking together for help at the shop, so trust stays intact and the shop's need is covered.
How might Reena's mother have felt standing at the shop alone for 12 hours?
She was probably exhausted and hurt, and later betrayed on learning Reena had lied about where she was.

Monday, summer holidays. Mehak put a mango on the table. "Kunal, you can have it after lunch." Kunal sat and stared at it. He cried. He ate it before lunch.
Wednesday. Mehak put the mango in the fridge. "After lunch." Kunal asked about it three times, but he played with his blocks. He waited.
Saturday. Mehak said, "Mango after lunch. Want to play a counting game till then?" They counted cars from the balcony. Kunal counted to forty. "Lunch!" called Amma. Kunal ran in. "Mango time!" He had forgotten to cry.

Where did Mehak put the mango on Wednesday?
In the fridge.
Why did Kunal cry on Monday?
He was staring at the mango, so waiting felt too hard and he felt upset and impatient.
What helped Kunal wait longer each time?
Putting the mango out of sight and playing a counting game, which kept his mind busy until lunch.
How might Mehak feel on Saturday when Kunal forgot to cry?
Mehak probably felt pleased and proud that her ideas helped him wait.
Is it safe to use free Wi-Fi at a cafe?
It can be fine for simple browsing, but be careful. Public Wi-Fi may not be secure, so others on the same network might see what you send. Avoid logging into bank or other important accounts on it.
What if I really need to check something?
Use your mobile data instead for anything private. If you must use the cafe network, check that the website address starts with https, and log out when you're done.

In the waiting room of a community legal advice centre, Simran sat with a folder of printed screenshots. Weeks earlier, some posts had claimed her bakery used spoiled flour and made customers ill. That was false, and it had cost her orders. Other posts only called her cakes dry and overpriced. In the first angry week she had drafted a message threatening every critic; she deleted it, seeing that honest dislike is not harm. Maria, the volunteer at the desk, glanced at the folder as Simran said, 'I sorted them. These four are false and hurt my shop. The rest are just people who didn't like the cakes, and I won't touch those.' Each page had a date and a link noted on it. Inside, she asked only about the false claims and what lawful options existed.

How many posts did Simran count as false and harmful?
Simran counted four posts as false and harmful.
What did Simran realise when deleting the threatening draft?
Simran realised her anger had run ahead of her: honest dislike of her cakes was not harm and did not deserve a threat.
What other approach could Simran use for the honest critics?
Simran could reply politely to honest criticism and use the platform's report tool for the false claims, since that answers fairness with fairness.
How might the honest critics have felt if Simran had threatened them all?
They would probably have felt bullied and more likely to spread the story, turning a small dislike into a bigger fight.

“Amma, the milk is going to spill!”
“Let it, Hemant. Watch.”
The milk in the new clay pot rose, foamed, and bubbled over the edge.
Bhavna and Paati clapped. “Pongalo Pongal!”
Hemant, five, clapped too. “Why do we let it spill?”
“So our year overflows with good things. That's how our family does it.”
“Every year?”
“Every year. My Paati did it too.”
Hemant shouted it again, louder. “Pongalo Pongal!”

What did the milk bubble over?
It bubbled over the edge of the new clay pot.
How did Hemant feel when everyone clapped?
He felt excited and happy to be part of the celebration.
How could Bhavna help Hemant learn more about the tradition?
She could tell him stories of how her Paati celebrated and let him help with the next step.
How might Paati feel hearing Hemant shout “Pongalo Pongal”?
She probably feels proud and happy that the family tradition continues.
Give three reminders for keeping a desk tidy, numbered, each under eight words.

1. Put pens back in the box.
2. Stack your books neatly.
3. Throw away old paper.

Beta, you want to know about my oldest friend? I'm your Vandana Nani, and at ten I thought friends were just whoever sat beside me. Then, the monsoon I turned eleven, Gurleen moved into our lane. One wet afternoon under the neem tree, she told me she couldn't swim and was terrified of the school picnic at the river. She made me pinky-swear not to tell. At the picnic the other girls splashed and shouted, "Come in!" I said, "Gurleen's helping me collect shells," and we walked the bank together. She squeezed my hand. Sixty years later, she still calls me every monsoon.

What did Gurleen tell Vandana under the neem tree?
She told her she couldn't swim and was terrified of the school picnic at the river.
What did young Vandana want when she said Gurleen was helping her collect shells?
She wanted to spare Gurleen embarrassment, feeling loyal and protective of her friend's secret.
Which choice at the picnic mattered most, and why?
Keeping the promise and giving Gurleen a reason to stay on the bank protected her secret, and turned a new neighbour into a lifelong friend.
What was the picnic like for Gurleen?
Gurleen was scared of the water and the girls' shouting, so Vandana's help probably brought her huge relief.

Every Sunday evening, Neelam's family lit a lamp in the flat and said the same prayer together before dinner. Neelam had never questioned it before. Tonight, as Papa struck the match, the words felt unfamiliar in the mouth. Neelam stayed silent while the others chanted, then noticed that Seema, Neelam's mother, had noticed. At the table Seema asked quietly, “You weren't saying it. What's going on?” Neelam's heart thumped. “I love the lamp part. But I don't know if I believe the words, and I don't want to fake it.” Seema paused, then passed the rice. “Tell me more. I'd like to hear what you think.” Papa cleared his throat but said nothing.

What did Neelam's family do every Sunday evening?
They lit a lamp and said the same prayer together before dinner.
Why did Neelam stay silent while the others chanted?
Neelam seems unsure whether the words are believed and does not want to say them without meaning it.
What choice did Neelam make at the table, and what did it lead to?
Neelam answered honestly and respectfully, loving the lamp but unsure of the words, and Seema invited more, so the question became a conversation.
What might Papa have been feeling when Papa cleared his throat but said nothing?
Papa may have felt uneasy or unsure how to respond, though Papa let Seema lead the conversation.

Before: Mehak's resume listed every class she'd taken and every certificate, in tiny font. After her first interview, the panel said, "We couldn't tell what you actually did." She went home stung.

During: A week later, her senior Sudha went through it with her. "What did you build? What problem did you solve?" Mehak realised her best work, a small app for the college canteen, was buried at the bottom. They moved it to the top. Sudha also made her practise answering in two minutes.

After: At her next interview, a month later, Mehak explained the canteen app clearly. Her voice was steady. The panel asked follow-up questions, and she answered them. She walked out smiling.

What did Mehak build for the college canteen?
She built a small app.
How did Mehak feel after the first panel's comment?
She felt stung and hurt, realising her resume hadn't shown what she could actually do.
What changes made Mehak's second interview better?
Putting her best project first and practising short, clear answers helped her present her skills confidently.
How might Sudha feel knowing Mehak's interview went well?
She'd probably feel pleased and proud that her help made a real difference.

I'm Tejas, Vinita didi's younger brother. I'm only writing what I saw, because I don't really know what she's thinking.
In August she started going to the 'wellness collective' after her office hours. By October she'd quit the job. She said the collective needed her full-time and that her boss was 'stuck in the old frequency'.
She keeps her phone locked now, face down. When Mummy calls her name she sometimes doesn't answer, like she's somewhere else.
She stopped seeing Rhea and Sonal. When I asked why, she said the leader told them outside friendships 'drain the energy'.
At dinner last week Papa asked who decides things there. Didi said, 'Our leader sees what we can't. Doubting him is how you fall.' Then she said a girl had been made to clean the hall alone for a month for asking about money.
She said it like it was normal. It didn't sound normal to me.

When did Vinita quit her job?
By October she'd quit the job.
What might Tejas be feeling as he writes this account?
Tejas seems worried and unsettled, especially after hearing that a girl was punished for asking about money.
What could the family do with what they have noticed?
They could stay warm and in contact with Vinita, avoid mocking the group, and speak to a counsellor or helpline about the warning signs.
How might Rhea and Sonal experience Vinita's sudden silence?
They may feel hurt and confused, not knowing that the group has been pushing Vinita to drop outside friends.

I'm Yusuf. After Nani died in March, I put every photo of her in a drawer, even the one on the fridge, because seeing her face felt like a slap. When Amma started a sentence with “Remember when Nani...”, I got up and left the room. Jahnavi, my little sister, would say, “Bhaiya, please stay,” and I would close my door. I thought if I didn't look, it would stop hurting. It didn't. It sat there, sharper, and came out at strange moments, like when I smelled her cardamom tea in a shop. Meanwhile dinner grew quiet. Amma and Jahnavi shared stories without me, and I felt a wall growing between us. Looking back, running away made the pain last longer and made me lonelier.

What did Yusuf do with every photo of Nani?
Yusuf put every photo of her in a drawer.
What was Yusuf feeling when he saw Nani's face?
Yusuf felt deeply hurt, since seeing her face felt like a slap, so he hid the photos.
What could help Yusuf now?
Yusuf could stay for one short story and let the sadness come, maybe with a photo in view, since sharing memories can soften the pain over time.
How might Jahnavi feel when Yusuf leaves the room?
Jahnavi probably feels sad and shut out, since she asks Bhaiya to stay and he closes his door.

messages.content:
Read this:

At the coaching hostel in Kota, everyone knew Rajni and Wasim talked every night on the common room phone and messaged all day. Then, one Monday, nothing. He stopped replying. He looked away in the corridor.
By Thursday Rajni felt like she'd been erased. She checked her phone every minute. At night she whispered to her roommate Sunita, "Maybe I'll make a new account. Just to see if he's online."
"No," Sunita said. "That will only hurt you more."
"Then what did I do wrong?"
"Maybe nothing. Some people vanish because they can't handle saying things. That's about him, not you."
Rajni cried into her pillow. Sunita didn't leave. The next evening, two other girls from their floor came to Rajni's room with chai and cards. They played until lights-out. Rajni still checked her phone once or twice. But the new account never got made.

Where did Rajni and Wasim talk every night?
On the common room phone at the coaching hostel in Kota.
How did Rajni feel when Wasim vanished?
She felt hurt and erased, anxiously checking her phone every minute and wondering what she had done wrong.
Which choices helped Rajni cope?
Listening to Sunita, grieving openly instead of making a fake account, and spending time with friends who came with chai and cards.
How does Sunita see Wasim's silence?
Sunita sees it as Wasim's avoidance, a way of not facing hard conversations, rather than proof that Rajni did something wrong.

For six weeks Rajni's portfolio site had stayed in draft. The fonts were not right, and the case studies were not quite finished. Then Nitin, a peer from her old course, posted his half-finished site with typos in the footer and landed an interview. Rajni felt envy heat her face, then confusion, then shame at being stuck. She had been sure that only flawless work counted. Who had made that rule? She realised it was hers, and nobody else had signed it.

On Sunday she set a timer for ninety minutes, and when it rang she emailed the rough draft to her friend Irawati with the message, "It's rough. Tell me what you think." Her stomach rolled all afternoon. Irawati replied that evening: "Love the second project! Fix the footer." Nothing terrible had happened.

Over the following months Rajni kept high standards but held them loosely. She asked what a piece of work taught her more than whether it was flawless. She finished the site, took feedback from an interviewer without sinking, and, when the fear still spiked before deadlines, booked a session with the college counsellor.

How long did Rajni's site stay in draft?
It stayed in draft for six weeks.
How did seeing Nitin ship imperfect work lead to Rajni's experiments and her later approach?

Nitin's typo-filled site earned an interview, which showed Rajni that the flawless-only rule was her own. She then sent a rough draft after a timer and saw that nothing terrible happened, and later held high standards loosely, finished things and took feedback.
What was Rajni feeling when she saw Nitin's site?
She felt envy, confusion and shame at being stuck.
What could Rajni do if the fear before a deadline stays intense?
She could book a session with a counsellor and keep using time limits and rough drafts.

Read this:

Sharmila slammed the door of her room in their Hyderabad flat and threw her bag on the bed. Keerthana had told the whole project team that Sharmila's slides were "messy". In front of everyone! "She's always been like this," Sharmila told her mother through the door. "Selfish. Showing off." That night, hunting for a charger in her drawer, she found a crumpled card: 'Get well soon, I'll bring your notes every day. K.' Class 7, when she'd been ill for a month. Under it lay a friendship band from Class 8 and a photo of the two of them at Keerthana's cousin's wedding, dancing badly. Sharmila sat on the floor holding them. 'Always like this' didn't fit. One mean comment today; years of notes, bands and bad dancing before it. She picked up her phone and typed, 'Can we talk tomorrow?'

What did Keerthana say about Sharmila's slides?
Keerthana told the whole project team that Sharmila's slides were 'messy'.
Why did Sharmila feel sure that Keerthana had 'always been like this'?
Sharmila felt angry and humiliated, and the fresh quarrel felt like the whole truth about Keerthana, crowding out years of kindness.
What did Sharmila do that was wise, and what could she do tomorrow?
She let the old card, band and photo remind her of the whole friendship before acting; tomorrow she could tell Keerthana how the comment hurt and listen too.
How might Keerthana see the quarrel?
Keerthana may think the comment was just honest feedback on slides, without knowing how public and hurtful it felt.

Tutor's note: Pema, Wednesday evening session

Pema had the fractions worksheet in front of him at 5:00. By 5:40 he had not written a single answer. In that time he re-arranged his pencil case twice, sharpened four pencils to tiny points, lined up his erasers by size, and asked to fill his water bottle. When I asked about question 1, he looked at the page and his shoulders went up to his ears. "It's too hard," he said very quietly. Gurpreet, his mother, came in at six and saw the blank sheet. I suggested we do the first question together, slowly, and let him try the second alone. He managed three before the session ended.

How many pencils did Pema sharpen?
Four pencils, to tiny points.
What did Pema's shoulders going up to his ears suggest?
They suggested he felt scared and tense about the fractions, which is why he kept doing easy things instead.
What small step helped Pema start?
Doing the first question together slowly, then letting him try the second alone.
How might Gurpreet feel seeing the blank sheet?
Gurpreet may feel worried or disappointed at first, then relieved once Pema managed three questions.

metadata.subtype: Approach: puts off an unpleasant task by doing something easy [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Results day, and the college server was crawling. Kunal sat cross-legged on the floor of Bhavna's room with his laptop, the loading wheel spinning. Bhavna's face was blank. Her tea had gone cold in her hand. Her mother had called twice, and she had let it ring. When the page finally loaded, she read it silently, her face unchanged. Kunal glanced at her, wondering if she was indifferent or upset. She put the cup down very carefully. "I got it," she said, in a completely flat voice. Then her hands started to shake and she pressed them under her arms. Kunal grinned. "You're allowed to scream now." She did, quietly, into a cushion.

How many times had Bhavna's mother called?
Her mother had called twice.
What was Bhavna feeling behind her blank face, and what shows it?
She felt strong excitement or anxiety, shown by her shaking hands after the flat voice, so the blank face was control, not indifference.
What could Kunal do beyond guessing from Bhavna's face?
He could ask her how she's feeling and give her room, as he did by telling her she was allowed to scream.
How might Bhavna's mother see her not picking up the phone?
She may worry or think Bhavna is upset, though Bhavna was probably too tense to speak.

In their small town, the cricket match against the next village had become a legend. Mohit's friends told it at every tea stall: the dog that ran onto the pitch, the six that broke a bicycle bell, the umpire falling off his chair.

Mohit loved the story. By the third week, he was telling it too, adding the dog's name and the colour of the bell.

Then his cousin Tanuja, who had filmed some of it, showed him the video. No dog. The bell was fine. The umpire only wobbled.

"But I remember the dog!" Mohit said.

"You were there, Mohit. But the dog came from Suresh's version."

Mohit watched the video twice, feeling oddly cheated by his own head.

What did Tanuja's video show about the bell?
The bell was fine.
Why did Mohit feel cheated by his own head?
He felt shocked and a bit let down, because the story he had heard from friends had mixed into what he truly remembered.
What could Mohit do next time the group retells a big event?
He could enjoy the story but check photos or videos before adding details as fact.
How might Tanuja feel showing Mohit the video?
Tanuja might feel amused, and maybe a little sorry to spoil the legend.

Wednesday, hostel room
The canteen contract went to the union president's uncle today. Everyone knows it. Mahima's proposal was cheaper, had a menu for vegetarians, and she'd spent a month on it. She didn't even get a reply. At the meeting, the president said his uncle was "trusted". Honestly, part of me gets it. If Chacha's shop needed work, I'd want to put in a word too. That pull is real. But watching Mahima pack up her files so carefully, not looking at anyone, made my stomach turn. Loyalty felt nice for the president. It felt like a closed door for her. I'm going to ask at the next meeting how bids are chosen. Politely. I just want there to be a rule.
— Mridul

Who got the canteen contract?
The union president's uncle.
What does Mridul mean by "made my stomach turn"?
Mridul felt upset and uneasy seeing Mahima treated unfairly, even while understanding the pull of family loyalty.
Is Mridul's plan to ask how bids are chosen a wise next step? Why?
Yes, because asking politely for a clear rule addresses fairness for everyone without attacking the president personally.
What is it like for Mahima after a month of work gets no reply?
Mahima likely feels dismissed and discouraged; she packs her files carefully and avoids looking at anyone.
