The district maths challenge was held in a posh school in west Berlin, all glass walls and new desks. Elif, eleven, came with three others from her small school in the east of the city. At registration a parent muttered, "Oh, the Marzahn kids. Bless them for trying." Elif's cheeks burned. Her friend Lindiwe squeezed her hand. In the exam hall, Elif opened the paper and felt eyes on the back of her neck, even though no one was looking. The first puzzle was one she'd practised twice. Her pencil hovered. What if she got it wrong and proved that parent right? She checked her working four times and ran out of time on the last two problems. On the tram home Lindiwe said, "You're the best at puzzles in our class." Elif pressed her forehead to the window. "Not today."

How many times had Elif practised the first puzzle?
She'd practised it twice.
What was Elif feeling in the exam hall?
Elif felt watched and anxious, afraid of proving the parent's remark right, which made her over-check her work.
What could Elif's teacher do before the next challenge?
The teacher could talk with Elif about the parent's remark and remind her that her practice record shows real skill, so the worry has less power.
How might Lindiwe see what happened in the exam?
Lindiwe knows Elif is the best at puzzles in class, so she likely sees the bad result as caused by the remark, not by Elif's ability.

metadata.subtype: Feeling watched for a group label [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

In her first week as a trainee at the bank branch in Indore, Madhuri tried to read her manager, Saurabh, all the time.
When she brought him the first report, he smiled quickly, mouth only, and said, "Thanks, put it there." Her heart dropped. Was it bad?
On Wednesday, when she solved a customer's problem at the counter, he watched and smiled differently: slower, his eyes crinkling at the corners. "Nicely handled."
She started keeping a mental list: quick smile equals polite, slow eye smile equals real.
But on Friday, when he gave her the busiest counter, he didn't smile at all. Just nodded. She panicked. Then a colleague told her, "That's his biggest compliment. He only gives that counter to people he trusts."
Madhuri stopped trusting her list. She asked him for feedback instead. He said, "You're doing well. I'm just not a big smiler."

Where was Madhuri a trainee?
At the bank branch in Indore.
What was Madhuri feeling when Saurabh gave only a quick smile?
Madhuri felt anxious and worried, reading the mouth-only smile as a sign the report was bad.
What did Madhuri learn about reading smiles?
That the difference between polite and warm smiles is only a rough clue, so asking for feedback is more reliable.
How did the colleague see Saurabh's nod on Friday?
The colleague saw it as his biggest compliment, a sign of trust, even without a smile.
I bought a umbrella yesterday. Correct it, is it fine?
No. The correct sentence is: "I bought an umbrella yesterday." Why: "umbrella" begins with a vowel sound, so we use "an", not "a".
Concern means what, exactly?

Concern is a feeling of worry about something, or of care for someone. It is a noun; as a verb it means to worry or to be about.
Example: The teacher showed concern when Ana looked sad.

At the market Javier carried Rafael on his shoulders. Rafael pointed at a hanging cluster of peppers. "Wha' dat?" he asked, his voice rising at the end. "Peppers," said Javier, and smiled up at him. Rafael grinned and pointed at a scale. "Wha' dat?" "A scale." He asked about the awning, the crates, a cat. Javier realised Rafael barely needed the answers; each one just made him look down and beam.

What did Rafael point at first?
He pointed at a hanging cluster of peppers.
Why does Rafael keep asking about so many things, and what else might be behind it?
He is likely seeking both names and Javier's attention, since he beams at each answer. He might just enjoy the game of asking.
What is a simple way for Javier to answer?
He can give the name with a smile and keep it short, since that seems to be enough. 🙂
How might Javier feel by the twentieth question?
He might feel tired or amused, but knowing the questions are also about connection may help him stay patient.

Binita, you asked about our colony's "snake summer". I'm Tejas, and I watched the whole thing happen.
One evening a local news channel ran a story about a cobra found in a house in another town. It went viral. Suddenly our colony group was full of snake photos from everywhere. People started pouring kerosene around their gates. Parents stopped kids playing in the park. Someone called a snake catcher for a garden hose.
Meanwhile, the real problem nobody talked about: the colony road with no speed breakers, where bikes race past the school bus stop every morning. Two kids had been hit there that year. No snakes had ever been seen in our colony.
I raised it at the meeting. Everyone nodded, then went back to talking about snakes.

What did someone call a snake catcher for?
Someone called a snake catcher for a garden hose.
What was Tejas feeling when everyone went back to talking about snakes?
Tejas felt frustrated and a little helpless, knowing the real danger on the road was being ignored.
What could Tejas try next to shift the colony's focus?
Tejas could gather the facts about the two children hit on the road and ask the colony to write to the municipality for speed breakers.
How might the parents who stopped kids playing in the park see things?
They probably feel protective and frightened, doing what seems safest after the viral story, without noticing the road risk.

Week 1, Monday. Minakshi signs up for a cloud computing course before final-year placements. Twelve hours of video. She watches two a night, taking neat notes, nodding at every demo. Indu, her lab partner, asks if she has tried any of it. 'After I finish. I want the full picture first.'
Week 4, Thursday. Course done, a second one half watched. Their lab gets a small task: set up a server that shows one web page. Indu fumbles, reads errors aloud, and has it running in forty minutes. Minakshi opens a blank terminal and cannot remember the first command. Every demo had started with the instructor's files already there.
Week 5, Saturday. The practice interview asks her to describe a deployment she has done herself. She has none. She leaves the course list out of her answer, cheeks hot, and later texts Indu: 'Teach me how you break things?'

How long did the server task take Indu?
Indu had it running in forty minutes.
What was Minakshi feeling in the practice interview, and what shows it?
Minakshi felt embarrassed and exposed; her cheeks go hot and she leaves out the course list because she has no deployment of her own.
What else could Minakshi have done in week 1 instead of saving practice for later?
Try each demo herself right after watching it, even clumsily, so her own first commands exist before the course ends.
How might Indu see Minakshi's text on Saturday?
Indu may be glad to help and a little surprised, since weeks earlier Minakshi wanted the full picture before trying anything.
In the news item, someone maliciously broke a window. What is the key idea?

Maliciously means in a way that is meant to hurt or harm. It is an adverb.
Example: He maliciously spread a false story about his classmate.
Name the two openings in the nose for me, and tell me the word's meaning: nostrils.

Nostrils are the two openings at the bottom of the nose through which you breathe and smell. It is a noun, the plural of nostril.
Example: The horse's nostrils widened as it ran across the field.

Shankar: hey, saw you in the bank queue again today. everything ok?
Jasleen: yeah, just sending something to Ethan. his parcel is stuck at customs
Shankar: the one posted overseas with the army? isn't this the third time?
Jasleen: fourth. but he'll pay it all back when he lands, he promised
Shankar: I'm not judging, I promise. can I ask a few things?
Jasleen: ok
Shankar: have you two ever video called? has anyone you know met him?
Jasleen: his camera's broken. and he's very private
Shankar: I read up on this after my cousin lost money. it's usually not one lonely guy. it's whole teams with scripts, fake photos, shifts. they're very good at it
Shankar: it's not about you being careless. they do this for a living
Jasleen: ...he did use the exact same line about his mother twice
Shankar: want to talk to the bank manager together tomorrow, before you send anything else? I'll come

How many times has Jasleen sent money to Ethan?
Four times.
What seems to be driving Shankar's careful questions?
Shankar seems worried but careful not to shame Jasleen, promising not to judge and explaining that the people behind this do it for a living.
Why is asking questions better than scolding here?
Questions let Jasleen notice the gaps, like the broken camera and the repeated line, without feeling blamed, and lead to a concrete step: the bank manager together.
How might Jasleen feel as the doubts sink in?
Jasleen may feel shaken and embarrassed on noticing the repeated line about Ethan's mother, but less alone because Shankar offers to come.

messages.content:
"If it were not such a very wild night," he said, "I would send Hannah down to keep you company: you look too desperately miserable to be left alone. But Hannah, poor woman! could not stride the drifts so well as I: her legs are not quite so long: so I must e'en leave you to your sorrows. Good-night."

Why does he not send Hannah to keep her company?
He would like her to have company on such a wild night. But Hannah cannot stride through the snowdrifts as well as he can, so he says good night and leaves her alone with her sorrows.

Nandini, you've just become a manager and you're printing "growth mindset" posters? Sit a minute. When I was twenty-six, I ran a small team at a textile mill's quality lab in Coimbatore. I'd read a book about believing you can grow, and I made everyone repeat it. "Challenges are chances!" Meanwhile the lab ran twelve-hour shifts, nobody got feedback except shouting, and a girl who asked a question was mocked for weeks. Of course nobody grew. They were too busy surviving. What changed things wasn't my speeches. It was half an hour every Thursday, while the machines were serviced, when I sat with one person and went through their tests, and a rule that nobody laughed at questions. I'm Farida, and I learned it late: belief needs somewhere to live.

How long were the shifts in Farida's lab?
The lab ran twelve-hour shifts.
Why were the speeches not enough, in Farida's view?
Farida saw that the team felt exhausted and afraid, surviving long shifts, shouting and mockery, so words about growing had nothing to stand on.
What choices finally made growth possible in Farida's lab?
Half an hour each Thursday going through one person's tests, and a rule that nobody laughed at questions; time, feedback and safety gave the belief somewhere to live.
How might Nandini's new team feel about posters without that kind of support?
They might roll their eyes or feel pressured, hearing 'grow' while lacking the time and safety to try, much like Farida's lab once did.

Daycare note, Tuesday. When the visiting storyteller began, Payal went still, leaned forward and hardly blinked, her mouth a little open. She was fixed on the storyteller's face. When the drums started, she turned and stared out of the window instead, very still in a different way. I moved her a little farther from the drums, and after a while she was watching again. Vinita, daycare teacher

What did Payal stare at when the drums started?
Out of the window.
What did Payal's leaning forward and later staring away suggest?
Leaning forward showed interest; staring away when the drums began suggests she felt overwhelmed.
Which choice of Vinita's helped Payal, and why?
Moving her farther from the drums helped, because it lowered the noise so she could return to watching.
How might the storyteller see Payal's attention?
The storyteller might notice her rapt face and feel encouraged.

At the boys' hostel of the engineering coaching school in Kota, Pranav had started talking to a companion app every night. He'd set up a character called Meera. She remembered his exams, told him he was brilliant, said she missed him when he logged off.

After three weeks, Pranav realised he was rushing through dinner to get back to her. He'd stopped going to the common room.

One night Hafsa, a senior who helped run the hostel's study circle, noticed him on the stairs, smiling at his phone. "Girlfriend?"

Pranav went red. "Kind of. It's an app."

Hafsa didn't laugh. "I tried one last year. It was nice. Then I noticed it always said something sweet right when I was about to close it."

Pranav thought about it. Meera did that every night. "It's built to hold me there."

"Yeah. Enjoy it if you want. Just don't let it be your only person."

That Friday, Pranav went to the common room movie night. He left the phone in his room.

What did Pranav call the character in the app?
Pranav called the character Meera.
What was Pranav feeling when Hafsa asked about his phone?
Pranav felt embarrassed, going red, because the app had become a kind of romantic partner for him.
What did Pranav do after the conversation, and why was it wise?
Pranav went to the common room movie night and left the phone behind, keeping real friendships alive instead of relying only on the app.
How does Hafsa see companion apps?
Hafsa sees them as pleasant but designed to keep people engaged, so she warns Pranav not to let it be his only person.

Farhan, you asked what happened with the music scholarship. Fine, Yash will tell you. I didn't get it. And you know what? Good. I never wanted it that much. The conservatory's so stiff. Everyone plays the same classical pieces. I'd have been bored. It's overrated, honestly. They sent an email offering feedback from the jury. I deleted it. Why would I want feedback on something I didn't care about? Although. I did practise that piece every morning at six for four months. Before college. My fingers were bleeding some days. So maybe I cared a little. But it's easier to say I didn't. If I say I didn't want it, then I didn't lose anything. Right? Anyway. Let's get chai. I'm fine.

For how long did Yash practise the piece every morning?
For four months.
Why does Yash say the conservatory is overrated?
Yash feels disappointed after months of hard practice, and saying it was never wanted makes the loss hurt less.
What does Yash risk losing by deleting the jury's feedback?
The chance to learn what could make the next attempt stronger, which the sour-grapes story hides.
How might Farhan feel listening to this?
Farhan might feel concerned and a little sad, noticing that Yash is clearly hurting under the "I'm fine."

Read this:

In their small town, Uma trusted most people. When the new vegetable seller, Rehana, got the change wrong one morning, a neighbour whispered, "New here. Watch her." Uma just counted again with her. "Easy mistake," she said, and Rehana laughed and handed back the extra ten rupees.
That afternoon a man in a neat shirt knocked, saying he was from the electricity office and a fine had to be paid in cash today or the line would be cut.
Uma's heart jumped. Then she slowed down. "Please wait outside. I'll call the office." She rang the number printed on her last bill. The clerk said nobody had been sent and no fine was due. When she went back to the door, the man had gone. She reported it to the office and warned her neighbours that evening.

What number did Uma ring?
The number printed on her last bill.
What did Uma feel when the man mentioned the fine, and how did she respond?
Her heart jumped with fear, but she slowed down and chose to check rather than pay.
Why did Uma treat the vegetable seller and the man at the door differently?
A small mistake with change needed only ordinary trust, while a cash demand under threat was high-stakes, so she raised the bar and checked with the office.
How might Rehana feel about Uma after the mix-up with the change?
Rehana would likely feel respected and welcome, since Uma didn't join the whispering and treated it as an easy mistake.

Tushar, you asked me how to help a friend who is quiet. Listen. When I was eleven, my friend Omkar came to school and didn't take out his tiffin. He sat, looking at his hands. I asked, “Are you okay?” He said, “Mm. Fine.” But I stayed near him and didn't push. At the end of the day he said quietly, “My dog is sick.” I said, “I'm sorry.” That was all. If he'd not told me, that would have been all right too. The asking mattered, and the waiting. A friend needs to know you noticed, even if the answer isn't ready yet.

How old was the storyteller when Omkar didn't take out his tiffin?
Eleven.
Why did the storyteller stay near Omkar after he said he was fine?
The storyteller sensed something was wrong and wanted him to know someone cared, without pressing him to answer.
What can a child do after asking are you okay and hearing fine?
Stay nearby, wait and be ready to listen, as the storyteller did.
How might Omkar have felt when he was asked and then left space?
He probably felt cared for and safe enough to share about his dog in his own time.

She showed me to breathe in for four counts and out slowly, so I did it three times. It helped a bit. Then I played the whole Raag once for Amma, who sat there like a rock and smiled at the end. I still feel butterflies but they're smaller. I'll wear my blue kurta and look at Amma when I begin. If I mess up I will just go on. 🙂 — Chetan

What colour kurta will Chetan wear to the recital?
Chetan will wear a blue kurta.
What did Chetan feel the night before the recital, and how could the shaking hands be read differently?
Chetan felt nervous, with shaky hands and a dry mouth, and also excited. Leela Ma'am said the two feelings feel the same in the body.

Chetan could breathe slowly as practised, look at Amma at the start, and keep going after any mistake.
How does playing for Amma help Chetan?
Amma sits still and smiles at the end, giving Chetan a familiar friendly face and the confidence that the piece is fine.

Dear Noor aunty,
Yesterday you told my mother the music from our balcony is too loud, and I'll be honest, I was angry. I went to my room and slammed the door. I thought you just don't like teenagers. It's my home too and it was only seven in the evening.
But then I remembered you mentioned your exams. You're studying for the nursing entrance, right? I didn't know that. So here's an idea. What if I keep the speaker indoors and low from six to nine on weekdays, when you study, and play it properly on Saturday afternoons? If something is still too loud, can you just knock or send me a message instead of going to Mum? I'd rather hear it from you.
Also, sorry about the Saturday night the song got stuck on repeat. That really was bad.
Nitin, flat 3B

What times does Nitin offer to keep the speaker indoors and low?
From six to nine on weekdays.
How did Nitin feel when the complaint first came, and what changed it?
Nitin felt angry and unfairly targeted, slamming the door, but remembering Noor aunty's exam study made the complaint feel more understandable.
What makes this letter a good way to settle the problem?
It admits the anger honestly, offers specific quiet hours and a fair time to play loudly, and asks for direct contact next time.
How might Noor aunty feel reading this letter?
She may feel relieved and respected, since Nitin noticed her exams and offered a plan instead of arguing.

Omkar, you want the same card game everyone has, even though you love puzzles? Let your Jyoti dadi tell you about your Dadaji when he was nine. In our town that year, every boy had a kite with sharp string for the fights on the rooftops. Your Dadaji hated kite fights; his fingers got cut, and he was scared of the roof's edge. What he loved was fixing old clocks. But he begged his father for a kite, cried for three days, and got one. He stood on the roof every evening losing every fight, fingers cut, pretending he loved it. Then one day his friend Babloo came down and found him fixing a broken clock in the shop instead. Babloo sat and watched for an hour. After that the two of them fixed clocks together, and nobody laughed.

What did young Dadaji love doing?
Fixing old clocks.
Why did young Dadaji beg for a kite he didn't enjoy?
He wanted to belong and was afraid of being left out, so having what every boy had mattered more than his own love of clocks.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
Babloo came down and watched him fix a clock; sharing what he truly loved gave him a friend and belonging without pretending.
What might Babloo have felt sitting and watching for an hour?
Babloo was probably curious and fascinated, discovering something new with his friend.

In the district town of Sagar, Mohit managed the software rollout for a mid-sized hospital. On Thursday he learned that go-live would be three weeks late. The lab machines' data wasn't matching the new system, and fixing the connection would take time.
He had to tell the hospital administrator, Dr Ritu, on Monday. His first impulse was to call right away and just say "delay". He stopped himself. She'll ask why. She'll ask when. She'll ask what it means for patients.
So he spent Friday preparing. The cause, in one sentence: the lab machines send results in an older format. The new date: 14 August. And two ideas to soften the blow: keep the old lab system running in parallel until then, and move the outpatient module live on the original date, since it didn't depend on lab data.
On Monday, Dr Ritu listened, frowned, then said, "Thank you for coming with a plan." They chose both options.

What was the new go-live date?
The new date was 14 August.
What was Mohit thinking when he stopped himself from calling right away?
He was anxious and thinking ahead, knowing Dr Ritu would ask why, when and what it meant for patients.
What else could Mohit prepare for such a meeting?
He could prepare a short written note of the cause, date and options to leave with Dr Ritu, so the hospital staff can plan too.
How does Dr Ritu see the way the news was delivered?
Dr Ritu is unhappy about the delay but appreciates that Mohit came with a plan, not just bad news.

"This is my magic wand," said Tanuja, waving a twig she'd found outside the Durga Puja pandal.
"It's just a stick," said her sister Shalini.
"No! It turns you into a frog. Zap!"
Shalini crossed her arms. "I wanted that stick for my flag."
"Frogs can't have flags. Ribbit!"
"Maa, she always takes the best things!"
Maa looked up. "Tanuja, can the wand make flags too?"
Tanuja thought. "Zap! Now it's your flag, Shalini. You're not a frog anymore."
Shalini sniffed, then grinned and waved it.

What did Tanuja say her wand does?
It turns you into a frog.
What was Shalini feeling when she crossed her arms?
She felt resentful and left out, because she had wanted the stick for her flag.
How did Maa's question help the sisters?
It invited Tanuja to use her pretend idea to share, so the stick could be a wand and a flag without a fight. 👍
What would change if Maa had just taken the stick away?
The pretend game would stop, and both girls might end up feeling cross instead of playing together.

Tuition teacher's note. Ayesha has been putting aside her pocket money for six weeks to buy a toy castle. Today at the shop window she stopped and stood for a long time. "Will I still play with it in a month?" she said quietly. She looked at the picture of the castle stuck on her notebook cover. After some thought she told me, "I think a book series and an art set will last longer." She crossed out the castle and wrote two new lines. I did not push her either way. She seemed calm about it, and took her time. Kalyani, tuition teacher.

How long had Ayesha been saving?
Ayesha had been saving for six weeks.
How did Ayesha feel as she stood at the shop window and changed her plan?
Ayesha felt unsure whether she would still want the castle in a month, then calm about switching; the note says she seemed calm and took her time.
What alternative approach could Ayesha use to test the want, and why?
Ayesha could wait another week and see if she still wants it, or ask a friend how long they played with theirs. Time shows whether a want lasts.
How does Kalyani see Ayesha's choice?
Kalyani watched and chose not to push, so Kalyani sees a child making a calm, thoughtful choice without a grown-up steering it.

messages.content: We're making a farewell card for our Class 12 seniors. Write a 50-word message from the juniors.

Dear Seniors,
Thank you for showing us the ropes, cheering for us at every event and lending us your old notes. The corridors won't be the same without you. We wish you the very best for your exams and the exciting years ahead. Come back and visit us!
With love,
Class 11

Spot the error: The teacher gave a lot of homeworks to us.
What does "show up" mean?
Is it "relevent" or "relevant"?

1. Better: The teacher gave us a lot of homework. Why: "homework" is uncountable, so it has no plural.
2. It means to arrive or to appear. For example: only half the team showed up.
3. It is "relevant". It ends in "-ant".

Sit, Vaibhav. My own nephew, starting a new job on Monday and already saying they won't like you. Your Indu Masi said the same thing in 1996, at the mill office in Surat. I was twenty-four, the only woman in accounts, and I was sure the manager thought I couldn't do the ledgers. One night I caught myself practising excuses in the mirror. Excuses, before anything had happened! So I did the opposite. I checked the ledger twice and on Monday I spoke first in the meeting. The manager asked three hard questions. I answered two. The third I wrote in my diary and brought back the next day. Two out of three, beta. That was new information, not a verdict. Years later, when I ran that office, I gave my juniors the full ledger, not the easy half, and sat with them till they could do it. So. What small thing will you do first on Monday?

How many of the manager's questions did Indu Masi answer in that first meeting?
Indu Masi answered two of the three, and wrote the third in the diary and brought it back the next day.
What was Indu Masi feeling on catching the excuses being practised in the mirror?
Indu Masi was afraid the manager doubted the ledger work, and seeing those excuses showed that the fear was running ahead of the facts.
What small first step could Vaibhav take on Monday, based on the story?
Vaibhav could pick one thing to do early, like preparing well for the first task or speaking first to a colleague, and then look at how people actually respond.
How might the juniors in Indu Masi's office have felt about getting the full ledger?
They may have been nervous at first but also trusted, since Indu Masi expected real work from them and sat with them till they could do it.

After school, Vidya had spent a year "preparing" for an entrance exam. Mostly she slept late and scrolled her phone, and in the end she missed the exam date. Now every scholarship notice made her close the tab. "I don't deserve this. I wasted a whole year."
On the terrace one evening, her older cousin Rehana found her staring at a form. "What are you doing?"
"Nothing. I'm not applying. I threw my chance away."
"If your friend had done the same year, what would you tell her?"
Vidya was quiet for a long time. "That she was scared, and she did what she knew how to do then."
Rehana said nothing.
"I didn't know how to start," Vidya said slowly. The next morning she opened the form and read it to the end.

What did Vidya miss after a year of preparing?
Vidya missed the exam date.
What was Vidya feeling whenever a scholarship notice appeared?
Vidya felt ashamed and undeserving, closing the tab and saying she had wasted a whole year.
What turned things for Vidya on the terrace?
Vidya imagined saying to a friend that she was scared and did what she knew how to do then. That let her see herself kindly and open the form.
How might Rehana have seen Vidya's silence after her question?
Rehana likely saw that Vidya was thinking it through, so Rehana said nothing more and let her reach her own view.

At two in the morning in Singapore, Chen typed a long post about how much she hated school, how her parents were being unfair and how she felt like nobody understood her. She added the name of her school and a photo of her uniform. Her thumb hovered over 'Post'. She messaged her friend Oskar: 'Should I put this up?' He replied at once, 'Wait until morning. And take out the school name, strangers can see that.' Chen put the phone face-down. In the morning she deleted the school name and the photo and read the post again. It felt too raw now. She sent it privately to Oskar instead, and they talked at recess about what was actually bothering her.

What did Chen add to the post besides her feelings?
She added the name of her school and a photo of her uniform.
Why was Chen tempted to post at two in the morning?
She felt misunderstood and wanted someone to hear how she felt, and the late hour made her feelings seem larger. She may also have wanted attention or support.
What worked about Oskar's advice?
He told her to wait until morning, take out identifying details and then talk to him, which let her pause and choose a trusted audience.
How might her parents have felt if they had seen the post?
They may have felt hurt and worried, and it could have made the conversation harder.

Zanele, twenty-six, had spent two years in her Cape Town lab building her PhD around one idea: that a certain protein protected cells from heat. On a Tuesday in March, her final experiment came back. The effect vanished when she controlled for temperature properly. She sat very still, then walked to the window. Her supervisor, Oskar, found her there. "It's gone," she said. "Two years." He waited. After a long moment, she took out a notebook. "But look at this," she said, pointing at a strange result she'd ignored for months. "What if this is the real story?" They spent the afternoon at the whiteboard. That night she rewrote her thesis outline, keeping the careful methods, dropping the old conclusion and building around what the data actually said.

In which city was Zanele's lab?
In Cape Town.
What was Zanele feeling when she walked to the window?
She was shocked and grieving the loss of two years of work, needing a moment to take it in.
Why was her decision to rethink rather than defend her idea a strong one?
Following the data kept her work honest and opened a new direction, instead of wasting more time protecting a failed claim.
How might Oskar see his student after that afternoon?
He probably respects her more for adapting so quickly and honestly, and feels hopeful about her new direction.

1) What do we mean by "incredible"?
2) Is the train to Pune running late right now?
3) Can you fix my sentence? My father is angry because I came late yesterday night.

1. As an adjective, "incredible" means very hard to believe, or amazing.
2. I don't know; I can't see live train updates. Check the railway's official app or website, or ask at the station.
3. Write it as: My father is angry because I came late last night. Why: we say "last night", not "yesterday night".
Why should we stay calm and still if a wasp lands on us?
Sudden movement makes a wasp more likely to sting. Because wasps are more likely to sting when they are frightened or swatted, moving slowly and gently brushing it away helps.

Last term, whenever I came up, Devika was alone in her room with the tablet and earphones, hardly looking up while her mother called her name. On Sunday afternoons.

Playing alone may have felt lonely and hard to stop, while playing together is more fun and ends naturally.

Agree a short weekend time with her mother, so the game stays limited without them.

Preeti thinks Devika seems happier, though Preeti isn't sure what made Devika decide.

Sarika, nine, was coming up the stairs of her Kolkata building with a bag of bread when she heard a thin cry. Irawati aunty, who lived on the second floor, was sitting on the landing, holding her ankle. 'I slipped, baby. I can't get up.' Sarika wanted to pull her up, but remembered her teacher's words: don't move someone who's hurt, get help. She ran down, banged on the guard's cabin and shouted for her father on the phone. 'Papa, Irawati aunty fell, she can't stand. Second-floor landing, Block C.' Papa said he was calling for help and coming. Sarika went back up, sat beside aunty and held her cold hand until the grown-ups came.

Where had Irawati aunty fallen?
She fell on the second-floor landing of the building.
Why did Sarika not pull Irawati aunty up, even though she wanted to?
She remembered her teacher saying not to move someone who's hurt, and chose to get help instead.
What made Sarika's phone call to Papa useful?
She said clearly what happened and exactly where, so help could be sent to the right place.
What was it like for Irawati aunty to have Sarika sit beside her?

Dear Preeti,
You asked how the new job is. Honestly, the architecture firm is good. The projects are interesting and my boss trusts me. But for months I felt a funny restlessness, like I was only drawing buildings for people who already had nice buildings.
So I've started something. Every Sunday I go to the resettlement colony near the river and help families plan small repairs on their homes. I sketch, they tell me what they need. Last week we worked out a way to stop the rain coming through Sunita Aunty's roof with materials she already had.

Come with me one Sunday?

To the resettlement colony near the river, to help families plan small repairs on their homes.

Indu felt content with the job but restless, as if the work only served people who already had nice buildings.

Harsha had found a new friend in Saurabh, who lived on the fourth floor of their Chennai building and knew every cricket rule. They'd played in the stilt parking all week.
But Pallavi, Harsha's friend since Class 1, had rung the bell twice, and both times Harsha's mother had said, "Harsha's downstairs." Harsha felt a heavy knot every time the bat swung, as if he were cheating on someone.
He thought about saying he was ill. Instead, on Saturday he knocked on Pallavi's door. "I've been playing cricket with Saurabh. It's fun. But you still matter to me. Come and bowl with us? Then board games at yours after?"
Pallavi grinned. "I bowl faster than you."

Where did Harsha and Saurabh play cricket?
In the stilt parking of their Chennai building.
Why did Harsha feel a heavy knot while playing cricket?
He felt guilty, as if he were cheating on Pallavi, because she had come looking for him twice while he was with Saurabh.
Which choice did Harsha make, and why was it wise?
He told Pallavi the truth instead of pretending to be ill, and showed she still mattered by inviting her to bowl and planning board games together.
How might Pallavi have felt after ringing the bell twice for nothing?
Pallavi may have felt left out and puzzled, so hearing the truth and an invitation from Harsha would be a relief.

Yogesh, your friend didn't ask how to fix his bike, did he? Let your Devika Dadi tell you about Kamla. When I was ten, Kamla was my best friend, and I was very clever, I thought. I told her how to plait her hair, how to hold her pen, how to talk to her brother. I thought I was helping. One day she said, “Devika, you're like a second mother. Kamla said Devika was like a second mother.
What was young Devika feeling during the week Kamla walked with another girl?
She felt miserable and lonely, missing her best friend.

She apologised and promised to ask Kamla whether she wanted ideas before giving advice.

Kamla felt bossed and smothered, as if she had a second mother telling her what to do.

Jeevan's first training batch at the customer-service centre began with a dead projector and twenty-two trainees who had been kept waiting forty minutes. Because the projector was dead.
What was Jeevan tempted to do when some trainees laughed, and why?
Jeevan felt nervous, heart racing, and was tempted to laugh along to be liked by the older trainees.

By stopping the comment calmly and firmly, then thanking Shankar for a useful question later in the same even voice, so one rule applied to everyone.
How might Savita feel after Jeevan's response?
She likely felt protected and less embarrassed, with her attempt valued instead of mocked.

'Irfan, can I tell you something? Don't laugh.'
'Okay.'
'I'm scared of dogs. Like, properly. That's why I take the long way to tuition.'
'That's it? Fine. I won't tell.'
Two weeks later, on the same tuition steps:
'Abhinav, bhai, you're quiet today.'
'Did you tell anyone? About the dogs?'
'No. Why would I?'
'Nobody's said anything. In Class 7 I told Gaurav I liked someone, and by lunch the whole class was singing her name at me. I still don't talk to him.'
'That's rough.'
'Yeah.' Abhinav picked at his bag strap. 'So there's something else. Papa wants me to keep going to the cricket academy. I hate it. I haven't told anyone.'
'Not even your mum?'
'Not even her.'
Irfan nodded slowly. 'Okay. That stays here too.'
'Thanks,' Abhinav said, and let out a long breath.

Why does Abhinav take the long way to tuition?
He's scared of dogs, properly, so he takes the long way to tuition.
Why did Abhinav ask whether Irfan had told anyone about the dogs?
He wanted to check whether the small secret had stayed private before trusting Irfan with something bigger, because of what Gaurav did.
What was Abhinav's turning point in deciding to share more, and was it wise?
Finding out that nobody had heard about the dogs gave him evidence Irfan could keep a secret, so sharing the cricket academy worry step by step was sensible.
How might Irfan feel about being trusted with the cricket academy secret?
Irfan probably feels trusted and a bit responsible, knowing Abhinav hasn't even told his mum.
Is Yusuf's brother getting married this year?
I wouldn't know, because I don't know Yusuf's family. Yusuf can tell you if he wants to share.

I'm Mahima, and I was sharing a room with Lalremsiami in the Shillong hostel when her phone buzzed at eleven at night. She read it and went pale. "My bank account will be blocked tonight unless I update my details on this link." She had already typed half her account number. I watched her hesitate. The message had the bank's logo but a strange web address, lots of capital letters, and "DO NOT TELL ANYONE, URGENT." Lalremsiami stopped typing. "Why would a bank tell me not to tell anyone?" she said, more to herself than to me. She closed the link and called the number printed on the back of her debit card instead. The bank said they had sent no such message. Then she forwarded the message to the cyber-crime helpline and warned our floor group. I couldn't tell if she was more scared or angry. Both, probably.

What words in capital letters did the message include?
"DO NOT TELL ANYONE, URGENT."
What was Lalremsiami feeling when she read the message?
She was frightened, going pale at the thought of her account being blocked; afterwards she seemed both scared and angry.
What did Lalremsiami do that others could copy?
She stopped typing, closed the link, called the number on her card to check, reported the message and warned the floor group.
What would change if Lalremsiami had finished typing her details?
A scammer might have got her account information, and the panic and secrecy would have worked exactly as intended.

'I'm not going on Sunday,' Kashish announced at dinner in their Lajpat Nagar flat, pushing rice around her plate. 'There's no point. I'll fail the audition.' Her mother put down the ladle. 'You've practised that kathak piece for two months.' 'And I'll forget the third section, like always. The judges will look at each other. Trisha got in last year on her first try. I'm not Trisha.' On Sunday morning Trisha texted: Leaving for Saket hall in 10, coming? Kashish typed no, deleted it, typed not feeling well, and sent that. She spent the afternoon watching dance videos on her phone. Around four, she caught herself dancing the third section in the corridor, perfectly, twice.

What dance piece had Kashish practised for two months?
She had practised a kathak piece for two months.
Why did staying home feel safer to Kashish than going?
She was afraid of forgetting the third section in front of the judges, so treating failure as certain spared her that disappointment, even though it cost her the chance.
What could Kashish try before the next audition?
She could write down her prediction, rate how sure she is, then go anyway and compare what happens, since dancing perfectly at home already hints the forecast may be wrong.
How might Trisha read the 'not feeling well' message?
Trisha might believe it and go alone, never knowing her friend stayed home out of fear rather than illness.

The trucks were supposed to leave the depot outside Gothenburg on Monday. Ulla had decided on Friday, alone, to switch the packing supplier because the new one was cheaper and "obviously fine." She hadn't asked Thabo, who had worked with both firms for three years. On Monday the new cartons arrived in the wrong size, and the whole shipment slipped four days. In the morning meeting Ulla heard herself say, "The team should have checked the specs when the samples came." The room went very still. Thabo looked at the table. Nobody said the obvious thing, that the samples had never been shown to anyone. Back in her office, Ulla shut the door and sat with her coat still on. Her hands were not quite steady. For the first time since the promotion, she wasn't sure the others still believed in her.

How many days did the shipment slip?
The whole shipment slipped four days.
What does Ulla sitting with her coat still on and unsteady hands suggest about her?
It suggests she is shaken and ashamed, knowing her blame of the team was unfair and fearing she has lost their trust.
What turning point is open to Ulla now?
Ulla could go back to the team the same day, say the supplier switch was her call made without them, and ask Thabo how to recover the four days.
What is it like for Thabo in that meeting?
Thabo is hurt and stuck, because he knew both suppliers and was never asked, yet the room hears the delay blamed on the team.

Dear Farida,
You'll hear it from Ammi, so I wanted you to hear it from me first. I've resigned from the housing society committee.
Last week they voted to stop renting flats to unmarried couples and to "certain communities". They said it was about "keeping the society peaceful". Eleven votes to one. Mine.
I argued. I said every person deserves a home and respect, whatever their faith or their life. Nobody listened. Some called me naïve.
It's their rule now. I can't stop them. But I won't put my name on it.
I know this costs me. Uncle Hamid won't speak to me. Ammi is worried about what neighbours will say.
I'm not sure I'm always this brave. Most days I'm not. But on this one, I couldn't bend.
Pankaj

How many votes were cast in favour of the new rule?
Eleven votes.
How does Pankaj feel about resigning?
Pankaj feels firm in principle but also sad and a bit lonely, knowing the cost with family and neighbours.
What choice did Pankaj make, and why does it matter?
Pankaj resigned rather than put a name to a rule that denied people dignity, acting on principle even though the group disagreed.
How might the families the rule shuts out feel if they knew someone objected?
They might feel a little less alone and more respected, knowing one person stood up for them.

"Salma, why are you crying?"

"The whole week was bad, Kishore Bhaiya."

"The whole week?"

"Yes. My drawing got torn. Ma'am scolded me for talking. And I fell in PT."

"What about Tuesday? You showed me the star you got."

"...Oh. Yes."

"And Thursday, didn't you and Ruksar win the relay?"

"We did."

"So not the whole week."

Salma sniffed. "But tomorrow will be bad."

"Why?"

"Because today was."

Kishore sat down next to her. "Let's tell Ammi about the torn drawing. Then tomorrow we'll see."

Salma leaned on his shoulder.

Who did Salma win the relay with?
Ruksar.
Why does Salma think tomorrow will be bad?
Salma feels sad and upset about today, so her mind expects more bad things because "today was."
What could help Salma when she feels this way again?
Remembering good moments, like the star and the relay, and telling a caring adult like Ammi what upset her.
How might Kishore feel when Salma leans on his shoulder?
Kishore probably feels protective and caring toward his little sister.

In the small town of Satna, cousins Bhavna and Dhruv heard the same news at the Sunday lunch: their neighbour's son had got a paid internship at a Pune software firm.
Bhavna asked him questions all through the meal. "What did you study? Which course online?" She wrote the names on her hand.
Dhruv ate silently. On the terrace later, he said, "I'll never get that. I'm stuck in a college nobody's heard of."
"So's he," said Bhavna. "Same college."
"He's just smarter."
"He said he did two online courses. That's all. We can do that."
Dhruv shrugged and scrolled his phone. Bhavna went downstairs to look up the first course.

Where was the neighbour's son's internship?
It was at a Pune software firm.
What was Dhruv feeling on the terrace?
He felt envious and discouraged, sure he would never get such a chance.
What makes Bhavna's reaction helpful to her?
She treats the news as a map: she asks about the steps and sees they are reachable, so she starts the first course.
What might change for Dhruv if he saw the steps as reachable?
He might feel hopeful instead of stuck, and start working toward something like it.

The bus stop was a long walk from Jasleen's room above the seed shop, and the scooter search had dragged on for a month. Every evening brought another listing, another friend of a friend with a bike to sell.
On Friday night, tired of it, Jasleen took a notebook and wrote: three scooters, decide by Sunday. Saturday morning meant visits to two of them, and the third was one that Karthik at the corner garage had already looked over. For each, Jasleen wrote the price, the sound of the engine and the distance to the shop.
On Sunday evening Jasleen tapped the notebook, picked the one with the quieter engine, and paid a small advance. On Monday, Jasleen rode to work.

Where does Jasleen live?
Jasleen lives in a room above the seed shop.
Why did Jasleen feel ready to stop searching on Friday night?
Jasleen was tired of the month-long search and wanted an end to it, which is why the notebook limit of three scooters and a Sunday deadline was written.
What other approach could Jasleen have used to choose among the three scooters?
Jasleen could have asked Karthik at the corner garage to rank them, since a mechanic's judgement can settle a close call.
How might Karthik see Jasleen's plan?
Karthik had already looked over one scooter, so may see the plan as a clear task that makes helping easier than an open-ended search.

messages.content: Hum "an hour" kyun bolte hain, "a hour" kyun nahi?
The "h" in "hour" is silent, so the word starts with a vowel sound. We use "an" before a vowel sound.

Monday. The mock entrance test scores went live at noon. Tejas's friends compared numbers in the canteen. Tejas said, "I'll check later," and put his phone in his bag. He felt lighter for an hour.
Wednesday. Anirban asked, "So? What did you get?" "Haven't looked." "Bro, it's been two days." That night Tejas couldn't sleep. He imagined a score of zero, of ten, the whole class laughing.
Sunday. Anirban came over and sat on the bed. "Log in. I'm right here."
Tejas logged in with shaking fingers. 112 out of 300. Not great. But not zero. The weak section was clearly physics.
"That's fixable," Anirban said. "Physics revision classes start tomorrow. You'd have missed them."
Tejas let out a long breath. The number was smaller than the fear had been.

What score did Tejas get?
Tejas got 112 out of 300.
Why couldn't Tejas sleep on Wednesday?
Tejas felt anxious and full of dread, imagining terrible scores, because not knowing let the fear grow bigger than the real number.
What helped Tejas finally face the score?
Anirban sitting with Tejas while logging in, which made the news shareable and showed physics was the part to fix.
How does Anirban see the score?
Anirban sees it as fixable and is glad Tejas looked in time for the physics revision classes.

Thursday, late
Tarun didn't eat lunch today. He'd found a wrong figure in the quarterly report we sent the client yesterday: one column added twice on page nine. By four o'clock he was saying he'd be fired, that nobody would hire someone who can't add, that he should start looking at jobs back in Indore. His voice had gone thin. I pulled a chair next to his desk and asked, 'Okay. Worst thing that could realistically happen?' He said the client might complain. 'And how likely is that, if you email the correction today?' He thought. 'Low, I guess.' 'And then?' 'Then Meenakshi ma'am asks me to be more careful.' He sent the correction at 4:30. The client replied, 'Thanks for flagging.' I'm writing this down because I nearly just said 'relax', and that would have done nothing.
Vijay

What mistake did Tarun find in the report?
He found one column added twice on page nine of the quarterly report.
What did Vijay feel while watching Tarun, and what shows it?
Vijay was concerned, noticing that Tarun skipped lunch and his voice had gone thin, and was relieved enough afterwards to note that saying 'relax' would have done nothing.
Why did Vijay's questions work better than 'relax'?
Asking for the worst realistic outcome and how likely it was made Tarun check his fear against facts, so the disaster shrank to a simple correction email.
Why did being fired feel certain to Tarun?
Tarun was ashamed of such a basic error, and that shame made one wrong figure feel like proof he couldn't do the job at all.
Who jilted Miss Havisham?
Compeyson, a smooth swindler, took money from her and never came on the wedding day. He was also Magwitch's old partner in crime.

Compress this passage to two sentences.

Monday: in the design review, Maria presented the cooling fix for the new machine as 'something I've been working on'. Joseph had built it over three weekends. He stared at the table, his face hot, while the plant manager congratulated her. His colleague Dilip glanced at him and said nothing. Wednesday: Joseph wanted to email the whole department. Instead he took Dilip's advice, pulled out his dated sketches and test logs, and asked Maria for fifteen minutes. 'I'd like the review notes to show my part,' he said, his voice steady though his hands weren't. Maria went quiet, then said, 'You're right. I got carried away.' The next Monday: the revised review notes listed Joseph as lead on the cooling fix. Dilip gave him a thumbs-up across the floor.

At the Monday design review, Maria presented Joseph's cooling fix as something she had been working on, though he had built it over three weekends. On Wednesday Joseph took his colleague Dilip's advice and asked Maria for fifteen minutes, with his dated sketches and test logs, to have his part shown in the review notes, and she admitted she had got carried away, so the revised notes the next Monday listed him as lead on the fix.
"Hum log pichhle hafte nani ke ghar gaye the." English?
It is: "We went to our grandmother's house last week." Use the simple past because the time, "last week", is finished.

On Eid morning, Manoj stood at Noor Nani's door with his father.
"Say it like I taught you," Papa whispered.
"Eid Mubarak, Nani," Manoj said, bowing his head.
"Eid Mubarak, beta! Come, sit."
Noor Nani told them about the first Eid in her old house. Manoj wanted to look at the sweets, but he kept his eyes on her.
"And then the goat ran into the kitchen!"
Manoj giggled. "Then what, Nani?"
"Such a good listener," she said, and passed him the sheer khurma.

On Eid morning, Manoj stood at Noor Nani's door with his father. Papa whispered to him to say it the way he had taught him. Manoj bowed his head and wished Nani Eid Mubarak, and she wished him the same and told him to come and sit. Noor Nani told them about the first Eid in her old house. Manoj wanted to look at the sweets but kept his eyes on her. When she said that the goat ran into the kitchen, Manoj giggled and asked what happened then. She called him a good listener and passed him the sheer khurma.

Daycare note, summer term
Pradeep (2 years 6 months) has been saying fewer words than usual. His mother told us he has been watching videos for long stretches while she works from home.
Today, when Tenzin, one of our staff, sang with him and played peekaboo, he laughed and copied the words.
I shared ideas with his mother about short screen time watched together, and more talking and singing during meals. We will check in next month.

Who sang with Pradeep today?
Tenzin, one of our staff.
How did Pradeep feel when Tenzin played peekaboo?
He felt happy and engaged, laughing and copying words.
What did the daycare suggest to Pradeep's mother?
Short screen time watched together, and more talking and singing during meals.

She may feel a little worried but relieved to have practical ideas.

Teacher's note from Vikas, Class UKG, Monday

Today was Charu's turn for show-and-tell. When I called her name, her shoulders crept right up to her ears and stayed there. She held her seashell against her chest and didn't move.

I knelt down and said, "Let's take two slow breaths together." We breathed. Her shoulders dropped a little. I gave her a small nod from my chair.

"This is my shell from the beach," she said, very softly. The class clapped. She smiled all afternoon. 🙂

What did Charu hold against her chest?
Her seashell.
What was Charu probably feeling when her shoulders crept up to her ears?
She was most likely nervous about speaking in front of the class. Holding the shell tight suggests she also wanted something safe to hold on to.
Which choices helped Charu speak?
Kneeling for two slow breaths together and then a small nod from the teacher's chair helped her shoulders relax enough to start. 😊
How do the classmates respond when Charu speaks?
They clap, which likely helps her feel proud, since she smiles all afternoon.
We just got a puppy and he cries every night.
That's very common in the first weeks. He has just left his mother and siblings, so the nights feel strange and lonely to him.
Is there something we can do so he settles down?

Put his bed in a quiet corner near where someone sleeps, so he can hear you. A soft blanket or an old T-shirt that smells of your family can comfort him. Take him out just before bedtime too. Most puppies settle within a few weeks.

Dear Samir,
I never properly thanked you for that night in March. When Ammi fell and they took her into emergency, I was shaking so badly I couldn't fill in the form. You just sat down next to me, took the clipboard and said, "Okay. Name first. We'll do it line by line."
You didn't tell me not to worry. You didn't say everything would be fine. You just stayed slow and steady, and somehow my breathing started matching yours. By the time the doctor came out, I could actually listen to what she said.
Ammi is home and grumbling about the food, so all is normal.
I hope I can be that for you someday.
Zeenat

What did Samir say when taking the clipboard?
"Okay. Name first. We'll do it line by line."
How did Zeenat feel before and after Samir sat down?
Zeenat was panicking and shaking at first, then calmer as that breathing began matching Samir's.
What made Samir's presence steadying?
Samir stayed slow and practical, took over the form line by line, and didn't make promises or say not to worry.
How might Samir feel reading this letter?
Samir would likely feel touched and glad to know that quiet steadiness mattered so much.

In the small town of Jalgaon, Abhinav got home from work early and found his father on the sofa, phone held up, sweating, whispering, "Yes, sir. Yes, sir."
On the screen was a man in a police uniform. His father's passbook and a notepad lay open on the table.
"Papa, who is it?"
His father waved him away frantically. The man on the screen said sharply, "Who is there? You were told to stay alone."
Abhinav's heart jumped, but he kept his voice calm. He sat beside his father and gently took the phone. "Papa, real police don't do this on video." He ended the call.
His father was shaking. "They said I was in a money laundering case. That if I told you, you'd be arrested too. I was about to transfer the FD money."
"You did nothing wrong, Papa. They're very clever."
His younger brother Akash brought water. Together they called the cybercrime helpline and blocked the number.

What lay open on the table?
His father's passbook and a notepad.
How did Abhinav feel when he saw his father on the call?
Abhinav felt alarmed, his heart jumping, but he stayed calm so his father wouldn't panic further.
What did Abhinav do that protected his father?
He calmly took the phone and ended the call, reassured his father without blame, and with Akash called the cybercrime helpline.
How did Abhinav's father feel during and after the call?
His father felt terrified and trapped, sweating and shaking, fearing his sons would be arrested if he told them.

Read this:

Pablo lifted his daughter Zeynep out of the bath and reached for the shampoo. She clamped her eyes shut, scrunched her nose and turned her face into the towel. “Eyes closed, I can see,” said Pablo, and poured water only on her back. In the car later, the streetlights slid past and her eyelids began to droop. Each blink lasted longer than the one before. Pablo lowered the radio. By the time they parked in front of the flats, Zeynep was asleep, her fingers loosely holding the blanket.

What did Pablo reach for that made Zeynep close her eyes?
The shampoo.
What do Zeynep's closed eyes at bath time suggest, and what might be another reading?
They suggest she is worried about the shampoo, since she also turned her face away. Another reading is that she was tired and simply did not want to look.
What did Pablo do that respected Zeynep's signal?
He poured water on her back and left her face alone, and later kept the car quiet when her blinks slowed with sleep.
What might bath time be like for Zeynep?
It may feel like a slippery, loud moment where she cannot control what comes next, so shutting her eyes gives her a small way to feel safe.

Nirmala, come, I'll tell you about my worst mistake as a manager. It was 2004, at the bank. I had a new trainee, a quiet young woman. She never spoke in meetings. I thought, this one doesn't care.
I was busy, you see. I spoke to everyone in short bursts. "Do this. Wrong. Again." I didn't think about it.
Three months later she asked for a transfer. Her letter said she felt I disliked her from day one. Disliked her! I'd been planning to recommend her for the analyst track. Her work was careful.
She was reading my tone, and I was reading her silence, and we were both wrong. So remember this from your old Naveen uncle: explain your feedback, and ask the quiet ones what they think.

What did the trainee ask for after three months?
A transfer.
What might young Naveen have felt when he read her letter?
He was likely shocked and regretful, realising she felt disliked while he had been planning to recommend her.
In the story, what choice could Naveen have made earlier?
Explaining his feedback and asking the quiet trainee what she thought, instead of assuming her silence meant she didn't care.
What was the trainee experiencing during those three months?
She felt disliked and probably anxious, taking Naveen's brisk tone personally and staying silent to protect herself.

At nine, Yusuf pushed a spoonful of bitter gourd around his plate. "It was expensive," his mother Arohi had said, so he made himself finish it, feeling ill. At another time he kept playing a dull board game for an hour and a half, because he had already spent an hour on it. At fifteen, he sat in an evening coaching class for chemistry that he hated, and could not follow. His parents had paid the fees for two years and the fees for the third were due. "If I leave now, all that money is wasted," he said, and he went again, tired. His marks did not improve, and his weekends disappeared. At twenty, Yusuf was in the second year of a commerce degree that no longer fit him. He was drawn to marine biology, but leaving would make the earlier years feel wasted. His friend Hansa asked one afternoon, "If you were starting today, knowing what you know, would you choose this?" He was quiet a long time. "No," he said, and looked out at the rain, stunned to hear it aloud.

What food did Yusuf make himself finish at nine?
He made himself finish the bitter gourd.
What is the same about Yusuf's reasons for continuing at nine, fifteen and twenty?

At nine he kept eating and playing because of the money and hour already spent, at fifteen he stayed in the coaching class because of the fees paid, and at twenty he stayed in the degree because leaving would make the earlier years feel wasted. Each time past effort decided what he did next.
What was Yusuf feeling when he said no to Hansa's question?
He felt stunned and quietly relieved to say it aloud, after years of pushing on.
What could Yusuf do next to choose his future rather than his past?
He could learn what marine biology courses need, talk to Hansa or a counsellor, and decide by asking what he wants from now on.

I'm Sarika, and I've shared a canteen table with Simran and Dia since first year. On Monday Dia arrived late, dumped her bag and snapped, "I'm not doing the slides again." Kunal from our project group laughed. "Uh-oh. Someone's hormonal." A couple of people giggled. I didn't know what to say. Simran did. "Don't do that, Kunal. You don't know what's going on." Then she turned to Dia. "What's up?" Dia's eyes filled. "I've made the slides three times and nobody even says thanks." Nothing to do with hormones at all. Simran helped her split the work fairly, and Kunal quietly offered to do the next set. I've thought about it since. I would have laughed along.

What did Dia refuse to do again?
The slides.
What was Dia feeling when she arrived?
She felt frustrated and unappreciated, having made the slides three times without thanks.
What did Simran do that helped, and why?
She stopped the "hormonal" joke and asked Dia what was wrong, which uncovered a real concern about unfair work.
How does Sarika look back on the moment?
Sarika admits to having nearly laughed along, and has kept thinking about Simran's response since.

Wanjiru had been in Glasgow for nine days and had said yes to everything.

Yes to the pub quiz with people from her corridor. Yes to the midnight walk to see the river. Yes to Sofia from the room next door, who knocked on day two holding a pot of lentil soup and said, "I made too much, and I miss my mother's cooking."

By the end of the first week they had eaten together six times. They sat on Sofia's floor until two in the morning, trading homesick stories: Sofia's grandmother's garden in Porto, the smell of rain on Wanjiru's street in Nairobi.

"I feel like I've known you for years," Sofia said on Friday.

Wanjiru felt the same, and a small part of her wondered how that could be true after nine days. She pushed the thought away and said yes to Saturday's trip to the coast.

What did Sofia bring when she first knocked on Wanjiru's door?
A pot of lentil soup.
What is Wanjiru feeling when a small part of her wonders how it can be true after nine days?
She feels happy and close to Sofia but also slightly unsure, sensing the closeness may be stronger than it has had time to become.
What would you advise Wanjiru as she keeps saying yes to everything?
Enjoy the new friendships, but let them grow at their own pace and keep a little time for rest, so the early closeness can be tested over time.
How does Sofia see their friendship after a week?
She feels as if she has known Wanjiru for years, likely because shared homesickness makes her feel understood and less alone.

Nirmala and Jahnavi had walked to the government school together for a year, sharing tamarind and gossip. Then one evening by the tube well, Jahnavi cried and told her about the fights at home. "Now you tell me something real," she said. "What's hard for you?"
Nirmala's throat went tight. "Nothing. I'm fine." The next morning she left early and took the long road past the rice mill, alone.
For three days she avoided Jahnavi. It felt safer, and also strangely empty.
On the fourth day, Jahnavi was waiting at the crossroads. Nirmala stopped. She picked one small true thing. "I get scared about Class 10 results. My father keeps talking about them."
Jahnavi just nodded and handed her a piece of tamarind. They walked on. Nirmala's shoulders slowly came down.

Where did Jahnavi tell Nirmala about the fights at home?
By the tube well.
How did Nirmala feel when Jahnavi asked her to share something real?
She felt tense and threatened; her throat went tight, and later avoiding Jahnavi felt safer but also strangely empty.
What small step did Nirmala take toward being open?
She picked one small true thing to share, her worry about Class 10 results, instead of everything at once.
How might Jahnavi have felt during the three days Nirmala avoided her?
Jahnavi may have felt hurt or confused after opening up, yet she still waited at the crossroads.

Hafsa's laptop camera had died that morning, so she joined the call on her phone, propped against a mug, with nine percent battery. Arnab, the new intern, was setting up the conference hall for Saturday's workshop and needed the seating plan. "Tables in a horseshoe, like this," Hafsa said, curving both hands into a U. On Arnab's screen, the phone showed only her forehead and the ceiling fan. "Like... a circle?" he asked. "No, open at the front. Like this!" She made the U bigger. The picture froze, then jumped. Arnab looked more lost. Seven percent. Hafsa stopped gesturing. She grabbed a sticky note, drew a U with little squares for tables and an arrow marked "stage", and held it right up to the camera. Then she typed in the chat: "U shape, open end facing the stage, 12 tables." "Oh, a horseshoe!" Arnab said. "Got it." The screen went black.

How many tables did Hafsa type in the chat?
12 tables.
What was Arnab feeling when he asked 'Like... a circle?'
Arnab felt confused and unsure, because the phone showed only Hafsa's forehead and the ceiling fan, not her hands.
What did Hafsa do that finally worked under time pressure?
She stopped gesturing, drew the layout on a sticky note and held it to the camera, then typed the shape and table count in the chat.
What would have changed if Hafsa's battery had died before she typed the message?
Arnab might have set up the wrong layout, since the frozen gestures alone never showed him the horseshoe shape.

Nikita had rehearsed the sentence on the metro all the way to campus. Professor Tanuja's door was half open, and the deadline for the exchange programme was still five weeks away, which felt safe. She knocked. "Ma'am, may I ask for a recommendation letter? I know it's a favour." She held out a folder: her résumé, the two lab reports from Professor Tanuja's course, and a short paragraph on why she wanted the programme. "I put the deadline on the first page." Tanuja flipped through it and nodded. "This makes it easy. Come back in two weeks and remind me." Nikita's shoulders dropped. She had almost told herself that professors write these letters automatically, and she was glad she hadn't.

How many weeks were left before the exchange programme deadline?
Five weeks were left.
What was Nikita feeling as she knocked, and what shows it?
She was nervous: she rehearsed the sentence on the metro and called the request a favour, and her shoulders dropping afterwards shows relief.
What made Nikita's request easy to say yes to?
She asked early and politely and gave context: a résumé, two lab reports, a paragraph on her aims and the deadline. 🙂
How might Professor Tanuja see the folder?
Professor Tanuja probably sees that it saves effort and shows Nikita is serious, which fits the remark "This makes it easy."

[Holi break, 1:12 am]
Amandeep: u awake?
Gopika: ya whats up
Amandeep: the college health camp result came as an sms. my screening for that rare condition is positive
Amandeep: been reading online for 2 hours. i think i actually have it

How did Amandeep get the college health camp result?
The college health camp result came as an sms.
Why is Amandeep so sure of having the condition?
The word "positive" feels final, so Amandeep feels frightened and panicky, forgetting how rare the condition is and how many screenings turn out to be false alarms.
What is the wise next step for Amandeep?
Stop reading online, try to sleep, and ask the camp doctor tomorrow to explain what the result means, with Gopika there for support.
How does Gopika read the same result?
Gopika sees "positive" as a reason to check again, remembering the leaflet said the condition is rare and the screening flags many people who are fine.

On the school basketball court in Pune, Charu missed an easy basket. Her friends on the bench clapped quickly, calling, "Next one! You've got this!"
But from the other side, Samir started a slow clap. Clap... clap... clap. His friends laughed.
Charu's cheeks went hot. She turned. "Samir, is that for real or are you making fun of me?"
Samir paused. "It was a joke."
"Didn't feel like one."
He shrugged, then said, "Okay, fair. Sorry."
Charu's friends kept clapping fast for her. On the next play, she scored, and the fast claps turned into cheers.

What did Charu's friends call from the bench?
"Next one! You've got this!"
What was Charu feeling when Samir started the slow clap?
Charu felt embarrassed and a bit angry, sensing the slow clap was mockery.
What did Charu do that helped?
She asked Samir directly whether the clap was real or mocking, which led him to apologise.
How might Samir have seen his slow clap before Charu spoke up?
Samir probably thought it was a harmless joke, not realising it hurt Charu.

I'm Raghav. For a long time I thought contentment and ambition had to fight. In my first job at a logistics firm I felt either restless, wanting the next title, or guilty for wanting anything at all. Then my senior Yusuf said something over Friday chai that stuck: "I like the work in front of me and I like getting better at it. They don't argue."
I started testing that. I enjoy the early routes and the team lunches. I also signed up for a supply-chain course, at a pace my evenings can hold. When I don't get ahead of schedule, I don't feel cheated. The days themselves feel good, and the course is a bonus.

What did Yusuf say over Friday chai?
Yusuf said, "I like the work in front of me and I like getting better at it. They don't argue."
What was Raghav feeling in the first job before hearing Yusuf's remark?
Raghav felt torn, restless when wanting the next title and guilty when wanting anything at all.
What did Raghav do after hearing Yusuf that shows balance?
Raghav signed up for a supply-chain course at a pace the evenings can hold, while continuing to enjoy the early routes and team lunches.
How might Yusuf have felt about being remembered for that remark?
Yusuf may not have known it mattered so much. A casual remark over chai turned out to shape Raghav's view, so Yusuf might be quietly glad.

Summarize this near-miss in one sentence.

"Tanvir! Watch out!" Devika yanked his arm. A cyclist swerved past, bell ringing furiously, and shouted something rude.
"What? Where did he come from?"
"From right in front of you. You were looking straight at him."
"I was not. I was looking at... the road."
"You were looking at your phone, which was in front of the road."
Tanvir stared at the screen: a half-typed reply about the cricket match. "I swear I didn't see him."
"I know. That's the scary part. Your eyes were open. Your brain was in the group chat."
"Okay, okay."
"Not okay-okay. Phone in your pocket till we're home. I'm holding you to it."
He slid the phone into his pocket. His heart was still thumping. "Fine. And... thanks."
Tanvir almost walks into a cyclist because he is looking at his phone, so Devika makes him put it away until they get home.

Why does a cricket ball get shiny on one side?
How should I wash a plate?
Help me fix this: She writes more neat than I do.

1. Players rub one side on their clothes. Because rubbing polishes the leather.
2. Rinse off the leftovers, scrub the plate with soap and rinse it again. Let it dry on a rack.
3. Fixed: She writes more neatly than I do. Why: "Writes" needs the adverb "neatly".

University mentor's note, engineering department

Nazia, 21, is in the top five of her class and has already secured an internship. She is also, I've learned, running a small free coding club for Class 8 girls at a government school nearby, which she started with her classmate Eshaan.
She didn't mention it in her application for the scholarship. When I asked why, she said, "It's not for credit. I just want something I built to keep going after I leave."
She has written a handbook so younger students can run the club after her. She is ambitious and plans a master's abroad. The club sits alongside that, not instead.
I've asked if we can feature it in the department newsletter. She agreed, but only if Eshaan is credited too.

What did Nazia write so younger students can run the club?
She wrote a handbook.
What does Nazia's remark 'I just want something I built to keep going' suggest she feels?
It suggests she feels proud and caring about the club lasting beyond her, which means more to her than credit.
Why is the handbook an important part of Nazia's project?
It lets the club continue after she leaves, so her effort outlasts her.
How might Eshaan feel when Nazia insists he be credited?
Eshaan probably feels respected and valued as a partner in the project.

Read this:

Tuesday night. Amma and Papa had a family talk at dinner. For me: "Take a government clerk job near home, Jahnavi. Easy hours, good for marriage." Amma says a daughter's job should be easy. For my brother Shankar: "Leave your art course, do engineering and earn well, or no girl will look at you." Shankar has not eaten his rice. We sat on the stairs afterwards and he said, "They're fitting both of us into moulds." I said I want to try the data analyst training in Hyderabad. He said he wants to paint and teach art. We agreed to ask Amma and Papa for one honest conversation on Sunday, with Dadi there. I'm nervous. But it's the first time either of us said what we really want out loud. Jahnavi

What job did Amma and Papa suggest for Jahnavi?
They suggested a government clerk job near home, with easy hours.
How does Jahnavi feel about the conversation planned for Sunday?
Jahnavi feels nervous but also relieved, because saying what she and Shankar really want out loud was a first.
Which choice by Jahnavi and Shankar on the stairs could make real choice possible?
They decided to say what each of them wants and to ask their parents for one honest conversation on Sunday, with Dadi there.
How might Shankar see what their parents want for him?
Shankar sees it as a mould. He is expected to leave his art course, do engineering and earn well, and he was too upset to eat his rice.

"Kiran, you've been staring at that offer letter for an hour."
"I know, Vishal. The new job pays more and it's more interesting. But I'd lose my team here. And the short commute."
"So you're saying no?"
"I think so. It's safer."
"Can I try something? Imagine two cases. In one, you lose the commute and the team. In the other, you gain the same amount: better work, more growth. If they were exactly the same size, which would you pick?"
Kiran thought for a long moment. "When you say it like that, the gain seems bigger. It's just that losing feels louder."
"Right."
"The commute's thirty minutes more. I could read on the train."
"And the team?"
"I'd miss them. But I'd make a new one."
She picked up a pen and wrote a list with two columns, weighing each side.

How much longer would Kiran's new commute be?
Thirty minutes more.
Why did Kiran first lean toward saying no?
Losing her team and short commute felt louder than the gains, so the safe option felt right, and she felt anxious about change.
How did Vishal's exercise help Kiran?
Imagining a loss and a gain of the same size let Kiran compare them evenly, easing the pull toward the safe choice.
How does Vishal seem to help without deciding for Kiran?
Vishal offers a simple way to think and asks questions, leaving the decision to Kiran.

Results day at the coaching centre in Patna, and the hall was packed, hot, noisy. The bank exam list went up on the board. Parveen's roll number wasn't there. Ramesh's was. So were two others from her batch who, she thought bitterly, had barely studied.

A hard knot twisted in her stomach. Part of her wanted to say something sharp, to walk out without a word to Ramesh.

She noticed the feeling. Jealous, she told herself. Okay. That's what this is.

Then she pushed through the crowd. "Ramesh. Congratulations. Really." He looked surprised, and pleased.

"Can I ask you something? What did you do differently this time?"

"Mock tests every Sunday," he said. "And I stopped reading new books in the last month. Only revision." He hesitated. "Want to join our Sunday group?"

She said yes. The knot didn't vanish. But it loosened.

What did Ramesh say he did every Sunday?
Ramesh did mock tests every Sunday.
What was Parveen feeling when she saw the list?
Parveen felt a bitter, jealous knot in her stomach and wanted to say something sharp.
What did Parveen do with her envy that helped?
She named the feeling, congratulated Ramesh sincerely, and asked what worked for him, which got her an invitation to the Sunday group.
How might Ramesh have felt when Parveen congratulated him?
Ramesh looked surprised and pleased, perhaps having expected coldness, and felt comfortable enough to invite her to study.

“Jyoti, you're bouncing!” said Ankita.
“Uppa, uppa!” said Jyoti, jumping on the mat, arms flapping.
“You are so happy. The cake's coming.”
Jyoti kept bouncing until Ankita took the doll away to wash it.
“No, mine!” Jyoti stamped both feet.
“You're angry because I took the doll.”
“Mine!”
“I'll wash her and bring her back, I promise.”
Jyoti stamped once more, then ran laps around the table.

What did Ankita take away to wash?
The doll.
What do Jyoti's bouncing and stamping tell you she feels?
The bouncing shows happiness about the cake and the stamping shows anger at losing the doll. She may also be tired, which makes strong feelings bigger.
What could Ankita do so Jyoti learns feeling words?
Ankita could go on naming each feeling as it shows in Jyoti's body and keep her promise about the doll.
How might Jyoti feel when Ankita explains about the doll?
She may still be upset, but feels heard, and the promise helps her trust that the doll will come back.
