So, Sachin, you asked why I've stopped doing the shrug. Okay. Last month at the café, a birthday cake came out with the wrong name iced on it: "Rina" instead of "Rinu." The woman who'd ordered it held it up, and I did the thing. Shoulders up, palms out, like, what can I do, the kitchen wrote it. In my head I meant, "I'm so sorry, this is awful." But her face went hard. She said, "So nobody's responsible?" and walked out with it. Ojas, the shift manager, shrugging at a birthday cake. Great. Next week, a similar slip, a spelling on a card with a tray of cupcakes. I felt that helpless shrug coming again, but this time I said, "That's our mistake. I'm sorry. I'll redo it in ten minutes, on the house." The customer actually thanked me.

What was wrong with the birthday cake?
It had the wrong name iced on it, 'Rina' instead of 'Rinu'.
What did Ojas mean by the shrug at the birthday cake?
Ojas felt sorry and helpless and meant it as an apology, but without words the woman read it as dodging responsibility.
What changed the second time, and why did it work?
Ojas added words that owned the mistake, apologised and offered to redo it within ten minutes, so the customer felt taken seriously.
How did the woman with the cake see the shrug?
She saw it as 'nobody's responsible', felt dismissed and angry, and walked out.

On the way home from the village school, Seema walked with her classmate Deepika. "Four days until the Social Studies test," Seema said. She stopped and counted on her fingers. "Six chapters. Four days." She drew a chart in the dust with a stick. "Four into six. A chapter and a half each day." Deepika looked at the lines. "That's not so much." "No," said Seema. "It looked big before." At home she wrote it on the back of her notebook: Monday, chapters one and half of two. She tied a string around the page to mark it.

How many chapters did Seema count for the test?
She counted six chapters.
What did Seema feel when she saw her plan was a chapter and a half each day?
She felt relieved and more confident, since she said the work looked big before and now seemed smaller.
What alternative approach could Seema use if she falls behind, and why?
She could move the plan for the next day and add a short extra session. Small changes keep the plan working.
How does Deepika see Seema's plan?
Deepika sees the chart in the dust and thinks the work is not much. Deepika may feel less worried about the work too.

messages.content: My teacher said my handwriting is barely legible. What is she asking for?

Legible means clear enough to read. It is an adjective. She is asking you to write more neatly.
Example: Write your name in legible letters so that the examiner can read it.

"Why did you send me a crying face, Zubin?" Ritu asked, holding up the tablet at dinner.
"Because I was sad. My tower fell."
"But it was the laughing-crying one. I thought you were laughing."
"It was crying and laughing. Both."
"Then how do I know?"
Zubin thought about it. "Maybe I'll write 'sad' next to it."
"Or send me the heart," said Ritu. "The heart means you love me."
"Bhaiya sent a heart to his teacher yesterday," said Zubin. "Does that mean he loves her?" Ritu burst out laughing. "Ask Papa!" 😄

What happened to Zubin's tower?
Zubin's tower fell.
What was Zubin feeling when he sent the crying face, and why did Ritu read it differently?
Zubin felt sad and a bit amused that the tower fell, so Zubin meant both feelings. Ritu saw a laughing-crying face and thought Zubin was laughing.
What could Zubin add so that Ritu understands the emoji better?
Zubin could write a word like 'sad' next to the emoji, or say his feeling aloud, so the message does not depend on Ritu guessing.
How might Ritu feel about needing to guess what the emoji means?
Ritu feels confused and a little left out of Zubin's feelings, because Ritu cannot tell whether to comfort Zubin or laugh along.

Subject: Request for a short extension

Dear Baljeet,

Thank you again for the offer. I am very glad to have it and I want to answer properly. I have another decision still pending, and I expect to hear from them by Monday. Could I please have three more days, until Tuesday evening, to reply to you? In that time I plan to compare both offers on role, team and learning, and I will give you a clear yes or no by then. If the original date has to stand, I understand and will let you know.

Warm regards,
Yash

How many extra days did Yash ask for?
Yash asked for three more days.
What is Yash feeling as the email is written?
Yash feels grateful but a little nervous: the wording is warm and careful because Yash does not want to lose the offer by asking.
What alternative approach could Yash use if the extension is refused, and why?
Yash could do a quick pros-and-cons comparison at once, because a refusal shortens the time and a short structured list still allows an honest answer.
How might Baljeet see this request?
Baljeet reads a polite, honest message that names a reason and a plan, which makes it easier to say yes than a vague delay would.

messages.content:
Read this:

Lokesh, sit. You asked why I pushed you to tell me about those messages. Let me tell you why.
When I was fifteen, a boy in my class took a photo of me on the school trip, changing my shoes behind the bus, and passed it round on phones with an ugly caption. I found out on a Tuesday. I felt so ashamed I wanted the ground to swallow me. I thought, if I tell Amma, she'll look at me differently.
But that night I told her anyway, crying into her sari. She didn't ask why I was behind the bus. She said, “This is not your shame, Sudha.” Next morning she took me to Mrs Iyer, my class teacher. The three of us sat together and made a list: who had the photo, who to speak to, what the principal must do.
It wasn't easy. But I wasn't carrying it alone any more. So now, show me those messages.

What did Amma say when Sudha told her?
This is not your shame, Sudha.
What was young Sudha afraid of before telling Amma?
Sudha felt deeply ashamed and was afraid Amma would look at her differently.
What choice in the story changed things for Sudha?
Telling Amma that night despite the shame, which led to Mrs Iyer and a shared plan instead of carrying it alone.
How might Amma have felt hearing Sudha's story that night?
Amma was likely hurt and angry on Sudha's behalf, but steady, making sure Sudha knew the shame was not hers.

"You said you'd pay half the cake," Tanvir said at the dining table, holding the bakery bill.
Sudha paused. "I remember it differently. I think I said I'd pay for the flowers."
"No, it was the cake. I'm sure."
"You might be right. Let's check." She scrolled back through the family chat. "Here. Sunday: 'I'll do flowers, you do cake.' That's me."
Tanvir frowned at the screen. "Huh. I really remembered cake."
"I remember lots of things wrongly," Sudha said. "Last year I was sure Mummy's anniversary was on the ninth."
"It's the seventh."
"Exactly." She smiled. "Still, I'll pay a third of the cake."
"You're not calling me a liar?"
"Why would I? You remembered it your way. The chat just remembered it better."

What did the Sunday message in the family chat say?
It said, "I'll do flowers, you do cake."
Why doesn't Sudha call Tanvir a liar?
Sudha feels calm and understanding, because she believes Tanvir genuinely remembered it that way and knows her own memory has slipped too, like the anniversary date.
Which choice by Sudha kept the disagreement calm?
She said "I remember it differently" and checked the family chat instead of insisting, so the record settled it without blame.
How might Tanvir feel after seeing the message?
Tanvir may feel a little embarrassed but not attacked, since Sudha shares her own mistake and still offers to pay a third.

In the college canteen in Kolkata, Vidya drew three columns on a paper napkin: 'Plan', 'If late', 'If rain'. The group of five was going to Gangtok in September, and Tushar wanted to fill every day.
'Buses and jeeps on that highway can be hours late,' Vidya said. 'If we plan every hour, one delay ruins everything.' Under 'If late' she wrote: one spare day before the train back. Under 'If rain': the monastery museum, a tea tasting, the flower show. And next to each booking: free cancellation, yes or no.
Tushar sighed but moved the monastery trek to day two.
On the way up, their shared jeep was stuck behind a broken-down truck for five hours. They reached Gangtok at midnight instead of seven. Day one was gone, but day four was spare. Nobody had to rebook the train, and the guesthouse, booked with free changes, shifted their first night at no cost.

How many hours was the jeep stuck?
Five hours.
What was Vidya feeling when she said one delay could ruin everything?
Vidya was cautious and a little worried about a tight plan, and wanted a spare day and backups so she could feel calm about it.
What else could Vidya add to the napkin plan?
Share the plan and a contact number with each family, so people at home know about any delays.
How does the delay look to Tushar, who wanted to fill every day?
Tushar loses day one but sees the spare day save the rest, without rebooking the train.

I'm Vidya, and I share Room 214 in the hostel with Ayesha. This term she has lived on late-night chai and videos in bed, then slept through her morning lectures. Last week she snapped at me for asking about the laundry, then sat on her bed staring at nothing. On Friday she said, "I just feel flat. Maybe I need a new study app, or one of those morning-routine videos." I didn't know what was going on inside her, so I only said, "You've barely slept all week." She looked surprised, as if she hadn't connected the two. Since Sunday she has set one alarm for the same time every day and put the kettle away at night. She's laughing at my jokes again, though I can't say for sure that's why.

What did Ayesha snap at Vidya for?
For asking about the laundry.
What was Ayesha feeling on Friday, and what did she think would fix it?
She felt flat and low, and thought a new study app or morning-routine videos might help, without linking her mood to sleep.
Which change seems to have helped, and why?
A steady alarm time and putting the kettle away at night; small, regular sleep changes seem to lift her mood more than a motivation trick would.
How is Vidya affected by Ayesha's sleepless weeks?
Vidya gets snapped at over small things and is unsure what is going on inside Ayesha, but cares enough to point out the missing sleep.

At the bus stand, Eshaan waited with his mother, Arohi, for his father's bus from the city. It was late. Eshaan chewed the corner of his nail, then picked at a loose thread on his shirt till it made a hole. Arohi saw it but didn't scold. She found a smooth, cool pebble near the tea stall and put it in his hand. “Rub this. And let's breathe like a balloon.” They breathed in and out. When the bus horn sounded, Eshaan dropped the pebble and ran.

What did Arohi put in Eshaan's hand?
A smooth, cool pebble.
What was Eshaan feeling while he waited for the late bus?
He was probably anxious and impatient about his father's bus being late, and picking the thread soothed him.
Why did giving the pebble work better than scolding?
It gave his hands something calming to do and treated the picking as worry, not naughtiness.
How might Arohi have been feeling while they waited?
She may have been a bit anxious too about the late bus, but she stayed calm to help Eshaan.

My name is Vaibhav, and for months the words 'just have faith' made my jaw clench. My best friend Nitin said them every time I talked about my mother's surgery or my failed semester. I'd go quiet and think, That's not an answer, that's a slogan. Once I nearly told him his belief was a crutch for people who couldn't think. I'm glad I didn't. One night on the hostel terrace, instead of arguing, I asked him, 'What does faith actually give you, when you say that?' He took a long time to answer. He said it gave him a feeling that he wasn't carrying everything alone, and that when his father lost his job, it was the only thing that let him sleep. I didn't feel that. But I understood him better. Then I told him what I needed from him: not advice, just, 'That sounds hard, I'm here.' He said he'd try. He does, mostly.

What words made Vaibhav's jaw clench?
The words 'just have faith' made Vaibhav's jaw clench.
What did Vaibhav feel when Nitin said 'just have faith'?
Vaibhav felt irritated and unheard, as if Nitin were offering a slogan instead of an answer.
What did Vaibhav do instead of calling Nitin's belief a crutch?
Vaibhav asked what faith gave Nitin, listened, and then said plainly what support Vaibhav needed.
What does faith give Nitin, according to Nitin?
A feeling that he isn't carrying everything alone, which helped him sleep when his father lost his job.

Supervisor's note, procurement team review

Tushar joined us in March. In his first two vendor meetings, I noticed he said little and took notes. Afterwards he told me something: "In both meetings, the vendor named a figure first and we spent the entire time bargaining around it."

He was right. I'd not seen it.

Before the third meeting, Tushar asked Avni in finance for past contract data and built a range himself. When the vendor opened at 40 per unit, Tushar calmly said, "Similar suppliers are charging 28 to 32. Here's the data." The vendor paused, then offered 33. We settled at 31.

What I noticed was his calm. He didn't argue harder. He argued from a different starting point.

I've asked him to run a short session for the team on preparing ranges before negotiations.

Recommendation: confirm and consider for lead role.

What figure did the vendor open at in the third meeting?
When the vendor opened at 40 per unit.
What was Tushar feeling when the vendor opened at 40?
Tushar seemed calm and confident, because he had already built a range from data and didn't need to react to the vendor's number.
Why did Tushar's preparation work better than bargaining harder?
It replaced the vendor's figure with research as the starting point, so the talk centred on 28 to 32 instead of 40.
How might Avni in finance feel about Tushar's success?
Avni might feel pleased and appreciated that the past contract data made such a clear difference.
Which line on page 18 of my storybook is underlined?
I can't see your book, so I don't know. Open page 18 and read it.

Give this passage a two-sentence summary.

"Master Heathcliff," I resumed, "have you forgotten all Catherine's kindness to you last winter, when you affirmed you loved her, and when she brought you books and sung you songs, and came many a time through wind and snow to see you? She wept to miss one evening, because you would be disappointed; and you felt then that she was a hundred times too good to you: and now you believe the lies your father tells, though you know he detests you both. And you join him against her. That's fine gratitude, is it not?"

The speaker reminds Master Heathcliff how kind Catherine was last winter, bringing books and songs and coming through wind and snow to see him. Now, believing his father's lies, he joins his father against her, which the speaker bitterly calls fine gratitude.

Mentor's note, fellowship check-in, 9 January
Noor has been planning her community health-literacy workshops since August. Her folder is thick: maps of the ward, lists of partners, draft posters, three possible timetables. At our last two check-ins, nothing had actually started. She seemed tired and a bit embarrassed about it.
Today I asked her to look through the whole folder and find one thing she could do tomorrow without waiting for anything else.
She turned pages for several minutes. Then she stopped at a list of partners, took my red pen and circled one line: "Ask the anganwadi worker in Ward 7 for a room." She wrote beside it: "Thursday, 10 a.m."
She looked lighter when she left. I will ask on Friday how the conversation went.
— Vishal

What did Noor write beside the circled line?
"Thursday, 10 a.m."
How did Noor seem to feel at the earlier check-ins?
She seemed tired and a bit embarrassed that nothing had started despite the thick folder.
What else could Noor do after Thursday's visit?
She could circle the next single step in the folder and give it a time, so planning keeps turning into action.
How might Vishal see the change in Noor today?
Vishal notices she looked lighter when she left and plans to check on Friday how the talk went.

Dear Sachin,
The washing machine stopped last week, and the technician who came said the main board had burnt out. He quoted a big price and said it was urgent. I felt helpless because I could not check. But I remembered what you said, so I asked him to show me the fault. He pointed at the board and said, "See?" I saw only a green plate. I said I would think about it, and asked for the quote in writing. Then I called another repairer, who found a loose belt and fixed it in half an hour for a tiny fraction of the price. What did the first technician say had burnt out?
The first technician said the main board had burnt out.
What was Bhupen feeling when the technician quoted a big price and said it was urgent?
Bhupen felt helpless, because Bhupen could not check the claim.

Bhupen asked the technician to show the fault, asked for the quote in writing and called another repairer for a second opinion.

The second repairer found a loose belt and fixed it cheaply, so probably saw a simple job that did not need a costly part.

Can you tell me who wrote this poem?

Sahil,
You asked why my marks jumped this term. Honestly, it's embarrassing how simple it was.
Last term I studied on my bed with the TV on in the next room, my phone beside me and music with lyrics in my ears. I thought I was studying for three hours every night. But in tests, whole chapters were blank. I felt stupid.
Then our physics teacher said something in class: your brain can hold only a few things at once, and every buzz and every lyric takes a slot. So I tried an experiment. One evening: phone in Mummy's room, no music, desk instead of bed, fifty minutes.
I learned more in those fifty minutes than in three noisy hours. It was almost annoying.
Try it before your exams. Put your phone somewhere it can't see you.
Ritu

Where did Ritu put the phone during the experiment?
Ritu put the phone in Mummy's room.
How did Ritu feel when whole chapters were blank in tests?
Ritu felt stupid and confused, having studied three hours a night without much sticking.
What changed in Ritu's study routine, and why did it help?
The phone out of the room, no music, a desk instead of the bed and fifty focused minutes, which freed attention for learning.
How might Sahil react to Ritu's advice?
Sahil might be doubtful at first but curious to try it before exams.
Put this in the past tense, please: Hamid fixes his bicycle and rides to the market.
Hamid fixed his bicycle and rode to the market.

Last March my roommate Ojas met someone at a dance workshop, and by the next Saturday I barely recognised our flat. Our Sunday grocery run? Cancelled. The group trip to the waterfall? Ojas stayed back to wait for a call. Every dinner story was about Kiran: Kiran's poems, Kiran saying they were soulmates, Kiran wanting Ojas to move in by summer.
I'm Reena, and I'm bad at hard talks. I wrote three versions of what to say and deleted them all. In the end I just said, over chai, "I've noticed you've stopped doing the things that were yours. I might be wrong. I'm not going to lecture. I just miss you."
Ojas went quiet, then said I didn't understand real love. I said maybe not, and that the Sunday grocery run would still happen at ten.
Three Sundays later, Ojas showed up at ten, eyes puffy, holding the cloth bags.

Where did Ojas meet Kiran?
Ojas met Kiran at a dance workshop.
Why did Reena delete three versions of what to say?
Reena was nervous about hurting Ojas or sounding like a lecture, and admits to being bad at hard talks.
Why was Reena's reply to "you don't understand real love" a wise choice?
Reena did not argue or try to win; keeping the Sunday grocery run open at ten gave Ojas a way back without losing face.
What might it have been like for Ojas to show up at ten, three Sundays later?
Ojas likely felt hurt and embarrassed, but also relieved that the old plan was still there and that no one would say "I told you so".

I'm Vandana, and for eight months I lied to Jagdish about Tuesdays. I told him I had a pottery class. Really, I was visiting my brother Raju, who Jagdish hasn't spoken to since Raju skipped our wedding. I deleted Raju's messages every night. I told myself I was protecting Jagdish from being upset.

But the lies grew. The pottery teacher's name. Why I never brought anything home. I started feeling far from him, even sitting on the same sofa.

Last week Jagdish said, "Can I see what you made in class?" My stomach dropped.

That night I told him everything. I said, "I've been seeing Raju on Tuesdays. I lied because I was scared of how you'd react. I'm sorry. I don't want secrets between us anymore."

He was hurt, more by the lying than by Raju. He went for a long walk. When he came back he said, "I'd rather be upset than lied to."

What did Vandana tell Jagdish she did on Tuesdays?
Vandana told him she had a pottery class.
What was Vandana feeling when Jagdish asked to see the pottery?
Vandana felt a sinking dread, her stomach dropping, afraid the lies would be exposed.
Why was ending the secrecy the wise step?
The lies were slowly deadening their closeness, and telling the truth, even at a cost, let Jagdish choose to be upset rather than deceived.
How did Jagdish feel about the truth?
Jagdish felt hurt, more by the lying than by the visits, but preferred honesty to being protected by lies.

The placement cell at the engineering college in Guwahati held mock group discussions every Friday. In the first one, Bhupen said "database" when he meant "data set" and a girl across the table corrected him. He nodded, smiled, and didn't speak again for the rest of the session. Nor the next Friday. Nor the one after. He was sure the whole group had filed him as the boy who didn't know basic words. In the fourth week, the placement officer pulled him aside. "Bhupen, your written summaries are among the best. Why don't you speak?" He admitted the mistake. The officer smiled. "I sat in that first session. I have no idea what you're talking about." Later, Bhupen asked Ankita, who had been in the group. She didn't remember either. She remembered her own stammer.

What did Bhupen say instead of "data set"?
He said "database".
What was Bhupen feeling during the weeks he stayed silent?
He felt embarrassed and anxious, sure the whole group remembered him as the boy who didn't know basic words.
How did the placement officer help Bhupen, and what could he try next?
The officer praised his summaries and admitted not remembering the slip; Bhupen can now speak in discussions, knowing small errors fade fast.
What does Ankita remember from that first session?
Ankita remembers her own stammer, not Bhupen's word mix-up.

messages.content:
Tell this to a child in two simple sentences.

Covered with many kinds of creepers, it was the resort of diverse kinds of birds. It had a large trunk from which numerous branches extended in all directions. Delightful to look at, the shade it afforded was very refreshing. It stood in the midst of the forest, and animals of diverse species lived on it. A mouse of great wisdom, named Palita, lived at the foot of that tree, having made a hole there with a hundred outlets. On the branches of the tree there lived a cat, of the name of Lomasa, in great happiness, daily devouring a large number of birds.
A big, shady forest tree is home to birds, animals and a wise mouse called Palita. A cat named Lomasa also lives in its branches and eats many birds.

(1) Quick one: how can I stay calm when someone teases me?
(2) Is "panorama" a hard word? What does it mean?
(3) Why do we feel nervous before an exam?
(4) Did the flight to Delhi land on time?
(5) Please correct: He said me that he was tired.

1. Take a slow breath and answer calmly, or walk away. If it keeps happening, tell a trusted adult such as a teacher.
2. Panorama is a noun that means a wide view of a whole area.
3. The body switches on its alert mode, so the heart beats faster and the stomach feels tight. Because it is getting ready for something important.
4. I don't know that. I can't see live flight data. Check the airline's website or the airport's arrival screen.
5. Fixed: He told me that he was tired. Why: "tell" takes a person directly, while "say" does not.

Shreya's phone buzzed on the table while she was in the kitchen. Deepak saw the name: Aman. Third time today. His hand actually moved towards the phone. He pulled it back.
When she came out with two bowls of instant noodles, he said, 'Can I ask something without it sounding bad?'
'That's a scary start.'
'I've been feeling suspicious, and I hate it. You've been texting Aman a lot. I nearly looked at your phone just now. I didn't.'
Shreya put the bowls down slowly. 'Thank you for not looking. And for asking.' She unlocked the phone and held it out. He shook his head.
'I don't want to read it. I want to hear it.'
'Aman's organising the surprise for my sister's graduation. I've been hiding it from her, not from you.'
Deepak let out a long breath. 'My brain made a whole movie out of three texts.'
'Next time, ask sooner. Movies are worse than questions.'

Who is Aman, according to Shreya?
The person organising the surprise for her sister's graduation.
What was Deepak feeling when the phone buzzed?
He felt suspicious and anxious, enough that his hand moved towards her phone.
What did Deepak do instead of spying?
He pulled his hand back and calmly told Shreya his worry, asking to hear the truth rather than read her phone 👍
How does Shreya respond to Deepak's question?
She thanks him for not looking and for asking, and explains openly.

Dear Ira,
Remember I said Nani was coming for Lohri? She stayed up with me after everyone slept, rubbing her knees by the heater, and told me something I can't shake. She topped her village school, but when her brothers went to college she was kept home. "I wish I'd argued," she said. "I wish I'd just asked once." She wasn't crying. She said it like a weather report.
For a day it felt heavy, like now I have to succeed for both of us. But I don't think she meant it that way. She squeezed my hand and said, "Don't carry mine. Just don't make your own."
So I'm doing the scary thing: I'm applying for the exchange semester, even though Papa thinks it's too far. If I don't get it, fine. At least I asked once.

Nani said, "I wish I'd argued," and "I wish I'd just asked once."
How did Gurpreet feel at first after hearing Nani's regret?
At first Gurpreet felt it as a heavy burden, as if success now had to count for both of them.

It turns Nani's regret into a warning about not asking, so Gurpreet takes one worthwhile risk now, accepting that a no is fine as long as the question was asked.

From her chin to her cheek.

Monday. Karthik sat beside Lalremsiami on the college fest organising committee's interview panel. The first candidate, a smooth talker in a sharp shirt, charmed the room. Lalremsiami gave him top marks for creativity, planning and budgeting. Karthik noticed he hadn't said a word about budgets.

Wednesday. The committee picked him as events head. Karthik felt uneasy but stayed quiet.

Two weeks later, Monday. The events head had missed three vendor deadlines and overspent on posters. Lalremsiami was furious. "He interviewed so well!"

Karthik finally spoke. "He was charming. That made us see him as great at everything. We never actually tested budgeting."

"So what now?"

"For the next roles, can we score each skill separately? Ask one budgeting question, one planning question, and mark each before moving on?"

Lalremsiami nodded slowly. "And not look at the other scores while marking."

How many vendor deadlines did the events head miss?
Missed three vendor deadlines.
What was Karthik feeling when the committee picked the charming candidate?
Karthik felt uneasy, having noticed that budgeting was scored high without being asked, but he stayed quiet.

Karthik proposed scoring each skill separately with its own question, which stops charm from lifting every rating.

Lalremsiami felt furious and surprised, because he had interviewed so well.

In Kumily, where their small spice-packing unit smelled of cardamom all day, Elizabeth and Sarita had stopped talking about anything except orders. The fight was about shares. Elizabeth had put in her savings; Sarita had found every farmer who supplied them. Each thought the other was asking for too much.
They went together to Varghese uncle, who had run a tea-trading business for thirty years. He sat them on his verandah with black tea and said, "Before you tell me what you want, tell me what she wants. And why."
Elizabeth struggled. "Sarita thinks her work built the supply, and without it my money would just sit in a bank." Sarita was slower. "Elizabeth thinks she took the risk. If we failed, she lost her savings, not me."
Varghese uncle nodded. "Good. Now you've both heard it. Here are three ways other people have split this."

Where did Varghese uncle hear them out?
On his verandah, over black tea.

Elizabeth struggled and felt uncomfortable at first, having to speak up for the person she was arguing with.
Why did asking each to restate the other's view help?
Each heard their own contribution recognised by the other, which calmed the fight before any options were put forward.
How might Sarita feel hearing Elizabeth say her work built the supply?
Sarita would likely feel understood and valued, having wanted her work to count as much as the money.

On the last school day before Christmas, Leela carried her report card home through the cold Delhi fog. Nine teachers had written kind things: "excellent reader", "helpful in class", "beautiful handwriting", "asks great science questions". The music teacher had written: "Talks too much during practice." At dinner, Leela pushed her rajma around her plate. "Music ma'am hates me," she said. Her brother Sumit picked up the card. "It says excellent reader. It says helpful." "But it also says I talk too much." "That's one line, Leela. There are nine good ones." Leela nodded, but in bed she could still see only that one line, glowing behind her eyes in the dark.

What did the music teacher write?
"Talks too much during practice."
Why does Leela keep thinking about the music teacher's comment?
The one critical line feels hurtful and grabs her attention, so she feels upset and sure music ma'am hates her, while the nine good comments fade.

Reading the good comments aloud, perhaps writing all ten on a sheet, and asking the music teacher how to do better at practice.

Sumit sees mostly good news, with nine kind comments and only one line to work on.

Half the room had tears in their eyes, showing how strongly the emotional appeal worked on them.

She met the question with interest, said doubt is old and common, used no shame, and invited him to read and disagree, so he felt safe to keep talking.

You want to know how faith and questions fit together for me? I'm Maria, and I learnt that the hard way.

I go to Mass every Sunday in Margao, and I volunteer at the shelter on Wednesdays. That part of my life has never wavered.

Two years ago I joined a healing prayer group at a friend's house. At first it felt warm. Then the leader said doubting him was a sin, and asked each of us to sign over our savings "to the mission."

I couldn't sleep that night. So I went to talk to the old parish priest, who has known me since I was a baby. He listened and said, "God doesn't need you to stop thinking. Faith that forbids questions isn't asking for faith."

I left the group. I still pray, still go to the shelter. And when something asks for my obedience and my money together, I slow down and ask.

On which day does Maria volunteer at the shelter?
Maria volunteers at the shelter on Wednesdays.
What was Maria feeling on the night after the leader's request?
Maria felt troubled and anxious, unable to sleep after being asked to hand over savings and stop doubting.

Maria talked to a trusted priest, left the group, and kept Maria's own worship and service while staying wary of demands for obedience and money.
How does the old parish priest see the prayer group's demands?
The priest sees them as a warning sign, saying faith that forbids questions isn't truly asking for faith.

“Anjali, wake up. Six-thirty: shower. Seven: breakfast. Seven-fifteen: revise chemistry. Eight: bus.”
“Mumma, I know.”

She felt controlled and trapped by the timetable, so refusing was a way to protect her sense that her choices were her own.

She took the timetable down and asked what Anjali would like to plan herself, giving back some ownership.

You tell me about everything that affects us: money, plans, your family, how you feel about us. You've never lied to me about anything that matters. Asha is going through a divorce. Those late messages were hers to share, not yours.

Darshan's college friend Asha.

Hi Zubin,
You asked how I finish translation jobs so fast now. It isn't speed. It's fewer switches.
Here's my day. From nine to eleven I translate one document, only that. Notifications off, chat closed, phone in the other room. Opens email and messages and answers everything in one go, maybe twenty minutes.

Observation note, Thursday. Divyansh, nursery teacher. Mridul has checked his bean cup six times today. Each time he crouches, crosses the fingers on both hands and whispers, “Please come up, please come up before Friday.” Friday is when the children take their cups home. What was Mridul feeling as he whispered to his bean cup?
He felt hopeful and anxious, wishing hard for the seed to come up before Friday; his wobbling lip later shows disappointment starting.

Microeconomics.

His sisters were very anxious for his having an estate of his own; but though he was now established only as a tenant, Miss Bingley was by no means unwilling to preside at his table; nor was Mrs. Hurst, who had married a man of more fashion than fortune, less disposed to consider his house as her home when it suited her. Mr. Bingley had not been of age two years when he was tempted, by an accidental recommendation, to look at Netherfield House. He did look at it, and into it, for half an hour; was pleased with the situation and the principal rooms, satisfied with what the owner said in its praise, and took it immediately.

Mr. Bingley's sisters want him to own an estate, but meanwhile they happily treat his rented house as their own. Not two years after coming of age, he looked at Netherfield House on a chance recommendation and took it after half an hour.

The women's meeting under the peepal tree in Kalwa village had grown tense. Two lanes were arguing over the new water tap timings, voices rising. Jahnavi, the young coordinator, raised her hands. "At this rate, the tap will retire before we decide!" A few women laughed, then more, and the shoulders around the circle loosened. They settled on alternate mornings within ten minutes. Then Yamini-bai asked to speak. Quietly, she told them her husband had been in the district hospital for a month and she was struggling to manage the fields alone. Just then a rooster strutted into the middle of the circle and crowed at full volume. Jahnavi felt a laugh bubble up and saw two girls at the back biting their lips. She pressed her own lips together, kept her eyes on Yamini-bai, and waited until the rooster wandered off. Then she said, "We'll make a rota for your fields."

What did the women decide about the water tap?
Alternate mornings.
What was Jahnavi feeling when the rooster crowed during Yamini-bai's words?
Jahnavi felt a laugh bubbling up but also respect and concern for Yamini-bai, so she held the amusement back.
Why was Jahnavi right to laugh at one moment and hold back at the other?
The joke about the tap eased a tense argument, but laughing during Yamini-bai's hard news would have seemed dismissive of her struggle.
How might Yamini-bai have felt if the circle had burst out laughing at the rooster?
She might have felt hurt and unheard, as if her husband's illness and her struggle were being brushed aside.

When the science-fair model collapsed an hour before judging, Hemant's heart hammered. Two classmates were shouting at each other and someone was close to tears. Devika just looked at the pieces, took a breath and said, "Okay. What do we still have?" Her voice was flat.
"She doesn't even care," Hemant muttered to another boy.
Then he noticed her hands sorting screws into a lid, and that she had tied her hair back before anyone spoke. She wasn't indifferent. She was steady. By judging time the model stood, slightly crooked.
Hemant felt ashamed. "Sorry," he told her. "I thought you didn't care."
"I saw all of it," said Devika. "I just didn't want to add to it."

What happened an hour before judging?
The science-fair model collapsed.
How did Hemant feel afterwards about what he said?
Ashamed. He realised Devika had been steady, not uncaring, and apologised.
What could Hemant do differently the next time a classmate stays composed in a crisis?
He could watch what the person does, such as sorting screws and tying back hair, before deciding they don't care, and ask instead of assuming.
How does Devika see her own calm?
She sees it as a choice not to add to the panic. She noticed all of it but did not want to make it worse.

Day 1. Zainab read Aditi's message, "Are you free after school?", and put her phone in her bag. She didn't want to hurt Aditi, but she'd been feeling suffocated lately, and she didn't know how to say she needed some space. So she said nothing.

Day 4. Aditi wrote, "Did I do something?" Zainab's stomach twisted. She walked to class a different way to avoid Aditi's corridor. Her chest felt tight every time the phone buzzed, and she felt like a coward.

Day 9. She finally typed, "I'm sorry I went silent. I need some space right now. It's not about anything you did." Sent. Aditi replied an hour later: "Thanks for telling me. It hurts, but I'd rather know." Zainab breathed out slowly.

What did Zainab do when Aditi asked if she was free after school on Day 1?
She read the message and put her phone in her bag, saying nothing.
Why did Zainab avoid replying at first?
She wanted distance but did not know how to say it and did not want to hurt Aditi, so she stayed silent. She also felt like a coward.
What did Zainab do on Day 9 that was kinder than silence?
She sent a short honest message saying she needed space and that it was not about anything Aditi did.
How might Aditi have felt during the days of silence?
Confused and worried, since Aditi asked, "Did I do something?" Afterwards Aditi said it hurt but was better than not knowing.

Sarita's slate pencil box had gone missing from the village school for the second time that week. Walking home past the mustard fields, her grandfather Deepak Dada asked, "Why did it get lost?"
"I left it on the bench."
"Why?"
"I forgot it."
"Why did you forget?"
Sarita kicked a pebble. "Because the bell rang and everyone ran for the bus, so I ran too."
"And why was it still out when the bell rang?"
She stopped walking. "Because I only pack after the bell."
Dada smiled and waited.
"So if I pack before the bell," she said slowly, "I won't have to rush."
The next day, when Masterji said, "Five minutes left," Sarita put her slate, pencils and box into her cloth bag. When the bell rang, she walked out with everything.

What did Masterji say when Sarita started packing?
Masterji said, "Five minutes left."
How was Sarita feeling when she kicked a pebble?
She was frustrated and a bit embarrassed about losing her box again and being asked why.
Which approach did Dada use, and why did it work better than telling her the answer?
He kept asking why, so Sarita found the deeper cause herself and was more likely to remember the fix.
How might Deepak Dada see Sarita walking out with everything the next day?
He would feel proud and pleased that his granddaughter found her own solution and stuck to it.

Read this:

Jahnavi, you're asking for your podcast what surprised me most as senior designer at an export house in Jaipur? Okay, it's Akash, your data bhaiya, talking. Every season, our buyers pick which block prints will sell in Europe. They're so sure. "This one will fly." "This one's dead." They've done it for twenty years. So last winter I got curious. I went back through three seasons of their picks and the actual sales sheets. Their hits and misses were almost a coin toss. Fashion abroad changes with a hundred things nobody here sees, and the sales figures arrive months later, mixed up with other reasons. Twenty years of guessing hadn't sharpened much. I didn't embarrass anyone. At the next meeting I just said, "Let's keep your pick, and also test twenty samples with two shops first." One buyer grumbled. The samples are selling differently from what anyone guessed.

How many seasons of picks did Akash check?
Three seasons of their picks and the actual sales sheets.
What does Akash's quiet approach at the meeting suggest about his feelings toward the buyers?
He seems to respect their experience and doesn't want to embarrass them, but he is also curious and doubtful, since the data showed their confidence wasn't matched by results.
Which step did Akash add, and why does it suit this kind of decision?
Testing twenty samples with two shops alongside the buyers' picks, because in a field with slow, mixed feedback, real data helps more than confident guesses.
How might the grumbling buyer feel about the new sample test?
The buyer may feel doubted or a little threatened after twenty years of trusting their own eye, even if the test is fair.

"How was school?" Sabina asked.
"Fine." Naveen dropped his bag and went straight to his room, shoes still on.
"Fine with your shoes still on?" She followed and sat on the floor by his bed. "You don't have to talk."
"...Nobody picked me for kabaddi."
Sabina opened her mouth, then closed it. She waited.
"They picked Bunty before me. Bunty!"
"Hmm."
"And then I sat alone by the tap." He rubbed his eyes quickly.
"That sounds rotten," Sabina said quietly. "Want to practise raids with me after tea?"
Naveen's shoulders dropped. "Maybe."

Which game was Naveen not picked for?
Kabaddi.
How did Sabina seem to feel when Naveen said "Fine" and went straight to his room?
She seemed concerned, because his going straight to his room with his shoes still on suggested something was wrong.
Which of Sabina's choices helped Naveen open up?
Saying he didn't have to talk and then waiting quietly gave him space, instead of pushing him with questions.
What might Naveen feel when his shoulders drop?
Some relief, because his sister listened without judging and offered something to do together.

Hansa had wanted to start a weekend pottery class for children for over a year. Her flat in Ahmedabad had a small balcony, and she only had Sundays free from her bank job.
She had three notebooks full of plans. Diagrams of where the wheels would go. Lists of clay suppliers. A rough budget. Lesson ideas for twelve weeks. Colour-coded timetables.
Every Sunday she sat with a notebook and added more. It felt like progress. Her friend Minakshi asked in March, "So when's the first class?"
"Soon. I'm still planning the lessons for weeks nine to twelve."
"Have you called the clay supplier?"
"Not yet."
By September, the notebooks were thicker. She still hadn't ordered clay, cleared the balcony or told a single parent.
One Sunday, flipping through all three, she felt a heavy sinking. It was a year of plans, and not one child had touched clay.

How many notebooks of plans did Hansa have?
She had three notebooks full of plans.
How did Hansa feel flipping through the notebooks in September?
She felt a heavy sinking, realising a year of planning had produced no class at all.
What would you change first in Hansa's approach?
Pick one concrete step, like calling the clay supplier this week, and do it before writing any more plans.
How might Minakshi see Hansa's plans?
Minakshi seems gently doubtful, asking when the first class is and whether the supplier has been called.

Hrithik, two, bumped his head on the table and wailed.
"Aa ja, beta," called Dadi, arms out.
"I've got him," said Chachi, scooping him up. "Oof, big bump."
Hrithik cried louder, then reached for his cousin. "Tenzin!"
Tenzin, eight, made a funny face. "Look, a fish!"
Hrithik hiccuped, then giggled.
Dadi laughed. "Whoever is closest wins."
He fell asleep on Chachi's shoulder, one fist holding Tenzin's shirt.

Who scooped Hrithik up first?
Chachi scooped him up.
How did Hrithik seem to feel when Tenzin made a funny face?
He seemed comforted and safe, stopping crying and giggling.
What does this home do well when Hrithik cries?
Whoever is nearest comforts him, so he has many familiar people to feel safe with.
How might Tenzin feel when Hrithik reaches for him?
Tenzin probably feels proud and loved, being trusted to cheer up his little cousin.

Dhruv: where were u this morning, we had cricket
Rafiq: visarjan cleanup at the beach. 6 am 😴
Dhruv: on a SUNDAY?? after ten days of festival crowds?
Rafiq: colony uncle asked if anyone could help. i thought i'd go for 1 hour
Rafiq: stayed 4

Rafiq: idk. the little kids from building C followed me around asking which bag the plastic goes in
Rafiq: one of them told the others "Rafiq bhaiya knows everything"

Rafiq: today i felt like i actually mattered
Dhruv: ok that's actually nice 🙂
Dhruv: next sunday wake me up
Rafiq: 6 am. no excuses

At what time did the beach cleanup start?
At 6 am.
How did Rafiq feel at the cleanup compared with after the maths test?
After the 58 in maths he felt like nothing, but at the cleanup, with the little kids following him, he felt needed and quietly proud, as if he mattered.
What could help Rafiq keep this sense of worth going?
He could keep a regular slot for helping, like the next Sunday cleanup, so his sense of being useful does not rest only on marks.
What might the little kids from building C think of Rafiq?
They see him as someone who knows things and is worth following, like a big brother they can ask anything.

Aparna found out from the lunch queue that Arohi had told the group about her crush on the new boy in 11B. By sixth period, three people had made jokes.
After school, at the bus stop outside the mall, Arohi said, "Look, I'm sorry you feel that way. I didn't think it was such a big secret."
Aparna felt her face go hot. "That's not an apology. That's saying I'm the problem for feeling it."
Arohi opened her mouth, then shut it.
"You told something I asked you not to tell," Aparna said. "That's the bit I need you to say."
The bus came and went. Arohi stood there, fiddling with her bag strap.
"Okay. I told your secret. You asked me not to, and I did it anyway. I'm sorry. No excuse."
Aparna breathed out. "Thank you. That's the one I needed."

Where did Aparna and Arohi talk after school?
They talked at the bus stop outside the mall.
What was Aparna feeling when Arohi said "I'm sorry you feel that way"?
Aparna felt hurt and angry, her face hot, because the words seemed to put the blame on her feelings instead of on what Arohi did.
What made Arohi's second apology work?
It named exactly what she did, admitted she knew it was wrong, and had no excuse attached.
How might Arohi have been feeling as she fiddled with her bag strap?
She was probably embarrassed and uncomfortable, realising her first apology had shifted blame and that she needed to own what she did.
What does deportment mean?

Deportment is the way a person stands, walks and behaves. It is a noun, and it sounds a little old-fashioned now.
Example: The old school report card had a grade for deportment.

Friday: Nikita arrived from Dubai for the summer. At the door, her Dada Ramesh waited. Nikita didn't know what to do, so she hung her head and stared at the floor. “Is she upset?” Dada whispered to Papa. Sunday: On the veranda, Dada showed her. “Palms together, a small dip of the head, then look up and smile. It says, I respect you. Hanging the head says, I'm sorry, or I'm sad.” Nikita practised on the cat. Tuesday: When the neighbour aunty came with sweets, Nikita pressed her palms together, dipped her head, looked up and smiled. The aunty beamed. Dada winked at her from his chair.

Where did Nikita arrive from?
Nikita arrived from Dubai.
What was Nikita feeling when she hung her head on Friday?
She felt unsure and shy, not knowing the greeting, so her hanging head looked like sadness even though it was confusion.
How did Dada's lesson on Sunday help?
He showed the difference between a small respectful dip with a smile and a hanging head, giving her a clear way to greet elders.
How did Friday's greeting look to Dada Ramesh?
It looked to him as if she might be upset, since a hanging head can mean sadness or shame.

Only ten minutes till the Lohri bonfire, and Gurpreet begged for one more round of hide-and-seek. Aditi counted by the gate. Gurpreet crouched behind the pile of quilts on the cold verandah, then peeked out. "She can't see me," he whispered. When Aditi walked past twice, he pressed a hand over his mouth to keep from giggling. At last he leapt out: "You didn't know!" Aditi laughed. "Next time I'll trick you." Then Mummy called them to the fire.

Where did Gurpreet hide?
He crouched behind the pile of quilts on the cold verandah.
Why did Gurpreet press a hand over his mouth?
He was trying not to giggle, feeling excited and proud that Aditi didn't know where he was.
How could the adults keep this kind of playful trick fun and safe?
They could mark hiding areas well away from the bonfire and laugh along with both children.
How does Aditi feel about being tricked?
Aditi takes it in good spirit and even plans a trick back, so the game stays playful for both.

It was the day before the annual exams, the staff room was chaos, and Siddharth sir had forty papers to check. Then Pallavi appeared at the door, eyes red. "I can't read the news at assembly tomorrow. Everyone will stare at me. Nobody has ever been this nervous." Siddharth felt the urge to say, "Not now, Pallavi." Instead he pushed the papers aside. "That sounds really hard. Sit." He listened for five minutes. Then he asked, "Remember who read the news last week?" "The boy from 9C." "How was he?" "His voice shook the whole time." "Did you laugh?" "No. I felt bad for him." Pallavi paused. "Oh." The next day she read, her voice shaking a little, and nobody laughed.

What did Pallavi say she couldn't do tomorrow?
Read the news at assembly.
What did Siddharth feel when Pallavi appeared?
He felt the urge to say "Not now", stressed with forty papers, but chose patience.
How did Siddharth widen Pallavi's view?
He listened first, then asked about last week's reader and how she felt about his shaky voice, letting her see that others weren't judging her.
How does Pallavi's view change?
She realises she felt sympathy, not scorn, for the last reader, so others will probably feel the same about her.
What was the print run of the first edition of a small poetry book from 1932?
I don't know the print run, because it is hard to confirm for old, small books. A library catalogue or a rare-book dealer may have it.

At ten, Tenzin opened a steel tiffin of home-made dumplings, and Bhupen wrinkled his nose loudly. "What is that? Smells weird!" A few classmates giggled. Tenzin closed the lid halfway and ate the rest quickly, eyes down. The next day Tenzin asked Amma for plain biscuits and carried those instead, the tiffin buried at the bottom of the bag.

At fifteen, Preeti leaned across the back bench. "Everyone's skipping the last period. Come on, don't be boring, or we'll go without you." Tenzin's stomach sank. The threat was no bigger than standing alone at the gate, but it felt like standing on a cliff. "I'll pass," Tenzin said, voice wobbling, and walked to class. The seat felt lonely for ten minutes. Then Bhupen slid in beside Tenzin and whispered, "Honestly, I didn't want to go either."

What did Tenzin carry to school the day after the tiffin was mocked?
Tenzin carried plain biscuits instead.
How does the pressure on Tenzin at ten differ from the pressure at fifteen, and what does Tenzin do each time?

At ten Bhupen's remark about the home-made dumplings made Tenzin hide the tiffin and copy the others with plain biscuits. At fifteen Preeti's push to skip the last period came with the threat of going without Tenzin, and this time Tenzin said, "I'll pass" and stayed, though the seat felt lonely.
What was Tenzin feeling when Preeti said everyone was skipping?
Tenzin felt afraid of being left out, and the social threat felt far bigger than the act itself.
What could Tenzin do after Bhupen's whisper?
Tenzin could accept the company and later suggest another plan for that period, showing there are choices besides skipping or being alone.

Anjali Bua looked at Ojas over her glasses when he said the family shouldn't talk about Nani's illness, to keep her spirits up. "Let me tell you about my father, beta. When I was twenty-five, the doctors told us his illness was serious. And we decided, all of us, not to talk about it. My mother said it would make him lose hope. So we smiled and spoke about weddings and cricket.
Nobody asked him whether he wanted to be in hospital or at home at the end. Nobody asked where his papers were, or what he wanted done with the shop. We thought we had time.
Then one night he couldn't breathe. At the hospital, strangers asked us questions only he could have answered. We made choices in ten minutes in a corridor. I still don't know if they were the ones he would have made.
Hope is good, Ojas. But ask Nani what she wants while she can tell you."

What did the family talk about instead of the illness?
Weddings and cricket.
How does Anjali feel about the choices made in the corridor?
She still feels uncertain and regretful, not knowing if they were what her father would have wanted.
Which choice in the story could have changed the ending, and why?
Asking her father about his wishes and papers while he could answer, so the family wasn't deciding for him in ten minutes.
How might Anjali's father have felt being kept in cheerful talk?
He may have felt protected but also unheard, never asked what he himself wanted.

The hostel common room was loud with a cricket match on TV, but Kunal sat by the window holding the letter from the pilot selection board. Not recommended. Since he was nine he had pictured himself in a flight suit; he had even practised the salute in the mirror. Now that future had simply closed. On his phone, a batchmate was posting photos from the academy gates, grinning, and Kunal felt a sharp stab of envy, then guilt for feeling it. Irfan dropped onto the sofa beside him. "Bro, forget it. You'll crack something better. It's a sign." Kunal nodded and said nothing. Later, alone on the terrace, he let himself cry for the nine-year-old in the flight suit. He didn't know yet what came next. For tonight, not knowing was allowed.

What did the letter from the pilot selection board say?
Not recommended.
What did Kunal feel seeing the batchmate's photos?
A sharp stab of envy, then guilt for feeling it.
Why is Kunal's crying on the terrace a healthy step?
Letting himself grieve the lost future, instead of rushing to Irfan's positive story, is part of moving on.
How does Irfan seem to see Kunal's loss?
Irfan means well and wants to cheer Kunal up quickly, not seeing that Kunal first needs to grieve.
Can an occurrence be good as well as bad?

Yes. An occurrence is something that happens, good or bad. It is a noun, and it often refers to events that happen now and then.
Example: Rain in April is a rare occurrence in this town.
Our residents' association meetings always turn into shouting matches.
That makes it hard to get anything done. Is there a set agenda for the meetings?
Not really. People just raise whatever they want.
A short written agenda, shared a few days before, can help a lot. Give each topic a time limit, and let one person act as chair to call on speakers.
People still interrupt each other.
You could agree on a simple rule: raise a hand to speak, and only one person talks at a time. Write key decisions down and read them out at the end, so everyone knows what was agreed.

Damini, look at this small diary I still keep. I'm Pankaj, and when I was ten, my teacher, Mr Kulkarni, called out what we needed for the next day's science class: a torch, a spoon, a small mirror and a piece of black paper. Most children nodded and hoped to remember. I took out my little diary and wrote the four items at once, in a hurry, before the next lesson began. That night I checked it twice, once at dinner and once before sleep. In class, I was the only one with all four things. Writing had made my head free to think about the experiment.

What four items did the teacher ask for?
The teacher asked for a torch, a spoon, a small mirror and a piece of black paper.
Why did the narrator write the items at once?
Pankaj wanted the list safe in the diary instead of in a head that might forget, and felt sure this would help.
What choice in the story helped the narrator have all four items, and why?
Writing them down at once and checking twice helped, because the list stayed correct and the narrator could check it later.
How did the other children in the class fare?
Most children only nodded and hoped to remember, and Pankaj was the only one with all four things, so the others probably missed some items.

Anand was the agriculture extension officer for six villages around Sirsi, and for months his monthly reports were late. He blamed himself: lazy, careless, bad with paper.
In April he noticed something. By two in the afternoon, after the field visits in the heat, he could barely read a form. At dawn, with the crows and the cool air, his head was sharp.
So he changed the day. Reports from five-thirty to seven, before anyone else woke. Every night he packed his field bag, filled the water bottles and wrote the next day's village list on a chit. Evenings were for easy things: dinner, the radio, a phone call home.
His brother Uday, who used to tease him, found him one morning writing by the window. "You? At this hour?"
"Me," Anand said. "Report's done. Go back to sleep."

When does Anand now write his reports?
He writes them from five-thirty to seven in the morning, before anyone else wakes.
How did Anand feel about himself before he changed his day?
He felt ashamed and frustrated, blaming himself as lazy, careless and bad with paper.
What steps helped Anand, and why are they wise?
He moved the reports to the cool, sharp dawn hours and packed his bag and wrote the village list each night, so hard work fits his best time and evenings need few decisions.
How might Uday see Anand now?
Uday, who used to tease him, is likely surprised and a bit impressed to find Anand finished with his report so early.

Subject: I said yes to the smaller offer
Hi Vaibhav,
You asked why I didn't take the higher package. Here's my thinking.
I asked myself one question: what do I want to be able to do three years from now? My honest answer: build and ship a product feature end to end, and explain every decision in it.
Offer A pays about 30% more, but it's a support team, and nobody I met there writes code daily. Offer B has a senior engineer, Farooq, who has built two payment systems and told me he reviews every junior's code personally.
So I put mentoring and skill growth first and the package second. B won easily. I know A would feel nicer on payday. But in three years I think B makes me better at the work, and that matters more to me.
Tell me if I'm being naive.
Darshan

How much more does Offer A pay?
Offer A pays about 30% more.
How does Darshan feel about choosing the lower package?
Darshan feels fairly confident but a little unsure too, asking Vaibhav whether it is naive.
What else could Darshan confirm before joining?
Darshan could ask B for a written plan of the first months, including how often Farooq's reviews happen.
How might Vaibhav read the email?
Vaibhav can see clear reasoning based on Darshan's three-year goal, and may reassure Darshan or point out anything missing.

The stream-choice form was due at school on Monday, and it was already Saturday night. Lalit's father wanted Science, his mother thought Commerce was safer, and Lalit himself kept drifting toward History books. His cousin Chaitanya, visiting from Pune, pulled out a notebook. "Stop arguing in your head. Score them." They made columns for Science, Commerce and Humanities, and rows for interest, how his marks had moved over two years, careers, coaching costs and family support. Lalit scored each from one to five. "Now, which rows matter most to you?" Lalit thought. "Interest. And careers." They doubled those. Science won on family support, Humanities on interest by a mile, Commerce sat in the middle. Totals: Humanities 29, Commerce 26, Science 24. Lalit looked at the gap for a long time. "So it's not just a feeling. There's a real difference."

When was the stream-choice form due?
It was due at school on Monday.
How does Lalit seem to feel looking at the totals?
He seems surprised and a bit relieved that his pull toward Humanities shows up as a real difference, not just a feeling.
What could Lalit do next with the grid?
Show it to his parents, so they can all see the trade-offs, including the low family-support score, and talk them through together.
How might Lalit's father see the totals?
His father may feel disappointed that Science came last, but the scores give a clear starting point for talking instead of arguing.

Dhruv rubbed his face with both hands. "Amandeep, you know how long I prepared for the army. Since Class 9. Morning runs, pushups on the terrace, the medical, the written test, the interview. I thought I'd done well. Yesterday the final list came out. My name wasn't there. And I'm over the age limit for trying again. That's it. Done. I didn't cry in front of Mummy. I went to the ground where I used to run and sat there till it got dark. It's not just the job, you know? It's the picture I carried of myself in uniform, making Papa proud. That picture's just... gone. I don't know what I want now. I'm not asking you to fix it. I just needed to say it out loud to someone."

Since which class had Dhruv been preparing for the army?
Since Class 9.
Why did Dhruv go to the ground and sit there until dark?
He was grieving deeply and needed a place to feel the loss privately, away from his mother.
How could Amandeep best respond right now?
By listening and staying with him instead of offering quick solutions, as Dhruv asked, and checking in over the next days.
What would change if Dhruv's father were in the room hearing this?
Dhruv might feel he had failed him, or he might realise his father cares about him more than the uniform.

Study hour at the girls' hostel ran from six to half past eight. Himani spread out her homework and chose the nicest bits first: a poster of the solar system, then copying a poem in her best writing. The glitter pens came out. Urmila, at the next desk, was already scratching away at fractions. By eight the poster was beautiful and the poem neat, but eight sums still waited. Himani's eyes kept closing. She rushed through them, guessing at two. Next day the teacher returned the notebook with three red crosses and a note: 'Careless. Were you tired?' Himani stared at the crosses, cheeks hot.

What were the first two things Himani did during study hour?
A poster of the solar system, then copying a poem in her best writing.
What was Himani feeling when she stared at the red crosses?
Her hot cheeks suggest she felt embarrassed and disappointed, since the mistakes came from rushing while sleepy.
What would you change first in Himani's plan?
Do the fractions at six while fresh, and keep the poster and poem for the end when she's tired; the fun parts need less thinking.
How might Urmila see Himani's evening?
Urmila did the fractions first, so Urmila might admire the poster but wonder why the hard sums were left so late.

metadata.subtype: Approach: doing the easy fun parts first [Pitfall]

At the end of the day at playschool, the van was honking outside. Kalyani sat on the low bench with one sandal on the wrong foot. Ritu Miss knelt to help. "No! Me do it!" Kalyani pulled her foot away. She tugged the strap, it slipped, she tugged again. Her tongue poked out. Ritu Miss sat back on her heels, waited, and called to the driver, "Two more minutes!" At last the strap clicked. Kalyani stood up, stamped both feet, and marched to the van, chin high.

What did Kalyani say when Ritu Miss knelt to help?
"No! Me do it!"
What does Kalyani's stamping and chin held high suggest she felt?
She felt proud and strong because she had done the strap by herself 😊.
What choice did Ritu Miss make, and why was it a good one?
She sat back, waited and asked the driver for two more minutes, letting Kalyani finish on her own.
How might the van driver feel about the two extra minutes?
The driver may be a bit impatient, but a short wait lets a small child leave feeling capable instead of upset.

Baljeet sat on the edge of her bed in their Chandigarh flat, rehearsing. Vasudha would be home from work any minute, and Baljeet had to tell her she was moving out to be closer to her new job. They'd shared this flat for three years.
Her jaw was clenched. Her shoulders were hunched forward. She caught herself and sat up, let her hands rest open on her knees, pressed her feet into the floor and breathed out slowly, like blowing through a straw.
The key turned in the lock.
"Vasu, got a minute? I need to tell you something hard."
Vasudha's face fell as Baljeet explained. She was quiet for a long time, and a few tears came. It was still sad. But Baljeet didn't ramble or apologise ten times. They made tea and started talking about how to find a new flatmate.

How long had Baljeet and Vasudha shared the flat?
They had shared the flat for three years.
What was Baljeet feeling before Vasudha came home?
She was tense and nervous, with a clenched jaw and hunched shoulders, dreading the conversation.
Which choice helped Baljeet in the conversation, and why?
Sitting up, pressing her feet into the floor and breathing out slowly steadied her, so she could explain clearly instead of rambling.
How does Vasudha feel when she hears the news?
She is sad and hurt at first, with a few tears, but she can still talk it through calmly.

Charu: just landed!! my flat is empty and the SIM shop closes soon 😅
Rekha: breathe. Take the tram to the mall, there's a shop by the pharmacy. I'll send the exact stop
Rekha: also come Saturday, we're cooking for Ugadi, bring nothing
Charu: really? thank you, I was dreading the first weekend 🥺
Rekha: same when I came. Someone did this for me, so now I do it for you
Charu: what about my colleagues? they keep inviting me to trivia night
Rekha: go!! I love our group but I don't want to only ever go to the dinners from home. trivia sounds fun
Charu: ok. trivia Thursday, Ugadi Saturday
Rekha: perfect. and next year you'll help the next newcomer 🙂

What is Rekha's group cooking for on Saturday?
They are cooking for Ugadi.
How does Charu feel about the first weekend, and what changes it?
Charu was dreading the first weekend, and feels relieved and grateful when Rekha invites Charu to cook for Ugadi.
How can Charu enjoy the group from home and still avoid living in a bubble?
Go to the Ugadi cooking on Saturday and also say yes to the colleagues' trivia night on Thursday.
Why might Rekha push Charu toward trivia night instead of only the group dinners?
Rekha loves the group but does not want to only ever go to the dinners from home, and wants Charu to mix with colleagues too rather than stay in a bubble.

For seven weeks the cross-body lead had been Hrithik's embarrassment at the Thursday salsa class in a Pune studio above a bank. He counted out loud, stepped on Ayesha's toes, apologised, counted again.
This Thursday the instructor put on a song nobody knew and said, "No counting tonight. Just listen."
Hrithik panicked for eight beats. Then something odd happened. His feet moved before he thought about them. His hand went up, Ayesha turned under it and came back exactly on the beat. They did it again. And again, without a stumble.
"Who are you?" Ayesha said, laughing.
He didn't know. It felt like it had arrived from nowhere. But in the auto on the way home, watching the wet streets, he understood it hadn't: all those clumsy Thursdays had been teaching his feet in the background while his head was busy counting.

What did the instructor tell the class this Thursday?
No counting tonight. Just listen.
How did Hrithik feel when the turn finally worked?
He felt surprised and delighted, as if the skill had arrived from nowhere after weeks of embarrassment.
What might help Hrithik keep this breakthrough going?
Keep dancing to new songs with less counting and trust his feet, so the lead becomes steady rather than a one-night fluke.
What is the change like for Ayesha as Hrithik's partner?
Ayesha is delighted and amused; after weeks of stepped-on toes, dancing with Hrithik suddenly feels easy and fun 😊

Deepak had kept the credit card statements in his office drawer for eight months. The balance had grown after his friend's wedding, the new phone, a few dinners he'd insisted on paying for. He meant to clear it quietly, a little every month, before Anjali ever needed to know.
Then the bank called their home number while he was at work.
When he came back to the Dwarka flat that evening, Anjali was sitting at the table with the notepad she'd written the amount on.
"Is this true?"
"Yes. I was going to fix it before—"
"Before I found out." She didn't raise her voice. "Deepak, I'm not even upset about the number. We could have handled it together. What I can't handle is eight months of you pretending."
That night she slept in the other room. The balance could be paid in a year. Trust, he realised, would take longer.

How long had Deepak kept the statements in his office drawer?
For eight months.
What was Anjali feeling when she said she wasn't upset about the number?
Anjali felt hurt and betrayed; the hiding mattered more to her than the amount.
What else could Deepak have done when the balance first grew?
He could have told Anjali early and worked out a plan together, perhaps with advice from a qualified adviser, instead of hiding it.
How does the hidden debt affect Anjali's view of Deepak?
Anjali now questions whether she can trust what he tells her, which is why she sleeps in the other room even though the amount could be paid off.

metadata.subtype: Approach: hiding a debt or spending to avoid a fight [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Behind the government school in their village near Nashik, the pond was strictly out of bounds. At recess Pankaj kicked the school football there anyway, waded in after it, and lost it in the weeds. Now Masterji was asking the class, 'Who had the ball?' Pankaj stared at Asif, begging with his eyes. Asif could say they'd played by the well. It would be easy. His chest tightened. After class, he pulled Pankaj behind the water tank. 'I won't lie for you. But if you tell Masterji, I'll come and stand with you.' Pankaj kicked the dust. 'I'll have to clean the classroom.' 'Then I'll help clean.' They went together. Masterji listened and gave Pankaj a week of sweeping. Asif swept beside him every day.

What did Pankaj lose in the pond weeds?
The school football.
Why did Asif's chest tighten?
He felt torn between loyalty to Pankaj and not wanting to lie to Masterji.
How did Asif show real loyalty?
He refused to lie but urged Pankaj to own up, went with him, and helped with the sweeping.
What was Pankaj feeling when he stared at Asif?
Scared of being caught and hoping Asif would cover for him.
Dawat se jaldi jaana hai. Host ko kaise bolun?
Say: "I'm sorry, I have to leave early. Thank you so much for inviting me."
Change "must" to a softer word: You must call your grandmother this weekend.
You should call your grandmother this weekend.

Read this:

Sangeeta: Rhea is so upset about the trip money. Not my fault the bus tickets went up
Ayesha: You said you'd book them a week ago
Sangeeta: Not my fault the site kept crashing
Ayesha: And the missed rehearsal last month was "not my fault, the alarm didn't ring"
Sangeeta: because it wasn't??
Ayesha: Maybe partly! But the group paid extra because the tickets were booked late. Can we say that part out loud?
Sangeeta: ...I did leave it till the last night
Ayesha: Thanks for saying it. Could you tell Rhea that?
Sangeeta: ugh. fine. I feel awful
Ayesha: Awful is what owning it feels like at first. I'll wait with you 🙂

What did Sangeeta first say about the bus tickets?
Sangeeta said the bus tickets went up, and that it was not Sangeeta's fault.
What is Ayesha noticing and feeling as Sangeeta keeps blaming the tickets, the site and the alarm?
Ayesha is patient but a little frustrated, having heard the same reply about the tickets, the site and the alarm, and hopes Sangeeta will own part of it.
What did Ayesha do that moved Sangeeta from an excuse toward owning the harm?
Ayesha named the part that was Sangeeta's, the late booking, and asked to say it out loud, without accusing. Sangeeta then admitted it.
What might Sangeeta be feeling on writing that it feels awful?
Sangeeta feels guilty now that the late booking has been admitted, and is probably uncomfortable about telling Rhea. The excuses had kept that feeling away.

Mentor's note, plant 2, 14 March.
I was at the inspection bench this morning when Darshan, the line manager, told Payal to "keep the hairline cracks off the report — they're cosmetic, the client won't notice." The parts were brake-lever brackets.
Payal is in her first year. She went red and was quiet for a few seconds. Then she said, "I hear you, sir. But if I sign this, I'm the one saying they're fine. I'm not able to do that."
Darshan said it was his decision, not hers. She answered that the decision might be his, but her signature was hers.
She logged the cracks, then came to me and asked how to raise it formally. I walked her through the quality escalation form and we submitted it together at noon. The quality head held the lot by 3 p.m. and has called Darshan in tomorrow.
Payal's hands were unsteady afterward. I told her she had done her job well.

What parts had the hairline cracks?
The cracks were in brake-lever brackets at the inspection bench.
How did Payal feel when Darshan gave the instruction, and what did she believe?
She was nervous, going red and silent for a moment, but she believed her signature was her own responsibility even if the decision was his.
What did the mentor do that helped?
The mentor showed Payal the quality escalation form, submitted it with her at noon and reassured her afterward.
Why might Darshan react the way he did?
He likely felt pressured and saw the cracks as cosmetic, so passing the decision upward to himself felt normal to him.

Read this:

Dear Madhuri,

Guess what I finally did today? I switched my phone plan.

I know, very exciting. But listen. I had been on the same plan since Class 11. It cost more than double what the new ones cost, and gave half the data. Every month I'd see the bill and think, I should change. Then I'd think about calling customer care, the forms, the new SIM, and I'd just... not.

I told myself I was fine with it. "It works, why change?" But I wasn't fine. I just didn't want the effort.

This morning I timed it. The switch took twenty-two minutes.

Four years. Twenty-two minutes.

I'm now looking at everything else I've been "fine" with. My gym I never go to. The coaching I don't like. Maybe some of those are just inertia too.

Love,
Himani

How long did the switch take?
The switch took twenty-two minutes.
Why did Himani stay on the old plan for so long?
Himani felt the effort of switching was too much, and kept saying it was fine, so inertia felt like contentment.
What could Himani do about the other things called "fine"?
Himani could check each one, like the gym and coaching, and ask whether staying is a choice or just to avoid effort.
How might Madhuri react to this letter?
Madhuri might feel amused by the twenty-two minutes and encouraged to check Madhuri's own habits.
Please pick up him at the station at six. Is the word order right?

Please pick him up at the station at six.
Why: A pronoun object goes between verb and particle: "pick him up".

Read this:

At the village school's drawing competition, the teacher pinned all the pictures on the wall. Mahima ran to see.
Her mango tree had got a star. Nandini's peacock had two stars. Mahima's tummy sank. Then she saw that the boy next to her had no stars at all, and she felt a little better.
All afternoon she kept looking. Who had more? Who had less? She counted the stars twice.
Walking home past the fields, Nandini said, "I liked your mango tree. The leaves looked real."
Mahima was quiet. She had been so busy counting stars, she hadn't really looked at anyone's drawing, not even her own.

How many stars did Nandini's peacock get?
Nandini's peacock had two stars.
How did Mahima feel when she saw the boy with no stars?
She felt a little better, because being above someone made her feel less small.
What could Mahima try at the next competition?
She could look at what she likes in each drawing, including her own, instead of only counting stars.
How does Nandini seem to see Mahima's drawing?
Nandini sees it warmly, admiring how the leaves looked real, without comparing stars.

Read this:

Zainab, you young people think only old uncles fall for these calls. Listen. When I was branch manager in Kochi, a college boy, Anand, came in shaking. Someone had called "from the bank" saying his account would be frozen, and asked for the OTP to "verify". Anand was sharp, top of his engineering class. He gave it. Why? Because the caller knew his name, his birthday, even his last transaction. People forget how much they have scattered about themselves online. We blocked the card in time, luckily. But Anand's real lesson came after. He went home and removed his birthday, phone number and hometown from every public profile. He told me, "I handed them the key years ago, bit by bit." So, Zainab, before you fill in that online quiz asking your first pet's name, think of Anand. Your Karthik Uncle has seen what happens next.

What did the caller ask Anand for?
The OTP, to verify.
What was Anand feeling when he came into the branch?
Anand was shaking, frightened and probably ashamed that a clever student like him had been tricked.
What was Anand's turning point after the call, and why was it wise?
Removing his birthday, number and hometown from public profiles, because scammers build trust from such scattered details.
How might Karthik, as branch manager, have felt seeing Anand shaking?
Karthik likely felt concerned and protective, acting quickly to block the card, and wanted Anand to see it wasn't about intelligence.
