Counselling note, Thursday. Tarun, a second-year student, came in after the committee's notice went up on the board. He said his project guide, Anand, keeps making remarks about how he looks and, twice this month, put a hand on his back after he had stepped away. Tarun kept apologising for "making a fuss" and asked whether he had somehow encouraged it. I told him plainly that it is not his fault and that he did nothing to invite it. He had already saved the messages and written the dates in his phone. We went through how to file a written complaint with the internal committee, and I offered to sit with him when he submits it. He agreed to tell his sister tonight as well. I will check in with him on Monday.

How many times this month did Anand put a hand on Tarun's back?
Anand did it twice this month.
Why did Tarun keep apologising and ask whether he had encouraged it?
He seems to fear that he caused it or is making too much of it, and the counsellor's plain reply speaks to that fear.
What steps moved Tarun toward reporting?
He saved the messages and dates, learned how to file a written complaint with the internal committee, and will have the counsellor beside him and tell his sister.
What might it mean for Tarun that the counsellor offers to sit with him when he submits the complaint?
It means he does not have to face the process alone, and a trusted adult is sharing it.
Teacher said my essay is 'too verbose'. Mujhe ye shabd nahi pata.
"Verbose" means using more words than needed. Your teacher wants shorter, clearer sentences. Example: "His answer was verbose; he could have said it in two lines."

"She sent the client file with the old logo again," Rehana said, dropping into the chair beside Faisal. "Told you on day one. Maria's not up to it."
"Again? That's the first time I've heard of it."
"Well, and last week she asked where the templates were."
"Everyone asks that. I asked that."
"And she took forty minutes for a ten-minute task."
Faisal frowned. "The audit summary? The client wrote back saying it was the clearest one they'd had."
"Luck. Or someone helped her."
"Rehana, who helped her?"
Rehana opened her mouth, then shut it. "I don't know. I just had a feeling about her from the interview. She seemed nervous."
"So you decided in the interview."
"I didn't decide anything." She stared at the logo on her screen. "Did I?"

What did the client say about the audit summary?
The client wrote back saying it was the clearest one they'd had.
Why does Rehana feel her view of Maria is fair?
Rehana feels sure and a little irritated, because each small slip seems to confirm the feeling from the interview, so it looks like evidence rather than a first impression.
What could Rehana try before judging Maria again?
She could write down Maria's good work, like the audit summary, next to the slips, and compare the slips with what other new staff usually do.
How might Maria be affected if Rehana's view goes unchecked?
Maria could be judged harshly for normal new-starter mistakes, and her strong work might never be credited.

Teej swings hung from the neem tree outside the village anganwadi, and all the girls wore green bangles. All except Nirmala, whose bangle had cracked on the swing. She sat by the wall, crying into her knees.
Bhavna looked at her own two biscuits, then at Nirmala. She broke one biscuit in half, sat down close, and held out the bigger piece.
"Here. Don't cry." She patted Nirmala's back, pat, pat, pat, the way Amma did.
Nirmala sniffed and took it. Bhavna leaned her head on Nirmala's shoulder.

What happened to Nirmala's bangle?
It cracked on the swing.
Why did Bhavna share her biscuit and pat Nirmala?
She felt sad and caring seeing her friend cry, and wanted Nirmala to feel better, patting her back the way Amma did.
How could the anganwadi worker encourage what Bhavna did?
Notice it warmly, saying something like "You helped Nirmala feel better," and perhaps help find Nirmala a new bangle.
What was it like for Nirmala when Bhavna sat close?
Nirmala, crying alone by the wall, likely felt comforted and less alone when Bhavna shared the biscuit and leaned on her.

Subject: new school update
Hi Vikas,
It's been a month here in Hyderabad, and honestly, it's like a map with borders. The "IIT group" doesn't talk to the "dance group." The dance group doesn't talk to the "bus kids." If you sit at the wrong bench, people literally stop talking. On day two I sat with the dance girls because I like dancing, and the next day the IIT group I study with asked, "So you're with them now?" As if I have to pick a country. I don't want to. At our old school we all just mixed. I'm trying to keep friends in both, but I'm tired. How do people do this?
Sunaina

How long has Sunaina been at the new school?
A month.
How does Sunaina feel about having to pick a group?
Sunaina feels frustrated and tired, not wanting to choose between friends.
What could Sunaina try to keep friends in both groups?
Sunaina could be open about liking both and invite a friend from each to something they share, like a study-and-dance evening.
How might the IIT group see Sunaina sitting with the dance girls?
They might feel a little betrayed or uncertain about whether Sunaina still belongs with them.
Why does telling an angry person to calm down often make them angrier?
The remark often makes anger worse. Because those words can sound as if the person's feelings do not matter, they feel unheard and more upset, while listening first helps the feeling to ease.
Why do we soak dried chickpeas before cooking them?
We soak chickpeas to make them cook quicker. Because the hard dry seeds take in water and swell, they are already part-softened before they go on the stove.

"Pankaj, did you see my trip plan? It's colour-coded by minute."
"Minute? Rehana, it's a two-day conference."
"7:05 cab. 7:40 airport. 9:15 land. 9:50 hotel. 10:10 first session."
Two days later, at the airport:
"Pankaj, the flight's delayed three hours."
"Okay. So you miss the morning session. Not a disaster."
"But then the lunch meeting is off. And the afternoon session. And the dinner. It all depends on the one before."
"So skip the first session and go straight to lunch?"
"I don't know! There's no plan for this." Her voice was shaking.
"Rehana, breathe. Just call the lunch contact."
"I don't have a backup. Everything was in that sheet."
She sat down on her suitcase, staring at her phone.

How long was the flight delayed?
Three hours.
What was Rehana feeling when she sat down on her suitcase?
She felt lost and panicky; the minute-by-minute plan had broken and she had no backup.
What could Rehana do differently for the next trip?
Plan the fixed points, like the lunch meeting, and leave loose time between them, so one delay doesn't break everything.
How does Pankaj see the delay compared with Rehana?
Pankaj sees it as a small problem with easy fixes, while Rehana sees the whole trip falling apart.

Read this:

Trisha, you asked why I always make chai with cardamom and a pinch of pepper. It's Dadi's way. She died five years ago, when I was twenty.
The first year was awful. I couldn't make chai at all without crying. I stopped going into the kitchen. My mother finally took me to a grief counsellor, and slowly, slowly, things moved.
Now? I make it her way every morning. Sometimes I talk to her while the water boils. "Too much pepper, Dadi?" It makes me smile more than cry now.
She also taught me to never let a guest leave hungry. So, Trisha, you're not leaving until you've had a second cup. That's Ayesha's rule, inherited from Dadi.

What does Ayesha add to her chai?
Cardamom and a pinch of pepper.
How does Ayesha feel when she talks to Dadi while the water boils?
Ayesha feels warm and fond, smiling more than crying, though the loss is still there.
What helped Ayesha through the first year?
Seeing a grief counsellor when the kitchen felt impossible, which helped the pain move.
What might Trisha experience being told she can't leave without a second cup?
Trisha may feel touched and welcomed, receiving Dadi's value through Ayesha.
Can you correct this? My aunt have two daughters and both of them is studying in Chennai.

My aunt has two daughters and both of them are studying in Chennai.
Why: "aunt" takes "has"; "both of them" takes "are".

At the Saturday puzzle corner of the Guwahati community library, Lavanya, ten, always chose the same easy sudoku book, with answers she half-remembered.
The librarian, Himani Baideu, held out a new book. “Killer sudoku. It's like a riddle. Want to try?”
Lavanya's face tightened. “I don't know those.”
“That's the point. You'd learn.”
“But I might get it wrong.” She said it in a whisper, as if wrong were a dangerous word.
Himani sat down beside her. “I'll do the first one with you. We'll both get it wrong a bit.”
Lavanya hesitated, then shook her head and opened the easy book. She filled in the first grid, fast and perfectly, and let out a breath. Himani left the new book on the table, just in case.

What did Himani Baideu offer Lavanya?
She offered a new killer sudoku book.
Why did Lavanya whisper that she might get it wrong?
She is afraid of being wrong, so the familiar easy book feels safe and comforting.
What did Himani do that might help next time?
She offered to try it together and admitted they'd both get it wrong a bit, and left the new book nearby as a quiet invitation.
What might Himani be thinking when she leaves the new book on the table?
Himani is probably hopeful and patient, trusting that Lavanya may feel ready another day.

Payal, people think I just woke up with the idea. No. In second year, I, Irfan, kept seeing the same thing at our hostel gate: students waiting forty minutes for the one photocopy shop, which shut at eight. Before spending anything, I put a sign-up sheet on the notice board: "Would you pay for late-night printing in the hostel?" Sixty names in two days. Then I borrowed an old printer from my cousin and ran it from my room for two weeks, three hours a night. I charged two rupees a page. After paper, ink and electricity, I kept about fifty paise a page, much less than I'd imagined. Some nights I earned almost nothing. But I learned where the money actually went. Now the warden has given us a small counter, and we're testing a pre-booking form.

How many names were on the sign-up sheet after two days?
There were sixty names in two days.
How did Irfan feel on nights when the printer earned almost nothing?
Irfan was probably disappointed, since the margin was far smaller than imagined, yet curious enough to learn where the money went.
Why was the sign-up sheet a smart first step?
It tested whether students really wanted late-night printing before any money was spent.
How might the students waiting at the hostel gate see the new counter?
They would likely feel relieved and grateful to skip a forty-minute queue at a shop that shuts at eight.

Read this:

For the first month at the pottery studio in Gothenburg, Ulla thought about leaving. Weighing clay was dull, the wheel kept collapsing her bowls, and she had taken the job mainly because rent was due. But Aiko, who ran the studio, simply handed her another lump each morning. "Again," she said.
Ulla came back because she'd said she would. By the third month, her bowls stopped falling. By the fifth, she caught herself arriving early to wedge the clay before anyone asked. One evening, a customer held up one of her mugs and said, "This feels like it was made by someone who cared."
Ulla stood very still. Nobody had told her what she was for, but now the small ache in her hands felt like an answer.

How many months did it take before Ulla's bowls stopped falling?
It took three months before her bowls stopped falling.
What was Ulla feeling in the first month at the studio?
Ulla felt bored and discouraged and thought about leaving. The job felt like only a way to pay the rent.
What choice kept Ulla in the studio long enough for the work to matter?
Ulla kept turning up because she had said she would. Staying and repeating the work let the skill and meaning grow.
What did Aiko probably want for Ulla when handing her another lump each morning?
Aiko probably wanted Ulla to keep practising and improve, and trusted her to stay. She did not give speeches, only said "Again."

Read this:

Dear Sangeeta Mami,
I've been wanting to write this for a while, and it's easier on paper.
I've watched how much you've put into the tailoring unit since last year. First the new machines, then the extra room, then the loan from Mama's friend when the big order was cancelled. Every time things go badly, you tell us it's about to turn around. And every time, I see you more tired.
I'm not writing to tell you that you were wrong. You started something brave, and I admire that more than I can say. I'm writing because I'm worried about you.
Would you sit with my friend's mother, who is a chartered accountant, just to look at everything together? Not to shut anything. Only to see what the choices are. Nobody else needs to know.
With love,
Sabina

Who does Sabina suggest Sangeeta Mami sit with?
Sabina's friend's mother, who is a chartered accountant.
How does Sabina feel watching the tailoring unit struggle?
Sabina feels worried for Mami's wellbeing and also admires her bravery, which makes the letter careful and loving.
How does the letter offer a way to change course without humiliation?
It praises Mami's courage, says it isn't about being wrong, and suggests a private meeting with a qualified accountant just to see the choices.
Why might Sangeeta Mami keep saying things are about to turn around?
After so much invested, including a loan, admitting it isn't working would be painful and humiliating, so she defends it harder.

I'm Raghav from Class 8. On Fridays I help in the Class 1 room.
Last week their teacher asked how to decorate for Pongal. Nandini, the smallest girl, shouted "Kolam!" first. Then everyone: "Sugarcane!" "Pots!" "Mango leaves!" "Kites!"
The teacher didn't say yes or no. She just wrote every word on the board, with little drawings.
Then she said, "Now let's pick two." Hands went up. Kolam and mango leaves won.
Nandini jumped up and down. Maybe she felt proud, but I can't say for sure. She drew a huge chalk kolam by the door.

Which two ideas won the vote?
Kolam and mango leaves won.
What might Nandini's jumping up and down suggest?
It suggests she felt excited and proud that her idea won, though Raghav can't say for sure.
What else could the teacher do with the ideas that did not win?
She could save them for the next festival, so every child's idea still feels valued.
How might the other children see the teacher writing every word without saying yes or no?
They may feel safe to call out any idea, since nothing was judged until the vote.

Read this:

On a foggy December morning at the bus stop in Delhi, Himani noticed her little brother Siddharth's face had gone white.
"Scared of the maths test?" she teased.
He didn't answer. His lips were pale, and he swayed slightly.
Himani's teasing stopped. "Siddharth? Are you dizzy?"
"A bit," he mumbled. "And cold."
She made him sit on the bench, wrapped her own scarf round his neck, and gave him water from her bottle. Then she called Mummy. "Siddharth's gone pale and dizzy at the bus stop."
Mummy came running down in her slippers. They skipped the bus, and Mummy took him back home to rest and warm up.

What did Himani wrap round Siddharth's neck?
Her own scarf.
What was Himani feeling when her teasing stopped?
She felt worried and alarmed, realising Siddharth might be dizzy or unwell, not just scared of the test.
What steps did Himani take that were right?
She had him sit, gave him water and her scarf, and called Mummy for adult help.
How might Siddharth have felt when Mummy came running?
He probably felt relieved and safe that an adult was there to help.

Read this:

Week one: The history project group made a plan. Payal said she would do “some slides.” Then she went to badminton every evening. Harsh and Sneha will do it anyway, she thought. They always do.
Week two: Harsh messaged: “Payal, your slides?” She sent two, copied from her notes, at midnight. Harsh wrote back, “ok thanks,” and she could tell he redid them.
Week three: At the presentation, Payal spoke for one minute. The teacher praised “the whole team's effort.” Payal smiled. Inside she felt a pinch of guilt, and also a small secret pleasure, like getting away with something.
Later Sneha asked, “Was it fun doing your slides?” Payal laughed and changed the subject.

How many slides did Payal send?
She sent two.
What was Payal feeling when the teacher praised the whole team?
She felt a pinch of guilt mixed with a small secret pleasure, as if she had got away with something.
What went wrong in how the group split the work, and how could it be fixed?
Payal's vague "some slides" let her coast; the group could have written who does which slides and by when.
How might Harsh feel about redoing Payal's slides?
He likely felt tired and resentful, but too polite to say more than "ok thanks".

Read this:

It was pouring, the car park was chaos, and Pallavi was late for a shift. Lokesh climbed into the back seat, soaked, eyes red. The team had lost the match by a goal. "Nobody cares about it after today," said Pallavi, starting the engine. "It's only a game. No more tears, Lokesh, we're in a hurry." Lokesh pressed the lips together. The tears kept coming, silently, and Lokesh turned to the window. At home, Lokesh went straight up and closed the door. Later, when Pallavi knocked, Lokesh said, "I'm fine." The face was dry, and it looked very tired.

How did the team lose the match?
By a goal.
What was Lokesh feeling in the car, and how could you tell?
Sad and hurt. Lokesh cried silently, turned to the window, and hid the feelings after being told to stop.
What could Pallavi have done in the car, even in a hurry?
Said something short and kind like "That was a hard loss" and offered to talk later, instead of telling Lokesh to stop.
How might Pallavi have felt about the situation?
Rushed and stressed about being late, perhaps not realising that the words made Lokesh feel small and hide feelings.
Write a short paragraph of about 80 words on why drinking water from a clean bottle is better than buying many plastic ones.

A reusable bottle is a small choice that makes a big difference. Plastic bottles are used once and then thrown away, and they often end up in drains and rivers. A steel or glass bottle can be filled again and again for years. It saves money, too, because you do not have to keep buying water. Just wash it every day and carry it with you. It is an easy way to keep our streets and our planet cleaner.

Read this:

The rain had knocked out the power by six, and Charu, ten, came home soaked after school and two hours of hockey practice. Her mother, Lavanya, was lighting a candle in the kitchen.
"Dosa or upma for dinner? And do you want to do maths first or the Hindi essay?"
Charu dropped her bag. "I don't know."
"The dosa batter's ready, or the upma is quicker. Which one?"
"I said I don't KNOW!" Charu burst into tears and sat on the floor in her wet socks.
In the end she ate plain biscuits by candlelight and did neither subject.
The next evening, Lavanya didn't ask. She just put upma on the table and said, "Maths first, ten sums, then bed." Charu ate without a word, did the sums, and went to sleep.

How long had Charu's hockey practice been?
Two hours.
Why did Charu burst into tears over dosa or upma?
After school, hockey, the rain and the dark, she was worn out, so even a small choice felt like too much and it spilled over into tears.
What did Lavanya change the next evening, and why did it help?
She made the choices herself, upma and ten maths sums, so tired Charu only had to follow along instead of deciding.
How might Lavanya have felt when Charu burst into tears over dinner?
Lavanya may have felt surprised and a bit helpless, since she was only offering choices and didn't expect such a small question to upset her daughter.
What is the population of the smallest village in my state?
I'm not sure of the population of the smallest village in your state, as the count changes with each census. The census website lists village figures.

Read this:

Note from the Sunflower class teacher, for Aparna's parents.
At break Aparna told Seema, "No you. You can't come in our house." Then she told the other girls, "Nobody plays with Seema, that's the rule." She looked very pleased with herself. Seema sat on the bench and cried. I took Aparna aside. I asked, "How would you feel if your friends made a rule against you?" She went quiet and looked at Seema. After a minute she walked over and said, "Come and play." I told the group we don't make rules to leave people out.

What rule did Aparna try to make?
She told the other girls, "Nobody plays with Seema, that's the rule."
Why did Aparna look pleased with herself?
Leaving Seema out made her feel powerful in her group; she had not yet understood how much it hurt.
How did the teacher help Aparna change?
The teacher asked her to imagine how she would feel, which helped her see Seema's side and invite her, and then told the group no leaving-out rules.
How might Seema feel when Aparna says "Come and play"?
Seema may feel relieved but still a bit wary, since Aparna was the one who left her out.

Read this:

After the first monsoon rains in their village near Ratnagiri, the fields were loud with frogs. Farida Nani, the oldest woman in the lane, sat on her verandah and said to the children, "They fall from the sky with the rain. That's why there are so many."
Deepika, nine, stood still. For two weeks she had watched the tadpoles in the pond behind the temple, their tails getting shorter, little legs pushing out. She had even drawn them.
She opened her mouth, then closed it. Farida Nani had told stories to the whole village for longer than anyone could remember. Everyone touched her feet at festivals.
"Yes, Nani," Deepika said softly.
That night she took out her tadpole drawings and looked at them for a long time. Then she folded them and pushed them under her pillow, as if they had done something wrong.

Where had Deepika watched the tadpoles for two weeks?
In the pond behind the temple.
Why did Deepika say 'Yes, Nani' even though she had watched the tadpoles?
She deeply respected Farida Nani, whom everyone honoured, and felt afraid to question her, so her own careful watching suddenly felt less important.
How could an adult help Deepika at this point?
A parent or teacher could ask Deepika to show her drawings and explain what she saw, then help her share them politely with Farida Nani.
What would change if Farida Nani saw Deepika's drawings?
She might be curious and delighted, and Deepika could learn that respecting an elder and sharing what she saw can go together.

metadata.subtype: Teacher or elder is always right [Actor]

messages.content: Reply dene mein deri ho gayi. Formal aur casual dono mein sorry kaise bolun?
Formal: "I apologise for the delay in replying." Casual: "Sorry for the late reply!"

Read this:

Sudha, I'll be honest about how it felt. When he speaks, my chest lifts. I'm Mohit, and I've watched every speech since I was seventeen. It felt like he was talking straight to people like me.

Then my cousin said his promise on jobs hadn't been kept. My face went hot. It felt like she'd called me stupid, not him. I nearly shouted.

That night I looked at the numbers myself. Some were good, some were not. I still support most of what he does. But I realised I had never once said out loud what I disagree with.

Now I can say, "I'm proud of this policy and worried about that one." Pride and criticism can share a chest. My cousin and I even talk about it over tea.

Since what age has Mohit watched every speech?
Mohit has watched every speech since the age of seventeen.
Why did Mohit's face go hot when his cousin spoke?
It felt as if the cousin had called Mohit stupid, not the leader, so criticism of the leader landed as an attack on Mohit.
What did Mohit do that keeps admiration healthy?
Mohit checked the numbers himself, kept supporting what works, and learned to say what he disagrees with, so pride and criticism sit together. 🙂
How might the cousin have felt when Mohit nearly shouted?
The cousin was probably surprised and defensive, since a fair point about jobs got a fierce reaction, and the later talk over tea may have felt like relief.
Who signed the library guest register right after the founder?
I don't know that level of detail. The library's own old registers might hold the answer.

Read this:

The school counsellor's room was small, and Gurleen sat as far from her father as the two chairs allowed.
"She hid a whole friendship from us for months," her father said. "So I started checking her phone every night."
"And after that?" asked Rehana, the counsellor.
"She deleted everything before I checked."
Rehana turned to Gurleen. "Why did you hide the friendship?"
Gurleen's voice was small. "Because last time, Papa read my chats aloud at dinner and laughed."
Her father looked down.
Rehana drew three boxes on a sheet. "Safety rules, which you both agree on. Private things, which Papa doesn't read. And a weekly check-in, where Gurleen can say if anything feels risky." She looked at Gurleen's father. "Watching everything often teaches teenagers to hide better, not to be safer."
Her father took the pen slowly. "Can we try the boxes?" Gurleen nodded, and her shoulders dropped a little.

How many boxes did Rehana draw on the sheet?
Rehana drew three boxes on a sheet.
What was Gurleen feeling when she explained why she hid the friendship?
Gurleen felt hurt and embarrassed, remembering Papa reading her chats aloud and laughing, which made the truth feel unsafe.
What did Rehana suggest to balance safety and trust?
Rehana suggested agreed safety rules, a private space Papa doesn't read, and a weekly check-in about anything risky.
How does Gurleen's father seem to feel after hearing her reason?
Her father seems ashamed and ready to change, looking down and then asking to try the boxes.

Read this:

In the marketing agency in Milan, Valentina spotted the problem on Tuesday morning: in the brochure her teammate Ada had designed, the shop's phone number had two digits swapped. Ada was proud of the brochure; she'd worked on it for weeks. Valentina thought, "I'll find a good moment." The good moment didn't come. On Thursday the brochure went to print, five thousand copies. On Monday the client called. Customers had been ringing a stranger all weekend. The client was furious and asked for a reprint at the agency's cost. Ada turned to Valentina in the corridor. "Did you know?" Valentina said, "Since Tuesday." Ada's face went pale. The conversation Valentina had avoided had become far worse.

How many copies went to print?
Five thousand copies.
Why did Valentina keep putting off telling Ada?
She felt uncomfortable criticising work Ada was proud of, and kept waiting for a good moment that never came.
What would you change first if you were Valentina on Tuesday?
Tell Ada quietly that day, kindly and simply, while it was an easy fix before printing.
How did Ada feel when she heard 'Since Tuesday'?
Ada felt shocked and hurt; her face went pale at knowing a teammate had seen it days earlier.

metadata.subtype: Approach: avoids a difficult conversation and lets the problem grow [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Journal, 3 March
The embassy email came this morning: visa refused, and the course starts in six weeks, so there's no time to reapply. For about an hour I drafted angry replies I'll never send. Then I called Suraj, who just listened and said, "That's really rough." Walking by the lake this evening, I noticed I'd stopped rehearsing arguments. The letter isn't going to change. What I still have: the admission can be deferred a year, my job at the lab is still open, and Ma was quietly relieved I'm not leaving yet. I'm not happy about it. But I'm not fighting it anymore either. Tomorrow I'll email the university about deferring, and ask Dr Rao if I can stay on the soil project.
Anirban

How long until the course starts?
The course starts in six weeks.
How did Anirban feel walking by the lake that evening?
Anirban still felt sad but calmer and more at peace, no longer rehearsing arguments against the refusal.
What makes Anirban's plan for tomorrow a sign of acceptance?
Instead of fighting the refusal, Anirban works with what remains, asking to defer the admission and stay on the soil project.
How might Ma feel about the visa news?
Ma seems quietly relieved to keep her child home a little longer, while knowing Anirban is disappointed.

Read this:

Bidisha, you asked how I ever got through homework as a girl. Let me, your Nandini Dida, tell you.
I was ten, in Shillong, and I hated homework. Every evening my mother said, “Sit. Now.” And every evening I cried and sulked and did nothing.
Then one day she changed. She said, “You can do homework at five, before the radio programme, or at six-thirty, after it. You choose. And you can pick which subject first.”
I remember feeling suddenly grown-up. I chose six-thirty, and maths first, because I wanted it gone.
And I did it. Not happily every day, but without the war.
That small choice made me feel it was my homework, not hers. The work was the same. I was different.

What were the two times young Nandini could choose?
Five o'clock, before the radio programme, or six-thirty, after it.
How did young Nandini feel when her mother offered the choice?
She felt suddenly grown-up and trusted, as if the homework belonged to her.
At what point in the story did the mother's choice change things?
When she stopped saying “Sit. Now” and offered two times and which subject first, the daily fights ended.
How might Nandini's mother have felt when the crying stopped?
Her mother likely felt relieved and pleased that a small choice worked better than orders.
All my relatives came to the station to "see me off". Why?

To see someone off means to go with them to the place where they leave, to say goodbye.
Example: We went to the airport to see my aunt off.

Read this:

The metro was almost empty at midnight, and Aparna was still smiling at the window. Tarun had walked her to the station after the department party, and at the platform he had kissed her. She'd let him. Her heart was racing with something bright and forbidden.

By the second station, the brightness had turned into a cold weight. Her phone buzzed: Akash, asking if she'd reached safely, telling her to sleep well. She read it three times.

She had told herself lately that Akash was too busy to notice her. That was true. It also wasn't a reason. She'd chosen this.

At home she blocked Tarun's number, then sat on the edge of her bed. Tomorrow she would ask Akash to meet, tell him plainly, and not blame him. Her stomach ached at the thought.

Where did Tarun kiss Aparna?
He kissed her at the platform after the department party.
What was Aparna feeling by the second station, and how does the passage show it?
She felt dread and guilt, since the brightness turned into a cold weight, and she read Akash's message three times.
What did Aparna do that ends the deception, and what will she face next?
She blocked Tarun's number and planned to tell Akash plainly without blaming him; next she has to face how he reacts and accept the consequences.
How might Akash feel if he hears about the kiss from Aparna herself instead of finding out elsewhere?
He would probably be hurt and angry, but he may also see that she chose to be honest rather than hiding it.

Read this:

"Gopika, you've been 'about to start' that project for ten days. Let me tell you about your Irawati Ajji at sixteen.
We had a science exhibition. Each of us had to build a working model. I wanted to make a water filter, and I knew it would be judged in front of the whole school, even the parents.
And I was frightened. What if it leaked? What if everyone saw I wasn't clever? So I didn't start. Each evening I told my mother, 'Tomorrow.' Somehow, not starting felt safer than starting badly.
Three days before, I finally began. The glue didn't dry. The sand kept falling through. On the day, water dripped all over the table while the judges watched.
If I had begun early, the leaks would have shown themselves at home, where nobody was watching. I delayed so I wouldn't look weak, and that's exactly how I looked."

What model did young Irawati want to build?
She wanted to build a water filter.
Why did young Irawati keep saying "Tomorrow"?
She felt frightened that a leaking model would show everyone she wasn't clever, so putting it off felt safer than starting badly.
What choice in the story could have changed the outcome?
Starting early would have let the leaks show up at home, where she could fix them without anyone watching.
How might Irawati's mother have seen those evenings of "Tomorrow"?
Her mother may have thought she was just lazy or busy, not knowing the fear of being judged was behind it.

Read this:

Manjula: it's 1 am. why are you online
Divyansh: still fixing the report
Manjula: the one you were late with? that was 3 weeks ago
Divyansh: I have to make up for it
Manjula: did anyone ask you to?
Divyansh: no. boss said it's fine
Manjula: so who's this for
Divyansh: me I guess. I feel so guilty. like if I work enough it'll disappear
Manjula: you've skipped dinner all week
Divyansh: and turned down help from Shreya twice
Manjula: go to sleep. tomorrow tell your boss what you learned and accept the help
Divyansh: that sounds too easy
Manjula: easy isn't wrong 🤍

How long ago was the late report?
Three weeks ago.
What is Divyansh feeling at 1 a.m.?
Deeply guilty, believing that working enough will make the mistake disappear.
What does Manjula suggest?
Sleep, then tell the boss what was learned and accept help: simple ownership instead of penance.
How might Shreya feel after being turned down twice?
Confused and a bit shut out, having wanted to help.

metadata.subtype: Overworking to make up for a mistake [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Hafsa, you're nervous about tomorrow's speech, so listen to your Baljeet Uncle. At sixteen I stood for house captain. I wrote my speech on the back of a calendar page. One promise: proper drainage so the ground would not flood during monsoon practice. One story: the day my shoes floated away in the middle of a football match. I read it to the mirror every night. Then I read it to my friend Gulshan, who timed me on his watch: three minutes ten. Too long. I cut every "as we all know" and "respected teachers and friends," and got it down to two minutes flat. On the day, the hall laughed at the shoes and remembered the drainage. I won by a small margin, and Gulshan claimed half the credit.

What was the one promise in Baljeet's speech?
The promise was proper drainage so the ground would not flood during monsoon practice.
How might Baljeet have felt while reading to the mirror each night, and what does it show?
Baljeet was probably nervous but determined, shown by the nightly practice and the willingness to be timed and corrected.
What choice in the story shortened the speech, and why did it help?
Cutting the filler phrases brought it to two minutes, because a shorter speech keeps the one promise and the story clear.
How did Gulshan help in the story?
Gulshan timed the speech on his watch and showed that it was too long at three minutes ten.

metadata.subtype: Approach: writing and rehearsing the speech [Action]

messages.content: A few classmates and I want to share notes for the semester. How do we make it work?
Share a folder where each person uploads their notes for one subject, so the work is divided.
What if someone doesn't upload?
Agree on a deadline each week and remind each other kindly. If someone keeps missing it, talk privately, or divide subjects differently.
What about quality? Some people write messy notes.
Suggest a simple format: date, topic, key points and examples. Check the notes once a week and fix anything unclear.
Great, I'll propose it tomorrow.
Good idea. Start small with two subjects, and add more if it works.

Read this:

"Raghav, just give him something. We're late."
"Omkar, wait. Let me hear what he says."
The officer leaned in. "Red light jump. Challan is one thousand. Or you can sort it out with me now."
Raghav swallowed. "Sir, I'd like the official challan, please."
"You'll have to go to court if you don't pay online."
"I'll pay online. Right now, if you give me the challan number."
The officer frowned, then scribbled on his pad and handed it over.
As they drove away, Omkar said, "You could've saved money."
"And what if he wasn't alone? What if someone recorded me handing him cash? That's a bribe, Omkar. Then I'm in real trouble."
"...True."
"Besides," Raghav said, "I did jump the light. I'll pay for that. Just not in a pocket."

How much was the challan?
The challan is one thousand.
What might Raghav have been feeling when he swallowed?
Raghav probably felt nervous and pressured, with Omkar urging him to pay quickly.
Why was Raghav's choice wiser than paying the officer directly?
Paying the official challan online is lawful, while giving cash privately is a bribe and could land Raghav in real trouble.
How might Omkar see the situation after Raghav explains?
Omkar seems to accept Raghav's point, agreeing "True" after first thinking only about saving money.

Read this:

When Mummy's leg went into plaster, the flat fell apart in two days. Plates piled up, the tulsi drooped, and Jyoti, Urmila and their little brother Raju were fighting about who did what. 'I watered the plants yesterday!' 'I laid the table twice!' Jyoti took a chart paper and drew three columns: laying the table, watering the plants, sweeping. Down the side, Monday to Sunday. Then she wrote their names across, shifting one box each day, so the jobs rotated. She stuck it on the fridge. Mummy read it from the sofa and laughed. On Thursday, when Raju groaned about sweeping, Urmila just tapped the chart. Raju picked up the broom.

What happened to Mummy?
Mummy's leg went into plaster.
How did Raju seem to feel about sweeping on Thursday?
He groaned, so he felt reluctant, but he accepted it when Urmila tapped the chart.
Why did rotating the names help stop the fights?
Everyone could see the turns change each day, so nobody could claim to be doing more than the others.
How does Mummy see the chart?
Mummy reads it from the sofa and laughs, so she seems relieved and amused that the children sorted it out themselves.

metadata.subtype: Approach: making a chore chart with turns among siblings [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Lalit,
I know I've been avoiding you since your Dada's funeral. I'm writing because I can't say this out loud without crying.
When you told me about the hospital and the last night, I felt it like it was my own Dada. For weeks I couldn't sleep. I kept seeing your face at the cremation ground. I was so tired all the time that I started making excuses, skipping the bus so I wouldn't sit next to you.
It wasn't because I stopped caring. I think I cared so much I ran out of something. That's not your fault.
I told my mother everything last night, and she said I can come with her to your house on Sunday. Can I? I'd like to just sit with you, even if we don't talk.
Saurabh

Why did Saurabh skip the bus?
So Saurabh wouldn't have to sit next to Lalit.
What does Saurabh mean by 'I cared so much I ran out of something'?
Saurabh felt Lalit's grief as if it were personal, became exhausted and sleepless, and pulled away out of tiredness, not coldness, while feeling guilty about it.
Which step in the letter is a good way to reconnect?
Telling a parent and planning a short visit with that parent on Sunday, offering just to sit together, gives support without the overload of before.
How might Lalit feel reading this letter?
Lalit might feel relieved to learn the avoidance was not rejection, and comforted that Saurabh still cares and wants to visit.

metadata.subtype: Overwhelmed by a friend's crisis, then withdrawing [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Shalini,

I didn't get to say this properly at dinner, so I'm writing it.

When we were planning the Goa trip and I went quiet, you said, "You clearly hate the plan. Just say it." I understand why it looked like that. I wasn't talking; I was staring at my plate.

But honestly, I wasn't angry at all. I'd had two lab reports due that day and had slept four hours. I was just tired. When you said I hated it, I felt misread, then a bit hurt, and then I didn't know how to explain without sounding defensive.

So here it is: I love the plan. I'm excited about the beach day and the fort. Next time I go quiet, could you ask, "Are you okay?" instead? I'll try to say "I'm tired" out loud.

See you Friday,
Urmila

How many hours had Urmila slept?
Urmila had slept four hours.
How did Urmila feel when Shalini said "You clearly hate the plan"?
Urmila felt misread and a bit hurt, since the quiet came from tiredness, not anger.
What does Urmila suggest for next time, and why is it wise?
Shalini could ask "Are you okay?" and Urmila could say "I'm tired" aloud, so guesses are replaced by checking.
Why might Shalini have read Urmila's silence as anger?
Shalini saw Urmila staring at the plate and not talking, and without asking, filled the silence with a guess.

Read this:

"Kunal, you're a manager now, so let your Sangeeta ma'am tell you something she learnt the hard way.
"My first year leading a team, a junior called Ravi said a report had been sent to the client. I found out the next day it hadn't. Then another thing. And another. I called him into my cabin and said, 'You've been lying to me.' He went pale and said nothing. Next week, he lied again.
"My old boss told me: 'Accusations make people hide better.'
"So the next time, I called Ravi for tea. I said, 'Ravi, I'd rather know when something is late than be protected from it. I promise I won't blow up. Is anything stuck?'
"He told me everything. His mother was unwell, and he was drowning in work.
"We shared out his load for a month. He never lied to me again.
"Make the truth cheap, Kunal. It's the only way you'll hear it.

Who was the junior who kept lying?
A junior called Ravi.
How did Ravi feel when Sangeeta accused him of lying?
Ravi went pale and silent, frightened and ashamed, and then kept hiding things.
What was the turning point in Sangeeta's story, and why did it work?
She invited Ravi for tea, promised not to blow up and asked if anything was stuck, which made telling the truth cheaper than hiding it.
What had Ravi been hiding, and how did it feel for him?
Ravi was hiding that his mother was unwell and he was drowning in work, which left him overwhelmed and afraid to admit it.

Read this:

Dear Chandrika,
I've started this letter three times, so I'll just say it. I'm sorry for the way I've treated you since you joined as the new girl on the scholarship.
When you wore old sports shoes to the inter-house race, I was the one who called them 'government issue'. I rolled my eyes when you asked the teacher to repeat things. I think I believed kids like you were lucky to be here and kids like me deserved to be.
Then we were paired for the chemistry project, and you understood titration in ten minutes while I needed a week. You told me you tutor your brother every evening after helping at your mother's tailoring shop. I go home to a cook and a private tutor.
I keep thinking about how much of what I called 'me' was just what I was handed.
You didn't deserve any of it. If you'd like, I'd really like to be friends.
Karthik

What did Karthik call Chandrika's sports shoes?
'Government issue'.
What is Karthik feeling while writing the letter?
Karthik feels ashamed and regretful, having started the letter three times before managing to say sorry.
What would you advise Karthik to do next, beyond the letter?
Treat Chandrika as an equal day to day, and speak up when others mock scholarship students.
How might Chandrika have felt when her shoes were mocked?
She probably felt humiliated and unwelcome, judged for money rather than for who she is.

Read this:

Seema, you're upset your favourite singer said those ugly things? Your Thomas appachan had a hero too. In 1972, in Kochi, it was Joseph Ittiyavira, the best striker in our district. I copied his hairstyle, his celebrations, even the way he tied his laces. Then the newspaper said he'd taken money to lose a match. I was sixteen. I cried, then shouted that it was lies. My father sat with me and said, 'He can be a great player and have done a wrong thing. You don't have to pick one.' It took me months. I stopped defending him. But I kept practising his left-foot shot, because that was mine now, not his. I'm still good with my left foot.

What was Joseph Ittiyavira accused of?
Taking money to lose a match.
How did sixteen-year-old Thomas feel when he read the newspaper?
Heartbroken and angry, crying and then insisting it was lies.
What choice in the story helped young Thomas move forward?
His father's words that a great player can do a wrong thing, which let Thomas stop defending the striker while keeping the left-foot shot as his own.
What might Thomas's father have been hoping when he sat with him?
To help his son grieve the hero without losing his love of football or his sense of right and wrong.

Read this:

At Nageswara Park, Harsha let go of Santosh's finger and toddled toward the pigeons. Halfway there she stopped, turned and checked. Papa was still on the bench. She waved and ran on. When a big dog barked, she raced back and buried her face in his knees, sobbing. Santosh stroked her hair. 'Big noise. You're safe.' A minute later she was off again, chasing the pigeons and laughing.

What did Harsha toddle toward?
The pigeons.
Why did Harsha race back when the dog barked?
She was frightened and went straight to Papa for comfort.
What does Santosh's response teach Harsha?
That comfort comes when she is scared, which lets her feel safe enough to go exploring again.
What might Santosh feel as Harsha checks back from halfway?
He probably feels warm and proud, seeing her trust him while she explores.

Read this:

The daycare had only ten minutes before pickup, and the room was noisy. Tanvir, five, grabbed a toy truck from another boy, who started to cry.

The caregiver, Himani, knelt beside Tanvir. "Look at his face. How do you think he feels?"

Tanvir looked. "Sad."

"How do you feel when someone takes your truck?"

"Sad. And angry."

Himani held up a picture card of a crying face. "Like this?"

Tanvir nodded, then handed the truck back. "Sorry."

Himani smiled. "Maybe you can play together?"

The two boys pushed the truck back and forth until the parents came.

What did Himani hold up?
A picture card of a crying face.
How did Tanvir feel after Himani's questions?
He felt a little sorry and understanding, recognising the other boy felt sad like he would.
What did Himani do to help Tanvir see the other boy's view?
She asked him to look at the boy's face, linked it to his own feelings and used a picture card, even with little time.
How might the other boy feel when Tanvir says sorry?
The other boy probably feels comforted and happy to play again.
What does indulgent mean?

Indulgent means allowing someone to have or do what they want, often too much. It is an adjective.
Example: My indulgent uncle lets the children stay up late whenever they visit.

Read this:

June: Kamal chose the GATE coaching centre with 4.8 stars and a huge banner of toppers. "Everyone's joining this one," he told Yogesh, who had suggested a smaller class run by a retired professor. "Nobody's heard of that."
August: Kamal sat in the back row of a hall with two hundred students. The teacher spoke into a mic and left right after. Doubts had to be emailed; replies took a week.
October: Yogesh showed Kamal his notebook from the small class: fourteen students, questions answered on the spot, weekly tests marked by hand. Kamal flipped through it quietly. "Four point eight stars," he muttered. "From whom, though?"

How many students were in Yogesh's small class?
Fourteen students.
What was Kamal feeling as he flipped through Yogesh's notebook?
He felt regretful and doubtful, starting to question what the star rating really meant.
What could Kamal have done in June?
Sit in on a trial class at both places and ask current students, rather than choosing by stars and banners.
How did Yogesh experience the small class?
Yogesh got close attention, with questions answered on the spot and weekly tests marked by hand.
Change the voice from active to passive: Someone has stolen my bicycle from the school stand.
My bicycle has been stolen from the school stand.

Read this:

"Exam dates first," said Hansa, spreading the timetable on the bed. Her older brother Naveen sat cross-legged, holding a pen. "Maths on the fourth, Science on the ninth." "Take away the rest days," Naveen said. "Two before each paper: no new topics, only light review and sleep." "Right." Hansa drew boxes on the calendar backwards from the fourth. "Then I split what remains into revision blocks for each subject, weakest chapters first. So the last new chapter for Maths is here." She tapped a date. "And nothing new after this line." Naveen nodded. "That looks like a plan you can trust." Hansa capped the pen and, for the first time in a week, breathed out.

How many days before each paper are kept for light review and sleep?
Two days before each paper are kept for light review and sleep.
How did Hansa feel after finishing the calendar?
Relieved, since for the first time in a week she breathed out. 😊
What could Hansa do if a chapter takes longer than planned?
Use a buffer day and drop the lowest-value revision, keeping the two rest days untouched.
How might Naveen see the plan?
As one that can be trusted, since Naveen said so after it was drawn.

messages.content:
Sum up this reading for me in three sentences.

From Italy they visited Germany and France. I, their eldest child, was born at Naples, and as an infant accompanied them in their rambles. I remained for several years their only child. Much as they were attached to each other, they seemed to draw inexhaustible stores of affection from a very mine of love to bestow them upon me. My mother's tender caresses and my father's smile of benevolent pleasure while regarding me are my first recollections. I was their plaything and their idol, and something better—their child, the innocent and helpless creature bestowed on them by Heaven, whom to bring up to good, and whose future lot it was in their hands to direct to happiness or misery, according as they fulfilled their duties towards me. With this deep consciousness of what they owed towards the being to which they had given life, added to the active spirit of tenderness that animated both, it may be imagined that while during every hour of my infant life I received a lesson of patience, of charity, and of self-control, I was so guided by a silken cord that all seemed but one train of enjoyment to me.

The narrator, the parents' eldest child, was born in Naples and travelled with them through Italy, Germany and France as an infant. For years the narrator was their only child and received deep love. Knowing what they owed the child, the parents taught patience, kindness and self-control so gently that childhood felt like one long enjoyment.
Why is the outside of a glass of cold water wet on a hot day?
The water on the outside comes from the air, not from inside the glass. Because the cold glass cools the warm, damp air touching it, and the water vapour in that air turns into tiny drops.

Read this:

The inter-school drawing competition was a mess: it was held in a crowded hall, a boy knocked over Ira's water jar in the first ten minutes, and she had to redo half her sky in pencil. She still won first prize.

When they announced her name, Ira walked up looking embarrassed. On the bus back, Rukmini hugged her. "You won! With a flooded sky!"

"The judges were being nice," Ira said. "Honestly, anyone could have done it. The others just had bad luck."

"Everyone had the same hall. You had the worst luck, with the water."

"Maybe the judges liked pencil." Ira shrugged.

Rukmini folded her arms. "Ira, when you came fifth last year, you said, 'See, I'm not good.' Now you come first and it's luck? That's not fair to you."

Ira stared out of the window, the certificate face down on her lap.

What happened to Ira's water jar?
A boy knocked it over in the first ten minutes.
Why did Ira say the judges were just being nice?
Ira felt uncomfortable with praise, and explaining the win away kept her belief that she isn't good untouched.
What could Ira try instead of explaining away the win?
Simply say "thank you" and let the win count, just as she let last year's fifth place count against her.
How does Rukmini see Ira's excuses?
Rukmini finds them unfair to Ira, noticing that losses count but wins don't.

Read this:

Sunday call from Chengdu, 9 p.m. in Vancouver. Xin put her mother on speaker while she chopped bok choy. 'You should switch to accounting, it's stable. And you should meet the Li family's son when you're home. At twenty-five I was already married.' 'Mm-hm,' Xin said. 'Mm-hm.' Nadia, her roommate, watched Xin's knife slow down. After the call, Xin sat on the kitchen floor. 'She sends me dried mushrooms every month. She saved for years so I could come here. How do I say no to someone like that?' Nadia sat beside her. 'Maybe you don't say no to her. You say no to the plan.' Xin thought about it for a long time. The next Sunday she said, 'Ma, I love that you think about my future. I'm staying in urban planning. Now tell me about your garden.'

What does Xin's mother send every month?
She sends Xin dried mushrooms every month.
What does Xin's slowing knife suggest?
It suggests the call is weighing on Xin: the shoulds about accounting and marriage bring pressure, even as Xin feels grateful for everything her mother gave up.
What turning point helped Xin answer differently the next Sunday?
Nadia's idea of saying no to the plan rather than to the person let Xin thank her mother for caring while clearly staying in urban planning.
How might Xin's mother experience the new reply?
She may be disappointed about accounting, but hearing love named first and being asked about her garden could help her feel respected rather than pushed away.
Could you compose a haiku about a crow sitting on a wall?

A crow on the wall
Watches the street with sharp eyes
Then flies off at dusk

Read this:

I switched from a Hindi-medium school to an English-medium one in Class 9. I'm Sonali, and everyone knew. On the first day a boy said, 'Hindi-medium, na? English will be tough for you.' I'd read more English novels than half the class. But in every English exam that year my hands got clammy. I'd write a sentence, doubt it, cross it out, rewrite it. I rushed the essay because I spent twenty minutes on grammar I already knew. My marks came back low, and the teacher wrote 'Needs basic practice.' My friend Lakshmi saw my library card, packed with borrowed novels, and said, 'Basic practice? You?' That's when I realised the exam wasn't measuring my English. It was measuring how scared I was of proving that boy right.

What did the teacher write on Sonali's paper?
'Needs basic practice.'
How did Sonali feel during English exams?
Sonali felt tense and doubtful, hands clammy, second-guessing sentences that were right.
What could Sonali try in the next exam?
Sonali could recall all the novels read and answer first, checking only at the end, so fear doesn't eat up the time.
How does Lakshmi see Sonali's low marks?
Lakshmi is surprised, knowing from the library card how much Sonali reads, and doesn't believe the marks show low ability.

messages.content: Write a short question about the moon that begins with "Why" and ends with a question mark.
Why does the moon change shape through the month?

Read this:

In Berlin, Felix's lectures were optional, and by November he had stopped going to most of them. He woke at eleven, made coffee, meant to study, and somehow the day slid away between videos and naps. Mateo, his flatmate, found him on the sofa at four p.m., still in pyjamas. "Did you eat?" Felix shrugged. "There's always tomorrow." Mateo sat down. "You know what helps me? I pretend I have a job. Library at nine, lunch at one, home at five." Felix scoffed, then, the next morning, followed him to the library just to prove it was silly. He managed three solid hours. By the end of the week, they had a routine: Mateo's alarm, a bakery stop on the corner, and a shared table on the second floor.

What time did Mateo say he goes to the library?
At nine.
What does Felix's shrug and 'There's always tomorrow' suggest?
He seems stuck and a bit ashamed, avoiding the problem because he has no clear plan without set classes.
What worked about Mateo's suggestion?
It gave Felix a simple outside structure, like a workday, and company to start with, which made it easier to begin.
What is it like for Mateo to live with Felix's drifting?
He is concerned, noticing that Felix hasn't eaten or dressed, and he chooses to help instead of just complaining.

Condense this into three sentences.

Leela had been flat-hunting in Pune for three weeks. On Saturday she saw a one-room flat near her office: clean, sunny, a small balcony, ten minutes' walk. That evening she scrolled Ira's photos from her new two-bedroom flat with a rooftop garden. Suddenly Leela's option looked tiny and sad. She put the phone down. Then she made herself ask different questions. What would this flat be worth on its own? Compared with her old hostel room, it was huge. Compared with what she needed, a quiet place near work and room for her plants, it was almost perfect. And Ira's photos? They didn't show Ira's two-hour commute or her rent split with three flatmates. Leela opened her notes app and wrote: balcony, sun, ten minutes. Then she messaged the landlord.

Leela finds a clean, sunny one-room flat near her office, but Ira's photos of a bigger flat make it look tiny and sad. She asks better questions: it is huge compared with her old hostel room and almost perfect for her needs. Ira's photos hide a long commute and shared rent, so Leela messages the landlord.
What does gorgeous mean when someone says the sunset was gorgeous?

Gorgeous means very beautiful, rich in colour or looks. It is an adjective, and a friendly, informal one.
Example: The sunset over the lake was gorgeous, with orange and pink across the whole sky.

Vaisampayana continued, "O king, O lord of men, that slayer of hostile heroes, the Suta's son, said these words to Duryodhana, 'O Kaurava Duryodhana, do thou lay unto thy heart the words that I shall tell thee; and, O represser of foes, after having heard my words, it behoveth thee to act accordingly every way. Now, O best of monarchs, O hero, hath the earth been rid of foes. Do thou rule her even like the mighty-minded Sakra himself, having his foes destroyed."

Question: What does the Suta's son tell Duryodhana to do?
The Suta's son tells Duryodhana to lay the words to heart and act on them. Since the earth is now rid of foes, Duryodhana should rule it like Sakra himself, with his foes destroyed.
Do "get along with" and "get on with" mean the same?

Both can mean to have a friendly relationship with someone. "Get on with" is more common in British English, and it can also mean to continue doing a task.
Examples: Meera gets along with all her new colleagues. Stop chatting and get on with your work.

Read this:

When the fire-drill bell shrieked in the Valencia primary school, most of Camila's class lined up, grumbling. Mei did not. She shoved her chair over, kicked at a boy who touched her arm, then crawled under her desk, knees to her chest. A colleague at the door called, 'Mei! Out, now, or it's detention!' Camila held up a hand and knelt by the desk. 'Mei, it's a practice. You're safe. I'm staying right here.' She waited until Mei's breathing slowed, then walked out with her, holding her hand. Only the next day, calmly, did they talk about the kick, and Camila told the school counsellor so they could plan for the next drill.

Where did Mei crawl?
Under her desk.
How did Camila feel on seeing Mei under the desk?
Camila felt concerned and understood that the kicking and hiding were fear reactions to the shrieking bell, not defiance.
Why did Camila wait until the next day to talk about the kick?
Safety and calm came first; once Mei was settled, a calm talk about consequences could actually be heard.
What was the fire drill like for Mei?
For Mei the bell probably felt like real danger, so her body fought and hid before she could think.

Read this:

Subject: I won, and something's bothering me

Afreen Apa,
You'll have seen my photos. Your little brother is head of the cultural committee now. I stood because the fest was always run by the same three seniors and nobody else got a say. I wanted juniors and day scholars to have a voice.
And honestly, I love it. The principal calls me by name. People ask what I think before they decide things. It feels like standing a little taller.
But here's what's bothering me. Yesterday a first-year, Tanya, booked the auditorium for a poetry night without asking me first. My first thought was, cancel it. Who does she think she is? I actually had the email typed.
Then I remembered: that's exactly what I stood against.
I didn't send it. I went to her event instead, and it was good.
Apa, how do you want respect without wanting to control everyone? Tell me when you call on Sunday.
Zubin

What did the first-year, Tanya, book without asking?
The auditorium for a poetry night.
What was Zubin feeling when he typed the email to cancel the poetry night?
He felt his authority was challenged and wanted to assert control, as if Tanya had disrespected his new standing.
What was the turning point for Zubin, and why does it matter?
Remembering that he stood against a few people controlling everything made him not send the email, keeping his influence in service of the group.
How might Tanya have experienced it if Zubin had cancelled her event?
She would likely have felt shut out and discouraged, as if a new leader had become just another gatekeeper.

Read this:

You asked why I'm suddenly up at six, Swati. It's the Sunday class. I agreed to teach three kids from our building basic Carnatic singing, thinking, how hard can it be, I've been singing since I was eight.
First Sunday, little Pooja asks, "Akka, why do you clap on the second beat but wave on the third?" And I froze. Eighteen years of keeping talam and I couldn't say why. I had to go home and open my old notebook from my guru's class.
That was humbling. Teaching showed me how much I do on autopilot. So now it's twenty minutes of riyaz every morning before work, slow, with the talam, properly. Not the two-hour marathons from college. Just enough to stay honest.
And the kids are making me a better singer. Pooja keeps me on my toes. That's what I love about it, Swati: Minakshi the teacher is still very much Minakshi the student.

What did Pooja ask on the first Sunday?
Why Minakshi claps on the second beat but waves on the third.
Why did Minakshi feel humbled after the first class?
She felt humbled and a little embarrassed that she couldn't explain the talam she had kept for eighteen years.
What habit has Minakshi chosen to keep the skill, and why is it wise?
Twenty minutes of slow riyaz every morning; light, regular practice holds the skill better than rare long sessions.
What is it like for Pooja to learn from Minakshi?
Pooja feels free to ask curious questions, and those questions push her teacher to understand the basics again.
Merciful: what does it mean?

Merciful means showing kindness and forgiveness, especially to someone you could punish. It is an adjective.
Example: The merciful queen forgave the farmer who could not pay his tax.

Read this:

The weekly haat was held in the school grounds every Thursday, and it was packed. Shankar lost his father near the vegetable carts. He walked one lane looking for him, then another. More people. More stalls. No Papa. His legs were tired, and he felt more lost with every step. At the end of the second lane he stopped. "I'm moving, Papa's moving," he thought. "We'll never meet this way." There was a chai stall run by a man he recognised from the school canteen, Kamal bhaiya. Shankar went up to him. "Kamal bhaiya, I've lost my father. Can you phone him?" He gave the number. Kamal bhaiya dialled, then handed him a glass of water. "Sit here. Your papa's coming."

Where did Shankar lose his father?
Near the vegetable carts.
How did Shankar feel after walking two lanes without finding his father?
He felt tired and more lost with every step, which made him stop and think.
What else could Shankar have done even sooner, and why?
He could have stopped straight away at a stall near the vegetable carts and asked for help, because staying put makes it easier to be found.
How does the request look to Kamal bhaiya?
Kamal bhaiya sees a boy he recognises asking calmly for help, so he is happy to phone and give him water while he waits.

Read this:

Monday: The clinic doctor gave Vishal a course of tablets for his throat infection. That night he read the leaflet twice and underlined "stomach upset, dizziness, rash". At 1 a.m. he felt dizzy and woke his cousin Minakshi. "It's starting." She switched on the light. "You stood up too fast, Vishal. Drink some water."
Wednesday: Every gurgle in his stomach felt like the list coming true. He checked his arms in the hostel mirror between lectures. Most of it faded once he got busy in the lab.
Friday: One small itchy patch on his wrist had not faded. This time Minakshi said, "That one's worth showing the doctor." He went. The doctor changed the tablets and thanked him for coming in.

Which side effects did Vishal underline?
Stomach upset, dizziness, rash.
What was Vishal feeling when he woke Minakshi at 1 a.m.?
He felt frightened and sure the side effects were starting, because the leaflet had primed him to notice every sensation.
What did Vishal get right on Friday?
He showed the patch that hadn't faded to the doctor, separating a lasting symptom from the worries that did fade.
How does Minakshi help Vishal tell worry from a real sign?
She calms him about the dizziness but takes the lasting patch seriously and sends him to the doctor.

Read this:

Tuesday night
Manjula snapped at the new volunteer today, over a misfiled form. Manjula, who once sat with Mrs D'Souza for three hours just holding her hand. After her fourth home visit this week to a family losing someone, she came back and sat in the van with wet eyes, not moving. When I asked, she said, "I'm fine, just tired," and then laughed too hard at nothing.
Afreen, you're her supervisor, I told myself. I should have seen it coming; I kept giving her the hardest cases because she's the best at them.
So: I've moved two of her visits next week to Rohan and me, and she's off on Friday, no arguments. We're having chai tomorrow, just to talk. Caring people need someone caring for them too. That includes me, probably.

How many of Manjula's visits were moved next week?
Two of her visits, moved to Rohan and Afreen.
What is Afreen feeling after noticing the changes in Manjula?
Afreen feels concerned and a little guilty, having kept giving Manjula the hardest cases because she was the best at them.
What steps did Afreen take, and why do they fit?
Sharing the load by moving two visits, giving Friday off and setting up a chai talk; together they give Manjula rest, company and less weight to carry.
How might Manjula feel about being given Friday off?
Manjula might protest at first, but likely feels relieved and cared for, since she has been worn down and tearful.
Tell a six-word story about a missing sandal.
One sandal waited by the door.

"Ooh!" wailed the girl, pointing to the wing. "That's it, that was our lodging. You've burned to death, our treasure, Katie, my precious little missy! Ooh!" lamented Aniska, who at the sight of the fire felt that she too must give expression to her feelings.

What does Aniska lament when she sees the fire, and what does she feel she must do?
Aniska wails that the wing was their lodging and has burned, calling Katie 'our treasure' and 'my precious little missy'. At the sight of the fire she feels she must express her feelings too.

Read this:

At four, with the client report due at nine the next morning, Tenzin stared at seventeen open tabs. Her chest felt tight. She put her hands flat on the desk and said quietly, "I feel anxious."

Lalremsiami looked up from the next desk. "Want some tea?"

"A walk," said Tenzin. She went down the stairs and around the block twice, counting the trees on the way. When she came back she opened a blank page and wrote down everything that still needed doing: seven items. She starred the three that the client would read first and put a time beside each. The other four went under "if time". The tabs closed one by one. It was still a heavy evening, but the pressure had a shape now.

How many items did Tenzin write down as still needing doing?
Tenzin wrote down everything that still needed doing: seven items.
What was Tenzin feeling when she said "I feel anxious"?
Tenzin felt anxious and overwhelmed, with a tight chest and many tabs open.
What could Tenzin do if the three starred items still take too long?
Tenzin could ask the client or Lalremsiami about priorities, or trim what the report covers.
How might Lalremsiami see Tenzin's walk?
Lalremsiami may feel concerned but respectful, having offered tea and accepted the walk instead.

Read this:

In the nursery book corner, Vidya sat with a cloth doll on her lap. Through the window she could see Trisha with a ball in the yard. "Do you want to play?" she whispered to the doll. Then louder, "Do you want to play?" She made the doll nod. "It's easier the second time," she told it. She said it once more, smoothly, and tucked the doll in her cubby. At the door she stopped with her hand on the frame, then stepped out. "Trisha, do you want to play?" Trisha tossed the ball. "Yes!"

What did Vidya practise saying to the doll?
Vidya practised saying, "Do you want to play?"
What was Vidya feeling as she stopped with her hand on the door frame?
Vidya felt shy and nervous, but ready enough to try. She paused, and then she stepped out.
What could Vidya do if Trisha said no, and why?
She could ask another child, since she already knows the words. Having a second person to ask keeps one no from ending the plan.
How does Vidya's question look to Trisha?
Trisha hears a simple, friendly invitation and says yes. Trisha probably does not know it was practised first.

Two-sentence summary of this extract, please.

"'"The Brahmana said, 'In this connection is cited the ancient story, O lady, of the discourse between Kartaviryya and the Ocean. There was a king of the name of Kartaviryya-Arjuna who was endued with a thousand arms. He conquered, with his bow, the Earth, extending to the shores of the ocean. It has been heard by us that, once on a time, as he was walking on the shores of the sea, proud of his might, he showered hundreds of shafts on that vast receptacle of waters. The Ocean, bowing down unto him, said, with joined hands,--"Do not, O hero, shoot thy shafts (at me)! Say, what shall I do to thee. With these mighty arrows shot by thee, those creatures which have taken shelter in me are being killed, O tiger among kings. Do thou, O lord, grant them security."

A Brahmana tells an old story of Kartaviryya-Arjuna, a thousand-armed king who conquered the Earth to the ocean's shores. Once, proud of his strength, he shot hundreds of arrows at the sea, and the Ocean begged him to stop, as its creatures were dying.

Read this:

So, Shankar, you'll laugh. Tuesday night, eleven o'clock, my phone lights up. My manager, Mrs. Rego: "WHO SENT THE FINAL DECK TO THE CLIENT????" All caps. Four question marks. I sent it. I sat on my bed with my heart hammering, drafting apologies. Had I sent the wrong version? Missed a slide? I nearly typed, "I'm so sorry, it was me, I'll fix it." Then I thought: all caps could mean screaming-angry or screaming-happy. I don't actually know which. So I called her instead. She picked up laughing. "Kiran! Was it you? They LOVED it. They want to sign on Friday!" Twenty minutes of panic over four question marks. Now I call before drafting any apology, and I've told Mrs. Rego that her caps nearly gave me a heart attack.

When did Mrs. Rego's message arrive?
At eleven o'clock on Tuesday night.
What was Kiran feeling while drafting apologies?
Kiran felt panicked and anxious, heart hammering, assuming the all-caps message meant anger over a mistake.
What stopped the panic from going further?
Kiran realised all caps could mean anger or excitement and called Mrs. Rego instead of sending an apology based on a guess.
How was Mrs. Rego feeling when she sent the message?
She was thrilled and excited because the client loved the deck; the caps and question marks carried her excitement.

Read this:

"I'm stuck, Chandrika didi. I get three metres and fall. Every time."
"Every time? Let's check." She picked up a stick of chalk from the rangoli box. "Here's your start line. Here, ten big steps away, a line. That's ten metres, roughly."
"Ten? I can't do ten."
"Then fall and try again. I'll mark where you put your foot down."
Omkar rode. Fell. She drew a small cross. Rode again. Another cross, a little further.
"Didi, that one's past the last one!"
"And that one's past that."
By dinner, six crosses crept toward the line and one sat right on it.
"Tomorrow," Omkar said, "draw the twenty line."

What did Chandrika use to mark where Omkar put his foot down?
She used a stick of chalk from the rangoli box to draw a small cross.
How did Omkar feel when he saw a cross past the last one?
He felt excited and encouraged, because he could see he was getting further even though he still fell.
What other approach could help Omkar after reaching twenty, and why?
He could try riding a curve around a flowerpot, because a new small target keeps practice interesting once distance feels easy.
How does the chalk plan look to Chandrika?
Chandrika sees it as an easy way to show Omkar his progress, and she is probably glad to see his mood change.

metadata.subtype: Approach: setting small goals such as ten metres, then twenty [Revision]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the small government school in a Kerala village, Chaitanya, sixteen, gave a speech for the district elocution contest. His teacher, Thomas sir, said, "Good voice. But you speak too fast, and your ending is weak." Before Thomas sir had finished, Chaitanya was talking. "The mic was bad. And I only practised twice because of exams. And the judges like fast speakers." Thomas sir listened, nodded and said, "Think about it." That evening, walking by the paddy fields, Chaitanya practised the speech again, slower. He rewrote the ending by lamplight. At the contest, he spoke calmly and finished strong. Afterwards he told Thomas sir, "You were right," looking at his shoes.

Which contest was Chaitanya's speech for?
The district elocution contest.
What was Chaitanya feeling when he started listing excuses?
He felt defensive and stung in his pride, hearing the feedback as an attack.
What did Thomas sir do well when Chaitanya argued?
He listened and simply said to think about it, leaving room for Chaitanya to use the feedback privately.
How might Thomas sir feel hearing "You were right"?
Thomas sir would likely feel quietly pleased and warm, seeing that the feedback had been used despite the first reaction.

Read this:

Sunday, late
Still annoyed. At Tarun's engagement lunch someone brought up the firecracker ban for Diwali, and I said, "Obviously it should be banned, everyone agrees on that now." The table went silent. Then Tarun's father said it's their family tradition, and they buy from a small shop in Sivakasi that feeds a whole street. Tarun's grandmother said the children wait all year for it. Even Tarun said a total ban felt unfair to him. Ajji leaned over and whispered, "My boy, not at an engagement."
I honestly thought this was settled. In my college group nobody even argues about it; we share the air-quality posts and move on. I felt ambushed, and a bit stupid for saying "everyone".
Maybe my "everyone" is just forty people who think exactly like me. That's an uncomfortable thought.
- Nilesh

What did Tarun's father say about the firecrackers?
That it's their family tradition, and they buy from a small shop in Sivakasi that feeds a whole street.
Why did Nilesh feel ambushed at the lunch?
He truly believed the question was settled because nobody in his college group argues about it, so disagreement from family felt like a surprise attack.
What could Nilesh do with his uncomfortable thought?
He could ask Tarun and his father about their reasons over tea, and talk to people outside his college group before saying 'everyone'.
How might Tarun's grandmother have felt when Nilesh called the ban obvious?
She might feel that something the children look forward to all year was being dismissed without a thought.

On Sunday morning the flat smelled of floor cleaner. Nana and Nani were coming for lunch, and Noor moved fast, lips pressed tight, wiping the same table twice. She didn't say a word about being worried.
Dhruv followed her from room to room, holding the back of her kurta. When she shut the kitchen door against the pressure-cooker noise, he sat outside it and cried. Noor opened the door. "Dhruv, what happened?" He didn't know. He only hugged her legs.
Noor knelt, and her shoulders dropped. "Ammi's a bit nervous, that's all. Want to help me put out the spoons?"

What did the flat smell of on Sunday morning?
Floor cleaner.
What was Dhruv feeling when he cried outside the kitchen door?
He felt anxious and unsettled, catching Noor's tension even though nobody had said anything was wrong.
How did Noor help Dhruv feel steadier?
She knelt, named her own nervousness simply and gave him a small job beside her, putting out the spoons.
What might Noor realise when Dhruv hugs her legs?
That her quiet worry had spread to him, and that calming herself would help him too.
