messages.content:
Read this:

Ten minutes before the client call, Sumit was pasting the last numbers into the slides when Lalremsiami leaned over his desk. "Run the spell-check and read the numbers aloud once. Last time there was a typo in the total."
Sumit felt the bristle rise up his back. He didn't need a checklist; he'd been doing slides for three years. The office was loud with someone's birthday song, and he wanted to snap, "I know."
Instead he took a breath and asked himself the question he'd been practising: is she wrong, or do I just hate being told?
She wasn't wrong. Last month's typo had cost them an awkward apology.
"Fair," he said. He read the numbers aloud under the birthday noise and found one: 1,450 where it should have been 1,540.
"Thanks," he said, fixing it with two minutes to spare. The bristle was still there, a little. But he had chosen what to do with it.

What wrong number did Sumit find?
Sumit found 1,450 where it should have been 1,540.
What did Sumit feel when Lalremsiami gave the advice?
Sumit felt irritated and defensive, a bristle rising up his back, because he didn't like being told after three years of slides.
What question helped Sumit, and why?
'Is she wrong, or do I just hate being told?', which separated the useful advice from the feeling of being told, so he checked the numbers.
How might Lalremsiami feel when Sumit says 'Fair'?
Lalremsiami probably feels relieved and respected, since the advice was taken without an argument.

Read this:

Note from the art teacher, Thursday.
We coloured mango trees today. Vinita sat beside Disha and kept glancing at Disha's page, which was very neat. Halfway through, Vinita stopped colouring, folded her page in half and pushed it into her bag. When I asked to see it, she shook her head and said Disha's was "the good one".
I took out Vinita's tree from June, a few green scribbles, and put it beside today's, with a brown trunk and leaves in two greens. I said, "Look how far you have come." Vinita unfolded her page and added orange mangoes. I will keep showing children their own old work.

What did the class colour on Thursday?
They coloured mango trees.
What was Vinita feeling when she folded her page into her bag?
She felt embarrassed and discouraged, because she thought Disha's page was the good one and hers was not.
How could a teacher help other children who compare like Vinita?
A teacher could put the child's old work next to the new, as this teacher did, so the child sees their own growth.
How might Disha see what happened at the table?
Disha may not have noticed at all, since the comparison was happening quietly in Vinita's head and on Vinita's side of the table.

Read this:

In the lift of their Bengaluru apartment block, Uday stood next to Pallavi from the eighth floor, rehearsing in his head: "Want to go to the book fair on Saturday?" He'd practised it all week.
Floor three. Floor four. If she said no, he'd have to see her in this lift every day and remember it. If he never asked, nothing could go wrong.
Floor seven. Pallavi smiled, said, "Bye, Uday," and stepped out at eight.
Uday rode up to the twelfth floor alone, the sentence still in his mouth. That evening he saw her photo from the book fair with friends on the building group and wondered what she would have said.

Where did Uday want to invite Pallavi?
To the book fair on Saturday.
Why did staying silent feel safer to Uday in the lift?
He imagined the sting of a no every day in the same lift, so not asking felt like it protected him from any regret.
What small step could help Uday next time he wants to ask?
He could ask early in the ride instead of waiting for the right floor, and remind himself that not asking also leaves a 'what if'.
How might things look from Pallavi's side?
Pallavi only sees a quiet neighbour in the lift; she never knew about the invitation, so she had no chance to say yes or no.

Read this:

Warden's note, Block C, Room 14. Rukmini Iyer, 7 March.
Heard raised voices at 10 pm and went up. Sujay, pointing at the bins, had said that Kamal "never does anything around here." Kamal did not answer about the bins. Instead he listed, fast and loud: he had paid for the gas cylinder, fixed the fan, cleaned the bathroom twice last week, carried Sujay's parcel up four floors. His hands were shaking. Every item was a defence, as if he were on trial. The bins were still full when I arrived. I asked both to sit. I said to Kamal, "It sounds like you felt called lazy." He nodded, jaw tight. To Sujay: "What do you need, specifically?" "Just the bins on Tuesdays." Plan: rota on the door by tomorrow. Will check in on Friday.

What did Kamal say he had fixed?
He said he had fixed the fan.
Why did Kamal answer with a list instead of talking about the bins?
He felt hurt at being called lazy, so, hands shaking, he defended himself with everything he had done instead of talking about the bins.
How did Rukmini Iyer turn the trial back into a request?
Rukmini named Kamal's hurt, "you felt called lazy", and asked Sujay for a specific need, which turned out to be only the bins on Tuesdays.
What was it like for Sujay to hear a long list in reply?
Sujay probably felt unheard, since the bins were never addressed and the complaint became a contest over who does more.

Read this:

Sunday night: Jahnavi lay on her bed scrolling through the beach villas and rooftop dinners of a travel influencer. Her own room, with its cracked wall and exam timetable, looked very grey.
Wednesday: Rafiq caught her sighing at the phone. "Look at the corner of the reel. It says paid partnership. The villa is free, and the ten bad takes were cut out." 🤔 She looked again and saw the small tag she had never noticed.
Saturday: Instead of comparing, she watched the influencer's tutorial on colour editing. Then she walked to the lane behind her house and filmed steam rising from the tea stall at sunrise. Rafiq texted: "Post it 👍"

What small tag did Jahnavi notice on the reel on Wednesday?
She noticed the paid partnership tag in the corner of the reel.
What was Jahnavi feeling about her own room on Sunday night?
Her room looked grey and dull next to the villas and dinners, which suggests envy and a sense that her own life was boring.
How did Jahnavi turn her admiration into something useful?
She took a skill instead of a lifestyle: she watched the colour editing tutorial and filmed her own lane at sunrise. 😊
How might Rafiq have felt watching Jahnavi sigh over the feed?
Rafiq probably saw a friend being made to feel small by an edited feed and wanted to gently show what sits behind it.
I'm writing my first poem and I can't get it to rhyme.
Poems don't have to rhyme at all. Many fine poems don't. What is the poem about?
The rain on my window.
Then start by writing what you see and hear, in short lines. 'Drops tap on the glass' is already a line of poetry.
It sounds plain, though.
Plain can be powerful. To add colour, try comparing the rain to something, like a drum, or a tiny dancer. Use only one comparison, so it stays fresh.
I'll say the rain is a drummer. What comes after?
Decide what the drummer plays, maybe a slow tune on the window and a quick one on the roof. Let your lines follow the feeling of the rain.
I like 'a drummer with no sticks'. It feels right.
It does, and it's your own idea, which is the best kind. Read the poem aloud and cut any word that doesn't help the picture.

Read this:

Note by Saurabh, KG teacher.
Today was Siddharth's birthday. When we sang and he blew out the candles, he asked, “Why do we blow them?” I said, “In many families, it's a way to mark that you're one year older and to make a wish.” He thought, then asked if he could blow them again for his friend's birthday next week. I told him the candles belong to the birthday child, but he could sing loudest. He practised singing all afternoon.

What did Siddharth ask if he could do next week?
Blow the candles again for his friend's birthday.
What was Siddharth feeling when he asked why they blow the candles?
He was curious about the ritual, wanting to understand it, not just copy it.
How did Saurabh help the ritual's meaning grow?
Saurabh explained simply that it marks being a year older and making a wish, and that the candles belong to the birthday child.
How might Siddharth's friend feel next week?
The friend would likely feel special, blowing the candles while Siddharth sings loudest.

Read this:

In the kasba, Salma's father runs a small cycle-repair shop beside the bus stand. Chandrika, Salma's friend from Class 6, started coming after school to wait for her bus. At first she only sat on the tyre pile, bored. Then one day a boy's chain slipped, and Salma's father was busy. Chandrika picked up a spanner. "Show me?" Salma laughed, but her father nodded. Chandrika watched how he hooked the chain back, then did the next one herself, grease up to her wrists. After that she missed two buses in a week. At home her mother scolded her for her black nails. Chandrika only said, "Amma, I want to learn how the gears work."

Where is Salma's father's shop?
It is beside the bus stand in the kasba.
Why did Chandrika miss two buses in a week?
She was so absorbed in fixing the cycles that she lost track of time; the repair work had caught her interest in a way sitting on the tyre pile never did.
How could Chandrika's mother respond to this new interest?
Instead of only scolding about her nails, she could ask what she is learning and help her plan her time so she doesn't miss the bus.
How does Salma's father seem to see Chandrika's interest?
He takes it seriously, nodding and letting her try, which suggests he respects her wish to learn even though she is a young girl in his shop.
Please write this in a formal tone for an email to the college office: hi, my fee receipt has the wrong name on it, can u fix it asap

Dear Sir or Madam,
My fee receipt shows the wrong name. Could you please correct it at your earliest convenience?
Thank you for your help.

Read this:

Ada had been best friends with Tomasz since primary school in Leeds, long before Emeka came along. They had inside jokes Emeka didn't understand, a Friday film night, and a way of finishing each other's sentences that made his stomach tighten. Twice he'd almost said, 'Maybe you should see less of him.' He knew how that would land: as an order. So one Sunday, walking back from the market, he said instead, 'Can I tell you something a bit embarrassing? I feel insecure about Tomasz. It's not anything he's done. You two just have so much history.' Ada squeezed his arm. 'Thank you for telling me. Why don't you come to film night?' He went. Tomasz had made terrible popcorn and an even worse pun about it. By the end of the evening the two of them were arguing happily about football. Walking home, Emeka realised the unease had shrunk to something small and ordinary.

How long had Ada and Tomasz been best friends?
Since primary school in Leeds.
What was Emeka feeling about Ada and Tomasz's closeness?
He felt insecure, his stomach tightening at their shared history and inside jokes.
What did Emeka do instead of asking Ada to see less of Tomasz?
He shared his feeling honestly and then got to know Tomasz at film night.
How does Ada respond to Emeka's confession?
She thanks him and invites him to film night, including him rather than defending herself 😊

Read this:

Thursday. Thomas handed Bidisha an envelope with a hand-drawn egg on it. 'Easter lunch at our place, Sunday. Amma says you have to come.' Bidisha felt a flutter: she had never been to an Easter anything.
Sunday. Thomas met her at the gate and explained everything patiently. 'We went to church this morning, that's why Appachan is still in his white shirt. The eggs are for new life. Want to help hide them for the little ones?' At lunch his grandmother said a short prayer. Bidisha bowed her head politely and didn't pretend to say the words. Nobody minded. She felt welcome all the way through the appam and stew.
Monday. Bidisha told Ma, 'Their prayers are different from ours. But I didn't feel I had to change anything. I just felt invited.'

What was drawn on Thomas's envelope?
An egg.
How did Bidisha feel at Thomas's Easter lunch?
Welcome and comfortable, all the way through the appam and stew.
How did Bidisha join respectfully?
She helped hide the eggs and bowed her head politely during the prayer without pretending to say words she didn't share.
How did Thomas make Bidisha feel included?
He explained each thing patiently and gave her a job hiding eggs.

Read this:

Dear Papa,
I know you said no to the school trip to Rishikesh. I'm writing instead of arguing because last time I shouted and that didn't help.
I understand you're worried about the river and about me being away for three nights. Here's what I've found out. There are four teachers going. The rafting is only for students whose parents sign a separate form, so you can say no to that part. We'll stay in a school-approved hostel.
Here's what I can promise. I'll call you every night at nine. I'll share my location. I'll stay with my group.
If you still say no, I'll accept it. But please think about it.
Your daughter, Ishita

How many teachers are going on the trip?
Four teachers are going.
How does Ishita feel about her last argument with Papa?
Ishita seems regretful about shouting last time, which is why the letter is calm.
What makes Ishita's letter a respectful way to negotiate?
She acknowledges Papa's worries, gives facts, offers promises and accepts his final decision.
How might Papa feel reading Ishita's letter?
He may feel touched and reassured, more willing to trust her with the trip.

Read this:

I'm Alka, and I sat next to Rukmini during the riddle hunt at the community centre.
The clue said: "I am behind the thing that holds water, but not in the kitchen."
Rukmini tapped her pencil on her chin. "Holds water: tap, bucket, pot, tank." She crossed out "tap" and "pot". "Those are in the kitchen."
"Bucket's in the bathroom," I said.
"Tank's on the roof." She looked at the ladder. "But the roof's locked. So… bathroom."
She ran off. She came back waving the next clue from behind the bucket. I couldn't tell if she was proud or just happy, but she was grinning.

What things did Rukmini list that hold water?
A tap, a bucket, a pot and a tank.
What might Rukmini have been feeling when she came back waving the clue?
Rukmini seemed excited and pleased with herself for solving the clue by ruling things out.
Which step in Rukmini's thinking was most useful, and why?
Crossing out answers that didn't fit, like kitchen items and the locked roof, narrowed it to the bucket.
How does Alka see Rukmini during the hunt?
Alka watches closely and can't be sure of Rukmini's feelings, but sees her grinning after solving it.

On the bus home in Nairobi, Wanjiru bounced on her seat. “Tomas, listen! Wiggle-waggle-woggle-wee! Nobody stinks as much as me!” She collapsed with giggles. Her big brother Tomas groaned. “That doesn't make sense.” “It rhymes!” she said. “Now you!” He sighed. “Jiggle-jaggle-jungle-jee…” “Nobody sings as loud as me!” she finished, and shrieked. A lady in front turned and smiled. By their stop, Tomas was laughing too, and they had a whole song about stinky socks.

What did Wanjiru and Tomas have a song about by their stop?
Stinky socks.
What was Wanjiru feeling when she collapsed with giggles?
She felt joyful and silly, delighted by the sound of her nonsense rhyme.
What would you advise an older sibling when a little one tells silly rhymes?
Play along, as Tomas did in the end, because the fun is in the sound and pattern, not in making sense.
How did Tomas's view of the rhymes change on the bus?
At first he found them silly and senseless, but he ended up laughing and joining in.

Read this:

Tutor's note. In Tuesday's video seminar Vinita went silent for nearly a minute after I asked a question about the reading. Her camera stayed on, but her eyes moved to a corner of the screen and she did not unmute. In a physical room I would have read the frown as confusion, but online it could also have been a slow connection or a distraction at home. I typed in the chat, "Vinita, no rush. Do you want me to rephrase, or would you like to think and type your answer?" She unmuted and said the audio had lagged and that she'd also been unsure of one term. I explained the term. Tejas, another student, added a quick example. I will use direct check-ins more often on video.

What did the tutor type in the chat?
The tutor typed, "Vinita, no rush. Do you want me to rephrase, or would you like to think and type your answer?"
What might Vinita have been feeling during the silence, and what other reasons did the tutor consider?
She may have felt unsure about one term, but the tutor also considered a slow connection or a distraction at home.
What could a teacher do on a video call when a student goes quiet?
They could check in with words, offer options like rephrasing or typing an answer, and avoid guessing from the face.
How might the tutor see video seminars after this one?
The tutor seems to realise that silence on camera is hard to read, so the tutor plans to use direct check-ins more often.

Read this:

At the community centre in Guwahati, Kalyani ran the evening computer class for women who had never used email. On Thursday, one learner, Mrs Baruah, complained to the coordinator, Arnab, that Kalyani moved too fast and she felt left behind.

Kalyani's first thought was to hand over the class to someone else.

Instead, after the last learner left, she sat in the empty room with a notebook and drew a line down the middle. On the left, what had worked: eleven of twelve learners sent their first email this month. Two asked for an extra class. Mrs Deka printed a photo of her grandson by herself and cried a little.

On the right, the one thing that didn't: Mrs Baruah felt rushed.

She looked at both sides. The criticism was real. It just wasn't everything.

Next week, she decided, she'd keep the class and add ten minutes at the end for anyone who wanted to go slower. She'd ask Mrs Baruah to stay.

How many learners sent their first email this month?
Eleven of twelve learners.
What was Kalyani probably feeling when her first thought was to hand the class over?
She likely felt hurt and ashamed after the complaint, as if one learner's frustration proved she was failing. Quitting seemed like a way to escape that feeling.
Why did listing three good things before deciding help, without ignoring the complaint?
It gave Kalyani the full picture, so she could see the class was working and still take Mrs Baruah's point seriously. That led to a practical fix, a slower extra ten minutes, rather than quitting.
How might Mrs Baruah feel when Kalyani asks her to stay for the slower time?
Mrs Baruah would probably feel heard and relieved that her complaint led to real help. She may also feel less alone in finding it hard.

Read this:

In the Class 10 group chat, someone posted a photo of Kalyani's cracked old phone with the caption "museum piece". Laughing faces poured in. Anand, lying on his bed in their Pune flat, saw it all. He didn't laugh. He didn't add anything. He also didn't write "not cool". Not my joke, he thought, and scrolled on. The next morning Kalyani wasn't in class. Her best friend said she had cried all evening and didn't want to come. Anand felt sick. If he had posted the photo himself, he'd know he was guilty. But he had only watched, and somehow that had let him feel clean. At lunch he went to their class teacher, Mr Kulkarni, and showed him the chat. Mr Kulkarni thanked him, spoke to the class that afternoon, and phoned Kalyani's parents before the day ended.

What caption was posted with the photo of Kalyani's phone?
The caption was 'museum piece'.
Why did Anand feel 'clean' after the chat?
Anand felt less guilty because he hadn't posted or laughed; watching silently seemed innocent, until Kalyani's absence made him feel sick.
What did Anand do at lunch, and why was it the right move?
He showed the chat to Mr Kulkarni, who spoke to the class and phoned Kalyani's parents that day, so an adult could stop the harm.
How did Kalyani experience the chat?
Kalyani felt humiliated and hurt, crying all evening and staying home the next day.

Read this:

Saturday, 9:30 pm
This afternoon I was supposed to revise the geometry chapter. I opened the book, looked at the theorems and felt like lying down on the floor. Then Vishal shouted from the next terrace that the wind was perfect for kites. I told myself I'd revise after.
The second I shut the book, I felt SO light. Like taking off a heavy school bag. We flew kites till sunset and I laughed so much.
But since about 7 there's been this small buzzing feeling in my stomach, like when you can't remember if you locked the door. Through dinner, through TV. It's still here.
Funny thing is, last Saturday I did exactly the same with the history chapter, and it felt exactly the same. Light, then buzzing.
Test is Tuesday. I'll do it tomorrow. Probably.
Rajni

What did Vishal shout from the next terrace?
That the wind was perfect for kites.
How did Rajni feel the moment the book shut, and later that evening?
Rajni felt light, like taking off a heavy school bag, and then from about 7 a small buzzing guilt that stayed through dinner and TV.
What could Rajni try tomorrow so the pattern doesn't repeat?
Rajni could do one theorem before any break, so the light feeling comes after starting rather than after avoiding.
What might Vishal have noticed about Rajni on the terrace?
Vishal probably saw a friend laughing and relaxed, with no idea that a geometry chapter was waiting and guilt would follow.
Meeting mein bolna hai "Kripya dobara bataiye." English?
Say: "Please say it again."
Say this in the past tense: Our teacher gives us a quiz.
Our teacher gave us a quiz.

Read this:

In the playschool the week before Christmas, the classroom tree had paper bells. Divyansh knocked down Gautam's block tower, and Gautam raised the plastic hammer. Then he stopped and looked at Miss Rao. 'You can't hit,' he told Divyansh, 'or you go to the thinking chair.' Miss Rao came over. 'Is that the only reason?' Gautam nodded hard. 'Hitting is bad. Because of the chair.' He put the hammer down and started stacking again, lips pressed tight.

What did Divyansh knock down?
Gautam's block tower.
What do Gautam's tightly pressed lips suggest?
They suggest Gautam was still cross about the tower, holding the anger in because of the thinking chair.
How could Miss Rao build on Gautam's answer?
She could praise him for stopping, then ask how Divyansh's head would feel if hit, adding a reason beyond the chair.
What is it like for Divyansh when Gautam raises the hammer?
Divyansh might feel scared for a moment, then relieved when the hammer goes down.

Read this:

"Madhuri, you're still coughing? It's been a month."
"I know, Keerthana. I thought if I stayed positive, it would go."
"Positive is good. But a month?"
"My aunt says it's just the weather and I should think happy thoughts."
"And do you feel better?"
"Some days. But at night it's worse."
"Then call the doctor tomorrow. Tell them everything, even the worry."
"What if they say it's nothing?"
"Then you'll be relieved. And if it's something, you'll know."
"You're right. I'll ask what it could be and what I should watch for."
"And keep the happy thoughts too."
"Hope and a doctor. Okay."

How long has Madhuri been coughing?
It's been a month.
What is Madhuri feeling about the cough?
Madhuri feels hopeful some days but worried, especially as it gets worse at night.
What makes Keerthana's advice balanced?
Keerthana supports staying positive but insists a month-long cough needs a doctor, and encourages sharing worries and asking questions.
How might Madhuri's aunt see the cough?
The aunt sees it as just the weather, which may lead Madhuri to dismiss a lasting symptom.

Read this:

Last December, Jomon invited me to midnight mass at his church in Kochi. I'm Pradeep, and I'd never been inside a church in my life. I was curious, and a little nervous about doing something wrong.
Before we went, I asked him, "What should I not do?" He laughed and said, "Don't take communion, just sit, and stand when we stand." I wore a plain shirt and left my phone on silent.
Inside, the candles and the choir were beautiful. I didn't know the words, so I just listened. At one point an old lady handed me her hymn book, open to the right page. I thanked her with a nod.
Afterwards, over plum cake at Jomon's house, I asked his father about why the carols mattered to him. He talked for an hour.
I'm still who I was. But I understand Jomon a little more.

What did Jomon tell Pradeep not to do?
Jomon said, "Don't take communion, just sit, and stand when we stand."
How did Pradeep feel before going to the mass?
Pradeep felt curious and a little nervous about doing something wrong.
What made Pradeep's visit respectful?
Pradeep asked about etiquette beforehand, dressed plainly, silenced the phone, followed the congregation, and asked Jomon's father questions afterward with real interest.
How might Jomon's father feel when Pradeep asks about the carols?
He would likely feel pleased and respected that his son's friend was genuinely interested, which is why he talked for an hour.

Read this:

Dear Varun bhaiya,
I'm writing this because if I say it out loud I'll start making excuses, and I don't want to.
Since January I have not been going to my CA coaching. I stopped after the first exam went badly. When you asked on the phone every Sunday, I said classes were fine. When you sent money for the books in March, I said I'd bought them. I didn't. It's still in my account.
That's four months of lying to you, every week.
It wasn't because of pressure from you or Papa. I was ashamed, and lying was easier than saying I'd failed.
I'll return the book money this week. I'm going to tell Papa on Sunday myself.
I know you might need time before you believe what I say again. You can ask me anything, and I'll answer honestly, even if it's slow.
Sudha

Since when had Sudha stopped going to coaching?
Since January.
Why did Sudha lie, according to the letter?
Sudha felt ashamed after the first exam went badly, and lying felt easier than admitting failure.
What makes Sudha's letter own it fully?
It names exactly what was hidden and for how long, refuses to blame family pressure, plans to return the money and tell Papa, and accepts that Varun bhaiya may need time.
How might Varun bhaiya feel reading the letter?
Varun bhaiya may feel hurt by four months of Sunday lies, but also that Sudha is finally being honest without excuses.

Read this:

Harish finished Class 12 in his small town and joined a distance-learning BCom. There were no bells, no teachers checking attendance, just a box of study material and his father's hardware shop downstairs. For two months he drifted: shop in the morning, phone in the afternoon, a guilty page of accounts at midnight. His sister Reena, who taught at the village school, noticed him yawning at breakfast. "You need your own bell," she said. So Harish used the ones he had. When the temple bell rang at six, he studied for an hour before opening the shop. When the afternoon bus from the district town honked past, he went back upstairs for another hour. By the time the exam date came, he had finished every unit.

What did Harish's father own?
A hardware shop, downstairs from where Harish studied.
How did Harish probably feel during his first two months of drifting?
He likely felt guilty and scattered, since he only managed a guilty page of accounts at midnight.
Why did using the temple bell and bus horn work for Harish?
They gave him fixed signals in his day, replacing the structure that school bells used to give.
How might Reena see her brother's change?
As a teacher she may feel satisfied that her small nudge helped him build his own routine and finish every unit.

Read this:

I spent four years as a conductor on the number 21 bus in Coimbatore, and on the last route of each day I'd watch the electricians working on the streetlights and think: that could be me.
At twenty-four I finally sat down with my sister Aadhya and a school notebook. She made me write the end first: licensed electrician by twenty-seven. Then we filled in the middle. Year one: night classes, three evenings a week. Year two: an apprenticeship on weekends with a contractor near our house. Year three: the licence exam.
Each year got a month-by-month page. Aadhya checked it every Sunday.
Year two was the hardest; I nearly quit when the contractor shouted at me. I looked at the notebook instead and turned a page.
I sat the exam last month. I'm Karthik, and I'm waiting for the result now.

What did Aadhya make Karthik write first?
She made Karthik write the end first: licensed electrician by twenty-seven.
How did Karthik feel in year two, and what kept the plan going?
Karthik felt discouraged and hurt when the contractor shouted and nearly quit, but looking at the notebook gave a reason to keep going.
What made this plan easier to follow than a vague wish?
Breaking it into years and month-by-month pages, with Aadhya checking every Sunday, made each step clear and kept Karthik accountable.
How might Aadhya feel while waiting for the exam result?
She is likely hopeful and proud, since she helped build and check the plan for three years.
Make a chore chart with three lines in the form "Day: task", for Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday.

Monday: water the plants
Tuesday: sweep the floor
Wednesday: wash the dishes
Why does a torch with weak batteries give a dim yellowish light?
The weak cells push less current through the bulb. Because the filament stays cooler, it glows less brightly and looks yellower.

Read this:

Interviewer: What got you through that quarter?

Honestly, Ishita. I'm Aditi, and last winter the company was running out of money, and I stopped sleeping. I sent Ishita a message at midnight saying, "I don't know what to do." She didn't tell me it would be fine. She said, "I can't promise a rescue. But I'll sit with you while you look at the numbers." And she did, every Thursday for three months.

She told me some hard things. That I was avoiding a difficult conversation with my co-founder. That I hired too fast. I didn't like hearing it, but I wrote it all down.

I thanked her at the time, but I also wrote to her afterwards with what I changed. I cut two costs, I had the conversation with my co-founder. Thanks matter more when they turn into action.

How often did Ishita meet Aditi during the dark quarter?
Ishita met Aditi every Thursday for three months.
Why did Aditi message Ishita at midnight, and what was Aditi feeling?
Aditi was overwhelmed and not sleeping because the company was running out of money, and wrote 'I don't know what to do.'
What did Aditi do to show gratitude that lasts?
Aditi listened to the hard truths, changed things such as costs and the co-founder conversation, and reported back to Ishita with the outcomes.
How might Ishita have felt about telling Aditi hard truths?
Ishita may have felt it was risky to say them, but offering honesty without a promise of rescue shows care more than easy comfort would.

Read this:

Samir: Varun, is it ok if I come to the church tomorrow for your Dadi's funeral?
Varun: of course. she'd have liked that
Samir: I've never been to one there. what do I do?
Varun: nothing special. sit anywhere. when the priest prays, most people bow their heads
Varun: you don't have to pray. just bowing quietly is respect
Samir: and at the end?
Varun: people go up to the coffin. some bow, some touch it. you can just bow your head and move on
(next evening)
Samir: I hope it was alright that I stood at the back
Varun: I saw you bow your head when they carried her out
Varun: it meant a lot. my mum noticed too
Samir: I'm really sorry about your Dadi. she always fed me when I came over

What do most people do when the priest prays?
Most people bow their heads.
What was Samir feeling before the funeral?
Samir felt unsure and a little anxious about doing the wrong thing in an unfamiliar place, while wanting to show care for Varun.
What helped Samir show respect at the church?
Samir asked Varun ahead of time, then followed the local custom by quietly bowing the head without having to pray.
What did Samir's bowed head mean to Varun?
Varun felt comforted and grateful, taking the bow as Dadi was carried out as real respect; it meant something to Varun's mum too.

metadata.subtype: Bowing the head in respect and mourning [Expressing]

messages.content:
Read this:

You asked why Vikas and I stopped fighting, Rashmi? Sit, I'll tell you.
Vikas is twenty-six. Four jobs in three years: a bank, a startup that shut, a travel company, now something with maps. And still in the room with the cricket posters. Every Sunday I'd say, "At your age your father and I had a flat and a child." Every Sunday a door would bang.
Then one night I couldn't sleep, and I actually read his CV. In every job he'd learned one thing and carried it forward. The maps job uses all of it. It wasn't drifting. It was a longer road than ours, with more turns.
Now on Sundays I ask one question instead: "What are you learning this month?" Last week he talked for an hour. He's still at home. I still worry sometimes. But I'm Kashish the mother again, not Kashish the judge.

How many jobs has Vikas had in three years?
Four jobs in three years.
How did Kashish feel when she read Vikas's CV?
She felt reassured, seeing that he had learned one thing in every job and carried it forward, so it was a longer road, not drifting.
What question did Kashish start asking, and why did it work?
'What are you learning this month?', which invited him to explain instead of defend himself, so he talked for an hour.
What might Sunday dinners have felt like for Vikas before the change?
They probably felt like a weekly verdict on his life, which is why a door banged every time.

Read this:

Jeevan, you slammed your door three times this week. No, I'm not scolding. I'll tell you about me at fourteen. One minute I'd be laughing with my friends, and the next I'd want to throw my books out of the window. I once shouted at my father because the dal was too salty, then cried in the bathroom, not knowing why. My mother said, 'Rashmi, your body is changing, the storms will come. You can't stop the rain, but you can hold the umbrella.' She taught me to go for a walk around the building before saying anything. It didn't always work. But more often, by the end of the walk, the storm had passed. Want to walk with me now?

What did young Rashmi shout at her father about?
That the dal was too salty.
How did young Rashmi feel after shouting at her father?
She felt confused and upset, crying in the bathroom without knowing why.
What does Rashmi suggest Jeevan try when a mood hits?
Walking around the building before saying anything, to let the storm pass.
What might Jeevan feel when Rashmi says this is not a scolding?
Jeevan might feel relieved and understood, and more willing to talk about those moods.

Read this:

In the courtyard of their village house, Bhavna and her cousin Kunal shared her father's old phone. A bright box popped up over the game: "Golden skin, today only!" Bhavna's thumb hovered. Her character looked plain beside the others, and a win would look good too. "Everyone will laugh at the plain one," Kunal joked. She wanted it. She also knew the game wanted her to want it. "I'll ask Papa first," she said, and went to the shed where he was mending a wheel. Papa said not today. When she came back, Kunal shrugged. "I don't care what skin you have. I like playing with you."

Who did Bhavna go to ask before buying the golden skin?
She went to ask Papa in the shed.
What was Bhavna feeling as her thumb hovered over the golden skin?
She felt tempted but torn: she wanted to look good and win, yet she also sensed that the game was designed to make her want it.
Why is asking a parent before spending a wise step for Bhavna?
The game is built to tempt, and a parent can help her decide with a cooler head and an eye on what things really cost.
How does Kunal see the skin?
As no big deal: he joked about it at first, but then said he did not care what skin she has and just likes playing with her.

Read this:

Pankaj, you asked what to do first when everything's on fire. Let me tell you about my worst night, when I was twenty-five and on call alone. At two in the morning, a scheduled job I had set up started sending duplicate invoices to our customers. Hundreds. My first thought was, whose fault is this? Mine, probably. My second thought was better: what could still go wrong in the next ten minutes? The job was still running. So I stopped it. Then I asked again. Wrong invoices were already out. So I restored the billing records from the midnight backup and wrote a short message to the affected customers: ignore the duplicates, a correct one will follow. Only at six, with tea, did I start asking why it had happened. Blame can wait, beta. The fire can't. That's what your Tarun Chacha learnt.

What time did the scheduled job start sending duplicate invoices?
At two in the morning.
What was Tarun's first thought, and how was he feeling?
He felt a rush of guilt and blame, thinking the fault was probably his.
What was the key choice Tarun made that night?
Asking what could still go wrong in the next ten minutes and stopping the job first, which contained the damage before any blame.
How might the customers have experienced that night's message?
A quick note telling them to ignore the duplicates likely saved them worry or double payments, and showed the company was on top of it.

Read this:

On the first day of the coding club, Yash sat at the back of the lab in his new college T-shirt, laptop closed. Jasleen, a final-year student, noticed him leave early three weeks in a row.
She found him at the canteen. “Stuck?”
“Everyone already knows everything,” he muttered.
“I didn't, in first year. I cried over a missing bracket once.” She opened his laptop, looked at his half-built attendance app and said, “This is good. Want to finish it for the library?”
For a month she met him every Thursday for thirty minutes. Then she did something bigger: she started a help desk run by seniors, two evenings a week, and put up a sign-up sheet on the club noticeboard. By December, Yash was sitting at that desk himself, helping a nervous first-year from the hostel.

How long did Jasleen meet Yash every Thursday?
She met him every Thursday for thirty minutes for a month.
What was Yash feeling when he said everyone already knew everything?
He felt discouraged and out of place, comparing himself to others and thinking he did not belong.
Why did the help desk matter more than Jasleen's own meetings with Yash?
It meant help no longer depended on one senior, so newcomers after Yash could also find support.
What is it like for the new first-year when Yash sits at the help desk?
The nervous student gets help from someone who struggled recently, which may make asking feel less embarrassing.
What is a locksmith?

A locksmith is a person who makes, fits and repairs locks and keys. It is a noun.
Example: We called a locksmith when the key broke inside the door.
Remind me to water the tulsi plant. Under ten words, as a command.
Water the tulsi plant before the sun gets strong.

Read this:

The college corridor was packed and the principal's car was already waiting; Afreen ma'am had a train to Lucknow in forty minutes. Mridul, twenty, the student council rep, had one chance. She had just cancelled the cultural fest because two students fought last year.
"Ma'am, one minute, please."
She turned, irritated. "Quickly, Mridul."
He kept his voice low under the noise. "Ma'am, I respect your worry about safety. I see it differently. If we cancel, everyone is punished for two people. What if the council hires extra volunteers and we end at eight?"
She looked at her watch, then at him. "You think you can manage that?"
"Yes, ma'am. I'll send a written plan tonight."
"Tonight. Before ten." She got into the car. At 9:40 he emailed the plan. At 7 a.m. her reply came: "Approved, with conditions." Mridul let out a breath he felt he'd been holding all night.

How long before Afreen ma'am's train did Mridul catch her?
Forty minutes before her train to Lucknow.
How did Mridul feel when the reply came at 7 a.m.?
Mridul felt relieved, letting out a breath he felt he'd been holding all night.
What made Mridul's disagreement effective?
He kept a calm tone, said "ma'am" and "I see it differently", respected her worry and offered a practical plan, so she could hear him without feeling challenged.
How might Afreen ma'am have seen Mridul's request?
She was irritated at first but seemed to respect his calm, polite approach and the concrete plan, which made it easier to approve.

Read this:

In Ms Lindqvist's Grade 5 class in Vancouver, everyone was doing a coin experiment and recording the results. Hiroshi and Astrid shared a coin. Five heads in a row landed on their desk.
Hiroshi leaned over the tally sheet. "Next one's tails. It has to be. Five heads is too many."
"Why?" asked Astrid.
"Because it's supposed to be half and half. So now it'll catch up."
He wrote T in pencil before tossing, very lightly, just in case. Heads.
Astrid tapped the sheet. "Maybe it doesn't know it's supposed to catch up."
Hiroshi rubbed out the T and frowned at the coin, turning it over as if checking for a trick.

What did Hiroshi write before tossing?
He wrote T in pencil, very lightly.
Why does it feel true to Hiroshi that the coin will 'catch up'?
Hiroshi feels confident because he knows coins land half and half overall, so he expects the coin to fix the run of heads right away, as if it remembers.
How could Ms Lindqvist use the class tallies to help Hiroshi?
She could gather every pair's results and show what came after runs of heads, so Hiroshi sees tails isn't more likely then.
What would change if Astrid had agreed with Hiroshi instead of asking 'Why?'
Hiroshi would feel even surer, and the pair might never question the idea that the coin remembers.

Read this:

Pantry, after the Monday review.

Pradeep: You okay?
Siddharth: Fine. (pause) My face is still burning. He read my report aloud in that voice and said, "Is this what they teach at your college?" Everyone laughed. He calls it directness.
Pradeep: I saw. That wasn't directness, that was mocking. The mistakes in the report you can fix. The way he said it is on him.
Siddharth: I froze. I couldn't say a word.
Pradeep: Most people do. Write it down today: the date, what he said, who was in the room. Every time.
Siddharth: For what?
Pradeep: For when you talk to HR, or to me again. And keep your CV fresh, quietly.
Siddharth: So it's not just me being oversensitive?
Pradeep: No. Find me on Wednesday and we'll go through it together.

What does the boss call his mocking?
He calls it directness.
What was Siddharth worried about when asking whether it was just oversensitivity?
Siddharth worried that the hurt might be an overreaction, which shows how much the mockery had shaken Siddharth's confidence.
What steps did Pradeep suggest?
Pradeep suggested writing down the date, the words and who was there each time, keeping the CV fresh quietly, and talking to HR or to Pradeep.
How does Pradeep see the boss's behaviour?
Pradeep sees it as mocking rather than directness, and says the way he said it is on the boss, not on Siddharth's report.

Read this:

Class teacher's note, Class 11B, 18 November
Jatin joined us in August from another city and has not been let into any group. This week I noticed a pattern. When Trisha's group came back late from the canteen, the class monitor, who is part of it, wrote nothing. When Jatin came in two minutes late on Wednesday, she wrote his name on the board. During the group presentation, Trisha's friends praised each other's slides and called Jatin's section "confusing," though it was the clearest. He sat very still afterwards and skipped lunch. Today he asked me quietly if he could do the next project alone. I said I would think about it. I will speak to the monitor about applying the late rule equally, and I will set the next groups myself.

What did the monitor do when Jatin came in two minutes late?
Wrote his name on the board.
Why did Jatin ask to do the next project alone?
He felt hurt and excluded, seeing the group excuse each other while judging his clear work as confusing.
What steps is the teacher taking, and why do they help?
Asking the monitor to apply the late rule equally and setting the next groups, so the same rules apply to all and Jatin isn't left outside.
How might Trisha's group see their comments on Jatin's section?
They may think they were being honest, without noticing they judged him more harshly than their own friends.

Read this:

In the corridors of their Nairobi secondary school, Chen had a new habit: whenever Wanjiru walked by, he suddenly needed to tie a shoelace that was already tied. In chemistry he teased her about her spiky handwriting, then went red to the ears when she laughed. At night he typed long messages and sent only "did u get the homework". Otieno said, "She likes you, obviously. She sat next to you on the bus." Chen wasn't sure. She sat next to everyone. On Friday, by the bike rack, he made himself ask. "I kind of like you. Like, like-like. Do you feel the same, or no?" Wanjiru looked surprised, then kind. "I like you as a friend, Chen. Not that way. Sorry." His face burned. "Okay. Thanks for telling me straight." On Monday he said hi to her normally, and meant it.

What did Chen send at night after typing long messages?
Chen sent only "did u get the homework".
What was Chen feeling each time Wanjiru walked by?
Chen was most likely nervous and shy because of a crush, shown by the fake shoelace tying and going red; it could also be plain awkwardness, which is why asking mattered.
Which choice worked, and why?
Chen asked directly instead of trusting Otieno's guess, and accepted Wanjiru's no politely, so their friendship could carry on.
What might Wanjiru have needed when Chen asked?
Wanjiru needed room to answer honestly without pressure, and Chen thanking her and greeting her normally on Monday gave her that.

Read this:

Mum shouted "Amandeep, dinner!" at the exact moment I found my remote car behind the sofa with one wheel snapped off. I knew who did it. Pooja, my little sister, had been driving it into walls all afternoon.
I stomped into the kitchen ready to yell. Pooja was sitting very still, not eating, looking at her plate. When she saw the car in my hand, she started crying before I said anything.
I wanted to be angry. I was angry. But she looked like I look when I break something of Mum's and wait for trouble.
So I just said, "It was an accident, na?" She nodded so fast.
I'd like to say I stayed nice. I didn't. At bedtime the wheel still wouldn't click in, and I told her she ruined everything.

What was broken on Amandeep's remote car?
One wheel was snapped off.
What was Amandeep feeling on seeing Pooja at the table?
Amandeep was angry but also recognised Pooja's fear, because she looked the way Amandeep looks when waiting for trouble, so the anger softened for a while.
What could Amandeep try at bedtime when the anger comes back?
Amandeep could take a few breaths, put the car down for the night and say 'I'm still upset, let's try fixing it tomorrow' instead of blaming Pooja.
What might it have been like for Pooja at dinner?
Pooja was probably scared and guilty, sitting still and not eating while she waited to be shouted at.

Read this:

Saturday night
Irfan got the Bengaluru internship!!! The one he's wanted since first year. He called me from the bus stop, half shouting, and I was grinning so wide my face hurt.
It means eight weeks apart this summer. I know. I did the maths while he was still talking. No evening walks, no Sunday dosas.
And honestly? I don't mind as much as I thought I would. When I pictured him walking into that office, I felt proud, like my own chest was going to burst.
I used to think loving someone meant wanting them close all the time. Tonight it felt like wanting them to fly.
We'll video call. I'll send him terrible memes.
– Mridul

How long will Mridul and Irfan be apart?
Eight weeks this summer.
How did Mridul feel when picturing Irfan walking into the office?
Mridul felt proud and overjoyed, as if Mridul's own chest would burst.
What could Mridul do to stay close during the eight weeks?
Mridul could keep regular video calls and small messages, like the promised memes, while cheering Irfan on.
How might Irfan feel when Mridul reacts with such joy?
Irfan probably feels loved and free to go after the internship without guilt.

metadata.subtype: Delight in a partner's or friend's joy [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Suraj had known Chinmay since school, so he noticed every small change once Chinmay started dating Fatima.

At first it was little things. Chinmay, who used to eat anything, learned to order the vegetarian thali when they all went out, because Fatima didn't eat pork and he'd decided to make meals simpler for everyone. Fatima started coming to their Sunday cricket and cheering badly.

Then, one evening at Suraj's flat, Chinmay went quiet over dinner. "Mom asked me yesterday what Fatima's 'community' is. Just like that."

Fatima put down her spoon. "My father asked the same thing about you last week."

They looked at each other across the table. Suraj waited for someone to change the subject.

Instead Fatima said, "So we tell them together. Not separately." Chinmay nodded slowly.

Suraj realised they weren't just a couple anymore. They were a team facing something.

What did Chinmay's mom ask him?
What Fatima's "community" is.
How does Suraj feel when Chinmay and Fatima look at each other across the table?
Suraj feels a little tense and uncertain, waiting for someone to change the subject, and then quietly impressed that they face it together.
What choice did Chinmay and Fatima make, and why does it matter?
They decided to tell their families together, not separately, which tests and strengthens whether they can face the outside as a couple.
What might it be like for Fatima to hear Chinmay's mother's question?
She may feel hurt and wary, recognising the same worry her own father has, but also determined not to let it split them.

Read this:

Monday: Harish and Ojas argued over whose turn it was on the carrom board at the society clubhouse. It ended in a sulk.
Tuesday: The argument started again at the bus stop, with six kids from their building watching. Ojas said Harish cheated. Harish felt every eye on him, and his chest went tight. "At least I didn't cry on sports day in Class 2 like you," he said, loudly. Someone laughed. "And your dad's scooter sounds like a sick goat." More laughter. Harish didn't care about carrom anymore; he only needed to win.
Friday: Ojas sat at the far end of the bus. Harish kept looking at the back of his head. The laughter from Tuesday didn't feel so good now.

Where did the second argument happen, and who was watching?
It happened at the bus stop, with six kids from their building watching.
Why did Harish bring up Ojas's dad and sports day at the bus stop?
With every eye on him he felt cornered, so winning mattered more than the carrom game and he picked words meant to hurt.
What could have stopped the stakes rising at the bus stop?
Harish could have noticed his tight chest and said "Let's sort it later", or an older kid could have split them up before the crowd made it a show.
What is it like for Ojas by Friday?
Ojas seems hurt and wants distance, sitting at the far end of the bus after being laughed at about his dad in front of everyone.

Make this passage shorter.

"Whoa, it fell again," said Farhan.
"I hate this!" Arohi swept an arm across the mat and sent every block skidding.
"Hey, my foot!"
"Stupid tower!" Arohi's voice cracked.
"You got it up to six last time."
"Don't care." Arohi crossed both arms and stared at the wall.
Farhan sighed, Arohi's big brother, and began collecting the blocks.

Arohi's tower fell again, and she said she hated it and swept every block off the mat, hitting her big brother Farhan's foot. He reminded her that she had got it up to six last time, but she said she did not care and stared at the wall. He sighed and began collecting the blocks.

Read this:

Supervisor's note, Operations team. Written by Mehak.
This quarter I watched Pallavi, 25, carry more than her job title shows. Her grandmother moved in with her family in April after a fall, and Pallavi shifted her hours to cover mornings at home. She told me plainly and asked for a flexible start, which I approved. At work, she took our two newest hires under her wing without being asked, walking them through the supplier files and letting them make small calls on their own. She also noticed how much packaging we throw away and started a small reuse shelf in the storeroom; three teams now use it. I did notice she looked tired in June and skipped our team lunch twice. I asked, and she said she was managing, but I have suggested she take her leave days. Next: I will formally name her mentor for the new hires.

Why did Pallavi shift her hours in April?
Her grandmother moved in after a fall, so Pallavi covered mornings at home.
What might Pallavi be feeling in June, and what is the evidence?
She may be stretched and tired from caring at home while mentoring at work; Mehak noticed she looked tired and skipped team lunch twice.
What did Mehak do well as a supervisor, and what else could Mehak try?
Mehak approved flexible hours and suggested leave; Mehak could also check whether Pallavi's workload should be lightened during the mentoring.
How are the two new hires affected by Pallavi's mentoring?
They get patient guidance and the chance to make small decisions themselves, which likely helps them settle in and grow confident.
'Wo hamesha haar ke rota hai' matlab sore loser? Sahi word hai?
Yes. A "sore loser" is someone who gets upset or angry when they lose a game. Example: "Don't be a sore loser; shake hands and play again tomorrow."

Read this:

"Close your eyes, Dhruv," Ritu said. "Which hand has the toffee?"
Dhruv, four, opened them and pointed. "That one!"
Ritu opened her right hand. Empty. "Wrong!"
"Again!"
This time Ritu, six, hid both hands behind her back and swapped the toffee twice. "Which one?"
"That one. I saw it there before."
"But I moved it! You didn't see!" She opened the other hand.
Dhruv stared, then grinned. "My turn to trick you."

Which hand did Ritu open first?
Her right hand.
What does Dhruv's grin suggest when he says "My turn to trick you"?
He was amused rather than upset and eager to try the trick himself.
How could a parent keep this game fair and fun for both?
Let them take turns hiding and guessing, and give the toffee to share at the end.
What is it like for Ritu when Dhruv guesses wrong?
She enjoys knowing something he doesn't and feels clever about her swap.

In merchantmen, oil for the sailor is more scarce than the milk of queens. To dress in the dark, and eat in the dark, and stumble in darkness to his pallet, this is his usual lot. But the whaleman, as he seeks the food of light, so he lives in light. He makes his berth an Aladdin's lamp, and lays him down in it; so that in the pitchiest night the ship's black hull still houses an illumination.

Answer from the text. How does the passage contrast a merchant sailor with the whaleman?

The merchant sailor, short of oil, dresses, eats and stumbles to bed in the dark. The whaleman seeks the food of light and lives in light, making his berth an Aladdin's lamp, so even the blackest night finds the hull lit within.

Read this:

When Sarika got back to the Pune flat after her evening lecture, Irawati was waiting on the sofa, arms crossed. "You've been angry with me all week. You're so cold. Just admit it."
Sarika put down her bag and thought back. She'd left early every day for lab, texted "running late" twice, and bought the milk they'd run out of. She didn't feel angry at all.
"I don't think I'm angry," she said slowly. "I've had labs every morning. Did something I did feel cold?"
Irawati looked away. "You didn't even mention the rent."
Sarika remembered: last week she'd paid her half late and Irawati had covered it. "Oh. Are you still upset about that? I'm sorry. Let's talk."

What did Sarika buy that they had run out of?
The milk.
Why might Irawati accuse Sarika of being angry and cold?
Irawati seems to be the one holding a grudge about the rent, and it may feel easier to see that anger in Sarika than to admit it herself.
What choice helped Sarika avoid simply accepting the charge?
Sarika checked the facts of her week, calmly said she didn't feel angry and asked what felt cold, which brought the real issue out.
How might Sarika feel on being told she is angry and cold?
Sarika may feel surprised and confused, since she didn't feel angry at all, yet she stays calm and asks what she did that felt cold.

metadata.subtype: Being accused of hostility one does not feel [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Uday, Ishita's older brother. Last month I noticed she'd stopped eating properly and jumped every time her phone buzzed.
One night she came to my room, shaking, and showed me her messages. Someone she'd met in a game, who said he was sixteen, had got a photo of her face and made it into a fake picture. Now he was saying, "Send more or I share this with your school. Don't tell anyone."
I told her, "This isn't your fault. You did right by showing me." We woke Mummy and Papa right then. Papa took screenshots, and they reported the account on the cybercrime portal that night. Next morning they went to the police station and told her class teacher, just in case.
She blocked him and hasn't replied since. I don't know everything she felt, but she slept in Mummy's room for a week, and slowly started laughing again.

What did the person threaten to do?
He said he would share the fake picture with her school.
What was Ishita likely feeling before she showed Uday the messages?
She was likely terrified and ashamed, jumping every time her phone buzzed and not eating properly.
Which choice protected Ishita best, and why?
Telling her brother, who woke their parents that same night to save evidence and report it, because trusted adults could stop the blackmail and she didn't face it alone.
How does Uday respond to seeing his sister in this situation?
Uday stays calm and protective, telling her it isn't her fault and bringing in their parents straight away.

Read this:

You asked me, Sumit, how we got Amma and Appa to stop arriving every weekend without warning. I'm Kavitha, and honestly, we tried everything first.
Rajesh talked to them. I talked to them. We even made a calendar. Every time, Amma heard it as us not wanting her.
Then Rajesh said, "What about Shanthi aunty?" She's his mother's older cousin. She's fair, she's calm, and my own mother trusts her too. Everyone listens to her.
We went to her house with sweets and explained. She didn't take our side. She just listened.
A week later, she had tea with Amma. She said something like, "The children are working so hard. Why don't you visit on the first and third Saturdays? Then you'll find them rested and happy to see you."
Amma agreed. Just like that. The same idea we'd suggested, but from Shanthi aunty, it sounded like care, not rejection.

Which Saturdays did Shanthi aunty suggest for visits?
The first and third Saturdays.
How did Kavitha feel when Amma agreed after Shanthi aunty's visit?
Kavitha felt relieved and a little amazed, since the same idea from the couple had been heard as rejection.
What else could Kavitha and Rajesh do to keep the new arrangement working?
They could make the planned visits warm and welcoming, so Amma sees the change as better time together, not less love.
How did the suggestion look to Amma when it came from Shanthi aunty?
From a calm, fair elder, it sounded like care for the children rather than being pushed away, so Amma agreed more easily.

metadata.subtype: Approach: asking a trusted elder to mediate [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the start of Class 5, I promised to get good at maths. I wrote “MATHS!!” on my bedroom wall in pencil.
Nothing happened. For a month I felt guilty every time I saw it.
My friend Ujjwal is good at maths. I asked him how he did it. He said, “I do five sums every day after tea. Then I play.”
Five sums? That's all?
So I tried. After tea, five sums from the book. I drew a small box on the wall under “MATHS!!” and ticked it each day.
Some days it took ten minutes, some days half an hour. But I always knew when I was done.
After a month, there were thirty ticks. In the next test I got 16 out of 25. Last time it was 8. I, Harish, think five is a very good number.

What did Harish write on the bedroom wall?
Harish wrote “MATHS!!” in pencil.
How did Harish feel during the first month of the vague promise?
Harish felt guilty every time Harish saw the word, because nothing had actually been started.
What made Ujjwal's advice work for Harish?
It gave a small, specific target, five sums after tea, that was easy to start and to tick off.
How might Ujjwal feel if he heard about the 16 out of 25?
Ujjwal might feel happy and proud that his simple routine helped a friend.
