The new phone app promised to identify crop disease from a single photo, and the agriculture department had asked Chetan, the young extension officer, to use it in the villages around Solapur. At Sonali's pomegranate orchard he photographed a spotted leaf. The app said "bacterial blight, 94 percent" and suggested a spray. Sonali, who had farmed these trees for nine years, frowned. "Blight spots look different. These came after the hailstorm." Chetan hesitated. It would be easy to trust the screen. But if the spray was wrong, Sonali would lose money and the soil would take the chemicals for nothing. He took three samples to the district lab instead. The result came back a week later: hail damage, no disease. Chetan wrote to the department suggesting that every app result be checked by an officer or lab before any spray was advised. Sonali sent him a box of pomegranates.

How long had Sonali farmed the trees?
Nine years.
What was Chetan feeling when the app and Sonali disagreed?
Chetan felt uncertain and tempted to trust the screen, but uneasy about the cost of being wrong.
How did Chetan keep accountability while using the app?
He treated its answer as a lead, sent samples to the district lab, and proposed that every app result be checked before a spray is advised.
How might Sonali see the app after this?
Sonali probably sees it as a tool that can be wrong, and feels respected that her experience was taken seriously.

Read this:

Team-lead advice, Kiran? Here's the one story I always tell. I'm Usha, and last year my colleague Gautam flew back from a two-week client visit in Chicago and walked straight into our Monday review. He looked fine, in a crisp shirt. But he nodded off twice during the budget slides, snapped at the intern over a typo, and then agreed to a vendor contract he had argued against for months. I was annoyed at first. Then I felt uneasy, because this wasn't the Gautam I knew. After the meeting I spoke to our manager, and we paused the contract till Thursday. Gautam was embarrassed when he read his own notes later. Now our team has a simple rule: after a long trip, the first day back is for email and sleep, and no big decisions.

Where had Gautam been on his client visit?
In Chicago, for two weeks.
How did Usha's feelings shift during the Monday review?
Usha was annoyed at first, then uneasy, sensing this wasn't the Gautam Usha knew.
What fair, practical step did Usha take, and what rule came from it?
Usha asked the manager to pause the contract till Thursday, and the team now keeps the first day back for email and sleep with no big decisions.
How did Gautam feel when he read his own notes later?
He felt embarrassed at the poor judgment he had shown while so tired.

metadata.subtype: Business traveller and a tired mind [Observer]

messages.content:
"You think too much of your 'toilette,' Adele: but you may have a flower." And I took a rose from a vase and fastened it in her sash. She sighed a sigh of ineffable satisfaction, as if her cup of happiness were now full. I turned my face away to conceal a smile I could not suppress: there was something ludicrous as well as painful in the little Parisienne's earnest and innate devotion to matters of dress.

What does the narrator give Adele, and why does the narrator turn away?

The narrator tells Adele she thinks too much of her dress, then fastens a rose in her sash. Adele sighs with deep satisfaction, and the sight is so funny, as well as sad, that a smile must be hidden by turning away.
Wary or weary: how do I say I am very tired?

Use "weary" for tired. "Wary" means careful because you suspect danger.
Examples: The travellers were weary after the long journey. Be wary of crossing the river after heavy rain.

Read this:

Week 1: Vasudha joined the design studio. Omkar, her lead, spoke in quick half-sentences. "Colours, too many. Fix." Vasudha went home thinking, He doesn't like me.
Week 2: In reviews, Vasudha stopped offering ideas. She did exactly what was asked, silently. Omkar told a colleague over coffee, "The new intern doesn't seem that into it."
Week 3: The colleague mentioned it to Vasudha, gently. Vasudha stared. "Not into it? I'm scared of him." That afternoon she stayed after the review and said, "Omkar, I'm very interested. I just thought you found me annoying." Omkar blinked. "Annoying? I talk like this to everyone."

What did Omkar say about the colours?
"Colours, too many. Fix."
What was Vasudha feeling in week two when she stopped offering ideas?
She felt hurt and scared, believing Omkar disliked her, so she kept quiet to stay safe.
What turning point did Vasudha reach in week three?
She named the misreading directly, telling Omkar she was interested and had thought he found her annoying.
How might Omkar feel when he hears he seemed to dislike her?
He is probably surprised and a bit embarrassed, realising his brisk style was taken personally.

Read this:

On the tram in Rotterdam, Tuan checked his phone for the third time in ten minutes. Across from him sat Tomas, an old friend visiting for the weekend, halfway through a story about his mother's illness. Tuan's thumb scrolled without reading. His stomach felt tight; he was waiting for a message about his own job contract and could not concentrate. Tomas trailed off. "Am I boring you?" he asked, and Tuan flushed. He put the phone away. "No. I am sorry. I am waiting for news on my contract and my hands keep reaching for it. Your mother matters. Please, go on." Tomas nodded, and this time the story was heard properly.

What was Tomas talking about when Tuan checked his phone?
Tomas was talking about his mother's illness.
Why did Tuan keep reaching for his phone, and how did Tomas read it?
Tuan was anxious about his contract and could not concentrate, and Tomas read it as boredom. Both readings were possible until Tuan explained.
What helped repair the moment?
Tuan put the phone away, explained what he was waiting for and asked Tomas to go on.
How might Tomas have felt when Tuan scrolled during his story?
He probably felt unimportant or hurt, since he trailed off and asked if he was boring Tuan.

Read this:

Tuesday night

Bijli did it again. Stopped dead at the Deccan signal, with a bus honking behind me. I patted her tank and said, "Come on, don't sulk, I washed you on Sunday." Kicked twice. Nothing. Third kick, she coughed and went. I swear she was punishing me for parking her in the sun all week.
Francis says she's a secondhand scooter with a dirty spark plug. Also says I'm mad for talking to her. But when I say she's in a mood, it at least makes sense to me. If it's just random, I'd go crazy at every signal.
Taking her to the mechanic on Saturday. I'll tell him she's been moody. He'll say spark plug. We'll both be right.
Samir

Where did Bijli stop dead?
At the Deccan signal, with a bus honking behind.
Why does Samir talk about Bijli being in a mood?
Giving the scooter a motive makes the breakdowns feel explainable instead of random, which keeps Samir calmer at signals.
What is the sensible step Samir is taking, alongside the coaxing?
Taking Bijli to the mechanic on Saturday to check the spark plug, since coaxing won't fix a real fault.
How might Francis see Samir patting the scooter's tank?
Francis finds it a bit mad and funny, seeing only a secondhand scooter with a dirty spark plug.

metadata.subtype: Blaming the laptop or the car [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday: The coach pinned up the team list for the inter-school final. Hrithik's name wasn't there. He tore the paper off the board, crumpled it and shouted, "This is a joke!" in front of everyone, then kicked the dustbin.
Tuesday: Himani, his closest friend on the team, messaged him three times. Nothing. At school he walked past her like she was a wall. Cold. His jaw clenched every time someone mentioned the final.
Wednesday: Himani found him sitting alone on the back steps. She didn't say anything. She just sat one step below and waited.
Thursday: Hrithik came to her before class. "Sorry for ignoring you. I was so angry I couldn't talk to anyone. If I'd talked on Monday I'd have said something awful."
"I know. I've done it too."
"I'm going to ask Coach what I need to work on."
He did, calmly, that afternoon.

What did Hrithik kick on Monday?
He kicked the dustbin.
What was Hrithik feeling on Tuesday when he walked past Himani?
Hrithik was still furious, now in a cold, silent way, with his jaw clenching whenever the final came up.
What helped Hrithik's fury turn into a useful conversation?
Taking time away, Himani's patient presence without pressure, and returning days later to apologise and ask the coach calmly.
What was it like for Himani to be ignored by her closest friend?
It was probably hurtful and confusing, but she stayed patient and understood from her own experience.

Read this:

The power went out in the middle of the Class 5 half-yearly exam, and the room went dim. In the confusion, Naveen knocked over his ink bottle. It splashed across the answer sheet of the boy next to him.
Siddharth Sir walked over with his torch. "Who spilled this?"
Naveen's mouth went dry. A month ago, when he had confessed to breaking the class globe, Siddharth Sir had made him stand on the bench for the whole period while the class laughed. He still remembered every face.
"I don't know, Sir," Naveen said. "It was dark."
His neighbour stared at him. Naveen stared at his paper. His hands were shaking.
He knew he was lying. He also knew, very clearly, that the truth had cost him more last time. That evening he told his mother everything, crying, and she said she would speak to the principal the next morning.

What did Naveen knock over?
He knocked over his ink bottle.
Why did Naveen say "I don't know, Sir"?
Naveen felt afraid of being humiliated again, because the last time he told the truth he was made to stand on the bench while the class laughed.
What could make it safer for Naveen to tell the truth in class?
If Sir responded to confessions calmly and privately instead of shaming, and with his mother and the principal involved, Naveen would learn truth is safe.
How might Naveen's neighbour feel when Naveen says he doesn't know?
The neighbour probably feels angry and unfairly treated, staring at Naveen because his answer sheet is ruined.
What are remnants when you find them after a party?

Remnants are small pieces or amounts that are left over after the rest has been used or gone. It is a noun.
Example: We swept up the remnants of the paper streamers when the party ended.

Read this:

Mentoring programme, session notes. Written by Vasudha, mentor.
Pooja (25), four months into the strategy team. Asked how meetings were going, she said, 'Fine. I mostly listen.'
When I pushed a little, it came out in a rush. 'Everyone in that room talks like they already know the answer. Rohit quotes numbers from memory. Sheetal just says, "Obviously we should…" and people nod. Inside I'm checking my point five times, and by the time I'm sure, the meeting has moved on.'
She said she'd had an idea about the pricing slide on Tuesday, and someone else said something similar ten minutes later, and it went into the plan. 'So maybe it wasn't special. Maybe I'm just not adding much.'
She laughed when she said it, but she didn't look up.
Next session: we'll talk about how everyone's outside looks, compared with her own inside. And one small point to say aloud next week.

What did Pooja have an idea about on Tuesday?
She had an idea about the pricing slide.
What does Pooja believe about her place in the team, and what shows it?
She feels discouraged and unsure she adds much, which shows when she says, 'Maybe I'm just not adding much,' without looking up.
What small step could Pooja try to break the pattern of silence?
She could say one point aloud early in a meeting, even before she is fully sure, so her ideas are heard and credited.
How might Rohit and Sheetal look from their side of the table, compared with how Pooja sees them?
They may have their own doubts too; Pooja only sees their confident outside, not whatever uncertainty they feel inside.

Read this:

I'm Naveen, and until last year I believed that eating bread crusts gives you curly hair. Everyone in my class said it. Suraj said it, the twins said it, my cousin in Pune said it on the phone. I heard it so often it stopped feeling like a story and started feeling like a fact, like the sky being blue. So I ate every crust and checked the mirror. My hair stayed straight as sticks. Then one day in the library Suraj asked, "Who actually got curly hair from crusts?" We went round the class in our heads. Nobody. And Suraj's own hair is curly, and he hates crusts. We laughed until the librarian shushed us.

What did Naveen believe about eating bread crusts?
That eating bread crusts gives you curly hair.
Why did the crust fact feel true to Naveen?
Naveen felt certain and comfortable with it, because hearing it from so many people so often made it as familiar as the sky being blue.
What question helped Naveen see through the fact, and when could it help again?
Suraj's "Who actually got curly hair from crusts?" is worth asking whenever something is repeated a lot but no one has seen it happen.
How might Suraj have felt hearing the crust fact all those years with his curly hair?
Suraj may have found it quietly funny, since he hated crusts and still had curly hair, which was proof against it all along.
"Speed up" and "slow down": are they just opposites?

Yes, they are opposite phrasal verbs. "Speed up" means to go or happen faster, and "slow down" means to go or happen more slowly.
Examples: The bus sped up on the empty road. Please slow down; I cannot write that fast.

Read this:

In their Mumbai flat, Kavitha had a pattern: homework till eleven, then chatting with Sabina till two, then alarm at six. She told herself her body just liked nights.
At school she dozed in chemistry and snapped at her mother at breakfast.
The school nurse, seeing her yawning, said, "Teens' body clocks do shift later. But your school starts at seven-thirty. The clock doesn't change that."
That evening, Kavitha texted Sabina: "New rule. Chat stops at 11:30."
Sabina replied, "Thank god. I'm dying."
The first nights were hard; Kavitha lay awake. But by the second week, she wasn't dozing in chemistry. She even laughed at breakfast.

What time does Kavitha's school start?
At seven-thirty.
What was Kavitha feeling in the mornings before the change?
Kavitha felt exhausted and irritable, snapping at her mother.
What small step helped Kavitha get more sleep?
Setting a clear end time for chatting with Sabina, even though the first nights were hard.
How does Sabina see the new rule?
Sabina is relieved, because she was also exhausted by the late chats.

Read this:

For a month, two boys in the Mumbai school corridor had been snatching Yamini's water bottle and emptying it on her shoes. She hadn't told anyone. "Telling is for babies," one of them had sneered.
On Friday, her friend Disha walked her to the staffroom. "It's not tattling if someone's being hurt," Disha said.
Yamini's heart was hammering. "Mrs Kapoor, can I talk to you? Alone?"
Mrs Kapoor closed the door. She listened, then said, "I believe you. Thank you for telling me." That same afternoon she moved the boys' lockers away from Yamini's and spoke to them privately. On Monday, Yamini's bottle stayed full.

What were the boys doing with Yamini's water bottle?
Snatching it and emptying it on her shoes.
What was Yamini feeling as she went to the staffroom?
She was scared and nervous, her heart hammering, after being told that telling is for babies.
How did Mrs Kapoor handle it without making Yamini look like a snitch?
She talked with her alone, believed her, and acted quietly that same afternoon by moving the lockers and speaking to the boys privately.
How might Disha see her part in helping Yamini?
Disha seems to see herself as a supporter, reminding Yamini it is not tattling and walking with her.

Read this:

My first job offer came with a salary lower than my classmates got. I'm Thomas, and I almost accepted it on the spot because I was scared they'd take it back.
My friend Ishita, who'd done this before, said, "Ask. Politely. The worst they say is no."
I spent a night preparing. I wrote what I'd bring: the internship project, two languages, willingness to travel. I practised saying the number out loud until it stopped sounding rude.
On the call, my voice shook. I said I was excited to join and asked if there was room on the salary. The HR manager said the salary was fixed, but she could offer an earlier review and a laptop allowance.
I took it. Not everything I wanted. More than I'd have got by staying silent.

What did Thomas write down before the call?
The internship project, two languages and willingness to travel.
How did Thomas feel before and during the call?
Thomas felt scared and nervous; the voice shook, but Thomas asked anyway.
What did Thomas's preparation make possible?
It gave Thomas clear reasons to ask, so the HR manager offered other benefits even though the salary was fixed.
How might the HR manager see Thomas's request?
She may see it as professional and reasonable, since Thomas was polite and showed enthusiasm first.

Read this:

Anjali: did u see Kunal in the corridor today
Raghav: the fight? yeah. it looked like messing around tbh
Anjali: his lip was bleeding
Raghav: everyone was just standing there chill. i thought if it was bad someone would stop it
Anjali: i thought the same. that's the problem
Raghav: ...ya. i'm messaging Nair sir now
Raghav: Sir, sorry to text late. Kunal was hit in the corridor near the lab today, his lip was bleeding. A lot of us saw.
Mr Nair: Thank you for telling me, Raghav. I'm calling Kunal's parents now, and I'll speak to the boys first thing tomorrow. You did the right thing.
Raghav: thank you sir

Where was Kunal hit?
He was hit in the corridor near the lab.
What was Raghav thinking during the fight?
Raghav felt unsure and assumed it was fine because everyone looked calm, thinking someone would stop it if it was bad.
What made Raghav's message to Mr Nair helpful?
It was clear about where it happened and that Kunal was hurt, so Mr Nair could call Kunal's parents that same evening.
How might Anjali feel about Raghav's decision to message sir?
Anjali probably feels relieved, having also frozen, and knew the calm faces were the problem.
Why is it better to ask the teacher when you are stuck than to guess and move on?
Asking clears up the problem at once, while a guess may leave a gap. Because a guess may be wrong and later lessons often depend on earlier ones, a small gap can grow bigger if it is left alone.

Monday: Disha got home at nine after a double shift at the pharmacy. Rohit was late again, the third night that week. She ate alone.
Tuesday: At 6:40, mid-meeting, Rohit got a call from Vidya's flatmate: Vidya had collapsed and was being taken to the hospital. He typed quickly to Disha: "will be late, don't wait." Then the meeting restarted and he forgot everything else.
Disha read it at the pharmacy counter, her feet aching. Don't wait. As if she ever did anything else. She put the phone in her pocket without replying.
Wednesday: At breakfast Rohit said, "Vidya's better, by the way." Disha stared at him. "Vidya? What happened to Vidya?"

Who did Rohit get a call from on Tuesday?
Vidya's flatmate.
What was Disha feeling when she read the text at the pharmacy counter?
She felt tired and resentful, reading it as one more sign she didn't matter.
What small step could Rohit have taken on Tuesday?
Adding one line about Vidya being taken to hospital, so Disha knew the reason.
What might Rohit be experiencing when Disha stares at him on Wednesday?
He may feel surprised and then uneasy, realising his short text left out the most important part.

metadata.subtype: Stage 1: A terse message in a busy hour [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

"You asked why I visit Seema Bua every month. I'm Deepika, and honestly, it's partly for her and partly for me.
She's sixty-eight. Every visit she tells me the same stories: how her sister got the better marriage, how she was never allowed to finish college, how her son doesn't call. Her voice goes hard.
I used to want to fix it. 'Bua, why not forgive?' That made it worse. Now I just listen. I hold her hand when she gets to the part about college.
I feel sorry for her, really sorry. And I leave thinking: I don't want to spend my old age polishing my wounds. So when something hurts me now, I try to talk it through while it's fresh.
She's not a lesson. She's my Bua. But I learn from her anyway."

How old is Seema Bua?
She's sixty-eight.
What does Deepika feel after visiting Seema Bua?
Deepika feels real compassion and sorrow for her, and a resolve not to spend old age polishing old wounds.
What did Deepika learn about how to respond to Seema Bua?
That lecturing her to forgive made things worse, while listening and holding her hand helped.
What might it be like for Seema Bua when Deepika holds her hand at the part about college?
She probably feels comforted and understood, even as the old hurt comes back.

Read this:

At the temple fair, the magician pulled a white pigeon out of an empty basket. Damini gasped, her hands flying to her cheeks, her eyes shining. Simran Didi smiled; that was a happy gasp. Later, walking home past the fields, something slithered across the path. Damini gasped again, the same sharp breath, but this time she grabbed Simran's arm and froze, face pale. Simran looked: only a long rope a farmer had dropped. “It's a rope,” she said, holding Damini's hand. Damini's face relaxed.

What did the magician pull out of the basket?
A white pigeon.
What was Damini feeling each time she gasped, and how can you tell?
The first gasp came with shining eyes, showing joy and awe at the trick; the second came with a pale face and a grip on Simran's arm, showing fear.
What did Simran do that helped Damini on the path?
She looked to check what it was, told Damini it was only a rope and held her hand, which calmed her.
What would change if Simran had only listened to the gasps and not looked at Damini's face?
She might not have known which gasp was joy and which was fear, since the sound was the same.

Read this:

Dear Binita,
You were right, and I'm writing to tell you so.
When you visited, you noticed my eye twitching, my jaw clenched and that I was getting headaches every afternoon. I brushed it off. But it got louder: my stomach started playing up too, and I was waking at four every morning.
So this month I finally listened. I saw the doctor, who checked me carefully and said it looked like stress. I told my manager I couldn't take on the new project and gave one away. I've started seeing a counsellor on Thursdays. And I go to bed at eleven, no phone.
The symptoms haven't vanished, but they're quieter. Thank you for noticing when I wouldn't.
Love,
Damini

What time was Damini waking up every morning?
At four.
How does Damini feel about Binita now?
Damini feels grateful to Binita for noticing when Damini would not.
What steps did Damini take after listening to the signals?
Seeing the doctor, giving away a project, seeing a counsellor on Thursdays and going to bed at eleven without the phone.
How might Binita feel reading this letter?
Binita is likely to feel relieved and touched that Damini listened and is doing better.

At the end of the day in the preschool, Miss Kaur rang the little bell. "Pack-up time."
Pooja pushed in her chair. Lunchbox in the bag. Water bottle… she looked around. It was under the table. Into the bag.
Shoes next. She sat and pulled them on, left then right.
Gargi was still colouring. Pooja tapped her. "Chair, box, bottle, shoes!"
Gargi jumped up.
Miss Kaur looked over. Pooja was already standing in line, bag on her back, without a single reminder.

Where was Pooja's water bottle?
Under the table.
What does Pooja tapping Gargi suggest about how she feels?
Pooja feels confident and proud about knowing the routine, and wants to help Gargi too.
What could Miss Kaur do to support Pooja and Gargi?
Miss Kaur could name Pooja's steps with a smile and let Pooja keep saying the list for friends who need it.
How might Gargi feel when Pooja reminds her?
Gargi might be a little startled but glad of the help, since she had forgotten while colouring.

Read this:

At the Dussehra fair in Sirsa, Neelam saw Kashish before Kashish saw her, and ducked behind the bangle stall.

Kashish had cleared the state service exam in June. Her photo had been in the local paper. Her father had distributed laddoos to the whole mohalla. Neelam had failed the same exam twice. She hadn't called Kashish once since the result.

Standing behind the bangles, Neelam felt jealousy burn in her throat, and under it something sadder. She wanted it too. Not Kashish's life. Her own chance.

That was useful to know. It meant she should sit the exam once more, and maybe ask Kashish how she'd prepared.

She stepped out. "Kashish!" Kashish turned, her face lighting up, then uncertain.

"Congratulations. Really. I should have called. I was jealous and I'm sorry."

Kashish hugged her, bangles clinking. "I missed you so much. Come for tea tomorrow. I'll give you all my notes."

Which exam had Kashish cleared?
She had cleared the state service exam.
What did Neelam feel standing behind the bangle stall?
Neelam felt jealousy burning in her throat and, under it, sadness and longing for her own chance.
How did Neelam turn her envy into something useful?
She saw it showed what she wanted, decided to try the exam again, and congratulated Kashish sincerely instead of avoiding her.
How did Kashish feel when Neelam stepped out?
Kashish was glad but unsure at first, then warm and relieved, saying how much she had missed Neelam.
What does persevere mean?

To persevere means to keep trying to do something even when it is difficult. It is a verb. The noun is perseverance.
Example: Arnav kept falling off his skateboard, but he persevered and learnt the trick.

Ten days before Ganesh Chaturthi, Pradeep, five, tried to shape a small clay Ganpati with his mother, Lakshmi. The trunk fell off. He squashed the whole thing and cried.
Five days later, he tried again, patting slowly. The ears were uneven, but the trunk stayed on.
On festival morning, his little Ganpati sat beside the big one on the altar. When his Mama visited, Pradeep stood very straight and said, "I made that one. By myself. Mostly."

What fell off Pradeep's first clay Ganpati?
The trunk.
What does Pradeep standing very straight on festival morning show?
Pradeep felt proud of making the Ganpati himself.
How could Lakshmi encourage healthy pride?
Praise his patience in trying again and his honest 'mostly', not just how it looks.
How might Pradeep's Mama feel hearing 'By myself. Mostly'?
Mama would likely feel charmed and amused by his pride and honesty.

So, I'm Tushar, and last term I finally learnt how to hand work over properly. Our civil engineering group had traffic counts from four junctions, typed by four different people. Total mess. Indu offered to clean it. Earlier I'd have said "just sort it", then lain awake wondering what she was doing. This time I sat with her for ten minutes. I showed her exactly what I needed: times in 24-hour format, one junction per tab, and vehicle types spelt the same way every time, "two-wheeler", never "bike" or "scooty". Then I said, "Don't spend more than an hour before you show me. Send me Junction B by Wednesday lunch." She sent it Wednesday at noon, and there was one problem: she'd merged buses and vans. We fixed it in five minutes, not five days.

Which junction did Indu send first, and when?
Junction B, on Wednesday at noon.
How did Tushar feel about handing over work in the past?
Tushar felt anxious and out of control, lying awake wondering what the other person was doing after just saying "just sort it".
What would you change first if the group had missed the Wednesday check?
Set a new short check straight away on one small piece, so a mistake like merging buses and vans is still caught early.
What is it like for Indu to get such clear instructions?
Indu can work confidently without guessing, and the early check means her one mistake was cheap to fix rather than embarrassing at the end.

metadata.subtype: Approach: hands over a task with clear expectations and a check-in time [Action]

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Sunaina, and I'm writing down what I've seen in Vikas since his Dadu died, because I'm scared I'm missing something. Every evening at seven, the time Dadu used to call, he checks my phone. Twice this week he asked, 'But where exactly is Dadu now?' I said, 'He died, beta. His body stopped, and he can't come back.' He nodded, then asked again the next day. Yesterday I saw him make a garland of paper flowers and lay it on Dadu's chair. I don't know what goes on in his head. At first I tried distracting him with cartoons. It didn't help. Now I just answer, simply, every time he asks. He seems calmer afterwards.

What time does Vikas check his mother's phone every evening?
At seven, the time Dadu used to call.
Why is Sunaina scared, and what shows it?
She worries his repeated questions and garland-making mean something is wrong; she even writes it all down in case she's missing something.
Which approach seems to help Vikas more, and why?
Answering simply and honestly every time, rather than distracting him with cartoons, because it lets him make sense of the loss and he seems calmer afterwards.
What might Vikas be looking for when he checks the phone at seven?
He may half-expect Dadu's call, a sign that he is still searching and slowly learning the calls won't come 🤍.

In a cafe near the university in Buenos Aires, Layla had the group project spreadsheet open and was colour-coding it again. "Valentina, you'll do the survey by Tuesday. Actually, send it to me first, I'll check it."
"I've done surveys before," Valentina said.
"I know. I just like to be sure." Layla's knee was bouncing under the table. Last year one group member had vanished before a deadline, and she'd stayed up two nights fixing everything.
Valentina put her cup down. "Layla, you check everything. It's like you think we'll ruin it."
Layla felt her face go hot. Under the bossiness was fear, cold and familiar. "I'm scared it'll fall apart," she admitted.
"So try trusting me with one thing. Just the survey. No checking."
Layla breathed out. "Okay. Just the survey."
On Tuesday, the survey arrived. It was good.

What was Valentina given to do by Tuesday?
The survey.
What was Layla feeling beneath the checking?
She was scared the project would fall apart, a cold, familiar fear from last year, shown by her bouncing knee.
What small step helped Layla practise trust?
Agreeing to let Valentina do the survey with no checking, which ended with a good result on Tuesday.
How does Valentina experience Layla's constant checking?
Valentina feels doubted, as if Layla thinks the group will ruin the project, even though she has done surveys before.

Read this:

Dear Diary,
Today at PT, team picking again. I stood on the line while names got called: Rahul, Vicky, Sam, everyone. My shoes got really interesting.
When three of us were left, I joked about being "saved for last like the best sweet". Everybody laughed. I laughed too, even though my stomach felt like a stone.
Then Joseph, captain of the blue side, said, "Anirban! I wanted you. You always pass instead of hogging." He said it like he meant it, and gave me a high five.
I passed to him twice and he scored once. At lunch he sat next to me.
Maybe I'm not bad at football. Maybe I'm just not fast.
Anirban

What did Anirban joke about being saved for last like?
Like the best sweet.
How did Anirban feel while making the joke?
Anirban felt hurt and embarrassed, stomach "like a stone", and used the joke to hide it.
How could the PT teacher make team picking kinder?
Make teams by counting off or drawing names, so nobody has to stand on a line waiting to be chosen.
Why might Joseph have picked Anirban so warmly?
Joseph seems to value passing, and may have seen how the waiting hurt, so he made Anirban feel wanted.
Why does the bathroom mirror mist over after a hot shower?
Tiny water droplets cover the glass. Because warm, damp air from the shower meets the cooler glass and the water vapour turns into liquid, the clear surface becomes blurred.

Read this:

Chetan, listen, it's me, Saurabh, and you'll laugh. Yesterday's match against B section. Last over, eight to win, everyone shouting from the boundary. I hit it to cover and just ran. Didn't look, didn't call, just ran, because everyone was screaming "RUN!" Run out by a mile. Lost the match. I was so angry at myself I kicked my own kit bag. Papa just said, "That's my boy, fast feet, no brain." But here's the strange part. Last night at home I sat with the maths problem set, the probability one, and took forty minutes on one question. Drew a table, checked each case, got it right. Calm as anything. Same brain! When the whole ground is yelling, my head goes fast and hot. Alone at the desk, it goes slow and careful. So next match, before each ball, I'm going to take one breath and look at the fielder. Just one breath.

How many runs did Saurabh's team need in the last over?
Eight to win.
Why did Saurabh run without looking?
Everyone was shouting "RUN!" and the moment was tense, so excitement and the crowd pushed him into a snap decision.
What plan did Saurabh make for the next match, and why might it help?
Taking one breath and looking at the fielder before each ball, which gives his slower thinking a moment to join in.
How might Chetan see the way Saurabh tells this story?
Chetan might find it funny but also be impressed that Saurabh noticed the difference between his hot and calm moments.

Give me the gist of this verse in three sentences of modern English.

Close followed by his Rakshas train
Through Lanka's gate he reached the plain.
Then down he leapt, and bade a band
Of giants by the chariot stand:
Then with due rites, as rules require,
Did worship to the Lord of Fire.
The sacred oil, as texts ordain,
With wreaths of scented flowers and grain,
Within the flame in order due,
That mightiest of the giants threw.

Followed closely by his Rakshas, he left Lanka's gate and reached the plain. He jumped down, ordered a band of giants to stand by the chariot, and worshipped the Lord of Fire with the proper rites. As the texts command, the mightiest giant then threw sacred oil, scented wreaths and grain into the flame.

"Aadhya, come, sit. You've been quiet all week. Is it your team lead again? Let Binita di tell you what happened to me.
"At twenty-four I worked under a man who shouted. Not at everyone. At me. 'Useless.' 'Even a child could do this.' In front of the whole floor. I would freeze. My mind went blank, and by evening I believed him.
"A senior, Mrs D'Souza, saw me crying on the stairs. She said, 'Start writing it down. Date, time, words, who was there.' So I did. Every night, in a small diary.
"Two colleagues had seen it too. They agreed to speak up if asked.
"After six weeks I took the diary to HR. The HR head read every page, thanked me, and started a formal inquiry that same week. She moved me to another team while it ran.
"Keeping quiet did not stop him, Aadhya. Writing it down and finding my people did.

What did Mrs D'Souza tell young Binita to write down?
She said, "Date, time, words, who was there."
What was young Binita feeling after being shouted at?
Young Binita felt frozen and ashamed, her mind going blank until she began to doubt herself and believe the insults.
What was the turning point in Binita di's story, and why did it matter?
Mrs D'Souza's advice to keep a written record, with colleagues willing to speak, gave her proof and allies to take to HR, which led to a formal inquiry.
How did Mrs D'Souza likely feel seeing Binita on the stairs?
Mrs D'Souza likely felt concern and sympathy, and wanted to protect the younger colleague.

Honestly, I still cringe. I'm Indu, and this is my most embarrassing flood story. The water on our lane was up to my knees and moving fast, and Moti, our puppy, was stuck on the wall of the empty plot across the street. I didn't think. I just went. My little brother Vishal was yelling, his voice cracking, “Didi, wait, call Papa!” but I had already stepped in. Halfway across the current pulled my legs from under me and I went down, swallowing muddy water. Vishal grabbed the railing and my hand, and two rescue men in orange jackets, who had been going door to door, had to pull both of us out. Moti, by the way, was lifted off the wall ten minutes later, perfectly fine. Calling for help would have taken one minute. Instead I made two emergencies.

Who pulled Indu and Vishal out of the water?
Two rescue men in orange jackets, who had been going door to door, pulled both of them out.
What was Indu feeling when she stepped into the water, and how does she feel now?
She was driven by worry for Moti and did not think, and now she cringes with embarrassment.
What could Indu have done instead, and why?
She could have called Papa and the rescue workers first, because a call takes one minute and trained people can handle the current safely.
What might Vishal have felt during it?
Vishal was probably frightened, since he yelled for Indu to wait and then had to hold the railing and her hand to keep her from being swept away.

Read this:

Kishore, when I was your age I once visited a friend's family in Calcutta for tea. After an hour I was tired, but I didn't want to be rude, so I looked at my watch and said to his mother, "It is getting rather late." She smiled and said, "Oh yes, the evenings are short in winter," and brought out more sweets. My friend's father, who'd noticed, said, "Ujjwal, do you want to go home?" I said, "Yes, uncle, if it's not a bother." Everyone laughed kindly. I've thought about it ever since. A hint saves face, but it often slips past. Now I say, "I'll have to leave in ten minutes," and people are grateful for the clarity.

What did Ujjwal say to the friend's mother?
Ujjwal said, "It is getting rather late."
Why did Ujjwal hint about the time instead of saying he wanted to leave?
He did not want to be rude and hoped a hint would spare everyone's face. His relief when the father asked plainly suggests he was tired and uneasy.
What does Ujjwal do now?
Ujjwal now tells people plainly, for example, "I'll have to leave in ten minutes."
How might the friend's mother have understood the hint?
She probably thought Ujjwal was commenting on the season, and did not realise Ujjwal wanted to leave.

During the paddy harvest, the courtyard in the Kerala village was full of drying rice. Jeevan, two, sat on a mat trying to stack four steel tumblers. They kept falling. He whined and hit the mat.
His grandfather Uday knelt and held the bottom tumbler still with one finger. Jeevan put the next one on. Then the next. Then the last.
Jeevan clapped and shouted, "Me! Me did it!" He looked around for everyone to see.

What was Jeevan trying to stack?
He was trying to stack four steel tumblers.
How did Jeevan feel when the tower stood?
He felt proud and delighted, shouting that he did it, as if the win were all his own.
What did Uday do that helped just enough?
He held the bottom tumbler still with one finger, so Jeevan could stack the rest himself.
How might Uday feel when Jeevan shouts 'Me did it'?
Uday probably feels warm and amused, happy to let Jeevan take the credit.

At lunch in the school cafeteria in Vancouver, Javier eyed Chen's dumplings. "Can I have one?" Chen was eyeing Javier's chocolate chip cookie. "Only if I get half your cookie." "Half? For one dumpling?" "It's a big dumpling." Javier thought about it very seriously. "Okay. One dumpling, half cookie. Deal." They shook hands across the table like businessmen. Later, a new boy sat alone with no lunch at all. Javier noticed him. He looked at his remaining half cookie. Then he looked at the new boy. "He doesn't have anything to trade," he told Chen, and kept the cookie in his box.

What did Chen want in exchange for a dumpling?
Half of Javier's cookie.
Why did Javier keep the cookie when he saw the new boy?
He thought sharing only made sense as a trade, and the new boy had nothing to give back, so to Javier it wasn't a fair deal.
What could Javier try if he wanted to be kind next time?
He could offer part of his cookie to the new boy without asking for anything, just because the boy has no lunch.
How might the new boy feel sitting alone with no lunch?
He probably feels lonely and hungry, watching others trade food while nobody offers him anything 😔

At the bank branch near the market, Hemant was waiting in line to deposit a cheque when he saw his uncle, Jagdish Chacha, at the counter, phone on video call, telling the clerk, "Transfer all of it. Quickly. It's urgent."
The man on the screen was in uniform. Hemant heard him say, "Don't tell the clerk why."
Hemant's heart pounded. He walked over calmly. "Chacha, namaste. Who's this?"
Jagdish Chacha's eyes were full of fear. "Police. They say I'm in a case. I must pay to clear my name. They said not to tell family."
Hemant gently took the phone and ended the call. "Chacha, real police never do this on video. You haven't done anything wrong."
The clerk nodded; she had seen three cases this month. She stopped the transfer. Hemant sat his uncle down with water, and together, from the branch manager's office, they called the cybercrime helpline.

What did Jagdish Chacha tell the clerk to do?
Transfer all of it. Quickly.
How did Hemant feel when he saw his uncle at the counter?
Hemant felt alarmed, his heart pounding, but he walked over calmly so as not to frighten his uncle.
What did Hemant do that fits the right response?
He calmly ended the call, reassured his uncle without blame, and with the bank staff stopped the transfer and called the cybercrime helpline.
How did Jagdish Chacha feel during the call?
He felt fearful and pressured, believing he was in a police case and must not tell family.

How would you explain this text to a young child, in three sentences?

In the evening we had a dance. Cathy begged that he might be liberated then, as Isabella Linton had no partner: her entreaties were vain, and I was appointed to supply the deficiency. We got rid of all gloom in the excitement of the exercise, and our pleasure was increased by the arrival of the Gimmerton band, mustering fifteen strong: a trumpet, a trombone, clarionets, bassoons, French horns, and a bass viol, besides singers. They go the rounds of all the respectable houses, and receive contributions every Christmas, and we esteemed it a first-rate treat to hear them. After the usual carols had been sung, we set them to songs and glees. Mrs. Earnshaw loved the music, and so they gave us plenty.

In the evening there is a dance. Cathy asks for someone to be freed to partner Isabella, but this fails, so the narrator takes the place. The Gimmerton band of fifteen players arrives, plays carols and songs, and Mrs. Earnshaw loves the music.

My name is Ira, and I’m in Class 4. Our whole class loves the same film hero, and on Fridays we all wear his colour. I wear an orange band on my wrist and a scarf. At lunch we do his dance, and even Rohan, who is shy, joins in.
Only Reena wears green because she likes a different hero. She sits at the edge and eats quietly. Yesterday I asked her to show us her favourite song. She looked surprised, then hummed it, and we clapped.
I like being part of something big. It feels like all of us are in the same story, even when the story has two heroes.

Which colour does Ira's class wear on Fridays?
The class wears the colour of their favourite hero, and Ira wears an orange band and a scarf.
How does Ira feel about being part of the class group?
Ira feels happy and proud to belong, saying it feels like everyone is in the same story.
What small choice did Ira make that changed things for Reena?
Ira asked Reena to show the class her favourite song, which gave Reena a way to join in even though Reena likes a different hero.
How might Reena feel sitting at the edge while the others do the dance?
Reena may feel a little left out, but not sure, since she eats quietly and looked surprised when Ira asked her. Being invited seems to have been welcome.

In the village school, Vinita Ma'am had one rule for mistakes: whoever confessed stood on the bench for the whole period. One Monday morning Hafsa admitted forgetting her sums and stood there while the class giggled, ears burning.
After lunch Ma'am asked for the spelling homework. Hafsa had forgotten that too. She said, "I did it, Ma'am, but the goat ate the page." Her voice was steady. Inside she was shaking.
The new head teacher had seen Hafsa on the bench through the window that morning. That afternoon she called Hafsa in and said, "I think you were afraid of the bench. You won't be punished for the truth." Hafsa cried and told her. Before the bell, the head teacher spoke with Vinita Ma'am, and the bench rule ended that day.

What was Vinita Ma'am's rule for mistakes?
Whoever confessed stood on the bench for the whole period.
Why did Hafsa lie after lunch?
She feared being humiliated on the bench again while the class giggled, so a lie felt safer than confessing.
What did the head teacher do that helped?
She called Hafsa in calmly, named the fear, promised no punishment for the truth, and spoke to Vinita Ma'am the same day to end the rule.
How might the other children change after the bench rule ends?
They may feel safer admitting mistakes, instead of learning, like Hafsa, that lying is safer than the truth.

The call came as Jahnavi, twenty-four, was stuck in a Bengaluru traffic jam in the rain, late for her own failed interview's follow-up. Mohit, her closest friend since school, was shouting with joy. "I got it! Senior designer at the studio!" Jahnavi's heart dropped and lifted at the same time. She was thrilled for him. And after three rejections this month, she also felt small, like someone left on the platform while the train pulled away. "Congrats, Mohit! That's amazing!" she said, too brightly. After she hung up, she sat with the wipers thudding. Then she texted: "I'm really happy for you. Honestly, I'm also a bit jealous right now. Rough month. But mostly proud." He replied: "Thank you for saying that. Dinner on me, and we'll plan your next move." Jahnavi smiled, properly this time.

How many rejections had Jahnavi had this month?
Jahnavi had three rejections this month.
What was Jahnavi feeling when Mohit shared his news?
Jahnavi felt thrilled for him and small at the same time, like someone left on the platform.
Why did Jahnavi's honest text work better than her too-bright reply?
Admitting the jealousy along with pride made her congratulations genuine and invited Mohit's support.
How did Mohit respond to Jahnavi's honesty?
Mohit was grateful and offered dinner and help planning her next move, showing their friendship could hold both feelings.

Read this:

Dear Raghav,

I've been thinking about the argument after our marketing project presentation, and I owe you a proper message.

When the professor asked who led the project, I said I did. You looked hurt. I was annoyed that you looked hurt. In my head, I'd done most of it: the research, the slides, the late calls.

Then last night I went back through our chat history, from week one. You'd drafted the survey. You'd done all the data cleaning. You'd fixed my slides twice at midnight. I honestly didn't remember most of it.

I remembered my work because I was tired while doing it. Yours happened while I was asleep or busy.

I think if we'd both written down what we did each week, neither of us would have been so sure. Can we do that for the next project? And I'm sorry.

Eshaan

What did Raghav do at midnight?
You'd fixed my slides twice at midnight.
What was Eshaan feeling when Raghav looked hurt?
Eshaan felt annoyed at first, sure of having done most of the work, and later felt sorry after checking the chat.
What does Eshaan propose, and why is it fair?
Eshaan proposes writing down what each person does every week, so credit rests on a record instead of memory.
How might Raghav feel reading this letter?
Raghav might feel relieved and respected that Eshaan checked the record and apologised.

"Amma, I'm not going to school tomorrow." "Why, Kartik?" "Everyone saw me drop the trophy on stage. Everyone. They're all talking about it." "Everyone?" "The whole school, Amma. Nobody has ever been this humiliated. Ever." "Aparna, didn't you fall off the stage in Class 9?" "Into the flower pots. In a sari. In front of the chief guest." "Akka, that's different. It's not the same for me." "Kartik, how many people mentioned it today?" "...Two. But they were all thinking it." "Or thinking about their own lunch." "You don't understand." Aparna ruffled his hair. "Maybe not. But I still remember the flower pots, and nobody else does." Kartik almost smiled. "The chief guest, really?" "Front row." Rukmini, their Amma, put a plate of murukku between them.

How many people mentioned the trophy to Kartik that day?
Two.
Why is Kartik so sure the whole school is talking about him?
He feels that everyone is watching him and that his embarrassment is unlike anyone else's, so two comments seem like the whole school.
What was the turning point in the conversation for Kartik?
Aparna's flower-pot story and her saying nobody else remembers it, which made him almost smile and see others have felt this too.
How might Aparna feel sharing her own embarrassing fall with her brother?
She seems warm and a little amused, willing to laugh at herself so that he feels less alone.

"Is this yours?" Bhupen held out a folded note.
"My lunch money!" Alka had been checking every pocket for ten minutes. "Where was it?"
"Under the bench."
"Thank you, thank you! Take half my sandwich, please."
"No, it's fine. Eat it."
At home Bhupen told Mama, "Alka thanked me three times."
"How did that feel?"
"Really good. But I wish I didn't keep hoping for it. I think I'd have given it back anyway."
"Would you?"
"Yes. I think it would still feel right, only quieter."

Where was Alka's lunch money?
It was under the bench.
What does Bhupen feel when Alka thanks him, and what does he tell himself about it?
He feels really good, but he tells himself not to keep hoping for thanks each time; he thinks giving it back would still feel right, only quieter.
What could Bhupen do if nobody thanks him next time?
He can remember that returning the money was right on its own, and let the quiet good feeling be enough.
How might Alka have been feeling before Bhupen held out the note?
Worried about the lost lunch money, since Alka had been checking every pocket for ten minutes, so the thanks came out of relief.

Jasleen's uncle Harbhajan arrived late for Sunday lunch and I, Keerthana, Jasleen's friend, sat opposite. Every time Jasleen spoke, the uncle waved a hand: "You don't know the world yet, puttar."
The third time, Jasleen's fork stopped. I saw a jaw tighten. I don't know if it was anger or hurt.
Then, quiet and steady, Jasleen said, "Uncle-ji, I probably don't know everything. But could you give me two minutes without interrupting? Then tell me what I've missed."
Nobody moved. Harbhajan blinked, then sat back. "Two minutes. Go."
Jasleen spoke. The uncle asked one question at the end, and it wasn't dismissive.

How many minutes did Jasleen ask for?
Jasleen asked for two minutes without interrupting.
What might Jasleen have been feeling when the fork stopped and the jaw tightened?
Jasleen may have felt hurt or angry, though Keerthana says the cause is not certain. The stopped fork and tight jaw show something was building.
What did Jasleen say that opened the way to be heard?
Jasleen said "I probably don't know everything" and asked for two minutes without interruption, then to be told what was missed. That was calm and specific.
How might Harbhajan have felt when Jasleen asked for two minutes?
Harbhajan may have felt surprised, since Harbhajan blinked and sat back. The calm respect probably made it easy to listen without feeling attacked.

Kamal: are you going to ask Ma'am about the pendulum problem?
Jeevan: no
Kamal: it's been three weeks, you keep saying you'll get it
Jeevan: everyone else gets it. if I ask it looks like I've been sleeping in class 😶
Kamal: no it doesn't. I asked about circuits last month
Jeevan: you're smart, it's different
Kamal: I'm not smart, I asked. that's the whole difference
Jeevan: hm
Jeevan: what if she says “you should know this by now”
Kamal: then you'll know she said it, and you still get the answer. coming to her table with me tomorrow?
Jeevan: ...maybe

How many weeks has Jeevan been stuck on the pendulum problem?
Jeevan has been stuck on the pendulum problem for three weeks.
What is Jeevan afraid of about asking Ma'am?
Jeevan is afraid of looking like someone who was sleeping in class and worries that Ma'am might say “you should know this by now”.
What did Kamal say and do that made the request feel possible?
Kamal shared having asked about circuits, said “I asked, that's the whole difference”, and offered to go to Ma'am's table together.
How might Kamal feel about Jeevan's replies?
Kamal is probably patient and caring, gently answering each fear while hoping Jeevan will say yes.

There the son recognised not the sire, the sire (recognised not) the son of his loins, the brother (recognised not) the brother, the sister's son (recognised not) the maternal uncle. The maternal uncle (recognised not) the sister's son, the friend not the friend. The Pandavas and the Kurus fought as if they were possessed by demons.

How bad was the confusion in this battle?
So bad that fathers and sons, brothers, uncles and nephews, and even friends could not recognise each other.

Subject: The thing I've been going back and forth about

Hi Sahil,

You asked what I decided about the master's in Leeds. Here's where I am.

I talked to four people. Your cousin, who went abroad and came back, said it changed how she thinks. My old manager said skills matter more than the degree. Kavitha aunty, who did hers at thirty, said don't rush. And Papa said, quietly, that he'd be fine alone, which is exactly what someone says when they won't be.

Everyone was right about their own life. None of them were living mine.

So I wrote down what I care about: learning, being near Papa while his knee heals, not waiting forever. I've deferred by one year. It's my call, and I feel strangely calm about it.

Talk soon,
Jaya

How many people did Jaya talk to about the master's?
She talked to four people.
How did Jaya feel after making the decision?
Jaya felt strangely calm, because the choice came from her own list of what she cares about.
What would you advise someone facing a choice like Jaya's?
Ask a few people who have lived through something similar, then list your own values and decide from that list, as Jaya did.
What might Papa have been feeling when he said he'd be fine alone?
He was probably trying to protect Jaya's plans while quietly worrying about coping alone with his knee.

The queue for the giant wheel at the Durga Puja fair was forty minutes long, the evening was sticky, and Anirban's feet hurt. Right beside it, the toy train had no queue at all. "Let's just go on the train," said his friend Siddharth, tugging his sleeve. Anirban looked up at the wheel's lights turning slowly against the dark. Last year he'd have given up. This year he'd waited his turn at the pani-puri stall without once whining, and his mother had noticed. "I'm staying," he said. He and Siddharth played word games to pass the time. When they reached the top of the wheel, the whole fair glittering below, Anirban felt a proud warmth. "Worth it," he whispered.

How long was the queue for the giant wheel?
Forty minutes long.
How did Anirban feel at the top of the wheel?
He felt a proud warmth, pleased that his waiting had paid off.
What helped Anirban and Siddharth get through the wait?
Playing word games to pass the time.
How might Siddharth feel at the top of the wheel?
Siddharth is probably glad they stayed, even though he wanted the train.

It was harvest time in their village near Hoshangabad, and Dadaji's small grain shop was piled with sacks. Seema and her cousin Ritu were told to label the tins. Ritu wrote "rice", "wheat", "moong", "masoor" and "chana" and lined them up in a row. Seema frowned. "Rice and wheat are grains. Moong, masoor and chana are dals. And all of them are food we sell." On the slate she drew a big circle marked FOOD, and inside it two smaller circles, GRAINS and DALS. Dadaji peered over his glasses. "And where do moong sprouts go?" Seema thought. "Inside dals, in a smaller circle." Ritu clapped.

What did Seema write in the big circle on the slate?
She marked the big circle FOOD.
Why did Seema frown at Ritu's row of labels?
She was dissatisfied because the row didn't show how the items belonged together, and she wanted a clearer order.
How could Dadaji use Seema's circles in the shop?
He could arrange the shelves by the same groups, grains on one side and dals on the other, so customers find things quickly.
What is it like for Ritu to see Seema's circles?
Ritu is impressed and delighted, clapping when Seema fits the sprouts into a smaller circle.

The community hall in Wakad was full of fairy lights for Pooja's wedding reception. Jahnavi was laughing with her college friends by the dessert counter when she saw him: Kunal, her ex, by the stage, in a navy kurta.

Her stomach flipped. They hadn't spoken since the breakup a year ago. Her friends were watching her, and she felt the urge to laugh louder, look busier, prove something.

She didn't. When their paths crossed near the photo booth, she said, "Hi, Kunal. Good to see you."

"Hi, Jahnavi. You look well."

"Thanks. Pooja looks so happy, doesn't she?"

"She does."

"Enjoy the evening." She moved on to her friends.

It had taken thirty seconds. Her heart was still racing, but nothing had exploded. Her friend Tina squeezed her arm. "Very classy." Jahnavi laughed, properly this time, and went back for another gulab jamun.

What was Kunal wearing?
He was wearing a navy kurta.
What did Jahnavi feel when she saw Kunal?
Jahnavi felt anxious, her stomach flipping, with an urge to prove something to the watching friends.
Why did Jahnavi's short greeting work well?
She was polite and brief and didn't perform happiness or anger for the audience, so the moment passed calmly.
How did Tina see Jahnavi's greeting?
Tina admired it, squeezing her arm and calling it "Very classy".

what is the difference between "practice" and "practise"?
Which shops are closed today in my town because of a holiday?
How can I finish a long project on time?
Could you explain what destitution means?

1. In British English, "practice" is the noun and "practise" is the verb. For example: I practise the guitar, and daily practice helps.
2. I don't know that. I can't see your town's notices. Ask a shopkeeper or check the town's local page.
3. Break it into small tasks and give each one a day. Start early, because the last part often takes longer than you expect.
4. Destitution is a noun that means extreme poverty.

In the student union office, Kiran pinned up the plan for Friday's sit-in against the library's shorter hours: two hours, outside the library, no blocking doors, first-aid kit by the pillar. Afreen, the union secretary, wanted more. 'Let's lock the library gates. They'll have to listen.' Kiran shook her head. 'That blocks other students and could get people suspended. We sit, we speak, we leave.' Kiran had also asked the university's legal-aid cell about students' right to gather on campus, and printed their helpline on every flyer. On Friday, two hundred students sat reading library books aloud. When a group from another hostel arrived shouting and kicking the gate, Kiran stood up and ended the sit-in. The next week, the dean agreed to a meeting.

How long was the sit-in planned to last?
Two hours.
How might Afreen have felt when Kiran refused to lock the gates?
Frustrated and impatient, wanting stronger pressure to force the administration to listen.
What did Kiran do to keep the action safe and lawful?
Kept it peaceful and time-limited, avoided blocking doors, checked students' rights with the legal-aid cell and ended the sit-in when others turned aggressive.
How might the other students using the library see a peaceful sit-in?
They can still get in and study, so they are more likely to sympathise with the cause.

Nirmala: sure. what's up

4:10 pm

Jyoti: team cheered when I told them. first time in weeks 😊

The loyalty points and dark mode.
How did Jyoti feel before the meeting with the manager?
She felt very nervous, as if admitting the delay meant admitting she had failed.

She could check progress against the plan every sprint and raise risks earlier, before two sprints slip.

The team feels relieved and happier, cheering for the first time in weeks when they hear the news.

The wedding hall in Prague was booming with brass music, and a hundred guests were clapping on the beat. Two-year-old Ada pressed both hands over her ears, then started to wail and clung to the leg of her mother, Jana. When Jana lifted her, Ada went stiff and hid her face. Jana carried her out to the quiet cloakroom, sat on a bench among the coats and hummed their bedtime tune. Slowly Ada's fists loosened, and she began to play with a coat button.

Where did Jana carry Ada?
Out to the quiet cloakroom.
How was Ada feeling in the hall, and what shows it?
She felt overwhelmed and scared; she covered her ears, wailed and clung to Jana's leg.
What helped Ada calm down?
A quiet space away from the noise, being held by a familiar adult, and their bedtime tune.
What would have changed if Jana had kept Ada in the hall to join the dancing?
Ada would likely have cried harder or shut down, since the noise was already too much for her.

Rostov saw that it had been well considered by them. Sonya had already struck him by her beauty on the preceding day. Today, when he had caught a glimpse of her, she seemed still more lovely. She was a charming girl of sixteen, evidently passionately in love with him (he did not doubt that for an instant). Why should he not love her now, and even marry her, Rostov thought, but just now there were so many other pleasures and interests before him! "Yes, they have taken a wise decision," he thought, "I must remain free."

Question: Why does Rostov decide that he must remain free?
Although he finds Sonya lovely and thinks she loves him, he feels there are so many other pleasures and interests ahead of him just now.
I tried pressing flowers in a book, but they went brown and mouldy.
That's disappointing. Were the flowers fresh and wet when you put them in?
Yes, I picked them right after the rain.
Moisture is the problem. Use flowers that are dry on the surface, and put them between sheets of blotting paper or plain paper before closing the book.
How long does it take?
About two weeks in a heavy book, and a change of paper after a few days helps. Don't open it too often.
I'll try again with thin flowers, as thick ones may be harder.
Good thinking. Flat, thin flowers such as small daisies press best. Choose them on a dry, sunny day.

I'm Lokesh, and I live across the lane from Dolma. Every evening for months I saw Dolma on the front steps, scrolling, head bent, not even looking up when the ball rolled past. Then something changed. Last month I saw Dolma at the end of the lane with a borrowed bat, asking if there was room in our neighbourhood cricket game. At half past five each day since, there's been a figure in the field, chasing badly at first. And on Saturday mornings I've seen Dolma leave with a guitar case. I don't know if Dolma misses the phone. But the front steps are empty in the evenings now, and I've heard Dolma laughing.

What two activities did Dolma sign up for?
Evening cricket and a Saturday guitar class.
What might Dolma have been feeling about the empty hours before joining?
Bored and restless, though Lokesh can only guess; the scrolling on the steps and the later laughter hint at a change.
What else could help Dolma stay with the new habits, and why?
Invite a friend to join the guitar class, since company makes new routines easier to keep.
How does the change look to Lokesh?
Lokesh, who plays in the lane, gains a new player and sees the steps empty, and is glad to hear laughter even without knowing what Dolma felt.

metadata.subtype: Approach: replacing the habit with an appealing alternative [Action]

Read this:

Friday night

I've been sick in my stomach for two days. On Wednesday I saw an offer for cheap game coins: "90% off, today only." I used Mummy's phone payment app while she was bathing, because I knew her PIN. 1,500 rupees. No coins came. The site vanished.

I kept thinking, she'll kill me. She'll never trust me again. So I said nothing. Every time her phone buzzed, my heart jumped.

Today Himani didi found me crying behind the water tank. When I told her, she said, "The longer you wait, the harder it is for the bank to do anything. Tell her now."

So I did, at dinner. My voice shook. I said, "Mummy, I got scammed and I used your money. I'm really sorry."

She went quiet. Then she said, "I'm upset you used my phone. But I'm glad you told me." She called the bank helpline straight away and reported it to the cybercrime number too. We'll change her PIN tomorrow.

I feel lighter than I have in two days.

Divyansh

How much money did Divyansh lose on the fake game coins?
Divyansh lost 1,500 rupees.
What was Divyansh feeling in the two days before telling Mummy?
Divyansh felt sick with fear and shame, scared she would never trust Divyansh again.
Why was Himani didi's advice important?
She pointed out that waiting makes it harder for the bank to act, so telling early could limit the damage.
How did Mummy react, and why did it help?
Mummy was upset but glad to be told, and called the bank and cybercrime number straight away, which showed that the truth was better than hiding it.

Teacher's note, Class 4B, class shop week Rafiq priced the pencils beautifully; his labels had drawings of each item. But when Mehak bought an eraser for seven rupees with a ten-rupee coin, Rafiq froze. He counted the coins in the box three times, went red and whispered, "I can't do it." He left the counter and hid in the reading corner. In writing time the same afternoon he wrote a funny story about a shopkeeper parrot, full of lively words. What I did next: I gave Rafiq a tray of real coins and a number line, and we practised change privately, one small amount a day. No one is timed at the shop now. By Friday he gave three rupees change, checked it twice, and grinned. - Madhuri, class teacher

How much did the eraser cost in the class shop?
Seven rupees.
What does Rafiq hiding in the reading corner suggest he was feeling?
It suggests he felt panic and embarrassment when he couldn't work out the change in front of others.
What small steps did Madhuri take that helped Rafiq?
Madhuri gave him real coins and a number line, practised privately one small amount a day, and stopped timing children at the shop.
How might Mehak have been affected if Madhuri had scolded Rafiq at the counter?
Mehak and the other children might have learned to see Rafiq as slow, and his shame would have grown.

The canal water in Rampura came by turns, one field after another through the week, and Kishore, twenty-six, kept the register for the water committee. This summer Gurleen's turn fell between one and four at night. Since her husband's death she farmed alone, and she had stopped going out at night after a pack of stray dogs chased her.
Some men told Kishore to quietly swap her turn. Others said a turn is a turn.
Kishore called the committee to the panchayat ghar on Sunday. He wrote two lines on the board: every field's fair share of water; every farmer's safety in getting it. Then he asked Gurleen to speak, and after her, Harbans, whose day turn would move.
The rules said any change needed two-thirds of members. They voted to let Harbans swap with her for one season. Kishore then proposed a standing swap list for anyone who cannot irrigate at night, to be voted on next month.

What two lines did Kishore write on the board?
Every field's fair share of water, and every farmer's safety in getting it.
What might Gurleen have been worried about before the meeting?
She was probably worried about going to her field alone at night after the dogs chased her, and perhaps that asking for a change would look like special treatment.
When men told him to quietly swap her turn, what did Kishore choose, and why was it wiser?
He called the committee and followed the two-thirds rule, so the change was agreed openly and Harbans had a say instead of being overruled.
How is Harbans affected by the way the swap was decided?
Harbans gives up a day turn for a season but was asked to speak and saw the vote, so the loss comes with a fair hearing rather than a quiet deal.

Preschool note, Christmas party, by the class teacher.

At the party, Chaitanya grabbed a paper crown from Ayesha's head. When Ayesha cried, Chaitanya shouted, "Ayesha is angry! She's mean!" He kept saying it, even louder.

I knelt beside him. "Chaitanya, I saw you take the crown. I think maybe you feel angry, or bad, inside." He looked at me and his face went red. Then he cried too.

I stayed with him until he calmed down. He gave Ayesha the crown and we made a new one for him. I'll let his parents know today, so they can help at home too.

What did Chaitanya grab from Ayesha's head?
A paper crown.
Why did Chaitanya keep shouting that Ayesha was angry?
He felt bad and angry about taking the crown, and it was easier to say those feelings belonged to Ayesha.
What did the teacher do that helped Chaitanya?
The teacher calmly named what happened and his feelings, stayed with him until he calmed, and helped fix it with a new crown.
How might Ayesha feel after getting the crown back?
Ayesha probably felt relieved and happy again.
It's our first Diwali in a new city and we don't know anyone here yet.
A new place can feel quiet at festival time. Many apartment buildings and neighbourhoods hold small gatherings, so check the notice board or ask a neighbour what is planned.
I'm shy about knocking on doors.
A short, friendly greeting is enough: say you are new and wishing neighbours a happy Diwali. You could also leave a small box of sweets with a note. Most people respond kindly to a welcome.

In her first week at a design studio in Coimbatore, Ira kept waiting for Pema, her new teammate from Thimphu, to say whether he liked her logo drafts. He only said, 'Hmm, this one is also interesting,' and smiled. Ira, used to her old Delhi office where people said 'no, redo it' bluntly, assumed he approved. She sent the draft to the client. The next day Pema quietly showed her his own notes: three concerns he had hoped she would notice. Ira felt her face heat. That evening, over chai, she asked him how feedback worked where he grew up. 'We don't like to embarrass someone,' he said. 'But I should have been clearer.' They agreed he would write one clear concern per draft, and she would ask directly, 'What would you change?' By Friday Ira found she admired how gently he said hard things.

Where is Pema from?
Thimphu.
Why did Ira's face heat when Pema showed his notes?
She felt embarrassed, realising she had read his polite 'interesting' as approval and sent the draft too soon.
What agreement helped them work across their styles?
Pema writes one clear concern per draft and Ira asks directly what he would change, bridging indirect and blunt habits.
How might Pema have felt when Ira sent the draft to the client?
Perhaps uneasy and partly responsible, since he admits he should have been clearer.

Friday. Tanuja screamed at her father when he said no to the school trip. "You never trust me! You're the worst!" She slammed the door.
Saturday. Tanuja woke at six. She mopped every floor, washed the scooter, ironed Papa's office shirts and made him ginger tea. She placed it on the table and walked away before he could say anything. When her friend Zeenat called, Tanuja said, "I'm busy. Being a perfect daughter."
Sunday. Papa found her polishing the steel almirah for the second time. He sat on the bed. "Beta, the house has never been cleaner," he said gently. "But I've been waiting for something else." Tanuja's hands stopped. She stared at the cloth. "I'm sorry I called you the worst," she whispered. Papa nodded. "Thank you. Now sit. Let's talk about the trip."

What did Tanuja make Papa on Saturday?
Ginger tea.
What does Tanuja's remark 'Being a perfect daughter' suggest she was feeling?
Guilty about the outburst and trying to make up for it through work, half aware that she was performing instead of apologising.
What turning point on Sunday finished the repair, and why?
Papa gently said he was waiting for something else, and Tanuja apologised; the words did what the cleaning couldn't. 🤍
How might Papa have felt on Saturday, receiving tea from a daughter who walked away?
Touched by the effort but still hurt, sensing her guilt yet missing the sorry he needed.

When the society notice came saying my balcony grille broke building rules and had to go within the month, my first instinct was to fight it on the residents' group. Suraj, my colleague, even offered to draft a strong reply; he'd "handled a landlord once". I almost let him. Then Papa said on the phone, "Sangeeta beti, don't sign or send anything in a hurry." I read the notice again and understood maybe half of it. So I went step by step. I found the purchase agreement and the builder's approved plan in Papa's steel cupboard. I asked the society office, politely, for the rule they were quoting, in writing. I photographed the grille and the builder's letter. Then I booked one session with a lawyer who handles housing matters. It turned out the grille was in the approved plan. I'm glad Suraj's reply was never sent.

Where did Sangeeta find the purchase agreement?
In Papa's steel cupboard.
How did Sangeeta feel on first reading the notice?
Sangeeta was upset and ready to fight it, then uneasy on realising only about half of the notice made sense.
Which step did the most to settle the matter, and why?
Finding the builder's approved plan and taking it to a lawyer, because it showed the grille was allowed, which arguing on the residents' group never could.
How might Suraj feel when the grille turns out to be in the approved plan?
Suraj might feel a little sheepish that the strong reply would have been wrong, and perhaps relieved it was never sent.

In Aizawl, the hill roads are steep and wet most of the year. Lalremsiami, sixteen, had started riding her cousin's scooter to tuition without a helmet. "It's only five minutes," she told her uncle Jagdish when he saw her.

"Five minutes is enough," he said.

"Nothing will happen. I'm careful."

On Thursday, a car came round the bend too fast. Lalremsiami braked hard, skidded, and stopped inches from the drain. Her knee was scraped. Her head was fine, but only by luck.

That evening Jagdish sat with her on the steps. He didn't shout. "Everyone your age feels like nothing bad will happen. Your brain is built to think the ride matters more than the risk. That's normal. But the road doesn't care how careful you are."

Her hands were still shaking. She nodded.

The next morning, he left his old helmet on her scooter seat. She wore it.

Where did Lalremsiami stop after skidding?
Inches from the drain.
Why did Lalremsiami believe nothing would happen without a helmet?
Lalremsiami felt confident and safe, believing that being careful meant accidents happen to other people.
What did Jagdish do after the skid, and why was it wise?
Jagdish talked calmly instead of shouting, explained why teens feel invincible, and left her a helmet the next morning.
How did Jagdish seem to feel when he first saw her riding without a helmet?
Jagdish seemed worried, warning her that five minutes is enough for an accident.
I was asked to fill in for a colleague next week, and I don't know all her tasks.
That's a fair thing to feel unsure about. Can you ask her for a handover list before she leaves?
She's already on leave.
Then ask your manager for the main tasks and who to contact when something is unclear. Make a list and tick items off.
Should I tell my manager that I'm unsure?
Yes, plainly and calmly. For example, 'I'd like to do this well. Could you tell me which tasks are most urgent?' That's professional and clear.
My manager says the tasks are on a shared sheet and I can't make sense of it.
Ask your manager or a teammate to walk you through it for ten minutes. Note which columns matter, and ask what each colour means.
Colour-coded, of course. I'll ask someone.
Sensible. Write the key on a sticky note so you remember it.

Tarun: did u see the comment on my drawing
Sahil: which one? there's like 30
Tarun: the one that says "mid, my little brother draws better"
Sahil: bro there are 29 comments saying it's amazing

Tarun: ok. not deleting. but i'm redrawing the hands 😅
Sahil: redraw them because u want to, not because of him 👍

What did the unkind comment say?
It said, 'mid, my little brother draws better.'
Why has Tarun been staring at one comment for two hours?
Tarun feels stung and insecure, and the one negative comment feels truer than the 29 kind ones.
What does Sahil suggest, and why is it useful?
Screenshotting the 29 kind comments and reading those instead, which gives the praise as much attention as the criticism.
How does Sahil see the single comment?
Sahil sees it as one random voice against the art teacher and 28 others, and wants Tarun to keep the post up.

Devika: how did it go with Mrs Rao?
Shalini: I told her about Nani. Just said it flat, then cried in the corridor
Devika: oh Shali. what did she say
Shalini: that I don't have to perform normal right now. Extra time on the two assignments, four weeks
Devika: that's good?
Shalini: I think so. I wasn't sleeping and I kept staring at the page
Shalini: we made a lighter plan. One subject a night, weekends free
Devika: want me to sit with you at lunch?
Shalini: yes please
Shalini: it felt like putting a bag down. I'm still sad but I can breathe a bit
Devika: I'm here

How long is the extra time on the two assignments?
The extra time on the two assignments is four weeks.
How does Shalini feel after the talk with Mrs Rao?
Shalini feels some relief, as if putting a heavy bag down, though still sad.
What else could support Shalini besides the lighter plan?
Shalini could talk to the school counsellor and keep friends close, since a lighter plan eases the work but not the grief itself.
How might Mrs Rao see Shalini's request?
Mrs Rao seems understanding, since she tells Shalini there is no need to perform normal right now.
