messages.content: Please revert back to me soon. Is it good English?
Not quite. Say: "Please reply to me soon." Why: "revert" means go back to an earlier state; "back" repeats the idea.

After a while, finding that nothing more happened, she decided on going into the garden at once; but, alas for poor Alice! when she got to the door, she found she had forgotten the little golden key, and when she went back to the table for it, she found she could not possibly reach it: she could see it quite plainly through the glass, and she tried her best to climb up one of the legs of the table, but it was too slippery; and when she had tired herself out with trying, the poor little thing sat down and cried.

Give me a one-line version of this text.
Alice finds she has left the key on the table, cannot reach it or climb the slippery leg, and sits down and cries.

Rewrite this in modern English, in four sentences.

Sumantra thus, palm joined to palm,
Poured forth his words of bane and balm,
With keen reproach, with pleading kind,
Striving to move Kaikeyi's mind.
In vain he prayed, in vain reproved,
She heard unsoftened and unmoved.
Nor could the eyes that watched her view
One yielding look, one change of hue.

Sumantra, with his palms joined, spoke words of both warning and comfort, scolding her sharply and pleading kindly, in the hope of changing Kaikeyi's mind. He begged and reproved her in vain. She listened without softening or moving. Those who watched her could see no yielding look and no change in her colour.

Give the gist of this in three sentences.

The drought had lasted all June in the village near Bijapur. Pankaj, restless, climbed onto the flat roof and did the silly rain dance his friend Vikas had made up: three stamps, a spin, and a shout. That evening dark clouds rolled in, and it poured. Pankaj ran down, soaked and shouting, "I did it! My dance brought the rain!" The next day he danced again, twice as long. The sky stayed blue. "You didn't dance properly," Vikas said. Pankaj frowned. His grandfather called him over. "The radio said rain was coming on Monday," he said. "You danced on Monday too." Pankaj sat down beside him, thinking. "So it would have come anyway?" "The clouds don't watch you dance, beta."

During a June drought in a village near Bijapur, Pankaj did a silly rain dance on the roof, and that evening it poured, so he shouted that his dance had brought the rain. The next day he danced twice as long and the sky stayed blue, and his friend Vikas said he had not danced properly. His grandfather reminded him that the radio had said rain was coming on Monday and that he had danced on Monday too, so Pankaj asked if it would have come anyway, and his grandfather said the clouds do not watch you dance.

"They said nothing is needed," Papa said, folding the newspaper. "Only a hall for four hundred, a car for the couple, and gold as per custom. That's just how it is." "Papa, that is a demand," said Ritu, her voice shaking. "If nothing is needed, why is there a list?" "Suresh-uncle down the road did the same, and his daughter is happy." "Maybe she is. We don't have to copy anyone." Ritu swallowed. "It's dowry, Papa. It's against the law, and it starts my marriage with a price." Her mother set down a cup. "Madhav, drink your tea." Papa looked at the fan for a long time. "I don't want you to suffer." "I won't suffer for saying no. Let me speak to Rohan first. If he wants me only with a car, better to know now." Papa sighed. "Tell your mother. We'll ask them together."

What did Papa say the list asked for?
Papa said the list asked for a hall for four hundred, a car for the couple and gold as per custom.
What is Ritu feeling when her voice shakes?
Ritu feels nervous and angry but determined. She is afraid of upsetting her father, yet she cannot accept a marriage that starts with a price.
What turning point comes when Ritu says she will speak to Rohan first?
Ritu shifts from arguing to a concrete step, asking to speak to Rohan so the family can learn whether the demand is really his. Papa then agrees to ask together.
How does Papa see the situation?
Papa is afraid that Ritu will suffer and thinks copying Suresh-uncle is the safe path. After staring at the fan he softens and agrees to ask together.

The school bus to Mahabaleshwar lost network every few kilometres, and Payal was secretly glad. Aman had called four times since breakfast.
"Network's bad," she texted when a bar came back. It was true, but not the whole truth.
Vandana, squashed beside her, watched Payal's phone light up again. "u ok? why so quiet? did I do something?" Then: "call me when u reach. pls. pls."
Payal turned the phone face down. She wasn't angry at him. She just felt something pressing on her chest whenever his name appeared. She didn't know how to say "I think I'm bored" without it sounding cruel.
"You're not replying?" Vandana asked.
"Later," Payal said, and looked out at the hills. Behind her silence, she knew, Aman was getting more worried, and more worry meant more messages, and more messages made her want to disappear.

How many times had Aman called since breakfast?
Aman had called four times since breakfast.
What is Payal feeling when Aman's name appears?
Payal feels a pressure on her chest, bored and trapped, and doesn't know how to say it without sounding cruel.
What could Payal do to stop the cycle of hints and worried messages?
When she's back, Payal could tell Aman honestly and gently that her feelings have changed or that she needs space, instead of using the bad network as cover.
How is Aman experiencing Payal's silence?
Aman senses a change, worries he did something wrong and sends more messages, which only pushes Payal further away.

People think a real founder lives on noodles and hope. I tried that for two months. I'm Avni, by the way. What actually saved the company was taking two part-time programming contracts, ten hours a week each, that paid my rent and food. That meant every rupee in the startup account went to the product: the designer, the servers, the testing. It felt like a step backwards at first, like admitting the startup wasn't enough. But it bought us about five more months of runway. Bhavna, my co-founder, said it best: "You're not leaving the startup. You're refuelling it." I still write code for other people on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the product is better for the time it got.

How many part-time contracts did Avni take?
Avni took two part-time programming contracts.
How did Avni feel at first about taking the contracts?
Avni felt uneasy about it, since it seemed like a step backwards and like admitting the startup wasn't enough.
What should Avni watch out for while doing this?
Avni should keep the contract hours fixed so that the outside work does not eat the time the product needs.
How might Bhavna see Avni's decision?
Bhavna seems supportive, describing it as refuelling the startup rather than leaving it.

In the clinic waiting room, Amandeep slid the tablet into his bag. "Time's up, Chandrika. The doctor will call us soon."
Chandrika screamed, "No! It's mine! Five more minutes!" A few families glanced over.
"I hear you. You love that game," Amandeep said quietly. "The answer is still no. The tablet is finished for now."
"Five more minutes, please, please!"
"Not again. But you can pick a picture book from the shelf."
She kicked the chair leg, cried louder, then slowly took a book, tears still on her cheeks.

Where did Amandeep put the tablet?
He slid the tablet into his bag.
Why did Chandrika scream when the tablet was put away?
She felt something she loved was taken from her, and she hoped begging for five more minutes would bring it back.
What did Amandeep do to keep the rule steady?
He stayed calm, named her feeling, refused the extra minutes, and offered a book instead.
What would change if Amandeep gave in to five more minutes?
Chandrika would learn that screaming and begging works, so she would likely try it again next time.

It was Margazhi season in Chennai, and every sabha was packed. In the hostel common room, Lakshmi mentioned that a senior had quit engineering to study Carnatic music full time. Indu put her tea down so hard it spilled.
"That's so selfish. Her parents paid for three years, and now she'll sing at weddings? People like that just want attention."
Lakshmi blinked. "You sound really angry about someone you've never met."
"Because it's irresponsible," Indu snapped, and went back to her room.
She had left the door open. Lakshmi saw, under the bed, the old veena Indu never mentioned, its cover freshly dusted. That night Lakshmi heard her humming a varnam, very softly, until nearly midnight.

What did Lakshmi see under Indu's bed?
The old veena Indu never mentioned, its cover freshly dusted.
What might Indu's strong anger about the senior suggest?
Her anger is far bigger than the situation, hinting that she is secretly drawn to music herself and feels envious or torn about a path she did not take.
How could Lakshmi respond wisely?
Avoid confronting Indu about the veena; later, gently ask whether she still plays, leaving room for her to talk.
How does Lakshmi see Indu's outburst?
Lakshmi is surprised and puzzled, noticing the anger is too strong for someone Indu has never met.

It was Holi in a dry March, and the colony's overhead tank was half empty because the water tanker hadn't come for two days. Everyone knew. But the pichkari fight was on, and Pallavi kept running back to the common tap to refill, leaving it gushing while she shot at Pradeep. 'Close it!' Pradeep shouted. 'One tap won't matter,' she yelled back. A dozen other children were thinking the same thing at six other taps. By evening the tank was dry. Nobody could wash off the colour. Pallavi stood in the bathroom, green-faced and itchy, with an empty bucket, while her grandmother wiped her face with a mug of drinking water.

Why was the overhead tank half empty?
The water tanker hadn't come for two days.
How did Pallavi feel when she said 'One tap won't matter'?
Pallavi felt carefree and caught up in the fun, sure her own share was too small to matter.
What could the children have agreed before the Holi fight?
To fill buckets once and keep the taps closed, so the shared tank would last for washing afterwards.
How might Pradeep feel when the tank runs dry?
Pradeep would feel frustrated and annoyed, since he had warned Pallavi to close the tap.

In the village of Kheda, Hansa, twenty-six, had set up two sewing machines on the verandah of the panchayat office. Four afternoons a week she taught young women to cut and stitch. Farida, her first student, now helped teach.
Hansa had worked five years in a garment unit in Surat. She knew collars, darts, how to price a blouse. Now she was using it for something that felt like hers.
One evening, folding cloth, she said to Farida, "I'm happy. Really. But I keep thinking we could teach embroidery too. And maybe sell to shops in town together."
Farida laughed. "You just started!"
"I know," Hansa said, smiling. "That's the thing. It doesn't feel like I've arrived. It feels like the road just opened."

Where did Hansa set up the sewing machines?
On the verandah of the panchayat office.
What was Hansa feeling while folding cloth?
She felt content and happy, but also restless to grow the work further.
What does Hansa's approach show about using skills well?
She turned her factory experience into teaching others, and she keeps finding new ways to serve rather than seeing it as finished.
How might Farida see Hansa's new ideas?
Farida seems amused and a little surprised, but she is already part of the work and may grow with it.

Student counselling note. Sarita, 20, second year. Came in at the suggestion of her roommate, Himani.
Sarita said nothing is "wrong" with Nitin, whom she has been seeing for four months. But she is noticing things she didn't at first: he keeps money very tight and gets irritated when she spends on friends; he is warm with her but short with waiters; he wants to settle near his parents, while she has always planned to study abroad.
"At first it just felt amazing to be with him," she said. "Now I'm asking whether I actually like the person, not just the feeling." She seemed relieved, and a little sad, saying it.
We talked about how this shift is normal and useful, and that she can raise differences with Nitin directly. She plans to ask him about the study-abroad plan this weekend. Follow-up in two weeks.

Where does Nitin want to settle?
Nitin wants to settle near his parents.
How did Sarita seem to feel as she described the shift?
Sarita seemed relieved and a little sad: relieved to say it aloud, sad that the early glow is fading.
What step did Sarita plan, and why is it useful?
Sarita planned to ask Nitin about the study-abroad plan this weekend; talking directly about differences shows who he is, not just how the relationship feels.
How might Himani have seen things before suggesting counselling?
Himani probably noticed Sarita seemed unsettled about the relationship and wanted her to have someone neutral to think it through with.

metadata.subtype: Stage 3: Getting to know the real person [Actor]

messages.content:

I'm Irfan, and I sit behind Pranav in history. When our teacher announced the essay on Thursday, Pranav told me, “Two evenings, easy. I know the topic.” I said nothing, because I remembered the map project in September, which he'd said would take one night and which took six days. On Sunday night Pranav was still gathering sources, and the second evening was gone before the introduction was done. I saw him on Monday morning, writing the conclusion on the school bus with his notebook on his knees. I don't know what he was thinking. He looked tired, but he also said, “It'll be fine.” The teacher gave it a mark he didn't seem to like.

How many evenings did Pranav say the essay would take?
Pranav said the essay would take two evenings.
What might Pranav have been feeling on the school bus on Monday?
Pranav seemed tired and perhaps worried, though “It'll be fine” suggests hopeful confidence; Irfan cannot be sure about Pranav's inner state.
What could Pranav do before the next essay?
Look back at how long the map project and this essay really took, and plan the start date from that instead of from the best-case picture.
Why did Irfan say nothing about the map project?
Irfan may have felt awkward correcting a classmate, and wanted to avoid sounding critical, so kept quiet.

"Vaibhav! What was that noise?" Papa called.
"Nothing!"
"That was Nani's blue glass."
Vaibhav stood with milk on his socks. His cousin Zeenat was beside him, holding her doll.
"Zeenat did it," he said in a tiny voice.
"I did not!"
Papa came to the doorway and saw Vaibhav's fists squeezed tight.
"Are you scared I'll shout?"
Vaibhav nodded, chin wobbling.
"I won't shout. I promise. Tell me."
"I wanted to carry it myself. It slipped."
"Thank you. That's brave. Let's say sorry to Zeenat, then tell Nani together."

Whose glass broke?
It was Nani's blue glass.
What was Vaibhav feeling when Papa came to the doorway?
Vaibhav was frightened that Papa would shout, which is why his fists were squeezed tight and his chin was wobbling.
What did Papa do that helped Vaibhav tell the truth?
Papa named the fear, promised not to shout, and thanked him for being brave, so the truth felt safer than the lie.
How might Zeenat feel about being blamed?
Zeenat feels upset and unfairly accused, since she was only holding her doll.

Tuesday: Maa said no to the park because of homework time. Usha yelled, "You're mean! I hate you!" and ran to her room. Under her blanket, she felt hot and shaky.
Wednesday: At breakfast, Usha would not look at Anirban, her father. He sat beside her. "You were angry yesterday. I still love you. So does Maa." Usha peeked out. "Even after hate?" "Even after."
Saturday: Maa said no to more ice cream. Usha scowled. "I'm angry at you." Then she hugged Maa's leg anyway.

Why did Maa say no to the park on Tuesday?
Maa said no because it was homework time.
How was Usha feeling under her blanket?
She felt angry and afraid at the same time, hot and shaky about the hard words she had shouted.
What did Anirban do that helped?
He sat beside Usha, named her anger and told her they both still loved her, so she learned hard words do not end love.
How does Maa probably see Usha's hug on Saturday?
She likely feels warm and relieved, seeing Usha can say she is angry and still stay close.

Farhan, you asked how I made peace with my parents. Let me, Preeti, tell you. After three years of silence over my marriage, my mother called and said, "Come home for Diwali, but come alone." I sat with that for a whole night. Then I called her back and said, very slowly, "Ma, I would like to see you. I miss you. And I will not accept insults about my husband. If that happens, we will leave, calmly." She was quiet. Then: "That is your condition?" "That is my condition." We went together. When my uncle made a remark about Arun's family at dinner, I stood up, and Ma said sharply, "Enough." We stayed. A condition like that protects the relationship; it does not end it. But understand this too: some homes are truly unsafe, and there, keeping your distance is the right choice.

What did Preeti's mother first say on the phone?
She said, "Come home for Diwali, but come alone."
How was Preeti feeling during the night she sat with her mother's invitation?
She was torn and hurt, longing to see her mother but unwilling to go without her husband.
What choice did Preeti make when she called her mother back, and why did it work?
She said she wanted to visit and set one calm, clear condition about insults to her husband, which protected both her marriage and the bond with her mother.
What might Ma have felt when she said 'Enough' to the uncle?
Ma may have felt protective and determined to keep the fragile peace, honouring the condition she had accepted.

The community hall was full of wedding lights and the smell of halwa, and Siddharth had been bouncing since breakfast. His cousins from Amritsar had arrived! He dragged Gurpreet and three smaller cousins to the corner where he'd hidden his box of cars. 'Okay, rules. I'm the race boss. Gurpreet, you're only allowed the blue truck. You little ones just watch.' Within five minutes the little ones had wandered off, and Gurpreet was sitting on the stage steps, chin in his hands. Siddharth's excitement drained away. This wasn't how he'd imagined it. He picked up the box and walked over. 'Sorry. Everybody picks one car. And you choose the track.' Gurpreet grinned and built a ramp from a chair cushion, and the little ones came running back.

Where had Siddharth hidden his box of cars?
In the corner of the community hall.
What happened to Siddharth's excitement after five minutes, and why?
It drained into disappointment, because bossing everyone around made them leave.
What fixed the game?
Apologising, letting everyone pick a car and letting Gurpreet choose the track.
How did Gurpreet feel about being allowed only the blue truck?
Bored and left out, so he sat on the stage steps with his chin in his hands.

Dear Shreya didi,
Today was a whole year in one day. Morning: someone I like on the school bus smiled at me and I felt like I could fly. Noon: Sir punished our whole row for talking when it was only two boys, and I was so angry I shook. I nearly threw my bottle. Evening: I came home and cried in the bathroom for no reason I could explain, just this heavy grey feeling.
Is this normal? It scares me how fast it changes.
I told Mummy a bit at dinner. She didn't laugh. She said she felt like this at sixteen too, and that if the grey stays a long time or feels too heavy, we'll talk to the school counsellor together.
Write back?
Baljeet

What did Sir do at noon?
Sir punished the whole row for talking when it was only two boys.
What worries Baljeet most about the day?
Baljeet is scared by how fast the feelings change, from flying to shaking with anger to a heavy grey sadness.
What choice did Baljeet make that evening, and how did Mummy respond?
Baljeet told Mummy a bit at dinner; she listened without laughing, said she felt this way at sixteen and offered to see the school counsellor together if the grey stays long or feels too heavy.
How might Shreya didi feel reading this letter?
She may feel trusted and want to reassure Baljeet that these swings are common, while backing Mummy's plan.

In the quiet corner of the school library, Payal wrote on the back of her maths notebook, crossing out and rewriting.
Not: “What's wrong with you lately?” Too sharp.
Better: “I've noticed you seem low these days, and I'm worried about you.”
Then: “You don't have to tell me anything. I'm just here.”
She thought about Akash, who had stopped coming to band practice and snapped at everyone last week. What if he gets angry? she thought. Then I don't argue. I say, “Okay, I'm not going anywhere,” and I try again tomorrow.
What if he shuts down completely? Then I tell Mr Pereira, the music teacher, today, not someday.
And if he says something really scary? Then I stay with him and get an adult straight away.
She read the lines under her breath twice. At the bell, she found Akash by the lockers and said them.

Which line did Payal cross out as too sharp?
What's wrong with you lately?
What might Payal be worried about while planning?
Payal is worried Akash might get angry or shut down, and nervous about saying the wrong thing.
What else could Payal prepare before talking to Akash?
A quiet, private place and time, so Akash doesn't feel watched by others at the lockers.
How might Akash feel hearing Payal's words?
Akash may feel caught off guard, but noticed and cared for rather than accused, since the words are gentle.

Sonali saw the number before she saw anything else: 29 out of 80 in the chemistry pre-board. She walked home through the market without noticing the crowds.

In her room she whispered, "Useless. Papa told everyone at the office I'd get ninety." She pictured his face, then her grandmother's. She felt she had brought shame on the whole house.

Her younger brother Yash knocked. "Didi? Dinner." Then, seeing her face, "It's just one paper, na?"

She almost snapped at him. Instead she sat with it. One paper. Not her. She took a sheet and wrote what had gone wrong: skipped two chapters of organic, panicked on the numericals, ran out of time on the last section.

Seeing it on paper, it looked less like a verdict and more like a to-do list.

The next morning she waited outside the staffroom for Mrs Gill. "Ma'am, I got 29. Can you help me make a recovery plan for the boards?" Mrs Gill pulled out a chair for her.

What mark did Sonali get in the chemistry pre-board?
Sonali got 29 out of 80.
What was Sonali feeling when she whispered "Useless"?
Sonali felt worthless and ashamed, afraid she had let down her father and grandmother and the whole house.
What steps helped Sonali move from shame to action?
Sonali wrote down exactly what went wrong and then asked Mrs Gill for a recovery plan, turning the result into a list of fixable problems.
How does Yash see his sister's result?
Yash sees it as just one paper, which shows he does not think it defines Sonali the way she fears.

Monday: Usha tried to climb the shelf for the pickle jar. Her sister Sangeeta pulled her down. "Ask Papa!"
Wednesday: Usha pointed at the jar. "Papa, can you get the jar down?" Papa did.
Friday: Papa was out, so Usha asked Sangeeta, pointing. "Can you get it?" She didn't climb at all.

Who pulled Usha down on Monday?
Her sister Sangeeta.
What was Usha feeling on Wednesday when Papa got the jar?
She was probably pleased and glad it was so quick.
What else could Usha do if nobody tall is home?
Wait until someone comes, since climbing a shelf isn't safe.
How does Usha's asking look to Sangeeta?
Sangeeta is relieved that Usha asks instead of climbing.

Salma unzipped her bag in the classroom and her stomach dropped. The maths notebook was still on the dining table at home. Ramesh Sir checked homework right after prayer. He'll shout in front of everyone, she thought. Maybe he'll hit my hands with the ruler. Then he'll send me to the principal. The principal will call Ammi, and Ammi will cry, and they'll say I can't come back to this school. Everyone will remember me as the girl who got thrown out. Her hands were cold when Ramesh Sir reached her desk. 'Forgot it?' he asked. She nodded, eyes stinging. 'Bring it tomorrow and show me first thing,' he said, and moved to the next desk. Salma stared at her empty hands for a long time.

What did Salma leave at home?
Salma left her maths notebook on the dining table at home.
Why did being thrown out of school feel so certain to Salma?
She was scared and ashamed, and each imagined step, from shouting to the principal to Ammi crying, seemed to follow from the one before, so the fear felt like fact.
What could Salma try the next time her mind races ahead like this?
She could ask herself what usually happens when someone forgets homework, and remember that Ramesh Sir only asked her to bring it the next day.
How might Ramesh Sir see the forgotten notebook?
To him it is a small, ordinary slip, which is why he simply asks for it first thing tomorrow and moves on.

Pradeep's manager.

It was about consent to share Pradeep's photos, so a clear request, 'please don't post without asking', left no doubt and got them taken down.

"Gopika, can I ask you something? I keep saying mistakes are part of learning. Why doesn't anyone on the team try the new approach?"
"You want the honest answer, Abhinav?"
"Yes."
"Last month Ramesh tried it on a client report. One number was wrong. He got a written warning."
"That came from finance, not me."
"We don't see the difference. We just see a warning."
"Okay. What else?"
"We're asked to learn the new system but there's no training time. We do it at night."
"And feedback?"
"You're in meetings all day. We send questions and wait a week."
Abhinav was quiet for a while. "So the slogans are just... slogans."
"Pretty much. Sorry."
"Don't be. I needed to hear it." He opened his calendar. "Let's start with two hours of training time on Tuesdays, and I'll talk to finance about Ramesh."

What happened to Ramesh last month?
One number in his client report was wrong and he got a written warning.
How did Abhinav seem to feel after hearing Gopika's answer?
Abhinav seemed quiet and a bit shaken, then grateful, realising his slogans weren't matched by real support.
What first steps did Abhinav take to support learning?
He set two hours of training time on Tuesdays and planned to talk to finance about Ramesh's warning.
What is it like for Gopika to give the honest answer?
Gopika seems a little nervous, even apologising, but relieved to share what the team really experiences.

The college magazine office smelled of old paper and marker ink. Sonali, the new student editor, had split the issue three ways: features to her, photos to Aman, interviews to Sudha. Two deadlines had passed without Sudha's interviews, and the others were muttering. Sonali could have posted about it in the group chat. Instead she found Sudha alone after the Thursday meeting. "The interviews are late, and I need them by Monday for the printer. What's getting in the way?" Sudha's eyes went to the floor. "My mother's been in and out of hospital. I didn't want to use it as an excuse." Sonali let that sit for a moment. "Thanks for telling me. Can you do two interviews instead of four? I'll take the other two." Sudha breathed out. "Two I can do." That evening Sonali updated the plan without mentioning why.

By when did Sonali need the interviews?
She needed them by Monday for the printer.
What was Sudha feeling when Sonali asked what was getting in the way?
She felt ashamed and anxious, looking at the floor and worried that her mother's illness would sound like an excuse.
What did Sonali's approach get right as a team lead?
She raised the problem privately, stated the deadline clearly, asked what was blocking, and cut the load instead of blaming Sudha in public 👍
How might the muttering teammates see the updated plan?
They may just see the work moving again without knowing Sudha's private reason, which protects her dignity.

Tuesday night. Ramesh here. I've watched eleven videos by the same finance influencer since dinner. Luxury car, beach villa, him saying, 'My trading course changed my life, and it can change yours.' The course costs more than two months of my stipend. I felt that pull, like if I don't join, I'm choosing to stay small. I had the payment page open. Then I texted Wasim, who's studying accounting. He replied: 'Ask how he actually makes money. From trading, or from selling courses to you?' Good question. I searched his name on the market regulator's list of registered advisers. Not there. I looked for any record of his trading returns. Only screenshots. The cars might be real. The evidence isn't. I closed the page. I'm annoyed, and a bit embarrassed at how close I came. Wasim sent me the free basics course from the stock exchange's own site instead. Starting it tomorrow.

How many videos had Ramesh watched since dinner?
Ramesh had watched eleven videos.
What pull did Ramesh feel with the payment page open?
Ramesh felt drawn in and anxious, as if not joining meant choosing to stay small.
What checks did Ramesh make, and why do they matter?
Searching the regulator's list of registered advisers and looking for real records, because a dream is not evidence.
How does Wasim see the influencer?
Wasim suspects he earns from selling courses rather than from trading, and pushes Ramesh to ask.

Usha was supposed to be asleep, but her eyes were wide open under the blanket. "Mummy, why are we here?"
Her mother, Lavanya, switched on the small lamp. "Here in this room?"
"No. Here. On earth. And what happens to Dadu now that he's gone?"
Lavanya sat on the bed. The flat was quiet, except for the fridge humming. "I love that you ask this. I don't know all the answers, Usha. Some people believe Dadu is at peace, some believe he's part of everything around us. What I know is that we remember him, and he is still part of who we are."
Usha thought. "I remember his tea-stirring."
"So do I. Tell me more."
Usha curled up against her mother's arm and started to tell it.

What did Usha remember about her grandfather?
She remembered his tea-stirring.
What was Usha probably feeling as she lay awake asking why we are here?
Usha was curious and probably a little sad and unsettled about Dadu having gone. The wide-open eyes suggest she couldn't rest with the questions.
What did Lavanya do that helped Usha feel her questions were welcome?
Lavanya said she loved the questions, admitted she did not know all the answers and shared what she knew. She then invited Usha to say more about the memories.
How might Lavanya have been feeling as she answered?
Lavanya may have felt tender and a bit sad herself, since Dadu is gone. She stayed calm and honest and did not brush the questions off.

When I was ten, I used to eat lunch with Francis. Before he ate, he always closed his eyes for a moment. I thought it was weird.
One day I asked. He said, "I say thanks. For the food, and for Mummy who made it."
The next day I tried it, secretly. I just thought, "Thanks, Amma, for the lemon rice." It felt silly. Then it felt nice.
Now I'm older, and I still do it. Just a pause, a few seconds of quiet, before I eat.
My name is Kiran, and I learnt that small habit from a boy in Class 5.

What did Kiran silently thank Amma for?
The lemon rice.
What was Kiran feeling the first time trying the pause?
Kiran felt silly at first, then found it pleasant and calming.
How could Kiran pass on this habit?
Kiran could share it with a friend or younger cousin the way Francis did, just by explaining it simply.
How might Francis feel if he knew Kiran still does it?
Francis would probably feel touched and pleased that a small habit of his mattered.

The wedding hall in Jaipur was hot and packed, the band was deafening, and Ishita had been handed four trays of sweets to serve. Every relative she served had a "should".

"You should be next, beta. Twenty-three is the right age."
"You should take the government exam, not this start-up nonsense."

Binita Masi, fanning herself, caught her arm. "Ishu, you should let me find you someone. I only want you settled."

Ishita's throat tightened. She loved Masi; Masi had sat with her through every childhood fever. But the shoulds were piling up like the trays.

She set the tray down, knelt by Masi's chair and spoke under the music. "Masi, I know you want me happy, and that means a lot. I'm happy in my job, and I'll know when I'm ready to marry. Can you trust me a little?"

Masi blinked, then patted her cheek. "Okay. But you'll tell me first."

How many trays of sweets was Ishita handed?
Ishita was handed four trays of sweets.
What did Ishita feel when Binita Masi caught her arm?
Ishita felt love and pressure together, her throat tightening, because Masi meant well but the shoulds kept piling up.
How did Ishita keep both respect and her own choice?
She knelt, spoke gently, thanked Masi for caring, and clearly stated her own plans while asking for trust.
How might Binita Masi see Ishita's words?
Masi seems a little surprised but reassured, choosing to trust Ishita as long as she's told first.

Pallavi was twenty-six and Hansa, her junior on the team, was thirty-four. Whenever Hansa's reports came in with figures missing, Pallavi's stomach knotted at the thought of correcting someone who had been working since Pallavi was in school. "I'll mention it after festival week," she told herself. Then after the quarter-end. Then after Hansa's birthday. Four months went by with the small comments never made. At the annual review, the manager asked for examples, and Pallavi handed over a long list. Hansa read it, blinked, and said quietly, "Why didn't you tell me in March?" The room in the Pune office felt very small.

How old was Hansa?
Hansa was thirty-four.
Why did Pallavi keep postponing the feedback?
Pallavi felt awkward about correcting someone older, and her stomach knotted at the thought.
What could Pallavi have done in March, and why?
Pallavi could have mentioned the missing figures in a short, kind chat when they first appeared, because small feedback early does not turn into a surprise later.
How might Hansa have felt reading the list at the review?
Hansa was probably surprised and hurt, wondering why nobody had said anything for months.

messages.content:
Read this:

I'm Vandana, and my first big home-staging client, Sabina, nearly broke me. Three days after I finished her flat for sale, she messaged: "I'll only release the final payment if you also style my sister's flat. Otherwise, my review will say you're unprofessional."
I read it on the bus and felt sick. My first instinct was to reply with something sharp, or threaten her back.
I didn't. Looking back, that was the best thing I did. I screenshotted every message: the original agreement, her approval photos, this one.
I replied, "Thank you for your message. The staging was completed and approved on 3 May, as per our agreement. The final payment is due. I'd be happy to quote separately for your sister's flat."
She didn't pay. So I filed a complaint through the consumer helpline, with the evidence attached. It took two months, but the money came. And the review never appeared.

When was the staging completed and approved?
On 3 May, as per the agreement.
What was Vandana feeling when reading Sabina's message on the bus?
Vandana felt sick and angry, tempted to reply sharply or threaten back.
What steps helped Vandana deal with the threat?
Keeping screenshots as evidence, replying courteously but firmly, offering a separate quote, and using the consumer helpline when payment was withheld.
How might Sabina have seen Vandana's calm reply?
Sabina probably expected Vandana to give in under pressure and may have felt thwarted by the firm, polite answer.

Uncle Jagdish pinned a printed article to our fridge: fake officers, fake job offers, fake parcels. I read it twice and then did something a bit silly. In front of the bathroom mirror, out loud, I practised. “I will call the police station myself.” “I don't discuss money on the phone.” “Thank you, no.” I said them until they sounded boring, which was the point. A week later my phone rang. A grave voice said there was a parcel in my name with something illegal inside. My hands shook. But the lines were already in my mouth, and I said, “I'll call the station myself,” and ended the call. Then I told Mama and sat down. — Mehr

Where did the narrator practise the lines?
In front of the bathroom mirror.
How did Mehr feel when the real call came?
Nervous: Mehr's hands shook, but the practised words came out anyway.
What else could Mehr add to the plan, and why?
A rule to hang up and tell an adult whatever the caller says, since a calm exit works even when the story sounds frightening.
How might Jagdish feel on hearing what happened?
Jagdish, who pinned the article, may feel relieved and proud that the reading turned into a calm refusal.

Read this:

Imran, it's Kashish. Before your first flu season here, let me tell you about mine. Last year I came into the office with a fever because I didn't want the team to think I was unreliable. New job, big client, you know. I sat there sweating, drinking tea after tea, and sent the client a report with last quarter's figures. Twice. Then I snapped at our manager when she asked if I was okay. By Friday, three people on our floor were ill, including an intern who had just started. So what did I actually prove? That I was reliable at spreading germs. This year, when I felt it coming on, I messaged the team: "Unwell, resting today, here's where my files are." Nobody minded. The work waited. That's the more responsible choice, honestly.

What did Kashish send the client by mistake?
A report with last quarter's figures, twice.
Why did Kashish come in with a fever last year?
Kashish was afraid of seeming unreliable in a new job with a big client.
What did Kashish do differently this year, and why was it better?
Kashish messaged the team, rested and shared where the files were, which protected colleagues and avoided mistakes.
How were Kashish's colleagues affected by last year's choice?
Three people on the floor fell ill, including a new intern, and the manager got snapped at for asking kindly.

"Ammi, can I eat in my room?" "Since when? Sit. What happened, Imran?" "Nothing." Parveen put down the ladle. "Your face says something." "There's a new boy, Joel. The group decided nobody sits with him. He tried to sit with us and Faisal said the table was full." "Was it?" "No." Imran pushed his rice around. "I wanted to move my bag. But then they'd say I'm not with them. Faisal's been my friend since Class 3." "And what do you want to be, beta?" "A good friend. And a good son. You'd be ashamed if I was mean." "Would I?" "Yes, Ammi." He looked up. "So what do I do when I can't be both?" Parveen sat down beside him. "Tell me what a good friend would do for Joel."

What did Faisal say when Joel tried to sit with them?
Faisal said the table was full.
Why is Imran pushing his rice around instead of eating?
He is torn: he wanted to move his bag for Joel but feared the group would think he wasn't with them, and he doesn't want Ammi to be ashamed of him.
What choice does Imran face at lunch tomorrow, and what small step could he take?
He must choose between the group's approval and fairness to Joel; he could start by moving his bag and saying hello, even if Faisal frowns.
What is it like for Joel when Faisal says the table is full?
Joel is shut out on purpose and likely feels embarrassed and alone, without knowing Imran wanted to move his bag.

I'm Uma, the neighbour aunty, and I watched this from my doorstep. Tejas, who is five, got a plain red toy car in a birthday bag. Ten minutes earlier he hadn't cared about it. Then Jaya's little girl offered her shiny blue car for a swap. Tejas hugged the red one to his chest. "No! Mine is the best one!" The blue car was bigger and had working lights. He still wouldn't swap. I'm not sure what he was thinking, but he held that red car all evening.

What did Jaya's little girl offer Tejas?
She offered her shiny blue car for a swap.
Why did Tejas hug the red car and call it the best one?
Tejas felt protective of the red car once it was his, so it seemed more precious to him even though the blue car was bigger and had working lights.
How could a grown-up help Tejas and the girl play together?
A grown-up could suggest taking turns with both cars, so Tejas keeps his red car safe while trying the blue one.
How might Jaya's little girl feel when Tejas refuses?
She may feel disappointed or confused, since she offered a car with lights and got a loud no.
I caught cold after getting wet in the rain. Do I need an article?

I caught a cold after getting wet in the rain.
Why: "Catch a cold" is the usual phrase; it needs "a".

"Okay Sachin, you want the honest version? Fine. During Durga Puja the campus clinic put up that notice about the flu shot, remember? Free, five minutes, and the doctor said it was a good idea for hostel people. I walked past it every day for two weeks.
It's not that I'm against vaccines. I read about one person who had a rare reaction, and I kept thinking: if I take the shot and that happens, it's my fault. I did it. But if I get the flu, well, that's just the flu. It happens to everyone.
Then in November I got it. Nine days in bed, missed my practical exam, and Ma took leave to come and look after me. The whole time I felt oddly less guilty than if the shot had given me a sore arm. That's messed up, right? So Anirban here is booking a proper talk with the doctor this time."

What did Anirban miss because of the flu?
Anirban missed the practical exam.
Why did skipping the flu shot feel safer to Anirban?
A rare reaction from the shot would feel like Anirban's own fault, while the flu just happens, so doing nothing felt less frightening and less blameworthy.
What would be a wise next step for Anirban?
Anirban could have that proper talk with the doctor, bring up the worry about the rare reaction, and weigh it against what the flu actually cost.
How was Ma affected by Anirban's choice?
Ma had to take leave to come and look after Anirban, so the choice that felt like doing nothing still cost her worry and time.

Hi Manoj da,
Quick update from the alumni meet you told me to attend. I got ten minutes with Ms Iyer from the design firm. At first she turned her whole body toward me, feet and shoulders, and asked lots of questions. I felt on top of the world. Then, halfway through my portfolio story, her shoulders swung toward the door while her face stayed on me. I panicked and thought, She's bored, I've lost her. I nearly stopped mid-sentence. Remembering your advice, I asked, "Should I wrap up? You look like you might need to be somewhere." She laughed, relieved. "Yes, my cab's waiting outside. But send me your portfolio tonight. I liked the bus-stop project." So the turn meant the cab, not me. I sent it at nine.
Thanks for pushing me to go.
Arnab

Which of Arnab's projects did Ms Iyer say she liked?
The bus-stop project.
What did Arnab feel when Ms Iyer's shoulders swung toward the door?
Arnab panicked, worried that she was bored and the chance was lost, though the turn could mean other things, as it did.
What did Arnab do instead of trusting the guess?
Arnab asked politely whether to wrap up because she might need to be somewhere, which gave her an easy way to explain.
How might Ms Iyer have felt when Arnab asked?
She likely felt relieved, since she needed to reach her cab and the question let her leave without seeming rude.

Vidya, sit, let me tell you about your Nilesh Chacha at twenty-five. I worked at the bank all day and ran a night school for mill workers' children from seven to ten. Three months of that. I ate dinner at midnight, and I was so proud of myself.
Then one afternoon I fell asleep at my counter while a customer was counting notes. My manager woke me, not angrily, just worried. That shook me more than a scolding would have.
That night I sat with a notebook and asked myself a plain question. If I break, who teaches those children? Nobody. So I cut the school to Tuesday and Saturday, two hours each, and I asked two college boys from our street to take the other days.
The school ran eleven more years, beti. It would not have lasted one more winter with me running it alone.

How long did Nilesh run the night school every evening before things changed?
For three months Nilesh ran it from seven to ten, eating dinner at midnight.
What did Nilesh feel after the manager woke him at the counter?
Nilesh felt shaken, because the manager's worry, more than any scolding, showed how worn out the long nights had made him.
At the moment he sat with the notebook, what other choice could Nilesh have made, and how might it have gone?
Nilesh could have pushed on alone out of pride, but would likely have broken down within the winter and the school would have closed.
How might the two college boys from the street have seen the invitation to teach?
They may have felt trusted and proud to be asked, and their joining is what let the school keep going for eleven more years.

Sunday night.
Scary thing today. I was driving Aditi back from the station, and my boss called about Monday's shift. I answered. Just a short call, I told myself.
At the roundabout a boy on a cycle came from the left. He was right there, in plain view, in a bright red shirt. I didn't see him until Aditi shouted. I braked, he wobbled, nobody was hurt. He glared at me, and he was right to.
I keep thinking: I'm not a careless person. I was looking. But my attention was on my boss's voice, not the road.
Aditi said, "You don't need to feel like a villain. You need a rule." So here's the rule, written down so I remember: phone in the boot on every drive. If someone calls, they can wait twenty minutes.
Kishore

What colour was the boy's shirt?
The boy's shirt was bright red.
How did Kishore feel after the near-miss?
Kishore felt shaken and guilty, knowing there had been looking but no real attention on the road.
What rule did Kishore write down, and why does it help?
Phone in the boot on every drive, so calls can't pull attention from the road.
How might the boy on the cycle have felt?
The boy was likely frightened and angry, which is why he glared.

Chandrika's diary, Thursday, 1 a.m.
Disha asked for the whole brochure in Tamil AND Hindi by Monday. I said "Of course, no problem!" in that bright voice I use when I'm panicking.
She's my biggest client. If she walks, rent is gone.
But I've already promised three other things this week. I haven't eaten dinner. My neck hurts from sitting. Last month I sent her a translation with two mistakes because I was this tired, and she noticed.
I'm scared of her. That's the truth. Not of her exactly, of losing her.
So tomorrow, first thing, I'm calling her. Script:
"I can do Tamil by Monday, done properly. Hindi by Thursday. If you need both Monday, I'd rather tell you now than do it badly."
Also: I'm messaging that school that asked for translations last month. One client shouldn't feel like my whole life.
Going to sleep. Actually going.

What languages did Disha ask for the brochure in?
Tamil and Hindi, by Monday.
What was Chandrika feeling when saying "Of course, no problem!"?
Chandrika was panicking and scared of losing the biggest client, hiding it behind a bright voice.
What is Chandrika's plan to stop overpromising?
Calling Disha with a realistic timeline, Tamil by Monday and Hindi by Thursday, and contacting another potential client to spread the risk.
How might Disha have felt about last month's translation mistakes?
Disha probably felt annoyed and less confident in the work, which is why an honest timeline may rebuild trust.

Dear Diary,
We got our maths test back. I got 9 out of 25. I folded it very small and pushed it inside the torn lining of my school bag.
At dinner Ritu didi asked. I said, "Ma'am hasn't given it back yet." My heart was going so fast. Didi looked at me for a long time.
Last time I got a low mark, Papa shouted for half an hour and took away cricket for a month. So now I hide. I don't even feel bad about the lie. I feel bad about the 9.
But it needs a signature by Friday.
Tonight Didi sat on my bed. "Kamal, whatever it is, I'll sit with you when you tell Mummy." I nearly cried.
Maybe tomorrow.

What did Kamal get on the maths test?
I got 9 out of 25.
Why did Kamal hide the test paper?
Kamal was afraid of being shouted at and punished again, as after the last low mark.
How could Kamal's parents help Kamal stop hiding things?
They could respond calmly to low marks and help with the maths, so telling the truth no longer feels dangerous.
How might Ritu didi feel sitting on the bed?
Ritu didi seems worried and caring, sensing the lie and gently offering to sit with Kamal while telling Mummy.

Friday. Disha wrote her birthday plan: a game with chairs, quiet and neat, and cake after. She liked how tidy it looked.

Saturday. Ten friends sat in a ring. Two minutes in, Meera was yawning, someone kept peeking at the garden, and a boy tapped his feet. Disha looked around and put the whistle down. "New game! Catch the ribbon in the garden!" The chairs stayed in the hall and everybody ran outside, shouting.

Sunday. Gopika phoned. "That garden game was the best part. Can we play it at my house?"

What did Disha change the game to when the chairs stopped working?
Disha switched to catching the ribbon in the garden.
What did Disha notice about her friends during the quiet game, and what might Disha feel?
Disha noticed yawning, peeking at the garden and tapping feet; Disha probably felt worried the party was going flat but decided quickly.
What alternative approach could Disha have used, and why?
Disha could have prepared one quiet and one active game in advance, so a switch would be easy. Having a spare game means the party need not depend on a single idea.
What did the change mean for Gopika?
Gopika enjoyed the garden game most and wants to play it again, so for Gopika the switch saved the afternoon.

messages.content: What is rangoli and why do people make it?
Rangoli is a pattern drawn on the floor with coloured powder, rice flour or flower petals. It is made at the entrance of homes, especially at festivals, to welcome guests and bring good fortune.
Does it have to be a fixed design?
No. Some families follow traditional patterns, but many people create their own. Dots, flowers and lamps are popular, and the designs differ across regions.

Monday: "There's a snake under my bed!" Dilnaz cried. Her mother, Deepika, laughed. "Don't be a baby. There's nothing there." Dilnaz's face went hot. She turned to the wall.
Wednesday: Dilnaz lay awake, still afraid, but said nothing. She didn't want to be laughed at again. In the morning, her eyes were puffy.
Friday: Deepika noticed. "You're not sleeping. Is it the snake?" Dilnaz nodded. Deepika sat on the bed. "I'm sorry I laughed. I believe you're scared. Let's look together." They checked with a torch. Dilnaz slept with Mummy's scarf tucked beside her.

What did Dilnaz think was under her bed?
She thought there was a snake under her bed.
Why did Dilnaz say nothing on Wednesday?
She felt ashamed after being laughed at and hid her fear so she wouldn't be mocked again.
What did Deepika change on Friday, and why did it help?
She apologised for laughing, said she believed Dilnaz was scared and checked with her, which helped the fear shrink.
How might Deepika feel when she sees Dilnaz's puffy eyes?
She may feel worried and guilty, realising her laugh made Dilnaz keep quiet.

Dear Amma and Appa,

I'm writing this so you can read it properly before we talk.

You know about the paper leak in the state board exam. Thousands of us studied for months, and now some people bought the questions. I'm so angry I can't sleep. Imran and some seniors are organising a silent march on Saturday from the school gate to the education office to ask for a fair re-exam.

Before saying yes, I checked. The march has written police permission; Imran showed me the letter. It's from ten to twelve, on the main road, no shouting, just placards. Two teachers are coming. I've read the news reports and the board's statement, so I know what we're actually asking for.

I want to go. I'll walk with the teachers, keep my phone charged, and send you my location every half hour. If anything feels unsafe, I'll leave and call you.

Can we talk tonight after dinner?

Dolma

What time does the silent march run?
The march runs from ten to twelve.
What was Dolma feeling about the paper leak?
Dolma felt so angry about the unfairness that sleep was hard.
What did Dolma do that made the plan safer and wiser?
Dolma checked the permission letter, read the news and the board's statement, planned to walk with teachers and share a location every half hour.
How might Amma and Appa feel reading this letter?
They might feel worried about the march, but also reassured and proud that Dolma checked the facts and made a safety plan.

Maria, twenty, was eating toast on the balcony of her Bengaluru PG when the headline popped up on her phone: "Coffee drinkers live longer, huge study finds."
By lunch she had bought a bag of filter coffee powder and a steel tumbler set. By the evening she was on her third cup.
"You hate coffee," Simran said from the doorway.
"I'm learning to like it. It's science. The study had half a million people."
"Did it say why they lived longer?"
"Because of the coffee, obviously."
Simran picked up the phone and scrolled. "It says coffee drinkers in the study also walked more and smoked less."
Maria took the phone back and scrolled up to the headline again. "Yeah, but the big number is about coffee." She poured another cup, grimacing at the bitterness.

How many people did Maria say the study had?
Half a million people.
How does Maria feel about the coffee headline, and what shows it?
Maria feels convinced and eager, buying coffee powder by lunch and drinking a third cup by evening, even grimacing at the bitterness, because the huge study sounds like proof.
At which moment could Maria think again, and what could she ask?
When Simran reads that coffee drinkers also walked more and smoked less; Maria could ask whether those habits, not the coffee, explain the longer lives.
How might Simran feel watching Maria drink coffee she dislikes?
Simran is probably amused and a little puzzled that Maria forces down a bitter drink because of a headline, especially after pointing out the other habits.

"Bhaiya, you missed the whole week," Sunaina said, leaning on the kitchen door. "So that's it? You're quitting?"

"No." Lokesh pulled out his notebook. "I looked at the ticks. Every session I skipped was in the evening. Late meetings, tired, hungry. The mornings, I never missed."

"So?"

"So it's not me, it's the timing. I'm moving everything to six-thirty in the morning."

"And if you miss again?"

"New rule. I can miss once, but never twice in a row."

Sunaina grinned. "You've turned a failure into a spreadsheet."

"It's data," he said. "Tomorrow, six-thirty. Bang on my door if I'm not up."

What time will Lokesh move his sessions to?
Six-thirty in the morning.
What is Lokesh feeling after looking at his ticks?
Lokesh feels determined and a bit relieved, since seeing the pattern shows the problem was timing and not a lack of effort.
What could Lokesh do if the morning slot also fails, and why?
Lokesh could note the reason again and test another time or a shorter session, because each missed session gives new information to adjust the plan.
How might Sunaina see Lokesh's response to the missed week?
Sunaina may be relieved and amused that Lokesh did not quit, and the joke about the spreadsheet shows a wish to help.

Sarita, you think you're the first one to fail an exam? Come, let me tell you about your Manoj mama.

Second year of engineering, I failed Fluid Mechanics. Thirty-one out of a hundred. I came back to the hostel and lay on the bed and asked the ceiling, why? Why me? Was I stupid? Had my father wasted his money? My roommate Gopal went to dinner, came back, and I was still asking the same questions. For two weeks I did that. I didn't open a single book. I felt worse every day.

Then Gopal threw the question paper on my chest. "Stop asking why. Circle the questions you couldn't do." I circled six. Four were from the same chapter I'd skipped.

That's all. A chapter, not my whole worth. I cleared the supplementary in October. So, Sarita beta, which chapter did you skip?

What mark did Manoj get in Fluid Mechanics?
Manoj got thirty-one out of a hundred.
What was young Manoj feeling during those two weeks of asking why?
Young Manoj felt ashamed and low, fearing he was stupid and had wasted his father's money, and the questions only made him feel worse each day.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
Gopal telling Manoj to circle the questions he couldn't do turned vague self-blame into a concrete finding: four were from one skipped chapter.
How might Gopal have seen Manoj during those two weeks?
Gopal probably watched with growing worry as Manoj lay there asking the same questions, until he decided to push him toward the question paper.

When Charu started explaining the savings sheet she had made, Yogesh rolled his eyes. "Here we go, the accountant." He mimicked the way she hummed while she chopped onions, and felt superior and very tired. It was easier than saying that he had been feeling unseen since the job changed.

Charu felt herself shrink. She stopped in the middle of a sentence, and for a moment she thought about answering in kind, with a sneer of her own. She swallowed it. Speaking felt risky, as if anything she said would be turned into a joke. She told her friend Ishita about it at lunch, and Ishita said, "That's a pattern, not one bad evening."

That night Charu said, quietly, "When you roll your eyes and copy me, I feel small. I would like us to talk with respect. If this keeps happening, I would like to see a counsellor together."

Yogesh went quiet. Then, after a while, he said, "I've been feeling like nobody notices what I do since the transfer, and I took it out on you. I'm sorry." He turned off the television. "Tell me about the sheet."

Where did Charu tell Ishita about it?
She told Ishita at lunch.
How did Yogesh's eye-rolling look from his side and from Charu's side?

Yogesh felt superior and tired but was really hiding that he felt unseen, while Charu felt small and unsafe to speak. She named the pattern and asked for respect, and he then named the hurt beneath it.
What was Charu feeling when she stopped in the middle of her sentence?
She felt small and unsafe to speak, afraid her words would be turned into a joke.
What could Charu do if Yogesh's sneering returns after this talk?
She could calmly point to the pattern again, ask for respect without sneering back, and suggest they see a counsellor together.

I'm Parul, and I teach in the department Vasudha heads. Last term the school gave new laptops to the senior teachers only. We were all paid on the same scale and nobody was underpaid, but the junior staff went quiet in a way I hadn't seen before. They stopped volunteering for events. Someone left a note on the staffroom board: "Seniors: laptops. Juniors: chalk." Vasudha noticed. I saw her read the note twice and leave it up. At the next meeting she laid out exactly how the laptops had been allotted, by years of service, and admitted the rule had never been explained. Then she got the management to publish when the juniors would get theirs. I can't say what she felt, but her voice was steady. The note came down on its own a week later.

What did the note on the staffroom board say?
"Seniors: laptops. Juniors: chalk."
What does Vasudha reading the note twice and leaving it up suggest?
She seemed to take the junior staff's resentment seriously rather than wanting to hide it.
What did Vasudha do at the next meeting, and why did it help?
She explained how laptops were allotted by years of service, admitted it hadn't been explained, and got a published date for juniors, making the criteria transparent.
How might the junior staff feel once the date for their laptops was published?
They may feel less left behind, since the rule was now clear and they could see when their turn would come.

You asked how I run reviews on my team, Akash. I'm Sumit, and I lead a small sales team at a furniture company. Here's the one habit that changed everything.

Before any big decision, like which city to open in or which client to chase, I write a short note. What we expect to happen. How sure we are. Why we think so. It takes five minutes.

Last year we opened in Nashik. I wrote, "60% chance this works. Main risk: a big competitor might arrive." Six months later, one did, and sales fell.

In the review, one manager said it was obvious we'd fail. I opened the note. "We said 60%. We named this risk. The decision was reasonable. We were unlucky." Nobody got blamed.

But in another case, the note showed we'd ignored a warning. That one, we learned from properly.

Without the notes, everything looks obvious afterwards.

What chance of success did Sumit write for opening in Nashik?
60% chance this works.
How did Sumit feel when the manager called the Nashik result obvious?
Sumit felt calm and confident, because the note showed the decision had been reasonable and the risk was named.
Why is writing forecasts before outcomes a fair practice?
It shows what was known at the time, so reviews can separate bad luck from bad decisions and avoid wrongly blaming people.
How might Sumit's team members feel about this habit?
Team members probably feel safer taking reasonable risks, knowing they won't be blamed for bad luck.

The prize distribution at the school hall in Indore ran late because the sound system kept crackling. Rukmini, five, walked back from the stage with her medal, chest out, chin up, marching like a soldier. Her father Kamal, holding a cold drink, clapped. On the way out, a group of older children crowded near. Rukmini's chest sank, and she stepped behind Kamal's leg, holding the medal against her tummy. He said quietly, "You can show them when you're ready." After a minute, she peeked out and held the medal up.

What did Rukmini do with her chest when she walked back from the stage?
She walked back with her chest out and her chin up.
What does Rukmini's stepping behind her father's leg suggest she felt when the older children crowded round?
It suggests she felt shy or wary, since her chest sank and she held the medal to her tummy. She might also simply have been tired after the long event.
What could Kamal do to help Rukmini in a crowd?
He can let her take her time behind him and invite her to show the medal when she is ready, as he did.
How might the older children see Rukmini's marching walk?
They may see a proud small girl, and might not realise she felt shy when they crowded round.

Monday: At break, Simran sat alone on the steps, picking at her shoelace. The teacher, Mrs Nair, sat down beside her and said nothing for a bit. Then she asked, "Want to help me count the ducks on the pond?"
Tuesday: Mrs Nair and Simran were counting again when Imran came over. "What are you counting?" "Ducks. Want to help?" Mrs Nair asked. Imran squatted beside Simran. "I see seven!"
Friday: Simran and Imran counted ducks by themselves. Mrs Nair waved from the gate and did not come over.

How many ducks did Imran count?
Imran said, "I see seven!"
What was Simran feeling when she sat on the steps?
She felt lonely and alone, picking at her shoelace while others played.
How did Mrs Nair help without embarrassing Simran?
She sat beside her quietly, offered a simple job and let another child join naturally, without forcing anyone to be friends.
Why might Mrs Nair stay back at the gate on Friday?
She can see Simran is less lonely now, so she steps back and lets the friendship grow on its own.

Vidya, you're a new mother now, so let me tell you something about your uncle Ravi. Come, drink your tea.
When I was twenty-five, Ravi was four, and I was certain he was shy. I said it everywhere: "He's shy, he won't talk." At the doctor's, I answered for him. At school I asked the teacher not to make him stand up.
One day his class had a play. The teacher, Madhuri, came to our door. "Let him be a tree, at least. Trees don't speak." I nearly said no. Then I thought: what if I'm wrong about him?
He was the tree. The next year he was the shopkeeper, with two lines. Now he argues cases in court. I had been so sure. My certainty was the thing keeping him quiet.

What role did Ravi play the first year?
He was the tree.
What was the elder feeling when nearly saying no to the play?
The elder felt protective and certain, then a flicker of doubt about whether the shy label was really true.
What was the turning point in the story?
The turning point was deciding to say yes to Madhuri's idea of the tree role instead of shielding Ravi again.
How might Madhuri, the teacher, have seen Ravi before the play?
Madhuri probably saw a child who could do more if given a small, safe chance, which is why she came to the door.

When Wei moved from Shanghai to a school in Johannesburg, a group of boys adopted him in the first week. They loved his sneakers. They loved his accent. They said he was the smartest guy in the class. Then they asked him to buy the tickets for the cinema, again and again.
Zanele sat next to him in maths. She laughed at his jokes when they were funny and rolled her eyes when they weren't. When he said he wanted to try out for the debate team, she said, "You'd be good. But you talk too fast when you're nervous. Practise with me."
One afternoon, Wei told the boys he couldn't pay for the cinema this week. The group chat went silent.
Zanele texted: "Debate practice tomorrow? Bring snacks, I'll bring the timer."
Wei smiled at the screen. He knew now which kind of friend he wanted to keep.

What did Zanele say Wei does when he's nervous?
She said he talks too fast when he's nervous.
What was Wei feeling when the group chat went silent?
Wei felt hurt but also clear, seeing that the boys' praise had been tied to what he paid for.
What did Wei learn about telling warmth from steering?
He learned that Zanele, who praises and also disagrees without asking for anything, is the friend to trust.

Sunday night
Finished the last of the eight Science board papers today, the 2016 one, timed, at the dining table while Jasleen did hers on a video call. Then I did what Sir told us: added up my lost marks by reason. I've been writing each one at the back of my rough book since January. Totals: slow writing, 38. Didn't know the concept, 14. The 2016 Science paper, the last of the eight.

Study how marking schemes award points and practise matching them, so each long answer covers the key points in fewer words.

Jasleen gets to support a friend and may pick up the same point-form habit for her own papers.

Read this:

Every evening in the Chandigarh flat, Gurleen's father, Manoj, asked the same question. "Where's your mother? She's late from the gurdwara."
Mummy had died two years ago. Papa's memory had been slipping since spring, and the doctor had said to keep him calm.
The first time, Gurleen told him the truth, and he cried as if hearing it for the first time. In a way, he was. The next evening he asked again.
Her cousin said, "Just say she's at the market. It's kinder." Gurleen didn't want to lie to her father. She also couldn't watch him grieve fresh every night.
She thought about it for a week. Then she found a middle path. When he asked, she would sit beside him, hold his hand and say, "You're thinking of Mummy. Tell me about her." He would smile and talk about the day they met at the fair.
She wrote her choice in the notebook she kept for the doctor, so it was on record and hers. Some nights it still felt heavy. But it felt honest enough to live with.

Where did Papa think Mummy was?
At the gurdwara, late.
What was Gurleen feeling as she weighed her cousin's advice?
Gurleen felt torn, unwilling to lie to her father yet unable to watch him grieve fresh every night.
How did Gurleen find the least deceptive path?
She neither repeated the painful news nightly nor invented a lie; she held his hand, said 'You're thinking of Mummy', invited him to talk, and noted the choice for the doctor.
What was it like for Papa when Gurleen first told him the truth?
Papa cried as if hearing of Mummy's death for the first time, because in a way he was.
Our lane wants to put on a small street play about keeping the area clean. I'm supposed to write the script.
That's a great way to share a message. Keep it short, around ten minutes, with simple scenes and a few characters.
What should the story be?
Maybe a person who throws litter and meets a funny 'garbage monster' who shows the effect of mess. It can be humorous but have a clear point at the end.

Summarize what Wickham tells Elizabeth here, in one or two sentences.

"We were born in the same parish, within the same park; the greatest part of our youth was passed together: inmates of the same house, sharing the same amusements, objects of the same parental care. My father began life in the profession which your uncle, Mr. Philips, appears to do so much credit to; but he gave up everything to be of use to the late Mr. Darcy, and devoted all his time to the care of the Pemberley property. He was most highly esteemed by Mr. Darcy, a most intimate, confidential friend. Mr. Darcy often acknowledged himself to be under the greatest obligations to my father's active superintendence; and when, immediately before my father's death, Mr. Darcy gave him a voluntary promise of providing for me, I am convinced that he felt it to be as much a debt of gratitude to him as of affection to myself."

Wickham says he grew up alongside Darcy at Pemberley, where his father managed the estate for old Mr. Darcy. Before his father died, old Mr. Darcy promised to provide for Wickham out of gratitude and affection.

After Jonas told her by the bike racks that he just wanted to be friends, Astrid cycled home through the sleet in Gothenburg without her gloves. She didn't text him. She didn't post anything. She sat at her desk with her grandmother's old notebook and wrote until her hand cramped. A poem about a lighthouse that nobody visited. Another about the bike racks, with every bike leaving but one.
On Saturday, her friend Ingrid read them at the kitchen table over cinnamon buns. "These are really good," Ingrid said quietly. "Sad, but good."
Astrid looked at the page. It still hurt. But the hurt had edges now, a shape she could hold up and show someone. That evening she signed up for the school poetry night.

What did Astrid's first poem describe?
A lighthouse that nobody visited.
Why did Astrid write instead of texting Jonas or posting something?
She was hurt, and writing let her give the pain a shape without lashing out at him or exposing it online.
Which choice turned Astrid's pain into something she could share?
Letting Ingrid read the poems, and then signing up for the poetry night, so others could see the feeling she had shaped.
What might it have meant to Ingrid to read the poems?
Ingrid got to understand how much Astrid was hurting without having to ask, and could answer with honest, gentle praise.

Every Saturday at nine, Eshaan unlocked Room 3 of the Kalyan Nagar community centre for the adult reading class. He had signed up in first year of college mostly to have something for his CV. The first months were dull: flashcards, slow syllables, learners who missed weeks. Most volunteers drifted away. Eshaan kept going, partly because Avni aunty, sixty-two, always brought him a steel tumbler of filter coffee and asked, "Same time next week?" In March, on the walk to the bus stop, Avni aunty stopped under a signboard. She moved her finger along the letters. "Ma-ja-staic. Majestic." Then she turned to him, eyes bright. "I can go to my daughter's house alone now." Eshaan laughed, then had to look away. On the bus home he opened his CV and deleted the line. It wasn't about that anymore.

What did Avni aunty always bring Eshaan?
A steel tumbler of filter coffee.
Why did Eshaan delete the line from his CV?
He felt moved and proud after Avni aunty read the sign, and realised the class now meant far more to him than a CV line.
What small step could the community centre take to keep volunteers like Eshaan?
They could ask volunteers to commit to one learner for a few months, so each one gets to see a moment of progress like the signboard.
What is it like for Avni aunty to read the signboard?
It gives her a new freedom and pride, since she can now travel to her daughter's house alone.

Subject: About the photo of Ira

Dear Mrs Fernandes,
You asked me to write down what happened, so here it is.
On Tuesday at the science fair, Tamanna took a photo of Ira mid-sneeze, braces showing, glasses slipping. Tamanna is house captain, and she said, 'Send it to the Class 10 group, it's hilarious.' So I sent it. I didn't take it and I didn't write the caption. I only forwarded it because she told me to.
I know Ira didn't come to school on Wednesday or Thursday. But I think Tamanna and the forty people who reacted should be asked about that too, not only me.
Honestly, when a house captain tells you something, you don't really argue.
I keep checking whether Ira has seen the group.
Aadhya, 10B

According to Aadhya, who gave the instruction to send the photo?
Tamanna, the house captain, who said, 'Send it to the Class 10 group, it's hilarious.'
Why does forwarding the photo feel reasonable to Aadhya from the inside?
Aadhya feels uneasy, still checking whether Ira has seen the group, but since Tamanna took the photo and gave the order, Aadhya's own part feels like just going along.
What choice could Aadhya make now that would actually help Ira?
Aadhya could own the one step that was Aadhya's, pressing send, then ask the group to delete the photo and apologise to Ira directly.
How might Ira see the question of who 'only' forwarded the photo?
For Ira it hardly matters who took it or who gave the order; every forward spread the sneeze photo further, and Ira stayed away from school for two days after it.

At the school science fair, Indu's water-filter model stood on Table 6 with a neat chart beside it. Ms. Fernandes stopped and read the chart twice.
"Indu, did an AI help write this?"
"No, Ma'am," Indu said, too fast. Her partner Vikas looked at his shoes.
Ms. Fernandes moved on to the next table. Indu's cheeks prickled. The chart had come from the AI. She and Vikas had built the filter, tested the gravel layers and timed the drips, but the words weren't hers.
Before the judges arrived, she walked over. "Ma'am, I said no, but that wasn't true. The AI wrote the chart. We did the model and the tests."
Ms. Fernandes smiled. "Thank you for coming back. Explain the tests to the judges yourself. That part is all yours."

What did Indu and Vikas build for the fair?
A water-filter model.
Why did Indu's cheeks prickle after she said no?
She felt guilty and uneasy, knowing the chart had come from the AI.
How did Indu fix her first answer, and why did it help?
She went back before the judges arrived and told the truth, which kept her teacher's trust and let her show her own tests.
How might Ms. Fernandes see Indu coming back?
She sees an honest student who corrected herself, so she thanks her and guides her to present her real work.

Wednesday, 9.40 p.m.
Almost sent it. The AI summary of the sixty-page market report looked perfect: five bullet points, three figures, two citations. Rehana wanted the client note by 10 tomorrow.
But I've read enough about these tools making things up, so I went back to the original report, figure by figure. Market size: 4,200 crore. Matches page 12. Growth rate: the summary said 18%. The report says 18% for one segment only; overall it's 11%. Citation two: a 'government survey, 2022' that isn't in the report at all. I searched. I can't find it anywhere.
So two of five points would have gone to the client wrong. I fixed the growth rate, cut the fake citation and put page numbers next to every figure.
Tomorrow I'll tell Rehana what I found. Tired, but glad.
Kavitha

What does the report say overall growth is?
Overall it's 11%.
How does Kavitha feel at the end of the evening?
Kavitha feels tired but glad and relieved, having caught two wrong points before they reached the client.
What else could Kavitha suggest to Rehana for future summaries?
Kavitha could suggest that every AI summary carry page numbers for each figure, so anyone can check it against the source quickly.
How might the client have been affected if the note had gone out unchecked?
The client could have acted on a wrong growth rate and a citation that doesn't exist, damaging trust in the firm.

It was their first night in the new house in Lima. Rosa lay in her cot, wide awake, stroking the satin edge of her old blanket between finger and thumb, over and over.
Daniel sat by the cot. He didn't take the blanket or tell her to sleep. He just sat.

What did Rosa stroke between finger and thumb?
The satin edge of her old blanket.

She was likely unsettled and a little worried in a strange room, and stroking the familiar blanket helped her feel safe enough to sleep.

He stayed nearby and left the blanket with her, letting her use her own comfort without rushing her.

"So in the church part, you'll say 'till death do us part'," Charu said, spreading the order of service on the bed. "Mummy is very serious about that line."
Irawati looked at it. "In our pheras we take seven steps and seven vows. My Aaji says each step is a promise. But honestly, I don't know what your mother hears in that line."
"What do you mean?"
"For my family the vows matter, but so does everything around them, the families, the feasts. For yours, it sounds like the words themselves are the whole thing."
Charu thought. "For Mummy, yes. She says once you say it in church, it's before God and the law both. No going back."
"Then I want to understand it properly before I say it. Can we ask her tomorrow what it means to her?"

How many steps and vows are in Irawati's pheras?
Seven steps and seven vows.

Irawati felt uncertain and a little anxious, not knowing what Charu's mother heard in 'till death do us part', and wanted to understand before saying it.

Asking Charu's mother what the vows mean to her, and having Aaji explain the seven steps, so each side understands the other's commitment.

"Coming, Mohit." Footsteps. Suraj sat on the bed. "Cold?"

Mohit felt safe and secure, trusting that Papa is there.

He comes every time, meets each need, warmth and water, and says calmly that Papa always comes.
