In their Haifa apartment, Yosef had noticed the boxes in the storeroom and the long phone calls behind closed doors. For a week the ten-year-old had been quiet, eating little.
Daniel finally sat on the edge of his bed. "Yosef, you look worried. Want to tell me?"
"Are you and Ima getting divorced?" Yosef whispered.
Daniel's chest tightened. "No. No, we're not. I'm sorry you've been carrying that." He took a breath. "Here's what's really happening. I got a new job in Toronto. We're moving there in August. The boxes are for that. We didn't tell you because we weren't sure yet, and that was a mistake."
Yosef stared. "Toronto? Is there snow?"
"Lots."
"Will I have friends?"
"Not at first. It'll be hard. We'll help."
Yosef let out a long breath and leaned against his father.

When is the family moving to Toronto?
They are moving there in August.
What was Yosef afraid of before Daniel explained?
Yosef was scared and anxious that his parents were getting divorced, imagining the worst from the boxes and closed doors.
What went right in how Daniel explained the move?
He asked about Yosef's worry first, told the truth simply, admitted keeping quiet was a mistake, and was honest that making friends would be hard.
What would change if Daniel had kept the move secret longer?
Yosef's divorce fear would likely have grown, and he might have trusted his parents less when he finally found out.
Only people with a library card can borrow books. Zara could not borrow a book today. What can we say?

"Nirmala, can you close the door for a minute?"
"Is it about the salary, Damini? It's fine, I know things are tight."
"It's not fine. It's the second month late. You've been here since we started, and you've never asked once."
"I believe in this place."
"I know you do. That's why I have to be honest. We have enough to pay what we owe you and the others by the fifteenth, and that's being paid first. After that, I don't know if we'll make it past August."
Nirmala looked at her hands. "Oh."
"I've written you a reference. It's in your inbox. If you get an offer, take it. I'd never want you to stay out of guilt."
"But what about you?"

Nirmala was quiet, then nodded. "Thank you for telling me straight."
"You earned that much. You earned more."

By what date will Damini pay what she owes the staff?
By the fifteenth.
What was Nirmala feeling when she said "Oh"?
Nirmala felt shaken and worried, looking at her hands after hearing the company might not last past August.
How did Damini treat Nirmala's loyalty with respect?
Damini was transparent about the future, paid dues first, wrote a reference, and urged Nirmala to take any offer without guilt.
How might Damini be feeling as she speaks?
Damini seems guilty and responsible, which is why she insists the risk is hers to carry and not Nirmala's.

Seema, you asked why I always say 'ask me anything'. Let me tell you. When I was twelve, in our village, nobody explained anything to girls. One morning I saw blood and thought I was dying. I hid in the cowshed and cried. My mother just said, 'Keep quiet, don't tell anyone,' and gave me old cloth. I felt dirty for months, as if I'd done something wrong. Only when my aunt came visiting did she sit me down, say 'Leela, listen,' and tell me it was my body growing up, that it happens to every girl. I promised myself my girls would know before. So, Seema, your voice-changing brother, your own body, all of it: ask me anything.

Where did young Leela hide when she first saw the blood?
She hid in the cowshed and cried.
Why did young Leela feel dirty for months?
She felt ashamed and frightened, because nobody explained what was happening and she was told to keep quiet, so she believed she had done something wrong.
What is Leela doing differently for Seema?
She is inviting open questions about body changes early, so Seema can learn facts before any fear or shame sets in.
How might Seema feel hearing Leela's story?
Seema might feel sad for young Leela and more comfortable bringing questions to Leela.

After the match in Lisbon, Ines sat with her head down and her friend Bao gave her shoulder a light squeeze. "Rough one." Ines nodded, grateful. It felt like being held up. But when the assistant coach patted her shoulder the same way, then let his hand slide down her back, Ines went rigid. Something felt wrong. She stepped away and said, "Please don't." The coach shrugged and left. Ines's hands were shaking. Bao noticed. "Are you okay?" "I don't like what he did." "You said stop, that was right. Let's tell the head coach and your parents." That evening the head coach listened to Ines and her parents, told Ines it was not her fault, and reported it to the club's safeguarding officer the same day.

In which city did Ines sit with her head down after the match?
Ines was in Lisbon.
What was Ines feeling when the coach's hand slid down her back?
She felt uncomfortable and alarmed, and went rigid, and her hands shook. This felt different from Bao's welcome squeeze.
What could Ines do next?
She can keep talking to the head coach, her parents or another trusted adult, and keep away from that coach. She did right to say stop, and it was not her fault.
How might Bao have felt hearing Ines?
Bao was worried and supportive, checking on Ines and backing what she did. Bao points Ines toward trusted adults.

A samosa evening, and she sat with him.

Come here, Arnab, you look worried about the results. Sit. I'm Joseph, and I have been where you are. At sixteen I failed my whole year and I hid it. I took the report card out of the letterbox before anyone saw it and told my parents "results next month." I dreaded every dinner.

In the end my older sister found the crumpled card and just sat with me. I cried for an hour. My parents were sad, but they helped me plan the repeat year. I wish I had told them sooner.

How long was Joseph alone with the secret?
Joseph was alone with it for six weeks.

Joseph felt afraid and lonely, dreading every dinner and feeling sick when the phone rang. Hiding seemed safer at first but grew heavier.

Joseph's older sister found the crumpled card and sat with Joseph, who cried for an hour. The parents were sad but helped plan the repeat year.

Joseph's sister was probably worried and gentle, choosing to sit beside Joseph without scolding. Being calm made it safe to cry and tell the truth.

He folded the studio's form into his pocket without filling it.

Elizabeth may see that he wants the studio path but something holds him back, since she invited him with “Coming?” and glanced at him.

Four lakh.

"Uday! Can you like my page? New skincare business," Lavanya said over coffee.
"Sure." He tapped it.
"And come to my demo evening on Friday? Just an hour."

On Friday, after the demo, Lavanya handed him a form. "Starter kit! You'd be amazing at selling this. Only eight thousand to join."

Only eight thousand to join.

In Accra, Kofi, nine, knocked over a tin of blue paint on the church steps while decorating for Easter. His grandmother, Auntie Vera, gasped. "Kofi! What will people say? The whole church will talk about our family!"
Kofi's stomach twisted. He didn't think about the steps. He thought about the faces of the ladies in the choir.
The next week, he broke a cup at home and hid the pieces under the sink.
When his father found them, he sat Kofi down. "Why did you hide it?"
"So nobody would talk about us."
His father sighed. "Kofi, the cup matters because it was Grandma's, not because of neighbours. When you make a mistake, you own it and fix it. Not because of what people say. Because it's right."
Kofi went to Auntie Vera and told her about the cup himself.

What did Kofi knock over on the church steps?
He knocked over a tin of blue paint.
What was Kofi thinking about when his stomach twisted?
Kofi felt ashamed and afraid, thinking about the faces of the choir ladies rather than the steps.
What did Kofi's father teach him that fear of gossip didn't?
He taught Kofi to own and fix mistakes because it is right, not because of what people might say.
How might Auntie Vera feel when Kofi tells her about the cup himself?
She might feel surprised and touched by his honesty, and perhaps rethink how she reacted about the paint.

Read this:

"Ritu, my friend's café needs a website. Can you do it by Friday? I told him you're fast."
Ritu looked up from her laptop at her brother. "Zubin, before I say yes, give me two minutes."
"Two minutes to say yes?"
"To check." She opened a spreadsheet. "Last three small websites. The bakery: I guessed four days, it took nine. The yoga studio: guessed five, took eight. The tailor: guessed three, took seven, because the photos came late."
Zubin leaned over. "Okay, that's… a lot."
"So I break it down. Menu page, photos, contact form, mobile check, his changes. And I add a few days for surprises." She typed. "Realistic date: the Friday after next."
"He'll be disappointed."
"Less disappointed than if I promise this Friday and miss it."
Zubin nodded slowly and picked up his phone to call his friend.

How long did the bakery website actually take?
The bakery: guessed four days, it took nine.
Why did Ritu insist on checking before agreeing to Friday?
She knew from her own record that her guesses were usually too short, and she seemed to care more about keeping a promise than pleasing her brother right away.
What steps did Ritu take before giving a date?
She looked at how long three similar sites really took, broke the job into parts like the menu page and photos, and added a buffer for surprises.
What would change for Zubin's friend if Ritu had simply said yes to this Friday?
The friend might be happy at first but let down when the site was late, and Zubin would look bad for having said Ritu was fast.

Read this:

I sit next to Vandana at the customer service centre, and I've been watching her since she joined three months ago. She's the first one at her desk every morning, headset on before the shift bell. Last Tuesday, a customer's refund got delayed because a form was filled in wrong. The team leader asked who'd done it. There was silence. Some people looked at the new boy, who looked terrified. Vandana raised her hand. "It was me. I'll call the customer and fix it today." I thought she'd get into trouble. The team leader just nodded and said thank you. At lunch some of the others were gossiping about the manager's favourites. Vandana ate quietly and changed the subject to cricket. I don't know what she was thinking. But I noticed.

What went wrong with the customer's refund?
It got delayed because a form was filled in wrong.
What might Vandana have been feeling when she raised her hand?
She was probably nervous about getting into trouble but felt it was right to own her mistake, especially when the new boy was being looked at.
Why was changing the subject during the gossip a wise move?
It kept her out of office politics without lecturing anyone, protecting both her reputation and her colleagues.
How might the new boy have felt when Vandana spoke up?
He likely felt relieved, since people were looking at him as if he'd made the mistake.

Read this:

Launch night at the Bengaluru startup, 2 a.m., the servers glitching, and everyone exhausted. Anirban, twenty-five and team lead, looked at Lokesh's code and heard himself say, "Is this the best you can do?" His father's words, his father's tone. Lokesh flinched. Anirban stopped. He'd grown up with that sentence every exam season, and it had never once made him better; it had only made him scared. His father had also taught him to check every line twice, to never leave a job half-done. That part he wanted. With the clock ticking, he took a breath. "Sorry, Lokesh, that came out wrong. This bit's close. Let's check the loop together, line by line." They found the bug in twenty minutes. At 4 a.m., as the site went live, Anirban said, "Good work tonight." Lokesh grinned, tired.

What time was it when Anirban looked at Lokesh's code?
2 a.m.
Why did Anirban stop after saying "Is this the best you can do?"
He recognised his father's harsh words and felt uncomfortable, remembering that they had only made him scared, never better.
How did Anirban keep his father's diligence while dropping the sharpness?
He apologised, then checked the code line by line with Lokesh, keeping the careful habit without the harsh tone.
How might Lokesh feel hearing "Good work tonight"?
Lokesh likely felt relieved and valued after a stressful night that started with a sharp remark.

metadata.subtype: Choosing which parental traits to keep [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Shankar Mama,

I saw the flood video you shared on the family group this morning, with "Today in Guwahati!! Pray!!" I know you sent it because you were worried about people there, and that's why I'm writing to you directly and not replying in the group.

I checked it. The same video is on a news site from 2019, from a different country. The shop signs are in another language if you pause it. There is no flood in Guwahati today; the weather office shows light rain.

I'm not upset. These videos are made to look urgent so people share them fast. I've nearly shared a few myself. What I do now: pause and look at signs, search a frame of it, and check one reliable news source first.

Could you delete it from the group? If you like, I'll call you on Sunday and show you how I check. It takes two minutes.

With love,
Rekha

Where did the flood video actually come from?
The same video is on a news site from 2019, from a different country.
How did Shankar Mama likely feel when he shared the video?
He was probably worried and anxious for the people in Guwahati, which is why he shared it quickly with "Pray!!"
What made Rekha's way of correcting the video kind and effective?
Rekha wrote privately, assumed good intentions, explained the evidence, shared simple checks, and offered to help on Sunday.
How might the family group be affected if the video stayed up?
Relatives might panic or pass it on further, spreading false alarm and making real warnings harder to trust.
Two sentences on the Moon, please. The first must start with "The" and the second with "It".
The Moon travels around the Earth. It shines because it reflects sunlight.

We discerned Linton watching at the same spot he had selected before. My young mistress alighted, and told me that, as she was resolved to stay a very little while, I had better hold the pony and remain on horseback; but I dissented: I wouldn't risk losing sight of the charge committed to me a minute; so we climbed the slope of heath together. Master Heathcliff received us with greater animation on this occasion: not the animation of high spirits though, nor yet of joy; it looked more like fear.

One line only: what happens in this passage?
The narrator and the young lady in their care meet Linton Heathcliff, who seems livelier than before but looks afraid, not happy.

Read this:

In the glass cabin of the Andheri office, Tejas held up the printout. 'Vinita, I asked for the regional numbers only. Why is there a national summary?' 'On Thursday you asked me to add it,' Vinita said. 'For the board.' 'I don't think so. You must have misunderstood.' Two colleagues glanced up through the glass. Vinita felt her ears burn. She wanted to snap, 'You said it in front of everyone.' Instead she opened her email on her phone. After every meeting she sent a short 'as discussed' note, a habit from her first job. There it was: 'Thurs: add national summary for board (Tejas).' She turned the screen towards him. 'This is what I noted. If it's changed, I'll take it out now.' Tejas looked at it for a long second. 'Okay. Keep it,' he said, and moved on to the next slide.

What did Vinita's 'as discussed' note from Thursday say?
The note said: 'Thurs: add national summary for board (Tejas).'
What did Vinita feel when told she must have misunderstood?
Vinita felt embarrassed and angry with colleagues watching, and wanted to snap back, because she knew Tejas had asked for it.
Why is Vinita's habit of 'as discussed' notes so useful here?
The dated note let her show what was agreed without accusing Tejas, and offering to change it kept the focus on the work rather than on who was wrong.
Why might Tejas have said 'You must have misunderstood' instead of 'I forgot'?
Saying Vinita misunderstood let Tejas avoid feeling like a leader who forgets his own instructions, especially with the board meeting close.

Read this:

Ritu Api,
Confession time. Remember the eight thousand rupees the university refunded from my hostel deposit? Gone. In a week. A concert ticket, a smartwatch, dinner for five people.
The weird part is how careful I am with small things. I walk forty minutes to save a thirty-rupee auto. I skip the canteen tea because ten rupees adds up. I've been doing that all month and feeling very responsible.
Then tonight I added it up. All my walking and tea-skipping this month saved maybe six hundred rupees. The refund was eight thousand. It's like I have two wallets in my head: real money that I guard, and bonus money that doesn't count.
I'm not asking for money. I just needed to say it out loud. Next time something extra comes in, I'll ask Abbu to sit with me before I touch it.
Wasim

How much did the university refund?
The university refunded eight thousand rupees from the hostel deposit.
Why did Wasim feel responsible while the refund vanished?
Wasim felt proud and careful skipping tea and walking, while the refund felt like bonus money that didn't count, so the bigger loss went unnoticed.
What does Wasim plan for next time, and why is it sensible?
Asking Abbu to sit together before touching any extra money, so a trusted adult helps look at the whole picture.
How might Ritu feel reading the confession?
Ritu might feel amused and a little worried, and glad Wasim noticed the two wallets and is being honest.

Read this:

Nitin: did you submit the lab report?
Kunal: not yet. still fixing the first graph
Nitin: it's been three days on that graph
Kunal: the axis labels look off by a pixel
Nitin: a PIXEL 🙂 the deadline is in two hours
Kunal: what if the marker thinks I'm careless
Nitin: what if the marker just wants a report? and you haven't even started the second lab
Kunal: I'd forgotten about the second one 😬
Nitin: exactly. send this one now, fix things after feedback
Kunal: ok. ok. sending. my hands are sweaty
Kunal: sent
Nitin: proud of you. now go do lab two 😅

How long had Kunal been working on the first graph?
Kunal had worked on the first graph for three days.
What is Kunal worried about when asking "what if the marker thinks I'm careless"?
Kunal is anxious about being judged as careless, so the fear of criticism keeps the report from going out.
What helped Kunal press send?
Nitin reminded Kunal of the deadline and the unstarted second lab, and suggested sending it and fixing things after feedback.
How does Nitin see Kunal's graph problem?
As over-polishing that eats the time needed for the second lab.

Read this:

A firecracker exploded in the lane outside the school, so loud the windows rattled. Chetan screamed and dived under the table, shaking. Vikas Sir crouched down and held out his arms. Chetan crawled into them. Vikas didn't say, “Stop crying, it's nothing.” He held him and said quietly, “That was loud. You were scared.” Chetan nodded against his shirt. “Very scared.” “I know. You're safe now.” Slowly Chetan's shaking stopped. He sat on Vikas's lap for the rest of story time.

What exploded in the lane?
A firecracker.
What was Chetan feeling when he dived under the table?
He was very frightened by the sudden loud bang, and his shaking showed it.
Why was naming the feeling better than saying “Stop crying”?
It helped Chetan understand and accept his fear and settle, instead of learning to hide it.
What would change if Vikas Sir had said “Stop crying, it's nothing”?
Chetan might learn to hide his fear, and he wouldn't have felt safe enough to calm down on his lap.

messages.content:
Read this:

School counsellor's note, Class 6.
Madhav came to see me today. He said his voice keeps cracking in class and two boys call him "squeaky". He'd also noticed hair growing under his arms and asked if something was wrong with him.
I told him these changes are normal, that everyone's body changes at a different time, and that he's not the only one. I gave him a simple book about growing up and suggested a daily bath and a clean vest.
He asked if I could tell the class that teasing about bodies isn't okay. I spoke to the class teacher this afternoon, and we'll do a puberty session next week. — Hafsa Qureshi

What did the two boys call Madhav?
"Squeaky".
What was Madhav feeling when he asked if something was wrong with him?
Madhav felt worried and embarrassed about his body changing and being teased.
What did Hafsa Qureshi do that helped Madhav?
She told him the changes are normal, gave him a book and simple hygiene tips, and acted on his request about the teasing.
How might the boys who tease see things after the puberty session?
They might understand that everyone's body changes and that teasing about it is unkind.

Read this:

Baljeet: they're fighting again
Ayesha: your parents?
Baljeet: yeah. about the car loan I think. I can hear it through the door
Ayesha: I'm sorry
Baljeet: it's my fault
Ayesha: how is it your fault??
Baljeet: if I'd got better marks they wouldn't have had to pay for tuition. and I left the gate open last week and papa got a fine
Baljeet: if I was better they'd be happier
Ayesha: Baljeet. parents fight about money and stuff that has nothing to do with you
Ayesha: you're 15. you didn't make their loan
Baljeet: but I feel like I should fix it
Ayesha: you can't fix it. that's their job
Ayesha: can you talk to your masi? or the school counsellor tomorrow?
Baljeet: maybe masi. she's coming for dinner tonight
Ayesha: tell her how you feel. not about the fight. about you

What does Baljeet think the parents are fighting about?
Baljeet thinks they are fighting about the car loan.
Why does Baljeet feel the fight is Baljeet's fault?
Baljeet feels guilty and over-responsible, linking the marks and the open gate to the parents' conflict.
What did Ayesha suggest, and why is it wise?
Talking to Baljeet's masi or the school counsellor about Baljeet's feelings, because a trusted adult can help with guilt Baljeet shouldn't carry alone.
How does Ayesha see the family conflict?
Ayesha sees it as the parents' problem to solve, not something a fifteen-year-old caused or can fix.

Read this:

Hey Ujjwal,
I'm sorry about the family photo at Diwali. When everyone lined up, you had your lips pursed tight and your arms crossed, and I said loudly, "Look, Ujjwal's doing his duck face for the camera!" Everyone laughed, even Bade Papa.
I didn't know then that you'd just had a fight with your mum about the trip you couldn't go on. You weren't posing. You were upset.
In the photo you look miserable, and I made it worse.
I get it now. Sometimes a pout is just for the camera, and sometimes it isn't, and I didn't check. Next time I'll just ask if you're okay.
Want to play badminton on Sunday?
Ramesh

What did Ramesh say loudly when the family lined up?
"Look, Ujjwal's doing his duck face for the camera!"
What was Ujjwal likely feeling during the photo?
Ujjwal was upset and hurt after the fight about the trip, and Ramesh's joke probably made him feel embarrassed and mocked.
What will Ramesh do differently next time?
Ramesh will check whether someone is okay instead of assuming a pout is only for the camera.
How might Bade Papa see the photo now, if he knew the story?
Bade Papa might feel sorry for laughing, seeing that Ujjwal's pursed lips showed real hurt, not a pose.

Read this:

Nana sat on the bench at the colony park in Lucknow, watching Neelam and her brother Kiku. They had fought all morning over the swing.

Then Thomas, a big boy from the next building, pushed Kiku off the slide. "Move, shorty."

Before Nana could get up, Neelam was there. She stood in front of Kiku, hands on hips. "Don't push my brother."

Thomas laughed. Kiku stood up beside her. "Yeah. Don't push my sister either."

Thomas shrugged and wandered off.

Nana watched them walk back to the swing, arguing again about whose turn it was. He smiled. The same two who fought at home had stood shoulder to shoulder in thirty seconds.

What did Thomas say when he pushed Kiku?
"Move, shorty."
How does Nana feel watching Neelam and Kiku stand together?
He feels warm and amused, smiling at how quickly they defended each other despite their fighting.
What could Nana say to the children later?
He could tell them he noticed how they stood up for each other, so they see the loyalty behind their fights.
How might Kiku feel when Neelam steps in front of him?
He probably feels protected and proud of his sister, and brave enough to stand beside her.

Read this:

Every Sunday at noon, Marek, twenty-five, video-called his mother, Valentina, in Kraków from his flat in Dublin. She always answered on the first ring, already smiling, hair brushed.
"I'm fine, everything's fine," she said, every time.
This Sunday, Marek noticed things. The table behind her was set for one. His father's chair was pushed against the wall. She laughed a little too quickly at his stories, and asked three times when his next holiday was.
"Mama, are you lonely?"
"Me? No, no. Busy, busy."
Marek looked at the single plate. He'd been so wrapped up in his new job that he'd left a gap of three weeks without calling.
"I'm booking a ticket for May," he said. "And let's talk Wednesdays too, not only Sundays."
His mother's smile wobbled. "Only if it's not a trouble."
"It isn't," Marek said.

How many times did Valentina ask when his next holiday was?
She asked three times when his next holiday was.
What was Marek feeling when he looked at the single plate?
Marek felt guilty and concerned, realising his mother was lonely and he had gone three weeks without calling.
What steps did Marek take after reading the signs?
He booked a ticket for May and added a Wednesday call, so his mother would feel less alone.
What is it like for Valentina between calls?
She seems lonely, setting the table for one, but she hides it so she won't burden Marek.

Read this:

At the Dasara sports day in Kushalnagar, the kabaddi coach put Zubin and Tenzin, from the Tibetan settlement, on the same team. Zubin's older cousins had always said the settlement boys were 'rough' and 'kept to themselves'. For the first round Zubin wouldn't even look at him. Then in the second round Zubin got trapped by three raiders, and Tenzin dived in and pulled him free, grinning, grass in his hair. At the break they shared Tenzin's butter tea and Zubin's chakli. They found out they both hated maths, both had grandmothers who scolded in two languages and both wanted a new cricket bat. By sunset they had won the cup, and Zubin couldn't remember what 'rough' was supposed to mean.

What did Tenzin do when Zubin got trapped?
He dived in and pulled him free, grinning.
What was Zubin feeling in the first round?
Zubin felt wary and uneasy about Tenzin, carrying his cousins' idea that settlement boys were rough.
What could the coach do to build on this?
Keep mixing children from the town and the settlement in teams with a shared goal, so more friendships like this can grow.
What might Tenzin have felt when Zubin wouldn't look at him?
Tenzin may have felt hurt or used to it, yet he still helped Zubin, which opened the way to friendship.

Bessie's presence, compared with the thoughts over which I had been brooding, seemed cheerful; even though, as usual, she was somewhat cross. The fact is, after my conflict with and victory over Mrs. Reed, I was not disposed to care much for the nursemaid's transitory anger; and I was disposed to bask in her youthful lightness of heart. I just put my two arms round her and said, "Come, Bessie! don't scold."

Why does the narrator not mind Bessie's anger?

After the clash with Mrs. Reed and the victory over her, the narrator does not care much about the nursemaid's passing anger and wants to enjoy her youthful light-heartedness. Both arms go round Bessie with the words, "Come, Bessie! don't scold."

By Rail.--There is no one in charge of the box. It would have to take its chance of being delayed; and delay would be fatal, with enemies on the track. True, he might escape at night; but what would he be, if left in a strange place with no refuge that he could fly to? This is not what he intends; and he does not mean to risk it.

Keeping to the passage, why does the writer rule out sending the box by rail?

No one would be in charge of the box, so it would take its chance of being delayed, and delay would be fatal with enemies on the track. Even if the one being sent escaped at night, that one would be left in a strange place with no refuge to fly to.

Read this:

I'm Bhavna, from the ground floor. This morning a street dog chased Damini at the gate, barking. It didn't touch her, but she ran screaming to her mother and buried her face in her dupatta. Her mother didn't say, “Don't be silly.” She picked her up, sat on the step, and said, “You were scared. The dog ran at you.” Damini sobbed, “It was so loud.” Her mother rocked her. I don't know how long it took, but by the time I came back from the shop, Damini was waving at the dog from her lap.

What did Damini bury her face in?
Her mother's dupatta.
What was Damini feeling when she ran screaming to her mother?
She was frightened by the barking dog, even though it didn't touch her.
What did Damini's mother do that helps later self-soothing?
She held her and named the feeling, “You were scared,” instead of calling it silly.
How did Bhavna see the change in Damini?
When Bhavna came back from the shop, Damini was already calm enough to wave at the dog from her mother's lap.

messages.content: Our neighbours are very kind peoples. What is wrong?

Our neighbours are very kind people.
Why: "people" is already plural.

Read this:

Sabina: Hey. I saw the thread. You don't have to explain anything.
Tanvir: I can't stop reading it. Two thousand comments about my talk.
Sabina: Okay. Can we do one thing? Mute the thread and turn notifications off for tonight. I'll stay on this chat.
Tanvir: What if it gets worse
Sabina: Then we deal with it together. I've saved the ones that are plain abuse and I'll report them from my side too. You don't have to look at them.
Tanvir: Rohan posted a joke about it. Meher liked it. Kunal hasn't said anything at all.
Sabina: That's on them. I'm bringing dinner at 8. Just food, no talking about it unless you want to.
Tanvir: ok. thank you
Sabina: I'm here till you fall asleep.

At what time is Sabina bringing dinner?
Sabina is bringing dinner at 8.
Why might Tanvir keep reading the thread even though it hurts?
Tanvir feels exposed and may fear missing the next comment, so reading feels unavoidable even though it deepens the hurt.
What did Sabina suggest first to help Tanvir?
Sabina suggested muting the thread and turning notifications off for the night while staying on the chat.
What might Sabina be feeling while promising to stay on the chat till Tanvir falls asleep?
Sabina is probably worried about Tanvir and protective, which is why Sabina saves and reports the abusive comments and plans to bring dinner at 8.

Read this:

Supervisor's note, Ward 4 — Anjali
Harish told me in April he wanted to pass the critical care certificate by the end of the year. I asked him to write it on the duty-room board and then break it down.
He set one module a month and two practice sets a week, done on his days off. Every Friday after handover we spent ten minutes on his chart. He ticked what he finished and circled what slipped, without scolding himself.
In August he was moved to nights for five weeks. His practice sets stopped. I expected him to give up. Instead he came to me on a Friday morning, tired but calm, and said, "I'll do one set a week till nights end, and push module six to October."
He passed in December. I have asked him to show the new trainees his chart.

What did Harish set as his monthly and weekly actions?
He set one module a month and two practice sets a week, done on his days off.
How did Harish seem to feel when his practice stopped during night shifts?
He seemed tired but calm and steady rather than defeated, because he already had a habit of adjusting the plan instead of scolding himself.
What could new trainees learn from Harish's chart?
They could set one big aim, split it into small weekly actions, and review it kindly each week, adjusting when shifts change instead of dropping the aim.
How did the note-writer see Harish's change of plan in August?
The note-writer expected him to give up, so his calm offer to cut to one set a week and push module six to October came as a welcome surprise.

metadata.subtype: Linking the goal to the next step [Response]

messages.content:
Read this:

Family counsellor's note, final session

Rekha first came in March, distressed that her daughter Seema, twenty, had moved into a shared flat in Pune against her wishes. "She doesn't need me anymore," she said then.

Over the sessions, Rekha has worked on changing her role. She described three changes today. First, she now asks Seema, "Do you want my advice?" before giving it. Second, when Seema chose a college course Rekha disagreed with, Rekha said her piece once and then stopped. Third, when Seema's first month's budget went wrong, Rekha did not say "I told you so"; she only asked what Seema had learned.

Today Rekha said, "She calls me more now, not less. She asks what I think." She was smiling. "I think I'm actually proud of her for leaving."

I have closed our sessions.

— Anjali Kulkarni, counsellor

Where did Seema move to?
A shared flat in Pune.
How does Rekha feel now compared with March?
In March she felt distressed and unneeded; now she feels proud of Seema's independence and happier, smiling.
Which of Rekha's changes helped most, and why?
Asking before advising, saying her piece once, and not saying "I told you so" helped, because they let her become an adviser rather than a decision-maker.
How has Seema responded to her mother's new role?
Seema calls more, not less, and asks what Rekha thinks, showing the relationship of two adults is growing.

Read this:

The results list went up on the college noticeboard in the kasba, and Parul's roll number wasn't in the accounts pass column. She walked home past the sugar mill with the old voice loud in her head: you're useless, you'll never pass. At home, her younger brother Nilesh asked, "Didi, what happened?" She told him. Then, instead of crying on the cot, she took out her paper and checked. The theory questions: good marks. The ledger problems: nearly zero. She remembered she had never finished the ledger chapter. "It's not all of accounts," she said aloud. "It's ledgers." Nilesh brought her tea. She wrote on the back of the paper: two ledger problems every day before the supplementary exam.

Which column was Parul's roll number missing from?
The accounts pass column.
What was Parul feeling on the walk home?
She felt hopeless and worthless, with the inner voice calling her useless.
What did Parul do to test the inner voice?
She checked her paper, found the theory was fine and only ledgers were weak, and planned two ledger problems a day.
How does Nilesh react to his sister's result?
He is concerned, asking what happened, and supportive, bringing her tea while she works it out.

Read this:

In the boarding school hostel, phones were allowed for one hour on Sunday. Ojas spent his whole hour scrolling.
Aditi, from his old day school, had posted photos from a national debate. Her certificate. A new haircut. A crowd of friends. Every post seemed to shine.
Ojas looked at his own week: dal-rice in the mess, a failed chemistry quiz, mud on his football boots. He felt like he was falling behind everyone.
When the hour ended, the housemaster collected the phones. He saw Ojas's face. "Bad news?"
"No. Just... everyone's doing better than me."
"Everyone's posting better than you," the housemaster said. "Different thing. Come, the match is starting."

How long were phones allowed on Sunday?
Phones were allowed for one hour on Sunday.
What was Ojas feeling as he looked at his own week?
He felt discouraged and behind, comparing his ordinary week with Aditi's shining posts.
How did the housemaster help Ojas?
He pointed out that people post their best moments, and invited him to the match, pulling him back into real life.
How might Aditi see her own week?
Aditi's week probably had ordinary or hard moments too, which she didn't post.

Read this:

Note from Bidisha, class teacher. At lunch, Lakshmi's friend wrinkled her nose while Lakshmi was unpacking her tiffin. Lakshmi shut the box and stopped eating. I sat beside her and asked quietly what was wrong. She said, “She thinks my food smells.” I asked the friend, gently, what the face was about. She said the bin near their bench smelled sour. Lakshmi opened the box again. I suggested to them that when a face worries you, you can ask, “Was that about my food?” They tried the sentence together.

What did Lakshmi do after her friend wrinkled her nose?
She shut the box and stopped eating.
What was Lakshmi probably feeling when she shut her tiffin, and what else could the friend's face have meant?
Probably hurt and self-conscious, thinking her food was being rejected. The friend's face was actually about the sour smell from the bin.
What small step did Bidisha suggest for next time?
That when a face worries them, they ask something like “Was that about my food?” instead of assuming, and she had them practise it together.
How might the friend have felt on learning Lakshmi had been hurt?
Probably surprised and sorry, since she did not mean anything by it. She joined in practising the question, which suggests she wanted to make it right.

Rain hammered the tin roof of the bus stop. Yamini had twenty minutes before the portfolio deadline at the design institute, and Vaibhav's folder was still in her bag; he had left it on her desk that morning. Her phone buzzed with a message from friends: "Anniversary pic?? 🎉" She thumbed it away and ran for the auto, holding the folder under her dupatta.

She reached the gate as he was pacing outside. He looked at the folder, then at her, and laughed with relief.

"If you get in, it means Ahmedabad for two years," she said, catching her breath. "I'll be sad. I'll also be proud. Let's figure out calls now, and tell each other honestly if it gets hard."

She posted nothing that day. He'd made the deadline; that felt like enough.

Why was Yamini running through the rain?
She was bringing Vaibhav the portfolio he had left on her desk, so he could submit it before the deadline at the institute.
What was Yamini feeling about the possible move to Ahmedabad?
Mixed feelings: she says she will be sad but also proud, which shows she wants him to go without hiding her own side of it.
What could Yamini and Vaibhav do if he does move for two years?
Agree on realistic times for calls, keep telling each other honestly when it gets hard, and plan visits.
How might Vaibhav see Yamini turning up at the gate with his folder?
He probably feels backed by her, and reassured that his ambition is welcome and not something that threatens them.

In their flat in Istanbul, Elif played her racing game under the blanket until almost midnight. The next morning she yawned through maths and missed an easy question. At football, she tripped twice.
Her brother Sami found her dozing on the sofa after school. "You're a zombie."
"I'm fine," she mumbled.
That evening, the new level unlocked. Elif's thumb hovered over the button. She looked at her bag, still packed with homework, and at the football by the door.
She put the tablet on the kitchen shelf. "Sami, don't let me take it to bed."
"Deal," said Sami. "Want to kick the ball first?"

Where did Elif put the tablet?
On the kitchen shelf.
What was Elif feeling when her thumb hovered over the button?
Elif felt tempted and torn between the new level and her homework and football.
Which choice helped Elif, and why?
Keeping the tablet in the kitchen at night took away the temptation, so she could sleep and do her homework.
How does Sami see Elif's tiredness?
Sami notices she's like a "zombie" and supports her plan by agreeing not to let her take the tablet to bed.

At the common service centre in the kasba, Sahil had trained three operators before Rukmini. With her he wanted to be perfect. So he hovered. "Check the ID number twice." "Did you save?" "Don't forget the receipt." Every few minutes, a reminder. By Thursday Rukmini's answers had shrunk to "Yes, bhaiya," and she stopped asking him anything. On Friday she printed a farmer's certificate with the wrong village name, because she'd been afraid to ask how to change the default. Sahil realised the hovering had made her hide, not learn. On Monday he tried something different. "Here are two ways to change the village name: the drop-down or the settings page. You choose. I'll only remind you about the receipt, because that's the one people forget." He went back to his own desk. At noon Rukmini came over. "Bhaiya, the drop-down is faster. And can I ask about the pension form?"

What mistake did Rukmini make on Friday?
She printed a farmer's certificate with the wrong village name.
How did Rukmini seem to feel under Sahil's constant reminders?
Rukmini seemed nervous and discouraged, her answers shrinking to 'Yes, bhaiya' and too afraid to ask questions.
What did Sahil change on Monday, and why did it work?
He offered two options, let her choose and kept only one reminder, which gave her room to decide and made her willing to ask again.
What would have happened if Sahil had kept hovering?
Rukmini would likely have kept hiding her questions and making silent mistakes instead of learning.

Dear Seema didi,
You asked how the district chess tournament went. I lost in the second round. And I have to tell you the truth, because I've been lying to everyone else.
The night before, I watched chess videos and then random videos until 2 am. Mummy called out three times. I kept saying, "Just five more minutes." In the morning my eyes burned and I blundered my queen in move fourteen.
To everyone, I said, "I was so tired, I didn't sleep." Which is true. But I chose not to sleep. I think I was scared. If I'd slept well and lost, it would mean I'm just not good. Being tired meant I had a reason.
But now I don't know if I could have won. That feels worse.
Next tournament is in March. I'm going to sleep at ten the night before, even if I'm nervous.
Bhavna

In which move did Bhavna blunder the queen?
Bhavna blundered the queen in move fourteen.
Why does Bhavna think staying up till 2 am happened?
Bhavna was scared that losing after a good sleep would mean not being good enough, so tiredness became a ready reason.
What is Bhavna planning for March, and why is it a good choice?
Sleeping at ten the night before, even if nervous, so the result will show real ability and something to learn.
How might Seema didi feel reading this letter?
Seema didi would likely feel proud of Bhavna's honesty and hopeful about the March tournament.

Playgroup note, Tuesday. Chandrika, the older of the two sisters who come together, was stacking blocks when her little sister Pema toddled over and picked up the red one. Chandrika snatched it back, shouted and raised her hand. I knelt beside her and said, "You are angry. You were using that block." She stopped, breathing hard. I added that being angry is fine but hitting is not. Then I helped her ask Pema for a turn with the green block. She nodded slowly. 🙂

Which block did Pema pick up?
Pema picked up the red block.
What was Chandrika feeling when she snatched the block back, and how do we know?
She was angry that her sister took something she was using, shown by the shouting and the raised hand. She calmed after her feeling was named, which suggests she felt understood.
What did the adult who wrote the note do that helped?
They named the feeling, held the limit against hitting, and gave Chandrika words to ask for a turn instead.
What might Pema have understood from the moment?
Pema is very small and may only have seen a block she wanted, so the shout could have surprised her.

First week: Siddharth started telling Chaitanya about his grandfather's hospital stay. Chaitanya cut in about his own cousin's broken leg. Siddharth went quiet and looked at the floor.
Next week: Siddharth mentioned it again, shoulders hunched. Chaitanya wanted to jump in, then noticed the hunched shoulders and just said, "Tell me."
A month later: Siddharth talked for a long time about visiting his grandfather. Chaitanya listened all the way to the end, watching his face. When Siddharth smiled at the end, Chaitanya smiled too.

What did Chaitanya talk about in the first week?
His own cousin's broken leg.
What was Chaitanya feeling in the second week when he wanted to jump in?
He felt eager to talk, but seeing Siddharth's hunched shoulders made him concerned, so he held back.
What helped Chaitanya become a better listener?
Noticing Siddharth's hunched shoulders and holding back his own story.
How might Siddharth feel about Chaitanya after a month?
He likely feels more comfortable and trusting, because Chaitanya now listens properly.

In their Chennai flat, Chandrika hid behind a cushion and popped out. "Boo!" Sachin grinned for a flash, then looked up at the ceiling fan. Again. Grin, then gone.
"He's bored of me," Chandrika sighed to her husband.
Then she started "round and round the garden" on Sachin's palm. This time his smile stayed and grew. He giggled all the way to the tickle and held his hand out for more.

What game made Sachin smile for a long time?
The "round and round the garden" game on his palm.
Why did Chandrika think Sachin was bored, and was she right?
She felt a bit disheartened because his peekaboo grins vanished fast and he looked at the fan; but quick smiles are normal, and he was still enjoying himself, as the long smile later showed.
What would you advise Chandrika about short smiles?
Treat a quick grin as real joy and keep playing, rather than deciding the child is bored.
How might Sachin experience the two games differently?
Peekaboo gives him a sudden burst of surprise that fades fast, while the palm game builds up slowly, so his joy lasts longer.

Hansa had practised her Annual Day speech on water conservation for two weeks: a story to open, three points, a question to close. She was on third. Then, as she reached the podium, the microphone died with a squeal. Four hundred students and parents stirred and started chatting.
Her hands went cold. Her friend Jomon, running the sound desk, mouthed, "Two minutes!"
Hansa didn't wait. She stepped to the front edge of the stage, planted her feet like her drama teacher taught, and said loudly, "Raise your hand if your tap ran dry this summer."
Hands shot up. The chatter stopped.
She spoke slower than in practice, looking at the back row, pausing after each point. When the mic crackled back on halfway through, she waved it away.
Afterwards, Jomon handed her a bottle of water. "You didn't even need me."

How many students and parents were in the audience?
Four hundred students and parents.
What was Hansa feeling when the microphone died?
Hansa felt nervous, her hands going cold, but she chose to act instead of freezing.
What choice kept the audience with Hansa, and why?
Asking a question that everyone could answer with a raised hand, because it pulled attention back to her without needing the microphone.
How might Jomon feel watching from the sound desk?
Jomon probably felt stressed about the broken mic at first, then relieved and proud when Hansa held the audience on her own.

When my recipe blog had just three pages, I did something that felt too early: I showed it to five relatives at Nani's house one Sunday. I'm Samir, and the blog was meant to collect our family's Konkani dishes.
I didn't explain anything. I handed my phone to each person and said, “Find the fish curry.” Then I just watched and wrote in a notebook.
Saurabh Mama went straight to About and got lost. Nani kept pressing the photo, thinking it was a button. Two of my aunts scrolled to the bottom looking for a menu that was hidden behind three little lines at the top. Only my cousin found it in under a minute.
That night I didn't add a single recipe. I put the menu as plain words across the top, made the photos open the recipe, and sent it to Saurabh Mama again. He found the curry in seconds.

What did Samir ask each person to find?
The fish curry.
What might Samir have felt watching Nani press the photo like a button?
Samir was probably surprised and a little embarrassed, but also curious, since each wrong tap showed where the blog confused people.
What other approach could have found the same problems, and would it work as well?
Asking relatives what they thought would mostly get polite praise; watching them try a task shows real confusion, so watching works better.
What was the first version like for Saurabh Mama?
It was confusing: he went to About and got lost, but after the fix he found the curry in seconds.

In the village lane, three elders sat on a charpai under the neem tree. Gurpreet, five, was racing past with a hoop when Rehana Aunty, his mother's friend, called, "Gurpreet, look who's here." He stopped, joined his hands and said, "Sat Sri Akal, Bebe ji. Sat Sri Akal, Chacha ji." Bebe ji blessed him. He stood and listened while she told him about the buffalo calf born that morning, answering "Ji, Bebe ji" in a small, soft voice. Only when she waved him off did he run back to his hoop.

Where were the elders sitting?
On a charpai under the neem tree.
Why might Gurpreet have stayed to listen instead of running off?
He seems to respect Bebe ji and wanted to show it, even though he was keen to get back to his hoop.
How could Rehana Aunty encourage him afterwards?
She could tell him Bebe ji was happy he stopped to greet her and listen, so he links his politeness with her warmth.
How might Bebe ji see Gurpreet's soft "Ji, Bebe ji"?
She probably feels respected and cared for, and enjoys sharing the calf news with him. 🙂

Kiran, you're sighing like the whole world is against you. Let your Sachin Dada tell you something about your Papa. When he was sixteen, before his board exams, he sat at that same desk from morning till night. By evening he'd bite anyone's head off. Your Dadi would scold, and he'd shout, and the whole house would be on fire. I had no clever words. So one evening I just wheeled out my old cycle and said, 'I'm going to the lake. Coming?' He grumbled but came. We didn't talk much. We cycled round the lake twice, watched the boats, and came back. He was a different boy. After that, every evening we cycled. No lectures, just company. He passed, and he still calls those rides the best part of that year.

Where did Sachin and his son cycle?
Round the lake.
How did Kiran's Papa feel after long days at the desk?
He was irritable and snappy, biting anyone's head off.
What was the turning point in Sachin's story?
Sachin stopped scolding and simply invited his son on a cycle ride as company.
How might Kiran's Dadi have seen the evening rides?
She probably felt relieved that the house was calmer and the shouting had stopped.

Farhan,

I'm not going to send this. I'm writing it because I've been carrying you around for two years, and my shoulders are tired.

When you left our design studio and took the three biggest clients with you, I waited for an explanation. Then I waited for an apology. I rehearsed what I would say when it came. It never came, and I finally understand it may never come.

Last week I caught myself checking your new studio's page at two in the morning, and I thought: this is my life I'm spending, not yours.

So here is what I'm choosing. I'm not saying what you did was fine. It wasn't. I'm saying I'm done feeding it. I'm setting the grudge down, for my own sleep and my own work.

I hope your studio does well. I actually mean that, mostly.

Arohi

What did Farhan take when leaving the design studio?
Farhan took the three biggest clients.
What was Arohi feeling when checking the new studio's page at two in the morning?
Arohi felt worn out and a little ashamed of how much space the resentment was taking, which is what sparked the decision to let it go.
What makes this letter a useful step for Arohi?
Writing it without sending lets Arohi say clearly that the act was wrong while choosing to stop carrying it, without needing Farhan to respond at all.
What would change if Farhan did apologise one day?
The apology might be welcome, but Arohi's peace would no longer depend on it, since the decision to release the grudge has already been made.

messages.content: Is it right to say "Don't take tension"?

"Take tension" is an Indian English usage, and many people will understand it. Standard alternatives are "Don't worry" or "Don't get stressed".
Example: Don't worry; we have plenty of time.
Dukaan mein bolna hai "Mujhe ye wali nahi, doosri wali chahiye."
Say: "I don't want this one. I would like the other one, please."

Mohit, an engineer, was curious about data analysis but did not trust the shiny job descriptions. So he messaged four people in the field, including Siddharth, a friend's cousin, and asked what they actually did each day, how people got in, and what the pay looked like at the start. Their stories were plainer than any advert.

Next he saved ten job listings and wrote the skills that kept coming up. He compared them with his own list: strong on statistics and programming, weak on dashboards and business questions. Each gap became a course on his calendar for the evenings.

Nandini did it another way. Bored with her office, she resigned to study all day, with no plan and nothing saved. For three months she drifted between videos and half-finished notebooks while her money ran low. In the end she took the first job that came, and the switch she had wanted slid back by a year.

Mohit's own applications drew several rejections. Instead of taking them as a verdict, he emailed the recruiters for feedback. One replied that his portfolio showed clever code but no business context. He rebuilt the project around a real question about a shop's sales, and the next interview lasted an hour.

How many people did Mohit message about their work in the field?
He messaged four people.
How did Mohit's route differ from Nandini's, and what happened to Nandini's plan?
Mohit gathered first-hand accounts and worked backward from job listings, while Nandini resigned with no plan or savings, drifted for three months, took any job and delayed the switch.
What was Nandini feeling when she took the first job that came?
She was likely discouraged and pressed by dwindling money, and she had to set aside her switch for a while.
What did Mohit's feedback request change about how he used rejection?
He treated it as information instead of a verdict, learned his portfolio lacked business context, and rebuilt it around a real question.

From the next room, I have heard Vijay's alarm every morning for three years. This term it rings and rings. Vijay used to bring the group's notes to my door every Sunday, with jokes; now the notes have stopped, and when I asked about the internship report the answer was, "Who even reads them?" Vijay sleeps a full night and still has a face like Monday at midnight. Vijay skipped my birthday dinner and did not text back, which never happened before. I cannot say what is going on inside. I knocked, put a cup of tea on the desk and said, "This term looks heavy. Is it the load, or something else?" Vijay looked up. "Maybe just the load." We sat for a while, and I suggested speaking to our faculty mentor about dropping something.
Sarika

What did Sarika put on Vijay's desk?
Sarika put a cup of tea on Vijay's desk.
What might Vijay be feeling, judging by the cues Sarika describes?
Drained and detached, suggested by the flat "Who even reads them?", the unanswered texts and the skipped dinner, though Sarika cannot be sure.
What did Sarika suggest, and why is it sensible?
Speaking to the faculty mentor about dropping something, since lightening the load early is a reasonable response to lasting tiredness.
How might Sarika have felt when Vijay stopped answering texts?
Worried and a little hurt, which fits with knocking and bringing tea.

At the Kolkata newspaper office, Pradeep noticed the change first on the notice board: freelance photographers' names would no longer be printed with their photos.
In the canteen, reporters grumbled. "Typical." "Let's all stop crediting anyone." One joked about leaking it online.
Anirban didn't join in. At the Monday editorial meeting, he stood up with a folder. "I've worked here five years. I care about this paper," he said. "That's why I'm raising this. Freelancers depend on credits to get their next job. Here are three other papers' credit policies. I'd like us to reconsider."
The editor frowned but listened. "Put it in writing. We'll discuss it at the board."
Pradeep watched Anirban sit down, calm. He'd always thought objecting meant being against the paper. Anirban had just shown him it could mean caring for it.
Three weeks later, credits were back.

How long had Anirban worked at the newspaper?
Five years.
What was Pradeep thinking as Anirban sat down?
Pradeep felt admiring and a little surprised, realising objection could come from caring for the paper.
What made Anirban's objection effective?
He raised it in the proper meeting, explained who was harmed, brought other papers' policies and followed the editor's process.
How might the freelance photographers see the change?
They would probably feel relieved and respected, getting credit they need for future work.
Which one is cheapest, this bag or that one? Correct my question.

Which one is cheaper, this bag or that one?
Why: two things need the comparative "cheaper".

After overnight snow in Seoul, the kindergarten yard was slippery. Rosa, a new girl from Spain, slid and landed on her bottom with a shriek.
Soo-ah, holding her mitten, froze. She screamed and cried so loudly that the teacher ran out thinking she was the one hurt. Soo-ah could not step forward.
The teacher helped Rosa up. Rosa was fine and already laughing.
Soo-ah was still sobbing. The teacher knelt. "You were scared for Rosa?" Soo-ah nodded hard.
Later, inside, Soo-ah drew a picture of Rosa with a big plaster and gave it to her.

Why did the teacher run out?
Soo-ah was screaming and crying so loudly that the teacher thought she was the one hurt.
What was Soo-ah feeling when Rosa slipped?
She was scared for Rosa and so overwhelmed by her own distress that she froze and could not step forward.
How could the teacher help Soo-ah next time she freezes like this?
The teacher could calm her first, name the fear kindly as she did, and later practise simple steps like calling a grown-up.
How might Rosa feel when she gets Soo-ah's drawing?
Rosa might feel touched and happy, seeing that the new friend cared about her fall.

Vasudha, you think I was always this careful? Ask your Deepak mama about the ghat road. I was fifteen, in Kodaikanal, and my friends bet I wouldn't cycle down the ghat without touching the brakes. Six boys, all shouting. I didn't think for one second. I just went. I hit gravel at the second bend and flew into the bushes. Twelve stitches on my knee, and my father's face in the hospital, I still remember it. But here's the other half. That same year I had to choose between science and arts. I sat alone on the roof for three evenings with a notebook. I listed what I loved and what I was good at. I talked to my teacher. I chose arts, against everyone's advice, and it was right. Same boy. Different room. That's what I want you to see.

How many stitches did Deepak get on his knee?
Twelve stitches.
Why did young Deepak not think before cycling down the ghat?
With six boys shouting and a bet on, Deepak felt excited and dared, and the pressure of friends watching pushed him into a snap choice.
What was different about how Deepak chose between science and arts?
Deepak decided alone and calm over three evenings, making lists and talking to a teacher, which let careful reasoning guide him.
How might Deepak's father have felt at the hospital?
He was likely frightened and shaken seeing his son hurt, and perhaps angry that a bet had led to it.

"Ting-ting!" Madhuri, two, rang the puja bell.

"Gently," Karthik said. "Like this."

Madhuri rang it softly, then clapped when Amma did.

"Namaste to God," Amma said, folding her hands.

Madhuri folded hers, peeking at the lamp.

What did Madhuri ring?
Madhuri rang the puja bell.
What was Madhuri feeling during the puja?
Madhuri felt happy and curious, drawn by the lamp, the bell and her family's faces.

How does Grandma see Madhuri's actions differently from Karthik?
Grandma thinks Madhuri is praying, while Karthik sees it as copying the family, which is enough.

Debate coach's notes, college society. Yogesh Tiwari.
Mahima, second year, opened today's inter-college debate. Last month she rushed her first line and lost her thread. Since then we have practised one thing: reach the podium, breathe out slowly, let the shoulders fall, and pause before the first word.
Today I watched from the back row. She stepped up, placed her notes, and I saw her shoulders lower. There was a pause, barely a second. Then her first sentence came out clear and unhurried. I doubt anyone else in the hall noticed a thing; they simply heard a confident speaker. She kept her thread through all four minutes, even when heckled.
Next step: I'll ask her to lead a short breathing warm-up for the first-years before the next round.

Where did Yogesh watch from?
Yogesh watched from the back row.
How might Mahima have felt stepping up, given what happened last month?
Mahima was probably nervous, remembering how she rushed her first line and lost her thread, but she felt prepared.
Why does Yogesh plan to have Mahima lead a breathing warm-up?
Mahima has shown the routine works, and teaching it lets first-years learn the same quiet steadying before they speak.
How did the audience see Mahima's start?
They simply heard a confident speaker and most likely did not notice the brief pause at all.

Sarita wrote three dates on the whiteboard of the college magazine room in Delhi: 10th, all articles in. 18th, rough layout. 22nd, full proof. Underneath, in red: Printer, 28th.
Lokesh laughed. "You've invented deadlines nobody asked for."
"Nobody has to. I asked."
On the 18th the rough layout was done, ugly but complete. On the 23rd the sports writer withdrew his match report, and the cover photo turned out blurred. Lokesh went pale. Sarita pulled in the spare poetry page and reshot the cover in the corridor the next morning. The last four days went on fixing typos and choosing fonts. On the 28th the files reached the printer before lunch.
"Fine," Lokesh said, leaning back. "Your fake deadlines saved us."

When did the files have to reach the printer?
On the 28th.
How did Sarita seem to feel when the report was withdrawn and the cover was blurred?
Sarita stayed calm and steady, because the early rough layout left room to swap in the poetry page and reshoot the cover.
Which choice worked, and why?
Setting her own earlier dates meant the layout was finished before the surprises hit, so the final days were spent improving, not scrambling.
How does Lokesh's view change over the story?
Lokesh starts amused, thinking the extra dates are pointless, panics when the problems appear, and ends relieved and grateful for them.

At two, Parveen watched bright, fast cartoons on the tablet every night after dinner. By bedtime her cheeks were flushed, she kicked the blanket and cried for another one. Her father Jomon switched the screen off and read her a picture book in the dim room, and after a few nights of quiet play and books, she settled sooner. At fifteen, Parveen lay in bed scrolling. "One more video," she told herself, and then another, afraid she would miss something in the group chat. It was past midnight when she put the phone down, and she still lay awake, with her mind buzzing. The next day she was snappy and everything seemed heavy. At twenty-five, she answered emails from her bed at eleven at night. Afterwards her head kept running through tomorrow's tasks and she woke unrested. Her friend Nandini said, "Try closing the laptop at nine and doing nothing with a screen for half an hour." Parveen tried a week of it. She kept a paperback on the pillow, and her mind began to slow by ten.

What did Parveen's father do when he switched the screen off?
He read her a picture book in the dim room.
How do screens affect Parveen's sleep at two, fifteen and twenty-five?

At two bright, fast cartoons left her wired and crying, at fifteen scrolling and fear of missing out kept her awake and snappy, and at twenty-five late emails kept her mind buzzing. In each case the screen before bed delayed her settling, and a screen-free wind-down helped.
What was Parveen feeling when she kept scrolling one more video at fifteen?
She felt anxious about missing something in the group chat, so she kept going even when tired.
What could Parveen do to keep her evenings calm on busy work days?
She could set a time to close her laptop, keep the phone out of the bed, and use a book or quiet music for the last half hour.

The next day commenced as before, getting up and dressing by rushlight; but this morning we were obliged to dispense with the ceremony of washing; the water in the pitchers was frozen. A change had taken place in the weather the preceding evening, and a keen north-east wind, whistling through the crevices of our bedroom windows all night long, had made us shiver in our beds, and turned the contents of the ewers to ice.

Why do the writer and the others skip washing that morning?

The weather turned in the evening and a keen north-east wind whistled through the window cracks all night. The water in the pitchers froze to ice, so they dressed by the dim light of a rush candle without washing.

Examples: She packed her rucksack for the trek. She packed her backpack for the trek.
"Mere dada ji roz subah park mein tahalte hain." Translate.
It is: "My grandfather walks in the park every morning." In English, "grandfather" is the usual word, and "grandpa" is casual.
Aur dadi ke liye?
Use "grandmother" for the polite form and "grandma" for the casual one.
Aur nana-nani?
They are also "grandfather" and "grandmother". English does not separate the mother's side from the father's side.

I'm Tenzin, Binita's roommate, and I watched her decide how to vote in the student council election. Two weeks before, she had a list on her desk: hostel water, library hours, the women's safety committee. She'd even read both manifestos. Then, three days before polling, the whole corridor started wearing Rakesh's yellow badges. Posters on every door. In the mess, people just said, "Everyone's voting Rakesh." Binita came back one evening with a yellow badge. When I asked what his plan for the library was, she said, "Honestly, no idea. But half the campus can't be wrong." Her list was still on the desk, and his name wasn't on it. I don't know exactly why she changed. Maybe she just didn't want to be on the losing side.

What colour were Rakesh's badges?
They were yellow.
What does Binita's 'half the campus can't be wrong' suggest about her thinking?
It suggests she was treating the number of supporters as proof, even though she didn't know his plan for the library.
What could Binita do before polling day?
She could check Rakesh's plans against her own list about water, library hours and safety, then vote for whoever matches it best.
How does Tenzin see Binita's change?
Tenzin notices the list still on the desk and wonders whether Binita just didn't want to be on the losing side.

Dear Sonali,
You kept asking, and I kept saying 'I'm fine'. I wasn't. It's been nine weeks since Neel and I ended things. I thought I'd bounce back in a fortnight. Instead I stopped going to the library, I missed two assignment deadlines, and some mornings I just sat on my bed until lunch.
Last Monday my tutor asked, very kindly, if everything was okay. I nearly said 'fine' again. Instead I asked her how to see the college counsellor. She walked me to the office herself, and I booked a slot for that Wednesday.
The counsellor didn't tell me what to feel. She asked questions and let me talk, and for the first time in weeks I cried in front of someone. We've planned to meet every week for now.
I'm telling you because I don't want to keep pretending with you either. Chai this weekend?
Ishita

How many assignment deadlines did Ishita miss?
Two assignment deadlines.
What was Ishita feeling when the tutor asked if everything was okay?
Ishita felt the pull to hide again but also some relief at being asked kindly, which gave the courage to ask for help.
What could Sonali do after reading this?
Say yes to chai, listen without trying to fix things, and keep checking in while Ishita continues the counselling.
How might Sonali feel reading 'I don't want to keep pretending with you'?
Sonali may feel sad about the weeks of 'I'm fine' but grateful and closer, now that Ishita has been honest.

"Ninety rupees a plate is too much," Yogesh said. "Every canteen in the area charges ninety," Jyoti replied. "But that doesn't mean ninety is what it costs."
She opened her laptop. They were planning to run a small mess for the forty students in their PG building, two meals a day.
"Let's build it from scratch. Rice, dal, sabzi, roti. How much of each goes on one plate?"
They weighed a sample plate from the hostel kitchen. Rice, a hundred and fifty grams. Dal, one bowl. Then they checked grocery prices, added gas for a month, paid helpers, disposable plates, and ten percent thrown away.
"Fifty-four," Jyoti said. "Even with waste."
"So canteens make thirty-six on every plate?"
"Some of that is rent and electricity, which we don't pay. But yes, part of that ninety is just what people accept."
They priced the plate at sixty-five.

What price did they set for the plate?
They priced the plate at sixty-five.
How can you tell Jyoti felt confident about her method?
Jyoti calmly builds the cost from a weighed sample plate and explains the gap, sure that the usual price is not the real cost.
What else could Jyoti and Yogesh check before starting the mess?
They could run a one-week trial to see if their waste guess of ten percent is right, since a higher waste would raise the cost.
How might the PG residents see the sixty-five rupee plate?
Residents used to paying ninety may be pleasantly surprised and see the mess as fair, especially if the numbers are shown to them.

messages.content: Is it "collegue" or "colleague" for people I work with?

It is "colleague", spelled c-o-l-l-e-a-g-u-e. A trick: "a colleague" has "ague" at the end, like "league".
Example: My colleague shared her notes with me.

Dear Preeti didi,
I need to tell someone, and you're the one I trust most after Mummy.
Last month, someone called "Coach_Arjun" messaged me on the football forum. He said he was a scout, that I had real talent, that he could get me into an academy. He asked for my school name, then my address, then photos of me "in kit, for the file." Then he said, "Don't tell your parents yet, it'll ruin the surprise."
That's when my chest went tight. You always said: if someone online wants secrets, it's a trap.
I didn't send anything more. I blocked him. And I told Mummy the same evening. She held my hand and said, "You did exactly right, Pradeep. This isn't your fault." She reported it to the cyber cell that night and told my school.
I'm okay. A bit shaky, and embarrassed I believed him at first. Can you call me on Sunday?
Your brother,
Pradeep

What did the contact claim to be?
A scout.
How did Pradeep feel when the contact asked to keep it from his parents?
Pradeep felt alarmed, his chest going tight, recognising the request for secrecy as a trap, and later a bit embarrassed.
Which steps did Pradeep take, and why were they right?
He stopped sending anything, blocked the contact and told Mummy the same evening, so she could report it and protect him.
How does Mummy respond when Pradeep tells her?
She reassures him it isn't his fault, reports it to the cyber cell that night and informs his school.

Counsellor's note.

Sonali came to see me on Monday. Last week she reported to her teacher that a group of friends had shared answers during the unit test. Since then the group has stopped talking to her, and Saurabh, who she considered her closest friend, walked past her in the corridor. She said she feels like a traitor. I noticed she kept her voice level and did not blame anyone loudly, and she did not regret it, but she was lonely. I told her that acting on a principle can cost belonging, and that this hurts. We discussed spending time with people who share her values. She agreed to join the library club and will come back next week.

What did Sonali report to her teacher last week?
That a group of friends had shared answers during the unit test.
How does Sonali feel about what she did, and what is the evidence?
She feels like a traitor and lonely, but she does not regret reporting. She kept her voice level and did not blame anyone loudly.
What did the counsellor suggest Sonali do?
Accept that acting on principle can cost belonging, stay steady, and spend time with supportive people, starting with the library club.
How might Saurabh see Sonali's report?
Possibly as a betrayal, since Saurabh walked past her in the corridor. Saurabh may be angry or ashamed, but the note does not say.

Friday: Indu and Vasudha had their worst fight in months, about Vasudha's night shifts. Vasudha went silent for the whole weekend, as she often did.
Monday: They sat with the counsellor Indu had found. Indu said, "I never know if the silence is ending in an hour or a week." The counsellor asked them to agree on what a fair pause looks like. They settled on two rules: pauses are okay if you say when you'll be back, and nobody is left guessing.
Thursday: A smaller argument. Vasudha said, "I'm too upset. I'll come find you at nine." At nine, she knocked on Indu's door. Indu found she was not scared this time.

What did Vasudha say during Thursday's argument?
"I'm too upset. I'll come find you at nine."
What was Indu feeling on Thursday when Vasudha asked for a pause?
Indu felt calm and not scared, because this time she knew when Vasudha would come back.
What turning point helped Indu and Vasudha?
Seeing a counsellor and agreeing that pauses need a return time and no one is left guessing changed silence from a threat into a signal.
What was Vasudha experiencing when she knocked on the door at nine?
She was likely still upset but calmer, and able to keep her promise to come back.

Mehak: hi. I saw your photo from Nani's funeral
Sonali: yeah. Someone took it when I was laughing
Mehak: you were smiling so much. I wasn't sure if I should say anything
Sonali: I understand. We were sharing stories about her cooking. It was the first time in days I felt light
Mehak: that makes sense. I was worried you were only pretending
Sonali: partly, maybe. It's both. I'm happy remembering her and I'm also really sad
Mehak: thank you for telling me. I'm sorry I guessed
Sonali: it's fine. Most people look at the photo and just see the smile
Mehak: I won't. Do you want to talk later or is it easier not to?
Sonali: later would be good. Thank you for asking

What were the family sharing stories about?
They were sharing stories about Nani's cooking.
What was Sonali feeling when smiling at the funeral, and how does Sonali explain it?
Sonali felt happiness and sadness together, saying it was happy remembering Nani and also really sad.
What could Mehak do to keep supporting Sonali?
Mehak could check in later as Sonali agreed, listen and avoid guessing feelings from the photo.
How might other people who see the photo interpret it?
They might think Sonali was simply happy, as Sonali says most people see only the smile.

In Lagos, the French results were pinned to the classroom door, and Chidi pushed through the crowd to find a seventy-eight, up from fifty-two. "It's the app," Chidi told Oskar, holding up the phone. "Ten minutes of flashcards a day for a week. Look at that jump!" Oskar scanned the list. "Everyone jumped. Tunde went up twenty, and he doesn't even have a phone." "Tunde's different." "Madame Okafor said this test was only on the easy chapters." Chidi frowned at the list, then at the phone. The flashcards had felt like magic. "Okay. So I don't know yet if it helped." "Keep using it. See what happens on the hard chapters." Chidi nodded, a little deflated, and set a reminder for seven o'clock.

What mark did Chidi get in French?
Chidi got a seventy-eight, up from fifty-two.
Why did the app feel like the reason for the jump to Chidi?
Chidi felt excited and proud, and since the higher mark came right after a week of flashcards, the app seemed like magic.
What is a fair way for Chidi to find out whether the app helps?
Keep using it and watch the marks on the hard chapters, comparing with classmates who don't use it, like Tunde.
How does Oskar see the jump in marks?
Oskar notices that everyone's marks jumped because the test covered only the easy chapters, so the app may not explain it.

At the inter-school cricket match, I sat two rows behind Asif. He was the one who started the rhythm: bang the plastic bottles twice, clap once, shout our school's name. Soon the whole stand was doing it, and Asif was grinning so wide you could see his missing tooth.
Then the other team's fielder dropped an easy catch. The big boys behind us yelled, "Butterfingers! Go home!" and started banging the bottles for that instead.
Asif turned and looked at them. He put his bottle down between his feet and sat back down. He didn't clap again until our batsman hit a four.
I don't know exactly what he was thinking. Maybe he felt sorry for the fielder. Maybe he just didn't like the big boys taking over his beat.
- Sumit

What rhythm did Asif start in the stand?
Bang the plastic bottles twice, clap once, shout the school's name.
What might Asif have been feeling when he put his bottle down?
He may have felt uncomfortable or sorry for the fielder being mocked; he might also have felt annoyed that the big boys took over his beat, and Sumit cannot tell which.
What could Sumit try next time the stand turns mocking?
Sumit could stop joining in too, and restart the school cheer so the noise goes back to supporting their own team.
How might the fielder who dropped the catch feel hearing the stand?
He probably felt embarrassed and low, since an ordinary mistake became a reason for a whole crowd to shout at him.
