messages.content:
Three-sentence summary of this extract, please.

The list went up at 3:55, five minutes before the school bus left. Binita's name wasn't on the debate team. She had practised for three weeks. On the crowded bus, wedged between bags, Divyansh leaned over. "Were you on it?" Her automatic answer was ready: "It's fine, I didn't even care." Instead, with the engine roaring and a Class 6 kid kicking her seat, she heard herself say, "No. I'm really disappointed. And kind of embarrassed, because I told everyone I'd get in." Divyansh nodded. "Yeah. That's rough." That was all. No pep talk, no fuss. Binita stared out at the traffic for two stops. By the fourth stop she was arguing with him about a cricket score. At home she told her mother the same words, and it came out easier the second time.

Binita's name is not on the debate team list, though she practised for three weeks. On the bus, Divyansh asks if she was on it, and instead of saying she did not care, she admits she is disappointed and embarrassed. He only says it is rough, and by the fourth stop they are arguing about cricket.

Teaching assistant's note, chemistry lab, Week 9.
I have noticed a change in Jaya, a second-year student. She has forgotten to record data twice this week, which is unlike her careful work earlier in the term. She sighs often and I saw her skip the lunch break to finish another course's worksheet. She mentioned a part-time job and a family function. I did not want to lecture her about time management; I think she knows. Instead I asked, "Is there something here I can take off your plate?" She asked if the lab report deadline could move by three days. I agreed and informed the professor, Ujjwal sir. I will check in with Jaya next week.

How many times did Jaya forget to record data this week?
She forgot to record data twice this week.
How does the teaching assistant seem to feel about Jaya?
The teaching assistant seems concerned and caring, noticing the change and choosing not to lecture.
What did the teaching assistant do, and why did it help?
They asked what could be taken off Jaya's plate and moved the lab report deadline by three days, easing one real demand.
How might Jaya feel when the deadline is moved?
Jaya would likely feel relieved and grateful, with one less thing pressing on an overloaded week.
"Kal match mein hum haar gaye" kaise kahte hain?
It is: "We lost the match yesterday." Remember: you win a match, and you lose a match.
Aur "hum jeet gaye"?
It is: "We won." You can add the match: "We won the match."
My class teacher said, "Don't just mug up the answers." Is "mug up" good English?

"Mug up" is informal British and Indian English and means to learn something by repeating it again and again, without really understanding. The standard words are "memorise" or "cram".
Examples: Don't just mug up the dates; try to understand the events. Tara crammed for the test.

"Charu didi, look at this study influencer. She has two million followers."

"What's she saying, Anirban?"

"She says toppers never revise. Just read once and trust your brain. She topped her state."

"And you believe her?"

"She's a topper. She must know."

"She might be right for herself. But does she show any evidence it works for others?"

"...No. She just sounds really sure."

"Sounding sure isn't the same as being right. What does your teacher say?"

"Mrs Das says revise at least twice."

"And who has seen more students?"

"Mrs Das. Thirty years of students."

"So?"

Anirban scrolled down. The comments were full of people saying it didn't work for them. He hadn't noticed before.

"I feel stupid."

"Don't. Everyone falls for confident people. The trick is asking how they know."

How many followers does the influencer have?
She has two million followers.
Why was Anirban inclined to believe the influencer?
Anirban felt impressed and trusting, because she was a topper who sounded very sure.
What question did Charu didi suggest, and why is it useful?
Charu suggested asking how the influencer knows and whether there's evidence, which separates confidence from truth.
How does Charu didi seem to see Anirban's mistake?
Charu didi seems kind and understanding, telling him not to feel stupid because everyone falls for confident people.

The bus to school was cancelled because the road had flooded, so everyone in Manjula's lane had to walk the long way through the rain. Her friend Shreya had a fever, and the girl could barely keep up.
Manjula, ten, took Shreya's heavy bag without asking and hung it on her own front, so she looked like a turtle with two shells. Water splashed over her sandals. Her shoulders ached.
"You'll get tired," Shreya said weakly.
"I'm fine. Hold the umbrella."
At the school gate, Kusum's gang ran up. "Shreya, is it true you sleep with a toy rabbit? Manjula knows. Tell us, Manjula!"
Shreya had told her that on a sleepover, whispering. Manjula's face went hot. "I don't know anything," she said, and walked Shreya straight to the sick room.

Why did everyone have to walk the long way?
The bus to school was cancelled because the road had flooded.
What was Manjula feeling when Kusum's gang asked about the toy rabbit?
She felt hot-faced and uncomfortable under pressure, but she was determined not to betray what Shreya had trusted her with.
What choice did Manjula make at the school gate, and why did it matter to Shreya?
She refused to reveal the secret and took Shreya to the sick room, protecting both Shreya's trust and her health.
How might Shreya feel about Manjula after that walk?
Shreya would likely feel deeply grateful and safe, knowing her friend carried her bag in the rain and kept her secret.

Read this:

You want the embarrassing story, Eshaan? Fine. I'm Maria, and in Year 9 I shot up, suddenly taller than every boy in class. I became convinced the whole school was mocking me. If someone laughed in the corridor, it was about my height. If the PE teacher smiled, it was pity. I started slouching so hard my back hurt. Then one day a girl I barely knew told me, "I always wanted to be tall like you." I actually thought she was being sarcastic! It took me months to realise that the cruel commentary running in my head all day was mine. Nobody else was saying it. I was saying it, and hearing it in everyone's voice.

Who did Maria become taller than in Year 9?
Every boy in class.
Why did Maria think the girl was being sarcastic?
Maria felt so insecure about height that even a compliment sounded like mockery; the self-criticism coloured everything.
What could help a teenager in Maria's position sooner?
Talking to someone trusted and checking the evidence: who has actually said anything unkind? Often no one has.
How might the girl who complimented Maria feel if she knew it was taken as sarcasm?
Surprised and a little sad, since she meant it sincerely.

Wednesday night

Last night I spent the whole bus ride and then an hour in bed looking at bridal makeup pages. Every bride has glass skin and eyes like a cartoon. Then I opened my front camera and nearly threw the phone. My nose! My eyebrows! I actually asked Ammi if I could get my face 'fixed', and she just stared at me.

Then school today. Sharmila had a pimple on her chin the size of a ber. Rehana's eyebrows are two different shapes, I noticed for the first time. Nobody's skin looks like glass. Everyone looks like... people. And I looked like one of them, totally normal. Sharmila even said my plait looked nice. My face is the same face as yesterday. It's what I was looking at that changed.

Zainab

What pages was Zainab looking at the night before?
Bridal makeup pages.
How did Zainab feel after opening the front camera last night?
Zainab felt ugly and upset, nearly threw the phone and even asked Ammi about getting the face 'fixed'.
What could Zainab try before bed next time?
Zainab could put the phone away earlier, or remember that those pages show edited faces, not ordinary ones like the classmates at school.
What does Ammi's stare suggest about how she saw the request?
Ammi was probably shocked and worried, seeing nothing wrong with the face she looks at every day.

'Lokesh, lights off at ten? Your test is tomorrow.'
'That's the plan, Papa. Sleep is in it.'
'In my day we studied till the milkman came.'
'And did it work?'
Ramesh laughed. 'Sometimes.'
'I wrote down every day I missed this month. Look. Monday I planned five hours after tuition. I did one. Wednesday, same.'
'So you were lazy on Mondays and Wednesdays?'
'No. Tuition finishes at seven on those days. Five hours was never possible. Now I plan one hour on those days and more on Saturday. Every day since, I've done what the plan says.'
Ramesh looked at his son's notebook, columns of small ticks. 'Every day?'
'Not perfectly. But every day.'
'Hm.' Ramesh switched off the light himself. 'Goodnight, planner sahib.'

What time does tuition finish on Mondays and Wednesdays?
At seven.
What does Lokesh's calm reply to 'lazy' show about how he feels about the missed days?
He feels settled, not guilty; he treats the missed days as information about his tuition schedule, not proof of laziness.
Why is Lokesh's change to one hour on tuition days sensible?
It fits the plan to real life so he can keep it every day; consistency counts for more than an impossible five hours.
How might Ramesh feel as he switches off the light himself?
Ramesh seems amused and a little impressed, even proud, won over by his son's plan.

When I sat down to write Sudha's half-yearly review last October, my first draft said "excellent" in every box. Sudha is our star: she closed the biggest client, everyone likes her, and her presentations make the room go quiet. Then I stopped at the box marked "reliability" and couldn't name a single example. So I did what I'd started doing for everyone: one trait at a time, an example before any rating. Communication: easy, three client emails I'd genuinely admired. Reliability: two missed handover notes and a report a week late. I rated those honestly. In our meeting I asked Sudha for examples I might have missed. She brought one I hadn't known about, and I changed that rating. The rest stayed. She was quiet for a moment, then said, "Thanks, Devika. Nobody has ever told me the handover part." I'm glad her shine didn't cover it.

What did Devika find under reliability?
Two missed handover notes and a report a week late.
Why did Devika hesitate at the reliability box?
Devika felt uneasy and uncertain, realising the 'excellent' came from Sudha's overall shine rather than from any real example.
Which steps made Devika's review fairer?
Rating one trait at a time, finding an example before each rating, and asking Sudha for examples Devika might have missed.
How might Sudha feel about the honest review?
Sudha may feel a small sting at first, but also respected and grateful, since nobody had told her about the handover problem before.

Thursday, 11:50 pm
Kashish's father died three weeks ago. The first week I was on the phone with her every night till 2. She cried and cried and I cried too. I couldn't sleep after. I kept seeing her face at the funeral.
Second week I was so tired I fell asleep in chemistry. Mum asked if I was ill.
This week she called four times. I didn't pick up twice. I told her my phone was on silent. It wasn't.
I feel horrible. She's my best friend. But every time her name comes up on the screen my chest goes tight and I just want to hide.
I don't know how to help her without drowning.
Maybe I'll tell Mum tomorrow. She'll know what to do.
– Sangeeta

How long ago did Kashish's father die?
Three weeks ago.
Why does Sangeeta not pick up Kashish's calls?
Sangeeta feels exhausted and overwhelmed by Kashish's grief, and guilty for hiding.
What would be a wise next step for Sangeeta?
Sangeeta could talk to Mum as planned and get help to support Kashish in a way that doesn't drain Sangeeta, like shorter calls and involving other adults.
How might Kashish feel when Sangeeta doesn't pick up?
She might feel hurt and lonely, missing her best friend just when she needs her most.

metadata.subtype: Overwhelmed by a friend's crisis, then withdrawing [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

The heavy traffic outside the Toronto clinic drowned out every sound, and Tobias, five, screamed "Hamid, look, a helicopter!" at his uncle, standing right beside him. Hamid smiled and touched his ear. "Here, outdoors, that voice is fine." He took out a small card with a finger-on-lips drawing. "Inside the clinic, use the quiet one." Inside, Tobias remembered, pointed at the card his uncle had shown him, and whispered, "Shh voice." "Well done," whispered Hamid. When the nurse called them, Tobias held the card up to show her.

What did Tobias see outside the clinic?
He saw a helicopter.
What was Tobias feeling when he screamed about the helicopter?
He was excited and wanted to share it. The traffic was loud, so he may also have thought he needed to shout to be heard.
What could Hamid do to help Tobias use the right voice in future?
He can keep using the card and a friendly reminder, and praise Tobias whenever he tries.
How might the nurse see Tobias holding up the card?
The nurse might find it charming and understand that Tobias is learning to control his voice.

Thursday, 10 pm
Something's off, and I've stopped pretending it isn't. For about a month I've been exhausted even after long nights of sleep. And thirsty, weirdly thirsty, finishing a whole bottle and still wanting more. I've tried everything I can think of: early nights, less screen, more water, fewer coffees. Nothing has changed.
Tonight Lalit found me asleep on the sofa at eight with my shoes on. He said, very gently, "Arohi, this isn't a willpower thing. Please get it checked." I wanted to argue that I'm just busy. But I've been saying that for a month.
So. Booked the clinic for Saturday morning. Writing down what I've noticed so I don't forget: tired, thirsty, up at night to pee, since roughly early June.
Scared, a bit. Also relieved I've stopped guessing.

When is the clinic appointment?
Saturday morning.
How does Arohi feel after booking the clinic?
Arohi feels a bit scared, but also relieved to have stopped guessing.
Why is writing down the symptoms a sensible step?
It gives the doctor a clear picture of what has been happening and since when, so nothing is forgotten in the appointment.
How does Lalit see Arohi's tiredness?
Lalit sees it as something to be checked rather than a willpower problem, and gently urges a visit to the doctor.

"How's the treadmill-and-series plan?" Asif asked, dropping onto Avni's couch.
"Great," Avni said. Then, "Okay. Not great."
"What happened?"
"I was so good for a month. The fantasy show only at the gym. I was running like crazy to find out who the traitor was."
"And?"
"And then I had a cold, so I watched one episode in bed. Just one. Because I was sick."
"And now?"
"Now I've finished the season. In bed. And I haven't been to the gym in two weeks."
Asif laughed. "So the show got free and the gym got dumped."
"Don't. I feel like such an idiot."
"You're not. You just gave it away. Next season, the laptop stays at the gym locker?"
Avni groaned into a cushion. "Next season."

How long had Avni been away from the gym?
Avni hadn't been to the gym in two weeks.
How does Avni feel about the plan now?
Avni feels embarrassed and frustrated, saying "I feel like such an idiot" after finishing the season in bed.
What could Avni do next season to keep the bundle working?
Avni could make the show truly gym-only, for example by only watching on a device kept at the gym, so there is no "just one episode" at home.
How does Asif see what happened?
Asif sees it with gentle humour: the show got free and the gym got dumped, and Asif does not think Avni is foolish.

Read this:

In the Monday meeting, the manager blamed Devika for the late report. Devika went quiet and stared at her screen. The delay had come from another team, but nobody said so. Ganga felt her pulse quicken. She could see how easily silence would let it become the story. That afternoon she went through the email trail and marked the dates. She asked Bidisha, another colleague, whether she had seen the same, and Bidisha nodded. The next day, the two of them sent the manager a short, factual note with the timestamps, and Ganga asked to talk it through.

Devika had not asked anyone for help. She hadn't slept properly, and she'd been half decided to give up and look for another job. When Ganga stopped by her desk and said, "I sent the dates to the manager, and Bidisha backed it up," she found she could hardly speak. She said, "Thank you. Really." Then, "If anything comes back at you, tell me. I'll say I asked you to check." She wrote a card the same week and left it on Ganga's desk, and she kept the debt in mind. When Bidisha needed cover on a Friday, Devika offered without being asked.

What did Ganga and Bidisha send the manager?
They sent a short, factual note with the timestamps.
How did Ganga's speaking up and Devika's response connect, and what difference did it make to Devika?

Ganga checked the emails, involved Bidisha and sent the facts, and Devika thanked her and offered to take responsibility if anything came back. Devika had been half decided to give up, so the support made the difference in her continuing.
What was Ganga feeling as she watched Devika stare at her screen?
She felt her pulse quicken and worried that silence would let the blame become the story.
What could Devika do to return the support later?
She could help when a colleague needs cover, as she did for Bidisha, and remember the debt.

Read this:

Tejas, you think those boys are laughing at you. Sit, and let your Yusuf Nana tell you about my first night at the hostel in Aligarh. I was eleven. When the lights went out, I heard tittering from the beds across the room, and whispering, and more tittering. I lay stiff as a plank, sure they were laughing at my torn trunk and my village accent. By midnight I was ready to fight all of them. Instead, I sat up and said, “What's so funny?” A voice said, “Nothing. We're scared of the dark, so we're laughing instead of crying.” By morning, the four of us were friends. Still, Tejas, if it's the same boys every day, you tell your teacher.

Where was the hostel?
The hostel was in Aligarh.
What was young Yusuf feeling as he lay stiff in bed?
Young Yusuf felt hurt and angry, sure the boys were laughing at his torn trunk and village accent.
What choice did young Yusuf make, and why did it matter?
Yusuf sat up and asked what was funny instead of fighting, which showed the laughter was nerves, not mockery, and led to friendships.
What was the first night like for the boys across the room?
They were scared of the dark and laughing to keep from crying, not thinking about Yusuf at all.
'Main paise bacha raha hoon nayi cycle ke liye' English mein?
Say: "I'm saving up for a new bicycle." "Save up for" means keeping money aside to buy something later.

Read this:

June, first day as prefect: Hafsa pinned the shiny badge on her kurta and felt taller. She was nervous about telling anyone off; she even said 'please' when asking juniors to walk, not run.
August: she had started standing at the corridor corner with her arms folded, the way the head prefect did. She wrote names in the late book without listening to excuses. When a junior said her bus had broken down, Hafsa said, 'Not my problem,' in a voice she didn't recognise, and felt, oddly, powerful.
October: her old friend Zeenat watched Hafsa snap at a crying Class 6 girl for untied laces. 'Since when do you shout at little kids?' Zeenat asked. Hafsa opened her mouth to defend herself and realised she couldn't remember when it had started. It just felt normal now.

What did Hafsa say to the junior whose bus had broken down?
'Not my problem.'
How did Hafsa feel in October when Zeenat questioned her?
Hafsa felt startled and unsettled, realising she couldn't remember when the harshness began.
What could help Hafsa step back from the role?
Asking whether she'd treat a junior this way without the badge, and inviting honest feedback from friends like Zeenat.
How might the crying Class 6 girl see Hafsa?
The girl probably sees her as frightening and unkind, not someone to ask for help.

metadata.subtype: Playing a role until it takes over [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Gargi, you said your friend is "just slow" because she didn't follow your chemistry explanation. Come, sit on the swing; the Onam pookalam can wait. When I was fifteen, I was the maths girl of our class in Thrissur. Shobha asked me to explain quadratic equations before the exam. I rattled it off: "Discriminant, roots, just plug into the formula, it's obvious." Two minutes, done. She looked at me with such a lost face that I got irritated. I told the others she was slow. The next week our teacher explained it to her, slowly, with mangoes drawn on the board, and Shobha got full marks. I had forgotten that I once needed mangoes too. So, Gargi, before calling her slow, try again from the very first step. That is what your Aparna maasi learned the hard way.

What did the teacher draw on the board to explain quadratic equations?
Mangoes.
Why did young Aparna get irritated with Shobha?
The steps felt obvious to Aparna, who had forgotten being a beginner, so Shobha's lost face looked like slowness and made Aparna impatient and annoyed.
What choice in the story could young Aparna have made differently?
She could have started from the first step, used plain words and examples like the mangoes, and checked whether Shobha was following.
How might Shobha have felt when Aparna rattled off the formula?
Shobha probably felt lost and embarrassed, and later hurt at being called slow, though she got full marks once it was explained slowly.

Read this:

Thursday
Sonali's diary. Parveen didn't come to lunch, so I found her behind the library, knees up, not crying, just staring. Her abbu's shop is closing and they're moving to her uncle's town in June. "Everything's finished," she said. "My friends, school, all of it." I almost said "It'll be fine!" but it won't be, not all of it, and she'd know I was lying. So I just sat. I didn't talk. After a long time she told me about the new school, and that her ammi cries in the kitchen at night. I asked what one thing would make June less scary. She said, "Knowing when I'd see you." So we made a plan: first holidays, she visits. I walked her home, and her ammi came to the gate and hugged her. Parveen said she'd talk to her ammi properly tonight.

Where did Sonali find Parveen?
Behind the library, sitting with her knees up.
Why did Sonali stop before saying "It'll be fine!"?
Sonali felt it would be dishonest, since not all of it would be fine, and was worried Parveen would know it was a lie.
Which part of Sonali's response helped most?
Sitting quietly and then asking about one thing that would make June less scary, which led to a real plan instead of empty cheer.
What was it like for Parveen to have Sonali just sit with her?
She probably felt less alone and safe enough to talk about the new school and her ammi crying at night.

Read this:

The power went out at nine, the night before the school council speeches, so Mahima practised by candlelight in the room she shared with her older sister. Zainab listened from the top bunk, then said, "The middle part is boring. And you say 'basically' about eleven times."
Mahima's face went hot. She blew out the candle a little too hard. "Wow. Thanks."
"What? You asked."
In the dark, Mahima counted her breaths. Then she said, "When you say it like that, it sounds like the whole speech is bad. Is it?"
Zainab was quiet for a moment. "No. The opening is really good. I just meant the middle drags."
"Then say that part too, okay? It helps me hear the rest."
Mahima relit the candle, crossed out the extra 'basically's and cut the middle paragraph in half. Zainab climbed down to hold the page steady.

Why was Mahima practising by candlelight?
The power went out at nine, the night before the school council speeches.
What was Mahima feeling when Zainab called the middle part boring, and how can you tell?
She felt stung and hurt: her face went hot, she blew out the candle a little too hard and said a flat "Wow. Thanks."
Which step helped Mahima most, and why?
She told Zainab how the words sounded and asked if the whole speech was bad. That let her keep the useful points about the middle and the 'basically's without carrying the sting.
How does Zainab see her own comment?
Zainab thought she was just being honest because Mahima asked. Once she heard how it landed, she said the opening was good and came down to help.

messages.content: Write me a haiku on a monkey sitting on a roof.

A monkey sits still
Watching the street from the roof
Then it takes my fruit

Read this:

Sit down, beta. Mahima aunty will tell you about my second year at the packaging firm. I was twenty-four, and my manager Chandrika slid a delivery form across her desk and said, "Just date it the twenty-eighth, the truck was basically there." The truck had reached on the second. My hands went cold. Chandrika had helped me get that job, and I thought of my loan. So I signed. Six weeks later an auditor asked for the gate records, and the mismatch carried my signature. Chandrika said, "You should have told me no." I still hear that. If I could go back, I would ask for the order in writing, or say I am not comfortable, and go to the head of accounts if pushed. Instead I learned it late, and at a cost.

When did the truck actually arrive?
The truck had reached on the second.
What was Mahima feeling when the form was slid across the desk?
Frightened and torn: Mahima's hands went cold and the thought of the loan pressed on the decision.
What choice could Mahima have made at the desk instead of signing?
Mahima could have asked for the order in writing, said she was not comfortable, or gone to the head of accounts if pushed.
How might Chandrika have felt when the auditor found the mismatch?
Probably worried and defensive, since Chandrika answered by saying, "You should have told me no."

"You've eaten breakfast at midnight three days running," Rukmini said as Nitin came in, still in his hospital scrubs.
"Rotation. Nights this week, mornings next, then evenings. My body doesn't know what day it is."
"Neither does your temper. You shouted at the cooker yesterday."
"The cooker deserved it." He sank onto the sofa. "I'm so tired my eyes hurt."
"Can you ask for the same shift for longer? Even two weeks at a time?"
"Maybe. Jaswant in my ward did."
"Then ask. And book that health check you keep postponing."
"I'm fine."
"You're grey, Nitin."
He was quiet. "Okay. I'll talk to the ward in-charge tomorrow. And book it."
"I'll come with you."

What does Nitin's rotation look like?
Nights this week, mornings next, then evenings.
How is Nitin feeling after weeks of changing shifts?
He is exhausted and short-tempered, so tired his eyes hurt, and he shouted at the cooker.
What steps does Rukmini push Nitin to take?
Asking for longer blocks of the same shift and booking the postponed health check.
What is it like for Rukmini to live with Nitin's shifting hours?
Rukmini sees the midnight breakfasts and flashes of temper and worries about Nitin's health.

Read this:

I'm Pema, and I sit two benches behind Varun. Every time Varun answered a question, the bigger boy from 7C laughed loudly and copied his voice in a squeak. The back row kept glancing over, waiting. Varun's ears went red and his hands stayed still on the desk. I thought he would snap or cry. Instead he finished his sentence, packed his bag, and walked to the front bench near the teacher, without looking at the boy. At lunch I saw him talking to the class teacher. I can't tell what he was really feeling, but the boy stopped getting his laugh.

Where did Varun move to after the boy laughed?
He walked to the front bench near the teacher.
What might Varun have been feeling, judging by his red ears and still hands?
He was probably hurt or embarrassed, but Pema cannot be sure; finishing his sentence and walking away suggests he chose not to give the boy a reaction.
What could Varun keep doing if the name-calling starts again?
He can keep moving away, stay near the teacher and friends, and tell an adult again if it continues, since the boy's words do not say anything true about him.
How might the bigger boy see the moment when Varun does not react?
He may feel his laugh has lost its point, because the back row stopped waiting and he no longer got the reaction he wanted.
Where does my classmate Ritu live?
I don't know, because I can't see a private person's address and shouldn't share one. If you need it for an invitation, ask Ritu directly.

Read this:

I'm Kunal, and I was on the college bus the week it happened. An older man kept leaning over the seat toward a junior, Mitali, making comments about her clothes. She kept staring out of the window. Leela, who sat beside me, went stiff. I expected her to shout at him; she's like that. She didn't. At the stop, she walked beside Mitali and asked quietly, "Are you okay? Do you want me to do anything? Report him, say something to him, or just walk with you?" Mitali said she wanted to report it. Leela went with her to the college's complaints cell that same afternoon and waited outside. I don't know what either of them felt exactly. But Mitali looked less small on the walk back.

Where did the older man make comments to Mitali?
On the college bus.
What does Leela going stiff suggest about how she felt?
It suggests she felt angry and alarmed at the harassment, but she chose to hold back rather than take over.
Why was asking Mitali what she wanted a wise move?
It gave Mitali control over what happened next, and she chose to report, with Leela beside her that same afternoon.
How might Mitali have felt being given options rather than a rescue?
Mitali may have felt respected and steadier, making her own choice with support instead of being spoken for.

Read this:

The bus from Thrissur broke down, and Elizabeth walked into the panchayat hall in Kuttanad twenty minutes late, sweaty and flustered, apologising as she tripped over a bench. Siddharth, who had come with her from the NGO, saw the elders exchange a look. From his seat by the door he watched the meeting play out: every idea she raised about the new water filters got a short "we'll see". It was as if the first minute had already given the answer. Then old Thomas chettan asked about upkeep, and Elizabeth answered in easy Malayalam with a story about her own grandmother's well. Siddharth saw two elders lean forward. On the ride home he said, "Next time we leave an hour early, and you open with the well story." Elizabeth laughed tiredly. "And they did change their minds, a little."

Why was Elizabeth late?
The bus from Thrissur broke down.
What was Siddharth thinking as he watched from the door?
Siddharth felt uneasy, sensing that the elders' look in the first minute had already shaped their answers to every idea.
What does Siddharth suggest for the next meeting, and why is it sensible?
Leave an hour early and open with the well story, so the first minutes create warmth instead of fluster.
How did the elders' view of Elizabeth shift during the meeting?
They started cool after her late, flustered entrance, but the story about her grandmother's well made two of them lean forward.
I tried this board game for first time yesterday, and I loved it. What is missing?

I tried this board game for the first time yesterday, and I loved it.
Why: "For the first time" needs "the".

Read this:

In the school's PE period, Madhuri, the teacher, gave each child a hula hoop. "Stand in your bubble. Move around without popping anyone else's." Deepika, five, walked, then skipped, carefully keeping her hoop from bumping others. When her friend dropped his hoop and she ran to hug him, he stepped back. "No hug." Deepika froze, then nodded. "Okay. High five?" He smiled and held up his hand.

What did Madhuri give each child?
A hula hoop.
What was Deepika feeling when she froze after "No hug"?
She was probably surprised and a little hurt, but she accepted his choice.
Which choice by Deepika worked, and why?
Offering a high five instead, because it kept the friendship warm while respecting his wish.
How does Deepika's friend experience her response?
He feels his "no" was respected, which makes him happy to connect in another way.

I took what Joe gave me, and found it to be the crumpled play-bill of a small metropolitan theatre, announcing the first appearance, in that very week, of "the celebrated Provincial Amateur of Roscian renown, whose unique performance in the highest tragic walk of our National Bard has lately occasioned so great a sensation in local dramatic circles."

What does Joe hand over, and what does it announce?

A crumpled play-bill of a small theatre. It announces the first appearance that very week of a celebrated provincial amateur, praised for a unique performance in the highest tragic walk of the national bard.

Read this:

Dear Dr. Sarita,
For the last six months I've come to every meeting asking you what I should do next, and you've always answered patiently. I realised last week that I've never once come with my own plan. That isn't fair to you, and it isn't helping me grow as a researcher.
So this time I'm sending an idea first. For the next chapter, I'd like to compare the flood records from the two districts using the rainfall data I cleaned in April. I've written a one-page outline with two possible methods. I lean towards the second because it handles the missing years better, but I'm unsure about the sample size.
Could we discuss this on Monday? I'd value your view on the weak points. And if you think it's the wrong direction, I'd like to understand why, so I can judge better next time.
Thank you for your patience with me.
Bhupen

When did Bhupen clean the rainfall data?
In April.
What did Bhupen realise last week, and how does it seem to feel?
That every meeting had been spent asking what to do; Bhupen feels a little embarrassed and determined to grow as a researcher.
How does Bhupen's email move from dependence towards independence?
It brings a proposed chapter, a one-page outline with two methods and a reasoned preference, and asks for critique rather than instructions.
How might Dr. Sarita read this email?
Pleased and encouraged to see Bhupen thinking independently, and ready to discuss the weak points on Monday.

"Sanjaya continued, 'Hearing these words of Radheya, king Duryodhana then, accompanied by his brothers, O monarch, proceeded towards Drona's car. The noise there was deafening, of Pandava warriors returned to the fight on their cars drawn by excellent steeds of diverse hue, all actuated by the desire of slaying Drona alone.'"

Answer from the text. Where does Duryodhana go after hearing Radheya's words, and what is the scene there?
Duryodhana goes with his brothers toward Drona's car. The noise there is deafening from Pandava warriors returned to the fight on cars drawn by excellent horses, all wanting to kill Drona alone.
I'm 19 and just had my first heartbreak. Write a diary entry, about 100 words, that sounds real but hopeful.

Dear Diary,
It's been a week since Aditya and I ended things. Everyone says it gets easier, but right now, every song on the radio seems to be about us. I keep reaching for my phone to tell him something funny and then remembering. Today, though, was a little better. I went for chai with Ruhi, and I laughed properly for the first time in days. I also finished a painting I'd abandoned months ago. Maybe this is how it heals: one small, ordinary good day at a time. I'm still sad. But I'm also still me.
What time did I wake up today?
I can't tell, as I have no way of seeing your day. If you note it down each morning, you can look back.

Read this:

The family counselling centre had a fish tank, and Ira watched the fish instead of Tenzin.
The counsellor had asked Tenzin to describe an ordinary day. Tenzin spoke slowly. "I send Ira a photo when I reach work. I share my location. Ira checks my expenses every Sunday. I don't wear the blue kurta any more, because Ira said it looked like I was trying to impress someone. I stopped the pottery class."
Ira's face burned. "I do all that because I worry. The city isn't safe. Money goes so fast."
"What would happen," the counsellor asked Ira gently, "if Tenzin didn't send the photo one day?"
Ira meant to say I'd be worried. What came out was, "I'd feel like I was losing her."
The room went very quiet. Tenzin looked at Ira for the first time that hour.

What does Tenzin send Ira on reaching work?
Tenzin sends Ira a photo on reaching work.
What did Ira truly feel when asked about a missed photo?
Ira felt afraid of losing Tenzin; the words "I'd feel like I was losing her" came out instead of "worried".
What could Ira do after this honest moment in counselling?
Ira could keep working with the counsellor on the fear itself and start giving Tenzin back choices, like the pottery class and privacy with money and location.
What is it like for Tenzin to hear Ira's admission?
Tenzin looks at Ira for the first time that hour, perhaps surprised, and maybe a little hopeful, to hear the fear named instead of excused as worry.

Read this:

Note from Raghav, sports coach. Hemant talks loudly in the huddle when he's excited. I press my palms gently downward with a smile, and he now lowers his voice. Today I saw a teammate make the same gesture with a flat face in the middle of a game. Hemant went silent and stared at his shoes. I asked him privately afterwards. He said, “It felt like he thought I was silly.” I explained that the same gesture can be kind or dismissive and that the face and tone tell you which. Next practice I will invite the two of them to talk it through.

What does Raghav do with his palms to get Hemant to lower his voice?
He presses his palms gently downward with a smile.
What was Hemant feeling when he went silent after the teammate's gesture, and what else could explain it?
Hurt and embarrassed, since he said it felt like the teammate thought he was silly. He might also have been just focusing on the game, but he told Raghav how it felt.
What did Raghav do that helped, and what will he do next?
He asked Hemant privately and explained that face and tone show whether the gesture is kind, and he will invite the two boys to talk it through.
How might the teammate have meant his gesture?
Possibly as a simple, quick request for calm in the middle of a game, without noticing his flat face looked dismissive.
Two classmates tell the teacher different stories about a broken chair. How can the teacher find out what happened?

The teacher can ask each of them careful questions and listen for details that fit together. Because other students or the chair itself may offer evidence, checking facts is fairer than simply believing one side.

Read this:

So you asked about the scariest shift I've had at the warehouse. Okay, I'm Kishore, I run the evening dispatch team, and this is the one I still think about.

Shreya takes a phone call near loading bay three. Next minute she's white as chalk, one hand on the rack, knees kind of wobbling. Some of the lads assumed she was furious, because she'd been arguing with a driver earlier.

I didn't know. Could be anger, could be she was going to faint, could be bad news. So I just asked, "Are you hurt? Do you need to sit?" She shook her head, then sat on a pallet anyway. I got water, asked if she wanted anyone called.

Turned out her father had been taken to hospital. Shock, not temper. I called our supervisor to cover her line and booked her a cab. The feelings could wait; getting her safely off the floor couldn't.

Where did Shreya take the phone call?
She took the phone call near loading bay three.
Why did Kishore ask about Shreya's safety before anything else, and what was Kishore feeling?

Kishore felt uncertain and concerned, because her paleness and wobbling knees could mean anger, faintness or bad news, so Kishore checked she was not hurt or about to fall before guessing her feelings.
How could the other workers handle a moment like this next time?
They could stop assuming it is anger, ask a simple question about whether the person is hurt or needs to sit, and help get them somewhere safe.
What was it like for Shreya when some of the lads thought she was furious?
She had just heard frightening news about her father, so being read as angry would have left her more alone at a moment of shock.

Read this:

"Gurleen, switch off the torch."
"Why, Manjula Didi?"
"Just do it. Now look up."
Gurleen tilted her head back. Above the Spiti valley, the sky was so full of stars it looked like spilled salt. The Milky Way stretched from one mountain to another.
"Oh," she whispered. "Oh my god."
"I know."
"I've lived twenty-five years in Delhi and never seen this."
"It's been there all along."
Gurleen felt her throat tighten. "I feel... so small. But not in a bad way."
"Like you're part of something huge."
"Yes." She laughed shakily. "I don't have words."
"Then don't use any."
They stood there in silence, breath fogging, for a long time.

Where were Gurleen and Manjula?
In the Spiti valley.
What was Gurleen feeling when her throat tightened?
She felt awe and profound wonder, small but part of something huge.
What did Manjula do that let Gurleen fully experience the moment?
She had Gurleen switch off the torch, look up, and then encouraged silence instead of talk.
How might Manjula feel watching Gurleen's reaction?
She likely feels happy and moved to share something she already loved.

Read this:

"You didn't pick up. Three times," Madhuri said at the door of the library reading room.
"I was in the lab, phone in the locker. I called back at six."
"Six was too late. You're useless, Asif. Honestly, you're like everyone else."
Asif blinked. "Last week you said I was the only one who gets you."
"Well, I was wrong."
He felt the floor tilt. Part of him wanted to snap back, "Fine, then find someone else." He took a breath instead. "I'm sorry I missed it. I can't always pick up in the lab. I do care. What happened at three?"
Madhuri's jaw worked. "Forget it."
"Okay. I'm around after seven if you want to talk. I'm not going anywhere, but I'm also not useless."
She walked off. Asif sat down, heart pounding, and went back to his notes.

Where was Asif's phone when Madhuri called?
Asif's phone was in the locker while Asif was in the lab.
What was Asif feeling when Madhuri called him useless?
Asif felt bewildered and hurt; a week earlier he was the only one who understood her, and now the floor seemed to tilt.
What did Asif's reply get right?
He apologised without grovelling, explained his limits, stayed open to talking after seven, and refused the "useless" label without snapping back.
What might Madhuri be feeling behind "you're like everyone else"?
Madhuri seems hurt and let down, perhaps by whatever happened at three, and the disappointment flipped Asif from perfect to useless.

These were on my mind:
How can I learn the names of many new people?
Fix my grammar: They arrived to the airport at night.
Why do we put a stamp on a letter?
How would you explain "tendencies" to a child?

1. Repeat each name when you hear it, and use it in the conversation. Link the name to something about the person.
2. It should be: They arrived at the airport at night. Why: we use "arrive at" a place such as an airport.
3. It shows that the postage is paid. Because the post office needs payment to carry a letter and deliver it.
4. Tendencies is a noun that means habits or ways that someone is likely to act.

Reena: did you finish the physics lab report
Vikas: yes. wrote it myself first, then asked the AI for feedback
Reena: feedback how
Vikas: I pasted my draft and asked "what's unclear, don't rewrite it"
Reena: and?
Vikas: it said my method section skips how I measured the time. and my conclusion doesn't mention the error
Reena: ooh that's what Sir always cuts marks for
Vikas: exactly. so I rewrote those two parts myself. took 40 min
Reena: why not just let it fix them
Vikas: because then next lab I'd make the same mistakes. now I actually get why the error goes in the conclusion 🙂
Reena: ok I'm doing the same. draft first, then feedback
Vikas: and don't paste your name or roll number in it
Reena: noted 👍

What did the AI say the method section skipped?
It skips how Vikas measured the time.
Why did Vikas choose to rewrite the parts personally?
Vikas wanted to understand the mistakes rather than repeat them next lab, and is pleased to finally get why the error belongs in the conclusion.
What else could Reena do after getting feedback?
Reena could check the feedback against the teacher's marking points, since the AI's comments may not match exactly what Sir looks for.
How might Reena see Vikas's method?
Reena is convinced and decides to copy it, drafting first and asking for feedback after.

messages.content:
Read this:

"Yamini, you've skipped lunch all week."
"Not hungry, Sabina."
"You said that last week too. And you left the dance group. You loved dance."
Yamini picked at her sleeve. "I just feel… empty. Every day. I can't sleep, and then I can't get up. It's been like this since the holidays."
Sabina sat down beside her on the bench. "That sounds really heavy. Thank you for telling me."
"Don't make it a big thing."
"I care about you, so I think it is. Can we go to Ms D'Souza together? Right now? I'll stay with you."
Yamini hesitated, then nodded.
In the counsellor's room, Ms D'Souza listened to all of it. "You did the right thing coming in," she said. "Feeling this way for weeks is something we can get help for." She called Yamini's mother that afternoon, and they set up a meeting for the next day.

When did Yamini say she had been feeling like this since?
Since the holidays.
What does Yamini asking Sabina not to make it a big thing suggest she felt?
It suggests Yamini felt ashamed and worried about being a burden, even though she was really struggling.
What did Sabina do well when she noticed the signs?
Sabina noticed the changes over weeks, listened without judging, and went with Yamini to the counsellor the same day instead of keeping it secret.
How does Ms D'Souza respond to Yamini?
The counsellor listens fully, tells Yamini she did the right thing, and calls her mother that afternoon to set up support.
Is "my cousin and I" okay as the subject? My cousin and I walked to the lake after breakfast.

This is already correct.
Why: "I" is the subject; naming the other person first is polite.
Write a 60-word message to my flatmates asking everyone to wash their own dishes on time. Friendly, not bossy.

Hi all,
Quick request: could we each try to wash our own dishes on the same day we use them? The sink has been full most mornings, and it's making breakfast a bit difficult. I know everyone is busy, so even a quick rinse helps. Thanks, and I'll keep doing my share too!
Ankita
She asked me to not to go. Please correct.
The correct sentence is: "She asked me not to go." Why: after "asked me", "not to" comes before the verb.
To "to not go" bolna galat hai?
It is understood, and some people use it, but "not to go" is the usual and safer form.
amusing - meaning?

Amusing means funny enough to make you smile or laugh. It is an adjective.
Example: Kabir told an amusing story about his dog chasing its own tail.

Manoj: yeah. sitting next to me would help
Ira: done. and your voice is fine btw

How many times had the joke happened this week?
It was the third time this week.
What was Manoj feeling when writing 'it was funny'?
Manoj was most likely hurt and embarrassed, using the laugh as a shield so as not to look weak; part of the joke may still have seemed funny in the moment.
What did Ira do that made it easier to talk?
Ira asked privately, didn't insist Manoj was hurt, accepted 'I'm fine' while leaving the offer open, and then suggested concrete support. 🤍
What might Karan have missed by seeing only the laugh?
Karan probably took the laugh as a sign the joke was harmless, missing that it was the third time and that Manoj went quiet afterwards.

Sit, Swati, I'll tell you about Manjula, my best friend when I was your age. Our lane had a small gurdwara at one end. Every Sunday we could smell the dal from the langar kitchen. Manjula was curious, but her father said, "That's their place, not ours." One day she walked in with her head uncovered, and a lady gently handed her a scarf. Manjula went red. The lady just smiled and showed her where to wash her hands. After that, Manjula helped roll rotis there every week, and she still lit her diya at home every evening. When I asked if she had changed religions, she laughed. "No, silly. I just learned their rules so I don't hurt anyone."

What did the lady hand Manjula when she walked in?
She gently handed her a scarf to cover her head.
Why did Manjula go red when the lady handed her the scarf?
She felt embarrassed because she realised she had broken a custom of the place without knowing, and she worried she might have been disrespectful.
What could Swati take from Manjula's story if she visits another faith's place?
She could ask or watch for the customs, like covering her head or washing hands, and follow them while still keeping her own practices at home.
How might Manjula's father have seen her weekly visits?
He may have worried at first that she was crossing a line, but he might see over time that she kept her own diya and simply learned to respect her neighbours.

"Kiran, stay back a minute. You're not in trouble."
"Okay, Ma'am."
"You yawned all through science. And you told Riya to shut up. That's not like you."
"Sorry. I'm just tired."
"What time did you sleep last night?"
"Twelve. After abacus class and Hindi tuition I still had my project."
"Is it like that every night?"
"Most nights. I keep saying I'll be fast, but I'm slow when I'm sleepy."
"That makes sense. Tired brains are slow brains. Can I talk to your mother about the homework load?"
"Will she be angry?"
"I'll tell her you were honest. And today, no extra practice sheet. Go home and rest."
Afreen Ma'am wrote a reminder on her hand before the next bell rang.

What time did Kiran sleep last night?
Twelve.
How can you tell Afreen feels concerned rather than annoyed?
She tells Kiran there is no trouble and calls the rude words "not like you", which shows care and worry rather than anger.
What did Afreen do that was more useful than a punishment?
She asked gently about bedtime and homework, found the real cause, and planned to talk with Kiran's mother about the load.
How might Kiran feel walking home without the extra practice sheet?
Kiran is likely relieved and understood, because the tiredness was noticed instead of punished.

messages.content: Sentence: 'First you boil the milk and then you put the sugar in it.' Ok for recipe?
It is correct, but recipes usually use short commands: "Boil the milk. Add the sugar and stir." Leave out "you" and start each step with a verb.
My budgie sleeps with his head tucked in his feathers. Is something wrong?
That's normal. Many birds sleep with their head turned back and tucked under a wing. It keeps them warm and comfortable.
Okay. I was worried.
It's kind of you to notice. If he seems sleepy all day, puffed up or stops eating, ask a vet who treats birds. Otherwise, sleeping like this is part of his routine.

During Makar Sankranti in the village near Solapur, Zeenat, eleven, and Ankita, nine, were flying kites on the roof.

Zeenat, the older one, took Ankita's best kite. "I'll fly it better."

Ankita crossed her arms. "It's mine. You always take things because you're bigger."

Zeenat stopped. Nobody had ever said that to her.

"Okay," she said. "You fly it, and I'll hold the spool."

Ankita was surprised. They flew it together, and it went higher than any other kite on the street.

Who held the spool?
Zeenat held the spool.
How did Zeenat feel when Ankita said she always takes things?
Zeenat felt surprised and a bit ashamed, since nobody had said it to her before.
What helped the girls resolve the argument without adults?
Ankita spoke up clearly, and Zeenat listened and offered to share the job.
How might Ankita feel when Zeenat agreed?
Ankita was surprised and likely happy to be listened to.

He took it. "You give it up very gleefully," said he; "I don't quite understand your light-heartedness, because I cannot tell what employment you propose to yourself as a substitute for the one you are relinquishing. What aim, what purpose, what ambition in life have you now?"

Using nothing beyond this text, what puzzles him about the speaker's light-heartedness?
He cannot tell what employment the speaker plans in place of the one being given up, and he asks what aim, purpose or ambition lies ahead.

Here is a short passage from Great Expectations. What is the narrator sure of after seeing the housekeeper?

Only twice more did the housekeeper reappear, and then her stay in the room was very short, and Mr. Jaggers was sharp with her. But her hands were Estella's hands, and her eyes were Estella's eyes, and if she had reappeared a hundred times I could have been neither more sure nor less sure that my conviction was the truth.
He is sure that her hands and eyes are Estella's hands and eyes. He feels so certain that seeing her many more times would not change his mind.

Near the hospital, with mostly visitors.
What was Uma thinking before deciding not to copy the card?
Uma felt curious and a bit cautious, wanting to know why the card worked for the rival before copying it.

Uma checks who the customers are and what the café's costs are, then adapts the idea to visitors instead of students.

Saturday. Vishal opens a blank sheet. Three countries across the top: the Netherlands, Ireland, the UAE. Down the side: pay, visa path, cost of living, distance from family, work culture. His friend Madhav asks, 'Aren't they all equal?' 'Not to me,' Vishal says, and gives the visa path 30 percent, because his last application was rejected.
Tuesday. He fills in scores from one to five, using official pages and two friends' replies. Ireland: 3.9. The Netherlands: 3.7. The UAE: 3.4. Under the totals he writes: 'rough scores, could swing'.
The next Sunday. Madhav finds him lowering Ireland's living-cost score after reading about rents. The total drops to 3.6. Vishal just shrugs. 'That's why I wrote rough. Now the Netherlands and Ireland are close, so I'll look at the jobs themselves.'

What score did Ireland get on Tuesday?
Ireland got 3.9.
How does Vishal feel when Ireland's total drops?
He seems calm and unbothered, having expected the scores to be rough, so the drop doesn't upset him.
What would you advise Vishal now that two countries are close?
Compare real job offers and talk to people working in both places, since the matrix has narrowed the list but can't choose for him.
How does the matrix look to Madhav?
Madhav first thought the factors were equal, but watching Vishal adjust scores he sees a careful, personal method.

I'm Dolma, Asif's lab partner this year. He used to rewrite our lab reports five times and miss deadlines. This term I've watched him change. He sets his phone timer for one hour, writes a rough version, and then stops. Stops! Last week he deliberately handed in a report with the graph colours not matching, which would have killed him in August. His hand hovered over the submit button for a long time, then he clicked. He also mentioned, quickly, that he's been talking to the campus counsellor about the anxiety. I don't know how hard it is inside his head. But he laughs more in the lab now.

How long is Asif's timer?
He sets his phone timer for one hour.
What does Asif's hand hovering over the submit button suggest?
It suggests he felt anxious about sending imperfect work, even while choosing to do it.
Which practice is helping Asif most, and why?
Setting a time limit, writing a rough version and deliberately sending small flaws builds his tolerance, while the counsellor helps with the anxiety.
How might the lab teacher see Asif's reports now?
The teacher probably notices them arriving on time, which matters more than matching graph colours.

At the end of badminton practice at the sports club, the coach said the court was free till seven for anyone who wanted to stay. Pooja was already bouncing. "Parul, doubles! Come on!" Parul looked at the big clock over the scoreboard. Six. Both her parents worked late on Thursdays. Lucky had been in the flat since two, with food and water but nobody to lean against. "He eats fine," she thought, "but he's a dog, not a plant. He needs a walk and someone around." She zipped her racket bag. "Not today, Pooja. Lucky's waiting, and he's been alone all afternoon." Pooja groaned, then said, "Saturday, then?" "Saturday morning. I'll bring him to watch."

When do both of Parul's parents work late?
On Thursdays.
What was Parul feeling as she zipped her bag?
A little sorry to miss doubles, but responsible and sure Lucky needed her.
What else could Parul arrange for Thursdays?
She could ask a neighbour to take Lucky for a short walk, so she can sometimes stay late.
How does Pooja react?
Pooja groans at first, then accepts and suggests Saturday instead.

"...so the report can't go out like this, Naveen. The data section needs to be redone."
Naveen nodded. He opened his mouth to answer and found his eyes had filled. "Sorry. I... sorry."
Dolma pushed the tissue box across the desk. "No need. Take your time."

"Of course. The water cooler's free. Come back when you're ready."
He came back five minutes later, face washed, carrying a notepad.
"Better?" Dolma asked.
"Yes. Thanks. Can we go through exactly what's wrong in the data section? I'd like to fix it by Thursday."
"That's a good plan." She turned her screen toward him. "And Naveen, the structure is strong. It's only the data. I should have said that first."
He let out a breath. "That helps."

By when does Naveen want to fix the data section?
By Thursday.
Why did Naveen's eyes fill up?
He felt hurt and disappointed, having worked all weekend on the report, and the criticism hit hard.
What did Naveen do that helped him recover?
He asked to step out for a few minutes, washed his face, then came back with a notepad and a plan to fix the data by Thursday.
What did Dolma realise about how she gave feedback?
Dolma realised she should have mentioned the strong structure first, and tried to make up for the harshness by saying it now.

Salma had read Arman's messages over his shoulder twice that week, and last night she'd picked a fight about a colleague's 'good morning' text, just to see if he'd still say he loved her. He did. It didn't help. On Sunday, over coffee at a Bandra café, her friend Nikita asked why she looked so tired. Salma found herself saying it: 'I keep thinking he'll leave. So I either cling or I push, to test him.' Nikita didn't laugh. 'What would you tell me if I said that?' 'That he's not the problem. The fear is.' Salma went quiet. That evening, instead of checking his phone, she told Arman the truth: 'I'm scared you'll leave, and I've been acting badly because of it. It's not about you. I'm working on it.' Arman held her hand. 'Thank you for saying it. I'm not going anywhere. But I'd like you to talk to someone too, not just me.' She booked a counselling session the next day.

What did Salma pick a fight about?
A colleague's 'good morning' text to Arman.
What was Salma afraid of underneath the clinging and testing?
She felt anxious and afraid that Arman would leave.
What did Salma do instead of checking his phone?
She named her fear honestly to Arman, took responsibility, and booked a counselling session.
How does Arman respond to Salma's honesty?
He thanks her, reassures her, and gently suggests she talk to someone besides him.

Chinmay's last week at the design firm was calm, almost too calm. At Tuesday's lunch he explained his layoff to Aparna like a case study: the lost client, the forty-person cut, why his team was the logical choice. "It's not personal. From a cost view it makes sense."

Aparna noticed his lunch box went back full, two days in a row. On Wednesday he was in the office at seven, with emails timestamped two in the morning.

On Thursday she found him at his desk, sorting files. She didn't ask about his plan. She pulled up a chair and asked, "Setting the logic aside for a minute, how does it feel?"

Chinmay kept sorting. Then his hands stopped. "Like I wasn't worth keeping," he said, very quietly.

How many people were cut at the design firm?
It was a forty-person cut.
What made Aparna worried about Chinmay?
Aparna felt concerned because Chinmay's calm talk didn't match the full lunch box and the emails sent at two in the morning.
Why was Aparna's question a good choice?
Asking how it feels instead of what the plan is gave Chinmay room to say the hurt, which the logic had been holding back.
What is it like for Chinmay when Aparna asks how it feels?
Chinmay seems caught off guard and, for the first time, lets the hurt show: feeling he wasn't worth keeping.

For the third Saturday running, Sharmila's towel was missing from the bench at the swimming club, and Avni's group sang "Drippy Sharmila" as she stood shivering by the pool. Avni flicked water at her. "Go on, cry." Sharmila's hands curled. She wanted to push Avni straight into the deep end. Instead she breathed out slowly and walked to the lifeguard's chair, where Coach Latha was writing lap times. "Coach, it keeps happening. The towel, the song, every week." Coach Latha put her clipboard down and listened to all of it. "Thank you for telling me. None of this is your fault." Before the session ended, she spoke to Avni's group, found the towel stuffed in a locker, and that evening she rang Sharmila's mother.

How many Saturdays in a row had Sharmila's towel gone missing?
It was the third Saturday running.
Why did Sharmila walk to the lifeguard's chair instead of pushing Avni?
She was angry enough to want to push Avni, but she held it in and moved next to a safe adult; she was probably also hurt and tired of the weekly song.
How did Coach Latha support Sharmila?
She stopped, listened to everything, said it was not Sharmila's fault, and acted the same day: she spoke to the group, found the towel and rang Sharmila's mother.
What would change if Sharmila had pushed Avni into the pool?
Avni could have been hurt, Sharmila might have been the one blamed, and the repeated taunting could have been hidden behind the push.

Preeti, sit down. You're off on this trekking trip, and your Vijay Mama has a confession. When I was twenty, in Indore, my friend Ashok announced he was taking a year off to travel the Himalayas by bus. I was furious. I told everyone he was a loafer, that his father's hard-earned money was being wasted, that travellers were just people running from responsibility. I went on about it for months, far more than anyone needed. Finally your Nani asked me, "Vijay, why do you keep talking about Ashok's trip?" I had no answer. That night I took out the map I'd hidden inside my accounts textbook, with routes marked in pencil. I had been planning that same trip for years and was too scared to go. The anger was about me, beta, not Ashok. So go, and send me photos.

Where had Vijay hidden his map?
Inside his accounts textbook, with routes marked in pencil.
Why did Vijay's anger at Ashok last for months?
Ashok was doing the very trip Vijay secretly longed for and feared; condemning it kept his own wish buried.
What turning point helped Vijay see the truth?
Nani's simple question about why he kept talking about Ashok's trip, which sent him back to the hidden map.
How might Ashok have felt hearing he was called a loafer?
Probably hurt and confused, since his friend's anger was much bigger than a travel plan deserved.

"Have you seen this?" Simran held out her phone. It was a video of Siddharth from Class 8, pretending to be a teacher with a fake accent.
Siddharth went pale. "Where did that come from? I deleted it."
"Someone saved it. It's going round the Class 11 group."
"But that was three years ago. I was stupid."
"People don't know that. They just see it now."
Siddharth put his head in his hands. "The teacher I was copying is still here."
Simran sat down. "Then maybe say sorry to her first, before she sees it from someone else."
Siddharth was silent for a long time. Then he stood up. "Okay. Come with me?"
"I'll wait outside the staff room."

How long ago did Siddharth make the video?
Three years ago.
What was Siddharth feeling when he put his head in his hands?
Siddharth felt ashamed and worried about how the teacher would see it.
What did Simran suggest, and why is it wise?
She suggested apologising to the teacher before she saw it from others, which shows responsibility and respect.
How might the teacher feel if Siddharth apologises before she sees the video?
The teacher might still be hurt, but she'd likely respect him for coming to her first.

Wednesday
Something happened today that I keep thinking about. In the science quiz, Ishita, who always comes first and whose father is on the school committee, gave a wrong answer, and Joseph Sir said, "Not quite, try again," exactly the way he says it to me. Then when I mixed up a Hindi word, nobody laughed, because he never lets anyone laugh at mistakes, not even at Ishita's.
At my old school the teacher had favourites. I used to feel invisible there.
Here I feel safe to put my hand up, even with my accent. I answered three questions today!
I think Joseph Sir decides to be fair every morning. Like brushing his teeth.
Harish

How many questions did Harish answer today?
Three questions.
How does Harish feel in Joseph Sir's class compared with the old school?
Safe and confident, whereas at the old school Harish felt invisible.
What does Joseph Sir do that makes the class fair?
He responds to everyone's mistakes the same way and never lets anyone laugh at a mistake.
How might Ishita experience Joseph Sir's fairness?
She gets no special treatment, which might surprise her, but she is also protected from being laughed at.
Three rhyming couplets for a children's toothbrush song, about 40 words; mention the front and the back, and sugar bugs.

Brush your teeth, up and down,
Chase the sugar bugs from town.
Brush the front and brush the back,
Keep your smile upon the track.
Brush each morning, brush at night,
Make your teeth all clean and bright.

It was Bonfire Night in Leeds, and the fractions sheet had been on Daniel's desk since tea. He sharpened three pencils. He lined up his rubbers by size. He went down for water, then again because the first glass was "too warm". From the window he could see rockets bursting over the park.
"Done yet?" called Siddiq, the older boy from next door who helped him with homework.
"Nearly," Daniel said. He hadn't written a single number. Every time he looked at question one, his tummy went tight, and tidying made the tight feeling go away.
By eight his desk was spotless and the sheet was blank. Next week, he thought, he would tidy the drawers first.

How many pencils did Daniel sharpen?
Three pencils.
Why did Daniel keep tidying instead of starting question one?
Looking at the fractions made his tummy tight with worry, and tidying brought quick relief, so escaping felt good.
What small step would help Daniel?
Ask Siddiq to sit with him for just question one, or set a timer for five minutes of trying 🙂, so he learns the tight feeling passes.
What might Siddiq think when Daniel says "Nearly"?
Siddiq probably believes him or hopes it is true, and may be surprised later to find the sheet blank.

At the community centre's pottery class, Lavanya lifted her little bowl off the wheel and held it up. “Is it right, Dilnaz Aunty?” She had asked after every step: after centring the clay, after opening the hole, after pulling up the walls. Another parent in the room murmured, “She's so unsure of herself.” Dilnaz Aunty didn't think so. She turned the bowl slowly in her hands. “The base is even, well done. The rim is thick on this side; next time press gently with your thumb here.” Lavanya watched her thumb. “Like this?” She tried it on a scrap of clay. “Exactly,” said Dilnaz Aunty.

Where was the pottery class?
The pottery class was at the community centre.
What was Lavanya feeling as she held up her bowl?
Lavanya felt hopeful and eager to learn, wanting to know if she had got each step right.
How did Dilnaz Aunty's answer help Lavanya learn?
She gave specific feedback, praising the even base and showing exactly how to fix the thick rim.
How did the other parent read Lavanya's questions?
The other parent saw them as a sign of being unsure of herself, not as effort to learn.
The teacher corrected all our homework and gave us a feedback. Anything wrong?

The teacher corrected all our homework and gave us feedback.
Why: "feedback" is uncountable, so no "a".
The number of students in our club are increasing. Is the verb right?

The number of students in our club is increasing.
Why: "the number of" is singular, so "is".

I'm Bhupen, and last winter a man I'd met in an online chess group started telling me about his "crypto arbitrage". He was friendly, sent me screenshots, said my money would double in sixty days. I'd had a bad year. The idea of doubling felt like a door opening.
I told my friend Sangeeta about it over chai. She didn't laugh. She just asked, "Why would he share a secret that makes money for free?" I didn't have an answer.
That night I looked up the platform he recommended. It wasn't registered with any regulator I could find. Its website was two months old. The "reviews" all used the same sentences.
Looking back, what hooked me wasn't greed exactly. It was hope. I wanted something to go right. That's what the scam was built on. I stopped replying to him, reported his profile to the group admins, and told Sangeeta she'd probably saved me a lot.

How long was the platform's website, according to Bhupen?
Two months old.
What made Bhupen want to believe the offer?
Bhupen felt hopeful after a bad year, and the idea of doubling money felt like a door opening.
How did Bhupen check the offer?
Bhupen asked why a stranger would share free money, looked for the platform's registration, and noticed the website was new and the reviews repeated.
How might Sangeeta see her own question afterwards?
Sangeeta may feel relieved and glad that one simple question helped Bhupen step back.

The first time Salma heard the qawwali at her cousin's engagement in Lucknow, she thought it was too long and too loud. Yamini Aunty, who sang it at every family function, clapped and swayed while Salma counted the ceiling fans.
Then came her uncle's wedding, then Eid lunch, then Nani's birthday. The same song every time. By Nani's birthday, Salma knew when the claps came. One evening, doing homework, she found herself tapping her pencil to it.
At the next function, when Yamini Aunty began, Salma sat right in front.
"I thought you hated this one," Aunty said.
Salma shrugged, smiling. "It grew on me."

Who sang the qawwali at every family function?
Yamini Aunty.
What was Salma feeling when she sat right in front?
She felt happy and attached to the song, enjoying what she once found too long and loud.
What does Salma's change suggest about first reactions to music?
That a first dislike can fade with repeated listening, so it's worth giving songs a few chances.
How might Yamini Aunty feel about Salma sitting in front?
She is likely pleased and a little amused, having seen Salma bored before.
How many copies did the first edition of that old poetry book print?
I'm not sure, and a made-up figure would not help you. A library catalogue or the publisher's records may list print runs.
What does borders mean on a map, and what does it mean on a notebook page?

A border is an edge. On a map it is the line that separates one country or state from another; on a page it is a line or pattern drawn around the edge. It is a noun. The plural is Borders.
Example: The map showed the borders of every state in a different colour, and Sneha drew a blue border around her title.

For four months, Madhuri did everything herself. After work she drove to her father's flat, cooked, sorted his tablets, phoned the pharmacy and slept badly. It was her job, she told herself. By spring she was writing wrong figures in reports, snapping at her mother over small things, and crying in the car park.

One Sunday she opened a notebook and wrote down what her father needed: which clinic visits, which daily jobs, who in the family was free and what each thing cost. The list showed her something. The real gap was weekday mornings, when nobody was there.

She rang her brother Tanvir and their aunt that evening. "Here is what's needed and how many hours it takes," she said. "Can you each take a part?" Tanvir agreed to handle the money and hospital visits. Madhuri kept the daily calls and organised the medicines. Their aunt offered to cover two mornings.

In autumn, when her father's condition worsened, they met again. With her parents and Dr Varun, they discussed replacing the morning attendant with trained professional care. Her father asked questions, her mother nodded, and the family agreed to review it again in a few months.

How long did Madhuri do everything by herself?
She did everything herself for four months.
How did Madhuri's first approach differ from her call to Tanvir and her aunt, and what did the notebook show?

At first she carried all the care alone, which left her exhausted and making mistakes, while the notebook showed weekday mornings as the real gap and the call shared the tasks and hours between the family members.
What was Madhuri feeling when she cried in the car park?
She was exhausted and overwhelmed, worn down by doing everything alone.
What did the autumn meeting do well?
It reviewed the arrangement when her father's condition worsened and discussed changing to professional care with her parents and Dr Varun rather than deciding without them.

The week after I saw the bus hit the boy on the cycle, I couldn't sleep properly. I kept replaying it. Other people had helped. I had stood on the footpath with my hands shaking, trying to remember if the emergency number was 100 or 108 or something else.
My friend Tushar asked what was bothering me most. I thought about it and said, "Not knowing. Not the blood, not the noise. Just not knowing what to do."
So I made a list for myself. What would make next time different? Numbers I don't need to remember. So I saved 112 and the local hospital's ambulance line under "A" for "Accident". And some actual skill. I found a first-aid course at the community hall, with a certificate at the end, and signed up for the next batch.
I'm Jeevan. I did the course in two weekends. I still hope I never need it. But the fear feels smaller now that it has a plan.

Under which letter did Jeevan save the emergency numbers?
Jeevan saved them under 'A' for 'Accident'.
What did Jeevan feel most troubled by after the accident?
Jeevan felt most troubled and helpless about not knowing what to do, more than the blood or the noise.
What else could Jeevan do to keep the skills fresh?
Jeevan could refresh the course when it's offered again, so the steps stay clear instead of fading.
How might Tushar feel after asking what was bothering Jeevan?
Tushar may feel glad that one question helped Jeevan find the real worry and turn it into a plan.
