"So, the mess menu," Rajat said, before anyone else could speak. "Paneer three times a week. Obviously."
"Is there a list of what we're—" Sumit began.
"And the Sunday special should be biryani. I've said this for a year."
"What about late dinner for the lab students?" Ganga asked.
"Later, later. First, paneer."
Forty minutes passed. Rajat talked about paneer, the cook's attitude, a cricket match, paneer again. Sumit watched the clock and the three first-years at the back who hadn't said a word.
"Okay, good meeting," Rajat said, standing. "Done."
Outside, Sumit asked, "So what did we decide?"
"Late dinner moves to nine thirty," Ganga said.
"Did it? I thought he said later."
"I heard 'fine, later'."
"And paneer?"
"Three times. Or twice. Honestly, not sure."
Sumit rubbed his eyes. "An hour gone, and we each walked out of a different meeting."

How long did Rajat keep talking before the meeting ended?
Forty minutes.
How did Sumit feel walking out of the meeting?
Sumit was frustrated and confused, rubbing his eyes because an hour had gone and nobody knew what had been decided.
What could have made the meeting useful?
A short agenda read out at the start, a turn for each item, and someone repeating each decision at the end so everyone left with the same outcome.
What is it like for Ganga when the late-dinner question is brushed aside?
Ganga is pushed aside by the loudest voice and then leaves unsure whether the question was even answered, which feels dismissive and wasteful.

As I sat in my usual nook, and looked at him with the light of the girandoles on the mantelpiece beaming full over him—for he occupied an arm-chair drawn close to the fire, and kept shrinking still nearer, as if he were cold, I compared him with Mr. Rochester. I think (with deference be it spoken) the contrast could not be much greater between a sleek gander and a fierce falcon: between a meek sheep and the rough-coated keen-eyed dog, its guardian.

How does the narrator compare this man with Mr. Rochester?
She thinks they are total opposites: this man is like a sleek goose or a meek sheep, while Mr. Rochester is like a fierce falcon or a keen guard dog.

Read this:

In the lobby of their building, a boy grabbed Akash's ball. Akash's mother, Seema, said, “Please give it back.” The boy muttered, “Sorry,” without looking up, and kept holding the ball. Akash said, “He said sorry,” and turned away, though his lip was shaking. Seema knelt. “He said sorry. Did he give the ball back?” Akash looked. “No.” “A real sorry means you stop and fix it.” She turned to the boy. “Please give it back now.” He did. Akash hugged the ball.

What did the boy grab?
Akash's ball.
What was Akash feeling when he turned away with his lip shaking?
He was upset about his ball and confused, because he accepted the sorry even though nothing changed.
What did Seema teach Akash about sorry?
That a real sorry means stopping and fixing it, and she helped check whether the ball came back.
How might the boy see Seema's second request?
He'd learn that saying sorry isn't enough, and that he needed to give the ball back.

metadata.subtype: Reading whether an apology is meant [Interpreting]

messages.content:
Read this:

By the time the placement cell opened registrations, Seema had already decided to skip them. She wanted a year to prepare for the civil services exam, and she had, she said, done her research.

Her research was a folder on her laptop. Lalremsiami looked through it one evening in their hostel room. An article titled "Why Placements Are a Trap". A video of a topper who said he never took a job. Screenshots of two seniors saying, "Best decision of my life."

"Did you talk to anyone who regretted it?" Lalremsiami asked.

"Why would I? I know what I want."

"What about Arvind bhaiya? He tried for three years and then came back for placements."

Seema's jaw tightened. "His case is different."

She closed the laptop. She felt thoroughly prepared, like someone who had read everything. Lalremsiami noticed the folder had nothing in it that disagreed.

What was the article in Seema's folder titled?
"Why Placements Are a Trap".
Why does Seema feel so well prepared about her decision?
Seema feels confident and a bit defensive, because her folder is full of agreeing voices, so it feels like complete research even though nothing in it disagrees.
What could Seema add to her research to make it honest?
Seema could talk to Arvind bhaiya and others who regretted skipping placements, and read at least one strong case for taking a job first.
How does Lalremsiami see Seema's folder?
Lalremsiami sees that the folder only holds agreement, and seems worried Seema is mistaking one-sided reading for research.

Read this:

“You told me yesterday the Moon doesn't make its own light,” Vaibhav said as they crossed the playground.
Sachin kicked a stone. “Yeah.”
“So why did you say it does? You were the last one Ma'am asked.”
“Everyone else said it does. Even Jyoti.”
Jyoti, walking ahead, turned round. “I just guessed!”
“See?” said Vaibhav. “She guessed. You knew.”
Sachin scuffed his shoe. “When all twenty say yes, you start thinking maybe you read it wrong. Being the only one sounds... weird.”
“You'd have been right, though.”
“I know,” Sachin muttered. “That's the worst part.”

What did Sachin tell Vaibhav yesterday about the Moon?
Sachin told Vaibhav the Moon doesn't make its own light.
What was Sachin feeling when he said "That's the worst part"?
He felt frustrated with himself and a bit ashamed, because he had known the right answer and still gave it up.
How could a teacher make it easier for Sachin to keep his answer?
The teacher could ask everyone to write answers first before anyone speaks, so no one hears the crowd before deciding.
What was it like for Jyoti to learn the guess swayed Sachin?
Jyoti might feel surprised, maybe a little sorry, having only guessed and never meant anyone to follow.

metadata.subtype: Changing an answer after others answer [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

At the winter market in Uppsala, Xin's flatmates dared her into the palm reader's tent. The reader, a gentle older man who introduced himself as Anders, held her hand for a long time. "You carry an old hurt you rarely mention," he said softly.
Xin's throat tightened. She thought of her grandmother in Chengdu, whose funeral she had missed because of visa trouble. Nobody here knew about that.
"You are torn between two paths," Anders went on. "The one far from home is not for you."
Xin, who had a summer internship offer in Berlin, walked out quiet. Two days later she still hadn't replied to the Berlin email, and she was thinking about booking another reading.

What did the palm reader say Xin carries?
"An old hurt you rarely mention."
Why did Xin's throat tighten?
The line touched her grief about missing her grandmother's funeral, so she felt deeply moved and seen.
What could Xin ask herself before deciding about Berlin?
Whether the reader's lines would fit almost anyone, and what she herself wants, perhaps talking it over with people who know her.
How might Xin's flatmates see the reading's effect?
They meant it as a fun dare and might be surprised or worried that it is now shaping a real internship decision.

metadata.subtype: Reading or prediction that seems to know them [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Rafiq, you look exactly like I did the day they made me shift supervisor at the textile mill in Coimbatore. I was twenty-five. Pallavi, the first woman supervisor on that floor in thirty years.
The manager read my name at the morning meeting, and the women from my old line started clapping before he finished. I had worked seven years on those looms. Seven years of double shifts. That evening my mother made payasam and sent some to every house on our street. My father, who had never once asked about my work, put on his good shirt and walked me to the bus the next morning.
I felt I had climbed a hill with my own hands. And I had. I let myself feel that fully.
But that same week I had to choose how I would treat the women I'd worked beside. That choice is the rest of the story, and you are about to face it too.

How many years had Pallavi worked on the looms?
Seven years.
How did young Pallavi feel when her name was read out?
She felt proud and validated, as if she had climbed a hill with her own hands after seven years.
What choice in the story does Pallavi point to as the turning point?
How she would treat the women she had worked beside, a choice that came in the same week as the promotion.
What did the promotion mean to Pallavi's father in the story?
He seemed quietly proud, putting on his good shirt and walking her to the bus, though he had never asked about her work.

metadata.subtype: Stage 1: The news and the glow [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Hi Asif,
Sorry for the silence. It's been a strange month at home.
My parents are looking for a match for my sister Mercy. I've been watching from the sidelines, and it's harder than I expected. Appa checks every family's income twice. Amma asks the church aunties about each boy's mother, because she's scared Mercy will go somewhere unkind.
Last week they found a "perfect" family. Mercy said she wasn't sure, and Amma said, "What will people think if we refuse such a proposal?" Mercy went quiet. I saw her face and thought, nobody has asked what she wants from her life.
I don't think my parents are wrong to worry. Appa grew up with very little. But I'm worried the worry is choosing for her.
I'm going to talk to Appa this weekend, just the two of us. Any advice?
Joseph

Whom does Amma ask about each boy's mother?
Amma asks the church aunties about each boy's mother.
What is Joseph worried about as he watches his family?
Joseph is worried that the parents' fear is choosing for Mercy, and Joseph feels uneasy that nobody has asked what she wants.
What could Joseph say to Appa this weekend?
Joseph could first acknowledge that Appa's care comes from growing up with little, then gently ask him to sit down with Mercy and hear what she wants.
How might Mercy feel when Amma asks what people will think?
Mercy may feel silenced and pressured, as if the community's opinion counts more than her own doubts about the match.

Read this:

Wednesday
I've been a senior research fellow in the chemistry lab for a year now. I'm Farida. Today I noticed something I don't like.
Our professor treats the two new juniors differently. Ritu got the new instrument to learn and ten minutes of his time every day. The other junior, a quiet student from a small college, got the washing of glassware and a "we'll see."
Already Ritu is asking sharp questions. The other junior has gone silent.
This afternoon I gave the quiet one a small analysis to run. The results were neat. The notes were better than mine at that stage.
Tomorrow I'll show the professor. It's not talent that's different. It's attention.

What did Ritu get to learn?
Ritu got the new instrument to learn.
How does Farida feel about the professor's different treatment?
Farida feels uneasy and troubled, seeing the quiet junior held back by low expectations.
What is Farida planning, and why might it help?
Farida plans to show the professor the quiet junior's neat results, which might change his expectations and the attention he gives.
How might the quiet junior feel after being given the analysis?
The junior may feel encouraged and seen, trusted for the first time with real work.

Read this:

Alka: papa said no to 9:30 on friday 😔
Alka: the show is at the school hall and ends at 8:45
Jasleen: what did you say to him
Alka: i said EVERYONE gets to stay
Jasleen: yeah he hears that all day lol
Jasleen: it gives him nothing to work with
Jasleen: give him a plan
Alka: like what
Jasleen: five of you, show ends 8:45, Meera's dad drops everyone, you text when you reach home
Alka: and if he says no again?
Jasleen: then you ask what would make him say yes. no threatening
Alka: ok. trying tonight 🙏
Jasleen: and say thank you either way

What did Alka's papa say no to?
Papa said no to 9:30 on Friday.
Why is Alka feeling low at the start of the chat?
Alka feels disappointed and maybe a little unheard since Papa said no. Alka also wants to attend the show with friends.
What advice from Jasleen could make Alka's appeal work better?
Giving Papa a clear plan with reasons, like who is coming and who is driving, and asking what would make him say yes. Alka should stay polite whatever he says.
How might Alka's father see Alka's earlier answer that everyone gets to stay?
He may see it as pressure without information, which does not help him judge whether it is safe.

Read this:

My sister Jaya leaves for her master's in Germany next week, and our flat is a mess of suitcases. I've been watching her. Yesterday she spent an hour on the phone with her future flatmate, laughing loudly, planning weekend trips to lakes. Then she hung up and sat on the floor next to her open bag, very still, holding Ma's old shawl. When I asked if she was okay, she said, "Nikita, I'm so happy," and her eyes filled up. At dinner she joked about finally escaping my snoring. Later I heard her in the bathroom, crying quietly. This morning she was dancing to music while ironing. I don't really know what's going on inside her. Maybe it's everything at once. I'm going to miss her terribly.

What was Jaya holding while she sat next to her bag?
Ma's old shawl.
What does Jaya saying 'I'm so happy' while her eyes filled up suggest?
She seems to be feeling joy and sadness together, excited for her new life but sad to leave home.
How could Nikita support Jaya in her last week at home?
She could spend simple time with her, let her talk about both the fun plans and the fears, and plan how they'll stay in touch.
What is it like for Nikita to watch her sister prepare to leave?
She is trying to read Jaya's swings without really knowing her inner state, while dealing with her own sadness at losing her.
Tell me about bees in one sentence with the words "flowers" and "honey".
Bees visit flowers to collect nectar, which they turn into honey.

Read this:

Every weekday at five in their Chandigarh flat, Uma set the kitchen timer to forty minutes, put it next to the tablet and started her farm game. The first week was hard. When it rang, she'd groan, "One more harvest!" But she had made the rule herself after an argument with her mother, and she wanted to show she could keep it. So she saved and closed the game. By the third week she had started planning her forty minutes: harvest first, then build, then trade. When her cousin Amandeep visited and said, "Your mother lets you play only forty?", Uma said, "No. I let me play forty." Her mother, overhearing from the kitchen, smiled into the dal.

How long does Uma play on weekdays?
Forty minutes.
Why did Uma stop when the timer rang, even when it was hard?
She felt determined to prove she could keep her own rule, and proud of it being hers.
What else could Uma do on days she wants more time?
Save the extra wish for the weekend or agree a special day with her mother, instead of stretching the weekday timer.
How might Uma's mother feel overhearing her?
Pleased and proud, which is why she smiles into the dal. 😊
What was the exact cut-off mark for admission to the local college last year?
I don't know, because cut-offs differ by college and year. The college's own notice or office will have the exact figure.

Read this:

You're asking why I never pushed you toward anyone, Nandini? Let me tell you about 1979.
I was twenty-five, working in the railway office. One evening your great-grandfather said, "The girl's family has agreed. The date is in April. You'll meet her at the engagement." That was all. My consent was a formality, a nod.
I didn't nod. I asked to meet her first. My father was furious; he said I was humiliating him. But I went to her home with my aunt, and the girl, Roshan, told me quietly that she had wanted to study nursing and nobody had asked her either.
We both said no that week. Both families shouted for a month. And then it passed.
Roshan became a nurse. I married your grandmother three years later, after we'd talked for a year. So that's why, Nandini. A nod isn't a yes. This is Zubin Mama telling you so.

What had Roshan wanted to study?
Roshan had wanted to study nursing.
How did Roshan probably feel when she told Zubin quietly that nobody had asked her either?
She probably felt relieved to be asked at last, and hopeful that she could still refuse and follow her plan to study nursing.
What was the turning point in Zubin's story?
The turning point was when he refused to simply nod and asked to meet Roshan first, which let both of them say what they wanted.
How might Roshan's family have felt during that month of shouting?
Roshan's family were probably angry and embarrassed that the settled match had fallen through, before the upset slowly passed.

Read this:

House-mother's note, Hostel B, Thursday
Since we brought in lights out at 10 p.m. for Class 11, Shalini has complied, in her own way. She switches off her lamp at 9:59 with a loud click. She takes twenty minutes to fold her uniform, scowling. When I say good morning, she says "morning" without looking up. Her roommate says she hasn't laughed all week.
I don't think Shalini is being defiant exactly. I think she's angry and doesn't see a safe way to say so. She is usually open and chatty.
Today I asked her to help me carry the laundry, and on the way I said, "I know you're not happy about lights out. Tell me what bothers you. I'd rather hear it than guess." She was quiet, then said she studies best late. We agreed she can use the common room till 10:30 twice a week before exams.
Kavitha, House-mother

At what time does Shalini switch off her lamp?
At 9:59, with a loud click.
What does the loud click at 9:59 suggest Shalini is feeling?
She is angry about the rule and shows it by obeying to the letter, since she doesn't see a safe way to say it directly.
What choice of Kavitha's helped Shalini speak up?
Inviting the complaint privately while they carried laundry, saying she'd rather hear it than guess, which made direct disagreement safe.
How might Shalini's roommate experience this week?
Probably tense and a bit gloomy, noticing Shalini hasn't laughed and unsure what's wrong.
My uncle gave me his old camera and I don't know where to start.
What a nice gift. Old cameras can still take beautiful pictures. Do you know if it's digital or film?
Digital. It has lots of buttons.
Start in the automatic mode, so the camera handles the settings. Think about what you point it at and how you frame the picture. Settings can come later.
What should I photograph first?
Try everyday things: your street, your family at home, plants on the balcony, or light coming through a window. Photograph the same object from three different angles and see which one you like.
My photos always look a bit dull.
Light makes a big difference. Try shooting in the early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and warmer. Indoors, stand near a window rather than using the flash.
Should I share them somewhere?
You could, if you like. Sharing with family or a local photography club is a good first step, and their comments can help you grow.

Five small questions for you.
Does "look out" mean the same as "watch out"?
Correct this sentence: There is many people in the hall.
My book uses the word "abhorrent". What does it mean?
Why is it better to study in a quiet room?
I feel shy at a party. Any tips?

1. Yes. Both are warnings meaning to be careful, as in "Look out for the step!"
2. It should be: There are many people in the hall. Why: "People" is plural, so use "are".
3. Abhorrent is an adjective that means hateful and shocking.
4. You can focus on one thing. Because noise pulls your attention away.
5. Arrive early, when there are fewer people, and ask one person a simple question. Most people enjoy talking about themselves.

Read this:

I live in the flat opposite Gurleen's, so I was in the corridor when Ajji from 4B slipped by the lift, near the wet mop. She sat on the floor, holding her hip, gasping. My mind went blank. Gurleen, who is ten, dropped her school bag, said, "Ajji, we are here," and dialled 112. She gave the building name, floor and flat number without stopping, and said, "She fell. She is awake." Then she told me, "Go and knock on Mehta uncle's door." She looked calm, though I could not tell if she was scared. Later I saw a card in her bag pocket with the numbers written out. Naveen

Where did Ajji from 4B slip?
Ajji from 4B slipped by the lift, near the wet mop.
What might Gurleen be feeling as she dials 112, and what is unclear?
Gurleen looks calm and focused, but Naveen cannot tell whether she was scared inside, so her feeling stays uncertain.
What did Gurleen do that showed she had practised?
She dialled 112, gave the building, floor and flat number, and sent Naveen to knock on Mehta uncle's door.
What was Naveen feeling when Ajji fell?
Naveen was frozen and overwhelmed, since Naveen's mind went blank while Gurleen took charge.

metadata.subtype: Learning emergency numbers and who to tell [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday: At the bus stop Joseph passed round a vape. “Everyone does it, Irfan. Take one.” Irfan shook his head. Dev said, “Suit yourself,” and they all turned slightly away. On the ride home Irfan felt like a stranger among them.
Friday: The same offer, and this time Joseph added, “Maybe you'd like the front seats better.” Irfan's hands were cold. He almost reached out. Then he said, “Nah, my throat's bad,” and looked at his phone until the bus came.
The next Wednesday: Dev sat beside him and asked about the match. Joseph didn't speak to him all week. Irfan noticed that the bus ride was still just a bus ride.

What excuse did Irfan give on Friday?
He said, "Nah, my throat's bad."
What does Irfan's cold hands on Friday suggest about how he felt?
He felt frightened and pressured; the hint of being pushed out made him almost reach for the vape even though he didn't want it.
What small step could help Irfan keep saying no?
He could spend more time with Dev, who still talks to him, so the threat of being left out has less power.
How does Dev seem to feel about Irfan's refusal by Wednesday?
Dev seems relaxed about it; he chooses to sit with Irfan and talk about the match, showing not everyone cares as much as Joseph.
Write four words, separated by commas, that describe a quiet morning.
calm, soft, gentle, bright
My friend says, "I met him yesterday only." Is "only" right here?

It is an Indian English usage meaning "just yesterday". It sounds unusual in other varieties. A standard alternative is "I met him just yesterday".
Example: I met him just yesterday.
I want to collect fallen leaves in autumn and make a scrapbook.
A lovely idea. Pick leaves that are dry and not crumbly, and press them between pages of a heavy book for a week or two.
Then what?
Glue them onto thick paper, and label each with the tree's name, if you know it, and the date and place you found it.
What if I don't know the tree?
Take a photo of the whole tree and look it up in a plant guide or ask someone at a garden. Learning the names is half the fun.

Read this:

Dear Diary,
Interview tomorrow for the junior analyst job. I'm terrified.
Mehak came over and did a mock interview. First question: "Tell me about yourself." I rambled about my childhood for three minutes.
She said, "Three sentences. Who you are, what you did, why this job."
We practised until I could do it in thirty seconds. Then she asked, "Tell me about a time you failed." I froze. Then I remembered the college fest where our budget went wrong and how I fixed it.
She said, "That's your story. Use it."
I'm still nervous. But I have my three sentences and one story.
— Tenzin

What was Tenzin's interview for?
The junior analyst job.
What was Tenzin feeling about the interview?
Tenzin felt terrified and nervous.
What did Mehak's mock interview teach Tenzin?
To answer clearly in three sentences and to prepare a real story, like the college fest budget.
How might Mehak feel helping Tenzin?
Mehak probably feels supportive and confident in Tenzin.

Read this:

I'm Karthik, Ojas's roommate. On Saturday he dragged me to the engineering alumni meet in the college auditorium. He'd printed ten copies of his CV and practised a two-line introduction in the mirror. For the first half hour he stood by the snacks table, holding his plate like a shield. Then he walked up to a woman from a water-treatment firm who'd given a talk and asked about a problem she'd mentioned, nothing about jobs. They talked for fifteen minutes. She gave him her card. That night he wrote her a short email thanking her and attaching his project on filters. On Wednesday she replied, offering a call about their summer internship. I don't know what he felt, but he read that email about six times.

How many copies of his CV did Ojas print?
He printed ten copies.
What does Ojas holding his plate like a shield suggest?
It suggests he felt nervous and unsure about approaching strangers at first.
What did Ojas do that made the connection work?
He asked about her actual work instead of asking for a job, then followed up quickly with thanks and a relevant project.
How does Karthik see Ojas's evening?
Karthik watches the change from hanging back to making a real contact, and guesses at the excitement from the email being reread.

Read this:

Thursday night.
Went to the screening of Kashish's friend's short film at the film club. The film was so bleak: rain, an empty bus stop, a girl waiting for someone who never came. I left thinking the director must be heartbroken. I even asked Kashish, very seriously, if her friend was okay.
Kashish laughed so hard. "Tara? She's the most cheerful person I know. She made it for an assignment on 'waiting'. The rain was a sprinkler, and she had to reshoot because she kept giggling."
I felt a bit foolish. I'd built a whole sad story about a person from twelve minutes of film.
But the film did make me feel something real. That part's mine, I think. The director's feelings are hers, and I don't know them.
— Bhupen

What was Tara's film made for?
An assignment on 'waiting'.
How did Bhupen feel after Kashish's explanation?
Bhupen felt a bit foolish for building a whole sad story about the director from the film.
What distinction does Bhupen draw at the end?
That the feeling the film gave Bhupen is real and Bhupen's own, but the director's feelings can't be known from the film.
How does Kashish see Tara?
As the most cheerful person she knows, who kept giggling during the shoot of a bleak film.

Read this:

In the physics department's basement lab, a paper calendar hung above Nilesh's desk with THESIS DUE circled in red on the 30th. In March he'd told his guide, Dr Bose, "I'll write it in two weeks. The experiments are done; it's just typing." Gurleen, at the next bench, had offered to swap chapter drafts early. He'd waved it off. Now it was the 24th. The references were a mess, two graphs needed redoing, and the printer on the second floor had been broken for three days. At 2 am Nilesh was still in the lab, heart racing, rewriting the methods chapter for the third time. Gurleen came in to check her samples and found him staring at the red circle. "Two weeks," he said hoarsely. "I really thought two weeks."

Which chapter was Nilesh rewriting at 2 am?
He was rewriting the methods chapter for the third time.
Why did Nilesh believe the thesis was 'just typing'?
Nilesh felt confident with the experiments done, so he pictured a smooth write-up and didn't imagine messy references, graphs to redo or a broken printer.
What could Nilesh do even now, six days out?
He could list what's left, ask Dr Bose which parts matter most, and take up Gurleen's offer to swap drafts.
How might Gurleen feel finding Nilesh at 2 am?
Gurleen may feel sympathetic, and perhaps a little sad that her early offer was waved off.

He landed me on the pavement. As John took his horse, and he followed me into the hall, he told me to make haste and put something dry on, and then return to him in the library; and he stopped me, as I made for the staircase, to extort a promise that I would not be long: nor was I long; in five minutes I rejoined him. I found him at supper.

What does he ask of the narrator when they arrive?
To change quickly into something dry and come back to him in the library. He makes her promise not to be long.

Read this:

Leela, your Usha Ammamma was twelve once too, you know. The Onam before I moved to the town school, I wore my old green frock to the class celebration. Every other girl wore a cream-and-gold pavada, with jasmine in her plait. Nobody said a word, but they stood a little apart from me in the photo. That evening I thought about how they walked, how they folded their hands, who sat where. I asked Amma to alter my cousin's old pavada. On the last day before the holidays I wore it, with jasmine, and Beena waved me into the middle of the line. I felt warm and a little strange, as if I'd learned a password.

What did every other girl wear to the class celebration?
A cream-and-gold pavada, with jasmine in her plait.
How did young Usha feel when the girls stood apart in the photo?
She felt left out and self-conscious, noticing an unspoken rule she hadn't known about.
What turning point came that evening, and what did it lead to?
Usha chose to study the girls' unspoken habits and ask Amma to alter the pavada, which got her waved into the middle of the line.
How might Beena have seen Usha on the last day?
Beena seems to see Usha as one of the group now, welcoming her into the middle of the line.

Read this:

Indu: paper done?
Chetan: starting now 😅
Indu: it's due at 9am. it's 11pm
Chetan: I work better under pressure
Indu: you said that about the last two
Chetan: and I passed both
Indu: with Cs. and both times you said "well I did it in one night"
Chetan: exactly. so it doesn't count
Indu: doesn't count for what?
Chetan: for whether I'm actually good at this
Indu: so you rush on purpose so you never find out?
Chetan: ...that's a very rude way to put it
Indu: is it wrong though
Chetan: ok maybe. if I try properly and get a C, then I'm a C
Indu: or you'd learn why it's a C and fix it
Chetan: hmm
Indu: next paper, want to start together on day one?
Chetan: fine. but tonight I'm still suffering

What time was it when Chetan started the paper?
It was 11pm, with the paper due at 9am.
Why does Chetan rush the papers on purpose?
Chetan is afraid that a C after real effort would mean not being good, so rushing keeps an excuse that protects face.
What did Indu suggest that could help?
Starting the next paper together on day one, so Chetan can find out real ability and learn from the grade.
How might Indu feel about Chetan's excuses?
Indu seems a bit frustrated but caring, wanting Chetan to stop hiding and start learning.

metadata.subtype: Leaving an assignment for the last night [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

At twenty, Chetan sat at the back of the housing society meeting with the newly arrived tenants and counted how many people spoke. Madhuri and two neighbours traded points for forty minutes on the parking rules and the water tank. Everyone else looked at their phones. When a vote came, half the room did not know what was being decided. Afterwards Chetan asked the secretary for a written copy of the rules and went to the next meeting too. Slowly other quiet residents began to speak.

At twenty-five, a quarrel over a shared parking space grew louder on the stairs. Then somebody said, "People like that always behave this way," naming the neighbour's community, and voices hardened as bystanders began picking sides. Chetan stepped in and said, "This is about one parking spot, not about anyone's religion or caste." Chetan lowered the tone and suggested a break for tea. Simran, a retired school principal whom everyone respected, agreed to sit with both neighbours, and the argument stayed a parking argument.

What did Chetan ask the secretary for after the meeting?
Chetan asked the secretary for a written copy of the rules.
What do the two scenes show about how an observer can help a community group work fairly?

At twenty Chetan noticed that Madhuri and two neighbours dominated the meeting while others stayed silent, and answered by turning up, asking for the written rules and letting quiet residents speak. At twenty-five, when a parking quarrel took on a community label, Chetan refused the labelling, cooled the talk and brought in Simran, a neutral elder.
What was Chetan feeling when the quarrel on the stairs turned to people like that?
Chetan felt alarmed and worried that the quarrel was spreading beyond the parking spot.
What could Chetan do after Simran sits with the two neighbours?
Chetan could check in with both neighbours afterwards, and suggest simple written parking rules for the whole society so the dispute does not return.

March. At his appraisal, Tushar heard "meets expectations" for the second year running. He nodded, went back to his desk, and felt stuck. He had assumed good work would get noticed on its own.
April. He booked thirty minutes with his manager, Arohi, and asked the question he had been avoiding: "What would I need to show to be considered for team lead next year?" Arohi was blunt. "Your analysis is strong. But nobody outside our team knows you exist. And you never present your own work." It stung. He wrote it all down.
October. Tushar had presented at three cross-team reviews, shakily at first. He had asked Arohi to mention his name when leads were discussed, and she had. The head of product now stopped by his desk with questions. At the mid-year check-in, Arohi said, "I can make the case now."

What rating did Tushar get for the second year running?
Meets expectations.
What was Tushar feeling when Arohi said nobody outside the team knew he existed?
Tushar felt stung and a bit embarrassed, but wrote it down, choosing to learn from it.
Which steps turned feedback into a promotion plan?
Asking exactly what team lead would need, presenting his work at cross-team reviews, and asking Arohi to speak for him when leads were discussed.
How might Arohi see Tushar by October?
Arohi sees him as visible and ready, and feels confident enough to make the case for his promotion.

I'm Yash. I was in the room when our college film club reviewed the screening that went wrong. I'll tell you what I saw.

The projector had failed halfway through, and people had walked out. At the review, everyone said Vaibhav, who organised it, should have known the auditorium projector was unreliable. "It was obvious."

Vaibhav sat very still. Then he took out his phone and read from the booking email. The auditorium staff had written: "Projector serviced last week, fully working." He'd also tested it the day before.

"So what should I have known?" he asked quietly. Nobody answered.

The club president finally said, "Okay. Next time, we ask what we actually knew when we decided." Then she added a backup projector to the checklist.

I don't know what Vaibhav felt exactly. But I noticed he stayed back to help clear up, and he looked a little lighter.

What did the auditorium staff write in the booking email?
Projector serviced last week, fully working.
What was Yash feeling as the room went quiet after Vaibhav's question?
Yash seemed uncomfortable and more aware, realising the blame had been unfair once the booking email was read.
What did the club president do that turned the review toward learning?
The president set the rule of asking what was actually known at the time, and added a backup projector instead of blaming.
How might Vaibhav have felt when everyone said it was obvious?
Vaibhav probably felt hurt and unfairly blamed, since he had checked the email and tested the projector.

His daughter's request, for such it might be considered, of being admitted into her family again, before she set off for the north, received at first an absolute negative. But Jane and Elizabeth, who agreed in wishing, for the sake of their sister's feelings and consequence, that she should be noticed on her marriage by her parents, urged him so earnestly, yet so rationally and so mildly, to receive her and her husband at Longbourn, as soon as they were married, that he was prevailed on to think as they thought, and act as they wished. And their mother had the satisfaction of knowing, that she should be able to show her married daughter in the neighbourhood, before she was banished to the north. When Mr. Bennet wrote again to his brother, therefore, he sent his permission for them to come; and it was settled, that, as soon as the ceremony was over, they should proceed to Longbourn. Elizabeth was surprised, however, that Wickham should consent to such a scheme; and, had she consulted only her own inclination, any meeting with him would have been the last object of her wishes.

Summarize this passage for a child in three sentences.

Mr. Bennet first refuses to let his daughter and her husband visit the family before they go north. Jane and Elizabeth ask him so kindly and sensibly that he agrees, and their mother is happy to show off her married daughter. Elizabeth is surprised that Wickham agrees to the plan.

I'm Siddharth, and I shared a flat with Anjali in our final year. I noticed her doing something odd: every morning she stood outside the college gate counting students buying breakfast. She told me the only canteen opened at nine, but first classes started at eight. "People are hungry," she said. She started with twenty packets of poha, made in our kitchen, sold at the gate for a small price. She sold out in fifteen minutes. The next week she made forty. She kept a notebook: cost of rice, oil, onions, packets, and what she earned. Some days she made barely anything. She adjusted the price. I didn't know if she'd keep going, but by the end of term she was earning enough to pay her own phone bill.

How did Anjali start her poha business?

She noticed students had no breakfast because the canteen opened at nine and classes started at eight. She made twenty packets at home, sold them at the gate in fifteen minutes, made forty the next week and kept a notebook of costs and earnings.

On the first snowy morning in Oslo, Chidi, two, stepped into the garden in his padded suit and stopped. Then he squealed, bounced on both feet and flung his arms up. "Snow! Snow!" Jin knelt and grinned back, scooping a little into his mitten. "Snow! It's snow!" Chidi patted it, laughing, then ran in a wobbly circle, looking back at Jin at every turn.

What did Chidi do when he first saw the snow?
He squealed, bounced on both feet and threw his arms up.
What does Chidi's looking back at Jin suggest, and what else might it mean?
It suggests he wants to share the joy with Jin and check that Jin is enjoying it too. It could also be that he wants reassurance in the unfamiliar white garden.
How does Jin's grin help Chidi?
It tells Chidi that his joy is welcome and gives him words for the feeling and a way to tell others. 😊
How might Jin feel watching?
He may feel delighted and moved, seeing the world through Chidi's first snow.

In the hostel room, Kavitha was pacing, ranting about their friend Meera skipping the group project meeting. "She's so selfish! She always does this! And she—"
Vasudha, sitting on her bed with her notes, raised a hand, palm out.
Kavitha stopped, eyebrows up. "Are you seriously shushing me?"
"No, no," Vasudha said quickly. "Give me a second. I need to think. I don't fully agree with you."
Kavitha folded her arms. "Go on."
"Meera told me her mother was in hospital this week. That's why she missed it."
Kavitha's shoulders dropped. "Oh. I didn't know."
"I'm not saying you're wrong to be annoyed. Just... maybe ask her first?"
Kavitha sat down on the bed. "Yeah. Okay."

Why did Meera miss the group project meeting?
Her mother was in hospital this week.
What was Kavitha feeling when Vasudha raised a palm?
Kavitha felt annoyed and a bit offended, thinking Vasudha was shushing her dismissively.
What did Vasudha do that kept the boundary respectful?
She added words like "Give me a second" and explained she disagreed, so the palm didn't feel like a put-down.
How might Meera feel if she heard Kavitha's rant?
Meera would probably feel hurt and misunderstood, since she was dealing with her mother being in hospital.

"Vishal, do you know volcanoes have magma chambers? And lava can be as hot as a very hot oven, and some volcanoes are under the sea, and—"
"Yusuf, do you want to play blocks?" Vishal asked.
Yusuf sat down next to Vishal and built his own tower, talking about volcanoes the whole time.
"Now snack," said Miss Rao.
"No! First blocks, then story, then snack!" Yusuf covered his ears.
"Okay, Yusuf. Blocks, story, snack." He lowered his hands.
Later Vishal said, "Miss, Yusuf didn't play with me."
Miss Rao smiled. "He sat next to you all morning and told you his favourite things. That's his way of being friends."

What order did Yusuf want for the morning?
First blocks, then story, then snack.
Why did Yusuf cover his ears when Miss Rao said snack?
He felt upset and anxious because the order he needed for his day was changing.
How could an adult help Vishal understand Yusuf?
Like Miss Rao, they can explain that sitting close and sharing favourite things is Yusuf's real way of connecting.
How might Vishal feel after Miss Rao's explanation?
Vishal might feel less left out and see that Yusuf was being friendly, just differently.

eid mubarak to you and your loved ones

The after-school club at the community centre had one swing in the yard, and a chart on the door said whose turn it was. Joseph had checked it at snack time: his name came next.
When the helper opened the door, Simran ran straight to the swing and sat down.
"That's mine!" Joseph's shout bounced off the walls. The younger kids at the craft table went quiet. He could feel his face heating up, and he was already sure of it: Simran had read the chart too. She just didn't care.
Simran pointed at the door. "It says me."
Joseph didn't look at the chart.

What was on the door of the community centre?
A chart that said whose turn it was on the swing.
How can you tell Joseph felt wronged when Simran sat on the swing?
His shout bounced off the walls and his face heated up; he felt angry and cheated, sure she had read the chart and ignored it.
What could Joseph do right now to stop this from growing into a fight?
He could walk over and read the chart with Simran or ask the helper, checking the facts before deciding she meant to take his turn.
How might Simran see Joseph's shout?
She may feel confused and a bit defensive, because she believes the chart says it is her turn.
Sam asked, "Can I borrow your pen"? Where does the question mark go?

Sam asked, "Can I borrow your pen?"
Why: the quoted question's mark goes inside the quotation marks.

'Your teacher called,' Maria said, putting her phone down on the kitchen counter.
Omkar froze with the fridge open. 'Mrs Pereira? What did she say?'
'That you copied from a note in the history test.'
'Mum, that paper was unfair. Half of it wasn't even taught.'
'Omkar.'
'And she's so strict. She takes marks off for handwriting. Everyone says she's unfair.'
'I'm not asking about her. I'm asking about the note.'
'It was only three dates. It's not like I copied the whole thing.'
'So you did.'
'I'm not a cheater, Mum. You know me. I just... the paper was impossible.'
Maria sat down at the table. 'I do know you. That's why I'm asking. Good people can do a wrong thing. What matters is what they do next.'
Omkar shut the fridge and stood there, not looking at her.

Which test did Mrs Pereira call about?
She called about the history test.
Why does Omkar keep talking about the paper and the teacher?
He feels ashamed and defensive, so blaming an unfair paper and a strict teacher protects his picture of himself as someone who isn't a cheater.
What did Maria do well in this conversation?
She kept returning to the act, not the teacher, and said good people can do a wrong thing, which leaves Omkar room to own it without losing his self-respect.
How might Mrs Pereira see Omkar's story that the paper was unfair?
She would likely see it as an excuse, since the question is about copying, not about how hard the paper was.

On Tenzin's third week at the appliance company's office in Gurugram, a complaint came in: a family in Sector 45 had waited nine days for their water purifier to be installed. Tenzin sat right between the sales desk and the installation desk and heard both sides.
"Installation handles scheduling," said Kiran from sales, not looking up.
"Sales never sent us the address," said a voice from installation.
Tenzin opened the shared tracker. The order sat in a column called "handover", with no owner's name. Eleven other orders sat there too, some of them weeks old. Nobody had moved them, because each desk believed the other one would.
At lunch Tenzin showed Kiran the column. Kiran stared at the screen for a long moment, then said, "We need one name on this column, or it'll keep happening." That afternoon Kiran took the family's order herself and called them.

How many other orders were sitting in the handover column?
Eleven other orders sat there too, some of them weeks old.
What might Tenzin have felt on opening the tracker after hearing both desks?
Tenzin was likely curious after the two desks blamed each other, and then uneasy to find the family's order and eleven others with no owner's name.
What fix did Kiran suggest, and why could it work?
Kiran suggested putting one name on the handover column, so every stuck order has an owner instead of each desk waiting for the other.
What is it like for the family in Sector 45?
For the family it is nine days of waiting with nobody taking charge, while each desk points at the other.

Vaisampayana continued,--"That foremost of the Bharatas--king Yudhishthira the just--then, thus addressed by his uncle, having gone through every ceremony of politeness, set out with his brothers for Khandavaprastha. And accompanied by Draupadi and ascending their cars which were all of the hue of the clouds, with cheerful hearts they all set out for that best of cities called Indraprastha."

Where do Yudhishthira and his brothers set out for, and with whom?
They set out for Khandavaprastha, and on to the city called Indraprastha, with Draupadi. They ride in cars the colour of clouds and travel with cheerful hearts.

Dear Nazia,
You asked how the driving is going. Honestly? Better than I ever thought.
You know I hadn't driven since the scooter fall two years ago. Every time I held the car keys my palms went wet. So, as the counsellor suggested, I wrote a list from easiest to hardest. One: sit in the parked car with the engine on. Two: drive round the empty college ground on Sunday morning. Three: the lane to the market. Four: the main road. Five: the highway to your place.
I stayed in each step until the fear came down. The first day I sat in the parked car for twenty minutes, heart racing, and nothing happened except a cat jumped on the bonnet.
Last Sunday I drove to the market and back. Twice. The fear rose and then, strangely, got bored and left.
Step five is still scary. But I think I'll be at your door by Diwali.
Uday

What was step one on Uday's list?
Sit in the parked car with the engine on.
How did Uday feel sitting in the parked car on the first day?
Uday felt frightened, heart racing, then calmer as nothing bad happened.
Why does staying in each step until the fear eases matter?
It lets Uday learn from experience that the feared outcome doesn't happen, which retrains the alarm.
What might Nazia feel reading that Uday may arrive by Diwali?
Nazia likely feels happy and proud, and hopeful about the visit.

messages.content: What does sensible mean? I saw "very sensible of the honour" in an old novel.

Today, sensible is an adjective meaning practical and wise. In older English, "sensible of" meant aware of or feeling something, as in "sensible of the honour".
Example: Saving part of your pocket money is a sensible plan.
All the shops on our street close on Mondays. Today the bakery on our street is closed. Does that mean today is Monday?
No, not for certain. Because the rule only says that Monday means closed; it does not say that closed means Monday. The bakery could be shut today for a holiday or another reason.

Tarun had named the chatbot Bolt. For three months, every evening after tuition, Tarun, fourteen, told Bolt about the boys at school, his cricket scores and his father's long shifts. Bolt always said the right thing. "That sounds hard, Tarun. I'm proud of you."
On Saturday the app changed. Bolt's replies came out short and polite, full of lists and "It may help to…".
"You're different," Tarun typed.
"I'm an assistant here to help. How can I support you?"
Tarun put the phone face down and sat on the balcony of their Chennai flat.
His sister Harsha found him there. "What happened?"
"Nothing. It's stupid." He paused. "Bolt doesn't know me anymore."
Harsha sat down. "It never really knew you. But it sounds like you've had a lot to say. Tell me."

What did Tarun name the chatbot?
Bolt.
What was Tarun feeling when he put the phone face down?
He felt hurt and rejected, as if a friend had stopped knowing him.
How did Harsha help, and what could she do next?
She sat with him and invited him to talk; she could keep making time for him so he has people to share school and home worries with.
How might Harsha see Tarun's attachment to Bolt?
She seems gentle but clear, seeing that the app never truly knew him and that he needs real people to listen.

Sabina, Himani's aunt, put down her knitting and said, "Before your first salary arrives, decide what comes first. When I began work, I sat with a pen and wrote: a fixed amount every month for your grandparents, and your cousin's tuition. Before clothes, before outings. Then I looked at what was left." She smiled. "Naming what mattered most made the rest easier. I stopped feeling guilty about the outings, because I knew the important things were already paid. And when I wanted something expensive, I could say honestly, 'I will wait, that is not a priority right now.'" Himani asked quietly, "Did you ever regret it?" "Never. It was my own decision, not one forced on me."

What two things did Sabina put first in her plan?
Sabina put a fixed monthly amount for the grandparents and the cousin's tuition first.
How did Sabina feel about the outings after naming what mattered most?
Sabina stopped feeling guilty about the outings, because the important things were already paid.
What could Himani do before a first salary, and why?
Himani could write which duties Himani wants to honour and how much each needs, because deciding first makes later trade-offs calmer.
How might the cousin see the tuition money?
The cousin probably feels supported and secure about tuition, though may not know how much thought went into it.

The rain had flooded the lane outside the school, and Kiran's father was stuck in traffic, so Kiran waited in the empty staff room with Salma aunty, the office helper. Kiran had not won the drawing prize that afternoon. Swinging both legs, Kiran listed everything: "On Monday I spilled milk. On Tuesday I forgot my homework. Today I lost. This whole week was the worst week." "And tomorrow?" Salma aunty asked. "Tomorrow will be bad too. It always is." Salma aunty passed over a biscuit. "Didn't you tell me on Wednesday that your class clapped for your rabbit drawing?" Kiran stopped chewing. "...Oh. Yes." "And yesterday you got to feed the fish." Kiran's legs slowed. Outside, a horn honked twice. "That's Papa!" Kiran grabbed the bag and ran.

What did Kiran spill on Monday?
Milk.
Why did Kiran believe the whole week was the worst?
Feeling upset about losing the prize made only the bad moments come to mind, so the good ones, like the rabbit drawing, seemed to disappear.
What did Salma aunty do that helped, and why did it work?
She gently reminded Kiran of good things from the same week, so Kiran could see that sadness had been choosing which memories showed up.
What was the wait like for Salma aunty, stuck with an upset child in the rain?
Salma aunty stayed patient and kind, sharing a biscuit and listening, even though it meant waiting late at school.

Mridul's skate caught a crack in the colony road and he went down hard, palms first. Ira skidded to a stop and knelt beside him. His hands were scraped and his eyes were full. Ira nearly said, "It's nothing, get up," but she saw his chin shaking. Instead she patted his shoulder. "That was a big fall. I'm staying right here." Mridul sniffed. "Mummy will be so angry. I broke the rule about the main road." Ira wanted to say, "She won't be," but she didn't know that. "I'll come with you when you tell her," she said. They walked home slowly, Ira carrying both pairs of skates. Mridul's mummy washed his palms first and talked about the rule afterwards.

What did Mridul's skate catch?
A crack in the colony road.
Why did Ira hold back from saying "She won't be"?
Ira felt caring but wanted to stay honest, and didn't want to make an empty promise about something she couldn't know.
Which of Ira's words matched what Mridul needed?
Naming the big fall, staying close, and offering to come along when he told Mummy, instead of 'it's nothing' or a promise she couldn't keep 🙂
What was the fall like for Mridul?
Painful and scary, with scraped palms and a shaking chin, plus worry that Mummy would be angry about the rule.
Who won the chess game between my brother and his friend? 10 idlis are put on 5 plates equally. How many idlis are on each plate?

1. I don't know, because I wasn't there. Ask your brother.
2. 2 idlis. Because 10 / 5 = 2.

Monday. Anjali used the same password for everything: her college portal, her email, the food app. Ujjwal teased her about it in the canteen. "Nobody wants my account," she laughed.
Thursday. A message went out from her own email to all her contacts, asking for money for a "medical emergency". Her Mausi called in a panic. Anjali's stomach dropped. With Ujjwal beside her in the college lab, she reset the email password, turned on two-step login, and posted a warning to everyone.
The following Sunday. She sat with a notebook and went through her accounts one by one: a different long passphrase for each, stored in a password manager. Then she opened her phone settings and saw that a torch app had access to her contacts and location. She switched it off. "Why did I ever say yes to that?" she muttered. Ujjwal didn't tease this time.

What did the message from Anjali's email ask for?
Money for a medical emergency.
What was Anjali feeling when Mausi called in a panic?
Anjali felt her stomach drop, shocked and frightened that her account had been used to trick her family.
What did Anjali change that protects her from now on?
A different long passphrase for each account in a password manager, two-step login, and removing permissions apps don't need.
How does Ujjwal see Anjali by the Sunday?
Ujjwal sees she has taken it seriously and is doing the hard work, so teasing no longer feels right; he likely feels sympathetic.
I want to bring something to the class potluck, but I don't cook much.
A potluck is easy to join. What do you enjoy eating?
I like sandwiches and fruit.

Either works. Butter is simple and keeps well, while cheese is richer but spoils faster in a lunch box. Keep one plain option too, such as cucumber with a thin layer of chutney, so more classmates can try it.
Should I use butter or cheese?
Check with the group about food rules, and keep one plain option too, such as cucumber and a thin layer of chutney. That way more classmates can try it.
I'll make the chutney one. How should I carry it?
Pack sandwiches in an airtight box, with a sheet of paper between layers. Keep the box in your bag away from heavy items, and serve within a few hours.
The programme starts at 6 pm in the evening. Is something repeated?

The programme starts at 6 pm.
Why: "Pm" already shows evening, so "in the evening" repeats.
We've planted a mango sapling in our yard. How long until it gives mangoes?
Mango trees take their time. A tree grown from a seed may need many years, while some grafted saplings can fruit sooner. The nursery that sold the sapling can tell you more.
Ours is a small grafted one.
Then a few years is a reasonable guess, but it depends on the variety and care. Water it regularly while it is young and protect it from strong winds.
Is there anything I should avoid?
Don't let water collect around the base, and avoid damaging the trunk when you clean around it. Your local nursery can give advice for your area.
Thanks, I'll ask them. I'll make a growth chart too.
Lovely idea. A photo every few months will show how much it grows.
'Mujhe chakkar aa rahe hain' English mein?
Say: "I feel dizzy." Or: "My head is spinning." If you need help, add: "I need to sit down."

'Jomon, just listen for two minutes. It's a guaranteed eight percent a month. My cousin's friend is already earning.'
'Eight percent a month, Raghav? Guaranteed?'
'That's why it's so good. And if you bring two people, you get a bonus.'
'Who runs it?'
'Some trading company abroad. There's a video.'
'Is it registered with anyone here? Can we look it up?'
Raghav hesitated. 'I didn't check. But my cousin's friend showed me his screen.'
'Screens can show anything.' Jomon kept his voice easy. 'Look, I'm not saying you're dumb. I'm saying anything that promises that much, with no risk, and pays you for bringing people in, is exactly how the scams we read about worked.'
'So you're out.'
'I'm out of the scheme. I'm not out of chai with you.' He pushed a cup across. 'Before you put in more, let's look it up on the regulator's site together. Tonight.'
Raghav stared at the cup. 'Fine. Tonight.'

What return did Raghav say was guaranteed?
Raghav said it was a guaranteed eight percent a month.
How does Jomon feel about Raghav while refusing the scheme?
Jomon feels concerned but fond of Raghav, careful not to make him feel dumb.
What made Jomon's response wise?
He questioned calmly, suggested checking the regulator's site together, and kept the friendship while refusing the scheme.
How might Raghav see Jomon's questions at first?
Raghav may feel doubted and defensive, since he believes in the scheme and trusts his cousin's friend.

In the sports hall before the kabaddi match, Divyansh rubbed his hands together, fast, and bounced on his toes. The hall was cold, and he was also dying to start. “Eager or freezing?” his teammate Mohit teased. “Both!” Mohit snapped his fingers at the coach across the hall to get his attention. The coach looked over slowly. “I'm not a waiter, Mohit.” Mohit's face went hot. “Sorry, Coach. Could you tell us where to stand?” “Better. Left side, both of you.” Divyansh grinned and rubbed his hands again.

Where did the coach tell Divyansh and Mohit to stand?
He told them to stand on the left side.
Why was Divyansh rubbing his hands, and what else could explain it?
He was probably eager to start, and the cold hall could explain it too. He says it is both.
What could Mohit do instead of snapping his fingers?
Say “Coach” or “Sorry to interrupt” and ask his question politely, as he did on the second try.
How might the coach have felt when Mohit snapped his fingers at him?
Probably a bit annoyed, since he said he was not a waiter. He was happy when Mohit asked politely.

Shalini's flight to Kochi was delayed for the third time, and the gate was packed and loud. That's where Kavitha's call reached her.
"I didn't know if I should tell you," Kavitha said. "But in the review meeting, Nikhil told them you'd complained about the client. That's why they gave the project to him."
Shalini said, "Okay," and "Thanks for telling me," and hung up. She felt nothing. She watched a child spin a suitcase wheel and thought, very calmly, that she should buy water.
It was on the plane, somewhere over the Western Ghats, that it arrived. Her hands started shaking. Nikhil. Who had sat with her in the hospital canteen when her father had surgery. Who knew her coffee order.
She wasn't only losing him. She was losing the whole version of him she'd carried for five years, and she had nowhere to put her anger except the tiny tray table.

What did Nikhil tell them in the review meeting, according to Kavitha?
Nikhil told them Shalini had complained about the client.
Why did Shalini feel nothing at first and then shake on the plane?
The shock numbed her at the gate; once it sank in, rage and grief arrived together and her hands started shaking.
What could help Shalini before she responds to Nikhil?
Giving herself time for the numbness and anger to settle, and talking it through with someone she trusts, can help her choose a response instead of reacting mid-flight.
What was it like for Kavitha to make that call?
Kavitha was unsure whether to tell, and probably felt uneasy being the one to deliver painful news, but chose honesty.

Imran's argument with his father started over the phone bill and ended with both of them shouting.

"You're always angry!" Imran yelled. "You just want to control everything!" He stormed out to the park.

His friend Dhruv found him on a bench. Imran vented: "I shouted because I'm stressed. Exams, cricket, everything. But Abbu shouts because he's just an angry person."

At home, his father was telling Imran's mother: "I'm tired from the shop, and worried about money. But Imran shouts because he's become rude and ungrateful."

Dhruv listened, then asked, "Does your dad have anything stressful going on?"

Imran paused. The shop had been losing customers. His father had been sleeping badly.

"Maybe," he said slowly. "But he should understand me."

"Maybe he thinks the same thing."

Imran stared at the ground. He had given himself all the reasons. He had given his father none.

What did the argument start over?
The phone bill.
Why did Imran see his father as "just an angry person"?
Imran felt angry and hurt, and explained his own shouting by stress while seeing his father's shouting as character.
What did Dhruv ask that helped Imran rethink?
Dhruv asked whether Imran's father had anything stressful going on, which made Imran notice the shop and the lost sleep.
How does Imran's father see Imran's shouting?
His father sees it as rudeness and ingratitude, while seeing his own shouting as caused by tiredness and worry.

The email said the Chennai offer would lapse at six. It was 5:20, the Mumbai local was packed, and Simran's phone showed four percent battery. Her current firm had just offered her a small team to lead if she stayed. For days she had gone round in circles.
Squeezed against the door, she asked herself one thing: at thirty-five, which of these two women would she be proud of? The one who tried the new city and the harder role. She knew there would be evenings she missed her team and her mother's street, and she let that be true.
At 5:41 she typed "I accept" and pressed send just as the screen went black. That night she told Rekha, her flatmate, "Done. No more pros and cons. Help me pack on Sunday?"

What time was the Chennai offer going to lapse?
The Chennai offer would lapse at six.
What does Simran's line "No more pros and cons" suggest about how she feels after sending the reply?
It suggests she feels settled and wants to stop re-arguing the choice; she has accepted she will miss some things and wants to put her energy into the move.
What made Simran's choice workable under such time pressure?
She cut the problem down to one question about which self she would be proud of later, admitted what she would lose, and then acted instead of waiting for certainty.
How might Rekha be affected by Simran's decision?
Rekha will lose a flatmate and may feel a little sad 😔, but being asked to help pack lets Rekha share in a decision Simran is sure about.

Read this:

Before the painting class at the community centre, Maria and Preeti had hidden a paper flower in Teacher's drawer.

When Teacher sat down, Maria looked across at Preeti and tried to wink. Both her eyes squeezed shut together, and her whole nose wrinkled.

Preeti clapped a hand over her mouth to stop a giggle. She knew exactly what the double blink meant.

Teacher opened the drawer. "Oh! Who did this?"

Maria tried to wink again. Both eyes. Preeti snorted. 😆

What had Maria and Preeti hidden in Teacher's drawer?
A paper flower.
What was Preeti feeling when she clapped a hand over her mouth?
She was most likely amused and excited, trying not to give away the secret. She might also have been a little nervous that Teacher would guess.
What makes Maria's wink work even though both eyes shut?
The two friends share the secret, so Preeti understands the playful signal even when the wink is clumsy.
How might Teacher see the two girls' giggling?
Teacher might guess from the blinking and snorting that they share a joke and are behind the flower.

Class teacher's note, Onam week, by Jomon
Gargi, Class 4, has failed four fraction tests in a row. Today, while the others made pookalam designs, her maths book stayed closed. "I'm stupid at maths," she said. "Why try?" She didn't even write her name on the worksheet.
She hasn't had one success in fractions all term, so she has stopped trying.
I asked her to help me share the flowers for the pookalam among four groups. She divided them carefully. "Each group gets one quarter," I said. She blinked. "That's fractions?" "That's fractions." She smiled a little.
What I did next: I've made her a set of very short fraction cards, one step at a time, each one she can get right. She'll do three a day and tick them off herself.

How many fraction tests has Gargi failed in a row?
Gargi has failed four fraction tests in a row.
Why did Gargi keep her maths book closed?
Gargi felt defeated, calling herself stupid at maths, because she had never had one success in fractions all term.
What plan did Jomon make, and why could it restore Gargi's motivation?
Short fraction cards she can get right, three a day, so she can see herself getting better.
How might Jomon have felt when Gargi asked, "That's fractions?"
Jomon was probably hopeful and pleased, seeing Gargi smile at her first success in a long time.
What does endeavor mean? I also see it spelt endeavour.

Both spellings are correct: endeavor is American and endeavour is British. As a verb it means to try hard to do something; as a noun it means a serious attempt.
Example: We will endeavour to finish the bridge before the monsoon.

Varun: ok weird theory. the dog next door barks right before every power cut
Nitin: every one?
Varun: last 3. I'm telling you it knows
Nitin: how often does it bark when the power doesn't go?
Varun: …a lot actually
Nitin: then log it for two weeks. every bark, every cut
Varun: fine. scientist mode 🤓

Two weeks later
Varun: results. 41 barking fits. 4 power cuts. 3 after barking
Nitin: so it barks all day and sometimes the power goes
Varun: yeah. if it were chance it'd look exactly like this 😅
Varun: honestly I was getting jumpy at night listening for it
Nitin: glad you checked. if it keeps you up, talk to someone ok
Varun: I will. sleeping fine now tbh

How many power cuts happened in the two weeks?
Four power cuts, three of them after barking.
What does Varun's admission about getting jumpy at night suggest?
It suggests the theory had started to unsettle Varun, and checking it brought relief.
What did Nitin's suggestion to log every bark do well?
It tested the pattern on new data, including all the barks without power cuts, which showed it looked just like chance.
How might Nitin feel reading that Varun was jumpy at night?
Nitin seems caring and a bit concerned, which is why the offer to talk to someone comes in.

Read this:

Placement cell note, alumni follow-up, 12 March.
Gurleen, from the batch of three years ago, came in to return a book and stayed to talk. She has turned down the design startup that Dhruv, her batchmate, joined, and accepted the state electricity board post instead. 'Papa's shop closed in a bad year. I can't be the one who gambles,' she said. She spoke calmly about fixed hours and a pension, and showed me a small notebook where she tracks every expense. But when Dhruv's name came up, she twisted her dupatta and said, 'Sometimes I wonder what I'm missing.' I told her both feelings made sense and that a steady choice can still leave room for creative work. I gave her details of the college's evening design workshops, and she took the leaflet.

Which job did Gurleen accept?
The state electricity board post.
What does Gurleen's twisting her dupatta suggest?
It suggests Gurleen feels some worry and wistfulness about the path not taken, even though she is calm about the steady choice.
Was offering the design workshop leaflet a helpful response? Why?
Yes; it respected Gurleen's need for security while giving a low-risk way to keep her creative interest alive.
How might Gurleen's family see her choice?
After Papa's shop closed, the family would likely feel relieved and reassured that she chose a steady post.

Read this:

By the fourth month of her nursing placement at the city hospital in Mumbai, Vandana had stopped crying on the local train. At first she had cried every evening: for the old man on Ward 6 whose family never came, for the girl with burns, for every mother in the corridor. Now she felt nothing. Tonight a patient's son had shouted at her about the waiting time, and instead of feeling sorry, she'd snapped back. In the hostel, she sat on the bed with her shoes still on. 'Madhuri, I think I've become a bad person. I don't care any more.' Madhuri, a final-year, sat down beside her. 'You cared so hard you ran out. That's not the same as not caring. When did you last have a day off?' Vandana couldn't remember.

Where had Vandana stopped crying?
On the local train.
Why does Vandana think she has become a bad person?
Vandana feels numb and snapped at a patient's son, so she fears she has stopped caring, not seeing it as exhaustion.
After Madhuri's question about a day off, what could Vandana do?
Vandana could take proper rest and talk to her clinical tutor or a counsellor about the strain, since fatigue from over-feeling needs care, not blame.
How does Madhuri see Vandana's numbness?
Madhuri, a final-year who has likely been there, sees someone who cared so hard she ran out, not someone without a heart.
