Read this:

Sunday, 30 June
Kiran's month-end accounts, done at last on the hostel bed. Hansa made me do it properly, with a table.
Tutoring, Class 7 science, Mon/Wed/Fri: 12 hours, ₹3,000.
Captions for a local news channel's clips: 9 hours, ₹1,800.
Data entry from home: 18 hours, ₹1,440.
I kept dividing because I didn't believe it. ₹250 an hour, ₹200 an hour, ₹80 an hour. The data entry is what eats most of my nights, eyes burning, earphones in so I don't fall asleep.
Hansa just said, 'So?'
So. I emailed the agency tonight to say July is my last month. Weird feeling. It was the first job I ever got, and I was proud of it. But I'd rather spend those eighteen hours on two more tuition kids, or on sleep.

How many hours did Kiran spend on data entry?
18 hours.
What mixed feelings does Kiran have about dropping data entry?
Kiran feels strange and a little sad letting go of a first job that brought pride, but relieved to free those hours.
What else could Kiran check before the next month's table?
Kiran could add travel and preparation time for tutoring, to be sure the ₹250 figure really holds.
How might Hansa see Kiran's decision?
Hansa probably sees it as the obvious result of the table, which is why the only reply is 'So?'

metadata.subtype: Approach: measuring results and dropping weak options [Revision]

messages.content: Is "recomend" spelled right?

No. It should be "recommend", with one c and a double m: re-com-mend.
Example: Could you recommend a good book for my little sister?

Read this:

Between the physics and chemistry classes at the coaching centre there was a seven-minute gap. Nazia's hand was on her phone before the teacher had finished saying "break". She didn't open anything in particular: a cat video, a meme, somebody's new haircut, next, next. When Bidisha asked what she'd been watching, Nazia honestly couldn't say. It happened again in the lunch queue, waiting for the lift, and during the few seconds while the projector warmed up. On Friday the teacher collected every phone in a basket before a test. In the first empty minute Nazia's hand went to her pocket, found nothing, and she laughed out loud. "My hand went looking on its own," she whispered to Bidisha.

How long was the gap between the physics and chemistry classes?
Seven minutes.
Why did Nazia laugh when her hand found an empty pocket?
She was surprised to see her habit so clearly; she had not decided to reach for the phone, and catching her hand doing it alone felt funny and a little unsettling.
What could Nazia try the next time a pause comes?
Treat the empty moment as the cue and keep a different small action ready, like stretching or talking to Bidisha, with the phone zipped in her bag between classes.
How does Bidisha experience Nazia's scrolling?
Bidisha asks what Nazia watched and gets no answer, so Bidisha sees a friend who is busy but not really present in the gaps they share.

metadata.subtype: Reaching for the phone when bored [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Vasudha worked at the district cooperative office in Bhiwani. Office hours were ten to five. Nobody had ever said anything else.
But her manager, Divyansh sir, posted in the team group at 10:40 p.m.: "Can someone check the loan list?" Someone replied in four minutes. The next night, at 11:15, another message. Someone replied in two.
Vasudha started keeping her phone on the pillow. On Sunday, at her cousin's engagement, she answered three messages under the table. Nobody had asked her to. It was just that everyone else did.
By the third month, she no longer painted on weekends, which she used to love. She checked the group before brushing her teeth. When her mother asked what she wanted for her birthday, she said, "Sleep."
One night, at 11:30, she started typing a reply and stopped. She looked at the message. It said, "No rush, tomorrow is fine." She had never noticed that line before.

What are the office hours?
Office hours were ten to five.
How did Vasudha feel by the third month?
Vasudha felt drained and uninterested, giving up painting and wanting only sleep for her birthday.
What could Vasudha try, and who might help change the team's habits?
Vasudha could mute the group after hours and reply in the morning, and ask Divyansh sir to say clearly that late replies are not expected.
How might Divyansh sir see his late messages?
He may think they are harmless reminders, even writing "no rush," without noticing the unspoken pressure they create.

Read this:

Monday: Four friends argued about the route for the hostel trip, and Uday sat at the end of the bench peeling the label off a bottle. Deepak noticed, and said nothing yet.
Wednesday: While the others argued, Deepak leaned over. "Uday, what do you think? No pressure, pass is fine too." Uday hesitated. "The night bus loses a whole day. The lake stop is better on the way back." The others paused. "Huh, that's actually smart," said Meghna.
Saturday: Uday sent a short plan to the group chat. Deepak was first to reply: "Booked it the way Uday said." Meghna sent three thumbs up, and Uday sent back a photo of the lake.

What was Uday doing at the end of the bench on Monday?
Peeling the label off a bottle.
What might Uday have been feeling while sitting at the end of the bench?
Left out or unsure about speaking. Uday stayed quiet and fiddled with the label while the others argued.
What made Deepak's question easy for Uday to answer?
Deepak asked what Uday thought and added "No pressure, pass is fine too," so Uday could say yes or no without being cornered.
What is it like for the others when Uday speaks up?
They are surprised and interested. They pause, and Meghna says it is actually smart, so the plan improves.

Read this:

In the Berlin school yard, two older boys kept knocking Abebe's football away and shoving him whenever he chased it. Abebe was new and didn't speak much German yet.
Felix watched from the bench. His stomach twisted. He felt sorry for him, but what could he do?
Then he remembered that small things count. He walked over and sat on the wall next to Abebe. "Do you want to play with us instead?" he asked, pointing to his friends.
Abebe nodded. The older boys went off to find someone else.
After the break, Felix told Frau Weber what he'd seen. She thanked him and said she'd watch the yard herself tomorrow.

What were the older boys doing to Abebe?
Knocking his football away and shoving him.
How did Felix feel watching from the bench?
He felt sorry for Abebe and unsure, with his stomach twisting as he wondered what he could do.
What small actions did Felix take?
He sat with Abebe, invited him to play with his friends, and told Frau Weber after the break.
How might Abebe see Felix's invitation?
Abebe, being new, may feel welcomed and safer with Felix's group.

Read this:

Monday: Santosh's boss says in the team meeting, "Honestly, Santosh, a trainee could have done this better." Santosh says nothing. At home he snaps at Tenzin for leaving the lights on, then again about dinner.
Tuesday morning: Santosh notices Tenzin moving around him carefully. He sits on the balcony and asks himself, "Who am I actually angry with?" The answer is obvious. He apologises to Tenzin, then goes for a long walk before work and writes down what the boss said and what felt unfair.
Thursday: Santosh asks his boss for fifteen minutes. Calmly, using his notes, he says the comment in front of the team felt unfair, and asks for specific feedback. The boss pauses, then agrees.

What did the boss say in the meeting?
"Honestly, Santosh, a trainee could have done this better."
What was Santosh feeling on Monday evening?
Stung and angry about the boss's remark, but the sharpness came out at home, at Tenzin.
What steps helped Santosh aim the anger fairly?
Noticing Tenzin moving carefully, asking who he was really angry with, apologising, walking and writing, then calmly raising it with his boss.
How might Tenzin have experienced Monday evening?
Tenzin was probably hurt and wary, moving carefully around Santosh without knowing what was wrong.

Read this:

"Where did the stipend go, Nikhil?" Lavanya asked, holding up his empty wallet at the dining table.
"Relax, didi. The hostel fee is paid."
"And the rest? Mummy sent you train fare because you said you were broke."
Their mother, Sarika, stopped rolling rotis. "Broke on the fifteenth again?"
"I needed the shoes. And the trip was a one-time thing."
"Last month it was the one-time concert," Lavanya said.
"I know, I know." Nikhil rubbed his face. "Next month I'm putting half into savings the day it comes. Promise."
"You said that in March."
"This time I mean it. I really want the laptop by December."
Sarika slid a roti onto his plate. "Meaning it isn't the hard part, beta."

What did Mummy send Nikhil?
Mummy sent him train fare because he said he was broke.
Why does Nikhil believe his promise this time?
Nikhil feels embarrassed at being caught and truly eager for the laptop by December, so in that moment meaning it feels like enough.
What would you advise Nikhil to do on the day the stipend arrives?
Move the laptop money out straight away, before shoes or trips come up, so the plan does not depend on how he feels that week.
What is it like for Sarika to hear the same promise again?
Sarika seems tired but kind; she serves him a roti and gently points out that meaning well is not what has been failing.

Read this:

“Pradeep, who am I supposed to copy on the vendor mail?” Urmila whispered at the coffee machine. “Nobody told me.”
Pradeep glanced at the corridor. “Nobody tells anyone. Copy the team lead on anything that goes outside. It's not written anywhere.”
“And in the Monday meeting? Sunita spoke over me last week.”
“Sunita speaks over everyone. Wait until the lead finishes, then say it plainly. If it matters, send it in writing after.”
Sunita walked in and both went quiet. She smiled, took her tea and asked, “New-joiner questions?” Urmila's ears went hot. “Something like that.”
“Ask me anytime,” Sunita said, and left.
Urmila let out a breath. “See?” Pradeep said. “Half the rules are people being nervous.”

Whom did Pradeep say to copy on anything that goes outside?
Pradeep said to copy the team lead on anything that goes outside.
Why did Urmila's ears go hot when Sunita walked in?
Urmila seems embarrassed at being overheard asking about Sunita's habit of speaking over others, and worried about a misstep.
What could Urmila try in the Monday meeting?
Urmila could wait until the lead finishes, say her point plainly, and send it in writing afterwards if it matters.
How might Sunita have felt when she asked, “New-joiner questions?”
Sunita seems friendly and at ease, offering help, and may not know how her interrupting comes across.

Read this:

Playschool note, Tuesday
At circle time, Jatin, 5, told us he saw a green monster behind the slide at the park, "with three eyes and a long tail". He wasn't joking; he looked worried.
Later I read our storybook. Its monster has three eyes and a long tail. Jatin pointed. "That's the one I saw!"
He remembers the monster clearly but has mixed up the book with the park.
I told him, "That monster lives in the book. Let's check the park together." We peeped behind the slide and found a green watering can. He laughed.
Amandeep

What was really behind the slide?
A green watering can was behind the slide.
Why did Jatin look worried at circle time?
He truly believed he had seen the monster at the park, because he remembered it clearly but had lost track that it came from the storybook.
What did Amandeep do to help Jatin, and why is it gentle?
Amandeep said the monster lives in the book and checked behind the slide with Jatin, so he could see for himself without being called a liar.
How might the other children at circle time feel hearing about the monster?
Some might feel scared of the park, so checking it together could help them feel safe too.

Read this:

On the first Sunday of every month, Tenzin's small Mumbai flat filled with people far from home: Jasleen from Ludhiana, a colleague from Guwahati, two students from Kochi. Each brought something: Jasleen's parathas, Tenzin's momos, a pot of fish curry. Nobody was related, and nobody had to explain a pause before a word in a mother tongue. Jasleen taught a Punjabi phrase for eat more and everyone tried it. Last month, when Tenzin's grandmother was unwell in Gangtok and Tenzin sat silent, Jasleen simply refilled the tea and stayed until midnight. Nothing was said about it. The next month a small brass bell appeared on the shelf, brought by whoever felt like it.

How often does the group meet?
The group meets on the first Sunday of every month.
What was Tenzin feeling while sitting silent, and how did Jasleen's action help?
Worried and alone; Jasleen's staying and refilling the tea eased the loneliness.
What makes this circle work?
Shared time and small kindnesses, like a potluck and phrases from each language.
Why might Jasleen have said nothing about staying until midnight?
Because the kindness needed no words; staying was enough to show care.
Why do fresh green leaves turn limp when left on a hot kitchen counter?
Warm air dries the leaves out, and they lose their crispness. Because plant cells are firm only when full of water, leaves that lose water go limp.

Read this:

Let me tell you, Hemant, about my first year in the city. Elder here, Raghav. I sent messages to a friend and saw the two blue ticks and no answer for days. I lay awake thinking, what did I do? When a video meeting started and the friend's camera stayed off, I assumed the coldness had grown. In my time we simply knocked at the door and asked. So I called. It turned out the friend's mother was unwell and that friend was answering nothing to anybody. Nothing personal. I am glad I asked and did not stew in silence. Now I tell young people, do not build a wall from a blue tick. A kind question costs one minute.

What did Raghav see after sending messages to a friend?
Raghav saw two blue ticks and no answer for days.
What was Raghav feeling when the friend's camera stayed off, and what was the truth?
Raghav feared coldness had grown and worried about having done something wrong, but the friend's mother was unwell and the silence was not personal.
What did Raghav do that helped?
Raghav called and asked directly instead of waiting in silence.
How might the friend have felt about the unanswered messages?
The friend was dealing with an ill mother and probably had no energy to reply, so may have felt overwhelmed and not thought about the ticks.

Read this:

"Yash, can you come and solve this one?"
In the Class 5 room of a Kota school, Yash's pencil rolled off his desk. He bent for it and took a long time coming up. "Ma'am, can I go to the washroom?"
Rashmi Ma'am had seen this three times this month. At lunch she sat beside him in the empty classroom. "Is it about the Independence Day assembly? When your voice cracked in the song?"
Yash looked blank. "Was I singing?" He wasn't joking; he really couldn't place it. Then he rubbed his palms on his shorts, again and again.
"Okay," she said. "Next time, I'll ask you to tell me the answer from your seat first."

What did Yash ask when he was called to the board?
"Ma'am, can I go to the washroom?"
What do Yash's palms rubbing on his shorts suggest?
Even though Yash can't recall the assembly, his body still seems to hold the embarrassment, so the mention makes him nervous.
What change did Rashmi Ma'am choose, and why might it help?
Letting Yash answer from his seat first lowers the spotlight, so he can rebuild confidence before facing the class at the board.
How might Yash's classmates read his trips to the washroom?
They may think he's dodging work, without knowing that being called up seems to set off an old embarrassment he can't even remember.
A friend is going on a weekend retreat in the hills. I only know retreat as running away.

As a noun, a retreat can be a quiet place to rest away from normal life, or a short stay in such a place. The other meaning is moving back from danger or a fight.
Example: After a busy term, she spent a calm weekend at a mountain retreat.

Read this:

Tanvir's diary, Wednesday night
Third day at the logistics firm. At four, Naveen, my senior, slid a delivery form across the desk and said, "Just put last Friday's date. The client needs it to show on time." My heart was pounding. Everyone was watching, or it felt like it. I said, "I can't put a date that isn't true. But I can write today's date and add a note saying the shipment was delayed by the port strike, with the port notice attached." Naveen stared at me for a second. Then he sighed and said, "Fine, try it. If the client shouts, you handle it." The client didn't shout. They just said thanks for the explanation.
I'm writing this down so I remember how it felt. Scary, but only for about a minute. If I'd said yes today, I think saying no next month would have been much harder.

What did Naveen ask Tanvir to put on the form?
Naveen asked Tanvir to put last Friday's date.
What was Tanvir feeling when Naveen slid the form across?
Tanvir felt nervous, with a pounding heart and the sense that everyone was watching, but was determined to stay honest.
Which of Tanvir's choices made refusing work?
Tanvir said the reason simply and offered a true alternative, today's date with a delay note and the port notice, so the client still got what they needed.
How might Naveen see the new hire after the client's reply?
Naveen may feel surprised and perhaps a little respectful, seeing the honest way worked without trouble.

Read this:

Arnab came up from the village pond with two fish on a string. Raghav toddled ahead of him into the house, straight to Maa, and stretched his arms wide, wide, wide.
"A big fish?" Maa asked.
Raghav nodded, then pinched his fingers close together and pointed at Arnab.
"And a small one too!" Arnab laughed, holding up the tiny one. Raghav bounced, arms wide again, looking from Maa to his brother.

How many fish did Arnab bring up from the pond?
Two fish on a string.
What was Raghav feeling as he stretched his arms wide for Maa?
He was excited and proud to share the news of the big fish, bouncing and looking from Maa to his brother.
How did Maa and Arnab help Raghav's language here?
They put words to his gestures, "a big fish" and "a small one too", matching his wide arms and pinched fingers.
How might Arnab feel seeing Raghav tell the story?
Arnab likely feels amused and proud that his little brother is so excited about his catch.

Read this:

After the harvest money came in, Pradeep and Pooja walked together to the post office savings counter in their kasba, the first time in eleven years of marriage they had gone there together.

At home that evening Pooja drew two columns in the back of a school notebook. "Everything that comes in, everything that goes out. Both of us write. Both of us can read it any time."

"For how long?" Pradeep asked.

"Until you don't need to read it every day. Then maybe once a month."

Then the harder part. Her brother would need help again; everyone knew it. They agreed that from now on any help to either family, his or hers, would be decided together at this table, never alone.

"Even for your sister?" Pooja asked, half teasing.

Pradeep smiled for the first time that week. "Even for my sister."

He picked up the pen and wrote the first line himself.

What did Pooja draw in the back of the school notebook?
Two columns, one for everything that comes in and one for everything that goes out.
Why does Pradeep smile for the first time that week?
Pooja's teasing about his sister shows the rule is mutual, not a punishment only for her, and he feels relieved and a little lighter.
What makes this arrangement likely to help rather than feel like a punishment?
Both write in the notebook and both can read it, the family-help rule applies to both families, and they agree the daily checking will ease over time.
How might this routine feel for Pooja?
It gives her a way to prove she has changed, and she is likely hopeful and relieved that it is shared and temporary rather than one-sided watching.
One word I always mix up in essays is responsibility. Please give its meaning.

Responsibility is a duty to take care of something or someone, or to be the one who must act. It is a noun.
Example: Feeding the class fish is Anika's responsibility this week.

Read this:

Monday: Tarun, nine, said Nanaji's story about the moon was wrong; his science book said otherwise. Mama snapped, "Respect your elders." Tarun went quiet, confused.
Thursday: He asked why he couldn't play at the park. "Don't argue. Respect your elders," said Mama again. Tarun muttered, "What does that even mean?" and got sent to his room.
Sunday: Indu masi, visiting, found him sulking. "Respect isn't being scared," she said. "It's being polite and caring. You can say, 'Nanaji, my book says something different, can I show you?' Gently." Tarun tried it at dinner. Nanaji put on his glasses, read the page and laughed. "Your book is cleverer than me." Tarun grinned.

What did Nanaji say after reading the page?
"Your book is cleverer than me."
How did Tarun feel when he was told "Respect your elders" again on Thursday?
He felt confused and frustrated, not understanding what it meant, and muttered back.
How did Indu masi help Tarun?
She explained that respect means politeness and care, not fear, and gave him gentle words to disagree with, so he kept his manners and his voice.
How might Nanaji have felt when Tarun asked politely?
He probably felt amused and pleased, happy to be shown something rather than argued with.

Read this:

Indu: Tushar, you free? Need you to be mean about something 😅
Tushar: always
Indu: I want to move our evening tutoring fully online. I'm like 80% sure. What would make me wrong?
Tushar: honestly? half the kids share one phone with the whole family
Tushar: and the volunteers love seeing the kids in person
Indu: ok the phone thing, I hadn't counted that
Indu: what would change my mind: if attendance drops in a two-week trial
Tushar: also read the district team's report, it says the opposite of you
Indu: already opened it. their best point is the phone thing again 🤔
Indu: fine. hybrid trial, two weeks, one centre. you check the numbers with me?
Tushar: deal. you're weirdly good at being argued with
Indu: learned it the hard way 🙏

What did Tushar say about the phones?
Half the kids share one phone with the whole family.
How can you tell Indu feels open rather than defensive about Tushar's points?
Indu admits not having counted the phone problem and calmly sets a test, so Indu seems curious and secure rather than hurt.
What small step does Indu take before committing, and why does it help?
A two-week hybrid trial at one centre with a clear sign of failure, so real attendance decides instead of confidence.
How does Tushar see Indu's way of handling criticism?
Tushar respects it, saying Indu is weirdly good at being argued with.
Is it right: 'I am very much excited for trip'?
Better: "I'm really excited about the trip." Use "really" or "very" with "excited", not "very much". Say "excited about", and add "the" before "trip".

Read this:

Dear Akash,
You asked how the weekend at the ashram near Rishikesh was. Mixed, honestly.
The talks were beautiful. Swami-ji speaks about kindness in a way that made me cry once. But something bothered me. When a woman asked a simple question about where the donations go, three devotees told her to 'surrender her doubts'. Swami-ji just smiled and changed the topic. Everyone kept saying he was beyond mistakes. People touched the chair he had sat on.
I thought about our old music teacher, who used to say, 'If a student can't question me, I'm not teaching, I'm performing.' A real teacher, I think, welcomes questions, answers to someone, and doesn't need your wallet or your obedience.
I'm not saying Swami-ji is a fraud. I'm saying I'll go back only if questions are welcome.
Come with me next time and tell me what you see?
Rafiq

What question did the woman ask?
The woman asked where the donations go.
What did Rafiq feel during the weekend?
Rafiq felt moved by the talks but uneasy about how questions were silenced.
What test does Rafiq decide to use before going back?
Whether questions are welcome, the teacher answers to someone, and no money or blind obedience is demanded.
How do the devotees seem to see Swami-ji?
They see him as beyond mistakes, even touching the chair he sat on.

Read this:

The phone line kept breaking, and Ammi was calling from the hospital night shift. Rehana, five, clutched Sangeeta Aunty's phone.

"Ammi, today we... we..." The line crackled. Rehana wanted to say everything at once.

Sangeeta Aunty whispered, "Start with the morning."

Rehana took a breath. "First I brushed teeth. Then Sangeeta Aunty took me to school. Then we planted beans. Then... I came here and ate khichdi."

"Beans!" Ammi said through the static. "Tell me the beans part again."

What did Rehana plant at school?
Rehana planted beans.
What was Rehana feeling at the start of the call?
Rehana felt rushed and flustered, wanting to say everything at once while the line kept breaking.
How did Sangeeta Aunty help Rehana tell about the day?
She gave a small prompt to start with the morning, which helped Rehana put the day in order.
What is it like for Ammi hearing Rehana's story on a bad line?
She is far away on a night shift, so hearing about Rehana's day, especially the beans, likely makes her feel close to Rehana.

Read this:

Note for Neelam's baby book — Tanuja, nanny

Annaprashan day, at last, at thirteen months. Neelam wore a tiny red-and-gold dress and a crown that slid over one eye. About forty pairs of hands held her before lunch.

When her Mama fed her the first grain of payesh, everyone cheered. She jumped, then laughed because they laughed.

She ignored the tray of objects and grabbed the marigold. By evening she was asleep on my shoulder, still holding it.

What did Neelam grab from the tray?
She grabbed the marigold.
How did Neelam feel when everyone cheered?
Neelam was startled and then happy, laughing because everyone else was laughing.
What could the family do to keep the day gentle for Neelam?
Let her rest between all the hands and follow her lead, as the nanny did by letting her sleep on a shoulder.
How might Mama feel feeding Neelam her first grain?
Mama likely feels proud and joyful to welcome her in this special way.

Read this:

In the kasba of Sehore, everyone knew Jyoti never said no. When her neighbour Sunaina came with cloth for 'my cousin's wedding, just two blouses, you're so quick', Jyoti stitched them at night after her own orders. Then two more, for another wedding. Then four. On Tuesday, at the weekly haat, Jyoti saw her own stitching, her neat double hem, on blouses hanging from Sunaina's stall with price tags. Her face went hot, then cold. She walked home slowly past the temple, thinking. She liked being the one who helped. She did not like being the one who was used. That evening Sunaina came with more cloth. Jyoti kept her hands on the sewing machine. 'I can't stitch these free any more. If you like, I'll teach you the hem on Sunday.' Sunaina's smile slipped. 'Oh. Okay.'

Where did Jyoti see her own stitching?
On blouses hanging from Sunaina's stall at the weekly haat, with price tags.
What was Jyoti feeling when she saw the blouses at the stall?
She felt shocked and used, her face going hot and then cold.
Was offering to teach the hem a good limit? Why?
Yes; it stops free work that was being sold, while still offering a fair, kind kind of help.
How might Sunaina have felt when her smile slipped?
Sunaina was probably caught off guard and a little embarrassed, realising Jyoti had noticed.

Read this:

Gopika, you ask why your Ammamma Manjula makes payasam at Onam and also a plum cake at Christmas? Sit. When I was ten, in Kottayam, my own Ammamma told me about Mahabali every Onam while I arranged the flowers. I kept asking, 'But why did Vamana push a good king down?' She never scolded. She said, 'Good question. Keep asking.' That December my friend Mary's mother let me help stir the cake and told me about a baby born in a stable. I asked why a king would be born among cows. She laughed. 'Good question.' I went home with two stories that year, both full of whys. I still keep both.

What did Mary's mother let young Manjula help with?
Stir the cake.
What was young Manjula feeling when she kept asking about Mahabali?
She felt curious and a little troubled, wondering why a good king would be pushed down.
Which choice by the adults in the story helped young Manjula most?
Ammamma and Mary's mother welcomed her questions instead of scolding, so the stories became her own and her friend's festival mattered too.
How might Mary's mother have felt when young Manjula asked about the stable?
She seemed amused and pleased, laughing and calling it a good question, glad to share her festival.

Read this:

Dear Kishore Sir,
I'm sorry I haven't come to Saturday football for a month. In January I decided I'd only let myself play once all my weekly revision was done, as a reward. It sounded smart. But the revision list never ended. Every Saturday there was one more chapter, so I stayed home. Now I'm studying more hours than ever and getting less done. I get headaches by evening and snap at my mother over nothing. My marks in the last test actually dropped. My friend said running around used to be the only time my head went quiet. I think she's right. Can I come back this Saturday? I'll keep the revision, but football will be a fixed slot, not a prize.
Kashish

How long has Kashish missed Saturday football?
A month.
How has Kashish been feeling since stopping football?
Kashish feels irritable and worn out, with evening headaches and snapping at home, and frustrated that more hours bring less done.
Why is a fixed slot better than football as a reward?
A fixed slot guarantees the exercise that clears Kashish's head, while a reward that depends on finishing never arrives when the list keeps growing.
How might Kishore Sir feel reading the letter?
Kishore Sir may feel glad the player wants to come back, and concerned about the headaches and the dropped marks.

metadata.subtype: Approach: treating sport as reward only after study [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Monday night. Thunder cracked. From his cot Akash whimpered, then sobbed, clutching the bars. Urmila went straight in, lifted him, and hummed until his breathing slowed.
Wednesday night. Thunder again. A whimper. She came, rubbed his back, and sat by the cot until he slept.
Saturday night. A rumble. One small whimper. Urmila called softly from the doorway, “I'm here, Akash.” He hugged his cloth rabbit and settled on his own.

What did Akash hug on Saturday night?
He hugged his cloth rabbit.
What was Akash feeling when he whimpered and sobbed on Monday night?
He was frightened by the thunder and wanted his mother close; the sobbing and clutching showed distress and a wish for comfort.
Why did Urmila's approach work over the week?
She soothed him every time instead of ignoring him, so he learned she would come, and by Saturday her voice alone was enough to help him calm down.
How might Urmila feel on Saturday night when Akash settles on his own?
She would likely feel relieved and proud that he is learning to calm down.

Read this:

In Class 8 I started telling Amma I'd eat in the canteen. The truth was, I was hiding my ragi mudde. The first day I opened it, Kishore said it looked like a grey cricket ball, and three people laughed. I ate it alone in the corridor for a week.
Then, this year, our teacher asked everyone to bring a traditional dish. I almost brought pasta. But I took ragi mudde with Amma's soppu saaru, and I explained how my Ajji ate it every day in the fields. Kishore tried it first. He asked for the recipe. I'm still a little shy about how it looks. But now I'm proud too.
Leela

What did Kishore say the ragi mudde looked like?
A grey cricket ball.
How does Leela feel about the ragi mudde now?
Leela feels proud of it now, though still a little shy about how it looks.
What helped Leela move from hiding the dish to sharing it?
The traditional-dish project gave a chance to explain its story, and a classmate trying it respectfully turned shame into pride.
How might Kishore have felt when he tried it and asked for the recipe?
Kishore probably felt curious and maybe a bit sorry for the old joke, and asking for the recipe showed real respect.

Read this:

In the study hall of the residential school, Damini leaned across the desk to read Lalremsiami's essay and gasped. "This is so good! Honestly, I thought sports-quota kids only cared about training." She laughed, meaning it as a compliment. Lalremsiami closed the notebook. "I'm in the reading club too. Since Class 6." "I know, I just meant..." "You meant you were surprised." The warden's bell rang for lights out. Damini lay awake on her bunk, stunned. She had been trying to be nice. She replayed the words and heard, for the first time, the "only" in them. In the morning she found Lalremsiami at the water cooler. "I'm sorry. I put you in a box. The essay's just good." Lalremsiami nodded slowly. "Okay. Thanks for coming back."

Since when has Lalremsiami been in the reading club?
Since Class 6.
What was Damini feeling as she lay awake on her bunk?
She was stunned and uneasy; she had meant to be nice and only now heard the "only" in her own words.
What was the turning point for Damini, and what made her morning apology work?
Hearing the "only" was the turning point; the apology worked because it named what she did, putting Lalremsiami in a box, without asking for reassurance.
What might "Thanks for coming back" show about how Lalremsiami felt?
Lalremsiami was hurt, but valued that Damini came back to own it instead of letting it slide.

Read this:

From our parenting-class notebook, written by Tenzin, Ritu's papa.
Sunday, the neighbours came for tea. Ritu saw the chocolate box and asked for three. I said one, after lunch. She began to cry very loudly, looking at the guests between sobs. Last month her Nani gave in when this happened, and now Ritu tries it every time we have visitors. This time I knelt and said quietly, "I hear you. One, after lunch." I did not change it. She cried a while, then went to play. At lunch she ate her dal and got her one chocolate.

How many chocolates did Ritu ask for?
Ritu asked for three chocolates.
Why did Ritu look at the guests between sobs?
She hoped the crying in front of visitors would pressure her papa into saying yes, because it had worked before; she was also genuinely disappointed.
What did Tenzin do that a wise parent would do?
He stayed kind and quiet, repeated the same answer and did not give in, so the loud crying did not win.
How might the neighbours see Tenzin's calm response?
They might feel relieved and a little impressed that the visit stayed calm, without a shouting match or a pile of chocolates.
Give me a pre-journey check for a long train trip: three dash bullets, each under six words.

- Your ticket and ID
- Phone charger
- Water for the trip

Read this:

Last semester I taught a six-week evening English class for adults at the community library as part of my internship. At the end, the coordinator, Rukmini ma'am, handed me the feedback forms. Twenty-nine of them. I remember flipping through fast, looking for something, and finding it on form seventeen: a frowning face drawn in the corner and 'too fast sometimes, hard to follow'. That was the one I took home. I didn't sleep well. I told my roommate the class had gone badly. A week later Rukmini ma'am asked, 'Nilesh, did you read the others?' So I did. Twenty-eight forms said things like 'patient teacher', 'I can fill a bank form now', 'please teach next year'. I'd let one frown outweigh twenty-eight thank-yous. I still think about form seventeen, but now I think about slowing down, not about failing.

How many feedback forms were there?
There were twenty-nine feedback forms.
Why did form seventeen stay with Nilesh that night?
Nilesh felt hurt and anxious about the frowning comment, and that sting made a whole successful class feel like a failure.
What did Nilesh eventually take from form seventeen?
A specific, useful point, slowing down, rather than a verdict of failure, once it was weighed against twenty-eight positive forms.
How might Rukmini ma'am see the feedback?
Rukmini ma'am probably saw an intern with overwhelmingly positive feedback and one fair tip about pace, which is why she asked about the other forms.

metadata.subtype: Only the negatives in a review [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Lavanya, come, sit by your Salma aunty. You think you're the only one whose mouth runs ahead? When I was ten, at our school in Bhopal, I shouted answers before the teacher finished. I pushed to the front of the water queue. Once I tore my friend's drawing because she laughed at mine, and then cried all night, because I loved that girl.
My Abba didn't beat me or call me bad. He taught me a trick. Before I did anything with a hot face, I had to press my thumb to each finger, one by one. Four little taps.
By the time I reached my little finger, the shout had usually gone quieter. Not always! But more and more.
I still do it, you know. In queues at the bank.

What trick did Abba teach Salma?
To press the thumb to each finger, one by one, four little taps, before doing anything with a hot face.
How did Salma feel after tearing the friend's drawing, and why?
She felt deep regret and cried all night, because she loved that friend.
Which choice by Abba helped Salma more than punishment would have?
He didn't beat her or call her bad; he gave her a simple pause, the finger taps, that widened the gap between the hot feeling and acting.
How might Lavanya feel hearing that Salma aunty once had the same trouble?
Lavanya might feel less alone and less ashamed, and more willing to try the four taps.

Read this:

On Sankranti morning in their village near Sambalpur, Rekha, five, held two fists behind her back. "Maa, which hand has the til laddoo?" Binita pointed left. Rekha opened it: empty. She giggled. "Wrong! Again!" This time Rekha switched the laddoo from hand to hand behind her back, very busy, and put on a serious face. Binita pointed right. Empty again. Rekha shrieked with glee. "You don't know! Only I know!"

What was hidden in Rekha's fist?
A til laddoo.
What does Rekha's shriek of 'Only I know!' show?
Rekha felt gleeful and proud, realising her mother couldn't know what she knew.
How could Binita keep this game good-natured?
She could keep playing along, then take a turn hiding the laddoo herself, so tricks stay a shared game.
How might Binita feel guessing wrong twice?
Binita probably felt amused and warm, enjoying Rekha's delight.
Using no more than ten words, tell me what a compass does.
A compass shows you which direction is north.

Read this:

Okay Pradeep, since you asked. Me, Siddharth, the guy who hid a sealed envelope for nine days. The school sent our report cards home sealed, and I just knew physics had gone badly. So I put the envelope under my cricket kit in the cupboard and didn't touch it.
Every day it sat there I felt worse. I couldn't eat properly, I kept checking whether Mummy had cleaned the cupboard. I'd tell myself, tomorrow, I'll open it tomorrow.
Then the class group chat said physics remedial classes had started, and the signed report card was due. Mummy saw that before I did. When we finally opened it, physics was bad, yes, but not the disaster I'd been imagining. And I had already missed three remedial classes. That's the part that really hurt.

Where did Siddharth hide the report card envelope?
Siddharth put the envelope under the cricket kit in the cupboard.
Why did Siddharth keep promising to open it tomorrow?
Not looking put off the sting of a bad physics mark, so each delay felt like a small relief, even though the worry grew every day.
What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
By hiding the result Siddharth missed three remedial classes; opening it on day one, maybe with Mummy, would make the bad news smaller and leave time to act.
What is it like for Mummy to learn about the report card from the class group chat?
Mummy may feel hurt and worried at finding out from other parents, and sorry that Siddharth carried the fear alone for nine days.

Read this:

I'm Hafsa, and Divyansh and I were in the same first-year batch. For a whole week he agonised over the sports elective: badminton, swimming or yoga. He made lists. He asked seniors. He went to see the pool twice. On Thursday evening I found him outside the sports office staring at the notice board. Then I watched his face change. He tapped a line on the notice and read it out: "Students may switch electives in the first two weeks." He laughed at himself. "So if I hate it, I just switch. Why am I treating this like marriage?" He wrote "badminton" on the form in about ten seconds and handed it in. That night he was back in the library, working on the coding assignment he'd been putting off.

What did the line on the notice board say?
"Students may switch electives in the first two weeks."
What might Divyansh have felt when he laughed at himself?
He seemed relieved and a bit embarrassed at how much worry he'd put into a choice he could undo.
What else could Divyansh ask himself before future choices?
Whether the choice can be reversed and what that would cost; if it's cheap to undo, choose a good-enough option quickly.
How might Hafsa see the change in Divyansh?
Hafsa seems amused and glad to see him drop the agonising and get back to the assignment.

metadata.subtype: Approach: asks what a good enough choice would be and what reversing it would cost [Revision]

messages.content: Why do teachers ask students to line up calmly before entering the science lab?
A calm line keeps the lab safer. Because the teacher can check everyone and give the safety rules before anybody touches the equipment, there is less chance of pushing, spills and mistakes.

Read this:

In the community centre craft room, Sunaina tipped a puzzle onto the table, sat back and frowned at the huge pile. Then she picked up one piece. "If a piece has one flat side, it is an edge." She turned it over. "Flat. Edge." Another: "Bumps all round. Not an edge." Pranav, from the next table, held out a piece. "Is this one an edge?" "Does it have a flat side?" "Yes." "Then it is," said Sunaina. Soon the edge pieces stood in their own row, and the middle pile was much smaller.

What was Sunaina's rule for finding an edge?
Sunaina's rule was, "If a piece has one flat side, it is an edge."
What was Sunaina feeling when she frowned at the huge pile before she made the rule?
Sunaina felt the job was too big to start and wanted a way to make it smaller. The rule gave her one.
What could Sunaina do next once the edges are sorted, and why?
She could make another small rule, like sorting the middle pieces by colour. A second rule shrinks the pile again.
How does the rule look to Pranav?
The rule gives a clear answer for each piece. Pranav only has to check for a flat side.

Read this:

The alarm clock in Binita's house in the village had stopped years ago and lay on the shelf like a dead beetle. On Sunday, her older brother Eshaan gave her a small screwdriver and a plate. "Unscrew only the back, and put every screw on the plate." Binita worked slowly. Inside were wheels with tiny teeth and a coiled spring. She turned one wheel with her finger, and another wheel moved. "They're holding hands!" she whispered. When she tried to close it again, the wheels would not line up. Dada came and showed her where the small wheel fitted. The clock ticked for a minute. Binita listened with her head on her arm.

What did Eshaan tell Binita to put on the plate?
Eshaan told Binita to put every screw on the plate.
What was Binita feeling when she said "They're holding hands!"?
Binita felt amazed and delighted at seeing how one wheel moves another.
What helped Binita understand the clock even though she could not put it back alone?
Eshaan gave her a small screwdriver and a plate, and Dada showed where the small wheel fitted.
How might Dada feel when helping Binita fit the wheel?
Dada is probably pleased and patient, glad that Binita is curious about how things work.

Read this:

By Saturday evening the outage at the Koramangala office had gone on for eleven hours. Avni, the incident commander, walked round the room. Chetan, who had taken the first alert at seven in the morning, was still at his desk, reading the same log line for the third time.
Avni stopped. 'Chetan, when did you last eat?'
'Lunch? I think.'
She thought it through aloud for the room. 'Long incidents are when tired people make the mistakes that start new ones. So: everyone who started before ten a.m. hands over by eight tonight. Write down what you've tried, what's running, what not to touch. Then go home and sleep. Back at eight tomorrow.'
Chetan opened his mouth to argue. Avni held up the handover template. He filled it in, slowly, and went home.

When had Chetan taken the first alert?
At seven in the morning.
What does Chetan reading the same log line three times suggest?
It suggests he was exhausted and foggy, too tired to take in information, even if he didn't feel ready to stop.
Why did Avni ask for what not to touch in the handover?
So the fresh shift doesn't undo work in progress or repeat risky steps, keeping the system state clear.
How might the fresh team arriving at eight see the handover notes?
They can start quickly with a clear picture instead of guessing what the tired team had already tried.
I snapped at a friend yesterday and I feel terrible.
Feeling bad shows that you care about the friendship. A sincere apology can repair a lot. Do you know what set you off?
I was stressed and took it out on them.
That explains it but does not excuse it, so be clear in your apology. Say what you did, that you are sorry, and that you will try to do better.
Should I text or talk in person?
In person or a call is warmer, but a thoughtful message is fine if that is easier. Whatever you choose, do it soon.
What if they're still upset?
Give them time. You cannot force forgiveness. Let them know you are there when they are ready to talk.
Should I explain my stress?
Briefly, yes, without making it sound like an excuse. 'I was stressed, but that is not a reason to snap' is honest and fair.

Read this:

I'm Farida, and last winter every aunt in the family had an opinion about my two offers. One from a consulting firm in Dubai with the bigger package. One from a housing nonprofit in Bhopal, where I'd grown up, with less money but real work on the projects I cared about.
Jyoti-phuppo called me every evening. "Take Dubai. Your father worked so hard. Why would you choose less?" I felt guilty. I also felt furious, and then guilty for being furious.
It took me a week to hear what was under it. My phuppo had seen my father work double shifts to pay my fees. She was scared for me, not controlling me.
So I told her plainly: "Phuppo, I'm choosing the job where I'll learn and stay healthy. I know you worry. I'll show you the plan." She was quiet, then said, "Just promise me you'll eat properly." I promised.

Where was the nonprofit job?
In Bhopal, where Farida had grown up.
What was Farida feeling during Jyoti-phuppo's calls?
Farida felt guilty and furious, and then guilty again for being furious.
How did Farida make the decision while respecting the family's worry?
Farida saw the fear behind the pressure, weighed growth and health along with pay, and explained the choice plainly with a plan.
How might Jyoti-phuppo see Farida's choice at the end?
She may still feel anxious, but her request to eat properly shows she accepts the choice and simply wants Farida to be safe.

Read this:

I saw the clip at 11 p.m., in the college meme page. Nandini tripping on the stage steps at the fest, slowed down, with a sad trombone and a caption about her walk.
The comments grew as I watched. Laughing faces. Someone guessed her roll number. Someone wrote her surname wrong on purpose.
I typed, “Guys, enough,” and deleted it. Surely somebody from her class would say something. There were four hundred of us looking. I told myself that someone else would handle it.
At 11:40 I saw a new comment from Indu, who sits behind me in stats: “She's my friend. She sprained her ankle there. Please take this down.” Calm, no insults.
Within ten minutes, three more people wrote “agreed.” Then the page admin removed it.
I still think about the “Guys, enough” I deleted. It would have taken four seconds.

What did Indu write in the comment?
Indu wrote, “She's my friend. She sprained her ankle there. Please take this down.”
Why did the narrator delete the comment “Guys, enough”?
The narrator felt unsure and hesitant, and with four hundred people watching it seemed safe to assume someone else would speak up.
What made Indu's message work?
It was calm, gave a human fact about the sprained ankle, and asked for one clear thing, which let others agree without a fight.
How might Nandini feel about the three people who wrote “agreed”?
She would probably feel relieved and less alone, knowing some classmates stood up for her instead of watching.

Read this:

The whole mohalla in their little town had been waiting for Sunday's cricket match against the boys from the station colony. At nine the sky opened. By ten the ground behind the temple was a pond. Swati stood at the door with the bat, her face falling. Her cousin Yogesh kicked the doorframe. "Spoiled. The whole day's spoiled." Swati watched the rain for a minute. Then she turned. "The carrom board is under Dadi's bed. And we have ludo." "Carrom isn't cricket." "No. But all eleven of us are here anyway." By noon, four were playing carrom on the verandah, four were at ludo on the charpai, and the rest were keeping score and shouting. Dadi sent out pakoras. Nobody mentioned cricket until the rain stopped at five.

Where was the carrom board?
Under Dadi's bed.
How did Yogesh feel when the match was rained off?
Angry and frustrated, kicking the doorframe.
What else could the children have done besides indoor games?
They could also fix a new date with the station colony boys, so the match is postponed, not lost.
How might Dadi see the day?
Dadi's house was full of noise and games, and sending out pakoras suggests she enjoyed it.

metadata.subtype: Approach: switching to an indoor activity [Revision]

messages.content: My British aunt said she will go to the "surgery". Is she having an operation?

Not necessarily. In British English "surgery" can also mean the place where a doctor or dentist sees patients. American English says "doctor's office".
Examples: The surgery opens at nine. The doctor's office opens at nine.
Write a sentence of exactly nine words about a sleeping baby.
The baby sleeps quietly while the fan hums softly.

Read this:

The doorbell rang in the Stockholm apartment and his mother's friend Mina came in, stamping snow off her boots.
Oskar stopped playing. His shoulders crept up towards his ears and he edged behind his father's legs.
“Hello, Oskar!” said Mina, reaching out.
“He needs a minute,” said his father gently.
Mina sat down on the floor, took off her scarf and started stacking his blocks.
Oskar watched. Slowly his shoulders came down. Then he walked over and handed her a red block.

What did Mina do after sitting down on the floor?
She took off her scarf and started stacking his blocks.
What was Oskar feeling when his shoulders crept up to his ears?
He was feeling shy and uneasy with someone new, and hunching was a way of protecting himself.
What did Mina do that helped Oskar warm up?
She stopped reaching for him, sat at his level and played nearby, letting him come to her in his own time.
How did Oskar's father see the moment?
His father saw that Oskar was shy and needed time, not that he was being rude.

Read this:

Note from Minakshi (Madhav's aunt), written for his school's "skills at home" project, Sunday.
This morning Madhav, fifteen, helped his uncle fix the leaking kitchen tap. His uncle first showed him how to close the main valve under the sink. Madhav watched closely as the tap was opened and a worn rubber washer taken out. His uncle explained why the washer wears out and let Madhav fit the new one himself. Madhav's hands were unsure at first; he dropped the washer twice. But when the tap was closed and the dripping stopped, he grinned widely and said, "I did that." He has asked to help with the cycle chain next weekend.

What part did Madhav fit himself?
The new rubber washer.
How did Madhav feel when the dripping stopped?
He felt proud and capable, grinning widely and saying, "I did that."
What made this a good way for Madhav to learn the repair?
His uncle showed each step, explained why the washer wears out, and let Madhav do the fitting himself, even with fumbles.
How might Madhav's uncle feel when Madhav asks to help with the cycle chain?
His uncle would likely feel pleased and proud that Madhav wants to keep learning with him.

metadata.subtype: Fixing something with a family member [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

The old-age home in Pune ran a Saturday storytelling hour, and Kiran, twenty-four, volunteered to record the residents' memories. One resident, Alka-ji, was ninety and sharp as a knife. She told Kiran about her husband, her classroom, the children she'd taught to read. Then she said, "When I go, these stories go too, unless you keep them." Kiran felt a chill, then a kind of steadiness. That night she couldn't sleep, thinking about her own life. What would she want remembered? Not her job, she realised. She began recording her own grandmother's stories on weekends. When Alka-ji died that winter, Kiran played her recording at the memorial. The room went very quiet. Kiran felt sad, but not afraid.

How old was Alka-ji?
Alka-ji was ninety.
What did Kiran feel when Alka-ji spoke of her stories ending?
She was shaken for a moment, feeling a chill, then felt steady and began thinking about what she would want remembered.
What did Kiran do with this new understanding?
She began recording her own grandmother's stories so they would be kept.
How might Alka-ji's family have felt hearing her recording at the memorial?
They likely felt moved and grateful that her voice and memories were preserved. 🤍

Read this:

Anand: Can we talk about tonight? Riya heard us arguing about the bowl.
Disha: I know. I said no screens and you said it was fine. She looked at both of us.
Anand: I did undermine you. Sorry. But I also felt you were being too harsh.
Disha: And I felt like you're always the fun one. I don't want to be the villain.
Anand: Neither do I. Let's pick three rules: no throwing, screens end at seven, we say sorry after.
Disha: Agreed. If we disagree in front of her, we say "let's talk after" and go with whoever spoke first.
Anand: Deal. I'll tell Riya tomorrow that we decided together 🙂
Disha: Thank you for listening 👍

What are the three rules Anand suggests?
No throwing, screens end at seven, and we say sorry after.
What is Disha afraid of becoming, and why?
Disha fears being the villain, because Anand is always the fun one.
What would you advise if the two disagree in front of Riya again?
Say 'let's talk after', back whoever spoke first in front of her, and settle the disagreement privately.
How might Riya have experienced her parents arguing about the bowl?
Riya looked at both of them, so she may have felt unsure which rule to follow; shared rules give her one steady message.

Read this:

Sit, Pallavi. You're scrolling while the radio talks about the river, and it reminds me of something.
When I was sixteen, in Guwahati, I had my first phone. The river was rising and the evening news said low areas should move to higher ground. Our lane had never flooded, not once. I lay on the charpai playing a silly game and told your Nani, my mother, "It's just the news making drama."
My friend Moni called at nine. Her family was leaving. I told her she was being dramatic too.
At midnight the water came under our door. We carried Nani's sewing machine up to the neighbour's roof in the dark. I remember my phone died up there, and I didn't even care.
So I'm your Sonali Masi, and I'm telling you: the river doesn't know what happened last year.

What did Sonali and her family carry up to the neighbour's roof?
They carried Nani's sewing machine up to the neighbour's roof.
What was Sonali feeling when she called the news "drama"?
She felt safe and a bit dismissive, sure their lane would stay dry because it never had flooded before.
When Moni called at nine, what could the young Sonali have done instead?
She could have taken Moni's leaving as a sign to pack up and move with her family to higher ground before dark.
How might Moni have felt when Sonali called her dramatic?
Moni might have felt hurt and worried for Sonali, since her own family was taking the warning seriously.

Read this:

Monday: Dolma hadn't replied since lunch. Ritu sent "?" then "hello??" then "are you mad at me". Her chest was tight all evening, and she couldn't focus on anything.
Thursday: Dolma was quiet again. Ritu's thumb hovered over a fourth message. She put the phone down and said out loud, "I'm scared she's pulling away." Then she typed one text: "Hey, I get worried when things go quiet. Can you tell me if we're okay?" Dolma replied an hour later: "We're fine!! Just exams."
Two weeks later: Ritu had joined the school pottery club on Wednesdays and started messaging Sonam from the club too. When Dolma went quiet on Sunday, Ritu noticed the worry, and went back to shaping her lopsided bowl.

What club did Ritu join?
The school pottery club on Wednesdays.
What was Ritu afraid of on Thursday?
She was scared that Dolma was pulling away from her, and she named that fear out loud before texting.
Which step on Thursday worked, and why?
Ritu paused instead of sending a fourth message, named the fear, and asked directly whether they were okay, which got a clear answer.
What might Monday's messages have been like for Dolma?
Dolma, busy with exams, might have felt pressured or confused by several worried texts in a row.

Winter in Shimla. Monday: Irfan, two, lost his red woolly cap somewhere on the Mall Road. At home he stood by the door calling "Topi! Topi!" and sobbed until his mother Binita rocked him to sleep. Wednesday: he wore his old grey cap, pulled it off twice, and cried quietly into her shoulder. Saturday: a shopkeeper had kept the red cap. Irfan grabbed it, hugged it to his chest and wouldn't let Binita put it on him.

Where did Irfan lose his red woolly cap?
Somewhere on the Mall Road.
What does Irfan hugging the red cap to his chest suggest?
He was relieved and happy to have it back after days of missing it.
What could Binita do while Irfan grieves the lost cap?
Comfort him, say that he misses it, and let him cry without rushing to replace it.
What would change if the shopkeeper hadn't kept the cap?
Irfan might keep missing it for a while, and Binita would need to help him slowly accept the loss.

Debate club notes, Friday. Vandana, club mentor
Mehak, Class 10, argued for school uniforms in the first round and against them in the second, and was sharper both times. She grinned when nobody could tell which side she really held. Afterwards she played me a clip of throat singing she has just discovered and asked why our assembly songs never change. Then she said, a bit too proudly, that she had skipped her cousin's engagement "because traditions are for sheep." I asked which part she actually disliked, the ceremony or being told to go. She went quiet, then said, "Being told, I think." We agreed she will write next week's motion on choosing traditions rather than just refusing them. Her energy is a gift, and I want to keep giving it room.

What did Mehak argue for in the first round?
Mehak argued for school uniforms in the first round.
What does Mehak's quiet pause after Vandana's question suggest she is feeling?
She seems caught off guard and unsure as she rethinks; she sees that what she disliked was being told, not the engagement itself.
What choice did Vandana make instead of lecturing Mehak about the engagement?
Vandana asked what she really disliked and then offered her a debate motion, turning a proud remark into real thinking.
How might Mehak's cousin see her skipping the engagement?
The cousin may feel hurt or left out, taking it as a rejection of them rather than of a custom.

"Sangeeta, it's Sachin. Can I come up? I brought the lunch you like from the canteen."
"You don't have to do this."
"I know." He set the tiffin on her dining table. "Three of us have forwarded your profile. The design head at Karan's firm wants to talk on Monday."
Sangeeta stared at the tiffin. "I feel like a charity case."
"Were you a charity when you rewrote my entire portfolio last year? For free, on a Sunday?"
"That was different."
"How?"
She didn't have an answer. She opened the tiffin. Aloo parathas, still warm.
"Okay," she said quietly. "Monday. Thank you."
"And when you're heading a design team somewhere, you'll do the same for someone else."
"I will." She tore a paratha in half and passed it to him. "Sit. Eat with me."

When does the design head at Karan's firm want to talk?
On Monday.
What was Sangeeta feeling when she said "I feel like a charity case"?
She felt embarrassed and small, uncomfortable accepting help after losing her job.
What changed Sangeeta's mind about accepting the help?
Sachin reminded her that she had rewritten his portfolio for free, showing that help between coworkers goes both ways.
How does Sachin see his visit?
Sachin sees it as returning a favour and keeping their working friendship human, not as pity.

I'm Tenzin, and I've worked with Chetan at the school for four years. For all that time he insisted on one thing: Class 8 homework every single night. When parents complained, he'd say, "Discipline builds character." When the counsellor raised stress, he'd list toppers who did homework daily.

Last month the school ran a survey. Chetan read it in the staff room, very slowly. Most students said they slept after midnight. His class's marks hadn't improved in three years.

I expected him to find a reason. Instead, at the next staff meeting, he stood up and said, "I was wrong about daily homework. The survey shows it. From next term my class gets three evenings a week, and one project instead." Someone clapped, awkwardly.

I don't know what it cost him inside. He went a bit red. But he looked lighter afterwards, and the Class 8 children definitely do.

How many evenings a week of homework will Chetan's class get?
Chetan's class will get three evenings a week.
What might Chetan have felt reading the survey slowly?
Chetan probably felt uncomfortable and embarrassed, seeing evidence against a choice he had defended for years.
What made Chetan's statement a real correction?
He named the mistake plainly, pointed to the evidence, and stated a specific change for next term.
How might the Class 8 students feel about the change?
They likely feel relieved and happier, with fewer late nights and a project instead.

Research log – S. Kale, Monday
Abhinav, a third-year, came to office hours two weeks ago with a regression model that kept giving strange results. We found the issue in fifteen minutes: two of his variables measured almost the same thing.
That same evening, he emailed: 'Thank you, sir. I removed one of the two variables and the results now make sense. The error went from 18% to 6%.' Short, specific, and he had clearly done the work.
Today he came back with a new version and one new question, about whether to include rainfall data. I noticed I was pleased to see him. It is not a one-time favour anymore; I know his project now and can help more quickly each time.
I have told him about the department's summer research list. I think he should apply.

What happened to the error after Abhinav removed one variable?
The error went from 18% to 6%.
What might Abhinav have felt sending the thank-you with specific results?
Abhinav likely felt grateful and proud, wanting to show that the professor's help was actually used.
What should Abhinav do after hearing about the summer research list?
Apply, and keep sending short progress updates, so the relationship grows around real work.
How does S. Kale feel seeing Abhinav return?
S. Kale is pleased and more invested, since the thank-you and new work turned a single favour into an ongoing relationship.

metadata.subtype: Approach: following up with a thank-you and progress [Revision]

Read this:

In the hostel mess, Vaibhav stared at the elective form. His father had texted: "Take Finance. We are paying, we decide." Vaibhav wanted Urban Design.
"Just tick Finance and hate it quietly," Trisha said, stealing his papad. "That's what I did."
"And spend two years sulking on their money?" Vaibhav said. "That's worse."
He had been turning it over for weeks. Last month he had spent their money on a phone he didn't need, half out of spite. It hadn't made him feel any freer.
After dinner he went to the department office and asked about teaching assistant posts. The coordinator said there was one opening for the first-year drawing labs, eight hours a week, with a small stipend. He took the form.
That night he called home. "Papa, I'm grateful you pay my fees. I've applied for a TA post to cover my own spending. I'd like to take Urban Design, and here's why." He had three reasons written down.
His father listened to all three.

What did Vaibhav's father text?
"Take Finance. We are paying, we decide."
How did Vaibhav feel about the phone he had bought?
It had been bought half out of spite, and it didn't make him feel freer; he felt stuck and a little ashamed.
What did Vaibhav do to speak more freely with his father?
He applied for a TA post to earn his own spending money and called home with gratitude and three written reasons for his choice.
How does Trisha handle the same kind of pressure?
She ticked what her parents wanted and hated it quietly, a path Vaibhav sees as worse.

In Class 6, Tarun started calling me "Balloon" because I was the roundest boy in the class. The whole row laughed, and so did I. I even puffed my cheeks out once, to be funny.
But every night, I pulled my shirt down over my stomach in the mirror. I stopped eating my tiffin at school. I didn't want anyone to see me eat.
I didn't say anything, because I didn't want to be the one who can't take a joke.
One day, the PE sir saw me sitting alone at lunch with my full tiffin. He sat down and asked, "Thomas, is something wrong?" I told him everything. He said, "Laughing along doesn't mean it didn't hurt. Thank you for telling me." That afternoon he spoke to Tarun and called my mother.
Tarun hasn't said it since.

What did Tarun call Thomas?
Balloon.
What was Thomas feeling while laughing along?
Thomas felt ashamed and hurt, hiding his stomach in the mirror and not eating at school.
What did the PE sir do that helped?
He noticed Thomas alone, listened, said laughing along didn't mean it didn't hurt, and that same afternoon spoke to Tarun and called his mother.
How might Tarun have seen the nickname at first?
Tarun probably thought it was just a funny joke, since Thomas laughed and even puffed his cheeks.

Monday night. New school, new uniform. Mine is the same as everyone's: grey trousers, white shirt, maroon tie. It felt strange but good, like being part of a team. At the gate the guard checked our ties, and I saw that Rohit's shoes were shiny and had a logo on the side. Mine are plain black and scratched. I tucked my feet under the desk in class. Then Sir said the house colours would be decided tomorrow and I got excited about being in a team. Maybe I'll be Red House. Amma polished my shoes tonight and said they looked new. I looked, and they did a bit. 🙂 — Chaitanya

What colour tie is part of Chaitanya's uniform?
The uniform includes a maroon tie.
Why did Chaitanya tuck both feet under the desk, and what else does the diary show Chaitanya felt about the uniform?
Chaitanya felt self-conscious about the scratched plain shoes next to Rohit's shiny ones. The diary also shows Chaitanya felt good about the uniform, like being on a team.
What could Chaitanya do if the shoe comparison keeps bothering Chaitanya?
Chaitanya could talk to Amma or a teacher, and remember that the uniform makes everyone look alike apart from small things like shoes.
How does Amma respond to Chaitanya's worry?
Amma polishes Chaitanya's shoes and says they look new, a small, warm gesture that helps Chaitanya feel cared for.

I'm Darshan, Jatin's roommate. Every Tuesday evening he says the same thing about his case-study write-up: 'Two hours, max. I'll do it after dinner tomorrow.'
Every Wednesday after dinner he opens the laptop at ten. By midnight he's still reading the case. At two he's making coffee, and at four the desk lamp is still on while I'm trying to sleep. On Thursday morning he submits just before the deadline, eyes red.
Last week I counted: seven weeks, seven all-nighters. I asked him once why he doesn't start on Monday. He said, 'It's only a two-hour job, it doesn't need a Monday.' He really seemed to believe it.
I can't tell what's going on in his head. But every Wednesday I put in earplugs, and every Thursday he says, 'Next week will be quicker.'

How many all-nighters did Darshan count?
Seven weeks, seven all-nighters.
What does Jatin's 'It's only a two-hour job' suggest about his thinking?
It suggests he feels overconfident and stuck in the same hopeful estimate, not letting past weeks change his plan.
What could Jatin try next week?
Look back at how long the last seven took, plan for that, and start on Monday with a first hour of reading.
What is it like for Darshan every Wednesday?
Darshan loses sleep to the desk lamp and has to use earplugs, watching the same pattern repeat.

metadata.subtype: Approach: planning fallacy about assignment length [Pitfall]

'I'm quitting tomorrow,' Irawati said, dropping her bag by the door.
Asif, her flatmate, looked up from the stove. 'Tomorrow? What happened?'
'Nothing happened. That's the problem. Same desk, same spreadsheets, same bus. I could move to Goa. Rent a room, teach surfing, whatever.'
'You don't surf.'
'I'd learn!' She pulled out her phone. 'Look, I've already found three rooms.'
'Iru, last month it was Canada. Before that, breaking up with Nikhil.'
She sat down hard. 'I know. I just feel like I'm dissolving.'
'Okay.' He turned the gas down. 'What would Goa give you?'
'Sea. Time. Not being bored out of my skull.'
'And if you quit tomorrow, what pays the rent there?'
She didn't answer. She scrolled the rooms again, slower.
'I'm not saying stay,' Asif said. 'I'm saying find out what you're hungry for first.'

Where did Irawati say she could move?
To Goa, to rent a room and teach surfing.
What does 'I just feel like I'm dissolving' reveal about Irawati?
It shows the urge to quit comes from feeling empty and bored, as if she is losing herself, rather than from a clear plan.
What question helps turn Irawati's restlessness into useful information?
Asif's question, 'What would Goa give you?', helps her name the needs behind the urge (sea, time, not being bored) so she can look for ways to meet them without a sudden leap.
What might Asif be feeling as he hears about Goa?
Asif seems concerned but patient; having heard about Canada and the breakup before, he wants to help Irawati find what is missing rather than brush her off.

Monday: Kashish reached for the biscuit tin. "More! More!" Mohit gave her one, and she munched happily.
Wednesday: after she tumbled off the step, she reached toward the tin again. "More!" But her eyes were wet and her lip shook. Mohit picked her up instead. "You want up. A cuddle." She clung to him.
The next Monday: she stood by his leg, raised both arms and said, "Up!"

What did Kashish reach for on Monday?
The biscuit tin.
What did Kashish really want on Wednesday when she said "More!"?
She was upset after tumbling and wanted comfort; her wet eyes and shaking lip showed she needed a cuddle more than a biscuit.
What habit of Mohit's helped Kashish learn to ask for comfort?
He named what she needed, "You want up. A cuddle," which gave her the word she later used.
What would change if Mohit had simply given her a biscuit on Wednesday?
She would have been left without the comfort she needed and might have stayed upset.

Mentor's note, first-year B.Com, Vaibhav
Vaibhav is the most responsible student in my group, and I am starting to worry about that. He is the eldest of four. Since his father's shop closed, he works evening shifts at a courier office and walks his sisters to school every morning. He has never once asked for an extension.
Today he fell asleep during the tutorial. When I asked, he said, 'I'm fine, ma'am, I'm used to it.' Then, very quietly, 'Sometimes I wish I could just go on the college trip like the others.'
What I did next: I told him that wish is normal, not selfish. I connected him with the fee-support office and asked whether an aunt or cousin could share the morning school run. He will ask his mother this weekend. I will check in next Friday.
Ayesha

What does Vaibhav do every morning?
He walks his sisters to school every morning.
What does Vaibhav's quiet wish about the college trip reveal?
It reveals that behind his sense of duty he is tired and longs for some freedom like the others.
What steps did Ayesha take after the tutorial, and why were they wise?
She told him the wish is normal, linked him with the fee-support office and suggested sharing the school run, easing his load without shaming his care.
How might Vaibhav's sisters be affected if a cousin shares the school run?
They would still get to school safely, and might see their brother less exhausted and more like himself.

Hrithik, you asked how Nishat and I didn't break up during finals. So here it is, from Asif, the man who used to call her every night even when she had a paper at nine.
Last semester was a disaster. She was studying, I kept calling, she'd pick up out of guilt, and we'd both be short with each other. Then she'd have a bad paper, and so would I.
This time we did it differently. In October we opened one shared calendar and each shaded our exam weeks. Hers began on the 18th of November, mine on the 25th. For those weeks we agreed: one good-luck message before each exam, and a ten-minute call on Sundays only. Nothing else, no guilt.
And we booked the evening of 12 December, the day after my last paper, for a long video call with dinner ordered on both sides.
Easiest exam season we've had. That dinner call went on for three hours.

What did Asif and Nishat agree for exam weeks?
One good-luck message before each exam, and a ten-minute call on Sundays only.
How does Asif feel now about last semester's nightly calls?
He feels regretful, seeing that calling every night made them both short-tempered and hurt their papers.
What else could Asif and Nishat add for the next exam season?
A simple way to say if one of them is struggling badly, so the reduced contact never leaves someone alone at a hard moment.
How might the new plan have felt for Nishat?
Nishat could study without picking up out of guilt, and still knew a long call was waiting on 12 December.

"Yogesh, you're eating lunch alone again? Mummy said your tiffin came back untouched."
"It's fine, Rashmi di. I'm not hungry."
"You've said that for three weeks."
"Okay. Nobody talks to me at the new school. They all have their groups. I sit on the bench and pretend to read."
"That sounds really lonely."
"Maybe I'm just boring."
"You're not boring. You made me laugh for an hour last night about your terrible cricket."
"That's different. You're my sister."
"Okay. What do you like doing there?"
"The art room, I guess. There's a sketching club on Fridays."
"Go. Just once. And ask one person what they're drawing."
"And if it's awful?"
"Then you tell me, and we tell Mummy, and she talks to your class teacher. But try Friday."
On Saturday, he burst in. "Di! There's this girl, Sana, she draws dragons. She asked me to help with the wings."

What did Yogesh pretend to do on the bench?
Read.
How is Yogesh feeling at the new school?
He feels lonely and left out, and has started to think he might just be boring.
What small step did Rashmi di suggest, and why is it wise?
Joining the Friday sketching club and asking one person what they're drawing, a small way to connect through shared interest, with adults as backup.
How does Rashmi di see Yogesh's loneliness?
She takes it seriously and cares, reminding him he's not boring and offering to involve Mummy if things don't improve.

Independence Day
Diary, Samir here. This morning at the flag hoisting, Madhuri whispered that the principal's hat looked like an upside-down bucket, right as the anthem started. I snorted. Then I couldn't stop. My shoulders were shaking, and I was pressing my lips together so hard they hurt. The old man next to us, Mr Bakshi from Block C, turned and looked at me. Not angry. Just sad. He was standing so straight, holding his walking stick, and I remembered Papa saying he'd been in the army for thirty years. My face burned. After the anthem I said sorry to him. He said, 'It's all right, son. Just remember it matters to some of us.' From now on I'm saving my jokes for the walk home.

What did Madhuri say the principal's hat looked like?
An upside-down bucket.
How did Samir feel when Mr Bakshi looked at him?
Ashamed and embarrassed; his face burned.
What did Samir do after the anthem, and what does he decide?
He apologised to Mr Bakshi and decided to save his jokes for the walk home.
How did Mr Bakshi feel about the giggling?
Sad rather than angry, because the anthem matters to him after thirty years in the army.
