I learned this one the hard way, last Diwali holiday. We were playing a board game I'd made up, with dice and paper coins. Every time Uma was about to win, I'd think of a new rule. 'Oh, landing on red means go back five.' 'Oh, you need a six to finish.' The first time, she laughed. The second time, she frowned. The third time, she put down the dice and said, 'Zubin bhai, you're just changing it so you win.' My cousin nodded. They both went to the balcony and started a card game without me. I sat there with my board, my new rules and nobody to play with. A game with moving rules isn't a game.

What was the new rule about landing on red?
Landing on red means go back five.
How did Uma feel by the third new rule?
Uma felt cheated and fed up, putting down the dice and saying he was changing the rules to win.
What should Zubin do next time he wants a new rule?
Suggest it before the next game starts, not in the middle of one, so everyone agrees and the rules stay fixed while playing.
How might Zubin's cousin have seen the game?
The cousin nodded along with Uma, so the cousin also seemed to find the game unfair and chose cards instead.

metadata.subtype: Approach: changing rules in the middle to win [Pitfall]

messages.content: My dog barks at every visitor and it's embarrassing.
Barking at visitors is natural for many dogs, because they guard the home. It can be improved with patient training.
How do I begin?
Teach a calm command like 'sit' or 'quiet', and reward the dog with a treat when it follows. Practise when no visitors are there, then with a family member acting as a visitor.
How long will it take?
It differs from dog to dog. Some learn in a few weeks, others in months. Short daily practice works better than long sessions.
Should I shout at the dog?
No. Shouting can make the dog more excited or fearful. Keep your voice calm and your praise warm when it behaves.
Is a trainer worth it?
A trainer can help if progress is slow or the barking looks like fear or anger. Ask a local vet clinic or animal shelter for trainers they trust.

I still remember standing outside the hostel gate in Nainital with our bags, reading a paper sign: "Full. Sorry." Our online booking had simply vanished. I'm Kamal, and for about a minute I wanted to sit down on the road and cry. Usha didn't. She pulled out our list of backup places, handed me one number and dialled the other. Mine was a dharamshala near the market, 300 a night. Hers was a homestay, 550. We put Usha's father on speaker and read him both addresses, and he asked to talk to the homestay owner himself. Ten minutes later he called back: "The homestay. The family sounds careful." That was 250 more each for our one night, so we cut it from our food money and ate street noodles instead of café meals. I updated the shared sheet sitting on a bench.

How much did the dharamshala cost a night?
The dharamshala near the market cost 300 a night.
What was Kamal feeling on reading the sign?
Kamal felt shocked and close to tears, wanting to sit down on the road and cry.
Which step would you keep for any future trip, and why?
Keeping a list of backup places with phone numbers, because it let them call two options within minutes instead of searching from scratch at the gate.
How did Usha's father see the choice?
He wanted to judge the place himself, so he spoke to the homestay owner and chose it because the family sounded careful.

metadata.subtype: Approach: replanning when a booking fails [Revision]

"Two minutes to pick your quiz partner, captains!" called Madhuri ma'am. Rain was drumming on the tin roof and half the class was absent with flu, so Omkar had only four boys to choose from. He looked fast. Chirag, quiet, round glasses, always reading: surely a genius. Rakesh, who made silly noises during assembly: surely hopeless. "Chirag!" Omkar said. In the quiz, Chirag froze at every buzzer. Rakesh, on the other team, answered six science questions in a row, laughing loudly each time. At the break Omkar muttered, "But he looks like a topper." Chirag heard and shrugged. "I like reading stories, not science." Omkar went red and didn't know where to look.

How many questions in a row did Rakesh answer?
Six science questions.
Why did Omkar go red at the break?
He felt embarrassed, because Chirag heard him say he looked like a topper, and it was clear the glasses had not meant what Omkar thought.
What could Omkar try next time he picks a team, even in a hurry?
Think of who actually answered well in past science lessons, instead of who looks clever.
What is it like for Chirag to be picked for his glasses?
Chirag probably felt awkward and under pressure, freezing at the buzzer in a quiz about something he doesn't love.
Text my mother that I reached school safely. Keep it under ten words.
Reached school safely, Mummy. Will call at lunch.

Van Helsing said solemnly, "You are always right; but this is life and death. All chambers are alike to the doctor; and even were they not they are all as one to me to-night. Friend John, when I turn the handle, if the door does not open, do you put your shoulder down and shove; and you too, my friends. Now!"

Answer from the text. What instructions does Van Helsing give about the door?

Van Helsing tells friend John that if the door does not open when the handle is turned, John should put a shoulder down and shove, and so should the others. Van Helsing adds that this is life and death.

Tuesday: Two weeks before the colony's Holi-eve open mic, Ira made the team play a strange game. "Imagine it's over and it was a disaster. Why?" Charu laughed, then answered: "Rain." Someone added, "Mic dies." Another: "Only three volunteers turn up." Ira wrote each one in her notebook, thinking aloud: "If rain is likely, we need cover. If the mic dies, we need a second one."

Saturday: They borrowed a tarpaulin tent from the gurdwara committee, asked Charu's uncle for his old karaoke speaker, and signed up six extra helpers from the building.

Event night, Friday: Clouds rolled in at seven and a drizzle started. The tent held. When the main mic crackled, Charu swapped in the backup within a minute. Ira caught Charu's eye across the stage and let out a long breath.

Where did the team borrow the tent from?
They borrowed a tarpaulin tent from the gurdwara committee.
What does Ira's long breath on event night suggest she was feeling?
It suggests relief, and perhaps pride, because the rain and the failing mic, which she had worried about, were handled by the backup plans.
What other planning step could the team add next time?
They could also plan a rough running order with spare acts, in case some performers drop out, since that was a risk they had not listed.
How did the pre-mortem look to Charu at first, and later?
At first Charu laughed at the game, but on the night Charu was the one swapping in the backup speaker, so the idea clearly proved useful.

Monday. A reporter quoted Pallavi out of context from a panel on hospital staffing, and by noon the clip was trending: "Young nurse says patients are a burden." She sat in the hospital locker room, heart pounding, writing a furious reply on her phone.

Her colleague Harsha found her. "Don't post that. Not today."

Tuesday. Pallavi barely slept. Would they fire her? She booked a meeting with HR and brought the full recording of the panel. The HR officer listened, then said, "We'll handle media questions. Please don't comment publicly for now."

Friday. The hospital released a short factual statement with the full quote: she had said overworked staff struggled to give patients the time they deserve. The clip slowly stopped trending.

Pallavi deleted the angry draft. Harsha brought her a samosa. "Silence and calm," Harsha said. "Hardest thing ever."

What did Pallavi bring to the HR meeting?
The full recording of the panel.
What was Pallavi worried about on Tuesday?
She was anxious and frightened that she might be fired and her reputation ruined over the out-of-context clip.
Which choices helped Pallavi through the controversy?
Not posting the angry reply, speaking with HR, and letting the hospital release a short factual statement with the full quote.
How does Harsha see the week?
Harsha sees how hard it was for Pallavi to stay silent and calm, and supports her with advice and a samosa.

Read this:

Friday, 11 pm.
I told exactly one person that I write songs. Imran. On the terrace last month I even sang him half of one. He said it was really good and that he wouldn't tell anyone.
Today in music class, Sir said, "I hear Vandana is a secret songwriter! Come, sing us something." Everyone turned. I said I had a sore throat. My face was on fire. At the back, Imran gave me a thumbs-up, like it was a present.
Maybe he thought he was helping. I don't care. It was MINE to share.
I'm not telling anyone anything again. Not Imran, not anyone in my class. It's safer to keep everything in here.
V.

What did Vandana tell Imran on the terrace?
Vandana told Imran about writing songs and sang him half of one.
What was Vandana feeling when Sir announced the secret?
Vandana felt exposed and embarrassed; the face was on fire and a sore throat became the excuse not to sing.
What could Vandana try instead of shutting everyone out?
Vandana could tell Imran calmly why it hurt, so he learns the difference between cheering someone on and sharing their private news.
Why might Imran have told the music teacher?
He may have thought he was helping, as his thumbs-up suggests, without realising the news was Vandana's to share.

Read this:

At the hostel orientation in the common room, Jasleen noticed that her new roommate Rajni pulled her chair back each time Jasleen leaned in to talk. Jasleen had grown up in a crowded home where people sat shoulder to shoulder, and she thought Rajni disliked her. She felt a small drop in her chest. During the tea break she asked, "Am I sitting too close?"

Rajni looked startled. "Oh, a bit. I'm from a small town where we sit apart when we're new. I like you, I just need a little room."

They laughed and moved their chairs to a distance both liked. Jasleen said she'd keep asking.

Where did Jasleen's orientation take place?
The orientation took place in the hostel common room.
What did Jasleen feel when Rajni kept pulling the chair back?
Jasleen felt a small drop in the chest and feared Rajni disliked her. The chair moving was a cue, not proof, and Rajni's later reply gave a different reason.
What did Jasleen do well?
Jasleen asked directly, 'Am I sitting too close?', instead of assuming Rajni was cold.
What was it like for Rajni when Jasleen leaned in?
Rajni felt crowded because Rajni comes from a small town where people sit apart when new, and only needed more room, not distance from Jasleen.
What grade did the boy at the next desk get in maths?
I don't know, because grades are private. Only he can choose to tell you.
Was the boxing match in the city stopped early tonight?
I wouldn't know, because I can't see tonight's fights. A sports news page will carry the report.

Read this:

Sunday, late. Today I told Hansa I hate my ears and the way my voice cracks. She said, "You look fine, honestly," and I nearly rolled my eyes. Then she told me she hides her forehead under her fringe every single day and hates how loudly she laughs. I'd never noticed either thing.
I realised I'd been carrying my worries around like they were only mine. We ended up laughing about our "flaws club" until Amma knocked to say lights out.
I'm still not sure my ears are fine, but I believe Hansa cares. Tomorrow I'll ask her about the science project instead of our faces.
Santosh

What does Hansa hide under her fringe?
She hides her forehead.
How did Santosh feel after Hansa shared her own insecurities?
Santosh felt less alone, having realised the worries weren't only theirs to carry. 🙂
How can Santosh support Hansa back without attaching worth to looks?
Santosh can listen, share honestly and turn to shared interests like the science project instead of ranking faces.
Why might Hansa have shared her own insecurities?
Hansa may have wanted Santosh to know they weren't alone, which made "you look fine" feel honest instead of just polite.

Read this:

At the bank's regional training centre, Vinita was to present the new loan-processing checklist to thirty branch staff. She had been a junior officer for a year and a half.
The week before, she had rehearsed aloud three times in the empty training room, timing herself on her phone. Her slides had one heading and three points each. Her main message was on the first slide: "The checklist cuts our processing from four days to two."
Halfway through, Madhav, the senior branch manager in the front row, raised his hand. "What happens to applications already in the system?"
Vinita felt her stomach drop. She didn't know. The room went quiet.
"That's a good question, sir. I don't know yet. I'll confirm with the head office and send the answer to everyone by Wednesday."
Madhav nodded. After the session, he came up. "Most people bluff on that one. I prefer your way."
She sent the answer on Tuesday.

What was Vinita's main message?
The checklist cuts our processing from four days to two.
How did Vinita feel when Madhav asked the question?
Vinita felt a sudden drop of fear, since she didn't know the answer and the room went quiet.
What did Vinita do instead of bluffing, and why was it wise?
Vinita said she didn't know yet and promised a confirmed answer by Wednesday, which kept her credible and calm.
How does Madhav see Vinita's answer?
Madhav respects it, saying most people bluff but he prefers her honest way.

Read this:

At the school counsellor's office in Gangtok, Disha sat twisting her dupatta. "It's probably nothing," she said. "I just wanted to check."

For two months she had chatted with Pema on a drawing forum. Pema said she was sixteen, from the other side of town, and loved the same comics. Disha liked her a lot. She'd been curious to meet her for weeks.

Then Pema had written, "Let's meet at the mall on Saturday. Just us. Don't tell your parents, they'll make it weird." And when Disha suggested a video call first, Pema said her camera was broken.

"That's what made me feel strange," Disha said. "If she's a real friend, why the secret?"

The counsellor nodded. "You noticed exactly the right thing. Wanting to meet a friend is normal. Being told to hide it isn't."

With Disha's agreement, the counsellor called her mother during the lunch break. That afternoon, at home, Disha and her mother blocked the account together and reported it to the forum.

What reason did Pema give for not doing a video call?
Pema said her camera was broken.
What was Disha feeling as she sat in the counsellor's office?
Disha felt uneasy and unsure, twisting her dupatta, worried that something was wrong with Pema's request.
What did Disha do that was wise?
Disha stepped back when Pema pushed for secrecy, asked the counsellor, and let her mother be called so they could block and report the account.
How does the counsellor see Disha's curiosity?
The counsellor sees wanting to meet a friend as normal, but sees the demand for secrecy as the real warning sign.

Monday. Deepika stared at x² + 5x + 6 = 0 for twenty minutes. The textbook's steps might as well have been in another language. She was close to tears when her brother Eshaan said, “Ask the AI to explain it like you're twelve.” She did, and it broke the steps into small pieces: find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5.
Wednesday. She asked for five practice questions and solved them all on paper before looking at the answers. Three right, two wrong. She asked why the wrong ones were wrong.
Saturday. Class test. Deepika solved four equations with no phone in sight and got three right. She told Eshaan, “It didn't do it for me. It sat next to me while I did it.”

How many practice questions did Deepika ask for?
Deepika asked for five practice questions.
How did Deepika feel on Monday?
Deepika felt frustrated and close to tears after twenty minutes with no progress.
What could Deepika do if the tool's explanation is still unclear?
Deepika could ask her teacher or ask the tool to explain in a different way, since another route may click when the first does not.
How might Eshaan see her progress?
Eshaan is probably pleased, since his suggestion helped, and her sentence about the tool sitting next to her shows she did the work.

metadata.subtype: Approach: using AI as a tutor by asking for explanations [Action]

Read this:

"Parth, it's nine. What happened to the geography map?"
"Tomorrow, Mummy. I'll do it in the morning before school."
"You said that yesterday."
"Yesterday I was tired. Tomorrow I'll be fresh."
Mehak put the dal on the table. "Sonali, what time did he get up today?"
"Seven fifty," Sonali said, grinning. "He ran to the bus with toast in his mouth."
"That was a one-time thing, didi."
"It's been a one-time thing every day this week."
Parth looked at the empty map lying on the chair. "Okay, but tomorrow morning will be different. I can feel it."
Mehak sat down. "What will be different about tomorrow's you?"
He opened his mouth, closed it, and reached for his phone.

What time did Parth get up that day?
Seven fifty.
How does Parth feel about doing the map, and what shows it?
Parth feels reluctant to start tonight and hopeful that tomorrow will be different, saying "I can feel it", even though it has happened every day this week.
What is the turning point in the conversation, and what could Parth do next?
Mummy's question about what will be different leaves him with no answer; he could start the map right away for fifteen minutes instead of reaching for his phone.
How does Sonali see Parth's promise about the morning?
Sonali finds it funny and unbelievable, since she has watched him rush to the bus with toast every day this week.

Read this:

Dear Naveen Sir,
You used to say college would be 'freedom with a hidden bill.' I get it now. In my first semester I had classes only in the mornings and nothing after two. No bells, no one checking. I slept through afternoons, watched series, and told myself I'd study 'in the evening.' The evening kept moving. I nearly failed the statistics mid-term. After that I sat down and made my day into a timetable I set for myself: library from three to five, a walk at six, calls home at nine. I even put in a 'lazy hour', so I'd stop feeling guilty about resting. It isn't perfect, but I passed the finals with a B. I wanted you to know your line stayed with me.
Regards,
Sharmila

What grade did Sharmila get in the finals?
A B.
Why did Sharmila add a 'lazy hour' to the timetable?
Sharmila wanted to rest without feeling guilty, making it easier to stick to the rest of the plan.
What would you advise a new college student based on Sharmila's letter?
Build your own timetable early, with fixed study blocks and planned rest, before a bad test forces it.
How might Naveen Sir feel reading this?
Touched and pleased that his warning stayed with Sharmila and helped. 🙂
Are turtles the same as tortoises?

Not quite. Both have shells, but turtles live mostly in water and have flat feet or flippers, while tortoises live on land and have rounded, heavy feet. This is a noun, and its plural is Turtles.
Example: The turtles slid into the pond when we came close.

Read this:

"Jomon, tell us what you found in the garden," said Yamini Miss.
Jomon held up his leaf. "A pillarcater!"
The class burst out laughing. "Pillarcater!" someone squealed.
Jomon's ears went pink and he pulled the leaf to his chest.
"Everyone is learning," said Yamini Miss. "I mix up long words too. Want to try again, Jomon?"
Jomon peeked at the giggling faces. The word did sound funny. A small smile crept up. "Pillarcater," he said slowly, and giggled too.
"Cat-er-pil-lar," Yamini Miss said with him.
"Caterpillar!" This time everyone laughed together, and Jomon laughed loudest.

What did Jomon call the creature on his leaf?
He called it a "pillarcater".
What was Jomon feeling when the class burst out laughing?
He felt embarrassed and small: his ears went pink and he pulled the leaf to his chest.
Which choice helped Jomon, and why?
Yamini Miss saying that everyone is learning, and Jomon choosing to giggle at the funny word, turned the laughter into something shared instead of hurtful.
How might Yamini Miss see the first burst of laughter?
She seems to notice it could hurt Jomon, so she reminds the class that she mixes up words too and gives him a kind second try.

Read this:

When Parveen-aunty wanted to drive us all to Agra last winter, I was the one who said, "Wait." I'm Jeevan, and I like lists. I drew three columns in my maths notebook: train, bus, car. The car meant Aunty driving six hours each way, fog on the highway, but stopping for parathas whenever we liked. The bus was cheap but cramped. The train cost less than fuel and tolls together, and nobody would have to watch the road in the dark on the way back. I showed Aunty. She read it twice, then booked the train. We never got those highway parathas. But on the ride home, in the fog, I watched her sleep with her mouth open, and I felt I'd done something useful.

How long would Aunty have driven each way?
Six hours.
How did Jeevan feel watching Aunty sleep on the ride home?
Jeevan felt useful and quietly pleased that the train let Aunty rest.
Which other approach might suit a trip with more stops?
The car, because it allows stopping for food and sights; it could work better on a daytime trip without fog.
What was the train choice like for Parveen-aunty?
She could rest instead of driving in fog, though she gave up the highway parathas.

metadata.subtype: Approach: comparing travel options by cost and comfort [Thinking]

messages.content: In around 75 words, describe a mountain lake covered in morning fog.

The lake lies silent under a thick white blanket of fog. You cannot see the other shore, only the dark outlines of pine trees that seem to float in the air. The water is still, like glass. A single duck glides through the mist and leaves a thin ripple behind. Cold air touches your cheeks, and everything sounds soft and far away. Slowly, the sun rises, and the fog lifts like a curtain.
Can you describe a gooseberry for me? I have never seen one.

A gooseberry is a small round green or pale berry with a sour taste, used in jams and desserts. It is a noun.
Example: Grandmother made a jar of gooseberry pickle for the winter.

Read this:

Tuesday
Tenzin's parents came to dinner with Ma and Papa tonight. First time both families in one room.
Tenzin's mother brought butter lamps as a gift. Ma had put a Ganesh idol by the door and then, at the last minute, a small Buddha beside it. I nearly cried.
Everything was fine until Papa asked what religion "the children" would follow. Tenzin and I aren't even married yet! His father went quiet.
Tenzin answered: "We've talked about it. Our children will learn both, the gompa and the temple, and decide for themselves." We had talked, three long nights, so I could nod and mean it.
Papa said, "That's very modern." Not happy. Not angry. Tenzin's father said, "It's sensible."
Driving back, Tenzin said, "One rule at a time." I think we'll be okay.
Trisha

What did Tenzin's mother bring as a gift?
Tenzin's mother brought butter lamps as a gift.
How did Trisha feel when Ma placed a small Buddha beside the Ganesh idol?
Trisha felt so moved and grateful that she nearly cried.
Why did it help that the couple had already talked for three nights?
Because they had agreed early, Tenzin could answer calmly and Trisha could nod and mean it, which showed both families a united, respectful plan.
How might Tenzin's father have felt when Papa asked about the children?
He went quiet, so he may have felt uneasy or worried, but he then called the couple's plan sensible.

Read this:

"That's the second time the dashboard milestone slipped, Nikita."
"I know, Lavanya. I'm sorry."
"I'm not asking for sorry. I'm asking why. Why isn't it done?"
"Because I had to redo the charts."
"Why?"
"Because on Tuesday Rohan said he wanted weekly data, and on Thursday you said monthly."
"...Did I?"
"You did. Why did we say different things?"
"Because we never wrote down what the dashboard is for."
"Why not?"
"Because we thought it was obvious."
"So it's not that you're slow."
"No. It's that nobody knew what finished looked like."
"Okay. Tonight we write one page. Who uses the dashboard, what it shows, weekly or monthly. And a definition of done: it works, it's tested, and all four of us have signed off."
"Can we add: nobody changes it without telling everyone?"
"Yes. That too."

What did Rohan want on Tuesday?
Rohan wanted weekly data.
How did Nikita feel at the start of the conversation?
Nikita felt guilty and on edge, apologising for the slipped milestone.
What else could the team do to stop this in other modules?
They could write a one-page spec for each module before starting, saying who uses it and what done means.
How does Lavanya see the missed milestone by the end?
Lavanya realises that a changing request from Lavanya was part of the cause, seeing unclear requirements rather than slowness.

metadata.subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis of a missed milestone [Revision]

Read this:

Suraj was sure he was right. In the science club he had told everyone that Bhavna's plant-growth table was wrong, and Bhavna had gone quiet. At home he re-measured the seedlings and found that his own ruler had started at the wrong end. His neck went hot. He thought about saying nothing.
The next morning in the school garden he found Bhavna. "I was wrong about your table. My ruler was upside down. Sorry I said it in front of everyone."
Bhavna blinked, then grinned. "I wondered if you'd notice. Help me redo the graph?"
They knelt over the pots together, and Suraj felt lighter than he had all week.

What was wrong with Suraj's ruler?
It had started at the wrong end.
What is Suraj feeling when he finds his own mistake?
Ashamed and uncomfortable, since his neck goes hot and he thinks about saying nothing.
What choice did Suraj make the next morning?
He found Bhavna in the garden, said he was wrong, explained the ruler and apologised for saying it in front of everyone.
How does Bhavna seem to feel when Suraj admits it?
Relieved and friendly. Bhavna blinks, grins and invites Suraj to redo the graph together.

Read this:

Gargi and Trisha's repair café had worked beautifully once: one Sunday, a borrowed hall, forty broken fans and toasters fixed by volunteers. Now three neighbourhoods wanted one, the festival was in two weeks, and the hall owner had backed out.

"We can't be at three places at once," Trisha said, pacing the bus stop in the rain.

Gargi pulled out her phone and started typing a checklist. What any host needs: a covered space, four tables, an extension board, a sign-in sheet, a safety rule that nothing with gas gets opened. What volunteers need: a one-page guide and a toolbox list. What they would do: train one lead per area on Saturday.

"So we stop being the café," Trisha said slowly, "and become the recipe."

"Exactly." Gargi hit send to the group. The rain kept falling.

How many broken fans and toasters were fixed on the first Sunday?
Forty broken fans and toasters were fixed by volunteers.
What was Trisha feeling as she paced the bus stop?
She felt stressed and overwhelmed, since they could not be at three places at once and had lost the hall with only two weeks left.
Why was Gargi's checklist a strong solution?
It turned a one-time event that depended on the two of them into simple steps any trained local lead could repeat.
What would change if the neighbourhood leads ignored the safety rule in the checklist?
The events could become risky and lose trust, so the rule is part of what lets the idea spread safely.
My phone keeps hanging, so I will restart it. Is "hanging" right?

My phone keeps freezing, so I will restart it.
Why: "Hanging" is Indian English; "freezing" is understood everywhere.
Please check the spelling: exagerate or exaggerate?

It is "exaggerate", with a double g.
Example: Don't exaggerate; the fish was not as big as a bus.

Read this:

Parveen, you're stuck because you decided on a volcano before looking in the cupboard. Let me tell you what I, Gautam, did in Class 5. Our teacher said, "Any model, due Monday." Everyone rushed to buy kits. We had no money for kits. So I tipped the junk box from under the bed onto the floor: a flattened cardboard carton, twelve bottle caps, a bundle of ice-cream sticks, and a coil of old wire from a broken radio. I sat and looked. The caps were round. Wheels? The sticks were straight. A frame? The wire could bend into an axle. By evening it wasn't a volcano or a rocket. It was a little cart that actually rolled. Your Dadi still has it somewhere.

What did Gautam find in the junk box?
A flattened cardboard carton, twelve bottle caps, a bundle of ice-cream sticks and a coil of old wire.
What was young Gautam thinking as he sat and looked at the pile?
Young Gautam felt curious, letting the shapes suggest uses: round caps as wheels, straight sticks as a frame.
Which choice inside the story made the difference?
Emptying the junk box and looking before deciding what to build, so the materials shaped the idea.
How might Gautam's mother have felt about the cart?
She has kept it all these years, which suggests she was proud of it.

metadata.subtype: Approach: looking at what is available before deciding [Thinking]

messages.content: Invite our relatives to a small thread ceremony for my son Aryan, about 55 words. It is next Saturday at 9 am at our house, followed by lunch. It is from Hema and Girish.

Dear Relatives,
We are happy to invite you to the thread ceremony of our son Aryan. It will take place next Saturday at 9 am at our house, and lunch will follow. We would be deeply grateful for your blessings and your presence. Please bring the whole family and share this special day with us.
Yours lovingly,
Hema and Girish

Nitin: thinking of quitting my job to join Reena's startup
Reena: yay!!
Nitin: wait. thinking.
Nitin: what's the runway
Reena: 8 months of funding
Nitin: and if it doesn't work?
Reena: we'd know by month 6
Nitin: i'd have to find a job again. my rent, my loan
Reena: true. it's a real risk
Nitin: what if i stay and work weekends first? 3 months. see if it's clicking
Reena: honestly that's smart
Nitin: i want to jump. but i don't want to crash 😅
Reena: we can revisit in march
Nitin: deal. i'll start this saturday

How many months of funding does the startup have?
Eight months.
How is Nitin feeling about the startup offer?
Nitin feels excited and wants to jump, but anxious about rent and the loan.
What choice does Nitin make, and why is it a sensible way to judge the risk?
Working weekends for three months first, which tests the startup before risking a full job and income.
How is Reena affected by Nitin's caution?
Reena is excited at first but respects it, calling it smart and agreeing to revisit in March.

Read this:

Santosh, you're new to reviewing people, so let me confess something. In 1999 I was a young man of twenty-five, a sub-editor at a Lucknow newspaper, and they put a new reporter, Kamini, on my desk. On her first day she spelt a minister's title wrong. That was it for me. I'm Lalit, and I decided she was careless. After that, every comma she missed went into my little notebook. Her scoop on the flooded school? I told myself someone had tipped her off. Her clean copy on budget day? Luck. At the six-month review I read out my notebook. The editor listened, then pulled out a folder of her bylines and asked, "And these?" I had no answer. I'd been collecting only one kind of fact. So before you write anyone's review, look for what you've been skipping.

What mistake did Kamini make on her first day?
She spelt a minister's title wrong.
Why did young Lalit put every missed comma into his notebook?
Having decided early that Kamini was careless, he felt annoyed by each slip and saw himself as simply thorough. Good work didn't fit, so he explained it away as luck or a tip-off.
What was the turning point for Lalit at the six-month review?
The editor pulled out Kamini's bylines and asked "And these?", showing him the evidence he had been skipping.
How might Kamini have felt if she had known about the notebook?
She would likely have felt judged unfairly and discouraged, since her scoop and clean copy were being dismissed.
Can you explain "see eye to eye" with an example?

To "see eye to eye" means to agree with someone. It is often used in the negative.
Example: My sister and I do not see eye to eye on music, but we both love the same films.

"Hold my hand, Karthik. Look, the light is red."
"Red means stop!"
"That's right, even for us," said Sabina, halting at the kerb. "Cars are big and cannot stop quickly."
"Why are you waiting, Mummy?"
"Because I follow the rule too."
A man hurried across in front of them. "He did not wait!" Karthik said.
"No. We wait, because the rule keeps us safe."
The little green man lit up. "Now?"
"Look left, look right first."
They crossed together, and Karthik puffed out his chest. "I stopped at the red!"

What did Karthik say red means?
He said red means stop.
How does Karthik feel after crossing?
He feels proud: he puffs out his chest and announces that he stopped at the red.
What helped Karthik understand the rule?
Sabina explained in simple words that cars cannot stop quickly and followed the rule herself even when someone else did not.
How might Sabina see the man crossing against the light?
Sabina probably sees it as unsafe and a poor example for Karthik, so she tells him they wait because the rule keeps them safe.

Read this:

In the courtyard of their village house, Kamal Mama held his dupatta over his face. “Where's Tanuja?” He dropped it. “There she is!”
Tanuja gave a quick flash of a smile, then looked at a hen.
“She's bored of you,” laughed his friend on the step.
But when Kamal set her on his knee and bounced her, “Horse ride, horse ride!”, Tanuja's smile stayed and stayed. She squealed for more.
“Not bored,” said Kamal. “The peekaboo smile is just quick.”

What did Kamal Mama hold over his face for peekaboo?
He held his dupatta over his face.
What was Tanuja feeling during peekaboo, even though her smile was quick?
She felt a quick burst of surprise and joy; the short smile fading as she looked at the hen does not mean she was bored, as the horse ride shows.
How could Kamal's friend read short smiles better next time?
The friend could watch across more than one game and remember that a quick smile at a surprise is normal, not a sign of disinterest.
How does Kamal's friend see Tanuja's quick smile?
The friend reads it as boredom and laughs about it, until the horse ride shows otherwise.

metadata.subtype: Sustained and fleeting smiles in play [Expressing]

Read this:

Class 4 observation note, 25 July.
Harish joined us three weeks ago. On his first day he cried at lunch, and some children, Chinmay among them, called him "a baby."
Since then he has settled well. He scored highest in the maths quiz, he organised a game of kho-kho at break, and he stood up for a younger child in the corridor. Yet today, when I asked Chinmay to pair with Harish for the science project, he said, "Not with the baby." When I asked why, he said, "He cries." I asked when. "On the first day." Nothing since.
I have asked Chinmay to write three things Harish has done this week. We will read them together tomorrow. I will also pair them for one task.

When did Harish cry at lunch?
On his first day.
Why did Chinmay not want to pair with Harish?
Chinmay still felt sure Harish was a baby because of the first day, and felt embarrassed to change that view even though nothing since supported it.
What is the teacher's plan, and why might it help?
Asking Chinmay to write three things Harish did this week and pairing them for a task, so Chinmay sees Harish as he is now.
How might Harish feel being called a baby three weeks later?
Harish might feel hurt and stuck, since he has done so much since then and is still judged by one hard day.

Read this:

Ujjwal, you won't step on the cracks before your cricket match? Let your Saurabh dadu tell you something.

When I was ten, I had a lucky marble. Green, with a white swirl. I kept it in my pocket for every exam and every match.

One day before the school race, I lost it. I cried and said, "Now I'll lose."

My mother said, "Did the marble run the race, or did you?"

I ran anyway. I came second. Without the marble.

I still kept looking for it for weeks. I knew it didn't really help. But having it made me feel less scared. That's okay, Ujjwal. Just don't forget who does the running.

What colour was Saurabh's lucky marble?
Green, with a white swirl.
Why did young Saurabh keep looking for the marble even after coming second?
He knew it didn't really help, but having it made him feel less scared and more comforted.
What turning point in the story helped Saurabh see the marble differently?
His mother asked whether the marble or he ran the race, and then he ran without it and came second.
How might Saurabh's mother have felt when he cried about the marble?
His mother probably felt sympathetic but wanted to help him see his own strength.

Read this:

Simran ran the small accounts team at the rice mill office outside Karnal. Every evening she stayed back after everyone left, redoing the ledger entries Gopal, the new junior, had made that day.
"Why are you so late again?" her sister Rashmi asked when she came home at ten, dal already cold.
"Gopal's entries have errors. The audit is next month. It's quicker if I fix them myself."
"Does he know?"
Simran shook her head. "He'd feel bad."
Two months later, Gopal's entries still had the same errors in the same columns. He had no idea anything was wrong; his work always seemed to come back fine. Simran had dark circles under her eyes and snapped at her mother over nothing.
One night, Rashmi found her asleep at the table with the ledger open.
"Didi, this isn't helping him either," she said softly.

What time did Simran come home?
At ten.
Why didn't Simran tell Gopal about his errors?
She was worried he would feel bad, and she wanted to avoid an awkward talk, even though fixing them herself was wearing her out.
What else could Simran try instead of fixing the entries herself?
She could go through one day's errors with Gopal, show him the pattern, and check his entries together briefly each evening until he improves.
How does Simran's approach look to Rashmi?
Rashmi watches her sister come home late and exhausted and sees that the quiet fixing isn't helping Gopal either, so she is worried.

Desk editor's note, fact-check team (Ritu):
On Tuesday a video spread showing a state minister apparently mocking flood victims. Three rival outlets had already posted it. Kalyani, 25, our newest fact-checker, asked for thirty minutes before we ran anything. I watched her work. She noticed the minister's lips drifted out of sync on two words, and the shadow on his collar didn't move with his head. She found the original speech on the government channel; the words weren't there. She traced the clip to an account created that week. She was nervous presenting it, since everyone else had run the story. We published a clear verification piece instead, showing each step so readers could learn to check. Two outlets later took their versions down. Next: I've asked Kalyani to run a short session for the desk on spotting synthetic video.

How long did Kalyani ask for before the team ran anything?
Thirty minutes.
Why was Kalyani nervous presenting her findings?
Everyone else had already run the story, so going against them felt risky for the newest fact-checker.
Which verification steps did Kalyani use?
Checking lip-sync and shadows for glitches, finding the original speech on the official channel, and tracing the clip to a newly created account.
How might readers benefit from the verification piece?
Seeing each step shown lets them learn how to check suspicious videos themselves before sharing.
The builder is digging the foundations of our new house. What are foundations?

Foundations are the strong base under a building, usually below the ground, that holds the whole building up. Foundations is the plural form of this noun.
Example: The builder dug deep to lay the foundations before putting up the walls.

NGO coordinator's note, literacy programme
Tanuja joined as a volunteer three months ago. In week one, she posted photos with the children and wrote, "Changing lives!" She was lively and enthusiastic.
By week six, she stopped coming to the evening classes, which were harder. When Binita, a senior teacher, suggested she try teaching the older, slower learners, Tanuja said it "wasn't really her style."
Last week, I overheard Binita tell Tanuja, gently, "You don't need to post about us. You need to listen to the children." Tanuja was upset.
I've spoken to Tanuja today. She admitted, "I liked the idea of helping more than the helping." We agreed she'll try two evening classes before deciding.

What did Tanuja write with her photos in week one?
She wrote, "Changing lives!"
What does Tanuja's admission suggest about how she was feeling?
It suggests she felt embarrassed but honest, recognising she enjoyed looking helpful more than doing the hard work.
What is a fair next step for Tanuja?
Trying the two harder evening classes, listening to the children and accepting correction, before deciding if she can commit.
How might Binita have felt about Tanuja's photos?
Binita may have felt frustrated, seeing the posts get attention while the difficult evening classes were left to others.

Saturday. Parul spread out four lab files and the practical notes. Instead of a bit of each subject every day, all the writing went into this afternoon: aim, procedure, observations, conclusion, one file after another. Yash brought tea and asked why. "Every time I switch from writing to reading, I lose ten minutes remembering where I was," Parul said.

Tuesday. The reading for the two theory papers was done in one long sitting in the library, with all the notes open at once.

Friday. The files were ready before the deadline, the papers had been read, and there had been two clear evenings in between. Yash said it seemed like a real change. Parul was pleased. 😊

What went into Saturday afternoon's work?
All the lab file writing went into Saturday afternoon, one file after another.
Why did Parul want to do all the writing at one time?
Parul feels pleased and less scattered, since switching between writing and reading wastes about ten minutes each time and keeping like with like saves effort. 😊
What could Parul do if a batch takes longer than planned, and why?
Parul could shorten the next batch or move one file to a free evening, since a fixed plan can bend without being dropped.
How might Yash see the change in Parul's week?
Yash saw that the week had two clear evenings and that the work still got done, which made batching look worthwhile.

'They're saying Abba's cart has to move by the first,' Farhan said, stirring the tea too hard. 'New no-vending zone. Twenty years on that corner.'
'Did they say why?' Leela asked.
'Traffic. School buses.'
'That part's fair. Kids crossing there is scary.'
'So you're on their side?'
'I'm on the side of what the law is for. It's meant to protect the kids and people like your Abba who earn there. If it only protects one, it needs fixing.'
'Fixing how? Abba can't fight the municipality.'
'Not fight. There's a ward vending committee; vendors are meant to have seats on it. We write it up: a spot twenty metres down, away from the gate. Photos, the school timings, the licence.'
'And if they say no?'
'Then we hear their reason and try the next proper step. Not a bribe, not a fight.'

Why did the no-vending zone come up, according to Farhan?
Traffic and school buses.
How does Farhan feel about the order to move the cart?
Farhan feels worried and angry, stirring the tea too hard, because Abba's cart has stood on that corner for twenty years.
Which steps does Leela suggest, and why are they wise?
Writing to the ward vending committee with photos, school timings, the licence and a nearby spot, which uses a fair process instead of a bribe or a fight.
How might parents of children at that school see the new rule?
They would likely be relieved the gate is clearer, which is why Leela says that part of the law is fair.

Dear Kishore-bhaiya,
You gave me your old guitar last Diwali and said, "Give it a year." I nearly didn't. For the first month my fingers hurt, the chords buzzed, and every video made it look easy. I shoved the guitar under my bed in March. Then last week I found the voice recording I made on the first day, trying to play "Happy Birthday". It was terrible! I recorded the same song again. It's not great, but it's a song now. I'd been comparing myself to people who've played for ten years, not to me in January. So it's back out from under the bed. Fifteen minutes a day. I'll play for you when you're home in May.
Jagdish

When did Jagdish put the guitar under the bed?
In March.
How did Jagdish feel in the first month?
Jagdish felt frustrated and impatient, with sore fingers and buzzing chords while videos made it look easy.
What changed Jagdish's mind?
Comparing the first-day recording with a new one, which showed real progress against Jagdish's own earlier self.
How might Kishore-bhaiya feel reading the letter?
Kishore-bhaiya would probably feel pleased and proud that the guitar is being played again.

Rain hammered the hockey field, and the final was ten minutes from full time, tied. In the huddle Coach Mridul murmured, "Their striker is the danger. When I nod, foul her hard. The umpire cannot see in this rain." Sabina felt the cold go through her. Keya and Rina stared at their sticks. Nobody spoke. Sabina had always respected Coach Mridul, and refusing him felt unthinkable. When the nod came, she froze and did nothing. The whistle blew at a draw. That evening she went to the PE teacher, Ms Dsouza, and told her everything. Ms Dsouza sat with her, said it was not her fault, and took it to the principal before dark.

Who spoke to the team in the huddle?
Coach Mridul spoke in the huddle.
Why did Sabina freeze when the nod came?
Sabina respected Coach Mridul and feared him, so refusing felt unthinkable, but doing it felt wrong; respect and fear were mixed together.
What turning point that evening helped Sabina?
Sabina told the PE teacher Ms Dsouza everything, and Ms Dsouza stayed with Sabina, said it was not Sabina's fault, and took it to the principal before dark.
How might Keya and Rina have felt in the huddle?
Staring at their sticks suggests discomfort and unease, perhaps fear of the coach; since nobody spoke, each may have thought the others agreed.

messages.content: Explain the word "overwhelm" simply. And how do I spell "pronounciation"? One more thing: can you correct this for me? "They was late for school."

1. As a verb, "overwhelm" means to affect someone so strongly that they cannot cope.
2. It is "pronunciation". Notice that there is no "o" in "nun".
3. Better: They were late for school. Why: "they" is plural, so the past form is "were".

From my balcony I saw it happen. Jomon, from the ground floor, fell off the swing and landed hard on the gravel. He lay there crying, holding his knee. Seema, his little playmate, was right beside him. She didn't go to him or call anyone. She just stood with her fists clenched and screamed, louder than Jomon, tears pouring, frozen to the spot. She looked as frightened as if she had fallen herself. By the time I ran down, both were sobbing. I picked Jomon up and held Seema's hand. After a while she whispered, 'Is he broken?'

Where did Jomon land?
Hard on the gravel.
What does Seema's whisper "Is he broken?" suggest about her feelings?
It suggests Seema cared about Jomon deeply but was so frightened that she couldn't move or help.
What could an adult teach Seema for the next time a friend gets hurt?
An adult could practise a simple plan with Seema, like taking a big breath and running to call a grown-up, so the caring can turn into help.
How might Jomon have felt with Seema screaming beside him?
Jomon may have felt even more scared, with his friend crying louder and nobody coming until the neighbour ran down.

Hafsa beta, you asked if I remember my Dadi. I remember the day she died better than any birthday. I was ten, it was Holi week, and I was sitting on the stairs with a pichkari full of yellow water. My uncle came up the steps, took the pichkari from my hand very gently, and said nothing. I remember his white kurta, the smell of gujiya from the kitchen, a crow on the railing. For sixty years your Pankaj nana was sure of every bit. Then last year my sister told me it was our father who came up the stairs, not our uncle. I still see my uncle's face. Both of us feel certain. Big days paint their pictures very brightly, beta.

What was young Pankaj holding on the stairs?
A pichkari full of yellow water.
Why does Pankaj still feel sure it was his uncle?
The grief and shock of that day made the scene feel sharp and permanent, so he still sees his uncle's face and feels certain after sixty years.
What turning point in the story shows the memory might have drifted?
His sister's remark last year that it was their father on the stairs: two people, equally certain, remembering different details.
How might Pankaj's sister experience the same memory?
She is just as certain it was their father, and may feel her own picture of that sad day is the true one.

In the small town, the notice on the college gate read "Student march against fee hike, Friday 11 am." Anirban, in Class 11, read it twice. Older students said everyone was going, but the notice named no demand. He read the college's statement: a rise of ten percent "for lab upgrades." The local paper called it a protest by the students' union. Another called it the work of "a political group." He phoned his older cousin Anand, a second-year at the college. "Who is behind it?" "The students' union, with the teachers' association. The police gave permission for the ground." "What do they ask?" "Roll back the rise, or set up a scholarship fund." Anirban wrote three lines on a sheet: who, what, permission. He was not yet sure, but it was clearer than the rumours.

Who is behind the march, according to Anand?
The students' union, with the teachers' association.
What is Anirban trying to work out, and how does he feel about it?
Anirban is trying to work out who organises the march and what it demands, and feels more confident because the facts are clearer than the rumours.
What else could Anirban do before deciding, and why?
Anirban could tell a parent where he wants to go and ask about the plan for the day, because safety and permission matter as much as the cause.
How might Anand see Anirban's questions?
Anand probably sees a careful younger cousin who wants facts and not a crowd, and is happy to answer.

Dear Dhruv-mama,
I'm writing because I didn't want to say this at the table on Sunday, with Nani's birthday cake still out.
When you said my views were 'brainwashed' by my college, I felt insulted, and my face went hot. You know I had an answer ready; I think you wanted it. But I didn't want Nani's eightieth to end in shouting, so I said, 'Mama, I don't want to argue tonight,' and asked about your new scooter instead. I know that annoyed you.
I'm happy to talk about politics with you, honestly. Not when we're both heated, and not with 'brainwashed' in it. I read, I think, I sometimes change my mind. So, I hope, do you.
Next month, when I'm home, could we go for a walk and talk properly? You can tell me what worries you, and I'll tell you what worries me.
With respect,
Abhinav

Whose birthday was it on Sunday?
It was Nani's eightieth birthday.
How did Abhinav feel when called 'brainwashed'?
Abhinav felt insulted, face hot, with a sharp answer ready.
What did Abhinav do at dinner that was wise?
Abhinav calmly declined to argue and changed the subject to protect Nani's birthday, then offered a calmer talk later.
How might Dhruv-mama feel reading the letter?
Dhruv-mama may feel a little embarrassed but respected, invited to a proper talk instead of a fight.

Hi Shalini,
After Friday's gig I said, in front of the whole band, that your drumming "dragged the entire second half". It was true, but I said it when you were tired, sweaty and proud, and I said it partly to sound sharp in front of the others. I'm sorry for that.
Here's what I should have said, and when. The tempo does slow in the second half, especially in the bridge of the last song. I think it's because we don't have a click track in the monitors. Could we try one at Wednesday's rehearsal? Your fills in the opener were the best they've ever been.
I'm sending this on Monday so you have time to think before we meet, not on stage and not in the group chat.
Chaitanya

When does Chaitanya suggest trying a click track?
At Wednesday's rehearsal.
Why does Chaitanya think the first comment went wrong?
Chaitanya realises it was said when Shalini was tired and proud, in front of everyone, partly to sound sharp, so the truth became a weapon.
Which choices make the email's feedback kinder and more useful?
It is private, sent on Monday with time to think, names the exact bridge, suggests a fix, and adds real praise for the fills.
How might Shalini receive the email compared with Friday's comment?
Shalini would likely feel respected rather than humiliated, and more open to trying the click track.
What is hypocrisy?

Hypocrisy is saying you believe in something or have good qualities, but acting in a different way. It is a noun.
Example: Telling others to save water while leaving your tap running is hypocrisy.

Friday night
Parul asked me today to co-run the college film festival. Three weeks of work, starting Monday. My heart jumped. I love films.
And then I opened my planner. Two quizzes next week. The research internship form due on the 20th. My café shifts on Saturday and Sunday. NSS on Wednesday. I'm already sleeping at one most nights.
I sat on the library steps for a long time. If I say yes, something gives, and I know what gives: sleep first, then the quizzes, then the form. I've done this before and it hurt everything.
So I texted Parul: 'I'd love to, honestly, but my weeks are full till the 20th and I'd do a bad job. Could I help with just the poster design after that?' She replied with a sad face and then, 'Deal.'
It stings a bit. But I'm going to bed at eleven tonight.
– Parveen

When is the research internship form due?
On the 20th.
How does Parveen feel after texting Parul?
Parveen feels a sting of disappointment at missing something loved, but relieved and settled about protecting sleep and studies.
What else could Parveen offer the festival later?
Once the form is done, a clear small role like the poster design, as agreed, with a fixed number of hours.
How might Parul feel receiving the reply?
Parul is briefly disappointed, sending a sad face, but values the honesty and accepts the smaller offer.

Exam month made the flat noisy and full: tuition at five, dinner at eight, cousins visiting. "When do I practise?" Sunita asked Jatin Sir at her lesson. Dear Rafiq,
I've owed you this letter for months.
When you told me in March that you'd been asked to join the other band, I panicked. Our band was the only place I felt like I mattered. So I said, "If you leave, I'll quit and tell everyone you stole the chorus of 'Monsoon' from me."
You didn't steal it. We wrote it together on your terrace. I knew that when I said it.
You stayed. You stopped laughing at practice, and you looked at me like you were scared of me. I told myself it worked. Really, I'd turned our friendship into a hostage situation because I was terrified of being left.
I've been talking to a counsellor about why being left feels like the end of the world to me.
Please join the other band if you still want to. I won't say a word against you. I'm so sorry.
Ramesh

What song did Ramesh threaten to say Rafiq stole?
The chorus of 'Monsoon.'
Why did Ramesh make the threat?
Ramesh felt panicked and terrified of being left, because the band was the only place Ramesh felt important.
What steps is Ramesh taking now?
Ramesh is talking to a counsellor about the fear of being left, admitting the threat was false, and freeing Rafiq to join the other band.

Rafiq seemed scared and unhappy, no longer laughing at practice and looking at Ramesh with fear.

At twenty-five, Ishita became manager of a small bank branch in a town in Himachal, with a team of five, most of them older than her. Chinmay, the youngest clerk, was friendly but slow with loan files, and customers had started complaining.
She didn't scold him at the counter. After closing, she asked him to stay for tea. "The loan files are taking too long. Two customers complained this week. I want to help fix it. Where do you get stuck?"
Chinmay was quiet. Then he admitted he was scared of making mistakes, so he checked everything three times.
Ishita sat with him and made a simple checklist for each file. For two weeks, she checked his first file each morning, then stepped back. She also gave the senior clerk the task of mentoring him.
By the end of the month Chinmay's files were on time. At the staff meeting, Ishita thanked him in front of everyone.

How many customers complained that week?
Two customers.
What was Chinmay feeling that made him slow?
Chinmay felt scared of making mistakes, so he checked everything three times.
Which of Ishita's choices were good people management?
She raised the issue privately and plainly, asked where he got stuck, gave a checklist, coached then stepped back, and praised him publicly.
How might the older team members see Ishita after this?
They might respect her more, seeing she handles problems fairly and helps people improve.

I share a bench with Gopika, so I saw most of it. Last Monday she was quiet all through maths. At lunch she told me she'd submitted the science project on renewable energy mostly written by an AI tool, and she couldn't stop thinking about it. "It's got my name on it and it isn't mine," she said. After lunch she went to Mr. Varghese. I waited outside the staffroom. When she came out, her eyes were red, but she looked steadier. She told me he'd given her a week to redo it, written by her this time, and the marks would be capped at half. Every evening that week she wrote in the library, and I saw a new line on the first page of her notebook: "AI: ideas and checking only. Never the writing." I'm Maria, by the way. I'm not sure I'd have been that brave.

What was the science project about?
Renewable energy.
Why did Gopika go to Mr. Varghese?
Gopika felt guilty and uncomfortable that work with her name on it wasn't hers, and couldn't stop thinking about it.
What else could Gopika do to keep her new rule?
She could tell Mr. Varghese about the rule and note how AI was used on each assignment, so it stays visible.

Maria admires it as brave and isn't sure of being able to own up in the same way.

messages.content: How can I feel more confident in class? Why do clever people still make mistakes? Explain the word "unaware" simply. What does "call it a night" mean?

1. Prepare well, sit where you can see and hear, and try raising your hand once a day. Confidence grows with practice.
2. Everyone is human and can miss a detail. Because cleverness does not stop tiredness or hurry.
3. As an adjective, "unaware" means not knowing about something.
4. It means to stop what you are doing and go to bed or go home.

It was 11:55 p.m. An email arrived for Mohit: "Your bank account will be blocked at midnight. Update KYC now." There was a link and the bank's logo.
Mohit panicked. Midnight was five minutes away. He clicked. The page asked for his card number and OTP.
He paused. His cousin Manjula, who worked in a bank, had told him: "Banks never ask for OTP."
He looked closely. The sender's address was a long string of random letters.
He closed the page, called the bank's official number from the back of his card, and they confirmed it was phishing. He forwarded it to the bank's report address and changed his password.
He texted Manjula: "Almost fell for it." She replied, "You didn't. That's what matters."

What did the page ask for?
His card number and OTP.
What was Mohit feeling when he clicked the link?
Mohit felt panicked by the midnight deadline.
What steps did Mohit take after noticing the warning signs?
He closed the page, called the official bank number, reported the email and changed his password.
How does Manjula see Mohit's near miss?
Manjula focuses on the fact that he stopped in time, not on the mistake of clicking.

When I got my English paper back in Class 6, I saw 38 out of 80 and wanted to crawl into a hole. I'm Farhan. I told myself I was the dumbest person in the whole school. I didn't go out for recess; I sat in the toilets reading the red marks over and over. My friend Ujjwal found me. 'You're not dumb. You beat me in science,' he said. That helped a little. Then I made myself actually look at the paper, not just the total. Most of the red was in one place: tenses. Past, present, all mixed up. That wasn't my whole brain. That was one thing. I asked Ma'am for extra worksheets on tenses. By the half-yearly, I had 61. Still not the top. But not a hole either.

Where did Farhan spend recess?
In the toilets, reading the red marks.
How did Farhan feel on seeing 38 out of 80?
Ashamed and crushed, wanting to crawl into a hole and calling Farhan the dumbest person in school.
What wiser step did Farhan take after the first shock?
Looking at where the marks were lost, tenses, and asking Ma'am for extra worksheets.
How does Ujjwal see Farhan?
As clever, since Farhan beat Ujjwal in science, not dumb at all.

In the living room in Addis Ababa, Yara, five, built a block tower, and it fell twice. She kicked the blocks and sat with her arms folded. "Stupid tower!" Her father Abebe crouched beside her. "It's hard to make it stand. You worked hard on the bottom. It's wide and strong. What if we do just the first three layers together?" They did, and it stood. "Now you add the fourth." She placed one block, very carefully.

How many layers did Abebe suggest doing first?
The first three layers.

Anger and frustration, and perhaps a wish to give up.

He praised her effort and broke the task into steps.

Subject: sorry, and a real question
Maria,
When Professor Rao tore into our joint poster on Tuesday, I'd shrugged it off by dinner. That's how I am: criticism rolls off, I fix the thing, I sleep fine. So on Wednesday I sent you a cheerful list of edits and a silly cartoon, and I didn't notice you'd gone quiet until Ana told me you skipped the lab meeting. By dinner.
What did Chaitanya think Maria was feeling after Tuesday?
Chaitanya assumed Maria had bounced back and felt as calm as Chaitanya did, so Chaitanya didn't notice Maria had gone quiet.

Take it slowly and keep it playful. Which game are you teaching?
A matching game with pictures.

Last month Rafiq Chacha from next door asked if I'd feed his parrots every evening while his leg was in plaster. I said, "Yes, yes, definitely!" And then, three evenings out of five, I "forgot". Mummy had to go instead, and she looked at me funny at dinner.
The truth, which I didn't even tell myself then, was that the parrots scare me. They screech and bite the bars when you open the cage. But Chacha is so kind, always giving me toffees, that saying no felt rude.
Last week Mummy asked why I kept agreeing. I cried a bit and told her. Then I told Chacha. He laughed and said, "Arre, just say so!" Now I water his plants instead. I'm Jahnavi, and plants don't bite.

What did Rafiq Chacha ask Jahnavi to do?
Feed his parrots every evening while his leg was in plaster.
Why did Jahnavi keep 'forgetting' instead of saying no?
Jahnavi was scared of the parrots but felt that saying no to kind Chacha would be rude, so the resistance came out sideways as forgetting.
What turning point let Jahnavi stop forgetting?
Telling Mummy the truth when she asked, then telling Chacha, which led to a new job Jahnavi could really do.
How might Mummy have felt going to feed the parrots herself?
Probably puzzled and a bit annoyed, sensing something was off, which is why she later asked Jahnavi why she kept agreeing.
I always drink tea in the morning. Is 'always' in the right place?

Your word order is fine.
Why: "always" goes after the subject, before the verb.

Thursday

Today at school I told Vaibhav that last week a boy in our class put a frog in the teacher's drawer and she screamed and fell off her chair.

Vaibhav said, "That never happened."

I said it DID. I remember the frog was green and slimy. But then Vaibhav said, "That's from the cartoon we watched at your house on Sunday."

I thought about it. The teacher in the cartoon had a big bun. Our teacher doesn't.

I wasn't lying. I really thought it happened at school! My brain just forgot where I saw it.

— Omkar

What colour was the frog Omkar remembered?
Green and slimy.
How did Omkar feel when Vaibhav said it never happened?
Omkar felt defensive and sure at first, then puzzled, realising the memory had come from the cartoon.
What clue helped Omkar work out where the memory came from?
The teacher in the cartoon had a big bun, but Omkar's teacher doesn't.
How might Vaibhav see Omkar's story?
Vaibhav might think it's funny or strange, but Vaibhav can see Omkar wasn't really lying.

When I started work in Bengaluru, I noticed things. I'm Sachin. I'd been to an English-medium school, my uncle knew the CEO's brother, and I'd never worried about rent. Aparna, who joined the same day, had come from a Kannada-medium school and sent half her salary home.
I didn't want to pretend I'd done it all alone. I also didn't want to spend my days feeling guilty. That helps no one.
So I did small things. When a hackathon came up, I forwarded it to Aparna first. When she spoke in meetings, I made sure nobody talked over her. When she said the English-only training was hard, I told HR.
Last month she got a promotion before me. I was genuinely glad.

What kind of school did Aparna come from?
Aparna had come from a Kannada-medium school.
How does Sachin feel about the head start?
Sachin feels aware of it without guilt, and genuinely glad when Aparna is promoted.
Which of Sachin's small acts seems most useful, and why?
Telling HR the English-only training was hard, because it could change things for others too.
How might Aparna see Sachin's actions?
Aparna may see Sachin as a fair colleague who shares opportunities and listens.

At the evening tuition centre, Mohit kept kicking Omkar's chair and calling him "brain box". Omkar hated it.
One evening Omkar waited downstairs for his mother. A car pulled up, and a man leaned out and shouted at Mohit, "Useless! Late again!" Mohit's shoulders went up to his ears.
Omkar felt something unexpected: a twist of pity.
Next day, Mohit kicked his chair again. Omkar didn't kick back, but he didn't pretend it was okay either. He moved to the front row and told Mahima Ma'am, who ran the centre. She thanked him, spoke to Mohit that same evening, and changed the seating. Omkar still felt a bit sorry for Mohit. But sorry wasn't the same as fine.

What did Mohit call Omkar?
"Brain box".
What mixed feelings did Omkar have about Mohit after seeing the man in the car?
Omkar felt pity for Mohit, sensing he might be hurt at home, while still being upset about the chair-kicking.
What did Omkar do that balanced understanding and safety?
He didn't fight back, moved to the front row and told Mahima Ma'am, keeping away from Mohit without excusing him.
How might Mahima Ma'am see the situation?
Mahima Ma'am sees a child being bullied who needs protection, so she speaks to Mohit and changes the seating that evening.
Sketch a stallholder who sells vegetables in the early bazaar, 50 words, with a warm eye for his hands.

The vegetable seller arranges tomatoes in a neat red pyramid. His hands are quick, and his voice rings out over the noise. He weighs each bag with a smile and adds one extra chilli for luck. The morning sun lights up his baskets, and the whole stall looks like a painting.

Dilnaz: haha glad. it was nothing really, just a template

Dilnaz fixed the peacock feathers at 1 a.m.
What did Elizabeth feel as Dilnaz kept deflecting?
Elizabeth felt warm gratitude and a growing determination for the thanks to land, which is why Elizabeth announced that this one couldn't be waved away.

It named concrete effort, three evenings and the 1 a.m. feathers, and the effect, a mother in tears, so the thanks were too specific to dismiss.

Dilnaz seems surprised and a bit shy, pausing with '...' before accepting the thanks instead of deflecting.

"Damini didi, you know when Nanu died last winter? Everyone kept telling me, 'Darshan, he's in a better place,' and I kept thinking, how do they know? I wasn't angry exactly. Just... it cracked something open. Where did he go? Does anything I do matter if we all end? I started reading at night, anything I could find: old stories from the Upanishads, a book on black holes, even Nanu's own diary in Gujarati, which took ages. I sat in the temple some evenings and in the library some afternoons. I don't have answers. Some days that scares me. Other days it feels exciting, like I'm allowed to decide what I believe instead of just copying. Is that weird? You're the only one I can say this to."

Whose diary did Darshan read?
Nanu's own diary, written in Gujarati.
What mixed feelings does Darshan describe about not having answers?
Some days the uncertainty scares Darshan, while on other days it feels exciting because Darshan gets to decide what he believes.
What could Damini say to support Darshan?
She could tell Darshan these questions are normal and worth having, listen without rushing to answers, and maybe share what she herself wonders about.
How might Darshan's parents feel if they knew about the reading?
They might be moved that Darshan is honouring Nanu, or uneasy about the questioning of what the family says, depending on how they see such doubts.

Class teacher's note, Monday
Tushar has missed PE twice this month and sits in the back row with his hood up. Some staff have called him lazy and moody. Today he snapped at a classmate who was drumming on the desk, then put his head down. When I spoke to him privately, he said he gets headaches most days, and when he told his coach, he was told, "It's nothing, toughen up." He looked close to tears saying it. I told him I believed him and that pain like that deserves a proper check. With his permission I called his mother this afternoon; she hadn't realised how often it was happening and is booking him with their doctor this week. I've asked staff to let him sit away from the window glare for now.
Vinita

Where does Tushar sit in class?
In the back row, with his hood up.
What did Tushar feel when his coach said "It's nothing, toughen up"?
He felt hurt and dismissed, close to tears, as if his pain did not count.
What made Vinita's response helpful?
Vinita believed him, spoke privately, told his mother the same day so he could see a doctor, and eased the glare in class.
How might Tushar's mother feel after the call?
Surprised and concerned, not having realised how often the headaches came.

Dear Tarun Sir,
I'm writing about something happening in our class chat group. Since Monday, some people have been posting mocking comments and edited pictures about Sabeena, mostly about her weight and her voice. I haven't added anything or passed any of it on.
On Tuesday I messaged Sabeena privately to ask if she was okay. She said she hadn't eaten lunch in two days because she didn't want to sit in the canteen. I have saved screenshots of the messages, with names and times, in a folder on my phone.
Sabeena is scared to come to you alone, but she has agreed to come with me. Could we both meet you tomorrow before assembly?
Gurleen, 9B

Reply, 6:40 pm, same day:
Gurleen, thank you. You did exactly the right thing. I have called Sabeena's parents this evening. Please both come to the staffroom at 7:45 tomorrow and bring the screenshots.
T. Singh

When does Tarun Sir ask them to come?
At 7:45 tomorrow, to the staffroom, with the screenshots.
What might Gurleen be worried about in writing the email?
Gurleen is worried about Sabeena skipping lunch and being scared, and wants help to come quickly.
What else could Gurleen do in the class group itself?
Stay out of it and not react, and perhaps quietly ask a few classmates not to forward anything.
How might Sabeena feel about going to the teacher with Gurleen?
Sabeena may still feel scared, but less alone, since a classmate stands beside her and has already gathered proof.

Read this:

Dear Ujjwal,
You asked how we finally got Dadu's pension restarted. Here's how, in case your family ever needs it.
His pension stopped in March because of a "verification issue." We went to the office five times. Each time, a different clerk said, "Come next week."
So I stopped arguing. I wrote a formal complaint to the pension office, listing every visit, date and name, and his pension number. I sent it by registered post and kept the receipt. Then I filed an RTI asking the status of his file and the reason for the stop.
It took six weeks. The reply said a form had been misfiled. They fixed it, and paid the arrears.
Dadu cried when the money came. Not because of the money, he said, but because someone had listened.
The secret, Ujjwal, is copies, dates and patience.
Chinmay

When did Dadu's pension stop?
His pension stopped in March because of a "verification issue."
How did Dadu feel when the money came?
Dadu cried, feeling moved and relieved that someone had listened, not just about the money.
What made Chinmay's complaint effective?
Chinmay stopped arguing, wrote a detailed formal complaint sent by registered post with a receipt, and filed an RTI, politely insisting on the process.
How might Ujjwal use this letter?
Ujjwal might keep it as a guide in case his own family faces a similar delay.

1) Is the road to the airport clear today?
2) Why do airports check bags?
3) A car goes 4 kilometres in one hour. How far does it go in 4 hours?

1. I don't know, because I can't see live traffic. Check a map with traffic or ask the local police.
2. To keep passengers safe. Because they look for dangerous things before anyone boards.
3. 16 kilometres. Because 4 x 4 = 16.

Class 4 note, Thursday

Sabina got 7 out of 10 in the maths test. When I handed it back, she went pale and asked if she could take it home tomorrow instead of today. I asked why. She said quietly, "Mummy only smiles when it's ten. If it's seven she'll be sad with me." Later I found the paper in the classroom dustbin.

Sabina is a careful, bright child. The mark is fine. But she seems to believe that her mother's love depends on it.

I kept her back after school, told her that seven is a good mark and that mistakes are how we learn. I also called her mother this evening, gently, to share what Sabina said. Her mother was quiet, then said she hadn't realised. We'll meet next week.

— Sangeeta

What mark did Sabina get in the maths test?
7 out of 10.
Why did Sabina throw the paper in the dustbin?
She felt afraid and ashamed, believing her mother would be sad with her and only smiles at full marks.
What steps did Sangeeta take, and why were they helpful?
Sangeeta reassured Sabina that seven is good and called her mother the same evening, so the belief could be addressed at home too.
How might Sabina's mother feel after the call?
Her mother may feel shocked and sad, not having realised how her reactions made Sabina feel.

Read this:

Friday. At dinner Sunaina's father Vikas announced that a match was "more or less fixed" and that the wedding would follow once her posting in Bhopal ended. Sunaina's rice went cold. "I would like to talk about this, Papa," she said. "What is there to discuss?" he replied.

Sunday. On the terrace she told her mother and her aunt that she was not refusing marriage; she wanted a say in whom and when. Her aunt said, "I will speak to your father."

Next Saturday. Sunaina asked her father to hear her for ten minutes without interrupting: two years to finish her fellowship, then she would gladly meet families. Vikas was silent a while. "Two years? Let me talk to your mother." She had no yes, but she had a maybe, and she had not shouted.

What did Sunaina ask her father for on Saturday?
She asked him to hear her for ten minutes without interrupting.
What was Sunaina feeling when her rice went cold?
Sunaina was shocked and pinned between love for her family and her own wishes.
How did Sunaina gather support?
She talked to her mother and her aunt on the terrace, and her aunt offered to speak to her father.
How might Vikas be seeing the situation?
Vikas assumed the match was settled and saw little to discuss, but his "let me talk to your mother" shows he is starting to listen.

"So are you going to apply to the science camp?" Jahnavi asked, putting the form on the table.
"Maybe." Akash raised one eyebrow at the paper.
"That's your third maybe this week."
"I know." He picked at the corner of the form. "The others have done coding for years. I'll be the one who doesn't know anything."
"Is it that you don't want to go, or that you're scared it'll go badly?"
He thought about it. "Scared, I think. But also I'm not sure it's even the right camp."
"Both of those are worth looking at. I won't push. Shall we read the syllabus together tonight and list what worries you?"
"Okay." He almost smiled. "Maybe that helps."

What does Jahnavi say about Akash's maybe this week?
Jahnavi says it's Akash's third maybe this week.
What might Akash be feeling about the science camp?
He is probably nervous about not knowing enough compared with the others, and also unsure about whether it suits him, so his doubt mixes fear and careful thinking.
What could Jahnavi and Akash do next?
They could read the syllabus together and list his worries, sorting the fears from the real questions before he decides.
Why might Jahnavi's choice not to push matter to Akash?
Pressure could make him feel he had to say yes to please Jahnavi, while open discussion lets him work out what he really thinks. 🙂
Bank ki line mein agar koi beech mein ghus jaye toh kya bolun?
Say: "Excuse me, the line starts there. Could you please join the end of it?"
