Last semester I won the college pitch contest with an idea for passing textbooks from seniors to juniors. I was proud. I told everyone, even my mother, that it came to me on a night bus. Two months later I was clearing out old voice notes and found one from Gargi, from our first week of college: "What if seniors just passed their books down, like a library, but between people?" I sat on my bed and played it four times. I had no memory of hearing it, yet there was my own reply: "Hmm, maybe." I called Gargi that night, embarrassed, and told her. Now I keep a notes file where I write down who said what. I'm still Madhav, who pitched it, but I'm no longer the only one who thought of it.

What did Madhav find among the old voice notes?
A voice note from Gargi from the first week of college: "What if seniors just passed their books down, like a library, but between people?"
How did Madhav feel after playing the voice note four times?
Madhav felt stunned and embarrassed: there was no memory of hearing the idea, yet Madhav's own reply was on the recording.
What habit did Madhav take up, and why does it help?
A notes file recording who said what, so ideas keep their sources and honest credit is easy to give.
How might Gargi feel when Madhav calls?
Gargi may feel surprised and a little hurt at first, but also respected, because Madhav owned up to it.

The college auditorium had been decorated with the old batch photo blown up huge on the stage, and Kishore stood under it holding a paper cup of juice. Five years since graduation. Around him, the talk moved fast. Hansa had just come back from a master's in Berlin. Two friends had a startup with an office. Someone showed wedding photos, someone else a new car key. "And you, Kishore? Still at the bank branch?" Hansa asked, kindly enough. "Yes," he said, and heard how small it sounded. A month ago he'd been proud of his promotion to assistant manager. Now it felt like standing still while everyone else ran. He laughed at the right moments and clapped for the slideshow, but his chest felt tight. On the drive home, he didn't turn the radio on.

Where had Hansa just come back from?
Hansa had just come back from a master's in Berlin.
How did Kishore feel when he answered Hansa's question?
Kishore felt small and suddenly behind, with a tight chest, although he had been proud of his promotion a month ago.
What could help Kishore after this reunion?
He could remind himself what he valued about his own path and talk honestly with a friend, remembering that a reunion shows others' highlights, not their whole lives.
How might Hansa have meant the question about the bank branch?
Hansa probably meant it kindly, as simple catching up, without realising how it landed after all the talk of degrees and startups.

In Belgrade, the software company planned to replace the free lunch with an equal amount of flexible hours. HR's Vera sent an email: "Great news, you'll gain two flexible hours a week!" Within an hour, angry messages flooded in. "You're taking away our lunch?" Ivan, who worked in the same team, noticed something. The flexible hours were worth the same, maybe more. But nobody wanted to lose what they already had. He went to Vera's desk. "People cling to the lunch much more than they want the new hours. Maybe say what stays the same first, and be honest about what's going." They rewrote it together: "Your total benefits stay the same. Lunch will end in March. In return, two flexible hours weekly." The next day, questions were calmer. Some people even said they preferred the hours.

What did the company plan to replace the free lunch with?
An equal amount of flexible hours.
How did Ivan seem to feel reading the angry messages?
Ivan seemed thoughtful and curious rather than annoyed, noticing that people reacted to the loss more than the gain.
Why was the rewritten message better?
It began with what was protected and honestly named what was ending, so people felt less threatened and could compare fairly.
How might Vera feel after the rewritten email?
Vera probably felt relieved and grateful for Ivan's help as the reactions calmed.

Note from Sharmila, playgroup teacher, Wednesday:

Today Gurpreet, two, noticed his face in the low mirror. He looked, then touched the paint on his own nose and giggled. "Gurpreet!" he said, pointing at himself. Later, when a friend took his blue truck, he held on and said, "Mine!" twice.

What I did next: I said, "Yes, that's you in the mirror," and gave him a turn timer for the truck. His mother may enjoy hearing about the mirror 🙂

What was on Gurpreet's nose when he looked in the mirror?
He had paint on his nose, and he touched it and giggled.
How did Gurpreet seem to feel when a friend took his blue truck?
He seemed upset and protective, holding on and saying "Mine!" twice.
What did Sharmila do that supports this stage well?
She confirmed he was seeing himself and used a turn timer, respecting his sense of "mine" while teaching turns.
How might Gurpreet's mother feel reading this note?
She would likely enjoy hearing that her son is starting to recognise himself 🙂

The power cut came ten minutes into the meeting, and monsoon rain hammered the tin awning over the Nagpur flat. Kavitha, twenty-one, sat in the candlelit hall with her parents on one side and Vikram's parents on the other. The visitors' train left at nine. Vikram's sister Sarika lit a second candle and whispered, "Ask him everything, we haven't got long." Kavitha did: would he mind her keeping her teaching post, who cooked at his house, what he did when he was angry. Vikram answered without glancing at his parents. When the taxi honked outside, Kavitha said, "I'd like to meet once more, just the two of us over chai, before I say yes or no." "And if it's no, that's an honest answer," Vikram said. Both mothers, surprised, nodded.

What happened ten minutes into the meeting?
The power cut came, and monsoon rain hammered the tin awning over the Nagpur flat.
What might Kavitha be feeling as she asks about her teaching post and his temper?
She is determined and serious, wanting to know the real person before deciding. She is probably a little nervous too, but she spends the short time on questions rather than politeness.
What choice did Kavitha make when the taxi honked, and why did it help?
She asked for a second meeting, just the two of them, before answering. It gave time and a chance to talk freely, and let both say plainly whether they want to go on.
How does Vikram seem to see Kavitha's request for another meeting?
He accepts it calmly and treats a no as an honest answer, so he sees the match as a decision for both of them.

In the sandpit of a São Paulo park, Priscila, five, had the red dump truck. Yesterday Sami had let her use his bucket all afternoon. Now Sami toddled over. Priscila pushed the truck straight to him. "Your turn!" Then Lucas came, the boy who never let anyone touch his digger. He reached for the truck. Priscila pulled it back. "No. You don't share." Lucas stamped. Priscila crossed her arms. "When you share, I share." She went back to building a sand road with Sami.

Who had let Priscila use his bucket yesterday?
Sami had let her use his bucket all afternoon.
What was Priscila feeling when she pulled the truck back from Lucas?
Priscila felt it was unfair and a little cross, remembering that Lucas never let anyone touch his digger.
What could a parent say to help all three children?
A parent could praise Priscila for sharing with Sami and suggest Lucas try sharing his digger, so everyone sees how sharing works both ways.
How might Lucas feel when Priscila said no?
Lucas felt frustrated and left out, stamping his foot, maybe not yet understanding why.

The truck for the Hyderabad order was due at the factory gate in two hours when Jyoti found it: the safety valves on batch 14 were sticking in the pressure test, eleven out of forty. She took the report to Farida, the production manager. Farida glanced at it. 'Mark the batch passed. We'll fix it in the next lot. If this order misses the truck, we lose the client.' Jyoti felt her hands go cold. 'I understand the instruction,' she said. 'But I'm the one signing the test sheet, and I'm responsible for what I sign. I can't mark it passed.' 'Then it's on you.' 'It is. That's why I'm raising it.' She emailed the quality head and the compliance officer with the test data, copying Farida. Within forty minutes the compliance officer, Mr Nair, came down to the floor himself, held batch 14, and told dispatch to send the other three batches on the truck.

How many valves on batch 14 were sticking?
Eleven out of forty were sticking.
What did Jyoti feel when told to mark the batch passed, and what shows it?
She felt alarmed and tense, her hands going cold, yet she stayed steady in refusing.
Why did Jyoti's response work?
She acknowledged the instruction, owned her signature, and raised it with the quality head and compliance officer with data, so the right people could act.
How might Farida feel after Mr Nair holds the batch?
Farida may feel frustrated about the order but also relieved not to be responsible for faulty valves reaching customers.
I have to wear a tie for an interview and I've never tied one.
It's a skill you can learn in one evening. Look for a step-by-step picture or video, and practise with the tie on a chair back first, so you are not rushing in front of the mirror.
I tried but one end is always much longer than the other.

That is common at the start. The wide end should hang a little lower than the narrow end, so begin with the wide end well below the narrow one and adjust from there. A few tries will show you the right starting point.
Got it. Should I practise a few times before the day?
Yes, three or four tries on separate evenings will help. By interview day, your hands will remember the steps and you can think about the conversation instead.
I'll do that. Any advice for the first minute of the interview?
Smile, say good morning, and give a firm but friendly hello. Keep your first answer short and clear. A calm start sets the tone for the rest.

Moon Over Water

Tuesday
Got 21 out of 80 in the Maths unit test. Again. Binita Ma'am said, "Ask yourself why, and keep asking." So tonight I tried it.
Why did I fail? Couldn't do the quadratic questions.
Why? Kept getting the factorising wrong.
Why? The minus signs and fractions mess me up.
Why? I never really got how negatives and fractions work with letters.
Why? Class 8. I copied the algebra homework from Sonu all year because I didn't understand it and was too scared to ask.
So it's not quadratics. It's Class 8. I've been building on a hole. Weirdly, that's a relief. Tomorrow I'm finding my old Class 8 book and starting with fractions, even if it feels babyish.
Pradeep

What did Pradeep score in the Maths unit test?
21 out of 80.
Why does Pradeep find the answer a relief?
Pradeep feels relieved because the problem finally has a clear, fixable cause, gaps from Class 8, rather than being hopeless at Maths.
What would you add to Pradeep's plan?
Tell Binita Ma'am about the Class 8 gap, so she can suggest which basics to practise first and check progress.
How might Binita Ma'am feel if Pradeep shares this?
Binita Ma'am would likely be pleased that the advice worked and that the real gap is now known, making it easier to help.

messages.content: When do I use "your" and when "you're"?

"Your" shows that something belongs to you. "You're" is short for "you are". If you can say "you are" in the sentence, write "you're".
Example: You're welcome to borrow your cousin's cycle tomorrow.

Supervisor's note on Nikita's seedling experiment.
The fifth run failed today, like the four before it. Nikita did not repeat it. She changed one detail each time: soil moisture after the second run, the hour of measuring after the third, the lamp distance after the fourth.
I asked why she keeps going. She said the first two runs both leaned the same way, so the effect is probably real and each failure tells her which detail to fix. She writes down what she changed and why, every evening.
I have given her the second growth room for next week and asked nothing else of her. I'll read the log on Friday.

What did Nikita change after the third run?
Nikita changed the hour of measuring after the third run.
How does Nikita seem to feel after five failed runs?
Nikita seems patient and hopeful, believing the effect is probably real since the first two runs leaned the same way.
What could Nikita try if the effect still did not show after many more changes?
Nikita could ask a colleague to run the same setup independently, since another pair of hands would show whether the problem lies in the method or in the idea.
How does the supervisor see Nikita's way of working?
The supervisor sees careful, patient work, and shows it by giving Nikita the second growth room and planning to read the log on Friday.

Read this:

Ankita, sit. You're angry with your mother about the phone rule, I know. Let me tell you something about her. When your mother was fifteen, she lied to me about a school trip and went to the beach with friends. I was furious. I locked away her radio, stopped her going out for three months, and read every letter that came to the house. I thought I was teaching her honesty. What I actually taught her was to post her letters from her friend's house and to smile at me at dinner. She told me years later, after you were born. I had wanted to know why she lied. I never asked. Your grandpa Francis was strict, but not very wise. Don't tell your mother I said so.

What did Francis lock away?
He locked away her radio.
What did Francis think he was teaching his daughter?
Furious at her lie, he thought he was teaching her honesty, but she learnt to hide things better instead.
What does Francis wish he had done differently?
He wishes he had asked why she lied instead of only punishing, since he never learnt the reason.
How might Ankita's mother have felt during those three months?
She probably felt watched and resentful, so she kept up smiles at dinner while quietly posting letters from her friend's house.
My boss's email asked for the "updation" of the file. Is that an English word?

"Updation" is used in Indian English, but standard English does not use it. Say "update" instead: "the update of the file" or "please update the file".
Example: Please update the file by Monday.

Dear Damini,
You asked why I crossed the road yesterday when the constable was standing at the corner. Honest answer: since I saw an officer shove the fruit-seller near our market last month, every uniform feels like a warning. I tense up before anyone has done anything. But yesterday I watched that same constable for a while. He walked a lost old woman to the bus stand and held the traffic for her. That doesn't cancel what I saw, and I'll still be careful. But I don't want to treat everyone as a threat when some are doing their job properly. I'm still working it out. Tell me what you think.
Tanvir

What did Tanvir see an officer do last month?
Tanvir saw an officer shove the fruit-seller near the market.
How does Tanvir feel about uniforms, and how is that feeling shifting?
Tanvir tenses up at every uniform as if it were a warning, but seeing the constable help a lost old woman makes Tanvir unwilling to treat everyone as a threat.
How can Tanvir stay careful without hating everyone?
By judging each officer by what they actually do, staying alert and polite, and remembering that one bad moment is not every officer.
How might Damini feel on receiving this letter?
Probably trusted and thoughtful, since Tanvir shares a hard feeling openly and asks what Damini thinks.

"Swati, I want to move to the new AI team," Anand said, closing the door.
Swati looked up from her screen. "Now? The launch is in three weeks."
"I know. That's why I'm telling you now, not just asking HR."
"The team needs you."
"And I won't leave them stuck. I'll stay through the launch, and I'll train Priya on the payment module before I go."
"Why this team?"
"Because it's what I want to learn. I've been doing the same work for two years. I don't want to be bored and bitter in another two."
Swati leaned back. "Fair. What if the launch slips?"
"Then I'll stay till it's done. You tell me honestly if I'm leaving a gap."
Swati nodded slowly. "Write me a handover plan. Then I'll talk to their manager."

How long is it until the launch?
Three weeks.
What was Anand feeling when explaining the reasons?
Anand felt determined to grow but also responsible towards the team, not wanting to leave them stuck.
What did Anand do that balanced independence with duty?
Anand explained reasons, offered to stay through the launch and train Priya, and asked Swati to say honestly if there was a gap.
How does Swati see Anand's request by the end?
Swati sees it as fair and responsible, and agrees to help if Anand writes a handover plan.

The bus broke down two stops early, so Ganga ran the last stretch and reached the clinic with four minutes to spare, out of breath and clutching a crumpled appointment slip. Inside, Dr Farhan asked, "What brings you in?" Ganga had rehearsed a line all week: "Just a bit of gaming, some late nights." The words sat in the air, only half true. Ganga's palms were damp. Then, quietly: "It's more than that. Some nights I play until the sun comes up. I missed two lab sessions." Dr Farhan nodded and wrote something down. "Thank you for telling me that. And if there's a slip next week, come back anyway." Ganga's shoulders dropped for the first time that day, and a shaky laugh came out.

Why did Ganga have to run to the clinic?
The bus broke down two stops early.
Why were Ganga's palms damp before speaking?
Ganga was nervous about admitting the whole problem, and the rehearsed line was only half true.
What would you advise Ganga to do if a slip happens next week?
Go back to Dr Farhan anyway, as invited, and stay honest about what happened.
How might Dr Farhan have seen Ganga's first answer compared with the second?
The first gave only a softer half of the story, while the second gave the doctor the real picture to work with, and Dr Farhan answered with thanks.

Every Monday in the glass meeting room above the Pune print shop, Imran's lips did the same thing. Ms. Kapoor would add another Saturday shoot to the calendar, and his mouth would press into a thin line while his head nodded. At the tea stall downstairs, Shreya handed him a cutting chai. "You do this thing," she said, pressing her own lips flat to show him. "Every week. Is it the Saturdays?" Imran laughed, caught out. "Fourth one this month. I keep thinking it's not worth a fuss." "It's a fuss inside you anyway," Shreya said. The next Monday, when a fifth Saturday appeared, Imran breathed out and spoke. "Before we lock that in, four Saturdays in a row is wearing the team down. Could we rotate who covers them?" Ms. Kapoor paused, then pulled up a rota.

Where did Imran and Shreya have tea?
At the tea stall downstairs.
What might Imran have been feeling when his lips pressed into a thin line while he nodded?
He was probably frustrated and tired of the Saturday shoots but held it back to avoid a fuss; the nod might also have been partial agreement mixed with reluctance.
How did Imran raise the concern, and why did it work?
He named the issue calmly before the date was locked and offered a fix, a rota, so Ms. Kapoor could respond without feeling attacked.
How did Shreya see Imran's pressed lips?
Shreya read them as a sign something bothered him each week and gently asked about it instead of assuming he agreed.
Describe the sound of a thunderstorm arriving over a village, around 70 words.

First, the wind rises and shakes the leaves. Dogs bark, and mothers call the children inside. Then a low rumble rolls across the fields, like a giant moving furniture in the sky. The thunder grows louder until the windows rattle. A flash of light lights up the lane, and big drops begin to fall on the tin roofs. Soon the whole village is filled with the loud, happy sound of rain.

Class teacher's note, Class 6B, Thursday.

Darshan joined us from a school in Surat three weeks ago. He often says, "At my old school, everyone was nice. We never had fights." Today he said it after a small quarrel over a cricket ball with Vijay.

I asked him gently, "Never any fights at all?" He thought and said, "Well... once a boy broke my kite." Then he smiled a little.

I think Darshan misses his friends and the old school feels perfect from far away. I've paired him with Vijay for the science project, and I'll check in with him again next week.

Who did Darshan quarrel with over a cricket ball?
Vijay.
Why might Darshan say everyone at his old school was nice?
He probably feels lonely and misses his friends, so the old school seems perfect and the fights have faded.
What did the teacher do to help Darshan settle in?
The teacher paired him with Vijay for the science project and plans to check in next week.
How might Vijay feel hearing that Darshan's old school never had fights?
Vijay might feel a bit hurt or annoyed, as if he's being compared unfairly.

Oskar was halfway through a friend's holiday photos when he caught himself sighing at his own Berlin flat: the one radiator, the crooked shelf, the view of the tram depot. Beach in Portugal. Rooftop dinner. New car. His thumb kept moving. He put the phone face down on the table. Elif, his flatmate, looked up from her laptop. 'You've got the face again.' 'Yeah.' He tried something his old football coach used to say: compare yourself with who you were. Two years ago he had been sleeping on his brother's sofa in Hamburg, with no contract. Now he had a job he liked and a room with a door. 'Honestly,' he said, 'this flat is fine. It's not a beach. It isn't meant to be.' Elif grinned and pushed the biscuit tin towards him.

Where had Oskar been sleeping two years earlier?
On his brother's sofa in Hamburg.
What was Oskar feeling while scrolling the holiday photos?
Oskar felt dissatisfied and a bit envious, sighing at his flat's single radiator and crooked shelf.
What small step broke the spell of the photos for Oskar?
Putting the phone face down and comparing his life with his own past, not with friends' best moments.
How does Elif see Oskar's change of mood?
Elif spots 'the face again' and is glad to see him settle; pushing the biscuit tin over shows warmth and relief.

Dear Bidisha,
You asked why I've been so slow replying lately. It's not you, I promise. I've changed how I use social media, and I want to explain before you think I'm ignoring you.
I noticed I was checking it about forty times a day, even in the middle of maths homework. It was in charge of me, instead of me being in charge of it. So now I have two windows: 7:30 to 8 in the evening, and fifteen minutes after lunch on weekends. That's when I check, reply and post. I've turned off all notifications except calls, so the phone doesn't pull at me in between.
During exam weeks I'm nearly offline. Just the class group once a day for homework updates.
It felt strange at first. Now I actually like knowing I'll see everything at 7:30.
So if I don't reply for a few hours, I'm not upset. I'll get back to you at 7:30.
Jeevan

When is Jeevan's evening window?
7:30 to 8 in the evening.
How does Jeevan feel about the new routine now?
Jeevan felt strange at first, but now enjoys it and feels in control rather than pulled.
What else could Jeevan add to make the windows easier to keep?
Keep the phone in another room outside the windows, so there's no temptation to check early.
How might Bidisha feel after reading the letter?
Bidisha would likely feel reassured that the slow replies aren't personal, and maybe curious to try it.

Summarize this Mahabharata scene in about three sentences.

When everyone had failed, Drona smilingly called Arjuna and said unto him, 'By thee the aim must be shot; therefore, turn thy eyes to it. Thou must let fly the arrow as soon as I give the order. Therefore, O son, stand here with bow and arrow for an instant.' Thus addressed, Arjuna stood aiming at the bird as desired by his preceptor, with his bow bent. An instant after Drona asked him as in the case of others, 'Seest thou, O Arjuna, the bird there, the tree, and myself?' Arjuna replied, 'I see the bird only, but nor the tree, or thyself.' Then the irrepressible Drona, well-pleased with Arjuna, the instant after, again said unto that mighty car-warrior amongst the Pandavas, 'If thou seest the vulture, then describe it to me.' Arjuna said, I see only the head of the vulture, not its body.' At these words of Arjuna, the hair (on Drona's body) stood on end from delight. He then said to Partha, 'Shoot.' And the latter instantly let fly (his arrow) and with his sharp shaft speedily struck off the head of the vulture on the tree and brought it down to the ground. No sooner was the deed done than Drona clasped Phalguna to his bosom and thought Drupada with his friends had already been vanquished in fight.

Drona tests Arjuna by asking what he sees while aiming at a bird on a tree. Arjuna says he sees only the bird, and then only its head. Drona tells him to shoot, Arjuna knocks the bird down, and the delighted Drona hugs him.
Describe a flower market just before a festival, in about 90 words.

The flower market is a flood of colour. Heaps of orange marigolds, white jasmine and red roses lie in baskets on the ground. Women thread garlands quickly, their fingers busy and quick. The scent is so strong that it makes you dizzy. Buyers bargain loudly, and sellers shout the price of a metre of flowers. A boy carries a huge sack of petals on his head. Bees buzz around in the morning light. Every stall seems to say that the festival will be beautiful.

Since her father's shop in Sirsa closed, Ishita had stopped going to evening badminton. At home there was only silence and the ceiling fan, and her Class 11 marks had slipped.
Then Mona didi noticed her outside the new dance studio near the bus stand. "You look like someone carrying a heavy bag," she said, and let Ishita join for free. The girls there called each other sister. They remembered her name, asked about her exams, bought her lassi after practice. On Sundays they sat in a circle while Mona didi talked about "real discipline" and "finding your purpose when the world forgets you".
Ishita walked home those evenings feeling taller than she had in months. Nobody had asked her for anything. That was the strange, good part.
Her cousin Irfan noticed she now said "sister" in every sentence. "Who are these people?" he asked.
"Just friends," she said, and smiled as if she meant it.

What did the girls at the studio call each other?
Sister.
Why did Ishita walk home feeling taller?
She felt seen and valued for the first time in months, after the loneliness and silence at home since the shop closed.
What might a trusted adult do at this stage?
Notice Ishita's loneliness, spend time with her, and ask gently about the group and its Sunday talks, without mocking it.
What might Irfan be sensing when he asks 'Who are these people?'
Irfan senses a sudden change in his cousin and feels curious and a little uneasy about a group he knows nothing about.

Read this:

Parul, you asked how I knew when to stop tiptoeing. When I was twenty-four I was engaged to Vinod. One week he'd send me poems and turn up at the bank with jasmine. The next he'd vanish, and when I called he'd say, "Why are you always after me?" I learned to watch his face before I spoke, to weigh every word. I stopped seeing my friends in case he needed me. My turning point was small: I fell ill with worry before an exam, and lying in that clinic I thought, I'm disappearing. I told him I loved him and that I'd keep my Sunday walks with my friends, no matter what. And I asked him, gently, to see a counsellor. We didn't marry, but I kept myself. That's Vandana-masi's one lesson.

What did Vinod bring to the bank?
Jasmine.
What was young Vandana feeling while she watched Vinod's face before speaking?
She felt anxious and confused, always on guard and afraid of setting off his coldness.
What was the turning point in the story?
Falling ill before an exam made her see she was disappearing, so she kept her friends and asked Vinod to see a counsellor.
How might Vinod have felt when Vandana kept her Sunday walks?
Vinod may have felt unsettled or hurt, but also met a steady limit instead of her tiptoeing.

Monday night
NSS review meeting today about the blood donation camp that got only eleven donors. Within five minutes everyone was saying, "Obviously nobody comes during mid-sems, Vikas should have known." Vikas kept staring at the table.
I almost joined in. Then I remembered: when he proposed the date in August, the mid-sem schedule wasn't even out. The exam cell posted it three weeks later. And last year's camp in the same week had forty donors.
So I said that. Out loud. My voice shook a little. I asked, "What did we actually know when we picked the date?" It went quiet, then Pooja said, "Nothing about exams." We ended up making a rule to check the academic calendar before fixing dates, instead of blaming Vikas.
He messaged me later: "thanks." Just that.
Avni

How many donors came to the camp?
Only eleven donors.
How did Avni feel speaking up in the meeting?
Avni felt nervous, with a shaking voice, but also uneasy about Vikas being blamed for something no one could have known in August.
What rule came out of the meeting, and why is it more useful than blame?
Checking the academic calendar before fixing dates, which prevents the problem next time without punishing a choice made before the schedule was out.
What might the one-word thanks say about how Vikas felt?
Vikas probably felt relieved and grateful that someone stood up for him, even if he didn't have words for more.
What usually happens to seeds that are planted but never watered?
Most of them will not grow. Because seeds need water to soften and sprout, and young plants dry out and die without it.

Wrap up this text in two sentences.

"I noted, in passing, that she had written a note before leaving home but after being fully dressed. You observed that her right glove was torn at the forefinger, but you did not apparently see that both glove and finger were stained with violet ink. She had written in a hurry and dipped her pen too deep. It must have been this morning, or the mark would not remain clear upon the finger. All this is amusing, though rather elementary, but I must go back to business, Watson. Would you mind reading me the advertised description of Mr. Hosmer Angel?"

The speaker notes that the woman wrote a note after dressing, because her torn glove and finger were stained with violet ink. The mark is still clear, so the note was written this morning, and the speaker asks Watson to read the advertised description of Mr. Hosmer Angel.

Tejas, it's Keerthana. Every notice date goes into my phone calendar the minute the letter arrives, and I add a second reminder a week before. That's the whole trick, honestly.
I used to feel my chest tighten whenever a notice landed. Once, a due date crept up on me because I'd put the paper on the fridge and forgot it. Since then, I keep a folder on my laptop called "Notices". Each reply I send gets scanned and saved there, with the date in the file name.
Last month a new notice came. I found last year's reply in two minutes, checked the date in the calendar, and answered in an hour.
It's boring. But boring is what I wanted.

What is the name of Keerthana's folder?
The folder is called "Notices".
How did Keerthana feel when notices used to arrive?
Keerthana's chest tightened, which shows fear and pressure that the calendar and folder later eased.
What could Keerthana do if a notice needs documents that are not in the folder?
Keerthana could add a list of usual documents to the folder and ask the office or a qualified person about what is missing.
Why might Tejas have wanted to hear how Keerthana handles notices?
Tejas may have wanted a simple habit to copy, since Keerthana calls it a boring trick that works.

Monday: Gautam, ten, played a racing game on his phone until midnight. At school he fell asleep in maths. His friend Devika poked him awake.
Wednesday: His mother made a deal: games only after homework, one hour, phone charges in the kitchen at nine. Gautam grumbled and slammed his door.
Saturday: Devika called him to the park for cricket. He went, and they played until dark. That night he slept by ten without meaning to. "Cricket's better than the racing game," he admitted to Devika. "Don't tell my mum."

Where does the phone charge at nine?
In the kitchen.
How did Gautam feel when his mother made the deal?
He felt annoyed and resentful, grumbling and slamming his door.
What helped Gautam balance games with play and sleep?
Clear limits at home and a friend inviting him to play outside.
How might Devika feel when Gautam says cricket is better?
Devika likely feels happy and a little triumphant.

At 11 p.m. on Thursday, Kavitha opened the folder for the essay due Friday at nine. Fear, finally, was loud enough to move her. She drank tea, typed until the birds started, and hit submit at 8:41. Her eyes stung and the last two pages were thin, but it was done, and she got a B-plus. That result whispered to her that leaving it late was fine.

By Sunday the mood had soured. "I'm so lazy," she told herself, folding laundry with her jaw tight. "Never again." Every ugly word made the next assignment feel heavier, and when her roommate Sumit asked about the next paper she changed the subject. She would start on Monday, she promised, and the promise slid away like the last one.

The next Wednesday, Sarita texted: "Library, 4pm? Just sit with me." Kavitha went. She set her phone timer for ten minutes and wrote one messy paragraph, bad on purpose, full of gaps. The timer rang. She kept typing. By six she had two pages, some awful, but all hers. Walking home, she noticed she was not dreading tomorrow the way she had for weeks.

What time did Kavitha submit the essay on Friday morning?
She hit submit at 8:41.
How did the all-nighter and the library session differ in how they got the work started, and what did the earlier self-blame add?

The all-nighter was driven by fear and ended with stress and thin pages, while the library session started with a ten-minute timer and a deliberately messy paragraph; the earlier self-blame had made the next task feel heavier.
What was Kavitha feeling on Sunday while folding laundry with her jaw tight?
She felt ashamed and frustrated with herself, calling herself lazy and vowing to change.
What made the library session easier to start than the overnight sprint?
She lowered the bar to one messy paragraph, worked beside Sarita, and used a short timer, so the dread eased and momentum did the rest.

In a classroom in Seville, Senora Ruiz held up a picture of a snail. "Who knows what this is?" Javier, five, bounced off his chair. "CARACOL! I know! I know!" Valentina kept her hand high and still, though her fingers wiggled. Senora Ruiz smiled at Javier. "Back on your chair, please. Hands up." Javier flopped down, arms folded, and kicked the table leg. "Not fair, I said it first." She called on Valentina, who said, "A snail, and it's slow." When the next picture came up, Javier's hand shot up, and he kept himself on his chair.

What picture did Senora Ruiz hold up first?
A picture of a snail.
Why did Javier kick the table leg?
He felt it was unfair because he had said the answer first, and he was cross at being asked to sit and wait.
What could Senora Ruiz try to help children like Javier wait their turn?
Give a quiet signal, like a thumb on the chest when they know the answer, and notice the first child who waits.
How might Valentina experience Javier's shouting?
She may feel her patient waiting goes unnoticed, so it matters that the teacher still chose her.

"Beep-beep-beep!"
"Lakshmi, don't stop now, we're about to win!"
"Sorry, Sonali. Timer's done."
"Your mother isn't even home. Nobody's watching."
"I know. It's my timer, not hers."

When will they play tomorrow?
At four-thirty.
How did Lakshmi feel stopping even though nobody was watching?
Calm and firm, a little sorry to stop but proud that the rule is her own.
What else could Lakshmi do if a level truly needs a few more minutes?
Save it for the next day's forty minutes, as she did, rather than stretching today's limit.
How does Sonali react?
Sonali is annoyed at first, calling Lakshmi weird, then agrees to start on time tomorrow.

Lokesh was twenty and leading a group of eight college volunteers at a flood relief camp in a small town in Assam. He set the plan each morning: two sorting supplies, three cooking, three with the local health team.
Irawati kept disappearing from the cooking shift. By day three, the others were grumbling. "Why do we cover for her?"
Lokesh found her sitting behind the school building, pale. "Irawati, what's going on?"
She admitted the smoke from the cooking fires gave her headaches and made her eyes stream, and she was embarrassed to say so when others were working so hard.
"You could've told me. Let's switch you to sorting supplies. Can you also keep the list of what we're short of?"
She did it brilliantly. At the evening meeting, Lokesh said only, "We've changed roles to fit people better," and the grumbling stopped.

How many volunteers was Lokesh leading?
A group of eight college volunteers.
How was Irawati feeling when Lokesh found her?
Irawati felt unwell and embarrassed, not wanting to complain while others worked hard.
Which of Lokesh's choices showed good team leadership?
He asked privately before blaming, moved Irawati to work that suited her, and explained the change to the team without exposing her.
How might the grumbling volunteers see Lokesh's explanation?
They might feel reassured that the workload was being handled fairly, even without knowing Irawati's reason.

Dear Sonali,
You'll laugh at this. Remember I told you my new manager, Mr Kurien, seemed annoyed with me? Short replies, no smiley in his emails, walked past my desk without saying hi. I spent the whole weekend imagining it. He thought my presentation was weak. He regretted hiring me. He was going to put me on a performance plan. I wrote imaginary replies in the shower.
On Monday I tried what you once told me: just ask. I knocked on his door and said, "Is something wrong with my work? I'd rather hear it directly." He looked genuinely puzzled. "Your work is fine. I've been dealing with a family thing. I'm sorry if I seemed short." It took two minutes. Two minutes, versus a whole weekend of arguments with someone who wasn't even arguing with me.
Thank you for the advice.
Farhan

Who was Farhan sure was annoyed with Farhan?
Farhan's new manager, Mr Kurien.
How did Farhan feel over the weekend, and what shows it?
Farhan felt anxious and insecure, imagining a weak presentation and a performance plan and even writing imaginary replies in the shower.
What did Farhan do that ended the worry?
Farhan knocked on the manager's door and asked directly whether something was wrong with the work.
What might Mr Kurien feel after Farhan's question?
He seemed puzzled and a little sorry, realising his short replies were being read as displeasure while he dealt with a family matter.

Monday: Aditi waved a pack of glitter stickers. “Everyone's buying these. Decide now; there are only two left!” Irfan almost handed over his canteen money. Then he asked, “What's the reason I need them?” Aditi shrugged. He kept his money. Wednesday: After school, some older kids said, “Everyone climbs the old water tank. You have to do it today, or you're a baby. And don't tell anyone.” Irfan's heart raced. Everyone, today, don't tell: the same pushing as the stickers, only scarier. He said, “No,” walked back inside and told Rao Sir at the gate. Rao Sir went straight to the tank, sent the kids home and had the ladder chained that evening. Friday: The ladder stayed chained.

What did Rao Sir have done to the ladder?
He had the ladder chained that evening.
What was Irfan feeling when the older kids pushed the dare?
Irfan felt scared, his heart racing, and recognised the same pushing as with the stickers.
What did Irfan do on Wednesday, and why was it right?
He said no, went inside and told Rao Sir the same day, because a pushed dare and a secret should always be told to a trusted adult.
How did Aditi respond when Irfan asked the reason?
Aditi just shrugged, showing she had no real reason beyond “everyone” and hurry.
He do not came yesterday. Fix it please.
The correct sentence is: "He did not come yesterday."

Vikas waited until the Monday meeting room emptied. "Deepak, do you have five minutes about the weekend rota?" Deepak glanced at the clock but nodded. Vikas slid over a one-page table: weekend hours for each team over the last two months, his own team's column clearly the longest. "I think this got uneven without anyone meaning it," he said. "Could we rotate it, so each team takes every third weekend?" Deepak frowned at the numbers, tapped his pen and said he'd think about it. Walking back to his desk, Vikas noted the date and the conversation in his own log. It was unfair, but nobody was at risk and nothing dishonest was going on, so going over Deepak's head was not something he wanted to spend on this.

What did Vikas bring to Deepak in the meeting room?
A one-page table of weekend hours for each team over two months, with a suggestion to rotate the weekends.
How did Vikas feel about the rota, and why did he not go over Deepak's head?
Vikas was frustrated because the rota was unfair, but he saw no danger and nothing dishonest, so he decided escalating was not worth it.
What could Vikas do if Deepak does not change the rota?
Follow up after a week with the same numbers, ask what would make a rotation workable, and escalate only if a real safety or ethics issue appears.
How might Deepak see Vikas's table?
Deepak might feel a little challenged, but since it came privately with a workable alternative, it may feel more like help than an accusation.
My sister called the shopkeeper dishonest. Is that a big accusation?

Yes, it is a serious thing to say about someone. Dishonest means not truthful, ready to lie or cheat. It is an adjective. It is better to say it only when you are sure.
Example: The dishonest seller gave less change than he owed.

March: Arnab, sixteen, and his friend Jeevan argued about whether sixteen-year-olds should vote. Arnab said yes, loudly, without really knowing why. April: after a class debate, he read both sides and realised he'd only listened to people who agreed with him. He wrote his reasons down, and some of them didn't hold up. May: he still wasn't sure about voting at sixteen, but he'd decided what mattered to him: that people know their rights. He signed up to help older neighbours check their names on the voter list. "You changed your mind," said Jeevan. "No," said Arnab. "I made it up properly this time."

What did Arnab sign up to help with?
Helping older neighbours check their names on the voter list.
How did Arnab feel when he realised he'd only listened to people who agreed with him?
He felt uncomfortable and a bit embarrassed, which pushed him to think again.
What made Arnab's final choice stronger than his first opinion?
He weighed both sides, tested his reasons in writing and chose something concrete to act on.
How might Jeevan see Arnab's change?
He might be surprised and even respect how seriously Arnab thought it through.

Why do plastic bags harm animals in the sea?
Can you fix my sentence? I am waiting for the bus since twenty minutes.
How should I say sorry to a friend I upset?
Is it "independance" or "independence"?
Is "prophetic" a hard word? What does it mean?

1. Animals can swallow them or get tangled in them. Because plastic looks like food to some animals and does not break down in the water.
2. Correct form: I have been waiting for the bus for twenty minutes. Why: a continuing action needs the present perfect continuous; use "for" with time.
3. Say clearly what you did and that you are sorry, without adding excuses. Then listen to your friend and give them time.
4. It is "independence", ending in "-ence".
5. "Prophetic" is an adjective. It means telling or showing what will happen in the future.

Mridul used to sit on the counter of Nirmala's small grocery shop in Ranikhet after school, chattering about cricket and eating peanuts from the sack. This year he walked straight past with his earphones in, rolled his eyes when she asked about his day, and slammed the door of his room behind the shop. One evening she stood outside that door with a plate of pakoras, her throat tight. Had she done something wrong? The neighbour, weighing out sugar, said, "My son was the same at fifteen. They come back." So Nirmala stopped knocking and asking. She just left the pakoras on his desk and kept the shop light on late. Two weeks later Mridul drifted to the counter at closing time, sat down, and started talking about a girl in his class who was "so annoying". Nirmala kept counting coins and listened.

What did Nirmala leave on Mridul's desk?
The pakoras.
What was Nirmala feeling outside Mridul's door?
She felt hurt and anxious, throat tight, wondering if she had done something wrong.
What helped keep the door open?
Dropping the pressure of knocking and questions, while staying available with food and the shop light on late.
How might Mridul see his mother's questions this year?
He seems to want privacy and space, so questions may feel intrusive, even though he still comes back to talk.

Read this:

In the staffroom of the Nagpur school, Rukmini caught her reflection in the glass of the trophy cupboard and barely recognised it: jaw locked, brows pinched, mouth a hard line. In ten minutes she had to tell Ojas that the science fair plan he had presented as his own was mostly hers.
If she walked in with that face, he'd get defensive before she said a word.
She sat down, put her palms flat on the table, and breathed in for four counts, out for six. She let her shoulders drop away from her ears. She unclenched her back teeth. Again. By the fourth breath her forehead felt looser.
When Ojas came in, she said, "Can we talk about the fair plan? I think some of my part got lost." Her voice came out even. He blinked, then nodded. "Okay. Show me."

Where did Rukmini see her reflection?
She saw it in the glass of the trophy cupboard.
Why did Rukmini want to soften her face before Ojas came in?
Rukmini felt tense and angry that her work had been passed off, and she feared a hard face would make Ojas defensive before she even spoke.
What steps did Rukmini use to relax her face?
She put her palms flat, breathed in for four and out for six, let her shoulders drop and unclenched her back teeth, repeating it until her forehead loosened.
What would change if Rukmini had walked in with a locked jaw?
Ojas might have felt attacked and turned defensive at once, making a fair talk about the plan much harder.

Friday night.

Finally did the thing I kept postponing. I saved ten job listings for the role I want, data analyst, and put them side by side in a spreadsheet. Then I listed every skill they asked for. SQL: nine of ten. A spreadsheet tool: ten of ten. A charting tool: seven. Basic statistics: eight. Storytelling with data: five, though in different words.

Then I marked what I already have. Spreadsheets: yes. Statistics: half. SQL: no. Charting: no. So the gap is clear, and it's smaller than I feared. Anjali says to start with SQL because it's what most listings want. I signed up for a course that begins Monday and put one hour every evening in my diary.

The target has picked my study plan.

Salma

How many listings asked for SQL?
Nine of ten.
How does Salma feel about the size of the gap after comparing skills?
Salma feels relieved and motivated, since the gap turns out smaller than feared and now has a clear order.
What could Salma do if the course turns out too slow, and why?
Salma could practise the same skill with a small real dataset alongside it, because the target skills are what count and there is more than one way to learn them.
How might Anjali see Salma's plan?
Anjali may be pleased that the advice about SQL was taken and that Salma built the plan from evidence and not guesswork.

metadata.subtype: Approach: work backward from the target role's required skills [Thinking]

messages.content: It's my first time cooking pasta and I'm afraid it'll stick together.
Use a large pot with plenty of boiling, salted water, and stir during the first minute or two. Does your pasta packet have instructions?
Yes, it says ten minutes.
Follow that, but taste a piece at nine minutes. When it's soft with a little bite, drain it and rinse with warm water if you're not adding sauce at once.
What if it still sticks?
Toss it with a spoon of oil. Next time, stir more at the start and keep the water bubbling.
I'll report back with pasta pictures.
I'd love to hear how it turned out. Good luck.

Read this:

Dear Parul,
Quick question, and I need your honest answer, not the polite one.
In the last month, nine people from my old college batch have signed up for the same six-month digital marketing certificate. Every week another one posts a photo of their welcome kit, and the comments are all "Me too!" and "Best decision!" I almost filled in the form last night.
Then I noticed something. Not one of them works in marketing. They joined because the others did. I can't tell if they know something or are just following each other.
You've hired marketing people for three years. Does this certificate actually matter when you look at a CV? I'll wait for your reply before paying anything.
Love,
Vasudha

How many people from Vasudha's old batch have signed up for the certificate?
Nine people from the old college batch.
What worry sits behind Vasudha's question to Parul?
Vasudha worries the rush is just people copying each other and doesn't want to pay for something only because it looks popular.
Why is asking Parul a wise choice at this point?
Parul has hired marketing people for three years and isn't part of the posting crowd, so Parul can say whether employers actually value the certificate.
What would change for Vasudha if Parul replied that the certificate matters little in hiring?
Vasudha could skip it without feeling left behind, knowing the crowd's excitement wasn't backed by real information.

metadata.subtype: Asking whether the crowd knows or just copies [Response]

messages.content:
He did not leave for Cambridge the next day, as he had said he would. He deferred his departure a whole week, and during that time he made me feel what severe punishment a good yet stern, a conscientious yet implacable man can inflict on one who has offended him. Without one overt act of hostility, one upbraiding word, he contrived to impress me momently with the conviction that I was put beyond the pale of his favour.

How does the man punish the narrator without any open hostility?
He puts off leaving for Cambridge for a whole week. Without any open act of hostility or a word of blame, he makes the narrator feel shut out of his favour.
Why do older relatives often ask many questions about our studies?
They are showing interest in us. Because they care about us and want to feel part of our lives, asking is their way of staying close.
My uncle bought a watch to me on my birthday. Which word is wrong?

My uncle bought a watch for me on my birthday.
Why: "Buy" takes "for" with the person.
Our neighbour's dog barks only at strangers. It barked at me yesterday. Am I a stranger to it?
Yes, I am a stranger to it. Because the dog barks only at strangers and it barked at me, the dog must see me as one.

In the May heat, Rashmi aunty brought over a bowl of raw mango with salt and chilli.
Pranav wrinkled his nose. "It's green. Green is yucky."
"You don't have to eat it. You can lick it," said Rashmi aunty.
Pranav licked a slice. His eyes screwed shut. "Sour!"
Then he licked it again.
"Still yucky?"
"Sour-yummy." He took a small bite and reached for another slice.
His mother laughed. "This from the boy who only eats white rice."

What did Rashmi aunty bring over?
A bowl of raw mango with salt and chilli.
What does Pranav licking the slice again suggest?
Pranav felt surprised but curious, and he began to enjoy the new sour taste.
Which approach helped Pranav try the mango?
Rashmi aunty didn't force him and let him just lick it, which made trying the new food feel safe.
How might Pranav's mother see this moment?
His mother is amused and pleased, since Pranav usually eats only white rice.

I'm Reena, and in March I got my first bonus: ₹60,000. The question was whether to put it into my education loan early or keep it.
So I made a list in two columns on the office whiteboard after hours.
For prepaying: less interest over the years, loan finished sooner, one less thing on my mind.
For keeping it: the interest on this loan gets a tax deduction, so it costs a bit less than the rate says; and I have almost no emergency savings.
My senior, Tarun, looked at it and said he'd kept his loan running for the deduction, but his situation was different: he already had savings. Then I booked a session with a fee-only adviser, someone paid by the hour who doesn't sell anything. The adviser asked for my actual numbers and went through them with me.
The list didn't decide for me. But I understood what I was choosing.

How much was Reena's first bonus?
Reena's first bonus was ₹60,000, in March.
How did Reena feel after the session with the adviser?
Reena felt clearer and more confident, not because the list decided anything but because the choice was finally understood.
Why was it wise for Reena to check with the adviser as well as Tarun?
Tarun's choice fit his own savings; a fee-only adviser could test the general reasoning against Reena's actual numbers.
Why might Tarun have chosen differently from what suits Reena?
Tarun already had savings, so keeping the loan for the deduction carried less risk than it might for Reena.

metadata.subtype: Approach: compare tax benefit and prepayment trade-offs with a pros-and-cons list [Thinking]

messages.content:
Read this:

Shankar, you say the manager was honest about the budget and you liked him. Good. Let your Sonali-aunty tell you why I still keep one old letter. At twenty-two I was offered a lab assistant post at a research institute in Pune. The head, Dr. Kulkarni, said plainly, 'This is all the budget allows. But you'll learn more here than anywhere, and I'll review your pay in six months.' I felt respected; nobody had ever been that straight with me. I thanked him warmly. Then, a little embarrassed, I asked, 'Could the six-month review be written into the offer letter?' He smiled and added a line by hand. Four months later he moved to Delhi. The new head knew nothing of any promise, until I showed him the letter. My review happened on time. So thank your manager, Shankar. And get it written.

What post was Sonali offered at twenty-two?
Sonali was offered a lab assistant post at a research institute in Pune.
How did young Sonali feel when Dr. Kulkarni was candid about the budget?
Sonali felt respected and grateful, since nobody had been that straight with her before.
What turning point in the story protected Sonali's review?
Asking for the six-month review to be written into the offer letter, which she could show the new head after Dr. Kulkarni moved.
What would have changed for Sonali if the review promise had only been spoken?
When Dr. Kulkarni left, the new head knew nothing of it, so her review might never have happened.
Why does the sea sound louder at night?
The waves are no louder, but we notice them more. Because the daytime noises of people and traffic have faded, the steady sound of the waves becomes easier to hear.

Read this:

Kishore had been at the Gurugram consultancy for four years, and Farida had been his closest ally for all of them: shared cabs, shared deadlines, shared jokes about their boss.

When the senior associate post came up, Farida's name was on everyone's lips. Kishore felt something tighten in his chest every time he heard it.

On Thursday, the partner called him in for a routine chat. Near the end, Kishore said, casually, "Farida's been saying the new client is a nightmare, by the way. Might be worth knowing, if she's leading it."

Farida had said it to him alone, half joking, at eleven at night over cold pizza.

Walking back to his desk, he passed her cubicle. She waved. He waved back.

He told himself it was just information. Business. She would have done the same. But he didn't stop at her cubicle for the rest of the week.

Where had Farida made her remark about the new client?
To Kishore alone, at eleven at night over cold pizza.
What does the tightening in Kishore's chest suggest?
It suggests he feels insecure and afraid of being left behind as Farida's name comes up for the post.
What could Kishore still do now?
He could admit to Farida what he told the partner before she hears it elsewhere, and take responsibility.
Why might Farida react so strongly if she learns about it?
She trusted Kishore as her closest ally and said it privately, so it would feel like a betrayal, not business.

Counsellor's note, Wednesday. Manjula (Class 10) arrived with a list of thirty jobs cut from a magazine. I asked her to put it aside and tell me how a working life would have to feel to suit her. She thought, then said: “Independence. A steady income. Work that helps people.” We wrote those three on the board. Only then did we test fields against them. Nursing and public health fitted well; teaching fitted; graphic design excited her but she was unsure about steady income. She said medicine sounds like helping but worried about the years it takes. I suggested she talk to people who do the work in the fields that stayed. She copied the three words into her diary. — Ojas

What three things did Manjula say she wants from work?
Independence, a steady income and work that helps people.
What might Manjula have felt when asked to put her job list aside?
A little surprised or unsure at first, but then engaged, since she quickly named what she wants.
What could Manjula do next, and why?
Talk to people who work in nursing, public health and teaching, because a real working day shows whether those fields truly match her values.
How does the conversation look to Ojas?
Ojas sees a student become clearer once the question changes from which job to what kind of life, so Ojas stays back and lets her lead.

metadata.subtype: Approach: values-first reflection before naming jobs [Thinking]

Read this:

Come here, Jyoti, and leave that chart for a moment. When your mother, Leela, was ten, she had to make a solar system chart for school. The chart paper was huge and white. She stood in front of it for an hour, not drawing, just staring. Then she went and played with the calf. I, her grandmother, found her crying behind the shed. "It's too big, Nani." So we cut it into a plan. First only the sun, in the corner, big and yellow. That was all for day one. The next day, Mercury and Venus. By Saturday, all eight planets. She still has it.

What chart did Leela have to make?
Leela had to make a solar system chart for school.
What was Leela feeling when her grandmother found her behind the shed?
She felt overwhelmed and hopeless, crying because the chart seemed too big to do.
What choice in the story helped Leela start?
Deciding to draw only the sun on day one gave her a small first piece, which made the big chart feel doable.
How did the grandmother see Leela's crying?
The grandmother saw that Leela was frozen by the size of the task, not lazy, so she helped break it into small steps.

metadata.subtype: Big task feels like a wall [Actor]

messages.content: Tailor ko bolna hai "Yeh kurta thoda dheela hai, ise tight kar dijiye." English?
Say: "This kurta is a bit loose. Please make it tighter."
I want to end a request with "Thanks in advance". Does that sound rude?

Some readers find it presumptuous, as if you are sure the person will help. It is common, though. A gentler line is "Thank you for your help" or "I would be grateful for your help".
Example: I would be grateful if you could send the form by Friday.

Ramesh: did u see ankit's sketch on the class group
Deepak: yeah i thought it was actually really good
Ramesh: lol everyone's saying it looks like a little kid drew it
Deepak: wait really
Ramesh: check the replies. 20 people laughing
Deepak: hmm
Deepak: the shading was nice tho
Ramesh: bro nobody thinks that
Deepak: ok maybe it's a bit weird
Deepak: yeah now that i look again the face is wonky
Ramesh: see
Deepak: ya lol
[Later that night, Deepak opened the sketch again. The shading still looked nice. He didn't post anything.]

How many people were laughing in the replies?
20 people were laughing.
What might Deepak be feeling when he opens the sketch again later that night?
He is unsure and uneasy, seeing the shading still looks nice after he agreed with the group.
What could Deepak do if he still likes the sketch?
He could send Ankit a private message saying he liked the shading, even if he doesn't argue in the group.
How might Ankit feel reading twenty laughing replies?
Ankit would likely feel humiliated and hurt, with no one saying anything kind.

In their Delhi flat, baby Charu was asleep when Yash, three, climbed into Amma's lap. "Me baby too. Carry like baby."

His aunt laughed. "Such a big boy wanting to be a baby!"

Amma didn't laugh. She cradled Yash sideways and rocked him for a minute. "There. My baby Yash."

Yash giggled, wriggled down and ran to his blocks.

Who was asleep when Yash climbed into Amma's lap?
Baby Charu was asleep.
Why did Yash ask to be carried like a baby?
Yash felt left out and needed reassurance, wanting to be held like his baby sister.
Why was Amma's response wiser than the aunt's?
Amma met his need gently and briefly without mockery, so he felt secure and quickly moved on.
How does the aunt see Yash's request?
The aunt sees it as funny, a big boy acting like a baby, rather than a sign that he needs reassurance.

Last year I was bad at history. Twenty dates for the Class 6 test, and I kept mixing them up. I'd read the chapter five times the night before and still forget.

Vikas, who sits next to me, showed me his notebook. For each chapter he wrote a short summary in three lines, and drew a little timeline with pictures. He said he looked at it for five minutes every evening, not all at once.

I tried it. It felt slow at first. But by the third week the dates felt like a story in my head. I got nineteen out of twenty. Now I make a timeline for every chapter, even science. Tanvir's timelines, my sister calls them.

How many dates did Tanvir have to learn for the Class 6 test?
Twenty dates.
How did Tanvir feel about the new method at first?
Tanvir found it slow at first, which suggests some doubt before it started working.
Why did Vikas's method work better than reading the chapter five times?
Short summaries, pictures and a few minutes of review every evening helped the dates stick, instead of cramming once.
How might Vikas feel seeing Tanvir use his idea?
He would likely feel happy and proud that sharing his notebook helped his friend.
Rewrite as an email to a teacher: I am Ravi from class eight. I missed the quiz because of a train delay. Can I take it again?

Subject: Request to retake the quiz

Dear Teacher,

I am Ravi from class eight. I missed the quiz because of a train delay. May I take it again?

Thank you,
Ravi

Dear Elizabeth Miss, sorry Mehak was late today. At 8:10 she came to me with one shoe on and said, "Mummy, I can't find my shoe." I was packing lunch, so I only asked, "Where did you last have it?" She stood still, then said, "I took them off to feed the cat on the balcony." She went to the balcony, looked behind the plant pots, and came back with it. It took four minutes, but she did the searching herself. I have told her that from now on shoes come off at the door. Mehak's mother

Why had Mehak taken off her shoes?
She took them off to feed the cat on the balcony.
What might Mehak have felt when she came back with the shoe?
She probably felt proud and relieved, having done the searching herself after just one question.
What else could help Mehak avoid losing shoes before school?
Taking shoes off only at the door, as her mother has now told her, so there is one place to look.
How might Elizabeth Miss see the late arrival after reading the note?
Elizabeth Miss would understand the four-minute delay and might see it as a small lesson in searching rather than carelessness.

Sunday, 10 p.m.
Chandrika's big social experiment, week six. Result: I now know four people in this building by name, which is four more than in March.
Today was the potluck I'd been nervous about. I put the note in the lift two weeks ago and was sure nobody would come. Seven people came. Indu from 5B brought lemon rice and her toddler, and stayed to help me wash up. She's a nurse, works nights, and said she's been lonely since moving from Madurai too. We swapped numbers. We've also started a building chat group, just for small things: a spare key, a parcel, someone sick.
It's not a best friend yet. But when my geyser broke last week, I didn't have a single number to call. Now I have four. Slightly proud of myself. Also exhausted. Being social is work.

How many people came to the potluck?
Seven people came.
How did Chandrika feel before and after the potluck?
Chandrika felt nervous beforehand, sure nobody would come, and afterwards slightly proud but exhausted.
What small steps helped Chandrika build a network in the building?
Putting a potluck note in the lift, swapping numbers with Indu, and starting a building chat group for everyday help 🙂
What might the potluck mean to Indu?
Indu has felt lonely since moving from Madurai, so a welcoming neighbour may bring relief and a sense of belonging.
Why was Devavrata given the name Bhishma?
To let his father marry Satyavati, he vowed never to claim the throne and never to marry. Because the vow was so terrible, he was called Bhishma.

Monday. "He's a fraud, Papa. Everyone can see it." Lokesh switched off the speaker's talk. "You don't know anything about him." Shankar left the room with a hot face, and neither ate much.
Wednesday. Shankar sat beside Lokesh on the sofa. "What do you like in his talks? I really want to know." Lokesh paused. "After a long day at work, they help me feel patient. I need that." Shankar nodded. "Okay. That I can see."
Saturday. "One thing bothers me, Papa. He asked people to give money for a hall, and I couldn't find any accounts. I'm not calling him a liar. Can we look together?" Lokesh sighed. "Fair. Bring the laptop."

What does Lokesh say the talks help with?
Lokesh says they help with feeling patient after a long day at work.
What was Shankar feeling on Monday, and how did it change by Wednesday?
On Monday Shankar was frustrated and doubtful, with a hot face; by Wednesday Shankar was curious enough to ask what Papa likes in the talks.
What worked better than calling the preacher a fraud?
Asking what Lokesh finds helpful and then raising one specific concern, about the hall money, kindly and without ridicule.
How might Lokesh have felt when Shankar first called the preacher a fraud?
Probably defensive and hurt, since Lokesh switched off the talk and said "You don't know anything about him".

Read this:

"So people think I'm restless. And fine, I am, a bit. My name's Vidya, I'm sixteen, and there's always a pen cap in my mouth. I tap my foot through every class. To study I need loud music, really loud, or my brain won't sit still. My best friend Nilesh is the opposite. At the school fest he wore ear defenders and ate only the plain parathas he brought from home. Some people laughed. But he knows himself. That's what we worked out together. We both have bodies that react strongly, just in different directions. So I carry a chewy bracelet instead of wrecking pens, and I ask to sit at the back so my tapping doesn't bother anyone. Nilesh plans his quiet corner before every event. It's not weird. It's a plan."

What did Nilesh bring from home to the school fest?
Plain parathas, and he wore ear defenders.
How does Vidya seem to feel about being called restless?
Vidya accepts it without shame and seems proud that Vidya and Nilesh understand themselves well enough to plan.
What choices does Vidya make to manage the need for movement?
Vidya carries a chewy bracelet instead of chewing pens and sits at the back so the tapping doesn't bother anyone.
How might the people who laughed at Nilesh see him if they heard Vidya?
They might see him as someone who knows what his body needs and plans for it, not as someone strange.

Retell this passage briefly in three sentences.

"To oblige you, I would try to believe almost anything, but no one else could be benefited by such a belief as this; for were I persuaded that Charlotte had any regard for him, I should only think worse of her understanding than I now do of her heart. My dear Jane, Mr. Collins is a conceited, pompous, narrow-minded, silly man: you know he is, as well as I do; and you must feel, as well as I do, that the woman who marries him cannot have a proper way of thinking. You shall not defend her, though it is Charlotte Lucas. You shall not, for the sake of one individual, change the meaning of principle and integrity, nor endeavour to persuade yourself or me, that selfishness is prudence, and insensibility of danger security for happiness."

The speaker would try to believe almost anything to please Jane, but not that Charlotte cares for Mr. Collins. The speaker calls Mr. Collins conceited, pompous, narrow-minded and silly, and says any woman who marries him thinks wrongly. Jane must not defend Charlotte or call selfishness prudence.

Manoj sat on the balcony of the Andheri flat with his laptop, frowning at a bug that wouldn't go away. Siddharth came out with two mugs of tea and put one beside him. Manoj rubbed his eyes.

"Long day?" Siddharth asked. Manoj nodded.

"Can I?" Siddharth held his hand near Manoj's hair, not touching. "Only if you want it."

"Yes, please."

He ran his fingers lightly through Manoj's hair a few times. Manoj's shoulders dropped and he leaned in a little, eyes closing. After a minute Manoj said, "That's enough, thanks," and Siddharth stopped at once, squeezed his shoulder, and picked up the tea.

What did Siddharth bring out to the balcony?
Siddharth brought out two mugs of tea.
What did Manoj's leaning in and dropped shoulders suggest?
They suggested Manoj felt comforted and safe with the touch, after a long day. Manoj also said yes when asked, so the reading is backed by consent, not just by posture.
What made this a caring way to offer a gentle touch?
Siddharth asked first, kept the hand still until Manoj said yes, and stopped at once when Manoj said enough.
What could Siddharth have done if Manoj had stiffened or said no?
Siddharth could have pulled back, put the hand down and checked in gently about what Manoj needed instead.

Jahnavi, you asked why I keep this old school badge. Let me tell you. When I was ten, my class decided to collect used books for a village school. I’m Neelam, and I had never organised anything.
We borrowed a handcart. Ravi, the strongest boy, pulled it. A quiet girl, Divya, kept the list and ticked every house. I only knocked on doors and felt my knees shake.
By evening we had three hundred books. Our teacher looked at the cart and said nothing for a while. Then she smiled. Divya put her pencil behind her ear and we all laughed.

What did Neelam's class collect?
Neelam's class collected used books for a village school.
How might Neelam have felt knocking on doors?
Neelam was nervous, since the knees shook. Neelam had never organised anything before but kept knocking on doors anyway.
Which choice by the class made the collection succeed?
They divided the jobs: Ravi pulled the cart, Divya kept the list and Neelam knocked on doors. Each child did the part that suited them.
What might Divya have been feeling as she ticked every house on the list?
Divya may have felt proud and focused, since her quiet job kept everyone's effort organised. Putting the pencil behind her ear at the end suggests a happy, satisfied mood.

metadata.subtype: Helping together at school or in a colony [Actor]

messages.content: The word chemical was in my English test. Can you explain it?

A chemical is a substance that is made by, or used in, chemistry. It is a noun; as an adjective it means "to do with chemistry".
Example: Teachers keep every chemical in a locked cupboard in the science lab.

Write a firm but polite request to the landlord not to enter the flat without informing me first, because it is a matter of privacy, and ask him to call or message before he comes. Around 40 words. From Ms Das.

Dear Landlord,
I request you not to enter my flat without informing me first. This is a matter of privacy. Please call or message me before you come, and I will be glad to arrange a time. I would appreciate your understanding.
Ms Das

The week before Christmas, Class 4 at the Andheri school was making cards, and Joseph Sir walked between the benches with a box of glitter. At the back, Anirban was guarding his twenty-four colour pencils with both arms.
"Tashi has none," Joseph Sir said quietly. Tashi had joined only on Monday.
"He can use them if he gives me his sticker sheet," Anirban said. "That's fair."
Joseph Sir crouched. "It is fair, in a way. You like things to be even. Can I ask you something? If you were new and had nothing, and everyone wanted a sticker first, how would you feel?"
Anirban looked at Tashi, who was colouring a star with a blunt pencil. "Bad, I think."
He slid the box to the middle of the bench.

How many colour pencils did Anirban have?
Twenty-four.
What did Anirban feel on looking at Tashi colouring with a blunt pencil?
He felt a pang of sympathy, answering "Bad, I think," as he imagined being new and having nothing.
What did Joseph Sir do well without shaming Anirban?
He agreed the deal was fair in a way, then asked Anirban to imagine being new, turning his attention from the trade to Tashi's feelings.
How might Tashi feel when the box slides to the middle of the bench?
Tashi, new since Monday and colouring with a blunt pencil, would likely feel welcomed and relieved.

On Diwali morning, Avni stood in the hallway of her grandparents' flat with her hand hovering. Jomon had come along as her friend and was watching everyone bend to touch Dadaji's feet. Avni had done it since she was small. This year she felt unsure; she had argued with her grandfather over her choice of course. Still, she bent, touched his feet and heard him say, "Khush raho." His hand rested briefly on her head. Jomon, from a Kerala family where people rarely did this, stayed back with folded hands. Dadaji smiled at him warmly and said, "That's alright, beta." Avni wasn't sure if her gesture had been respect or habit or both, and she noticed her eyes were wet.

What did Dadaji say when Avni touched his feet?
He said, "Khush raho."
What might Avni be feeling as she touches her grandfather's feet, and what else could her wet eyes mean?
She may feel respect mixed with lingering hurt after their argument, and the wet eyes could be emotion, relief or simply the moment, so it is not certain.
What is a good way for Jomon to handle a custom that is not his own?
He can show respect in a way that is comfortable for him, such as folded hands, and does not need to do the gesture just because others do.
How does Dadaji see Jomon's folded hands?
Dadaji seems to accept them warmly, since he smiles and says it is alright, so the gesture is not required of a guest.

The monsoon had turned the road to the Gurugram office into a river, and Parveen's shared cab took two hours each way. Still, she was at her desk by eight and left after ten, three weeks into her first job as a data analyst. She checked every spreadsheet three times. She read reports for meetings where she wouldn't even speak. On Friday her manager Jagdish praised her analysis in front of the team. For a moment she glowed. Then the thought came: it's only because I worked till midnight. If I stop, they'll see I'm not good enough. That weekend, with her feet up on a bucket to dry, she was back at her laptop, preparing Monday's report. Her mother called and asked if she'd slept. "I'll sleep once I've settled in," Parveen said, and kept scrolling through the numbers.

How long did Parveen's shared cab take each way?
Two hours each way.
Why did Parveen's glow at Jagdish's praise fade so quickly?
She felt relieved for a moment, but then fear returned, because she credited the praise to overwork rather than her own ability.
What could break Parveen's cycle of overwork?
Trying one week with normal hours and noticing whether her work is still good could show that her skill, not only extra hours, earns praise.
How might Parveen's mother feel on the phone?
Her mother likely feels worried about her tiredness and the long days.

I'm Vinita, and I sit two rows behind Kiran, who joined our class on Monday. This is what I saw. Kiran opened the lunchbox and closed it again. Kiran looked at our table three times and turned away three times. During the games period, Kiran stood near the wall with the ball in both hands, watching us, and mouthing something quietly, as if practising. I don't know what was going on inside. When I finally said, "Do you want to play with us?" Kiran said, "Yes!" so quickly that I was surprised. Now I say hello to anyone new before I overthink it, in case they are waiting too.

What did Kiran do three times near the lunch table?
Looked at the table and turned away.
What might Kiran have been feeling near the wall, holding the ball?
Nervous and wanting to join, though Vinita cannot know for sure what was going on inside.
What helped when Vinita spoke up?
Vinita offered a simple invitation to play, and Kiran answered yes at once.
How might Vinita have felt when Kiran said "Yes!" so quickly?
Surprised, as Vinita says, and probably glad, since Vinita now says hello to anyone new before overthinking it.

Mridangam classes.
How is Karthik feeling before the first class?
Karthik feels weirdly nervous but hopeful, awake since 4 after the talk with Appa.
Why did not quitting anything help the talk with Appa?
It showed Karthik wasn't rejecting the family's choice, only testing a small change, so Appa could listen instead of fear.

Appa worries about safety but appears to accept it, saying they only wanted Karthik safe.

"Rajni, why are you standing by the tree? The girls are skipping."
"I'm waiting, Mumma."
"Waiting for what?"
"For them to say come."
Sharmila sat on the bench. "What if you ask? Let's practise. I'm a skipping girl. Go."
"Can I... play too?"
"Louder, like you mean it."
"Can I play too?"
"Good! Being shy is okay. It gets smaller every time you try."
Rajni walked to the rope. Her voice was small but clear. "Can I play too?"
"Yes! You hold one end!"

What were the girls doing?
The girls were skipping.
Why was Rajni standing by the tree?
She felt shy and unsure, and she was waiting for the girls to invite her instead of asking.
What did Sharmila say about shyness that could help Rajni?
She said being shy is okay and gets smaller every time you try, and she let Rajni practise first.
How might the skipping girls feel when Rajni asks?
They seem pleased to include her, and happily give her a job holding the rope.
