Thursday night.
Saurabh's report card came today. Maths: 34. I am his mother, and I sat on the bed and felt sick. At the lift, Mrs Bhatia said her son "just does tuition, simple." I smiled and wanted to scream.
Part of me wants to sit with him for two hours every night and drill tables. Part of me wants to hide the report and tell him marks don't matter. Neither feels right.
I met his class teacher after school. She said he tries hard and suggested the school's learning support twice a week. We agreed to try.
Then Saurabh showed me the clay temple he made for art. Every tiny bell. I put it on the TV shelf where everyone will see it.

What mark did Saurabh get in maths?
He got 34 in maths.
How did the mother feel about pushing or protecting Saurabh?
She felt torn and anxious, wanting both to drill him every night and to hide the report and tell him marks don't matter.
What steps help keep the family steady?
Meeting the class teacher, agreeing to try learning support and proudly displaying Saurabh's clay temple to celebrate his talent.
How might Saurabh feel seeing the clay temple on the TV shelf?
Saurabh may feel proud and valued, knowing his mother celebrates what he is good at, not only his maths marks.

Ten minutes before the inter-school music round, with the hall already filling, Bhavna grabbed her friend Rekha's arm backstage. "Tell me honestly. Am I okay?"
Rekha prided herself on never sugar-coating. "Honestly? You go flat on the high notes. You'll probably embarrass yourself." She said it quickly, almost pleased with how clear it sounded.
There was no time to practise, nothing Bhavna could fix. Her face went pale. On stage she started too quietly and never recovered.
Afterwards Rekha told the others, "Someone had to be real with her." But on the bus home she remembered the small satisfied feeling she'd had while saying it, and it didn't feel like honesty any more. It felt more like winning.

When did Bhavna ask Rekha for an honest opinion?
Ten minutes before the inter-school music round, backstage.
What did Rekha realise on the bus home?
She realised her comment had come with a small satisfied feeling, so it felt more like winning than honesty.
What could Rekha have said ten minutes before the round?
With no time to fix anything, she could have offered encouragement, like reminding Bhavna to breathe, and saved honest notes for later when they could help.
How did Rekha's words affect Bhavna on stage?
They shook her confidence; she went pale, started too quietly and never recovered.

The stream behind the kasba school was swollen after two days of rain, and the fallen log across it was slick and dark. 'Race you across!' Pinky shouted, and the others cheered. Manjula felt her feet move forward on their own. With everyone watching, it seemed easy.
Then she remembered Amma at the kitchen fire last month: 'If your friends start something that scares your stomach, say you have to fetch the milk. Walk away with one person. Practise it now.' Manjula had rolled her eyes, but she had said it out loud three times.
'I have to get the milk,' she said now. Her voice wobbled. 'Nitin, walk with me?'
Nitin looked at the water, then nodded fast, as if he'd been waiting for someone to say it. Behind them, the cheering went on.

What excuse had Amma told Manjula to use?
To say you have to fetch the milk, and walk away with one person.
What does Nitin nodding fast suggest he was feeling?
It suggests he was nervous about crossing the log too and relieved that someone gave him a way out.
What choice did Manjula make at the stream, and why did it work?
She used the practised milk excuse and asked Nitin to walk with her, which let her leave without a fight in front of everyone.
How might Amma feel if she heard how the practice was used?
Amma would likely feel relieved and proud that the rehearsal Manjula rolled her eyes at helped in a real moment.

Session note, 14 October. Devika came in smiling for the first time in our six sessions. Her husband Manoj's parents have invited her to lead the Diwali lamp-lighting this year, a task that has always belonged to the eldest woman of the house. She described her mother-in-law pressing the brass diya into her hands. Her eyes filled as she told it. "I finally feel like I belong," she said, and her shoulders dropped as if she had put down a bag.

Then she listed her plans: cooking all the sweets herself, giving up her Saturday painting class to help at their shop, never disagreeing again. Her voice sped up.

I asked what she was afraid would happen if she did less. She paused. "That they'd take it back." We talked about warmth that is given rather than earned. By the end she had decided to keep her class and share the cooking with Manoj.

Which task did Manoj's parents invite Devika to lead?
They invited her to lead the Diwali lamp-lighting.
What was Devika feeling when she described the invitation?
Devika felt relief and belonging, her eyes filling and her shoulders dropping, though fear of losing it crept in.
How did the counsellor help Devika avoid over-pleasing?
The counsellor asked what she feared if she did less, which helped her see she could keep her painting class and share the cooking.
How might Manoj see Devika's plan to share the cooking?
Manoj may be glad to help and relieved that Devika is staying herself rather than working to earn his parents' warmth.

Ira, you know me, Minakshi who never stops talking, so it's strange that I can't say this at home. Siddharth and I still eat dinner together, mostly. But he eats with his laptop open, and I eat with my phone. He used to rub my feet while we watched something; I can't remember the last time. Yesterday I got a new haircut, quite short, and he said, "Oh, nice," without really looking up. Evenings, he's in the study with his headphones and I'm in the bedroom with a book I'm not reading. The strange part is, when I lived alone in Chennai I was never this lonely. Lonely with someone in the next room is a different kind. And I keep not saying it, because saying it means a big talk, and what if the big talk goes badly? So I just say, "Night," and he says, "Night," and the lights go off.

What did Siddharth say about the new haircut?
He said, "Oh, nice," without really looking up.
Why does Minakshi keep not saying anything to Siddharth?
Minakshi feels lonely but is afraid that naming it will start a big talk that goes badly, so staying silent feels safer for now.
What small step could Minakshi take at this stage of distance?
Minakshi could choose a calm moment and say one honest sentence, such as missing their evenings together, instead of waiting for a perfect big talk.
What might Siddharth be experiencing in these separate evenings?
Siddharth may not have noticed how far apart they have drifted, or may feel the same distance and be avoiding it behind the laptop and headphones.

Kunal's phone lit up: 'okay.' Just that, lowercase, with a full stop. He stared at it. Samir was usually all capital letters and exclamation marks. A full stop felt like a closed door. Kunal wrote back, 'you good?' Two minutes later, 'OKAY!!! sorry, was in the middle of football and my hands were muddy.' Kunal grinned and typed, 'sooooo you're not angry?' Samir sent, 'Lol no, I was just typing with one thumb.' Kunal put the phone away, half laughing at himself. On the walk to school he said, "Your full stops are scary, you know." Samir shrugged. "They're just how I type when I'm rushed." They agreed to ask when in doubt.

What was Samir's first message?
It was 'okay.' in lowercase with a full stop.
Why did Kunal write 'you good?' after the first message?
The lowercase word with a full stop felt cold to him, and he worried Samir might be upset. He could not tell the mood without checking.
What could Kunal do when a short message feels cold?
Ask a light question like 'you good?', because punctuation suggests a mood but does not prove it.
How might Samir have seen Samir's own message?
As an ordinary quick reply typed with one thumb, with no cold meaning. 🙂
I'm trying to read sheet music for the first time and the notes all look the same.
They start to look different with a little practice. Begin with just the notes in one clef and learn their names, one or two at a time.
Is there an easy way to remember them?
A rhyme can help. Many learners use a short sentence where each word's first letter is a note name. Make up your own, and it will be easier to remember.

At the chemistry lab door.
What was Ritu worried about before the end of school?
Ritu was worried that everyone would be at the gate doing the face from the sticker, and felt as if the whole class was laughing.
What choice did Jahnavi make about the people who made the sticker, and how did it help?
Jahnavi chose not to reply to them at all and simply walked Ritu out, arguing about question 6; with no scene to feed on, the teasers got bored.
How did the walk change the way Ritu saw the day?
Ritu had felt everyone was laughing; with Jahnavi alongside, it shrank to four people, and Ritu felt less alone and even asked to sit together at lunch.

Dear Diary, 14 August
Big panic today. At lunch my blue water bottle was gone. Afreen said, "Just take mine, Sangeeta," but Amma will ask where it is. So I sat on the stairs and thought backwards. Lunch: no bottle. Maths class: I don't remember drinking. PT: yes! Sir made us girls run three rounds, and I drank half the bottle on the bench by the ground. After that I ran to the line when the bell rang. So I went back down during the break. There it was on the bench, warm from the sun. Afreen and I shared it on the way up. Thinking backwards works!

Where did Sangeeta find the bottle?
On the bench by the ground, warm from the sun.
Why did Sangeeta sit on the stairs instead of taking Afreen's bottle?
Sangeeta was worried that Amma would ask about the lost bottle, so she wanted to find it and calmly thought backwards through the day.
What could Sangeeta do so the bottle isn't left behind after PT again?
Pick it up before joining the line, or check the bench whenever the bell rings; thinking back found it, but a habit would stop it happening.
How might Afreen see the search?
Afreen offered a quick fix with a spare bottle, but ended up sharing the found one, so Afreen likely felt glad it worked out.

Monday: No park, lunch at three, no nap. At bath time Jeevan, two, screamed and kicked. Rafiq, his father, felt helpless.
Thursday: Rafiq started a pattern: park after breakfast, lunch at twelve, nap after lunch, bath after dinner.
The next Monday: After dinner, Jeevan tugged Rafiq's hand towards the bathroom, singing his bath song. That night he fell asleep quickly.

What did Jeevan sing on the next Monday?
His bath song.
How did Rafiq feel on the first Monday?
He felt helpless as Jeevan screamed and kicked.
What changed between the first Monday and the next?
Rafiq built a steady day of park, lunch, nap and bath at regular times.
How might the regular day feel for Jeevan?
It probably feels safe and predictable, so bath time is no longer a shock to fight.

Dolma sits in front of me in Class 10. All last week she was busy with the dance competition and, I think, barely opened her history book. On Monday, before the test, she told our group, "This test is so unfair. They didn't even tell us the chapters properly." They had. The chapters were on the board for two weeks.
After the paper she said, "Honestly, unit test marks don't matter at all. Colleges never see them."
I can't know what she felt. But when the paper came back, she didn't look at it, just folded it into her bag. And she laughed a bit too much at lunch.
— Sahil

How long had the chapters been on the board?
Two weeks.
Why might Dolma insist that unit test marks don't matter?
Believing the marks don't count lowers the shame of not preparing, so Dolma doesn't have to feel it right now.
What could help Dolma before the next test?
Looking at this paper to see what she missed, and fitting a little history around dance practice, would lower the cost later.
How might Sahil feel hearing Dolma call the test unfair?
Sahil probably felt a bit uneasy, knowing the chapters had been on the board, and unsure whether to say so.

The corridor had emptied, but Madhuri Ma'am was still at the board with a marker. Vandana hovered at the door, cheeks warm. "I didn't get the integration steps," Vandana said. "I didn't want to ask in class." "Come, sit." Ma'am redrew the graph slowly and waited each time Vandana frowned. The tea on her desk went cold. Vandana felt thankful, and a little small for needing this. "Thank you, Ma'am. I know you have to go home." "Bring me whatever you get stuck on." Vandana walked out with the notebook still open, already starting the first sum.

What had Vandana not understood?
Vandana had not understood the integration steps.
What was Vandana feeling about needing help, and how can you tell?
Thankful but a little embarrassed; the warm cheeks, the hovering at the door and the earlier reluctance to ask in class show it. 😊
How could Vandana use the extra time well?
Bring whatever Vandana gets stuck on, and practise sums soon after, as Vandana began doing on the way out.
How might Madhuri Ma'am see a student who stays back to ask?
As someone willing to learn; Ma'am stayed while the tea went cold and invited more questions.

"You're back early," Rashmi said as Chandrika dropped her bag by the door.

"I argued with Didi today. At the discussion."

"The meditation Didi? Oh no. Are you in trouble?"

"That's what I expected. She said anger should always be swallowed. I said sometimes anger tells you something is wrong, like when my manager shouted at the new girl."

"And?"

"Everyone went quiet. Then Didi said, 'That's a fair point. Let's think about it together next week.'" Chandrika laughed. "I nearly cried with relief."

Rashmi grinned. "So they didn't throw you out."

"No. Someone even walked me to the bus and said she agreed with me."

"I like hearing that. You've been so much lighter since you joined."

"I know. But I'm glad I can disagree there. And I'm glad I still have you to tell."

What did Didi say after Chandrika disagreed?
"That's a fair point. Let's think about it together next week."
What was Chandrika feeling after the discussion?
Chandrika felt huge relief, nearly crying, after fearing trouble for disagreeing and being respected instead.
What does Chandrika's evening show about a healthy group?
A healthy group lets members disagree and still respects them, and Chandrika keeps outside ties like Rashmi to talk things over.
How does Rashmi see Chandrika's time with the group?
Rashmi is happy for Chandrika, noticing how much lighter things have been since joining, and glad the group did not punish the disagreement.

In the small flat in Cairo, Dalia, nine, sat on the floor surrounded by wires, a battery, and a broken torch she'd found in the drawer.
She wanted the tiny bulb to light up inside a cardboard lighthouse. She tried one wire. Nothing. She twisted it the other way. Nothing. She took the whole thing apart and started again, humming.
Her friend Chen from the floor below knocked. "Are you coming to the park?"
"In a minute," Dalia said.
Chen sat down and watched. An hour went by. The call to prayer drifted in from the mosque; Dalia didn't notice.
Then, click. The lighthouse glowed.
Dalia gasped and laughed. "Look! Look!"
"Is it for school?" Chen asked.
"No," Dalia said, surprised. "It's just for me."

What did Dalia want the bulb to light up inside?
A cardboard lighthouse.
What was Dalia feeling when the lighthouse glowed?
She felt joyful and thrilled, laughing after an hour of absorbed effort.
How could Dalia's family support this kind of interest?
They could give her space, old parts and time to tinker, without turning it into schoolwork or prizes.
What is it like for Chen to watch Dalia work?
Chen seems patient and curious, waiting an hour and then sharing the surprise when the lighthouse lights up.
Sketch with words the lights of a city at night, seen from a rooftop. 50 words.

From the rooftop, the city glows like a field of tiny stars. Windows shine yellow, and car lights crawl along the streets in red and white lines. The sound of horns rises and fades, soft as a hum. A cool breeze brushes my face, and for a moment everything below feels calm.
Is there a double c in vacuum?

No. "Vacuum" has one c and two u's: v-a-c-u-u-m.
Example: Mum used the vacuum cleaner on the carpet.

I'm Madhav, Ujjwal's cousin, and I stayed at their place the week they got Moti. For the first two days nobody knew who had fed the puppy. Ujjwal's mother fed Moti, then his father fed Moti again, and then nobody filled the water bowl. On the third evening Ujjwal sat at the dining table with a sketch pen and a sheet of paper. He wrote: FOOD 7 am and 6 pm. WALK after school. WATER BOWL check morning and night. Beside each line he drew little boxes for the days. He pinned it to the board by the front door, right where you take off your shoes. After that, whoever fed Moti ticked a box. I don't know if Ujjwal was proud, but he checked that sheet every time he came in.

Where did Ujjwal pin the sheet?
On the board by the front door, where you take off your shoes.
Why did Ujjwal make the sheet?
He seemed worried that Moti was being fed twice or left without water, and wanted the care to be steady.
What else could help the schedule work?
Writing a name beside each job, so everyone knows whose turn it is as well as what needs doing.
How does Madhav see Ujjwal after the sheet?
Madhav notices Ujjwal checking it every time he comes in, but is not sure whether Ujjwal feels proud.

I'm Vasudha, and I was hanging washing on the terrace when I saw my neighbour's daughter Elizabeth lying flat on her roof with a blanket, staring up. It was a clear night after the power cut, with stars everywhere. She didn't move for a long while.
When I whispered across and asked what she was doing, she said, "Just looking." Then, "It's so big, Aunty. It makes me feel tiny, but in a nice way." She was smiling.
Earlier that evening she had fretted loudly about a spelling test, and now she never mentioned it. I can't say exactly what she was thinking. I left her the quiet and went in.

What did Elizabeth lie on the roof with?
Elizabeth was lying flat on her roof with a blanket.
How does Elizabeth feel as she looks at the stars?
Tiny but happy. She says the sky is so big it makes her feel small in a nice way, and she is smiling.
What did Vasudha choose to do when she saw Elizabeth?
Vasudha whispered one question, listened, and then left Elizabeth alone with the sky instead of talking more.
How does Vasudha see Elizabeth's stargazing?
Vasudha notices the smile and that the spelling test worry has vanished, but admits she cannot say exactly what Elizabeth is thinking.

Monday night: Thunder boomed. Sunaina ran barefoot to Mumma's bed. Jasleen lifted the blanket and held her close. "I am here." Sunaina's heart slowed against Mumma's.
Wednesday night: Thunder again. Sunaina ran in, and Mumma held her. "Let's say it together: I am safe, I am here." They whispered it three times.
Saturday night: A rumble woke Sunaina. She hugged her teddy and whispered, "I am safe, I am here." She listened to the rain. Then she went back to sleep in her own bed. In the morning she told Mumma, and Mumma hugged her tight.

What did Sunaina hug on Saturday night?
She hugged her teddy.
How did Sunaina feel on Monday when Mumma held her?
She felt calm and safe, her heart slowing against Mumma's.
How did Jasleen's comfort teach Sunaina to calm herself?
She held her each time and taught her words to say, so by Saturday Sunaina could use them alone.
How might Jasleen feel when Sunaina tells her about Saturday night?
She likely feels proud and happy that her comfort helped Sunaina become braver. 😊
What does a ticket to the science fair cost this year?
I'm not sure, because the organisers set the price and I can't see this year's list. The fair's ticket page or its help desk will have the price.

I've been at the company six years, and I sit across from Akash, who joined in January. Last week he was asked to set up the new visitor ID cards for our office.
On Monday he showed me his plan on a single sheet: order blank cards Monday, print Tuesday, go live Wednesday. He looked pleased. It was neat.
I asked, "Who has to approve the card design?" He blinked. Security has to sign off, and they meet on Thursdays. I asked about testing the card printer; it hadn't been used since last year. And the blank cards come from a supplier in another city: four working days, minimum.
He went quiet and started writing in the margin. By the end, Wednesday had become the Wednesday after next.
I'm Jaya, by the way, and I did the same thing in my first year with a canteen contract. Nobody plans the waiting. It's always the waiting.

On which day does the security team meet?
They meet on Thursdays.
How does Jaya seem to feel watching Akash's plan change?
Jaya seems sympathetic rather than critical, remembering making the same mistake with a canteen contract.
What should Akash add to future plans?
Approvals, testing and waiting times, such as security sign-off, printer checks and supplier delivery, since those steps eat the schedule.
How might Akash have felt as Wednesday became the Wednesday after next?
Akash probably felt deflated and a little embarrassed, having been pleased with a neat plan that missed the hidden steps.

When Saurabh joined Class 10 on a scholarship, the others noticed his old shoes and the way he took the bus from the far end of the city. At lunch he ate alone near the water cooler. At the community kitchen near the railway station.

Hearing the boys call Saurabh a charity case made her angry and ashamed of doing nothing, so she felt she had to step in.
How could a class teacher support what Kiran began?
The teacher could arrange mixed seating or group work so Saurabh is included naturally, and speak to the boys about the name-calling.

At the maths club in Accra, the teacher put out a stack of new logic puzzles. Kwame picked the grid puzzle he'd already solved last week.
“That one again?” his friend Jamal asked.
“I like it.”

Kwame shook his head quickly. What if he got it wrong? What if everyone saw him stuck?
He filled in the grid he already knew, fast and neat, and felt calm.
Jamal took the pyramid puzzle and got it wrong three times. He groaned, laughed, rubbed out his answers, and tried a new idea. On the fourth try he got it and did a little dance.

He was afraid of getting it wrong and being seen stuck, so the known grid felt safer.

Saurabh, you asked how our final-year team didn't fall apart. I'm Raghav, so you'll get the honest version. Four of us, one crop-disease detection app, eight months. In the first week we broke the project into modules: image collection, the model, the app screens, and the report. Then we broke each module into tasks small enough to finish in under a week and put them on a shared online board. Every task had one owner's name and a date. Not "the team". One name. Every Monday and Thursday at 5, we met for fifteen minutes, standing, in the lab corridor. Each person said what they'd finished, what was next, and what was blocking them. That's it. When Pooja's image collection slipped by a week, we saw it on a Thursday, not in March. Honestly, the board did half the managing for us.

Pooja's delay was spotted early, so the team could help while there was still time, rather than it becoming a crisis later.

You want the honest version, Ifeoma? Fine. I'm Manoj, and last month I found out I'd been that guy. In robotics club I had this habit with Gopika. Whenever we debugged, I'd say, "Okay, let me explain it simply," and slow right down, just for her. I thought I was being helpful. Then one evening she waited till everyone had left and said, very quietly, "When you do that, it comes across like you think I can't follow. I wrote half the motor code." My face went hot. My first words were, "That's not what I meant, you're taking it wrong." She just nodded and picked up her bag. I lay awake thinking, I'm not that guy, I'm nice. Next morning I found her by the lockers and said, "You're right. It came across badly, and I'm sorry." I didn't ask her to tell me it was fine. I've just stopped doing it.

"Okay, let me explain it simply."

Manoj felt embarrassed and misjudged: the face went hot and the first words were "you're taking it wrong", because Manoj had believed the habit was helpful.

Manoj stopped defending the intent, apologised for how it came across without asking Gopika for reassurance, and then dropped the habit, putting the effect ahead of Manoj's own comfort.

Gopika risked an awkward moment with a clubmate and chose privacy so Manoj wouldn't be embarrassed, which shows care along with real frustration at being talked down to.

At the temple fair, Anjali, eight, let go of her mother Bhavna's hand to watch a puppet show. When the crowd moved, she was alone among strangers' legs. Bhavna always said, "Behave, or the police will take you." Now Anjali saw a constable near the bus stand with a stiff cap and a whistle, and her knees shook.
Then she remembered the school talk: find someone in uniform, say your name and number. She walked up with folded hands. "Namaste. I am lost. I am Anjali. My mother is Bhavna. Papa's number is..."

Anjali found a constable near the bus stand.

She remembered the school talk and walked up to the constable, said her name and number politely, and the constable dialled.

Bhavna saw that the fear she had put in Anjali nearly stopped Anjali from asking for help, and wanted to change it.

I'm Preeti, and Anjali sits two desks from me at the bank's back office. Last month she was about to start an evening walking habit, and she did something I'd never seen.
She pulled a sticky note off my desk and said, "Imagine it's a month from now and I've quit. Why did I quit?" Then she answered herself: "Late meetings on Thursdays. The monsoon. Being too tired after the commute."
Next to each she wrote a fix. Late meetings: walk in the morning on Thursdays instead. Monsoon: twenty minutes of a home workout video in the living room. Too tired: just ten minutes, no more, on those days.
She stuck the note inside her locker door. Three weeks later, during a downpour, I saw her leaving on time. She said she was going home to do the video. I can't say if she enjoyed it, but she didn't skip.

The same forty songs.

September: Indu, the volleyball coach, watched Jeevan throw the ball at the wall after a lost match and storm off. He'd been angry all season.
October: Jeevan changed. He trained twice a day, spiking until his palm was red, lifting weights before class. His game became powerful. The team called him the machine.
November: Indu noticed he'd lost weight, came in with dark circles, and hadn't laughed in weeks. After practice she called him over. "You've turned all that anger into brilliant work. I'm proud of that. But machines break without rest. Are you sleeping? Is there something under this you want to talk about?" Jeevan looked at the floor. "My brother's sick," he said quietly. Indu nodded. "Then take Sunday off. And let's talk to the counsellor together on Monday."

The machine.
Why did Indu speak to Jeevan in November?
Indu felt worried seeing his weight loss, dark circles and no laughter, signs the channel had become unhealthy without rest or talking.

Taking Sunday off and talking to the counsellor together, so he keeps the healthy outlet but also rests and faces what's underneath.

For Thursday.
What does Lalit realise while writing the letter?
Lalit feels uneasy and a little scared, realising the symptoms are the body warning about the schedule, not softness.
Why is booking the doctor a wise step at this stage?
It treats the headaches and stomach trouble seriously and may give Lalit support to change the schedule.
How might Reena feel reading this?
Reena would likely feel worried and relieved that Lalit is reaching out and seeing a doctor.

metadata.subtype: Stage 5: Body and mood sound the alarm [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Day one. Results were out at noon. Farida read her marks on the school portal, closed the laptop and said nothing at lunch. Her mother, Nandini, noticed she left her rice untouched.
Day four. Farida snapped at her younger brother over a borrowed pen, then muttered, "Don't bother with me, I'm useless. Everyone got more." Nandini stopped her chopping. She didn't lecture about studying harder or list other children's scores. She simply sat down by Farida and said, "That sounds heavy. Tell me more."
Day nine. Farida was still quiet and still saying she'd never be good at anything. Nandini called the school counsellor that morning and booked a time, and sat beside Farida while they spoke.

What did Farida leave untouched at lunch on day one?
She left her rice untouched.
What might Farida be feeling when she says 'I'm useless'?
She is probably deeply disappointed and hopeless, comparing herself with others; snapping at her brother may show the hurt spilling over.
Why did Nandini contact the school counsellor on day nine?
Because Farida stayed quiet and kept saying she'd never be good at anything, so the hopeless feeling wasn't fading and needed caring, professional attention.
How might Nandini have felt seeing Farida still quiet on day nine?
Nandini was probably worried that Farida's hopeless talk was lasting, which is why she called the school counsellor and sat beside her.

metadata.subtype: Distressed and disappointed by exams and comparison [Expressing]

messages.content:
Read this:

The Eid holiday was coming, and Jatin Sir's kindergarten class lined up for the sweet sevaiyan a parent had sent. Zainab stood very straight at the back. The boy in front of her tried to push forward. "Don't!" Zainab hissed. "Jatin Sir said whoever stands nicely gets the star badge." "So?" "And pushers sit on the bench." The boy stepped back. When Jatin Sir walked past and pinned a badge on her kurta, Zainab glowed and touched it the whole time she ate.

What did Jatin Sir pin on Zainab's kurta?
A star badge.
How can you tell Zainab felt proud of the badge?
She glowed and kept touching it while she ate.
How could Jatin Sir help the children see a reason beyond badges for waiting in line?
He could ask them how it feels when someone pushes in front, so fairness also matters.
What would change for the boy if there were no bench and no badge?
He might have kept pushing, since Zainab's warning worked only by naming the reward and the punishment.

Read this:

The rents in Aiko's Osaka neighbourhood had doubled in three years, and for most of last winter she had spent every night reading threads that blamed newcomers for it, reply after furious reply. In March she deleted the forum app. It was harder than she expected. Her friend Sofia, who lived two streets away, came with her to the ward office's free counselling hour, and the counsellor asked what Aiko wanted to change, not just who she hated. By May, Aiko was sleeping seven hours. She joined the local tenants' group that met in the community hall on Thursdays and learned how rent rules actually worked. At the June meeting, she sat beside a family who had moved in last year and were facing the same increase. They split the work of writing a joint letter to the landlord. Aiko was still angry. It just pointed somewhere useful now.

Where did the tenants' group meet?
The tenants' group met in the community hall on Thursdays.
How does Aiko feel by the June meeting?
She is still angry about the rents but steadier and more hopeful, because her anger now has a useful direction.
Which steps helped Aiko turn her anger into something useful?
Deleting the forum app, going to counselling with Sofia, sleeping properly and joining the tenants' group all shifted her anger from people to a real problem.
How might the family who moved in last year see Aiko at the meeting?
They likely see a neighbour facing the same increase and working beside them, not someone who once blamed people like them.

Read this:

"Trisha, remember at Onam when the elephant sneezed on you?"

"No..."

"Yes! Gopika chechi was there!"

"Was it a big sneeze?"

"Huge!"

Next day.

"Trisha, tell Ammamma about the elephant sneeze."

"The elephant sneezed on me! It was wet!"

Ammamma smiled. "Trisha, you stayed home with fever at Onam."

Gopika's eyes went wide. "Oh. I made that up."

Trisha frowned. "But I remember the wet."

Who said Trisha had fever at Onam?
Ammamma.
Why did Trisha say "But I remember the wet"?
She felt puzzled and sure, because the made-up story had started to feel like a real memory.
How could Gopika make things right?
Gopika could gently tell Trisha that it was a pretend story, and not ask about it again.
How might Gopika feel when she realised her story had become Trisha's memory?
Gopika seems shocked and a little guilty that her game changed what Trisha remembers.

Read this:

Dear Eshaan Bhaiya,
I saw the video you posted: no helmet, overtaking that truck on the highway, everyone commenting fire emojis. I'm writing because I can't say this on the phone without crying.
You know my friend Ritu from tuition. Last year she was riding pillion without a helmet. Her cousin was showing off. They fell near the flyover. She's okay now, but she spent three months in hospital and still has headaches. Her cousin still can't talk about it.
I know you think nothing will happen to you. Ritu's cousin thought so too.
You're the person I look up to most. Please wear the helmet. Please don't race. If your friends think it's boring, they're not really your friends.
I'll buy you a helmet for Rakhi if that helps.
Your sister,
Vandana

How long did Ritu spend in hospital?
She spent three months in hospital.
How does Vandana feel about Eshaan's video?
Vandana feels frightened and upset, unable to talk about it on the phone without crying.
Why might Vandana's letter change Eshaan's habit?
It tells a real story about someone they know and comes from a sister who looks up to him, which can matter more than friends' approval.
How might Eshaan feel reading the letter?
Eshaan might feel shaken and guilty, realising how much his sister worries.

Read this:

I'm Nandini. I bite the inside of my cheek when I concentrate or get nervous. In class today Sunaina looked at me and asked, “Are you cross with someone?” I said, “No, I'm thinking.” Then I realised my face looks like a grimace when I do it. So I told her, “It's just a habit when I'm nervous about the test.” She said, “Oh, I do something too. I twist my hair.” We both laughed. I didn't feel so odd after that.

What does Nandini do when she concentrates or gets nervous?
She bites the inside of her cheek.
What was Nandini feeling when Sunaina asked if she was cross, and what did Sunaina think?
Nandini was nervous about the test and concentrating. Sunaina thought Nandini looked cross, because the cheek biting looks like a grimace.
What worked when Nandini explained her habit?
She said plainly that it is a habit when nervous, so Sunaina understood and shared her own habit of twisting her hair.
How might Sunaina have felt when Nandini said she was only thinking?
Probably relieved that Nandini was not upset with someone. She was also comfortable enough to admit her own habit.

Read this:

Bhupen had planned it for weeks: on Makar Sankranti morning, the kite seller would bring the big red fighter kite he'd saved thirty rupees for. Waiting a month had felt easy when it was far away.
But the morning came thick with fog, and the seller's cart was late. Every roof already had kites up. Kunal leaned over the wall. "I'll sell you my small green one right now. Fifteen rupees."
"The big red one is coming," Bhupen said. Then a kite snapped overhead and the whole street cheered. His fingers itched.
"Fifteen," Kunal said. "Now."
Bhupen handed over the money. The small green kite went up. Twenty minutes later, the seller's cart came round the corner with the big red kite, and Bhupen had fifteen rupees left.

How much had Bhupen saved for the big red kite?
Bhupen had saved thirty rupees.
Why did Bhupen buy Kunal's kite?
Bhupen felt impatient and left out with every roof flying kites, so a small kite now felt better than the big one soon.
What could Bhupen have done during the wait?
Bhupen could have helped a friend fly or held the reel to keep busy until the cart came, instead of spending half the savings.
How might Kunal see the deal?
Kunal probably felt pleased, getting fifteen rupees for a small kite because Bhupen couldn't wait.
A cow give milk, and a hen lays egg. Please correct.

A cow gives milk, and a hen lays eggs.
Why: "cow" takes "gives"; general plural "eggs".

Read this:

The prices dropped the week Ritu's scooter needed a new part, and the bank's message about the monthly instalment arrived on the same morning. Hrithik, a colleague at the next desk, looked over. "Stop it for now. Wait till the bottom, then buy."
Ritu opened her notebook. On the first page, written before any fall: "Same amount, same date, every month. No guessing."
"I can't tell where the bottom is," Ritu said. "Nobody can. But if the price is low, the same money buys more units."
"And the scooter?"
"I'll cut something else for a month."
The instalment went through at ten, and Ritu turned back to work with her stomach still tight.

What did Ritu's notebook say on its first page?
The notebook said "Same amount, same date, every month. No guessing."
What was Ritu feeling as the instalment went through?
Ritu felt nervous, as the tight stomach shows, but she stuck to the rule she had set.
What could Ritu do if money ever feels too tight to keep the instalment?
Rather than changing the rule in a worried moment, Ritu could talk it through with a qualified adviser first and decide calmly.
How might Hrithik have seen Ritu's choice?
Hrithik probably thought it risky and wanted to protect Ritu from more losses, which is why Hrithik said to stop it for now.

Read this:

Monday: On TV, a cartoon lion lifted a bus after one bowl of Zoom Flakes. "Eat Zoom Flakes, be strong!" Deepika decided that was why she kept losing arm-wrestling to her friend Dolma.
Wednesday: At the supermarket, Deepika dropped the bright box into the trolley. "Mummy, I need it to get strong."
Mummy turned the box over. "Who made this ad, do you think?"
"The lion?"
"The company that sells the cereal. They want you to buy it. Let's ask the doctor on Friday whether it really makes children strong."
Friday: At Deepika's check-up, the doctor laughed kindly. "Lions don't eat cereal. Playing, sleeping well and ordinary home food do the job."
Saturday: Deepika arm-wrestled Dolma again, lost again, and giggled anyway.

What did the cartoon lion lift in the ad?
A bus.
Why did Deepika want the cereal so badly?
She believed the ad and felt hopeful it would make her strong enough to beat Dolma.
What did Mummy do that helped Deepika understand the ad?
She asked who made the ad, explained that the company wants to sell, and suggested asking the doctor.
What does the company behind the ad want children like Deepika to believe?
That the cereal will make them strong, so they will beg their parents to buy it.
My office is so noisy that I can't focus.
That's tough. Is the noise from people talking or from machines?
Mostly people chatting and phone calls.
Headphones, even without music, can lower the noise a little. Or you could find a quiet corner or meeting room for tasks that need focus.
My boss doesn't like headphones.
Then maybe ask him if you can use a quiet room for an hour or two each day. Say it's to do your best work on difficult tasks.

Describe this excerpt in just three sentences.

Your mother was exactly like you when she was nine, you know. I'm her big brother, your Saurabh Mama; I saw it all. She had rules for herself, written in her rough book: "I must come first. I must never cry. I must never forget my tiffin." During Durga Puja that year, the half-yearly results came. She came second, by one mark. She didn't cry, because crying was against the rules. She just went up to the terrace and sat very straight, and when I found her, her hands were shaking. "I broke the rule," she whispered. "I'm so bad." I sat with her and said, "Indu, who made these rules?" "Me." "Then you can make kinder ones." We crossed out "must" and wrote "try". She cried then, finally. She still came second sometimes. The sky never fell.

Saurabh Mama remembers his sister Indu at nine, who made strict rules for herself: come first, never cry, never forget her tiffin. When she came second by one mark, she sat very straight on the terrace, shaking, and said she had broken the rule. He helped her change "must" to "try", and then she finally cried.

Read this:

You want to know a secret? I'm Gautam, and in Class 10 I was the smartest lazy person in our group.
For the geography project, Afreen made the charts, Sid did the model, and Pallavi wrote the report. I said I'd “handle the printing.” That was two pages at the shop.
I knew Afreen would never let the project fail. She stays up till two for everything. So I just waited.
We got an A. The teacher said, “Great teamwork.” I felt a little guilty, sure. But honestly, also kind of clever, like I'd found a shortcut.
I never told them. You're the first person I've said this to, and my face is getting hot saying it.

What did Gautam say he would handle?
Gautam said he'd handle the printing.
How did Gautam feel after the teacher said "Great teamwork"?
Gautam felt a bit guilty but also clever, as if a shortcut had been found; now the memory brings embarrassment.
What could Gautam do now to make it right?
Gautam could thank Afreen honestly for carrying the project, and take a real share of the next group task.
How might Afreen feel if she learned the truth?
She might feel used and frustrated, having stayed up late while Gautam counted on her not letting it fail.

Read this:

Monday. Day 18!
Skipping rope on the terrace before school: done. It's harder when it's cold and my legs want to stay in bed, but I've marked every day on the calendar and I don't want a gap. Saurabh bhaiya tried it with me today and gave up after two minutes. 'Sonali, how?' HA.
What's changed: I'm less out of breath on the stairs. I eat breakfast now, poha or eggs, instead of skipping it. And I wash my face after every workout because sweat plus my oily skin was giving me spots.
What's not changed: I still want samosas. I had one on Saturday and didn't feel guilty. Mumma says that's the right attitude.
Goal: keep going through exams, even if it's just ten minutes.

What exercise does Sonali do on the terrace?
Skipping rope, before school.
How does Sonali seem to feel about the calendar streak?
Sonali feels proud and motivated, not wanting to leave a gap even on hard mornings.
What makes Sonali's habits likely to last?
Sonali is consistent but flexible, eats breakfast, looks after skin and doesn't feel guilty about a samosa.
What might Saurabh think after giving up after two minutes?
He might be surprised at how fit Sonali has become and a bit impressed.

Read this:

I'm Raghav, Sarita's big brother. On Sunday I saw her playing with Papa's spectacles on the dining table. Later I heard a crack.

That evening Papa was hunting everywhere for them. Sarita stood in the doorway, twisting her frock. Then she walked up to him, eyes full. "I broke them. I was wearing them and they fell."

I waited for Papa to shout. He didn't. He took a slow breath. "Thank you for telling me the truth. That was brave. Spectacles aren't toys, though. Next time, ask first."

Sarita cried, and then she hugged him. She looked lighter, somehow.

What was Sarita playing with on the dining table?
Papa's spectacles.
What was Sarita feeling when she stood twisting her frock before confessing?
She was most likely scared of being in trouble; her full eyes and twisting show it. After Papa's calm answer she seemed relieved, looking lighter as she hugged him.
Why was Papa's response wise?
He stayed calm, praised her honesty and still named the problem, spectacles aren't toys, which makes it more likely she will tell the truth next time.
What would change if Papa had shouted and punished Sarita harshly?
She might learn to hide her mistakes instead of owning up, and Raghav might learn the same lesson watching.

Read this:

Age five: after lunch, Jeevan's mother switched off the television and put out three books, a pad of paper and some soft music. 'Quiet hour.' Jeevan sighed loudly, then drew a whale, then a very long boat. When the hour ended he said, 'Can we do quiet time again?' His mother smiled. 'Every day.'

Age twenty-five: Anirban noticed that his Sunday scrolling left him more tired than before. He tried a walk by the river, then a pottery class, then Saturday tea with his old friend Afreen. In a notebook he wrote down what left him lighter: the walk and Afreen. He put them in his calendar like meetings: Wednesday walk, Saturday tea. 'It's maintenance, not a reward,' he told a colleague who asked why he was leaving on time.

On which weekday did Anirban schedule his walk?
Wednesday.
What do the two scenes share about learning to rest?

Jeevan found in quiet time that calm was not boring, and Anirban found by trying a walk, pottery and tea with a friend which rest restores him more than scrolling. Each learned that rest can be chosen and protected, not treated as laziness or reward.
What was Jeevan feeling when he asked for quiet time again?
Content and a little proud, having found that calm can be enjoyable.
What could Anirban do if his week gets busy?
Keep the walk and the tea as fixed appointments, because they are maintenance.
Diwali is close and the market is so crowded. I need to buy lamps and sweets.
Go early in the morning if you can, because the crowds are smaller. Make a short list so you don't wander.
Should I buy everything on the same day?
Not unless you must. Buy lamps first, since they are not perishable, and sweets closer to the day so they stay fresh. Keep your bag in front of you in busy lanes.

Read this:

After the interschool football match in Chennai, Suraj's friends were at the juice shop, going over the game.
“The referee was blind,” said Rakesh. “Totally biased.”
Suraj had thought the referee was fair. The penalty was a real foul; he'd seen it clearly. But everyone was nodding.
“Totally biased,” he said.
Then Rakesh started imitating the way Rekha, the girl who scored the other team's goal, celebrated. Everyone laughed. Suraj thought her celebration had been brilliant. He laughed too, because the table was laughing.
On the way home, he felt tired, as though he'd carried something heavy. At the signal, a boy on a cycle did the same celebration, joyfully. Suraj smiled, a real smile this time, and felt a sting of shame about the juice shop.

What did Rakesh say about the referee?
He said the referee was blind and totally biased.
Why did Suraj agree the referee was biased?
He was afraid of standing apart from his friends, so their approval felt more important than what he had seen.
What could Suraj try next time his friends mock someone?
He could simply not laugh, or say he thought Rekha's celebration was great, keeping hold of his own view.
How might Rekha feel if she knew the boys were mocking her celebration?
Rekha would probably feel hurt and belittled after a moment she was proud of.
What did the driver of our school bus say to my friend today?
I don't know, as I can't hear conversations on your bus. Ask your friend.

Why do we peel an orange before eating it? Then, what is "infallible"?
When does the next local festival start? Also, what is wrong with this: The childrens are playing outside. And one more: is it "peice" or "piece"?

1. The peel is bitter and tough. Because it is the fruit's protective skin, not the part meant for eating.
2. It is an adjective. It means never wrong and never failing.
3. I don't know the exact date, and I can't check calendars. Look at the town notice or ask a neighbour.
4. The children are playing outside. Why: "Children" is already plural, so it takes no "-s".
5. It is "piece". Think of "a piece of pie".
The children plays in the garden after school.

The children play in the garden after school.
Why: "Children" is a plural noun, so the verb has no -s: "play".

Read this:

At home on Sunday, Arohi's older brother Hemant kept changing the rules of snakes-and-ladders so that he always won. "That's not fair!" Arohi shouted, and she fetched their mother, Rajni. Rajni sat down with them. "Hemant, letting your little sister win sometimes is a kind thing to do," she said, and the game began again with the real rules. At school on Monday, Tanu peeked through her fingers during hide-and-seek, giggling and a little nervous. The teacher noticed. "The game is only fun if everyone plays fair," the teacher said. On Friday, at sports day, Arohi wanted to beat Tanu so badly that she darted off before the teacher said "go". The teacher called her back. Arohi's face went hot and she wanted to run away and hide. The teacher knelt and said, "Let's say sorry to Tanu, then run again, properly." Arohi whispered her sorry, and they ran. She lost, but the teacher smiled. "You can be proud that you tried your hardest," the teacher said.

What did Arohi shout when Hemant changed the rules?
She shouted, "That's not fair!"
How did Rajni's words to Hemant differ from the teacher's words to Arohi after the false start, and what did both stress?

Rajni told Hemant that letting his little sister win sometimes is kind and restarted the game with the real rules, while the teacher helped Arohi say sorry and run again, saying she could be proud she tried her hardest; both put fair play first without calling any child bad.
What was Arohi feeling when the teacher called her back from the start line?
She felt ashamed, with her face hot and a wish to run away and hide.
What could Tanu do next time in hide-and-seek?
She could keep her eyes closed and count properly, since the game is only fun if everyone plays fair.

1) My teacher used the word "likelihood". What is it?
2) What is the difference between "so" and "such"?
3) Can you correct this for me? "Do you know where is the post office?"
4) Who lived in my house before us?
5) Quick one: why do the days feel longer in summer?

1. As a noun, "likelihood" means the chance that something will happen.
2. Use "so" before an adjective alone, as in "so tall". Use "such" before a noun, as in "such a tall tree".
3. Better: Do you know where the post office is? Why: after "know where", the subject comes before the verb.
4. I don't know; I can't see your house's history. Ask a neighbour or the house owner.
5. Daylight lasts longer in summer. Because our part of the Earth tilts toward the sun then, so the sun stays above the horizon for more hours.

Read this:

Last Diwali, at my cousin's house, the uncles got into a debate about the economy, and I heard myself say, 'Well, you know what they say: India's youth are its biggest strength, and we're the fastest-growing everything.' Everyone nodded. My cousin Indu, who's doing economics, asked, 'Fastest-growing what? Where did you read that?' I opened my mouth and nothing came out. I'm Kamal, I'm twenty, and I'd heard that line a hundred times, on hoardings, in speeches, in forwards. It came out so easily that I thought I knew it. But I couldn't name one number or one source. It had just been in the air. Now when a line slides out of my mouth that easily, I stop and ask myself where it actually came from.

What was Indu studying?
Economics.
How did Kamal feel when Indu asked where the line came from?
Kamal felt caught out and embarrassed, unable to name a single source for something that came out so easily.
What habit did Kamal build afterwards, and why is it useful?
Kamal now stops when a line comes out too easily and asks where it came from, because ease of recall is not the same as accuracy.
How might Indu have seen the uncles nodding along?
Indu may have felt that everyone accepted the line because it sounded familiar, not because anyone had checked it.

Read this:

At the school sports day, while everyone waited for the relay, someone whispered loudly that Sahil liked Irawati. The group around her burst into giggles.
Irawati's cheeks flamed. She stared at her shoelaces.
Sahil walked off, his ears red.
At lunch, Irawati found him by the drinking water tap. "Sahil, I heard what they said. It's okay. Thanks for always helping me with maths. I'm just not thinking about that kind of thing."
Sahil nodded, looking at the ground. "Yeah. Okay."
"Still maths partners?"
He looked up. "Still maths partners."

Where did Irawati find Sahil at lunch?
By the drinking water tap.
How did Irawati feel when the group giggled?
She felt embarrassed, her cheeks flaming as she stared at her shoelaces.
What did Irawati do that was kind and honest?
She thanked Sahil for helping her with maths, gently said she wasn't thinking about that, and offered to stay maths partners.
How might Sahil have felt walking off with red ears?
Sahil likely felt embarrassed and exposed after his feelings were made public.

Read this:

Maria, you're scared of your brother's temper? Sit with your Manoj uncle. At nineteen, I was just like him. In Kolhapur, I'd pick fights at the bus stand, punch walls, shout at my mother. Everyone said I'd end up in trouble. Then one evening, the kabaddi coach at the akhada, an old wrestler, watched me shove a boy. He didn't shout. He said, "You've got fire. Come and use it on the mat, where there are rules." I laughed at him. But I went. And on that mat, my temper was welcome. The harder I raided, the more they cheered. But one foul, one push outside the rules, and I sat out. I learnt to hold my fire until the whistle. By twenty-two, I was captain. My temper didn't vanish. It just found a place where it belonged.

Where did young Manoj go to play kabaddi?
The akhada in Kolhapur.
Why did young Manoj stay with kabaddi after laughing at the coach?
On the mat his fierce temper was welcomed and cheered, so he felt valued rather than judged, while the rules taught him control.
What was the key choice in the story, and why did it work?
The coach inviting him to use his fire on the mat, which honoured the intensity instead of telling him to stop being angry.
How might Manoj's mother have felt as he found kabaddi?
His mother likely felt relieved and proud, seeing him move from punching walls to leading a team.

After the mummers' visit, how do the guests look, and what does Pelageya Danilovna do?

In an hour, all the costumes were crumpled and disordered. The corked eyebrows and mustaches were smeared over the perspiring, flushed, and merry faces. Pelageya Danilovna began to recognize the mummers, admired their cleverly contrived costumes, and particularly how they suited the young ladies, and she thanked them all for having entertained her so well. The visitors were invited to supper in the drawing room, and the serfs had something served to them in the ballroom.
Their costumes are crumpled and their painted eyebrows and mustaches are smeared on sweating, merry faces. She starts to recognize them, admires their costumes and thanks them for entertaining her.

Read this:

Sunday, late
Siami told me today she's taking the single room in the new block next year. I just said "oh, nice," walked back to our room and sat on my bed for an hour.
I was SO sure. We've shared since first year. I never even asked her. In August I told the hostel office not to put me on the list, because "Lalremsiami and I are sorted." I didn't look at any other room or ask anyone else. Now the list is closed.
She says she needs quiet for her final-year project. It makes sense. That's the annoying part. It's not even a betrayal. It's just a plan I never checked.
Tomorrow: go to the office, ask about the waitlist, text Ruth about sharing.
Bhavna

What did Bhavna tell the hostel office in August?
Not to be put on the list, because "Lalremsiami and I are sorted."
How did Bhavna feel after hearing Lalremsiami's news?
Bhavna felt hurt and stunned, sitting on the bed for an hour, because the plan had been treated as certain and never checked.
What are Bhavna's next steps, and why are they sensible?
Asking the office about the waitlist and texting Ruth about sharing, which builds the backup that was missing.
Why might Lalremsiami see the decision differently from Bhavna?
For Lalremsiami it is a practical choice, needing quiet for the final-year project, not a rejection of the friendship.

Read this:

Friday, early March: Keerthana spent her free evening in bed with her phone, thumb moving for hours. She went to sleep somehow more tired, jaw tight. Saturday, a week later: her friend Yamini dragged her to a pottery class above the bakery. Keerthana's hands were caked in clay, the wheel wobbled, and she forgot to check anything for two whole hours. Walking home, she noticed her shoulders had dropped. That night she made a list: pottery, walks by the sea, dinners with Yamini, plain quiet with the window open. Late April: Keerthana's work calendar had a block every Saturday afternoon marked 'maintenance'. When her manager asked for a weekend call, she offered Monday instead.

Where was the pottery class?
Above the bakery.
How did Keerthana feel after the evening on her phone?
She felt more tired and tense, jaw tight, as if the scrolling had not rested her at all.
What did Keerthana do to protect the rest that worked?
She listed what really refreshed her and blocked Saturday afternoons as 'maintenance', offering Monday instead of a weekend call.
What might Yamini have noticed about Keerthana after the pottery class?
Yamini may have seen a looser, lighter friend with dropped shoulders, compared with the tense one Yamini had dragged along.

Read this:

It rained all week in Shillong, so Yusuf's new babysitter arrived in a dripping raincoat. Yusuf took one look at her and screamed, clinging to his mother. Every day the new aunty tried; every day he turned away.
But when Lalremsiami, the neighbour he had known since birth, popped in with her umbrella, he ran to her, laughing. The babysitter noticed and began singing Lalremsiami's clapping song. Yusuf stopped crying and watched her hands.

Why did the babysitter arrive in a dripping raincoat?
It rained all week in Shillong.

Lalremsiami's face was familiar and felt safe, while the new aunty still felt strange and scary.

She sang Lalremsiami's familiar clapping song, borrowing something Yusuf already trusted.

Looking back, my anger was the loudest thing in the room that week. A "recruiter" had taken a registration fee for a job that did not exist, and when I understood, I shook with rage. I wanted to track the person down and make them suffer.

My cousin Vishal took the phone gently out of my hand. "That could go wrong in ways you can't see. Use that energy on the complaint."

So I did. I saved screenshots of the chats, the phone number and the transaction IDs, told my bank, and filed a report on the cyber portal. Then I posted a warning in my college alumni group.

The anger did not vanish, but it had a job now. Two friends wrote back to say they had seen messages from the same recruiter.

Rajni

The recruiter took a registration fee for a job that did not exist.

Rajni wanted to track the person down and make them suffer, which shows intense rage.

By saving screenshots, the phone number and transaction IDs, telling the bank, filing on the cyber portal, and warning friends.

Vishal worried that going after the scammer could go wrong in ways Rajni could not see, and wanted the energy to go into the complaint.

Wednesday
Got 9 out of 25 in maths again. The test was full of trick questions. Ankita Ma'am always sets the hard ones when it's my turn to be unlucky. Last year I told Sir I didn't understand fractions and he just said 'pay attention' and moved on. So what is the use.
But today something weird happened. Ma'am called me after class and said, 'Show me how you did number 4.' I showed her. She said my first two steps were right and I only forgot to carry the one. She let me fix it and gave me the marks.
So number 4 was not luck. It was me.
Maybe I will try number 5 tomorrow. Just to see.

9 out of 25, again.

Imran feels discouraged and helpless, believing results come from trick questions and bad luck, and remembering that asking for help last year only got 'pay attention'.

When Ankita Ma'am asked to see the working and let Imran fix the missed carry, Imran saw the marks came from Imran's own steps, not luck.
How might Ankita Ma'am see Imran after this talk?
She may see a student who can do the steps and mainly needs to be listened to and shown small fixes, not someone who doesn't care.

After dinner he went to the sink, pulled up his stool and washed his own hands with soap, humming.

She drew a windmill on plain paper first, blades, tower, base, with numbers beside each part: 12 cm, 8 cm. Then she cut paper shapes and laid them over the cardboard like a jigsaw. Two blades overlapped, so she moved the tower. Only then did she cut the cardboard, slowly, with no scraps wasted. I would have cut straight away. I cannot say what she felt, but she hummed. - Arnab

What did Irawati do before touching the scissors?
She drew a windmill on plain paper with numbers beside each part.

Every night in Mexico City, Rosa, two, climbed onto Abuela Esther's lap for the bedtime prayer.

Esther held Rosa's small hands together inside hers and whispered the words slowly. Rosa said the last word with her, "Amén," and giggled.

Then Esther kissed her forehead. "Good night, mi amor." Rosa snuggled into her shoulder, eyes closing.

What word did Rosa say with Esther?
Rosa said "Amén" with Esther.
What does Rosa snuggling into Esther's shoulder suggest?
It suggests Rosa felt loved, safe and close to her grandmother.
Why does this bedtime ritual matter for Rosa?
Shared warmly each night, it makes her feel part of the family and becomes a safe memory, not an obligation.
How might Esther feel holding Rosa's hands during the prayer?
Esther likely feels tender and joyful, passing on something precious.

"Knock knock!" "Who's there?" said her grandmother Indu. "Banana!" "Banana who?" "Banana... purple!" Payal, five, giggled so hard she slid off the sofa. "Why is that funny?" "Because purple!" "Say it again in a silly voice." "Zibbly zobbly purple!" Payal rolled on the rug, and Indu laughed until she had to wipe her eyes.

Why does Payal laugh so hard at the knock-knock joke?
Because the answer is just the silly word "purple". When Indu asks her to say it again in a silly voice, she rolls on the rug laughing.

Since the flu hit, Sahil had learned his wife Ankita's rhythm in their Hyderabad flat: warm water by the bed, the curtains half drawn, a quiet "I'm here" whenever she stirred. He set phone reminders to offer a drink, and each evening he checked the list of things the doctor had told them to watch for. On Wednesday she threw the remote when he asked, for the third time, whether she wanted khichdi. "Leave me alone, Sahil!" He felt the sting, then remembered his own fever last winter, when he had snapped at everyone. He covered the khichdi on the tray and said, "I'll be in the next room." Later she called him back, sheepish. "Sorry. Can I have that khichdi now?" "I'll warm it up," he said.

What did Ankita throw?
The remote.
What did Sahil feel when Ankita shouted at him?
He felt a sting of hurt, then understanding, as he remembered snapping at everyone during his own fever.
Which of Sahil's habits make him a good carer?
Offering drinks regularly, keeping the room calm, checking the doctor's list each evening and not taking her grumpiness personally.
How might Ankita have felt when she called Sahil back?
Sheepish and a little embarrassed, but relieved that he had given her space instead of arguing.

After the evening class at the training institute, the corridor was almost empty. Yogesh, the tutor, stopped Yamini at the door. "Stay ten minutes in the small room. I'll go through your assignment there, just us." His tone was easy, but her stomach flipped. "Could we do it at the front desk instead, sir?" she asked. "Or in office hours?" Yogesh asked Yamini to stay ten minutes in the small room.

I'm Zubin. At twenty-four I had a job in consulting that swallowed my weeks, parents in Surat who needed me for hospital visits, and a friend, Pankaj, whose wedding I'd promised to help plan. I loved all of them. And I felt guilty about whichever one I was ignoring that day. When I was at work, I thought of Mum's appointments. Zubin's parents lived in Surat.

Zubin felt guilty about whichever duty was being ignored, resentful at carrying everything, and then ashamed of that resentment.

Class 3 note, Christmas week. During the paper-star activity I asked, "Which clock shows half past three?" and held up two cardboard clocks. Tarun wrote A on his slate straight away, which was correct. Then he looked around. Most children were writing B, and Dilnaz was already giggling at a friend's slate. Tarun rubbed out his A with his thumb and wrote B. When I asked him later, he said quietly, "I thought A. But everyone put B, and I didn't want them to laugh." What I did next: I praised him for his first answer, privately. The next day I asked the class to answer on slates turned face-down and reveal together, so nobody could copy the crowd.

What did Tarun write on his slate at first?
He wrote A on his slate straight away, which was correct.
What made Tarun rub out his answer, and what was he worried about?
He saw most children writing B and Dilnaz giggling, and he felt nervous that they would laugh at him for being different.
Which choice by the note-writer worked, and why?
Having slates turned face-down and revealed together worked, because children answer before they can see and copy the crowd.
How might Dilnaz's giggling look from Tarun's side?
To Tarun it may have looked like proof that anyone who differs gets laughed at, even if Dilnaz was only laughing with a friend.
I need to email my professor about missing a class. How do I start?
Keep it short and polite. Start with a greeting, state your name and class, explain briefly why you missed it and ask how to catch up.
Could you show me an example?
For example: 'Dear Professor Rao, I'm Meera from your Tuesday class. I missed today's lecture because I was unwell. Could you tell me how I can catch up on the material? Thank you, Meera.'
Should I attach a note?
Only if your college asks for one. You can mention that you can bring it, if needed.
Okay, I'll write it now.
Good. Check the subject line, and read the email once before you send it.
Thanks. It feels easier now.
It does get easier after the first one. Clear and polite is all it takes.

Friday, last day before the Christmas holidays.
Dear diary, Mummy asked how my week was. I said "boring and bad", because today Vidya Ma'am gave us a surprise test and didn't let us go to the Christmas party early. She is the strictest teacher ever.

Okay, maybe my week was good and only today was bad. Maybe Vidya Ma'am is nice and only strict on Fridays.

Vidya Ma'am brought plum cake for everyone on Thursday.

Tushar felt cross and disappointed about today's surprise test, and that fresh feeling crowded out the good days earlier in the week.

Looking at the school diary with Mummy brought back Monday's star, Tuesday's snowflakes, Wednesday's reading and Thursday's cake.

In the maths test at their school in London, Emil nudged Kwame's elbow and mouthed, "Number six." Kwame shook his head a tiny bit. Emil's face hardened, and Kwame remembered last month, when Emil hadn't spoken to Tomasz for a whole week. So Kwame moved his arm and let his page show. Emil copied fast. Afterwards Emil grinned and slapped his back, but Kwame felt sick. That evening he kept thinking: Ms Adeyemi marks carefully. What if she noticed two identical pages? He couldn't finish his rice. The next morning he dreaded maths. By Friday, when Ms Adeyemi asked both boys to stay behind after class, the fear had grown so big he could barely look up.

Number six.

He was afraid Emil would stop talking to him; afterwards he felt sick and worried.

Kept his arm in place and talked to Emil after the test; a friendship that ends over a refusal was not safe anyway.

Rain had flooded the lane, the gas cylinder had run out, and dinner at Farida Nani's house was going to be very late. Aparna, five, had been whining for an hour. When her last biscuit snapped in two, she flung both halves on the floor and wailed, "Everything is broken!" Nani didn't scold. She found a handful of roasted chana in a tin and a banana gone brown at the edges. "Sit with me, gudiya. Eat this while we wait." Aparna chewed, sniffling, head against Nani's arm. By the time a neighbour lent them a stove, she was helping stir the dal.

The gas cylinder.

She was hungry and overwhelmed after a long wait, so the snapped biscuit felt like the last straw.

It met Aparna's real, physical need quickly, calming her better than a scolding could have while they waited.

The rain had flooded the underpass, and Binita, twenty-two, took two autos and waded the last stretch to reach the insurance office by nine. Her trousers were wet to the knees, but she signed the register at 8:58. At 9:10 her phone buzzed. Rashmi, from her team: 'Stuck in traffic. Sign me in pls? Everyone does it 🙏' Binita looked at the register, the pen on its string. She liked Rashmi; Rashmi had taught her the software in her first week. She typed and deleted twice. Then: 'Can't sign for you, sorry. I'll tell Ma'am you're stuck in the flood so she knows.' She went to the supervisor and did exactly that. Rashmi walked in at 10:05 and didn't talk to her till lunch. At lunch she slid a samosa across. 'Fair enough,' she said.

What time did Binita sign the register?
Why did Binita type and delete her reply twice?
She felt torn, liking Rashmi and owing her, yet not wanting to sign in falsely.

Offering to tell the supervisor about the flood, which was honest and still looked out for Rashmi.

Monday: Amma left for the bank, and Ganga howled at the gate. Devika Chithi lifted her onto a hip, and within minutes Ganga was patting the rangoli powder.

Wednesday: Ganga fell asleep on Paati's lap while Chithi fried vadas.

Saturday: Ganga toddled from room to room with a broken biscuit, pressing a crumb into Thatha's hand, then Chithi's, then her big cousin's, laughing each time.

Before: In the months after her younger brother died in a road accident, Dilnaz stopped going out. She kept his cricket bat by her bed and didn't answer her friend Sarika's calls.
During: In September, Sarika came to the door with two aprons. "The community kitchen near the station needs help on Sundays. Just come once." Dilnaz almost said no. She went. For four hours she chopped onions and served dal to workers and families. A small boy asked her for extra roti, and he had the same gap in his teeth her brother had had. She had to step outside for a minute. Then she went back in.
After: By December, Sundays at the kitchen were fixed. The grief was still there; some nights it was as sharp as ever. But she told Sarika, "When I'm serving, I feel like I'm doing something he'd be proud of. It gives the pain somewhere to go."

Where did Sarika take Dilnaz on Sundays?
Sarika took her to the community kitchen near the station.
How did Dilnaz feel when the small boy asked for extra roti?
She felt a sharp wave of grief, reminded of her brother's smile, and had to step outside for a minute before going back in.
Why did helping at the kitchen make Dilnaz's grief more bearable?
Serving others gave her pain a purpose and a feeling of doing something her brother would be proud of, even though the grief did not go away.
How might Sarika feel seeing Dilnaz keep going on Sundays?
Sarika probably feels relieved and quietly glad that her gentle push helped her friend find some meaning in the loss.

To the terrace, where it was quieter.

The sheet was dull and easy to postpone, so a short, bounded block made starting easy even in a noisy house.

I brought his old blue T-shirt to sleep in, and it still smells a bit like him. Nani saw me crying and didn't say, “Don't be silly.” She said, “Missing someone means you love them. Ankita brought Papa's old blue T-shirt.

Ankita felt homesick, missing Papa so much her chest hurt.

Talking with Nani, the comfort of Papa's T-shirt and a planned call every night at eight.

Our final-year team almost split up in the first month. I'm Chaitanya. Vishal and I both wanted the machine learning part, because it looked best on a resume, and nobody wanted the documentation. So our guide made the four of us sit in the library for an hour and say two things each: what we're good at, and what we want to learn. It felt awkward. But Vishal admitted he'd already done machine learning in an internship and actually wanted to learn app development. I admitted I was strong in data cleaning but had never trained a model. In the library for an hour.

Tutor's note, coaching centre, 3 April.
Nazia has a system I want the other students to see. Every Sunday she makes a list of the topics studied that week. On Monday she writes what she remembers of last week's list on a blank sheet, without looking, then checks it. Topics she gets right move to a 'two weeks' pile; topics she misses stay in 'this week'. messages.content:
What does scruple mean in simple words?
Why should you cover your mouth when you sneeze?
What will happen in the next episode of my favourite series?
How can I get ready for an exam the night before?
Fix my grammar: I and my sister are twins.

1. Scruple is a noun that means a feeling that stops you from doing something you think is wrong.
2. It is polite and healthy. Because sneezing throws tiny drops into the air, and covering stops them from reaching other people.
3. I don't know that. I can't see future episodes or your series. Wait for the next episode, or read an official preview.
4. Go over your short notes and pack your bag. Sleep on time, so that you can think clearly the next day.
5. Better: My sister and I are twins. Why: "I" is the subject form; name yourself last.

July. His old friend Rohit called Leela: Nitin had blocked him. Then Nitin told her he had skipped his exams. "The Guide says family ties are chains."

The evening her parents told her they were separating, Lalremsiami walked out of the room and shut her door. For weeks she would not eat dinner if her father, Eshaan, sat at the table; she blamed him for everything. At night she cried into her pillow for the house with two parents and the Sunday breakfasts, but at school she told her friends, "I'm fine, honestly." She kept up her football practice anyway. In her head one quiet question kept going: her fights with her mother, Uma, over marks, the exam she failed. Had she pushed them apart? One night Uma found her awake, and Lalremsiami finally asked. Uma said, "No. This is between your father and me. It is not your fault, and we both love you." Eshaan said the same on the phone the next day. Lalremsiami cried properly then, and told her best friend how much she missed the old family. Under the anger, she realised, she had mostly been sad. Months later, on a Sunday, she visited Eshaan's new flat, ate his lopsided pancakes and saw two flawed people who did better living apart. She still missed the old house. She said so, and Eshaan nodded.

What would Lalremsiami not do if her father sat at the table?

How did Lalremsiami's feelings toward her father change between the first weeks and the months afterwards?

At first she blamed Eshaan and would not sit with him while her grief and her secret question about her fights stayed hidden; after her parents said it was not her fault and time passed, she visited his flat and saw both parents as flawed people who did better living apart.
What was Lalremsiami feeling when she told her friends "I'm fine, honestly"?
She was hiding sadness and grief, trying to look fine while crying at night.
What could Lalremsiami do next to look after herself?
She could keep up her football practice, keep talking to a friend or counsellor, keep visiting Eshaan and stay honest with both parents.

There's a thunderstorm coming, and my little sister is scared.
Storms can feel scary, especially to small children. How old is she?
She's four. She hides under the bed when it thunders.

Shared rooms often cause friction. A calm talk about what bothers each of you is a good start.
We just argue when we try.
Try picking a time when you are both calm, and take turns speaking without interruption. Say what you need, such as quiet during study time.
What kind of rules could help?
Agree on things like a tidy-up time, quiet hours, and a space that is each person's own. Writing them down makes them easier to remember.
What if it still doesn't work?
Ask another family member to help you both talk it through. A neutral person can suggest a fair plan.

Please define "consolation". Why do we plant seeds a little below the surface of the soil? Correct this sentence: My friend invited me for his birthday. what should I do if I find a lost wallet on the street?

1. "Consolation" is a noun. It means comfort given to someone who is sad or has lost something.
2. Seeds should be covered with soil to sprout well. Because the soil keeps them moist and hides them from birds.
3. Fixed: My friend invited me to his birthday. Why: we are invited "to" an event, not "for" it.
4. Take it to the nearest police station or hand it to a responsible adult. Do not keep it, because it belongs to someone who needs it.

Read this:

I'm Devika. I share a flat with Kashish, and this year I watched her change, though I can't tell you exactly what was in her head.
It started after her uncle's funeral. She came home and sat on the balcony for hours. The next week she did three things I'd never seen before.
She called her sister, whom she hadn't spoken to in two years, and apologised. She started going to the Saturday literacy class at the community hall, teaching adults to read. And when she promised to help me move my cupboard, she actually did, on time.
Once I asked her why. She said, "I'd like to look back and be okay with it. Not perfect. Just okay."
She still forgets to buy milk. But something in her is steadier.

Where does Kashish teach adults to read?
At the Saturday literacy class at the community hall.
What might Kashish's hours on the balcony suggest she was feeling?
They suggest she felt shaken and thoughtful after her uncle's funeral, reflecting on her own life.
Which of Kashish's changes show a life she can accept?
Repairing things with her sister, teaching at the literacy class and keeping small promises, while accepting she's not perfect.
How might Kashish's sister feel after the apology call?
Her sister likely felt surprised and relieved after two years of silence.

metadata.subtype: Living so the story is one you can accept [Response]
