Read this:

I wanted my timetable app to be perfect before anyone saw it. So I added chat. Then badges. Then a dark mode, because a good app has one. Every evening there was one more thing, and I told myself I was almost done. But my exam-free weeks ran out, and the app never went live. Later my friend Simran told me what the class had actually wanted: a plain page with the timetable on it, something to open on the way to school. A photo of the timetable would have done the job. I had spent six weeks on features that nobody had asked for and forgotten to ask anyone what they needed. — Rashmi

What had the class actually wanted?
A plain page with the timetable on it.
How does Rashmi feel looking back?
Regretful and a bit embarrassed at spending six weeks on features nobody asked for.
What could Rashmi have done instead, and why?
Share a plain timetable page first and add features only when classmates ask, because real requests show what is worth building.
How does the situation look to Simran?
Simran, who knew what the class wanted, saw the extras as unnecessary and probably wished Rashmi had asked earlier.

metadata.subtype: Approach: overbuilding features before anyone uses it [Pitfall]

messages.content:
I don't understand "indifferently". Can you help?
Then, what colour are my teacher's shoes today?
And one more: how can I manage my time on the weekend?
Oh, and what does "sleep like a log" mean?
Make this correct: After the match we goes home tired and happy.

1. "Indifferently" is an adverb. It means in a way that shows no interest or concern.
2. I can't check that, since I can't see your teacher. Look at them next time you are in class.
3. Do the important task first, then plan some play and rest. A simple list for the day helps.
4. It means to sleep very deeply. For example: after the long walk, the children slept like logs.
5. Better: After the match we went home tired and happy. Why: the match is over, so use the past tense "went".

Read this:

"You're driving four hours to look at stars?" Afreen asked, holding the car door.
"To the observatory in the hills. They open the telescope on new-moon nights." Deepak tossed a blanket in the back. "Come."
"I have that client deck."
"You had that client deck last month too. And you snapped at the office assistant on Wednesday."
Afreen winced. "Fine. But if I'm bored, you're buying dinner."
At one in the morning they lay on the observatory terrace. Through the telescope Afreen saw Saturn, rings and all, small and perfect. She pulled back, looked up with her own eyes, and said nothing for a long time.
"Still thinking about the deck?" Deepak asked.
"What deck," Afreen said softly.

What did Afreen see through the telescope?
Saturn, rings and all.
What does Afreen saying "What deck" softly suggest?
It suggests she felt awe and calm, her work stress shrinking beside Saturn and the sky.
Why is Deepak's new-moon trip a wise habit?
Making time on purpose for awe, like nights at the observatory, eases petty stress before it builds.
Why might Deepak have pushed Afreen to come?
Deepak seems worried about Afreen's stress, having noticed the snapping on Wednesday and the same deck dragging on for a month.

Read this:

Rekha had planned a slide show. Then, on Thursday evening, the vice-principal moved the eco-club assembly to Friday morning, and the projector in the hall was still broken. Naveen stared at the laptop. "Twelve slides of graphs. Useless." Rekha pulled out the chart paper left over from Diwali decorations. "We only need three things. Why it's getting hotter. What our school wastes. What we'll do." They worked on the floor of her room until midnight: a sun over a grey blanket of smoke for the greenhouse effect, a tally of forty lights found on in empty classrooms, and a sign-up sheet for "Switch-Off Monitors". In the morning her hands shook holding the chart. But thirty-one names were on the sheet by lunch, and a Class 6 boy asked to be monitor for the whole corridor.

How many lights did the tally show on in empty classrooms?
Forty lights.
What was Rekha feeling as she held the chart in the morning?
Rekha felt nervous, with shaking hands after the rushed night, but went ahead anyway.
How did the group handle the broken projector, and why did it still work?
They cut twelve slides down to three simple ideas on chart paper, which kept the message clear and ended with an action students could join.
How might Naveen feel when thirty-one names appear on the sheet?
Naveen, who thought the plan was useless without slides, would probably feel relieved and proud that the simpler version worked.

Read this:

In their tiny café in Osaka, Yuki and her business partner Yosef had set aside one weekend and a small budget for safety. Yosef had a brochure for a second, very expensive gas detector. "Then there's no chance of a gas leak at all." Yuki made a list on the back of a receipt. The café already had one gas detector, checked last month. But the tall shelves of cups and jars weren't bolted to the wall, and the city had small earthquakes every few weeks. Falling shelves were the thing most likely to hurt someone. "The second detector would move a tiny risk from almost zero to zero," she said. "Bolting the shelves cuts a much bigger one." Yosef grumbled, then fetched the drill. That afternoon they bolted every shelf and moved the heavy jars to the bottom row.

What did Yosef want to buy?
A second, very expensive gas detector.
Why did Yuki push for bolting the shelves instead?
Yuki felt calm and practical, seeing that falling shelves were the most likely danger while the gas risk was already very low.
What makes Yuki's receipt list a good way to decide?
Listing what already protects them and what is most likely to hurt someone shows which option removes the most total risk.
How did Yosef respond once the list was explained?
Yosef grumbled, then fetched the drill and helped bolt every shelf.
Why do runners lean forward when starting a sprint?
Leaning helps them push off the ground. Because the body tilts in the direction of the run, the legs can push backward and send the runner forward quickly.

Read this:

Naveen had been in bed with flu for three days in their Chennai flat, and his thoughts felt as if they were wading through syrup. When Karthik called about the group project, Naveen listened to his idea of changing the topic and exploded. "Fine, do whatever you want. I don't care about the stupid project!" He hung up and threw the phone onto the blanket. Ten minutes later he was staring at the ceiling, ashamed and worried: what if the others dropped him? What if he failed the term? His mother brought him rasam and found him close to tears. "You're sick, kanna. Everything looks worse right now. Don't settle anything today." The next evening, feeling a little better, he called Karthik back. "Sorry about yesterday. Your topic's actually good. Can we talk properly when I'm back?"

How long had Naveen been in bed with flu?
Three days.
How did Naveen feel staring at the ceiling after hanging up?
He felt ashamed and anxious, worried the group would drop him and he would fail the term.
What made the second call go better?
Waiting until he felt better meant he could think clearly, apologise, and see that Karthik's topic was good.
How might Karthik have felt when Naveen hung up?
Karthik was probably hurt and confused, having only suggested an idea.

metadata.subtype: Ill teen feeling foggy and cranky [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

The school library was Lalit's favourite hiding place now. At break, Pallavi found him in the back row with a book he wasn't reading. "We're all going for the inter-house match after school. Coming?" Lalit didn't look up. "I've got stuff." It was the third time this month. Since the class trip, when nobody had saved him a seat on the bus, he had stopped messaging the group first. If they wanted him, they could ask. When they did ask, like now, he said no anyway, before they could change their minds. "You used to love these matches," Pallavi said. Lalit shrugged. "I like being alone. It's easier." Pallavi stood there a moment longer, then left. Lalit watched her go through the glass door, and something in his chest dropped. He turned a page, though he hadn't read it.

Where did Pallavi find Lalit at break?
She found him in the back row of the school library with a book he wasn't reading.
Why does Lalit say no before the others can change their minds?
Lalit is afraid of being rejected again after the bus trip, so refusing first feels safer even though it leaves him lonely.
What turning point is available to Lalit or Pallavi here?
Lalit could say yes once, even for a short while; Pallavi could keep inviting him and tell him plainly that she wants him there.
How might Pallavi feel walking away from the library?
Pallavi may feel confused and a little hurt, wondering if Lalit is annoyed with her, since he used to love these matches.

Read this:

Sunday.
Tried my new rule today. Small stuff: gut. Big stuff: slow. Lunch at the dhaba? Gut said rajma, done in two seconds. Which shirt for Dolma's birthday? Gut, blue. Then the landlord messaged asking me to sign a two-year lease by tonight. My gut said yes, the flat's lovely. But two years is big and hard to undo. So I wrote a checklist: notice period, repairs, deposit terms, distance to work. Called Dolma, who rented last year, and she told me to ask about the notice clause. Told the landlord I'd reply on Tuesday, after sleeping on it. Felt weirdly grown-up.
Abhinav

What did Abhinav's gut choose for lunch?
Rajma.
How did Abhinav feel after telling the landlord Tuesday?
Abhinav felt weirdly grown-up and calm about slowing down on something big.
What is Abhinav's rule, and how was it used?
Small stuff by gut, big stuff slowly: for the lease, a checklist, advice from Dolma, and sleeping on it before replying.
How might the landlord see the delay?
The landlord might be a little impatient, but gets a considered answer instead of a rushed one that could fall apart.

Read this:

Thursday
Harsha got the same haircut as me today. Exact same. He even asked the barber for "Sahil bhaiya style." I rolled my eyes, but okay, it looks good on him.
He follows me everywhere. To the terrace, to the tuition gate, even to cricket, where he sits on the wall and cheers every ball like I'm famous. My friends think it's hilarious. Yesterday Pratik said, "Your fan club's here," and I laughed along and said, "Go home, baby." Harsha went home. He didn't eat much at dinner.
I felt terrible. He's eight. He copies me because he thinks I'm worth copying, which is a weird feeling, a bit heavy and a bit nice.
So new rule. Saturday mornings are his: I'll teach him to bowl. Weekday cricket is mine with my friends. I told him tonight. He nodded like it was a treaty.

What did Harsha ask the barber for?
"Sahil bhaiya style."
How does Sahil feel about Harsha copying him?
Sahil is annoyed but secretly flattered, finding it a bit heavy and a bit nice to be looked up to.
Which choice is Sahil making now, and why is it wise?
Sahil is giving Harsha Saturday mornings while keeping weekday cricket for his friends, a clear boundary that still shows care.
What was it like for Harsha when Sahil called him 'baby'?
Harsha felt hurt and embarrassed in front of the older boys, so he went home and barely ate dinner.

Although I saw him every day, it was for only a short time; hence, the regularly recurring spaces of our separation were long enough to record on his face any slight changes that occurred in his physical state. I do not recollect that I once saw any change in it for the better; he wasted, and became slowly weaker and worse, day by day, from the day when the prison door closed upon him.

How does the narrator know that the man's health is failing?

He is seen only briefly each day, so the gaps between visits are long enough to show slight changes. There has been no change for the better; he wastes away and grows slowly weaker each day since the prison door closed on him.

Read this:

Thursday. Minakshi's parents sat her down at the table. "We're going to a wedding on Saturday, just for the afternoon. You'll stay home. Door locked, no stove, no opening it to strangers. If anything worries you, call Bhavna Aunty next door." Minakshi nodded, sitting very straight.

Saturday. She turned the key behind them and felt tall. When the doorbell rang, she said through the door, "My parents aren't in. Please come back later." She read her book and ate the sandwich they had left.

The next Friday. Her father said, "You can walk to the library by yourself now. Just tell Bhavna Aunty." Minakshi hid her grin behind her hair.

Who could Minakshi call if anything worried her?
She could call Bhavna Aunty next door.
What was Minakshi feeling when she turned the key behind her parents?
She felt grown up and proud that they had left her in charge, with a little nervousness under it.
What helped Minakshi earn the library walk?
She followed the rules while nobody was checking, so her parents saw they could depend on her and offered more freedom. 😊
How might her parents have felt when they came home from the wedding?
Relieved and proud to find everything as agreed, which made it easier for them to offer her more independence.
I auditioned for the lead in our school play and got a tiny role instead.
That is disappointing, especially if you worked hard for it. How are you feeling about it?
Embarrassed. My friend got the lead and everyone keeps congratulating her.
It is hard to be happy for a friend while you are hurting, and both feelings can exist together. You don't have to pretend you are fine, but you can still congratulate her.
Is a small role even worth doing?

Yes. Small roles teach you how a show runs, and directors notice people who do them well. Use rehearsals to learn from the lead role too. Next time, you will go into the audition with more experience.

Could you explain what avarice means?
Can you fix my sentence? I like very much football.
How can I choose a gift for a friend's birthday?

1. Avarice is a noun that means a greedy wish to have more and more money.
2. Say it this way: I like football very much. Why: "very much" cannot sit between the verb and its object.
3. Think about what your friend enjoys and choose something useful or fun that fits your budget. A handwritten card makes any gift feel special.
Always I forget to bring my water bottle. How can I say it better?

I always forget to bring my water bottle.
Why: "always" goes before the main verb.

Read this:

The college bus was forty minutes late, stuck behind a waterlogged underpass, and everyone was short-tempered. In the back row, two seniors grabbed Eshaan's phone again, typed something from his account and tossed it back, laughing. The third time that week. Mridul, wedged by the door, felt his anger rise and started toward them. Then he stopped. Would a scene on a stuck bus help Eshaan, or just make him the centre of it? At the college gate, away from the crowd, he caught up. "I saw the phone thing. What do you want? I can go with you to the anti-ragging cell, or talk to them, or just sit next to you on the bus. Your call." Eshaan looked at his shoes. "Come with me to the cell? Now, before I lose my nerve." They went. The teacher on duty wrote down both seniors' names, asked Eshaan for screenshots, and called the seniors in that afternoon.

How late was the college bus?
Forty minutes late.
Why did Mridul stop himself from confronting the seniors on the bus?
He felt angry but also unsure, worried a scene would only make Eshaan the centre of attention rather than help him.
What made Mridul's help respectful?
He asked Eshaan privately what he wanted and offered choices, then followed his lead to the anti-ragging cell.
How might Eshaan feel being told "Your call"?
Eshaan likely feels respected and less powerless, able to choose the help he wants after days of having control taken from him.

Read this:

“Last one,” said Ritu, counting. “Manjula.”

“Ha, I'm always the bonus,” Manjula said, tugging her braid. Nobody laughed.

Salma, captain of Team Blue, stepped forward. “Manjula, come here. I've been saving you.”

“For what?”

“The goal circle. You never lose track of where the ball is. Last time you shouted ‘left!’ and we scored.”

“I only did that once.”

“Once was enough.” Salma nudged her shoulder. “Stand by me.”

Manjula stepped over slowly, hiding a smile. “Okay. But if I mess up, I go back to being the bonus.”

“Deal,” said Salma. “You won't.”

What did Manjula call herself when picked last?
Manjula said, “I'm always the bonus.”
Why did Manjula say she was always the bonus while tugging the braid?
Manjula was hiding hurt behind a joke, and tugging the braid shows nervousness about being measured in public.
What did Salma do that changed how Manjula felt?
Salma called Manjula over warmly, said Manjula had been saved for the goal circle and named a real contribution.
What might Salma have noticed that led Salma to choose Manjula for the goal circle?
Salma noticed that Manjula tracks the ball well and once shouted “left!” to set up a goal, a strength others had missed.
The waiter said the dessert was "on the house". Do we have to pay?

No. "On the house" means that the restaurant or shop is giving it to you for free.
Example: The owner brought us sweets, on the house.
What do swimmers wear on their heads in the pool? Answer in exactly two words.
Swimming cap

January, a quiet Sunday. Ira wrote a rule on an index card: "If shares fall so that they are much less of my mix, move a small slice from the steady holdings into shares." She stuck it inside the notebook.
March, the week of the crash. Ira's shares had dropped and the mix had drifted. Lokesh, her friend, texted, "You're not actually buying more now, are you?" Ira read the card twice. "I wrote this when I was calm," she replied. Her hands were cold as she moved the slice.
April. Prices were still unsteady, but the mix was back near the plan. Ira added a line to the card: "Review once a year." Lokesh sent a thumbs-up.

Where did Ira keep the rule?
Ira kept the rule inside the notebook.
What was Ira feeling when moving the slice in March?
Ira was nervous, shown by the cold hands, but held to the card because she wrote it while calm.
What could Ira do if she started to doubt the rule during a fall?
Ira could talk it over with a registered adviser before changing the card, rather than changing it in the heat of the moment.
How might Lokesh have felt seeing Ira follow the card?
Lokesh was worried at first, given the sharp text, and later relieved enough to send a thumbs-up.

Jyoti sat on the roof of her new house in a small town near Sangli, watching buffaloes cross the dusty road. She missed the noisy lanes of Mumbai and the way Rehana used to save half her tiffin for her. Her throat tightened. That evening she borrowed her aunt's phone and called Rehana, who laughed and told her all about the school play. Afterwards Jyoti wrote a long letter and drew the buffaloes in the margin. The next day a girl named Sunita from the next lane peeped over the wall and asked what she was drawing. Jyoti hesitated, then held up the page. She still missed Mumbai, but she let Sunita sit on the wall beside her.

What did Jyoti draw in the margin of her letter?
The buffaloes.
What was Jyoti feeling on the roof, and what does it show?
Jyoti felt homesick and sad, missing the noisy lanes of Mumbai and Rehana; her throat tightened, which shows how much she cared for them.
How can Jyoti keep her old friendship while making room for new ones?
Keep calling and writing to Rehana, and let Sunita sit beside her.
How might Rehana feel getting the call and the letter?
Rehana laughed on the call and shared news, so Rehana is probably glad that Jyoti keeps in touch, and may miss Jyoti too.

Read this:

In the fest committee's room, Seema noticed that Vasudha had sighed four times in an hour. Vasudha had sent the wrong date to the sponsors, misspelled a name on the banner and now sat with a packed lunchbox untouched beside the laptop. Seema thought about telling Vasudha to “take it easy” and “make a schedule”, and then dropped the idea; it would only be one more thing to carry. Instead she pulled a chair over and asked, “What can I take off your plate this week?” Vasudha stared, then laughed weakly. “The sponsor emails. Can you do those?” Seema nodded and drafted the first one right there while Vasudha finally opened the lunchbox.

How many times did Vasudha sigh in an hour?
Vasudha sighed four times in an hour.
Why did Seema drop the idea of telling Vasudha to take it easy?
Seema felt concerned for Vasudha and wary of adding to the load, sensing that such advice would only be one more thing for Vasudha to carry.
What did Seema do that helped?
Seema asked what could be taken off Vasudha's plate, then drafted the first sponsor email so Vasudha could eat lunch.
What might Vasudha be feeling when staring and then laughing weakly?
Vasudha is probably overwhelmed and relieved at being asked, and the weak laugh shows exhaustion and a little gratitude.

When the Sessions came round, Mr. Jaggers caused an application to be made for the postponement of his trial until the following Sessions. It was obviously made with the assurance that he could not live so long, and was refused. The trial came on at once, and, when he was put to the bar, he was seated in a chair. No objection was made to my getting close to the dock, on the outside of it, and holding the hand that he stretched forth to me.

Question: What does Mr. Jaggers apply for at the Sessions, and what happens?

Mr. Jaggers applies to postpone the trial until the following Sessions, obviously because the prisoner could not live so long, but it is refused. The trial comes on at once, and the prisoner sits in a chair holding the narrator's hand.

Read this:

I'm Harsha, and I've been mentoring new analysts at our firm for two years. I learned the hard way how not to do it.

My first mentee, I laughed when he made a mistake. "That's a rookie error," I said, in front of the team. He never asked me anything again. He also never admitted another error. He just got more confident and more wrong.

So when Aparna joined last month, full of confidence, I tried something else.

She'd built a sales forecast and said it was "bulletproof". Instead of pointing out the flaws, I said, "Walk me through it. Start from the first cell."

Halfway through, she stopped. "Wait, I've counted the same region twice." A few minutes later: "Oh, and these months are missing."

I didn't say anything. I didn't need to.

She fixed it that evening. The next week she came to me before submitting, asking, "Can I walk you through this one?"

What did Aparna call her sales forecast?
She said it was "bulletproof".
What did Aparna seem to feel when she found the double-counted region?
Aparna seemed surprised and a little embarrassed, discovering the gaps herself as she explained.
Why did Harsha's walk-through approach work better than the laughter used with the first mentee?
It let Aparna find her own mistakes without shame, so she stayed open, while ridicule made the first mentee defensive and hid errors.
How might Harsha's first mentee have felt after being laughed at?
The first mentee likely felt humiliated and defensive, which is why he stopped asking and never admitted errors.

Read this:

Monday: At school, Pooja's class learned the emergency number and practised saying their address clearly. She wrote both on a card and stuck it on the fridge at home.
Thursday: Nazia Aunty next door showed Pooja her first-aid box: bandages, antiseptic, cotton, and the doctor's number taped inside the lid.
The next Sunday: Pooja's grandmother slipped in the bathroom and couldn't get up. Pooja's hands shook, but she called the emergency number from the card, said the address slowly, then ran to fetch Nazia Aunty. Help arrived soon. Later, Nani squeezed her hand.

Where did Pooja stick the card with the emergency number?
She stuck it on the fridge at home.
What do Pooja's shaking hands suggest about how she felt?
They suggest she was frightened, even while she did the right things.
What preparation helped Pooja act in the emergency?
Learning the emergency number, practising her address and putting the card on the fridge.
How might Nani feel about Pooja?
She probably feels grateful and proud, which is why she squeezed her hand. 🙏

Read this:

On the night before Gurpurab the power went out in their lane in Amritsar, and the langar preparation moved to candlelight in the courtyard. Gurleen and her college friend Imran were chopping onions beside her Biji when the question she had been swallowing for weeks slipped out.
"Biji, what if the Gurus were just wise men? What if the stories aren't literally true?"
Her mother, stirring the dal, froze. Imran stopped chopping.
Biji didn't. She kept kneading, then laughed softly. "You think you're the first to ask that? Guru Nanak himself asked questions wherever he went. Asking is not a sin, puttar. Being afraid to ask is worse."
She told Gurleen about her own doubts as a young bride, and the granthi who had listened instead of scolding. "Come with me to the gurdwara tomorrow. Ask Bhai-ji too. He likes a good question."
In the flickering light, Gurleen felt something unknot in her chest. Imran grinned and went back to the onions.

Where did the langar preparation move during the power cut?
To candlelight in the courtyard.
What did Gurleen feel when her Biji laughed?
She felt relieved and lighter, the fear of asking unknotting in her chest.
What did Biji do that kept Gurleen close to the faith?
She welcomed the question with interest, said doubt is old and common, shared her own doubts, and invited Gurleen to ask the granthi.
What might Gurleen's mother have felt when she froze?
Her mother probably felt alarmed and worried, until Biji's calm response eased the moment.

Thursday

Today at school I was ME. I argued with Sir about the history project and won. I made the whole back bench laugh. Meghna said I should run for head of house. I said maybe.

Then I got home and became the other one. Amma asked, "How was school?" "Fine." Indu didi asked if I wanted to watch the match. "No, homework." I ate dinner with my head down. Nobody at home knows I do stand-up in the free period. Nobody at school knows Amma still checks my bag.

It's easier this way. At home nobody laughs at my jokes, and at school nobody sees me being small. No fights.

But tonight Indu didi said, "You used to be funny, you know." And I felt weird. Like she misses someone who's right here.

Chaitanya

What did Meghna suggest Chaitanya run for?
Meghna said Chaitanya should run for head of house.
Why does keeping the two worlds separate feel easier to Chaitanya?
Chaitanya feels safer that way: no one at home laughs at the jokes and no one at school sees the small side, so there are no fights, even if it feels lonely.
What small step could let Chaitanya be known at home?
Chaitanya could share one school story with Indu didi, like the stand-up or the head of house idea, and see how it lands.
How does Indu didi seem to feel about Chaitanya at home?
Indu didi seems wistful and a bit sad, missing the funny sibling who now goes quiet at home.

metadata.subtype: Different selves at school and home [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

In the girls' hostel common room, someone played a dance reel by Tina from the other hostel block.
“Attention-seeking,” said Mansi. “Who dances in a corridor?”
“Total drama queen,” agreed Pooja.
Vandana looked at Arohi, curled up on the sofa. Last Sunday Arohi had posted almost the same corridor dance, and the room had cheered, “So talented!”
Vandana didn't want a fight. She said, “Wait, isn't that the same step Arohi did last week? We loved hers.”
Arohi laughed, a little embarrassed. “Oh no. It is.”
Mansi paused. “Hm. Maybe we just like Arohi more,” she admitted. “That's... not really fair to Tina, is it.”

Where had Arohi posted her dance?
She had posted almost the same corridor dance last Sunday.
Why did Vandana choose her words carefully?
She felt uncomfortable with the unfairness but didn't want a fight, so she asked a gentle question instead of accusing.
What did Vandana's question help the group see?
It helped them notice they judged the same dance differently depending on who did it, and Mansi admitted it wasn't fair to Tina.
How might Arohi feel after the comparison?
She seemed a bit embarrassed but good-humoured, laughing as she realised the dances matched.

Read this:

At the temple fair in the kasba, Aparna kept stopping at the bangle stall mirror to fix her dupatta and smooth her hair. When a group of boys from her school came near the Ferris wheel, she took out her phone and stared at it, though there was no signal.
Her cousin Darshan grinned. "Getting ready for your fans?"
Aparna's cheeks burned. She tugged the dupatta over her head and turned away.
Darshan saw her face go tight. He stopped grinning. "Hey. Sorry. Something wrong?"
"The wind keeps messing my hair, and those boys laughed at my braces last week," she muttered. "I just don't want them to look."
Darshan stepped to stand between her and the boys. "Then let's go to the jalebi stall. They can't see us there."

Where did Aparna keep fixing her dupatta?
At the bangle stall mirror.
What was Aparna feeling when she stared at her phone?
Aparna felt self-conscious and anxious, not wanting the boys who had laughed at her braces to look at her.
What did Darshan do that turned it around?
He noticed her tight face, stopped teasing, asked what was wrong, and shielded her by moving them away.
How did Darshan first read Aparna's grooming?
He thought she was preening to look good for the boys, not realising she felt insecure.

Read this:

After the cricket bat went missing from the school sports room, Sumit wouldn't look at anyone. At lunch he stared at his tiffin. When Kishore asked if he'd seen the bat, Sumit looked at his shoes.
Kishore wondered: was Sumit guilty? Or just shy? Sumit was always a bit quiet.
After school, Kishore asked gently, "Are you okay? You've been really quiet today."
Sumit swallowed. "I broke the bat. By accident. I was scared to tell Sir."
Kishore thought for a moment. "Want me to come with you to tell him?"
Sumit finally looked up. "Would you?"
They went together. Sir said, "Thank you for telling me. Accidents happen." Sumit's shoulders dropped with relief.

What did Sumit break?
The cricket bat.
What was Sumit feeling when he wouldn't look at anyone?
Sumit felt guilty and scared about the broken bat.
What did Kishore do that helped?
He asked gently instead of accusing, and offered to go with Sumit to tell Sir.
How might Sir have felt when Sumit told him?
Sir was probably glad Sumit was honest and understood it was an accident.

messages.content:
Write this out as simple modern prose for me.

As when the woodman's axe has lopped
A Sal branch in the grove, she dropped:
So from the skies a Goddess falls
Ejected from her radiant halls.
She dropped like a branch of a sal tree cut off by the woodman's axe in the grove. It was like a goddess falling from the sky, thrown out of her shining halls.
Is it "recipie" or "recipe"?

It is "recipe", ending in "-pe". There is no "ie" at the end.
Example: My grandmother has an old recipe for lemon rice.

Read this:

Senior teacher's note, Class 5 trip to the zoo, Thursday.
During the afternoon, Ujjwal, ten, wandered off near the aviary. Our new teacher, Amandeep, 24, who had told me that morning that police "never help anyone, only trouble people," was the one who noticed he was missing. She panicked.
We approached a police officer at the zoo gate. He calmly radioed his colleagues, asked for Ujjwal's description and checked the exits. Within twenty minutes, another officer found Ujjwal near the snack stall, crying, and brought him back, crouching to talk to him gently.
Amandeep thanked the officer twice. On the bus back, she said quietly, "I was so sure they were all the same. I was wrong about him."
Next step: I've suggested Amandeep lead a short class talk next week on what to do if lost, including approaching police.

Where was Ujjwal found?
Another officer found him near the snack stall, crying.
What was Amandeep feeling when she noticed Ujjwal was missing?
Amandeep felt panicked and frightened for the child.
What does Amandeep's changed view show?
Seeing the officers help calmly made her realise that not all police are the same, so fair judgement avoids painting everyone alike.
How might Ujjwal have felt when the officer crouched to talk to him?
Ujjwal was probably scared and then comforted by the officer's gentle way.

Read this:

I'm Disha, Sudha's classmate, and I watched her do something I wouldn't have thought of. We both went to a one-day energy conference in Chennai. At lunch she pointed at a speaker, Dr Iyer, and said, 'Everyone will send him a thank-you. What would actually help him?'
She had heard him say he'd miss the afternoon panel because of a flight. So during that panel she took careful notes, and that night she wrote a one-page summary of the three main arguments and the audience questions. I saw her cut it twice to keep it short.
She emailed it to him the next morning, with one line: 'You mentioned missing this panel, so I thought this might be useful.' He wrote back the same day, thanked her, and asked about her own project. They've exchanged messages every few weeks since. I can't know what she felt, but she read his first reply aloud to me twice.

Why did Dr Iyer miss the afternoon panel?
Because of a flight.
What might Sudha have been feeling when she read the reply aloud twice?
She was probably excited and proud that her useful summary had opened a real conversation.
What else could Sudha offer Dr Iyer as the contact grows?
Share a short note on a related paper or event now and then, keeping the relationship about give and take rather than only asking.
How does the summary look from Dr Iyer's side?
For Dr Iyer it fills a real gap, the missed panel, so a student's email becomes something useful rather than one more thank-you.

metadata.subtype: Approach: reciprocity by offering something useful [Thinking]

Read this:

In the waiting room of the eye clinic, while Dadi was inside, Gurpreet unfolded a tourist map of Jaipur across his knees. "Papa, the weekend: the fort, the palace of winds, the zoo, the water palace, the wax museum and the village dinner place. Six places! Two days!" His father smiled and borrowed the map. "Look. The fort is here, the zoo is here, the dinner place is way out here." He traced the roads with a finger, then pointed at the big wall clock. "Each drive is about an hour in traffic. The fort alone takes a morning. Count." Gurpreet counted on his fingers, and his grin slipped. "That's more hours than we're awake." Nurse Manjula called Dadi's name. Gurpreet folded the map slowly and crossed out two places.

How many places did Gurpreet want to visit in two days?
Six places.
What does Gurpreet's slipping grin show?
He felt disappointed as he realised his exciting list could not fit into two days.
What would you change first in Gurpreet's planning?
Checking the distances and how long each stop takes before choosing, then picking only two or three places a day.
How might Papa see the list?
Papa takes the excitement kindly, but uses the map and clock so Gurpreet can see the problem for himself.

metadata.subtype: Approach: making a wish list without limits [Pitfall]

messages.content:
Read this:

Come, sit, I'll tell you about Arnab. We were in the same hostel in Shillong, both doing botany, when I was about your age. Every evening in the mess, Arnab said the same thing: "From tomorrow I'll start the herbarium file." The next evening, again tomorrow. I noticed he ate less each time he said it, and once he just stared at his plate and said, "What's wrong with me?" I felt sorry and also a little annoyed, I won't pretend. I didn't know what to do. Then one night I said, "Arnab, bring your file. We'll sit in the common room for twenty minutes. Just press one leaf." He came, grumbling. That leaf became six. In the end he submitted before me. So when you watch a friend going round and round, remember that, beta. Lalremsiami learned it at nineteen.

What did Arnab keep saying he would start from tomorrow?
The herbarium file.
How did Lalremsiami feel watching Arnab say 'tomorrow' again and again?
Lalremsiami felt sorry for him and also a little annoyed, and unsure what to do at first.
At what point in the story did things turn, and why did it work?
The turn came when Lalremsiami invited Arnab to sit together for twenty minutes and press just one leaf; a small, shared start broke the cycle of 'tomorrow'.
How might Arnab have felt each time he said 'from tomorrow'?
He probably felt hopeful saying it, then worse each time it didn't happen, which showed in eating less and asking what was wrong with him.

Read this:

Vishal had already typed three paragraphs to his manager, Usha, explaining why he should not present the quarterly review to the client. The client deserved a senior voice. His numbers needed another week. The team would benefit from hearing someone new. In the office pantry, waiting for the kettle, he peeled off a sticky note and wrote the reason without polish: I'm scared I'll freeze in front of them. Seven words. He reread the email and asked himself: if his friend Rohit sent him this, would he buy it? He could hear his own reply: "You're nervous, yaar, just say so." Vishal deleted two paragraphs, then the third. The new message was one line: "Honestly, I'm nervous about presenting. Could we do a practice run first?" Usha answered in ten minutes; she had already booked the small conference room for Thursday. "Of course. 4 pm. 🙂"

What did Vishal write on the sticky note?
I'm scared I'll freeze in front of them.
Why did the three-paragraph email feel reasonable to Vishal while he was writing it?
Every reason sounded mature and focused on the client and the team, so it let him avoid the less flattering truth that he was afraid of freezing.
Which choice turned things around for Vishal, and why did it work?
Asking whether he would accept the same email from Rohit; he knew he wouldn't, so he sent the honest one-line version and got the practice run he actually needed.
What might Usha have done if she had received the original three paragraphs?
She might simply have handed the presentation to someone else, never learning that Vishal was nervous or that a practice run could help him.

Read this:

I'm Himani, and last year, when Kalyani Mausi came to live with us, she asked me to peel the potatoes every evening. I always said, "Yes, Mausi, sure!" with a big smile. Then I'd forget. I'd be in the bath. Or doing homework. Or I'd peel two potatoes and leave the rest.

It wasn't really forgetting. I didn't want to do it, because before Mausi came, evenings were my drawing time. But she was a guest, and I didn't know how to say no to a grown-up.

One evening she found me drawing and said, "Himani, if you don't want to peel, you can tell me." I burst into tears and said everything. She laughed and said, "Then draw me a picture instead, and peel only on Sundays." Now I peel on Sundays, properly, and she has my drawings on her wall.

What did Kalyani Mausi ask Himani to do every evening?
Mausi asked Himani to peel the potatoes every evening.
Why did Himani keep forgetting the potatoes?
Himani felt resentful about losing drawing time but was too nervous to say no to a grown-up guest, so the refusal came out as forgetting.
Which choice worked, and why?
Mausi made it safe to say no, and they agreed on Sundays, so the resistance could be said openly instead of sideways.
How might Kalyani Mausi have felt about the half-peeled potatoes?
Mausi may have felt puzzled and a little unwelcome at first, before understanding how much the drawing time mattered.

Read this:

In the corridor after science, Mehak caught Disha's sleeve. "You looked like you knew the answer. Why did you say 'maybe, I guess, it could be the mitochondria'?" Disha laughed. "What if I was wrong and everybody heard?" Mehak thought about it. "You said it in a tiny voice. Sir moved on to Rohan." Disha looked at her shoes. "I revised it yesterday. But I wasn't sure enough." "What would make you sure?" asked Mehak. "If I saw the diagram again." "Then let's look at it at lunch," Mehak said, opening her notebook. Disha nodded, and for the first time that day her shoulders came down. Later she found she had been right all along, and wrote 'sure' in the margin.

Where did Mehak stop Disha?
She stopped Disha in the corridor after science.
Why did Disha hedge with words like maybe and I guess?
She was probably afraid of being wrong in front of everyone, even though she had revised. It could also be that she truly was unsure about one detail.
What small step helped Disha here?
Looking at the diagram together at lunch gave her a concrete way to check, so her certainty could come from evidence rather than from tone.
How might Sir have read Disha's tiny-voiced answer?
He may have taken it as not knowing and moved on to Rohan, missing that she had studied.

Read this:

Note from Devika, class teacher:
For a week Wasim has stopped colouring in class and put his crayons away. On Thursday he said quietly, "Papa says the neighbour's boy can already write his whole name." His jaw was set and he would not look at me. I asked if he could tell Papa how it made him feel. At pick-up I stood nearby. Wasim said, "I feel sad when you say that." His father paused, then apologised and said he would look at Wasim's own progress. The next morning Wasim took out his crayons.

What did Wasim stop doing in class for a week?
He stopped colouring and put his crayons away.
What was Wasim feeling when he said Papa compared him with the neighbour's boy?
He was hurt and stubborn: his jaw was set and he would not look at Devika, and he stopped trying.
What did Wasim say to his father that helped?
He said, "I feel sad when you say that," which told his father honestly what the comparison did, and Papa apologised.
How might Papa have seen his comment before Wasim spoke?
He may have meant to encourage Wasim and not seen the hurt, since he paused and apologised once he heard it.

There were but eight; yet, somehow, as they flocked in, they gave the impression of a much larger number. Some of them were very tall; many were dressed in white; and all had a sweeping amplitude of array that seemed to magnify their persons as a mist magnifies the moon. I rose and curtseyed to them: one or two bent their heads in return, the others only stared at me.

Question: What impression do the eight people make as they enter?
They seem a much larger number. Some are very tall, many are dressed in white, and their sweeping, ample dress makes them look bigger, like a mist magnifying the moon.
What mood is associated with Raga Mishra Khamaj?
Raga Mishra Khamaj is associated with a romantic, expressive mood.
Rewrite politely, as a waiter would say it: You can't sit there. That table is taken.
I'm sorry, but that table is already taken, so we cannot seat you there.
I used my roommate's phone charger without asking and left it at college. Write a short, sincere sorry message to her, about 50 words.

Hi,
I am sorry that I took your phone charger without asking, and I am even sorrier that I left it at college. I should have asked first. I will bring it back as soon as I can. Please tell me if there is anything else I can do to make up for it.
Your roommate

Republic Day morning on the village school ground was cold and bright. The flag climbed to the top of the pole and snapped open in the wind. When the anthem began, Dhruv stood so tall his neck ached, and goosebumps ran up both arms. Beside him, Manoj leaned on his crutch, standing as straight as he could, his hand trembling with effort. After the last line, sweets were handed out. Dhruv carried a stool across to Manoj. "Sit. The sweets are coming." "I was fine," said Manoj, sitting anyway, grinning.

What did Manoj lean on during the anthem?
He leaned on his crutch.
What was Dhruv feeling during the anthem?
Deep pride: he stood so tall his neck ached and goosebumps ran up both arms.
How did Dhruv show love for his country in a caring way?
He noticed a classmate's effort and carried a stool over to Manoj after the anthem.
How might Manoj have felt about the stool?
He said he was fine but sat anyway, grinning, so he probably appreciated the thought while not wanting to be fussed over 😊.
Why is my father quiet these days?
I can't tell what he is thinking, so I don't know. Choose a calm moment and ask him how he is.

Write it in formal English, with no sentence fragments.

I keep replaying it. Last month I honestly thought the election was a formality. Half the school says hi to me in the corridor. The cricket team, the drama lot, my whole tuition batch. I didn't make a single poster because what's the point, everyone knows me.

I keep replaying it in my mind. Last month, I honestly believed the election was a mere formality. Half the school greets me in the corridor, including the cricket team, the drama group and my entire tuition batch. I did not make a single poster, because I thought there was no point when everyone already knew me.

Read this:

Monday. Pankaj pressed his nose to the car window. "Are we there yet? Are we there yet?" When Mama said the ice cream shop was after the bridge, he kicked the seat and cried.
Wednesday. Before leaving for Nani's, Mama gave him a paper strip with five stickers. "Each time we pass a petrol pump, peel one off." Pankaj counted pumps and asked only twice.
Saturday. Damini, his cousin, whined in the queue for the merry-go-round. Pankaj took her hand. "Let's sing the elephant song. When it ends, we'll be closer." They sang it three times, and then it was their turn.

What did Mama give Pankaj on Wednesday?
She gave him a paper strip with five stickers to peel off at each petrol pump.
Why did Pankaj kick the seat and cry on Monday?
He was frustrated and impatient; the ice cream shop still felt far away and he could not bear the wait.
What could a parent borrow from Mama's idea for a long wait?
They could make the wait something a child can see and count, like stickers, a song or a small game.
How might Damini feel when Pankaj starts singing with her in the queue?
She probably feels comforted and less bored, because the song gives the wait a clear end she can hear.
Please don't waist water while washing the car. Check the spelling.

Please don't waste water while washing the car.
Why: "Waste" means misuse; "waist" is a body part.

Read this:

Last week Vijay called me "Speedy Gonzales" because I run fast in PT class. I laughed so hard my water bottle fell. Then he did it again at lunch, and I laughed again, and Vijay did a little bow. It felt like our secret club joke. But when Rohan from the next bench said, "Preeti, why is your lunchbox always the same dal-roti?" I went quiet and stared at the steel dabba. Rohan kept grinning and repeated it. Vijay noticed my face before I said anything. He said, "Arre Rohan, that's not funny, stop." I still felt hot in my ears. I'm not sure whether Rohan meant harm.

What nickname did Vijay give Preeti in PT class?
Vijay called Preeti "Speedy Gonzales" for running fast in PT class.
What was Preeti feeling when Rohan asked about the lunchbox, and what else might explain the silence?

Most likely Preeti felt embarrassed and hurt, shown by going quiet, staring at the dabba and the hot ears. Preeti might also have been unsure how to answer, since Rohan was grinning and may not have meant harm.
What could Preeti try next time someone teases about something sore?
Preeti could say calmly, "I don't like that joke," or tell Vijay or a teacher afterwards. Speaking up early makes it easier for the teaser to stop.
How might Rohan see the lunchbox comment, compared with Preeti?
Rohan may think it was harmless banter like Vijay's nickname, so Rohan keeps grinning. Rohan may not realise the topic was a sore spot for Preeti until seeing Preeti's quiet face.

Read this:

In the kasba, Karthik had been going to the meditation house behind the grain market for two months. This week the leader made three requests in one breath: a donation "for your growth", the phone handed over "to quiet the mind", and no more visits to old friends who "drag you down".

Karthik walked to Sabina's tea stall afterwards with the phone still in a pocket, and sat without ordering.

"You look like someone swallowed your tongue," Sabina said.

Karthik repeated the three requests slowly. Said aloud, they sounded different.

Sabina put down the kettle. "Money, phone, friends. That's how you control someone, not how you grow them. Keep your phone. Keep your own money. Keep coming here. And call your uncle in the city before you decide anything."

For the first time all week, Karthik took the phone out.

Where did Karthik walk after the leader's requests?
Karthik walked to Sabina's tea stall.
Why did Karthik sit at the stall without ordering?
Karthik was unsettled by the three requests and needed someone outside the meditation house, which the silence and slow repeating of the requests show.
What would you advise Karthik about the phone, money and friends?
Keep the phone and own money, keep seeing old friends, keep a way to leave, and call the uncle in the city or another outsider before deciding.
How does Sabina see the leader's three requests?
Sabina sees money, phone and friends together as a way to control someone, not help them grow.

Read this:

At the district post office, Darshan stamped letters harder than he needed to. During the tea break, behind the counter, he opened his phone and scrolled to Vaibhav's page. A photo from Pune: his son with paint on his hands, laughing with strangers. Darshan zoomed in on the face, then shut the phone quickly when a clerk passed.
"Your son is in Pune now, na?" the clerk asked.
"Ungrateful boy," Darshan said. "He made his choice."
That evening, as every evening, he went into Vaibhav's old room and straightened the bedsheet nobody slept on. He had not called in eight months. Calling first, he told himself, would mean begging, and a father does not beg. He sat on the bed a long time, waiting for a phone that didn't ring, and called it dignity.

How long had it been since Darshan called?
He had not called in eight months.
Why does Darshan shut his phone quickly when the clerk passes?
He feels ashamed to be seen longing for his son, since his pride insists he is only angry at an ungrateful boy.
What turning point is available to Darshan now?
He could see that his waiting is hurt rather than dignity, and send one small message or ask a relative to carry a soft word.
What might Vaibhav imagine about his father's silence?
Vaibhav may believe his father has truly given up on him, with no idea that the room is kept ready and his photos are read in secret.

Read this:

Subject: Almost signed something today
Hi Tanvir,
You asked how the bank visit went. Honestly: badly, then okay.
I went in to open a salary account, and within ten minutes a man at the next desk was showing me a "wealth plan". He kept saying things like "surrender value" and "guaranteed bonus structure", and every time I frowned he said, "Don't worry, it's standard." Then: "This offer ends today. Just sign here and here."
My face went hot. I didn't want to look stupid by asking what anything meant, so I nodded, and the pen was actually in my hand.
Then I remembered your dad saying, "If you can't explain it back, don't sign." I said I'd take the papers home to read. He said they couldn't be printed. I left without them.
Can we sit with your dad this weekend?
Darshan

Why did Darshan go to the bank?
Darshan went in to open a salary account.
Why did Darshan nod instead of asking what the words meant?
Darshan felt embarrassed and did not want to look stupid; the hot face and the nodding show the shame of not following the jargon.
What protective step did Darshan take, and what should come next?
Darshan asked to take the papers home and left when they could not be printed; next, going over any offer with a trusted person such as Tanvir's dad before signing.
How might the man at the desk read Darshan's nodding?
He may take the nodding as agreement and push harder, since his 'offer ends today' line depends on Darshan not stopping to ask.

Read this:

In Baljeet Chacha's pottery shop in the kasba, Samir was told not to touch the drying pots. When Chacha went to the back, Samir picked one up, and it slipped and cracked in two. His heart thumped. He could hide it behind the sacks. Instead, when Chacha came back, Samir held out the pieces, shaking. “I broke it. I'm sorry.” Chacha looked at the pot, then at Samir. “Thank you for telling me the truth. That was brave. Pots stay on the shelf. Help me sweep?” Samir nodded, relief flooding his face.

What happened to the pot Samir picked up?
It slipped and cracked in two.
What was Samir feeling when he held out the pieces, shaking?
He was frightened of getting into trouble, and then felt relieved when Chacha thanked him for telling the truth.
What did Chacha do that encourages future truth-telling?
He praised Samir's honesty calmly, restated the rule about the pots, and let him help clean up.
What would change if Chacha had punished Samir harshly?
Samir might learn to hide mistakes next time, behind the sacks, instead of telling the truth.

Read this:

Tejas, put the phone face down for a minute and listen to your Ganga Masi.
When I was sixteen, there was a boy called Sunil. We had those small phones then, only texts. If he didn't reply in ten minutes, my stomach dropped. I'd check the phone under my pillow, in the bathroom, during prayers. Once, when he went quiet for an evening, I told him another boy had walked me home. It wasn't even true. I just wanted him to feel as scared as I did.
He was hurt, and we nearly broke up.
That night I made myself a small rule. When the dread came, I would write it in my diary first, then call my friend Lata or walk round the colony. Only after that could I text him.
It was hard. Some nights I wrote three pages. But the texts I sent after were kinder, and so was I.

Where did young Ganga check her phone?
Under her pillow, in the bathroom and during prayers.
How did young Ganga feel when Sunil didn't reply?
She felt dread and fear; her stomach dropped if he didn't reply in ten minutes, and she wanted him to feel as scared as she did.
What choice did young Ganga make after nearly breaking up, and why did it help?
She decided to write in her diary, call Lata or walk before texting, which calmed the dread so her texts were kinder.
How was Sunil affected when she invented the story about another boy?
He was hurt by it, and they nearly broke up, because the jealousy test made him doubt her.

Read this:

In their small apartment in Vancouver, Chen dropped his backpack and held up his worksheet like a trophy. "Done. All of it. So can I walk to Leo's by myself?"
His mother, Wei, looked up from the rice cooker. "It's four blocks, and it's getting dark early now."
"Everyone in my class walks alone. Literally everyone."
Wei raised an eyebrow. "Everyone? Maya's dad picks her up every day."
Chen's shoulders dropped. "Okay, most people. But I know the way, and I'll text you when I get there."
Wei nodded slowly. "Finishing your homework is a good reason, and knowing the way is too. The dark is my reason. Go now, text me from Leo's door, and I'll pick you up at six."
Chen was already tying his shoes.

How far away is Leo's place?
It is four blocks away.
Why did Chen's shoulders drop when Wei mentioned Maya's dad?
He felt caught out and deflated, because his claim that everyone walks alone was an exaggeration; he still wanted to go, so he offered better reasons.
Which part of Wei's reply worked, and why?
She took Chen's real reasons seriously, named her own reason, the dark, and set clear limits: go now, text on arrival, pick-up at six 👍
What might change if Wei had just said no without explaining?
Chen would likely feel dismissed and keep pushing with bigger exaggerations, instead of learning which of his reasons counted.

Read this:

"Only three rules now?" Urmila asked, reading the sticky note on her sister's monitor.
"I had fifteen and remembered none," Payal said. "So: if someone asks for something urgent, I ask when they really need it. If I finish a call, I write one line of notes. And after lunch, I plan tomorrow."
"And do you?"
Payal sighed. "The first two, yes. Plan tomorrow after lunch? Not once in two weeks. After lunch everyone pings me."
"So when is your day quiet?"
Payal thought. "Four o'clock. When the stand-up ends and I close my laptop to get tea."
"Then that's your trigger."
Payal peeled off the note and rewrote the third line: When I close my laptop at four, plan tomorrow.
A week later, Urmila saw a neat list for the next day on the desk. "Working?"
"Five days out of five," Payal grinned.

When does Payal close her laptop to get tea?
Four o'clock, when the stand-up ends.
How did Payal feel admitting the after-lunch rule never worked?
She felt frustrated and a little defeated, sighing that she hadn't planned once in two weeks.
What else could Payal check after a few weeks?
She could look again at which rule is being skipped and move its trigger too, since a rule only works if its moment really happens.
How does Urmila see her sister's new plan?
Urmila is curious and helpful, and pleased to see the neat list a week later.

metadata.subtype: Approach: keeps three key if-then rules and revises them when they fail [Revision]

Read this:

Three weeks after Omar reported that the warehouse supervisor in Mississauga had been signing forklift safety checks that never happened, the break room went quiet whenever he walked in.
Nobody said it to his face. But his name vanished from the weekend overtime list. Someone left a sticky note on his locker: "Snitch." A man he'd trained for a month called him "Mr Loyalty" and got a laugh.
The checks were real now. Nobody had been hurt. He had been right. And he ate lunch in his car.
Kaito, who worked at a different site, came over on Saturday with dumplings. "You kept notes, right?"
"Everything. Dates, the report number, the overtime list."
"Good. Keep doing it. My cousin volunteers at a workers' legal clinic. They know the whistleblower protections. Call them Monday."
Omar laughed for the first time in days. "You're the only person who's said anything nice to me since."

What was written on the sticky note on Omar's locker?
The sticky note said "Snitch."
How was Omar feeling in the weeks after the report?
Omar felt isolated and lonely, eating lunch in his car, even though he knew he had been right.
What support does Kaito offer that could help Omar?
Kaito encourages Omar to keep dated notes of what is happening and to call a workers' legal clinic about whistleblower protections.
How might the man Omar trained see him now?
That man seems to see Omar as disloyal rather than as someone who made the site safer, which is why he mocked him as "Mr Loyalty".

Read this:

Sonali: are you awake? did you hear that scream just now?
Francis: yes. from the lane behind the PG?
Sonali: I think so. a woman's voice. then a crash
Francis: could be the family in 3B, they watch horror films really loud
Sonali: it came again. it doesn't sound like a TV
Sonali: I want to go down and check

Her stomach felt tight, but she waited before replying. A colleague, Mohit, had once told her about fake notices, so she opened the official portal by typing its address herself. The same notice sat in her account, with the same date. It was real: her freelance income did not match what a client had reported.

The date came and went. When he finally opened it, a penalty had been added to what was a small difference, and he now needed weeks to sort out something that would have taken an afternoon.

What was the deadline for answering in the notice Bidisha received?
It was the twentieth of the month.

Bidisha read the details, checked the notice on the official portal and settled it, while Irfan hid his letter in a drawer, missed the date and faced a penalty on a small difference.

Fear, shown by the cold drop in his chest, and a hope that it was a mistake.

Now Sami didn't trust anything Omar did. When Omar laughed, it sounded fake.

Tonight Omar brought a big box of dates for everyone. Sami refused. "He's just trying to look good."

His older sister said, "Sami, he cheated in a game. That doesn't mean everything he does is bad."

"But he's a cheater."

A big box of dates for everyone.

Sami felt distrustful after seeing Omar cheat, so that one flaw made everything Omar did seem bad.

She pointed out that cheating in one game doesn't make everything Omar does bad, and showed Sami that Omar was sharing kindly.

Freya felt thrilled at the cake and upset at Astrid's tears, and those two moments crowded out two hours of games.

We played a little choice game before the lesson on time. Question one: ten stickers today, or twenty tomorrow? Suraj shot up his hand. "Today!" Most of the class agreed. Question two: ten stickers in thirty days, or twenty in thirty-one? Suraj frowned, then said, "Thirty-one, obviously. It's only one more day." Kunal laughed. "Today it was also only one more day!" Suraj opened his mouth, then shut it. He looked genuinely puzzled. I told the class this is very normal: waiting feels easy when the reward is far off and hard when it's right in front of us. Tomorrow everyone gets the stickers they chose for question one, and we'll talk about how the choice feels a week later.

On Tuesday he pretended to fan his red face in front of the whole row, and Manjula's ears burned. After that she stopped raising her hand, ate lunch in a corner of the library and told her mother she had a stomach ache.

The picture scared her a little, so at break she took her notebook to the teacher and read out what she had imagined. She ate her lunch in a corner of the library.
How did Jahnavi's way of handling her anger differ from Manjula's way of handling her hurt, and what did Manjula's stairwell moment add?

Jahnavi's anger became a picture of the drain, but she told the teacher instead of acting on it. Manjula first withdrew, then said stop and went to sit near the teacher. Hearing Wasim's father shout explained his jokes to Manjula, but it did not make them fair.

She was angry, and also frightened by how strong the picture was, which is why she wanted an adult to hear it.

Saurabh stayed back again today. He's bright and he works hard in class, but his practice sheets come back half empty. When I asked, it poured out: "Sir, what if the paper is lengthy? In meetings, he began sentences with "When I decided to move us to the new database..." and let his eyes rest on the room until someone nodded. He noticed he enjoyed that nod. When it did not come, he felt vaguely short-changed.

The Friday lunches with Jagdish and Chaitanya thinned out. First a client call, then a planning session, then "you guys go ahead." When he did join them, he corrected Chaitanya's phrasing and said nothing about the offer he had just been sent. Jagdish stirred his rice and glanced across the table at Chaitanya. Subject: Update on project delivery

Dear Mr. Ghosh,
I wanted to inform you that the project will be delivered three days later than planned. An issue was found in the data, and I want to fix it properly before sending anything to you. I sincerely apologise for the delay, and I understand that it may cause inconvenience. Thank you for your patience and understanding.
Sincerely,
Pallavi

With the school bus leaving in ten minutes and rain drumming on the tin roof, the class hunted for the missing lab register. Mehak watched Swati, who stood by the window twisting her dupatta and staring at the floor. "She's hiding something," Mehak whispered to her bench-mate. "Look, she won't even look at Ma'am." Meanwhile Rudra, who had been the last to use the register, answered every question with an easy smile. The teacher asked everyone to check their bags anyway. The register slid out of Rudra's folder. He shrugged. "Must have picked it up by mistake." Mehak felt her cheeks burn. On the bus she sat beside Swati, who admitted she always went stiff when a teacher asked questions, even when she had done nothing. Mehak stared at the wet window, thinking how sure she had felt, and how wrong.

What was Swati doing while the class searched for the register?
Swati stood by the window twisting her dupatta and staring at the floor.
What was Mehak feeling when the register slid out of Rudra's folder?
Mehak felt embarrassed and ashamed of her quick judgement; her cheeks burned because she had been so sure Swati's fidgeting meant guilt.
What could Mehak do next time she is tempted to read guilt from someone's body language?
She could remind herself that nervousness is not proof, wait for facts such as who last used the register, and keep her guess to herself instead of whispering it.
What is it like for Swati when classmates read her stiffness as guilt?
Swati goes stiff whenever a teacher asks questions, even when she has done nothing, so being suspected for it would feel unfair and make her even more tense.

The photo was blurry: Astrid asleep on the school bus in Tromsø, mouth open, a string of drool on her scarf.
Noa had taken it for a laugh. That evening Liv messaged, “Send it to the class chat, it's hilarious,” and Noa did.
By morning it had a hundred reactions and someone had made it a sticker. Astrid walked into the classroom and everyone went quiet in the way that tells you something.
At break, Astrid found Noa by the lockers. Her voice was very flat. “Did you post that?”
“Liv told me to,” Noa said quickly. “It was her idea. I just sent it.”
“You took it,” Astrid said. “You pressed send.”
Noa opened her mouth to say Liv's name again, then closed it. Astrid's eyes were wet. Liv wasn't the one standing here.

Where was Astrid when the photo was taken?
She was asleep on the school bus in Tromsø, with her mouth open.
Why did it feel reasonable to Noa to say “Liv told me to”?
Blaming Liv made her feel less guilty; if the idea belonged to someone else, the harm seemed less hers.
What could Noa do now to take responsibility?
She could say sorry to Astrid without mentioning Liv, ask the class to delete the photo and sticker, and tell a teacher so it can be removed.
How does Astrid see what happened?
Astrid feels humiliated and holds Noa accountable, because Noa took the photo and pressed send, whoever suggested it.
He asked for a permission to leave early today. What should I change?

He asked for permission to leave early today.
Why: "Permission" is uncountable; drop "a".

In his first week as a trainee at a Bengaluru software company, Asif was given a database task he'd never seen before. Everyone else seemed to be typing fast.
He was tempted to copy something from the internet and hope. Instead he walked to Thomas, a senior developer. "I don't know how to start. Could you give me an approach I can try myself?"
Thomas drew a quick diagram on the whiteboard: "Understand the tables, write a small query, test, then scale." He didn't write any code.
Asif spent two days on it. He got stuck twice, solved one on his own. Then he went back. "My join is slow on big tables. Should I index this column?"
Thomas smiled. "Now you're thinking. Try it and tell me."

What did Thomas draw on the whiteboard?
He drew a quick diagram: understand the tables, write a small query, test, then scale.
What was Asif feeling in his first week when given the database task?
He felt unsure and tempted to copy something, since he'd never seen such a task and everyone seemed fast.
Why was Asif's way of asking better than copying from the internet?
He got a framework, worked through it himself, and came back with a specific, sharper question, which built real skill.
How might Thomas feel when Asif returns with his indexing question?
Thomas probably feels pleased and encouraged, seeing Asif learning to think for himself.

"Aunty, can I ask you about the weaving?" Vandana said, setting her notebook on the kitchen table.
Madhuri smiled. "Ask."
"How did you learn it?"
"My mother sat me at the loom when I was nine."
"What was that like for you?"
Madhuri thought. "Slow. Then it wasn't."
"Slow how?"
"My fingers hurt. But there was a day the pattern came out right on its own."
Vandana crossed out her next question, "Weren't you forced?" and wrote, "Tell me about that day."
"Now that," said Madhuri, leaning forward, "I remember."

At what age did Madhuri's mother sit her at the loom?
Madhuri was nine when her mother sat her at the loom.
Why did Vandana cross out 'Weren't you forced?'
Vandana wanted to learn Madhuri's own view and saw that the question was leading and could sound accusing. She replaced it with a curious open request.
What could Vandana keep doing in her research interviews?
Keep asking open questions, follow up with 'how' and 'tell me about', and avoid questions that suggest an answer.
How might Madhuri have felt about the first question versus the last?
Madhuri might have felt defensive at a leading question, while the open one made her lean forward and remember a proud moment.

The volleyball court behind the Champhai school was still muddy from rain when the girls lost the district semi-final, 21–25 in the last set. Nobody spoke on the walk to the bus. Lalremsiami, who had missed the last serve, kept her face to the window.
Vinita, the captain, stood at the front of the rattling bus. "That last set is on me. I called the wrong rotation and put Mawii out of position. We'll fix it in practice." Then she went down the aisle. "Mawii, your blocks in the first set were unreal. Lalremsiami, your serves won us the quarter-final. Tlangi, you kept us calm."
Lalremsiami looked up. "I missed the last one."
"And I put you in a bad spot to serve it," Vinita said. "We lost together."
At practice on Monday, Mawii was the first to say, "I think I'm late on my jumps. Can we work on that?"

What was the score in the last set?
21–25 in the last set.
What does Lalremsiami keeping her face to the window suggest?
Lalremsiami felt ashamed and guilty about missing the last serve, expecting to be blamed.
What did Vinita get right as captain?
She took her share of the blame first, praised each player's specific part, and told Lalremsiami they lost together.
What does Mawii's question on Monday show about how the team feels now?
Mawii feels safe to admit a weakness, because the captain showed that mistakes can be named without shame 🙂
Why did my cousin Zara stop calling me?
I'm not sure, because I can't see her reasons or her life. A kind message asking how she is might open the conversation.

Last Ramzan, after iftar, we played football in the lane every night under the tube light. I'm Irfan, and I was usually goalkeeper. One night Francis from the church end of the street came with his own ball and asked to join. Someone said, 'This is our game, go play with your people.' Everyone laughed. I didn't. My stomach felt hot. I said, 'He brought a ball. And it's everybody's lane. Anyone can play.' It came out louder than I meant. For a second I thought they'd kick me out too. Then Sameer shrugged and said Francis could be on my side. Francis scored twice. When I think about it now, I'm glad I said it, even though my voice shook.

What did Francis bring when he asked to join?
His own ball.
How did Irfan feel just before speaking up?
Irfan felt a hot anger at the laughing, and fear of being kicked out too; the shaking voice shows how nervous it was.
What could the lane's players agree so this doesn't depend on one person speaking up?
They could agree that anyone from the lane who turns up gets a turn, so nobody has to argue it each night.
What would it be like for Francis if nobody had spoken up?
Francis would have walked away laughed at and shut out of his own street, likely feeling hurt and unwelcome.
My friend said, "This is just for timepass." What is "timepass"?

"Timepass" is used mainly in Indian English and means something done only to fill free time, often without a purpose. In standard English you could say "a way to pass the time" or "just for fun".
Example: We played cards just to pass the time while it rained.

Jasleen came home from her office in Chandigarh, lay on the sofa and pressed her fingers to her forehead. The TV stayed off. Sonali, four, stopped building her tower. She stared at her mother's closed eyes, then fetched her own small pillow and pushed it under Jasleen's head. Next she brought her soft rabbit and tucked it under Mumma's arm. "Rabbit makes it better," she whispered, and patted Jasleen's hair very lightly, as if touching a bubble.

What did Sonali tuck under her mother's arm?
She tucked her soft rabbit under Mumma's arm.
What was Sonali probably thinking when she stared at her mother's closed eyes?
She seemed to sense that Mumma was hurting and wanted to make her feel better.
How could Jasleen show Sonali that her comfort mattered?
She could open her eyes for a moment and say, "Thank you, that helps," so Sonali learns her caring works. 🤍
If you were Jasleen, what would you want in that moment?
Probably quiet and gentle care, which is just what Sonali's whisper and light touch offered.

Okay, I'll tell you how it went online. I'm Abhinav, and I was in the middle of it.

In class we'd just mimic Nitin's walk. Stupid, but face to face, you could see when he'd had enough, and you'd stop.

Then someone made a fake account with his photo, calling it "Nitin the Nerd." We'd post edited pictures: his face on a cartoon penguin, his head on a baby's body. I did some of the editing. It took two minutes. It felt like nothing. Just pixels.

We made a group for the class trip and didn't add him. He found out from the photos.

What I didn't see, behind my screen, was his face. I never saw him reading those posts at night. His cousin told me later he'd stopped eating dinner with his family.

That's the thing about screens. They made it light for me. It was never light for him.

What was the fake account called?
"Nitin the Nerd."
How did the online cruelty feel to Abhinav at the time?
It felt light, even amusing, to Abhinav, just pixels, because the screen hid Nitin's reactions; only later came guilt.
What turning point could have stopped this, looking back?
Refusing to edit the pictures or to leave Nitin out of the trip group, and reporting the fake account to a teacher or parent.
How did the online bullying affect Nitin?
It hit him much harder than Abhinav realised; he read the posts at night and stopped eating dinner with his family.

Monday: Damini, one and a half, knocks over the three wooden blocks her uncle Mridul builds, and laughs.

Wednesday: She puts one block on top of another. It wobbles and falls. She pushes it away.

Saturday: Mridul holds the bottom block still. Damini sets two blocks on top, slowly, pressing each one down with her fingers. The tower stands. She claps and looks at Mridul, then points for more.

How many blocks did Damini set on top on Saturday?
She set two blocks on top.
What was Damini feeling when she pushed the blocks away on Wednesday?
She was probably frustrated when her block wobbled and fell.
What small step did Mridul take that helped Damini?
He held the bottom block still, making it easier for her to stack.
What would change if Mridul had built the tower for her every time?
Damini would have fewer chances to practise stacking and might not learn it as quickly.

In the Class 11 ethics elective, the teacher posed the old problem: a runaway train will hit five people unless you pull a lever to send it toward one.
Sonali said, "Pull it. Five lives are more than one."
Samir said, "But then you choose to kill someone. It's wrong to use a person like that."
The teacher smiled. "Sonali is thinking about consequences. Samir is thinking about duties and rules. Both are real ethical systems."
Sonali tapped her pen. "What if the one person is a doctor who could save hundreds?"
Samir said, "Then you're deciding who's worth more. That's dangerous."
They didn't agree. But after class, Sonali said, "I understand your side better now."

How many people would the train hit unless the lever was pulled?
Five people.
What was Sonali feeling when she said she understood Samir's side better?
Sonali felt more open and thoughtful after hearing Samir's reasons.
How did the teacher help them compare ethical systems?
The teacher named their positions as focusing on consequences and on duties, showing both are real ways of reasoning.
How might Samir see Sonali's doctor example?
Samir sees it as dangerous because it means deciding who is worth more.

Midterm week was in four days when the second milestone slipped. Salma stood at the board in the project room. "Why did the report module miss its date twice?" Because Manu was late finishing. "Why?" He redid it. "Why?" Because the requirement changed. "Why did it change?" There was a silence. Afreen said slowly, "Because we never wrote down what it should do. Each of us remembered it differently." Salma wrote it on the board: unclear requirement, not laziness. Nobody looked defensive now. Between two study sessions they wrote a single page describing each module and a short list of what "finished" would mean for each module. Then they sent the page to their guide, and the next milestone was met.

What did the team write between the study sessions?
They wrote a single page describing each module and a short list of what 'finished' would mean for each module.
What is Afreen feeling when saying the requirement was never written down?
Afreen seems reluctant but honest, speaking slowly because it names a shared mistake rather than blaming Manu.
What alternative approach could the team use in future, and why?
They could review each requirement together at the start of every milestone, because short check-ins catch differing memories before work is redone.
How might Manu see the five-why questions?
Manu is asked why he was late and might have felt blamed at first, but the answer shows the cause was the unwritten requirement, so nobody points at Manu.
