Emeka's class in Lagos wanted an end-of-term party, and Emeka had volunteered to organise it with Leila. First he listed every cost he could think of: drinks, snacks, decorations, a speaker, paper plates. Then he asked the class, anonymously on slips of paper, what each person could comfortably give. Some wrote very little. So they set one small contribution everyone could manage, and agreed that nobody had to explain giving less. With that total, hiring a speaker was out; Leila's cousin would lend one. Bought snacks cost too much, so Leila priced home-made puff-puff and chin chin against shop packets. Home-made won easily, and four parents offered to help fry. Every naira spent went into a shared sheet the whole class could see. At the party there was even a little left over for next term.

Who would lend the speaker?
Leila's cousin.
Why did Emeka ask about contributions anonymously?
He was worried that some classmates would feel embarrassed saying how little they could give in front of others.
What makes the shared sheet useful?
Everyone can see where the money goes, which builds trust and keeps spending within the agreed total.
How might classmates who could give only a little feel about the plan?
They are likely relieved and included, since the amount was set for everyone and no one had to explain giving less.

In the school staffroom, Gautam marked papers while the principal praised Baljeet's new science club plan in the staff meeting. Gautam had suggested the idea in June. Nobody mentioned it. He said nothing.
Afterwards, at the tea urn, he muttered to the maths teacher, "Some people are good at collecting credit."
The next week Baljeet asked for the lab timetable. Gautam sent it without the Saturday slots. Baljeet's messages got "ok" in reply, nothing more.
On Wednesday Baljeet sat down beside him. "Gautam, you've been different with me. Did I do something?"
Gautam kept marking. "Not everything is about you, Baljeet."

What did Gautam leave out of the lab timetable?
The Saturday slots.
What was Gautam feeling during the staff meeting?
He felt overlooked and resentful that his June idea went unmentioned, but kept it to himself.
What could Gautam do instead of answering "Not everything is about you"?
Accept Baljeet's opening and say calmly that he had suggested the idea in June and felt left out.
How might Baljeet be experiencing Gautam's replies?
Baljeet is probably confused and hurt, reading the coldness as hostility without knowing the cause.

The bus home from the weekly haat was late and crowded. Bhupen, not yet two, arched his back and wailed when his sister took the window seat. Alka told him gently to take turns. He screamed louder, rubbing his eyes with both fists. She stopped talking, broke open a boiled sweet potato from her cloth bag and held him on her shoulder. He ate half, slumped, and slept before the river bridge. At home he woke smiling and patted his sister's cheek.

What did Alka break open from her cloth bag?
She broke open a boiled sweet potato from her cloth bag.
What do Bhupen's eye-rubbing and arching suggest about how he felt?
They suggest he was tired, hungry and frustrated after the long day at the haat, so losing the window seat felt like too much for him.
What was the turning point on the bus, and why did it work?
Alka stopped explaining about taking turns and gave him food and her shoulder to sleep on; his body needed that first, and afterwards he was sweet to his sister again.
What is the bus ride like for Bhupen's sister?
At first she may feel blamed or bothered by his screaming over the seat, but later she gets a friendly pat on the cheek from a rested, happier brother.

"Noor, did I do something wrong? Pieter left hungry."
"What happened, Eshaan?"
"I asked if he wanted more biryani. He said, 'No, thank you.' So I said, 'Arre, have a little.' He said no again. Then I put some on his plate anyway, like my mother does."
"And?"
"He looked really uncomfortable. He didn't eat it."
Noor laughed softly. "In your mother's house, a guest says no twice to be polite, and the host insists. Here in Amsterdam, no means no."
"So I was forcing food on him?"
"A bit, yes. And your aunt last month in Lucknow, remember? I said 'no, thank you' once and she never offered again. I went to bed hungry."
Eshaan groaned. "So it's the opposite for each of us."
"Exactly. Ask once here. Ask three times in Lucknow."
"I'll message Pieter tomorrow. And save him some biryani."

What did Eshaan do after Pieter said no twice?
Eshaan put some on Pieter's plate anyway, like Eshaan's mother does.
How might Noor have felt when the polite no in Lucknow was taken as final?
Noor probably felt embarrassed and a bit awkward, too polite to ask again and going to bed hungry.
What rule does Noor suggest, and why is it useful?
Ask once in Amsterdam and three times in Lucknow; knowing the local rule avoids both offence and awkwardness.
How did Pieter probably experience the extra biryani?
Pieter probably felt uncomfortable and pressured, since for him a first no was final, so he left it uneaten.
I'd like to organise my wardrobe.
Take everything out, and sort it into keep, give away and mend. Seeing it all at once makes decisions easier.
How do I decide what to give away?
Set aside things that no longer fit, that you have not worn for a long time, or that you do not like. Be honest, but do not rush.
What's a good way to arrange the rest?
Group similar items together, with the ones you use most at easy reach. Folding clothes upright in drawers lets you see everything at a glance.
How do I keep it tidy afterwards?
Put each item back as you use it, and do a quick check every month or so. A small habit keeps the order from slipping.

Chinmay, you asked what helped me most in my first year of teaching. Not a training course. A person: Mrs D'Souza, the senior teacher in the staffroom.
The day the inspection team came, I was a wreck. My lesson plan was crumpled, my hands were sweating, I'd forgotten the register. I sat next to her, babbling. She didn't react. She just poured two cups of tea, pushed one to me and said, "Drink. Then show me your first activity."
Her voice was so slow and even. By the time I finished the tea, my heart had come down from my throat. We went through the lesson once. She said, "That's good. Go."
I, Parveen, now try to be that for the new teachers. Just slow. Just tea.

What did Mrs D'Souza push towards Parveen?
A cup of tea.
How was Parveen feeling before the inspection?
Parveen was panicking, a wreck, with sweating hands and babbling.
What can a person learn from Mrs D'Souza's way?
Staying slow and even, offering something simple like tea, and focusing on one next step helps a panicking person settle.
What might Mrs D'Souza have noticed about Parveen that day?
She likely noticed the panic and chose not to react to it, knowing her own steadiness would help more.

Dolma read the offer letter for the third time on the terrace of their Delhi flat: a research post in Hyderabad, starting in April. Her younger sister Avni sat cross-legged nearby with a maths book, watching her.
"You've been quiet since morning."
"Papa and Mama are used to me being around on Sundays. If I go, it feels like leaving them."
"Or like doing your work," said Avni. "Did you ask them?"
At dinner Dolma put the letter on the table. Her father read it slowly. "We will miss you at Sunday lunch. But we would miss more if you stayed and grew sour." Her mother laughed. "Video call every Sunday, and you come in Losar." Dolma exhaled for the first time in days.

Where is the research post that Dolma was offered?
The research post is in Hyderabad.
What was Dolma feeling as she read the offer letter on the terrace?
She felt torn and guilty, worried that going would feel like leaving her parents even though the post was work she wanted.
What choice moved Dolma from worrying alone to a shared plan?
She took Avni's advice to ask her parents and put the letter on the table at dinner, and they agreed on Sunday video calls and a visit at Losar.
How does Dolma's father see her leaving?
He says the family will miss her at Sunday lunch but would miss more if she stayed and grew sour, so he treats her growth as important too.

The night before his thermodynamics exam, Joseph's post about a film had gone the wrong way. Strangers mocked his accent, called him names, and their comments were still arriving. His hands shook over the keyboard. He typed a long reply, and Reena, from the next bunk, looked over. "Don't send that." "They're lying about me!" "They'll only get more to pile on." She showed him how to screenshot the worst messages, block the accounts, and switch off notifications until tomorrow. Joseph felt hot behind his eyes. "It hurts, though." "I know. It says nothing true about you." She made two cups of tea, and they went through his formulas until midnight. In the morning, he still felt bruised, but he walked into the exam.

What did Reena tell Joseph not to do?
She told him not to send his long reply.
What was Joseph feeling as he typed his long reply?
He was angry and hurt, and wanted to defend himself against people he felt were lying about him. His shaking hands and hot eyes show it.
What steps could Joseph take if the comments continue?
He can keep his screenshots as evidence, keep the accounts blocked, avoid replying, and report the abuse to the platform and, if it continues, to a trusted adult or the college.
How does Reena see the trolling?
Reena sees it as something that says nothing true about Joseph. She helps him step away and studies with him.

Read this:

At the coaching centre in Kota, the chemistry teacher paired Kamal and Seema for a joint problem set worth ten marks, one grade for both. Kamal looked at the forty problems and did the maths: if Seema did most of it, he could spend the week on physics, where his marks were worse. Seema, across the room, was doing the same maths about her biology. Each did eight problems and waited. On Thursday night they compared. Sixteen done, twenty-four blank, deadline at nine. They argued in the corridor, each sure the other had cheated them. In the end they submitted half a set and got four out of ten. Kamal's physics hadn't improved either; he had spent the week worrying. 'If we'd split it twenty-twenty,' Seema muttered, 'we'd both have had eight and a free weekend.'

How many problems were in the set?
Forty problems.
What was Kamal feeling during the week?
Kamal felt tempted at first, then worried, spending the week anxious instead of improving his physics.
What would have been the better strategy for both?
Splitting the forty problems twenty each and trusting each other, which would have given both a good mark and free time.
How does Seema see what happened?
Seema is frustrated and sees that their mutual shirking left both worse off than cooperating.

Read this:

Dear Maria,
I don't know if you'll read this. I just need to ask: what did I do?
Two weeks ago we were all fine. Then someone told Ms Das about the bunk, and the next morning you and the others moved to another bench. In the group chat, Sonam wrote, “Some people can't keep secrets.” Everyone liked it. You liked it.
I didn't tell. I swear. But I keep going over everything I said, wondering if I'm the reason.
Last night Mum found me crying in the bathroom. She sat with me for an hour, said none of this was my fault, and she's taking me to meet Ms Rao, our counsellor, tomorrow morning.
I still miss you.
Deepika

Who did someone tell about the bunk?
Someone told Ms Das.
How has Deepika been feeling since the group turned?
Deepika feels bewildered, betrayed and ashamed, going over every word and wondering if Deepika is the reason.
What did Mum do that was right?
She stayed with Deepika, said it wasn't Deepika's fault, and arranged a meeting with the counsellor for the next morning.
How might Maria feel reading this letter?
Maria might feel guilty and uncomfortable, realising that the group joined in blaming a friend without proof.
A two-line rhyme, please, that reminds a child to wash their hands before eating.

Before you eat your rice and dal,
Wash your hands with soap, that's all!
Why do shadows nearly vanish on a cloudy day?
Clouds soften the sunlight. Because clouds scatter the sunlight so it reaches us from every part of the sky, there is no bright spot to make a sharp dark patch.

Looking back, I should have noticed sooner. I'm Kashish. Last winter my best friend Parul stopped coming to the canteen. She said she wasn't hungry. She stopped answering my messages for days, then sent long ones at 3 am saying she felt like a burden. I thought she was just in a mood. But it went on for weeks. One day she said, "Nothing feels worth doing anymore," and my stomach dropped. I didn't know what to say. That evening I told my mother, who told me I did the right thing. Together we spoke to our class teacher, who called Parul's parents and the school counsellor. Parul was angry with me for a while. Now she says she's glad I told.

At what time did Parul send long messages?
She sent long messages at 3 am.
What made Kashish's stomach drop?
Parul saying nothing felt worth doing made Kashish realise Parul's sadness was serious and not just a passing mood.
What was the right thing Kashish did?
Kashish told a parent that evening and then the class teacher, so trusted adults and the counsellor could step in, instead of carrying it alone.
Why might Parul have been angry at first?
She may have felt exposed or embarrassed that others knew, before she felt the relief of getting help. 🤍
How would you describe the reading corner of our community library in 40 words? It has thirty chairs, a green rug, a window facing the garden and a plant on the front desk. Make it feel calm.
The reading corner is a calm place. It has thirty chairs and a green rug. A window faces the garden, so soft light falls on the books. There is a plant on the front desk, and the room is quiet.

You asked how I finished the picture book in six months while working at the print shop? I'm Salma, and honestly, I used to think I was just undisciplined. Every night I'd sit down to draw at ten and end up reorganising my pencils. My friend Elizabeth, a nurse on rotating shifts, watched this once and said, "When do you draw best? Not now, clearly." I thought about it. Mornings. Before the shop, the light is good and my head is quiet. So I moved drawing to 6:30 till 8:30. At night I did only small stuff: scanning, emails. And on Sundays I laid out the week's pages on the table, so there was no deciding in the morning. It felt like cheating at first. It isn't cheating. It's just knowing when I'm at my best.

What did Salma do on Sundays?
Laid out the week's pages on the table, so there was no deciding in the morning.
Why did Salma once feel undisciplined?
Salma felt frustrated when drawing at ten each night never worked, and blaming character was easier than noticing the time of day was wrong.
Which choices let Salma finish the picture book?
Moving drawing to the quiet morning hours, keeping only small tasks for night, and laying out pages on Sunday to cut down choices.
Why might Elizabeth, with rotating shifts, notice timing so quickly?
Working changing shifts, Elizabeth probably knows how energy rises and falls, so Elizabeth spots that ten at night wasn't Salma's time.

Read this:

Friday. Nirmala's diary. Today in Tenzin's class I forgot to look at Sir when he signed, and looked at my book instead. Tenzin tapped my shoulder twice and waited. I felt hot because it seemed rude, but he only smiled and pointed at his eyes. He explained that in sign language you keep looking at the signer's hands and face the whole time, and looking away means you are not listening. Then he flicked the lights to get everyone's attention when Mr Rao came in. It's clever! Tomorrow I'm going to keep my eyes up even when my pencil drops. 🙂

How did Tenzin get Nirmala's attention?
Tenzin tapped Nirmala's shoulder twice and waited.
What was Nirmala feeling when Tenzin tapped Nirmala's shoulder, and what did Nirmala learn?
Nirmala felt embarrassed, thinking it was rude, shown by feeling hot. Then Nirmala learned that keeping eyes on the signer is expected, not an insult.
What could Nirmala do next time Nirmala's pencil drops during a signed lesson?
Nirmala could keep watching the signer, then pick the pencil up at a pause or ask quietly by signing 'wait' before looking away.
How does Tenzin see Nirmala's mistake?
Tenzin is kind about it. Tenzin smiles and points to the eyes, treating it as something Nirmala has not learned yet.

I sit next to Devika, and last month I watched Devika try to plan the next five years. Devika wants to be a software architect before thirty. On a big sheet taped to the wall, in three columns, went what that job needs: designing whole systems, leading a team, and knowing one field really well.
Then came the years. Year one: system design, with a course and one design document a quarter. Year two: lead a small team on a project. Year three: go deep on one business area. Later years were pencilled in lightly.
Devika stepped back and said, "Okay." I couldn't tell if that meant excited or scared. Probably both.
— Swati

What three things did Devika list as needed for the job?
Devika listed designing whole systems, leading a team and knowing one field well.
What might Devika have been feeling when stepping back from the sheet and saying "Okay"?
Devika might have felt excited and scared at once, though Swati cannot tell which.
What could Devika do if year one's course turns out weaker than expected?
Devika could swap it for another way to learn design, such as a design review with a senior colleague, and keep the yearly slot.
What is it like for Swati to watch Devika plan?
Swati feels curious and a little impressed, and also uncertain about what Devika feels.

On a wet Sunday, Aadhya sat on the sofa with her cheeks puffed and her chin high, watching her mother Ira pack the umbrella away. The park trip had been cancelled. The puff looked like theatre: Aadhya glanced sideways to see if Ira noticed, and one corner of her mouth twitched. "Very dramatic!" said Ira. Aadhya let out a giggle, then puffed again and let her voice wobble. "But it's raining, Amma." Ira sat beside her. "I'm sad about it too. Shall we build a fort?"

Why was the park trip cancelled?
It was raining.
What does Aadhya's sideways glance suggest about her puffed cheeks, and what else might they mean?
The glance and the twitching mouth suggest she was partly acting for her mother's reaction. Her wobbling voice later hints that some disappointment was real too.
What could Ira do to help with the disappointment?
She could name her own sadness about the trip and offer a fun alternative, such as building a fort.
How might Ira feel when Aadhya puffs her cheeks at her?
She may feel amused at first, then a little sorry for the real disappointment beneath the theatre.

In the small town of Hosapete, Kiran had saved from his tuition job for a new phone. For three weeks he compared models every night: thirty-one tabs, battery charts, camera tests.
At the mobile shop near the bus stand, Salma, the shopkeeper, laid out five boxes. He held each one, checked his notes, and asked about another model that wasn't in stock. At last he chose the blue one.
Walking home past the temple, he was already watching a review of a different phone, frowning.
"Happy?" asked his cousin at dinner.
"It's fine," Kiran said, and scrolled through the other phone's photos again.

How many tabs did Kiran have open while comparing phones?
Thirty-one tabs, with battery charts and camera tests.
Why does Kiran feel only 'fine' about the phone he chose?
After comparing so many models, he keeps imagining the other phones might have been better, so the blue one feels less satisfying.
What could Kiran do next time before comparing phones?
He could list the three things he most needs and look only at phones that meet them, so there are fewer options to second-guess.
How might Salma feel after Kiran asks about a phone that isn't in stock?
Salma might feel a little tired or worried about losing the sale, having already laid out five boxes for him.

Counsellor's note, Digital Life elective, Class 9. For the attention-trap project, Afreen (14) logged every notification on her phone for three days. She came to me looking shaken: 'Ma'am, 212 in one day. Most were from one game app telling me my streak would die.' She had never noticed the streak made her open the game even when she was bored with it. In her presentation, she showed the class a slide of her tally and asked, 'Who decided I had to keep a streak?' Several students laughed nervously. I saw two quietly open their settings. Next step: I'll invite Afreen to help design a class challenge on switching off non-essential alerts, and ask the class to reflect afterwards rather than preach. — Mrs Jagdish

How many notifications did Afreen log in one day?
212 in one day.
Why did Afreen look shaken when she came to the counsellor?
She realised how many alerts were steering her, especially the streak pushing her to play a game she was bored with.
Why is Mrs Jagdish's plan to have the class reflect rather than preach a good one?
Students are more likely to change their habits when they discover the traps themselves, as Afreen did.
What might the two students who opened their settings have been thinking?
They were probably recognising the same patterns in their own phones and wanting to switch some alerts off.
I found a feather on my morning walk and I don't know which bird it came from.
A nice find. Feathers can tell you a lot. Look at its size, colour and shape.
It's long, black and shiny with a slight blue tint.
That sounds like it could be from a crow or a similar black bird, though I can't say for sure from a description. A local bird guide or a nature club can help you check.
I'll look in the library. Is it okay to keep it?
For one feather, it's usually fine, but wash your hands afterwards, since feathers can carry dust and germs. Local rules may differ, so ask at the library or the nature centre if you are unsure.

I'm Charu, Hemant's lab partner, and I watched him make his college decision table in the canteen last week.
He had three colleges: the one in Manipal he'd been talking about since first year, one in Vellore, one in Pune. Columns for fees, placements, campus feel, faculty, location.
The fees and placement numbers came from websites, and Pune was actually better on both. But then he got to campus feel and faculty. He gave Manipal a ten for campus feel. Pune got a four. Faculty: Manipal nine, the others five. He hadn't visited any of them.
When he added up, Manipal won by six points. He looked so happy. "See? Numbers don't lie."
I didn't say anything. But I'd seen him erase the Pune faculty score twice, going lower each time.

What score did Hemant give Manipal for campus feel?
He gave Manipal a ten for campus feel.
What does Hemant looking so happy suggest about him?
It suggests he felt relieved and pleased that the table confirmed the choice he already loved, though Charu can only guess.
What would you change first in Hemant's table?
I would ask someone neutral to score campus feel and faculty, or visit first, since those made-up scores decided the result.
How does Charu see the table?
Charu sees that the numbers were bent toward Manipal, but stays silent, perhaps unsure whether to spoil Hemant's excitement.

At the preschool, Suraj Sir covered his eyes and counted. Keerthana tucked the class teddy inside the dress-up basket, then pressed a finger to her lips at her friends. "Shh! Don't tell." Suraj Sir looked under the mats and behind the curtain, muttering, "Where could Teddy be?" Keerthana bounced on her toes. "He doesn't know!" she whispered. When he finally opened the basket, she shrieked with laughter and begged, "Again! Now you close your eyes!"

Where did Keerthana hide the class teddy?
She tucked it inside the dress-up basket.
How can you tell Keerthana felt delighted to know something the teacher didn't?
She bounced on her toes, whispered "He doesn't know!" and shrieked with laughter when he found it.
How could Suraj Sir extend this game for the class?
He could let children take turns hiding the teddy and ask, "Who knows where it is, and who doesn't?"
What would change if Suraj Sir had peeked while counting?
The trick would be spoiled, and Keerthana would miss the fun of seeing that others don't know everything she knows.

You want to know what my first month at the hospital taught me? I'm Sunaina.
Before I'd even worked a shift with Salma, I'd heard about her three times. "Salma covers for you when you're sick." "Salma never leaves a mess for the next shift." "If Salma says she'll check a patient, she checks."
So when I finally worked with her, I trusted her from the first hour. I hadn't seen anything yet. It was all what others said.
And then I thought: people are already saying things about me. Do I leave a mess? Do I do what I say?
That night I stayed ten minutes to finish my handover notes. Small things. That's how it spreads.

How many times had Sunaina heard about Salma before working with her?
Three times.
What was Sunaina feeling on realising people were already talking about Sunaina?
Sunaina felt a jolt of worry and self-awareness, wondering what reputation was already forming.
Why might staying ten minutes for handover notes matter?
Because reputation builds from small consistent actions, and others will pass on what they see.
How might Salma feel if she knew what colleagues said about her?
Salma would likely feel proud and appreciated that her small, reliable habits were noticed.

"Seema, you think you have to be strong all the time? When I, your Omkar Mama, was sixteen, I had a stammer, worst on words starting with 'p'. I never talked in groups. My friends thought I was just quiet. One evening on the riverbank, my friend Sadanand asked why I never told stories. My heart was hammering. I could have made a joke. Instead I said, slowly, 'Because I'm scared of getting stuck in front of you.' He didn't laugh. He said, 'Then get stuck. We'll wait.' That was the first time I told a story in front of anyone."

Which words did young Omkar's stammer affect most?
Words starting with 'p'.
What was young Omkar feeling when his heart was hammering?
He felt scared and exposed, afraid of being judged if he told the truth.
What turning point in the story came from opening up?
Admitting his fear instead of joking, which led Sadanand to offer patience.
How might Sadanand have felt when Omkar opened up?
Touched and trusted, and glad to understand why his friend stayed quiet.
Describe the waiting room of a clinic in three short sentences, each under ten words.
The chairs are arranged in neat rows. A fan hums softly overhead. Patients wait quietly for their turn.

In their Kochi colony, Saurabh spent the whole week before the maths unit test playing football in the park until the streetlights came on. "Revise?" he laughed when Jomon asked. "People who fail are the ones who panic. I'll be fine. I'm always fine." Jomon stayed home with the fractions chapter. On the morning of the test, Saurabh looked at question three, adding fractions with different bottoms, and his mind went white. He tried to remember what Miss had said, then guessed. When the papers came back, he had 11 out of 25. He stared at the red number for a long time. "But I'm always fine," he said quietly. Jomon, who had 21, didn't say anything, just slid his fractions notes across the desk.

What did Saurabh get in the test?
11 out of 25.
Why was Saurabh sure he didn't need to revise?
He felt carefree and certain that failing happens to people who panic, not to him.
What small step could help Saurabh before the next test?
Study the fractions chapter with Jomon's notes a few days before, instead of trusting that he'll always be fine.
How might Jomon feel sliding his notes across?
Jomon probably feels sorry for Saurabh and wants to help without rubbing it in.

In their hostel room in Hyderabad, Siddharth had tried fourteen planner apps in three weeks. Each promised to finally organise his life. He would download one, spend an evening setting up colours and tags, read that another was better, delete it, and start again. His actual assignments sat untouched. "Which one are you on now?" Samir asked from the other bed, writing in a cheap spiral notebook. "The one with the tree that grows. But the one with the calendar view might be better." "You said that about the tree." Siddharth sighed. None of them felt right, because there was always another. Samir held up the notebook. "One. Never looked at another." Siddharth laughed, then stopped. He deleted all the apps but one, and opened his first assignment.

What does Samir write in?
Samir writes in a cheap spiral notebook.
Why does no planner app feel right to Siddharth?
Siddharth feels restless and unsatisfied, because with so many options there is always another app that might be better.
What did Siddharth finally do, and why was it a good move?
He deleted all but one app and opened his first assignment, ending the search so the actual work could start.
How does Samir see Siddharth's search?
Samir sees it as time lost choosing tools, and shows that one plain notebook, never compared, works fine.

Saturday night
The whole class is doing the umbrella dance trend. Every single person has posted one. Even Sachin, who hates dancing, posted his yesterday with his little brother. My feed is just umbrellas.
I don't want to do it. I feel stupid dancing and I hate how I look in videos. But today at lunch Meghna said, "Usha's the only one left," and everyone laughed, and I laughed too, and my stomach felt like it was folding.
So tonight I filmed it eleven times in the bathroom. I posted the least bad one. Twelve likes so far. I feel relieved and also kind of gross, like I did it for them, not for me.
Maybe I'll ask Sachin tomorrow if he actually wanted to.
Usha

How many times did Usha film the video?
Eleven times, in the bathroom.
How does Usha feel after posting the video?
Usha feels relieved and also kind of gross, sensing it was done to fit in rather than out of wanting to.
What might help Usha the next time a trend sweeps the class?
Asking whether it is wanted or only done to avoid standing out, and talking honestly with a friend like Sachin who may feel the same.
What might it have been like for Sachin to post the trend?
Sachin hates dancing too, so he may also have felt pushed into it by everyone else posting.
What makes pushing a trolley up a ramp easier than lifting it straight up?
A ramp makes the climb gentle. Because the trolley goes up a long slope instead of a sudden steep climb, the push needed at any moment is smaller.

Week one: Vikas, a data analyst at a hospital software firm, was asked by a sales colleague for a spreadsheet of patient emails to 'send a friendly offer'. Vikas said he'd check. That night he couldn't sleep.

Week two: He read the company's privacy policy twice and asked his manager, Jasleen. She said clearly that patient data could not be used for sales. Vikas felt relieved, then worried the sales colleague would be annoyed.

Week four: The sales colleague did grumble. But at the next team meeting, Jasleen reminded everyone of the rule without naming anyone. Two other analysts admitted they'd been asked too. Vikas started keeping a small note of every data request he received and who approved it.

What did the sales colleague ask Vikas for?
He asked for a spreadsheet of patient emails to send a friendly offer.
Why couldn't Vikas sleep after the request?
He felt uneasy that sharing patient data for sales might be wrong, but he wasn't sure yet.
What habit did Vikas build to protect data in future?
He began keeping a note of every data request and who approved it.
How might the patients be affected if Vikas had shared the emails?
Their private details would be used for sales without their consent, which could break their trust in the hospital.

messages.content: Is it "heirarchy" or "hierarchy"?

It is "hierarchy", with "ie" and not "ei". It means a system with people or things ranked above others.
Example: The company has a clear hierarchy.

I am sorry, Ma'am, I left my homework notebook at home today. I will bring it to you first thing tomorrow.

Vijay, you asked on this podcast how I think about pleasure. I'm Manjula, I'm twenty-six, and I have a mango rule.
In summer, I eat one Alphonso mango every evening. Standing at the sink, juice running down my arms, no phone, no TV. Ten whole minutes. It's the best part of my day.
I don't eat five. I tried that once. By the fourth, I couldn't taste anything.
That's how I try to do everything. Real lunch breaks. A nap on Sundays. Dancing at weddings until my feet hurt. I think joy is serious business.
But I don't chase the next thrill. I don't need a bigger party every weekend. I need to actually be at the one I'm at.
And I still go to work, pay my bills and see my doctor when I should. The mango doesn't replace those. It just makes them bearable.

How many mangoes does Manjula eat each evening?
One Alphonso mango.
How does Manjula feel eating the mango at the sink?
Manjula feels joyful and fully present, calling it the best part of the day.
What does Manjula's mango rule show about balance?
Savouring one thing fully brings more joy than chasing more, and Manjula keeps it alongside work and health commitments.
How might Vijay see Manjula's approach?
Vijay might find it surprising and appealing, a way to enjoy life without being ruled by pleasure.

I'm Rehana, and I share a flat with Pallavi, so I watched her yearly plan take shape at the kitchen table. The first version was all rules: no takeaways, no late nights before work, no extra projects, no arguing with her manager. It looked tidy. On Sunday, though, she read it aloud, stopped, and said, 'This tells me what to avoid, not where I'm going.' She took a blank sheet, wrote the twelve months down the side, and beside each one put a single aim: finish the first module of her design course in February, present at the team demo in March, and so on. The rules went at the bottom of the page in small writing. I can't tell what she felt, but she pinned it above her desk and looked at it every morning.

Where did Pallavi put the rules on the new sheet?
Pallavi put the rules at the bottom of the page in small writing.
What might Pallavi have been thinking when she stopped reading aloud?
Pallavi may have realised that the plan was only about avoiding things and felt a little disappointed, though Rehana can't be sure.
What could Pallavi do if she misses a monthly aim?
Pallavi could move the aim to the next month and ask what got in the way, since the aims should guide the year and not become a source of guilt.
How might Rehana have seen the change in the plan?
Rehana probably noticed the plan going from tidy to purposeful, though Rehana can't say how Pallavi felt.

"I'm sorry, Vikas. The budget's closed for this year. I can't raise your pay now."
Vikas nodded slowly. "I understand, Nitin. Can I ask something else, then?"
"Go on."
"Could we set a date to revisit this, in writing? And tell me exactly what would make the case strong."
Nitin looked surprised. "Most people just walk out upset." He thought. "Six months. Say, first week of July. If your team's bug backlog is halved and you handle the payments release, I'll take it to the committee."
"Can you email that?"
"Today."
—
"Nitin, it's July. You have a minute?"
"Sure. I remember."
Vikas put a printout on the desk. "Backlog halved in May. Payments release went live last week with no rollbacks."
Nitin read it twice. "That's exactly what we agreed. I'll take it to the committee on Friday."

When did Nitin suggest they revisit the raise?
First week of July.
How might Vikas have felt hearing that the budget was closed, and how can you tell Vikas stayed steady?
Vikas was likely disappointed but stayed calm and determined, nodding slowly and asking for a written date and targets instead of walking out upset.
What else could Vikas try if the committee still said no in July?
Vikas could ask what was missing and agree the next review date, or look at the market range for the role to understand the options.
How does Vikas's approach look to Nitin?
Nitin is surprised and seems to respect it, since clear written targets give Nitin a solid case to take to the committee.

The science model was due tomorrow, and the rain had soaked their cardboard on the balcony. Kamal and Payal had one evening to start again, and no money for new craft paper. "You cut, I'll glue," Kamal said. Payal stared at the kitchen shelf, then had an idea. "Let's use old bottle caps for the wheels." They worked until the cart rolled across the floor. At school the next day, the teacher spun a wheel and praised Kamal. "Great wheels!" Kamal said, "That was Payal's idea. I just glued." Payal smiled shyly.

With their cardboard soaked by rain, Kamal and Payal had one evening to restart the science model with no money for new paper, until Payal suggested old bottle caps for the wheels, and the cart rolled across the floor. At the summer holiday camp in her new school, Gopika sat apart during craft hour. The camp counsellor knelt beside her. "Missing your old school?" "It was perfect there," Gopika said. "Everyone liked me. We never argued." A boy at the next table, Hrithik, looked up; he had moved from the same old school a year earlier. "Gopika, remember the class monitor fight? You didn't talk to anyone for a week." Gopika's cheeks went warm. She did remember, now. It seemed small and far away, like a faded picture. "That was only once," she muttered. The counsellor smiled. "Old places get prettier when we miss them. Want to make a card for someone new here?"

What was Gopika doing during craft hour?
Sitting apart.
What did Gopika feel when Hrithik mentioned the monitor fight?
Her cheeks went warm; she felt embarrassed and a bit defensive, because it didn't fit her perfect picture of the old school.
How did the counsellor help, and what could come next?
By saying old places get prettier when we miss them, and inviting her to make a card for someone new, a small step toward the present.
What is it like for Hrithik to hear Gopika's version?
He remembers the real quarrels, so he may feel he should be honest, and perhaps a bit amused.

On the school bus, Noor mentioned that Aryan had a nice smile, and Hafsa's stomach dropped like a lift. She had liked Aryan since the start of term and had never told a soul. She stared at the traffic, said, "Oh, he's okay," and felt her cheeks go hot. For two days they walked to class with strange gaps in their talk. Finally, over a shared packet of chips at the tuck shop, Hafsa said, "I like him too. It feels weird." Noor blinked, then laughed with relief. "It IS weird! Let's not fight over this. Where did Noor say Aryan had a nice smile?
Noor said it on the school bus.
How did Hafsa feel when Noor mentioned Aryan, and why did she say "Oh, he's okay"?
Hafsa felt anxious and embarrassed, since her stomach dropped and her cheeks went hot; she liked Aryan too and was not ready to say so.
What did Hafsa and Noor do that kept their friendship safe?
Hafsa admitted honestly that she liked him too, and they agreed not to fight over him, since the two of them came first.
How might Noor have felt on hearing Hafsa's confession?
Noor blinked and then laughed with relief, so Noor probably felt relieved and glad to have it out in the open.

Boss aur dost ko promotion ki badhai alag-alag kaise dun?

In Nani's kitchen in Jodhpur, Wasim, four, reached for the steel glass of milk and knocked it over. Milk spread across the floor and under the stove. Wasim stared, then ran and squeezed behind the grain bin. "I'm bad," he whispered. "I'm a bad boy." His big brother Madhav peeked in. Nani put down the rolling pin and crouched by the bin. "Wasim, come here, my sparrow." He shook his head. "The milk fell," Nani said softly. "That was an accident. You are still my good Wasim." Slowly, Wasim crawled out. Nani handed him a cloth. Together they wiped the floor.

Where did Wasim hide after spilling the milk?
Behind the grain bin.
What was Wasim feeling when he whispered 'I'm bad'?
He felt ashamed and scared, treating the spilled milk as proof he was a bad boy.
Why did Nani's response help Wasim?
She crouched down, spoke softly, separated the accident from who Wasim is, and let him help clean up.
How might Madhav understand Wasim hiding?
Madhav might see that little Wasim was frightened, and learn from Nani how to respond kindly.

The Republic Day rehearsal in the school yard at Kheda was running late, and Bhupen sir's voice was already hoarse. "Sabina, you're group leader," he said. "Tell Motilal he's out of the drill. He ruins every line. Make sure he knows it's because he doesn't practise." Sabina looked at Motilal, who was mouthing the counts to himself at the edge of the dust. Her stomach tightened. But sir had trained twenty batches; he must know. She walked over. "Sir says you're out. You don't practise." Her voice came out louder than she meant. Motilal's face crumpled, then went blank, and he sat down under the peepal tree. For the rest of rehearsal Sabina kept missing her own steps, telling herself, It was sir's order, not mine.

What was Motilal doing at the edge of the dust?
Motilal was mouthing the counts to himself at the edge of the dust.
Why did Sabina go along with the order even though her stomach tightened?
Sabina felt uneasy but reasoned that sir had trained twenty batches, so he must know better than she did.
At which moment could Sabina have chosen differently, and how?
When she saw Motilal quietly mouthing the counts, Sabina could have told sir that Motilal was trying and asked sir to speak to him instead.
What might Motilal think when the message comes from Sabina?
Motilal may feel shamed in front of the group, since he was practising and still heard 'You don't practise' from a classmate.

The village school had one big room and a long mat. Pankaj sat at the very end of it on his first day. He looked at the boys by the door, then at the girls near the blackboard, then at a boy with a torn slate who was humming. Pankaj pulled his knees up and did not say anything.
The teacher poured a heap of seeds onto the mat. "Two by two! Sort the tamarind from the beans. Pankaj, you go with Hrithik."
The humming boy shuffled over. They sorted in silence, then raced. Hrithik let out a laugh. So did Pankaj.

What did the teacher ask the pairs to sort?
Tamarind seeds from the beans.
What does Pankaj pulling his knees up suggest about how he felt?
It suggests he felt shy and a bit unsure, even while he was curiously looking round at who might be a friend.
How could a teacher help other new children like Pankaj?
Give them a simple job with a partner, like sorting seeds, so they have something to do together before they have to talk.
What might it be like for Hrithik to be paired with the new boy?
Hrithik may feel curious about Pankaj too, and the race turns the silence into shared fun.

What time was Gautam's exam?
At nine.
How did Gautam feel when his phone buzzed again?
He felt irritated and then guilty, worn out from weeks of being Joseph's main support.
What did Gautam do that balanced care and his own health?
He set a short, kind time limit, promised a proper talk later and encouraged Joseph to involve his brother and the counsellor.
How might Joseph have felt hearing "You deserve more than just me"?
Joseph may have felt a little hurt but also cared for, and agreed to call his brother.

The red cup.
What was Pooja feeling when she said "No!" to everything?
She seemed to enjoy the sense of control that "no" gave her, rather than really opposing things; climbing onto the swing with a grin shows she was happy.
Which of Jahnavi's choices worked, and why?
Offering two cups worked, because Pooja got to decide something and happily went along.
How might Pooja's parents feel reading this note?
They may feel amused and relieved that a day full of "no" is normal and manageable.

Read this:

"Disha, you're always in a hurry when you show me the phone. Let your Nani tell you about Tejas.
"Last winter your cousin Tejas came to stay for a week. On the first day I asked him how to send a photo to your Mama in Canada. I expected him to grab the phone, press-press-press, and hand it back like you all do.
"He didn't. He sat beside me and said, 'Nani, you do it. I'll just tell you.' Slowly. Tap the little picture. Choose the photo. Tap the arrow. When I pressed the wrong thing, he didn't laugh. He said, 'Happens to me also.'
"I sent the photo myself. Your Mama called in ten minutes. I felt like a young girl again.
"Tejas even wrote the steps in big letters on a card and stuck it on my almirah. It is still there. Go and see.

Where did Tejas stick the card with the steps?
Tejas stuck it on Nani's almirah.
What did Nani feel after sending the photo herself?
Nani felt proud and happy, like a young girl again, especially when Mama called within ten minutes.
Which of Tejas's choices made the difference, and why?
He let Nani do the steps herself, explained slowly and didn't laugh at mistakes, so she learned and kept her dignity.
How might Disha feel hearing this story?
Disha might feel a little embarrassed about rushing Nani, and inspired to slow down next time.
Name four school subjects. Write them on one line separated by a vertical bar.
Maths | Science | History | Art

Dear Mahima,
I heard about the company shutting your whole department. I'm so sorry. I also heard what some people in the old group chat said, that you "should have seen it coming." Please don't carry that. You worked harder than anyone I know. Sometimes the ground just moves under good people, and it has nothing to do with what they deserve.
What can I do? I can look over your CV this weekend, I can send your name to two teams I know are hiring, or I can just come over with biryani and not talk about jobs at all. You choose.
I've also written to our alumni group asking if we can start a proper referral list for anyone who's laid off, so it isn't just about who knows whom.
With love,
Lavanya

What did people in the old group chat say?
That Mahima should have seen it coming.
How does Lavanya feel about what happened to Mahima?
Lavanya feels sad and sorry for Mahima, and protective against the blame from the group chat.
How does Lavanya combine support with working for fairness?
Offering help with the CV, referrals or simply company, and starting an alumni referral list so help isn't only about who knows whom.
How might Mahima feel reading the letter?
Mahima might feel comforted and less ashamed, with real choices of help and no blame.

In the coaching centre's counselling room in Kota, the ceiling fan pushed hot May air around. Joseph stared at a poster of a beach.
"I just wish I was eight again," he said. "No tests, no ranks. Just cycling and mangoes. Everything was easy."
Shalini Ma'am, the counsellor, nodded. "That sounds lovely. What else do you remember about being eight?"
He smiled. Then the smile slipped. "I was scared of the dark. I slept in Amma's room till I was ten. And I cried every morning before school because of that boy who took my tiffin."
"So not only easy."
"No." He laughed a little. "I forgot that part."
"The pressure now is real," she said. "Let's also talk about what would help this week."

What did Joseph say he was scared of at eight?
He was scared of the dark.
Why does being eight feel so easy to Joseph right now?
Under the weight of tests and ranks he feels tired and longs for comfort, so his memory keeps the cycling and mangoes and drops the fears.
What did Shalini Ma'am do well?
She let Joseph find the harder parts of childhood himself with one open question, without arguing, and then turned to real help for this week's pressure.
What would change if Shalini Ma'am had just said, "Childhood wasn't easy either"?
Joseph might have felt dismissed and defensive, and missed noticing for himself what he had forgotten.

Monday: The science chapter only said, "The moon has phases." Swati, eleven, frowned. "But why?" Her sister Pooja shrugged. "It's not in the exam."
Thursday: Swati borrowed a torch and an orange. In the dark bedroom she held the orange at arm's length and turned slowly while Pooja shone the torch. "Look, only half is lit, and I see different bits as I turn!"
The next week: Swati kept a moon diary, drawing the shape every night from the terrace. At the bottom she added her own question: "Why do we always see the same face?" Pooja started coming up to the terrace too.

What did Swati use to model the moon?
A torch and an orange.
Why did Swati frown at the chapter's one line?
She wanted to understand the reason behind the phases, and the bare statement did not satisfy her curiosity.
What would you advise a teacher who hears Swati's new question?
Welcome it, perhaps point her to a book or ask her to model it with the orange again, instead of saying it is outside the syllabus.
How did Pooja's view change over the week?
She began by saying it wasn't in the exam but ended up joining Swati on the terrace, drawn in by her sister's curiosity. 🙂

'You're really filing the nomination?' Zainab asked, holding the form down against the canteen breeze.
'I'm tired of decisions being made by people who never ask us. Library hours, the hostel curfew, all of it.'
'And you want to be the one deciding.'
Indu laughed. 'Is that bad? I want people to listen when I talk. I want the dean to know my name.'
'That's the part that worries me a bit.'
'Why?'
'Last year's president wanted the same. By March he was cancelling meetings whenever people disagreed.'
Indu was quiet, pen tapping. 'Okay. Then you be my conscience. If I start doing that, you say so. Loudly.'
'In front of everyone?'
'In front of everyone. Now sign here as my proposer.'

Which decisions did Indu say were made without asking students?
Library hours and the hostel curfew.
What does Indu want from standing for the post?
Indu is eager for influence and respect, wanting people to listen and the dean to know the name, as well as to change decisions made without students.
What did Indu's request to Zainab get right?
Asking Zainab to object loudly and in public builds a check against sliding into control, the way last year's president did.
What worries Zainab about Indu's ambition?
Zainab fears that wanting standing could turn into shutting down disagreement, as it did with last year's president.

"Mummy, you called Dr Iyer's office again?" Mahima asked.
"Only to ask about the reports. Beta, just eat, I'll handle the forms."
"Mummy, I love you, but I want the reports myself. Yesterday you hid the scan letter in the drawer."
Sharmila's hands stopped. "I didn't want you to be frightened."
"I'm more frightened when I don't know. Please come to the appointments, I'd like you there. But I'll decide about my treatment, and you can ask me anything."
"Anything?"
"The hard parts too. I can hold them."
Sharmila wiped her eyes on her dupatta. "I only know how to cook and worry."
"Then cook, and worry out loud. I'll answer."

Where did Sharmila hide the scan letter?
She hid the scan letter in the drawer.
Why did Sharmila hide the scan letter?
She did not want Mahima to be frightened. The hiding comes from fear and love, not from wanting to deceive.
What did Mahima ask for regarding the appointments and the decisions?
Mahima asked Sharmila to come to the appointments, said the treatment decisions would be Mahima's own, and invited questions about even the hard parts.
What might it be like for Sharmila to say "I only know how to cook and worry"?
She probably feels helpless and scared. Being invited to worry out loud gives her a role that Mahima can accept. 🤍

Jasleen, you called yourself lazy again today. Come, your Nikita Nani will tell you something. When I was nine, in Dehradun, I couldn't learn my tables. Everyone else sang them like songs. I got stuck after seven sixes. So I decided: I'm lazy. Lazy girls don't learn tables. And I stopped trying. Why try, if you're lazy?

My grandfather heard me say it. He didn't argue. He asked, "Which table, exactly?" I said the sevens and eights. He said, "That's not lazy. That's two tables." Every evening he wrote one line on a matchbox, and we practised it walking to the temple.

By Diwali I knew them. I still say "seven sixes are forty-two" when I climb stairs. So, Jasleen, which part exactly is hard?

Which tables did young Nikita find hard?
The sevens and eights.
Why did young Nikita stop trying?
Young Nikita felt discouraged and ashamed, and calling herself lazy made trying seem pointless.
What turning point in the story changed things?
Her grandfather asked, "Which table, exactly?", turned the label into two tables, and practised one line with her each evening.
How might Nikita's grandfather have felt hearing "I'm lazy"?
He was probably saddened but calm, choosing a question and patient practice over an argument.

The job offer from Singapore had a one-week deadline, and it arrived the same day Kalyani's father's shop flooded in the Chennai rains. For three years she had sent half her salary home and paid her brother Hrithik's college fees, and she had done it gladly, mostly. Now, standing in the soggy shop with a bucket, she felt guilty for even wanting to go, and a hot resentment she couldn't say out loud. That night Hrithik found her on the terrace. "Akka, you're thinking of not taking it because of us." She didn't answer. "Talk to Appa. Tell him what you want." Next morning, over coffee, she did: she'd take the job and keep paying Hrithik's final year, and the family would decide together, with the bank's advice, how to fix the shop.

How long was the deadline on the Singapore offer?
One week.
What was Kalyani feeling in the flooded shop?
She felt guilty for wanting to go and a hot resentment she couldn't say out loud.
What did Kalyani's talk with Appa achieve?
It set a clear limit: she'd take the job and pay Hrithik's final year, while the shop became a shared family decision with proper advice.
How does Hrithik see his sister's sacrifice?
Hrithik sees she's putting the family first and encourages her to say what she wants.

This talk is for an engineering college, so make it less casual.

I'm Manjula, and I've been a structural engineer for six years. People ask how I spot problems in a building so fast. Honestly, it's often a feeling first. A crack in the wrong place, a beam that looks slightly off.

My name is Manjula, and I have worked as a structural engineer for six years. People often ask how I identify problems in a building so quickly. In truth, it often begins with a feeling: a crack in an unusual place, or a beam that appears slightly out of line.
My elder sister is getting married. Draft a short toast, about 100 words, that I can give at the reception.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Ananya, the bride's younger sister and her lifelong partner in crime. Growing up, Meghna was the one who covered for me when I broke Ma's favourite vase and stayed up with me before every exam. She has always had the biggest heart in our family. Karthik, you are a lucky man, and from what I've seen, you know it. Thank you for making her laugh the way she does now. Please raise your glasses to Meghna and Karthik, and to a lifetime of love, patience and happiness.

Read this:

Wanjiru's report on the Nairobi water project was due to the donors on Wednesday. On Tuesday night she was still in the office, rewording the summary for the fourth time and adjusting photo captions.
Her colleague Chidi had sent the partner report on Monday, rough in places. The director had replied to everyone: "Chidi, fast and clear. Thank you!"
Wanjiru's report went out on Thursday morning. It was better written, better checked, better laid out. The director's reply was one line: "Received, thanks. A day late."
That weekend her friends went to the lake without her. She had told them she was too tired. She was.
On Sunday evening she opened the report again and read it through. She couldn't find anything wrong. She sat back and thought about the lake, and the one line from the director, and all the hours in between.

What did the director say about Chidi's report?
The director wrote, "Chidi, fast and clear. Thank you!"
How does Wanjiru feel on Sunday evening?
She feels tired and let down, realising her extra hours cost her rest and the lake trip while earning only a note that she was late.
What could Wanjiru try on the next report?
She could agree a send date with herself and stop polishing once the report is clear and correct, keeping her quality without missing deadlines or rest.
How might Chidi see Wanjiru's late nights?
Chidi might admire her careful work but also wonder why she spends so long on details the director doesn't notice.
How many shoes are there in 12 pairs?
24. Because 1 pair is 2, so 12 x 2 = 24.

How does Bhishma arrange the army for battle?

Vaisampayana continued, "These words spoken by the high-souled Bhishma were acceptable to them, and the king of the Kauravas acted accordingly without delay. And having sent away the king and then the kine, Bhishma began to array the soldiers in order of battle. And addressing the preceptor, he said, 'O preceptor, stand thou in the centre, and let Aswatthaman stand on the left, and let the wise Kripa, son of Saradwata, defend the right wing, and let Karna of the Suta caste, clad in mail, stand in the van. I will stand in the rear of the whole army, protecting it from that point.'"

Bhishma places the teacher in the centre, Aswatthaman on the left, Kripa to defend the right wing, and Karna, wearing armour, at the front. Bhishma himself will stand at the rear, protecting the whole army.

Pull three bullet points out of this section.

In the staffroom of a small primary school, Nikita laid out her plan for a reading corner. There was no budget, only an unused corridor and a headteacher who had turned down two similar ideas. Raghav folded his arms. "So, hopeless?" "No. Hard. Let's list what's real." She wrote: no money, no room, one doubtful boss. "And what do we have? Forty old books in the storeroom, two parents who offered time, and a wall." "So pilot it," Raghav said. "One shelf, one month, then show the headteacher the children reading." Nikita smiled. "If that doesn't work, we'll try a class library instead. I think we can adapt."

- Nikita proposes a reading corner at a small primary school with no budget and a headteacher who rejected similar ideas.
- She says it is hard, not hopeless, and lists what they have: old books, volunteer parents and a wall.
- Raghav suggests a one-month pilot with one shelf, and Nikita says a class library is the fallback.
Why does an iron gate rust but a gold ring does not?
Iron is easily changed by the weather and gold is not. Because iron slowly reacts with water and air to make rust, while gold hardly reacts with anything, the ring stays shiny.

The concert at the Bengaluru stadium was running an hour late, and when the rain started, the crowd at gate 4 began to push. Someone at the front shouted that the organisers were cheating people; a chant started, then the barrier rattled. Salma felt Naveen's hand tighten on her wrist. Behind them, a group of young men were shoving forward and yelling at a steward. Naveen turned, jaw set, as if to tell them off. Salma pulled his sleeve. "Don't. Not now." She looked around for space, not for the fight. To the left, the crowd was thinner along the fence, and she could see the green sign of a side exit. "That way. Slowly." They edged sideways, keeping their hands visible, not pushing anyone, apologising as they squeezed past. At the side exit a police constable was already directing people out. Salma told him, "Gate 4 is getting dangerous. The barrier's shaking." He radioed it in at once. From the road they watched more police walk toward the gate.

Which gate was the crowd pushing at?
Gate 4.
What was Naveen feeling when he turned toward the shoving group?
Naveen felt angry and protective, jaw set, wanting to tell them off.
What made Salma's response wise?
She stayed calm, stopped Naveen from provoking the group, found the thinner side of the crowd and a side exit, moved without pushing, and told a constable about the danger.
What would have happened if Naveen had confronted the young men?
It could have sparked a fight in a pushing crowd, putting both of them and others at greater risk.

Gautam,
You asked what happened after the fest, so here it is, honestly. By eleven you were slurring, tripping over chairs, and when a senior bumped into you, you squared up and shouted in his face. I've never seen you like that. Then, suddenly, you went very sleepy, slumped on the steps, and it was hard to wake you. That scared me more than the shouting.
I didn't leave you. I kept you sitting up and kept talking to you. Nisha and I got you into an auto and back to the hostel, and I slept on the floor next to your bed. I'd decided that if you stopped responding, I'd call an ambulance, no question.
You're not in trouble with me. I just want you safe. Can we talk about it over chai?
Naveen

How did Naveen and Nisha get Gautam back to the hostel?
They got Gautam into an auto and back to the hostel.
What scared Naveen most that night?
Naveen was most frightened when Gautam went very sleepy and was hard to wake.
Which of Naveen's actions were the caring ones?
Staying with Gautam, keeping Gautam sitting up and talking, getting Gautam home, sleeping nearby and being ready to call an ambulance.
How might Gautam feel reading this letter?
Gautam may feel embarrassed and shaken, but also cared for, since Naveen says Gautam is not in trouble.
Thank someone for a book they gave me, in two sentences; the second must start with "I".
Thank you for the lovely book you sent me. I have already started reading the first chapter.

In the Helsinki school canteen, Ulla sat two tables away from Valentina, who was eating alone again, her tray barely touched. Last week, when Jonas posted the video of Valentina tripping, Ulla had laughed. Just once. She still felt sick about it. Now the video was going round again, and Ulla's phone buzzed: "share it!!" Her thumb hovered. If she didn't share, Jonas might start on her next. She put the phone in her pocket. That evening, alone in her room, she typed a private message: "Hey, that video is horrible. I'm sorry I laughed. You don't deserve this." She stared at it for a long time. Then she pressed send. A minute later, Valentina replied: "thank you. really."

What did Ulla type in her private message to Valentina?
She wrote that the video was horrible, she was sorry she laughed, and Valentina didn't deserve it.
What feelings was Ulla torn between?
She felt guilty for laughing once, but she was also afraid Jonas would target her if she refused to join in.
Why do Ulla's small actions count as real help?
Not sharing the video and messaging Valentina privately supported her without Ulla having to face Jonas in public.
How might Valentina feel after reading Ulla's message?
She likely felt less alone, grateful that at least one person saw her side, as her reply shows. 🤍

Vandana sat on the terrace of her house in the small town, phone in hand, watching one grey tick under her message. Arun was in Toronto, half a day behind, and his replies came when she was asleep or in class. This was the third night that week. She began to type, "You clearly don't care," and stared at it.

"Madhuri, look at this," she called down to her friend, who ran the tailoring shop next door.

Madhuri read it and raised an eyebrow. "Do you know his timetable?"

Vandana deleted the line. She wrote instead: "I miss you, and this week I felt left out of your days. Can we fix Sunday 9 pm my time for a proper call? And can we plan a visit when your term ends in December?"

His reply came at dawn: "Yes. Sorry. Yes."

In which city is Arun living?
Arun is in Toronto.
What was Vandana feeling as she watched the single grey tick, and what did she nearly do?
She felt hurt and left out, and she nearly sent a message saying he clearly did not care before deleting it.
What agreement in Vandana's new message could ease the distance?
A fixed Sunday call time that suits them both, plus a planned visit when his term ends in December.
How might Arun see the silence that upset Vandana?
He may have been busy with classes or asleep because of the time difference, so the silence could be about schedules rather than neglect.

I'm Seema, Pankaj's big sister. At dinner Papa was telling a story about his office, and Pankaj kept babbling right over him, louder and louder. I thought he was being naughty. Papa stopped and picked up a spoon. "Spoon means your turn, Pankaj." He handed it over. Pankaj babbled into it. Then Papa took it back. "My turn." Pankaj waited, sort of. I don't know if he got it, but it was funny.

What did Papa use to show whose turn it was?
A spoon.
What might Pankaj have been feeling as he babbled over Papa?
He probably wanted to join in and be heard, feeling excited rather than naughty; he doesn't yet know how to take turns.
What did Papa do that builds the turn-taking habit?
He used a simple object and the words "your turn, my turn" to show when to talk and when to wait.
How does Seema see Pankaj's babbling?
Seema first thinks he is being naughty, then finds Papa's spoon game funny, though unsure if it worked.

Anirban's housewarming was loud, and the person he insisted Gargi meet turned out to be Samir, who was refilling the chutney bowl. They talked on the balcony for an hour. Gargi felt the fizz of it, and also her practical mind counting: he worked in Pune, she was three months from a promotion in Bengaluru, and neither of them used the word "serious." Excitement and caution shared the same evening.

Within a month they were texting from morning until night and cooking together on Sundays. What she noticed was small. Samir remembered her presentation on Thursday and messaged at seven: "Good luck, eat something." It meant more than flowers would have. Weekends began to be planned around each other.

Then came the first argument. Samir's parents wanted Gargi to visit for a festival week, and she had a work trip that same week. "You could move it," he said. "It's my job," she said. The voices did not rise, which was worse. He went quiet and defensive, and she reeled off reasons like a lawyer. Neither sent the usual goodnight text, and both noticed the silence.

Where did Gargi first meet Samir?
She met him at Anirban's housewarming, where Samir was refilling the chutney bowl.
How did the early weeks compare with the first argument in what they revealed about the couple?

The early weeks gave excitement, constant texting and small acts like Samir's message before her presentation. The first argument, over the festival week and her work trip, showed different expectations and how each behaved: he went quiet and defensive while she reeled off reasons.
What was Gargi feeling on the balcony?
She felt excited by the fizz but cautious, because her practical mind was counting his city and her promotion.
What could Samir and Gargi do after the first argument?
They could talk about what each expects from family time and work travel, listen without defending, and look for a plan that respects both.

Ishita here, from flat 4A. When Aditi moved into 4B, I barely noticed. Then she kept "happening" to be at the lift at eight. First there was only a nod. Next she asked where the laundry was. A few days later she carried my parcel up from the gate and set it at my door, hovering a second too long before a small smile. She looked nervous each time, but she kept coming back. On Friday she asked if I wanted to share an auto to the market, and I said yes. Honestly, I would never have knocked on her door myself; I'd have waited for the awkwardness to pass. I can't be sure what she felt, maybe she was only being polite, but now we have a market plan for Sunday.

What did Aditi carry up for Ishita?
Aditi carried Ishita's parcel up from the gate.
What might Aditi have been feeling as she hovered at Ishita's door?
Aditi was probably nervous and hopeful, since Ishita noticed the hovering and the small smile, though Ishita admits she cannot be sure.
What could Aditi try next after the shared auto ride?
Aditi could keep the small, repeated contact going, such as a chat at the lift or an invitation for tea, so the friendship keeps growing.
Why might Ishita not have started the friendship herself?
Ishita says she would never have knocked, so she may also fear awkwardness, and Aditi's small steps made it easy to say yes.

In Melbourne, on Thursday, Jamal hung back after science and held out his phone, looking uneasy. "I don't think this is okay. You should see it." It was a second group, "Year 10 real", with everyone from the old chat except Mei. Pinned at the top were screenshots of Mei's messages, her long one about the history project and her question about the formal, each with a row of laughing faces underneath. Mei's ears went hot. She handed the phone back and said, "Cool. Whatever." On the tram home she stared out the window with no music on. At dinner her dad noticed she wasn't eating and asked gently what was wrong. She showed him the screenshots Jamal had sent her. He sat beside her, said it was not her fault and that being talked about like that really hurts, and they emailed her year coordinator together. A reply came before nine: the coordinator would meet Mei first thing tomorrow.

What was the second group called?
It was called "Year 10 real".
What does Mei's "Cool. Whatever." suggest?
It suggests she felt deeply hurt and humiliated but was trying to hide it in front of Jamal.
How did Mei's dad support her that evening?
He sat beside her, said it was not her fault and that it really hurts, and emailed the year coordinator with her that same evening.
Why might Jamal have looked uneasy when he showed Mei the group?
Jamal was likely torn: he did not want to upset Mei, but he felt the group was wrong and that she deserved to know.

Chandrika, you're worried about your friend who became a school discipline officer and turned harsh. Let me tell you about my friend Gopal. At twenty-five he became a ticket inspector on the Mumbai locals. At home Gopal was the softest man I knew; he carried his mother's shopping and sang to his nieces. On the trains, in that black coat, he became another person: shouting at labourers without tickets, making a fisherwoman get off at the wrong station, laughing with the other inspectors about 'these people'. I watched it happen over a year. I didn't gossip, though others did. One evening at his house I said, 'Gopal, the man in the black coat isn't you. You're the one who sings to your nieces.' He was angry, then silent. Months later he told me he had started letting the old fisherwomen ride to their stop. Mridul's lesson, beta: speak to the person, not the coat.

What job did Gopal take at twenty-five?
Ticket inspector on the Mumbai locals.
What did Mridul feel watching Gopal change over the year?
Mridul felt troubled and sad, seeing a gentle friend become harsh in the black coat.
Mridul chose to speak to Gopal privately at home rather than gossip. Why was that wise?
It reminded Gopal of who he was outside the role without attacking him, which helped him soften over time.
How did Gopal react when Mridul spoke?
Gopal was angry, then silent, and months later began letting the old fisherwomen ride to their stop.

Supervisor's note, site office, Thursday.
Raghav has spent four days on the drainage drawings Jagdish left when he moved to the Pune project. Today I watched him with three versions of the same plan open, trying to work out which one the client approved. The file names say only "final", "final2" and "use this". A pipe size is crossed out in pencil with no reason written. Raghav rang Jagdish twice; Jagdish is on site all day and didn't pick up.
Raghav chose "final2" and ordered the site levels on that basis. By evening we found the client had signed "use this". Two days of levels to redo. He sat with his head in his hands for a while, then said quietly, "I did the best with what I had." He did.
Next steps: I have booked a one-hour call with Jagdish for tomorrow and told Raghav in writing that the delay is not on him.

Which version had the client actually signed?
The client had signed "use this".
What does Raghav sitting with his head in his hands suggest about how he felt?
It suggests he felt discouraged and frustrated at losing two days of work, even though he knew he had done the best with what he had.
What could have prevented the lost days?
A handoff note saying which file the client approved and why the pipe size changed, plus a short call before Jagdish moved, would have removed the guessing.
How does the supervisor see Raghav's mistake?
The supervisor sees it as not Raghav's fault, agreeing "He did" and putting in writing that the delay is not on him.

On Friday evening in the kasba, Sarita pinned a chart above her bed: "SATURDAY: all of physics. SUNDAY: all of chemistry. Done!" Her elder sister Charu read it and raised an eyebrow. "Last term one chapter of optics took you four days." "That was different. I was lazy then. This weekend I'm focused." By Saturday noon Sarita was still on the second chapter of physics. The electricity went at four, and she worked by lantern until her eyes ached. On Sunday morning she looked at the untouched chemistry book and felt her stomach drop. "How is it only Sunday and I'm not even half done?" Charu brought her tea. "Want to make a real plan? Using how long chapters actually take you?" Sarita nodded, close to tears.

How long did one chapter of optics take Sarita last term?
Four days.
How did Sarita feel on Sunday morning?
She felt shocked and panicky, her stomach dropping, because the bright weekend plan was nowhere near done.
What does Charu suggest, and why is it wiser?
Making a plan based on how long chapters actually take Sarita, rather than a hopeful picture of one focused weekend.
How does Charu seem to see the chart?
Charu doubts it from the start, remembering the four-day optics chapter, but comes with tea and help rather than blame.
There's a school choir audition tomorrow and I only know one song well.
One song you know well is a good choice. Pick one that suits your voice and that you feel comfortable singing.
Should I add a second one?
If you are asked for only one, one is enough. Prepare the second only as a backup. It is better to sing one song confidently than two nervously.
How do I prepare tonight?
Sing it a couple of times, drink some water, and rest. Warm up your voice gently in the morning. Walk into the room standing tall and take a slow breath before you begin.

By day four Pooja's sprint chart looked wrong. She had planned a full budgeting app: login, charts, reminders, shared accounts, export. Only login and half the chart worked. In her Pune flat she sat back and counted what remained: three days, and at her speed, roughly one feature a day.

By day four my sprint chart looked wrong. I had planned a full budgeting app: login, charts, reminders, shared accounts, export. Only login and half the chart worked. In my Pune flat I sat back and counted what remained: three days, and at my speed, roughly one feature a day.

Ankita: Saw Meher's post again. Her big internship. So smug 😒
Jyoti: You mention her ten times a day. What did she actually do to you?
Ankita: Nothing. That's what's so annoying. I just can't stand her.
Jyoti: Then why can't you stop looking?

Ankita: I know. I know. 😔

Ankita saw Meher's post about her big internship.

Ankita realises the dislike is tied to envy and hurt over the internship Ankita wanted, not to anything Meher did to Ankita.
What could Ankita do to loosen her hold on this?
Ankita can mute Meher for a while, not spread the cheating rumour, and put the energy into her own applications, with Jyoti's support. 🙂
How does Jyoti see Ankita's anger?
Jyoti sees it as hurt more than hatred and gently asks questions instead of judging. Jyoti also asks Ankita not to share the cheating claim with anyone.

The lights went out just as the guests arrived, so Dadi lit two lamps in the hall. Lavanya's mother lifted one toward the shelf of trophies won by Lavanya's older brother Abhinav. “Third one this year!” Uncles clapped Abhinav's shoulder. Lavanya's painting of the neem tree, which she had worked on for a week, leaned unnoticed against the wall behind them. She refilled the water jug, then straightened cushions no one had asked her to straighten. Nobody looked her way. Only Dada, sitting near the door, asked, “And what's that behind the shelf?” “Nothing,” Lavanya said, and carried the painting to her room.

How many cricket trophies had Abhinav won this year?
The mother said it was the third one this year.
Why did Lavanya say “Nothing” when Dada asked about the painting?
Lavanya seems to feel invisible and does not expect praise, so she brushes the question off even though she worked on the painting for a week.
What could the adults do at the next gathering so both children feel seen?
They could look at Lavanya's work as warmly as at Abhinav's trophies and ask her about it directly.
What might Dada have noticed that the others missed?
Dada noticed the painting leaning behind the shelf and asked about it, which suggests he saw Lavanya's quiet effort when the guests did not.

At the school library's puzzle table, Farhan tipped out a jigsaw. "Edges first," he said to Yusuf. "Then sky. Then the house." He picked out every flat-sided piece and made a frame. Then he found the blue pieces for the sky. "Now the house," he said. Yusuf watched. "How do you know where to start?" "The edges make a box," Farhan said.

What did Farhan say to do first?
"Edges first."
What was Farhan feeling as he explained his plan?
He was confident and proud of knowing where to start.
What else could Farhan add to his plan?
He could sort the pieces by colour before starting the middle, so each part is faster.
How does the plan look to Yusuf?
Yusuf is curious and impressed, wanting to know how Farhan knew where to start.

He ceased. The wondrous arrow flew,
And Jamadagni's offspring knew
Those glorious worlds to him were barred,
Once gained by penance long and hard.
Then straight the airy quarters cleared,
And the mid regions bright appeared,
While Gods and saints unnumbered praised
Rama, the mighty bow who raised.
And Jamadagni's son, o'erawed.
Extolled his name with highest laud,
With reverent steps around him strode,
Then hastened on his airy road.
Far from the sight of all he fled,
And rested on Mahendra's head.

He stopped speaking, and the wondrous arrow flew. Jamadagni's son realised that the glorious worlds he had won by long and hard penance were now closed to him. Then the airy quarters were cleared at once, and the middle regions looked bright, while countless Gods and saints praised Rama, who had lifted the mighty bow. Jamadagni's son, overawed, praised his name highly, walked around him with respect and hurried on his way through the air. He fled far from everyone's sight and rested on the top of Mahendra.
