I'm Amandeep, and I've watched this happen to my whole friend group. Nikita used to bake on Sundays just because the kitchen smelled nice. Now she has a baking page, a posting schedule and a spreadsheet of likes. Last month her cake sank and she almost cried, not because it tasted bad, but because "it won't photograph."
Sameer's running is all pace charts. Farah learned guitar for three weeks, then started pricing online lessons she could teach.
At Nikita's place on Saturday, I pulled out an old box of watercolours and said, "Let's paint something terrible." She hesitated, then painted a purple cow with five legs. She laughed so hard she snorted. I can't say what was going on inside her. But she didn't reach for her phone to take a photo, and at the door she said, "Can we do terrible painting again?"

What did Nikita paint on Saturday?
A purple cow with five legs.
What might Amandeep have felt watching friends turn hobbies into metrics?
Amandeep seems sad and a little worried, noticing that Nikita was upset about a sunken cake only because it wouldn't photograph.
Why was "Let's paint something terrible" a good invitation?
It removed any goal or audience, so Nikita could play badly just for fun.
What was the terrible painting like for Nikita?
Nikita seemed freed and delighted, laughing till she snorted, leaving her phone alone and asking to do it again.

For two months, at the rural bank branch in Sehore, Himani had watched Bidisha leave early every Friday. Himani stayed to close the cash. She said nothing. When Bidisha said, “Thanks, yaar, you're the best,” Himani smiled.
She smiled in meetings. She smiled when the manager praised Bidisha's customer numbers. She smiled when Bidisha borrowed her calculator and didn't return it.
Then one Friday, Bidisha picked up Himani's pen from her desk.
“That's MY PEN!” Himani shouted, so loudly that a farmer in the queue jumped. “And my calculator! And my Fridays!”
The branch went silent. Bidisha stared at her. Himani's face burned. She hadn't known how much had been piling up until it came out all at once.

What did Bidisha pick up from Himani's desk?
She picked up Himani's pen.
Why did Himani shout over a pen?
She had held back resentment and anger for two months behind smiles, so a small trigger released all of it.
What could Himani do to stop this happening again?
She could raise small issues early and calmly, like the Fridays and the calculator, before they build up.
How might Bidisha have felt when Himani shouted?
Bidisha was probably shocked and confused, not knowing Himani had been upset for weeks.

Mentor's note, June. Varun writing about Binita, a colleague I have coached this year.
March: prices fell, and Binita paused the monthly plan, saying "I'll restart at the very bottom." April: prices rose a little. "It's a trap, another dip is coming," Binita said. May: higher again, and Binita kept the same line, checking the numbers every evening.
June: prices are well above where the plan was paused. Binita sounded tense and said, "If I buy now I'll feel stupid, and if I don't I'll feel stupid."
I am not an adviser, so I only asked what price would count as the bottom. Binita could not name one. We agreed to talk again next week.
— Varun

When did Binita pause the monthly plan?
Binita paused the monthly plan in March.
What was Binita feeling in June?
Binita was tense and torn, saying that either choice would feel stupid.
What could Binita try instead of waiting for a lower price?
Binita could restart a fixed monthly amount on a set date, which does not need a guess at the bottom, and check with a registered adviser if unsure.
What is it like for Varun to watch Binita's waiting?
Varun feels concerned but careful, since Varun is not an adviser and can only ask questions and stay in touch.

Read this:

Jahnavi, since your podcast is about career turns, here's mine. At twenty-one I had two offers: a research assistant post at a marine lab in Kochi, and a support engineer job at a big IT company in Pune. I loved the ocean work. I'd spent two summers counting crabs on mudflats. But the IT job was the one my uncles understood. "Good boy, Akash, sensible choice," they said. If the lab post ended in a year and I was jobless, it would be my mistake, and everyone would remember it. If the IT job went badly, it was just the economy. So I took Pune. Three years later I'm good at it, and nobody has called it a mistake. But every time I see a photo of a mudflat, I feel a small ache, and now I know its name: I never tried.

What were Akash's two offers at twenty-one?
A research assistant post at a marine lab in Kochi, and a support engineer job at a big IT company in Pune.
Why did the IT job feel safer to Akash than the lab post?
If the lab post ended and he was jobless, he felt it would be his own mistake that everyone remembered, while a bad IT job could be blamed on the economy.
What small step could Akash take now so the ache doesn't simply grow?
He could look for weekend volunteering or a short course in marine work, testing the old dream without throwing away the job he's good at.
How might Akash's uncles see his career compared with how he sees it?
They likely see a sensible, successful choice, while Akash feels a quiet loss that they can't see.
Why does bread go stale even in a closed bag?
Staling is not just drying out. The starch in bread slowly changes and firms up as it sits, which makes the crumb hard and dry, even when moisture cannot escape.
Can I bring it back to normal?
Partly. Sprinkle a little water on it and warm it in a hot oven for a few minutes. It will feel fresh again, but only for a short time, so eat it soon after.

Last summer I started teaching maths to kids in the lane behind our building, mostly because Ammi wouldn't stop nagging me to do something useful. I'm Wasim, and honestly I thought it would be boring. Then I met Vijay, nine, who couldn't do subtraction and said he was 'dumb, everyone says'. We used marbles. We used cricket scores. On the fourteenth day he got a whole page right and threw his pencil in the air. I've topped tests before and felt nothing much. That day I walked home feeling like I actually mattered to someone. Now when my marks slip, it doesn't wreck me the same way, because on Tuesday and Thursday evenings there's a kid waiting for me with a sharpened pencil.

What did Wasim use to teach Vijay?
Marbles and cricket scores.
How did Wasim feel walking home on the fourteenth day?
Wasim felt proud and needed, as if truly mattering to someone, more than after topping tests.
How could Wasim keep this going after the summer?
Wasim could keep the Tuesday and Thursday sessions and perhaps bring a friend to teach other kids in the lane.
What might the sessions mean to Vijay?
Vijay, who thought he was dumb, may feel capable and cared for, proud enough to throw his pencil in the air.

Counsellor’s note, Thursday. Wasim came in after lunch and sat with his bag on his lap. Three weeks ago he reported a lab-marks entry that had been changed, and the lab in-charge corrected it. Since then the class chat has stopped including him, someone wrote “informer” on the lab board, and two groups go quiet when he passes.
He said, “I keep thinking I should have said nothing.” He also said Samir, who sits beside him, still shares notes and eats lunch with him, and that this helps.
I told Wasim that reporting was not his fault and that the isolation is what needs dealing with. That afternoon I spoke to the head of department about the board and the chat. The head had the board wiped before the last class and said the class chat will be raised with the whole group tomorrow.
Next week I will meet Wasim again.
— College counsellor

What did someone write on the lab board?
Someone wrote “informer” on the lab board.
What was Wasim feeling when he said he should have said nothing?
Wasim was feeling lonely and doubtful about having reported, since he was being shut out by the class. It shows the isolation weighs heavily on him.
What did the counsellor do that helped Wasim?
The counsellor told Wasim that reporting was not his fault and took the board and the chat to the head of department that same afternoon. They also planned another meeting for next week.
How might Samir's sitting beside Wasim matter to Wasim?
Samir's sharing notes and eating lunch together shows Wasim is not alone. One ally can make the labelling and gossip easier to bear.

Sunday night

Cricket trials for the under-15 team are tomorrow at seven. I'm not going.

I already know how it'll go. I'll drop the first catch. Coach will shake his head. Gautam and the others will get picked and I'll be standing there like an idiot. So why go? At least if I don't go, I can't fail.

Gautam called and said, "You bowled well in the nets last week." I said, "That was nets. Trials are different." He said, "How do you know? You've never been to trials."

I didn't have an answer for that.

I've set my alarm for six anyway. Not saying I'm going. Just... the alarm is set.

Ramesh

What time are the cricket trials?
The trials are tomorrow at seven.
Why does not going feel safer to Ramesh?
Ramesh feels afraid of failing in front of others, and not going protects against that disappointment, even though it removes any chance of success.
What small step keeps Ramesh's chance open?
Setting the alarm for six and treating the prediction as a guess to test by going to the trials.
How does Gautam see Ramesh's prediction?
Gautam doubts it, pointing out that Ramesh bowled well in the nets and has never actually been to trials.

The power went out at 4 pm in the middle of Amandeep's video call, and the laptop battery showed nineteen percent. On the screen, Jatin's face was red. "You breached the delivery terms. My lawyer will send a notice tomorrow."

Amandeep's chest went hot. The first reply that came to mind was a nasty one. Instead: "I'll look at the agreement now and reply in writing tonight. Please send me which clause you mean."

The call dropped. By torchlight, Amandeep opened the contract on the phone and found a delivery clause allowing a week's extension if the client's files arrived late. The files had arrived nine days late. Amandeep pulled up the email thread as proof, screenshotted it and saved it in a folder.

That night, on the phone's last few percent, Amandeep typed a calm message with the clause and the dates, and added, "I'd be happy to try mediation before this goes further."

Jatin answered the next morning: "Let me check."

What was the laptop battery level when the power went out?
The laptop battery showed nineteen percent.
What was Amandeep feeling at the accusation, and what did Amandeep do about it?
Amandeep felt angry, chest hot and tempted to reply nastily, but chose to say the agreement would be checked and a written reply sent that night.
Why was it wise to reply in writing with the clause and dates?
A written reply citing the clause and the email evidence stays calm and factual, and suggesting mediation avoids an expensive escalation.
How might Jatin see the accusation?
Jatin may honestly believe the terms were broken and feel anxious about the client, which could explain the red face and the threat, and the late files may not have been clear to Jatin.

Saturday: At the inter-school science fair, the judge spent ten minutes at Abhinav's solar dryer. 'Clever design. Good data. Very neat poster. Your costing is a little vague, though.' She moved on.
Sunday: Abhinav replayed only one sentence. Costing is vague. Costing is vague. He told Irfan on the phone, 'She basically said the whole thing was vague.' Irfan said, 'Didn't she say clever?' 'Just being polite.'
Wednesday: The score sheet came to school. Irfan read it out in the corridor: design 9, data 9, presentation 8, costing 5. 'That's your one weak spot. Everything else is top.' Abhinav took the sheet and looked at the numbers for a long time. Then he drew a small circle around the 5 and wrote next to it: ask Papa about prices.

What score did Abhinav get for costing?
Abhinav got 5 for costing.
Why did Abhinav dismiss 'clever' as 'just being polite'?
The criticism hurt, so it held Abhinav's attention, and the praise felt less believable beside it; the painful line seemed like the judge's real opinion.
What changed on Wednesday, and why did it help?
Hearing all the scores read out put the 5 next to three high marks, so Abhinav could see one weak spot and plan a fix instead of feeling the whole project had failed.
What might Irfan feel reading the score sheet aloud?
Irfan probably felt relieved and eager to show the full picture, since the numbers proved what Irfan had been trying to say on Sunday.

Monday of the summer camp, the Red Cross volunteer taught first aid on a doll. Tushar yawned. Aparna, his sister, wrote everything down: cool running water for burns, don't pop blisters, call an adult.
Wednesday, they practised on each other with pretend injuries. Tushar still mixed up the steps, and Aparna quizzed him on the bus. "Burn?" "Uh… butter?" "No! Water."
Saturday, at home, Aparna touched the hot pressure-cooker lid and yelped. Tushar grabbed her hand, held it under the cold tap and yelled for Ma. "Don't put anything on it," he told her.
Ma came running, checked it and said it was small. "Who taught you?"
Tushar looked at Aparna. "She did. On the bus."

What did Aparna touch on Saturday?
Aparna touched the hot pressure-cooker lid.
How can you tell Tushar felt the first-aid lesson didn't matter at first?
He yawned on Monday while Aparna wrote everything down, which suggests he felt bored and thought it didn't matter.
What went right on Saturday that could help other families?
Cooling the burn under the tap, not putting anything on it and calling an adult straight away, then letting the adult check it.
How might Aparna feel when Tushar says she taught him?
Aparna might feel proud and a little amused that her bus quizzes paid off on her own hand.

Dear Kashish Ma'am,
I wanted to explain about today's online class. When you asked me a question, I didn't answer for a long time. I know it looked like I wasn't paying attention.
Actually, my internet was lagging, and your voice kept cutting out. I clicked the raise-hand button twice, but I don't think it showed on your screen.
Also, I get really shy speaking on video. When everyone's camera is on and it's silent, I freeze.
Could I type my answers in the chat sometimes? Or use the hand emoji when I want to talk?
Thank you for understanding.
Varun

How many times did Varun click the raise-hand button?
Twice.
What was Varun feeling during the silence in the online class?
Varun felt shy and frozen speaking on video, and frustrated by the lag.
What did Varun suggest to make online class easier?
Typing answers in the chat or using the hand emoji when wanting to talk.
How might Kashish Ma'am have seen Varun's silence before the email?
Kashish Ma'am might have thought Varun wasn't paying attention, not knowing about the lag and shyness.

Sharmila eyed the wooden elephant on the low plank shelf in the village house. She jumped, and it stayed put. She grabbed the shelf edge with both fists and tugged: nothing. Then she pulled the woven mat under the elephant, and it slid a little. "Ah!" she said, and pulled the mat again, and again, each time getting the elephant closer. Rehana, the neighbour, shelled peas by the door and watched without a word.

What happened to the elephant when Sharmila pulled the woven mat?
The elephant slid a little each time Sharmila pulled the mat.
What does Sharmila's "Ah!" suggest she is feeling?
The "Ah!" suggests a small burst of delight and discovery, because after two moves that did nothing, one finally worked. 😊
What could Sharmila try once the elephant is near the edge, and why?
She could reach up again now that it is closer, or ask an adult to catch it, because the mat brought the toy nearer but she still has to get it down safely.
How might Rehana see Sharmila's way of solving it?
Rehana might see a small girl working things out alone and quietly enjoy it; her silent watching suggests patience rather than a wish to take over.

Dear diary,
Disaster. I swallowed my gum in PT. Dilnaz screamed, "Now it'll stay in your stomach for SEVEN YEARS!" Everyone knows that. My cousin says it, the bus boys say it, even Dilnaz's big sister. I've heard it about a hundred times, so it must be true.
I kept touching my tummy all through maths.
At home I told Mummy, almost crying. She laughed a little, then hugged me and said it just passes through like food, and if my tummy ever hurts I should tell her. She said lots of things people repeat aren't true; they only sound true because we've heard them so often.
I still feel weird. But Mummy doesn't lie.
Preeti

Where did Preeti swallow the gum?
In PT.
Why was Preeti so sure the gum would stay for seven years?
Preeti felt scared and certain, because hearing it so many times made it feel true.
What could Preeti ask the next time a playground fact is scary?
Where it comes from, and whether someone who really knows, like Mummy or a teacher, agrees.
How might Dilnaz feel if she learned the fact was wrong?
Dilnaz might feel surprised and a bit sheepish, having shouted it so confidently.

The rank list left no room for doubt. Harsha scrolled to the bottom of the admit list at six in the morning and did not find his number. By breakfast the sentence in his head had hardened: I am stupid, and Papa's money is wasted. He thought of the coaching fees, the extra tiffin his mother packed, and the way the whole family had planned its year around this one exam. A single test had become a verdict on all of him.

He told Lokesh, who texted twice, that the paper had been set unfairly and the invigilator had rushed them. Then he stopped replying to Lokesh and told nobody else. On Sunday his father asked, "Anything on the result?" and Harsha said, "Not up yet."

That evening at his aunt's house the truth reached the room anyway, through a neighbour's son. Over tea an uncle counted off cousins' ranks and glanced at Harsha. "Some children just don't apply themselves." His cousin Gopika, visiting from Hyderabad, watched Harsha's face go blank. She followed him to the balcony that same hour. "One result isn't you," she said. "Do you want to sit with me and work out what comes next?" He nodded without looking up, and then, to his own surprise, wept.

What did Harsha tell his father on Sunday about the result?
He said it was not up yet.
How did Harsha's shame and hiding lead to the moment on the balcony?

Harsha turned one failed test into a verdict that he was stupid and his father's money was wasted, then blamed the paper and hid the result. When the truth reached his aunt's house and an uncle counted off cousins' ranks, Gopika saw his face go blank and offered a quiet word that one result is not the person.
What was Harsha feeling when the uncle counted off the cousins' ranks?
He felt ashamed and numb, and his face went blank.
What could the family do to support Harsha now?
They could stop comparing him with cousins, say that one result is not the person, and sit down with him to plan next steps.

The baby had been crying for an hour, the power was out in the Lucknow flat, and Tushar's phone buzzed nonstop: the family chat group. Jasleen's aunt had forwarded a message about child-kidnappers dressed as balloon sellers in the city. Within minutes, eight relatives had replied in panic. "Don't take the baby out!" "Lock all doors!"

Tushar, bouncing his daughter in the dark, read it twice. He looked around by torchlight. The bucket of water in the bathroom, full to the brim. Jasleen's mother's pills on the low table. The balcony railing with a gap wide enough for a small child.

He typed: "Has anyone checked if this is true? What do the police say?" He searched. The city police had called the message fake that same morning.

He posted the link. Then he emptied the bucket, moved the pills to the top shelf, and made a note to buy a railing net. Jasleen watched him, surprised.

What did the forwarded message claim?
A message about child-kidnappers dressed as balloon sellers in the city.
What was Tushar feeling as the relatives panicked?
Tushar felt uneasy and doubtful, wanting facts instead of fear, and worried about the real risks he could see around him.
What protective steps did Tushar take, and why were they sensible?
Tushar checked the police, posted the link and then emptied the bucket, moved the pills and planned a railing net, focusing on common home dangers.
How might Jasleen see Tushar's actions that night?
Jasleen was surprised, and may feel reassured and grateful that Tushar turned toward the real dangers in the flat.

When my best friend Urmila moved to a different school in Class 9, I acted like it was nothing. At her farewell I shrugged and said, "We'll see each other around." My classmates were there, and I didn't want to look soft.
She looked at me like she'd expected more.
For a month, we texted a bit. Short stuff. I missed her so much it made my stomach ache, and I never said it.
Then I found the comic we'd drawn together in Class 5, about two detective pigeons. I sat on my bed and read it three times.
So I wrote her an actual letter. On paper. I said, "I didn't say it at your farewell because I'm an idiot. I miss you. School is boring without you."
She called the day it arrived. She was laughing and crying. "You're such an idiot, Yusuf," she said, and I'd never been happier to be called one.

What was the comic about?
About two detective pigeons.
What was Yusuf feeling during the month after Urmila left?
Yusuf missed her so much it ached, but was too embarrassed to say it, hiding it behind short texts.
What small step brought them close again?
Writing an honest letter on paper saying "I miss you," which Urmila answered with a call the day it arrived.
How might Urmila have felt at the farewell when Yusuf shrugged?
Urmila probably felt hurt and a little disappointed, since she expected her best friend to show some care.

I'm Chaitanya, and three weeks before my Class 10 prelims I couldn't sleep. My head felt like a browser with fifty tabs open. Maths revision. The science project. Return the library book. Hindi essay. Practical file. Pay the bus fee. It all kept spinning.
My older cousin Yogesh saw me lying awake at midnight and handed me a notebook. "Write everything down. Everything. Don't sort it yet."
I wrote for ten minutes. Twenty-three things. Seeing them on paper, they suddenly looked smaller. Just a list.
Then Yogesh said, "Now make two columns. Today. Later."
Today got four things: finish the practical file, return the book, one maths chapter, ask Papa about the bus fee. Everything else went to Later.
I slept that night. First time in a week.

How many things did Chaitanya write down?
Twenty-three things.
How did Chaitanya feel after seeing the list on paper?
Chaitanya felt calmer and relieved, since the tasks suddenly looked smaller once they were written down.
What else could Chaitanya do with the Later column?
Chaitanya could move three or four items into Today each evening, so the Later list keeps shrinking.
How might Yogesh see Chaitanya sleeping that night?
Yogesh would likely feel glad and relieved that the simple list helped a worried cousin rest.

The corridor of Jomon's hostel in Pune smelled of instant noodles and floor cleaner. In one month he had learned which day the mess sambar was edible and which lab record was due when. At nine, Ishita from his batch sat beside him in the common room with her laptop. "You never sleep before one. Why not shift your call to Amma earlier and stop scrolling after?"
Jomon looked at his phone: twelve messages from the old school group, none from home. Last night he had stood on the terrace, thrilled by the size of the city and aching for the smell of rain on his own road in Kottayam. He typed: "Amma, call at 8.30 tomorrow?" Then he asked Ishita if she wanted to join the football game on Sunday.

What did Ishita suggest Jomon change about his call to Amma?
Ishita suggested he shift the call earlier so he could stop scrolling afterwards.
What was Jomon feeling as he stood on the terrace the night before?
He felt both thrilled by the size of the city and homesick, missing the smell of rain on his own road in Kottayam.
What small steps did Jomon take that could make his shift steadier?
He asked Amma for an earlier call at a fixed time and invited Ishita to the Sunday football game, which builds a routine and a friendship.
Why might Ishita have raised the late nights with Jomon?
Ishita from his batch had noticed he never sleeps before one and probably wanted to help him settle, so she offered a practical idea.

I'm Omkar, Kalyani's brother. When our Nani died in October, Kalyani, fifteen, didn't cry at the funeral. Everyone said she was strong.
But after that, she stopped eating dinner with us. She kept Nani's grey shawl on her bed and slept wrapped in it. Some nights I heard her talking softly, as if to someone.
One Sunday, Amma found her in the garden, planting a tulsi cutting from Nani's old pot. Kalyani said, “Nani watered this every morning. Someone has to.”
Amma knelt beside her, and they both cried then, finally.
Now every morning Kalyani waters the plant before school. I don't know what she says to it. But she eats dinner with us again.

What did Kalyani plant in the garden?
A tulsi cutting from Nani's old pot.
How was Kalyani feeling in the weeks after the funeral?
She was grieving deeply and quietly, missing Nani even though she didn't cry at first.
What helped Kalyani begin to mourn?
Planting and caring for Nani's tulsi gave her a way to remember Nani and let her finally cry with Amma.
How might Amma feel crying with Kalyani in the garden?
She probably feels sad but closer to her daughter, sharing their grief at last 🤍

From my balcony I can see the pond behind our lane and the old jamun tree that leans over it. Last Sunday Kamal stood under it while Aparna and two boys chanted, "Darpok! Darpok!" He went red, spat on his palms and climbed. Halfway along the branch it dipped toward the water, and he froze, hugging the wood. I don't know what he was thinking up there. His face had gone from angry to scared. I shouted for Kamal's father, who came running with the long bamboo ladder. It took twenty minutes to get him down. His arms and knees were scraped raw. Aparna didn't chant on the way home.

How long did it take to get Kamal down?
It took twenty minutes to get him down.
How did Kamal's feelings seem to change once the branch dipped?
He seemed to go from angry and embarrassed at being called darpok to frightened, frozen and hugging the wood.
What else could Kamal have done when the chanting started?
He could have walked away or offered a safer contest, since trying to prove himself cost him scraped arms and knees and a scare over the water.
Why might Aparna be quiet on the way home?
She may feel guilty and shaken after seeing how the chanting pushed Kamal into danger.

messages.content: Old tins could become a garden, I think. I want to start gardening in old tins, but I'm not sure which plants are easy.
Tins are a nice cheap start. Make a few small holes in the bottom for water to drain. Easy plants are mint, coriander, marigold and tulsi.
Is tulsi hard to look after?
Not at all. It likes sunlight and regular water, but not a soggy pot. Pinch the tips now and then so it grows bushy.
I'll start with tulsi and mint then.
Good choices. Keep mint in its own tin, because its roots spread and take over other plants.

Eight months after the report, the inquiry was still going on, and Kunal's new job paid a third less than the old one. On Saturday the rain came in through the window frame of his rented room, and he had just enough left this month for rent and not much else.
Samir turned up at seven with a steel tiffin of rajma chawal and two umbrellas. 'Your mother said you'd skip dinner,' he said.
They ate on the floor, away from the leak. Kunal's phone buzzed: a message from a former colleague. 'They've fixed the brake checks on the buses. Thought you'd want to know.'
He read it three times. He was tired, down to his bones. But under the tiredness was something solid.
'Worth it?' Samir asked.
'Ask me next year,' Kunal said, smiling. 'But yes.'

What did Samir bring?
Samir brought a steel tiffin of rajma chawal and two umbrellas.
What does Kunal feel after reading the message three times?
He feels deep tiredness but also a solid pride and quiet vindication that the brake checks were fixed.
What helps sustain Kunal through the long aftermath?
Friends like Samir turning up with food, his mother keeping an eye on him, and knowing his action made the buses safer.
What might Samir be feeling as he asks 'Worth it?'
Samir is likely proud of his friend but worried about his money and tiredness, wanting to hear how he really is.

"Farhan, it's your fourth job in three years," Hansa said, drying dishes in their Bhopal kitchen.
"Ammi, please don't start."
She paused. She had rehearsed a speech about stability, about her friends' sons who were engineers with houses. But she put the towel down.
"I'm not starting. I'm asking. What went wrong at the last one?"
Farhan looked at her carefully. "Nothing went wrong. I didn't like sales. This one's in teaching. I think I'm good at it."
"Teaching," Hansa said slowly. "You did always explain things to your cousins."
"You're not angry?"
"I'm worried," she admitted. "At twenty-five I had you. But the world's different now. Just tell me when you need help."
Farhan hugged her from behind.

What is Farhan's new job in?
His new job is in teaching.
What was Hansa feeling when she put the towel down?
She felt worried about his job changes, but chose to set aside her rehearsed speech and ask instead.
What made Hansa's response respectful?
She asked what went wrong, admitted her worry honestly, recognised the world is different, and offered help instead of a lecture.
How did Farhan feel about his mother's response?
He was surprised and relieved she wasn't angry, and hugged her.

Dear Tenzin, You asked what I think of the new rule banning street vendors within 500 metres of our college. I've been arguing about it all week. My first reaction was anger. Aunty Rosy's chai cart has been there for twenty years. She feeds half the hostel. But I also get why the council did it: the road is narrow, ambulances get stuck. Laws are supposed to be agreements that protect everyone, right? Safety, but also people's right to earn a living. This rule protects one and crushes the other. So I don't think we should just obey it or just ignore it. We've written to the council asking for a vending zone around the corner. Forty students signed. There's a public hearing on the 12th. I'm going to speak. Usha

Rewrite this letter as a three-sentence summary.

Usha writes to Tenzin about the new rule banning street vendors within 500 metres of their college. Usha was angry, since Aunty Rosy's chai cart has stood there twenty years, but accepts the narrow road blocks ambulances. Forty students signed a request for a vending zone, and Usha will speak at the public hearing on the 12th.

Tuesday
Passport office. Third visit. I'm so angry I could scream.
First visit: wrong photo size. Second: my address proof didn't match the spelling on my ID card. Today: they wanted my birth certificate original, not a copy. Nobody told me! The man at counter 4 didn't even look up.
I nearly shouted. I felt it in my throat. Then I saw the old lady behind me, holding her whole file in a plastic bag, and I thought: shouting won't fix this.
So I asked, as calmly as I could, "Sir, can you please write down every document I need, so I don't come back again?" He looked up. He actually wrote a list.
Sonali Didi says she'll help me check everything twice before Thursday.
Fourth visit, Thursday. With the list. Patience.
Sarita

What did the man at counter 4 write for Sarita?
He wrote a list of every document Sarita needed.
What was Sarita feeling at the passport office?
Sarita felt angry and frustrated after three visits, nearly shouting.
What helped Sarita more than anger?
Asking calmly for a written list and planning to check the documents twice with Sonali Didi made the next visit more likely to succeed.
How might the clerk have felt when Sarita asked politely?
The clerk may have felt respected rather than attacked, which made him more willing to help.

At Ganga's cousin's engagement party in their Hyderabad colony, a friend of the groom's family, a man in his thirties, stopped by Dilnaz at the snacks table.
"You've grown up very nicely," he said, and his eyes moved slowly down and up. "Very nicely."
Dilnaz felt her skin crawl. On the surface it was a compliment. It didn't feel like one.
Ganga appeared at her side with two plates. "Dilnaz, come, my mother is calling you." She steered her away.
Behind the pillar, Dilnaz whispered, "Was that weird, or am I overthinking?"
"It was weird. The way he looked. You're not overthinking."
"Should I say something?"
"We'll tell my mother. Now."
Ganga's mother listened, said, "Thank you for telling me, you did nothing wrong," and kept both girls with her. She spoke to the man's host family before the party ended, and she called Dilnaz's mother that night.

What did the man say to Dilnaz?
He said, "You've grown up very nicely."
What was Dilnaz feeling after the man's comment?
Dilnaz felt uneasy and uncomfortable, her skin crawling, sensing a suggestive meaning behind the surface compliment.
What made Ganga a good friend in this moment?
She noticed, steered Dilnaz away, confirmed the feeling was real, and brought her straight to a trusted adult.
How did Ganga's mother respond, and why did it matter?
She listened, told Dilnaz she did nothing wrong, kept the girls close, and spoke to the hosts and Dilnaz's mother that night, showing that telling leads to protection.

What does "distrustful" mean?
Fix the mistake: Where do you comes from?
What does "cross that bridge when you come to it" mean?

1. Distrustful means not trusting. It is an adjective.
2. It should be: Where do you come from? Why: after "do", the main verb stays in its base form.
3. It means to deal with a problem only when it really happens. For example: we may miss the train, but let us cross that bridge when we come to it.

Neelam sat on her bed with a pencil and paper. The fire-safety aunty at school had said to start from the end. "The end is Francis Uncle's gate across the lane, where everyone meets." She drew a box there. "Before the gate, the lane. Before the lane, the flat door. Before the door, the stairs, not the lift, because lifts can stop. And before the stairs, nothing in my hands: no bag, no phone, no hunting for shoes." She drew arrows backward until they reached her bed, then read them forward. It looked like a short walk. She stuck the paper inside her cupboard door.

Where did Neelam decide the meeting place should be?
She chose Francis Uncle's gate across the lane.
What was Neelam feeling after reading her arrows forward?
Reassured and calm, since the way out looked like a short walk.
What other approach could Neelam use to check her plan, and why?
She could walk the route with her family and time it, because walking it shows any blocked or slow spots that a paper plan hides.
How might Francis Uncle see being the meeting place?
He is a fixed, familiar spot where neighbours can gather, so he can help count people and call for help.

I'm Mridul, and I've taught moral philosophy to undergraduates for three years. Sudha taught me something this term.
In week two, she argued that the hostel curfew should be obeyed because "without rules, there's chaos". Classic Stage 4.
In week six, she refused to sign a petition her friends wrote, because they'd included false claims. She stood alone. That looked like principle.
In week nine, she admitted she'd lied to a warden to protect a roommate. "She'd have been upset with me otherwise," she said. That was approval, Stage 3.
I used to want to place students on the ladder. Sudha broke that for me. She wasn't one stage. She was a young person reasoning, sometimes higher, sometimes lower, depending on what was at stake.
Now I tell my classes: the model shows how reasoning grows. It doesn't sort people into better and worse.

In which week did Sudha refuse to sign the petition?
In week six.
What was Mridul feeling as Sudha's reasoning changed across the weeks?
Mridul felt surprised and thoughtful, letting go of the wish to place students on a ladder.
How has Mridul changed the way the model is taught, and why is it better?
Mridul now teaches that the model shows how reasoning grows, not a ranking of people, which avoids labelling students.
How might Sudha have felt standing alone over the petition?
She probably felt lonely but firm, choosing honesty over going along with friends.

messages.content: Is it true that charging my phone overnight ruins the battery?
Modern phones stop charging once the battery is full, so overnight charging is usually fine. The battery does wear down over time with use, whatever you do.
Does heat matter?
Yes. Batteries age faster in high heat, so avoid leaving your phone in direct sun or under a pillow while charging. A cool, open place is better.
Should I use any charger that fits?
It is safest to use the charger that came with the phone or one made for it. A very cheap or damaged charger can harm the phone and may even be unsafe.

Thursday. Dear diary, swimming class was awful again. I'm the only one in our group whose body has properly changed already, and I spent the whole hour with a towel wrapped round me. Sunaina is still tiny, and she kept saying she wished she looked like me, which is funny because I wish I looked like her. At home I stood in front of the mirror comparing myself to the girls in our group, one by one. Then Mummy knocked. I told her, and she laughed gently, not at me. 'Beti, at your age I was the last one. Your Masi was the first. We both hated it.' She said bodies don't read the same calendar and nobody wins a prize for being early or late. I felt a bit better. Tomorrow I'm leaving the towel on the bench, at least for the first lap.
- Sharmila

What did Sharmila keep wrapped around her during swimming class?
A towel, for the whole hour.
Why did Sharmila feel so uncomfortable at the pool?
She felt self-conscious and alone, being the only one in her group whose body had already changed.
What small step could help Sharmila feel easier at the pool?
Leaving the towel on the bench for the first lap, a patient start rather than forcing herself to feel fine at once 🙂
How does Sunaina seem to see Sharmila's body?
Sunaina wishes she looked like Sharmila, showing the two are comparing in opposite directions.

Lalremsiami, when I moved to Hyderabad for this job I was twenty-four and knew nobody. So I named everything. The money plant was Mr Green, the office printer was Grumpy, and the home speaker that said "Good night, Rashmi" felt almost like a flatmate. One night I caught myself telling it about a bad review and waiting for something kind. It told me the weather. I laughed, but it stung. I kept the names, I still greet Mr Green every morning, but I started calling my sister every Sunday and joined the lake walkers at six. My sister still teases me: "Rashmi, did you tell the plant first or me?" And honestly, these days it's her first.

What did the speaker say when Rashmi told it about the bad review?
It told Rashmi the weather.
How did Rashmi feel when the speaker answered with the weather?
Rashmi laughed but felt a sting of loneliness, seeing that the friendly voice could not actually care.
What turning point did Rashmi reach in the story, and what choice followed?
After the weather reply, Rashmi kept the playful names but began calling the sister every Sunday and joined the lake walkers, keeping people alongside the plant and the speaker.
How might Rashmi's sister feel about the Sunday calls?
The sister probably feels close and a little amused, teasing about being told before the plant, and glad to be the first one Rashmi talks to.

You want to know the hardest thing anyone said to me at work, as the only woman on the design team? Thomas, my mentor. We were having chai and he said, "Farida, you disappear in meetings." Just like that.
I laughed, then I didn't. He gave me examples. The client call where I had the answer and let my manager say it. The design review where I nodded at a mistake. It stung so much that I nearly told him he didn't understand how loud that room is.
But I went home and wrote down every meeting from that month. He was right about most of them. Not all. So next week, in the review, I made myself speak first. My hands were shaking. Nobody noticed, except Thomas, who gave me a small nod.

What did Thomas say to Farida over chai?
"Farida, you disappear in meetings."
How did Farida feel when Thomas gave her examples?
She felt stung and defensive, almost telling him he didn't understand how loud the room was.
What did Farida do that helped her decide what was useful?
She wrote down every meeting from that month and checked the feedback, finding it right about most but not all.
What might Thomas have felt when he gave Farida the small nod?
He was likely pleased and proud that she took the hard feedback and spoke first.

"Lavanya, why is your door locked?"
"Go away, Amma."
"Your Paati's reading glasses are in two pieces under the sofa."
Silence.
"Lavanya?"
"I sat on them. This morning. I hid them there." Her voice cracked. "I'm such a horrible person. I ruin everything."
Usha sat down on the floor outside the door. "Okay. Two different things just came out. You broke Paati's glasses and hid them. That was a bad thing to do. Is that what you mean?"
"I mean I'm bad."
"That part I don't accept. A bad thing happened. You're my daughter, and you're not bad."
The lock clicked. Lavanya's face was blotchy. "She can't read her newspaper."
"No. So what could fix that?"
"...I could use my birthday money for new ones. And say sorry. And read her the paper till they come."
"That sounds like someone who cares, not someone who's bad."
"Will you come with me when I tell her?"
"Right behind you."

Where were Paati's glasses hidden?
The glasses were in two pieces under the sofa.
What was Lavanya feeling behind the locked door?
Lavanya felt deep shame, saying 'I'm bad' and hiding, not just guilt about the glasses; there may also have been fear of Paati's reaction.
How did Usha help turn shame into repair?
Usha separated the act from the person, 'A bad thing happened... you're not bad', then asked what could fix it, so Lavanya came up with sorry, new glasses and reading the paper.
What would change if Usha had said 'How could you be so careless?'
Lavanya would likely have hidden further behind the door, feeling confirmed as bad, instead of moving towards repair.

Hi Pankaj,

Thanks for asking about Nani. Here's what happened. She fell in the bathroom on Sunday and broke her hip. At her age surgery carries a lot of risk, and the doctors explained that chest infections often follow. That is what happened. Her oxygen dropped on Wednesday, and she died on Thursday morning. I read that this happens a lot with older people. So in a way it was predictable.

The funeral was on Friday. Mum cried a lot. I made sure everyone had water.

Anyway, how are your exams going?

Vishal

PS. I found her reading glasses in my pencil box today. I don't know why I'm telling you this. I had to stop writing for a while.

On which day did Nani fall?
Nani fell in the bathroom on Sunday.
What does the PS suggest about how Vishal is feeling?
The PS suggests Vishal's grief is breaking through; finding Nani's glasses brought the sadness that all the facts were holding off.
What would help Vishal now?
Pankaj could reply warmly and ask about Nani herself rather than the facts, and Vishal could tell Mum or another trusted adult when the sad moments hit.
How might Pankaj feel reading an email so full of facts?
Pankaj may feel puzzled by the calm details and then moved by the PS, sensing how much Vishal is holding in.

Class 8: Tarun's teacher held up his notebook. "This is how every notebook should look!" At home, his father framed his certificate. Tarun felt warm all over.
Class 9: Tarun rewrote pages at the slightest smudge. His friend Nilesh laughed. "Yaar, it's just homework." Tarun said, "It has to be perfect." He liked how his parents smiled at his report cards.
Class 10: Before the prelims, Tarun couldn't sleep. He kept imagining a less-than-perfect mark, his father's face falling. "What if they're disappointed?" he asked Nilesh, and his voice cracked. Nilesh stopped laughing.

What did Tarun's father frame?
His certificate.
What was Tarun feeling before the prelims?
Tarun felt anxious and scared, afraid his parents would be disappointed if he wasn't perfect.
What turning point could help Tarun now?
Telling his parents or a teacher about the fear, and hearing that their love doesn't depend on perfect marks.
What might Nilesh feel when Tarun's voice cracks?
Nilesh probably feels surprised and concerned, realising Tarun's perfectionism is about fear, not neatness.

What does "find your feet" mean?
Why do farmers plough the field before sowing?
Please correct: The woman who's bag was stolen went to the police.
Could you explain what wakeful means?

1. It means to become comfortable in a new situation. For example: it took Sana a week to find her feet in the new school.
2. Ploughing loosens the soil. Because loose soil lets seeds and roots go in easily and lets air and water reach them.
3. Correct form: The woman whose bag was stolen went to the police. Why: "whose" shows belonging, while "who's" means "who is".
4. As an adjective, "wakeful" means unable to sleep, or alert.

"Indu, you are studying all night again? Sit, let your Nani tell you something.
When I was twenty, I, Ganga, was doing my BSc in Madras. Before the final exams I lived on hostel tea and two hours of sleep. I thought it made me brave.
The night before chemistry, my best friend Rukmini asked to borrow my notes. I shouted at her in front of the whole corridor, called her lazy. Then I sold my good fountain pen to a senior for nothing, just to be rid of it, because it was leaking.
I passed, barely. But Rukmini didn't speak to me for a month, and I cried over that pen.
Afterwards I learned: after a meal and a real sleep, I could not even understand why I'd been so cruel. A rested mind forgives. A starving one bites."

What did Ganga live on before the final exams?
She lived on hostel tea and two hours of sleep.
How did young Ganga feel after the exams about what she had done?
She felt regret and sorrow, crying over the pen and hurt that Rukmini didn't speak to her for a month.
What choice inside the story could Ganga have made differently the night before chemistry?
She could have eaten and slept instead of pushing on with tea, so she would not have snapped at Rukmini or made a rash choice with the pen.
How might Rukmini have felt when Ganga shouted at her in the corridor?
Rukmini was probably hurt and humiliated, being called lazy in front of everyone just for asking to borrow notes.

Dear girls,

Could you write a short poem for my mother for her birthday? Simple words, about 50 words.

Dear Mother, you wake before the sun,
You smile until the day is done.
You cook with love, you hold my hand,
You always seem to understand.
Today is yours, so rest and cheer,
You are the best, my mother dear.

Bring joy and laughter, always near.

Looking back, the poem was the start of it. Preeti read it to me at the bus stop in March, her voice shaking a little. "Pranav, be honest," she said. The middle verse didn't make sense to me. I said, "It's really good, honestly." She smiled and folded it away.
After that I noticed how often I said things were fine. Fine after the football trials I didn't make. Fine when Dad asked about the new school. Each "fine" ended the awkward moment quickly, and I liked that.
In June Preeti told another girl in our class, not me, that the magazine had rejected her poem. It stung, but I understood. Why would anyone bring the hard stuff to someone who only ever says nice things?

Where did Preeti read her poem aloud?
Preeti read it at the bus stop in March, her voice shaking a little.
Why does Pranav keep saying things are "fine"?
Pranav wants to escape awkward moments; each "fine" ended the discomfort quickly, even though it hid what Pranav really felt.
What could Pranav have said about the poem that was both kind and honest?
Pranav could have praised a line that worked and gently said the middle verse was confusing, which might have helped Preeti before she sent it out.
Why might Preeti have taken her rejection news to another girl instead?
She may have felt Pranav only ever says nice things, so she needed someone who would respond honestly to hard news.

At the government school in the kasba, the other teachers had started calling Amandeep "the ghost". For three weeks she'd drifted through the staffroom looking flat and tired, answering in a word or two, never joining the tea-time gossip. "Lazy," the PT teacher muttered. "She's lost interest." Yusuf wasn't sure. She still corrected every notebook, and her classes were quiet and orderly. Maybe she was just a private person. Maybe something was wrong. He didn't want to guess or label. One afternoon, when the staffroom emptied, he put a glass of nimbu pani on her desk. "You've looked tired lately. Totally fine if you don't want to say, but is there anything that would help?" She looked up, surprised. "I'm getting over typhoid. The doctor said I could come back, but I'm exhausted by noon." Yusuf nodded. "Want me to take your after-lunch playground duty for a couple of weeks?" "Yes," she said, and her face finally softened.

What were the other teachers calling Amandeep?
'The ghost'.
What did Yusuf think Amandeep's flatness might mean?
Yusuf felt unsure and concerned, wondering whether she was simply private or something was wrong, and didn't want to label her.
How did Yusuf show kind curiosity instead of labelling?
He waited for a private moment, brought nimbu pani, gently named what he saw, gave her the option not to say, and offered practical help.
How had the PT teacher read Amandeep?
The PT teacher labelled her lazy and uninterested, missing that she was recovering from typhoid.

The school library had a new rule: each Class 4 pair would run the book-return box for a week and enter a quiz at the end. Himani wanted Pallavi as her partner before the teacher had even finished speaking. Pallavi was the tallest girl in class, and she laughed so easily that even the librarian smiled at her.
"She'll know all the quiz answers," Himani whispered to her friend. "And she'd never forget anything. She's too nice."
On Wednesday, Pallavi left the return box on the bench outside while she went to play. Three books slid out in the rain. In Friday's quiz, Pallavi guessed most answers with a big grin, and they came sixth.
Walking out, Himani looked at Pallavi, who was still laughing with everyone. "You're really fun," she said slowly. "But you're not so good at quizzes, na?"

Where did Pallavi leave the return box on Wednesday?
She left the return box on the bench outside while she went to play.
Why did Himani feel so sure Pallavi would know every quiz answer?
Pallavi was tall, cheerful and liked by everyone, so to Himani it felt natural that someone so nice must also be clever and careful.
What could Himani try next time she chooses a partner for a task?
She could ask herself what the task really needs, like remembering things or knowing answers, and look for who has shown that, not just who is the most fun.
How might Pallavi feel about being chosen and then hearing Himani's last comment?
Pallavi may have enjoyed being picked first, but the last comment might sting a little, or she might just laugh it off, since being fun was never a promise to be good at quizzes.

Paulo, who had won every race since Grade 4, finished first without even looking tired, and his parents cheered from the stands. Lindiwe sat on the grass and pulled at her laces. Why did Lindiwe run in her school shoes?
Her trainers had split.
What did Lindiwe believe about herself as she pulled at her laces?
She felt discouraged and inadequate, believing she would probably never be a real runner because everyone else seemed better equipped and supported.

How does Paulo see Lindiwe's race?

Gurpreet's manager had just agreed to remote work for a year, and the two of them sat in the office canteen over cold tea, writing the deal on a napkin. "A year, Vidya, not forever," Gurpreet said. "You take the offer in Hyderabad. I work from wherever you are and fly back for the quarterly meetings." "And in month six we sit down and check," Vidya added, "whether it's working for both of us." They wrote: Review, month six. No guilt, no scorekeeping. Vidya had been afraid to say yes to the offer, afraid Gurpreet would resent it. Now she looked at the napkin and felt something loosen. A year had an end. Gurpreet folded it and slid it into his wallet, next to a photo.

When did Gurpreet and Vidya plan to review the arrangement?
In month six.
What had Vidya been afraid of before agreeing?
Vidya had been afraid that Gurpreet would resent it if she took the offer.
What else could make the trial feel safer for both of them?
They could agree in advance on a visiting schedule and on what would count as it working, so the review stays fair and calm.
How might Gurpreet feel about working remotely for the year?
Gurpreet may feel willing but also a little uneasy about being away from the office, though the limited time makes it feel manageable.

metadata.subtype: Approach: designing a time-limited trial arrangement [Action]

Read this:

At five, Deepika held both shoulders up near the ears before answering in class. Kiran, the teacher, gave a friendly nod and breathed in slowly, and Deepika breathed with Kiran. The shoulders dropped, and the answer came out clear.

At sixteen, before the district football match, Deepika rolled both shoulders back and down in slow circles beside the tunnel, feeling the tightness loosen. Before the last exam, the shoulders had crept up again without Deepika noticing, until a pencil case fell and Deepika noticed the ache and let them go.

At twenty-five, with a report due, Deepika sat with shoulders locked hard around the neck. Preeti, a colleague, thought Deepika was irritated and stayed away. Deepika stood, stretched both arms overhead and took a short walk down the corridor. "Sorry if I looked cross," Deepika said on returning. "It's not you. My shoulders just hold the stress." Preeti laughed with relief and made a cup of tea.

What did Kiran do before Deepika answered in class?
Kiran gave a friendly nod and breathed in slowly.
How does Deepika's handling of tight shoulders develop from five to twenty-five?

At five the teacher's nod and slow breath loosen shoulders held near the ears; at sixteen Deepika rolls the shoulders back to release tension before a match and notices them creeping up before an exam; at twenty-five Deepika stretches and takes a walk, and explains that tight shoulders meant strain, not irritation. The skill moves from borrowed help to own tool.
What was Preeti thinking on seeing Deepika's locked shoulders?
Preeti was thinking that Deepika was irritated, and kept away to avoid a clash.
What could Deepika do to keep shoulder tension from building during future deadlines?
Deepika could set short breaks between tasks and stretch early, so the tightness never locks in. 🙂

Read this:

At the lunch table in their Istanbul school, Wei leaned in. "Did you hear about Selin? Her mum came to school because she stole from the canteen."

Elif put down her sandwich. She had heard. Everyone had heard it three different ways.

"I don't want to talk about it," she said. "It's Selin's business."

Wei blinked. "Everyone's talking about it."

"Then I don't need to."

Wei looked around for someone else to tell, but the girl next to Elif just shrugged and went back to her book.

At the end of lunch, Selin walked past their table with her tray, eyes down. Nobody at Elif's table looked up or whispered. Selin's shoulders dropped a little, as if she'd been bracing for something that didn't come.

What did Wei say Selin had done?
That she stole from the canteen and her mum came to school.
How did Elif feel about the story Wei wanted to tell?
She felt uncomfortable and firm, not wanting to spread something that was Selin's business.
Why did Elif's refusal matter?
Rumours need carriers; by refusing, Elif and the girl beside her gave the story nowhere to go at that table.
What was it like for Selin to walk past the table without whispers?
She seemed a little relieved, her shoulders dropping, as if she had been bracing for more whispering.

messages.content:
Read this:

"Didi, you look like a ghost. Did you sleep?"
"Some. I was watching stuff."
"Till when?"
"Three? Four? I don't know, Abhinav. Everyone from school is posting. Tanya's at a beach in Goa. Rohit got into some fest band. Everyone's having the best year."
"And you?"
"I'm having the best year of watching them." Bidisha laughed, but it came out flat. "It helps, you know. When the room's too quiet. It's like company."
"Is it?"
"For a bit. Then I feel worse. Like everyone moved on and I'm stuck watching."
"Did you go to that dance club you mentioned?"
"I was going to. Then I was on my phone, and it was nine."
"Didi, Maa's asking if you'll video call on Sunday."
"Yeah. Sure." She was already glancing at her other screen.

Where is Tanya?
At a beach in Goa.
What does Bidisha mean by 'the best year of watching them'?
She feels lonely and left behind, and the scrolling that numbs the quiet makes the comparison sting more.
What small change could help Bidisha?
Put the phone away by a set time and go to the dance club once, trading some scrolling for real contact.
How might Abhinav feel seeing his sister on the call?
Abhinav likely feels worried and helpless, noticing she looks tired and distracted even while talking to him.

Read this:

The paddy was nearly cut, and the whole village near Champhai had come to help Lalremsiami's family bring in the harvest. Lalremsiami's father told everyone at the tea break, "My daughter has passed all her nursing papers. First class!"
Lalremsiami smiled and handed around the cups. She had failed two papers in the last semester. She had written "passed" in her messages home, and it had seemed easier than hearing her father go quiet on the phone.
That evening her college friend Sarita called. "The re-exam form closes on Friday. Did you fill it?"
"Not yet."
"Siami, you have to. And your family?"
"They think I passed."
Sarita was silent a moment. "Every week it gets bigger."
Lalremsiami looked out at her father laughing by the fire. She felt the trap close a little more.

How many papers had Lalremsiami failed?
She had failed two papers in the last semester.
What was Lalremsiami feeling when she looked at her father laughing by the fire?
She felt trapped and guilty, afraid of disappointing him yet aware that each week the false story grew.
What would you advise Lalremsiami to do next?
Fill in the re-exam form before Friday and tell her family the truth soon, perhaps with a trusted relative or Sarita's support.
How does Sarita see the situation?
Sarita sees the lie growing every week and worries about her friend, which is why she reminds her about the form and the family.

Read this:

At the wedding in their village near Jodhpur, the courtyard was full of relatives Preeti had never met. Her mother led her from elder to elder. Preeti bent and touched each pair of feet, quick and neat, and got pats on the head. Then a tall man with a big moustache, Lokesh-ji, a distant uncle, laughed and grabbed her wrist. “Come, come, touch properly, and give me a hug too.” Preeti's body went stiff, and she pulled back. Her mother stepped between them at once. “She has greeted you with respect, Lokesh-ji. A namaste is enough.” She kept Preeti beside her all evening and later told her, “You were right to pull back.”

What did Lokesh-ji ask Preeti to give him besides touching his feet?
He asked her to give him a hug too.
What was Preeti feeling when her body went stiff?
She felt uncomfortable and uneasy at being grabbed and asked for a hug by a man she didn't know.
How did Preeti's mother protect her?
She stepped between them at once, said a namaste was enough, kept Preeti beside her and told her she was right to pull back.
How might the relatives nearby see her mother's words?
Some might think she was being strict, but others would see a mother making sure respect never means unwanted touch.

Read this:

Exam week, a power cut, and a house still full of relatives: it was the worst time for questions, but Sonali kept asking them.
"Masi, where did Mamma go? Is she in the sky? Can she hear me?"
Jahnavi Masi was lighting a candle so Sonali could finish her maths. "She died, Sonu. Her body stopped. She can't come back, but we can remember her."
"But where is she?"
The same question, for the fourth time that evening. Jahnavi answered again.
Later, Sonali lined up her teddies and covered one with a dupatta. "This is the funeral," she whispered. Then she looked at the door, as if someone might walk in.

What was Jahnavi Masi lighting?
A candle, so Sonali could finish her maths.
What does Sonali looking at the door suggest?
She still hopes and longs for her Mamma to walk in, as the loss is not fully real to her yet.
What is Jahnavi Masi doing well, even in a hard week?
Answering the same question honestly and patiently each time, which helps Sonali slowly make the loss real.
What might the teddy funeral mean for Sonali?
Playing it out may be how she tries to understand what happened to her Mamma, a normal part of grieving.

Read this:

"Kiran, you think you invented this 'bro, I'm so done yaar' way of talking? Let your Chandrika Dadi tell you.
"When I was fifteen, in Lucknow, our college crowd thought Hindi alone was for aunties and English alone was for teachers. So we mixed. 'Too much ho gaya.' 'Timepass kar rahe hain.' 'Don't be such a lallu.' My mother would shake her head at the dinner table.
"But one day my best friend Nargis lost her father. At the condolence, I wanted to tell her how I felt and English gave me 'sorry', and Hindi gave me 'dukh'. Neither was enough. I held her hand and said, 'Nargis, I'm here. Tu akeli nahi hai.'
"She told me years later that line stayed with her. Half one language, half the other. That was just how we spoke when we meant it most.

Which city did Chandrika Dadi live in at fifteen?
She lived in Lucknow.
What was young Chandrika feeling when she couldn't find the right word for Nargis?
Young Chandrika felt helpless and full of sorrow for her friend, finding that neither "sorry" nor "dukh" was enough.
What choice at the condolence mattered, and why?
Young Chandrika held Nargis's hand and spoke in mixed Hindi and English, which let her say what one language alone could not.
How did Nargis experience Chandrika's words?
Nargis felt comforted and less alone, and the mixed line stayed with her for years.

Read this:

"Dolma, you asked how I finally started reading again, so here's the embarrassing truth. For a year I kept promising myself an hour every night. Every night I was too tired, and every morning I felt worse about it. Then I stopped trying to feel motivated and changed the setup instead. First, I made it tiny: one page. Just one. Second, I tied it to something I already do without fail, my morning tea on the balcony. The book now lives on the tea tray, right next to the sugar. Third, I moved the phone charger to the kitchen, so the phone isn't in my hand while the kettle boils. Some mornings it's one page. Most mornings it turns into ten. My mother laughs and says, 'Sudha, the sugar is reading more than you.' But it works."

Where does the book live now?
On the tea tray, right next to the sugar.
How did Sudha feel during the year of promising an hour every night?
Sudha felt tired every night and guilty every morning, worse each time the promise broke.
Which change in the setup seems most useful, and why?
Tying one page to the morning tea, because it rides on a routine Sudha never skips instead of on motivation.
How does Sudha's mother seem to see the new habit?
She finds it funny and affectionate, teasing that the sugar reads more, which shows she has noticed the change.

Department head's note, 3 October
Hansa from the packaging team asked for fifteen minutes today. She brought a slim folder: dated sketches, her weekly update emails to the team since July, and a note of a conversation she had with Baljeet on 19 September. In that talk she told him calmly that two of her box designs had been presented under his name at the supplier meeting, and asked that it not happen again.
It happened again last week. Baljeet's deck for the retail pitch includes her folding-tray design with no mention of her.
Hansa did not raise her voice or call him a thief. She said, "I'd like the record corrected and a clear process for credit."
What I did next: I checked the file dates against the deck. They match her account. I have scheduled a meeting with Baljeet tomorrow, asked HR to sit in, and will have her name added to the retail pitch before it goes out.

When did Hansa first speak to Baljeet about the designs?
On 19 September.
What does Hansa's calm manner suggest about how she felt?
It suggests Hansa felt steady and determined rather than furious, confident that the dated records would speak for her.
What steps did Hansa take before going to the department head?
She kept dated sketches and weekly update emails, and spoke calmly to Baljeet first, asking that it not happen again.
How might Baljeet see tomorrow's meeting with HR present?
Baljeet will likely feel exposed and uneasy, since the file dates match Hansa's account and there is little room to argue.
Write a message, about 35 words, thanking my colleague Meena for covering my shift yesterday. I'm Rohan.

Hi Meena,
Thank you so much for covering my shift yesterday. It really helped me, and I am truly grateful. Please tell me when you need a favour, and I will gladly return it.
Rohan

Read this:

Mehak, your Ishita Bua was not born organised, you know. In my board year I made a timetable and followed it about as well as you follow your mother's rules. Then my Maths teacher told us to check it every Sunday: what I had planned against what I had done. First Sunday, I sat with two columns. Mornings, fine. Evenings, almost nothing: Chemistry planned from seven to nine, done maybe half an hour. Second Sunday, the same. By evening I was tired, the TV was on, my brothers were fighting. So I swapped. Chemistry and Maths went to six in the morning, when the house was quiet and my head was fresh. Evenings became light revision and flashcards. Third Sunday, the two columns almost matched.

When did young Ishita check her timetable?
Every Sunday, comparing what was planned with what was done.
How might young Ishita have felt seeing the evening column nearly empty?
Young Ishita probably felt frustrated and disappointed to see the evening Chemistry slipping two Sundays in a row.
Which change inside the story made the columns match, and why?
Moving Chemistry and Maths to six in the morning, when the house was quiet and the mind fresh, and leaving evenings for light revision that tiredness could not derail.
What would have changed if Ishita had kept Chemistry in the evening slot?
The evening column would likely have stayed nearly empty, and Chemistry would have fallen further behind every week.

"You look miserable," Disha said, sliding into the café booth.
"Saw my college group's posts," said Amandeep. "Everyone's a manager or in London."
"And you?"
"Still an analyst."
"What were you a year ago?"
Amandeep frowned. "An intern. Couldn't make a spreadsheet without crying."
"And now?"
"I lead the weekly report." A small smile.
"So you've moved."
"I guess. It doesn't feel like it when I scroll."
"Then maybe don't scroll everyone. Who do you actually learn from?"
Amandeep thought. "Rhea. She shares how she does her models. And my manager."
"Keep them. Mute the rest for a while."
Amandeep took out the phone, muted six people, and put it face down. "Okay. Next year I'll ask what I've learned since today."
"There you go."

What was Amandeep a year ago?
Amandeep was an intern.
What was Amandeep feeling after scrolling the college group's posts?
Amandeep felt miserable and behind, as if everyone else was ahead.
What did Disha help Amandeep do?
Disha helped Amandeep compare with last year's self, mute people who caused low moods, and keep a few peers worth learning from.
How might Disha see Amandeep's progress?
Disha seems to see clear progress and wants Amandeep to notice it too.

Read this:

The night before the district meet last year, I couldn't sleep, so I raced in my head instead. I'm Lakshmi, and I'd run the 400 m for two seasons without ever finishing well; the nerves ate me alive in the call room.
My teammate Zainab had taught me this. I lay on the hostel bed and walked through everything slowly: the warm-up jog on the back field, the drills, lacing my spikes twice. Then the stagger, the gun, the first bend, running tall on the back straight.
I planned the bad bits too. If someone drifts close, I hold my lane and keep my arms going. If I stumble, I get up and finish; one stumble doesn't decide a race. And in the call room: breathe in for four, out for six, until my shoulders drop.
Next morning my shoulders dropped on the third breath. I finished second. Zainab screamed louder than my coach.

What place did Lakshmi finish?
Second.
How did Lakshmi feel in the call room before learning this?
Lakshmi felt so nervous there that the nerves "ate me alive", spoiling two seasons of races.
What else could Lakshmi add to the rehearsal next season?
Practising the breathing during real training, not only in bed, so it becomes automatic under pressure.
How might Zainab feel seeing Lakshmi finish second?
Zainab is thrilled and proud, since the technique Zainab taught helped, which is why the scream was so loud.

metadata.subtype: Approach: visualising the race and rehearsing [Thinking]

Read this:

Imran, you asked why the family downstairs danced so much yesterday. Sit, and let old Pranav Dadu tell you what I learned at your age.

I was nine, in a village near Amritsar. My best friend Harjeet dragged me to the fields on Baisakhi morning. The wheat was gold and everyone was singing. I asked his Bapu, "Why dance for wheat?"

He laughed and handed me a sickle. "Cut one bundle, then you'll know." It took me ten minutes, and my hands blistered. "Now imagine a whole year of waiting for this," he said. "And on this day long ago, our Guru called people to stand together as equals."

That night I told my mother both stories. She said, "Now you have Harjeet's festival and your own."

So yesterday, you should have gone down and danced.

What did Harjeet's Bapu hand young Pranav?
He handed him a sickle.
How did young Pranav feel after cutting one bundle?
His hands blistered and he felt tired but newly curious, starting to see why people celebrate the harvest.
What turning point helped young Pranav understand Baisakhi?
Harjeet's Bapu letting him cut a bundle himself and then telling him the story of the day, instead of just answering.
How might Harjeet's Bapu have seen the boy's question?
He seemed amused and glad to be asked, and chose to teach by doing.

Read this:

“Five minutes, Mummy, just five minutes!” Kishore called, crayon already moving over the paper. The school bus came at 7:40, and it was 7:25. His mother Swati kept an eye on the clock while she packed the tiffin. The sun took three minutes. Then the mountains needed a river, and the river needed a boat with a flag, and the flag needed all the colours. At 7:38 the bus honked. Kishore looked up, astonished. “Already?” he said, and meant it. He grabbed the drawing, still wet in the corners, stuffed his shoes on the wrong feet and ran down the stairs with the picture smudging against his shirt.

What time did the school bus come?
The school bus came at 7:40.
Why was Kishore astonished when the bus honked?
Kishore sincerely believed only five minutes had passed and felt surprised and a little shocked that the time had run out so soon.
What could Kishore and Swati try tomorrow so the drawing does not collide with the bus?
Set a timer for the drawing, or start earlier, and decide which part gets finished before the bus.
How might Swati feel watching the clock while packing the tiffin?
Swati is likely anxious about the bus and patient with Kishore at once, since the promise of “five minutes” was sincere but unreliable.

Read this:

The summer holidays had just begun, and the colony park in Lucknow smelled of mango peels. Noor sat on the swing with her report card folded small in her pocket.
"Will you show your ammi the maths mark?" asked Payal.
"Not the maths." Noor had got fifteen out of twenty-five. Last time she'd got twenty-four, and Ammi had hugged her and cooked sevaiyan. When Noor had got eighteen in science, Ammi had only said, "Next time better," and gone to the kitchen without a hug.
"I'll say they're not out yet," Noor said. She pushed the swing higher so Payal wouldn't see her face.
That evening she quietly tore the maths page out of her rough book too, the one with the red crosses.

What mark did Noor get in maths?
Noor had got fifteen out of twenty-five.
Why does Noor want to hide the maths mark from Ammi?
She is worried and sad, because she remembers hugs and sevaiyan after a high mark and no hug after a lower one, so love seems to depend on marks.
How could Ammi support Noor better?
Ammi could show warmth whatever the mark, for example a hug first and then a calm talk about the red crosses, so mistakes feel safe to share.
What might Payal think when Noor pushes the swing higher?
Payal may sense Noor is upset and hiding something, and feel unsure whether to ask again.

Read this:

Note by Usha Menon, Class 6 teacher, Monday.
At lunch today I saw Bhavna carry her tray to the corner table where four girls sit. One of them put her bag on the empty chair and said, 'There's no place for you here.' The others laughed. Bhavna stood for a moment, then walked to the steps and ate nothing. Afterwards she came to me, eyes wet. 'They always do this,' she said. I thanked her for telling me and said it said nothing bad about her. I spoke to the four girls straight after lunch. I also introduced Bhavna to Lavanya, who usually eats alone with a book, and mentioned our Tuesday nature club. I called Bhavna's mother this evening and will watch that table all week.

What did one girl put on the empty chair?
Her bag.
How did Bhavna feel after being turned away, and how can you tell?
Deeply hurt; she ate nothing on the steps and came to the teacher with wet eyes.
What steps did the teacher take the same day?
Spoke to the four girls, introduced Bhavna to Lavanya, mentioned the nature club and called her mother that evening.
What might Lavanya feel when Bhavna is introduced?
Perhaps glad of company, since she usually eats alone with a book.

Read this:

Emil's little sister Hana had been in the children's hospital in Copenhagen for two weeks. Every afternoon Emil sat at the kitchen table with his felt-tip pens and drew her something: a whale, a rocket, their dog in a raincoat. Mum took the pictures in when she visited. On Friday his friend invited him to a birthday party at the swimming pool. Emil said no. 'It feels wrong to have fun,' he told Dad. Dad sat down. 'Hana asked me yesterday if you were still going to parties. She wants to hear about them. It's okay to be sad and to have fun in the same week.' Emil went. Afterwards he drew Hana a picture of himself on the big slide, with a speech bubble: 'Next time, you too.'

What did Emil draw for Hana after the party?
A picture of himself on the big slide, with a speech bubble.
Why did Emil first say no to the party?
He felt guilty about having fun while Hana was in hospital.
What did Dad help Emil understand?
That it's okay to be sad and to have fun in the same week, and that Hana wants to hear about his fun.
What might Hana want from her brother while she is in hospital?
To hear about his life and still feel part of it, which is why she asked about parties.

Read this:

Sunday night
Lavanya laughed at me this morning: three video calls before breakfast. Nani's weekly one, Khala asking about her son's college forms, and my cousin Imtiaz showing off his new puppy. I don't mind. Nobody lives in the same lane anymore; we're spread over four cities, so if I don't call, the thread just slips. Last month I took two days' leave when Chhoti Khala was in hospital and slept on the bench beside her bed. Next week is Eid, and the train ticket home is already booked. Living alone here is my choice. Staying close is also my choice, just one I have to keep making.
Rehana

How many video calls did Rehana make before breakfast?
Three video calls.
How does Rehana feel about the effort of keeping in touch?
Rehana feels content and committed rather than burdened; the calls are a chosen way to stay close to a family spread over four cities.
Which of Rehana's habits keep the family close, and why?
Regular calls, turning up in person when Chhoti Khala needed help, and going home for Eid, because closeness now depends on effort, not a shared lane.
How might Lavanya see Rehana's morning of calls?
Lavanya may find it funny or tiring at first, but might also admire how much Rehana cares for relatives who live far away.

Read this:

When the bus from the district school dropped Gargi at the Ranipur crossing, Rehana was waiting as always, arms open. Gargi stepped round the hug and fixed her bag strap. "Not here, Ammi. Everyone's looking." Rehana's arms fell. At home Gargi went straight to the roof. Rehana stood at the stove a long time, stirring nothing. That evening she didn't push. She carried two cups of tea up to the roof and sat beside Gargi on the parapet, shoulders not quite touching, watching the goats come home. After a while Gargi leaned her head on her mother's shoulder, just for a moment. Rehana kept very still and said only, "The tea's getting cold."

Where did Rehana carry the two cups of tea?
Up to the roof.
Why did Gargi step round the hug at the bus stop?
She felt embarrassed and self-conscious with everyone looking, and wanted her own space.
What did Rehana do that kept the connection alive?
She didn't push, sat beside Gargi with tea, and let Gargi come closer at her own pace.
How did Rehana feel when her arms fell?
She felt hurt and a bit lost, standing at the stove stirring nothing.
